manual.title: DC-10 Series Flight Manual
manual.summary: Systems, procedures, limitations, performance and handling for the DC-10, KC-10 and MD-10.

blocks.content: This manual gives you what you need to operate the DC-10, the KC-10 and the MD-10 in Microsoft Flight Simulator 2024: a working knowledge of the aircraft and every one of its systems, the normal, abnormal and emergency procedures, the limitations, performance planning, and how the aircraft handles. The three share most of their structure, systems and procedures, so they share one manual.

It is written at study level. Each system is described the way an instructor would teach it: what it is made of, how it works and why it was designed that way, how it interacts with the rest of the aircraft, how it fails, and what the crew sees and does about it. Basic flight principles are not explained; your experience is assumed.

The manual describes the aircraft as it is simulated. Where the simulation departs from the real aircraft in a way you would notice, the part concerned says so under **Simulation notes**. No manual replaces judgment: multiple failures, weather and terrain can call for a different course of action than the one written here.

blocks.title: Simulation use only
blocks.content: This manual is written for Microsoft Flight Simulator. It is not a real aircraft's flight manual and must not be used for real-world flight or training.

Pick your aircraft with the **DC-10**, **KC-10** and **MD-10** buttons at the top of the page. The manual then shows only what applies to it, and the section and topic numbers close up around what is hidden. Content that applies to some of the three but not all carries a badge such as **DC-10 / KC-10 only**.

rows: DC-10-10, -15, -30 and -40 passenger aircraft and freighters, the -10 and -30 air tankers (firefighting), the -40 Omega air-refueling tanker, and the KDC-10

The manual marks those differences the way airline manuals do, with the series in parentheses: "Center landing gear (-30, -40)". [Aircraft General](aircraft-general) describes every variant and what sets it apart.
The manual follows the arrangement of the KC-10's military flight manual. Its sections are fairly independent, so it can be read straight through or used as a reference.

blocks.content: Three kinds of highlighted text appear throughout. They keep their real-world meaning, because that is what makes the procedures realistic.
An operating procedure or practice that, if not followed, could result in injury or loss of the aircraft.
An operating procedure or practice that, if not followed, could damage equipment.
Information that helps but is not critical.

blocks.title: Words with a fixed meaning
rows: The procedure is recommended; depart from it only for a good reason.
Declare an emergency and land at the nearest suitable airport, weighing the severity of the problem against the weather, the airport's facilities, the aircraft's weight and the light.
The flight is to end, but the problem is less urgent: the crew may choose an airport that is not the nearest, such as one with better facilities.

blocks.content:
Procedures in this manual are **expanded**: each step with the reasoning and amplification behind it. The checklists in the cockpit EFB carry the same primary steps without the amplification.

In emergency procedures, **memory items** are boxed and printed bold. They are the first steps of the procedure, done from memory, before the checklist is read. Every step names the crew member who does it.

blocks.title: Crew designators
rows: First officer (the KC-10's copilot), in the right seat
Flight engineer, at the side-facing station behind the first officer (DC-10, KC-10). FedEx calls the DC-10's flight engineer the second officer, S/O
Pilot flying, whichever seat that is

blocks.content: On the three-crew aircraft the pilot flying keeps control of the aircraft and calls for the checklist; the flight engineer reads it aloud and each crew member answers for their own steps. The MD-10 has two crew and its procedures are driven by its alert messages. If you fly alone, the [Virtual Crew](virtual-crew) can take the flight engineer's and the first officer's parts.

The manual uses the units the aircraft's instruments show: weights and fuel in pounds (lb), speeds in knots (kt), altitudes in feet, pressures in psi, and engine and oil temperatures in degrees Celsius. Abbreviations are spelled out in the [Glossary](glossary).

chapters.title: Systems Description
chapters.summary: How the aircraft and each of its systems work, one part per system.

blocks.content: Each system has its own part, in the order of the KC-10 flight manual's systems section, starting with Aircraft General. The last three parts describe what the simulation adds to the aircraft: the electronic flight bag, the Virtual Crew, and ground operations.
Every part is laid out the same way, so you can find your way around any of them:

items: **Introduction**: what the system does, its architecture in one picture, and its main components on each aircraft.
**Description**: each subsystem and how it works, with the theory of operation behind it.
**Controls and indicators**: panel by panel, every control and indication with what it does.
**Operation**: the system through a normal flight, its automatic functions, modes and logic.
**Failures and non-normal operation**: how the system fails, how each failure shows, and which procedure deals with it.
**Simulation notes**: what the simulation models, what it simplifies, and the failures you can practice.

blocks.content: Where the three-crew DC-10 and KC-10 and the two-crew MD-10 work differently, as they do wherever the MD-10's systems controllers replace the flight engineer, each has its own subsections, marked with a badge. Pick your aircraft at the top of the page and the others drop out of view.

parts.title: Aircraft General
parts.summary: The DC-10 family, its dimensions and variants, and the layout of each flight deck.

blocks.content: This part is the orientation to the aircraft. It explains why the DC-10 family is built the way it is, sets out every variant in the simulation and what distinguishes it, lists the avionics fits you can choose for a DC-10, gives the principal dimensions and the structure, and walks through each of the three flight decks, naming the part of this manual that describes each panel. It closes with the conventions the rest of Section 1 relies on: light colors, alert levels, panel names and the way effectivity is marked.

Every member of the family is a low-wing, wide-body transport with three high-bypass turbofans: one under each wing on a pylon, and the third in the tail, carried above the rear fuselage in a nacelle that passes through the root of the fin. The fuselage is a pressurized semi-monocoque tube 19 ft 9 in across, with two floor levels: the main deck above, and the lower cargo holds, avionics and accessory compartments below. The wing is a 35° swept cantilever whose box structure doubles as the integral fuel tanks and carries the main landing gear, the engine pylons and every high-lift and roll control surface.

The systems are built around the number three. Each engine drives one AC generator through a constant-speed drive, drives the two engine-driven pumps of one hydraulic system, and supplies one bleed air source (the KC-10A takes no bleed air from engine 2). A Garrett TSCP700-4B auxiliary power unit in the tail cone, the same model on every variant, supplies electrical power and bleed air on the ground; in flight it is mainly a standby source of electrical power. The flight controls are fully powered by the three independent hydraulic systems. The landing gear is a tricycle with two four-wheel main bogies under the wings; the heavier, long-range aircraft add a two-wheel main gear on the fuselage centerline.

sections.title: The DC-10 family
sections.summary: How the family came to be built the way it is.

blocks.content: The history below is kept to what explains the aircraft in front of you: why it has three engines and where they are, why the long-range aircraft have a third main gear and a longer wing, and how the freighters, tankers and the two-crew conversion grew out of the airliner.

The DC-10 was designed in the late 1960s for the gap between the narrow-bodies and the four-engine 747: a wide-body that could carry a full cabin across the United States and still use the shorter runways of the big domestic airports. The engines available then could not give a twin enough thrust to meet the engine-out climb requirements at that weight, and four engines would have added weight, fuel burn and maintenance out of proportion to the payload. Three engines was the compromise, and it shaped everything that followed.

A third engine has to go on the centerline, and Douglas put it above the rear fuselage, in a nacelle through the root of the fin with a straight inlet and a straight exhaust, rather than burying it in the tail cone behind an S-shaped duct. The straight duct gives the engine clean, undistorted airflow, and the same engine can be fitted in any of the three positions. The price is a thrust line well above the wing engines', inclined at 4° to the fuselage reference plane, and a heavy tail that the structure and the balance have to allow for.

The number three then runs through the systems. Each engine drives one generator, the pumps of one hydraulic system and one bleed source, so an engine failure takes away one of each kind of source and never all of one kind. The systems are designed to finish the flight on what remains, and they are cross-connected so that a surviving source can carry a lost one's loads: bus ties for the electrics, reversible motor pumps that let one hydraulic system pressurize another without mixing their fluid, and isolation valves in the bleed manifold. Managing those three sets of sources is the work of the flight engineer on the DC-10 and KC-10, and of the automatic system controllers on the MD-10. The parts that follow describe each one: [Electrical](electrical), [Hydraulics](hydraulics) and [Pneumatics](pneumatics).

Douglas built the DC-10 in two basic forms: a domestic aircraft with a short wing and three wing tanks, and an intercontinental one with a longer wing, an extra tank in the center section and a third main gear. Engine choice then gave each form its sub-series.

blocks.title: The four series
rows: The -10 airframe for hot and high airfields
Three wing tanks and a center wing auxiliary tank
Three wing tanks and a center auxiliary tank, upper and lower compartments
Three wing tanks and the center auxiliary tank's upper compartment only

blocks.content: **Why the center gear.** The intercontinental aircraft's takeoff weights rose from the -10's 440,000 lb to as much as 580,000 lb. On two four-wheel bogies that weight would have overloaded runway and taxiway pavements and concentrated too much load at the wing's gear attachments, so the -30 and -40 carry a third main leg on the fuselage centerline between the wing gears, with two wheels and brakes of its own. It takes a share of the weight that depends on the aircraft's weight and center of gravity, adds braking, and must be extended for takeoff and landing unless the performance is planned for it retracted. [Landing Gear and Brakes](landing-gear) describes it.

**Why the longer wing.** The long wing adds almost 10 ft of span at the tips, which raises the wing area from 3,550 sq ft to about 3,647 sq ft and the aspect ratio from about 6.8 to about 7.5. The extra area carries the extra weight at the same speeds; the higher aspect ratio cuts induced drag in the cruise, which is worth most on the longest sectors. The extra fuel goes in a center auxiliary tank in the wing center section and the fuselage beneath it.

**The -15 and the -40.** The -15 is a -10 airframe with the -30's engine family, rated for hot and high airfields where the -10's thrust left too little margin. The -40 is the intercontinental airframe with Pratt & Whitney JT9D engines, built for Northwest and Japan Air Lines. Its engines set thrust by engine pressure ratio (EPR) instead of fan speed (N1), its bleed system is scheduled for the JT9D's compressor, and the lower compartment of its center auxiliary tank is not equipped. [Engines](engines) describes both engine families.

**Freighters.** Douglas built the -30F as a factory freighter and the -30CF as a convertible, and many passenger -10s and -30s were later converted. A freighter replaces the passenger cabin with a cargo main deck, loaded through a large main-deck cargo door on the left side ahead of the wing, and keeps a small crew compartment behind the flight deck with seats for supernumeraries. Its passenger oxygen, lighting and galleys shrink to suit.

**Fire tankers.** 10 Tanker Air Carrier converted -10s and -30s into very large air tankers for fighting wildfires: three retardant tanks in a fairing under the fuselage, a drop system controlled from the flight deck, and an empty main deck. The -30-based tanker flies without its center main gear.

**Air-refueling tankers.** The KC-10A Extender is the U.S. Air Force's tanker-transport, built on the DC-10-30CF. Its lower holds became fuel tanks, and it carries a refueling boom under the tail, a hose and drogue on the centerline, hose-and-drogue pods under the wings, and a receptacle above the flight deck so that it can itself be refueled. Two other tankers grew out of airliners: the Royal Netherlands Air Force's KDC-10, a converted DC-10-30 with a refueling boom, and Omega's DC-10-40, which refuels probe-equipped receivers from two wing pods.

**The MD-10.** FedEx and Boeing converted DC-10-10 and -30 freighters into MD-10s by replacing the three-crew flight deck with the MD-11's two-crew glass flight deck, the Advanced Common Flight Deck. The flight engineer's station gave way to automatic controllers for the electrical, hydraulic, fuel and air systems, worked from an MD-11-style overhead panel; six display units replaced the electromechanical instruments; and a flight management system replaced the inertial navigation units. The airframe, engines and systems hardware stayed the DC-10's, which is why an MD-10 flies like the DC-10 it was built from while its crew operates it like an MD-11.

sections.title: Variants
sections.summary: Every variant in the simulation, the airframe and flight deck it uses, and what sets it apart.

blocks.content: Three things describe any variant. Its **airframe** is one of seven: the DC-10-10, -15, -30 and -40, the KC-10, and the MD-10-10 and -30. The airframe decides the engines, the wing, the landing gear, the fuel tanks and the systems, and so how the aircraft flies. Its **flight deck** is the DC-10's (in a -10, -30 or -40 form), the KC-10's or the MD-10's, and decides what is in front of the crew. Its **fit** is what sets it apart from the plain airframe: a main-deck cargo door, retardant tanks, a refueling boom or pods, a head-up display.

Each variant is a separate aircraft in the simulator's aircraft selection, listed under the types DC-10, DC-10-40 Refueler, KC-10A, KDC-10 and MD-10. The aircraft recognizes which variant it is when it loads and builds the matching airframe and flight deck.

blocks.content: **Early and Late.** The Early and Late versions of the -10, -30 and -30F differ in exterior detail: the engine nacelles, the wing, and the wing-to-body fairings. Their systems and flight decks are identical in the simulation.

**Freighters.** The -10F Late, -30F Early, -30F Late and -40F Late replace the passenger cabin with a cargo main deck and a main-deck cargo door on the left side ahead of the wing, keep a crew compartment with a galley and supernumerary seats behind the flight deck, and give up the passenger aircraft's lower galley, so the forward lower hold runs its full length. Their passenger oxygen system shrinks to the supernumerary units. [Doors, Cargo and Cabin](doors-and-cabin) describes the cargo installation.

**Fire tankers.** The -10 Tanker and -30 Tanker carry three retardant tanks in a fairing under the fuselage. Their controls are tank control panels at the flight engineer's station (where other DC-10s have the AIDS panel), a drop control panel on the pedestal, two lights on the glareshield and drop buttons on the control wheels. The galley power buses feed the retardant pumps instead of galleys. They carry no cargo and no passengers, the -30-based tanker has no center main gear, and neither is offered the Extended Range tank, the AIDS panel or the MAC panel. [Aerial Firefighting System](aerial-firefighting) describes the installation.

**DC-10-40 Refueler.** Omega's DC-10-40 refuels probe-equipped receivers from two hose-and-drogue pods under the outer wings, the same pods the KC-10A carries. Both pod control panels are at the flight engineer's station. The pods draw fuel from the main tanks' boost pumps through the crossfeed valves: there is no boom, no centerline hose and no dedicated refueling pump. The main deck is an open cabin with a few rider seats. See [Air Refueling Systems](air-refueling-systems).

**KDC-10.** In every system the KDC-10 is a DC-10-30: center gear, three packs, the DC-10-30 flight deck and the same choice of avionics. Added to it are the KC-10A's refueling boom, its sighting door and its boom operator's station. The boom runs on the aircraft's own electrical buses and on hydraulic system 2, with its hoist on system 3; it can be lowered, flown and stowed (see the Simulation notes for what it does not do). The KDC-10 carries cargo in the forward lower hold only and is not offered the Extended Range tank.

blocks.alt: Three exterior views side by side: the DC-10-10 Tanker with the retardant tank fairing under the fuselage; the DC-10-40 Refueler with a hose-and-drogue pod under each outer wing; the KDC-10 with the refueling boom stowed under the tail. Labels point to each mission installation.
blocks.title: Mission variants on the DC-10 airframes

blocks.content: One variant flies the KC-10 airframe. It is built on the DC-10-30's long wing, CF6-50C2 engines and center gear, and differs from it in these ways:

items: **Fuel.** Three wing tanks, the center wing tank (upper and lower compartments) and two bladder-type body tanks, forward and aft, in what were the lower holds: about 365,000 lb in six tanks. The lower cargo doors are sealed. See [Fuel](fuel).

**Aerial refueling.** A refueling boom under the tail, a hose reel and drogue on the centerline, a hose-and-drogue pod under each outer wing, and six hydraulically driven refueling pumps. The boom operator works the boom and pods from a station in the lower aft fuselage. A receptacle above the flight deck lets the KC-10A take on fuel from another tanker. See [Air Refueling Systems](air-refueling-systems).

**Bleed air and air conditioning.** There is no bleed system behind engine 2 (its starter remains, fed from the manifold), and two air conditioning packs, 1 and 3. See [Pneumatics](pneumatics) and [Air Conditioning and Pressurization](air-conditioning).

**Main deck.** A cargo floor with a roller and restraint system, loaded through the main-deck cargo door; seats for extra crew and riders at the front; a crew galley and two lavatories. Five cabin doors are in use.

**Flight deck.** Pilot, copilot and flight engineer, with a forward station for the boom operator. A flight management system with GPS controls the three inertial navigation units, the TACAN and ADF receivers and the IFF; the pilots fly electronic ADIs and HSIs, TCAS/VSIs with enhanced TCAS, and an electronic control surface position indicator.
**Equipment.** One fixed configuration: see [KC-10A equipment](#kc-10-fit).

blocks.content: The four MD-10 variants are two airframes, each with and without the head-up display. All four are freighters with a main-deck cargo door, a two-crew glass flight deck, automatic system controllers, carbon brakes and no flight engineer.

sections.title: Equipment options
sections.summary: The avionics and panel fits you can choose for a DC-10, and the fixed fits of the KC-10A and MD-10.

blocks.content: Airlines specified their DC-10s' avionics to their own standards, and over thirty years the fleet collected several generations of navigation units, flight instruments, engine displays and radio heads. The simulation offers that range on every DC-10 variant: you choose the fit one category at a time, and the flight deck changes to match, down to which panels are in the pedestal. The KC-10A has one fixed configuration, and the MD-10s' glass flight deck has nothing to choose.

Almost every item changes only the instrument or panel the crew sees and works. Two change the aircraft itself: **Extended Range** fits an auxiliary fuel tank, and the **navigation system** choice decides which long-range navigation unit is installed.
The fit is chosen in either of two places, and both talk to the aircraft, which holds the fit:

items: **On the EFB**, in the Configuration app's **Aircraft Configuration** page. The page shows a line drawing of the flight deck divided into five zones: Glareshield, Pilots' Panels, Centre Panel, Pedestal and Engineer. Press a zone's label or its panel on the drawing to list the categories in it; the engineer's station is behind you, so its label sits at the bottom right with an arrow towards the flight engineer's desk. See [Electronic Flight Bag](efb).
**In the Infinity Manager**, on the aircraft's equipment page, while the simulator is running.

blocks.content: Each category is one row with its choice at the end, and exactly one option in a category is fitted at any time: selecting one removes the other. An option you cannot select is shown unavailable, either because this variant cannot carry it (the Extended Range tank on a -40, for example) or because it belongs to an edition you do not have. After a press, the option is ringed until the aircraft reports the change, for 8 seconds at most; if the aircraft refuses it, the reason appears under the page title.

Every DC-10 loads with the same default fit, marked as the default in the table below, and the fit is not kept from one flight to the next. Changes take effect at once, in the air or on the ground, but choose the fit before you start the flight:

items: A new **navigation system** is installed once the selection has stood for about 3 seconds. It arrives as a fresh unit with no route. On the ground with the engines stopped an inertial unit must then be aligned; fitted in flight, or with an engine running, it comes up already navigating. Changing back later gives you another fresh unit, not the one you had.

Selecting **Extended Range** adds the auxiliary tank empty. Deselecting it removes the tank and any fuel in it. The change waits while a refuel, defuel or fuel dump is in progress, and is made as soon as it ends.

blocks.content: The categories are listed by the zone the EFB puts them in. In each, the first option is the default. Options marked (Pro) need the Professional edition.

blocks.title: DC-10 equipment categories
rows: Backcourse adds the BACK CRS switches to the glareshield flight guidance panel, for localizer back-course approaches.

The attitude display. KSSU is the original electromechanical ADI. MFD is an electronic ADI, the upper screen of an electronic ADI/HSI pair. FPDS is a flat-panel display system: one wide screen per pilot with a PFD and an ND side by side, replacing all of that pilot's primary flight instruments.
The horizontal situation display: either of two electromechanical HSIs, or an electronic HSI with map, plan and compass modes.
The vertical speed indicator: the original instrument, a digital screen, or a TCAS/VSI that also shows traffic and resolution advisories.
The RMI on each pilot's panel and its DME distance windows: the KSSU RMI, an RMI with one DME readout, or an RMI with two.
A separate DME distance indicator on each pilot's panel: mechanical drums, none, or digital segments.
A separate ADF bearing indicator on each pilot's panel.
A separate terrain display on each pilot's panel.
The performance and failure assessment monitor's two screens.
The primary engine instruments: round dials, vertical-scale tape instruments, or the two liquid-crystal screens of the engine indicating display system (EIDS).
The control surface position indicator: mechanical pointers, or the electronic display the KC-10A uses.
With tape engine instruments, whether the center panel carries the standby attitude indicator. The dial and digital layouts always carry it.
AINS-70; CIV-A; INS-61B (Pro); HT-9100 (Pro); ANS-70S; ANS-70D (Pro); VOR Only

The long-range navigation unit and its control-display units: the AINS-70 area inertial navigation system, the Delco Carousel IV-A or Collins INS-61B inertial navigation systems, the Honeywell/Trimble HT-9100 GPS navigation management system, or the ANS-70 in a single or dual installation; VOR Only fits no long-range unit. ANS-70 and VOR Only are offered on the passenger and freighter -10s only.
The Delco performance management system's control-display unit. Only the -30 and -40 have the performance computer behind it.
The ADF control heads: drum frequency windows, or a digital display.
The dual transponder control head: code drums, or a keypad head with a digital display.
The fuel quantity indicators on the flight engineer's fuel panel: pointer gauges, or one round liquid-crystal display per tank.
The aircraft integrated data system's control panel at the flight engineer's station. Not on the fire tankers.

The weight and balance computer's panel, which on the aircraft shows gross weight and center of gravity in percent MAC. Not on the fire tankers. In the current release the panel is drawn but shows nothing; read weight and CG on the EFB.
An auxiliary fuel tank: the center wing auxiliary tank on the -10 (32,700 lb), the aft auxiliary tank on the -30 (22,200 lb). Offered on the passenger and freighter -10s and -30s only.
The retardant tanks and drop system, always fitted on the two fire tankers and never on any other variant.

blocks.content: Some items share space in the panels, or depend on each other. The flight deck follows these rules:

items: **PMS and the autobrake.** The PMS unit sits in the aft pedestal where the AUTO BRAKE panel otherwise is, and fitting it also removes the VHF-3 control head. With the PMS fitted the aircraft has no autobrake selector and no VHF-3 head.

**HT-9100 and the ILS control head.** With the HT-9100 fitted, the pedestal's ILS control head is removed and the ILS is tuned from the two navigation control heads on the glareshield instead. [Navigation](navigation) describes both arrangements.

**FPDS.** The flat-panel display replaces each pilot's ADI, HSI, airspeed indicator, altimeter, vertical speed indicator, RMI, DME indicators and radio altimeter. With the FPDS fitted, the choices in those categories make no difference to what you see.

**TCAS traffic.** Traffic and resolution advisories are drawn on the TCAS/VSI and on the electronic MFD and FPDS displays, not on the original vertical speed indicator. In the simulation no traffic reaches the TCAS yet, so no fit shows traffic symbols: see [Weather Radar and Surveillance](surveillance).
**Standby attitude.** The Standby Attitude choice applies only with tape engine instruments.
**Engine and surface indicators.** The control surface position indicator is laid out to suit the engine instruments, so changing either redraws the center panel together.
**Fuel gauges and the Extended Range tank.** The extra tank brings its own fuel quantity indication on the flight engineer's fuel panel, with either kind of gauge.

blocks.content: The KC-10A has one configuration, the same for every edition, and offers no equipment choices: the Configuration app opens on its Aircraft Setup page and has no Aircraft Configuration page. Its fit corresponds to these items:

rows: KC-10 FMS: the flight management system with GPS, three CDUs, three inertial navigation units
Normal: no auxiliary tank option (the body tanks are part of the airframe)

blocks.content: The rest of the KC-10A's flight deck is its own and not part of the catalog: the electronic ADIs and HSIs, the TACAN and VOR/ADF RMIs, the dual DME indicator, the UHF, VHF and HF radios, and the fuel quantity totalizer at the flight engineer's station.

The MD-10's flight deck is fixed: the six display units, the flight management system, the air data inertial reference system and the conversion's own radio, transponder and weather radar panels are the same on every MD-10, and none of the DC-10's equipment categories apply. The Configuration app opens on its Aircraft Setup page. The one choice is the head-up display, which comes with the variant: pick the MD-10-10 HUD or MD-10-30 HUD to fly with it.

sections.title: Dimensions and structure
sections.summary: Principal dimensions and areas, the structure, the compartments, the reference datum and MAC, turning, and a summary of weights.

blocks.content: The family has one fuselage, one tail and two wings. The short-span wing is the -10's and is used by the -10, the -15 and the MD-10-10; the long-span wing is the -30's and is used by the -30, the -40, the KC-10 and the MD-10-30. Everything else in the table below is common, give or take an inch. Heights and ground clearances vary with weight, center of gravity, strut extension and tire pressure.

blocks.content: **Fuselage.** The fuselage is a semi-monocoque aluminum shell of frames, stringers and skin, in which the skin carries a large share of the loads. The pressure vessel takes in almost all of it: left outside are the nose radome, the wheel wells, the wing center section, the air conditioning compartments and everything behind the rear pressure bulkhead. A floor divides it into the main deck and the lower level, which holds the cargo compartments, the avionics compartment and the accessory compartments. Each cabin window has two panes, and each pane is strong enough to hold full cabin pressure by itself.

**Wing.** The load-carrying part of the wing is a box of spars, ribs and skin panels with no internal bracing outside the fuselage. Sealed, the box itself is the fuel tank. Everything else hangs on it: the main landing gear, the engine pylons, and the lighter leading- and trailing-edge structure that carries the full-span slats, the spoilers, the ailerons and the flaps. Tanks and fuel lines are built to stay intact if a main gear leg or a flap is torn away. On the long-range airframes the center section also holds the center auxiliary tank, and the KC-10's center wing tank. The center gear, where fitted, is carried in the fuselage between the wing gears.

**Tail.** The whole horizontal stabilizer moves for pitch trim, pivoting near its trailing edge while hydraulic motors drive its leading edge up or down; each side carries an elevator in two sections. The fin does not move. Its rudder is split into an upper and a lower section, each of two segments. Below the fin, the tail engine's pylon carries engine 2 above the rear fuselage.

**Wing bending.** A wing is a cantilever beam: lift spread along the span bends it upward, and every pound hung on it, from the engines and the main gear to the fuel in the tanks, bends it the other way and so relieves the bending at the root. That is why the fuel system keeps the outboard compartments of tanks 1 and 3 full until their inboard compartments have drawn down: fuel near the tip relieves the most bending. On the ground the same weights make the wing droop; in flight, as the load factor rises, the wing's own inertia adds to that downward load, which is why both full tanks and a firm touchdown flex the tips down.

The wing is flexible enough for the motion to be seen from the cabin. Its first symmetric bending mode, measured in NASA's ground vibration test of a DC-10-10 with the tanks empty, is at about 1.6 to 1.7 cycles per second; fuel lowers the frequency, and the long wing is stiffer. The tips droop on a fueled aircraft at the gate, rise as the wing takes the weight on the takeoff roll, and flex on touchdown and in turbulence. Flaps and spoilers move the lift along the span and change the bending with it: extended flaps add lift over their part of the span, and raised spoilers dump it.

From nose to tail, the lower level holds the radome, the avionics compartment under the flight deck, the air conditioning compartments (where the packs are), the forward cargo hold, the center wing section with the main gear wheel wells behind it, the center cargo hold and the center accessory compartment, and the aft cargo hold with the bulk compartment. Aft of the rear pressure bulkhead are the aft accessory compartment, the APU compartment and the tail cone.

items: **Passenger DC-10s** have a lower galley in the forward part of the forward hold, which shortens that hold.
**Freighters and MD-10s** carry cargo on the main deck as well, loaded through the main-deck cargo door; their forward hold runs its full length.

**The KC-10A** keeps fuel where the other aircraft keep cargo: the forward and aft body tanks fill the lower holds, which are outside the pressure vessel, while the body tank access compartment and the center accessory compartment stay pressurized. The boom operator's compartment, in the lower aft fuselage below the rear of the main deck, is pressurized and entered through a hatch in the main deck floor.
**The fire tankers** carry no cargo: the retardant tanks fill the space under the fuselage.

Pressurized areas shaded, unpressurized areas left clear.
blocks.title: Compartment diagram

blocks.content: Positions along the fuselage are given as **fuselage stations** (FS), in inches aft of a datum plane, FS 0, which lies 239 inches ahead of the nose. On this scale the main gear center is at about FS 1442 and the rear pressure bulkhead at FS 2007. Weight and balance arms, tank centroids and the gear positions are all measured on it.

The center of gravity is expressed in **percent of the mean aerodynamic chord** (% MAC): the chord of an equivalent rectangular wing, placed where its aerodynamic center falls. For the long-span wing, the MAC is 295.8 in (24.65 ft) long and its leading edge (LEMAC) is at FS 1312.0, so a center of gravity at arm H inches lies at (H − 1312.0) ÷ 295.8 × 100 percent MAC. The short-span wing has a different MAC, and its loading data are not interchangeable with the long wing's. [Performance and Mission Planning](mission-planning) covers loading and balance; the center-of-gravity limits are in [Limitations](limitations).

The nose wheels are steered by the steering wheel (tiller) through 68° either side of center, and by the rudder pedals through 10° either side. Pedal steering is for small corrections on runways and straight taxiways; turns are made with the tiller. [Landing Gear and Brakes](landing-gear) describes the steering system.

blocks.content: The first row is the tightest turn recommended for routine use. The two maximum-steering rows are for a slow, continuous turn at maximum gross weight with an aft center of gravity, and are for occasional use only. The nose gear radius is measured to the outside face of the tire. The wing tip sweeps the widest circle, so watch the tips, not the nose, in a tight turn near obstacles.

The -15 and -40 have weights of their own, and the -30's limits fall when it operates with its center gear retracted: see [Limitations](limitations).

sections.title: Flight decks
sections.summary: The DC-10, KC-10 and MD-10 flight decks, panel by panel, and where each panel is described.

blocks.content: Three flight decks serve the family. The DC-10's and the KC-10A's are three-crew flight decks with a flight engineer's station and electromechanical or early electronic instruments; the MD-10's is a two-crew glass flight deck. Each subsection below names every panel area and the part of this manual that describes it.

DC-10-30 Early, Late, -30F Early, -30F Late, -30 Tanker; KDC-10
As above; the KDC-10 adds the boom operator's station

blocks.content: The DC-10 flight deck is laid out for three. The captain sits on the left and the first officer on the right, each with a full set of flight instruments, and between them the center instrument panel carries the engine instruments both pilots and the flight engineer watch. The flight engineer sits behind the first officer at a side-facing station along the right wall, in a seat that swivels between facing the panel and facing forward. Behind the captain are the first observer's seat and a folding second observer's seat, each with oxygen and an audio panel.

The division of work follows the layout. The pilots fly the aircraft from the glareshield, their instrument panels, the pedestal and the overhead panel; the flight engineer runs the electrical, hydraulic, fuel, pneumatic, air conditioning and pressurization systems and the APU from their station, monitors the engines, and reads the checklists. Systems with controls in both places, such as engine start and anti-ice, are split so that the pilots' overhead panel carries what the pilots need in flight and the engineer's panel carries the rest.

blocks.content: **By series.** The deck comes in three forms, which differ only where the airframe does:

items: **-10 deck** (the -10s and the -15): no center gear controls or indications. The -15 uses this deck unchanged.

**-30 deck** (the -30s, -30Fs, -30 Tanker and KDC-10): the center gear switch and indications, the center auxiliary tank's controls at the flight engineer's station, the center gear brakes' temperatures, and a working PMS when that option is selected. The -30 Tanker keeps the center gear switch but has no center gear behind it. The KDC-10 adds the KC-10A's boom operator's station in the lower aft fuselage, described in [Air Refueling Systems](air-refueling-systems).

**-40 deck** (the -40, -40F and Refueler): as the -30's, with the JT9D's engine indications and thrust set in EPR, and a rearranged flight engineer's station (below). The Refueler adds the two wing pod panels at the flight engineer's station.

blocks.content: The fire tankers add their tank control panels at the flight engineer's station, a drop control panel on the pedestal, two lights on the glareshield and drop buttons on the control wheels ([Aerial Firefighting System](aerial-firefighting)). Beyond that, many instruments and pedestal panels depend on the equipment fit: see [Equipment options](#equipment-options).

The KC-10A's flight deck keeps the DC-10's three-crew layout and its flight engineer's station, with military avionics in place of the airline's. The pilot sits on the left and the copilot on the right; the cockpit placards still read CAPT and F/O for their controls. The flight engineer sits at the side-facing station behind the copilot. Behind the pilot are the boom operator's forward station, where the boom operator sits for takeoff and landing, and a seat for an extra crew member or observer. The boom operator works the refueling equipment from their own compartment in the lower aft fuselage.

What sets this deck apart from the DC-10's is mainly navigation and display: a flight management system with three CDUs on the pedestal controls the three inertial navigation units, the GPS, the TACAN and ADF receivers and the IFF, and the pilots fly electronic ADIs and HSIs. The deck also carries the receiver and tanker air refueling lights, the KC-10A's own radios, and additions at the flight engineer's station for the refueling fuel system.

blocks.content: The air refueling operator's (ARO) compartment is a pressurized compartment in the lower aft fuselage, reached through a hatch at the rear of the main deck. It seats the boom operator at a wide sighting window, with seats beside the operator for an instructor and an observer, and is not occupied for takeoff and landing. From here the boom operator flies the boom with a control stick and extends it with the telescope lever, trails and rewinds the centerline hose, works the wing pods from their panels, and talks to the receiver.

The station has its own electrical bus controls, oxygen regulators, compartment temperature and window heat, and a lamp test for its lights. [Air Refueling Systems](air-refueling-systems) describes it control by control, and [Air Refueling](air-refueling) gives the procedures.

blocks.content: The flight engineer's station runs along the right wall behind the first officer (the KC-10A's copilot). It is where the aircraft's systems are managed: the generators and buses, the three hydraulic systems, every fuel tank and pump, the bleed air manifold and packs, the cabin pressure controller and the APU are all controlled and monitored here. FedEx calls the DC-10's flight engineer the second officer, and its manuals call this the second officer's station; the panels are the same.

The station is arranged in two rows. Three upper panels, numbered 1 to 3 from left to right, carry the electrical system and APU, the fire detection, air conditioning and pneumatic systems, and the miscellaneous systems. The lower panel, at desk height, carries the hydraulic system on the left and the fuel system on the right, with the engineer's work table below it. Circuit breaker panels surround the station: the avionics circuit breaker panel overhead, and the upper and lower main circuit breaker panels.

blocks.content: **On the DC-10s** the station also carries engine 2's bleed supply selector and pack 2's controls and gauges, the flight engineer's clock, and the panels that depend on the variant and fit: the AIDS panel and the MAC panel when fitted, the fire tankers' tank control panels in the AIDS panel's place, and the DC-10-40 Refueler's two wing pod panels. The fuel panel follows the series' tanks: the -30 and -40 carry the center auxiliary tank's pump selectors, and the -30 with Extended Range the aft auxiliary tank's pumps. Brake temperatures are shown for the eight wing gear brakes, plus the center gear's two on the -30 and -40. The -40's station differs from the others: its hydraulic panel is on upper panel No. 3 instead of the lower panel, and it has no potable water panel and no fuel flow counters.

**On the KC-10A** there is no engine 2 bleed column and no pack 2, because the tanker has neither. The station adds the aerial refueling block of the fuel panel (the six refueling pumps and their hydraulic pressure lights, the body tank and center wing tank controls, the isolation valves, manifold scavenge and offload indication), the WING AERIAL REFUEL panel for the wing pods, the APU generator controls and APU advisory panel, brake temperature for all ten brakes, the fuel quantity totalizer, cabin cargo smoke detection, the AVIONIC FLOW switch, and an oxygen regulator at the engineer's seat.

The flight engineer has their own MASTER WARNING and MASTER CAUTION lights in the status block. Certain warnings and cautions at the flight engineer's station also light the pilots' master lights, but each pair is reset only from its own station: see [Lights and annunciators](#lights-three-crew).

The MD-10's flight deck is the MD-11's two-crew glass flight deck fitted to a DC-10 airframe. The captain sits on the left and the first officer on the right; there is no flight engineer. Three observer seats are fitted: the left observer's seat behind the captain, the right observer's seat behind the first officer, where the DC-10's flight engineer station was, and on some aircraft a folding seat on the bulkhead left of the door. The right observer station also carries the main circuit breaker panels.

Six display units across the instrument panel replace the electromechanical instruments, and the glareshield carries the flight control panel for the autoflight system and an EIS control panel for each pilot's displays. The systems the flight engineer used to run are managed by automatic controllers, worked from the overhead panel; the crew sees their state on the system display and is told of faults by alerts on the engine and alert display. In normal operation the overhead panel is dark.

blocks.content: The six display units (DUs) are numbered 1 to 6 from left to right. Each is a full-color display with a 6.5 in square picture. What they show is drawn by three Versatile Integrated Avionics (VIA) computers in the avionics compartment. In the normal split the captain's side (DU 1 to 3) comes from VIA 1 and the first officer's side (DU 4 to 6) from VIA 2, with the third, auxiliary VIA held in reserve; the EIS SOURCE selectors on the source input select panels switch a side to another VIA. The same computers host the flight management system.

blocks.title: Display units in their normal arrangement

FCP and ECP on the glareshield
Navigation display (ND): position, route, navaids and airports
Engine and alert display (EAD): the primary engine instruments in the upper two-thirds, the alert list in the lower third
System display (SD): the secondary engine page, the system synoptics, and the status, consequences and miscellaneous pages
SDCP cue switches on the aft pedestal
[Warning and Recording Systems](warning-systems) and each system's part

blocks.content: The SDCP's seven system cue switches (ENG, HYD, ELEC, AIR, FUEL, CONFIG, MISC) call that system's synoptic to the SD; a cue switch lights white when its system has an alert. The CONSEQ switch shows the consequences of the alerts present, STATUS lists every system fault, and ND turns the SD into a third navigation display when fewer than six DUs are working. The same panel carries a brightness knob for each DU: brightness normally follows light sensors on each DU and on the glareshield, and turning a knob fully counterclockwise through its detent switches that DU off.

If a DU fails or is switched off, the remaining units take over its picture in a fixed order of priority, so that the attitude, flight path, engine and alert information needed to fly stays in view. [Flight Instruments](flight-instruments) gives the reversion rules.

DU numbers labeled beneath.

blocks.content: The MD-10's overhead panel replaces both the DC-10's pilots' overhead and its flight engineer's station. Each major system has one control panel of backlit pushbutton switches, and behind each panel sits an automatic controller in the avionics compartment that does the work the flight engineer used to do. In automatic operation the crew leaves the buttons alone: the controller configures the system for each phase of flight and reconfigures it after a failure, and its panel stays dark. Each panel has a manual mode in which the buttons command the system directly.

The reason is workload. On the DC-10 a generator failure, say, is handled by the flight engineer, who reads the indications, reconfigures the electrical system by the abnormal procedure and reports to the captain. On the MD-10 the electrical controller reconfigures the system at once, then raises an alert and lists the **consequences** on the system display: what has been lost and what the crew must still do. With the systems in automatic, the crew can complete the flight working from those consequences alone; the abnormal checklist adds what is needed to recover as much of the system as possible. If a controller itself fails, its panel's manual mode gives the crew the switches the flight engineer used to have.

blocks.content: The MD-10-10 HUD and MD-10-30 HUD have a head-up display for the captain: a combiner glass hung from the cockpit roof in front of the captain's eyes, on which flight symbology is projected focused at infinity, so that it lies over the outside view. The symbology is mostly conformal: the horizon and heading scale, the pitch ladder and the flight path vector sit where they belong in the outside world. Around them are the speed and altitude scales, the roll scale and slip indicator, angle of attack, the heading rose, and text for the selected speed and altitude, Mach, ground speed, vertical speed, barometric setting, minimums, wind and the active waypoint. Behind the symbology the HUD can show an infrared picture of the scene ahead.
The MD-10-10 and MD-10-30 without the HUD have no combiner and no mount for it. [Flight Instruments](flight-instruments) describes the HUD's symbology and controls.

sections.title: Conventions used in this manual
sections.summary: Panel and crew names, numbering, effectivity, light colors, alert levels, switches and instrument markings.

blocks.content: The rest of Section 1 relies on the conventions below. The three kinds of highlighted text (warnings, cautions and notes) and the crew designators are explained in the manual's introduction.

children.title: Panel names, crew titles and numbering

blocks.content: Controls, lights and messages are written in capitals exactly as they are placarded or displayed: the BUS TIE switch, set the selector to AUTO, the GEN OFF light, the APU FIRE handle. Panel areas are named as in [Flight decks](#flight-decks): the glareshield, the captain's, center and first officer's instrument panels, the forward and aft pedestal, the forward and aft overhead panels, and on the three-crew aircraft the flight engineer's upper panels No. 1 to 3 and lower panel. A control's location is given by its panel and, where needed, its group on the panel.

The DC-10's crew are the captain (CAPT), first officer (F/O) and flight engineer (FE). FedEx calls its DC-10 flight engineer the second officer (S/O) and the station the second officer's station; the panels are the same. The KC-10A's crew are the pilot, copilot, flight engineer and boom operator (BO); its placards read CAPT and F/O, and this manual uses those designators for the KC-10A's pilot and copilot. The MD-10 has a captain and first officer only.

items: **Left and right** are as seen from the flight deck, facing forward.

**Engines** are numbered 1 to 3 from left to right: engine 1 under the left wing, engine 2 in the tail, engine 3 under the right wing. Each engine's generator, hydraulic system, bleed source, fuel tank and AC bus take its number.

**Fuel tanks** 1 and 3 are the left and right wing tanks, each with an inboard and an outboard compartment; tank 2 is in two compartments either side of the fuselage. The auxiliary and body tanks are named, not numbered.
**Display units** on the MD-10 are numbered 1 to 6 from left to right.
**Doors** are numbered from front to rear on each side, L for left and R for right: 1L is the forward left door.

blocks.content: Content that applies to only some of the three aircraft carries a badge, such as **DC-10 / KC-10 only**. Pick your aircraft with the buttons at the top of the page and the rest drops out of view.

Differences inside one button are written into the text, the way airline manuals do, with the series in parentheses: "Center landing gear (-30, -40)." A series name covers all its variants unless the text says otherwise: "the -30" includes the -30F, the -30 Tanker and the KDC-10, and "the -10" includes the -10F and the -10 Tanker. The -15 is named separately wherever it differs from the -10. "Short-wing" means the -10, -15 and MD-10-10, and "long-wing" the -30, -40, KC-10 and MD-10-30. A particular variant is named as the simulator lists it: "the DC-10-30F Late".
Content that depends on the equipment fit names the item: "(HT-9100)", "(TCAS/VSI fitted)". The fits themselves are described under [Equipment options](#equipment-options).

On the DC-10 and KC-10 a fault light normally sits on or next to the switch or gauge it belongs to, so the crew member who must act finds the light at the control. The exception is a system worked from more than one station: its lights are collected on an annunciator panel, either the pilots' annunciator panel on the forward overhead panel or the status annunciator block on the flight engineer's upper panel No. 2. A light's color tells you how urgent it is.

blocks.title: Light colors
rows: Warning: a condition that needs immediate action
Fire warnings, landing gear not down and locked, CABIN ALT, the red summary lights, MASTER WARN
Caution: a condition that needs attention, but not immediately
System fault and low-pressure lights, MASTER CAUTION, the cue lights
Advisory: a switch or valve is in a position worth knowing about. Not a fault, and it does not light the MASTER CAUTION
ENG ANTI-ICE SW ON, APU FUEL PUMP SW ON, APU/ISOL VALVE OPEN, the crew call CALLING lights

blocks.content: **Master warning and master caution.** Each pilot has a red MASTER WARN and an amber MASTER CAUTION light on the glareshield. Any warning or caution light at the pilots' stations brings on the matching master light, and so do selected lights on the flight engineer's panel, which is how a fault the engineer is handling also reaches the pilots. A push on either pilot's master light cancels the pair on both sides and arms them for the next fault. The engineer's own MASTER WARNING and MASTER CAUTION lights, in the status block, are cancelled only at the engineer's station, and cancelling them leaves the pilots' lights alone. Cancelling a master light never puts out the fault light itself: that stays on until the condition is gone.

**Summary and cue lights.** The pilots' annunciator panel tells the pilots which part of the engineer's panel has a problem. Five red **summary lights** (EMER BUS OFF, PNEU MANFLD FAIL, CABIN ALT, PNEU TEMP HI and APU FIRE) follow their warnings and have no reset: each goes out only when its condition clears. Four amber **cue lights** (ELEC, FUEL, HYD and PNEU, each placarded PRESS TO RESET) point to a caution light lit in that system at the flight engineer's station. Pushing a cue light puts it out and takes the pilots' MASTER CAUTION lights out with it, unless another fault is still holding them on.

**Tests and brightness.** The ANNUN LT TEST switch on the forward overhead panel lights every annunciator on the pilots' panel and selected lights on the instrument panels. The flight engineer tests their station with the ALL TEST, or one area at a time with the AREA TEST selector (UPPER 1, UPPER 2, UPPER 3 and LOWER PNL), on upper panel No. 3. A PRESS TO BRT/DIM button at each station switches that station's annunciators between bright and dim, except the master lights. With every system normal in cruise, the annunciator panels are dark apart from any blue advisories that the switch selections call for.

blocks.alt: The pilots' annunciator panel on the DC-10 forward overhead panel during the ANNUN LT TEST: every legend lit, the five red summary lights (EMER BUS OFF, PNEU MANFLD FAIL, CABIN ALT, PNEU TEMP HI, APU FIRE) and the four amber cue lights (ELEC, FUEL, HYD, PNEU, PRESS TO RESET) identified with callouts, the ANNUN LT TEST and PRESS TO BRT/DIM buttons beside them.
blocks.title: Pilots' annunciator panel

blocks.content: The MD-10's overhead panel follows the **dark cockpit** philosophy: when the aircraft is configured for normal flight, almost every switch light on it is out. A dark panel means the system is in its normal configuration and has no fault, so a glance across the overhead for anything lit is a check of the whole aircraft. The legends on the pushbutton switch lights follow one color code:

blocks.title: Overhead switch light colors
rows: Every panel in AUTO with its systems working
Advisory: a switch selected to a position worth knowing about, usually one that is seldom used
ON (a pump commanded on, a crossfeed valve commanded open), ARM and FILL (a fill valve armed or open), MANUAL
Abnormal: a fault, a disagreement, or a system switched off that is normally on
FAULT, DISAG (a valve not where it was commanded), LOW (low pump pressure), OFF

blocks.content: Faults are reported as **alerts** on the engine and alert display (EAD), in the lower third of DU 3, graded in four levels. The highest level is shown first and is never overwritten.

blocks.title: Alert levels
rows: Red, boxed, with a leading triangle
An emergency: immediate crew action needed
An abnormal condition: immediate awareness, then corrective action
May need maintenance before takeoff, a logbook entry, or a check of the system configuration

blocks.content: A level 3, 2 or 1 alert also lights its system's cue switch white on the system display control panel. Pressing the cue switch shows that system's synoptic on the SD with the alert's **consequences**, the effects of the failure and the action required, and resets the master light. Level 3 alerts are acknowledged this way but stay on the EAD while the condition exists. Level 2 and 1 alerts are removed from the list and replaced by an amber **reminder** with the system's name (boxed for level 2) in the bottom rows of the right-hand column. [Warning and Recording Systems](warning-systems) describes the alerting system in full.

blocks.title: Display colors
rows: Scales and their figures; values and modes selected manually; inactive lines on the synoptics
Status messages; navigation database items available but not in use
Valid and active: the track diamond, autoland modes, landing gear safe, trend vectors, active lines on the synoptics
Computed or selected by the system: FMS targets, flight director commands, radio navigation data, localizer and glideslope deviation
Failures, cautions, abnormal sources and abnormal system conditions
Warnings, autopilot and autothrottle disconnects, airspeed, attitude and engine limits and exceedances, landing gear not safe

blocks.content: Lost data is removed from a display and, where it matters, replaced by an X: red where the crew must act at once to restore the data, amber where restoring it can wait. When the captain's and first officer's displays disagree on attitude, airspeed, altitude, barometric setting, radio altitude, ILS or heading, an amber miscompare appears beside the attitude display. A display fed from its pilot's own side's sources shows no source label; one fed from an alternate source labels it, in white if the two pilots' sources still differ and in amber if both now use the same one.

blocks.alt: Close-up of the lower third of the MD-10 engine and alert display with one example of each alert level: a level 3 alert in red with a box and leading triangle at top left, a boxed amber level 2 alert below it, an unboxed amber level 1 alert, a cyan level 0 advisory at the bottom right, and an amber reminder message (FUEL) in the bottom right rows.
blocks.title: Alert levels on the engine and alert display

blocks.content: Procedures use a small set of verbs: **set** or **select** a switch or selector to a position, **press** a pushbutton, **pull** a handle, **rotate** a knob. A **momentary** switch acts only while held and springs back; an **alternate-action** pushbutton changes state each time it is pressed, and its legend shows which state it is in.

Switches whose accidental operation would be hard to undo or would remove a system from service sit under a hinged **guard**, which must be lifted before the switch can be moved. On the DC-10 and KC-10 these include the constant-speed drive disconnects, the fuel dump switch and the pneumatic isolation valve switches; on the KC-10A, also the FMS BUS SPLIT switch. A guarded switch is normally left with its guard closed, in its normal position. Fire handles and the ADG release handle are pulled; the ADG handle works in one direction only, and the ADG can be stowed again only on the ground.
Gauges are marked with colored arcs and radials that reflect the operating limits. Read them as part of every scan:

rows: Warning or danger; a maximum or minimum limit

blocks.content: On the MD-10's display units the same idea is carried by the display colors: an engine parameter changes color as it reaches a caution or a limit. The limits themselves are in [Limitations](limitations).

blocks.content: **Choosing a variant.** Each variant is its own aircraft in the simulator's aircraft selection, under the types DC-10, DC-10-40 Refueler, KC-10A, KDC-10 and MD-10. The aircraft recognizes the variant as it loads and builds the matching airframe, systems and flight deck; there is nothing to set.

**What is interactive.** Every control and indication this manual describes works unless the part concerned says otherwise in its own Simulation notes. That includes the circuit breakers, several hundred on each aircraft, which can be pulled and reset. Items that exist in the 3D flight deck but do nothing are listed in the Simulation notes of the system they belong to.
**Early and Late.** The Early and Late variants of the -10, -30 and -30F share their systems and flight deck; only the exterior differs.

**The equipment fit.** A DC-10 loads with the default fit each time; choose the rest before you start the flight. The Professional equipment items are available only while the Infinity Manager is running and has confirmed your edition; without it, the aircraft offers the standard items only. Two DC-10 retrofits are simulated but not yet selectable: the enhanced ground proximity warning voice and its terrain database. By default a DC-10 has the basic GPWS. The PMS option can be selected on the -10 and -15, but those airframes have no performance management computer, so it fits a blank unit there and removes the autobrake selector and VHF-3 head as it does on the -30 and -40. The ANS-70 is simulated in simplified form.

**Editions.** The DC-10-30 passenger aircraft, freighters and fire tanker and the KC-10A come with every edition. The DC-10-10s, the DC-10-15, the DC-10-40s and the KDC-10, and the equipment items marked (Pro), need the Professional edition. The MD-10s need the Deluxe edition, which includes everything in Professional.

**Mission variants.** The real KDC-10's boom was flown from a remote operator's station using cameras; the simulated KDC-10 carries the KC-10A's boom operator's compartment in the tail instead. Its station's bus isolation switches, oxygen regulators, compartment temperature and window heat controls have no effect, because the DC-10-30 has none of the systems they control, and its boom offloads no fuel. The simulated KDC-10 has no main-deck cargo door. The DC-10-40 Refueler's pod installation is modeled on the KC-10A's. The DC-10-15's engines are modeled on the CF6-50C2's performance.

**MD-10 flight deck.** Three MCDUs show the flight management system, but only the first MCDU's keys work at present. TCAS is not simulated on the MD-10, and the weather radar picture is not yet drawn on the NDs. The head-up display does not yet show the flight mode annunciations or the flight director guidance cue. Alert consequences are not yet listed on the system display, and the single chime for a new level 2 alert is not sounded: see [Warning and Recording Systems](warning-systems).

**Structure and weight.** The wings flex. The simulation solves each wing's first bending mode under the loads it carries at the moment (its structure, the engine, the main gear, any refueling pod and the fuel in each tank compartment, against lift spread along the span), with the stiffness calibrated to NASA's ground vibration test, and the exterior shows the result. Only that one mode is modeled: the two wings always bend alike, the wing does not twist as it bends, and the engines do not move on their pylons. Every aircraft's weight is shared between its landing gear legs according to its weight and center of gravity, the center gear included where fitted. Percent MAC is worked out on the long-span wing's mean aerodynamic chord on every airframe, the short-span ones included.

**Pre-flight items.** An aircraft loaded cold and dark starts with wheel chocks, pitot covers, engine covers and traffic cones in place, as it was left parked. Remove them from the EFB's Ground Ops app; the chocks and covers can also be removed by clicking them on the walkaround. While they are on, the pitot covers block the pitot inlets and the chocks hold the aircraft whatever the parking brake is doing. Each item also comes off by itself when it no longer could stay on: the chocks and cones when the aircraft moves, the pitot covers when it moves with an engine running or leaves the ground, the engine covers when an engine starts. See [Ground Operations and Towing](ground-operations).

**EFB settings that apply to every part.** Settings in the EFB choose the navigation database (the simulator's or Navigraph's) and whether inertial alignment is realistic or instant. The Configuration app's Aircraft Setup page chooses which radio the simulator's COM 2 tunes, and offers a brake type setting that is stored but not yet used: each airframe flies its own brakes. See [Electronic Flight Bag](efb).

parts.title: Engines
parts.summary: The CF6 and JT9D turbofans: construction, fuel control, starting, thrust reversers and indications.

blocks.content: Every aircraft in the family has three two-spool, high-bypass turbofans. Engines 1 and 3 hang on pylons under the left and right wings; engine 2 sits in the tail, in a nacelle built into the base of the fin. Three engine families are fitted: the General Electric CF6-6D on the short-span DC-10-10 and the MD-10-10, the CF6-50 series on the DC-10-15, DC-10-30, KC-10A and MD-10-30, and the Pratt & Whitney JT9D-59A on the DC-10-40. The CF6 engines are set by fan speed (N1); the JT9D is set by engine pressure ratio (EPR).

Thrust is only part of an engine's job. Its high-pressure spool drives an accessory gearbox carrying the fuel pump and fuel control, the oil pumps, the generator drive and two engine-driven hydraulic pumps; its compressor supplies bleed air to the pneumatic system; and its fan nacelle carries a pneumatically driven thrust reverser. An engine lost therefore takes a generator, two hydraulic pumps and a pneumatic source with it, which is why the [electrical](electrical), [hydraulic](hydraulics) and [pneumatic](pneumatics) systems are each built three ways, one per engine.

blocks.alt: Functional schematic of one CF6 engine as installed on the DC-10, side section. The low-pressure spool (fan, booster and low-pressure turbine on the inner shaft) in one color, the high-pressure spool (high-pressure compressor and high-pressure turbine on the outer shaft) in another, the annular combustor between them. A radial drive shaft from the HP spool to the accessory gearbox, with each pad labeled: air turbine starter, main engine control and fuel pump, oil supply and scavenge pumps, generator drive, two hydraulic pumps, N2 speed sensor. Bleed ports on the HP compressor piped to the pneumatic manifold; fan reverser translating cowl at the rear of the fan nacelle. Inset: aircraft plan view numbering engine 1 (left wing), engine 2 (tail), engine 3 (right wing).
blocks.title: Engine arrangement and accessory drives
blocks.caption: Two independent spools, coupled only by the gas flow. The accessory gearbox and the starter are on the high-pressure spool.

blocks.content: This part works from the inside out: how each engine is built and why its cycle behaves as it does; how the hydromechanical fuel control meters fuel; how thrust limits are computed and set; starting and ignition; the oil system, vibration monitoring and the bleed, anti-ice and accessory interfaces; and the thrust reversers. It then covers the controls and indications for each flight deck, normal operation through a flight, failures, and what the simulation models.

sections.title: Construction and engine types
sections.summary: The two-spool high-bypass turbofan, the CF6-6D, CF6-50 and JT9D-59A, and the cycle that governs their behavior.

blocks.content: All three engine families share one layout: a large single-stage fan at the front, a low-pressure compressor (booster) behind it on the same shaft, a high-pressure compressor, an annular combustor, a high-pressure turbine driving the high-pressure compressor and a low-pressure turbine driving the fan. They differ in how the work is shared between fan and core, in the number of compressor and turbine stages, in how the compressor is kept stable at low speed, and in what the crew uses to set thrust.

A jet engine makes thrust by accelerating air: thrust equals the mass flow through the engine times the increase in its velocity. A given thrust can come from accelerating a little air a lot, as a turbojet does, or a lot of air a little. At subsonic speeds the second is far more efficient, because the kinetic energy left behind in the jet, which is wasted, grows with the square of the velocity increase while thrust grows only in proportion to it. Propulsive efficiency is roughly 2 ÷ (1 + Vj/V0), where Vj is the jet velocity and V0 the flight speed: the closer the jet is to the flight speed, the less energy is thrown away.

The high-bypass turbofan puts that idea into practice by splitting the air at the fan. A small **core stream** passes through the compressors, combustor and turbines and makes the power. A much larger **bypass stream** is compressed only by the fan and leaves through the fan nozzle at moderate velocity. The **bypass ratio** is the mass flow of the bypass stream divided by that of the core. On the CF6-50C2 it is 4.31 to 1, and at full rated power the fan makes about 73 % of the thrust and the core the remaining 27 %. The slower jet is also much quieter.

The fan has to turn slowly, because its blade tips approach the speed of sound long before the core compressor's small blades do. The core compressor has to turn fast to do its work in a reasonable number of stages. Each engine therefore has two independent shafts, or **spools**. The **low-pressure spool (N1)** carries the fan and booster and is driven by the low-pressure turbine at the back of the engine. The **high-pressure spool (N2)** carries the high-pressure compressor and is driven by the high-pressure turbine immediately behind the combustor. The LP shaft runs inside the hollow HP shaft and the two are coupled only through the gas: fan speed settles wherever the low-pressure turbine's share of the gas energy balances the fan's load. The accessory gearbox and the starter are on the HP spool, which is why a start begins with N2 and N1 follows.

N1 and N2 are shown as percentages of a reference rotor speed. **100 % is a reference, not a maximum.** The CF6-6D's N1 red line is 111 %; the CF6-50C2's takeoff N1 runs from about 103 % to about 116 % depending on temperature, and its N1 red line is 118.5 %.

The CF6-6 was developed for the DC-10-10 and has the highest bypass ratio in the family, about 5.8 to 1. The fan and its booster form the low-pressure compressor. The core is a 16-stage high-pressure compressor in which the inlet guide vanes and the first six stator rows are variable, followed by an annular combustor, an air-cooled high-pressure turbine, and the low-pressure turbine that drives the fan. The -6 has no variable bypass valves: its booster adds comparatively little pressure, so there is little surplus booster air to spill at low speed. Customer bleed air comes from the 9th stage (low) and the 13th stage (high).

Takeoff thrust is in the 40,000 lb class. The engine is flat rated: up to about +20 °C total air temperature its takeoff rating is a constant corrected fan speed, and above that the rating falls away. At sea level on a standard day the takeoff N1 is 101.8 % with the packs off and 101.2 % with them on.

The -6D also has an **automatic cutback system** against fan blade failure. A dead-ended manifold around the fan case is pressurized from the compressor discharge pressure (CDP) signal line to the main engine control. A blade that fails ruptures the manifold, the CDP signal falls to ambient pressure, and the control responds by cutting fuel to less than the ground idle schedule, slowing the damaged rotor without crew action.

Station numbers 2, 2.5, 3, 4 and 5.4 marked along the gas path; N1 and N2 shafts labeled.
blocks.title: CF6-6D

blocks.content: The CF6-50 is the -6 developed for more thrust from a fan of similar size. General Electric traded bypass ratio for core flow and pressure ratio: the bypass ratio falls to 4.31 to 1, the booster does more work, and the core is a 14-stage high-pressure compressor with the inlet guide vanes and the first five stator rows variable. To keep the bigger booster matched to the core at low speed, **variable bypass valves (VBVs)** are fitted in the core flow path ahead of the high-pressure compressor: they open at low speed to spill surplus booster air into the fan stream and close as speed rises. The main engine control positions both the stators and the VBVs as a function of core speed and compressor inlet temperature. Behind the annular combustor are a two-stage air-cooled high-pressure turbine and a four-stage low-pressure turbine; core and fan streams leave through separate fixed-area nozzles.

The CF6-50C2 is flat rated to 30 °C at sea level. Installed takeoff thrust is 51,800 lb (about 52,500 lb uninstalled) and maximum continuous thrust 46,300 lb. Because the -50 turns its fan fast relative to its 100 % reference, its takeoff N1 looks high by -6 standards: about 111 % at sea level on a standard day, from about 103 % at −40 °C to about 116 % at +20 °C. Customer bleed comes from the 8th stage (low) and the compressor discharge, the 14th stage (high).

The DC-10-15's CF6-50C2F is a -50C2 variant built for that aircraft, which put -50 power on the short-span -10 airframe for hot-and-high operation. The simulation runs it on the -50C2's data and limits.

Bleed ports at the 8th stage and compressor discharge labeled.
blocks.title: CF6-50C2

blocks.content: The DC-10-40 is the Pratt & Whitney DC-10. Two JT9D models flew on it: Northwest Orient's aircraft had the JT9D-20 and -20J, Japan Air Lines' the later JT9D-59A. The simulation models the **-59A**, certificated at 51,720 lb takeoff thrust (dry, five minutes) and 44,770 lb maximum continuous, flat rated at and below 86 °F (30 °C).

Its compressor has 16 stages counted through both spools: the fan, four low-pressure stages (one of them the inserted stage that P&W numbers 1.5) and an 11-stage high-pressure compressor. The turbine has six stages, two high-pressure and four low-pressure. The inlet guide vanes and the first three high-pressure stator rows are variable, and bleed valves in the compressor case open at low speed for starting and surge margin. The fuel control is a Hamilton Standard hydromechanical unit; like the CF6s, the -59A has no electronic engine control. The bypass ratio is about 4.9 to 1. Customer bleed comes from the 8th and 15th stages in P&W's through-numbering, the second being the last high-pressure stage.

Two things look different on the flight deck. Thrust is set by **EPR**, the ratio of the total pressure at the low-pressure turbine discharge (Pt7) to the total pressure at the engine inlet (Pt2), measured by probes that are part of the engine. And **EGT is measured at a different station**: at the low-pressure turbine discharge (Tt7) rather than between the turbines as on the CF6. The -59A's takeoff EGT limit of 685 °C is not a cooler engine but a cooler measuring point, downstream of turbine stages that have already taken the work out of the gas.

The Pt2 inlet probe and the Pt7 and Tt7 probes at the turbine discharge called out, with a note that EPR = Pt7/Pt2. Fan reverser translating cowl.
blocks.title: JT9D-59A

blocks.content: Limits in this table are summarized from the DC-10, KC-10 and MD-10 flight manuals and, for the JT9D-59A, its type certificate. The MD-10 FCOM lists the CF6-50C2's maximum N1 as 119.5 % (with its overspeed band starting at 119.6 %); the FedEx DC-10 and KC-10 books give 118.5 %. The governing figures are in Section 4, [Limitations](limitations).

children.title: The cycle, corrected parameters and flat rating

blocks.content: The core runs a Brayton cycle. Engineers number the stations along the gas path, and the numbers appear in limits and placards: **2** is the fan face; **2.5** the high-pressure compressor inlet, where the CF6 measures its compressor inlet temperature (CIT); **3** compressor discharge (CDP); **4** the combustor exit and high-pressure turbine inlet, the hottest point in the engine; **5.4** the low-pressure turbine inlet, where the CF6 measures EGT; **7** the low-pressure turbine discharge, where the JT9D measures EGT and EPR.

Air is compressed by the fan, booster and high-pressure compressor, which raises its pressure and temperature. Fuel is burned at nearly constant pressure, raising the temperature toward the turbine's limit. The gas then expands through the high-pressure turbine, which drives the compressor, the low-pressure turbine, which drives the fan and booster, and the core nozzle. The higher the overall pressure ratio and the hotter the turbine inlet, the more work each pound of air yields and the better the fuel consumption. Turbine inlet temperature is the engine's real limit, and since it cannot be measured in service, the exhaust gas temperature downstream stands in for it.

An engine takes its air at whatever temperature and pressure the day offers, so its parameters are compared in **corrected** form. Dividing a rotor speed by the square root of θ (inlet total temperature divided by 288.15 K) gives corrected speed; dividing a pressure or a thrust by δ (inlet total pressure divided by 14.696 psia) gives the corrected value. Two engines at the same corrected fan speed are at the same aerodynamic operating point and make the same corrected thrust. A cold day needs less physical N1 for a given thrust and a hot day more.

**Flat rating** follows from this. Up to the flat-rating break temperature, the takeoff rating is a constant corrected fan speed: physical takeoff N1 climbs with the square root of inlet temperature, rated thrust stays constant, and the turbine is still below its temperature limit. Above the break the turbine inlet temperature has reached its limit, rated corrected speed has to fall, and takeoff thrust falls with it. The CF6-50's takeoff N1 chart reduces to a single corrected fan speed, about 111 %, across its whole flat-rated range. A thrust rating computer is in large part a machine for turning that number into the physical N1 the day requires.

EGT follows the same logic. At flat-rated takeoff thrust, EGT climbs with ambient temperature up to the break and then stays close to its limit. Takeoff EGT margin is therefore smallest on hot days, and a hot-day takeoff on a deteriorated engine is where the 5-minute and 2-minute EGT bands are reached.

Thrust lapses with altitude, because the air is thinner (δ falls), and with speed, because the engine must first bring the incoming air up to its own velocity before adding any thrust (ram drag). In cruise near Mach 0.85 at FL350 an engine of this class makes roughly a quarter of its sea-level static thrust.

blocks.alt: Line chart for the CF6-50C2 at sea level against outside air temperature from −40 °C to +50 °C. Solid line, left axis: full-rated takeoff N1, rising from about 103 % at −40 °C to a peak of about 116 % near +20 to +30 °C and falling beyond. Dashed line, left axis: corrected takeoff N1, flat at about 111 % up to the break and falling above it. Dotted line, right axis: takeoff thrust, flat at 51,800 lb up to 30 °C and falling beyond. The flat-rating break at 30 °C marked with a vertical line.
