blocks.caption: Constant corrected fan speed up to the break gives constant thrust; the physical N1 the crew sets rises with temperature.

children.title: Compressor stability: variable geometry, bleed valves and stall

blocks.content: An axial compressor stage is a ring of small wings. Each blade must meet the air at the right angle of incidence: too little and it does no work, too much and the flow separates, exactly as a wing stalls. A multistage compressor is designed for high speed, where each stage receives air already compressed by the ones in front. At low speed the front stages compress less than the design assumes, so the air at the rear is less dense than intended and moves through faster. The rear stages are then starved of work while the front stages run at high incidence, close to stall.

**Variable stator vanes** solve the front-end problem. Closing the inlet guide vanes and the first stator rows at low corrected speed pre-swirls the air in the direction of rotation and reduces the incidence each blade sees; as speed rises the vanes open to pass full flow. The CF6-50's **variable bypass valves** solve the matching problem between booster and core: at low speed the booster delivers more air than the high-pressure compressor can swallow, and the surplus is spilled into the fan duct rather than forced into a compressor that would stall on it. The JT9D's compressor bleed valves do the same job for its low-pressure compressor. All are scheduled on corrected core speed, that is on N2 and compressor inlet temperature, and all are positioned by the fuel control.

A stall can stay local, as a **rotating stall** in which cells of separated flow travel around the annulus and the engine hangs at reduced airflow with rising EGT. Or it can collapse the pressure rise of the whole compressor: a **surge**. In a surge the compressed air in the combustor briefly flows backwards out of the compressor with a loud bang, sometimes with flame at the inlet or exhaust, a drop in N1 and N2 and a jump in EGT. A surge usually clears by itself as the compressor re-establishes flow; if the cause remains, it repeats in a cycle.

Anything that pushes the operating point toward the stall line can cause one: an acceleration faster than the fuel control allows; inlet distortion from a strong crosswind or tailwind at high power on the ground, a very high angle of attack, or reverser efflux re-ingested at low speed; compressor blades damaged by foreign objects or ice; heavy bleed extraction at low power; or a mis-rigged variable stator system. The fuel control's acceleration schedule exists to keep normal accelerations clear of the line.

children.title: Why the CF6 is set by N1 and the JT9D by EPR

blocks.content: Both are thrust indexes. Neither is thrust itself; each is chosen because it tracks thrust closely and can be measured reliably in service.

On a high-bypass engine most of the thrust comes from the fan, and the fan's thrust depends almost entirely on how fast it turns and on the air entering it. General Electric therefore rated the CF6 on corrected fan speed. N1 comes from a speed sensor and needs no pressure probes, so it cannot be fooled by an iced or leaking probe, and it stays a good thrust index as the core deteriorates: a worn core simply runs hotter and faster to drive the fan to the same speed. Its drawback is that the N1 for a given thrust depends on temperature, so every takeoff needs a chart or a thrust rating computer.

Pratt & Whitney's practice, carried from its turbojets to the JT9D, was engine pressure ratio. EPR compares the total pressure of the gas leaving the low-pressure turbine with the total pressure at the inlet. It responds to everything the core is doing, follows thrust closely through the operating range, and its rated value varies less with temperature than N1 does. Its weakness is that it is a pressure measurement: a blocked or iced inlet probe makes indicated EPR read high, and the crew sets less thrust than they believe. EPR-rated engines are therefore always cross-checked against N1, EGT and fuel flow, especially in icing.

On the DC-10-40, EPR is the primary thrust instrument: the thrust rating computer computes an EPR limit and the autothrottle holds EPR in its fixed-thrust mode. N1 is still displayed and still has its red line.

sections.title: Fuel control
sections.summary: Fuel delivery, the hydromechanical main engine control and its schedules, ground and flight idle, and fuel flow measurement.

blocks.content: Each engine has a hydromechanical fuel control, the main engine control (MEC) on the CF6 and a Hamilton Standard unit on the JT9D, with no electronic authority over it. The crew commands the engine with two levers, the throttle and the fuel lever. Everything between the levers and the fuel nozzles is the control's mechanical logic: flyweights, cams, servo valves and pressure-sensing bellows.

blocks.alt: Schematic of one engine's fuel system downstream of the wing tank: tank boost pumps, engine fire shutoff valve, two-stage engine-driven pump (centrifugal boost element and gear high-pressure element), fuel/oil heat exchanger, main fuel filter with its differential pressure switch and bypass valve wired to the FUEL FILTER PRESS DROP light, main engine control with its inputs drawn as arrows (throttle cable, fuel lever cable to the shutoff valve, N2 drive, CIT sensor, CDP signal line), outputs to the variable stator and VBV actuators, pressurizing and drain valve, fuel flow transmitter wired to the FF indicator and FUEL USED counter, fuel manifold and nozzles.
blocks.title: Engine fuel and control system

blocks.content: Fuel from the tank boost pumps enters a two-stage pump on the accessory gearbox: a centrifugal boost element raises the pressure, and a gear element delivers high-pressure fuel to the control. On the way the fuel passes through the **fuel/oil heat exchanger**, where it takes heat from the engine oil, cooling the oil and warming the fuel enough to keep ice crystals from forming, and then through the **main fuel filter**. Metered fuel leaves the MEC through the **pressurizing and drain valve**, which holds the flow back until manifold pressure is high enough for the nozzles to atomize properly and drains the manifold at shutdown, then passes the **fuel flow transmitter** and reaches the manifold and fuel nozzles (30 on the CF6).

The **fuel shutoff valve** is inside the MEC and is worked by the FUEL lever on the pedestal. Pulling an engine fire handle closes a separate fire shutoff valve upstream of the engine; see [Fire protection](fire-protection) and [Fuel](fuel).

A differential pressure switch across the main fuel filter lights **FUEL FILTER PRESS DROP** (ICING on the DC-10-40's panel, the ENG n FUEL FILTER alert on the MD-10) when the filter is close to clogging. If it clogs further a bypass valve opens and unfiltered fuel goes on to the control, with no further indication. Debris and ice crystals in very cold fuel both load the filter.
The engine fuel pump and the MEC are lubricated by the fuel passing through them. Do not motor an engine unless fuel inlet pressure is positive, with the tank boost pumps on.

The MEC senses four things: **power lever angle** from the throttle; **core speed** through a geared drive from the accessory gearbox to a set of flyweights (on the CF6-6D the drive turns at 5,998 rpm at 100 % N2); **compressor inlet temperature** (CIT) through a sensing bulb; and **compressor discharge pressure** (Ps3) through a signal line. From them it meters fuel, and it positions the variable stator vanes and, on the CF6-50, the variable bypass valves.

**The throttle commands a core speed, not a fuel flow.** A cam turns lever angle into a demanded N2, from the ground idle setting at the idle stop to the full-throttle setting at the forward stop, and the speed governor meters whatever fuel it takes to hold that speed. The governor is a droop governor: proportional only, with no integrating term, as flyweight governors are. Its steady speed sags slightly when the shaft load on the core rises, for instance when the hydraulic pumps or the generator take more power, and fuel flow rises to pay for it.

Customer bleed acts differently. Taking compressed air out of the core removes mass flow, not shaft torque, so N2 hardly moves while EGT rises, and N1, and with it thrust, falls a little: less air reaches the turbines for the same fuel, and the low-pressure turbine has less energy to drive the fan with. Same throttle, same N2, higher EGT, lower N1 is the familiar signature of packs and anti-ice on a CF6.

Both settings are **corrected**: the cam and governor work on core speed referred to compressor inlet temperature. The forward stop is therefore temperature-scheduled and corresponds to slightly more than full-rated takeoff N1 for the day, not to a fixed N2. Idle is scheduled the same way, so physical idle N2 rises on a hot day and falls on a cold one; on the CF6-6D's schedule, ground idle is about 54 % N2 at −30 °C and about 60 % at +40 °C.

Between the governor and the nozzles sit two stops. The **acceleration limit** caps fuel flow during a throttle advance, so that combustor temperature and the compressor's operating point stay inside their limits while the rotor spools up. The **deceleration limit** is a floor that stops a sudden throttle chop from leaning the combustor so far that the flame blows out while the compressor is still delivering high airflow. Both are scheduled as the ratio of fuel flow to compressor discharge pressure (Wf/Ps3) against corrected core speed. Because Ps3 carries both the altitude and the temperature of the air inside the engine, the schedules compensate for altitude and temperature with no separate term for either.

The schedules show on the gauges. A rapid advance from idle is paced by the acceleration limit: fuel flow leads, EGT rises ahead of N1, and the engine takes about 7 to 8 seconds from ground idle to approach takeoff N1. A slow advance keeps the governor in control the whole way and peaks lower in EGT; the 2-minute EGT band in the limits exists for the transient of a normal takeoff advance. A chop to idle drives fuel flow briefly below its idle value, held up only by the deceleration limit, before it recovers as the governor takes back control near idle.

During a start the control meters fuel on a separate schedule that rises with N2 below idle, held before light-off to a normal value of about 550 to 650 pph. More than 700 pph before light-off risks a hot start.

The fuel control has two idle settings. **Ground idle** is the lowest speed at which the engine runs reliably and keeps its accessories supplied; it minimizes thrust, fuel burn, noise and jet blast on the ground. **Flight idle** is a higher idle for use in the air. The reason for it is acceleration time. At low N2 the compressor has little stall margin to spare for extra fuel and the turbine little energy to spare for spooling up, so an engine accelerates slowly from ground idle. From flight idle it reaches go-around thrust in a few seconds. Flight idle also keeps bleed pressure up for anti-icing and pressurization in the descent.

Selection is automatic: there is no idle control in the cockpit. The ground control relays, driven from the nose gear ground shift mechanism, select **flight idle** as the nose strut extends at rotation and return to **ground idle** after landing. Flight idle is held for a short time after the nose gear touches down, so that the engines spool up quickly when reverse thrust is selected.

**Flight idle is a floor under the throttle, not a new starting point for it.** With the throttle above the flight idle setting the demanded N2 is the same in the air as on the ground, so the shift at rotation does not change takeoff or climb thrust. Only when the throttle comes back into the lower part of its travel does the floor take over and hold the engine at flight idle. At cruise altitude that can be the bottom third of the lever or more, so a mid-range lever sits a little further forward in the air than on the ground for the same N1.

Beyond the full-throttle setting of its cam, the hydromechanical control has no topping or overspeed governor that stops the engine at a thrust limit. The forward stop gives slightly more than rated takeoff thrust on a standard day, and on a cold day full throttle can take N1 past the takeoff setting the thrust rating computer computes. The crew sets thrust to the computed limit and respects the red lines; the computer's limits position bugs and cap the autothrottle, but they do not cap the engine.

Two mechanical stops do act on the engine. In reverse, a stop in the fuel control limits reverse thrust to 95 % N2 (see [Thrust reversers](#thrust-reversers)). On the CF6-6D the automatic cutback system described under the engine types cuts fuel to below ground idle after a fan blade failure. Overspeed and overtemperature are otherwise recognized by the crew and handled by the actions in [Failures](#overspeed-overtemperature).

Each engine's fuel flow transmitter, downstream of the pressurizing and drain valve, measures the metered flow in pounds per hour. It drives the pilots' fuel flow indication and, on the DC-10 and KC-10, the flight engineer's fuel flow counter and the **FUEL USED** counter, which totals the fuel delivered to that engine since the last reset. The number 2 counter does not include APU fuel.
Typical values per engine: about 550 to 650 pph before light-off on a start; about 1,100 to 1,200 pph at ground idle; in the order of 13,000 to 14,000 pph at takeoff power on a CF6-50 at sea level.

sections.title: Thrust limits and thrust setting
sections.summary: Who computes the N1 or EPR limit on each flight deck, and how the crew sets thrust against it.

blocks.content: Rated thrust for each mode (takeoff, go-around, maximum continuous, climb, cruise) is a function of the day: total air temperature, pressure altitude and bleed configuration. On the DC-10 and KC-10 a thrust rating computer works it out; on the MD-10 the flight management system does. Either way the result is a limit in the engine's thrust-setting parameter, shown as a number and as a bug on each engine's indicator, and used as the ceiling for the autothrottle.

The thrust rating computer (TRC) reads out on the **TAT/thrust rating indicator** on the center instrument panel. The crew selects a power mode with the mode buttons; the computer takes total air temperature and pressure altitude from air data computer 1, applies corrections for the bleed configuration, and computes the limit for that mode. The indicator shows TAT and the limit: **N1 LIM** in per cent on the CF6 aircraft, **EPR LIM** to two decimals on the DC-10-40. The selected mode's button lights when the computer has accepted it.

On the aircraft with T.O. FLX, the **ASSUMED TEMP** thumbwheels below the indicator set an assumed temperature for reduced (flex) takeoff thrust, and the computer gives the takeoff N1 for that temperature. An assumed temperature at or below the actual temperature gives full takeoff thrust. The DC-10-40 has no flex mode; its alternate modes give reduced takeoff and climb ratings.

The computer corrects its limits for the bleed configuration: on the CF6-50 for packs off and for wing and engine anti-ice in the takeoff, flex and go-around modes, and on the DC-10-40 by 0.01 EPR with all packs off. It drives the maximum limit index (the reference bug) on each N1 indicator, or EPR indicator on the -40, when that indicator's set knob is pushed in, and it is the ceiling the autothrottle will not exceed. In the autothrottle's N1 mode (EPR on the -40) the throttles are driven to the limit. See [Automatic flight](automatic-flight) and [Flight instruments](flight-instruments).

A red flag over the limit window means the limit is unusable. The window reads **199.9** when the computer has no computed data for the selected mode and **155.5** when its air data input has failed; the TAT readout has its own flag. If the computer loses power, its readouts freeze and the flags come into view.
The computed limit is advisory. Nothing in the engine stops at it: the throttles can be advanced past the bug, and the engine will go on toward its red lines.

blocks.alt: DC-10-30 TAT/thrust rating indicator on the center instrument panel, close-up: TAT readout reading +15, N1 LIM readout reading 111.0, the six lit-capable mode buttons (T.O., T.O. FLX, GA, MCT, CL, CR) with T.O. lit, the ASSUMED TEMP thumbwheels below, and the N1 LIM and TAT failure flags stowed. Inset: the DC-10-40 version with EPR LIM reading 1.58 and buttons T.O., ALTN T.O., GA, MCT, CL, ALTN CL.
blocks.title: TAT/thrust rating indicator

blocks.content: The MD-10 has no thrust rating computer panel. The flight management system computes the N1 limit, and the flight control computers sequence the mode through the flight: **TO** or **TO FLEX** (with the assumed temperature), **CLB**, **CRZ**, **GA** and **MCT**. The limit appears at the top of the Engine and Alert Display with its mode legend, magenta when the FMS computed it and white when it was set manually, and as a magenta V on each N1 dial. The autothrottle holds N1 between the FMS limit and a flight idle limit. See [Flight management](flight-management) and [Automatic flight](automatic-flight).

Thrust is set on the thrust-setting parameter, N1 on the CF6 aircraft and EPR on the DC-10-40, against the computed limit. EGT, N2 and fuel flow are then cross-checked across the three engines: an engine whose EGT or fuel flow stands out from the others at the same N1 is telling you something.

items: Set takeoff thrust before 80 KIAS. After 80 KIAS, do not adjust the throttles except to avoid exceeding a limit.
Takeoff thrust set before 80 KIAS may not be used more than 2,000 ft above the takeoff field's pressure altitude: select the next thrust mode.
Each engine is built and rigged slightly differently, so equal N1 can need slightly staggered throttles. Set the parameter, not the lever position.
The throttle's forward stop is not a thrust limit. At full throttle a CF6 makes slightly more than rated takeoff thrust on a standard day, and more than that on a cold day.

sections.title: Starting and ignition
sections.summary: The air turbine starter, the two ignition systems, the start sequence and its limits, abnormal starts and in-flight restarts.

blocks.alt: Schematic of the start and ignition system for one engine. Left: pneumatic manifold (fed by APU, ground cart or cross-bleed through isolation valves) to the starter shutoff valve and the air turbine starter on the accessory gearbox. Center: the ENG START switch with its holding coil, the N2 speed switch at about 45 % that drops the coil, and the START VALVE OPEN light. Right: ignition exciter A on the L EMER AC bus and exciter B on the R EMER AC bus, each to its igniter plug; the control path from the battery bus through the ENG IGNITION selector (CONT A, START A, OFF, START B, CONT B), the fuel lever ignition switch and the OVRD & AIR START switch. An MD-10 inset shows the ENG IGN A, B and OVRD push-buttons and the miscellaneous systems controller in place of the selector.
blocks.title: Start and ignition system

blocks.content: Each engine has an **air turbine starter** on its accessory gearbox, supplied from the engine's pneumatic manifold through a **starter shutoff (start) valve**. The air can come from the APU, a ground pneumatic cart, or a running engine through the isolation valves (a cross-bleed start). The start valve is electrically controlled and pneumatically operated. It opens at a controlled rate, raising pressure at the starter by about 22 psi per second, so that the shock of engagement stays within the strength of the drive; this matters most when the starter is re-engaged with the rotor already turning. An overrunning clutch lets the engine run away from the starter once it is faster, and a shear section in the drive shaft protects the gearbox if the starter seizes.

An air turbine starter's torque is greatest at rest and falls as speed rises. With normal duct pressure the starter alone would motor the core to only about 20 to 22 % N2: it cannot take the engine to idle. Its job is to turn the compressor fast enough to deliver air for light-off. After light-off the turbine adds power, and from roughly 25 % N2 to cutout it is the burning engine that does most of the accelerating. At about **45 % N2** a speed switch in the N2 indicating circuit drops the START switch's holding coil: the switch releases, the start valve closes and start ignition ends, all at once. The engine accelerates the rest of the way to idle on its own.

Normal starts need at least **25 psi** duct pressure; 40 psi or more gives the quickest acceleration and the lowest EGT peak. A start can be made down to 15 psi, slowly and with a higher EGT peak, provided N2 keeps increasing. Below −18 °C (0 °F), 35 psi gives assurance of a good start. A drop of about 5 psi when the start valve opens is normal. With the APU isolation valve open, selecting an ignition position for the start raises APU speed to give more starting pressure. See [Pneumatics](pneumatics) and [APU](apu).

Each engine has two independent high-energy ignition systems, **A** and **B**, each with its own capacitor-discharge exciter (about 15 joules) and igniter plug. Either system alone will light the engine. System A's exciters are powered by the **left emergency AC bus** and system B's by the **right emergency AC bus**, and the control circuits (ENG START & IGNITION CONT, ENG IGNITION OVERRIDE) are on the **battery bus**. Putting ignition on the emergency buses keeps a relight possible with every generator lost, when the static inverter is feeding the left emergency AC bus from the battery. See [Electrical](electrical).

On the DC-10 and KC-10 one **ENG IGNITION** selector on the pilots' overhead panel serves all three engines, with positions CONT A, START A, OFF, START B and CONT B. A guarded **OVRD & AIR START** switch beside it acts on all three engines at once.

blocks.title: Ignition logic (DC-10, KC-10)
rows: None, unless OVRD & AIR START is on.
That engine's START switch engaged and its fuel lever out of OFF, with N2 above the lever switch's arming speed
System A (B) on that engine, until starter cutout
Fuel lever out of OFF, N2 above the arming speed
System A (B) on each engine, continuously
Nothing: it bypasses the selector, the fuel lever switches and the START switches
A and B on all three engines; also powers the START switches for a starter-assisted air start

blocks.content: The fuel lever's ignition switch is gated by speed. On the CF6-6D its contacts close at about 11 % N2; on the CF6-50 and the JT9D, spark comes with the fuel lever at the 15 % N2 fuel-on point. A fuel lever moved earlier sends fuel into a combustor with no spark, and that fuel collects there and burns when the light finally comes, pushing up the start EGT. Follow the fuel-on speed.

Alternate the system used for ground starts (START A on odd-numbered days, START B on even) so that a failed system shows up on the ground rather than when it is needed for a relight. Continuous ignition is not required for a normal takeoff or landing. Select CONT, CONT A preferred, in heavy rain or severe turbulence and whenever a procedure calls for it; it has no time limit, though heavy use shortens igniter life.

The MD-10's overhead replaces the selector with **ENG IGN A** and **B** push-buttons, an **OVRD** push-button and an **ENG IGN OFF** light. Pushing A or B arms that system (its white legend lights) and supplies the ENG START switches; the miscellaneous systems controller (MSC) then turns the igniters on and off from the START switch, the fuel lever and N2. Both may be selected, and one is enough to start. **OVRD** bypasses the MSC and powers both systems on all three engines for as long as it is selected, and powers the START switches for a starter-assisted air start. ENG IGN OFF lights when neither A, B nor OVRD is selected. The FedEx limitations call for OVRD in severe turbulence and heavy rain, and the icing procedure uses it for the ice-shedding runs.

The real MD-10's MSC also provides continuous ignition automatically during takeoff and landing and for 60 seconds after engine anti-ice is selected. The simulation does not: with A or B selected, the igniters fire only during a start. Select OVRD whenever continuous ignition is wanted.

The normal ground start order is engine 3, engine 1, engine 2. Before the first start the fuel levers are OFF, the tank pumps on, the packs off and duct pressure checked. The table shows what a normal start looks like; the procedure itself is in [Normal procedures](normal-procedures).

blocks.title: A normal ground start
rows: Start valve opens (DC-10, KC-10: ignition selector at START A or B; MD-10: an ENG IGN system selected)
Light in the START switch; duct pressure drops about 5 psi; N2 starts to rise
Starter turns the core; the fan turns with it
N2 rising about 1 % per second; oil pressure rising; N1 still reads zero
Fuel flow about 550 to 650 pph; MD-10: cyan lightning stroke on the EGT display
Combustion established, within 25 s of steady fuel flow
EGT starts to rise; N1 appears as the fan passes about 9 %
Turbine and starter accelerate the core together
EGT climbs to its start peak, typically 500 to 600 °C on a CF6 (limit 750 °C)
Holding coil drops: start valve closes, start ignition ends
START switch releases and its light goes out
N1 about 20 to 25 %, EGT below 500 °C, fuel flow about 1,100 to 1,200 pph, oil pressure 15 psi or more, OIL PRESS LO out

blocks.content: From switch to stable idle takes roughly a minute with good air. Below −18 °C, acceleration from light-off to idle can take up to two minutes and is acceptable while EGT is within limits; oil pressure may peak at full scale after a very cold start, and if it stays above the normal range once oil temperature has stabilized, shut the engine down. Run each engine at idle or taxi power for at least 3 minutes before takeoff.

N1 reads zero until the fan passes about 9 %. That is the speed sensor's signal floor, not a fan that is not turning. On the MD-10, shut the engine down if there is still no N1 indication 30 seconds after N2 reaches idle.

On the MD-10 the Engine and Alert Display shows a cyan line on the N2 scale at the fuel-on speed during the start (10 % on the MD-10-10, 15 % on the MD-10-30) and a red start limit mark on the EGT scale, both removed once the engine reaches idle.

blocks.alt: Time history of a typical CF6-50C2 ground start, time from START switch engaged on the horizontal axis (0 to 70 s). Four traces: N2 (0 to 60 %), rising about 1 % per second to 15 % at 16 s, then faster after light-off, starter cutout marked at 45 % near 50 s, leveling at ground idle; N1, at zero until about 30 s then rising to about 22 %; EGT, flat until light-off about 10 s after fuel on, peaking near 560 °C around 45 to 50 s and settling near 420 °C at idle; fuel flow, stepping to about 600 pph at fuel ON and rising to about 1,100 pph at idle. Event markers: START switch, fuel ON at 15 % N2, light-off, starter cutout, stable idle. The 750 °C start EGT limit drawn as a horizontal line.
blocks.title: Typical ground start

rows: Up to 5 minutes continuous. Cool 30 seconds for each minute of use. After two 5-minute cycles, cool 10 minutes between further cycles.
At the lowest practical N2: normally below 20 % (0 % recommended on the ground). In an emergency, such as a fire indication, up to 30 %. Never above 30 % N2.
750 °C normal. 750 to 900 °C allowed for no more than 40 seconds, once, with a log entry and maintenance advised. Above 900 °C, or more than 40 seconds above 750 °C: terminate the start.
Above 700 pph risks a hot start; below 300 pph, a hung start
EGT rise within 25 seconds of steady fuel flow on the ground; within 45 seconds of fuel ON for an in-flight restart
25 psi minimum for a normal start; 15 psi absolute minimum

blocks.content: These are summaries. The governing limits are in Section 4, [Limitations](limitations).

The engine does not protect itself during a start: the fuel control has no automatic abort, and nothing shuts the fuel off on a hot start. The crew watches N2, fuel flow and EGT, and each abnormal start has a recognisable signature.

blocks.title: Abnormal start signatures
rows: Over-rich mixture: too much fuel before light-off, or a late light-off with fuel already collected in the combustor
EGT rising fast toward or past 750 °C; possibly past 900 °C
Fuel lever OFF. Keep motoring 30 seconds to purge. Record peak EGT and time above 750 °C.
Light-off, then acceleration that stops below idle
N2 stagnating somewhere between about 20 and 50 %; EGT high or rising; START switch still engaged
Slow but continuing acceleration and a long time to idle. Not a hung start.
Continue while EGT is within limits. For the next start, consider all ENG PNEU SUPPLY selectors OFF in case a check valve is leaking.
No spark (a failed exciter or its power), or no fuel
Fuel flow but no EGT rise within 25 seconds
Fuel lever OFF. Motor 30 seconds. Select the other ignition system and start again.
Fuel left in the turbine or exhaust of an unlit engine ignites, on a start or after shutdown
EGT rising on an engine that should be cooling; flame from the exhaust reported from outside; no fire warning
Fuel lever OFF. Motor the engine with the starter (re-engage below 20 % N2) until EGT falls. The fire handle does not help: its agent goes into the nacelle, not the gas path.

blocks.content: Do not attempt another start if N2 did not reach 15 % while motoring or if a start EGT limit was exceeded: maintenance is required. If fuel flow before light-off was above 700 pph, a second attempt may also run hot. The procedures are in [Abnormal procedures](abnormal-procedures).

A failed engine windmills: ram air keeps both spools turning. N2 settles at a few per cent at approach speeds and in the mid-teens at cruise, and the fan turns in proportion to airspeed. A **windmill relight** needs at least **10 % N2**. Below that, use a **starter-assisted** air start, with air from another engine through the pneumatic isolation valves, or increase airspeed.

The OVRD & AIR START switch (MD-10: OVRD) gives dual ignition on all three engines and powers the START switches for a starter assist. Expect an EGT rise within 45 seconds of fuel ON; if there is none, or the start is abnormal, put the fuel lever OFF. After a successful relight allow one minute's warm-up before using power, unless safety of flight requires it. If an engine failed or flamed out for an unknown reason, do not restart it unless it is needed for safety of flight. Turning the engine's hydraulic pumps off reduces the load on a windmilling core and raises its speed. The procedures are in [Emergency procedures](emergency-procedures) and [Abnormal procedures](abnormal-procedures).

sections.title: Oil system
sections.summary: A self-contained dry-sump system per engine: pumps, filters, cooling by fuel, and what the indications mean.

blocks.content: Each engine has its own self-contained, dry-sump oil system. A gear-type **supply pump** on the accessory gearbox draws oil from a tank on the engine and delivers it through a supply filter to the bearing sumps and gearboxes, where jets spray it onto the bearings and gears. **Scavenge pumps** draw it back out of the sumps through the **scavenge filter** and the **fuel/oil heat exchanger** to the tank. Air from the compressor pressurizes the sump seals so that oil stays inside, and a vent system carries the air and oil mist away.

blocks.alt: Schematic of one CF6 engine oil system: oil tank with quantity transmitter, supply pump and supply filter, cold-start relief valve (300 psi), pressure transmitter and low oil pressure switch, jets into the A, B, C and D bearing sumps and the gearboxes, scavenge pumps, scavenge filter with its differential pressure switch (about 31 psid, to the OIL STRAINER CLOG light) and bypass valve, oil temperature sensor in the scavenge line, fuel/oil heat exchanger with its bypass valve, return to tank. Cockpit end: OIL PRESS, OIL TEMP and OIL QTY gauges on the flight engineer's panel, ENG OIL PRESS LO and ENG OIL STRAINER CLOG lights on the overhead annunciator panel; MD-10 inset showing the SD secondary engine page instead.
blocks.title: Engine oil system

blocks.content: The pumps are positive-displacement and turn with N2, so **oil pressure follows core speed**: lowest at idle, highest at takeoff. It also follows viscosity: cold oil is thick and reads high, and after a very cold start the gauge can go to full scale until the oil warms. A cold-start relief valve protects the system at about 300 psi. The gauge shows differential pressure (supply against sump), and the acceptable band widens with N2: on the CF6 the low limit rises from 10 psid at idle to about 34 psid at high N2.

Bearings and gears reject their heat into the oil, and the oil rejects it into the fuel in the heat exchanger. **Oil temperature** therefore rises with power and with anything that reduces cooling, and a heat exchanger bypass valve stuck open lets the oil skip the cooler altogether. The oil temperature indication measures **scavenge oil**, before the filter and the heat exchanger, so it reads the hottest oil in the circuit.

**Oil quantity** falls when the engine runs, because oil is spread through the sumps, gearboxes and lines. This **gulping** can take the reading up to 6 quarts below the static level, more at high N2 and briefly during the takeoff run and rotation, and the oil comes back after shutdown. A full tank shows about 18 quarts. Note the quantity once each engine is stable at idle (DC-10, KC-10: set the OIL QTY reference bug; MD-10: the cyan initial-quantity line on the SD) to judge consumption during the flight. A healthy CF6 uses about a quarter of a quart an hour.

blocks.title: Oil indications
rows: Scavenge oil temperature, °C, upstream of the scavenge filter and heat exchanger
ENG OIL PRESS LO light (MD-10: ENG n OIL PRESS LO alert)
Low oil pressure switch in the supply line: on at about 11 psi falling, off at about 14 psi rising
ENG OIL STRAINER CLOG light (MD-10: ENG n OIL FILTER alert)

Differential pressure across the scavenge filter has reached about 31 psid: the filter is close to clogging. Beyond that a bypass valve opens and dirty oil goes back to the engine, with no further indication. The MD-10 alert is inhibited below 35 °C oil temperature.

blocks.content: The low oil pressure switch and the pressure transmitter are separate sensors. A disagreement between the gauge and the light, or on the MD-10 between the SD and the alert, points to a sensor failure. When OIL STRAINER CLOG lights, retard the throttle toward idle: if the light goes out the filter is loading but not yet bypassing, and the engine may be run below the setting that lit it. If it stays on at idle, or comes with high oil temperature, abnormal pressure or rising vibration, the engine is shedding debris.

blocks.title: Oil limits
rows: 10 psi. Below 10 psi at idle, shut the engine down (30 seconds allowed under negative g).
A pressure change of more than 10 psi at constant N2 may mean pending failure

sections.title: Vibration monitoring
sections.summary: Two pickups per engine and tracking filters on each rotor: what the four channels show and how to read them.

blocks.content: Each engine has two vibration pickups (accelerometers): one on the forward, fan, flange and one on the aft, turbine, flange. A single signal conditioner serving all three engines passes each pickup's signal through **tracking filters** locked to N1 and to N2. Each displayed channel therefore shows only the once-per-revolution vibration of one rotor, which is what an out-of-balance rotor produces; combustion noise, gear mesh, buffet and rotating stall are rejected. The readings are in units of displacement.

An unbalanced rotor exerts a force that grows with the square of its speed, but the displacement the pickup sees levels out once the rotor runs above its critical (resonant) speed. Both rotors' critical speeds lie below idle, so the reading passes through a hump during a start and a shutdown and then sits near a steady value across the operating range rather than rising with power. A reading that changes with power, or creeps up at constant power, is therefore significant.
Each pickup senses both rotors to a degree, so the four channels (forward N1, forward N2, aft N1, aft N2) are four different numbers, and the crew can reason with them:

items: One channel at zero, or pegged at full scale, with the engine running: a failed pickup or channel, not the engine.
All channels rising together: bearing distress. Expect oil indications to agree (strainer clog, pressure or temperature changes).
N1 channels rising alone: the fan or low-pressure turbine, from blade damage or ice. A brief rise as thrust is increased after flight in icing is ice shedding from the fan, and normal.
N2 channels rising: the core, for example blade damage after a compressor stall.

blocks.title: Vibration controls and indicators (flight engineer's panel)
rows: 0 to 10 units, one per engine; all three show the selected channel
FAN: the forward pickup through the N1 filter. TURB: the aft pickup through the N2 filter.
EVM selector (KC-10): FWD N1 / FWD N2 / AFT N1 / AFT N2
Selects pickup and rotor. Normally left at AFT N1.
Drives all three indicators to the test value, 5 to 7 units
Vibration above 4.0 units on any of that engine's channels, whatever the selector shows. Time-weighted: a high reading lights it sooner than a marginal one, and a single brief spike does not.

blocks.content: Maximum running levels are 3.0 units on the N1 channels and 4.0 units on the N2 channels. The KC-10 has no HIGH VIB lights.
On the MD-10 the vibration monitor's compressor (COMP) and turbine (TURB) readings for each engine are on the SD secondary engine page, in amber when out of limits.

If vibration rises together with other abnormal indications, or after a compressor stall, reduce thrust on that engine and follow the procedure; a stall followed by increased vibration is a reason to shut the engine down.

sections.title: Bleed air, anti-ice and accessory loads
sections.summary: What the engine gives the pneumatic, anti-ice, electrical and hydraulic systems, and what that costs it.

blocks.content: Each engine supplies its pneumatic system from two ports on the high-pressure compressor: a **low-stage** port used in climb and cruise, and a **high-stage** port that takes over automatically when low-stage pressure is too low, at idle and low power. The pneumatic system's valves and their logic are described in [Pneumatics](pneumatics).

blocks.title: Bleed ports
rows: 15th stage (the last HPC stage, in P&W's numbering)

blocks.content: Bleed air is air the engine has compressed and then does not use to make power. At a given throttle the governor holds N2, so the cost shows elsewhere: less air reaches the turbines for the same fuel, the gas runs hotter, and the low-pressure turbine has less to drive the fan with. **Packs and anti-ice raise EGT and lower N1**, and the thrust rating charts and computers carry corrections for them. Extraction is limited by certification: the JT9D-59A, for example, may give up 10 % of its core flow (13 % maximum) from idle to 40 % of maximum continuous thrust, but only 5 % (6.5 % maximum) above that.
The KC-10 has no number 2 engine bleed system. The center manifold and the engine 2 starter remain, supplied by the APU and engines 1 and 3.

**Engine anti-ice** heats the nacelle inlet lip with engine bleed air. The fan blades and spinner are not heated: ice that forms on them is thrown off by centrifugal force, so fan speed is the protection. On the CF6 that means operating at 70 % N1 or more; a prolonged descent below 70 % N1 in moderate or severe icing calls for an ice-shedding run about every 10 minutes, one engine at a time, with ignition on, the throttle to idle and then up to at least 70 % N1 for 10 to 30 seconds. The JT9D-59A's certificated minimum in icing is 45 % N1 below 10,000 ft and 50 % N1 above. Engine anti-ice is required on the ground and in flight when the temperature is 6 °C or below with visible moisture. Low speed at high angle of attack, as in slow air refueling, is also a condition for induction icing. See [Ice and rain protection](ice-and-rain).

The accessory gearbox also carries the **generator drive** and **two engine-driven hydraulic pumps**, which feed that engine's hydraulic system. Their load is shaft power taken from the HP spool; the governor holds N2 by burning more fuel, so a heavy hydraulic demand shows as a small rise in fuel flow. See [Electrical](electrical) and [Hydraulics](hydraulics).

sections.title: Thrust reversers
sections.summary: The pneumatically driven fan reverser: construction, actuation, interlocks, indications and use.

blocks.content: Each engine has a **fan thrust reverser**. To deploy, the **translating cowl** at the rear of the fan nacelle, in left and right halves, moves aft and uncovers rows of **cascade vanes** in the nacelle wall, while **blocker doors** fold into the fan duct and close it. The fan air, which is most of the engine's thrust, is turned outward and forward through the cascades. The core exhaust is not reversed and still pushes forward, so net reverse thrust is the fan's reversed flow less the core's forward thrust. The three reversers are alike except for engine 2's cascades. The CF6's original turbine (core) reverser was deactivated across the fleet in 1971; neither the CF6 nor the JT9D in this aircraft has one.

blocks.alt: Two-part schematic of the fan thrust reverser. Top: side section of the fan nacelle stowed and deployed, showing the translating cowl moving aft, the cascades exposed, the blocker doors folding into the fan duct and arrows of fan air turning forward through the cascades while the core exhaust continues aft. Bottom: pneumatic control diagram: engine bleed supply, pressure regulator (50 to 60 psi), overpressure inlet shutoff valve (latches at about 75 psi), directional control valve, pneumatic drive motor with brake, flexible shafts to the ballscrew actuators; stow and deploy switches wired to the REV PRES, REV U/L and REV THR lights; the throttle interlock actuator releasing the reverse lever at about 95 % deployed; the gear-down and (engine 2) nose gear ground shift inputs.
blocks.title: Fan thrust reverser

blocks.content: The reverser is driven by a **pneumatic drive motor** running on regulated air through a **pressure regulator** that holds 50 to 60 psi. In flight and on the landing roll the air comes from the reverser's own engine; on the ground the system can also be run from the APU or a ground cart for checks. Flexible shafts and ballscrews move the cowl, and a brake on the drive holds it in position. An **overpressure inlet shutoff valve** guards against a failed regulator by closing and latching at about 75 psi; it then needs a manual reset on the ground. Air loads and mechanical loads tend to hold the reverser where it is, so after a failure **it stays in the last selected position**. The reverser lights are powered from the DC buses.
The reverser is commanded by the **reverse lever** mounted on each throttle. Deployment and stowing follow this sequence:

items: Throttle at idle and landing gear down. The reverse lever cannot be raised otherwise, and an in-flight interlock prevents deployment with the gear up.
Raise the reverse lever to the reverse idle detent. The inlet shutoff valve opens (REV PRES), the drive runs, and the cowl leaves its stow position (REV U/L). The engine stays at idle.

At about 95 % deployed the interlock releases and the lever can be raised past the detent for reverse power. Engine 2's interlock also needs the nose gear compressed (ground shift), so it waits for nosewheel touchdown.
Fully deployed: REV THR (green) lights; REV U/L and REV PRES go out. On the three-crew aircraft the FE calls “reverse available”.
Apply reverse up to the reverse stop. A stop in the fuel control limits reverse to 95 % N2, which is about 95 % N1 at sea level on a 0 °C day; on a colder day N1 can exceed 95 % at full reverse.

To stow, bring the lever down to the reverse idle detent and then through it to forward idle. REV THR goes out and REV U/L and REV PRES light while the cowl moves, and both go out when it is stowed. There is no interlock or stop on the way out of reverse.

blocks.title: Reverser indications
rows: REV PRES (amber; FE panel: REVERSER VALVE OPEN)
Inlet shutoff valve open: air is being supplied to the drive
Cowl out of stow but not fully deployed
MD-10: amber U/L / green REV in the N1 dial
In transit / fully deployed. Shown in red if either occurs in flight.

blocks.content: **Using reverse.** Reverse is most effective at high speed. Raise the levers to reverse idle at touchdown, apply reverse as required once REV THR is lit, and starting at 80 kt reduce so as to reach reverse idle by 60 kt. Reverse idle is about 25 % N1. At low speed the reversed efflux is drawn back into the inlets with hot gas and debris, and high reverse power at low speed is a known cause of compressor stalls that need a hot section inspection. Reverse operation is normally limited to 60 seconds. Selecting reverse disengages the autothrottle.

Reverse thrust is prohibited in flight and must not be used to back the aircraft. It is not authorized for normal taxiing. A reverser light in flight, or any sign of an inadvertent deployment, is an emergency: see [Emergency procedures](emergency-procedures).

sections.title: Controls and indicators
sections.summary: The pedestal levers, the start and ignition panels, the pilots' engine instruments on each flight deck, the flight engineer's engine panel and the annunciators.

blocks.content: The pedestal levers are the same on every flight deck. The start and ignition controls, the engine instruments and the annunciators differ between the three-crew DC-10 and KC-10 and the two-crew MD-10, and on the DC-10 the pilots' engine instruments are one of three equipment options chosen in the EFB.

blocks.alt: DC-10-30 center pedestal, engine controls, seen from above and behind the throttles: three throttles with the reverse levers mounted on their fronts (engine 1's raised to the reverse idle detent, the others stowed), the TO/GA button on the number 2 throttle and the ATS disengage buttons on the outboard throttles, and below them the three FUEL levers at ON with their ON/OFF placards and lock release, engine 2's lever showing its red light. Labels legible: FUEL, ON, OFF.
blocks.title: Throttle quadrant
blocks.caption: The MD-10 pedestal carries the same throttles, reverse levers and FUEL levers.

rows: Set the fuel control's demanded core speed, and so the thrust. Moved by the autothrottle when it is engaged. The forward stop is not a thrust limit.
Stowed / reverse idle detent / reverse power

Can be raised only with the throttle at idle and the gear down. To the detent: deploy, engine at idle. Past the detent, once the interlock has released at about 95 % deployed: reverse power, up to the 95 % N2 stop. Down through the detent to forward idle: stow. Selecting reverse disengages the autothrottle.

ON opens the fuel shutoff valve in the fuel control and enables ignition for that engine (start ignition with the START switch engaged, or continuous ignition on the DC-10 and KC-10 with CONT selected). OFF closes the valve and removes start and continuous ignition, shutting the engine down. Each lever locks at ON and at OFF; push its lock release button to move it.
Lights with that engine's fire warning, and when its fire handle is pulled with the FUEL lever not at OFF. See [Fire protection](fire-protection).

blocks.content: The engine fire handles (one per engine, on the overhead panel) shut off fuel and hydraulic supply to their engine and trip its generator field. They are described in [Fire protection](fire-protection).

blocks.alt: DC-10-30 pilots' overhead panel, engine start section: the ENG IGNITION rotary selector with its five positions CONT A, START A, OFF, START B, CONT B (set to START A), the guarded OVRD & AIR START toggle (guard closed, OFF), and the three ENG START switches 1, 2 and 3 with engine 3's integral START VALVE OPEN light lit. Placards legible.
blocks.title: Engine start and ignition panel (DC-10, KC-10)

rows: Pushing the switch in opens that engine's start valve, and a solenoid holds it in. Select START A or B on the ENG IGNITION selector first: it arms the switches and provides the start ignition. The switch pops out by itself at about 45 % N2, or if its holding power is lost, and can be pulled out by hand at any time to abort the start.
START VALVE OPEN light (in each switch)
That engine's start valve is open. It should go out when the switch releases at cutout; a light that stays on means the valve has not closed.
No ignition (unless OVRD & AIR START is on).
Arms the START switches. The selected system fires on an engine whose START switch is engaged and whose FUEL lever is out of OFF, until starter cutout.
The selected system fires continuously on every engine whose FUEL lever is ON.

Bypasses the selector, the fuel lever switches and the START switches to give both systems on all three engines; also powers the START switches for a starter-assisted air start. Use it for in-flight restarts.

blocks.content: If a START switch will not stay engaged, check the ENG START & IGNITION CONT circuit breaker, which powers the holding coils. With OVRD & AIR START on, the switches hold even with that breaker out.

blocks.alt: MD-10 forward overhead panel: on the left side the ENG IGN panel with the amber ENG IGN OFF light, the A and B push-buttons (A selected, white A legend lit) and the OVRD push-button with its amber ON legend; on the right side the three ENG START switches with engine 3's amber light lit, and the ENG MAX POINTER RESET button. Legends legible.
blocks.title: Engine ignition and start panels (MD-10)

rows: No ignition system selected (neither A, B nor OVRD): no power to the igniters.
ENG IGN A and B push-buttons
Select ignition system A or B (or both). Selection arms the START switches and stays until the engines are shut down. With the APU isolation valve open, it also raises APU speed for starting.
Ignition override: both systems on all three engines for as long as it is selected, bypassing the MSC; powers the START switches for a starter-assisted air start.
Pull to start: a coil holds the switch out and the start valve opens (light on). At about 45 to 52 % N2 the switch pops in and the light goes out as the valve closes.
Clears the maximum exceedance values shown on the N1, N2 and EGT displays.

blocks.content: The standard presentation, and the KC-10's only one, is a stack of four round instruments for each engine on the center instrument panel: **N1, EGT, N2 and fuel flow** on the CF6 aircraft, read across the three engines. The REV PRES, REV U/L and REV THR lights for each engine sit above the stack, and the TAT/thrust rating indicator beside it. On the DC-10 the pilots' engine instruments are an equipment option in the EFB: **Dials** (this presentation), **Tapes** or **Digital** (the EIDS); see [EFB](efb).

blocks.alt: DC-10-30 center instrument panel, engine instrument area, all three engines stable at ground idle: rows of N1 (about 21 %), EGT (about 410 °C), N2 (about 58 %) and fuel flow (about 1,100 pph) indicators for engines 1, 2 and 3, the REV PRES / REV U/L / REV THR lights above each column (all out), the ENG IND MAX POINTER RESET button, and the TAT/thrust rating indicator to the right. All needles, counters and red lines legible.
blocks.title: Engine instruments, round dials (DC-10-30)

blocks.alt: Close-up of one DC-10 N1 indicator at takeoff thrust: pointer and digital counter reading 111.0 %, the dial numbered 0 to 120 and graduated to 125, the red radial at 118.5 %, the max limit index (reference bug) on the outer edge at 111.0 % following the thrust rating computer, the N1 max pointer resting on the red line, the max limit set knob at lower right pushed in with its window shuttered, and the OFF flag stowed.
blocks.title: N1 indicator
Round-dial instruments
rows: Fan speed, per cent, to a tenth. The dial is numbered to 120 and graduated to 125. Reads zero below about 9 % N1.

With the set knob pushed in, follows the thrust rating computer's limit for the selected mode; parks at zero when the computer has no valid limit. With the knob pulled, the crew sets it by turning the knob, and the value shows in the max limit window.
Rests on the red line. Dragged up by the needle if N1 goes past it, and holds the highest value reached until reset.
N1 data unusable, or the indicator unpowered.
Exhaust gas temperature, °C, dial 0 to 1,000 (× 100), three-digit counter. Yellow caution band and red line for the fitted engine.
Indicator unpowered (the EGT indicators share one supply from the left emergency AC bus).
Pointer, counter, max pointer, OFF flag
Core speed, per cent, dial to 120. As on the N1 indicator.
Fuel flow, pounds per hour, dial to 25 (× 1,000) graduated to 27, five-drum counter.
Returns the N1, N2 and EGT max pointers to their limit marks.

blocks.content: Instrument markings follow the flight manual convention: a red radial is a maximum or minimum limit, a yellow band a caution range, and a green or white band the normal operating range.

On the DC-10-40 the round-dial stack reads, from top to bottom, **EPR, EGT, N1 and fuel flow**. The EPR indicator, scaled to 2.00, is the primary thrust instrument; with its knob in, its bug follows the thrust rating computer's EPR limit, and its counter reads to two decimals. The N1 indicator takes the place of the N2 indicator, so there is no N2 indicator at the pilots' station in this presentation. The EGT dial reads the JT9D's turbine discharge temperature, with limits far lower than the CF6's (685 °C for takeoff).

In the tape and digital presentations the -40 has all five parameters, N2 included: the tape columns are EPR, N1, EGT, N2 and FF, and the EIDS shows EPR and N1 on one display unit and N2, EGT and FF on the other.

blocks.content: The Digital option is the **Engine Indicating Display System**: two flat-panel display units on the center panel showing N1, N2, EGT and fuel flow for all three engines, and on the DC-10-40 EPR, N1, N2, EGT and FF. Oil and vibration stay on the flight engineer's panel. In the normal format each display unit carries part of the parameters (on the -30, N1 and N2 on one, EGT and FF on the other); the LEFT / NORM / RIGHT selector moves everything onto one unit, in the reversion format, if the other fails.

Each parameter has its scale and limits. A parameter that reaches its limit lights its **ENG IND MAX** light red; when it comes back below, the light turns blue and stays blue until reset with the max pointer reset button. Fuel flow has no limit light. The system records exceedances of the N1, N2 and EGT limits (up to 16 on each display unit, each with the engine, parameter, duration and, for EGT, its category) and stores up to 24 snapshots of every parameter on every engine, one of them taken automatically at the peak EGT of the takeoff.

blocks.content: The procedures themselves are in [Normal procedures](normal-procedures). This section explains what the engines are doing at each stage and what to watch.

Near idle; the flight idle floor holds the engines at flight idle. In moderate or severe icing below 70 % N1, ice-shedding runs every 10 minutes, one engine at a time. Continuous ignition (MD-10: OVRD) in heavy rain or severe turbulence.
Oil temperature; engine anti-ice; any engine rolling back at idle in heavy precipitation.

Flight idle is held briefly after nose gear touchdown, then ground idle. Engine 2 may be shut down for taxi if its thrust is not needed.

blocks.content: Because each engine drives its own generator, hydraulic system and bleed supply, an engine failure is also a partial failure of those three systems. The procedures for an engine failure therefore also deal with those systems: the electrical load on the remaining generators, the pressure in the affected hydraulic system (its reversible motor pumps and the windmilling engine's pumps), and bleed and packs on the remaining engines.

blocks.content: If any engine indication is abnormal at minimum thrust, consider a precautionary shutdown. Record every overspeed and overtemperature, its magnitude and duration, for maintenance. Time spent above maximum continuous EGT counts against the 5-minute total: time in the 2-minute band is part of it, not in addition to it.

A flame goes out when the fuel-air mixture in the combustor falls outside what it can sustain: fuel interrupted (a closed valve, starvation, a fuel lever moved), or too much air or water for the fuel, as when a sudden chop at high airflow outruns the deceleration schedule or when heavy rain or hail floods the combustor at low power. Water and hail ingestion take heat out of the flame and raise the fuel flow needed to keep it alight, so an idle descent through very heavy precipitation is the classic case. In extremely heavy rain N1 can also wander up or down by as much as 6 % at constant throttle.

With continuous ignition on (DC-10, KC-10: CONT A or B; MD-10: OVRD), a flame that blows out while the core is still turning fast relights by itself on the compressor's own airflow, often with no more than a brief rollback. Without it, the engine runs down to windmilling and needs a restart within the envelope (see [In-flight restart and windmilling](#inflight-restart)). That is why continuous ignition is selected for heavy rain and turbulence.

A stall is recognized by noise (a single bang or a series), sluggish or no response to the throttle, fluctuating N1 and N2, and an EGT that is high or rising fast because the combustor is still being fueled for air that is no longer arriving. Bring the throttle to idle and watch EGT and N2. When the stall clears, advance the throttle slowly and check that N1, N2 and EGT follow it. If the stall comes back at some setting, operate the engine below that setting or shut it down; shut it down if EGT rises rapidly or vibration increases. After any compressor stall the engine is unserviceable for dispatch until maintenance has inspected it, so record the conditions: TAT, altitude, airspeed, N1 and the weather.

Damaged compressor blades lower the stall margin from part power upward, so such an engine typically runs clean at idle and stalls again on a slow advance past some intermediate setting. Distortion stalls depend on the cause: very high angles of attack far beyond the stall warning, crosswind or tailwind at high power on the ground, and re-ingested reverser efflux at low speed.

children.title: EGT exceedances and the hot section

blocks.content: The EGT limits are time-at-temperature limits because turbine damage is cumulative: blades creep and their coatings degrade with time at high temperature. The CF6 limits therefore come in bands (maximum continuous, 5-minute takeoff, 2-minute acceleration) and the start limit allows a brief excursion above 750 °C. Time at temperature is not cancelled by a moment below the limit, so a sawtooth around a limit still counts. On the MD-10 the EAD turns EGT amber after 5 minutes over the amber line and red at the red line, and the maximum value reached stays at the top of the scale until reset.

An EGT that climbs at constant thrust, or runs higher than the other engines at the same N1, is the signature of a deteriorating hot section or a bleed leak; one that rises with a stall or after shutdown is an emergency in its own right.

items: **Leak downstream of the pump**: pressure falls quickly, OIL PRESS LO lights and quantity falls. Below 10 psi the engine must be shut down.

**External oil loss** (a weeping line, a loose cap): the tank drains while the pump keeps full pressure, so for a long time the falling quantity is the only clue. Only when the tank is nearly empty do pressure fall and temperature rise together. Watching quantity against the bug catches it early.

**Restriction** (contamination in the jets): pressure reads high at a given N2, and the bearing behind the restriction slowly distresses, which in time shows as heat and vibration. The strainer light may not come on.
**Heat exchanger bypass stuck open**: oil temperature rises with power and quantity stays normal. Reducing thrust brings it down.
**Contamination**: the scavenge filter loads and OIL STRAINER CLOG lights, first at high power. A filter that is only loading puts the light out at idle; one that is bypassing does not.

blocks.content: Whatever the cause, an engine that runs without oil pressure is consuming its bearings. A short interruption (up to 30 seconds, as under negative g) is harmless. Beyond that the bearings wear, the governor burns more fuel to overcome the growing friction, vibration rises on all channels, and eventually the core seizes. A seized core will not windmill or restart.

A sheared accessory gearbox stops every pad on it while the engine itself keeps running: the oil pumps (oil pressure goes to zero), the generator drive (GEN OFF), both hydraulic pumps, and the N2 tachometer, so N2 reads zero on an engine that is plainly still turning, with N1, EGT and fuel flow present. Combined with fan damage it brings high N1 vibration. The engine will seize within minutes as its bearings fail. Shut it down using the engine fire or severe damage procedure.

A reverser control valve that fails to its deploy position drives the cowl out with no lever command, and the in-flight interlock cannot stop it, because the interlock acts on the lever. REV U/L and REV PRES light, then REV THR, and on the MD-10 the legends are red. Because the reverse lever was never raised, neither the interlock nor the reverse N2 stop is in play: reverse thrust blends in at whatever power that engine's throttle holds. Bringing the throttle to idle and shutting the engine down removes the air from the drive, and the cowl then stays where it is.

A reverser whose stow side fails deploys normally on the landing roll and then does not stow when the lever comes down: REV THR stays lit. Takeoff is not permitted until the reverser is stowed and secured.

**Modeled in depth.** Each engine is a full thermodynamic model: a stage-by-stage compressor with its variable stator and bypass valve schedules, a combustor energy balance, the turbine work split between the spools, and EGT with the lag of real thermocouples. The CF6-6D is calibrated against the DC-10-10 maintenance manual's trim and power-assurance tables and the CF6-50C2 against the KC-10 flight manual's limits and setting charts. The hydromechanical fuel control is modeled as described in this part: a droop governor on corrected core speed, the Wf/Ps3 acceleration and deceleration stops, the start schedule, and the dual idle. Packs, anti-ice and the hydraulic pumps' load cost the engine in EGT, N1 and fuel flow as they do on the aircraft; the generator's load is not charged to the engine.

items: Starting: starter torque falls with speed and scales with duct pressure, the start valve opens at its controlled rate, and the starter's duty cycle and cooling time are tracked. Ignition A and B run on the emergency AC buses with battery-bus control. Fuel admitted before light-off collects in the combustor and burns at light-off, so hot starts, hung starts, slow starts on weak air and no-light starts arise from their causes. Nothing aborts a start for you.
Windmilling and relight: both spools windmill with airspeed, and the restart envelope of the KC-10 flight manual applies to every engine type.

Oil: pressure follows N2 and oil temperature, quantity gulps and is consumed, the strainer clog switch, leaks and restrictions all behave as described, and running without oil wears the bearings until the core seizes.
Vibration: four channels per engine, each pickup sensing both rotors, with imbalance, bearing distress, stall damage and fan ice shedding as causes.
Rain and hail lower the flameout margin at low power and make N1 wander in extreme rain; continuous ignition relights a flameout at power.

Compressor stalls arise from blade damage, from very high angles of attack at speed (from about 27° upward, never at stall warning angles), and from reverser efflux re-ingested below 80 kt or while rolling backwards.
Each engine is built and rigged slightly differently (a fleet-typical spread), so equal N1 can need slightly staggered throttles and the three engines' gauges do not read exactly alike.
While the simulator is slewing, the engines hold the airflow they had before the slew.

blocks.content: **Simplified.**

items: JT9D-59A (DC-10-40): its certificated thrust ratings and EGT limits are real, but the gas path underneath is the CF6-50's. EPR is computed from corrected fan speed on a fixed schedule (1.00 stopped, about 1.03 at idle, about 1.60 at takeoff); the EGT shown is mapped to the JT9D's turbine discharge station; and the N1 and N2 red lines and oil pressure and temperature limits shown are the CF6-50's. Its takeoff thrust is not perfectly flat across temperature, and its fuel burn in cruise is roughly a quarter lower than a real JT9D's. The thrust rating computer's EPR limits are approximate.
The DC-10-15's CF6-50C2F uses the CF6-50C2's data and limits.
Every CF6-50C2 has its N1 red line at 118.5 %, the MD-10-30's included; the MD-10 FCOM gives 119.5 % for that aircraft.

Every engine type uses the CF6-6D's ground and flight idle schedule. Idle selection follows the KC-10 logic on all aircraft: flight idle whenever the nose strut is extended and for about 10 seconds after nose gear touchdown. The in-flight reversion to ground idle that some DC-10-30s have, and the 5-second shift delay of the Northwest aircraft, are not modeled. In flight the floor takes up more of the lever's travel than on the ground (see [Ground idle and flight idle](#idle-schedules)).

Reversers deploy and stow at one speed, in about 0.7 seconds each way (the real reverser takes about 2 seconds to deploy and up to 5 to stow). Engine 2's reverser does not start to deploy until the nose gear is compressed, rather than deploying and waiting for the nose gear before reverse power. Reverse thrust magnitude is an estimate. The 60-second reverse limit is not annunciated. REV PRES (and the FE's REVERSER VALVE OPEN) lights only while the reverser deploys, not while it stows. Loss of DC power puts the reverser lights out but does not stop the reverser.

ENG FAIL arms at 85 % N1 on every aircraft, the MD-10 included (the MD-10 FCOM describes it as active between 80 kt and V1). Running one engine above 85 % N1 on the ground with the others at idle lights ENG FAIL.

On the DC-10 and KC-10 the START switches hold at any ENG IGNITION position, not only at START A or B as on the aircraft. With the selector at OFF an engine cranks without ignition and will not light.

The START switches move the opposite way to the aircraft's. On the DC-10 and KC-10 the switch is pulled out to engage and drops back in at cutout (on the aircraft it is pushed in and pops out); on the MD-10 it is pushed in and pops back out (on the aircraft it is pulled out and pops in).

MD-10 ignition: there is no automatic continuous ignition, and the blue MANUAL legends never light; use OVRD. A START switch with neither IGN A nor B selected starts on system A, and A and B together act as A.
Exceeding the 2-minute EGT band is recorded as hot section damage but does not change the engine's performance. Exceeding the starter duty cycle is recorded but does not fail the starter.
A sheared accessory gearbox leaves the engine running until it seizes; on the real engine the fuel pump, also on the gearbox, would usually stop it at once.
A windmilling engine's N1 and N2 are shown on the gauges, but the flight model treats an unlit engine as making no thrust. Turning a windmilling engine's hydraulic pumps off does not raise its speed.

On the DC-10-40 with round dials there is no N2 indicator, so the N2 cues of a start are not displayed; select the Tapes or Digital presentation to see N2. The EPR dial's reference knob has no manual mode: the bug follows the thrust rating computer only.
With the Tapes presentation, a latched EGT warning light is reset by the round dials' max pointer reset button, which that presentation hides; the light stays on until the presentation is changed.
Damage from motoring an engine with no fuel inlet pressure is not modeled.

blocks.content: The EFB's **Reset Aircraft** repairs engine wear and damage: bearings, oil, the hot section record, starter duty, stall damage and both filter elements. Active failures stay active and go on acting. See [EFB](efb).

**Keyboard and hardware.** Throttle axes and keys move the throttles. The simulator's reverse commands, or a hardware lever moved into its reverse range, raise the reverse levers to reverse idle, from idle only; the throttle input then meters reverse power, and the interlock still holds reverse idle until the cowls are out. The simulator's mixture lean and condition lever cut-off commands move all three FUEL levers to OFF and so shut down every engine; mixture rich and condition lever idle move them to ON, and the per-engine fuel valve and engine master commands move individual levers. The simulator's starter commands move the deck's START switches; on the DC-10 and KC-10 a keyboard start with the ENG IGNITION selector at OFF turns it to START A, and a start with no air available is refused. The N1 reference increase, decrease and set commands turn the reference knobs of whichever DC-10 or KC-10 presentation is fitted. On the DC-10, the engine instrument presentation (Dials, Tapes or Digital) is chosen in the EFB's equipment options.

parts.title: Auxiliary Power Unit
parts.summary: The TSCP700-4B auxiliary power unit: its two-spool construction, start sequence, speed and bleed control, protection, the controls on each flight deck, and how the simulation runs it.

blocks.content: The auxiliary power unit (APU) is a small gas turbine engine in the tail of the aircraft. It gives the aircraft two things it would otherwise have to get from ground equipment or from its main engines: **electrical power**, from a 90 kVA generator identical to the three engine-driven generators, and **low-pressure bleed air** for the engine air turbine starters and the air conditioning packs. It starts from the aircraft battery and draws its starting fuel from a battery-powered pump, so a DC-10, KC-10 or MD-10 with charged batteries and fuel in tank 2 can power itself up, cool its cabin and start its engines on a ramp with no support at all.

On the ground the APU normally carries the whole electrical load and the air conditioning before engine start, then supplies the air for the starts. In flight it is an emergency or backup source of electrical power, and at low and medium altitude it can still supply some bleed air. Electrical demand has priority: when electrical and pneumatic demand together exceed what the machine can deliver, the bleed load is shed so that the generator stays on speed.

Architecturally the unit is a **two-spool** engine, and that choice explains most of its behavior. The high-pressure spool (N2, the gas generator) runs at a governed, constant speed and drives the accessory gearbox, the generator among the accessories, so the generator frequency stays at 400 Hz without a constant-speed drive. The low-pressure spool (N1) carries the load compressor that makes the bleed air; its speed is varied by a ring of variable turbine nozzle vanes so that the air output follows demand. An electronic control unit (ECU) sequences the start, trims both speeds, and shuts the APU down automatically when it sees a hazardous condition.

blocks.alt: Functional schematic of the TSCP700-4B APU. Left to right: inlet door, three-stage axial load compressor on the N1 spool, transition duct with the bleed plenum tapping off to the load bleed valve, surge valve (dumping overboard) and air flow and reverse flow sensors, then the single-stage centrifugal high-pressure compressor on the N2 spool, reverse-flow annular combustor with two igniters and primary and secondary fuel nozzles, single-stage high-pressure turbine (N2), variable turbine nozzle vanes with their actuator, two-stage low-pressure turbine (N1), exhaust muffler and exhaust door. Below the N2 spool: tower shaft to the accessory gearbox driving the 90 kVA AC generator, permanent magnet generator, fuel pump and fuel control unit, oil pump and cooling fan, and the DC starter motor. The ECU sits above with signal lines to the fuel control, nozzle actuator, load bleed valve, surge valve, igniters, starter and door actuator. The bleed duct leaves through a check valve and the APU isolation valve into the pneumatic manifold. Label N1 and N2 spools in different colors.
