blocks.content: The APU has its own unpressurized compartment in the lower aft fuselage, behind the aft pressure bulkhead and beneath the No. 2 engine and the horizontal stabilizer, sealed against fire and lined against noise. Air enters through an inlet door on the underside of the tail cone and leaves through an exhaust door. The compartment access door doubles as a pressure relief panel: a burst duct inside the compartment blows it open rather than overstressing the structure. On the DC-10 and MD-10, engine 2's bleed duct also runs through this compartment, which matters for fire detection (see [Fire Protection](fire-protection#apu-fire)); the KC-10 has no engine 2 bleed supply.

blocks.alt: Exterior view of a DC-10-30 tail cone from below and behind the left main gear, APU running: the inlet door on the underside of the tail cone open, the exhaust door open with a faint heat shimmer, the APU compartment access door closed, and the cooling air inlet on the left side of the tail cone visible.
blocks.title: APU inlet and exhaust doors

sections.title: Construction and gas path
sections.summary: A load compressor on a free low-pressure spool, a constant-speed gas generator, and the gearbox that hangs off it.

blocks.content: Air passes through the APU in one line. It enters the inlet duct, is compressed first by the load compressor on the N1 spool, then by the centrifugal compressor on the N2 spool, burns in the combustor, and expands through the high-pressure turbine (which drives N2) and then the low-pressure turbine (which drives N1). Between the two compressors a plenum taps part of the load compressor's output off as bleed air. Everything the aircraft takes from the APU therefore comes from one of two places: shaft power from the N2 spool through the gearbox, or compressed air from the N1 spool.

The low-pressure compressor is a three-stage axial compressor. It does two jobs at once: it supercharges the high-pressure compressor behind it, and it supplies the bleed air. It is driven by a two-stage low-pressure turbine at the back of the engine. A ring of **variable turbine nozzle vanes** sits ahead of the first low-pressure turbine stage. Moving those vanes changes how much of the gas energy leaving the high-pressure turbine the low-pressure turbine can extract, and that is how the ECU sets N1. In service N1 runs from roughly 17,000 to 28,100 rpm as the bleed demand changes.

The vanes are moved by a nozzle actuator, powered by fuel pressure and commanded by an electrical torque motor from the ECU. If the torque motor is de-energized (in the standby control mode, for example) the actuator settles the vanes on a mechanical park detent.

The high-pressure compressor is a single-stage centrifugal impeller, driven by a single-stage high-pressure turbine with an air-cooled inlet nozzle. A tower shaft and bevel gear take power from this spool down to the accessory gearbox. Because the gearbox and the generator turn with N2, N2 is held at a constant 100% whenever the APU is running: the generator's 400 Hz depends on it.

The combustor is a reverse-flow annular can. It carries two igniters and two sets of fuel atomizers, nine primary and nine secondary. Only the primary nozzles flow during light-off, when the airflow is small and a fine spray is needed to ignite; the secondary nozzles join in as N2 passes about 35%, once combustion is stable and the fuel flow needed for acceleration outgrows the primary circuit.

Exhaust gas temperature (EGT) is measured downstream of the low-pressure turbine by two thermocouple rakes. The ECU and the indicator both use the hotter of the two rakes, so a cold or failed rake cannot hide an over-temperature. Losing both rakes is itself a shutdown condition.

The gearbox on the forward left side of the APU is turned by the DC starter motor during a start and by the N2 spool afterwards. It drives the AC generator, the permanent magnet generator (PMG), the fuel pump and fuel control unit, the oil pump and the cooling air fan. The cooling fan draws air through an inlet on the left side of the tail cone and blows it over the oil cooler, through the generator, around the engine and into the exhaust mufflers, and ventilates the compartment.

The **PMG** is a small generator with permanent magnets, so it needs no excitation. Once N2 passes 95% it powers the ECU, which until then has run from the aircraft battery. After that point the APU no longer depends on aircraft DC power to keep running its own control system.

A single-shaft APU has to run at one speed, because its generator does, so its compressor always pumps roughly the same air whether anything needs it or not. Surplus air is dumped overboard, and the machine burns fuel compressing air it throws away. Worse, when a large bleed demand arrives (an engine start), the only way to deliver more air is to burn more fuel at the same speed, and the turbine runs hot.

The TSCP700 separates the two products. The gas generator stays at constant speed for the generator. The load compressor's speed floats: with no bleed demand it idles at about 63% N1, where it moves little air and costs little fuel, and when bleed is wanted the ECU closes the nozzle vanes and N1 rises to the speed that delivers the flow. The price is control complexity, a second spool and an actuator, which is why the APU has an ECU and why it has a standby mode for when that control fails.

The two spools are coupled through the gas path. When the vanes move to raise N1, the low-pressure turbine takes more work out of the gas; the high-pressure turbine then has less available, N2 starts to sag, and the N2 governor adds fuel to hold it. So more bleed air always means more fuel and a higher EGT, even though N2 never moves. That coupling is what the crew watch on the gauges during an engine start: N1 up, EGT up, N2 steady.

sections.title: Speed control and the electronic control unit
sections.summary: N2 is governed by the fuel control with electronic trim; N1 is scheduled by the ECU through the nozzle vanes.

blocks.content: The ECU is the APU's brain. It sequences the start, trims N2, schedules N1, controls the load bleed valve, watches every protective limit and commands the automatic shutdowns. It contains two independent channels: the **normal** channel does all of that; the **standby** channel, selected by the crew, keeps the start sequence and the protection but gives up the fine speed controls.

Fuel is metered by a hydromechanical fuel control unit driven from the gearbox. During acceleration a scheduling governor meters fuel against N2 so that the engine accelerates without surging or overheating. From about 95% N2 a flyweight (flyball) proportional governor takes over and terminates the acceleration at 100%. A proportional governor alone settles slightly below its set speed when loaded (droop), so in the normal mode the ECU trims it electrically through a torque motor in the fuel control. The result is N2 held at 100 ±1% from no load to full load.
In the standby mode the electronic trim is lost and the flyweight governor works alone. N2 then holds 100 ±4% and moves with load, and the generator frequency moves with it.

In the normal mode the ECU commands a target N1 and holds it closed-loop by moving the nozzle vanes. What it targets depends on what the aircraft is asking for. Below 95% N2 the load compressor is held unloaded so the engine can finish accelerating; above it, the ECU picks the highest applicable row of the schedule. Two of the rows are not speeds at all: for main engine start the ECU drives the vanes to their stop and lets N1 settle where the gas path puts it, which is why that row is a band rather than a number.

blocks.content: The APU-air row is worth understanding. The packs' temperature controllers send the ECU a demand signal: a hot day with a full cabin raises it, and the ECU raises N1 toward 91% so the packs get the airflow they need; a cool day lowers it toward 78%. Selecting the engine ignition with APU air selected is the ECU's cue that an engine start is coming, and it opens the vanes fully so the starter gets the maximum flow and pressure the load compressor can deliver.

blocks.alt: Diagram of the APU N1 schedule. Horizontal bar chart of N1 percent from 50 to 105: ground idle 63 ±2, APU air band 78 to 91 with a marker at 85.5 for no demand signal, altitude idle 89 ±3, main engine start band 75 to 100 with a marker at about 97 on a standard day, standby band 75 to 100 hatched to show it is not regulated. A small inset flow chart shows the selection order: standby, then N2 below 95 percent, then main engine start, then the highest of ground idle, APU air and altitude idle.
blocks.title: N1 schedule

blocks.content: The standby mode exists so that a failure of the normal electronic channel does not take the APU away. Selecting it substitutes the ECU's second channel for the normal one. The start sequence, the ignition and fuel scheduling and every automatic shutdown remain; what is lost is the N1 schedule (the vanes are parked on their detent) and the electronic fine control of N2 (the flyweight governor holds N2 alone).

With the vanes parked, N1 no longer responds to bleed demand. It does respond to electrical load: a heavier generator load makes the N2 governor add fuel, more energy reaches the low-pressure turbine, and N1 rises. Cold air is denser and makes the same effect stronger, so at low ambient temperatures, about 7 °C and below with a full electrical load, N1 can reach its overspeed limit and the APU shuts itself down. The cure is to reduce the electrical load. Because N1 does not rise for an engine start in standby, the crew raise it, when needed, by adding electrical load.

Standby is a fallback, not an alternative: it is for an APU that the normal channel will not start after repeated tries, keeps shutting down, or runs unsteadily. Standby starts are approved to 10,000 ft. FedEx restricts in-flight use of standby to emergencies. Change between NORM and STBY only with the APU shut down: switching modes with the APU running can damage the transfer relays.

sections.title: Bleed air and surge control
sections.summary: How load compressor air gets into the pneumatic manifold, and what keeps the compressor out of surge.

blocks.content: Bleed air is tapped from the plenum between the load compressor and the high-pressure compressor. From there it can go three ways: into the aircraft through the **load bleed valve**, overboard through the **surge valve**, or onward into the core. The load bleed valve is a butterfly valve, spring-loaded closed and opened by a solenoid that admits regulated control pressure. It has two positions, closed or fully open. Downstream of it a check valve stops manifold air flowing backwards into the APU, and the APU isolation valve joins the APU duct to the pneumatic manifold (the center manifold on the DC-10 and KC-10, manifold 2 on the MD-10; see [Pneumatics](pneumatics)).

A compressor has a minimum flow below which it surges: the flow breaks down and reverses in pulses that can damage blades. The surge valve keeps the load compressor above that line. An air flow sensor in the plenum measures the flow; when the aircraft takes less than the compressor is pumping at its current N1, the surge valve opens and dumps the difference overboard. It is open during the start, modulates as the load valve opens and closes, and is what makes the noise from the surge duct when the APU runs at a high N1 with little demand. A reverse flow sensor in the same duct detects air flowing back towards the APU, which means the load compressor has stopped delivering (failure, or a manifold pressure higher than the APU can push against), and commands a shutdown.

rows: APU/ISOL VALVE switch OPEN (DC-10, KC-10); APU air switchlight selected (MD-10)
The manifold is asking for air
Pneumatic demand above about 5%; once open the valve stays open until demand falls below about 2.5%

blocks.content: The N2 condition is the APU's **electrical priority**. If the combined load drags N2 below 95%, the load valve closes, the load compressor is unloaded and N2 recovers, and the generator stays on line. The valve reopens when N2 is back above 95%. The crew see this as APU air dropping out and returning, and it is the signal to reduce the pneumatic load.

APU air is low-pressure air compared with engine bleed. It is enough to turn an engine's air turbine starter and to run the packs, and in an engine start the manifold sits at about 44 psig. Its temperature comes from the work the load compressor does: the higher N1, the hotter the air, and the hottest delivery is at a high N1 on a hot day. On the ground the APU can run all three packs (both packs on the KC-10) before or after engine start, and in most conditions it can carry the full electrical load while running the air conditioning. The KC-10's APU has run both packs at FL250 in testing, but its air output falls with altitude and APU air is not recommended above 18,000 ft.

Do not use APU air for wing anti-ice: the APU cannot supply the temperature or the flow to keep the wings clear. If the APU suffers compressor damage, debris can travel down the bleed duct into a pack or an engine starter. With the APU as the only pneumatic source, a manifold pressure lower than usual for the N1 shown can be the first hint.

sections.title: Start sequence
sections.summary: From the run command to a governed 100% N2, step by step.

blocks.content: Once the crew command the start, the ECU runs it automatically. The start is powered entirely by the aircraft battery: the starter motor, the ignition unit, the door actuator and the ECU itself all run on battery bus power until the PMG takes over. It needs fuel pressure at the APU's fuel inlet, which on a dark aircraft only the 28 V DC start pump can provide (see [Fuel supply](#fuel-supply)).

blocks.content: From doors fully open to 100% N2 a healthy start takes 12 to 23 seconds on the KC-10, and longer on a cold day: below about −40 °C starter time can approach 80 seconds. The EGT normally peaks somewhere between 80 and 90% N2 and then falls back as the airflow catches up with the fuel; that peak is the moment of the start most worth watching.

blocks.alt: Chart of a normal APU start against time from the crank: N2 percent (solid), N1 percent (dashed) and EGT in degrees C (red) on twin axes. Vertical markers at 6.5 percent N2 (fuel and ignition), about 35 percent (secondary fuel), 50 percent (starter cut-out), 95 percent (ignition off, PMG, generator available) and 100 percent (governing). blocks.title: Normal APU start

blocks.content: Three start faults are classic. A **hung start** is an engine that lights but stalls below governed speed: it has too little energy to accelerate against its own compressor, usually because of low battery voltage (weak cranking), a fuel schedule fault, or a restart attempted while the engine was still turning hot. A **hot start** is an over-fueled light-off in which the EGT climbs too fast. A **no light** is an engine that cranks but never shows an EGT rise. The ECU's start timers catch all three (see [Protection](#protection)), so the crew's job is to watch, to abort with the APU MASTER (or START/STOP) if the ECU has not, and to respect the starter's duty cycle before trying again.

After any APU shutdown, do not attempt a restart until the shutdown cycle is complete and the inlet door has closed: about 100 seconds on the DC-10 and KC-10, with APU DOOR OPEN out; about 3 minutes from STOP on the MD-10, with OFF out. A start into a still-turning, still-hot engine can hang and over-temperature.

sections.title: Protection and automatic shutdowns
sections.summary: What the ECU watches, and what it does when a limit is crossed.

blocks.content: The APU runs unattended, often with nobody on the flight deck, so it protects itself. The ECU compares a set of signals against limits; when any of them is crossed it closes the fuel solenoid, which stops the engine, and it latches the shutdown so that the APU cannot restart itself. The first cause to trip is the one recorded. The latch is cleared only by removing the run command: the APU MASTER to OFF on the DC-10 and KC-10, the START/STOP switchlight to STOP on the MD-10. A condition that is still present latches again at once.

The EGT limit is a schedule rather than a single number. During a start the engine passes through transient temperatures that would be damaging if held, but are harmless for seconds, so the ECU applies an acceleration limit that varies with N2 through the start. Once N2 has reached 95% and a further 8 to 12 seconds have passed, the limit drops to the 585 °C run limit and stays there for the rest of the run, even if N2 later sags. That delay lets the end-of-start transient settle before the strict limit applies.

blocks.content: On the DC-10 and KC-10 there is no single APU FAIL light: an automatic shutdown shows as the gauges winding down, APU PWR AVAIL going out and APU GEN OFF coming on, plus the specific light where there is one (APU FIRE, or APU OIL PRESS LO/TEMP HI, which stays latched while the APU MASTER remains at RUN). On the MD-10 the FAIL legend on the APU panel and the APU FAIL alert announce any automatic shutdown.
Do not restart an APU that has shut down automatically for fire, or with APU OIL PRESS LO/TEMP HI (DC-10, KC-10) illuminated. On the MD-10, an APU FAIL alert means a restart should not be attempted.

The APU burns fuel from main tank 2. It has two ways to get it. When AC power is available, any tank 2 boost pump pressurizes the No. 2 engine feed manifold, and the APU line taps off it through a check valve; the right aft tank 2 pump is the preferred one. Before AC power exists, a **28 V DC start pump** in tank 2 supplies the APU directly. On the DC-10 and KC-10 the FE switches it with the FUEL PUMP switch on the APU panel, and it runs only while the APU MASTER is at RUN or START; on the MD-10 it runs automatically. Once a boost pump is carrying the APU the start pump is no longer needed, and the fuel system's interrupt logic takes it off line (see [Fuel](fuel)).

The APU sits above the fuel, at the top of the tail, so it cannot draw fuel up by suction the way a wing engine can when its boost pumps fail. It needs fuel pressure at its inlet at all times: with no pump running, the line runs dry and the APU flames out. A pressure switch on the line lights APU FUEL PRESS LO (FUEL on the MD-10) when inlet pressure falls below about 2 psi and puts it out above about 4 psi. A low pressure on its own only lights the lamp; it is no pressure that stops the APU.

On its way to the APU the fuel passes two fire shutoff valves in series, which close when the APU fire controls are operated, and then the fuel control unit, whose solenoid is the ECU's on/off valve. Typical consumption on the ground is 350 to 500 lb/hr, depending on electrical and pneumatic load.

Before an APU start with no electrical power on the aircraft, check that the No. 2 crossfeed valve is closed. If it is open, start pump pressure leaks into the crossfeed manifold and the APU may not get enough. Without DC bus 2 the valve can be closed from the wing refueling panel using battery direct power.

The APU has its own self-contained lubrication system in the gearbox. A wet-sump reservoir holds up to 10 quarts, of which about 8 are usable. A gerotor pump driven by the gearbox delivers oil through a filter (with a bypass for a clogged element) and a pressure regulator to the bearings and gears; normal pressure is about 80 to 100 psig. The oil is cooled by fan air in an oil cooler. A chip detector at the low point of the reservoir collects metal particles, and an oil level sensor drives the OIL QTY gauge on the FE panel (the OIL readout on the MD-10 Systems Display).

Two switches protect the engine. The **low oil pressure** switch is made whenever pressure is low, including on a stopped APU; the ECU only acts on it once N2 has passed 95% and pressure has stayed low for about 20 seconds, so that a normal start does not trip it. The **high oil temperature** switch closes at about 149 °C and shuts the APU down after about 10 seconds. Both drive the single APU OIL PRESS LO/TEMP HI light on the DC-10 and KC-10, which is armed only while the APU MASTER is out of OFF.

Expect the gauge to fall by roughly 2.5 to 3 quarts during a start, as oil leaves the reservoir to fill the bearing cavities and passages; this gulping is normal. About a quart comes back once N1 is above about 64%. That is why the minimum before a start is 6 quarts, while 2 quarts is enough once the APU is running.

An electric actuator, powered from the battery bus on the run command, opens the inlet door; a torque tube from the inlet door drives the exhaust door with it. A proximity switch at the inlet door's fully open position tells the ECU it may crank, and lights the blue APU DOOR OPEN light on the DC-10 and KC-10 FE panel. On the aircraft the doors take about 20 seconds to travel each way.

The doors stay open after a shutdown while the engine runs down, so that it keeps breathing and cooling; on the aircraft they start to close about a minute after the APU stops, and the APU DOOR OPEN light goes out when they leave the open position. The ECU treats the doors as part of its protection: a door that has not opened 30 seconds after the run command stops the start, and a door that starts to close on a running APU shuts it down at once, because an APU starved of air would surge and over-temperature.

The APU generator is the same 90 kVA, 115/200 V, 400 Hz brushless machine as the engine generators, with its own generator control unit (GCU). It has no constant-speed drive because it needs none: the N2 governor holds the gearbox at constant speed. It becomes available at 95% N2, and it is protected by its GCU in the same way as the engine generators. How it is connected differs by flight deck.

On the DC-10 and KC-10 the FE connects it with the three APU GEN BUS switches, one per generator bus. Each closes an APU power relay (APR) that ties the APU generator to that bus; the APU PWR IN USE light for that bus confirms it. The FedEx procedure closes them one at a time, checking the engine instruments as each load transfers. An APU GEN RESET switch resets the APU GCU after a protective trip; the simulated KC-10 has it, the simulated DC-10 cockpit does not (see [Simulation notes](#simulation-notes)).

On the MD-10 the APU PWR switchlight on the electrical panel connects the APU generator to the generator buses, and the electrical power control unit then gives each generator bus the best source it has: its own engine generator first, then the APU, then the tie bus. Its AVAIL legend flashes during the start and goes steady at 95% N2, and its ON legend shows the APU powering at least one bus. APU GEN RESET on the APU panel resets the APU GCU.
For the generator itself, its control unit, its protections and the bus switching logic, see [Electrical](electrical).

Two continuous fire detector loops line the APU compartment walls, monitored by their own fire detection control unit. A fire warning from them shuts the APU down automatically, with no crew action. Operating the APU fire control then closes the APU fire shutoff valve, removes the generator field and discharges agent. The APU has no extinguisher bottles of its own: its agent comes from engine 2's two bottles in the aft fuselage, through outlets of their own into the APU compartment. Any agent used on the APU is therefore unavailable to engine 2, and the other way round. Detection, the warnings on each flight deck and the extinguishing controls are described in [Fire Protection](fire-protection#apu-fire).

The DC-10 and KC-10 put everything APU-related on the flight engineer's upper panels: the start controls and gauges on upper panel No. 1 with the electrical panel, the blue status lights and the APU/ISOL VALVE switch on upper panel No. 2, and the APU fire controls with the fire detection panel. The MD-10 puts a compact APU panel on the aft overhead panel and shows the APU's parameters on the Systems Display.

blocks.content: This section describes how the APU is used through a flight and why. The checklists themselves are in [Normal Procedures](normal-procedures).
A ground start on battery power follows a fixed order, and each step has a reason:

items: **Battery on**, and check battery voltage on the VOLT/AMP/FREQ selector (at least 23.5 V DC for a start). The battery powers the ECU, the doors, the igniters and the starter, so a weak battery means a slow crank and a hot or hung start.
**APU fire detection tested** if it has not been, so that the automatic fire shutdown is known to work before the engine lights.
**APU/ISOL VALVE CLOSED.** The APU must start unloaded; air drawn off during the start robs the acceleration and raises the EGT.
**No. 2 crossfeed closed**, so that the start pump's pressure goes to the APU.
**APU GEN BUS switches OFF**, so the generator does not take load the moment it comes on speed.
**APU fire controls at rest, CONT SYS at NORM.**
**FUEL PUMP on** (APU FUEL PUMP SW ON lights). On a dark aircraft this is the APU's only fuel.
**APU MASTER to RUN.** APU FUEL PRESS LO goes out and APU GEN OFF comes on; the doors open, and after about 20 seconds APU USING BAT PWR and APU DOOR OPEN light.

**APU MASTER momentarily to START**, then release to RUN. APU OIL PRESS LO/TEMP HI comes on and goes out during the start; N1, N2 and EGT rise; APU USING BAT PWR goes out and APU PWR AVAIL comes on at the end of the start.
**Check volts and frequency** on the APU position of the VOLT/AMP/FREQ selector, then close the **APU GEN BUS switches one at a time**.

Once AC power is on, **turn a tank 2 boost pump on** (the right aft pump is preferred) and then the **FUEL PUMP off**, and check that APU FUEL PRESS LO stays out. Check the oil quantity again (at least 2 qt).

blocks.content: If the APU shows no rise in speed or EGT after START, return the APU MASTER to OFF. If idle speed is not reached within 3.5 minutes, or N2 passed 10% but the start could not be completed, observe the starter duty cycle before another attempt.

On the MD-10 the APU start is one push. With the battery on, push START/STOP: ON flashes, the doors open, and the ECU cranks the engine as soon as the inlet door is open. The start pump runs automatically while there is no AC power. When the APU is on speed ON goes steady and APU PWR AVAIL goes steady; push APU PWR to put the APU generator on the unpowered buses (APU PWR ON lights). The APU box appears on the Systems Display. A drop in oil quantity during the start is normal.
MD-10-10: the APU must be off before the takeoff roll, in flight and during landing, even though the manual contains APU takeoff and in-flight procedures. See [Limitations](limitations).

With the APU running, selecting APU air (APU/ISOL VALVE OPEN on the DC-10 and KC-10, the APU air switchlight on the MD-10) lets the load valve open as soon as something draws air. N1 climbs from 63% to the APU-air speed the packs' temperature demand asks for, between 78 and 91%. The packs then run on APU air before engine start and, where takeoff performance is critical, the APU can supply the packs through the takeoff instead of engine bleed.

For an engine start, select APU air before the start. With the engine ignition selector out of OFF, the ECU drives the nozzle vanes fully open and N1 rises to about 97%; the manifold pressure the starter needs comes from that. Watch the EGT: an engine start is the APU's heaviest load, and the EGT during it is typically around 520 °C, well up towards the 585 °C limit on a hot day. Reducing the pack load during an APU-air start keeps margin.

Running the APU at a high N1 with little of its air being used sends the surplus overboard through the surge duct: very noisy, wasteful of fuel, and hard on the surge ducts and the APU's hot section. Ground personnel should stay clear of the APU area whenever N1 is above 91%.

In flight the APU is started the same way as on the ground, with the APU air and the APU generator deselected. Normal-mode starts are dependable up to 25,000 ft; standby starts up to 10,000 ft. There is no windmill start: the inlet door must open and the starter must turn the engine. Above about 7,000 ft the ECU raises the no-load N1 from 63% to 89% (altitude idle).

In flight its main use is electrical: a standby source when a generator is lost, or before an approach when only one engine generator remains. The in-flight operating envelope limits the generator load with altitude and temperature: the KC-10 chart marks regions where the APU may shut down above 67% or above 50% generator load, and does not recommend APU air above 18,000 ft. The APU must not be used during air refueling on the KC-10, or with a known fuel leak in the boom pivot area.

Open the APU GEN BUS switches, set the APU MASTER to OFF, and close the APU/ISOL VALVE. On the aircraft the ECU delays the shutdown until the APU has run for 90 seconds with the APU/ISOL VALVE closed, so that a hot machine cools before it stops. The normal shutdown works by sending the ECU a false overspeed signal, so every stop also tests the overspeed protection. Turn off whichever fuel pump was feeding the APU unless engine 2 needs it. The doors stay open while the engine runs down, then close; APU DOOR OPEN going out marks the end of the cycle.

Push START/STOP. OFF lights and the load valve closes. On the aircraft the APU keeps running for 90 seconds after it stops supplying air, to cool, and OFF stays lit until the whole cycle is complete and the door is closed, about 3 minutes after STOP was selected. The APU box leaves the Systems Display and the APU status line clears.

blocks.content: **Modeled in depth.** The simulation runs the APU as a two-spool gas turbine: both spools with their own inertia, the compressors, combustor and turbines, the variable nozzle vanes, the hydromechanical fuel control with its governors, the oil system, the load bleed and surge valves against the real pneumatic manifold, the doors and the thermocouple rakes. The ECU runs the start sequence, the N1 schedule and the automatic shutdowns described in [Protection](#protection), with the first cause latched until the run command is removed; of those shutdowns only the overcurrent and ECU fault cases never occur. APU fuel comes from the simulated fuel system, so an APU with no pump running starves, and bleed air goes into the simulated pneumatic manifold, where it starts engines and runs packs.

**Typical readings.** At 15 °C a battery start peaks at about 460 °C EGT and settles near 395 °C with no load; with the packs on APU air the EGT sits around 505 °C, and an engine start on APU air reads around 520 °C on a warm day. N1 idles at 63%, takes about 78 to 91% with APU air on the DC-10 and KC-10, holds 85.5% with APU air on the MD-10 (whose temperature demand signal is not connected), and about 96% for a main engine start on a standard day.

items: A start in the simulation follows a recorded start trace and takes about 50 seconds from the crank to 95% N2, longer than the 12 to 23 seconds the KC-10 manual quotes. The generator becomes available as the APU reaches governed speed, near 99% N2, rather than at 95%.
The doors take about 12 seconds to travel, not 20. After a stop they close once N1 has fallen below about 20%, roughly 90 seconds later.
The 90-second cooling delay after APU air is shut off is not modeled: OFF (or STOP) begins the shutdown at once.

Electrical load on the APU generator does not load the APU: N2, fuel flow and EGT do not change with generator load. Bleed load does raise fuel flow and EGT. The electrical priority is implemented as the load valve closing whenever N2 drops below 95%.
The load shedding the real ECU performs on a rising EGT (it throttles the load valve against a reference temperature) is not modeled; the over-temperature shutdown is the only EGT protection.
Altitude idle (89% N1) is applied only between about 5,500 and 8,500 ft; above that the APU idles at 63% N1 unless APU air is selected.

The standby control mode is not usable yet: with STBY selected on a running APU the simulated APU cannot hold its governed speed and shuts itself down (LOSS OF SPEED) within about ten seconds. On the MD-10 the CONT SYS STBY switchlight is not connected.

The APU OIL PRESS LO/TEMP HI light comes on as soon as the APU MASTER reaches RUN rather than at START, and goes out near the end of the start rather than at 50% N2, because the simulated oil pressure rises slowly.

Other lamps differ in timing. APU FUEL PRESS LO (FUEL on the MD-10) comes on at RUN and goes out only once the crank has the APU turning, and it lights again after any automatic shutdown once the APU has run down with RUN (START/STOP) still selected. APU USING BAT PWR comes on at RUN rather than with the doors open. APU GEN OFF lights only when the generator has been tripped off (a protective trip, the APU fire controls, or the KC-10's APU GEN RESET held), not on a stopped or starting APU.
An overspeed shutdown is not cleared by the APU MASTER (START/STOP on the MD-10): the APU stays unavailable until the EFB's Reset Aircraft.

There is no PMG model: APU USING BAT PWR follows the start sequence and cannot show a PMG that failed to take over. The APU gauges need no aircraft power in the simulation, so the OIL QTY gauge also reads on battery power alone.
On the MD-10 the APU generator is not connected automatically after the start, as the FCOM describes: push APU PWR to connect it.
The starter duty cycle is not enforced. Respect it anyway; the simulation will not stop you.

There is no hours meter display, and the APU FIRE CONTROL switch (APU OFF/AGENT ARM) of the real DC-10 and KC-10 panels is not fitted; the FE's APU agent discharge controls include its function (see [Fire Protection](fire-protection#apu-fire)).
The DC-10 cockpit has no APU GEN RESET switch (the KC-10 has one, as did the real DC-10), so an APU generator lockout on the DC-10 cannot be reset from the flight deck.

On the MD-10 the APU air switchlight works in the opposite sense to the FCOM's: released is APU air on, pushed in is APU air off with USE ENG AIR lit. The FCOM's USE ENG AIR caution (APU air on with the cabin pressurized) is not shown.
On the MD-10 the DOOR legend flashes while the doors travel.

blocks.content: **Failures you can inject** from the EFB Failures page: APU fire, an APU fire detection loop fault (a false alarm on one loop), APU generator off line, APU generator bearing failure (GEN FAIL; DC-10 and KC-10), and oil smoke in the APU bleed air. Running the tank 2 fuel dry, or leaving the fuel pump off on a dark aircraft, also produces the matching failure naturally. See [EFB](efb).

The sim's own APU keys work: APU starter turns the FE's APU MASTER to START (or presses the MD-10's START/STOP), APU off turns it to OFF, the APU generator keys move the three APU GEN BUS switches together (APU PWR on the MD-10), and the APU bleed keys operate the APU/ISOL VALVE switch (the APU air switchlight on the MD-10). The Virtual Crew starts and stops the APU as part of its checklists; see [Virtual Crew](virtual-crew).

parts.title: Fire Protection
parts.summary: Fire and overheat detection and extinguishing for the engines, the APU and the cargo compartments, cabin smoke detection, the fire handles, the warnings and the tests, on each flight deck.

blocks.content: The fire protection system finds fires and puts them out in the places where a fire is most likely and least visible: the three engine nacelles, the APU compartment and the cargo compartments. It also detects smoke in the main deck cargo compartment of the freighters and the KC-10, where nobody may be present to see it. It is two functions joined by the crew: **detection**, which is automatic and continuous, and **extinguishing**, which on the engines and in the cargo holds is always a crew action. The APU is the one exception: detection of an APU fire shuts the APU down automatically, because it often runs with nobody on the flight deck.

Every engine and the APU is watched by **two continuous detector loops** routed side by side through the compartment, each feeding its own channel of a fire detection control unit (FDCU). A fire warning normally needs both loops to agree, which is what keeps the false-alarm rate low; the logic also recognizes a fire that has burned through a loop, and lets the crew run on one loop when the other has failed. The extinguishing agent is Halon 1301, stored in pressurized bottles near the zones they protect and released by electrically fired cartridges. The engines have two bottles each; engine 2 and the APU share one pair; the lower cargo holds share a pair of their own.

blocks.alt: Schematic of the DC-10 family fire protection system on a plan view of the aircraft. Engines 1 and 3: dual detector loops in each nacelle (fan, core and pylon detectors), each engine's FDCU, and two Halon bottles in the wing leading edge inboard of each pylon with one capped outlet. Engine 2 and the APU: dual loops in the engine 2 nacelle and in the APU compartment, two bottles in the aft fuselage each with two outlets, one to engine 2 and one to the APU compartment, drawn so the sharing is obvious. Lower cargo: smoke detectors in the forward and center/aft compartments, heat detectors in the vent exhaust ducts (some aircraft), two cargo bottles of different sizes in the center accessory compartment feeding a manifold with directional outlets to either compartment. Main deck: ceiling smoke detectors, no bottles. FDCUs and the cargo controller in the avionics compartment, with signal lines to the flight deck warnings.

blocks.content: There is no fire detection in the wheel wells. Brake temperatures are watched by the brake temperature monitoring system, described in [Landing Gear](landing-gear). A tailpipe fire, fuel burning inside an engine's gas path after a failed start or shutdown, is not seen by the nacelle loops either; it is an engine problem, dealt with by motoring the engine (see [Engines](engines)).

sections.title: Engine fire and overheat detection
sections.summary: Gas-filled sensing tubes, a control unit that compares two loops, and the selectors that let the crew run on one.

blocks.content: Each engine nacelle carries two complete, independent detector loops, A and B, mounted close together on the same supports. In the simulation each loop is made of three detector segments, one each in the fan compartment, the core compartment and the pylon, so a fire in any of the three areas is sensed by both loops. Each loop drives one channel of that engine's FDCU, in the avionics compartment below the flight deck.

The engine detectors are pneumatic: a sealed stainless steel tube filled with helium, with a core of material charged with hydrogen running along its length. One end is sealed; the other carries a responder with two pressure switches, an alarm switch and an integrity switch. The tube works in two ways at once.

items: **Average (overheat) sensing.** The helium is a fixed mass in a fixed volume, so its pressure rises in proportion to its absolute temperature (Charles's law). When the average temperature along the whole tube reaches the detector's average alarm setting, the pressure closes the alarm switch. This catches a general overheat, such as a burst bleed duct or a leak of hot gas into the compartment.

**Local (fire) sensing.** A short section of tube heated far above the average setting, by a flame playing on it, makes the core release a burst of hydrogen. That raises the pressure and closes the alarm switch even though most of the tube is cool. This catches a concentrated fire that an averaging detector would miss.

blocks.content: Both effects reverse as the tube cools: the helium contracts and the core reabsorbs its hydrogen. A detector therefore reports a fire going out as well as one starting, and the warning goes out by itself when the fire is extinguished, which is what the fire procedures rely on when they ask whether the light is out after 30 seconds. If the tube is cut or burned through, the helium escapes, the integrity switch opens and the loop reports a **fault** rather than a false fire.

blocks.title: Engine detector alarm settings (simulation calibration, approximate)

blocks.content: The settings rise from front to back because the normal running temperature does: the core compartment surrounds the combustor and turbine cases, and a setting that suited the fan compartment would alarm on every takeoff there. Each setting sits above the hottest normal temperature of its compartment and well below what a fuel fire produces.

Each FDCU watches both loops of its zone for two signals per loop: **alarm** (the loop sees fire or overheat) and **fault** (the loop is open, shorted or has lost its gas). A fire warning normally requires both loops to see it, because a false alarm from one loop, a chafed wire or a failed responder, is far more likely than a real fire seen by only one. But a real fire can also destroy a loop before the other alarms, so the logic accepts a fault as a vote for fire under the right circumstances.

blocks.title: FDCU decision table (LOOPS selector at BOTH)
rows: Fault, within 5 seconds of loop A
FIRE: two loops failing together means a fire has burned through both
No fire; that loop's LOOP light only. After 15 seconds the FDCU declares the alarming loop unsatisfactory
No fire; detection fault (no light on the DC-10 and KC-10)

blocks.content: The 5-second window is what separates a burn-through from two unrelated failures: a fire destroys loops that run side by side within moments of each other, while two independent wiring faults almost never arrive together. Losing the FDCU's power, or a loop's own supply, is never read as a fire: a pulled loop circuit breaker takes that loop out of circuit as an unsatisfactory loop, so pulling both breakers at once cannot create a warning.

blocks.alt: Logic diagram of one FDCU. Inputs: loop A alarm and fault, loop B alarm and fault, the LOOPS selector (A, BOTH, B), the LOOPS A and B TEST inputs, loop A and loop B supply. Four AND gates for the fire cases (A alarm and B alarm, A alarm and B fault, A fault and B alarm, A fault and B fault with a 5 second window timer) into an OR giving FIRE; a single-loop path enabled when the selector is at A or B; a 15 second timer on single-loop alarm into the detection fault output. Outputs: FIRE (handle light, master warning, bell or aural, EAD alert, APU shutdown relay for the APU unit), LOOP A and LOOP B lights. The test inputs are drawn injecting at the loop alarm lines, after the loop integrity check.
blocks.title: FDCU dual-loop logic

blocks.content: Each engine and the APU has a three-position LOOPS selector: A, BOTH and B. BOTH is the normal position and gives the dual-loop logic above. Selecting A or B takes the other loop out of circuit entirely: with only one loop left there is nothing to cross-check, so the selected loop's alarm alone becomes a fire warning. That is what lets an aircraft with one failed loop be dispatched or continue: the crew select the good loop and keep full fire detection, at the cost of the protection against false alarms.

The amber LOOP A and LOOP B lights, two per zone, show each loop's **alarm**. In a real fire both lights of the zone come on together with the fire warning. One LOOP light on its own, with no fire warning, means one loop is alarming and the other is not: almost certainly a false alarm. The crew's response is to select the LOOPS switch to the loop whose light is out. A loop with a fault (open or shorted) does not light its LOOP light; it shows up instead as a light that fails to come on during the loop test.

With a zone's LOOPS selector at A or B, any alarm on the selected loop is a fire warning, and for the APU that means an automatic APU shutdown. Select the loop whose LOOP light is out, never the one that is lit.

The APU compartment uses a different kind of detector: a **resistive** (thermistor) cable. A center conductor runs inside a stainless sheath, packed in a semiconductor material whose electrical resistance falls steeply as it heats. The FDCU measures the resistance between conductor and sheath; when it falls below the alarm setting, the loop alarms. Each loop is made of three detector segments connected in parallel along the compartment walls, so the hottest part of the compartment dominates the reading. A uniform temperature of about 218 °C (425 °F) sets off the alarm, and so does a smaller area heated much more.

The same FDCU logic applies as for the engines, with its own LOOPS selector and LOOP A and LOOP B lights. A loop that reads an extremely low resistance is treated as shorted, and one that reads an extremely high resistance as open; both are faults rather than fires. A cold resistive cable has a very high resistance, which is why the open-circuit threshold has to sit far above anything a cold-soaked compartment produces.

On the DC-10 and MD-10, engine 2's bleed duct runs through the APU compartment (the KC-10 has no engine 2 bleed supply). The alarm temperature is above any normal bleed air temperature, so a duct leak only sets off the APU loops if it is hot enough to be hazardous; but when it does, the result is an APU FIRE warning. That is why the DC-10 and MD-10 APU fire procedures shut off engine 2's bleed air and close an isolation valve as well as dealing with the APU.

sections.title: Engine and APU extinguishing
sections.summary: Three pairs of Halon bottles, one of them shared by engine 2 and the APU.

blocks.content: The engine and APU extinguishing system is three fixed, two-bottle systems of Halon 1301, a high-rate-discharge agent that stops combustion chemically and leaves no residue. Engines 1 and 3 each have two bottles in the wing leading edge, inboard of the pylon near the front spar; each bottle has two outlets, one of them capped, and the open outlets join so that either bottle can discharge into that engine. Engine 2 and the APU share the two bottles in the aft fuselage; each of those bottles has two open outlets, one to the engine 2 nacelle and one to the APU compartment.

Each outlet has a discharge head with an electrically fired cartridge. Firing it ruptures the outlet and the nitrogen-pressurized agent leaves the bottle in a few seconds, through distribution lines that spray it into the compartment. A pressure switch on each bottle lights its **AGT LOW** light (AGENT LOW) when the bottle pressure falls, which normally confirms a successful discharge; a slow leak lights it too. The firing circuits are powered by the battery, so the engines and the APU are protected even on a battery-only aircraft during an APU start.

Because engine 2's pair serves two zones, an agent shot into the APU is gone from engine 2, and the reverse. Engine 2's AGT 1 LOW and AGT 2 LOW lights on the overhead come on whichever compartment the bottle was discharged into. The procedures carry the consequence: if both of engine 2's bottles have been used, do not start the APU, and use the second bottle on the APU only if the first did not put the fire out.
Only engine 2's fire bottles are available to the APU. Using both of them on the APU leaves none for engine 2, and using both on engine 2 leaves none for the APU.

children.title: Why the handle comes before the agent, and why the 30 seconds

blocks.content: Halon puts a fire out by interrupting the chemical chain reaction of combustion. It does so only while it is present at a high enough concentration, and in a ventilated nacelle that lasts a couple of seconds. If fuel is still spraying onto hot metal when the agent has gone, the fire re-ignites. That is why the procedures always shut off the fuel, hydraulic fluid and bleed air with the fire handle before discharging agent: the agent knocks the flame down; removing the fuel stops it coming back.

The 30-second wait after the first bottle gives the detectors time to cool and report that the fire is out. A fire caught early usually goes out with one bottle. A fire that has burned for some time has heated the surrounding structure past the point where leftover fuel and oil re-ignite on contact, so it can come back once the first bottle's agent has cleared; the second bottle deals with that.

Each engine has a red fire handle on the overhead panel, with its engine's AGT 1 LOW and AGT 2 LOW lights beside it. The handle light comes on with that engine's fire warning and stays on for as long as the warning exists, whether the handle has been pulled or not. The handle moves through a sequence of detents, each adding an action to the one before, so that the crew isolate the engine progressively.

blocks.title: Engine fire handle positions
rows: Nothing. The handle light shows that engine's fire warning
Removes the engine generator's field, so the generator drops off line. Fuel, hydraulics and bleed air are unaffected

Closes the engine's fuel shutoff valves at the firewall, so the engine runs down; shuts off its hydraulic supply; shuts off its bleed air and cowl anti-ice; keeps the generator field off; on the MD-10, ends that engine's aural fire warning; and frees the handle to rotate
Fires the cartridge of that bottle's outlet into this engine's nacelle. Each bottle fires once; the handle has to be fully pulled for a rotation to count

blocks.content: On engines 1 and 3 the firewall fuel valve is electrically operated by a switch in the handle; on engine 2 the handle works two valves in series directly through cables, so that the center engine is isolated even with no electrical power. The light in the engine's fuel lever on the pedestal (the START lever on some DC-10s, the FUEL SHUTOFF lever on the KC-10) comes on with the fire warning and also whenever the handle is fully pulled with the lever still on. It tells the crew which lever to shut off, and once the warning has gone it stays lit until they do.

blocks.alt: Close-up of one engine fire handle and its placard: the red T-handle lit, shown in three ghosted positions (stowed at NORM, pulled to GEN FIELD DISCONNECT, pulled fully to FUEL & HYD OFF) and with arrows for rotation to AGENT 1 and AGENT 2; the AGT 1 LOW and AGT 2 LOW lights beside it, out.
blocks.title: Engine fire handle

blocks.content: Do not twist an engine fire handle while pulling it: a rotation during the pull can fire a bottle before the handle has reached FUEL & HYD OFF, before the fuel is off.

An APU fire warning from the APU's FDCU shuts the APU down with no crew action: it energizes the fire signal relay, and the APU's control unit latches a FIRE shutdown and cuts the fuel at its own solenoid. Closing the APU fire shutoff valve, removing the generator field and discharging agent are done by the APU fire controls. The warning also raises the alerts: the APU FIRE lights, the APU LOOP A and B lights, the MASTER WARNING lights, and, with the aircraft on the ground, a horn and an APU FIRE light at the external APU control panel behind the left main gear. The crew's part is to make sure the APU is off, to operate the fire control and discharge agent, and, where engine 2's duct shares the compartment, to remove the possibility that it is the duct.

The agent for the APU comes from engine 2's two bottles, through their APU outlets (see [Engine and APU extinguishing](#extinguishing)). Discharging one lights engine 2's AGT LOW light for that bottle on the overhead as well as the APU panel's own indication.

children.title: APU fire controls, DC-10 and KC-10

blocks.content: The FE's APU fire controls sit beside the APU section of upper panel No. 1: the red APU FIRE light and two APU fire agent discharge controls, one for each of engine 2's bottles. Operating either control does everything an APU fire calls for at once: it shuts the APU down, closes its fuel shutoff valves, removes its generator field, and discharges that bottle into the APU compartment. On the pilots' overhead annunciator panel the red APU FIRE summary light repeats the warning.

blocks.alt: DC-10-30 flight engineer's upper panel No. 1, APU fire block during an APU fire warning: the red APU FIRE light illuminated, the two APU fire agent discharge controls (cylinder 1 and cylinder 2) at rest, beside the APU gauges which show N2 running down.
blocks.title: FE APU fire controls

blocks.content: There is no fire bell for the APU on the DC-10 and KC-10: the aircraft's central aural warning unit generates every aural warning except the APU's, which is the external horn for ground personnel. In the air, the APU FIRE lights and the MASTER WARNING lights are the whole warning.

On the MD-10 the APU FIRE control is on the APU panel of the aft overhead. It lights red with an APU fire warning. On the aircraft it is a handle that is pulled (APU emergency shutdown, fuel valve closed, generator field off, agent armed) and then turned clockwise for bottle 1 or counterclockwise for bottle 2. In the simulation the handle is not pulled: turning it to AGT 1 or AGT 2 does the whole of that in one movement, and it springs back to its center position.
An APU fire raises the APU FIRE level 3 alert, the MASTER WARNING lights, the APU LOOP A and B lights, the aural warning, and FAIL on the APU panel for the automatic shutdown.

Behind the left main gear well, in the wing fillet, the external APU control panel lets ground personnel deal with an APU fire. It has an APU FIRE light, AGENT 1 LOW and AGENT 2 LOW lights, an APU OFF/AGENT ARM switch that shuts the APU down and arms the bottles, two FIRE AGENT DISCHARGE switches, a HORN switch that silences the fire horn, and a service interphone jack. The panel can stop the APU but cannot start it. The horn sounds on the ground only, and stops when the fire signal clears.

sections.title: Cargo and cabin smoke protection
sections.summary: Smoke and heat detection in the holds and on the main deck, and how the lower holds are flooded with agent.

blocks.content: The lower cargo area is two class C compartments, forward and center/aft (the center and aft holds are separated only by a net or barrier and are protected as one). Class C means the compartment must have detection and a built-in extinguishing system that the crew can operate. The main deck of the freighters and the KC-10 is class E: detection only, with no built-in extinguishing, on the principle that the crew can starve a main-deck fire of air and land. Any single detector in a compartment is enough to raise the warning.

The smoke detectors are photoelectric. A light source and a photocell sit in a chamber that air from the compartment passes through; normally the cell sees no light, but smoke particles scatter light onto it and the detector alarms. Heat detectors, where fitted, are bimetallic thermostats in the ventilation exhaust ducts, which see the temperature of air that has passed through the hold.

children.title: DC-10 lower cargo detection and extinguishing

blocks.content: Each equipped lower compartment has four ceiling smoke detectors, each with its own amber detector light on the FE's upper panel No. 2: lights 1 to 4 for the forward compartment, 6 to 9 for the center/aft. Some aircraft add bimetallic heat detectors in the ventilation exhaust ducts, one forward and two aft, shown on HEAT DET lights 5 (forward) and 10 (center/aft); in the simulation the DC-10-30 has them. Any detector lights its own light, the red FWD CARGO FIRE or AFT CARGO FIRE light, and the MASTER WARNING lights.

blocks.title: Lower cargo fit by series
rows: One forward, two aft (one light each)
Both compartments; arming shuts off that compartment's ventilation

blocks.content: Two Halon bottles in the center accessory compartment serve both holds through one manifold: cylinder 1 holds the main charge and cylinder 2 a smaller one, about half the size, to make up agent that leaks out of the compartment over time. The FE first selects the compartment with the AGENT ARM switch (FWD CARGO or AFT CARGO). On the DC-10-30, arming a compartment also shuts off its ventilation, which starves the fire of oxygen and keeps the agent in. Only then does the AGENT DISCH switch do anything: turned to CYL 1 it discharges cylinder 1 into the armed compartment; it must be pulled out to reach CYL 2. AGENT 1 LOW and AGENT 2 LOW confirm each discharge.

On the DC-10 the discharge is entirely the FE's decision, and there is no timer for the second cylinder: the procedure keeps it for later in the flight, or for just before approach and landing, to restore the concentration.

blocks.alt: DC-10-30 flight engineer's upper panel No. 2, lower cargo fire section, during a forward cargo smoke warning: forward smoke detector lights 2 and 3 lit, the red FWD CARGO FIRE light lit, AGENT ARM switch at FWD CARGO, AGENT DISCH switch at OFF, AGENT 1 LOW and AGENT 2 LOW out, the CARGO FIRE switch at its normal (arm) position, the FWD and AFT compartment test buttons and the AGENT DISCH TEST switch at rest. All placards legible.
blocks.title: DC-10 lower cargo fire panel

children.title: MD-10 lower cargo and main deck

blocks.content: The MD-10 keeps the same two lower compartments and the same two different-sized bottles in the center accessory compartment, each with two outlets so that either can discharge into either hold. What changes is the control. The cargo fire system is run by the miscellaneous systems controller (MSC), and the crew have four AGENT DISCH pushbuttons on the cargo fire panel of the aft overhead: FWD 1, FWD 2, AFT 1 and AFT 2.

items: Smoke (or heat in the forward hold) lights the red SMOKE or HEAT light for that compartment, the MASTER WARNING lights and the CRG FIRE LWR FWD or AFT alert, with the aural tone.
The controller then flashes FWD 1 or AFT 1 to show which button to push, and raises DISCH CARGO AGENT.
Pushing it discharges bottle 1 into that compartment. After the discharge LOW lights on the button and the flashing cue goes out.

About 90 minutes after bottle 1, FWD 2 or AFT 2 flashes to call for bottle 2. It flashes at once instead if bottle 1's LOW was already lit from low pressure, since that bottle can no longer provide the first shot.

blocks.content: Bottle 1 takes about 28 seconds to empty and bottle 2 about 15. Together they hold an extinguishing concentration in the compartment for three hours. Discharge is never automatic. On some -30s the controller also shuts off the forward hold's heating and ventilation as long as smoke is detected, and restores it when the smoke clears.

The main deck is class E. Its smoke detectors, powered from the left emergency DC bus, raise the CABIN SMOKE level 3 alert, the MASTER WARNING lights and the aural tone. There is no extinguishing: the response is the smoke procedure, starving the compartment of air and landing.

blocks.alt: MD-10-30 aft overhead panel, CARGO FIRE panel on the left side, during a forward lower cargo smoke warning: the red forward SMOKE light lit, the FWD 1 AGENT DISCH pushbutton flashing (shown lit), FWD 2, AFT 1, AFT 2 dark, both LOW legends out, MANUAL TEST button dark, HEAT light out, FWD FLOW switch with DISAG lit. Legends legible.
blocks.title: MD-10 cargo fire panel

blocks.content: The KC-10's cabin cargo compartment has sixteen smoke detectors in its ceiling. Any one of them turns on the cabin cargo smoke caution: the CAB CARGO SMOKE lights on the pilots' overhead and on the FE's panel, the MASTER CAUTION lights (two on the glareshield, one on the FE's panel) and the FE's twelve smoke DETECTOR lights. It is a caution, not a warning. The KC-10 has no lower cargo fire protection at all: its extinguishing systems are the engines' and the APU's.

On the DC-10 the cabin smoke detection is the forward and aft cabin detectors, shown on detector lights 11 and 12 of the same panel as the lower cargo lights, with the CAB CARGO SMOKE light and the MASTER WARNING lights.
The CABIN CARGO SMOKE switch on the FE's upper panel No. 2 has three positions: OFF (detection off; the parked position after shutdown), ARM (detection active; the in-service position) and TEST.

blocks.alt: KC-10 flight engineer's upper panel No. 2, cabin cargo smoke section: the twelve amber DETECTOR lights 1 to 12, the CAB CARGO SMOKE light, and the CABIN CARGO SMOKE switch at ARM, all lights out. Legends legible.
blocks.title: Cabin cargo smoke detector panel

children.title: Why the indications outlast the fire

blocks.content: A smoke detector cannot tell smoke from a fire that is still burning from smoke left behind by one that is out. After a cargo fire has been knocked down, smoke, agent and soot stay suspended in the closed compartment for a long time, and with the ventilation shut off nothing clears them. The smoke lights therefore stay on although the fire may be out, and the crew cannot confirm by the lights that it is. That is the reason for the second bottle: it restores the agent concentration after leakage has reduced it, so that whatever is smouldering stays suppressed until the aircraft is on the ground.

Each DC-10 lavatory has a photoelectric smoke detector in its ceiling, some with a built-in high-temperature sensor, and a sounder in the detector that alarms until the condition clears or the power is removed. There is no flight deck indication of a lavatory smoke or overheat warning; the cabin crew (or, on a freighter, whoever is on board) hear it.

Under each lavatory sink, a small disposable Halon extinguisher points into the waste bin. When the temperature at its discharge tips reaches about 170 to 177 °F, the tips melt and it empties into the bin within a few seconds. It needs no electrical power, and its discharge is not shown on the flight deck.

The FedEx DC-10 freighter carries four portable Halon extinguishers: a 9 lb bottle on the flight deck and three larger bottles in the main cargo compartment. The cargo compartment bottles have quick-connect fittings that plug into the hazardous material containers, so a fire inside a container can be flooded without opening it.

The KC-10 carries eleven portable Halon 1211 extinguishers: nine small bottles of about 2 lb of agent, in the flight compartment, the galley area, along the cabin and at the boom operator's station, and two large gaseous extinguishers of 16 lb with extension wands, in the forward and aft emergency equipment panels, for fires in confined spaces and cargo.
Halon applied to a fire produces toxic decomposition products. Use oxygen and smoke protection when fighting a fire, and ventilate the area afterwards.

sections.title: Fire warnings and the aural interface

blocks.content: A fire warning has to tell the crew three things at once: that there is a fire, where it is, and which control deals with it. The system therefore lights the warning in several places at the same time. The general alert (MASTER WARNING and the aural warning) gets attention; the localizing lights (the handle, the fuel lever, the LOOP lights, the compartment lights) say where; and the lit handle or lever is itself the control to use.

blocks.title: Fire indications by aircraft
rows: Fire bell; captain's ENGINE FIRE light (glareshield); MASTER WARNING lights (pilots and FE); handle light; fuel lever light; that engine's LOOP A and B lights
Fire bell and ENGINE n FIRE voice; MASTER WARNING lights; ENGINE n FIRE alert (level 3); handle light; fuel lever light; LOOP A and B lights
FE's APU FIRE light; APU FIRE summary light (pilots' overhead); MASTER WARNING lights; APU LOOP A and B lights; no cockpit aural; external horn on the ground
APU FIRE control light; APU FIRE alert (level 3); MASTER WARNING lights; APU LOOP A and B lights; aural warning; external horn on the ground
DC-10: detector light(s); FWD or AFT CARGO FIRE light; MASTER WARNING lights
SMOKE or HEAT light; CRG FIRE LWR FWD or AFT alert; MASTER WARNING lights; aural tone; flashing AGENT DISCH cue
Detector light(s); CAB CARGO SMOKE lights (FE and overhead); MASTER CAUTION lights (KC-10), MASTER WARNING lights (DC-10)
CABIN SMOKE alert (level 3); MASTER WARNING lights; aural tone
That LOOP light; ENG n LOOP A or B alert after the FDCU's 15-second check

blocks.content: On the DC-10 and KC-10 the fire bell is the highest-priority sound of the central aural warning unit; it rings for engine fires only. The captain's red ENGINE FIRE light on the glareshield is the bell cutout: pushing it silences the bell and puts that light out, but leaves the handle light and the MASTER WARNING. The cutout is armed again for the next fire, so a second engine fire rings the bell again. If an overspeed warning arises during a fire, the unit alternates the bell and the overspeed clacker so neither is lost.

On the MD-10 the central aural warning system announces an engine fire with the fire bell and the ENGINE n FIRE voice message, repeating until the fire is out, the warning is silenced, or that engine's handle is pulled. Either pilot's MASTER WARNING light is a push-to-reset: pushing it silences the aural warning and resets the MASTER WARNING for the next warning. Lower cargo fires and main deck smoke sound the level 3 tone.
For the master warning and caution system and the aural warning units as a whole, see [Warning Systems](warning-systems).

blocks.alt: DC-10-30 glareshield, captain's side, during an engine 2 fire warning: the red MASTER WARN light and the red ENGINE FIRE (PRESS FOR BELL OFF) light both illuminated; above them on the overhead, the engine 2 fire handle lit red.
blocks.title: Engine fire warning, DC-10

sections.title: Fire detection tests
sections.summary: The tests exercise the loops and the warning circuits, and what does not light is the finding.

blocks.content: The loop test does not heat anything. It connects each selected loop's alarm line through a test relay inside the FDCU, after the loop's integrity has been checked, so a healthy loop presents an alarm and the FDCU's own logic produces the warning. A loop that is open, shorted or out of circuit stays dark under test. That makes the test a real check of the loops and of everything downstream of them: a light that does not come on is the result to act on, not a bulb to ignore. An engine and APU fire test is required before the first flight of the day.

A test fire never shuts anything down. It lights the warnings exactly as a fire would, but the APU keeps running and no valve closes: the shutoff valves are worked by the handles, and the APU's shutdown relay responds only to a fire that is still there when the test signal is taken away. A real fire during a test still shuts the APU down.

The FE holds the LOOPS A TEST and LOOPS B TEST switches on upper panel No. 2. Each tests its own loop in every zone (the three engines and the APU) whose LOOPS selector includes it. Holding one switch lights that loop's LOOP lights and, in any zone whose selector is at that single loop, a fire warning. With the selectors at BOTH, the warnings need both switches held together, because both loops must alarm.

blocks.title: A valid test with both switches held, selectors at BOTH
rows: All eight LOOP lights (six engine, two APU); APU FIRE light; MASTER WARNING light
All three fire handle lights; all three fuel lever lights; APU FIRE summary light; ENGINE FIRE light; MASTER WARN lights
AGT LOW lights (they are tested with the annunciator light test); the APU keeps running

blocks.content: Releasing the switches puts every light out and stops the bell. A LOOP light that stays dark marks the loop to deselect; a handle or lever light that stays dark is a lamp or circuit to write up.

blocks.alt: DC-10-30 flight engineer's upper panel No. 2, ENG FIRE DETECT SYS section, during a loop test with both LOOPS A TEST and LOOPS B TEST held: all six engine LOOP A and LOOP B lights and both APU LOOP lights illuminated amber, all four LOOPS selectors at BOTH. Inset: the FE's APU FIRE and MASTER WARNING lights lit.
blocks.title: Loop test, both loops

children.title: Engine and APU fire test, MD-10

blocks.content: The MD-10 has the same LOOPS A TEST and LOOPS B TEST switches on its fire detection panel. With the selectors at BOTH, both must be held together: one switch alone tests nothing. The simulated cockpit also has an ENG/APU FIRE TEST button that runs the both-loops test in every zone whatever the LOOPS selectors say.

A valid test lights all the LOOP lights, all three ENG FIRE handle lights, the APU FIRE control light and all three fuel lever lights, flashes the MASTER WARNING lights, raises the ENGINE 1, 2 and 3 FIRE and APU FIRE alerts, and sounds the aural warning. The external APU horn does not sound during the test.

blocks.alt: MD-10 engine and alert display during the engine and APU fire test: red boxed alerts ENGINE 1 FIRE, ENGINE 2 FIRE, ENGINE 3 FIRE and APU FIRE at the top of the alert area; inset of the aft overhead fire detection panel with all eight LOOP lights lit and both LOOPS TEST switches held.
blocks.title: MD-10 fire test

blocks.content: On the DC-10 the CARGO FIRE switch at TEST tests the lower cargo detectors: every fitted detector light comes on (a series without heat detectors leaves the HEAT DET lights dark), with both CARGO FIRE lights and the MASTER WARNING lights. The FWD and AFT compartment test buttons test one hold each, lighting only that hold's detector lights and its CARGO FIRE light. The CABIN CARGO SMOKE switch at TEST tests the cabin detectors (lights 11 and 12) and the CAB CARGO SMOKE lights. The AGENT DISCH TEST switch checks the continuity of each compartment's cartridges; on the aircraft both AGENT LOW lights come on if the circuits are good. The FE does not normally operate it, because a fault during the test could fire a bottle.

On the KC-10 the CABIN CARGO SMOKE switch is held at TEST: all twelve DETECTOR lights, the CAB CARGO SMOKE light and the MASTER CAUTION light on the FE's panel come on, and the pilots' MASTER CAUTION and CAB CARGO SMOKE lights with them. Back at ARM, everything goes out.

On the MD-10 the cargo controller tests the whole cargo fire system automatically when the first of the three IRS mode selectors is moved out of OFF: for a few seconds the cargo warnings come on, with one cycle of the aural tone. The MANUAL TEST switchlight on the cargo fire panel runs the same test on demand: MASTER WARNING, the SMOKE and HEAT lights, the LOW lights and the MANUAL TEST legends light, the tone sounds and the alerts appear, with CARGO FIRE TEST in cyan. A failed test raises CRG FIRE TEST FAIL, and the manual test is then required.

A detector that flashes during the test is starting to deteriorate. It still works, but it must be written up so that maintenance can replace it. A detector light that does not come on at all marks a dead detector.

On the DC-10 and KC-10 the pilots have the engine fire handles, the fuel lever lights and the warning lights; the FE has everything else: the detection panel and its tests, the APU fire controls, and the cargo fire and smoke panels. On the MD-10 all the controls are on the overhead panel, with the alerts on the EAD.

blocks.alt: Overhead panel fire handle strip of a DC-10-30 with an engine 1 fire warning: the three red engine fire handles (ENG 1 FIRE lit), each with AGT 1 LOW and AGT 2 LOW lights beside it, all agent lights out. Placards PULL, NORM, GEN FIELD DISCONNECT, FUEL & HYD OFF and AGENT 1 / AGENT 2 legible.

rows: NORM / GEN FIELD DISCONNECT / FUEL & HYD OFF / AGENT 1 / AGENT 2
See [Engine fire handles](#fire-handles). The handle light shows that engine's fire warning
AGT 1 LOW, AGT 2 LOW lights (2 per engine)
That bottle's pressure is low: normally a completed discharge. Engine 2's pair also lights for a discharge into the APU
That engine's fire warning, or its fire handle fully pulled with the lever on
ENGINE FIRE light (captain's glareshield, DC-10 and KC-10)

blocks.content: The fire protection system needs nothing from the crew in normal operation beyond its tests and its switches at their normal positions. What follows explains how it is used and how the fire procedures exploit its design. The procedures themselves are in [Emergency Procedures](emergency-procedures) and [Abnormal Procedures](abnormal-procedures).

Before the first flight of the day, and before an APU start if it has not yet been done, the crew test the engine and APU fire detection. The LOOPS selectors are checked at BOTH, the cargo and cabin smoke detection is tested and left armed, and the AGT LOW lights are checked out. The detection and the firing circuits all work on battery power, so the test can be done before any other power is on the aircraft.

The engine fire procedure follows the order the handle imposes. The throttle comes to idle and the fuel lever goes off (the lit one), which removes the fuel at its source; the handle is pulled fully, which closes the firewall valves and isolates the hydraulic, bleed and electrical connections; then the handle is rotated to discharge the first bottle. If the handle light is still on 30 seconds later, the second bottle goes in. On takeoff the KC-10 procedure waits until 400 ft above the ground before the memory items, because flying the aircraft comes first; a fire left that long is more likely to need the second bottle.

The handle light going out means the detectors have cooled below their alarm settings: the fire is out, or at least no longer heating them. The fuel lever light then stays on only if the lever has been left on. A light that stays on after both bottles leaves the crew with an uncontrollable fire and the procedure's last items: land at once.

The APU shuts itself down on the warning, so the crew's first job is to make sure it has, then discharge the first of engine 2's bottles into the APU compartment and isolate the bleed air: the APU isolation valve on the KC-10; on the DC-10 and MD-10 engine 2's bleed air and an isolation valve as well, in case the warning is engine 2's duct. If the APU FIRE light remains after 30 seconds, the second bottle goes in, at the cost of engine 2's last protection. The APU is not restarted after a fire warning.

A lower cargo fire is fought with the cargo bottles and by starving it: on the DC-10 the FE arms the compartment, which on the -30 also shuts its ventilation, and discharges cylinder 1; on the MD-10 the crew push the flashing button. Expect the smoke lights to stay on (see [Why the indications outlast the fire](#smoke-persistence)); the second bottle is kept for later, at the controller's 90-minute cue on the MD-10, or before the approach. A main deck fire has no bottles: the smoke procedures reduce the airflow to the compartment, protect the crew with oxygen and smoke goggles, and get the aircraft on the ground. Smoke can also come from a bleed source, oil in an engine's or the APU's air; that is isolated by shutting the pneumatic supplies off one at a time.
