blocks.content: **Modeled in depth.** The simulation models each engine's two pneumatic loops (fan, core and pylon detectors, with the helium average path, the hydrogen local path and the integrity switch), the APU's resistive loops, the four FDCUs with their full fire and fault logic including the 5-second burn-through window and the 15-second single-loop check, the LOOPS selectors, the loop test injected at the loop, the six engine and APU bottles with their pressure switches and per-outlet cartridges (engine 2's pair genuinely shared with the APU), the handles' detent sequence, the cargo bottles, the DC-10 arm-and-discharge interlock and the MD-10 cargo controller, the photoelectric and bimetal detectors, and the smoke in each compartment. The detectors respond to the modeled nacelle temperatures, so a fire reaches them physically and the warning clears only as the compartment cools.

**How a simulated fire behaves.** A nacelle or APU fire keeps burning while its fuel feed is open: the engine's firewall valve (closed by the handle) or the APU's fuel (stopped by its automatic shutdown). Once the feed is cut, the fire burns on its residue for about three minutes and then goes out by itself. A bottle knocks it down for a couple of seconds. A fire hit within its first minute goes out with one bottle and the handle light goes out in about 15 seconds; a fire left burning longer than a minute comes back once after the first bottle, and the second bottle puts it out. Discharging with the feed still open always lets it re-ignite. All of this is deterministic, so both branches of the procedures' 30-second decision can be practiced. A cargo fire's smoke lingers for a long time after it is knocked down, as in the aircraft, and a cargo shot reaches only the compartment it was directed into.

items: Engine bottles reach AGT LOW within about ten seconds of discharge. The cargo bottles' AGENT LOW lights come on within about a second, much faster than the real 28 and 15 seconds.
The detector alarm settings in the table above are the simulation's calibration and are approximate.
The hydraulic fire shutoff is not modeled as a valve: a pulled handle stops the engine, and its pumps with it, and on the MD-10 the hydraulic system controller treats that system as failed.

On the aircraft the handle's GEN FIELD DISCONNECT detent also silences the fire bell. In the simulation it only drops the generator: the bell is silenced with the ENGINE FIRE light on the DC-10 and KC-10, and with a MASTER WARNING light or the fully pulled handle on the MD-10.

The DC-10 and KC-10 FE panels have two APU fire agent discharge controls but no APU FIRE CONTROL (APU OFF/AGENT ARM) switch; each discharge control does that switch's work as well. The FE's APU FIRE light is not latched.

The MD-10's APU FIRE control is turned, not pulled, and its red light may not show in the 3D cockpit. On the MD-10, the APU FIRE AGENT LO alert appears whenever engine 2's bottles are low; on the aircraft that alert belongs to an optional third, APU-only bottle, which is not modeled.
The APU fire horn and the external APU control panel are not simulated: the horn is not heard, and the panel cannot be operated.
An engine 2 duct rupture in the APU compartment does not set off the APU loops; APU fires come only from the APU FIRE failure.

On the MD-10 a zone whose LOOPS switch is at A or B is not tested by the LOOPS TEST switches; only zones at BOTH are tested (the FCOM describes a single-loop test). An open or shorted loop raises no MD-10 alert.
The DC-10's AGENT DISCH TEST lights nothing. The DC-10 AGENT DISCH and CABIN CARGO SMOKE switches stay where they are put rather than springing back from CYL 1, CYL 2 and TEST.

The MD-10's FWD FLOW switch is not connected. The MD-10 cargo fire test cannot fail, and its LOW legends do not light during the test. DISCH CARGO AGENT appears only when the controller calls for bottle 2, not with the first FWD 1 or AFT 1 cue as on the aircraft.
The DC-10's overhead annunciator panel has no CARGO FIRE summary light; the lower cargo warning is on the FE's panel and the MASTER WARNING lights.

The simulated DC-10 has two main deck (cabin) smoke detectors and treats cabin smoke as a master warning; FedEx DC-10 freighters had eight to sixteen detectors and a master caution. The KC-10's twelve detector lights all come on together, because which of its sixteen detectors drives which light is not documented.
Detector deterioration (a light flashing during the test) and dead detectors are not among the failures you can inject.
Lavatory smoke detection is not presented (on the DC-10 the aircraft has no flight deck indication of it anyway), and the portable extinguishers are not interactive.

blocks.content: **Failures you can inject** from the EFB Failures page: an engine fire on any engine, an APU fire, a detection loop false alarm on any engine or the APU, air conditioning smoke from any bleed source (engine 2 excepted on the KC-10, which has no engine 2 supply), and smoke in the main deck, forward or aft lower cargo compartment (lower holds not on the KC-10). The Failures page also offers the engines' tailpipe fire, which the fire detection system does not see. See [EFB](efb).

The Virtual Crew runs the fire tests as part of its checklists: the flight engineer's LOOP A and B tests and the loop selectors to BOTH on the DC-10 and KC-10, and the engine and APU fire test on the MD-10; see [Virtual Crew](virtual-crew).

parts.title: Fuel
parts.summary: Tanks, engine feed, crossfeed and transfer, fueling, jettison, quantity indication and CG management, with the MD-10's automatic controller and the KC-10's tanker fuel system.

sections.title: Introduction
sections.summary: What the fuel system does, how it is laid out, and what each aircraft carries.

blocks.content: The fuel system stores the fuel, delivers it to the three engines and the APU at the pressure they need, moves it between tanks to keep the aircraft within its structural and center of gravity limits, takes it on from the ground (and on the KC-10 from another tanker), and gets rid of it overboard when the aircraft must land below its maximum landing weight. It also tells the crew how much fuel is aboard, where it is, how warm it is and how much each engine has used.

The architecture is the same on every aircraft in the family. Three integral wing tanks, numbered for the engine each one feeds, are the **main tanks**. Each main tank has its own boost pumps and its own engine feed line, so in normal operation every engine draws from its own tank and the three feeds are independent of each other. Running spanwise across the wing between them is a single pipe, the **fill/crossfeed manifold**. Every tank-to-tank movement of fuel goes through it: a pump pushes fuel into the manifold, and a fill valve lets it out into the receiving tank. The same manifold is where the ground fueling adapters deliver, where the crossfeed valves connect any engine to any tank, and where the two dump valves take fuel overboard.

What varies between the aircraft is the fuel stored outside the three main tanks, and how the system is controlled. The DC-10-10 carries only the main tanks. The DC-10-30 and -40 add a large **center auxiliary tank** in the wing center section, the -15 a smaller one, and the extended-range -30 an **aft auxiliary tank**. The KC-10 adds two fuselage **body tanks** to a center tank of its own and carries the aerial refueling system on top. On the DC-10 and KC-10 the flight engineer runs the whole system by hand from the fuel panel. On the MD-10 a two-channel **fuel system controller** runs it automatically, and the pilots monitor it on the systems display.

sections.title: Tanks, vents and capacities
sections.summary: Where the fuel is stored, how much each tank holds, and how the tanks breathe.

blocks.content: All the wing tanks are **integral**: the wing structure itself, front spar to rear spar and upper skin to lower skin, is the tank, sealed at its joints. Only the center tank's lower compartment and the KC-10's body tanks are flexible bladder cells installed inside the fuselage. Fuel is measured and displayed in pounds; the capacities below are usable fuel at the standard density of 6.7 lb per US gallon that the type certificate and the operators' limitations use.

**Tanks 1 and 3** occupy the outer wing. A **vent box**, a small sealed compartment spanning the tank, divides each into an **outboard compartment** (about 5,000 lb) and a much larger **main compartment** inboard of it. Further inboard, a rib fitted with hinged **flapper check valves** divides the main compartment again. The flappers open freely inboard and close against fuel trying to run outboard, so in a nose-high, wing-low or yawed attitude the fuel cannot slosh away from the inner section where the pumps are. They have no springs and no controls: the weight of the fuel on the flapper is all that works them. The result is a reservoir that keeps the pump inlets submerged in every normal attitude.

The outboard compartment is kept full until the main compartment is down to about 5,000 lb, and only then empties inboard. The reason is structural. Fuel in the outer wing hangs where the lift bending moment on the wing is greatest, and its weight relieves that moment; burning the outboard fuel last keeps the wing root bending and the fatigue damage of every flight as low as possible. A small bleed of pressurized fuel from the engine feed line keeps topping the outboard compartment up during the flight, because the water scavenge jet pump draws a little out of it continuously (see [Continuous scavenge](#scavenge)).

**Tank 2** is the inboard part of each wing box, a left half and a right half either side of the fuselage, joined by large-diameter lines so that it fills and empties as one tank and has one gauge. It feeds the center engine and the APU, and it is the largest of the three. Because the two halves cannot equalize completely by gravity, tank 2 carries a boost pump in each half.

The long-range aircraft carry additional fuel in the wing center section between the two halves of tank 2. On the -30 and the MD-10-30 this **center auxiliary tank** has two parts: an **upper compartment**, integral, above and within the wing box (87,100 lb), and a **lower compartment**, a bladder cell in the fuselage barrel underneath it (10,700 lb). They are one tank with one gauge, which shows their sum, but they are not interconnected: the lower compartment has no route to the manifold of its own, and its fuel is meant to be pumped up into the upper compartment before it can go anywhere else. A transfer from lower to upper therefore changes nothing on the gauge. The upper compartment is further divided by a baffle bulkhead with flapper checks, with the fill entering forward and the pumps standing aft.

The -40 has the upper compartment only; its lower compartment is not equipped, which makes its center tank 87,100 lb. The -15 carries the certificated **center-wing auxiliary tank** offered for the Series 10, a smaller upper tank of 32,727 lb with no lower compartment, and the same tank is the Extended Range option on the -10. The MD-10-10 has no center tank at all.

The KC-10's **CTR WING tank** is the same arrangement one size larger: 98,108 lb in an upper compartment over the wing torque box and a lower bladder compartment in the barrel below, again not interconnected. Its fuel belongs to the aerial refueling system as well as to the engines, which is why it has its own isolation valve (see [Tanker fuel system](#kc10-tanker-fuel-system)).

The extended-range -30 adds an **aft auxiliary tank** in the fuselage, with two transfer pumps of its own and one fill valve. The tank fitted is the larger of the two the books give, 22,200 lb (some aircraft had a 10,200 lb tank). Its pumps discharge into the fill/transfer manifold, so its fuel reaches the main tanks the same way the center tank's does. It is fitted when **Extended Range** is selected in the aircraft configuration, which on the -10 fits the center-wing auxiliary tank instead.

The KC-10 carries two **body tanks** in the lower fuselage, the **FWD tank** ahead of the wing (55,300 lb) and the **AFT tank** behind it (66,100 lb). Each is a string of interconnected bladder cells; jet pumps scavenge the forward cells into the aft one, where the pumps stand. Each body tank has one electric transfer pump and two hydraulically driven aerial refueling pumps, its own fill valve, and an isolation valve between its local manifold and the rest of the fuel system. Together with the CTR WING tank they hold the fuel the tanker carries to give away, half as much again as the three main tanks together. There are no cargo-compartment tanks.

Because the FWD tank is far forward of the wing, its fuel has a large effect on the center of gravity. The tanker keeps balance fuel in it, and the system stops transfer out of it at 15,000 lb (see [CG management and ballast fuel](#cg-management)).

blocks.title: Usable fuel per tank, lb (US gal at 6.7 lb/gal)

blocks.content: Published capacities differ by up to a few percent between documents and service bulletins, because a tank holds a volume and the pound figure depends on the density assumed and on how the unusable fuel was counted. The FedEx limitations, for example, list 40,116 lb for tanks 1 and 3 on the -10 but 40,704 lb on the -30, with 65,438 lb for tank 2 and 87,106 and 11,005 lb for the auxiliary compartments on the -30, and the KC-10's own books print 40,700 and 65,400 lb for the same wing tanks. The simulation carries one set of wing tank figures for the whole family, the ones in the table. At a lower density the tanks fill to fewer pounds; the gauges always show pounds actually aboard.

The fuel in the lines is not in any tank and is not counted by the gauges. The DC-10's crossfeed manifold alone holds several hundred pounds, which can be drained into tank 2 late in a flight (see [Manifold drain and outboard fill](#manifold-drain)).

A tank must breathe: air has to come in as fuel is used or dumped and as the aircraft descends into denser air, and has to go out as the tank fills and as the aircraft climbs. The vent system is open to the atmosphere through a non-icing, drip-free outlet in the lower wing surface, placed away from the wing tip and trailing edge where lightning strikes and streamering are most likely. It keeps the tanks close to ambient pressure, inside the few psi their structure is built for.

Each wing has a **vent box** between the outboard and main compartments of tank 1 or 3, a sealed trap of about 100 to 140 US gal between the vent lines and the overboard standpipe. Fuel that sloshes into the vent lines in a turn, a climb or a taxi is caught there rather than spilled, and drains back into the tank through float or check valves once the fuel in the line stands about an inch above the tank level. The vents are crossed: tank 1 and tank 2 vent to the vent box in the right wing, tank 3 and the center tank to the one in the left wing, so a wing-low attitude that floods one wing's vents leaves the tank venting through the high wing. Each tank has an open bellmouth vent with no valve that could fail shut, plus alternate climb vents with float valves for the attitudes that submerge the bellmouth. A flame arrestor with pressure and vacuum relief bypasses protects each standpipe.

A vent box also catches the overflow if a tank is overfilled, for instance through a fill valve that fails to shut. The **TANK OVERFILLED** light comes on when either box is about half full, which is the warning to stop the transfer or refueling before fuel goes overboard. On the MD-10 the same condition is the TNK WING OVERFILL alert.

Fuel always carries some dissolved and free water, which settles to the low points of the tanks. A **jet pump** at each low point keeps it moving: a small flow of pressurized fuel from the boost pump outlet passes through a nozzle into a venturi, and the low pressure in the venturi draws fuel and water from a rake laid along the tank bottom. The mixture is discharged toward an aft pump inlet and burned in the engine in small, harmless amounts instead of collecting. Tanks 1 and 3 have one jet pump for the outboard compartment and one for the main compartment, tank 2 one in each half, and the center tank's upper compartment two per side driven from its own pumps; the bladder compartments have none.

The jet pumps run whenever a boost pump in their tank runs. A spring-loaded check valve in each motive line stops air being drawn back into the engine feed when the pumps are off, and a pressure-operated valve in the outboard compartment's scavenge line closes without boost pressure so that the outboard compartment cannot drain inboard on the ground.

sections.title: Engine and APU feed
sections.summary: Boost pumps, the physics of pump and suction feed, the shutoff valves, APU fuel and fuel temperature.

blocks.content: Each engine has its own feed system. The boost pumps in its main tank discharge into a short **pump discharge manifold**, which runs forward to the front spar, through the engine's fire shutoff valve and out along the pylon to the engine-driven pump. Nothing else is connected to it in normal operation: the crossfeed valve that joins it to the fill/crossfeed manifold is closed, so a failure in one feed cannot starve another engine.

The boost pumps are three-phase, 115 V AC, 400 Hz induction motors driving centrifugal impellers, each in a canister mounted to the tank structure so that the motor and pump can be changed without draining the tank. Each motor phase has a non-resettable thermal protector. Tanks 1 and 3 each have two boost pumps: an **AFT** pump at the rear spar, whose inlet is at the low point when the aircraft is level or nose-up in the climb, and a **FWD** pump low in the forward part of the tank, whose inlet is the low point in the descent. Tank 2 has three: a **FWD** pump and an **L AFT** pump in the left half and an **R AFT** pump in the right half. All the pumps are interchangeable.

One boost pump can supply two engines at takeoff fuel flow. A tank's pumps are therefore heavily redundant, and the redundancy is spread across the electrical system on purpose: no single AC bus carries both pumps of a tank, and tank 2's L AFT pump is on the **right emergency AC bus**, which the air-driven generator can power. With every generator lost, tank 2 keeps one pump for the center engine, which cannot run without one.

On the KC-10 the FWD body tank's electric transfer pump is on AC bus 1, the AFT body tank's on AC bus 3, and the wing-tip pumps on AC buses 2 and 3. The six aerial refueling pumps are hydraulic and draw no electrical power at all.

Each pump has a **pressure switch** that compares the pump's discharge pressure with the fuel pressure in the tank. When the pump is switched on and the difference falls below about 2 psi, the switch makes and the pump's low pressure light comes on. Switching a pump on lights its lamp for about two seconds until the impeller is up to speed and pressure has built, which is the crew's confirmation that the pump started. A pump switched off has its light inhibited, so the light means one thing only: a pump that has been asked to run is not producing pressure, because it has failed, lost its power, or run out of fuel at its inlet. Running a pump dry overheats it, so a main tank pump whose light stays on is switched off; only the auxiliary tank pumps are allowed to run on with their lights coming on (see [Auxiliary tank transfer](#auxiliary-transfer)).

A centrifugal pump adds pressure, not flow. Its impeller raises the fuel's pressure by an amount that depends on its speed (roughly with the square of the speed, so with the square of the supply frequency) and falls off as the flow through it rises. Two pumps in parallel on one manifold give the same pressure as one at low flow and share the flow between them, which is why pumps can be added and removed without any control action. The boost pumps' job is to deliver the fuel to the engine-driven pump at a few tens of psi above the tank's pressure, so that it arrives there as a solid liquid with a comfortable margin above its **vapour pressure**.

That margin is the point of the whole arrangement. Jet fuel carries dissolved air and boils at a pressure that rises steeply with temperature. If the pressure in the line falls toward the vapour pressure, air comes out of solution and vapour forms, the line fills with bubbles, and a pump fed with froth delivers almost nothing; this is **cavitation**. At altitude the tanks are vented to an ambient of only three or four psi absolute, so a warm fuel, a wide-cut fuel such as JP-4 or Jet B, or a long lift from tank to engine leaves very little margin. The boost pumps put that margin back.

With the boost pumps off, the wing engines can still draw fuel by **suction feed**. The engine-driven pump's own inlet pulls the line below tank pressure, and fuel flows from the tank through a bypass with a check valve around each AFT pump, so a stopped impeller is a restriction rather than a plug. The FWD pumps are deliberately kept out of this path: their outlet relief valves are heavily spring-loaded and stay shut under suction, because in a nose-up, low-fuel attitude a forward pump inlet can be uncovered and would admit air to the engine. Suction feed works for engines 1 and 3 because they hang under the wing, roughly level with the tanks that feed them. The real aircraft may not sustain it at high altitude: the MD-10 books give about 38,000 ft as the ceiling, and warn that with wide-cut fuels the wing engines may not run satisfactorily at altitude without pumps.

**Engine 2 cannot suction-feed at all.** It sits in the tail, tens of feet above tank 2, and no engine pump can lift fuel that far against a few psi of ambient pressure. The APU, at the very tail, is in the same position. That is why the limitations require at least one of tank 2's AFT pumps to be on whenever engine 2 runs, and why the APU has its own start pump.

blocks.alt: Side-elevation diagram of the engine feed. Left: a wing tank with its AFT and FWD boost pumps at the rear spar and forward, the AFT pump's suction bypass check valve, the FWD pump's heavily spring-loaded outlet relief valve, the discharge manifold, the crossfeed valve to the fill/crossfeed manifold, the mechanical fire shutoff valve on the front spar and the line to engine 1's engine-driven pump. Right: tank 2 with its three pumps and the long riser up the fuselage to engine 2, two fire shutoff valves in series, and the APU branch with its DC start pump and two solenoid shutoff valves. Annotations: pump feed (boost pressure), suction feed (wing engines only, through the AFT pump bypass), height of engine 2 and APU above tank 2.
blocks.title: Engine feed and suction feed

blocks.content: Each engine feed line has a manually operated gate valve driven by cable from the engine's fire handle: one on the front spar for each wing engine, and two in series for engine 2, one on the left rear spar and one in the aft fuselage, both moved by the same handle. Being purely mechanical, they close the instant the handle is pulled and need no electrical power. Each valve body has thermal relief valves that let trapped fuel bleed round the closed blade if it expands in the heat, opening at about 70 psi and reseating at about 40 psi. The APU's fuel line bypasses engine 2's forward valve, so pulling the engine 2 handle does not shut the APU down.

Pulling a fire handle does not stop the boost pumps: they go on running against the closed valve at their no-flow pressure, which a centrifugal pump tolerates. The engine's own fuel lever closes the fuel shutoff valve in the engine's fuel control; see [Engines](engines) and [Fire Protection](fire-protection).

The APU takes its fuel from tank 2 through two normally closed, 28 V DC solenoid shutoff valves in series, one at the rear spar and one in the aft fuselage near the APU, which open when the APU is selected to run and close when it is shut down or its fire handle is pulled. Because the APU cannot suction-feed, it always needs a pump behind it. Once AC power is available any tank 2 boost pump does the job, feeding the APU through the engine 2 supply line. Before that, on a battery-only start, the only pump that can run is the **APU start pump**: a pump in the right half of tank 2 with a built-in inverter that turns 28 V DC from the battery bus into three-phase AC for its motor.

Running both is pointless and wears out the start pump, so an interrupt relay takes the start pump off once a tank 2 boost pump is holding the line pressure up, or ninety seconds after the start if something else is holding it up. The relay lets go again if the line pressure is lost, so the start pump is always the backstop. A pressure switch at the APU inlet lights **APU FUEL PRESS LO** when the line pressure falls below about 2 psi, and puts it out again above 4 psi.

On the DC-10 and KC-10 the flight engineer's **TANK 2 APU FUEL PUMP** switch is in series with the start pump's control, and its blue **APU FUEL PUMP** light shows it is on. It is turned ON for an APU start and OFF once a tank 2 boost pump is running; turning it off and on again also re-arms the interrupt. With the switch off and no AC power the APU has no fuel and will not start.

On the MD-10 the APU START/STOP switch opens both shutoff valves and runs the start pump. In AUTO the fuel system controller recognizes the running APU, turns on tank 2's boost pumps, and lets the interrupt take the start pump off once they are holding the pressure. The APU control panel's FUEL light reports low inlet pressure.

Fuel temperature matters at both ends. Cold fuel thickens and, near its freeze point, forms wax crystals that clog filters and stop flow; hot fuel has a high vapour pressure and cavitates. In a long cruise at altitude the wing skin sits near the total air temperature, often −25 to −35 °C, and the fuel in the thin outer wing follows it, because the outboard compartment has the most skin and the least fuel and is the last fuel to be burned. The coldest fuel on the aircraft is in the outboard compartment of the wing tanks. The single tank temperature probe is placed there, in the outboard compartment of tank 3.

The fuel is warmed on its way to each engine by the engine's fuel/oil heat exchanger, which cools the engine oil with the fuel and prevents ice in the fuel control. On the CF6 aircraft this is continuous and has no crew control. On the DC-10-40, whose JT9D engines heat fuel with engine bleed air, the flight engineer has a FUEL HEAT switch for each engine. Neither warms the fuel in the tanks. When the tank fuel gets too cold, the remedy is to circulate the warmer fuel from the main compartments out through the outboard compartments, or to descend or slow down to raise the total air temperature.

The limits keep a margin above the freeze point: 6 °C on the KC-10, 3 °C on the MD-10. FedEx DC-10 crews start circulating fuel when the gauge reads −35 °C, which is 5 °C above Jet A's freeze point. See [Limitations](limitations).

sections.title: Manifold, crossfeed and transfer
sections.summary: How fuel moves between tanks and engines: the manifold, crossfeed valves, transfer pumps, fill valves and the outboard compartment transfer.

blocks.content: There is no tank-to-tank line on this aircraft. Every movement of fuel between tanks, every crossfeed, every refuel and every dump goes through the **fill/crossfeed manifold**, a single pipe running across the front of the tanks from tank 1 to tank 3. To put fuel into a tank, some pump must push it into the manifold and that tank's fill valve must be open. To feed an engine from another tank, that engine's crossfeed valve and a pump in the supplying tank must put the two on the same manifold. Once that idea is clear, every procedure in this part is the same move with different subscripts.

blocks.alt: Simplified diagram of the fill/crossfeed manifold as a horizontal trunk with three segments (left, center, right). From each main tank: the transfer pump discharging into its segment, the fill valve from the segment into the tank, and the crossfeed valve connecting the segment to that tank's engine feed. The fill/transfer manifold from the center tank joining the center segment through a plain pipe. Three worked examples drawn as colored arrows: tank 2 to tanks 1 and 3 (tank 2 transfer pump, fill valves 1 and 3 open); engine 1 fed from tank 2 (tank 2 transfer pump, crossfeed 1 open, tank 1 pumps off); lateral balance tank 1 to tank 3 (tank 1 transfer pump, fill valve 3 open).
blocks.title: Moving fuel through the manifold

blocks.content: Each main tank's transfer pump discharges into its own part of the manifold, and the center and aft auxiliary tanks' pumps into a **fill/transfer manifold** that joins it in the center section. The manifold is normally full of fuel and, with no pump running into it, sits at roughly tank pressure. A **surge relief valve** at each end protects it from the pressure spikes of a fill valve slamming shut during a high-rate refuel, opening at about 145 psi and reseating at about 125 psi and dumping into the outboard compartment of tank 1 or 3. Thermal relief valves in the crossfeed valves relieve pressure built up by trapped fuel warming in the sun, cracking at about 90 psi.

The manifold holds several hundred pounds of fuel (436 lb on the -30 and -40 by the Northwest figures) that no gauge counts. It is kept full on purpose, because an empty manifold would deliver air to an engine the moment a crossfeed valve opened. Only at the end of a flight, when tank 2 is nearly empty, is it drained into tank 2 to make that fuel usable.

Three **crossfeed valves**, one per engine, connect each engine's feed line to the manifold. They are DC motor-driven gate valves, each on a different DC bus (1, 2 and 3 for engines 1, 2 and 3), with a manual override lever for maintenance. A motor-driven valve stays where it is if it loses power, so a crossfeed valve that was open stays open. The **X-FEED DISAGREE** light beside each control comes on whenever the valve's position does not agree with its selection: it lights briefly during every normal stroke (the confirmation that the valve moved) and stays on if the valve fails to reach the selected position.

Opening a crossfeed valve joins two pump groups to one manifold, and then the physics of parallel pumps decides who feeds whom. Pump groups that discharge into a common pipe settle at a common pressure; the group with the higher delivery pressure carries more of the flow, and if one side's pumps are switched off the other side carries all of it. That is how a healthy tank carries a dead tank's engine. It is also why a crossfeed must be set up deliberately: switch off the pumps of the tank you do not want to use, or the stronger group will feed every engine. With tank 2 and a wing tank both feeding through the manifold, tank 2 can be expected to take over. If a tank's quantity falls while another tank's rises, fuel is going back through an open path; close the crossfeed and use the transfer pump instead.
Do not open crossfeed 2 unless the manifold is pressurized by a pump. Engine 2 cannot suction-feed, and opening its crossfeed to an unpressurized manifold can reduce its fuel pressure.

On the aircraft the crossfeed valves also close by themselves when the dump low-level floats act and when the ground refueling panel is armed, and each DISAGREE light then stays on until its control is returned to closed (see [Simulation notes](#simulation-notes)).

Each main tank has one **transfer pump** (TRANS), the same pump as a boost pump, that discharges straight into the manifold instead of into the engine feed. It moves fuel to any other tank without opening any crossfeed valve, or to any engine by opening that engine's crossfeed valve.

Fuel enters a tank through its **fill valve**, the same valve the ground refueling uses. The valve is not a simple motor valve. It is a **fill shutoff controller**: a poppet held shut by a spring and pushed open by a diaphragm that is worked by the manifold's own fuel pressure. A solenoid decides whether manifold pressure reaches the diaphragm, and **pilot float valves** in the tank decide whether it stays there. While the tank has room, the pilot floats are down and the pilot line is closed; as the fuel reaches the float, the float lifts, opens the pilot line, the pressure behind the diaphragm decays, and the poppet shuts. Tanks 1 and 3 have two pilot floats in series (the last to open shuts the valve), tank 2 one in its left half. The result has three requirements for a fill valve to open: an open signal, pressure in the manifold, and room in the tank. It is fail-closed: lose the signal or the pressure and it shuts.

A latching overpressure controller shuts the valve if the tank pressure rises abnormally, for instance about 9 psig on the KC-10, and has to be reset by maintenance. The **HIGH LEVEL FLOAT TEST** button floods the pilot floats' chambers as if the tanks were full: with fill valves open and their FILL VALVE OPEN lights on, holding the button closes the valves and puts the lights out, and releasing it lets them open again. It proves the automatic full-tank shutoff before the tanks are filled to the top. The ground refueling panel's pre-check does the same.

**The 40,000 lb rule.** Tank 2 is filled before the wing tanks are emptied, so early in a long flight tank 2 holds more fuel than the wings. Fuel above about 40,000 lb in tank 2 is treated as auxiliary fuel: it is transferred into tanks 1 and 3 to keep them full, which keeps the wing bending relief, until tank 2 is down to about 40,000 lb. At that point all three main tanks hold about the same amount (a full wing tank is just over 40,000 lb), the transfer stops, and the three tanks burn down together. A float switch in tank 2 at 40,000 lb marks the point. On the MD-10 the controller ends the transfer itself. On the DC-10 the FILL VALVE switches are spring-loaded to CLOSE and held at OPEN by a solenoid only while an auxiliary tank pump is running (all three switches) or tank 2 holds more than 40,000 lb (tanks 1 and 3); when the float is uncovered the tank 1 and 3 switches drop to CLOSE, the transfer ends, and the flight engineer turns tank 2's transfer pump off. See [Simulation notes](#simulation-notes) for how this works in the simulation.

blocks.alt: Diagram of a main tank fill system: the manifold, the fill shutoff controller with its solenoid poppet, diaphragm-operated plunger, latching overpressure controller and manual override, the poppet fill shutoff valve in the tank, and the pilot line threading two pilot float valves in series in tank 1 (one in tank 2's left half). The pre-check line from the HIGH LEVEL FLOAT TEST / refuel panel pre-check solenoid into each pilot float can. Annotated states: filling (floats down, pilot closed, diaphragm pressurized, valve open) and full (float up, pilot pressure decayed, valve shut).
blocks.title: Fill shutoff controller and pilot floats

blocks.content: The outboard compartment of tank 1 or 3 is held full while the main compartment holds more than about 5,000 lb. Two independent systems then let it empty inboard and keep the main compartment at about 5,000 lb until the outboard fuel is gone. A **gravity transfer valve**, opened by a float at the 5,000 lb level in the main compartment, lets the outboard fuel run downhill through the vent-box bulkhead. A **jet transfer system**, armed by a second float, pumps out the fuel trapped on both sides of the vent box and is the primary path in a nose-up attitude. Either system can transfer faster than the engine burns at cruise power. The bleed flow that kept the compartment topped up is shut off by the same float.

That transfer rate is enough for the engine on its own, but not for more. So **do not plan to transfer or crossfeed out of tank 1 or 3 below about 11,000 lb**: once the outboard fuel is the only fuel replenishing the main compartment, a transfer pump or a second engine drawing on the tank can empty the main compartment faster than the outboard fuel refills it.

A **fuel schedule monitor** watches the transfer: a high-level float in the outboard compartment and two low-level floats at 4,000 and 6,000 lb in the main compartment. If the outboard compartment empties while the main compartment is still above about 6,000 lb (premature transfer, which throws away the bending relief) or stays full while the main compartment drops below about 4,000 lb (failure to transfer, which traps about 5,000 to 5,800 lb), the **FUEL SCHED** light for that tank comes on after a delay of about 22 seconds. A nose-high attitude with between 5,000 and 11,000 lb in the tank, or a transfer in progress when the engine's burn stops, can light it for up to ten minutes without a fault.

The KC-10 adds a **wing-tip pump** in each outboard compartment. Selected by its switch or by TRANS PUMP OVRD, it runs only once the tank is below about 11,000 lb and pumps the outboard fuel inboard, so that the outboard fuel can be transferred out of the wing as well as burned. The TIP PUMP TRANS and TIP PUMP LOW PRESS lights report it.

At each end of the manifold, in the outboard compartment of tanks 1 and 3, is a 28 V DC solenoid poppet, the **manifold drain and outboard fill valve**, with two jobs. As a drain valve it lets air into the end of the manifold so the manifold can empty downhill into tank 2 through a **manifold drain float valve** at its low point, which opens only when tank 2 is below about 2,000 lb. That recovers the several hundred pounds in the manifold at the end of a flight. The float valve is purely mechanical and needs no switch.

As an outboard fill valve it is a second, slower way into tank 1 or 3, used to keep the tanks balanced when the main fill valve has failed closed. It has no pilot float and does not close itself when the tank is full, so a transfer through it must be stopped by hand about 3,000 lb short of full to avoid venting fuel overboard.

Once the manifold has been drained, do not open a crossfeed valve or run a transfer pump: an empty manifold can deliver air to an engine. Below about 2,000 lb in tank 2, a transfer or crossfeed can also open the drain float valve and send manifold fuel into tank 2; trying to feed engine 1 or 3 from it can reduce the fuel pressure to engine 2.

The center tank's fuel reaches the engines only by transfer into the main tanks. Its upper compartment has two pumps, left and right, that discharge into the fill/transfer manifold; its lower compartment, where fitted, has two more. The intended sequence is lower into upper, and upper into tanks 1, 2 and 3 through their fill valves, keeping them full. With the lower compartment empty, the upper pumps carry on alone, and once the center tank is empty normal tank 2 transfer resumes. The -30ER's aft auxiliary tank and the KC-10's body tanks transfer the same way, through the fill valves of whichever tanks are to receive.

The auxiliary pumps' low pressure lights do not trigger the master caution, because a center tank running dry is a normal event: on the real aircraft the lights begin to blink as the pumps start to uncover, and FedEx allows the pumps to run for up to ten minutes after that so that the last fuel can be used.

On the DC-10 the flight engineer works the center tank's pumps with two selectors, **L** and **R PUMPS AUX TANKS**. **UPR** runs that side's upper pump. **ALL** runs that side's upper and lower pumps together, so the lower compartment's fuel is moved as well. **OFF** stops them. The -40's selectors have only OFF and UPR; on the -15, and the -10 with the center-wing tank, there is no lower compartment, so ALL and UPR do the same thing.

sections.title: Fueling and defueling
sections.summary: Single-point pressure fueling, automatic shutoff, defueling, and loading fuel from the EFB.

blocks.content: The aircraft is pressure-fueled through four **refuel/defuel adapters**, two under each wing, which deliver into the fill/crossfeed manifold. There are no gravity filler caps. From the manifold the fuel enters each tank through the same fill valves used for transfer, and each tank's pilot floats shut its fill valve when it is full, so one operator can fill every tank to the top from a single point without anyone in the cockpit. Each adapter has a spring-loaded poppet opened by the fueling nozzle and a check valve behind it, two barriers against fuel running back out.

The fuel enters the main tanks through diffusers low in the tank, below the normal low-fuel level, which keeps the velocity and splashing down and with them the build-up of static charge in the fuel. The fill valves are designed to close at a controlled rate so that a full tank does not send a pressure surge back into the fueling hose; the manifold's surge relief valves protect it if one does.

Fueling is controlled from a **fueling control panel** under the leading edge of the right wing, near the right-wing adapters. It is powered when its access door is open and its power switch is set to ARM; with no other power on the aircraft it runs from the battery through the static inverter, which is why a cold aircraft can be fueled without ground power. For each tank the panel has a quantity repeater, a **fuel load selector** to preset the quantity wanted, and a fill valve switch: OPEN fills the tank to full, AUTO fills it to the preset quantity and then shuts its fill valve, CLOSE keeps it shut. A VALVE OPEN light shows each fill valve's position. A **fuel level shutoff test** switch floods the pilot floats as if the tanks were full; every fill valve should close and every VALVE OPEN light go out, proving the automatic shutoff before the tanks reach it. A gauge test switch drives the quantity indicators so their movement can be checked.

Arming the panel closes any open crossfeed valve and takes the fill valve control away from the cockpit for the duration. Tank 2 may not fill completely from a low-capacity source: FedEx wants at least 250 US gal/min into tank 2 alone, and filling is easier if tank 2 starts with less than 15,000 lb. A fill valve needs pressure to open; on a dry system at a low delivery rate it can take up to a minute, and below about 25 psi at the adapters not every valve will open. If fueling must be done a few tanks at a time, fuel tank 2 and the auxiliary tanks first, so the center of gravity does not move too far aft while cargo is being worked.

The KC-10's panel has a selector and fill valve switch for each of its seven fill points: tanks 1, 2 and 3, the FWD and AFT body tanks, and the CTR WING tank's upper and lower compartments. Two fuselage fill receptacles forward of the left main wheel well connect to the same manifold. The body tanks' isolation valves open automatically with their fill valve switches as long as MASTER FUEL ISOL is at NORM. The cockpit's **GND REFUEL VALVE OPEN** light shows that the ground refuel shutoff valve is open.

On the MD-10 the right-wing panel's repeaters are fed by the fuel quantity processing unit. While the refueling system is armed the fuel system controller stops everything except engine and APU support, the REFUELING alert is displayed, and the crossfeed valves are held closed, with a DISAG light on any crossfeed switch selected open.

A tank is defueled through an adapter with its check valve held open by its manual override. Either that tank's transfer pump pushes the fuel into the manifold and out, or its boost pumps do so with its crossfeed valve open; this way each tank can be emptied selectively. Alternatively the ground equipment can apply suction to an adapter and draw fuel back through the suction defuel check valves; that cannot select a tank and cannot empty the tanks completely. The center tank is defueled with its own pumps.

In the simulation the fueling panel is worked for you by the EFB's Ground Ops **Fuel** page. Enter a block fuel, or fetch the ramp fuel from your latest SimBrief flight plan, and **Distribute** spreads it over the fitted tanks in the books' loading order: on the DC-10 and MD-10 the three mains equally until tanks 1 and 3 are full, then tank 2, then the center tank (upper compartment, then lower), then the aft auxiliary tank; on the KC-10 the seven-step loading schedule of its weight and balance manual, which puts 5,000 lb in each main tank and 15,000 lb in the FWD tank before filling the mains, then tank 2, then the body tanks and CTR WING tank. Each tank's target can then be adjusted by hand, and the page shows the fuel load, gross weight and center of gravity it gives.

**Refuel** pumps the fuel in through the aircraft's own adapters, manifold and fill valves, at a rate of a few thousand pounds a minute, and needs ground service power on the aircraft. A fill valve that has failed shut will not let its tank fill. The page shows progress, rate and time to go, and **Cancel refuel** stops it where it stands. A refuel only adds fuel; to lower a tank use **Instant**, which sets the quantities directly. Fuel loaded from the simulator's own fuel page or by GSX reaches the aircraft too. See [Electronic Flight Bag](efb) and [Ground Operations](ground-operations).

blocks.alt: The in-sim EFB, Ground Ops app, Fuel page, on a DC-10-30: block fuel entry with SimBrief button and Distribute, one row per fitted tank (Tank 1, Tank 2, Tank 3, Center aux) with target slider and typed value, the resulting total fuel, gross weight and CG in %MAC, and the Refuel and Instant buttons; a refuel in progress showing progress bar, rate and time to go with Cancel refuel.
blocks.title: Fueling from the EFB

sections.title: Fuel jettison (dump)
sections.summary: How the dump system works, its rates, the low-level shutoff and its limits.

blocks.content: The aircraft can take off far heavier than it may land, so it carries a system to jettison fuel. Fuel dumping uses the same manifold as everything else. The transfer pumps, and with the crossfeed valves open the boost pumps too, pump fuel into the fill/crossfeed manifold; at each end of the manifold a **dump valve** lets it out into a dump line that runs aft to an outlet in the **dump island** on the trailing edge between the outboard aileron and the flap, well clear of the engines' exhausts. The center tank's pumps empty into the manifold through the fill/transfer manifold and can be dumped completely.

The two dump valves are 28 V DC motor-driven gate valves, the left on DC bus 1 and the right on DC bus 3, so one electrical failure cannot leave both open or both shut. A spring-loaded flapper check valve downstream of each seals the end of the dump line when it is not in use. One guarded switch controls both. On the aircraft, selecting the dump does three things: it opens both dump valves, it arms the **low-level shutoff** floats in the three main tanks, and it closes any main tank fill valve that was open so that dumped fuel does not go into a tank instead of overboard (the center tank's upper fill valve is the exception). An **L** and **R FUEL DUMP VALVE OPEN** light shows each valve's position.

The dump switch only opens a path. The fuel moves only if pumps are pushing it into the manifold and the crossfeed valves are open to let the boost pumps join in, which is why the dump procedure on the DC-10 and KC-10 starts with every tank and transfer pump on and every crossfeed open before the switch is moved.

The dump rate is not a fixed number: it is whatever the running pumps can push through the two outlets. With every pump running it starts at about **5,800 lb/min**, and it falls as tanks reach their floats and their transfer pumps stop and as the center tank runs dry, giving an average for a complete dump of about **5,000 lb/min**. A pump lost or a crossfeed left shut lowers it further, and pumping a nearly empty tank in a nose-high attitude makes the low pressure lights flicker before the float is reached. The KC-10 adds its aerial refueling pumps: about 6,000 lb/min with the AR and electric pumps together, about 5,000 lb/min on the electric pumps alone, and its book adds five minutes to the planned dump time below 90,000 lb total because of the falling rate.
