blocks.content: A dump that ran on would empty the main tanks. Each main tank has a **dump low-level float**, about 11,000 lb in tanks 1 and 3 and 11,500 lb in tank 2 on the DC-10 (12,000 lb on the KC-10). When a tank's float is reached with the dump selected, that tank's transfer pump stops and it is cut off from the dump manifold, so it goes on feeding its own engine and dumps no more. On the real aircraft that transfer pump's low pressure light then stays on until its switch is turned off, and the first float to act closes **all** the crossfeed valves, each X-FEED DISAGREE light staying on until its control is turned to closed (see [Simulation notes](#simulation-notes)). The other tanks go on dumping through their transfer pumps until each reaches its float. The design leaves about 33,000 to 35,000 lb in the main tanks; FedEx plans on about 40,000 lb remaining (13,000 lb in tanks 1 and 3 and 14,000 lb in tank 2, allowing for the floats' tolerances and attitude).

The low-level shutoff and the FUEL DUMP VALVE OPEN lights are powered from DC bus 2. With DC bus 2 lost they do not work: monitor the quantity indicators and stop the dump by hand before the tanks go below the undumpable fuel.

On the KC-10 the FWD body tank also stops at its 15,000 lb balance level during a dump unless AR PUMP OVRD is selected. **TRANS PUMP OVRD** takes the main tank floats out of the loop: the main tank pumps then carry on dumping until tank 2 is empty and tanks 1 and 3 are down to about 4,000 lb each.
After a dump, if a FUEL DUMP VALVE OPEN light stays on, opening a crossfeed valve or turning a transfer pump on will dump fuel from that tank.

On the MD-10 the guarded **DUMP** switch on the fuel panel starts a sequence run by a dedicated dump control network, independent of the fuel system controller: the main fill valves close, the tank and transfer pumps start in a staggered order so the electrical system does not see one large transient, the crossfeed valves open, and the two dump valves open. The controller has no command over the dump valves, which keeps a controller fault from ever dumping fuel, but in AUTO it backs up the pump and crossfeed commands and monitors the sequence. Pushing DUMP again closes the dump valves and crossfeeds and stops the transfer pumps. If the switch itself fails, the dump emergency stop (the **MANF STOP** switchlight in this cockpit) reverses the signal and stops the sequence; pushing it again restarts it.

The low-level floats stop the dump at about 11,000 lb in tanks 1 and 3 and 11,500 to 12,000 lb in tank 2; if they do not, the crew must stop it. On the aircraft the first dump of a flight also stops at the dump-to-gross-weight value entered in the FMS (by default the maximum landing weight). FUEL DUMP ON is displayed while the switch is on, and DUMP VLV L or R DISAG if a valve disagrees with its command. Dumping in a high nose-up attitude can make a float act early. The center of gravity usually moves slightly forward during a dump; in AUTO the controller reschedules the remaining fuel afterwards.

sections.title: Quantity indication
sections.summary: Capacitance gauging, the indicators and totalizer, fuel used, and the MD-10's displays.

blocks.content: The quantity in each tank is measured by **capacitance probes**: pairs of concentric metal tubes standing from the bottom of the tank to the top, open to the fuel between them. Each probe is a capacitor whose dielectric is partly fuel and partly air. Jet fuel's dielectric constant is about 2.1 against air's 1.0, so a probe's capacitance rises in proportion to the depth of fuel around it. The probes in a tank are wired in parallel and shaped to the tank's cross-section, so that their total capacitance tracks the tank's volume of fuel, and they are spread across the tank so that the errors of a nose-up or wing-low attitude largely cancel. Tanks 1 and 3 have fifteen probes each and tank 2 ten.

Volume is not what the crew need: the engines burn mass, and range and weight are computed in pounds. Fortunately a fuel's dielectric constant and its density rise and fall together, so the system can measure mass directly. A **compensator**, a small fully immersed capacitor low in each tank (two in tank 2, one per half), measures the dielectric constant of the fuel actually in the tank, and the indicating circuit uses it to convert the probes' reading into pounds of that particular fuel. The DC-10's analog system is a three-wire, null-balancing bridge; the KC-10's digital system computes the same answer electronically. The compensator only works submerged, and the maintenance checks assume at least 12,000 lb in a tank for it to be; at very low quantities or high pitch angles the reading becomes unreliable, which is why the minimum fuel procedures caution against trusting the last few hundred pounds in a nose-high attitude.
The system runs on 115 V AC, 400 Hz, from **AC bus 1** normally and from **AC bus 2** as the alternate. With only the battery on, an inverter supplies it so that the tanks can be fueled.

The flight engineer selects the supply with the FUEL QTY IND PWR switch (NORM for AC bus 1, ALTN for AC bus 2), above the upper main circuit breaker panel; it must be at NORM for a battery-only refuel. Two independent electronic channels, A and B, compute the quantities, and one is enough; FedEx and the KC-10's digital system have disabled the FUEL QTY CHAN SELECT switch that used to choose between them.

children.title: Indicators, totalizer and fuel used (DC-10, KC-10)

blocks.content: The flight engineer has one quantity indicator per tank on the lower part of the fuel panel, above that tank's pumps and valves, plus a **totalizer / gross weight indicator** showing the sum of the tanks and the gross weight, which is the total fuel plus the zero fuel weight the flight engineer has set into it. Because it adds the tanks, the totalizer is only as good as the worst of them: with any tank indicator failed, the total and the gross weight are unreliable, and the actual figures must be found by adding the working indicators and the computed quantity in the failed tank.

The DC-10 offers two sets of indicators, selected in the aircraft configuration under **Fuel Gauges**. The **Analog** set has electromechanical counters, five drums per tank and six for the totalizer and the gross weight, driven by servos; the gross weight counter is set by its knob, and an unpowered counter freezes where it stands. The **Digital** set has round liquid-crystal indicators like the FedEx and KC-10 retrofit: a digital readout in pounds with a ring of segments around the rim showing the tank's fill at a glance, from the 7 o'clock position (empty) to the 5 o'clock position (full). The ring is for convenience only; the digits are the reading. A failed digital indicator shows dashes. The DC-10's digital set has no totalizer.

The KC-10's digital fuel quantity indicating system has six round LCD tank indicators, reading to 100 lb, and a landscape **TOTAL FUEL / GROSS WT** indicator reading to 200 lb. The flight engineer sets the zero fuel weight with the three-position, spring-centerd GROSS WEIGHT SET switch beneath it: a touch shows the zero fuel weight in place of the gross weight, and holding it up or down for more than about three seconds slews the figure, in 200 lb steps at first and in 1,000 lb steps once it has moved 1,000 lb. The system tests itself continuously; an indicator whose test finds a fault that could give a wrong reading stops showing a quantity and stays that way until maintenance, and the total fuel and gross weight can then no longer be trusted.

The **FUEL QTY TEST** button tests the indicators. On the digital indicators a press starts a fixed sequence: every segment lit for four seconds (the tank indicators read 188880, the totalizer 888880), all segments blank for one second, then each indicator shows its test value for five seconds (99900, or 199900 on the large center tank's indicator) before returning to the real quantity. On the analog counters the drums wind toward zero while the button is held and return when it is released. The totalizer is not itself tested; it shows the sum of whatever the tank indicators are showing.

A **FUEL USED** counter for each engine, fed by that engine's fuel flow transmitter, counts the fuel the engine has burned since it was last reset; engine 2's counter does not include the APU. Holding the **FUEL USED RESET** button winds all three counters back to zero; it must be held until they stop. Fuel used is the independent cross-check on the quantity system: total fuel at engine start minus the sum of the counters should agree with the totalizer, and a growing difference is the first sign of a gauging fault or a leak.

On the MD-10 the probes feed a **fuel quantity processing unit**, which sends the quantities to the display units, to the repeaters on the refueling panel and to the fuel system controller. The total fuel is shown on the engine and alert display, and the **FUEL synoptic** on the systems display shows each tank's quantity, the fuel used by each engine, the fuel temperature and the state of every pump and valve (see [Fuel synoptic](#md10-fuel-synoptic)). An invalid quantity is replaced by an amber X. The quantity system has a fuse on the battery bus as well, so the displays keep their fuel data with the generators off.

The fuel temperature shown is the probe in tank 3's outboard compartment, in °C: the FUEL TEMP gauge on the flight engineer's panel, or the temperature readout on the MD-10's FUEL synoptic, which turns amber and boxed below the limit. When tank 3 is low the probe can be out of the fuel and then reads closer to air temperature. If the indication fails, the total air temperature is a safe substitute in climb and cruise: the fuel will be at least as warm as the TAT.

sections.title: CG management and ballast fuel
sections.summary: How the fuel moves the center of gravity, ballast and balance fuel, and the Virtual Crew's cruise CG.

blocks.content: Fuel can be 40 percent of the aircraft's weight, and more than half of a KC-10's, so where it sits moves the center of gravity a long way. The wing is swept back about 35 degrees, so the further outboard a tank is, the further aft its fuel is. The outer wing tanks 1 and 3 lie well behind the mean aerodynamic chord's quarter point, roughly at 60 percent of the mean chord; tank 2 and the center tank, in the wing root, lie close to or slightly ahead of its leading edge. The CG limits themselves run from about 8 to 12 percent MAC at the forward end to about 24 to 31 percent at the aft end, depending on weight and series. So:

items: Burning or transferring fuel **out of the wing tanks** moves the CG **forward**.
Burning or transferring fuel **out of tank 2 or the center tank** moves the CG **aft**.

The normal schedule (center tank into the mains, then tank 2 down to the wing tanks, then all three together) therefore moves the CG aft through the first half of a long flight and forward in the second.

blocks.content: The schedule exists for structural reasons first, keeping fuel in the outer wing for bending relief, and its CG effect is accounted for in the loading limits. A flight that keeps to the schedule stays within the CG limits it was loaded to. Deviations, such as a trapped outboard compartment, a fill valve failed shut or a large imbalance, move both the CG and the structural loads and are why the abnormal procedures care about them.

**Lateral balance** matters too. Tanks 1 and 3 should burn down together; the limits are 2,000 lb on FedEx's DC-10s, 2,900 lb (Series 10) and 2,500 lb (Series 30) on the MD-10, and 4,000 lb on the KC-10 (2,000 lb above 556,000 lb gross weight). An imbalance is corrected by transferring from the heavy tank to the light one, or by feeding an engine on the light side from the heavy tank through the crossfeed.

An empty or lightly loaded DC-10-30 freighter has its CG well aft: the heavy tail engine is far behind the wing and there is no cargo forward to balance it. FedEx therefore carries **ballast fuel** in the -30's upper auxiliary tank, which sits ahead of the CG; about 45,000 lb is needed to ferry an empty aircraft. Ballast fuel is declared unusable and added to the zero fuel weight. Normal fuel management continues, except that the auxiliary tank pumps are turned off before the auxiliary quantity reaches the ballast figure, and the same applies during a dump; the auxiliary quantity indicator must therefore work. An INOP sticker with the ballast quantity is placed on the flight engineer's panel.

The MD-10 may carry ballast in tank 2 (up to 25,000 lb) or, on the -30, in the upper auxiliary tank (up to 75,000 lb), but in only one tank at a time. The crew enter the amount and the tank on the FMS FUEL INIT page; the FUEL synoptic shows the ballast in cyan under the total fuel, and on the aircraft the controller then keeps that fuel in its tank and leaves it out of the schedule.

On the KC-10 the FWD body tank carries **balance fuel**. The loading schedule puts 15,000 lb in it early, the system stops transfer out of it at 15,000 lb, and the limitations require the crew to keep whatever balance fuel the CG needs until tank 1 or 3 is down to about 5,000 lb; the FUEL SCHED light for the FWD tank warns of usable fuel still in it when the wing tanks are below 4,000 lb. To move the balance fuel into the main tanks, TRANS PUMP OVRD arms the FWD tank's transfer pump below 15,000 lb; AR PUMP OVRD lets the tank's AR pumps run below it (see [Simulation notes](#simulation-notes)). Above 556,000 lb gross weight, or when the zero fuel weight plus the body tank fuel exceeds 414,000 lb, the main tanks must be kept full, and tank 2 should never hold less than tank 1 or 3. Fuel sloshing in a part-full FWD tank can excite a gentle 0.4 Hz yaw oscillation above about M0.85; moving fuel out of the FWD tank, preferably into the AFT tank, stops it.

A further aft CG in the cruise means less tail download and less drag. On the DC-10 the Virtual Crew can hold a cruise CG for you. On the EFB's Virtual Crew page, **Target Cruise CG** is set to the present CG with Set and stepped by half a percent between 8 and 30 percent MAC; Off turns it off. With the second officer on (MANUAL or AUTO), no checklist running, and the aircraft level at or above 20,000 ft for a minute, the second officer keeps the CG within 1 percent MAC of the target by moving fuel with the fuel panel, exactly as a flight engineer would, and stops once it is back within 0.3 percent:

items: To move the CG **aft**, tank 2 into tanks 1 and 3: tank 2's transfer pump on and fill valves 1 and 3 open.
To move it **forward**, tanks 1 and 3 into tank 2: both wing transfer pumps on (so the wings stay level) and fill valve 2 open.
The crossfeeds stay closed, and each transfer runs at least 30 seconds.

The second officer stops short when tank 2 is down to the wing tanks' level, when a wing tank reaches 11,000 lb, when a receiving tank has less than 1,000 lb of room, or when tanks 1 and 3 differ by 1,500 lb, and leaves the panel alone while tank 2 holds more than 40,000 lb, when the normal transfer out of tank 2 has priority.

blocks.content: The page shows the CG now and what the second officer is doing. While a target is set they own the transfer pumps and fill valves in the cruise: a transfer you start by hand will be stopped or reversed at the next change, so turn the target off before managing the fuel yourself. See [Virtual Crew](virtual-crew).

sections.title: Fuel system controller (MD-10)
sections.summary: The automatic controller that replaces the flight engineer: its channels, modes, schedule and reversion to manual.

blocks.content: The MD-10's plumbing is the DC-10's, pump for pump and valve for valve. What changed in the conversion is who works it. The flight engineer's fuel panel is gone; a **fuel system controller** (FSC) does the engineer's job automatically, and a small **Fuel System Control Panel** on the forward overhead gives the pilots one button per function per tank for when they need to take over. The controller schedules the fuel, feeds the engines and APU, runs the transfers and the cold fuel recirculation, balances the wings, supports the dump, tests the system after refueling, and reverts to manual if it cannot cope.

The FSC contains two microprocessor channels, A and B. Both run all the time, but only one controls; the other monitors it and the system, and takes over if the active channel fails. Each time AUTO is selected the channels change roles, so both get used. An **ancillary fuel system controller** (AFSC) carries part of the output relays: some pumps and valves are driven by the FSC, some by the AFSC and some by both, arranged so that either controller alone can run the fuel system.

In **AUTO** the controller commands every pump and valve, and the panel's unguarded buttons have no effect. In **MANUAL** each pump and valve follows its button on the panel, exactly as on the DC-10's flight engineer panel but with one button per tank function instead of one switch per pump. Two things stay with the crew in both modes: the guarded **DUMP** switch, because the controller is deliberately given no command over the dump valves, and the dump emergency stop. The crew select MANUAL with the **SYSTEM** button; its **MANUAL** legend shows the controller in manual, and its **SELECT** legend shows that the controller has reverted on its own and is waiting for the crew to acknowledge (see [Reversion to manual](#fsc-reversion)).

The controller decides what to do from the phase of flight, which it works out for itself from airspeed, altitude, vertical speed and the gear and slat positions. The climb and descent bands overlap the cruise band on purpose, so that a slow level-off does not make the phase chatter.

blocks.title: FSC flight phases
rows: On the ground, below 50 kt, all fuel levers off
On the ground, below 50 kt, any fuel lever on
Above 50 kt, gear down or slats extended, below 17,750 ft
Clean or above 17,750 ft, climbing faster than 600 ft/min; held until the climb rate falls below 400 ft/min
Clean or above 17,750 ft, vertical speed within ±400 ft/min
Clean or above 17,750 ft, descending faster than 600 ft/min; held until the descent rate falls below 400 ft/min

children.title: Engine feed and the fuel schedule

blocks.content: **Engine and APU feed.** With any engine running, the controller runs the boost pumps of every main tank that has fuel in it. In T/O-LAND and DESCENT it makes sure every forward pump is on as well, for the two phases where a pump failure or an uncovered aft inlet matters most. When the APU is running it turns on tank 2's pumps, and the start pump interrupt takes the APU start pump off once they are holding the pressure; tank 2's pumps keep running for the APU after the engines are shut down.

**The schedule.** The controller works its way down a fixed ladder, always starting from wherever the fuel actually is, so a partial fuel load or a refuel mid-trip simply joins the ladder at the right rung. The first condition that is true decides what is moving:

blocks.title: FSC fuel schedule
rows: Runs the lower pumps and cycles the upper fill valve to keep the upper compartment full; at the same time runs the upper pumps into the main tanks
Runs both upper pumps and opens the three main fill valves; their pilot floats keep tanks 1, 2 and 3 full. With only a few thousand pounds left, it runs one pump so both do not cavitate
Runs tank 2's transfer pump and opens fill valves 1 and 3, keeping them full until tank 2 is down to about their level
No transfer: each tank feeds its own engine
Tank 1 or 3 down to about 11,500 lb
Stops all transfer and crossfeed and opens both manifold drain / outboard fill valves so the manifold drains into tank 2

blocks.content: In T/O-LAND the controller suspends every auxiliary transfer and lets the auxiliary transfer manifold depressurize, so that nothing but engine feed is going on at takeoff and landing. With no engine running it schedules nothing. While the refueling panel is armed it stops all functions except engine and APU support.

children.title: Cold fuel recirculation and lateral balance

blocks.content: **Cold fuel recirculation.** The outboard compartments' fuel is the coldest and the last burned, and the controller keeps it from freezing by moving warmer fuel into it. When the tank 3 probe falls to within about 5 °C of the freeze point (−35 °C for Jet A), with all three mains burning down together and more than 13,500 lb in tank 3, it runs the tank 1 and 3 transfer pumps and opens their fill and outboard fill valves. The warm fuel from the main compartments goes up the manifold and back into the wings, and the COLD FUEL RECIRC alert is displayed. It stops when the fuel is 11 °C above the freeze point, when the tip transfer phase begins, when the aircraft is parked, or after fifteen minutes, when it gives up. If the fuel continues to cool to within 3 °C of the freeze point with more than 10,000 lb in tank 3, FUEL TEMP LO is displayed.

**Lateral balance.** There is no wing-to-wing line, so the controller balances the wings the only way the plumbing allows: it runs the heavy tank's transfer pump and opens the light tank's fill valve, until the two are close. It does not balance during a dump, when every transfer pump is already pumping overboard, or once the manifold is being drained at the end of the flight.

After the first refueling of the day, with no engine running and each main tank holding more than 5,000 lb, the controller can run a **preflight test** of the components used on every flight (pumps, crossfeed and fill valves, pressure and temperature sensors) and of those the coming flight will need (the auxiliary tank pumps and fill valves if there is auxiliary fuel). FUEL SYS TEST is displayed while it runs and FUEL SYS TST FAIL if it fails. The test can move a few percent of fuel between tanks; once the engines start the controller puts it back on schedule.

During a dump the controller backs up the dedicated dump network's pump and crossfeed commands in AUTO, and when the dump is stopped it shuts the transfer pumps, closes the crossfeeds and reschedules what is left. See [Dump sequence (MD-10)](#md10-dump).

Some failures leave the controller unable to run the system safely, and then it reverts to manual by itself. The triggers include losing all fuel quantity data; losing the tank 2 quantity together with its 40,000 lb float or with a tank 2 pump and an empty auxiliary tank; a main tank quantity invalid for more than 90 seconds; an outboard transfer failed closed; auxiliary fuel trapped off schedule; and a crossfeed valve stuck open in flight. A reversion is latched until maintenance resets the controller.

On a reversion the SYSTEM button shows **SELECT** and **MANUAL** together and the SEL FUEL SYS MAN alert appears. Pushing SYSTEM acknowledges it and locks the system in manual: SELECT goes out, MANUAL stays, and FUEL SYS MANUAL replaces the alert. From then on the crew run the fuel system with the panel's buttons, with the pump low pressure messages at the higher level that manual operation calls for. The same applies when the crew select MANUAL themselves, for instance to work a non-normal procedure.

sections.title: Tanker fuel system (KC-10)
sections.summary: The body tanks' plumbing, isolation and alternate transfer, the hydraulic aerial refueling pumps, the receiver plumbing and manifold scavenge.

blocks.content: The KC-10 is a DC-10-30F fuel system with an aerial refueling system grafted onto it. The flight engineer still runs everything by hand; there is no automatic controller and nothing schedules the body tanks. This section describes the fuel-side plumbing: where the fuel the tanker gives away is stored and how it gets to the boom, the hose and the pods, and how fuel taken on through the receptacle reaches the tanks. The boom, the hose reels, the pods, the receiver signal system and the refueling procedures are described in [Air Refueling Systems](air-refueling-systems) and [Air Refueling](air-refueling).

blocks.alt: Schematic of the KC-10 aerial refueling fuel system: the FWD, CTR WING (upper and lower) and AFT body tanks, each with its local manifold, electric transfer pump, fill valve, ISOL valve to the fill/transfer manifold and (FWD and AFT) ALT TRANS valve to the AR manifold. Two hydraulic AR pumps in each body tank with their hydraulic system labels (FWD L sys 1, FWD R sys 3, CTR L sys 1, CTR R sys 3, AFT L sys 3, AFT R sys 2) discharging into the AR manifold, the AR ISOL valve on the CTR WING pumps, the FPCU with left and right channels and its pressure transducers. From the AR manifold: the boom valve to the boom, the drogue valve to the centerline hose reel, and the route to the wing crossfeed manifold and the two wing drogue valves. The UARRSI receptacle on top of the fuselage with its poppet, the AR MASTER valve and the aerial receiving manifold into the fill/transfer manifold. The three manifold scavenge drains (RCVR to tank 2, TANKER to the AFT tank and tank 2, BOOM to the AFT tank) and the boom bypass line.
blocks.title: Tanker fuel system

blocks.content: Each body tank gathers on a short manifold of its own. Its electric transfer pump discharges into it, its fill valve is fed from it, an **isolation valve** connects it to the fill/transfer manifold, and (on the FWD and AFT tanks) an **alternate transfer valve** connects it to the aerial refueling manifold. Every tank on the aircraft has at least one transfer pump that can reach the fill/transfer manifold, and fuel moves into any tank through the same fill valve the ground refueling and the onload use. So, for example, the FWD tank's fuel goes into the main tanks with its TRANS PUMP on, its ISOL VALVE open, and the receiving main tanks' FILL VALVEs open.

The isolation valves exist so that the tanker can carry a different grade of fuel for its receivers than it burns itself, without the two mixing. They are worked by the FWD, CTR and AFT **ISOL VALVE** switches, interlocked through the **MASTER FUEL ISOL** switch: at ISOL it locks all three valves closed whatever their own switches say, a deliberate second action before fuel grades can mix; at NORM each valve follows its own switch. There is a deliberate **ten-second delay** between selecting a valve closed and the valve starting to close. Its **ISOL VALVE DISAGREE** light compares the valve with the switch, so it stays on through that delay and the stroke, and steady if the valve does not get there. A FWD or AFT isolation valve failed shut stops that tank's transfer; a CTR isolation valve failed shut stops fuel going into the CTR WING tank but not out of it.
The aircraft's normal loading states start with the three ISOL VALVE switches closed. The FWD and AFT tanks cannot transfer to the main tanks until their isolation valves are opened.

The **CTR WING tank** has four pump switches, one per pump: **UPR L**, **UPR R**, **LWR L** and **LWR R**, and separate **UPR** and **LWR** fill valves. Its lower pumps discharge onto the tank's own manifold, behind the CTR isolation valve, so with that valve shut they can only reach the upper fill valve: lower to upper transfer is unaffected and cannot pressurize the rest of the system. Its upper pumps discharge straight onto the fill/transfer manifold, so transfer out of the CTR WING tank and offload from it are not affected by its isolation valve either; what the closed valve stops is fuel going **into** the tank. The lower compartment should be emptied into the upper as early as possible.

If a body tank's transfer pump fails, its fuel can still be moved two ways: with the main tank crossfeed valves open the main tanks' feed pumps can do the work in the other direction, or the tank's **ALT TRANS** and **ISOL** valves can both be opened so that its AR pumps push the fuel from the AR manifold back through its own manifold into the fill/transfer manifold.

children.title: Aerial refueling pumps and the FPCU

blocks.content: The fuel for the receivers is pumped by six **AR pumps**, two in each body tank, discharging into the **AR manifold** that feeds the boom and the hose. They are hydraulically driven, each by a variable-displacement motor on one of the three hydraulic systems, so that losing one hydraulic system or one engine still leaves pumps in every tank. Because the hydraulic systems are driven by the engines, an offload costs fuel twice: the fuel given away, and the extra fuel the engines burn to turn the hydraulic pumps. They draw no electrical power.

blocks.title: AR pumps and their hydraulic systems

blocks.content: A two-channel **fuel pressure control unit** (FPCU) runs them. The left channel controls the three left pumps and the right channel the three right pumps, one in each tank, so one channel failing costs half the pumping capacity and nothing else. The flight engineer arms each pump with its switch; the armed pumps start when contact is made with a receiver (or when **AR PUMP OVRD** replaces the contact signal for an internal transfer) and stop on disconnect. A pump takes about six seconds to start: its blue hydraulic pressurization light comes on at two seconds and the motor reaches breakout torque at six. If its pressure is not above 10 psi within seventeen seconds the pump shuts down and its LOW light stays on until it is reset, and the next pump is started no sooner than seventeen and no later than thirty-four seconds after the one before.

The FPCU regulates pressure, not flow. It holds **50 ±5 psi** at the station being used: at the boom nozzle when the boom valve is open, at the centerline drogue's venturi when the drogue valve is open, or on the wing crossfeed manifold for the pods (enough to keep at least 10 psi at a pod inlet at full flow). With the boom and drogue valves shut, during a dump, an internal transfer or a reverse refuel, it holds the AR manifold at **40 ±5 psig**. The receiver takes what it can at that pressure, so the offload rate is set by the receiver and the pumps simply keep up until they run out of authority. The **AR ISOL** valve, when closed, keeps the CTR WING tank's AR pumps from running, so CTR WING fuel cannot be offloaded by mistake when it is a different grade.

**Offload.** From the AR manifold the fuel goes to the boom through the **boom valve**, to the centerline hose through the **drogue valve**, and to the wing pods through the alternate transfer and isolation valves into the wing crossfeed manifold and each wing's drogue valve. The flight engineer's BOOM VALVE and DROGUE VALVE switches **arm** their valves; the valve itself opens on the coupling, when the receiver is in contact with the boom or has pushed the hose in about five feet. A boom bypass line drains the boom into the AFT tank when the boom valve is shut. The **FUEL PRESS** gauge shows the AR manifold pressure from two transducers, and the fuel flow / **OFFLOAD** gauge shows the offload rate and the total offloaded, with a reset knob. While offloading, fuel from any tank can still be transferred into the body tanks.

**Onload.** The KC-10 takes fuel through the **UARRSI** receptacle on top of the fuselage above the flight engineer's station. The fuel goes through the receptacle's spring-closed poppet, which opens only with a nozzle latched in and the tanker delivering, through the **AR MASTER** valve (opened by the AR MASTER switch, whose light shows the valve open) and along the aerial receiving manifold into the fill/transfer manifold, the same manifold the ground fueling uses. From there it goes into whichever tanks have their fill valves open. With all valves open the onload can reach about 1,200 US gal/min, roughly 7,800 lb/min; into the body tanks alone it is about 3,200 lb/min.

children.title: Manifold scavenge, tip pumps and the overrides

blocks.content: After refueling, the AR manifold, the boom and the receiving manifold are full of fuel that no gauge counts and no engine can use, and that would feed a fire in a crash landing. The **MANF SCAV** selector drains them with a small scavenge pump: **RCVR** drains the receiving manifold into tank 2, **TANKER** the AR manifold into the AFT tank and tank 2, **BOOM** the boom into the AFT tank. Each line can take up to about ten minutes. The **MANF SCAV PRESS LOW** light comes on when the pump has emptied the line and lost its prime, which is the signal to move to the next position and finally to OFF.

The guarded **TRANS PUMP OVRD** switch exists to get more fuel out of the main tanks than the dump floats allow. During a dump it takes the floats out of the loop and lets the main tank pumps carry on until tank 2 is empty and tanks 1 and 3 are down to about 4,000 lb each, and at any time it turns on both wing-tip pumps, which run once their tank is below 11,000 lb, and arms the FWD tank's transfer pump below its 15,000 lb stop, which is how the balance fuel is moved into the main tanks late in the flight. The guarded **AR PUMP OVRD** switch replaces the receiver contact signal to the FPCU, so the AR pumps can be used for an internal transfer or a dump, and it lets the FWD tank's AR pumps run below 15,000 lb (see [Simulation notes](#simulation-notes)).

sections.title: Controls and indicators
sections.summary: Every fuel control and indication, panel by panel: the flight engineer's fuel panel, the KC-10's aerial refueling block, and the MD-10's overhead panel, synoptic and alerts.

blocks.content: The fuel panel is the flight engineer's lower instrument panel. It is laid out as a mimic of the system: one column per fuel system, FUEL SYS 1, 2 and 3 from left to right, each with that tank's quantity indicator, its pump and fill valve switches and lights, its crossfeed control and the engine's fuel pressure and fuel used gauges above. The fill/crossfeed manifold is drawn across the panel joining the columns, so a glance at which lights are lit along it shows how the fuel is moving. The totalizer, the temperature gauge, the dump controls and the auxiliary tank controls are to the right.

blocks.alt: DC-10-30 flight engineer's lower panel, fuel section, with the aircraft in cruise: FUEL SYS 1, 2 and 3 columns each showing FUEL USED counter, FUEL PRESS gauge (about 70 psi), X-FEED knob closed with X-FEED DISAGREE dark, TANK PUMP switches (TRANS, FWD, AFT on tanks 1 and 3; TRANS, FWD, L AFT, R AFT on tank 2) all ON, TANK PUMP PRESS LO lights out, FILL VALVE switch and FILL VALVE OPEN light, FUEL QTY indicator, FUEL SCHED lights under tanks 1 and 3. Right side: TOTAL FUEL QTY and GROSS WT indicator with set control, FUEL TEMP gauge, three FUEL FILTER PRESS DROP lights, guarded FUEL DUMP switch with L and R FUEL DUMP VALVE OPEN lights, TANK OVERFILLED light, FUEL QTY TEST button, UPR and LWR TANK PUMP PRESS LO lights, L and R PUMPS AUX TANKS selectors at ALL, AUX TANK FILL VALVE OPEN lights, center auxiliary FUEL QTY indicator, guarded MANIFOLD DRAIN & OUTBD FILL switches for TANK 1 and TANK 3 at NORM, FUEL USED RESET button. All legends legible.
blocks.title: Flight engineer's fuel panel, DC-10-30

blocks.alt: KC-10 flight engineer's fuel panel, full width: the three main FUEL SYS columns with push-button TANK PUMP switch-lights (LOW legends), X-FEED switches with DISAGR lights, FILL VALVE switches with OPEN legends, FUEL PRESS gauges, FUEL USED counters, round LCD FUEL QTY indicators for tanks 1, 2 and 3, TIP PUMP TRANS and LOW PRESS lights. The body tank block: FWD TANK, CTR WING TANK and AFT TANK LCD indicators, TRANS PUMP and FILL VALVE switches, the four CTR WING pump switches (UPR L, UPR R, LWR L, LWR R), UPR and LWR fill valves, ISOL VALVE switches with DISAGR lights, L AR and R AR pump switches with LOW lights, ALT TRANS valves, AR ISOL valve. The TOTAL FUEL QTY / GROSS WT strip with its SET switch, guarded TRANS PUMP OVRD and AR PUMP OVRD switches, MASTER FUEL ISOL switch at NORM, MANF SCAV selector at OFF with MANF SCAV PRESS LOW light, AR FUEL SYS FUEL PRESS gauge and FF/OFFLOAD gauge, BOOM VALVE and DROGUE VALVE switches, BOOM/DROGUE ENGAGED light, guarded FUEL DUMP switch.
blocks.title: Flight engineer's fuel panel, KC-10
Fuel panel controls and indicators (shared)
rows: TANK PUMP switches, tanks 1 and 3: FWD, AFT; tank 2: FWD, L AFT, R AFT
Each runs one boost pump feeding its own tank's engine. On the KC-10 they are push-button switch-lights
TANK PUMP TRANS switch (each main tank)
Runs the tank's transfer pump into the fill/crossfeed manifold
TANK PUMP PRESS LO light (one per pump; LOW legend on the KC-10)

blocks.content: On the KC-10 the pump and valve switches are push-button switch-lights. A lit bar across a switch, the **flow line**, shows what the flight engineer has selected; a separate OPEN legend or DISAGREE light shows what the valve actually did. So with a fill or isolation valve selected open, a lit flow line with no OPEN legend, or a steady DISAGREE, means the valve has not followed. The fuel system's annunciator lights are not push-to-test: pushing on a FUEL SCHED or FUEL DUMP VALVE OPEN light disengages it. They are tested with the ALL TEST switch or the panel's area test.

blocks.content: The pilots have no fuel controls beyond the engine fuel levers and fire handles. A fuel fault reaches them through the **FUEL** cue light on the overhead annunciator panel and the **MASTER CAUTION** lights, triggered by any main tank boost or transfer pump PRESS LO light and by any FUEL FILTER PRESS DROP (ICING) light; on the KC-10 also by BOOM/DROGUE NOT STOWED with the gear down. An auxiliary or body tank pump's low pressure does not trigger them. Pressing a MASTER CAUTION light resets it.

On the MD-10 a fuel alert on the engine and alert display lights the white **FUEL** cue switch on the aft pedestal and the MASTER CAUTION or MASTER WARNING lights according to its level. Pushing the cue switch puts out the master lights, replaces the alert with a reminder and brings the FUEL synoptic onto the systems display.

The **FUEL** panel on the forward overhead has a row of switchlights for each main tank, left to right for tanks 1, 2 and 3: FILL, PUMPS and XFEED, and a TRANS button under each tank, followed by SYSTEM, the guarded DUMP switch and MANF STOP. Each switchlight has two legends: the upper one a condition or the command, the lower one a fault or the crew's selection. In AUTO the unguarded buttons do nothing; in MANUAL each one commands its pumps or valve.

sections.title: Operation
sections.summary: Fuel management through a flight on each deck, the standard transfers, the system logic and how fuel interacts with the other systems.

blocks.content: Fuel management has three aims, in this order: every engine fed from a tank with fuel in it, the fuel distributed to protect the wing structure and the center of gravity, and enough fuel accounted for at every point to finish the flight. The schedule in this part serves all three. The expanded procedures and checklists are in [Normal Procedures](normal-procedures); this section explains what they do to the fuel system and why.

children.title: Normal operation through a flight (DC-10, KC-10)

blocks.content: **Preflight.** The flight engineer checks the fuel load against the release and the quantity indicators against each other and the totalizer, sets the zero fuel weight into the gross weight indicator, and resets the FUEL USED counters. The pumps are checked one at a time: each switched on should light its PRESS LO light for a moment and then put it out as the pressure builds, and the engine's FUEL PRESS gauge should rise to the boost pumps' no-flow pressure, about 20 to 30 psi. Each crossfeed control is moved open and closed, its DISAGREE light lighting briefly and going out. Every pump is then switched off except one tank 2 boost pump if the APU is running, the crossfeeds are closed and the fill valves are closed.

**APU start.** On battery power alone, the TANK 2 APU FUEL PUMP switch ON is the only way to get fuel to the APU. Once AC power is on the buses, a tank 2 boost pump takes over, and the APU fuel pump switch goes OFF.

**Before start.** All four aft boost pumps ON: tank 1 AFT, tank 2 L AFT and R AFT, tank 3 AFT. The aft pumps' inlets are the low points in the level and nose-up attitudes, and they are the pumps the jet pump scavenging works into. Engine 2 must have a tank 2 aft pump running before it is started, and whenever it runs.

**Before takeoff.** The aft pumps on and the crossfeeds closed. If tank 2 holds more than 40,000 lb, its transfer pump is turned on and the tank 1 and 3 fill valves opened, so the transfer into the wing tanks is already running at takeoff and the wings stay full. On the -30 the auxiliary tank transfer is normally started after takeoff (see [Auxiliary tank transfer](#auxiliary-transfer-procedure)).

**Takeoff and climb.** Each engine feeds from its own tank. The forward pumps may light their PRESS LO lights in the climb and in a go-around when a wing tank is below about 14,000 lb (tank 2 below about 24,000 lb): the nose-up attitude uncovers their inlets, and the lights mean nothing more. Likewise an aft pump's light may come on during a hard deceleration, such as a landing, a rejected takeoff or an emergency descent, as the fuel surges forward; keep the aft pumps on and add the forward pumps.

**Cruise.** The flight engineer runs the transfers in schedule order: the auxiliary tanks into the mains, then tank 2 into tanks 1 and 3 until the three are even, then all three burning together. The engineer watches the FUEL SCHED lights as the wing tanks come down past 11,000 lb, keeps tanks 1 and 3 within the lateral balance limit, compares the fuel used with the fuel remaining, and watches the fuel temperature on a long, cold flight (see [Fuel temperature](#fuel-temperature-technique)).

**Descent and approach.** All seven boost pumps ON, so that each engine has both a forward and an aft inlet whatever the attitude; the crossfeeds closed; tanks 1 and 3 within 2,000 lb of each other. Transfers are completed before the approach. Do not try to balance fuel once the approach has begun.

**After landing and shutdown.** If engine 2 is shut down for a two-engine taxi and the APU will not be used, tank 2's pumps go off. At shutdown every pump goes off except one tank 2 aft pump to keep feeding a running APU.

Moves fuel from one main tank to another: tank 2 into tanks 1 and 3 in the normal schedule, or between tanks 1 and 3 to correct an imbalance. Plan so that no transfer or crossfeed out of tank 1 or 3 is needed below about 11,000 lb. Before transferring into a tank that is not full in the simulation, read [Simulation notes](#simulation-notes).

If the receiving tank's fill valve will not open, either feed its engine from the heavy tank through the crossfeed instead, or for tank 1 or 3 use its MANIFOLD DRAIN & OUTBD FILL switch, stopping about 3,000 lb short of full.

If a fill valve's light stays on after its switch is closed, treat the valve as open: do not open a crossfeed or turn on a transfer pump unless fuel going into that tank is acceptable. blocks.content: When the fuel is balanced:

Turning off the receiving engine's tank pumps is what makes the supplying tank carry the engine; leave them on and the receiving tank's own pumps go on feeding it. If the supplying tank's quantity falls while another tank's rises, fuel is going where it should not: close the crossfeed and transfer with the transfer pump instead.

If the FUEL TEMP gauge reaches −35 °C (with Jet A), the flight engineer circulates warm fuel through the wing tanks: the tank 1 and 3 transfer pumps ON, the tank 1 and 3 fill valves held OPEN until the temperature has risen 5 to 10 °C, then the fill valves closed and the transfer pumps off. If the temperature cannot be held and the flight will continue at that level for half an hour or more, descend to warmer air, or slow down: total air temperature, and with it the skin temperature, falls with Mach number.

The controller handles cold fuel itself (see [Cold fuel recirculation](#fsc-temperature-and-balance)). If FUEL TEMP LO appears, the fuel is within 3 °C of its freeze point: descend or reduce speed to raise the total air temperature.
The KC-10 is managed by hand, against a set of structural and CG rules rather than one fixed schedule:

items: Above 556,000 lb gross weight, or when the zero fuel weight plus the body tank fuel exceeds 414,000 lb, keep the main tanks full.
Never let tank 2 hold less than tank 1 or 3.
Empty the CTR WING tank's lower compartment into the upper one as early as possible.
Keep the balance fuel the CG needs in the FWD tank until tank 1 or 3 is down to about 5,000 lb.
Keep the CG within limits and the lateral imbalance within 4,000 lb (2,000 lb above 556,000 lb).

blocks.content: To feed the engines from the body tanks, open that tank's ISOL VALVE (the aircraft's loading states start with them closed), turn on its TRANS PUMP, and open the FILL VALVEs of the main tanks to receive. The CTR WING tank's upper pumps transfer the same way and do not need its isolation valve. To move CTR WING lower fuel up, run the LWR pumps with the UPR fill valve open. For an offload, the AR pumps are armed and draw from the body tanks; fuel can be transferred into the body tanks from any tank while offloading, through each body tank's FILL VALVE. With different fuel grades aboard, MASTER FUEL ISOL at ISOL and the AR ISOL valve closed keep them apart. See [Air Refueling](air-refueling) for the tanker procedures.

The fuel system is flown in AUTO. Before start the crew check the SYSTEM button shows neither SELECT nor MANUAL and the FUEL synoptic shows the fuel on schedule; the PUMPS buttons are in. From then on the controller feeds the engines and the APU, runs the auxiliary and tank 2 transfers, balances the wings, warms cold fuel and drains the manifold at the end of the flight, and the crew monitor it on the synoptic and the alerts. A partial fuel load needs no action: the controller joins its schedule wherever the fuel is. The crew act on the fuel system directly only to dump fuel, and in MANUAL when a reversion or a procedure calls for it.

In MANUAL the panel's buttons drive the system and the crew run the schedule themselves, exactly as a flight engineer would: TRANS and FILL buttons for transfers, XFEED and PUMPS buttons for crossfeed. Before selecting MANUAL, make sure the PUMPS buttons are in.

sections.title: Failures and non-normal operation
sections.summary: How fuel system failures show and what the crew do about them.

blocks.content: The fuel system is built so that no single failure stops fuel reaching an engine. Each tank has two or three boost pumps on different buses, each able to feed two engines; the wing engines can suction-feed; and any tank can feed any engine through the manifold. Most failures therefore cost redundancy rather than an engine, and the crew's job is to recognize which component has failed, rearrange the feed so every engine stays on a healthy supply, and account for any fuel that has become unusable. The procedures are in [Abnormal Procedures](abnormal-procedures) and, for fire and multiple failures, [Emergency Procedures](emergency-procedures).
Do not reset, or trip and reset, a fuel pump circuit breaker. A pump that has tripped its breaker may have an electrical fault inside a fuel tank.

blocks.title: Electrical failures and the fuel system
rows: Tank 1 FWD, tank 2 FWD and tank 3 transfer pumps; center tank upper R pump; KC-10 FWD body tank transfer pump; the quantity system's normal supply
Tank 3 AFT, tank 2 R AFT and tank 1 transfer pumps; center tank upper L and lower L pumps; the quantity system's alternate supply
Tank 1 AFT, tank 3 FWD and tank 2 transfer pumps; center tank lower R pump; KC-10 AFT body tank transfer pump
Crossfeed valve 1 control; left dump valve
Crossfeed valve 2 control; dump valve indication and low-level shutoff
Crossfeed valve 3 control; right dump valve
Every AC pump except tank 2 L AFT (if the air-driven generator powers the right emergency AC bus); wing engines on suction feed; auxiliary fuel unusable

blocks.content: A crossfeed valve whose control bus fails stays where it was. Losing any single AC bus leaves every main tank at least one boost pump; this is the reason for the spread of pumps across the buses.

**Modeled in depth.** The fuel system is a hydraulic network solved continuously: pumps produce pressure according to their speed and supply frequency, valves stroke in two to three seconds, check valves and floats act on the pressures and levels the solution finds, and fuel moves only where the pressures send it. Crossfeed, suction feed, a weakening pump on a sagging bus, a dump rate that falls as tanks empty and an engine starving when its supply cannot keep up all arise from that, not from scripts. Engines 1 and 3 can suction-feed and engine 2 and the APU cannot. Each tank is divided into its real compartments, with the flapper bulkheads, the outboard compartment held full by the bleed flow and released at 5,000 lb, and vent boxes that hold fuel and overflow overboard. Each compartment has its own temperature, warmed or cooled by the skin and by the fuel flowing into it. The gauges show the quantity system's indication, which can differ from the fuel actually in the tank when the gauging fails. Every pump is a real load on its circuit breaker and bus. The fuel aboard sets the simulator's weight and center of gravity once a second.

The KC-10's aerial refueling fuel system, with its hydraulic pumps, pressure control unit, isolation delay, receptacle and manifold scavenge, is modeled in the same way. Its aerial refueling lines hold fuel, which the manifold scavenge really recovers.
**Different from the aircraft.**

items: The main fill valves deliver into the inboard part of the main compartment of tanks 1 and 3 (and into the left half of tank 2); on the aircraft the fill enters tanks 1 and 3 through the outboard compartment. The outboard compartment is reached only through the MANIFOLD DRAIN & OUTBD FILL valve and the bleed flow. The two procedures that work through it therefore do not act as on the aircraft: circulating fuel for a low fuel temperature warms the tank 3 temperature probe little, if at all (if the FUEL TEMP does not rise, descend or slow down), and the premature-transfer procedure does not refill the outboard compartment.

Fuel sent into a main tank that is not full can be lost. A transfer refills only the part of the receiving tank its fill valve delivers into; once that part is full, the fuel the pumps go on sending disappears from the aircraft, while the FILL VALVE OPEN light stays on and the receiving tank's quantity stops rising. This applies to every transfer into a main tank that has burned down from full, including the keep-the-mains-full transfers (auxiliary or body tank into the mains, tank 2 into tanks 1 and 3) when they are started after the wing tanks have begun to burn down. Start those transfers while tanks 1 and 3 are still full, watch the receiving tank's quantity during any transfer, and close its fill valve as soon as the quantity stops rising. Compare the total fuel with the fuel used to catch a loss.
As a tank reaches full, its pilot float throttles the fill valve's flow rather than shutting it, so a fill valve's OPEN indication can stay on over a full tank.
The simulation adds a little heat from the hydraulic systems to the tank fuel; the aircraft's hydraulic systems shed their heat through their own lines and reservoirs instead.

The dump works only in flight. When a tank reaches its low-level float, its transfer pump stops and only its own crossfeed closes; the other crossfeeds stay open, and no X-FEED DISAGREE or PRESS LO light comes on for it. When all three main tanks have reached their floats, the dump valves close by themselves, even if the center tank still holds fuel, which can then no longer be dumped. Closing the DUMP switch reopens any crossfeed whose control is still at OPEN, so close the crossfeeds and turn the transfer pumps off after a dump as the procedure says. Losing DC bus 2 puts out the DUMP VALVE OPEN lights but does not disable the low-level shutoff.
Arming the refueling does not close open crossfeed valves. Refueling needs ground service power on the aircraft rather than the battery and inverter.
After an Instant fuel load the outboard compartments of tanks 1 and 3 can be part full; the bleed flow fills them slowly.
Suction feed is not limited by altitude.
The crossfeed manifold of the DC-10 and MD-10 holds no fuel, so draining it recovers nothing.

The FILL VALVE switches stay where they are set: there is no spring return and no solenoid hold, so the tank 2 transfer does not end by itself at 40,000 lb and the fill valves do not close when the auxiliary pumps are turned off. Close the switches and turn tank 2's transfer pump off yourself when the three tanks are even.
The dump switch does not close open fill valves: close them before dumping.
The FUEL SCHED lights respond only to the lamp test: the outboard compartment schedule monitor is not modeled, and the outboard transfer failure listed in the EFB's failure menu has no effect yet.

The FUEL QTY IND PWR and FUEL QTY CHAN SELECT switches are not modeled: the quantity system is powered while either AC bus 1 or AC bus 2 is. With any tank indication invalid, the total fuel and gross weight show invalid rather than a short sum.

The Virtual Crew's second officer starts the tank 2 transfer before takeoff when tank 2 holds more than 40,000 lb but does not end it when the three tanks are even: end it yourself. With a Target Cruise CG set, the second officer acts on it only once the CG has moved more than 1 percent MAC from the target.

With the PUMPS AUX TANKS selectors at ALL, the lower compartment pumps deliver into the transfer manifold directly instead of opening the upper compartment's fill valve and filling the upper compartment first. The center tank still empties into the main tanks; the AUX TANK FILL VALVE OPEN lights stay out during a transfer.

DC-10-15: the center-wing auxiliary tank is fitted and the EFB loads it, but the flight engineer's panel shows neither its quantity indicator nor its L and R PUMPS AUX TANKS selectors and their lights (on the -10 they appear only with Extended Range, which the -15 does not offer), so fuel in it can be neither seen in the cockpit nor transferred. Load the -15 with no more fuel than the three main tanks hold, 145,375 lb.
DC-10-30 Extended Range: the AFT TANK PUMP selectors' AUTO position runs the pumps as OVRD does, and the UPR TANK BYPASS and AFT TANK BALLAST FUEL switches are inoperative.
DC-10-40: the FUEL HEAT switches and the four-position FUEL TEMP selector are inoperative; the gauge always shows the tank 3 probe, and the ICING lights report the engine fuel filters.
TRANS PUMP OVRD does not arm the FWD tank's transfer pump below 15,000 lb; AR PUMP OVRD releases it instead. To move the FWD tank's balance fuel into the main tanks, select AR PUMP OVRD.
Selecting TRANS PUMP OVRD, the dump, the boom or the drogue does not close open crossfeed valves, as it does on the aircraft below the dump shutoff level.
The FWD TANK FUEL SCHED light responds only to the lamp test. Reverse refueling and the forward tank slosh oscillation are not modeled.

The panel's AUX TANKS L and R TRANS buttons, the MANF DRAIN switch and the FUEL USED RESET switch are not functional, so in MANUAL the auxiliary fuel cannot be transferred and the manifold drain is left to the float valve. The MANF STOP switchlight acts as the fuel dump emergency stop.

Selecting MANUAL hands every pump and valve to its button at once, without the aircraft's standard manual configuration; in MANUAL the dump runs only the pumps and crossfeeds whose buttons are in. The MANUAL legend does not flash when a button is pressed in AUTO.
The controller does not switch off a failed pump (no PMP OFF messages), its lateral balance thresholds are approximate, and it assumes Jet A (freeze point −40 °C).

The FMS ballast entry is shown on the synoptic, but the controller does not hold the ballast fuel back from the schedule, and the FMS dump-to-gross-weight value does not stop a dump: the floats or the crew do.
The synoptic's gross weight and CG lines and its TIP messages are not shown.

blocks.content: **Settings and failures.** Fuel is loaded from the EFB's Ground Ops Fuel page (see [Fueling from the EFB](#fueling-from-the-efb)). The EFB's Failures app offers, under Fuel: a boost pump pressure low (each of the seven pumps), a transfer pump inoperative (each tank), a center tank upper pump and a lower pump (the left ones), fuel filter clogging (each engine), the main tank fill valves failing closed (all three, or tank 1 or 3), all quantity indicators inoperative, and tank overfilled (tank 1's fill float failed). Electrical failures in the same app take away the pumps on the failed buses.
The KC-10 adds the FWD tank's isolation valve and alternate transfer valve failing closed.

On the DC-10 the EFB's Configuration app (Aircraft Configuration) chooses the **Fuel Gauges** (Analog or Digital) and the **Range Options** (Normal or Extended Range, which fits the center-wing auxiliary tank on the -10 and the aft auxiliary tank on the -30). Extended Range can be changed at any time except during a refuel or a dump; fuel in a tank that is removed is lost with it. The Virtual Crew's second officer can hold a cruise CG target (see [Cruise CG target](#cruise-cg-target)).

parts.title: Electrical
parts.summary: AC generation and distribution, paralleling, the DC system, and standby and emergency power.

blocks.content: The electrical power system generates, converts, distributes and protects all of the aircraft's electrical power. Its primary product is three-phase 115/200 V AC at 400 Hz from three engine-driven generators. Direct current at a nominal 28 V is derived from that AC by four transformer-rectifier units (TRs). On the ground the same network can be supplied by an APU-driven generator or by a ground power cart through the main external power receptacle, and the APU generator can also supplement the engine generators in flight. When every normal source has failed, a nickel-cadmium battery, a static inverter and a ram-air-driven generator (ADG) keep the essential instruments, radios and controls alive.

The architecture is three identical channels, one per engine. In each channel the engine's accessory gearbox drives a **constant speed drive (CSD)**, the CSD drives the generator at a fixed 8,000 rpm, and the generator feeds its own **generator bus** through a **generator relay (GR)**. Each generator bus supplies its main AC bus, its transformer-rectifier and the heavy, centrally located loads such as the fuel boost pumps. The three generator buses can be joined through their **bus tie relays (BTR)** to a common **AC tie bus**, so that any operating generator can carry a bus whose own generator has failed, or all three can run in parallel and share the load. External power enters at the tie bus; the APU generator reaches each generator bus through its own **auxiliary power relay (APR)** and never touches the tie.

The DC side mirrors the AC side. TR 1, TR 2A and TR 3 supply DC buses 1, 2 and 3, TR 2B supplies the DC ground service bus, and a four-segment **DC tie bus** lets the crew connect a dead DC bus to a working TR. Two pairs of emergency buses carry the flight-essential loads: the left emergency AC and DC buses serve the Captain's side and are normally fed from channel 1, with the battery and static inverter as their standby source; the right emergency AC and DC buses serve the First Officer's side and are normally fed from channel 3, with the ADG as their standby source.

Protection is automatic on every aircraft: each generator has a **generator control unit (GCU)** that regulates its voltage, trims its drive for load sharing and synchronizing, and trips it off line within milliseconds to seconds of a fault. What differs is who runs the rest. On the DC-10 and KC-10 the flight engineer configures the system from the electrical section of upper panel No. 1, with a bus control unit handling the preferential and paralleling logic. On the MD-10 the flight engineer's panel is gone: an **electrical power control unit (EPCU)** works with the GCUs to manage sources, paralleling and transfers by itself, the crew's panel on the forward overhead normally stays in AUTO, and the state of the system is drawn on the ELEC synoptic page.

blocks.alt: Block diagram of the whole electrical power system, common to all three models. Left to right: three engines, each with CSD and generator, feeding GEN BUS 1, 2 and 3 through GR 1-3; each generator bus joined to a horizontal AC TIE BUS by BTR 1-3; external power entering the tie bus through EPR and BTR-EP; the APU generator feeding each generator bus through APR 1-3. Below: AC BUS 1-3 hanging off the generator buses; L EMER AC off GEN BUS 1 with the static inverter as alternate; R EMER AC off GEN BUS 3 with the ADG as alternate; AC GND SVC off GEN BUS 2 (AGSTR) or external power (GSR). Bottom row: TR 1, TR 2A, TR 2B, TR 3 feeding DC BUS 1, DC BUS 2, DC GND SVC and R EMER DC / DC BUS 3, the four-segment DC tie bus with DC TIE 1, DC X TIE and DC TIE 3, the battery bus, battery direct bus and battery. blocks.content: **Three channels, any one sufficient.** Each generator is sized to carry every essential load on the aircraft, so the system is designed around losing generators one at a time. A generator that fails takes nothing with it but its own output: its generator bus is picked up through the tie bus by whichever generator is supplying it, and the loads on that bus never know. With only one engine generator left, all three generator buses are carried by that one machine through the tie.

**Paralleled, unparalleled or isolated.** Running the generators in parallel gives one stiff bus whose frequency and voltage are held by three machines at once, shares the load evenly, and means that the loss of one machine causes no interruption at all, because the other two are already connected. The price is coupling: a machine with a runaway governor or a collapsed field tries to drag its partners with it. The protection is therefore arranged in stages. The faults that only matter when machines are paralleled (load unbalance, over- and under-excitation, the first stage of over-frequency) open the **bus tie relay** first, separating the sick channel from the healthy ones while it keeps its own bus; only if the fault persists does the GCU open the generator relay and the field, and the tie then rescues the bus. The bus tie relays are, in effect, the fuses of the parallel system. Unparalleled operation (one generator on the tie, the others each on their own bus) and fully isolated operation (all bus tie relays open) trade that stiffness for independence, and are the configurations the crew falls back to when the parallel system misbehaves.

**DC isolation versus DC paralleling.** On the DC-10 and KC-10 the DC buses are electrically isolated in normal operation: each has its own TR, and the tie bus is a recovery path the flight engineer closes only to restore a dead bus. A short on one DC bus cannot pull down another, and the battery bus is fed from two TRs through diodes, so neither TR can back-feed the other. The MD-10's EPCU keeps the four DC tie contactors closed instead, so the four TRs share the DC load and every DC load stays powered without a break through starts, source transfers and shutdown, the design choice of an aircraft without a flight engineer to manage transfers by hand.

**Left and right segregation.** The Captain's essential instruments are on the left emergency buses, the First Officer's on the right. Each side has a different normal source (channel 1 or channel 3) and a different kind of standby source: the battery and inverter on the left, finite but available instantly and at any airspeed, and the ADG on the right, unlimited while the aircraft is flying fast enough but taking seconds to deploy. No single failure removes both sets of instruments.

**Ground service without powering the aircraft.** The AC ground service bus and its DC counterpart carry what the ground crew needs (cargo and cabin doors, cargo loading, service lighting, the battery charger, the auxiliary hydraulic pumps) and can be powered from external power alone, without energizing the main distribution. In flight the AC ground service bus rides generator bus 2.

sections.title: AC generation
sections.summary: Constant speed drives, the generators, voltage regulation and protection, the APU generator and external power.

blocks.content: Four machines can generate AC on board: the three engine generators and the APU generator. All four are the same brushless three-phase machine, rated 90 kVA at 115/200 V and 400 Hz. The engine generators are driven through constant speed drives, because engine speed varies; the APU runs at a governed speed of its own, so its generator needs no CSD. Each machine has its own GCU. A fifth source, external power, is accepted at the main receptacle only after a monitor has proved its quality.

A generator's frequency is set by its shaft speed and its number of poles: f = poles × rpm / 120. The aircraft's generators are six-pole machines, so 8,000 rpm gives exactly 400 Hz. Hold the speed and the frequency holds; let the engine drag the speed around and the frequency follows it.

Aircraft use 400 Hz rather than the 50 or 60 Hz of a ground grid because the size of every magnetic component falls with frequency. A transformer's induced voltage is proportional to frequency × turns × core area × flux density, so at 400 Hz the same transformer needs about one-seventh of the core of a 60 Hz unit, and motors, TRs and generators shrink in proportion. The cost is reactance: a conductor's inductive reactance rises with frequency, so long 400 Hz feeders drop more voltage. The design answer is visible in the bus layout: heavy loads are grouped close to the generator buses in the center of the aircraft, and lighter, distributed loads are fed through the main AC buses and the emergency buses.

Constant frequency is not optional. Paralleled generators must run at exactly the same frequency; synchronous and induction motors, gyros, synchros, clocks and the TRs' output voltage all depend on it. That is the CSD's whole job.

Each engine generator is driven by a **constant speed drive** mounted beside it on the engine's accessory gearbox, which turns at a fixed ratio to the high-pressure spool (N2). Between ground idle and take-off thrust N2 changes by nearly half, yet the generator must turn at 8,000 rpm throughout. The CSD is a hydromechanical transmission that adds or subtracts speed as required: a differential gear train combines the engine's input with the output of a small variable-displacement hydraulic unit, and a governor sensing output speed positions that unit. When the engine is slow, the hydraulic unit adds speed (overdrive); when it is fast, it subtracts speed (underdrive); near the straight-through point it hardly works at all and losses are least. The GCU can trim the governor's setpoint by a few hertz either way, which is how load is shared and generators are synchronized (see [Paralleling](#paralleling)).

The CSD has its own oil system, about 8.5 US quarts with charge and scavenge pumps, which lubricates the gears, works the hydraulic unit and carries away the heat the drive makes. That heat (gear and bearing friction, churning, and a few percent of all the power passing through) is rejected in an air-oil heat exchanger on the engine's fan case, cooled by fan air.

Below the governed range the drive cannot hold speed: output speed, and with it frequency, simply follow the engine down. An **underspeed switch**, worked by governor oil pressure, opens the generator relay within 150 ms once output speed falls below about 96 % of governed speed, and at the same time inhibits the GCU's under-frequency and under-voltage protection, so a normal engine shutdown never latches a protective lockout. The underspeed hold-off resets itself: when the engine comes back up (after a relight, for example), the generator returns to its bus with no crew action. During a normal start the generator comes on line by itself as the drive reaches governed speed, a little below ground idle, and the GEN OFF light goes out with the GEN switch already at ON.

rows: From just below ground idle N2 to maximum

children.title: Reading the CSD temperatures: outlet and rise

blocks.content: Two temperatures tell two different stories, and the dual-scale CSD TEMP gauge shows both. The **outlet temperature** (outer scale) is the oil leaving the drive. Its level is set by the cooler: how warm the fan air is and how well the heat exchanger is passing heat to it. The **rise** (inner scale, shown while PUSH FOR RISE is held) is outlet minus inlet, the temperature gained by the oil in one pass through the drive. It is the heat the drive is making divided by the heat capacity of the oil flow through it, so it depends on the drive itself and on its electrical load, and hardly at all on altitude, airspeed or the cooler. A healthy, normally loaded drive shows a rise of about 20-25 °C.

blocks.title: What outlet and rise together mean
rows: Heat is not being removed: a blocked or degraded oil cooler, or very hot fan air. The drive itself is making normal heat.
The drive is making abnormal heat (internal friction, slipping, a failing bearing), or the oil flow through it has fallen, as it does when the drive is losing oil.
Rising, with frequency or load oscillating
Governor or mechanical failure in progress: the drive should be disconnected

blocks.content: A high reading with the generator unloaded points at the drive; a high reading that falls when the generator is switched OFF points at the load. That is why the abnormal checklists begin by switching the generator off and then watching the rise.

A drive that is overheating, losing oil or failing mechanically can be disconnected from the engine with the guarded **CSD disconnect** button (DC-10 and KC-10: CSD PRESS TO DISC on the flight engineer's panel; MD-10: the DRIVE button on the ELEC panel). Holding the button energizes a solenoid that releases a pawl into the drive's input coupling; the coupling's own rotation then separates it, and the drive and generator spin down. The GCU opens the generator field within 60 ms of the disconnect. A successful disconnect shows as CSD OIL PRESS LO (DC-10, KC-10) or DRIVE DISC (MD-10), GEN OFF, a falling outlet temperature and a dead generator on the meter.

Do not disconnect a CSD with the engine below idle or stopped. The disconnect mechanism relies on the input shaft turning; actuated below idle it damages the coupling's teeth and the input seal. A disconnected drive cannot be reconnected in flight, or on the ground with the engine running.

The disconnect is the one irreversible action on the electrical panel, so the button must be held: a brush past the guard does nothing. The checklists call for holding it for 3 seconds. Reconnection is a maintenance action on the ground with the engine stopped.

The GCU watches each drive and latches a **drive fault** if any of four conditions is met. On the MD-10 the fault lights the DRIVE FAULT legend and raises GEN DRIVE n FAULT, telling the crew that the drive should be disconnected. On the DC-10 and KC-10 the crew reads the same conditions directly from the CSD OIL PRESS LO light and the CSD temperature gauge.

blocks.title: Drive fault conditions
rows: Oil temperature rise of 89 °F (49 °C) or more, with generator current at or below 348 A per phase, for 300 seconds
A drive making far more heat than its load explains: slipping or internal friction
Charge pressure falling to about 13 psi with the drive at speed
Charge pump failure or oil loss
Metal in the oil: internal wear

blocks.content: Each generator is a **brushless** machine: three generators on one shaft, with no sliding contacts to wear at 8,000 rpm. A small **permanent magnet generator (PMG)** produces power as soon as the shaft turns; it supplies the GCU and the exciter field, so the channel needs no outside power to come alive. The **exciter** has a stationary field and a rotating armature; its AC output is rectified by diodes mounted on the rotor and fed straight into the rotating field of the **main generator**, whose stationary three-phase armature delivers the output. The GCU controls output voltage by controlling the small exciter field current, which is amplified twice before it reaches the main field.

Two relays switch each channel. The **generator control relay (GCR)** is the field switch: opening it de-excites the machine, which is how the GCU kills a faulty generator. The **generator relay (GR)** is the line contactor that connects the generator's output to its generator bus. A generator can therefore be excited but not on line (GCR closed, GR open), which is how the flight engineer checks a machine on the meter before putting it on its bus.

blocks.title: Generator data
rows: Up to 1.0 continuously; 1.0 to 1.5 for 5 minutes; above 1.5 for 5 seconds only
Allow about 5 hours of operation after a main bearing fails

blocks.content: A generator's main bearings are monitored. If a bearing starts to fail, the generator's **GEN FAIL** light comes on (DC-10, KC-10) while the machine keeps running on its auxiliary bearings; it does not trip itself off. The GEN FAIL RESET button tests whether the signal was spurious: a real failure lights the lamp again on the next turn of the shaft. A confirmed bearing failure is dealt with by disconnecting the drive before the auxiliary bearings wear out.

children.title: Voltage regulation, the GCUs and protection

blocks.content: There is one GCU per engine generator and one for the APU generator. Each GCU regulates its generator's voltage, trims its drive for load sharing and synchronizing, decides when its relays may close, protects its channel, and drives that channel's lights. On the DC-10 and KC-10 a **bus control unit** adds the system-wide logic (external power, the preferential circuit, automatic paralleling); on the MD-10 the **EPCU** does that and more.

**Voltage regulation.** The GCU's regulator compares the line voltage with 115 V and adjusts the exciter field to hold it. The exciter field takes a fraction of a second to respond, which smooths the regulation and is part of what keeps paralleled machines stable. Under paralleled operation the regulators also share the reactive load (see [Paralleling](#paralleling)).

**Protection.** Each GCU runs a ladder of protective functions, each with its own pickup and time delay. The delays are graded so that the right relay opens first: faults that concern only paralleled operation open the bus tie relay; faults in the generator or its feeder open the generator relay and kill the field. Most trips latch (a **lockout**) until reset; two are self-resetting hold-offs. A bus tie relay locked out by a generator fault is released by itself once the generator relay has locked that generator out, so the tie can rescue the bus; a bus feeder fault (differential zone 2) never hands over, because the fault is on the bus itself.

blocks.title: GCU protection

Inverse time: faster the higher the voltage

blocks.content: Under-frequency and under-voltage protection are inhibited while the underspeed switch is actuated, so an engine running down never leaves a lockout behind it.

blocks.title: Lockouts and how they are cleared
