blocks.content: Reset a tripped generator once only. A trip that returns after one reset means a real fault; repeated resets drive the contactors onto it.

The APU generator is mechanically and electrically the same machine as the engine generators. It has no CSD: the APU's own governor holds its gearbox, and therefore the generator, at the speed that gives 400 Hz. It has its own GCU with the same voltage regulation and protection. It is rated 90 kVA in flight; on the ground the simulation allows it to carry up to about 110 kVA. How the APU itself is started and operated, and its in-flight envelope (the APU may shut down if heavily loaded at altitude), are in [APU](apu).

The APU generator connects to the three generator buses through three **auxiliary power relays (APR 1, 2, 3)**, one per bus, and to nothing else: it is never connected to the AC tie bus, and it is never paralleled with an engine generator or with external power. Its rules are simple. An APR closes onto a generator bus that is not being supplied by its own engine generator, and the APU outranks the tie bus: a bus being carried through the tie gives that connection up when the APU is selected onto it (a brief break while the bus tie relay opens and the APR closes). When an engine generator comes on speed, it displaces the APU from its own bus, and only that bus. While the APU supplies a generator bus, that bus's bus tie relay is held open, so APU power cannot reach the tie.

On the DC-10 and KC-10 the flight engineer selects the APU onto each bus separately with the three **APU GEN BUS** switches, and the APU generator's field is permanently enabled unless the KC-10's APU GEN RESET switch is held. On the MD-10 one **APU PWR** button arms all three APRs together.

On the MD-10 the transfer between the APU and an engine generator is a **no-break power transfer (NBPT)**: the GCUs and the EPCU bring the incoming source into phase with the outgoing one, close the incoming relay while the two are momentarily paralleled, and open the outgoing relay immediately afterwards, so the bus never loses power. Transfers between the APU and external power are break transfers; the battery-backed DC system rides through them.

Ground power arrives through the **main external power receptacle** aft of the nose wheel well. The receptacle's own copper, the external power bus, is live whenever a running cart is plugged in, and carries a few service items such as the receptacle relays and the service light. Before any of that power is allowed further, an **external power monitor** checks that its voltage is between about 104 and 122 V, its frequency between about 393 and 407 Hz and its phase rotation correct (reversed rotation would drive every three-phase motor backwards), and proves it for about a second. Only then does EXT PWR AVAIL light.
External power then has two separate paths:

items: **To the AC tie bus**, through the **external power relay (EPR)** and the **bus tie relay - external power (BTR-EP)** in series, when EXT PWR is selected and the battery switch is ON. From the tie it reaches every generator bus whose bus tie relay is allowed to close. BTR-EP waits until the tie bus is free of engine generators: external power is never paralleled with a generator.

**To the AC ground service bus**, through the **ground service relay (GSR)**. This path does not need the battery switch, so a cart with the battery off powers the ground service bus, and through TR 2B the DC ground service bus and the battery bus, and nothing else. When external power is not on it, the AC ground service bus is supplied from generator bus 2 through the **AC ground service tie relay (AGSTR)**, which is interlocked with the GSR so that the cart is never paralleled with generator 2.

blocks.content: The ground power unit is simulated as a machine, not as an ideal source. When the ground crew connect it, its diesel cranks for a couple of seconds, runs up to governed speed, closes its output breaker and builds voltage, so EXT PWR AVAIL comes on roughly eight seconds after the plug goes in. The cart is a 90 kVA unit; it has an output breaker that trips on sustained overload, a cable that drops a little voltage under load, and a fuel tank. Ground power is called from the EFB's Ground Ops page, with the simulator's own request-ground-power command, or through GSX if you use it (see [Ground operations](ground-operations)).
The DC-10 also has a **galley external power receptacle** beside the main one, which can supply the galley buses alone (see [Galley power](#galley-power)). The main cart can supply galley bus 1 only.

sections.title: Paralleling, synchronization and load sharing
sections.summary: How three generators share one bus, how a generator is brought into phase before it connects, and the logic that decides which bus tie relays close.

blocks.content: Every source on the aircraft follows the same priority rules, whoever is running the system. A generator bus takes its power from its own engine generator first, from the APU generator second, and from the AC tie bus last. The AC tie bus takes external power first and an engine generator second, and never both at once. Within those rules, the bus tie relays decide whether the three engine generators run separately or as one paralleled system.

blocks.title: Source priority
rows: APU generator; external power together with a generator

blocks.content: Once paralleled, the three generators feed one bus with one frequency and one voltage. How the load divides between them is then a question of control, not of wiring, and real power (kW) and reactive power (kvar) are divided by two separate mechanisms.

**Real power is shared through the drives.** Each CSD governor has a slightly drooping characteristic: the more power its generator delivers, the slightly lower the speed it holds. On a common bus every machine must run at the same frequency, so the system settles where the three droop lines cross the total load. Identical machines with identical settings share equally; raise one drive's speed setting a fraction and it takes a larger share of the kilowatts. The GCUs' load-division circuits compare each machine's share with the others' and trim the governors until the shares match, so the three AC LOAD needles stand together.

**Reactive power is shared through the excitation.** On a common bus every machine must also hold the same voltage. A machine whose field is stronger than its partners' pushes reactive current into them: its own kvar rises, theirs fall, and current circulates between the generators without doing any work for the loads. The voltage regulators' reactive-division circuits trim each field so the reactive load divides evenly.

This is also why the excitation faults need care. A machine that loses its field does not simply stop contributing; it becomes a reactive load on its partners, absorbing magnetizing current from them and pulling the common bus voltage down. A machine whose regulator runs away does the opposite, forcing reactive current into its partners and pushing the bus voltage up. In either case the partners see an abnormal reactive share too, so a reactive measurement alone cannot tell which machine is at fault. The GCUs therefore look at the bus voltage as well: under-excitation protection acts only with the bus low, over-excitation protection only with it high, and only the faulty machine's bus tie relay opens.

The loadmeters are the crew's best paralleling indication. Paralleled, the three AC LOAD needles agree; unparalleled, each shows only its own channel's load and they usually differ, and a generator that is also carrying another bus through the tie reads correspondingly higher.

Two live AC sources may only be connected when their voltages, frequencies and phase angles all match closely. Closing a contactor between two sources whose waveforms are out of step connects two voltage sources through almost no impedance: the voltage across the open contacts is 2 × V × sin(δ/2), where δ is the phase difference, and the current that flows at closure is that voltage divided by the machines' small internal reactance. At 15° the difference is about 30 V on a 115 V system, a manageable surge that pulls the incoming machine into step; at 180° it would be 230 V, twice the system voltage, with a current surge and a torque shock to the drive large enough to damage it.

A bus tie relay or generator relay joining two live islands may therefore close only when the frequencies are within **3 Hz** and the phase difference is within **15°** and closing. Closing onto a dead bus needs no synchronizing. When several live buses are waiting to close onto a dead tie, only one goes first; the others then see a live tie and must synchronize to it. Without that rule the first instant would join unsynchronized generators in one stroke.

The **synchronizer** in each GCU brings the incoming generator into step by trimming its drive's governor. It works on phase, not just frequency. Matching the frequencies exactly would freeze the phase difference wherever it happened to be, perhaps well outside the 15° window, and the relay would never close. The synchronizer instead pulls the incoming machine toward the tie in proportion to the phase difference, and then integrates that difference so that it holds the phase at zero even while its own load tries to drag it away. Once phase and frequency sit inside the window the relay closes, typically within about three seconds of the bus tie relay being armed.

children.title: Bus tie logic: DC-10 and KC-10

blocks.content: The engine generators can be run in three ways, and which one is the flight engineer's choice.

items: **Unparalleled** is the resting state on generator power. Each generator supplies its own generator bus, and exactly one of them also supplies the AC tie bus. The **preferential circuit** picks that generator in the order 2, 1, 3: the first operative generator in that order connects to the tie. Any generator bus that loses its own source is picked up from the tie automatically.

**Paralleled** operation is armed by pressing **PARALLEL GENS**, with all three AC BUS TIE switches at NORM. As each generator meets the synchronizing conditions, its bus tie relay closes, until all three generators share the tie bus. Paralleling is not self-sustaining: any event that opens a bus tie relay disarms it, and the system drops back to unparalleled operation until the button is pressed again.

**Isolated** operation is selected channel by channel with the AC BUS TIE switch at ISOL. The bus tie relay is held open, the preferential circuit ignores that channel, and its generator bus can neither feed the tie nor be rescued from it.

blocks.content: **The sitting donor keeps the tie.** The preferential order chooses a donor only when the tie has none; it does not take the tie away from a generator already carrying it. So an aircraft whose generators came on line one at a time ends up with whichever generator reached the tie first as the donor, not necessarily generator 2. Cycling AC BUS TIE switches 1 and 3 to ISOL and back to NORM makes generator 2 the donor.

blocks.title: Example: the preferential circuit with generators switched off and on (all AC BUS TIE switches NORM)
rows: Only one left; it carries all three buses

The tie needs a new donor: first in the order

blocks.content: **Returning to its own generator.** A bus being carried from the tie gives the tie up as soon as its own generator is ready: the bus tie relay opens, the bus is dead for an instant, and the generator relay closes onto the dead bus. Unparalleled operation never needs a synchronized closure for this.

blocks.content: In the simulation the AC BUS TIE ISOL light annunciates a channel that has been taken off the tie (switch at ISOL, APU on the bus, relay locked out, or relay failed to close), not a bus tie relay that is merely open. In normal unparalleled operation, with the switches at NORM, two relays are open by design and all three ISOL lights are out. Read paralleling from the loadmeters.

On the MD-10 the EPCU and the GCUs manage the sources themselves. With the ELEC panel in AUTO the crew's GEN, AC TIE and DC TIE buttons sit un-pressed and are not read at all: the EPCU treats every relay as armed and lets the source priorities decide what closes.

items: **The engine generators parallel automatically.** Whenever two or more engine generators are on line and external power is neither on the tie nor selected for it, each bus tie relay closes as its generator synchronizes with the tie. There is no PARALLEL GENS button and nothing to re-arm.

**External power stands paralleling down.** The tie bus prefers external power, and external power is never paralleled with a generator. With EXT PWR selected, the bus tie relays of the generator-fed buses open, and the cart takes the tie once it is free of generators. Deselecting external power lets the EPCU parallel the generators again within seconds, one bus at a time.
**The APU keeps its buses to itself.** An APU-fed generator bus stays off the tie, so with the APU alone on the buses the AC TIE ARM legends are lit.
**Transfers between the APU and an engine generator are no-break**, made by momentarily paralleling the two sources inside the synchronizing window before the outgoing relay opens.

**In MANUAL** each AC TIE button commands its bus tie relay: at ARM the GCU still closes the relay automatically, at OFF it is held open. The GEN and DC TIE buttons likewise command their relays directly.

blocks.content: The real MD-10 also splits the buses automatically for a dual-channel autoland. That split is not simulated: the generators stay paralleled through an autoland.

sections.title: AC distribution
sections.summary: Generator buses, main AC buses, the tie bus, the emergency and ground service buses, and the galley and ARO buses.

blocks.content: AC power is distributed in two layers. The three **generator buses** carry the heavy, centrally located loads and feed everything else: their main AC bus, their TR, and (for buses 1 and 3) an emergency AC bus. Each **main AC bus** hangs off its generator bus through its own feed circuit breakers and carries the lighter, more widely distributed loads. The two are different copper: a generator bus failure takes its main AC bus with it, but a main AC bus can be lost on its own (a tripped feed) while its generator bus, and everything else on it, stays up.

blocks.alt: One-line schematic of the AC system as simulated, common to all three models with fit notes. Middle: AC BUS 1-3 below their generator buses through feed breakers; L EMER AC off GEN BUS 1 through the L EMER AC feed, with the static inverter on the LECR contact; R EMER AC off GEN BUS 3 through the RETR, with the ADG bus (ABCR from the ADG) on the RETR's other pole; AC GND SVC fed by AGSTR from GEN BUS 2 or GSR from external power; cabin ground service buses (DC-10, KC-10); ARO AC bus off GEN BUS 3 (KC-10); galley buses 1-3/4 off their generator buses through GLCU and GTR, with the galley receptacle (DC-10). Bottom: the TR inputs (TR 1 from GEN BUS 1, TR 2A from GEN BUS 2, TR 2B from AC GND SVC, TR 3 from R EMER AC) and the 28 V AC transformer buses. Relays drawn in their normal in-flight positions; legend for contactor symbols.

blocks.content: **The emergency AC buses** are where the system's redundancy is concentrated. The left bus is fed from generator bus 1 through a feed contactor that opens when emergency power is selected; the static inverter then carries it from the battery. The right bus is fed from generator bus 3 through the **right emergency transfer relay (RETR)**, whose other pole is the ADG bus: when the ADG is released and selected to R EMER ELEC, the RETR moves the bus onto the turbine. Because TR 3 takes its input from the right emergency AC bus, the ADG keeps the right emergency DC bus alive too (see [Standby and emergency power](#standby-power)).

**The AC ground service bus** is normally carried from generator bus 2 by the AGSTR, which opens whenever generator bus 2 is dead, and is taken over by external power through the GSR whenever good external power is selected. Because the battery charger, TR 2B and both auxiliary hydraulic pumps live here, a generator bus 2 failure in flight costs battery charging, the DC ground service bus and the auxiliary pumps' normal supply as well as everything on AC bus 2.

The DC-10's galleys have buses of their own: four **galley buses** on the -10 and -15, three on the -30 and -40, each switched from the flight engineer's panel. Galley bus n is fed from generator bus n (the -10's fourth bus from generator bus 1) through a **galley load control unit (GLCU)** contactor and the GEN pole of a **galley transfer relay (GTR)**. With GLY EXT PWR selected and a galley cart connected to the galley receptacle, the transfer relay moves the bus onto that cart instead, which lets the galleys be stocked and run on the ground without loading the aircraft's sources.

Each bus's control circuit (the GLCU and transfer relay coils, and a latching control relay) runs on DC bus n. Galley power therefore needs both AC and DC: a galley cart plugged into an aircraft with only its battery on lights GALLEY EXT PWR AVAIL and powers nothing.
Galley loads are large and can be shed without affecting the flight, so they are the first loads the system gives up:

blocks.title: Galley bus protection
rows: Any generator supplying a galley bus runs above its rating for a few seconds
The GALLEY BUS switch's RESET position, once the overload has gone
One galley bus above its 30 kVA rating for a few seconds

RESET, once the fault has cleared

blocks.content: The simulated GALLEY BUS switches have no RESET position, so a tripped galley bus stays off for the rest of the session (see [Simulation notes](#simulation-notes)). A trip opens the generator side only; a bus already on the galley cart stays up. Main external power, arriving through the tie bus, can supply galley bus 1 only; the others are inhibited while their generator bus is on the cart's tie, and are released as soon as an engine generator or the APU takes their generator bus.

The KC-10's aerial refueling operator station has its own AC and DC buses. The **ARO AC bus** is fed from generator bus 3. The **ARO DC bus** is normally fed from the TR 3 side (DC bus 3); in flight, if that side fails, the **ARO DC bus transfer relay** moves it automatically to the TR 1 side (DC bus 1). The ARO also has its own ground service sub-buses off the AC and DC ground service buses.

Three guarded switches at the boom operator's station work these buses: **AR BUS ISOL** locks out both ARO buses, **GND SVC BUS ISOL** locks out the ARO's ground service sub-buses, and **AR DC BUS ALTN PWR GND TEST**, held on the ground, tests the transfer to the TR 1 side (all DC-powered lights at the station blink as it changes over). Details are in [Air refueling systems](air-refueling-systems).

sections.title: DC system
sections.summary: Transformer-rectifiers, the DC buses and tie bus, the battery bus, the battery and its charger.

blocks.content: Four **transformer-rectifier units (TRs)** are the normal source of 28 V DC. Each is fed from a different AC bus, so the loss of any one AC source costs at most one TR:

blocks.title: TR inputs and outputs
rows: DC BUS 2, battery bus (L TIE feed)
DC GND SVC, battery bus (R TIE feed)
R EMER DC, and DC BUS 3 and the DC cabin bus through the REIR

Below: the DC tie bus drawn as four segments, segment 1 (TR 1) joined to segment 2 (TR 2A) by DC TIE 1, segment 2 to segment 3 (TR 2B) by DC X TIE, segment 3 to segment 4 by DC TIE 3. DC BUS 1 and the L EMER DC normal feed off segment 1; DC BUS 2 off segment 2; DC GND SVC off segment 3 (NORM) or segment 2 (ALTN) through the DC ground service transfer relay; segment 4 joined to R EMER DC through the REIR, with DC BUS 3 and the DC cabin bus off it; TR 3 output on R EMER DC. Diodes from segments 2 and 3 to the BATTERY BUS (L TIE and R TIE feeds, breakers OH A-14 and A-15); the battery through the CBR (OH A-13) to the battery bus and to the charger; the BATTERY DIRECT BUS hot from the battery; the LECR from battery direct to L EMER DC; the static inverter off the battery. KC-10 inset: ARO DC bus with the ADBTR selecting DC BUS 3 or DC BUS 1 side. Ties drawn OPEN as on the DC-10/KC-10 in normal flight, with a note that the MD-10 keeps them closed.
blocks.title: DC system schematic

blocks.content: Each TR is a three-phase step-down transformer followed by a six-pulse rectifier bridge. Rectifying three-phase 400 Hz power gives DC with a ripple at 2,400 Hz and of small amplitude, which is easy to smooth. The TRs are **unregulated**: their output voltage is simply the transformer ratio times the input voltage, less the drops in the windings and diodes, so it sags as load increases, from about 29.5 V unloaded to about 27 V at the rated 75 A. That droop is not a defect. When TRs are paralleled through the DC tie bus, the one carrying more current sags further, so the load spreads itself across them without any control circuit. A blocking rectifier at each TR's output stops a working TR from back-feeding a dead one.

blocks.title: TR data
rows: About 29.5 V unloaded to about 27 V at rated load

A TR drops out when its AC input fails

blocks.content: A healthy aircraft typically shows about a third of rating on each DC LOAD meter. Closing a DC tie to recover a dead bus puts that bus's load on another TR as well, so watch its loadmeter after any tie is closed.

blocks.content: The **DC tie bus** is four segments joined by three contactors: **DC TIE 1** between segments 1 and 2, the **DC X TIE** between segments 2 and 3, and **DC TIE 3** between segments 3 and 4. Each TR lands on its own segment and each main DC bus hangs off one, so closing a tie connects a dead bus to a working TR on the next segment.

On the DC-10 and KC-10 the three tie switches are normally at **OPEN**, so the DC channels run isolated, each on its own TR, with the battery bus fed from both TR 2A and TR 2B through its diodes. The flight engineer closes a tie only to restore a bus whose TR has failed. A DC TIE CLOSED light that is on with its switch at OPEN means the system is running paralleled where it should not; it changes no procedure but should be written up.

On the MD-10 the EPCU keeps all the DC tie contactors closed in AUTO, so the four TRs run in parallel and share the DC load, and any DC load can be supplied by any TR. The DC X TIE has no button; DC TIE 1 and DC TIE 3 can be opened with their buttons in MANUAL, and the SMOKE ELEC/AIR selector opens the DC X TIE in any position other than NORM.

**Why the right side is built the way it is.** TR 3 is fed from the right emergency AC bus and lands on the right emergency DC bus, and DC bus 3 is supplied from there through the **right emergency isolation relay (REIR)**. Normally the REIR is closed and TR 3 carries both. When the ADG takes over the right emergency AC bus, the REIR opens, so the turbine's limited output carries only the right emergency DC bus and is not drained by DC bus 3 and the cabin. The same arrangement explains a familiar failure: losing TR 3, or its AC input, puts out R EMER DC and DC BUS 3 together, and closing DC TIE 3 restores both from TR 2B through segment 4.

The **battery** is two nickel-cadmium batteries in series, twenty cells, 28 V nominal and 50 Ah in all, in the center accessory compartment. A NiCd cell rests at about 1.2-1.4 V depending on its state of charge, holds a remarkably flat voltage through most of its discharge, and then falls away quickly toward its end-of-discharge voltage of about 1.0 V per cell (20 V for the battery). Its usable capacity shrinks at high discharge rates and in the cold, and its internal resistance rises as it cools, so a cold, heavily loaded battery sags noticeably. On charge, a nearly full NiCd turns more and more of the charging current into gas instead of stored energy, and its voltage climbs steeply; held on a constant voltage while hot, it can go into thermal runaway. That is why the charger controls the charge in stages and watches the battery's voltage and temperature.

The **battery direct bus** is connected straight to the battery and is live whenever the battery has charge, whatever the battery switch says. The **battery bus** is normally supplied by TR 2A and TR 2B through diodes; the battery reaches it, and the charger reaches the battery, through the two-coil **charger battery relay (CBR)**, controlled by the battery switch, the emergency power switch and two relays that sense whether the DC tie segments are powering the battery bus.

blocks.content: On the DC-10 and KC-10 the charger is also disconnected from the battery while the refueling panel at the right wing station is switched on, so a refuel on ground power does not also charge the battery.

The **battery charger** takes its power from the AC ground service bus and nothing else. Each time it is powered, or whenever the battery has been below 26 V for half a second, it runs a short self-test and then a fresh charge cycle:

blocks.content: In practice: after an APU start or a power-up on a partly discharged battery, the battery ammeter (BAT & L EMER AC on the meter selector) shows about 60 A of charge for around five minutes, the battery voltage climbs to about 31.5 V just before Bulk ends, and the charge current then falls to almost nothing. On the MD-10 the BAT CHARGING alert covers the Bulk phase and goes out on its own.

sections.title: Standby and emergency power
sections.summary: The battery and static inverter on the left, the air-driven generator on the right, and the relays that put them on the emergency buses.

blocks.content: When the normal sources fail, two independent standby sources keep the flight-essential buses alive. On the left, the **battery** carries the left emergency DC bus directly and the left emergency AC bus through the **static inverter**. On the right, the **air-driven generator (ADG)** carries the right emergency AC bus, and through TR 3 the right emergency DC bus. The two are deliberately independent: either can be used without the other, and the battery can be held in reserve while the ADG carries the right side.

blocks.alt: Schematic of the emergency power system, common to all three models, in three panels side by side. Panel 1, battery and inverter: battery, battery direct bus, LECR to L EMER DC, static inverter riding the LECR contact to L EMER AC, L EMER AC feed from GEN BUS 1 shown open, CBR to battery bus. Panel 2, ADG at HYD: ADG turbine deployed, ABCR open, ADG bus dead, AHXR closed to auxiliary hydraulic pump 1. Panel 3, ADG at R EMER ELEC: ABCR closed, ADG bus live, RETR transferred so R EMER AC rides the ADG bus, TR 3 feeding R EMER DC, REIR open isolating DC BUS 3 and the DC cabin bus, AHXR open. Each panel labeled with the switch positions that produce it (EMER PWR ON; ADG handle pulled, ADG switch HYD; ADG switch R EMER ELEC).
blocks.title: Emergency power configurations

blocks.content: Selecting emergency power closes the **left emergency control relay (LECR)**. One pole of the LECR connects the battery direct bus to the left emergency DC bus, and the left emergency DC feed from tie segment 1 opens. The other pole connects the **static inverter**, which turns battery DC into 115 V, 400 Hz single-phase AC, to the left emergency AC bus, and the feed from generator bus 1 opens. The transfer takes about 0.4 s, and the old source always lets go before the new one connects, so the inverter is never paralleled with generator bus 1 and the battery is never connected to a dead DC tie segment. Emergency power also disconnects the charger from the battery; the battery bus stays on the battery whenever the TRs are not supplying it.

Because both left emergency buses hang off the battery direct bus, they survive the battery switch being OFF on the DC-10 and KC-10. The inverter is a small unit that draws its power from the battery: a heavy left emergency AC load visibly speeds up the battery's discharge, and the inverter drops out if the battery falls below about 18 V.

**Endurance.** The books give about 30 minutes of left emergency bus power from the battery and inverter on the DC-10 and KC-10, and about 15 minutes for the MD-10's Captain's essential equipment. In the simulation endurance follows the battery's actual state of charge and the actual emergency load, and a fully charged battery carries the emergency loads for more than 30 minutes on all three models. On the DC-10 and KC-10 the inertial units have internal batteries of their own, and the Captain's INS-driven attitude and heading become unreliable when the unit's own battery is exhausted, whatever the aircraft battery is doing.

On the DC-10 and KC-10 the guarded **EMER PWR** switch on the pilots' overhead panel has two positions. At **OFF** the left emergency buses take their power from the main system. At **ON** they are transferred to the battery and inverter, and the EMER PWR IN USE lights (on the flight engineer's panel and the pilots' overhead) come on. There is no automatic transfer: the crew select it. When the normal source returns, return the switch to OFF to stop the battery discharging and let the charger work.

On the MD-10 the **EMER PWR** selector on the ELEC panel has three positions. At **OFF** the battery may not supply the left emergency buses, and the OFF legend is lit. At **ON** the left emergency buses are transferred to the battery and inverter. At **ARM**, the normal in-flight position, the EPCU makes the transfer automatically if the left emergency AC or DC bus loses power, provided the BAT switch is ON, ground power is not on the ground service bus, and the SMOKE ELEC/AIR selector is not at 1/2 OFF. The ON legend lights whenever the transfer is made.

The automatic transfer latches. Once it has happened, the left emergency buses stay on the battery even after normal power returns, until the selector is turned to OFF and back to ARM. For the same reason, do not leave the selector at ARM when shutting the aircraft down, and select ARM only once the AC buses are powered during a power-up: at ARM on a dead aircraft the transfer latches, the charger stays off and the battery discharges.

The **ADG** is a ram-air turbine driving a brushless three-phase generator, stowed flush in the lower fuselage. Pulling the **ADG release handle** on the aft pedestal (pull aft to break the safety wire, then lift) releases it; it swings into the airstream in about two seconds and locks down. The handle is the only way the ADG comes out: nothing deploys it automatically. Once deployed it cannot be stowed in flight; restowing is a maintenance task on the ground. Its drag costs about 1 % in range.

The turbine's pitch governor holds the generator at its rated speed, and with it 400 Hz, once there is enough airspeed. The power a ram-air turbine can extract is proportional to air density times the cube of the true airspeed, which in terms of calibrated airspeed means it grows with the cube of CAS and is no worse at altitude. In the simulation the turbine is stationary below about 50 kt, turns faster as speed increases up to about 90 kt where the governor takes over, delivers useful power from about 120 kt and its full rating of about 20 kVA from about 180 kt CAS. Ask more of it than the air can give and its voltage and frequency sag and collapse, exactly as an overloaded generator's would.
The **ADG switch** decides which one load the turbine carries:

items: **HYD**, the normal position: a released ADG drives **auxiliary hydraulic pump 1** (the hydraulic auxiliary pump transfer relay moves the pump onto the ADG), and its generator stays off line. No bus is powered.

**R EMER ELEC**: the ADG generator's line contactor (**ABCR**) closes onto the ADG bus, the **RETR** transfers the right emergency AC bus from generator bus 3 to the ADG bus, TR 3 then restores the right emergency DC bus, the **REIR** opens to isolate DC bus 3 and the cabin DC bus, and auxiliary pump 1 stops.

blocks.content: The ADG needs no emergency power selection: deploying it and selecting R EMER ELEC restores the right emergency buses whatever the EMER PWR switch is doing. That is the whole recovery for a generator bus 3 failure (DC-10, KC-10), and in a loss of all generators it lets the battery be kept for the left side only. The ADG never powers the left emergency buses, the battery bus or the battery charger.

Check the ADG on the meter before committing a bus to it. On the DC-10 and KC-10 the ADG position of the VOLT/AMP/FREQ selector reads the ADG generator itself, ahead of its contactor, so a turbine up to speed shows 115 V and 400 Hz before R EMER ELEC is selected, and a windmilling one reads nothing.

blocks.content: With all generators lost and no APU or external power, what remains depends on what the crew select:

blocks.title: Standby configurations after a loss of all generators
columns: ADG at R EMER ELEC only

blocks.content: In practical terms: emergency power alone gives the Captain their flight instruments, VHF 1 and VOR 1, the A ignitors, N2 and EGT for all engines, N1 for engine 1 and the lower yaw dampers; the ADG alone gives the First Officer the same on the right side, with VHF 2, VOR and ILS 2, HF 2, the B ignitors, N1 for engine 3, the upper yaw dampers and the tank 2 left aft boost pump. The battery bus, live in every case, keeps fire detection and extinguishing, the master warning and caution lights, engine start and ignition control, the APU controls and the standby horizon.

The fuel boost pumps are on the generator buses, except the tank 2 left aft pump on the right emergency AC bus. The center engine has no suction feed and will flame out without boost pump pressure. With all generators lost, the ADG at R EMER ELEC is what keeps that one pump, and engine 2, running.

sections.title: Circuit breakers
sections.summary: Where the circuit breakers are, how they protect the system, and how they behave in the simulation.

blocks.content: Every load circuit is protected by a circuit breaker, and the larger feeders by remote control circuit breakers (RCCBs) in the electrical compartments, worked from breakers or switches on the flight deck. The breakers are grouped on panels by the bus that feeds them, and each is identified by panel code, row letter and column number, as in UM B-17 (upper main panel, row B, column 17). Each simulated aircraft carries about 750 circuits, every one with its own breaker.

blocks.alt: Plan view of the DC-10 flight compartment showing the location of each circuit breaker panel, labeled with its code: OH pilots' overhead panel; AV avionics (F/E overhead) panel; UM upper main and LM lower main panels at the flight engineer's station; FE flight engineer's lighting panel; PC and CC pilot's and copilot's console panels. Inset: the nose wheel well external power panel (EP). KC-10 inset showing the ARO station (AR) and ARO ground service (AG) panels in the boom operator's compartment.
blocks.title: Circuit breaker panel locations
Circuit breaker panels
rows: Pilots' overhead panel (PO in the KC-10 manual)
Battery bus and battery direct bus circuits, emergency bus circuits (flight instruments, ignition, yaw dampers), fire detection and extinguishing, APU control, battery bus feeds
Avionics panel, over the flight engineer's station
Flight guidance, autothrottle, air data, navigation and communication units
Generator bus loads, the main AC bus feeds, emergency AC bus feeds, TR inputs and outputs, DC bus feeds, fuel pumps, hydraulics; the ELEC SYS RESET switches and GEN FAIL RESET button
Bus sensing breakers, AUTO PARALLEL CONT, 28 V AC transformers, CSD indication, lighting, landing gear and brakes, TR 2B input
Flight engineer's instrument and panel lighting
ARO station and ARO ground service panels (KC-10)

blocks.content: **Sensing breakers.** Each AC BUS OFF, DC BUS OFF and EMER BUS OFF light reports a sensing relay powered from its bus through a **sensing breaker**, not the bus itself. A pulled or tripped sensing breaker therefore lights the OFF light over a perfectly healthy bus. That is why the partial electrical failure checklists reset the sensing breaker before they go near the feeder breakers: if the light goes out, the bus was never lost.

Allow a tripped breaker to cool before resetting it (about 90 seconds in the KC-10 manual, about two minutes in the FedEx DC-10 and MD-10 manuals), and reset it once only; the MD-10 manual adds that a tripped fuel pump breaker is never reset. Several breakers tripping together on one system can mean a wiring fault; do not reset them unless the situation demands it.

items: Every breaker drawn in the 3D cockpit can be pulled and pushed in with a click; its tooltip names its panel and position and whether it is in or pulled. A pulled breaker removes power from its circuit exactly as on the aircraft.
Breakers trip on their own: each has a thermal model, so a sustained overload or a short pops it, and the 3D breaker is shown popped. A breaker that has tripped stays out until it is reset.
The EFB's Failures app lists every popped and pulled breaker with its position, and its **Reset Breakers** command pushes them all back in. A breaker whose fault is still present pops again at once.

Pulling the right breaker is a real crew tool: a sensing breaker lights a BUS OFF light over a live bus, an AUTO PARALLEL CONT breaker stops the generators paralleling, the three BATTERY BUS FEEDS breakers (OH A-13, A-14, A-15) each remove one of the battery bus's three supplies, and the emergency AC bus feed breakers (UM B-20, D-20) remove the normal feed to their bus.

sections.title: Controls and indicators
sections.summary: Every electrical control and indication, panel by panel, for the flight engineer's panel and for the MD-10 overhead and displays.

blocks.content: On the DC-10 and KC-10 the electrical system is the flight engineer's: nearly every control and indication is on upper panel No. 1, with the reset switches on the upper main circuit breaker panel beside the engineer. The pilots have the emergency power and ADG switches on their overhead panel, the ELEC cue and EMER BUS OFF summary lights on the overhead annunciator panel, and the ADG release handle on the pedestal. On the MD-10 the pilots have the whole system: the ELEC panel on the forward overhead, the ELEC synoptic and alerts on the displays, and the same ADG release handle.

The electrical controls and indications are grouped on the left half of the flight engineer's **upper panel No. 1**, laid out as a mimic of the system: the generators and CSDs along the bottom, the AC buses and ties above them, the DC buses and ties at the top, and the meter group and APU generator block to the right. The DC-10s and the KC-10 share this panel; the differences are listed at the end of this section.

blocks.content: The generator positions read the machine, not its bus. A tripped generator reads dead even though its bus is being carried from the tie at 115 V; a generator switched OFF still reads its own 115 V and 400 Hz. That is exactly the reading the abnormal checklists ask for when they say to select the affected generator.

blocks.title: ADG release handle

blocks.content: The **ADG release handle** on the aft pedestal is the same on all three models. Pull it aft to break the safety wire, then lift it: a cable releases the ADG, which swings out and locks in the deployed position. Deployment works in one direction only; the turbine cannot be stowed again in flight. On the DC-10 and KC-10 the ADG's output is then selected with the ADG switch on the pilots' overhead; on the MD-10 with the ADG ELEC button on the ELEC panel.

The MD-10's electrical controls are a row of backlit push-buttons and two rotary selectors on the forward overhead panel, with a BUS OFF light for each of the thirteen main buses laid out as a mimic. In AUTO the crew leave the GEN, AC TIE and DC TIE buttons alone; the EPCU runs those relays. BAT, EMER PWR, SMOKE ELEC/AIR, DRIVE, EXT PWR, APU PWR, ADG ELEC and CAB BUS work the same way in AUTO and MANUAL. Every legend on the panel except EXT PWR AVAIL is powered from the battery bus.

Inset: the GEN BUS FAULT RESET panel.
blocks.title: MD-10 ELEC panel
ELEC panel controls and indicators
rows: Alternate action: AUTO (legends out) or MANUAL. SELECT lights when the EPCU has given up on a function it manages in AUTO (in the simulation, a generator it could not reset) and wants the crew to take over; pressing the button selects MANUAL and puts SELECT out.

Electrical and air smoke isolation. Out of NORM it opens the DC X TIE and raises SMOKE SW IN USE; at 1/2 OFF it also inhibits the automatic emergency power transfer. See [Simulation notes](#simulation-notes).
Guarded, alternate action, normally in (ON). Pushed to OFF it disconnects the battery from the battery bus and the charger, inhibits the automatic emergency power transfer, and lights OFF.
OFF: the battery may not supply the left emergency buses; OFF lights. ARM: automatic transfer if a left emergency bus loses power. ON: transfer now. ON lights whenever the transfer is made.

In MANUAL, commands the generator: in, the GCU closes the generator relay when the generator's power is good; out, the generator is off. ARM: field on, generator relay open. OFF: generator relay open and not armed. Blank: generator on line. No effect in AUTO.

In MANUAL: at ARM the GCU closes the bus tie relay automatically; at OFF the relay is held open. ARM lights with the relay open and the button at ARM; OFF with the relay open and the button at OFF. Both out: relay closed. No effect in AUTO.

It shows the whole power system as a one-line diagram: the AC buses along the middle, the DC buses along the top, the generators, the APU and external power along the bottom, and the battery and ADG on the left and right emergency verticals.

DC-10-30F livery; the ground power cart visible at the edge of the frame.
blocks.title: Main external power receptacle

blocks.content: The main external power receptacle is on the lower nose, aft of the nose wheel well, behind an access door with its own small panel of lights. In the simulation the ground crew plug the cart in when it is called from the EFB's Ground Ops page or with the simulator's request for ground power; the cockpit then sees EXT PWR AVAIL once the cart has run up and been proved, and the crew connect it with the EXT PWR switch or button.

sections.title: Operation
sections.summary: The electrical system through a flight, from a cold aircraft to shutdown, with the automatic functions and the logic behind them.

blocks.content: This section follows the system through a normal day and explains what happens at each stage. The checklists themselves are in [Normal procedures](normal-procedures).

items: **BAT switch to BAT.** The CBR moves to its BAT position and the battery takes the battery bus; BAT BUS OFF flashes as the relay transfers, then goes out. The panel's lights come alive, powered from the battery bus and battery direct bus: AC BUS OFF, DC BUS OFF and all four EMER BUS OFF lights on (nothing is powering those buses yet), GEN OFF and CSD OIL PRESS LO on for all three channels.

**External power.** Call the ground power cart (EFB Ground Ops page or the simulator's ground power request). When the cart is plugged in, run up and proved, EXT PWR AVAIL comes on. Select **EXT PWR**: EXT PWR IN USE comes on, the EPR and BTR-EP close and the tie bus comes alive, all three bus tie relays close to pick up their generator buses, and the GSR puts the cart on the AC ground service bus. The AC, DC and emergency bus OFF lights go out together as all four TRs come up at once. The CBR moves to CHG and the charger starts a bulk charge.
**DC check.** DC TIE and DC X TIE switches OPEN, their CLOSED lights out; every DC LOAD meter below 1.0.
**Generators.** Each GEN switch to RESET and back to ON (this re-arms any field left tripped); AC BUS TIE switches at NORM.
**Battery check.** VOLT/AMP/FREQ selector to BAT & L EMER AC: left emergency AC voltage and frequency in the normal band, battery on charge.

**APU, if used.** Start the APU (see [APU](apu)). When APU PWR AVAIL comes on, select the three **APU GEN BUS** switches ON. The APU takes each generator bus from the tie: each bus tie relay opens and its APR closes, the three APU PWR IN USE lights come on, and the AC BUS TIE ISOL lights come on, because the APU's buses are now off the tie. With EXT PWR then selected OFF, the AC ground service bus moves from the cart to generator bus 2 (and so to the APU).

blocks.content: With the BAT switch OFF the cart reaches only the AC ground service bus. TR 2B then carries the DC ground service bus and the battery bus, and the AC, DC and EMER BUS OFF lights stay on while BAT BUS OFF is out.

items: **BAT** button in (BAT OFF out), the ELEC panel in AUTO, EMER PWR at OFF.

**External power.** When EXT PWR AVAIL is lit, push **EXT PWR**: ON lights, the AC and DC BUS OFF lights go out, and the three GEN ARM legends light (each generator armed but not on line, waiting for its engine).

**APU.** Start the APU from its own panel. APU PWR AVAIL flashes while it accelerates and goes steady. Push **APU PWR**: ON lights and the APU takes the generator buses. BAT CHARGING normally appears for a few minutes after an APU start; do not take off with it displayed.
**Emergency power.** Once the AC buses are powered, turn EMER PWR to **ARM**.

children.title: Engine start and transfer to the generators

blocks.content: As each engine accelerates through about 50 % N2 its CSD reaches governed speed, the generator's PMG brings the GCU alive, and the generator excites. If its bus is dead, the generator relay closes at once; if the bus is being carried by the APU, the relay closes the moment the generator and the APU are in phase, and the APU's relay to that bus drops out, a transfer the crew does not see. GEN OFF (DC-10, KC-10) or the GEN ARM legend (MD-10) goes out, and APU PWR IN USE for that bus goes out.

With the generators on line and the APU and external power off, the system runs unparalleled: one generator, normally the first to come on line, carries the tie bus, and the AC LOAD needles show three different loads. After the last engine start the flight engineer checks each generator on the meter, confirms the APU GEN BUS switches are OFF and external power is disconnected, and presses **PARALLEL GENS**. Within a few seconds each bus tie relay closes as its generator synchronizes, and the three AC LOAD needles come together. If they do not, the GENERATORS WILL NOT PARALLEL checklist applies.

The EPCU parallels the generators by itself as they come on line, unless external power is still selected; deselect EXT PWR and the AC TIE ARM legends go out within seconds as the bus tie relays close, one at a time, with no flicker on any bus. Push APU PWR to take the APU off when it is no longer needed.

In normal flight all three generators share the load, each typically well below half its rating, and the TRs each carry about a third of theirs. The CSD outlet temperatures settle well inside the gauge's normal range, colder at altitude where the fan air is cold, with a rise of about 20-25 °C. The things worth watching are the shares rather than the absolute numbers: a generator that carries noticeably more or less than its partners when paralleled, a CSD whose rise creeps up, or a frequency that wanders.

Paralleling must be re-armed after anything opens a bus tie relay. A generator trip, an ISOL selection, the APU put on a bus, or a protective trip all drop the system back to unparalleled operation, with no light to say so: the loadmeters spread apart. Once the cause is dealt with, press PARALLEL GENS again.

The APU generator can be used in flight as an additional source (for example with a generator inoperative), within the APU's in-flight envelope. It takes only buses that have lost their own generator, and on the DC-10 and KC-10 it cancels automatic paralleling while it is connected.

Before the engines are shut down, make sure another source is ready: the APU running with its generator available, or external power available. On the DC-10 and KC-10 select the APU GEN BUS switches ON or EXT PWR on; on the MD-10 confirm the APU or the tie bus can supply the buses. As each engine runs down, its CSD falls below governed speed, the underspeed switch opens its generator relay, and its bus is picked up by the APU or by external power through the tie. Because the underspeed switch also inhibits the under-frequency and under-voltage protection, a normal shutdown leaves no lockout behind.

If neither the APU nor external power is available and an engine must be kept running for electrical power, keep engine 2 running and shut down engines 1 and 3: generator 2 also feeds the ground service bus.
Turn EMER PWR to OFF before removing power. Left at ARM, the emergency transfer latches as the buses go dead and the battery is drained through the emergency buses.
In AUTO the EPCU and the GCUs do what the DC-10's flight engineer does by hand:

blocks.title: EPCU automatic functions
rows: Closes and opens the generator, APU, external power and bus tie relays to the priorities in [Source priority](#paralleling).
Parallels the engine generators whenever external power is not on or selected for the tie; brings them onto the tie one at a time.
Between the APU and an engine generator, by momentary paralleling in the synchronizing window.
Holds the DC tie contactors closed so the four TRs run paralleled.

After a protective trip, waits a few seconds and resets the generator itself, with up to three attempts at growing intervals. If the generator cannot be recovered, SYSTEM SELECT lights and SEL ELEC SYS MAN is displayed: the crew are being asked to take over in MANUAL. A channel that then stays healthy for a minute gets its full set of attempts back. Each automatic reset used raises EPGS FAULT.
Retries a bus tie relay locked out by a bus feeder fault once the fault has gone (the GEN BUS FAULT RESET switches are for maintenance on the ground).
With EMER PWR at ARM, transfers the left emergency buses to the battery and inverter when either loses power.

blocks.content: Switching to MANUAL changes only the GEN, AC TIE and DC TIE buttons, which then command their relays directly. The EPCU does not switch itself to MANUAL when it gives up on something: it keeps the relays where they are and lights SELECT, because handing the relay logic a row of un-pressed buttons would isolate every bus.

blocks.title: Main power relays

Protective trip, fire handle pulled, CSD disconnect

See [Bus tie logic](#bus-tie-logic) (DC-10, KC-10) or [EPCU source management](#md10-paralleling) (MD-10)

blocks.content: Contactors take time to move: about 50 ms to close and 30 ms to open for most relays, and about 0.4 s for the emergency power transfer relays. The outgoing relay of a transfer always opens before the incoming one closes, except in the MD-10's deliberate no-break transfers.

blocks.title: Interactions
rows: Each CSD is driven from its engine's accessory gearbox. An engine below governed speed, or a failed accessory drive, takes its generator off line through the underspeed switch.

Pulling an engine fire handle turns off that generator's field; pushing the handle back in restores it. The fire detection, warning and extinguishing circuits are on the battery bus and battery direct bus.
The APU generator; the APU's start, door and fuel controls are on the battery bus.
Boost and transfer pumps are on the generator buses, three per bus, except the tank 2 left aft pump on the right emergency AC bus. Engine 2 has no suction feed.
Auxiliary hydraulic pumps 1 and 2 run from the AC ground service bus; pump 1 moves to the ADG with the ADG switch at HYD. The engine-driven pumps' controls are on the battery bus.
A ignitors on the left emergency AC bus, B ignitors on the right.
Isolation valve 1-3 is controlled from the left emergency AC bus, isolation valve 1-2 from the right.
Lower yaw dampers on the left emergency buses, upper yaw dampers on the right; stall warning, stick shakers and auto slat extension on AC buses 1 and 3 and DC buses 1 and 3.
Captain's instruments on the left emergency AC bus, First Officer's on the right; the standby horizon on the battery bus.
The ELEC cue and EMER BUS OFF summary lights, MASTER CAUTION and MASTER WARNING; on the MD-10 the electrical alerts and the ELEC synoptic.
The pilots' gear warning is on DC bus 2, the flight engineer's on DC bus 3. In the simulation both sets of gear lights follow the DC bus 2 supply (see [Landing gear](landing-gear)).

sections.title: Failures and non-normal operation
sections.summary: How generators, drives, buses and TRs fail, how each failure shows, what is lost with each bus, and the loss of all generators.

blocks.content: The system is built so that most failures cost one channel and are absorbed by the others automatically. The crew's work is to recognize what has failed, confirm it is real (a sensing circuit can light a BUS OFF light over a live bus), restore what can be restored, and know what has been lost. The procedures are in [Emergency procedures](emergency-procedures) and [Abnormal procedures](abnormal-procedures); this section explains the failures behind them.

blocks.title: Generator and drive failures
rows: Generator protective trip (for example loss of field, over-voltage)
The GCU opens the field and the generator relay; the generator bus is picked up from the tie.
DC-10, KC-10: GEN OFF; the meter shows the generator dead; its AC LOAD at zero. MD-10: GEN n OFF, GEN OFF legend, generator amber on the synoptic.
Reset once (GEN switch RESET then ON; on the MD-10 the EPCU resets it in AUTO). If it trips again, leave it off.
The CSD underspeeds and the generator relay opens; the bus is picked up from the tie. The generator returns by itself if the engine is relit.
GEN OFF (MD-10: GEN ARM or OFF legend); low frequency on the meter.
The generator keeps running on its auxiliary bearings, for some hours at most.
DC-10, KC-10: GEN FAIL (APU GEN FAIL for the APU generator).
GEN FAIL RESET to check for a spurious signal; if it relights, disconnect the CSD per the checklist.
Charge pressure falls; the oil temperature rise climbs as the oil flow drops; a drive fault is latched.
CSD OIL PRESS LO (MD-10: DRIVE FAULT legend, GEN DRIVE n FAULT); ELEC cue.
Generator off, then disconnect the CSD.
The drive's heat is not removed; outlet temperature climbs with the rise normal, toward the over-temperature switch.
CSD outlet temperature in the yellow, rising; (MD-10: DRIVE FAULT at the over-temperature switch).
Generator off; if the outlet temperature keeps rising, disconnect.
The drive runs away high at about 1 Hz per second. Above 420 Hz the bus tie relay opens after 1.5 s and the generator after 4 s; the bus is then picked up from the tie.
Frequency high on the meter or synoptic; AC BUS TIE ISOL as the bus tie relay locks out; then GEN OFF.
Generator off, then disconnect the CSD.
PARALLEL GENS has no effect, or a bus tie relay will not close.
Loadmeters stay apart; AC BUS TIE ISOL on for a relay that will not close.
Check the AUTO PARALLEL CONT breakers and the AC BUS TIE switches; per the checklist.
The APU's relays open; its buses are picked up from the tie if a source is on it.
APU GEN OFF with APU PWR AVAIL out (MD-10: GEN APU OFF, APU GEN RESET OFF legend).
APU generator reset (KC-10: APU GEN RESET; MD-10: APU GEN RESET button) once the fault has cleared.

blocks.title: Bus and conversion failures
rows: Generator bus failure (a feeder fault on the bus)

Differential protection opens the generator relay and locks out the bus tie relay, so the faulted bus is isolated and is not rescued from the tie. Its main AC bus, emergency AC bus (buses 1 and 3), TR and boost pumps go with it.
DC-10, KC-10: GEN OFF, AC BUS TIE ISOL, AC BUS OFF, and the emergency and DC lights for that channel. MD-10: GEN BUS n FAULT.

Restore what can be restored: emergency power for the left emergency AC bus (bus 1), the ADG for the right emergency buses (bus 3), DC ties for the lost DC bus, and the APU generator where the checklist calls for it.
The main AC bus alone is lost; its generator bus, TR and emergency bus stay up.
AC BUS OFF (MD-10: BUS AC n OFF and the AC box amber on the synoptic).
Reset the sensing breaker first; then the feed breakers once only.
Nothing is lost; the sensing relay drops out.
An OFF light over a bus that is in fact powered.
Resetting the sensing breaker puts the light out.
All bus tie relays lock out; each channel runs isolated on its own generator.
All AC BUS TIE ISOL lights (MD-10: AC TIE FAULT).
Continue isolated; a generator loss can no longer be covered by the tie.
Bus tie relay fails to close
The preferential circuit hands the tie to the next generator; paralleling is inhibited.
That channel's AC BUS TIE ISOL (MD-10: ARM legend and AC TIE n OFF).
ISOL then NORM, or a BUS FAULT reset, retries the relay.
The TR's DC bus loses its source (TR 1: DC BUS 1 and L EMER DC; TR 2A: DC BUS 2; TR 2B: DC GND SVC; TR 3: R EMER DC and DC BUS 3).
DC BUS OFF and/or EMER DC BUS OFF; that TR's DC LOAD at zero (MD-10: TR n FAIL; DC ties already closed).
DC-10, KC-10: close the adjacent DC tie (DC TIE 1 for DC BUS 1, DC TIE 3 for DC BUS 3 and R EMER DC), watching the other TR's load.
Right emergency AC bus feed lost
R EMER AC, and with it TR 3, R EMER DC and DC BUS 3, are lost.
R EMER AC BUS OFF, R EMER DC BUS OFF and DC BUS 3 OFF together.
Close DC TIE 3 to restore DC BUS 3 and R EMER DC from TR 2B; the ADG at R EMER ELEC restores the AC bus.
The battery bus loses its supplies.
BAT BUS OFF (its lamp is powered from the battery direct bus), and loss of the battery bus loads.
Reset the three BATTERY BUS FEEDS breakers per the checklist.
TR 2B lost (for example its input breaker), or the AC ground service bus lost.

blocks.content: With every generator lost and no APU or external power, every AC bus and every DC bus fed from a TR goes dead at once. The flight and engine instrument flags come into view, every bus OFF light comes on except BAT BUS OFF (the battery takes the battery bus automatically), and the EMER BUS OFF summary light and MASTER WARNING come on. On the MD-10, GEN ALL OFF is displayed, and with EMER PWR at ARM the left emergency buses transfer to the battery by themselves.

The recovery has three strands, and the procedures take them in this order: restore the Captain's side at once with emergency power (battery and inverter); try to get a generator back (one reset each); and if the generator buses stay dead, deploy the ADG and select R EMER ELEC to restore the First Officer's side and, crucially, the tank 2 left aft boost pump that keeps engine 2 fed. Once the ADG is carrying the right side, emergency power need only be used as required, to save the battery. If generator bus 1 comes back, return EMER PWR to OFF.

What remains is listed in [What stays powered](#standby-configurations). Everything on the main AC and DC buses is lost, including the normal stabilizer trim, the elevator feel and flap limiter, and the flap and slat position indication; the checklists cover trimming with the longitudinal trim handles and the landing flap setting to use. Land at the nearest suitable airport.

Electrical smoke is fought by removing power from channels one at a time until the source is found. On the DC-10 and KC-10 the flight engineer does this with the GEN, AC BUS TIE and DC TIE switches and the circuit breakers, following the smoke checklist. On the MD-10 the SMOKE ELEC/AIR selector exists for the same purpose.

Most of the aircraft's wiring has polyimide insulation, which can carbonize and flash over along a bundle faster than a circuit breaker can open. Several breakers tripping together on one system can be the sign; do not reset them unless the situation demands it.

**Modeled in depth.** Each CSD (governor and its trim, oil system, charge pressure, outlet and rise temperatures against a fan-air cooler, underspeed switch, disconnect); each generator (PMG, exciter, bearings and the GEN FAIL indication, heating); every GCU protective function with its delay and its reset; the AC network solved every step as islands of buses with real voltages, frequencies, phase angles and loads, so load sharing comes from the drives' and regulators' droop and synchronizing is a real phase-locking process; the three bus tie modes of the DC-10 and KC-10, including the preferential order and the sitting donor; the MD-10's EPCU paralleling, no-break transfers and automatic resets; the DC network solved for real voltages, with TR droop, diode feeds and the battery picking up the load within a step; a NiCd battery with its charge curve, temperature and ageing; the battery charger's modes; the static inverter; the ADG's deployment, spin and power curve; the external power monitor and a diesel ground power cart; the DC-10's galley buses with load shedding; and about 750 circuits per aircraft, each with its own breaker, thermal trip and load.

**Simplified.** Several values are representative rather than taken from a maintenance manual: the inverse-time trip characteristics, the load-unbalance trip level, the TR output curve, the charger's rates and timings, the ADG's airspeed curve, and the APU generator's ground rating. Contactors move in about 50 ms (closing) and 30 ms (opening), the emergency transfer relays in about 0.4 s. The static inverter is modeled as a small single-phase source.

items: **Not modeled: the Dual Land bus split** for autoland, and the DUAL LAND SELECTED and DUAL LAND PWR ON lights (DC-10). The generators stay paralleled through an autoland.

**AC BUS TIE ISOL lights** (DC-10, KC-10) are out in normal unparalleled operation. On the real aircraft the two channels not on the tie show ISOL until PARALLEL GENS is pressed; in the simulation ISOL lights only for a channel taken off the tie. Read paralleling from the loadmeters.
**The DC GND SERVICE BUS PWR selector** (NORM/ALTN) is not in the cockpit: the DC ground service bus always takes its normal feed from TR 2B.
**The cabin ground service and ground power panels** are not in the cockpit. The flight engineer's EXT PWR switch also puts external power on the AC ground service bus.

**CSD disconnect** needs the button held for about one second (the checklists' three seconds work too). A disconnected CSD, and a deployed ADG, are restored on the ground with the EFB's **Reset Aircraft**.
**The engine fire handle's** generator cut-off resets itself when the handle is pushed back in; no GEN switch reset is needed.

**APU GEN RESET** is fitted on the KC-10 deck only; the DC-10 deck has no APU generator reset switch. The APU GEN OFF light (DC-10, KC-10) reports the APU generator's field contactor, so it does not light during a normal APU start as it does on the aircraft; it lights after a protective trip.

**Galley power** (DC-10): the GALLEY BUS switches have no RESET position, so a shed galley bus stays shed for the rest of the session; and no galley cart can be connected to the galley receptacle, so GLY EXT PWR cannot be used.

**MD-10 ADG:** as on the DC-10, the ADG carries only the right emergency buses. The MD-10 manual describes its ADG ELEC switch as also powering the left emergency buses, the battery bus and the battery charger; that is not simulated.

**MD-10 SMOKE ELEC/AIR selector:** out of NORM it opens the DC X TIE, raises SMOKE SW IN USE and drives the EIS displays to full brightness, and at 1/2 OFF it inhibits the automatic emergency power transfer. It does not yet de-power the generator channels or turn off the air conditioning packs.

**MD-10 generator reset:** in AUTO the EPCU makes up to three automatic reset attempts (the FCOM describes one). The GEN buttons in MANUAL do not reset a tripped generator in this build, and the GEN BUS FAULT RESET panel is not modeled (the EPCU's retry covers bus faults).

**MD-10 panel details:** the CAB BUS button lights its OFF legend and raises CABIN BUS SW OFF but has no cabin buses to remove; the GLY EXT PWR AVAIL legend follows the main receptacle; the MANUAL legend does not flash when a button with no effect in AUTO is pressed; EPCU load shedding is not modeled; the GEN LOAD HI, ELEC ALERTS and EMER PWR TST FAIL alerts are not yet implemented.
**Battery endurance** on emergency power is more than 30 minutes on all three models with a fully charged battery (the MD-10 manual quotes about 15 minutes for that aircraft).

blocks.content: **Simulator controls.** The simulator's generator key commands move the GEN switches (DC-10, KC-10) or, in MANUAL only, the GEN buttons (MD-10) between ON and OFF, never to RESET; the external power commands move the EXT PWR switch or button; the APU generator command moves all three APU GEN BUS switches together (DC-10, KC-10) or the APU PWR button (MD-10); and the request for ground power calls and connects the ramp's cart. An aircraft loaded with its engines already running starts with its battery switch on.

blocks.title: Electrical failures available in the EFB Failures app
rows: A loss of field: the generator trips on under-excitation or under-voltage.
Generator fault (1, 2, 3, APU), DC-10 and KC-10
A bearing failure: GEN FAIL, the generator keeps running.
A governor runaway: frequency climbs past 420 Hz until the protection trips the channel.
Generators will not parallel, DC-10 and KC-10
An AUTO PARALLEL CONT breaker trips.
Two generators trip, leaving single-generator operation.
A feeder fault on the generator bus.
A bus tie relay sticks open.
The bus's feed breaker trips (left emergency DC: its feed relay sticks open).
The right emergency AC bus feed breaker trips.
The three battery bus feed breakers trip.

blocks.content: Clearing a failure in the app removes its cause; breakers it tripped stay out until **Reset Breakers** is used, as a real popped breaker would. See [EFB](efb) for the Failures app.

parts.title: Hydraulics
parts.summary: Three independent 3,000 psi systems, their engine and electric pumps, the motor pumps that pass power between them, what each one powers, and how they are controlled and fail.

blocks.content: The hydraulic power system moves every flight control surface, the flaps and slats, the horizontal stabilizer, the landing gear, the wheel brakes and the nose-wheel steering. The DC-10 family has no manual reversion: no cable from the control column or the rudder pedals drives a primary surface directly, and every surface is positioned by hydraulic actuators. Hydraulic pressure is therefore the aircraft's controllability, and the whole system is designed around keeping some of it available after any credible failure.

There are three separate hydraulic systems, each named for the engine that drives it: **system 1** (engine 1, left wing), **system 2** (engine 2, tail) and **system 3** (engine 3, right wing). Each operates continuously at a nominal 3,000 psi and has its own reservoir, two engine-driven pumps, an accumulator, a system manifold with filters and a relief valve, and its own pressure and return lines. **No fluid ever passes from one system to another.**

What can pass between them is power. Two **reversible motor pumps** (1-3 and 2-3) couple system 3 mechanically to systems 1 and 2, in either direction. Two **non-reversible motor pumps** (2-1 and 3-2) give the two rudder segments and one stabilizer trim motor a standby supply from a second system. Two AC electric **auxiliary pumps** pressurize system 3 on the ground and in an emergency, and through the reversible motor pumps they can reach systems 1 and 2 as well.

Each aileron and elevator surface is moved by a tandem actuator with one half on each of two systems, and the pairs are chosen so that no single system serves every actuator of an axis. The two rudder segments have one system each, and each is backed by a standby motor pump from another system. The result is the design's central property: any one system can be lost with no loss of function, and the aircraft remains controllable with any two lost.

blocks.alt: Functional schematic of the DC-10 hydraulic power system drawn as three vertical columns: system 1 on the left (color band red), system 2 in the center (yellow), system 3 on the right (green). In each column, from bottom to top: reservoir with its pressurizing line from the accumulator, hydraulic fire shutoff valve in the suction line, the engine's left and right engine-driven pumps feeding through the engine hydraulic manifold (pressure and case-drain filters, check valves, PRESS LO switch, TEMP HI switch), the firewall check valve, the system manifold with return filters, relief valve and pressure transmitter, and the accumulator. sections.title: System architecture
sections.summary: Why three systems, how they are kept apart, and the physics of a constant-pressure hydraulic system.

blocks.content: The DC-10 was designed with fully powered flight controls and no manual reversion, so hydraulic redundancy has to do the work that a manual backup does on older types. Three systems give two levels of protection: after one failure every function is still available on the other two; after a second, enough remains to fly and land. Tying each system to one engine keeps an engine failure from costing more than one system's pumps, and a reversible motor pump then restores that system from a healthy one.

Keeping the fluid separate is as important as having three systems. A leak, a ruptured line or contaminated fluid in one system cannot drain or contaminate another, because nothing connects their fluid volumes. Every cross-system device transfers mechanical power through a shaft rather than fluid through a pipe, and each reservoir supplies only its own system.

The systems are also kept apart physically wherever the airframe allows: system 1 is based in the left wing and left main gear wheel well, system 3 in the right, and system 2 at the tail engine and the aft accessory compartment. The exception is the tail itself, where all three systems must reach the elevators, the rudders and the stabilizer trim close to the number 2 engine. That single area of common exposure is the reason for the system 3 elevator shutoff valve (see [System 3 protection](#system-3-protection)).

blocks.title: The three systems
rows: AUX PUMP 1 (ADG) and AUX PUMP 2; both reversible motor pumps
Upper rudder and stabilizer trim motor 2, from system 2 through the 2-1 motor pump
Lower rudder, from system 3 through the 3-2 motor pump
KC-10: feeds the air refueling alternate supply
Landing gear; brake system 2; auxiliary pumps; flight control bypass valve; elevator shutoff valve

blocks.content: System 3 is the busiest of the three. It alone moves the landing gear, it carries the auxiliary pumps, and through the reversible motor pumps it is the route by which electric power reaches systems 1 and 2 on the ground. Because it is pressurized for so much ground work, it is also the system with a flight control bypass valve, which lets maintenance keep its flight control actuators still while the rest of the system works.

Each system is a **constant-pressure** system: its pumps hold the pressure line at about 3,000 psi whatever the users take from it. Two quantities describe what the system can do. **Pressure** sets force: an actuator piston of area A produces a force of p × A, so pressure decides whether a surface can be held against its air load. **Flow** sets speed: the piston moves at Q / A, so the flow the pumps can deliver decides how fast surfaces, flaps and gear move.

Hydraulic power is the product of the two. One US gallon per minute (gpm) at 3,000 psi carries about 1.75 hp, so an engine-driven pump delivering its rated 37.5 gpm at 3,000 psi is passing roughly 65 hp from its engine's gearbox into the fluid. The figure explains why flow, not pressure, is the scarce resource: pressure is free to hold, flow costs power.

Because the pumps regulate pressure, the gauge stays near 3,000 psi while demand rises, until demand exceeds what the pumps can deliver. Only then does pressure fall. A falling gauge therefore means one of three things: demand greater than supply (a large transient such as gear retraction, or a system running on a weaker source), a source that has stopped delivering, or fluid leaving the system. The accumulator covers short transients; the relief valve caps the top.

No hydraulic system is perfectly tight. Every servo valve and control valve passes a small clearance flow from pressure to return across its spool lands, and actuator seals pass a little more. This **internal leakage** is small, under 1 gpm per system on a serviceable aircraft, but it never stops, so a system with no pump running loses its pressure in seconds rather than hours. Once the last pump of a system stops, the system falls through 2,400 psi within about 5 to 8 seconds and is below 1,000 psi within about half a minute. The brake accumulators are separate, sit behind check valves, and keep the brakes and the parking brake pressurized long after the systems have bled down.

Every loss in the system ends up as heat in the fluid: pump inefficiency carried away in the case drains, the pressure drop across every valve that meters flow, and above all flow through a relief valve, which turns its full 3,000-plus psi into heat. Fluid temperature is therefore a health indication as well as a limit.

The systems use a fire-resistant phosphate-ester fluid to Douglas specification DMS 2014 (the KC-10 manual names Skydrol 500B-4, Skydrol LD-4 and Hyjet IV). It resists burning far better than a mineral oil, which matters for a fluid whose lines run through the engine nacelles. Like any hydraulic fluid it is slightly compressible, so a sealed, pressurized line acts as a stiff spring that stores a little energy, and its viscosity rises steeply in the cold, which slows a cold-soaked system.

sections.title: Engine-driven pumps
sections.summary: Six pressure-compensated piston pumps, two per engine: one working, one in standby.

blocks.content: Each engine carries two hydraulic pumps on its accessory gearbox, the **left** (pump 1) and the **right** (pump 2), both feeding that engine's system. They are variable-displacement, nine-piston axial pumps, driven at a fixed ratio to the high-pressure spool, so their speed is proportional to N2. In normal operation the left pump pressurizes the system and the right pump runs in standby: turning, but held at zero output until it is needed.

Each pump's pressure and case-drain lines pass through the engine hydraulic manifold in the nacelle, which carries a filter and a check valve in each line, the pump's low-pressure switch (PRESS LO) and its case-drain temperature switch (TEMP HI). Both pumps draw from one suction line from the reservoir, through the system's hydraulic fire shutoff valve. The check valve in each pump's outlet lets either pump run alone without driving fluid back through the other.
