Arrows and labels show: yoke angle sets piston stroke; compensator tilts the yoke back as outlet pressure approaches 3,025 psi; case flow cools and lubricates the pump.
blocks.title: Engine-driven pump
blocks.caption: Outlet pressure, not the crew, sets the stroke: the compensator tilts the yoke back until the flow delivered just matches the flow being used.

children.title: Theory of operation: the pressure-compensated pump

blocks.content: The pump's cylinder block turns with the drive shaft. Its nine pistons ride on shoes against a yoke that can be tilted. When the yoke is square to the shaft the pistons do not move in their bores and the pump displaces nothing. As the yoke tilts, each piston is drawn out over one half of the revolution, filling from the suction port, and pushed back over the other half, discharging through the pressure port. The yoke angle therefore sets the **displacement** per revolution, and the delivered flow is displacement times shaft speed, less internal slip.

The yoke angle is set by a **compensator**: a spool held by a spring and pushed by outlet pressure. Below its setting the spring wins and the yoke stays at full angle, so the pump delivers all it can. As outlet pressure approaches the setting, the spool ports pressure to a piston that tilts the yoke back, reducing the stroke until the flow delivered equals the flow being used. At zero demand the yoke sits almost square and the pump makes only enough flow to cover its own internal leakage, holding the system at about 3,025 psi. The loop acts within a few hundredths of a second, so the pressure the crew sees barely moves while demand swings from nothing to full.

blocks.title: Pump pressure and flow
rows: All the pump can deliver at its shaft speed (rated 37.5 gpm at 2,850 psi at full speed)
Falls steeply as pressure rises; this narrow band is where the pump normally works
Internal leakage and case flow only

blocks.content: A compensated pump takes power from the engine only when the system uses flow. A fixed-displacement pump would deliver full flow all the time and dump the surplus over a relief valve, turning tens of horsepower into heat. The price is that pressure always sits near the top of the band, so every component is designed for 3,000 psi continuously.

Some fluid always leaks past the pistons and the valve plate into the pump case. The **case drain** returns it, about 3 gpm, through its own filter and past the TEMP HI switch to the reservoir. This flow is the pump's cooling and lubrication: it carries away the heat of the pump's own losses and keeps the case full. A worn pump leaks more internally, turns more of its power into heat and warms its case drain, which is why a TEMP HI light is an early sign of a failing pump.

Flow capacity is proportional to shaft speed and so to N2. At ground idle a pump can deliver a little over half its full-speed flow, which is ample for normal ground demands: the compensator simply works at a larger stroke. A windmilling engine turns its pumps slowly, and they can still hold their system's pressure when little is being used. Below about 5 % N2 the pumps deliver nothing.

A pump is switched off not by stopping it, since its drive is permanent, but by **depressurizing** it. The electric depressurizing valve ports the compensator so that the yoke goes to zero stroke and the pump is feathered. It keeps turning with the engine and its case flow keeps it cool. The valve is energized to depressurize: if its 28 V DC control power fails, the pump goes to full pressure whatever its switch says, and a pump that was switched off starts by itself. Losing a pump unexpectedly is far worse than being unable to switch one off, so the valve fails to the pressurizing state.

The power a pump delivers comes out of its engine's gearbox. A single pump holding a quiet system takes little; during a large demand, such as a flap or gear transit, both pumps of a system working at full stroke take tens of horsepower from their engine.

children.title: Pump control and the standby pump

blocks.content: Each pump's depressurizing valve is worked through one of two control circuits, one for all three left pumps and one for all three right pumps (the ENG HYD PUMPS CONT LEFT and RIGHT breakers, on the battery bus). Losing either circuit, by a tripped breaker or a dead battery bus, sends all three pumps on that side to full pressure. The pumps go on working; the crew simply cannot switch those pumps off until the power returns.

The right pump at **AUTO** is an on-demand standby. It stays depressurized while its system is healthy and comes on the moment the system needs it. It returns to standby 20 seconds after the demand has passed, so that a marginal left pump does not make it cycle rapidly. The same automatic circuit serves all three aircraft: on the DC-10 and KC-10 the flight engineer can override it with the R selector; on the MD-10 the hydraulic system controller supervises it.

blocks.title: Right pump selector overrides

blocks.content: With a left pump switched off or failed, the 20-second hold can make a system's pressure cycle regularly between about 3,000 and 2,400 psi: the right pump restores the system, drops back to standby, and comes on again when internal leakage has taken the system back down to 2,400 psi. If a pressure gauge fluctuates like this at regular intervals, select that system's R pump ON.

blocks.alt: Two cutaway drawings side by side. Left: a DC-10 hydraulic reservoir, a vertical cylinder with the small bootstrap piston at the top connected by a rod to the large diaphragm over the fluid, the small pressurizing port from the accumulator line, the supply and return ports at the bottom, the relief and sampling valve with sight glass, the quantity transmitter and its linkage on the cover, the low-level switch, the temperature sensor and the air breather; on the system 3 reservoir the two extra level switches for the elevator shutoff valve. Annotate the 50 to 1 area ratio and the 60 psi fluid head. Right: a spherical bladder accumulator with nitrogen precharge valve and gauge, shown at precharge (bladder filling the sphere) and at 3,000 psi (gas compressed into the top third).
blocks.title: Reservoir and accumulator
blocks.caption: The reservoir is pressurized by the system itself; the accumulator stores only a small volume at useful pressure.

blocks.content: The three reservoirs are identical and interchangeable: cylinders with a total internal volume of 12 US gallons including expansion space. How much of that each system uses depends on what it has to fill. Each reservoir carries a quantity transmitter linked to the fluid-level pointer, a low-level switch, a temperature sensor, a relief and sampling valve with a sight glass, and a filtered air breather.

A pump draws fluid in by lowering the pressure at its inlet, and fluid can only follow if something pushes it. At cruise altitude the outside air pressure is only a few psi, too little to keep a fast-turning pump's inlet full; the fluid would release dissolved air and vapour and the pump would cavitate. The reservoirs are therefore **bootstrap** pressurized: system pressure from the accumulator line acts on a small piston that is mechanically tied to a much larger diaphragm on the fluid. The area ratio of about 50 to 1 turns 3,000 psi into a head of about 60 psi on the fluid, at any altitude. A relief valve at the top limits reservoir pressure to 95 psi and is also where trapped air is bled off.

The quantity a reservoir shows depends on the state of its system. When the system pressurizes, the accumulator takes fluid from the reservoir; when actuators extend, their rods take more. The reservoir placards are therefore read with the system pressurized to 2,700 psi or more and the flaps, slats and spoilers retracted and the brakes off or parked. A serviced aircraft reads a little over half scale on the flight engineer's gauges: about 6.5, 6.25 and 6.7 gallons on systems 1, 2 and 3.

The **low-level switch** in each reservoir operates at about 1 gallon. In the aircraft it shuts down any reversible motor pump connected to that system, so that a system that has lost its fluid cannot draw a healthy one into driving a dry pump. The system 3 reservoir also carries the two level switches that work the elevator shutoff valve (see [System 3 protection](#system-3-protection)).

Each system has one accumulator: a welded steel sphere of 198 cubic inches divided by a bladder, with dry nitrogen precharged to 1,000 psi on one side and system fluid on the other. Below 1,000 psi the bladder fills the sphere and it holds no fluid. Above it, fluid compresses the gas and is stored under pressure. The accumulator smooths pump ripple, absorbs pressure surges, covers the instant between a sudden demand and the compensator's response, and keeps the reservoir pressurized for a while after the pumps stop.

The stored fluid follows the gas law. For a slow, isothermal change pressure times gas volume is constant, so at 3,000 psi the gas occupies a third of the sphere and the other two thirds, 132 cubic inches, is fluid. A rapid charge is closer to adiabatic and stores somewhat less, about 110 cubic inches. The important consequence is how little of it is available at a useful pressure:

Sixteen cubic inches is about a quarter of a quart. A serviceable system's internal leakage of roughly three quarters of a gallon per minute is about 3 cubic inches per second, so the accumulator alone keeps a system above 2,400 psi for about five seconds. That is why the PRESS LO lights come on so soon after a system's last pump stops, and why the accumulator is a buffer against seconds of excess demand rather than a reserve for flight. Below the precharge only the stiffness of the fluid and the lines remains, and the last of the pressure goes almost at once.

children.title: Relief valves, filters and check valves

blocks.content: A spring-loaded poppet relief valve at each system manifold protects the system against overpressure, which in practice means a pump compensator that has failed with its pump at full stroke. The valve cracks at about 3,600 psi, is fully open at about 3,700 psi with about 40 gpm going to return, and reseats no lower than 3,400 psi. The gauge then sits above 3,500 psi, and all the flow the relief valve passes is turned into heat. This is why the overpressure procedure removes the failed pump rather than leaving the relief valve to carry it.

Each system has six filters: one in each engine pump's pressure line and one in each case-drain line at the engine hydraulic manifold, and two in the return lines at the system manifold. The elements are non-bypassing, so a clogged filter restricts flow rather than letting dirt through. A pop-up differential-pressure button on each filter head shows maintenance a clogged element; the buttons are locked out below about 29 °C, because cold, thick fluid would raise them on a clean filter. None of this is indicated in the cockpit.

Check valves at each pump outlet, at the engine firewall and in the return lines keep fluid moving the right way and stop a failed component or an open line from draining the rest of a system. In the aircraft a combination relief and bypass valve in each accumulator line also closes as accumulator pressure falls through about 1,500 psi after shutdown, trapping fluid so that the accumulator keeps the reservoir pressurized for some time.

Most of the heat comes from the engine-driven pumps themselves. Their losses leave in the case-drain flow, so the hottest fluid in a system is in the case-drain line returning to the reservoir, and it sheds heat through the reservoir walls and the suction lines on its way back to the pumps. The rest of the plumbing, every pressure and return line in the airframe, adds more cooling surface. No dedicated cooler is fitted, so fluid temperature reflects how hard a system is working and how healthy its pumps are.

In cruise a normally operating system shows between about 0 °C and 60 °C. The temperature gauge has a yellow arc from 60 °C to 100 °C and a red line at 100 °C. Anything that throttles flow at high pressure for a long time heats the fluid: a pump with excessive internal leakage, flow through a relief valve, an engine pump dead-headed by a motor pump holding its system above the pump's own setting, or a non-reversible motor pump running continuously, whose motor side draws on the donor system and heats it. The case-drain TEMP HI lights catch a hot pump before the bulk fluid gets hot.

A cable-operated ball valve in each system's suction line (in the inboard leading edge of each wing for systems 1 and 3, in the aft accessory compartment for system 2) closes when that engine's FIRE handle is pulled. It stops hydraulic fluid flowing into the nacelle of a burning engine. That engine's pumps then stop delivering, while the rest of the system keeps its pressure from the accumulator, the motor pumps and, on system 3, the auxiliary pumps. See [Fire protection](fire-protection).

sections.title: Auxiliary pumps
sections.summary: Two AC electric pumps in system 3: ground power for the hydraulics, and the emergency source in flight.

blocks.content: Two AC motor-driven, variable-displacement pumps in the right main gear wheel well pressurize system 3, the only system with an electric pump. Each runs on 115/200 V AC, 400 Hz three-phase power and is rated at about 8 gpm at 2,200 psi or 6 gpm at 2,750 psi, a fraction of one engine pump's output. Their normal supply is the AC ground service bus, which is fed from external power or from generator bus 2 (see [Electrical](electrical)). AUX PUMP 1 is labeled **ADG** because the air-driven generator can power it when all normal electrical power is lost.

They have three jobs. On the ground with the engines stopped they are the source of all hydraulic power: they pressurize system 3 directly, and through the reversible motor pumps systems 1 and 2. They provide brake and steering pressure for towing. And AUX PUMP 1 is the last source of system 3 pressure in flight if every engine-driven pump is lost. One pump brings system 3 to pressure in a few seconds, two do it faster, and with little demand a system on its auxiliary pumps reads much like one on its engine pumps. Their small output is meant for ground work and for keeping the flight controls powered, not for heavy simultaneous demands.

The flight engineer controls each pump with its own spring-loaded START/STOP switch, AUX PUMP 1 (ADG) and AUX PUMP 2, and the blue AUX HYD PUMP 1 ON and AUX HYD PUMP 2 ON lights show each pump running. The pilots' overhead AUX HYD PUMPS switch starts or stops both pumps together; the three switches act on the same two pumps, and whichever was used last decides.

The AUX PUMP 1 (ADG) and AUX PUMP 2 switchlights on the overhead HYD panel start and stop the pumps in either controller mode; each shows a blue ON while its pump runs, and HYD AUX PUMP ON appears on the EAD.

In the aircraft, deploying the ADG with the ADG switch at HYD puts the turbine's output on AUX PUMP 1, which then pressurizes system 3 without crew action; moving the switch to R EMER ELEC gives the ADG to the right emergency AC bus instead and stops the pump. The turbine can power one load or the other, never both. See [Simulation notes](#simulation-notes) for how the simulation powers AUX PUMP 1 after a loss of all engines.

sections.title: Reversible motor pumps
sections.summary: The 1-3 and 2-3 units: power, never fluid, between system 3 and systems 1 and 2.

blocks.content: The 1-3 and 2-3 **reversible motor pumps** let a pressurized system power a depressurized one without exchanging a drop of fluid. Each unit couples system 3 to system 1 or system 2, and either side can drive the other. They exist chiefly for engine failure: an engine that stops takes both of its system's pumps with it, and the motor pump restores that system from a healthy one. They are also how the auxiliary pumps reach systems 1 and 2 on the ground. Both units are in the center wheel well.

blocks.alt: Functional diagram of one DC-10 reversible motor pump unit (1-3 shown): a fixed-displacement hydraulic unit on the system 3 side and a variable-displacement unit on the system 1 side joined by a common drive shaft; on each side a motor-operated shutoff valve in the pressure line, a flow control valve, suction, return and case-drain connections, and the pressure switch on the maintenance pressure line. Two panels: system 3 driving system 1 (system 3 side labeled MOTOR, arrows of fluid through it to return; system 1 side labeled PUMP, drawing from the system 1 reservoir and delivering into the system 1 pressure line), and the reverse. A note that no fluid crosses between the two sides.
blocks.title: Reversible motor pump
blocks.caption: Whichever side has the pressure becomes the motor. The shaft carries torque across; the fluid stays at home.

blocks.content: Each unit is two hydraulic machines on one shaft: a fixed-displacement unit on the system 3 side and a variable-displacement unit on the system 1 (or 2) side. Each side has a motor-operated shutoff valve in its pressure line, and both valves open and close together on one command. A flow control valve on each side limits the flow through whichever side is acting as the motor.

With the valves open, the side connected to the higher pressure becomes a **motor**: its fluid flows through it to return and turns the shaft. The other side, turned by the shaft, becomes a **pump**: it draws from its own reservoir and delivers into its own pressure line. Direction is set entirely by the pressure difference. A differential of roughly 100 to 150 psi is enough to set the unit turning, and if the pressures reverse, so does the unit. When the driven system reaches pressure and its demand stops, the torques balance and the unit stops delivering; it supplies only what the driven system uses.

The unit transmits torque, not fluid. A hydraulic machine of displacement D working across a pressure difference Δp exerts a torque proportional to D × Δp, so the pressure the pumping side can reach is roughly the driving pressure scaled by the ratio of the two displacements, less friction and leakage; the variable-displacement half lets that ratio adjust. Driven from a 3,000 psi system, the driven side delivers between about 2,600 and 3,300 psi, and a fully pressurized donor brings a dead system to 3,000 psi in about three seconds. A system on a motor pump may therefore read a little differently from one on its engine pumps, because the two sources regulate differently.

Power is conserved, less losses: every gallon per minute delivered into the driven system costs the donor's pumps somewhat more than a gallon per minute at its own pressure, so the donor system works harder. A donor system can carry its own users and a motor pump's load together, but heavy simultaneous demands on both systems are shared out of one engine's pumps.

If a motor pump holds a system above the setting of that system's own engine pumps, the engine pumps go to zero stroke and stay there, dead-headed, with only their case flow to cool them, and the system's temperature rises over time. This is why a motor pump valve that will not close is a defect to act on even though no pressure is lost.

children.title: Control from the flight engineer's panel

blocks.content: Each unit has a three-position selector on the flight engineer's hydraulic panel, **1-3 PUMP** and **2-3 PUMP**, marked ARM, OFF and ON.

blocks.title: Motor pump selector
rows: Valves open. The unit transfers power continuously, in whichever direction the pressures demand.
Valves driven closed. The unit is inoperative, whatever the system pressures.
Valves under automatic control: both units open while any engine is below 45 % N2 or the automatic slat extension is operating.

blocks.content: Two automatic signals override the selector whatever its position: an auto-slat extension opens the valves even at OFF, and a reservoir low-level switch on either side, or a deployed ADG with the ADG switch at HYD, closes them even at ON.

ARM is the normal position from after engine start to landing, so that an engine failure on takeoff is covered without crew action: as the failed engine runs down through 45 % N2, both units open and stay open. On the ground with the engines stopped every engine is below 45 % N2, so ARM opens both units and the auxiliary pumps carry all three systems. The engine failure procedure nevertheless selects the motor pump supporting the failed engine ON. In the simulation ARM works on system pressure instead and makes an armed unit cycle; see [Simulation notes](#simulation-notes).

The pilots' overhead HYD FLT CONTROL panel carries a second set of controls for the same valves, for maintenance: the guarded **1-3 PUMP** and **2-3 PUMP** pushbuttons (legend PUMP ON) beside **SYS 3 ISOL**, placarded DO NOT USE IN FLIGHT. Their wiring has three features that matter if one is ever found selected:

items: An overhead PUMP ON opens its unit's valves directly, whatever the flight engineer's selector says, even at OFF.

Each overhead PUMP ON also removes power from the **other** unit's flight engineer selector: overhead 1-3 PUMP ON takes away the F/E 2-3 PUMP selector, and overhead 2-3 PUMP ON the F/E 1-3. This is how maintenance pressurizes one system's flight controls at a time.
SYS 3 ISOL removes power from both flight engineer selectors, at ON as well as at ARM, so both units close unless held open from the overhead panel.

blocks.title: Motor pump valve logic
rows: Open while any engine is below 45 % N2 or the slats are auto-extended

blocks.content: The blue **1-3/2-3 PUMP VALVE OPEN** light on the flight engineer's upper panel comes on while the shutoff valves of either unit are in transit or disagree with their selector, and while either unit is operating, that is, actually passing power (a pressure switch on its pump side makes at about 600 psi). Every selector movement therefore flashes it, and a valve that sticks open keeps it on with its selector at OFF.

children.title: Control by the MD-10 hydraulic system controller

blocks.content: On the MD-10 the hydraulic system controller (HSC) commands the motor pumps. In its automatic mode the crew have no control of them: the controller runs them by the **phase of flight**, which it derives from whether the aircraft is on the ground, the engine FUEL switches, the airspeed, the altitude and the gear, flap and slat positions.

blocks.title: HSC phases of flight and the motor pumps
rows: On the ground, all engine FUEL switches OFF
On the ground, any engine FUEL switch ON, airspeed 80 kt or less
Both on while any engine is below 45 % N2
On the ground above 80 kt with any FUEL switch ON; or airborne at or below 17,750 ft with the slats, flaps or gear extended
Both on while any engine is below 45 % N2. Each on while a system of its pair cannot be held up by its own engine pumps (both pumps reading low)
Gear, flaps and slats retracted, or above 17,750 ft

blocks.content: The controller never reads the pressure it restores. Its two reasons for running a motor pump are an engine below 45 % N2 and a system whose two engine pumps both read low at their own outlet switches, and a pump that is not delivering reads low whatever the motor pump does to the system. Once on, a motor pump therefore stays on, steadily, until the condition that started it has gone.

items: During engine start both motor pumps run from the moment the first engine is running until the last is above 45 % N2.
With an engine shut down on the ground, for a two-engine taxi, both run.
A system that loses its engine pumps on the takeoff roll, or in the air in the land phase, is restored at once.
A system lost during taxi is left down until the takeoff roll passes 80 kt.
A system lost in cruise is left down until the aircraft enters the land phase.

blocks.content:
With the controller in MANUAL (SYSTEM SELECT pushed), each **1-3 RMP** and **2-3 RMP** switchlight opens its unit when pushed in and closes it when pushed again. In AUTO the switchlights have no effect.

The switchlight's blue **ON** shows the command, not the valve; the controller's command, in AUTO. Amber **DISAG** shows the valves not where they were commanded, for example stuck open with the pump commanded off. The HYD synoptic draws each unit as a pair of valves (see [HYD synoptic](#md10-hyd-synoptic)).

children.title: The 2-3 pump and the air refueling supply

blocks.content: On the KC-10 the 2-3 motor pump has a second role. The boom and the centerline drogue reel draw from an **alternate supply** fed by system 2: its own manifold behind a check valve, with an accumulator and an auxiliary reservoir. For boom or drogue refueling the flight engineer selects 2-3 PUMP ON when the boom operator's BOOM/DROGUE HYD PRSRZ light comes on, so that system 3 backs system 2 through the pump.

If system 2 loses its fluid, the system 2 reservoir's low-level switch closes an isolation valve on the system 2 side of the 2-3 pump. The pump then drives only the alternate supply, from system 3, so the boom keeps working while system 2 stays down. If the auxiliary reservoir runs low, its own switch stops the 2-3 pump whatever its switches say, so that a leak in the boom system cannot run the pump dry. See [Air refueling systems](air-refueling-systems).

sections.title: Rudder standby power
sections.summary: The 2-1 and 3-2 non-reversible motor pumps keep each rudder segment, and one stabilizer trim motor, powered after a system loss.

blocks.content: The two rudder segments are the only primary surfaces on a single system each: the upper rudder on system 1 and the lower rudder on system 2. Each is backed by a **non-reversible motor pump** that powers it from another system: the **2-1** pump (driven by system 2, for system 1's upper rudder and stabilizer trim motor 2) and the **3-2** pump (driven by system 3, for system 2's lower rudder). Together they are called rudder standby power. The 2-1 pump is in the aft fuselage compartment, the 3-2 pump in the aft accessory compartment.

Unlike the reversible motor pumps, these do not pressurize a whole system. Each supplies a small **standby loop**: the supply to its rudder actuator (and, for the 2-1 pump, to the stabilizer trim's control valve 2), fed from its own system through a check valve and provided with a small compensator reservoir for the motor pump. While the system is healthy the loop simply rides on it. When the system fails, the check valve keeps the motor pump's output in the loop, so the rudder goes on working while the rest of the failed system stays down. That is deliberate: the failed system's gauge and lights still tell the truth, and a leak in it is not fed.

Each motor pump has a pressure-operated shutoff valve that senses the system it assists. It opens when that system falls below about 2,000 psi and closes when it recovers above about 2,200 psi, and the donor system must itself be above about 1,500 psi to drive the pump. Rated output is 2,800 psi at 8 gpm, enough for a rudder actuator and a trim motor, and a restrictor on the motor side keeps the pump from overspeeding. Engagement is hydro-mechanical; no controller is involved.

blocks.title: Rudder standby power
rows: Upper rudder; stabilizer trim motor 2 (control valve 2)
Standby power disarmed; compensator low; pump failed; system 2 lost
System 3, behind the elevator shutoff valve

blocks.content:
The **RUDDER STBY PWR** switch on the flight engineer's panel is ARM or OFF, and ARM is its normal position from the cockpit preparation to shutdown. OFF disarms both pumps. Its relays are de-energized to arm: if the switch's circuit loses power, both pumps stay armed. A low compensator level closes that pump's shutoff valve to stop it cavitating.

The amber **RUD STBY PWR OFF** light shows that either or both motor pumps are inoperative: the switch at OFF, a compensator low, or a pump failed. It stays out when a pump is merely starved because its donor system has failed or the elevator shutoff valve has cut the 3-2 pump's supply. The light is therefore not a test of whether a rudder segment is powered: check the rudder itself, as the failure procedures do.

A motor pump running continuously draws on its donor system and heats it. After a system 1 or system 2 failure with RUDDER STBY PWR at ARM, monitor the donor system's temperature; the procedures allow the switch to be set OFF in cruise and returned to ARM before approach.

The MD-10 has no rudder standby switch: both pumps are always armed in flight. A pump that is inoperative is shown as RUD STBY UPR OFF or RUD STBY LWR OFF on the EAD, and a rudder segment with no supply from its system or its standby pump as RUDDER UPR INOP, RUDDER LWR INOP or RUDDER BOTH INOP.

Lower: the same arrangement for system 2's lower rudder loop, with the 3-2 pump's motor fed from system 3 downstream of the elevator shutoff valve. Show the RUDDER STBY PWR arming relay on each shutoff valve and the compensator low-level switches. Annotate: engages below about 2,000 psi in the assisted system, output 2,800 psi.

sections.title: System 3 protection
sections.summary: The elevator shutoff valve that keeps system 3 alive after tail damage, and the flight control bypass valve used on the ground.

blocks.content: On 19 July 1989 the fan disk of a DC-10-10's number 2 engine failed in cruise. Fragments passing through the tail severed lines of all three hydraulic systems where they converge near the horizontal stabilizer, and all three systems emptied. With no power to any flight control surface, the crew steered the aircraft to Sioux City using the thrust of the two wing engines alone. Douglas responded with a service bulletin (SB 29-128) that keeps enough of system 3 to fly with if the tail is damaged, by isolating system 3's lines into the tail before the system can empty.

The installation has four parts: a motor-operated shutoff valve in the system 3 supply to both inboard elevators and to the 3-2 motor pump, in the aft fuselage; a check valve in the matching return line, so that a broken line aft of the valve cannot drain the system backwards; two level switches on the system 3 reservoir cover; and a cockpit indication of the valve's closed position.

The switches read reservoir quantity. When system 3 falls to 19 quarts (4.75 gallons), the lower switch drives the valve closed. The valve reopens only when the reservoir is above a second, slightly higher switch, which in service means when maintenance has refilled the system. Between the two switches neither side of the valve motor is powered and the valve stays where it is; with no electrical power at all it also stays where it is. The indication comes on when the valve reaches its closed position.
Closure lights the amber **HYD SYS 3 ELEV OFF** light on the flight engineer's upper panel, the MASTER CAUTION lights and the HYD cue light.
Closure lights the MASTER CAUTION lights and the HYD cue light (see [Simulation notes](#simulation-notes) for the flight engineer's HYD SYS 3 ELEV OFF light).
Closure displays **HYD 3 ELEV OFF** on the EAD.

A leak **downstream** of the valve, in the tail, stops when the valve closes: the rest of system 3 keeps its remaining fluid and its pressure. A leak **upstream** cannot be isolated and empties the system, closing the valve on its way down. With the valve closed and systems 1 and 2 working, the only losses are system 3's half of the two inboard elevator actuators and the 3-2 standby for the lower rudder.

With systems 1 and 2 lost as well, the valve is what leaves the crew any control: pitch through the stabilizer trim at half rate (motor 1, on system 3 forward of the valve), roll through the right inboard, left inboard and right outboard ailerons, the slats, and nose-wheel steering after landing. All elevators are then inoperative.

blocks.alt: Schematic of the system 3 elevator shutoff installation: system 3 reservoir with the two level switches on its cover (lower switch at 19 quarts drives the valve closed, upper switch drives it open), the system 3 manifold, the motor-operated shutoff valve in the aft fuselage feeding the left and right inboard elevator power units and the 3-2 non-reversible motor pump, the return-line check valve, and the HYD SYS 3 ELEV OFF light fed from the valve's closed-limit switch. Shade the part of system 3 that remains powered with the valve closed (ailerons, slats, stabilizer trim motor 1, spoiler panel 3, landing gear, brakes, steering).
blocks.title: System 3 elevator shutoff valve
blocks.caption: A leak in the tail costs system 3 only the lines behind the valve.

blocks.content: System 3 is pressurized for much ground maintenance, often only to work the gear or the brakes. A two-position, motor-driven **flight control bypass valve** in the system 3 manifold lets maintenance keep system 3's flight control actuators still while the rest of the system is pressurized. In its bypass position it shuts the pressure port to the flight control line and connects that line to return. The landing gear, brakes, steering, auxiliary pumps and both reversible motor pumps are upstream and unaffected. The 3-2 motor pump takes its supply through the elevator shutoff valve, downstream of the bypass valve, so it loses its supply as well. With no electrical power the valve stays where it is.

The valve is selected with the guarded **SYS 3 ISOL** pushbutton on the pilots' overhead HYD FLT CONTROL panel, placarded DO NOT USE IN FLIGHT. The ISOL legend lights when the valve reaches its bypass position, and selecting ISOL also removes power from both of the flight engineer's motor pump selectors. All three HYD FLT CONTROL legends must be out during cockpit preparation; if any is on, call maintenance.

On the MD-10 the valve is commanded by maintenance through the MCDU on the ground; the crew has no control of it. HYD SYS 3 ISOL on the EAD shows it out of its normal open position, and the aircraft cannot be dispatched in that state.

blocks.title: Hydraulic users by system

blocks.content: Each aileron and elevator surface has a tandem power control unit: two pistons on one rod, each in its own cylinder on its own system, each with its own servo valve. Both systems normally share the load. With one system lost the surface still moves through its full range on the other, more slowly and with half the hinge-moment capacity. A surface whose two systems are both lost cannot be moved. An actuator half needs about 1,500 psi or more to count as powered. The crew's controls and the autopilot servos act through these same units (see [Flight controls](flight-controls)).

With no pressure, a surface goes where gravity and the air put it: the elevators droop trailing edge down, the inboard ailerons float trailing edge down, the mass-balanced outboard ailerons hold where they are, and a rudder segment trails with the relative wind, even parked in a crosswind on the ramp. The outboard ailerons are locked at neutral while the flaps and slats are retracted, and unlock when either extends or the main gear alternate extension lever is raised.

Each spoiler panel has one actuator on one system, arranged so that a system loss removes the same panels on both wings and spoiler operation stays symmetric. The panels receive their roll and speedbrake commands through two spoiler drive servos (the mixers), one in each main gear wheel well: the left one works from system 1 or system 2, the right one from system 1 or system 3. One serves three panels on each wing and the other the remaining two. A panel with pressure but no working drive servo gets no roll or speedbrake command, although the ground spoiler function, which bypasses the mixers, still extends it. FedEx's procedure for the loss of systems 1 and 2 expects panel 3 on each wing to remain operative. The simulation's arrangement differs in that case; see [Simulation notes](#simulation-notes).

The horizontal stabilizer is driven through a jackscrew by two hydraulic motors summed in a differential gearbox: motor 1 through control valve 1 on system 3 (primary and alternate trim), and motor 2 through control valve 2 on system 1's standby loop (primary and autopilot trim). Either motor alone drives the stabilizer at half rate. Each motor has a brake that holds it when its pressure falls below about 200 psi, so a stabilizer with no hydraulic power stays where it is.

Each flap segment is powered by systems 1 and 2, and the slats by systems 1 and 3, each pair able to drive its surfaces through their full travel. On one system the drive runs at a reduced rate; with both of a pair lost the surfaces stay where they are.

The landing gear (retraction and extension actuators, door actuators, downlocks and truck positioning) is on **system 3 alone**. There is no alternate hydraulic source for the gear: if system 3 cannot be restored by a motor pump or the auxiliary pumps, the gear is extended by gravity with the alternate extension handles and cannot be retracted. See [Landing gear](landing-gear).

Each main-gear brake has two sets of pistons fed by two independent **brake systems**: brake system 1 is supplied by hydraulic system 1, brake system 2 by hydraulic system 3. There is no brake system on hydraulic system 2. Either brake system alone can stop the aircraft at maximum landing weight. Each has its own anti-skid valves and its own accumulators, precharged with nitrogen to 1,000 psi: two per brake system on the DC-10 and KC-10, three on the MD-10.

The brake accumulators fill from their hydraulic system through a one-way restrictor and a check valve in the brake manifold. The check valve keeps their charge when the hydraulic system is lost or shut down, which gives a reserve of about six brake applications and keeps the parking brake set after shutdown. The restrictor limits how fast they draw on the system: refilling after a full application takes a few seconds, and holding the brakes on costs the system almost nothing once the pistons are filled. The autobrake, where fitted, uses brake system 1 alone in its landing modes and both brake systems for a rejected takeoff.

Nose-wheel steering takes pressure from system 1 directly and from system 3 through the nose gear down line, downstream of the gear selector, so system 3 reaches it only with the gear selected down normally (not after an alternate extension until the lever is stowed). On either system alone, rudder pedal steering is normal but tiller steering is limited to about 25° towards the side of the lost system: to the left with system 1 lost, to the right with system 3 lost, against 68° the other way. See [Landing gear](landing-gear).

blocks.content: The AR fuel pumps are hydraulic motors, and together they are a large load: an offload with several pumps running costs their systems a great deal of flow, and the engines the power to make it. The pump selection priority in the normal procedures spreads that load and avoids running more than two pumps from system 3 where possible. See [Air refueling systems](air-refueling-systems).
The KDC-10's boom has no alternate supply: with HYD SEL at BOOM it draws directly on system 2, and its hoist is on system 3. See [Air refueling systems](air-refueling-systems).

children.title: Not powered by the main systems

blocks.content: The thrust reversers do not use the hydraulic systems (see [Engines](engines)). The main deck cargo door, where fitted, has its own electric hydraulic power pack and a hand pump, independent of systems 1 to 3 (see [Doors and cabin](doors-and-cabin)).
The air tankers' retardant tank doors are worked by their own hydraulic power packs (see [Aerial firefighting](aerial-firefighting)).

The flight engineer operates the hydraulic system from the hydraulic panel and monitors it there and on the status lights of upper panel No. 2. The pilots have the auxiliary pump switch, the maintenance HYD FLT CONTROL panel and the HYD cue light on the overhead, and their own pressure gauges.
The MD-10 crew control the hydraulic system from the HYD control panel on the forward overhead panel and monitor it on the HYD synoptic and the EIS alerts.

The panel is laid out in three columns, one per system, each with its pressure, quantity and temperature gauges, the two pump switches with their PRESS LO and TEMP HI lights, and, between the columns, the motor pump selectors, the rudder standby controls and the auxiliary pump switches. It is on the flight engineer's lower panel on the DC-10-10, -15 and -30 and the KC-10, and on upper panel No. 3 on the DC-10-40.

blocks.content: The flight engineer sets up and checks the hydraulic system at each stage of the flight. The items below are the hydraulic parts of the normal procedures, gathered in one place with the reason for each; the checklists themselves are in [Normal procedures](normal-procedures). The Virtual Crew flies the same flow when it is acting as flight engineer (see [Virtual crew](virtual-crew)).

blocks.content:
The opening ARM-OFF cycles prove that each motor pump's valves move and that the valve light follows them, before anything is pressurized. The auxiliary pumps then bring up system 3.

The two rudder checks in the cockpit preparation are a quiet test of rudder standby power. With only the auxiliary pumps running, system 2 is still dead, so the 3-2 pump engages from system 3 and the lower rudder moves to center. Arming the 2-3 pump then brings up system 2, and with system 1 still dead the 2-1 pump engages and the upper rudder centers. The 1-3 pump finally brings up system 1.

With the left pumps off and the engines stopped, all six PRESS LO lights are on even though the systems are pressurized: each light watches its own pump, and no engine pump is delivering.

During each start, once the engine has stabilized at idle, the flight engineer checks the HYD PRESS gauges in the white band and the left pump PRESS LO lights going out as the left pumps are switched on, and confirms that one engine pump in each system gives at least 2,800 psi.

blocks.content: Switching the right pumps off proves each left pump on its own; returning them to AUTO restores the standby. The motor pumps are armed for takeoff to give adequate pressure in all systems if an engine fails during the takeoff.

blocks.content: If the 1-3/2-3 PUMP VALVE OPEN light stays on with both motor pump selectors at OFF, a valve is stuck open: maintenance is required. If the flight goes ahead, set the motor pumps ON for takeoff and landing and OFF for the rest of the flight.
In climb and cruise the flight engineer scans the gauges and lights; temperatures between about 0 °C and 60 °C are normal in cruise. Before descent the motor pump selectors are confirmed at ARM.

OFF (right pumps take over; left PRESS LO lights on)

blocks.content: This check proves every engine pump on its own before the next flight. Any pump not giving at least 2,800 psi is written up; a takeoff is permitted if either pump in each system gives 2,800 psi. If system 1 or system 3 is being held up by its motor pump, because its engine is shut down or has failed, that motor pump stays at ARM or ON to keep full nose-wheel steering and both brake systems. With engine 2 shut down for a two-engine taxi, system 2 is carried by the 2-3 pump in the same way.

items.action: START, if brake pressure or towing requires

blocks.content: Once the engines have run down, each system bleeds down to near zero within about half a minute and all PRESS LO lights come on. The brake accumulators keep the parking brake set.

The hydraulic system controller (HSC) runs the MD-10's hydraulics in AUTO for the whole flight. If the controller fails it reverts to manual, and the crew operate the pumps from the HYD panel for the rest of the flight. In AUTO it:

items: Keeps each system's left engine pump on and its right pump armed, with the same automatic standby circuit as the DC-10 bringing the right pump on whenever the system falls below 2,400 psi or the left pump fails.
Runs the two reversible motor pumps by the phase of flight (see [Control by the MD-10 hydraulic system controller](#rmp-control-md10)).
Leaves the auxiliary pumps to the crew.

blocks.content: On the ground before engine start, start the auxiliary pumps with the AUX PUMP switchlights to pressurize system 3. In AUTO the controller keeps the motor pumps off while parked; to pressurize systems 1 and 2 from system 3, for example for a flight control check, select MANUAL and push the 1-3 RMP and 2-3 RMP switchlights, then return the controller to AUTO before engine start.

As the first engine comes up the controller enters its taxi phase and both RMP ON legends light, with HYD 1-3 RMP ON and HYD 2-3 RMP ON on the EAD: the motor pumps carry the systems whose engines are not yet running. They go out when the last engine passes 45 % N2. With an engine shut down for taxi they come on again. On the takeoff roll above 80 kt and in the land phase the controller restores at once any system that loses both its engine pumps; in cruise it leaves such a system down until the land phase. After landing it returns to the taxi phase below 80 kt, and to the parked configuration a few seconds after the last engine has run down below 45 % N2.

On the synoptic, a cyan mark appears on each reservoir when its engine first reaches idle, recording the quantity at that moment. A reservoir level that falls away from its mark during the flight is the first sign of a leak.

In **MANUAL** the controller passes the crew's switchlights straight through. Each L PUMP runs unless its switchlight is pushed to OFF; each R PUMP runs continuously unless pushed to OFF, since there is no automatic standby in this mode; each RMP opens only while its switchlight is pushed in. If the controller reverts to manual by itself, the SELECT and MANUAL legends both light and SEL HYD SYS MAN appears: push the SYSTEM switchlight to lock the system in MANUAL, then set the pumps as the situation requires.

blocks.title: Interactions
rows: Engine N2 drives the engine pumps; their flow capacity follows it and stops below about 5 % N2. The pumps' load is taken from the engine's accessory gearbox. Pulling an engine FIRE handle shuts down the engine and with it that system's engine pumps. A failed engine's system is restored by its motor pump.

The engine pump depressurizing valves need 28 V DC (battery bus) to switch a pump off; without it the pumps pressurize. The auxiliary pumps run on the AC ground service bus; AUX PUMP 1 can be powered by the ADG. Rudder standby power arms when its circuit loses power. Each gauge has its own indicator supply.

Every surface actuator, the stabilizer trim motors, the flaps, the slats and the spoiler mixers draw on the systems as listed in [Hydraulic users](#users). Surface rates fall when an actuator half loses its system.
Gear actuation is on system 3 only. Brake systems 1 and 2 are fed from hydraulic systems 1 and 3 through their own accumulators. Nose-wheel steering uses system 1, and system 3 with the gear down.
PRESS LO, TEMP HI and HYD SYS 3 ELEV OFF light the MASTER CAUTION lights and the HYD cue (DC-10, KC-10). On the MD-10, hydraulic alerts appear on the EAD with the HYD cue switch.
KC-10: the alternate supply for the boom and drogue is fed from system 2 and the 2-3 motor pump; the boom hoist is on system 3; the AR fuel pumps are hydraulic motors on all three systems.

sections.title: Failures and non-normal operation
sections.summary: How the systems fail, what each failure costs, and what the crew sees and does.

blocks.content: The procedures themselves are in [Abnormal procedures](abnormal-procedures) and [Emergency procedures](emergency-procedures). This section explains what is behind them: how each kind of failure develops, what the aircraft loses with one, two or three systems gone, and how the indications tell the failures apart.

**Engine failure.** As N2 decays the engine's two pumps lose capacity and stop delivering below about 5 % N2; the right pump at AUTO cannot help, since it is on the same engine. The system bleeds down in seconds, both PRESS LO lights come on, and the system's motor pump is the way back: at ARM or ON it restores the system from system 3 (or system 3 from system 1 or 2). The system's fluid is intact, so a restored system is fully usable.

**Engine pump failure.** One pump stops delivering and its PRESS LO light stays on. If it is the left pump, the right pump at AUTO takes over; the system keeps its pressure and nothing else is lost. The failed pump is switched off.

**Failure of the automatic circuit.** The left pump stops and the right pump at AUTO does not answer. Pressure falls through 2,400 psi with both PRESS LO lights on, at a rate set by what the system is driving: within a few tens of seconds in flight with the controls moving. Selecting the R pump ON bypasses the automatic circuit and restores the system.

**Leak.** The pumps hold pressure while the reservoir empties, so the first sign is the quantity gauge falling (on the MD-10, the reservoir level leaving its cyan mark). When the reservoir is dry the pumps have nothing to draw and the pressure goes, quickly. A motor pump cannot restore a system with no fluid, and pumping into a leak only spreads fluid and heats pumps, so the procedure switches off the leaking system's engine pumps and its motor pump. Fluid is never drawn from another system. In system 3 the elevator shutoff valve closes at 4.75 gallons, which stops a leak in the tail.

**Overpressure.** A pump whose compensator fails high stays at full stroke past 3,025 psi, and the relief valve becomes the only limit: pressure settles between about 3,600 and 3,700 psi, above the gauge's normal band, and the relief flow heats the fluid. Switching the left pump off removes the failed compensator; the right pump at AUTO then takes over normally.

**Overheat.** A pump with excessive internal leakage heats its case drain (TEMP HI) and then the system fluid (the temperature gauge). Removing the heat means removing the pump: switching both of a system's engine pumps off stops it, and the system's motor pump can then keep it pressurized from another system.

**Motor pump valve stuck open.** The 1-3/2-3 PUMP VALVE OPEN light stays on with the selector at OFF (MD-10: DISAG). The unit will transfer power whenever the pressures differ, and can hold a system above its own engine pumps' setting so that they run dead-headed and heat up.

**Loss of pump control power.** With an ENG HYD PUMPS CONT circuit dead, all three pumps on that side pressurize and cannot be switched off. No pressure is lost; the crew loses the ability to depressurize those pumps.

**Standby pump failure.** A failed non-reversible motor pump, or one whose compensator is low, lights RUD STBY PWR OFF (MD-10: RUD STBY UPR OFF or LWR OFF). Nothing changes until the system it backs up fails, but from then on that rudder segment has no standby.

With one system lost every function remains, on its other source. Surfaces with one actuator half gone move more slowly and with less authority, the high-lift devices on that system run at a reduced rate (so they may need a lower speed to reach full extension), and the spoiler panels on that system are lost on both wings. The table assumes the system cannot be restored by a motor pump, as after a leak.

Each pair of losses has a different shape, which is why each has its own procedure. Use one hydraulic control at a time where possible, so that the surviving system's pumps are not asked for two large flows at once.

blocks.content: With systems 1 and 2 lost and the system 3 elevator shutoff valve closed, no elevator is powered. Pitch control is by stabilizer trim at half rate and by thrust.

The three-system architecture assumes the systems fail independently. The 1989 Sioux City accident showed the one place where they do not: an uncontained failure of the number 2 engine put fragments through the tail, where lines of all three systems run close together, and all three emptied. With no manual reversion there was no surface the crew could move. The aircraft was flown for some 40 minutes on the thrust of the two wing engines alone, using thrust together for pitch and differentially for roll and yaw, to a crash landing that most of those on board survived.

The design responses were aimed at keeping one system alive rather than at flying without any. The system 3 elevator shutoff valve isolates system 3's lines into the tail when its reservoir starts to empty, so that a leak behind the valve leaves system 3's ailerons, slats and stabilizer trim working (see [Elevator shutoff valve](#elevator-shutoff-valve)). The air-driven generator and AUX PUMP 1 give system 3 a source that needs no engine, and the reversible motor pumps can pass that pressure on to systems 1 and 2 if they still hold fluid.
With all three systems lost and no source left:

items: No flight control surface moves. The elevators droop, the inboard ailerons float down, the outboard ailerons hold where they are, and the rudders trail.
The stabilizer trim motors' brakes hold the stabilizer where it was.
The flaps and slats stay where they are.
The gear can only be lowered by gravity, with the alternate extension handles.
Braking is on the brake accumulators alone, a reserve of about six applications; there is no nose-wheel steering.
Control is by thrust: the crew's only remaining means of changing pitch, roll and yaw (see [Flight characteristics](flight-characteristics)).

blocks.content: A loss of all engines is a different case, because the systems keep their fluid. A windmilling engine still turns its pumps: above about 5 % N2 they deliver a small flow that can hold one system up while little is demanded, which is the basis of the procedure for operating on a single system powered by a windmilling engine. AUX PUMP 1 can power system 3, and through the motor pumps systems 1 and 2.

items: Each system is solved as a fluid network many times a second: pumps, accumulator, relief valve, internal leakage and the flow drawn by every surface actuator, the high-lift drives, the stabilizer trim, the gear and the brakes. Pressure falls only when the network says it should.

Engine pumps are pressure-compensated, their capacity follows N2 down to about 5 % N2, and the power they deliver loads their engine's accessory gearbox. The depressurizing valves fail to pressurizing on loss of their two control circuits.

Each engine pump has its own pressure switch (trip 2,400 psi, reset 2,800 psi) driving its PRESS LO light, so two lights of one system can disagree, as they do during the after-landing pump check. The right pump's automatic standby, with its 20-second hold, is modeled.
Internal leakage bleeds a system with no pump down in seconds: through 2,400 psi within about 5 to 8 seconds and below 1,000 psi within about half a minute, while the brake accumulators hold.

The reversible motor pumps transfer in whichever direction the pressures demand and cannot deliver into a system whose reservoir is dry. The overhead HYD FLT CONTROL panel is wired as in the aircraft, including the crossed override of the flight engineer's selectors and SYS 3 ISOL.
Rudder standby power: both standby loops, the pressure-operated engagement, the de-energize-to-arm relays, compensator low and the RUD STBY PWR OFF logic.
The system 3 elevator shutoff valve with its two reservoir level switches, its motor travel, and leaks upstream or downstream of it.
Every aileron, elevator and rudder actuator is modeled per system, and unpowered surfaces droop, float or trail; a dead rudder weathervanes on the ramp in a crosswind.
The MD-10 controller's phase-of-flight management of the motor pumps, and the KC-10's air refueling alternate supply.

DC-10 and KC-10 motor pumps at ARM open on low pressure in either system of the pair, not on the aircraft's N2 and auto-slat signals. An armed pump restoring a failed system therefore lifts it above 2,400 psi, closes, and opens again as soon as the system has bled back, so the system hovers near the bottom of the normal band and the 1-3/2-3 PUMP VALVE OPEN light comes and goes. On the ground with the engines stopped and the auxiliary pumps running, systems 1 and 2 sit near 2,400 to 2,500 psi with the valves cycling. Select ON when a system depends on its motor pump, or when a steady pressure is wanted, for example for a flight control check.

The right pump at AUTO is brought in by low system pressure (or a failed left pump) and released 20 seconds after the pressure recovers. With a left pump off this produces a regular cycle of about 25 seconds.

The motor pump shutoff valves move instantly, and the 1-3/2-3 PUMP VALVE OPEN light shows the valves open whether or not the unit is turning. The short flash of the aircraft's light while a valve travels is not seen.
The flow a motor pump can transfer is limited, so a system running on its motor pump recovers more slowly from large demands than one on its own engine pumps.

Reservoir quantity changes only with a leak. It does not change with pressurization, actuator positions or temperature, so lowering the gear cannot trip the system 3 elevator shutoff valve as it can in the aircraft.

Fluid temperature follows the outside air temperature slowly, over hours. The pumps' own heat and the heat of relief-valve flow are not modeled, so on a long flight at altitude the gauges drift towards and below 0 °C, and a hot system appears only with a failure.

The pump TEMP HI lights come on only with a pump overheat failure, which the EFB does not offer. The EFB's System temperature high failure heats the fluid and drives the temperature gauge, without the TEMP HI lights.
Brake force does not yet fall when a brake system's supply and accumulators are exhausted (see [Landing gear](landing-gear)).
Landing gear transit times do not depend on the flow available, and the gear takes less from system 3 than in the aircraft, so system 3's pressure barely dips during gear operation.
A hydraulic quantity or temperature gauge without indicator power reads zero. In the aircraft the quantity gauge freezes at its last reading and the temperature gauge goes below zero.

DC-10 and KC-10: the pilots' brake pressure gauges show hydraulic system 1 and 3 pressure. In the aircraft they read brake system pressure, which the accumulators hold up after the systems bleed down.

MD-10: the controller takes an engine at or above 45 % N2 as a FUEL switch ON, and an airspeed of 214 kt or less below 17,750 ft as the slats, flaps or gear being extended. A clean aircraft held below 214 kt below 17,750 ft is therefore in the land phase. A new phase is adopted only after it has held for about 2 seconds, and a system counts as having lost its engine pumps when both pump pressure switches have read low for about 2 seconds.
MD-10: in MANUAL the right pumps run continuously unless switched off; in the aircraft they remain armed.

The left spoiler drive servo (systems 1 and 2) serves panels 1, 3 and 5 and the right one (systems 1 and 3) panels 2 and 4. With systems 1 and 2 lost, this leaves no flight spoilers, where FedEx's procedure expects panel 3 to keep working; panel 3 still extends as a ground spoiler. With system 2 lost and the system 3 elevator shutoff valve closed, panel 3 keeps working, where FedEx lists it as inoperative.
The reservoir low-level switches (about 1 gallon) that shut down the motor pumps, the ADG's shutdown of the motor pumps, and the auto-slat command that opens them.
The ADG's automatic start of AUX PUMP 1. Select AUX PUMP 1 to START: with all three engines below about 50 % N2 it then keeps running on emergency AC power, whether or not the ADG is deployed.
The hydraulic fire shutoff valves. Pulling a FIRE handle stops the engine, and its pumps stop with it, but a windmilling engine's pumps go on delivering.

Pump overheating with both of a system's engine pumps depressurized for a long time, the heating of a donor system by a standby pump running continuously, and the relief and bypass valve that keeps the reservoirs pressurized after shutdown. The filters and their clog indicators are not represented.
Fluid viscosity: a cold-soaked system behaves like a warm one.
External hydraulic power. On the ground use the auxiliary pumps.

MD-10: the HYD PRESS TEST (the switchlight is inoperative) and the engine pump test after each start, with their alerts; the controller's own engine pump management by phase (turning off a pump with high pressure or depressurizing a hot or low system in cruise); and its quantity and ADG inhibits on the motor pumps. A pump overpressure therefore stays until the crew turn the pump off in MANUAL.
MD-10: the AUX HYD PUMP switchlight on the forward pedestal is inoperative; use the overhead AUX PUMP switchlights.
KC-10: the flight engineer's HYD SYS 3 ELEV OFF light is not fitted in this cockpit. The valve works, and its closure lights the HYD cue and MASTER CAUTION lights.
DC-10: the pilots' AUX HYD PUMPS ON light is not provided. The overhead AUX HYD PUMPS switch works; the flight engineer's lights show the pumps.

SYS 3 ISOL removes system 3 from the aileron and elevator actuators and the 3-2 standby pump, but not from the slats, spoiler panel 3 or stabilizer trim motor 1. On the KC-10 it does not operate the air refueling maintenance valve.
The loss of autopilot 2 pitch control when the elevator shutoff valve closes (DC-10, KC-10).
The nose-wheel steering angle limit on the captain's tiller with one system lost; steering is slower instead.
On the KC-10 the UARRSI receptacle does not load system 1.

parts.title: Flight Controls
parts.summary: Primary and secondary flight controls, high-lift devices, trim, spoilers and stall protection.

sections.title: Introduction
sections.summary: Fully powered, irreversible flight controls with artificial feel, on three independent hydraulic systems.

blocks.content:
Every flight control surface on the DC-10 family is moved by hydraulic power. The **primary flight controls** are the inboard and outboard ailerons, four elevator segments (an inboard and an outboard pair) and two rudders, upper and lower, each made of a forward and an aft segment. The **secondary flight controls** are the leading-edge slats, the inboard and outboard trailing-edge flaps, five spoiler panels on each wing and the adjustable horizontal stabilizer.

The crew's controls (control wheels, columns, rudder pedals, the flap/slat handle, the spoiler handle and the trim controls) are connected by closed-loop steel cables to the control valves of the hydraulic actuators. None of them is connected to a surface. The actuators are irreversible: air loads on a surface cannot move the cockpit controls, so all the forces the crew feel come from spring mechanisms designed to imitate them.

blocks.alt: Plan view of a DC-10-30 (long-span wing, center gear) from above, every flight control surface colored and labeled: inboard and outboard slats (eight segments each wing, the five outermost marked anti-iced), inboard and outboard flaps, spoiler panels 1 to 5 numbered inboard to outboard on each wing (panel 1 ahead of the inboard flap, 2 to 5 ahead of the outboard flap), inboard aileron between the flaps, outboard aileron at the tip, inboard and outboard elevators, the horizontal stabilizer pivot and jackscrew, and the upper and lower rudders each split into forward and aft segments. A small inset of the tail in side view shows the two-segment rudders.
blocks.title: Flight control surfaces
blocks.caption: The same surfaces on every DC-10, KC-10 and MD-10. The -10 and -15 have the shorter wing; the surface arrangement is unchanged.

blocks.content: The MD-10 conversion kept the DC-10 airframe's flight control system unchanged. What differs between the three aircraft is how the crew control and monitor it: the DC-10 and KC-10 have the flight engineer's panel, analog position indicators and lamps, while the MD-10 shows the same information on its system display (SD) and engine and alert display (EAD), and its flight control computers (FCCs) take over a few automatic functions.

A wide-body transport's control surfaces are too large, and their hinge moments at high speed too great, for a crew to move them directly. The DC-10 designers chose fully powered, irreversible controls, which brings three consequences that run through this whole part.

items: **There is no manual reversion.** With no cable to the surfaces, a surface with no hydraulic power cannot be moved by the crew at all. Safety therefore rests on hydraulic redundancy: every aileron, elevator, flap and slat is powered by two of the three hydraulic systems, the spoiler panels are spread across all three, and each rudder, which has a single system, has a standby pump that restores its pressure from another system. With any two systems lost, every axis keeps at least one powered surface.

**All feel is artificial.** Because the actuators block air loads from reaching the cockpit, the crew would feel nothing but cable friction. Spring feel units give the controls centering and a force gradient. The elevator's feel unit is varied with airspeed so that the column force needed to pull a given load factor stays roughly constant across the speed range.

**The autopilot drives the same actuators.** Its servo valves are built into the primary surface actuators, downstream of the cables. That is why the aircraft can still be flown through the autopilot after damage to the crew's cable runs (see [Failures](#failures)).

blocks.content: Hydraulic pressure also locks the surfaces. With the systems pressurized, the actuators hold every surface against gusts on the ground. With the systems depressurized, the surfaces are free and settle where gravity and the wind put them: the elevators and inboard ailerons hang trailing edge down on a parked aircraft, and the rudders trail with the wind.
The surfaces, actuators, hydraulic supplies, travel and rates are the same on all three aircraft. The differences are in crew interface and in a few automatic functions:

rows: ELEV FEEL selector (AUTO/MAN) and MAN SLEW selector, pilots' overhead; ELEV FEEL REF IAS indicator
One ELEV FEEL knob (2 LO, 1 LO, AUTO, 1 HI, 2 HI); ELF SPD shown on the SD CONFIG page

sections.title: Hydraulic power and actuation
sections.summary: Tandem power control units, which systems drive each surface, and what a surface does when it loses its supply.

blocks.content:
Each primary surface is driven by a **power control unit (PCU)**: a tandem actuator with two pistons on one rod, each piston in its own cylinder fed by a different hydraulic system. A control valve on the PCU meters fluid to the pistons. The crew's cable moves the valve's input lever; the actuator then drives the surface until the surface position, fed back mechanically to the valve, cancels the input. It is a follow-up servo: the surface goes where the input lever is, at a rate set by how much flow the valve can pass.

With the valve centerd, both cylinder ports are closed and the trapped fluid holds the surface rigidly. This is what makes the controls irreversible. The autopilot's servo valve and, on the rudders, the yaw damper's pistons act at the same summing linkage on the PCU, so their inputs move the surface without moving the cables.

blocks.alt: Functional diagram of hydraulic supply to the flight controls, systems 1, 2 and 3 color-coded (for example red, blue, green) as three vertical buses. Lines run to each PCU: left inboard elevator 2+3, right inboard elevator 1+3 (system 3 to both inboard elevators through the ELEV shutoff valve), outboard elevators 1+2, left inboard aileron 2+3, right inboard aileron 1+3, left outboard aileron 1+2, right outboard aileron 2+3, upper rudder from the system 1 standby loop with the 2-1 non-reversible motor-pump, lower rudder from the system 2 standby loop with the 3-2 motor-pump, spoiler panels 2 and 4 on system 1, 1 and 5 on system 2, 3 on system 3, flap drives on systems 1 and 2, slat drives on systems 1 and 3, stabilizer motor 1 on system 3 through control valve 1 and motor 2 on the system 1 standby loop through control valve 2. The RUDDER STBY PWR switch and both motor-pump shutoff valves are shown.

Hydraulic systems per surface

Standby: 2-1 non-reversible motor-pump, powered by system 2
Standby: 3-2 non-reversible motor-pump, powered by system 3
Either system moves them, at half rate
Either system moves them, at half rate
Used by every trim input except the autopilot
