blocks.content:
The arrangement is deliberate. The two inboard elevators share system 3 but each has a different partner, and the outboard pair shares systems 1 and 2, so any single system failure leaves all four elevators powered and any double failure leaves at least one pair. The ailerons follow the same pattern. Spoiler panels are spread across the three systems so that a system loss takes the same panels from both wings and never causes a spoiler asymmetry.

The two rudders are single-system surfaces, and the standby motor-pumps are what make that acceptable. Each **non-reversible motor-pump (NRMP)** is a hydraulic motor driven by one system, coupled to a pump that pressurizes a small, isolated loop of another system. When system 1 fails, the 2-1 motor-pump restores pressure to the upper rudder and stabilizer motor 2 loop from system 2 power, without any fluid crossing between systems. The 3-2 motor-pump does the same for the lower rudder. The RUDDER STBY PWR switch (ARM/OFF) on the flight engineer's panel controls both; see [Hydraulics](hydraulics) for the motor-pumps, their compensators and the RUD STBY PWR OFF light.

System 3's supply to the two inboard elevators passes through an **elevator shutoff valve** that closes automatically when the system 3 reservoir falls to a low level, so a leak in the tail cannot drain the whole system. The inboard elevators then run on their other system. The valve and its HYD SYS 3 ELEV OFF indication are described in [Hydraulics](hydraulics).

blocks.title: Rate, not travel
blocks.content: Losing one of a PCU's two systems roughly halves the surface's maximum rate but keeps its full travel: the remaining piston still drives the rod from stop to stop, only less quickly. A cylinder needs about 1,500 psi to contribute. Only when both of a surface's systems are lost does it stop following the controls.

A surface with no pressure on either cylinder follows gravity and the airflow. On the ground the elevators droop fully trailing edge down and the inboard ailerons hang about halfway down; the outboard ailerons are mass-balanced and stay where they were; the rudders center, or trail with a wind. In flight, an unpowered surface streamlines with the airflow. Spoiler panels have a **hold-down check valve** that stops a depressurized panel floating up, and an anti-cavitation valve that lets a deployed panel blow down to its retracted position under air load.

sections.title: Roll control
sections.summary: Inboard and outboard ailerons, the outboard aileron lockout, roll spoilers and aileron trim.

blocks.content: Roll control comes from four ailerons, helped on the down-going wing by the spoilers. The two control wheels are interconnected; their cable runs pass through the aileron load feel and centering mechanism, where the trim acts, to the four aileron PCUs, and to a spoiler drive servo in each main wheel well that feeds the spoiler mixers.

Each wing has an **inboard aileron**, between the inboard and outboard flaps, and an **outboard aileron** near the tip. Each moves about 20° either side of neutral. They work as a differential pair: for a roll to the left, the left ailerons go trailing edge up and the right ones trailing edge down.

The inboard ailerons work at all speeds. The outboard ailerons work only at low speed, when the high-lift devices are out; the rest of the time they are locked at neutral.

An aileron near the tip of a long, flexible wing has a large lever arm in roll, but at high dynamic pressure its hinge load twists the wing the opposite way: a trailing-edge-down aileron pushes the outer wing's leading edge down, which reduces the very lift increase it was meant to make. Above a certain speed the twist can cancel the aileron's effect or even reverse it, and it loads the outer wing in torsion. The DC-10 avoids this by locking the outboard ailerons faired at high speed and doing high-speed roll control with the inboard ailerons, which sit on the stiffer inner wing, and the spoilers, which do not twist the wing.

A mechanical **lockout mechanism** holds the outboard ailerons at neutral. It is released by an OR mechanism with cable inputs from the flap bus drum, the inboard slat drive drum and the alternate gear extension system. Because the drums follow the surfaces themselves, it is the position of the flaps and slats, not of the handle, that unlocks the ailerons.

Three consequences follow. An automatic slat extension moves only the outboard slats, so it does not unlock the outboard ailerons. If the flaps and slats fail retracted, the ailerons stay locked whatever the handle says, which is why the NO FLAP/NO SLAT landing procedure uses the alternate gear extension lever: raising it unlocks the outboard ailerons as well as dropping the gear. And with the ailerons locked, the surface position indicator's wing pointers can only reach half scale, because they show the sum of the inboard and outboard ailerons.
The flight control check before takeoff is not complete for the ailerons until the flaps and slats are out and the outboard ailerons are unlocked. Check for full scale on the wing pointers.

All five spoiler panels on each wing help in roll, in every mode of operation. A spoiler drive servo in each wheel well connects the aileron cable run to the spoiler mixer mechanism. As the wheel turns, the panels on the down-going wing rise in proportion, dumping lift on that wing; the panels on the up-going wing stay down.

The mixer adds the roll command mechanically to whatever the speedbrake handle is asking for:

items: **Speedbrakes out:** the down-going wing's panels extend further, up to their limit, and the up-going wing's panels retract toward stowed. Roll control stays available with the speedbrakes deployed.
**Ground spoilers out:** all panels are fully up, so the wheel retracts the panels on the up-going wing, which gives roll control for a crosswind rollout.
**Aileron trim beyond 5 units:** the excess is passed to the spoiler servo and raises the panels on the down-going wing (see [Aileron trim](#aileron-trim)).

blocks.content: The mixers are moved by hydraulic power. If a mixer loses its drive, the panels it serves get no roll or speedbrake command even if their own actuators still have pressure; the ground spoiler command does not go through the mixers. See [Spoilers and speedbrakes](#spoilers) for the panels themselves.

There are no trim tabs on the DC-10. Lateral trim works by moving the neutral point of the aileron load feel and centering mechanism: the mechanism then holds the ailerons at a new position with no force on the wheel. The AIL trim knob on the aft pedestal turns a cable drum that drives the trim actuator; there is no motor, no circuit breaker and no rate other than how fast the knob is turned. The trim needs no electrical power, although the ailerons still need hydraulic pressure to follow it.

items: The trim acts on the **inboard ailerons only**; the trim actuators are at the load feel mechanisms forward of the inboard ailerons.
Range **8 units either way**, LWD or RWD; one unit is one degree of aileron.
Up to **5 units**, only the ailerons move. A detrim actuator cancels the trim's input to the spoiler servo.
Beyond 5 units, the remainder reaches the spoiler servo and the spoilers on the down-going wing begin to rise.

blocks.content: The AIL trim indicator above the knob reads the trim in units. Aileron and rudder trim are set to zero before takeoff. A rigged aircraft needs very little: on the functional check flight the residual aileron and rudder trim in level flight must each be within 1 unit, so a larger steady need in normal flight points to an asymmetry such as a fuel imbalance or an engine out.

sections.title: Pitch control
sections.summary: Four elevator segments, the trimmable horizontal stabilizer, its four trim inputs and two-speed rate schedule.

blocks.content: Pitch is controlled by four elevator segments for maneuvering and an adjustable horizontal stabilizer for trim. The two control columns are mounted on a common torque tube; their cable run passes through the elevator load feel mechanism to the four elevator PCUs. The stabilizer is driven separately, by hydraulic motors and a jackscrew, and is commanded by trim switches, trim handles and the autopilot.

Each side of the stabilizer carries an **inboard** and an **outboard** elevator, all four moving together from the columns. Travel is about 23° trailing edge up and about 17° trailing edge down. Each segment has its own tandem PCU on two hydraulic systems (see [Hydraulic power](#hydraulic-power)), so a single system failure costs only rate, and any double failure leaves at least two segments working.

Because the elevators trim nothing, they normally sit near neutral in steady flight, with their whole travel available for maneuvering and the flare. An elevator held well away from neutral for long means the stabilizer is not where it should be.

Longitudinal trim is done by moving the whole horizontal stabilizer. The DC-10 carries a very wide range of loads and center-of-gravity positions, and its flaps produce large nose-down pitching moments. Trimming with the stabilizer keeps the elevators near neutral, so their full authority is always there for control; trimming with the elevators would use it up.

The price is power. The stabilizer is by far the most powerful pitch control on the aircraft, so its drive is slow, rate-limited by speed, watched by an aural warning, and given redundant motors and inputs.

blocks.alt: Functional schematic of the stabilizer trim drive: horizontal stabilizer pivot and acme jackscrew; a differential planetary gearbox summing two hydraulic motors, each with its own hydraulic brake (released above 200 psi); motor 1 fed through control valve 1 (CV-1) from hydraulic system 3; motor 2 fed through control valve 2 (CV-2) from the system 1 standby loop with the 2-1 non-reversible motor-pump from system 2. Inputs: the LONG TRIM handles by cable to both valves (CV-1 over the first half of travel, CV-2 joining over the second half), the control wheel trim switches, the ALTN LONG TRIM switch by wire to the CV-1 solenoids, and the autopilot auto pitch trim by wire to the CV-2 solenoids. The rate solenoids on each motor and the 250 kt switch on the elevator load feel mechanism are shown, with the autopilot trim disconnect microswitches on the pedestal cable.
blocks.title: Stabilizer trim drive

blocks.content:
An acme jackscrew moves the stabilizer. Two hydraulic motors drive the screw through a **differential planetary gearbox**, which adds their speeds: with both running the screw turns at the sum of the two, and with one stopped the other drives alone at half the speed. Each motor has a hydraulic brake that holds it until its supply exceeds about 200 psi, so a motor with no pressure cannot be back-driven by the other. Motor 1 is supplied through **control valve 1 (CV-1)** from system 3. Motor 2 is supplied through **control valve 2 (CV-2)** from system 1's standby loop, which the 2-1 motor-pump keeps pressurized from system 2 if system 1 fails and RUDDER STBY PWR is at ARM.

Stabilizer travel is **2° airplane nose down to 15° airplane nose up**. The limits are set by a mechanical shutoff linkage in each control valve and by stops on the jackscrew.
Four inputs can move the stabilizer. Which control valves each one opens decides how many motors run, and so how fast the stabilizer moves; the rate is not set by a separate rate selector.

rows: The primary trim control. Both halves of the split switch must be moved together. On the DC-10 and KC-10 the LONG TRIM handles move half travel when they are used; the MD-10 FCOM has them stay still
Half travel: motor 1. Full travel: both
Override authority over all other inputs. Both handles move together
Powered by HOR STAB ALTN TRIM CONT (DC bus 3). Inoperative without system 3
Does not move the LONG TRIM handles. See [Automatic Flight](automatic-flight)

blocks.content: Any input that works CV-1 (the trim switches, the handles, the ALTN switch) moves the cable to the pedestal handles and trips the autopilot pitch trim disconnect switches there. On the DC-10 and KC-10, with the autopilot in command that disconnects it; in CWS it does not, except in the turbulence mode. On the MD-10 a manual trim input disconnects the autopilot in any mode except SINGLE or DUAL LAND. The crew therefore always outrank the autopilot's trim.

**The two speeds.** A given change in stabilizer angle produces a pitching moment proportional to dynamic pressure. At high speed the same trim rate would pitch the aircraft much harder, and a runaway would be far more dangerous, so each motor has two displacements selected by a rate solenoid. Below the rate break the solenoid selects the high displacement and the fast rate; above it, or with the solenoid unpowered, the motor runs at half that speed.

The rate break is not the aircraft's airspeed. It is a switch mounted on the elevator load feel mechanism that opens when the mechanism's reference speed exceeds **250 kt** (see [Elevator load feel](#elevator-load-feel)). In AUTO the feel mechanism follows the airspeed within about 15 kt, so the two are nearly the same; with the feel in MAN, failed, or on the ground, only the mechanism counts. The slow rate is also selected above **33,000 ft** whatever the speed.

blocks.title: Stabilizer trim rates
columns: Fast band (feel reference below 250 kt, below 33,000 ft)
rows: Two (trim switches, LONG TRIM handles at full travel)
One (ALTN switch, handles at half travel, autopilot, or one motor failed)

blocks.content: The rates are checked on the real aircraft by timing 2° of stabilizer travel. The functional check flight tolerances are 3 to 5 seconds with both motors in the fast band, 6.5 to 9.5 seconds with one, 8 to 12 seconds with both in the slow band, and 16 to 24 seconds with one. The rate solenoids are powered by HOR STAB TRIM RATE CONT 1 (DC bus 1) and CONT 2 (DC bus 3); with one unpowered, its motor runs at the slow rate at every speed.

children.title: Stabilizer position and the takeoff green band

blocks.content: The LONG TRIM indicator beside the trim handles is a drum mechanically connected to the stabilizer. It needs no electrical power. Its scale reads from 2 nose down through 0 to 14 nose up, in degrees of stabilizer, which crews call units. A **green band** on the scale marks the range allowed for takeoff, and the takeoff warning sounds if the stabilizer is outside it when a takeoff throttle is advanced. The MD-10 also shows the stabilizer setting in digits on the SD CONFIG page (for example STAB 6.1 ANU).

The takeoff trim setting comes from the takeoff data card or the EFB's performance page and depends on the center of gravity and the takeoff flap setting. A forward CG needs more nose-up trim to rotate at VR. The published green band is 2.0 to 10.0 units for the -10 and 2.5 to 9.4 units for the -30.

After landing, FedEx crews set the stabilizer to 2 units nose up, which closes the fuselage opening around the stabilizer drive and keeps debris out.

Because a stabilizer moving when nobody meant it to is one of the most dangerous trim failures, an aural warning tells the crew whenever it moves for long. On the DC-10 and KC-10 a continuous deep-pitched air horn sounds after **more than 1° of continuous travel**: for manual trim, only if the rate exceeds 0.08° per second; in automatic pitch trim, at any rate. On the MD-10 the horn is followed by the voice STABILIZER MOTION. The detector is powered by HOR STAB MOTION (DC bus 1).

Normal trimming rarely reaches 1° in one movement in cruise, so the horn means either a deliberate large trim change, such as after flap extension, or something the crew should look at.

sections.title: Yaw control
sections.summary: Upper and lower two-segment rudders, standby power, yaw dampers and rudder trim.

blocks.content:
The vertical fin carries two rudders, **upper** and **lower**, each made of a forward and an aft segment. Each forward segment is driven by its own PCU; the aft segment is hinged to it and geared so that it deflects further in the same direction, which gives the rudder an effective camber and more side force for its size. Total rudder travel is about 24° either way.

The pedals drive both rudders through a closed-loop cable system. The two sets of pedals are interconnected and individually adjustable. On the ground the pedals also steer the nose wheel through a limited range; see [Landing Gear](landing-gear) for nose wheel steering.

Each rudder PCU has a single hydraulic supply: the upper rudder from system 1, the lower from system 2. Each is fed from a small standby loop of its system, and each loop has a non-reversible motor-pump that takes over when its own system fails: the 2-1 motor-pump, powered by system 2, for the upper rudder (and stabilizer motor 2), and the 3-2 motor-pump, powered by system 3, for the lower rudder. Two rudders on two systems, each with a standby from a third, means yaw control survives any two system failures.

The RUDDER STBY PWR switch and the RUD STBY PWR OFF light are on the flight engineer's panel on the DC-10 and KC-10; the MD-10 shows the motor-pumps' state as RUD STBY alerts. Both are described in [Hydraulics](hydraulics).

Each rudder has two yaw damper channels, A and B. Each channel drives a modulating piston at the rudder PCU, limited to **±2.5° of rudder**, so the two channels together command up to ±5° on each rudder. The pistons act in series with the pedals at the PCU summing linkage: they move the rudder without moving the pedals. The upper rudder's channels are driven by one yaw computer and the lower rudder's by the other, on opposite electrical supplies, so a single failure leaves at least one rudder damped. Losing one channel halves that rudder's damper authority.

The yaw dampers damp the Dutch roll that a swept-wing aircraft develops at altitude and coordinate turns. At least two channels must be operative for takeoff (MD-10: two channels from a common FCC); see [Limitations](limitations). The computers, switches, tests and lights are described in [Automatic Flight](automatic-flight).

Rudder trim, like aileron trim, moves the neutral point of the feel mechanism. The rudder trim knob on the aft pedestal turns a cable drum that drives one trim actuator in the fin; it shifts the neutral of both the upper and lower rudder load feel mechanisms together. The range is **10 units either way**, NOSE L or NOSE R, one unit being one degree of rudder. There is no motor and no circuit breaker. The rudder trim indicator reads the trim in units, and the rudder pointers on the surface position indicator show the resulting rudder position. Rudder trim is set to zero before takeoff and before touchdown.

The systems descriptions for this family show no rudder limiter or ratio changer: a full pedal input commands full rudder at any speed (the KC-10 manual's flight characteristics section does mention rudder deflection being reduced by limiting at speed, which the systems sections do not explain; the simulation has no limiter). That is one reason the limitations confine full application of rudder or aileron, and maneuvers near the stall, to speeds below the design maneuvering speed VA (see [Limitations](limitations)). The side load on the fin grows with dynamic pressure, so the same pedal input that is harmless on approach loads the tail far more in cruise; the yaw dampers, not the pedals, are what deal with Dutch roll.

sections.title: Artificial feel
sections.summary: Why the controls need artificial feel, and how the elevator load feel system schedules column force with airspeed.

blocks.content:
With irreversible actuators, nothing of the surfaces' air loads reaches the cockpit. The feel units put a force back: they center the controls and make the force grow with displacement. For the ailerons and rudders a spring mechanism is enough. For the elevators it is not, and the reason is worth understanding.

The elevator deflection needed to pull one extra g falls roughly in inverse proportion to dynamic pressure: at high speed a small deflection produces a large load factor. With a fixed spring, the column force per g would therefore fall as speed rose. The aircraft would feel heavy on approach and dangerously light in cruise, where an over-controlled pull could overstress it. If instead the spring rate rises in proportion to dynamic pressure, the two effects cancel and the force per g stays roughly constant across the envelope. That is a **q-feel** system, and the DC-10's elevator load feel is one.

The **elevator load feel (ELF)** mechanism is a spring unit in the elevator cable run whose spring rate is set by a jackscrew. The jackscrew is driven by a **duplex actuator**: one actuator with two electric motors, M1 and M2, each with its own clutches. Two **ELF/flap limiter programmers**, one per channel, compute where the jackscrew should be from airspeed and command the actuator. Channel 1 takes its airspeed from CADC 1 and drives M1; channel 2 takes CADC 2 and drives M2. Each programmer also contains one channel of the flap limiter (see [Flap limiter](#flap-limiter)), and both halves share the channel's circuit breaker.

blocks.alt: Block diagram of the DC-10 elevator load feel system: CADC 1 and CADC 2 through the CADC instrument switching unit to ELF/flap limiter programmers 1 and 2; the ELEV FEEL selector (MAN/AUTO) and MAN SLEW selector feeding both; programmer 1 driving motor M1 and programmer 2 driving motor M2 of the duplex actuator; the jackscrew setting the load feel spring mechanism in the elevator cable run between the control columns and the elevator PCUs; a load feel transmitter on the mechanism driving the ELEV FEEL REF IAS indicator; a switch on the mechanism marked 'opens above 250 kt' leading to the stabilizer two-speed trim control; the mechanical stabilizer position input entering the mechanism downstream of the jackscrew; the CHANNEL INOP and SELECT ELEV FEEL MAN lights.
blocks.title: Elevator load feel system

blocks.content: Three facts about this design explain what the crew see:

items: **The indicator reads the jackscrew, not the command.** A load feel transmitter on the mechanism drives the ELEV FEEL REF IAS indicator. The needle shows the airspeed the feel is set for, which is why it can disagree with the aircraft's airspeed. In manual mode, that disagreement is the crew's to manage.

**A stopped jackscrew holds.** With no power and no command the motors do not turn, so the feel stays at the force level it had when it stopped. A failure never leaves the column without feel; it leaves it with the feel for a speed the aircraft may have since left.

**The two channels are two motors on one actuator.** They do not average their answers. In AUTO the lowest-numbered healthy channel drives; if both fail, the jackscrew stops. In manual, each motor is run from its own selector position.

blocks.content:
The feel also varies with stabilizer position, through a mechanical linkage that enters the mechanism downstream of the jackscrew and adds to the airspeed term. Even with the feel slewed to its minimum the stabilizer term remains, which is why an aircraft with the stabilizer stuck near its cruise setting still needs a strong pull, up to about 30 lb, as it slows for the approach.

The programmers take their airspeed through the CADC instrument switching unit. Moving the CADC selector to BOTH ON 1 or BOTH ON 2 therefore changes what both programmers read, which is how the crew clear an airspeed disagreement between the CADCs (see [Failures](#failures) and [Flight Instruments](flight-instruments)).

With the ELEV FEEL selector at AUTO, the programmers drive the jackscrew so that the reference speed follows the indicated airspeed. The reference range is **120 to 300 kt**; below 120 kt the mechanism sits on its minimum stop, which is where it rests on the ground, with the needle in the white band at the bottom of the dial. Each motor slews the reference at about 10 kt per second, so full travel takes some 18 seconds. In normal operation the needle stays within about **15 kt** of the airspeed, which is the acceptance tolerance for the system.

The spring rate grows as the square of the reference speed, as dynamic pressure does. At the 300 kt end of the scale the column needs roughly six times the force for the same displacement as at the 120 kt minimum.
Each programmer monitors itself and the other:

items: A channel that loses its power or its CADC airspeed is called inoperative at once.
A channel whose actuator does not follow its command for several seconds is called inoperative.

A **comparator** watches the two channels' airspeeds. If they differ by more than **12 kt for 9 seconds**, neither computer is trusted and both are taken out of the automatic mode. The condition clears as soon as the airspeeds agree again.

blocks.title: Elevator load feel monitoring
rows: Follows airspeed on the other channel
CADC airspeeds differ by more than 12 kt for 9 s
On, together with SELECT FLAP LIMIT OVRD

blocks.content: SELECT ELEV FEEL MAN and SELECT FLAP LIMIT OVRD coming on together point to an airspeed disagreement between the CADCs, not to two separate failures.

With the ELEV FEEL selector at MAN, the programmers' automatic command is cut off and the jackscrew moves only when the crew hold the **MAN SLEW** selector. The selector has five positions and springs back to the center. Its four dots are two **motors**, not two rates:

rows: Raises the reference speed and the feel
The same, on the other motor
Lowers the reference speed and the feel
The same, on the other motor

blocks.content:
Both motors slew at the same rate. If the first dot does nothing, that channel has no power; use the second. On release, the needle stays where it is.

In MAN the crew are the feel computer. The procedure is to slew the reference to the aircraft's indicated airspeed and keep the two in approximate agreement as the speed changes. The other use of MAN is to make the column lighter on purpose: with the stabilizer inoperative, slewing the feel to its minimum reduces the force needed to hold the out-of-trim elevator. The limitation is that the ELEV FEEL selector stays at AUTO except in an abnormal condition (see [Limitations](limitations)).

With the feel set well below the aircraft's speed, the column is light and a normal pull produces a much larger load factor than expected. Keep the reference close to the airspeed, and slew it down only when the procedure calls for it.

A switch on the load feel mechanism opens when the reference speed passes **250 kt** and selects the stabilizer's slow trim rate (see [Stabilizer trim inputs and rates](#stab-trim-inputs)). Because it is on the mechanism, it follows the jackscrew, not the aircraft. Maintenance checks it on a parked aircraft by slewing the feel above 250 kt in MAN and timing the stabilizer. In flight it means that slewing the feel by hand also changes the trim rate, and that a feel system frozen at a high setting leaves the trim on its slow rate on approach.

rows: Programmer channel 1 and motor M1 (feel and flap limiter)
The REF IAS transmitter and indicator. Lost: the needle stops; the feel still works

blocks.content: Pulling one programmer breaker lights both CHANNEL INOP lights (elevator feel and flap limit) at once, because the two share the box. That is a quick way to confirm the lights and the channel split on the ground.

The MD-10 keeps the DC-10's feel mechanism, duplex actuator and two channels, controlled by the FCCs and from an MD-11-style overhead panel. One **ELEV FEEL** knob replaces the DC-10's two selectors. Its center position is AUTO; either side are two positions, 1 LO and 2 LO, 1 HI and 2 HI, the numbers naming the motor just as the DC-10's dots do. Turning the knob out of AUTO selects manual mode. The amber **ELEV FEEL MANUAL** light comes on in manual mode, and also when both channels have failed with the knob at AUTO.

In manual mode the SD CONFIG page shows **ELF SPD**: a scale from 120 to 300 kt with a bug at the feel's reference speed. The bug is removed if the reference is not available.

blocks.title: MD-10 elevator feel alerts
rows: Feel in manual with the ELF speed above 200 kt and the airspeed below 200 kt
ELEV FEEL selector out of AUTO

blocks.content: SEL ELEV FEEL LO guards against the case that matters most: an approach flown with the feel left at a cruise setting, where the column is far heavier than normal in the flare. The MD-10's procedures for a feel failure follow the DC-10's: select manual and slew the ELF speed to the airspeed, or to minimum with the stabilizer inoperative.

The ailerons have an aileron load feel and override mechanism, a spring unit in the wheel's cable run that centers the wheel and gives it a force gradient. The rudders have a load feel mechanism of two springs that give the pedals their feel. Neither is scheduled with airspeed. The trim systems work by moving the neutral point of these mechanisms, so a correctly trimmed aircraft has no force on the wheel or pedals.

The aileron breakout force, the force needed to start the wheel moving, is 3 to 5 lb on the functional check flight.

sections.title: Spoilers and speedbrakes
sections.summary: Ten spoiler panels for roll, speedbrakes and ground lift dumping, and the automatic ground spoiler logic.

blocks.content:
Each wing has five spoiler panels on its upper surface, numbered **1 to 5 from inboard to outboard**. Panel 1 is ahead of the inboard flap; panels 2 to 5 are ahead of the outboard flap. Every panel has one hydraulic actuator on one system: panels 2 and 4 on system 1, panels 1 and 5 on system 2, panel 3 on system 3. All three systems are needed for full spoiler operation.

The panels do four jobs:

items: **Roll augmentation**, in every mode (see [Spoilers in roll](#roll-spoilers)).
**Speedbrakes** in flight, selected with the spoiler handle.
**Ground spoilers** after touchdown or in a rejected takeoff, automatically when armed.
**Ground spoilers** selected manually with the handle.

blocks.content: A panel whose system fails cannot float up: a **hold-down check valve** in its actuator holds it down. A panel that was extended when its pressure went blows back down under air load through an anti-cavitation valve.

blocks.alt: Close-up of the spoiler handle on the left side of the DC-10 center pedestal, seen from the captain's seat: the T-handle at RET in the forward detent, the detent placard RET, 1/3, 2/3, FULL and GROUND SPOILER legible, the red ARM placard with white letters visible on the side of the handle (handle shown lifted to ARM in an inset), and the gate between FULL and GROUND SPOILER.
blocks.title: Spoiler handle

blocks.content: The spoiler handle on the left of the center pedestal has six positions:

rows: Forward detent; the handle is spring-loaded to it
Lift the handle at RET; a red ARM placard shows on both sides
Stowed; ground spoilers armed for automatic deployment
Squeeze the T-handle and pull aft
Squeeze and pull to the stop; the handle stops at FULL
On the ground, pull up and aft past FULL; pull out to lock

blocks.content: The gate at FULL stops the speedbrake at half the ground spoiler deflection. That limit protects the wing: fully raised spoilers at high speed would load it beyond its design. On the KC-10, a mechanical lockout keeps the handle from reaching GROUND SPOILER until the nose gear strut is compressed. The DC-10 and MD-10 have no such gate; the handle can be put at GROUND SPOILER in flight if it is deliberately pulled up through FULL and aft, and the limitations forbid doing so.
Do not extend ground spoilers in flight. Speedbrakes may be used only with the flaps at 0°, with or without the slats extended (see [Limitations](limitations)).

In flight the handle's detents set all ten panels symmetrically, up to 30°. The panels add drag and reduce lift, so the aircraft descends more steeply at a given speed. The roll command adds to the speedbrake setting on the down-going wing and subtracts from it on the up-going wing, so roll control is kept.

The speedbrakes are for the clean wing. With flaps extended, raised spoilers spoil the airflow over the flaps they sit ahead of.

The amber **SPEED BRAKE** light below the flap/slat position indicator on the DC-10 and KC-10 **flashes** when the spoiler handle is out of RET and the flap handle is at 3° or more, as a reminder that the speedbrakes are out with flaps. It is inhibited on the ground, and it flashes during the pilots' annunciator light test. On the MD-10 the same condition raises the level 2 alert **SPD BRK/FLAP**.

At touchdown the wing is still carrying most of the aircraft's weight. Wheel braking force is the friction coefficient times the load on the tires, so until the lift goes the brakes and the anti-skid have little to work with. Raising all ten panels to 60° dumps the lift and puts the weight on the wheels within a second or two, as well as adding drag. On a contaminated runway it is often the difference between braking and sliding.

**Manual operation.** On the ground, pull the handle up and aft through FULL to GROUND SPOILER, then pull it out to lock it there. Manual deployment is mechanical: it works without the automatic system and without its electrical supplies.

**Automatic operation.** With the handle at ARM, a ground spoiler control unit and an electric actuator drive the handle itself aft to GROUND SPOILER when any one of three conditions is met. The handle moving aft is what deploys the panels, so the crew see the deployment as the handle moving.

blocks.title: Automatic ground spoiler conditions (handle at ARM, system operative)
rows: Main wheels spun up, with the aft main wheels at 45 kt or more; flaps at 30° or more; radio altitude below 7 ft
Aircraft on the ground (ground sensing); main wheels spun up, at 45 kt or more; two or more throttles at idle or in reverse; flaps less than 30°
Deploy when the throttles are closed in a reject
Aircraft on the ground; two or more throttles in reverse; main wheels **not** spun up
Deploy on a runway where the wheels are aquaplaning and cannot spin up

blocks.content:
The flap condition reads the flap position, not the handle. The 45 kt wheel speed floor keeps an armed handle from deploying the spoilers during an ordinary taxi at idle thrust; it only stops a deployment from starting, and does not retract spoilers that have deployed as the rollout slows.

One consequence of the flap condition: in a landing with less than 30° of flap, the LAND mode cannot fire, and the spoilers come out instead through the REJECTED TAKEOFF mode once the aircraft is on the ground with two throttles closed. In an aquaplaning touchdown, selecting reverse is what deploys them.
**The handle latches.** Once the handle has been driven aft it stays latched at GROUND SPOILER, and the spoilers stay out through a bounce or a skip. Only two things release it:

items: The crew pushing the handle in (or striking it down), which sends it forward to RET, disarmed.

The **No. 2 throttle** advanced in forward thrust. A knockdown cam on the No. 2 throttle unlatches the handle, which returns to RET and retracts the spoilers. This is the go-around path, and it works for manual and automatic deployments alike. The No. 1 and No. 3 throttles do not have it.

blocks.content: The cam can only reach the handle once the actuator has driven it aft. If the No. 2 throttle is not at idle when the wheels spin up, the spoilers deploy and the cam then immediately knocks the handle back down; the crew must then deploy them manually. On the real aircraft the autothrottle cannot advance No. 2 against the cam after spin-up, so the autothrottles must be disconnected for a balked landing.
Advancing the No. 2 throttle forward of idle after the spoilers have deployed retracts them. For the automatic deployment to stay out, the No. 2 throttle must be at idle by main wheel spin-up.

The amber **AUTO SPOILER DO NOT USE** light on the pilots' overhead annunciator panel, with MASTER CAUTION, means some part of the automatic ground spoiler system cannot be relied on, and the handle should not be armed. Manual ground spoilers and the speedbrakes are not affected. It comes on when:

items: The ground spoiler control unit (GND SPOILER CONT, DC bus 1) or the auto spoiler actuator (GND SPOILER ACTR, AC bus 1) has lost power or has failed. Either one also stops the automatic deployment.

The handle was armed at main wheel spin-up and the nose gear did not touch down within **8 seconds**. A touch-and-go flown on the main gear alone with the handle armed lights it, by design. This check is the KC-10's; the DC-10 books do not describe it, but the simulation applies it to the DC-10 as well.

blocks.content: The light goes out when the fault clears. The rule is to treat a light that is on, or has been on at any time in flight, as a reason not to arm the spoilers for landing.

On the MD-10 the FCCs control power to the automatic ground spoiler actuator and monitor it. There is no nose gear timer. When the automatic system has failed the EAD shows **USE MAN SPOILERS** (level 2) if the handle is not armed, or **DISARM SPOILERS** (level 2) if it is: an armed handle on a failed system may deploy the spoilers when they are not wanted. Pushing the T-handle down disarms the handle from any position; it runs forward to RET and latches. Moving the handle out of RET also enables the autobrake.

sections.title: High-lift devices
sections.summary: Slats and flaps, the coupled flap/slat handles and takeoff flap selector, the flap limiter, automatic slat extension and limit speeds.

blocks.content: Leading-edge slats and trailing-edge flaps give the wing the lift it needs at low speed. Both are hydraulic and both are commanded mechanically, by cable from the flap and slat handles; they need no electrical power to move. Electricity is needed only for the two automatic functions laid on top: the flap limiter, which can hold the flaps back at high speed, and the automatic slat extension, which brings the outboard slats out at the stall warning.

Each wing has an inboard and an outboard flap segment, traveling from 0 to 50°. Each segment is driven by two actuators, one on system 1 and one on system 2. The inboard flap control valve is connected to the flap handle by cable; the inboard flaps are tied together by a cable bus so that the two sides move symmetrically; and the outboard flap control valves are driven by the inboard flaps' position, so the outboards are slaved to the inboards.

With both systems, the flaps move at about 2° per second, so a full extension from 0 to 50° takes about 25 seconds. On one system they move at half that rate, and with neither they do not move.

**Asymmetry.** Position transmitters on each side feed the flap indicator. When the left and right flaps differ by more than **5°**, the FLAP DISAGREE flag comes into view on the DC-10 and KC-10 indicator; on the MD-10 the alert FLAP DISAG appears at 4°. An asymmetry rolls the aircraft, and the abnormal procedure returns the handle to the last position where the flaps were symmetrical.

Each wing has eight slat segments, in an inboard and an outboard group. Systems 1 and 3 each drive them through full travel; with one system they move at half rate. The inboard slat control valve is connected to the slat handle by cable, and the outboard slat valves are driven by the inboard slats' position, so the outboards follow the inboards.

The slats have three positions, retracted, **takeoff** (about 20°) and **land** (about 28°), moving at about 3° per second. The outboard slats have a fourth, the auto-extend position used by the automatic slat extension. The five outermost segments on each wing are anti-iced (see [Ice and Rain Protection](ice-and-rain)).

A slat opens a slot ahead of the wing's leading edge. Air accelerating through the slot keeps the flow attached over the upper surface to a higher angle of attack, so the wing stalls later and reaches a higher maximum lift coefficient. The takeoff position gives most of that gain for less drag, which matters for climb performance; the land position gives the most lift.

Three lights on the flap/slat position indicator (DC-10 and KC-10) show the slats against their handle: **TAKEOFF** (blue) with the slats at the takeoff position and agreeing with the handle, **LAND** (blue) at the land position, and **DISAGREE** (amber) whenever any slat group is not where the handle, or the automatic extension, has put it. DISAGREE is therefore normal for the few seconds of every transit and for the whole of an automatic extension. With the slats retracted and agreeing, no light is on. On the MD-10, the SD CONFIG page shows SLAT EXT, or SLAT DISAG in amber if the slats are still not in the selected position 13 seconds after an extension or 17 seconds after a retraction.

children.title: Flap/slat handle and takeoff flap selector

blocks.content: The flap handle and the slat handle sit side by side on the center pedestal and are mechanically coupled, so they normally move as one. The slat position follows the flap handle:

rows: Takeoff settings. 15 and 22 are fixed detents

blocks.alt: DC-10 center pedestal, right side, from above and behind: the flap and slat handles coupled at the 15 detent, the FLAP scale UP, 0, 15, 22, 35, 50 and the SLAT scale RET, T.O. EXT, LAND EXT legible, the slat retract gate at 0 and the go-around gate at 22 marked, the FLAP T.O. SEL thumbwheel and window reading 12.5, the mechanical flap/slat interlock thumbscrew, and the GEAR HORN OFF placard.
blocks.title: Flap/slat handles and FLAP T.O. SEL

items: **FLAP T.O. SEL.** A thumbwheel beside the handle sets a movable detent anywhere from 1 to 25°, shown in the window, in addition to the fixed 0, 15 and 22° detents. It lets the crew choose the flap setting that gives the best performance for the runway and conditions. At 0, 15 or 22 the flap handle drops into the fixed detent; at any other setting only the slat handle drops into the movable detent.
**Slat retract gate.** At 0 the handles stop. To go to UP/RET, raise the slat handle and push the flap handle down through the gate. It prevents an accidental retraction of the slats with the flaps.
**Go-around gate.** On retraction the handle stops at 22°. Let it drop into the 22 detent, then lift again to pass the gate. It prevents an inadvertent retraction past the go-around flap setting.

**Flaps without slats.** The handles can be split only at UP/RET, by raising both together. The flaps can then be extended with the slats held retracted, for a slat malfunction. The slat handle cannot move without the flap handle.

blocks.content: Repositioning the flaps by turning the FLAP T.O. SEL wheel with the handles in its detent can bind the handles; lift the handles to move the flaps. When retracting from a takeoff setting, a detent bypass normally stops the slat handle catching in the takeoff selector's detent; if the flaps are less than 20° beyond the selected setting, the bypass does not arm and the slat handle must be lifted out of the detent.

The **dual automatic flap limit system** protects the flaps from being extended, or left extended, above their limit speeds. It works only between **20 and 50°**: when the airspeed is too high for the flap angle selected, it retracts the flaps, or stops them extending, to the largest angle allowed for the speed, and never below 20°. As the speed comes back down, the flaps go on to the selected position by themselves; no reselection is needed.

The limiter does not move the flaps itself. Through a limiter actuator in the flap control linkage, driven by one motor per channel, it lowers the target the flap drive is chasing, and the drive does the rest at its normal rate. Each of the two ELF/flap limiter programmers carries one channel, on the same CADC airspeed and circuit breaker as the elevator feel.

blocks.title: Flap angle allowed by the limiter

blocks.content: The schedule follows the KC-10's flap placard speeds (220, 185 and 170 KIAS for the bands up to 25°, 35° and 50°). The DC-10 and MD-10 books do not publish their limiter's schedule; the MD-10 FCOM says only that nothing is limited below 175 kt. It is a structural backstop with a floor, not a guardian of every limit. Between 220 and 250 kt it still allows 20°, which is itself above the placard for that angle, and some placards sit below the limiter's 220 kt: the DC-10's 210 KIAS for 15.1 to 25° (220 KIAS only on the 572,000 lb and heavier -30) and the MD-10's 210 KIAS for 21 to 25°. The crew keep the flap speeds; the limiter catches a gross exceedance.

**Failures.** One channel failed lights the blue **FLAP LIMIT CHANNEL INOP** light on the flight engineer's panel, with no effect while the selector is at AUTO. With both channels failed the limiter can no longer judge the speed, so it holds the flaps at its **20° floor**, and the amber **SELECT FLAP LIMIT OVRD** light comes on with MASTER CAUTION. The signature for the crew is a flap extension that stops at 20°.

**Override.** The FLAP LIMIT selector on the pilots' overhead has three positions: AUTO, OVRD 1 and OVRD 2. OVRD 1 uses channel 1's motor to retract the limiter actuator to its no-limit position; OVRD 2 does the same with channel 2's motor. When the actuator has retracted, the blue **FLAP LIMIT OVRDN** light comes on, which can take up to **20 seconds**. If it does not come on at OVRD 1, select OVRD 2. With the override in, the flaps follow the handle all the way and there is no protection at all: the crew must observe the placard speeds. If neither override works, the flaps stay at 20° and the procedure plans a 22°/EXT landing.

On the MD-10 the FLAP LIMIT selector (AUTO, OVRD 1, OVRD 2) is on the overhead panel beside the ELEV FEEL knob. The amber **FLAP LIMIT MANUAL** light comes on when both limiter channels have failed or when an override is selected, and the EAD shows **SEL FLAP LIM OVRD** (level 2) for the same conditions.

With the wing clean, the stall warning point is at a lower angle of attack than with slats out, and the margin to the stall is small. The **automatic slat extension** buys margin when it is most needed: at the onset of stall warning in the clean configuration, the outboard slats extend to their auto-extend position, raising the angle of attack at which the outer wing stalls and so protecting roll control at the stall. The slat handle does not move, and the outboard ailerons stay locked.

blocks.title: Automatic slat extension: arming
rows: In flight, flap handle below 4°, slats retracted
FCCs, 5 s after the condition clears
FCCs, 5 s after the condition clears
SLAT RESET (amber) and slat DISAGREE lights

blocks.content:
On the DC-10 and KC-10 the extension **latches**: the slats stay out after the stall warning stops, and the amber **SLAT RESET** switch-light on the center instrument panel stays on. Pushing it in flight retracts the outboard slats, puts the light out and re-arms the system. Hydraulic pressure in system 1 or 3 is needed for the reset. If the stall warning is still active when the slats are back in, they extend again. On the ground, the real aircraft resets the system only with the flight engineer's AUTO SLAT EXTEND test switch held at TEST.

The system is electric, from AUTO SLAT EXTEND PWR (AC bus 3) and AUTO SLAT EXTEND CONT (DC bus 3). With either breaker out the extension can neither start nor be reset, and slats already out stay out.

On the MD-10 the FCCs extend the outboard slats to 14.35° within 3.3 seconds, and retract them by themselves once the condition has been clear for 5 seconds. **SLATS ASE** in the lower left of the PFD shows the extension and takes priority over SLAT DISAG. There is no SLAT RESET switch.

With the outboard slats out, the airspeed limit for the auto-extended slats applies: 260 KIAS (DC-10-10, MD-10-10) or 270 KIAS (DC-10-30, KC-10, MD-10-30), and M 0.75. If the slats cannot be retracted, flight can continue within those limits.
For reference, the maximum flap and slat operating speeds published for each series are summarized below. [Limitations](limitations) is the authority.
Speeds are KIAS; the Mach limit for the flap bands above 5° is M 0.51. The DC-10-15 and DC-10-40 values are in Section 4.

sections.title: Stall warning
sections.summary: Angle-of-attack stall warning, stick shakers, the stall test and the slat overspeed warnings.

blocks.content: A wing stalls at an angle of attack, not at an airspeed: the stall speed changes with weight, load factor and configuration, but for a given configuration the critical angle of attack does not. The stall warning system therefore watches angle of attack, compares it with a reference for the present flap and slat configuration, and shakes the control columns when the aircraft gets close. Extending the slats raises the angle at which the wing stalls, so the reference depends on the configuration.

children.title: DC-10 and KC-10 stall warning system

blocks.content:
The system has two independent channels, one in each autothrottle/speed control (AT/SC) computer, each with its own angle-of-attack vane on its side of the forward fuselage and its own supply (AT/SC STALL WARN 1, AC bus 1, avionics B-13; AT/SC STALL WARN 2, AC bus 3, avionics D-13). The stall warning circuits run independently of the autothrottle, which can be off.

Each channel's function generator produces a reference angle of attack for the configuration, one schedule for the clean wing and another with all the slats extended. When the vane's angle of attack exceeds the reference, the channel energizes its stick shaker relay, and either channel runs **both** stick shaker motors, the captain's (CAPT STICK SHAKER, DC bus 1) and the first officer's (F/O STICK SHAKER, DC bus 3). The stick shaker is the only stall warning: there is no light and no aural warning.

items: **Ground inhibit.** Stall warning and the automatic slat extension are inhibited while the nose gear is on the ground, and for **5 seconds after nose gear lift-off**, to prevent false warnings during rotation.
**Automatic slat extension.** In the clean configuration, the onset of stall warning also extends the outboard slats and lights SLAT RESET (see [Automatic slat extension](#auto-slat)).

**Failure.** A vane that fails to its full-scale end still reads as valid, so that channel shakes the columns and extends the slats with nothing wrong. The abnormal procedure isolates the channel with its circuit breaker.

blocks.content:
The STALL TEST selector on the pilots' overhead panel has positions L and R, spring-loaded to the center. Holding it at L drives channel 1's vane signal to a stall and lifts its ground inhibit; after the 5-second delay, both columns shake. R tests channel 2 the same way. Releasing the selector stops the shakers. The test is inhibited in flight.

The crew check expects the shakers within about 5 to 8 seconds; no shaking within the first 3 seconds is also part of a correct result, since it shows the delay works.

On the MD-10 the FCCs compute stall warning from angle of attack, compensated for its rate of change, roll, sideslip and longitudinal acceleration, and test the vanes and shakers at power-up. As the aircraft slows, the pitch limit indicator on the PFD meets the aircraft symbol and turns amber; at the stick shaker point it turns red, the airspeed digits are boxed in red, the shakers run and, in the clean configuration, the outboard slats extend (see [Automatic slat extension](#auto-slat)). The FMS's speed-based cues (the amber and red columns on the speed tape) are separate. See [Flight Instruments](flight-instruments) for the PFD.

On the DC-10 and KC-10 (not simulated: see Simulation notes), a slats-extended warning (the overspeed clacker) sounds if the slats are in the takeoff position and the airspeed exceeds the slat limit speed, and a slat handle extend warning sounds the same tone if the handle is moved out of UP/RET above that speed. On the MD-10 the central aural warning system sounds the clacker and the voice SLAT OVERSPEED with the slats out above 260 KIAS (-10) or 270 KIAS (-30).

sections.title: Takeoff configuration warning
sections.summary: The aural warning for an unsafe flight control configuration at the start of the takeoff.

blocks.content: The takeoff warning catches the configuration errors that have caused takeoff accidents: no slats, landing flaps, speedbrakes out, a stabilizer far from the takeoff setting. It arms only on the ground (ground shift mechanism in ground mode), when **throttle 1 or throttle 2** comes forward for takeoff, and it sounds if any one of these conditions exists:

rows: Slats not in the takeoff range
The slat position system: the TAKEOFF light condition
Flaps in the landing range (35° or more). MD-10: flaps not in a takeoff position (retracted, or 26° or more)
Handle at 1/3 or beyond (RET and ARM are both forward)
Stabilizer not in the green band

blocks.content:
On the DC-10 and KC-10 the warning is an intermittent horn, the same sound as the cabin altitude warning. It stops when the condition is corrected or the throttles come back. Throttle 3 does not arm it. On the MD-10 the central aural warning system sounds a beeper and a voice naming the item: STABILIZER, FLAP, SLATS, SPOILER or BRAKES.

It is tested before flight, by the captain on the DC-10, the flight engineer on the KC-10 and the first officer on the MD-10: with the spoiler handle forward, the stabilizer in the green band and the parking brake released, advancing the throttles sounds the warning because the slats are still retracted. The steps for each deck are in [the takeoff warning test](warning-systems#takeoff-warning-test). See [Warning Systems](warning-systems) for the aural warning unit.

sections.title: Surface position indication
sections.summary: The surface position and flap/slat indicators on the DC-10 and KC-10, and the MD-10's configuration page.

blocks.content: The crew never see the surfaces, so the position indicators are the only way to confirm that a control input, a trim input or an automatic function has done what it should, and the only way to see a surface that has stopped following.

blocks.alt: The DC-10 center instrument panel SURF POS indicator, electromechanical version, with the aircraft on the ground, hydraulics on, flaps and slats retracted, full left wheel applied: the L wing pointer at half scale up and R at half scale down (outboard aileron lockout), both ELEV pointers at neutral, the left SPOIL tape raised about two-thirds and the right at DN, the RUD UPR and LWR pointers at neutral; the TEST button and the spoiler tape reference marks legible. An inset shows the electronic version of the same indicator with its -, +, MODE and TEST buttons.
blocks.title: Surface position indicator

rows: The summed deflection of that wing's inboard and outboard ailerons. With the outboard ailerons locked (flaps and slats retracted, alternate gear lever stowed), full wheel shows only half scale
The summed deflection of that side's inboard and outboard elevators. A split between the two (one segment drooping) shows as a pointer that does not reach full scale

The spoiler panels on each wing, for roll, speedbrake and ground spoiler. Reference marks: retracted, one-third speedbrake, speedbrake upper limit, fully extended (one further mark is not used). Both tapes read DN only with the wheel neutral
Upper and lower rudder deflection, including trim and yaw damper inputs
Drives all pointers to their test marks

blocks.content:
The indicator is dual powered: the left half from L SURF POS IND (28 V AC bus 1) and the right half from R SURF POS IND (28 V AC bus 3). With one supply lost, that half's pointers stop where they are, which can look like an asymmetry that is not there.

The KC-10's indicator, and an option on the DC-10, is an electronic display showing the same information. Its TEST button drives the pointers to their test reference marks while held; the -, + and MODE buttons dim it and give maintenance pages, which revert to the normal display after five minutes.

blocks.alt: The DC-10 center instrument panel FLAP/SLAT position indicator, flaps at 15 and slats at takeoff: the left and right flap tapes at 15, the flap handle position pointer at 15 with its chevron pointing to 250 on the FLAP LIM SPD scale (270, 250, 220, 185, 170), the blue SLAT TAKEOFF light on, LAND and the amber DISAGREE light off, the FLAP DISAGREE flag out of view, and below the indicator the amber SLAT RESET switch-light and SPEED BRAKE light (both off).
blocks.title: Flap/slat position indicator

rows: The outboard flap angle on each side

Where the flap handle is. Its chevron points to the limit speed for that setting on the FLAP LIM SPD scale. Pointer and tapes apart means a transit, a flap held back by the limiter, or a flap that is not moving
The left and right inboard flaps differ by more than 5°
Slats at the takeoff position, agreeing with the handle
Slats at the land position, agreeing with the handle
A slat group not where the handle or the automatic extension put it: in transit, auto-extended, or failed

blocks.content: The flap indication is powered from two 28 V AC supplies (buses 1 and 3) and the slat lights from SLAT POS SYS 1 and 2 (DC buses 1 and 3). The SLAT RESET switch-light and the SPEED BRAKE light are beside the indicator (see [Automatic slat extension](#auto-slat) and [Speedbrakes](#speedbrakes)).

blocks.alt: MD-10 system display showing the CONFIGURATION synoptic on the ground after a flight control check: the plan-view aircraft outline with ailerons, elevators, upper and lower rudders and spoiler groups drawn as boxes (gray outlines faired, one white box part-deflected, a solid green box at full deflection), the flap boxes under each wing reading 15, the white SLAT EXT legend, STAB 6.1 ANU in the fuselage, the ELF SPD scale (300, 200, 120) with its reference bug, and the landing gear and brake temperature boxes.
blocks.title: MD-10 SD CONFIG page

items: **Surfaces.** Ailerons, elevators, rudders and spoilers are boxes: a gray outline when faired, a white box sized to the deflection when deflected, a solid green box at full deflection.
**Flaps** are boxes under each wing with the angle in digits; they are removed with the flaps retracted.
**Slats:** SLAT EXT in white when extended, SLAT DISAG in amber when not in the selected position after 13 seconds (extension) or 17 seconds (retraction). Nothing is shown with the slats retracted.
**Stabilizer:** STAB and the setting in units nose up or down.
**ELF SPD:** the elevator feel reference scale and bug, shown when the feel is in manual.

blocks.content: The CONFIG cue switch on the aft pedestal calls the page up and lights when a CONFIG alert is on the EAD. Below the airspeed tape on each PFD, a flaps/slats legend shows the configuration: FLAPS and the handle setting, with an arrow while the flaps move, boxed amber if the flaps are split or have not reached the setting; SLATS with an arrow in transit; NO SLATS with the slats locked retracted; SLATS ASE during an automatic extension.

sections.title: Controls and indicators
sections.summary: Every flight control, trim control, selector and light, panel by panel.

blocks.content: The primary controls and the pedestal controls are the same on all three aircraft. The elevator feel and flap limit panel, the lights and the displays differ between the DC-10/KC-10 and the MD-10. The yaw damper panel is described in [Automatic Flight](automatic-flight), the RUDDER STBY PWR switch in [Hydraulics](hydraulics) and the alternate gear extension lever in [Landing Gear](landing-gear).

rows: Interconnected. Roll: ailerons and roll spoilers. The autopilot moves the wheels when it is flying roll
On a common torque tube. Pitch: the four elevators, through the elevator load feel mechanism. The autopilot moves the columns when it is flying pitch. Stick shaker motor on each column
Split switch on each wheel; both halves move together. Nose up / nose down: both stabilizer motors, fast rate. Disconnects the autopilot in command
Both rudders; nose wheel steering on the ground; wheel brakes (toe)
Unlocks each pilot's pedals, which are spring-loaded aft; keep feet on the pedals while adjusting

blocks.alt: DC-10 center pedestal, left side, from the captain's seat: the spoiler handle at RET; the two LONG TRIM handles (suitcase handles) in their neutral position; the LONG TRIM indicator drum reading 6.0 nose up with the green takeoff band (about 2 to 10 units) legible on the scale from 2 NOSE DOWN through 0 to 14 NOSE UP; the ALTN LONG TRIM switch; the PARK BRK handle. Labels NOSE DOWN, NOSE UP and LONG TRIM legible.
blocks.title: Pedestal: spoiler handle and pitch trim

rows: Command flaps and slats through cables to the control valves. See [Flap/slat handle](#flap-slat-handle)
FLAP T.O. SEL thumbwheel and window
Sets the movable takeoff flap detent; the window shows the setting
Thumbscrew interlock; split only at UP/RET to run flaps without slats
Speedbrakes, ground spoilers and arming. See [The spoiler handle](#spoiler-handle)
NOSE DOWN / neutral / NOSE UP; spring-loaded to neutral

Mechanical control of both stabilizer control valves, overriding all other trim. Half travel: one motor; full travel: both. Both handles together. They follow the valves: half travel when the trim switches are used, still when the autopilot trims
LONG TRIM indicator and green band
Stabilizer position, mechanically driven; green band is the takeoff range
NOSE DOWN / off / NOSE UP; spring-loaded off

sections.title: Operation
sections.summary: The flight controls through a normal flight, and the automatic functions at a glance.

blocks.content: This section follows the flight controls through a normal flight. The checklists themselves are in [Normal Procedures](normal-procedures); what follows explains what each step is checking and what the systems are doing.

**On a cold aircraft** the surfaces are free. Expect the elevators drooped fully trailing edge down and the inboard ailerons hanging part way, on the surface position indicator and from outside; the spoilers stay down on their hold-down valves. The stabilizer and the elevator feel are wherever they were left, because both hold without power: after a normal flight, 2 units nose up on the trim indicator. Once the hydraulic systems are pressurized the surfaces come back to neutral.

**Selectors.** ELEV FEEL at AUTO, with the REF IAS needle driven to its minimum in the white band; FLAP LIMIT at AUTO; SELECT ELEV FEEL MAN, SELECT FLAP LIMIT OVRD and both CHANNEL INOP lights out (MD-10: no MANUAL lights, no feel or flap limit alerts).

**Stall test.** Each pilot's channel in turn: hold STALL TEST at L, then R; both columns should shake after about 5 seconds and stop on release.

**Takeoff warning test.** With the spoiler handle forward, the stabilizer in the green band and the parking brake released, advance throttle 1: the horn sounds, because the slats are retracted, and the slat DISAGREE light should be out. Retard it, and repeat with throttle 2. Throttle 3 is moved only to check its freedom.

items: **Flaps.** Set the takeoff flap with the handle; for an intermediate setting, set FLAP T.O. SEL first and bring the handle to its detent. The slats go to the takeoff position: SLAT TAKEOFF on (MD-10: FLAPS and the setting on the PFD, flap boxes and SLAT EXT on the CONFIG page). The outboard ailerons unlock.

**Flight control check.** At a moderate rate, take each control to full travel and back while watching the surface position indicator (MD-10: CONFIG page): the first officer the elevators, the captain the rudders, both pilots the ailerons, with the flight engineer monitoring on the DC-10 and KC-10. Suggested minimum times are 2 seconds from neutral to full and 4 seconds from stop to stop (1 second each way for the rudder). Rapid movements on the ground produce rates the surfaces cannot reach in flight against air loads. Expect full scale on the wing pointers now that the outboard ailerons are unlocked.
**Trim.** Aileron and rudder trim zero; stabilizer at the takeoff setting from the takeoff data, inside the green band.
**Spoilers.** AUTO SPOILER DO NOT USE out (MD-10: no spoiler alerts); lift the handle to ARM and check that it stays up.

blocks.content:
Advancing throttle 1 or 2 arms the takeoff warning; a horn (MD-10: beeper and voice) means the configuration is wrong. During the roll the stall warning is inhibited until 5 seconds after the nose gear lifts off. If the takeoff is rejected, closing the throttles with the spoiler handle armed deploys the ground spoilers (see [Ground spoilers](#ground-spoilers)).

After takeoff the flaps are retracted on schedule. The handle stops at the go-around gate at 22° and again at the slat retract gate at 0: each needs a deliberate lift. The spoiler handle is returned to RET (disarmed) in the after-takeoff check. With the flaps and slats up the outboard ailerons lock, and the automatic slat extension arms once the speed is below its limit.

The elevator feel follows the airspeed; as the reference passes 250 kt, the stabilizer trim rate halves.

In cruise the autopilot trims the stabilizer through control valve 2, one motor, at the slow rate above FL330 or with the feel reference above 250 kt. Small, frequent movements are normal and do not sound the in-motion horn. Any manual trim input with the autopilot in command disconnects it.

The speedbrakes may be used for descent with the flaps up. The roll spoilers keep working on top of them. Retract them before extending flaps; on the DC-10 and KC-10, the flashing SPEED BRAKE light (MD-10: SPD BRK/FLAP) is the reminder if the handle is left out with flaps.

The flaps are extended at or below the placard speed for each setting; the flap/slat indicator's chevron shows the limit for the selected position. If the speed is too high for the setting, the flap limiter will hold the flaps at a smaller angle and let them go on as the speed falls: the pointer and the tapes then disagree, which is normal while it lasts. Extending the flaps from 22 to 35 or 50 takes the slats to the land position: SLAT LAND on.

Before landing, arm the spoiler handle; the landing flap (30° or more) is what lets the LAND mode deploy them at touchdown. Zero the rudder trim before touchdown.

At touchdown, with all throttles at idle, the main wheels spin up and the handle runs aft to GROUND SPOILER: all ten panels to 60°. The handle stays latched through a bounce. Reverse thrust and braking follow. The wheel keeps roll control by retracting panels on the up-going wing.

After landing, push the spoiler handle forward to RET, retract the flaps and slats, and set the stabilizer to 2 units nose up (DC-10 FedEx practice).

A go-around after the spoilers have deployed: advancing the No. 2 throttle unlatches the spoiler handle and retracts the spoilers. On the real aircraft the autothrottle will not advance No. 2 against the spoiler knockdown cam once the wheels have spun up; disconnect the autothrottles and advance the throttles by hand.

sections.title: Failures and non-normal operation
sections.summary: How hydraulic losses, feel and limiter failures, flap and slat malfunctions and trim failures show, and what the crew do.

blocks.content: The flight control system is built so that single failures cost little: a second hydraulic system, a second channel, a second motor or a second rudder takes over. The failures that matter to the crew are the ones that change the aircraft's configuration or handling: a flap or slat asymmetry, flaps held at 20°, a stabilizer that will not move, feel set for the wrong speed. The checklists are in [Abnormal Procedures](abnormal-procedures) and [Emergency Procedures](emergency-procedures).

The table shows what each combination of lost systems does to the flight controls, assuming the rudder standby motor-pumps are armed and working. Where a surface keeps one system it works at half rate, with full travel.

blocks.content: Every double failure leaves some control in every axis, but each one changes the aircraft differently, and the landing configuration with it: no flaps after losing systems 1 and 2, no slats after losing 1 and 3. Unpowered elevator segments streamline with the airflow, so pitch authority falls in proportion to the segments lost, and more column is needed for the flare. With an inboard aileron unpowered and the flaps up, roll control is down to the other inboard aileron and whatever spoilers remain; extending the flaps unlocks the outboard ailerons and restores much of it. The hydraulic procedures, landing configurations and speed additives are in [Emergency Procedures](emergency-procedures) and [Abnormal Procedures](abnormal-procedures); the systems themselves in [Hydraulics](hydraulics).
With system 3 lost, the ALTN LONG TRIM switch does nothing, because it works only through control valve 1. Use the trim switches or the LONG TRIM handles at full travel.
