blocks.content:
A feel failure in cruise freezes the column at cruise stiffness. Nothing changes at the time, but as the aircraft slows the column becomes progressively heavier than normal, and the flare needs a hard pull. A failure on approach does the opposite on the go-around: the column stays light while the speed builds. The fix in both cases is manual mode and a reference kept near the airspeed.

A frozen feel also freezes the stabilizer's trim rate band. Frozen above 250 kt, every trim input runs at the slow rate for the approach; frozen below, the fast rate stays selected in cruise, below FL330.

An asymmetry produces a roll that the crew counter with wheel, and, because the flaps change lift and pitching moment on one side only, a trim change and possibly buffet. With the autopilot engaged the roll may not show at all; the autopilot holds the wings level, and the first sign is the wheel offset or the disagree indication. That is why the procedures disconnect it.

The cure is to go back to where the surfaces were last symmetrical. If the asymmetry appeared during retraction, a further extension may be tried, carefully, with the handle returned at once if a roll develops. The landing data is then computed for the smallest flap setting actually achieved. Asymmetric flap tapes with no FLAP DISAGREE flag and no roll point to a fault in the indication rather than in the flaps.

**Stabilizer inoperative.** If the stabilizer does not move with the trim switches, the ALTN switch or the LONG TRIM handles, it is jammed downstream of all three, at the jackscrew. The elevators must then hold whatever trim the stabilizer cannot, and as the aircraft slows from cruise the out-of-trim force grows. The procedure takes the elevator feel to manual and slews it down to make that force manageable; the stabilizer term of the feel remains. Autopilot CWS can help with the forces, but must be disconnected by the final approach fix.

**One motor or one valve lost.** The stabilizer runs at half rate on the remaining motor. A trim input that uses only the failed valve does nothing: the ALTN switch with control valve 1 or system 3 gone, the autopilot with control valve 2 gone.

**Uncommanded motion.** The design defends against a runaway in depth: the LONG TRIM handles override every electric input, any manual input disconnects the autopilot's trim, the rate is limited at high speed, and the in-motion horn sounds after 1° of continuous travel. A horn the crew did not cause is the cue to stop the motion and identify the source.

children.title: Loss of control by conventional pilot inputs

blocks.content: Severe structural damage can sever the cable runs from the cockpit while leaving the hydraulic systems and the autopilot working. The autopilot's wiring runs in the overhead and ends at servo valves mounted on the primary surface actuators themselves, downstream of the cables. If the crew cannot control the aircraft with the wheel, column and pedals, it may still be controllable through the autopilot: engaged in command (the AP lever at CMD on the DC-10 and KC-10), the autopilot rolls the wings level and holds heading and vertical speed, and its controls on the glareshield can then fly the aircraft. The trim systems and the yaw dampers keep working. See [Emergency Procedures](emergency-procedures) and [Automatic Flight](automatic-flight).

The redundancy of the surfaces is also the defense against a jam: two rudders, four elevator segments and four ailerons plus ten spoilers mean a single seized surface leaves others to fly with. The FedEx abnormal procedures cover a jammed flap/slat handle, a spoiler handle jammed in a speedbrake position and an unresponsive rudder pedal input; see [Abnormal Procedures](abnormal-procedures).

sections.title: Simulation notes
sections.summary: What is modeled, what is simplified, how the flight model is driven, and the failures you can inject.

blocks.content:
**How the flight model is driven.** The simulation models every surface's actuator, its hydraulic supplies and its rate. On a healthy aircraft, the primary surfaces in the simulator's flight model follow your control inputs directly, and the model's solved surfaces drive the indicators and the exterior animation. When a surface loses both its hydraulic supplies, or a control link is failed, the model's own surface positions are written to the flight model for that axis instead (the average of the four elevators, or of the two inboard ailerons), so a drooping or dead surface is felt in the handling. Losing a single system therefore changes nothing you feel, apart from surface rates on the indicators.

The flaps, slats and spoilers always reach the flight model from the model: their transit times, half rate on one system, asymmetries (left and right flaps and outboard slats separately) and the speedbrake and roll spoiler positions are all real to the flight model. The model's roll spoilers reach the flight model, and the simulator's own roll spoiler channel is also left active in the flight model, so above about half aileron the aircraft gets somewhat more roll power and spoiler drag than the modeled panels alone would give.

Pitch trim reaches the flight model only through the modeled stabilizer. Every trim input moves the stabilizer at its real rate, through its real valves and hydraulics, and stops at its real limits; the simulator's own trim is then set from the stabilizer's position. When you start a flight in the air, the stabilizer starts where the simulator's trim was. The aileron and rudder trim reach the flight model the same way, from the modeled trim positions.

**Your cockpit controls.** The control wheel, column and pedals in the 3D cockpit follow your hardware or keyboard and never follow hydraulic state. When the autopilot flies, the wheel and column move with its servos. The aileron and rudder trim do **not** move the wheel or pedals as they do on the real aircraft: the surfaces move, the indicators show it, but the 3D controls stay where your hardware is.

The flap lever, the spoiler handle and both trim knobs can be worked in the cockpit or from your bindings, and the two stay in step. Your flap keys step the lever through its detents and stop at the takeoff flap selector's setting if one is set. The spoiler arm key arms the handle. Your elevator trim keys, buttons and trim wheel act as the control wheel trim switches, which are not clickable on the 3D wheel: full rate, both motors, and they disconnect the autopilot. A trim wheel is followed: the stabilizer is driven toward the wheel's position at the drive's own rate. The aileron and rudder trim keys turn the trim knobs. The LONG TRIM handles, when clicked, always go to full travel; the half-travel position is not selectable.
**Simplified or different from the real aircraft:**

items: The elevator feel system is modeled in full (both channels, motors, monitors, comparator, indicator, the 250 kt trim rate switch, power holds), but without force feedback hardware the column force it computes cannot be felt. Its stabilizer position term is not modeled.
No wheel or pedal forces are computed for the ailerons and rudders.

The DC-10's automatic slat extension takes the outboard slats to the takeoff position, rather than to a separate, smaller auto-extend angle. The flight engineer's AUTO SLAT EXTEND test switch is not modeled, so a slat extension latched on the ground cannot be reset until the next flight.

The DC-10 and KC-10 stall warning reference angles are set against the simulator's own lift curve, which does not raise the stalling angle with slats, so the shaker fires about 1.5 to 2° of angle of attack before the simulator's stall, and less than 1° before it at full flap. The shaker is heard, not seen: the columns do not visibly shake. The MD-10's stick shaker follows the simulator's own stall warning; its FCC alpha-based logic is not modeled, and its automatic slat extension uses the angle-of-attack vanes.

The flap limiter uses the KC-10's placard schedule on every aircraft. On the DC-10 and MD-10 it does not protect the lower 16 to 25° placard; fly the placard speeds. If the two limiter channels read different airspeeds, the more restrictive limit is applied.
Roll spoiler deflection is held to the 30° speedbrake limit in flight and reaches it at about two-thirds of full wheel. The MD-10 FCOM gives about 60° for the roll spoilers of the real aircraft.
The stabilizer green band used by the takeoff warning is 2.0 to 10.0 units on every aircraft, so a DC-10-30 set between 2.0 and 2.5 units does not sound the horn.
Rudder trim is limited to 10 units on every aircraft; the MD-10 FCOM gives 13°.

The MD-10's pedestal keeps the ALTN LONG TRIM switch and its circuit breaker, which work as on the DC-10; the MD-10 FCOM does not list the switch. Autopilot pitch trim runs through control valve 2 on every aircraft, where the MD-10 FCOM has autopilot 1 trim on hydraulic system 3.
Each ELEV LOAD FEEL & FLAP LIMIT channel is powered from its AC breaker only; its DC breaker is not modeled.
The yaw dampers damp the Dutch roll only; turn coordination is not modeled (see [Automatic Flight](automatic-flight)).

The flap drive has a skew brake that stops a flap asymmetry growing much beyond 6°, while always letting the flaps move back toward symmetry, so returning the handle to the last symmetrical position works.
The outboard ailerons unlock as soon as the flaps or inboard slats leave their retracted stops. The real aircraft needs about 15° of flap, or the slats in the takeoff range.

The automatic ground spoilers use one set of logic for all aircraft (LAND, REJECTED TAKEOFF, ICE/WATER), with a 45 kt wheel speed floor. On the real DC-10 and KC-10, a rejected takeoff deploys them on reverse thrust with the nose gear strut compressed, not on idle; the KC-10's two-stage deployment (two-thirds at spin-up, full at nose gear touchdown) is not modeled, and the spoilers deploy fully at spin-up.
The GROUND SPOILER position can be reached only on the ground, on every aircraft. The real DC-10 and MD-10 handle can be pulled there in flight.
The autothrottle in TO/GA does release a latched spoiler handle as it advances No. 2; on the real aircraft it cannot.
On the DC-10 and KC-10 the SELECT FLAP LIMIT OVRD light does not come on for the FLAP LIMIT selector being out of AUTO, only for the failures. The FLAP LIMIT OVRDN light is one light, not two halves.

The slats-extended and slat handle extend warnings are not modeled on the DC-10 and KC-10. The MD-10's SLAT OVERSPEED warning is, at the takeoff slat placard (260 or 270 KIAS); the MD-10 FCOM gives 280 kt.

The MD-10's ELEV FEEL knob has no pulled position and does not spring back: any position other than AUTO is manual and keeps slewing while it is there, and returning to AUTO resumes automatic control. A manual setting between the stops cannot be held. The SD CONFIG page shows the stabilizer setting in white at all times; the green or amber takeoff band coloring is not modeled.
The MD-10 alerts AUTO SLAT FAIL, AUTO TRIM FAIL, FLAP LIMIT DISAG and SLATS INHIBITED are not modeled.

Which spoiler panels each spoiler drive serves is not published, and the simulation's split is an estimate. With hydraulic systems 1 and 2 lost it leaves no flight spoilers and panel 3 as a ground spoiler only, where the FedEx manual keeps both panel 3s working.

Primary surface jams, a stabilizer runaway and spoiler panel jams cannot be injected. The PRIMARY HORIZ STAB TRIM and AUTO PITCH TRIM circuit breakers called for by the STABILIZER INOPERATIVE procedure have no effect; HOR STAB ALTN TRIM CONT does.
The spoilers' small extension with flaps down, which keeps them clear of the flap vanes, is not modeled.

The flap/slat position indicator has no separate OFF flags; with the indicator unpowered on both sides, the FLAP DISAGREE flag comes into view instead. Losing one side's supply leaves the other side working.
Above about M 0.82 the model applies a small nose-down elevator bias, like a Mach trim compensator. It shows on the surface position indicator and the exterior model but does not affect the handling.
On the KC-10, when the boom operator takes the joystick and throttles for the boom (see Air Refueling Systems), your flight control inputs are held off the aircraft while the autopilot flies it.

blocks.content: Hydraulic failures (system pressure loss, leaks, engine pumps, the system 3 elevator shutoff and more) are injected from the hydraulic groups of the same app and act on the flight controls exactly as the table in [Effect of hydraulic system losses](#hydraulic-failure-effects) describes.

Pulling the circuit breakers listed in [Flight engineer's panel](#fe-panel) also works: for example, pulling one ELEV LOAD FEEL & FLAP LIMIT breaker lights both CHANNEL INOP lights and stops that channel's MAN SLEW motor, as in the real aircraft's functional check.

parts.title: Flight Instruments
parts.summary: Air data, attitude and heading references, and the instruments and displays that present them.

blocks.content:
The flight instruments give the crew the aircraft's state relative to the air mass and the earth: airspeed and Mach, altitude and vertical speed, air temperature, height above the ground, attitude and heading. The system splits into three layers. **Sensors** measure physical quantities (pitot and static pressure, total air temperature, radio height, the spin axis of a gyroscope, the earth's magnetic field). **Computers** turn those measurements into flight parameters and decide whether each one can be trusted. **Displays** present the parameters and, as important, flag the ones that cannot be trusted.

The architecture is the same on all three flight decks even where the hardware differs. Each pilot normally flies from their own side: captain's instruments on system 1, first officer's on system 2. A third, auxiliary source can replace either side by a switch selection. A set of standby instruments, on independent sensors and power, sits behind all of them. No single failure removes the crew's ability to cross-check what they are seeing.

blocks.content: This part covers the measurement chain and its displays. Related material lives elsewhere: probe heating in [Ice and Rain Protection](ice-and-rain); the flight director, autopilot and flight mode annunciations in [Automatic Flight](automatic-flight); navigation sources, radio deviations and map modes in [Navigation](navigation); TCAS in [Surveillance](surveillance); aural warnings, clocks and the GPWS in [Warning Systems](warning-systems); and the buses that power everything here in [Electrical](electrical).

sections.title: Air data system
sections.summary: Pitot-static plumbing, the air data computers, temperature, radio height and the altitude advisory.

blocks.content:
Every air data parameter comes from three measurements. **Static pressure** (ps) is the pressure of the undisturbed air around the aircraft; it gives altitude and, by its rate of change, vertical speed. **Total pressure** (pt) is the pressure of the air brought to rest in a forward-facing tube; the difference between the two, the **impact pressure** qc = pt − ps, gives airspeed and, divided by static pressure, Mach number. **Total air temperature** (TAT) is the temperature of that same air brought to rest; with Mach it gives the static air temperature and the true airspeed.

The aircraft measures each one more than once, in plumbing and probes that are as independent as the airframe allows, and computes the parameters in two air data computers whose outputs are monitored continuously. The standby instruments read the same physical quantities directly, mechanically, with no computer and no electrical power.

Three **pitot tubes** sit below the radome. The captain's, left of the centerline, feeds CADC 1. The first officer's, right of the centerline, feeds CADC 2. The **auxiliary** tube, on the centerline, feeds the standby airspeed indicator. Each tube has a drain hole that lets water out of the line and, as a side effect, vents the line to the local static pressure if the ram inlet is closed.

There are three **static systems**: the captain's, the first officer's and the **alternate**. Each has a port on the left side of the fuselage and a port on the right, plumbed together into one line. The cross-connection is deliberate. In a sideslip the port facing the relative wind sees a higher pressure and the sheltered port a lower one; averaged in one line the two errors cancel.

The alternate static system always feeds the standby altimeter and standby airspeed indicator. Two selector valves, one per side, can tee that side's air data computer onto the alternate line instead of its own: the **STATIC AIR** selectors (NORM / ALT) on the DC-10 and KC-10, the **ALT STATIC** switches on the MD-10. The selection changes the static source only; the computer keeps its own pitot tube.

The static lines run inside the pressure hull and carry moisture drains at the main radio rack. The whole network is passive. It works with every electrical bus dead, which is why the standby altimeter and airspeed indicator read correctly on a cold aircraft.

blocks.content:
An airspeed indicator is a pressure gauge. Impact pressure grows with the square of speed and in proportion to air density, and compressibility adds to it at high speed. The instrument is calibrated to read speed for sea-level standard air, so it reads **calibrated airspeed** (CAS) exactly only at sea level on a standard day; at altitude the same CAS corresponds to a higher true airspeed. Because the aerodynamic forces on the aircraft depend on impact pressure and not on true speed, CAS (or indicated airspeed, which differs from it by the small instrument and position errors) is the speed the aircraft flies to.

An altimeter is a barometer calibrated in the ISA standard atmosphere: it converts static pressure into the altitude at which that pressure occurs on a standard day (**pressure altitude**), then shifts it by the crew's barometric setting. A vertical speed indicator differentiates that altitude.

Every run of plumbing is a small volume behind a narrow orifice, so the pressure at the instrument end follows the probe with a short first-order lag. On a clean line that lag is a small fraction of a second and invisible. A **partial** restriction (ice beginning to close an inlet, water in a line) lengthens it sharply, because the time constant grows with the square of the restriction: the instrument still reads correctly in steady flight but lags in a climb or acceleration. A **complete** blockage traps the pressure in the line, and the instrument then reads whatever the trapped pressure implies.

The cross-connected static ports cancel sideslip error only while both are open. With one port of a pair blocked, the line reads the survivor alone and shows a small altitude and airspeed error proportional to sideslip and speed.

A static port also sees a **position error**: the airflow around the fuselage makes the local pressure differ slightly from true static, by an amount that depends on Mach and angle of attack. The air data computers correct for it with a programmed static source error correction. Separately, no two transducers are identical: each computer carries a small calibration offset and a slow thermal drift, and the standby instruments carry their own capsule errors. The two pilots' altimeters therefore never read exactly the same, and the difference grows with altitude because a fixed pressure error is worth more feet in thin air (about 2 ft per 0.001 psi at sea level, about 6 ft at FL350). Small differences are normal; the cross-check exists to catch large ones.

Each pneumatic failure has a recognisable signature, and the signature identifies the line. Only the instruments fed by the failed line are affected, so comparing the captain's, first officer's and standby instruments isolates it.

blocks.content: A blocked pitot with its drain also blocked gives a believable, rising airspeed in a climb and a falling one in a descent. An autothrottle or a pilot chasing that reading flies the aircraft toward the stall in the climb and toward overspeed in the descent. Fly attitude and thrust, and identify the failed side by comparison with the other side and the standby airspeed indicator.

The pitot tubes, static ports, TAT probe and angle-of-attack vanes are electrically heated; the switches, lights and heater monitoring are described in [Ice and Rain Protection](ice-and-rain). Three ground schedules matter here. The TAT probe heater is removed on the ground, so on the ground the TAT probe reads close to ambient. The pitot heaters run their two elements in series on the ground, at reduced power. The vanes change supply from 28 V AC on the ground to 115 V AC in flight.

An unheated pitot tube in icing freezes at its inlet first and at its drain later, so the first sign is usually an airspeed that decays, and only later one that freezes and starts behaving like an altimeter.

Two **central air data computers** (CADCs) convert the pressures and temperature into flight parameters. CADC 1 normally serves the captain's side and is powered from the left emergency AC bus; CADC 2 serves the first officer's side from the right emergency AC bus. Each has an absolute static-pressure transducer, a differential transducer that measures impact pressure directly, an input from the shared TAT probe, and the barometric setting from its own side's altimeter (the setting potentiometer is powered by the computer, not the instrument, so it survives an altimeter power failure).

The differential impact-pressure transducer is why a healthy airspeed indicator reads exactly zero on a parked aircraft: it measures the difference between two pressures, so a transducer offset scales with speed rather than adding knots at rest. After power is applied a computer takes about two seconds to initialize, and its outputs are invalid until it has.

blocks.content:
In the troposphere the standard atmosphere gives pressure altitude as h = 145,442 × [1 − (ps / 29.92 inHg)^0.1903] ft; above 36,089 ft the temperature is constant and pressure falls exponentially. The barometric correction is the altitude difference between 29.92 inHg and the set value, added to pressure altitude: raising the setting raises the indicated altitude, by roughly 1,000 ft per inch near sea level.

For subsonic flow the compressible Bernoulli relation gives calibrated airspeed from impact pressure alone, CAS = 661.5 × √(5 × [(qc / p0 + 1)^(2/7) − 1]) kt, where p0 is sea-level standard pressure, and Mach from the ratio of impact to static pressure, M = √(5 × [(qc / ps + 1)^(2/7) − 1]). Because Mach needs static pressure and CAS does not, a static failure corrupts Mach and altitude while a pitot failure corrupts both airspeed and Mach.

Air brought to rest in the TAT probe is heated by compression: TAT = SAT × (1 + 0.2 × r × M²) in kelvin, where r is the probe's recovery factor, close to one. At M 0.82 and −50 °C SAT the ram rise is about 30 °C. The computer inverts this for SAT and then computes true airspeed as TAS = 38.97 × M × √SAT(K) kt.

Vertical speed is the time derivative of pressure altitude. Differentiating amplifies any noise in the altitude signal, so the rate is passed through two equal smoothing stages. Two equal stages are critically damped: the reading cannot overshoot or lead the aircraft, and it settles to a new rate in about two seconds. The autopilot uses the computer's rate directly; the indicator adds its own light damping for the crew.

Ten monitors run continuously in each computer. When a monitor's condition persists for **2 seconds**, the outputs it covers are frozen at their last good value and marked invalid, and every instrument reading them shows its flag. When a hardware monitor's condition persists for **18 seconds**, the computer's own failure annunciator latches; it survives power cycles and is reset only by maintenance. The reasonableness monitors never latch it, because they detect bad inputs rather than a bad computer.

The outputs are grouped, and each monitor kills only its group. One detail matters in the cockpit: the computer sends altitude rate on two lines, a digital word and an analog line, and **no monitor covers the analog rate line**. A static transducer failure therefore flags a digital VSI or TVSI (which read the digital word) but leaves the needle of a KSSU VSI (which reads the analog line) moving.

blocks.content:
The overhead **CADC** selector (BOTH ON 1 / NORM / BOTH ON 2) drives two motor-driven wafer switches in the air data instrument switching unit. They change which computer feeds each pilot's **altimeter** and **Mach/airspeed indicator**, and with them the airspeed reference of each elevator load feel programmer. Both computers keep running whatever the selector says.

The selector does **not** move the VSIs (captain's hard-wired to CADC 1, first officer's to CADC 2), the TAS/SAT indicator (CADC 2), the barometric setting inputs or the transponder altitude feeds. The switching unit runs on the battery bus so that it can still be operated on emergency power. Its wafers are motor driven, so if the unit loses power they stay where they were rather than returning to NORM.

Each computer applies the barometric setting of its own side's altimeter knob. With both altimeters on one computer, that computer's knob sets both altimeters: on BOTH ON 1 the captain's knob controls both displays and the first officer's knob has no effect on what either pilot sees, and the reverse on BOTH ON 2. Re-set the operative side's knob after selecting.

The amber **CADC SWITCHED** light on the captain's instrument panel follows the actual wafer position. Selecting both programmers onto one computer also removes any split between them, which is why the ELEV FEEL CHANNEL INOP procedure uses this selector (see [Flight Controls](flight-controls)).

One **TAT probe** on the lower forward fuselage carries two platinum sensing elements, one for each computer. It is a single point of measurement: a fault in the probe head affects both computers at once. The probe responds to a temperature change in a couple of seconds.

The probe heater is powered only in flight. A heated probe at very low airspeed reads slightly high because the heater warms the element; the error washes out quickly with airflow.

Two probe failures look completely different. An **element failure** (open or short circuit) trips both computers' TAT monitors: SAT and TAS go invalid on both sides with their flags. An **iced probe** with its heater failed is silent: the element sits in melting ice and its reading drifts toward 0 °C over tens of seconds while remaining electrically valid. No flag appears. SAT and TAS go wrong together on both sides, and so does anything computed from TAT, including the thrust rating limits (see [Engines](engines)). A TAT that settles near 0 °C at cruise altitude is an iced probe.

Two independent radio altimeters measure height above the terrain directly below. No. 1 serves the captain and is powered from AC bus 1; No. 2 serves the first officer from AC bus 3. Each is a transceiver in the center accessory compartment with its own antennas, and there is no ON/OFF switch: each runs whenever its circuit is powered.

The transceivers are frequency-modulated continuous-wave radars. The transmitted frequency sweeps continuously; by the time the echo returns from the ground the transmitter has moved on, and the frequency difference between the two is proportional to the round-trip time and so to height. The measurement is independent of the barometric setting and of the air mass, which is what makes it the reference for decision height, the GPWS and the flare.

Each transceiver drives two outputs, one for the autopilot and one for the indicator and other users, and compares them; if they disagree the indicator's flag comes into view. Its height also feeds the GPWS, the flight guidance and the ADI's rising runway. The indicator reads to 3,000 ft on the tape fit; above that the scale is masked. The dial fit's pointer stops at the top of its scale.

Pressing the indicator's **SET TEST** knob switches a delay line into the transceiver that simulates a return from 100 ft: for a few seconds the indicator reads 100 ft with its flag in view. The **decision height** is set with the same knob, from −20 ft to about 550 ft; the counter shows 0 to 499 ft and is masked outside that range (striped below zero, black above 499). When the indicated height is below the set decision height the **DH** light comes on.
On the MD-10 the radio height is shown on the PFD (see [Primary flight display](#md10-pfd)) and the decision height is set with the MINIMUMS knob on each ECP.

The altitude advisory compares the captain's baro-corrected altitude (from the computer their altimeter is switched to) with the altitude set in the glareshield ALT preselect window. Pulling the preselect knob arms it. An amber advisory light on each altimeter and a 2-second tone from the central aural warning system tell the crew they are approaching the selected altitude; the light alone tells them they have left it.

blocks.content: A flashing light is cancelled by the **ALT RESET** button or by setting a new altitude; a steady light only by setting a new altitude.

Two fuselage vanes, captain's and first officer's, measure angle of attack. They feed the stall warning (stick shaker) and the automatic slat extension, which are described in [Flight Controls](flight-controls) and [Warning Systems](warning-systems). On the MD-10 the captain's vane also drives the angle-of-attack scale on the head-up display.

The MD-10 computes its air data in two air data computers that work exactly as the DC-10's CADCs described above, fed from the same three pitot tubes and three static systems; computer 1 is on the left emergency AC bus and computer 2 on the right. The captain's PFD reads computer 1 and the first officer's reads computer 2, vertical speed included. There is no air data source switching, so each PFD stays on its own computer.

The **ALT STATIC** switches put the respective computer on the alternate static system. The standby altimeter/airspeed indicator reads the auxiliary pitot and alternate static lines directly and needs no power. The thrust limits are computed by the flight management system (see [Engines](engines)).

sections.title: Attitude and heading reference
sections.summary: Vertical gyros, compass systems, inertial references, the ADIRUs and the standby attitude indicator.

blocks.content: Attitude and heading are measured against references that do not move with the aircraft. On the DC-10 those references are spinning gyroscopes kept vertical by gravity-sensing erection loops (the **vertical gyros**) and gyroscopes kept on magnetic north by a flux valve (the **compass systems**). On the KC-10, and on DC-10s fitted with electronic attitude displays and a long-range navigation unit, the electronic displays read the **inertial navigation units** instead. On the MD-10 three strapdown **ADIRUs** provide both. Every aircraft carries a **standby attitude indicator** on the battery bus and a **magnetic compass** that need nothing else.

blocks.content:
A spinning rotor has angular momentum H = I × ω, the product of its moment of inertia and its spin rate. Two properties follow. **Rigidity**: with no torque acting, the spin axis keeps its direction in space however the case around it moves. **Precession**: a torque applied to the axis does not tilt it in the direction of the push but turns it at right angles, at a rate equal to torque divided by angular momentum. An instrument gyro is built to exploit both: rigidity holds the reference, and small deliberate torques (erection, slaving) precess it slowly back onto the reference it is meant to keep.

Because every rate is torque divided by H, a gyro is only as good as its rotor speed. A rotor running up from rest has little rigidity and is easily knocked off; a rotor coasting down after a power failure stays rigid for minutes and is still worth reading. The rotors are driven by hysteresis-synchronous motors whose speed is set by the supply **frequency**, not its voltage, so a generator running below 400 Hz slows every gyro on its bus.

A rigid axis is fixed in space, but the earth turns under it at 15.04° per hour. A gyro whose axis is meant to stay vertical or on north therefore appears to wander. The horizontal-axis (directional) gyro drifts in azimuth at 15.04 × sin(latitude) degrees per hour: about 10.6°/h at 45°, nothing at the equator. Bearing friction and small gimbal unbalance add their own drift. A vertical gyro is kept vertical by an **erection** system: a liquid level switch on each gimbal senses tilt from the apparent vertical and switches a torque motor on at a constant rate (about 3° per minute) until the level nulls. Because the loop is on/off with a small dead band, an erected gyro settles within that dead band rather than exactly vertical.

The level switches sense the **apparent** vertical, the direction of gravity combined with the aircraft's own acceleration. That produces two classic errors. During a takeoff roll the apparent vertical tilts aft and the erection loop slowly precesses the gyro toward a nose-up error. In a coordinated turn the apparent vertical is the floor of the banked aircraft and the loop erects toward it, leaving the indicator leaning after the rollout. Erection **cutouts** stop the loop during significant acceleration and when the gyro is banked or turning beyond small limits. The gimbals limit the inner (pitch) ring to ±85° to prevent gimbal lock; the outer (roll) ring turns freely through 360°.

blocks.content:
Three vertical gyros provide attitude. **Vertical gyro 1** feeds the captain's ADI, flight guidance computer 1, speed control computer 1 and the weather radar stabilization, and is powered from the left emergency AC bus. **Vertical gyro 2** feeds the first officer's ADI and the No. 2 computers from the right emergency AC bus. **Vertical gyro 3**, the **auxiliary**, is powered from AC bus 1 and normally feeds nothing. Three gyros on three supplies means no single bus failure removes every attitude reference.

The overhead attitude transfer selector, placarded **INS** on this aircraft (CAPT ON AUX / NORM / F/O ON AUX), operates the attitude switching unit and puts vertical gyro 3 in place of gyro 1 or gyro 2 for everything that side normally receives. The switching unit is on the battery bus, so the crew can select the auxiliary gyro with the generators gone. Either pilot on the auxiliary source lights the amber **AUX ATT** legend on both pilots' panels.

From cold, a gyro rotor lies toppled against its stops. When power is applied the rotor runs up, and an automatic fast-erection relay brings the axis to the vertical within seconds, overriding the cutouts while the rotor is still slow, then drops out once the level switches null. The ADI's **ATT** flag stays in view until the rotor reaches believable speed, about half a minute to a minute later. The maintenance manual allows five minutes for run-up and erection together. There is no crew fast-erect control for these gyros.

After a power failure the rotor coasts down over ten minutes or more. For the first minutes it is still rigid and the ATT flag stays out of view; the flag comes in when the rotor falls below believable speed. A gyro that has toppled, reached a gimbal stop or failed internally shows the flag at once.

blocks.title: Vertical gyro supplies
rows: Captain's ADI, flight guidance 1, speed control 1, weather radar
F/O's ADI, flight guidance 2, speed control 2

blocks.content:
Two independent compass systems give stabilized magnetic heading. Each has a **flux valve** in a wingtip (No. 1 left, No. 2 right), a **directional gyro**, a **compass coupler** and a **compass controller** on the overhead panel. System 1 is powered from the left emergency AC bus, system 2 from the right. On the DC-10 each system drives its own side's HSI and RMI compass cards; on the KC-10 the compass systems drive the RMIs.

The flux valve is a pendulous three-legged core excited at 23.5 V, 400 Hz by its coupler. It senses the horizontal component of the earth's field and so knows magnetic north, but it is noisy, it swings in turbulence, and it tilts in turns and accelerations, when it senses part of the vertical field as well. The directional gyro is smooth and rigid but drifts. The coupler combines them: the heading output follows the gyro, and a slow correction pulls it onto the flux valve's average. The valves are aligned to the airframe at installation and need no compensation.

The correction is electrical. The gyro turns freely in azimuth for the whole flight; the coupler measures the difference between the gyro heading and the flux valve heading and drives a stepper motor that turns a differential synchro in the gyro's signal path. A follow-up servo then drives the compass cards and the heading transmitters until they agree with that corrected signal.

The correction runs at two rates. **Normal sync** at 1 to 2 degrees per minute is slow enough that the momentary swings of the flux valve in a turn barely move the card, so the gyro, not the valve, defines heading in maneuvers. **Fast sync** at 600 to 800 degrees per minute removes a large initial error; the coupler drops back to normal sync once the error is under 2°. Fast sync is entered only by specific events, never simply because the error is large, which is why a long turn does not drag the card onto the swinging valve.

blocks.content:
The heading output carries a validity signal (the superflag). The **HDG** flag on the HSI and the OFF flag on the RMI come into view whenever the heading should not be trusted: during a fast sync, while the SET HDG knob is out of center, with an invalid directional gyro or a failed coupler, and in SLAVED with the flux valve's excitation lost. The card keeps turning while the flag is in view: during a fast sync the crew see the card sweep onto magnetic heading under the flag, which is exactly what the maintenance functional test expects.

The **sync annunciator** on the controller shows the difference between the card and the flux valve. Its scale follows the sine of the error, so a 90° error is full scale and a small one moves it only slightly; a card reading high deflects it to the right. In cruise the needle fluctuates around center, which proves the flux valve is alive; in a turn it is displaced. In DG mode the annunciator is disconnected and sits at center whatever the error.

In **DG** mode the flux valve is ignored and the card follows the free gyro, drifting at the earth-rate figure plus the gyro's own drift. This aircraft's compass systems have no latitude correction; the crew reset the card against a known heading with the SET HDG knob. DG is the mode for high latitudes, where the horizontal component of the earth's field becomes too weak for the flux valve, and for a flux valve that is known to be wrong.

The magnetic dip angle grows with latitude. The flux valve's tilt in turns and accelerations makes it sense part of the vertical field, the cause of the northerly turning error familiar from a simple compass. The slow normal sync rate is the coupler's defense against it.

A flux valve that develops an error is quiet. The sync annunciator deflects when the error appears and then walks back to center as the coupler slaves the card onto the wrong heading at 1 to 2°/min. Cross-check the two compass systems and the standby compass; if one is wrong, select DG on that system and set it by hand.

On the KC-10, and on DC-10s fitted with the MFD or FPDS glass and a long-range navigation unit, the electronic attitude and heading displays read the inertial navigation units: the captain's unit 1, the first officer's unit 2, and unit 3 for either seat with the INS selector at CAPT ON AUX or F/O ON AUX. The electromechanical ADI and HSI, where fitted, stay on the vertical gyros and compass systems. The same overhead selector therefore transfers both kinds of display together.

An inertial unit gives no attitude until it has aligned. During alignment it levels its platform on its accelerometers and finds true north by sensing the horizontal component of the earth's rotation, which is 15.04°/h × cos(latitude): the alignment is slower at high latitude and impossible at the pole, and its heading accuracy is the unit's gyro drift divided by that same rate. The displays it feeds show their attitude flag until the unit has leveled and their heading flag until it is aligned and navigating. The units, their control panels and their alignment procedures are described in [Navigation](navigation).

Three **ADIRUs**, numbered 1, 2 and AUX, provide attitude, heading and inertial position. Each is a strapdown unit: its gyros and accelerometers are fixed to the case and a computer resolves the aircraft's attitude from their outputs, so there are no gimbals to topple and no erection errors. Under normal conditions the captain's display units use ADIRU 1 and the first officer's use ADIRU 2; ADIRU AUX is a hot spare that either seat can select with the **IRS** switch on its SISP.

ADIRU 1 is powered from the left emergency AC bus, ADIRU 2 from the right, and ADIRU AUX from generator bus 1. Each unit has its own backup battery that carries it for about 15 minutes after its AC supply is lost. Each draws power only while its selector is at NAV.

The **IRS control panel** on the left forward overhead carries an **OFF / NAV** selector and an amber **NAV OFF** light for each unit, ordered 1, AUX, 2. There is no ATT or ALIGN position: alignment is a submode a unit enters by itself. At NAV a unit aligns for about **10 minutes** with the aircraft stationary and, once it also has a present position from the FMS (INITIALIZE IRS on the F-PLN INIT page), enters NAV by itself; alignment in flight is not possible. While any unit is aligning the PFD speed tape shows **NO TAXI**, and the unit gives no attitude until it reaches NAV. The panel, the NAV OFF light logic and the alignment procedure are described in [Navigation](navigation#md-10-adirs).

In NAV the unit outputs pitch, roll, magnetic heading, true heading and its navigation data. Its attitude error is far below anything a display can show. North of 73°N or south of 60.5°S the heading output changes to true, and returns to magnetic through 72.5°N or 59.5°S. A failure of the navigation function alone leaves attitude valid (IRU NAV FAIL). A primary failure removes the unit's attitude and heading: its seat's PFD shows ATT FAIL and its ND HDG FAIL until the seat is switched to ADIRU AUX.

The ADIRUs raise these alerts: **IRU 1 FAIL**, **IRU 2 FAIL** and **IRU AUX FAIL** (Level 2), and **IRU 1/2 NAV FAIL**, **IRU 1/2 NO ALIGN** and **IRU 1/2 ON BAT** (Level 1). The navigation side of the ADIRUs is described in [Navigation](navigation#md-10-adirs) and [Flight Management](flight-management).

The standby attitude indicator on the center instrument panel is a self-contained electric gyro horizon and the one attitude reference that survives a total AC failure. Its rotor is an ordinary three-phase 115 V, 400 Hz machine, supplied by a static inverter that runs from the battery bus; it is the inverter's supply, not the motor's type, that keeps it alive. It erects at about 3° per minute and is independent of every other attitude system.

It reads pitch to 80° climb and 60° dive and is free through 360° of roll; its bank scale is marked to 60° each way. Its **OFF** flag comes into view whenever the gyro is not usable: no power, rotor below speed, internal failure, or caged.

blocks.title: Standby attitude indicator knob
rows: Moves the miniature airplane symbol up (C) or down (D) for pitch reference. A display adjustment only; the gyro is unaffected.
Fast erection: erection runs at many times its normal rate until the gyro is erect, or for at most 2 minutes
Cages the gyro: the gimbals lock to the case, the horizon reads level and the OFF flag comes into view

blocks.content: From a cold start the horizon comes up from its toppled rest to level in about half a minute, with a visible sway as the gimbals settle. Fast erection corrects an indicator that has been disturbed by prolonged bank or acceleration; it erects to the apparent vertical, so do it in wings-level, unaccelerated flight.

Do not pull the knob for fast erection until the indicator has been running for at least 60 seconds, and never hold fast erection for more than 120 seconds. If the indicator still shows more than about 3° of error after erection in level flight, it needs maintenance.

A direct-reading magnetic compass with its own deviation card gives heading with no power at all. It suffers every error of a simple compass (northerly turning error, acceleration error, deviation from the cockpit's own fields) and is read in steady, unaccelerated flight. Its light is on the lighting panel (see [Lighting](lighting)). The preflight heading check compares the primary compass cards with each other and with this compass.

sections.title: DC-10 and KC-10 instruments
sections.summary: The pilots' panels: electromechanical instruments, the optional DC-10 glass, and the KC-10's EADI and EHSI.

blocks.content: Each pilot's panel follows the basic T: airspeed left, attitude center, altitude right, heading below the attitude, with the vertical speed indicator below the altimeter. The captain's and first officer's panels are mirror images and each is fed from its own side's computers and gyros. Standby instruments sit on the center panel.

blocks.alt: DC-10-30 captain's instrument panel, KSSU fit, daylight, aircraft at cruise: Mach/airspeed indicator upper left, ADI upper center, altimeter upper right with the altitude advisory light, HSI below the ADI, VSI below the altimeter, RMI and radio altimeter (tape) to the left, marker beacon lenses (A, MM, OM) at the right edge, chronometer lower left, CADC SWITCHED light and AUX ATT legend legible, glareshield ENG FAIL / GPWS / BELOW G/S / WINDSHEAR / NAV legends above.
blocks.title: DC-10 captain's instrument panel (KSSU fit)

blocks.alt: KC-10A pilot's instrument panel, daylight, aircraft at cruise: Mach/airspeed indicator, EADI over EHSI in the center, altimeter with advisory light, TVSI below it, radio altimeter dial, TACAN RMI and VOR/ADF RMI, NAV and AUX ATT annunciators, chronometer. All flags out of view.
blocks.title: KC-10 pilot's instrument panel

blocks.content: The DC-10 fleet flew with several generations of flight instruments, and the simulation offers them as fits. On a DC-10 the fit is chosen in the EFB's Configuration app, Aircraft Configuration page, Pilots' Panels zone; the change applies to both seats. Some fits are available only in some editions of the product. The KC-10A has one fixed configuration.

blocks.title: Pilots' panel fits
rows: KSSU electromechanical ADI; MFD electronic ADI (EADI); FPDS flat panel
KSSU HSI; Biman HSI; MFD electronic HSI (EHSI). The FPDS takes this position too.
KSSU electromechanical VSI; digital VSI; TVSI (TCAS/VSI)
Follows the DME display fit: single, dual or KSSU arrangement

blocks.content: The EADI and EHSI can be fitted independently, so a panel may carry an electronic ADI over an electromechanical HSI. The **FPDS** is a whole-panel replacement: with it fitted, each pilot's Mach/airspeed indicator, ADI, HSI, altimeter, VSI and radio altimeter are removed and their functions move to one wide screen and its display control panel.

Each pilot's Mach/airspeed indicator is a servo instrument driven by the computer the CADC selector assigns to that side (captain's on the left emergency AC bus, first officer's on the right). An **airspeed pointer** reads calibrated airspeed on a 0 to 450 kt dial. A striped **Vmo pointer** on the same dial shows the maximum operating speed for the present altitude: Vmo at low altitude, and above the crossover altitude the airspeed equivalent of Mmo, so it moves down the dial in the climb. A **Mach counter** reads Mach to three decimals. Five crew-set **reference bugs** ride the bezel, and a sixth, the **command bug**, follows the speed selected on the glareshield speed control panel.

blocks.title: Mach/airspeed indicator failure indications
rows: Airspeed data invalid or lost for 2 seconds
A/S flag in view; airspeed pointer stops
Vmo data invalid, or indicator unpowered
Vmo pointer runs down to its 257.5 kt stop
Mach data lost for 2 seconds or more
Counter freezes at the last valid Mach with the flag in view; the airspeed pointer stops where it was

blocks.content: A Vmo pointer at 257.5 kt is a failure indication, not a limit. Use the placarded speeds in [Limitations](limitations).

Each pilot's **altimeter** is a servo instrument showing the baro-corrected altitude computed by its assigned CADC. A pointer turns once per 1,000 ft against a dial graduated every 20 ft, and a five-drum counter reads altitude directly, the last two drums stepping together in 20 ft increments. A shutter covers the counter below zero altitude. The barometric setting is set with the knob on the instrument and shown in two windows, millibars and inches of mercury. The amber altitude advisory light sits on the bezel, and a crew-set altitude reference bug rides the dial.

The **OFF** flag comes into view on loss of power, invalid computer data, no data for 2 ± 0.5 seconds, or an internal failure. The mechanism holds its last reading when power is lost rather than running to zero.

The barometric setting is not applied in the altimeter: the knob sets a potentiometer read by the CADC, which applies the correction and sends corrected altitude back. That is why, with the CADC selector at BOTH ON 1 or BOTH ON 2, the operating computer's own side's knob sets both altimeters.

The **standby altimeter** on the center panel is a pneumatic instrument on the alternate static line with its own setting knob and millibar and inch windows; a counter reads to the nearest hundred feet and a pointer turns once per 1,000 ft. It needs no power except for a small vibrator that keeps its mechanism free; with the vibrator dead the pointer sticks and moves in jumps of about 30 ft. The **standby airspeed indicator** beside it is a pneumatic instrument on the auxiliary pitot and alternate static lines and needs no power at all.

blocks.alt: Close-up, side by side: DC-10 Mach/airspeed indicator reading 280 kt and M .820 with the striped Vmo pointer near 330 kt, the five reference bugs and the command bug visible; servo altimeter reading 33,000 ft with the counter 33 000, 1013 MB and 29.92 IN HG windows, OFF flag out of view, altitude advisory light out. Every dial legend legible.
blocks.title: Mach/airspeed indicator and altimeter

blocks.content:
The VSIs are servo instruments, not the capsule-and-leak instruments of light aircraft. Each is **hard-wired** to its own side's computer (captain's CADC 1, first officer's CADC 2) and is not moved by the CADC selector. The pointer reads ±6,000 ft/min with zero at the nine o'clock position; the scale is expanded near zero and compressed beyond 2,000 ft/min, and the two ends meet at three o'clock. Because the rate is computed and smoothed in the CADC rather than measured through a calibrated leak, the indication settles to a new rate in about two seconds, far quicker than a capsule VSI.

The instrument flags on invalid rate data, an over-range input, loss of power or an internal failure.

blocks.title: VSI fits
rows: Keeps working through a CADC static transducer failure, because no monitor covers the analog line
Glass, octagonal screen: the same dial, a thin arrow pointer
Flags on any CADC failure that invalidates the digital word
Glass, square screen: vertical speed with the TCAS traffic display and resolution advisory bands on the same dial
The vertical speed and the traffic picture fail independently; see [Surveillance](surveillance)

blocks.alt: Three VSIs side by side, each showing a 1,500 ft/min climb: left, the KSSU electromechanical VSI; center, the digital VSI's octagonal glass with its thin arrow pointer; right, the TVSI's square glass with VERTICAL SPEED and 1000 FPM legends and an idle traffic area (own-ship symbol and two-mile ring). Scales 0 at nine o'clock, .5 1 2 4 6 both senses, legible.
blocks.title: VSI fits

blocks.content: The TAS/SAT indicator on the first officer's panel is hard-wired to CADC 2. It shows true airspeed (130 to 599 kt) and static air temperature (−99 to +50 °C) on drum counters. Holding the **TAT** button shows total air temperature (−50 to +99 °C) in the temperature window instead; it reverts on release. Below 130 kt the TAS drums sit at 130 with no flag.

blocks.title: TAS/SAT failure codes
rows: Invalid input from the computer (with OFF flag)
No computed data for 2 seconds or more (with OFF flag)
No computed data for 2 seconds or more (with OFF flag)

blocks.content: The KSSU ADI combines the attitude sphere with the flight director and approach information. The sphere is driven by the vertical gyro the INS selector assigns to that seat. The flight director's command bars, the fast/slow indicator and the radio deviations are fed through a separate circuit (**ADI RADIO & CMD INFO**: the captain's on 28 V AC bus 1, the first officer's on DC bus 3), so losing it removes every radio and command display while the sphere keeps flying on its gyro. The slip ball is a ball in a liquid-filled tube and needs no power at all.

blocks.title: ADI elements
rows: Airspeed error from the speed control system's target
ILS receiver; on the pedestal radio fit the captain's ADI reads ILS 2 and the F/O's ILS 1
Localizer deviation, rising toward the symbol below 200 ft radio height
ILS receiver and the seat's radio altimeter
Not fitted on this aircraft; stays centerd with no flag
Below the decision height set on the seat's radio altimeter
FD CMD selector out of NORM

blocks.title: ADI flags
rows: The assigned gyro is not usable (no power, running up, toppled, failed) or the instrument has failed
No RADIO & CMD INFO power, or an ILS is tuned and no glideslope is received
No RADIO & CMD INFO power, or an ILS is tuned and no localizer is received
A flight director is selected and its commands are not usable
No RADIO & CMD INFO power, or the speed control system has no valid airspeed error
Instrument unpowered (the rate-of-turn channel is not fitted)

blocks.content:
The flags are spring-loaded and held clear by current, so a dead instrument shows all six. A powered instrument shows only the flags for channels the crew are using and not receiving: the GS and RWY flags stay out of view until an ILS is tuned.

Pressing and holding **TEST** drives the instrument to its test picture: 20° right bank and 10° nose up, command bars commanding a climbing right turn, the rising runway at about 100 ft, and the ATT, FD and RWY flags in view. The SPD flag does not appear in the test. Releasing it returns the instrument to its normal picture.

blocks.alt: Close-up of the DC-10 KSSU ADI on an ILS approach at about 150 ft radio height: sphere at 2° nose up and wings level, command bars centerd, glideslope pointer half a dot high, rising runway close below the aircraft symbol with the localizer bar slightly right, fast/slow pointer centerd, DH light out, FD light out, all six flags (ATT, GS, RWY, FD, SPD, RT) out of view. TEST button lower left legible.
blocks.title: Attitude director indicator (KSSU)

blocks.content: Two electromechanical HSIs are offered, the KSSU and the Biman; both hang a compass card from the seat's compass system and neither has crew controls of its own. The **heading bug** follows the glareshield heading select, the **course arrow** the glareshield course, and the navigation source is selected on the glareshield (see [Navigation](navigation)). The compass card is driven whenever its compass coupler's servo is turning and flagged whenever its heading is not trustworthy, so during a fast sync the card can be seen sweeping round under its **HDG** flag.

blocks.title: HSI elements
rows: Bar, two dots each side; CRS flag lamp
Bar on the course arrow, four-dot scale; red and yellow striped flag; TO/FROM arrows
Window showing the ILS glideslope or the navigation unit's vertical path, with its own flag state
Pointer on a four-dot scale on the right; GS flag
Drum: INS, VOR TO, VOR FROM, ILS, or stripes
Window on the left: INS printed, RAD and ILS flags sliding over it, 1 or 2 below
Drum windows: DME distance and the navigation computer's ground speed; dashes when not available
Two digital windows: distance (left), ground speed (right)
CRS, HDG, ADF 1, ADF 2 flag lamps

blocks.content: The card is powered through the seat's HSI HEADING circuit from 26 V AC off the emergency buses. With that circuit open the card stops and its HDG flag comes into view, which is the first step of the compass functional test.

blocks.alt: Close-up of the DC-10 KSSU HSI on a VOR radial: compass card on 095, heading bug at 100, course arrow at 090 with the deviation bar one dot left, source drum reading VOR TO, DME window 23.4, ground speed window 412, MAG annunciator, HDG flag and CRS lamp out. Below it, inset, the Biman HSI in the same state with its digital distance and ground speed windows and the RAD source window.
blocks.title: Horizontal situation indicators

blocks.content: Each RMI combines a compass card with two bearing needles. The needles hang from the card, so each reads the magnetic bearing to its station directly. The card has its own OFF flag, which follows the compass system's heading validity, and each needle source has its own flag.

On the DC-10 each pilot's RMI card is driven by their own side's compass system. On the dual-DME arrangement each needle has a **VOR/ADF** switch on the instrument; on the single and KSSU arrangements needle 1 reads VOR 1 and needle 2 reads VOR 2.

Each KC-10 pilot has a TACAN RMI and a VOR/ADF RMI, the VOR/ADF instrument with selector knobs for its needles. The cards are driven by the compass systems. The needle sources are described in [Navigation](navigation).

The MFD fit replaces the ADI with an electronic ADI (**EADI**) and the HSI with an electronic HSI (**EHSI**): two octagonal color LCDs per seat, drawn by one symbol generator per seat with the symbology of the Astronautics EFIS retrofit. Each seat's generator reads its own side: its inertial unit (or, with no long-range unit fitted, its vertical gyro and compass system), its assigned CADC, its radio altimeter, its clock and its navigation sources. The INS selector transfers a seat's attitude and heading to unit 3.

Each screen is powered from its seat's emergency DC bus and runs a short self-test when power comes on. Inputs that fail affect only the part of the picture they feed; the screen stays lit. Brightness is set with the **BRT** and **DIM** buttons on each bezel and is reduced automatically at night by the screen's photocell.

blocks.title: EADI symbology
rows: Light blue sky over red-brown ground; pitch ladder every 2.5°, numbered every 10°, the rungs lengthening with pitch; red chevrons beyond ±40° pointing to the horizon
Marks at 10, 20, 30, 45 and 60°, fixed zero index, sky pointer
Black wing bars outlined in white, center square
Far left, F over S, with a disc that is filled on the scale and hollow beyond it
Bottom: three boxes with a T that moves between them
Top left: RAD, ILS, INS1 and so on
DME1 and DME2 readouts in the lower corners
Lower right: radio height with the selected DH in green (for example 200DH); passing DH, the value goes and a flashing yellow DH replaces it; the other seat's passed DH as a DH in a yellow circle

Localizer and glideslope scales only while a localizer is tuned; green pointers, filled inside the scale and hollow on the stop; expanded localizer scale on the approach; scale turns yellow and the pointer flashes on excessive deviation
Green, under the localizer pointer below 200 ft, reaching the symbol at touchdown

blocks.content:
Flags are yellow legends in yellow boxes. With no attitude the screen goes black under the bank scale and reference symbol and **ATT** is boxed below the symbol; the sphere, sky pointer, command bars and rising runway are removed. A director computing nothing shows **F/D**; a dead speed control source replaces the fast/slow scale with a vertical boxed **SPD**; a tuned receiver with no localizer or glideslope shows **LOC** or **GS** in place of its scale; a failed radio altimeter or DME is boxed where its reading stands.

The EHSI's MAP picture is track-up when a ground track is available, with the box at the top reading TRK, and heading-up with the box reading HDG when it is not (at rest on the ground, or with no inertial unit aligned). It shows true airspeed and ground speed, the wind, the active waypoint with its distance and time, the course deviation, the weather radar returns while the radar is transmitting and, if selected, the terrain picture. Its modes (MAP, FMS, PLAN, CHSI and the combined CADI picture) and overlays are selected on the display control panel ([MFD display control panels](#ci-mfd-control-panel)); the navigation sources it can show are described in [Navigation](navigation#rad-ins-switching).

blocks.alt: DC-10 captain's MFD pair in cruise: EADI above showing 2.5° nose up wings level, magenta command bars centerd, fast/slow disc centerd, INS1 source top left, DME1 and DME2 lower corners, no radio altitude; EHSI below in MAP mode, TRK box at the top, 366 TAS and 395 GS top left, wind arrow 280/30, active waypoint and distance top right, route in magenta, range ring labeled 20. Bezel BRT and DIM buttons visible.
blocks.title: MFD EADI and EHSI

blocks.content: The FPDS fit gives each pilot one wide flat-panel screen with a PFD on its left half and a navigation display on its right, in the style of the 757/767 flat-panel retrofits (it follows the upgraded cockpit of the Dutch KDC-10s). It replaces the Mach/airspeed indicator, ADI, HSI, altimeter, VSI and radio altimeter on both panels. The FPDS reads the same symbol generator feed as the MFD; its control panel beside each screen takes over the barometric setting and the radio minimums from the removed instruments, adopting their settings when the fit is selected.

blocks.title: FPDS PFD
rows: Flight mode annunciator in four boxes (autothrottle, armed, roll, pitch), the same words as the glareshield FMA

Blue over brown in a rounded window; black chevron aircraft symbol edged in white; single-cue magenta V-bar flight director; yellow pitch limit indicator showing where the nose would meet the stick shaker; open white bank pointer with a slip rectangle beneath it, both filling and turning amber beyond 35° of bank

Gray tape with the current speed boxed; hollow magenta target bug; speed references V1, V2, VFR (flap retract), VSR (slat retract) and VMM, white until set and green after; amber NO VSPD on the ground until V1 and V2 are set; current-speed box amber below the minimum maneuvering speed and red in either red-and-black band

Current altitude boxed, thousands in larger figures; target in magenta above; altitude alert from the altitude advisory (selected altitude boxed white approaching, current altitude box amber on a departure); barometric setting below, STD in green with the preselected setting in white under it
Arc beside the compass rose, with a magenta bracket for a selected vertical speed
Full rose under the sphere with the heading, track and selected heading
In the foot of the sphere window below 2,000 ft with the gear down; amber RA whenever the radio altimeter has failed
Green ILS pointers, expanded localizer, approach monitors (scale amber, pointer flashing); rising runway below 2,500 ft; radio minimums
Ground speed, TAS, wind, bearing source data

blocks.content:
The FPDS distinguishes a reading that is not there **yet** from one that is **lost**. An input still coming alive (an inertial unit aligning, a gyro erecting, a computer initializing, the screen's own self-test) shows its legend in black on an amber box. A failed or unpowered input shows a red box, and an area it fills (the sphere, a tape, the VSI, the rose) is crossed out with a red X. The legends are **ATT** in the sphere window, **SPD** and **ALT** on their tapes, **VERT** on the VSI and **HDG** on the rose and the map.

The navigation display half offers APPR, MAP and PLAN pictures, the weather radar and terrain overlays and the traffic display, selected on its display control panel ([FPDS display control panels](#ci-fpds-control-panel)).

blocks.alt: DC-10 FPDS captain's screen on climb-out through 4,000 ft: PFD on the left half with the four-box FMA (SPD | | HDG SEL | ALT HOLD), sphere at 8° nose up, magenta V-bar on the chevron symbol, speed tape at 250 kt with green V1 and V2 references, altitude tape 4,000 with 10,000 selected in magenta, VSI arc reading 2,000 ft/min, full compass rose; ND on the right half in MAP with the route and range arcs. Display control panel beside it with its knobs legible.
blocks.title: FPDS screen

blocks.content: Each KC-10 pilot has an electronic ADI over an electronic HSI, worked together from one display control panel on the center pedestal. Attitude and heading come from the seat's inertial navigation unit (INU 3 with the INS selector at CAPT ON AUX or F/O ON AUX). The pilot's EHSI and display control panel are on the left emergency DC bus, the copilot's on the right.

blocks.title: EADI symbology
rows: Blue sky over orange ground, pitch ladder, roll scale with sky pointer, two-wing airplane symbol, magenta wedge V-bars
Vertical deviation scale (glideslope, or the FMS vertical path)
Course deviation scale and rising runway
Flight guidance comparator flags; FD annunciation when the FD CMD switch is not in its center position
Radio altitude (white), DH, navigation source and its RNP; EGPWS warnings (red) and cautions (amber), flashing for 5 seconds then steady; WS and GPWS fault flags

blocks.content: The **comparator flags** (amber boxes, black letters) compare what the two seats' displays are showing. Each condition must persist for 2 seconds.

blocks.title: EADI comparator flags
rows: Pitch differs by more than 3° (localizer, back course or FMS approach mode) or 4° (otherwise)
Roll differs by more than 3° or 4°, as for pitch
Heading differs by more than 4° (approach modes) or 6° (otherwise)
Below 1,000 ft radio height, glideslope deviations differ by more than 0.4 dot
Localizer captured, below 1,000 ft, localizer deviations differ by more than 0.5 dot
Below 1,000 ft, radio heights differ by more than 25 ft

blocks.content:
Beyond +30° or −20° of pitch or 65° of bank the EADI **declutters** to the sphere, the ladder with red chevrons, the roll scale and the airplane symbol; it restores inside +25°, −15° and 60°. The **ADI/PFD** button gives a split picture: a half-size EADI over a half EHSI arc carrying only the course needles; the declutter removes it. Failure flags are black letters on red: **ATT**, **SPD**, **GS** or **VNV**, the navigation source (for example LOC1), **RA**, **DU** and **DCP**.

The EHSI is always heading-up with the boxed digital heading at the top and the FMS track as a cyan diamond on the rose. It has five formats: 360° HSI, 80° sectored arc, 360° map, 80° arc map and the tactical map. Its formats, data line and overlays are selected on the display control panel ([KC-10 display control panels](#ci-kc10-dcp)); its navigation source and bearing pointer are described in [Navigation](navigation#rad-ins-switching).

blocks.alt: KC-10 pilot's EADI over EHSI in cruise: EADI with saturated blue sky and orange ground at 2° nose up, magenta wedge V-bars centerd, speed deviation scale left, no comparator flags, radio altitude blank, FMS1 source; EHSI in the 80° arc map with the boxed digital heading at the top, the FMS track diamond in cyan, route and half-range arc. Every legend legible.
blocks.title: KC-10 EADI and EHSI

sections.title: MD-10 electronic instrument system
sections.summary: Six display units, the PFD and ND presentation of flight data, the head-up display and the standby instruments.

blocks.content: The MD-10 conversion replaced the DC-10's electromechanical panel with the MD-11's Electronic Instrument System: six identical display units (DUs) across the main panel, driven by symbol generators in the avionics bay and controlled from the glareshield EIS control panels (ECPs), the source input select panels (SISPs) outboard of each pilot, and the pedestal. The basic T survives on the PFD: attitude in the center, airspeed on the left, altitude and vertical speed on the right, heading at the bottom.

blocks.alt: MD-10 main instrument panel, all six display units lit in cruise: DU 1 captain's PFD, DU 2 captain's ND in MAP, DU 3 engine and alert display, DU 4 systems display, DU 5 F/O's ND, DU 6 F/O's PFD. Captain's SISP outboard left and F/O's outboard right, both ECPs on the glareshield either side of the flight control panel, standby altimeter/airspeed and standby attitude indicator on the center panel below the gear lever. DU numbers labeled.
blocks.title: MD-10 main instrument panel

blocks.content:
Each DU has a 6.5-inch square display area. Normally DU 1 and DU 6 show the captain's and first officer's PFDs, DU 2 and DU 5 their NDs, DU 3 the engine and alert display (EAD) and DU 4 the systems display (SD). The units are interchangeable: when one is switched off or fails, the system reallocates the formats among the units still available, keeping the PFDs and the EAD in preference to the NDs and SD. The allocation follows a fixed table that covers every combination of available units; for example, losing DU 1 and DU 3 moves the captain's PFD to DU 2 and the EAD to DU 4, turns DU 5 into a combined navigation and systems display, and leaves the first officer's PFD on DU 6.

The pictures are generated by the VIA computers (display electronic units). VIA 1 feeds DU 1 to 3, VIA 2 feeds DU 4 to 6, and an auxiliary VIA is a hot spare. A DU that is powered but has no working VIA behind it is blank.

Each DU has a brightness knob on the pedestal's display control panel. The knob sets a reference level that the remote light sensor holds as the outside light changes; turning it fully counterclockwise to its OFF detent switches that DU off and the panel reconfigures as if it had failed. With the SMOKE ELEC/AIR selector out of NORM every lit DU goes to full brightness.

The displays share one color vocabulary, which carries meaning on every page.

blocks.title: Display colors
rows: Scales and figures, pilot-selected values, pilot-initiated modes
Status information, the sky, the pitch limit indicator, the captain's bearing data
FMS-computed targets and data, flight director commands, ILS data
Normal operation: engaged dual-land, track, trend data, allowable configuration speed limits, the first officer's bearing data
Cautions and alerts, abnormal sources, readings below minimums, non-allowable configuration speed limits
Warnings, Vmo/Mmo and stick-shaker speeds, failure flags requiring immediate action

blocks.content: Each PFD reads its own seat's sources: attitude and heading from its ADIRU (1 or 2, or AUX when selected), air data and vertical speed from its own air data computer, radio height and minimums from its own radio altimeter, speeds and targets from the flight control computers and the FMS. The two PFDs can therefore disagree, which is what the comparison monitor exists to catch. The flight mode annunciator across the top and the flight director are described in [Automatic Flight](automatic-flight).

blocks.content: The EIS separates three kinds of bad data. **Failed** data (the source says it has failed) is removed and replaced by a flag, usually an X over the area it occupied: red where the crew must act at once, amber where action can wait a moment. **No computed data** (a valid source with nothing to say, or a value outside its display range) is simply removed, with no flag. **Miscompared** data, where the two seats' sources disagree, stays on the screen and is annunciated.

children.title: Navigation display: heading and air data

blocks.content:
The ND takes its heading and route from its own side. Above the compass it shows the boxed digital heading or track with MAG or TRU, the selected heading bug and the green track diamond; at the upper left the ground speed, true airspeed and the wind direction, speed and arrow. It also carries the UTC clock and the elapsed time or chronograph (the TIMER button below each clearview window starts, stops and resets the chronograph). Its MAP, PLAN, VOR, APPR and TCAS modes, ranges, overlays, weather radar and bearing pointers are described in [Navigation](navigation).

An ADIRU heading failure removes the digital heading, the compass scale, the map, the VOR bearings, the wind and the heading bugs and shows a red **HDG FAIL** at the top of the compass. The ADF bearings remain. Data that is merely not computed is removed with no flag.

Inset: the same ND after an ADIRU heading failure, compass scale, map, bugs and wind removed and a red HDG FAIL at the top of the compass. Callout numbers on every element.
blocks.title: MD-10 navigation display

blocks.content:
The MD-10-10 and MD-10-30 are each available with or without a head-up display; the HUD-equipped aircraft carry a combiner above the captain's glareshield. The HUD draws a monochrome green picture focused at infinity, so its conformal symbols lie over the features they mark in the outside view, one degree on the glass for one degree in the world. From the captain's eye the combiner shows about 7° above to 13° below the aircraft's axis and about 13° either side.

The HUD reads the captain's PFD data, the flight control panel's selected values, the captain's angle-of-attack vane, the stall warning reference and the flight path acceleration. It is powered from the captain's main AC and DC buses; with either lost, or with the combiner stowed, it is dark.

blocks.content:
The HUD has two crew controls. The **stow handle** lowers the combiner into view (LOWERED) or stows it (STOWED). A **brightness mode switch** beside the combiner selects automatic brightness, which follows the light outside, or a fixed manual level.

The HUD also shows an enhanced-vision (infrared) picture behind the symbology. The simulator has no infrared image of its own, so this picture is generated outside the simulator by the Infinity Manager from a camera view along the HUD's boresight and a thermal model of the scene; it is available only while the Manager is running.

blocks.title: Head-up display

blocks.content: The center panel below the gear lever carries the **standby attitude indicator** (see [Standby attitude indicator](#standby-attitude)) and the combined **standby altimeter/airspeed indicator**. The altimeter is an aneroid instrument on the alternate static system with a pointer, an altitude counter and millibar and inch setting windows set by its BARO knob; the airspeed indicator, on the auxiliary pitot, reads on a drum below. Neither needs electrical power. A standby magnetic compass completes the set.

sections.title: Instrument source switching
sections.summary: How each pilot's displays are moved onto the other side's or the auxiliary source, and how the selection is annunciated.

blocks.content: Source switching rests on one principle: each pilot's displays are normally fed by their own side's sources, and any departure from that is deliberate, visible and reversible. A selection moves a whole group of displays onto another computer or reference; it never mixes sources within one instrument. An annunciation tells both pilots that the aircraft is no longer in its normal split configuration, because with both sides on one source the crew have lost the ability to detect that source's errors by comparison.

blocks.content:
The navigation source for each HSI or EHSI (radio or the long-range unit, VOR or ILS) is selected on the glareshield or, on the KC-10, on the display control panel; see [Navigation](navigation).

The CADC and INS selectors work through switching units on the battery bus, so they remain usable on emergency power, and the CADC unit's motor-driven wafers hold their last position if their power is lost.

Each pilot has a **source input select panel** (SISP) outboard of their display units. On the aircraft it carries an EIS SOURCE rotary that chooses which VIA generates that pilot's three DUs, and a column of switch-lights (FLT DIR OFF, FLT DIR, CADC, IRS, FMS, VOR and APPR), each of which moves one kind of data onto the alternate source when pushed and returns it when pushed again. An alternate source is annunciated on the PFD or ND in **white** when it differs from the other pilot's source and in **amber** when both pilots are on the same source, because then the comparison monitor can no longer catch an error in it.

Of these controls the FLT DIR OFF, FLT DIR and IRS switches are operative; the others are listed in [Simulation notes](#simulation-notes).
