sections.title: Operation
sections.summary: Power-up and alignment, preflight checks, and normal use through a flight.

blocks.content:
**DC-10 and KC-10.** The pneumatic standby altimeter and airspeed indicator read correctly on a cold aircraft. With the battery bus powered the standby attitude indicator starts: its horizon comes up from its toppled rest in about half a minute and its OFF flag clears when the rotor is up to speed. When AC power reaches the emergency buses the CADCs initialize in about two seconds and the altimeter, Mach/airspeed and VSI flags clear; the radio altimeters come alive and read zero on the ground.

The vertical gyros erect within seconds and the ADI ATT flags clear within about a minute. The compass systems wait for their directional gyros to become valid, then fast-sync to the flux valves: the HSI and RMI cards sweep onto magnetic heading under their flags and the flags clear. Electronic attitude and heading displays fed by inertial units (the KC-10's EADI and EHSI, the DC-10's MFD and FPDS with a long-range unit) show their attitude and heading flags until the units have aligned; see [Navigation](navigation).

**MD-10.** With battery and emergency power on, DU 1 and DU 3 light; the rest follow as their buses come up. Set the three IRS selectors to NAV: the NAV OFF lights come on steady, the speed tapes show NO TAXI, and the PFDs show ATT FAIL and the NDs HDG FAIL until their units reach NAV. Load the route or type the present position on the FMS F-PLN INIT page and transmit it with INITIALIZE IRS. After about 10 minutes standing still each unit enters NAV, its NAV OFF light goes out and its displays come up. The standby attitude indicator is on the battery bus and starts at once.

A flight started in any state other than cold and dark (on the runway, taxiing or in the air) begins with the gyros erect, the compass systems synchronized and the inertial units aligned. A cold-and-dark start begins with every gyro at rest and every unit off.

items.item: CADC, INS and FD CMD selectors

items: **ADI test** (DC-10, KSSU ADI): hold TEST. The sphere shows about 20° right bank and 10° nose up, the command bars a climbing right turn, the rising runway about 100 ft, and the ATT, FD and RWY flags in view. Release and check the normal picture returns.

**Radio altimeter test**: with the aircraft on the ground the indicator reads zero. Set the DH bug to about 20 ft and check the DH lights come on. Push SET TEST: the indicator reads 100 ft, the flag comes into view and the DH lights go out. Release: the indicator returns to zero and the DH lights come on. Set the DH bug as required.
**Altimeters**: set the airfield altimeter setting. The primary altimeters should agree with field elevation within 75 ft.

**Altitude advisory test**: set the preselect 1,000 ft above field elevation and pull to arm, then turn the BARO knob slowly clockwise. At about 750 ft from the selected altitude the advisory light comes on with the tone; at about 250 ft it goes out. Turn back: at about 250 ft from the selected altitude the light flashes. Push ALT RESET: it goes out. Reset the altimeter setting.
**Heading check**: the HSI and RMI cards should agree within 4° of each other and within 10° of the standby compass. Magnetic anomalies at some gates can exceed this.
**Standby attitude**: check the OFF flag out of view, cage and uncage, and set the miniature airplane.
**MAX SPD WARN TEST**: hold at 1, then at 2; the overspeed aural sounds for each.

blocks.content:
**Altimeter setting.** Set the local setting on the ground, standard (29.92 inHg, 1013 hPa) passing the transition altitude, and the destination setting passing the transition level. On the DC-10 and KC-10 set each primary altimeter and the standby altimeter with its own knob; on the FPDS use STD on each display control panel; on the MD-10 pull each BAROSET knob for STD and push it back to the previous setting by the first detent. The air data computers accept settings from about 28.1 to 31.0 inHg; a setting outside that band fails the computer's barometric setting monitor after 2 seconds and flags the baro-corrected altitude (on the MD-10, a red X on the altitude tape).

The simulator's altimeter keys work these knobs as a hand would: the barometric key sets the simulator's own setting into both primary altimeters (or ECPs, or FPDS panels) and the standard-pressure key sets standard; the Kollsman increment and decrement keys move the knob of the altimeter they address one detent; the decision height keys move the radio minimums.

**Cross-checking.** Compare the two sides' airspeed, altitude, attitude and heading regularly, and the standby instruments with both. A small steady difference between the two altimeters, growing with altitude, is calibration and normal; a difference that changes, or that one side shows and the standby does not, is a failure. Before climbing out on an approach or departure, check the VSI and altimeter agree on the sense of the rate.

**Altitude advisory** (DC-10, KC-10). Set and arm the next altitude with each clearance; the steady light and tone at 750 ft are the cue to begin the level-off.

**Heading.** In normal flight the compass sync annunciators fluctuate about center and are displaced in turns, recovering slowly afterward. At high latitudes, or with a suspect flux valve, select DG on the affected system and reset it against a known heading every so often: the card drifts at about 15 × sin(latitude) degrees per hour. The MD-10's ADIRUs change to true heading automatically in the polar regions.

**Approach.** Set the decision height or minimums. The radio altitude appears on the PFD (MD-10) below 2,500 ft; the rising runway (DC-10 KSSU and MFD) rises toward the aircraft symbol below 200 ft; the DH light, the amber minimums readout or the flashing DH legend mark the decision height.

sections.title: Failures and non-normal operation
sections.summary: How each failure shows, what it takes with it, and what the crew do about it.

blocks.content: Flight instrument failures fall into two classes. **Annunciated** failures raise a flag, an X or an alert, and the crew's task is to switch to a good source. **Silent** failures leave a plausible, unflagged indication that is wrong: a blocked pitot with its drain blocked, an iced TAT probe, a flux valve that has slaved its card to a wrong heading. These are caught only by comparing independent sources, which is why the cross-check matters more than any flag. The procedures are in [Abnormal Procedures](abnormal-procedures) and [Emergency Procedures](emergency-procedures).

blocks.content:
An airspeed indication can be wrong without a flag, because the computer receives a pressure it has no means of distinguishing from a real one. The most dangerous case is the blocked pitot with its drain also blocked: in a climb the indicated speed rises, the natural response is to raise the nose or reduce thrust, and the aircraft decelerates toward the stall while its airspeed indicator says it is fast. In a descent the error reverses.

The defense is to fly a known pitch attitude and thrust for the phase of flight, which hold the aircraft at a safe speed whatever the instruments say, and then to diagnose at leisure. Compare the captain's, first officer's and standby airspeeds: a single failed side disagrees with the other two. Ground speed from the navigation system, the stick shaker and the angle-of-attack information (on the MD-10 HUD) are independent of the pitot-static system. Once the bad side is known, put both pilots' instruments on the good computer where the aircraft allows it.
Disconnect the autothrottle and autopilot when the airspeed is suspect. Both fly the airspeed they are given, and an airspeed that rises in the climb will lead them toward the stall.

The flight instruments are spread across buses so that losing one takes only one side. The captain's air data computer and air data instruments are on the left emergency AC bus and the first officer's on the right; vertical gyro 1 and compass system 1 on the left emergency AC bus, vertical gyro 2 and compass system 2 on the right, vertical gyro 3 on AC bus 1. Radio altimeter 1 is on AC bus 1 and radio altimeter 2 on AC bus 3.

The flight instruments are spread across buses so that losing one takes only one side. ADIRU 1 is on the left emergency AC bus, ADIRU 2 on the right and ADIRU AUX on generator bus 1, each with its own battery. Air data computer 1 is on the left emergency AC bus and computer 2 on the right; radio altimeter 1 is on AC bus 1 and radio altimeter 2 on AC bus 3. The display units are powered as listed in [Display units and reconfiguration](#md10-eis-architecture).

With every AC bus lost, what remains depends on emergency power (see [Electrical](electrical)). Independent of it, the crew always keep the **standby attitude indicator** (battery bus through its own inverter, for as long as the battery lasts), the **standby altimeter** and **standby airspeed indicator** (pneumatic; the altimeter's vibrator alone needs power, and without it the pointer moves in small jumps), and the **magnetic compass**. A gyro whose supply has gone stays rigid and readable for several minutes while its rotor runs down, and its flag does not appear until then; the flag, not the picture, says when to stop believing it. On the MD-10 a DU that is powered but has lost its VIA is blank.

**Modeled in depth.** The pitot-static system is simulated as pressures in plumbing: each line lags its probe, a partial blockage slows it, a full blockage traps its pressure, drains vent, leaks drift toward cabin pressure, and icing follows the probe heat and the weather. The air data computers solve the standard air data equations, initialize on power-up, run their ten monitors with the 2-second and 18-second timing, and send separate digital and analog lines. The two sides and the standby instruments carry small, different calibration errors and a slow drift, so they never read exactly alike on a serviceable aircraft. The gyros are simulated from rotor physics: run-up and run-down with speed set by supply frequency, precession, erection and its cutouts, earth-rate drift, acceleration and turn errors, and topple. The compass couplers follow the maintenance manual's synchronization rates and logic. The ADIRUs align, compare the entered position, run on their batteries and change to true heading near the poles; while the simulator is paused no inertial unit drifts or aligns, and a slew is treated as a reposition.

items: Static source position error is not simulated: the computers' correction and the ports' error are both zero.

The Vmo/Mmo schedule driving the Vmo pointer, the barber poles and the overspeed warning is a fleet-typical value (about 365 kt and M 0.88) on every variant. The operating limits are those in [Limitations](limitations).
The air data computers' barometric setting monitor accepts about 28.1 to 31.0 inHg; outside that band the baro-corrected altitude fails.
Standby attitude fast erection stops by itself once the gyro is erect or after 120 seconds; the caution against fast erection in the first 60 seconds is not enforced.
The transponders report the simulator's own altitude for Mode C; the CADC's altitude word is used by TCAS.
Magnetic dip is taken from a simple dipole model of the earth's field.

The radio altimeter tape reads to 3,000 ft. Its self-test reads 100 ft; some operators' checklists quote 40 ±5 ft. The DH light responds only to the indicator's decision height comparison and cannot be pressed to test or cancel.
The compass SET HDG knob does not spring back to center; return it by hand, or the card keeps slewing.
The CADC selector moves the Mach counter along with the airspeed pointer and altimeter.
The FD CMD selector lights the ADI's FD light but does not move the command bars. On the KC-10 the FD CMD knob is not operative.
No rate gyro is fitted: the ADI rate-of-turn pointer stays centerd, and the decrab (rudder monitor) pointer is not driven. The MFD derives its rate of turn from the heading.
There is no attitude comparator indication on the DC-10.
On a powered ADI the GS and RWY flags appear only when an ILS is tuned; a dead ADI shows all six flags.
Each DC-10 RMI card is driven by its own side's compass system. On the aircraft the RMI cards are crossed: compass system 1 drives the first officer's RMI and system 2 the captain's.
Air data comes from two air data computers of the DC-10 type rather than the ADIRUs' air data function; there is no air data source switching; two radio altimeters are fitted.
The BAROSET knob can be set beyond the air data computers' accepted band (about 28.1 to 31.0 inHg), and the altitude tape then fails.

On the SISPs the CADC, FMS, VOR and APPR switches and the EIS SOURCE selector are inoperative; only FLT DIR OFF, FLT DIR and IRS work. The IRS selection moves the displays but lights no switch-light and shows no source annunciation. Because the EIS SOURCE selector stays in its normal position, a powered display unit whose VIA has failed stays blank.
The IRS selectors have OFF and NAV only; alignment takes 10 minutes at any latitude; sending a refused position a second time overrides the comparison test.
The standby attitude indicator is the same instrument and knob as the DC-10's. The MD-10's own instrument is a DC-powered gyro on the battery bus with a separate FAST ERECT switch.
The ND chronograph counts up only.
HUD: no flight mode annunciations, guidance cue or pitch limit bracket are drawn. The enhanced-vision picture is produced by the Infinity Manager and needs it running; there is no EVS switch.

blocks.content: **Instrument fits.** On the DC-10 the instrument fits are chosen in the EFB's Configuration app, Aircraft Configuration page, Pilots' Panels zone (see [Instrument fits](#instrument-fits)).

**EFB.** On the Ground Ops app's Ramp page, **pitot covers** close the inlets of all three pitot tubes while leaving their drains clear: with them fitted every airspeed reads zero. They come off by themselves when the aircraft moves with an engine running or leaves the ground. The Failures app offers, among others: airspeed indication failure (captain's or first officer's pitot blocked), static system blocked (either side), loss of primary attitude, attitude display failure and HSI display failure (either side), inertial navigation unit failure (1, 2 or 3; on the MD-10 the ADIRUs), pitot heat inoperative (any of the three), and nose radome damage with all three pitot tubes blocked. See [EFB](efb).

parts.title: Automatic Flight
parts.summary: Autopilots, flight directors, autothrottle and speed control, yaw dampers, autoland and the PAFAM landing monitor.

sections.title: Introduction
sections.summary: What the automatic flight system does, how it is built, and how the three flight decks differ.

blocks.content:
The automatic flight system flies the aircraft, or tells the pilot how to fly it, from the takeoff roll to the landing rollout. It combines five functions that share sensors, computers and annunciation: the **autopilots**, which move the flight control surfaces; the **flight directors**, which display the same guidance as command bars for the pilot to follow; the **autothrottle and speed control system**, which moves the thrust levers and computes speed guidance; the **yaw dampers**, which damp the Dutch roll; and, on the DC-10, the **autoland** capability with its landing monitor (PAFAM).

Two different automatic flight systems are installed across the family, and this part describes both.

items: **DC-10 and KC-10: the Flight Guidance System (FGS).** Two independent flight guidance systems, each with a roll, a pitch and a yaw computer, controlled from the FGS panel on the glareshield. Each autopilot is engaged with its own OFF / CWS / CMD lever, each mode has its own pushbutton, and a four-window flight mode annunciator strip on each pilot's glareshield reports AUTOTHROTTLE, ARM, ROLL and PITCH modes. Two separate Automatic Throttle / Speed Control (AT/SC) computers drive the thrust levers.

**MD-10: the Automatic Flight System (AFS).** The FedEx conversion replaced the DC-10's guidance with the MD-11's: two Flight Control Computers (FCC) behind a glareshield Flight Control Panel (FCP). One AUTO FLIGHT switch engages both autothrottles and one autopilot; the knobs work on the turn-to-preselect, pull-to-select, push-to-hold principle; and the flight mode annunciator is drawn across the top of each PFD in three windows (speed, roll, altitude).

blocks.content: The airframe did not change between the two, so the control surfaces, the auto pitch trim through the horizontal stabilizer, the single thrust lever servo and the four-channel yaw damper are common. Where this part says "the autopilot" without qualification, the statement applies to both systems.

blocks.alt: Functional schematic of the DC-10/KC-10 Flight Guidance System. Left column: sensors (compass systems, vertical gyros or INS platforms, yaw rate gyros, CADC 1 and 2, radio altimeters 1 and 2, linear accelerometer units, VHF NAV/ILS receivers 1 and 2, surface position sensors, angle-of-attack vanes). Center: FGS 1 and FGS 2, each drawn as a box containing ROLL, PITCH and YAW computers with A and B channels, plus AT/SC computers 1 and 2 and the auto pitch trim computer. Right column: outputs to ailerons, spoilers, elevators (four, one per pitch channel), horizontal stabilizer (auto pitch trim), upper and lower rudders (series yaw damper and parallel autoland servos), the single duplex autothrottle servo with three clutches to the thrust levers, both ADIs (command bars, fast/slow), both FMA strips, and PAFAM (DC-10). The FGS panel on the glareshield feeds both systems. Line style shows that FGS 1 uses side-1 sensors and FGS 2 side-2 sensors.

blocks.title: Definitions
blocks.content:
**Fail-passive**: an automatic system that, after any failure not shown to be extremely improbable, is protected against hardovers, leaves the aircraft in trim, gives a warning and does not interfere with the pilot taking over. One autopilot (SNGL LAND, SINGLE LAND) is fail-passive.

**Fail-operational**: a system with redundant automatic channels, so that if one fails below the alert height the remaining channels can complete the flare and touchdown. Two autopilots in DUAL LAND are fail-operational.

sections.title: System architecture
sections.summary: Guidance computers, sensors, servos and the flight director, and the reasoning behind the redundancy.

blocks.content: The automatic flight system is a set of closed loops wrapped around the aircraft. Each loop compares what the crew asked for (a heading, an altitude, a speed, a beam) with what the sensors say the aircraft is doing, and moves a surface or the thrust levers to null the difference. The architecture is about three questions: which computer closes which loop, which sensors each computer trusts, and what happens when one of them fails.

The DC-10 and KC-10 carry **two independent flight guidance systems**. Each contains three computers, one per axis: a **roll computer** (ailerons and spoilers), a **pitch computer** (elevators, with the auto pitch trim computer driving the horizontal stabilizer) and a **yaw computer** (the yaw damper and, on the DC-10, the parallel rudder servo used in autoland). Each computer has two channels, A and B. Channel A computes every cruise mode; channel B joins it in the approach to make a self-monitoring pair for the landing.

Each system is wired to its **own side's sensors**: FGS 1 reads the captain's vertical gyro (the INS platform on INS-equipped aircraft), CADC 1, ILS receiver 1 and radio altimeter 1; FGS 2 reads the first officer's. Nothing is shared that a single failure could corrupt in both, which is why the second system is a real backup rather than a copy of the first.

Only one autopilot flies the aircraft at a time, except in DUAL LAND. The autopilot that was engaged first is the **coupled** one: its computers fly its own side's ILS receiver and air data, and it keeps that role as long as it stays engaged. If its attitude reference fails (a toppled or failed vertical gyro or platform), that autopilot disconnects on its own; the other, on its own gyro, can be engaged and will fly normally.

The MD-10 carries **two Flight Control Computers (FCC)**. Each contains an autopilot, a flight director, an autothrottle channel and an auto pitch trim channel. The FCCs read the three ADIRUs, the FMS, the radio altimeters and the ILS receivers, and drive the same surfaces and the same thrust lever servo as the DC-10's computers. One AP is engaged at a time (AP1 is FCC 1, AP2 is FCC 2) except in DUAL LAND, when both are engaged and the FMA reads AP.

Each AP needs its hydraulic systems: **AP1 requires hydraulic system 2 for the flight controls and system 3 for auto pitch trim; AP2 requires system 1 for both.** An AP whose hydraulics, FCC power or attitude reference fails is not available, and an engaged one disconnects.

The flight director is not a separate computer. Its pitch and roll commands are computed inside the guidance computers, in parallel with the autopilot's, and sent through isolated circuits to the attitude indicators as command bars. Following the bars by hand produces the same flight path the autopilot would fly; with the autopilot engaged, centerd bars show that the autopilot is doing what the guidance asks.

Because it is the same computation, the flight director captures and tracks everything the autopilot does (heading, radials, the localizer and glideslope) and can be used with the autopilot off or in CWS. It works on the ground too, which is how the preflight check of the bars is done.

Each pilot's FD switch selects that pilot's command bars. The **basic engagement mode** of the flight director, with nothing else selected, is HDG HOLD in roll and VERT SPD in pitch, or ALT HOLD if the vertical speed wheel is in its detent. Normally the captain's bars are driven by FGS 1 and the first officer's by FGS 2; the overhead **FD CMD** selector (BOTH ON 1 / NORM / BOTH ON 2) puts both pilots' bars on one system, and an amber **FD** light on each ADI shows that the selector is off NORM.

The bars are fly-to: the pitch bar above the aircraft symbol commands nose up, the roll bar right of center commands right roll; full deflection is ±1 inch. The KC-10's EADI draws the same guidance as V-command bars. Bars are biased out of view when the FD switch is OFF, when the TURB pushbar is in, when guidance is invalid, and on the side whose director disagrees with the mode of an engaged autopilot.

Both MD-10 flight directors are on unless selected off with the **FLT DIR OFF** switch on each pilot's source input select panel. FD1 drives the captain's PFD and FD2 the first officer's; the **FLT DIR** switch puts the other side's director on that PFD (CAPT ON 2, F/O ON 1). Turning a director off removes its bars; turning it back on brings them back in the mode of the AP or the other director. With both APs and both FDs off, a director turned on commands wings level and heading hold, and altitude hold if the vertical speed is below 300 ft/min or vertical speed hold above it. On a go-around or a windshear, both directors come into view even if selected off.

children.title: Servos, surfaces and auto pitch trim

blocks.content:
The autopilot flies with the **ailerons, spoilers, elevators, horizontal stabilizer and rudders**. Its servos act on the same hydraulic actuators as the pilots' controls, so they need hydraulic power to move anything, and the pilots can override them at any time.

The roll servo positions one inboard aileron, which moves the cable run and therefore the control wheels; the pitch servos position the elevators, which moves the columns. In the simulation the 3D column and wheel are drawn where the autopilot has them while it flies an axis. The rudder pedals do not move with the yaw damper; they move only with the parallel rudder servo used in the autoland's align and rollout.

**Pitch is a two-surface loop.** The elevator is the fast actuator: it gives the pitch channel its bandwidth. The horizontal stabilizer is the slow one: **auto pitch trim** drives it whenever the elevator has been out of its faired position (aligned with the stabilizer) for a while, until the elevator is faired again. The stabilizer therefore acts as the loop's integrator in hardware. A sustained climb, a change of weight or a change of speed all end with the stabilizer where it must be and the elevator back near neutral, with nothing wound up in the computer. Auto pitch trim moves the stabilizer through its own channel and **does not move the longitudinal trim handles**.

If the elevator stays out of fair for longer than the trim can catch up with (a stabilizer that cannot move, a trim motor failure, a heavy mistrim), the amber **AP OUT OF TRIM** light comes on (DC-10/KC-10). It goes out when the stabilizer has caught up.

VERT SPD flies the rate on the wheel and nothing else. If the selected rate needs more thrust than the engines have, as it can when heavy and high, the autopilot keeps pitching up to hold the rate and the airspeed bleeds away. Watch the speed throughout any climb in VERT SPD.

children.title: Control laws: what the autopilot is trying to do

blocks.content:
Every vertical mode folds into one quantity: a **commanded vertical speed**. VERT SPD (V/S) commands it directly; the altitude modes command a vertical speed proportional to the altitude error (about 4.5 ft/min per foot, so 100 ft below the target the aircraft climbs at about 450 ft/min and the rate decays to zero at the altitude); the speed modes command the vertical speed that trades the aircraft's kinetic energy for the speed error. That single command then feeds a cascade of three loops, each faster than the one outside it: vertical speed error commands a **vertical acceleration** (limited to about 0.2 g), acceleration error commands a **pitch rate**, and pitch rate error moves the **elevator**. Auto pitch trim then removes the elevator's standing deflection through the stabilizer.

The cascade explains the behavior a pilot sees: mode changes do not step the pitch attitude, captures are smooth arcs rather than corners, and the aircraft does not pitch harder than the acceleration limit however large the error.

blocks.alt: Block diagram of the autopilot control laws. Top row, pitch: five outer laws (VERT SPD from the wheel, ALT CAP and ALT HOLD from altitude error, IAS HOLD from airspeed error, MACH HOLD from Mach error, G/S from beam deviation with gain programming by radio altitude) feed one 'commanded vertical speed' box; then a vertical acceleration command limited to about ±0.2 g, a pitch rate loop, the elevator servo, and an 'elevator out of fair' detector driving the auto pitch trim to the stabilizer, with the stabilizer drawn as the integrator. Bottom row, roll: HDG HOLD, HDG SEL, RAD/VOR, FMS/NAV and LOC laws feed a 'bank command' box clamped by the bank limit selector and rate limited, then a roll rate loop and the aileron servo. A side box shows the gain schedules: pitch gains with (250/IAS), heading gain with true airspeed.
blocks.title: Autopilot control laws
blocks.caption: Every vertical mode becomes a vertical speed command; every lateral mode becomes a bank command.

blocks.content:
**Gain scheduling.** A degree of elevator produces more pitch rate at high dynamic pressure than at low, so the pitch gains are scheduled with indicated airspeed: they fall above about 250 KIAS and rise below it. Without the schedule the loop would be sluggish on the approach or oscillate in the cruise. In roll, the heading error is converted to a bank command with a gain referred to true airspeed, because the turn rate a given bank produces falls as true airspeed rises.

**The roll channel is a rate loop.** Heading error commands a bank angle, limited by the bank angle selector (never more than 30°) and rate-limited so that the bank comes in progressively; bank error commands a roll rate; roll rate error moves the ailerons. As the aircraft approaches the selected heading the bank is taken out early, by an amount that grows with turn rate and bank, so the roll-out arrives on the heading rather than past it.

**Capture logic.** An altitude, a localizer or a glideslope is captured at the point where the capture maneuver will ask for no more than the aircraft is already doing. For the altitude the capture starts where the altitude law's own command (4.5 ft/min per foot of error) has fallen to the present climb rate, so the vertical speed command does not step at the capture. For the glideslope the capture point depends on how fast the aircraft is closing the beam: a fast closure captures farther out, a slow closure near the center, and with no closure inside about one dot. Rates come from the aircraft's own inertial vertical speed and ground track, not from differentiating the beam needle.

**Mode reversions** are listed with each mode below. The general rule is that a mode the aircraft can no longer fly gives way to the basic mode for that axis (HDG HOLD in roll; VERT SPD or ALT HOLD in pitch), and the change shows on the FMA.

blocks.title: Design performance (check flight tolerances)
rows: Held within 50 ft/min or 2 % of the selection; overshoot under 150 ft/min or 6 %. Limits 4,000 ft/min climb, 8,000 ft/min descent; pitch 22° nose up, 10° nose down
Engaged from a 2,000 ft/min climb or descent, the arrest overshoot does not exceed 200 ft
Overshoot no more than 100 ft; level off within 20 ft of the selection
Within 3 kt from a stabilized climb or descent; within 10 kt from a changing speed or in a 30° banked turn
Within 0.015 stabilized; 0.03 from a changing speed or in a turn
Roll rate about 2.5°/s; bank 5° to 25° by the selector; on heading within 1° with no more than one overshoot under 10°
Reverts to CWS at 5 to 15 lb wheel force (roll) and 12 to 32 lb column force (pitch)

blocks.content: These are the aircraft's own check-flight criteria. The simulation's laws are tuned to meet them on the simulated aircraft; with an unusual center of gravity or an extreme weight the results can sit at the edge of these bands.

For an automatic landing the DC-10 becomes a four-channel aircraft in pitch. With both autopilots engaged in DUAL LAND, channels A and B of both pitch computers each drive one of the four elevators, so a single failed channel moves only one elevator a quarter of the way and the other three overpower it while the failed channel is disconnected. In roll the two systems' A and B channels form monitored pairs. In yaw, two servos share each rudder actuator; a yaw failure does not disconnect the rudder but reverts it from **parallel** operation (the autoland servo, up to ±23° of rudder, felt in the pedals) to **series** operation (the yaw damper, ±5°, not felt).

Each channel carries in-line monitors that compare its command with its partner and with its sensors. A monitor that trips alone would disconnect a healthy channel on a transient, so the PAFAM inhibits the disconnect until a second factor confirms the failure (see [PAFAM](#pafam)). If an autopilot drops out during DUAL LAND the landing continues in SNGL LAND on the remaining one, which is why DUAL LAND is fail-operational and SNGL LAND fail-passive.

The KC-10's guidance computers are the DC-10's, but its LAND switch is placarded INOP and the aircraft has no autoland or PAFAM. Approaches are flown coupled to the ILS down to the applicable minimums and landed by hand. Both autopilots are never engaged together on the KC-10.

Before a land mode engages, the MD-10 is flown by one channel of one AP; the second channel of that AP and both channels of the other stand by. At DUAL LAND engagement the three standby channels become active, both APs are engaged (the FMA reads AP) and both rudders engage in parallel. If a requirement for DUAL LAND is lost above 100 ft, the system reverts to SINGLE LAND (two channels of one AP and one parallel rudder), and from SINGLE LAND to APPR ONLY. Reversions are inhibited below 100 ft.

sections.title: Flight mode annunciator
sections.summary: The one place that says what the automatic flight system is doing. Read it after every selection.

blocks.content: The flight mode annunciator (FMA) shows the modes actually engaged and armed, not the buttons the crew pressed. A selection that the system refuses, or a mode it reverts from, shows here first. The discipline is the same on both decks: after any selection, read the FMA and call the change; after any unexpected change, find out why before doing anything else.

Each pilot has a strip of four windows on the glareshield, in front of the ADI. From left to right they are **AUTOTHROTTLE**, **ARM**, **ROLL** and **PITCH**. Both strips show the same modes; they are two displays of one answer.

The AUTOTHROTTLE, ROLL and PITCH windows are **green**: they show what is engaged and flying now. The ARM window is **amber**: it shows what will engage when its capture conditions are met, and it goes blank at the capture rather than changing legend, because from that moment the capture is reported in the ROLL or PITCH window. Pressing the overhead **ANNUN LT TEST** cap makes both strips spell **T-E-S-T** across the four windows, all in green.

blocks.alt: DC-10-30 captain's glareshield and upper instrument panel, close up: the four-window FMA strip reading SPD | ILS | LOC TRK | G/S TRK, green legends with the ILS legend amber; beside it the AP OUT OF TRIM light, the ATS 1 and ATS 2 warning lights (red upper and amber lower halves) and the AP 1 and AP 2 warning lights (red upper, amber lower). All legends legible.
blocks.title: FMA strip and autoflight warning lights (DC-10)

blocks.content: Each window is a backlit **film strip**, not a screen. When a legend changes, the backlight goes out, the strip rolls to the new legend and the light comes back: the window is dark for about half a second and you hear the strip move (the sound plays on a side only when its strip is lit and its FD switch is on). A change to blank is also a roll. Each strip's lighting has its own circuit breaker (CAPT'S FMA LTG and F/O'S FMA LTS); losing one darkens that strip only, and the modes are unaffected. The strips dim with the panel lighting.

blocks.title: AUTOTHROTTLE window (green)
rows: Autothrottle engaged on the ground with no thrust mode selected, or held by the servo brake from 80 kt on the takeoff roll. The servo does not move the levers.
Rating mode: the levers are driven until the highest engine reaches the limit on the thrust rating computer.
Speed mode: the levers are driven to hold the speed in the SPD window.
Speed mode with the selected speed below the safe computed speed: the autothrottle is holding the alpha speed instead.
Retard: the levers are closing for the landing.

blocks.title: ARM window (amber)
rows: Altitude preselect armed: the altitude in the ALT window will be captured.
Armed to capture the VOR or TACAN radial set in the course window (with the altitude preselect).
Armed to capture the long-range navigation unit's course (with the altitude preselect).
Armed to capture the localizer only (with the altitude preselect).
Armed to capture the localizer and the glideslope (with the altitude preselect). With LAND selected, ILS stands until the preland test answers.
Both beams captured, no automatic landing: ILS selected without LAND, or the preland test failed with one autopilot. Not on the KC-10, whose window goes blank at G/S TRK instead.
Tracking both beams with LAND selected, one autopilot good for the landing: fail-passive.
Tracking both beams with LAND selected, both autopilots good: fail-operational.

blocks.title: ROLL window (green)
rows: Basic roll mode: holding the heading the aircraft rolled out on.
Turning to and holding the heading in the HDG window.
TO/GA pushed on the ground: wings-level guidance (flight director only).
TO/GA pushed in flight with flaps out: wings level, then the heading held.
Capturing / tracking the selected VOR or TACAN radial.
Over the station or departing the radial: holding the course. Replaced by RAD TRK after 30 s to 3 min, or by HDG HOLD after 3 min.
Capturing / tracking the long-range navigation unit's course.
Capturing (inside about two dots) / tracking the localizer.
Autoland runway alignment: the forward slip that removes the crab (DC-10).
Autoland rollout: rudder and nosewheel on the localizer after main gear spin-up (DC-10).
CWS selected with the CWS button, FD switches off.
CWS H/SEL, CWS H/HLD, CWS RAD, CWS R/CRS, CWS FMS, CWS LOC, CWS G/A
CWS selected with the CWS button, flight directors on: the crew fly the wheel while the bars show the mode named.

blocks.title: PITCH window (green)
rows: Basic pitch mode: holding the rate on the vertical speed wheel.
Holding altitude (wheel in the ALT HLD detent, or the preselect captured).
Holding the airspeed / Mach that existed at selection, on pitch.
TO/GA pushed on the ground: speed guidance on the pitch bar, 22° limit (flight director only).
Go-around: speed guidance on pitch, 15° limit.
Capturing / tracking the glideslope. G/S TRK follows G/S CAP after 20 s.
CWS, CWS IAS, CWS MACH, CWS G/A
CWS selected with the CWS button (bare CWS with the FD switches off).

blocks.content:
**How CWS is annunciated.** CWS selected with the **CWS pushbutton** (lever left in CMD) shows the CWS legends above. CWS on the **lever** is not annunciated at all: with a flight director on, the windows show the director's modes without the CWS prefix; with both FD switches off, the roll and pitch windows are blank. An overpower or the TURB pushbar drops the lever to CWS and is shown the same way, except that TURB puts TURB in the pitch window and blanks the roll window.

In an autoland, both pitch windows go blank at main gear spin-up and the roll windows read ROLL OUT.

The MD-10 FMA is drawn across the top of each PFD in three windows: **speed** (left), **roll** (center) and **altitude** (right). Each window shows a mode and the target it is flying to. Armed modes appear in smaller letters above the engaged mode; the engaged autopilot (AP1, AP2, or AP with both engaged in DUAL LAND) appears below the roll window.

The speed window puts the target first and the mode after it (for example "230 PITCH"); the altitude window puts the mode first and the target after it, with the thousands large and the hundreds small ("CLB THRUST 15 000"). In the autoland the altitude window carries the pitch mode and the land status on one line ("G/S DUAL LAND").

blocks.alt: MD-10-30 captain's PFD, top strip close up, on an autoland: speed window '145 THRUST', roll window 'LOC' in green with 'AP' below it, altitude window 'G/S DUAL LAND' in green. A second inset shows a climb: '280 PITCH' white, 'NAV1' magenta with 'AP1' below, 'PROF TO 31000' small magenta above 'CLB THRUST 15 000'. Legends and colors legible.
