blocks.content: **Flashing.** A mode that changes by itself (an automatic reversion) flashes five times, then stays steady. The speed window alternates the target and the mode while the speed is more than 10 kt fast and increasing, or 5 kt slow and decreasing, with speed on the throttles in V/S or FPA: the aircraft cannot hold that speed at that rate. A disconnect boxes the affected windows with a red flashing **AP OFF** or **ATS OFF** until the matching disconnect switch is pushed; the box then turns white if the system can be re-engaged, amber if it cannot. A red **FD FAIL** under the roll window means that side's flight director has failed and its bars and FMA modes are removed.

sections.title: Autopilot engagement and disconnect
sections.summary: How each autopilot is engaged, what CWS does, every way it disconnects, and the warnings that follow.

blocks.content:
Each autopilot has its own engage lever on the pitch control panel of the FGS panel, **AP 1** on the left and **AP 2** on the right, each with three positions: **OFF**, **CWS** (control wheel steering) and **CMD** (command). The levers are electrically held: a lever stays up only while its autopilot accepts it, and drops on its own when the hold is lost. A lever that drops is the crew's primary cue that something has disconnected the autopilot, whatever the cause.

Moving a lever from OFF to CMD takes it through CWS; on the aircraft the pressure is released at CWS and reapplied to reach CMD. Each autopilot needs its own computer power to engage and a healthy attitude reference on its own side.

items: **Airborne only.** A lever moved to CMD on the ground annunciates its modes but the autopilot moves no surface until the aircraft is airborne. The FedEx minimum height for engagement after takeoff is 500 ft AGL (see [Limitations](limitations)).

**Engaging under a flight director** keeps the modes the director was showing, so the FMA does not change at engagement. The one exception is TAKE OFF, which is a flight director mode only: moving a lever to CMD in the climb-out ends it and the autopilot starts in HDG HOLD and VERT SPD at the climb rate it finds. Moving a lever only to CWS keeps TAKE OFF on the bars.
**Engaging with no director** starts in the basic modes: HDG HOLD (rolling wings level first if banked) and VERT SPD, or ALT HOLD if the vertical speed wheel is in its detent.

**One autopilot at a time**, except in LAND. Moving the second lever to CMD drops the first to OFF. A lever passing through CWS on its way to CMD disturbs nothing, but a lever held at CWS beside an engaged autopilot for a few seconds (about 3 s) takes the aircraft and drops the other.

**In LAND**, the second lever may be moved to CMD for DUAL LAND (see [Approach and autoland](#approach-and-autoland)). A lever left at CWS beside one in CMD during LAND drops to OFF. Giving LAND up, or pushing TO/GA, with both levers in CMD drops AP 2.

blocks.content: Control wheel steering lets the crew fly through the autopilot: the crew make the maneuver with the wheel and column, and the autopilot holds what they leave it with. It has two entries:

items: **The lever at CWS.** The autopilot is engaged in CWS. Any flight director modes stay on the bars and in the FMA (without a CWS prefix); with the FD switches off the roll and pitch windows are blank.

**The CWS pushbutton** with a lever in CMD. The lever stays in CMD and nothing lights. The roll channel reverts to CWS, and the pitch channel too unless ALT HOLD or VERT SPD was standing, which keep flying. The FMA shows the CWS legends. The button is refused once both the localizer and the glideslope are captured, so it cannot take the wheel from an autoland approach.

blocks.content: CWS selected with the button ends in both axes, and the autopilot returns to command, on the crew's next selection of IAS, MACH, HDG SEL or HDG HOLD; at the moment a radial, a localizer or an FMS course is captured; and when an altitude preselect levels the aircraft off. A heading stroke ends it with the pitch taking VERT SPD at the climb rate in force. Rolling the vertical speed wheel selects VERT SPD and leaves the roll in CWS.

**How CWS flies in the simulation.** In CWS the roll axis is entirely the crew's: the ailerons follow the wheel and the autopilot does not hold a bank when the wheel is released. The pitch axis is held by the autopilot in its standing vertical mode (with none standing, it levels off and holds the altitude it arrives at); a column input beyond a small dead band hands pitch to the crew, and releasing the column hands it back. CWS never disconnects the autopilot, and flying in CWS lights no warning.

Do not engage CWS for takeoff or landing (FedEx limitation). CWS is not a substitute for a disconnect when the autopilot is doing something unexpected: disconnect with the AP release button and fly by hand.

blocks.title: What disconnects or reverts the autopilot
rows: AP release button on either control wheel (in the simulation, the autopilot disconnect binding on your yoke or keyboard)
Disconnect: both levers to OFF, red AP lights flash.
Longitudinal trim handles, control wheel trim switches or alternate trim switches operated, with a lever in CMD (or in CWS with TURB in)
Disconnect, lever to OFF. In CWS without TURB, trimming does not disconnect.
Overpowering the autopilot in CMD (wheel or column moved firmly against it)
Reverts to CWS: the lever drops from CMD to CWS and the red light flashes. In DUAL LAND, AP 1 drops to CWS and AP 2 to OFF.
CMD reverts to CWS (lever drops to CWS), autothrottles off, command bars out of view.
Second lever moved to CMD (outside LAND)
The first autopilot drops to OFF.
Attitude reference failure on that autopilot's side
That autopilot disconnects; the other can be engaged.
Loss of the autopilot's computer power
Altitude-holding law unable to hold (error beyond about 400 ft for about 10 s)
Disconnect: the monitor hands the aircraft back rather than chase a runaway.

blocks.content:
Each pilot's panel carries two autopilot warning lights, **AP 1** and **AP 2**, each with a **red** upper half and an **amber** lower half; every seat shows both channels. They are warning lights with a reset, not engage buttons.

The **red** light flashes whenever an engage lever moves down: CMD to CWS, CMD to OFF or CWS to OFF, including an overpower or TURB reversion. It is put out by pushing the light or by moving that lever up again. (On the aircraft a second push of the AP release button also puts it out; in the simulation the disconnect binding only moves the levers, so push the light.) All red autoflight lights flash together from one flasher.

The **amber** light burns steady and is used only with both autopilots engaged in LAND: it comes on for the autopilot that drops out of DUAL LAND, or that fails the DUAL LAND conditions at the preland test while remaining engaged. The amber lights are inhibited below 100 ft radio altitude and go out when LAND is ended or the light is pushed.
On the aircraft an autopilot disconnect in LAND also sounds an aural warning. The simulation does not sound it; the flashing red lights and the dropped levers are the only cues.

The MD-10 has one **AUTO FLIGHT** switch on the FCP. With no AP engaged, a push engages **both autothrottles and the armed AP** in the flight director's present modes. With an AP engaged, each push **transfers** control between AP1 and AP2, unless the other channel is inoperative or a land mode is engaged. On the ground the push engages the autothrottles only, which is the takeoff set-up.

The armed channel alternates so that both are used equally: at power-up it is the first FCC to be powered; with one AP engaged it is the other; and it changes each time the AP is disengaged. A failed channel does not arm. The engaged AP shows below the FMA roll window.

items: AP engagement is inhibited on the ground and below 100 ft AGL; an attempt flashes the red AP OFF box until the AP disconnect switch is pushed.
Below 400 ft with NAV armed or engaged, the AP cannot be engaged until NAV is exited; an attempt gives an AP disconnect warning.
Engaged with both FDs off, the AP rolls wings level and holds the heading it rolls out on, and holds altitude if the vertical speed is below 300 ft/min, otherwise vertical speed.

Engaged with a director on, the AP takes the director's mode. In V/S, FPA, altitude hold or level change it synchronizes to the present conditions; in heading hold or takeoff roll it rolls toward wings level and holds the heading once the bank is below 3°.
Once engaged above 100 ft, the AP stays engaged below 100 ft only in a land mode or a go-around.

blocks.title: What disconnects the MD-10 autopilot
rows: AP disconnect switch on either control wheel
First push disconnects; a push with AP OFF flashing makes it steady and, after one cycle of the aural, silences the aural.
AFS OVRD OFF lever pushed down (one per FCC)
Emergency disconnect of that FCC's AP and autothrottle.
The AP disconnects (there is no reversion to CWS).
Control wheel trim switches or long trim handles
Except in SINGLE or DUAL LAND.
Bank beyond 60° or roll rate beyond 10°/s
Outside the land and go-around modes.
Below 100 ft AGL in any mode except a land mode or go-around
In APPR ONLY the AP disconnects at 100 ft.
FCC power, its hydraulic systems or its attitude reference.

blocks.content:
Every AP disconnect, intended or not, raises the **AP disengage warning**: a red flashing **AP OFF** box around the roll and altitude windows of the FMA and a cyclic aural warning from the central aural warning system. Pushing either AP disconnect switch changes the box to steady white (amber if the disconnect was a failure and no AP is available) and, once at least one cycle of the aural has played, silences it. Re-engaging the AP resets both.

The autothrottle has its own warning: a red flashing **ATS OFF** box around the speed window, reset by either ATS disconnect switch on throttles 1 and 3 (steady white if it can be re-engaged, amber if not). Reverse thrust disengages the autothrottle without a warning.

sections.title: Lateral modes
sections.summary: Heading, radio and FMS navigation, the localizer, and the takeoff and go-around roll modes.

blocks.content: Every lateral mode ends in a bank command. The modes differ in what they compare: a heading against the selected heading, a course deviation against the selected radial or the FMS track, or the localizer deviation against the beam. The approach modes (localizer capture and track, align and rollout) are described with the [approach and autoland](#approach-and-autoland).

**HDG HOLD** is the basic roll mode, and the one an autopilot or director starts in. If the aircraft is banked when it engages, the guidance first rolls the wings level and then holds the heading the aircraft has when the bank has fallen to a couple of degrees (the books give 3°). It is selected by **pushing** the HDG knob, and is the mode the autopilot falls back to when another lateral mode ends.

**HDG SEL** is selected by **pulling** the HDG knob. The aircraft turns the short way to the heading in the HDG window and holds it; turning the knob in HDG SEL moves the target with it. The bank is limited by the **bank angle selector** (the outer ring of the HDG knob: 5, 10, 15, 20 or 25°). At low true airspeed the simulation also limits the bank to that of a standard-rate turn, which matters only below about 180 KTAS. The bank is taken out early on the approach to the selected heading, so the roll-out arrives on the heading.
**The RAD/INS pushbutton** (RAD/FMS on the KC-10) arms one of three modes, and which one is decided by the coupled pilot's HSI navigation source:

rows: RAD CAP, RAD TRK, RAD CRS
LOC CAP, LOC TRK (localizer only, no glideslope)

blocks.content: The button latches: pressing it again gives the arm up. Pushing or pulling the HDG knob also gives up any of these three, armed or captured, so on an intercept select HDG SEL first and press RAD/INS after it. (On the aircraft the localizer could stay armed through a HDG SEL; in the simulation a heading stroke releases it.) Moving the HSI source off the selected unit releases the mode and the roll falls to HDG HOLD.

**RAD** flies the radial set in that pilot's course window. The capture is planned from the course deviation and the rate of closure, with intercept angles up to about 45°: RAD CAP is annunciated as the aircraft enters the capture and RAD TRK once it is established. A VOR radial converges on the station, so the same deviation means less and less distance as the aircraft closes. Over the station (the cone of confusion), or when departing the radial fast, the mode changes to **RAD CRS**: the deviation is ignored and the course is held. RAD TRK returns after a minimum of 30 seconds and up to 3 minutes; if the tracking criteria are still not met at 3 minutes, the roll reverts to HDG HOLD.

**FMS** flies the long-range navigation unit's steering (the INS, or the FMS on aircraft so equipped): its desired track, cross-track error and turn anticipation. FMS CAP is the intercept, FMS TRK the track. If the unit's steering is lost, the roll reverts to HDG HOLD.

**LOC (localizer only)** flies the localizer with no glideslope: the capture inside about two dots, LOC CAP, then LOC TRK once established. LOC TRK will not engage above 2,500 ft radio altitude. Retuning the receiver, or losing the localizer for more than about 2 seconds while armed, gives the arm up; the crew must press the button again. The same applies to the ILS arm until the glideslope is captured.

**Back course** (B/CRS) modes are not available in the simulation: the BACK CRS switch is inoperative.

**TAKE OFF** (TO/GA on the ground) commands wings level for the whole of the takeoff: on the runway the roll bar keeps the wings level, and after lift-off it continues to command wings level rather than a heading. It is a flight director mode only. Pulling the HDG knob during the takeoff takes the roll into HDG SEL and leaves TAKE OFF in the pitch window. When the takeoff roll mode ends any other way, HDG HOLD takes the heading the aircraft has at that moment.

**G/A** (TO/GA in flight with flaps out) rolls the wings level and then holds the heading the aircraft has when the bank is below about 3°. It can be flown by the autopilot or the director.

**HEADING / TRACK.** Turn the HDG/TRK knob to preselect (the PFD bug is hollow), **pull** to select (the bug fills, the FMA shows HEADING and the target, and the aircraft turns to it), **push** to hold (the aircraft rolls wings level and holds the heading it rolls out on). The aircraft turns in the direction the knob was turned: a knob wound more than 180° one way turns the long way round, otherwise the turn is the short way, and a dotted arc on the PFD heading scale shows which. Once a selected heading is captured (within about 1°) the mode becomes hold; turning the knob during the capture moves the target. The HDG/TRK button changes the window and the mode between heading and track. North reads 360.

**Bank limit.** The outer ring of the HDG knob selects AUTO or a limit of 5 to 25°. The commanded limit is the lesser of the selection and the FMS limit, which is 15° at or below 1.3 Vs. In AUTO the limit varies linearly from 5° at 340 KIAS to 25° at 210 KIAS. In NAV, LOC and the TO/GA modes the computed limits apply whatever the ring says.

**NAV.** The NAV switch arms the FMS lateral mode (NAV ARMED); at capture the roll window shows NAV1 or NAV2 (magenta) for the FMC in control, and the FCCs fly its steering with its own bank limit. NAV can be armed on the ground once the engines are running. Guidance is available to the director from 100 ft AGL and to the autopilot from 400 ft AGL. A HDG/TRK push or pull, APPR/LAND, or the VOR and LOC ONLY modes cancel it. See [Flight Management](flight-management) for the flight plan itself.

**VOR and LOC ONLY** are requested on the FMS NAV RAD page, not on the FCP. VOR ARMED, then VOR1 or VOR2 on the selected receiver, and VOR1 CRS or VOR2 CRS over the station; the mode does not track above 18,000 ft. LOC ARMED, then LOC ONLY (white) on the approach's localizer laws with the glideslope disabled; ALIGN, FLARE and ROLLOUT are not available in LOC ONLY.

**TAKEOFF** commands wings level on the runway heading. The AP's roll takeoff (above 100 ft) retains the heading if the aircraft is on it with wings level, otherwise rolls wings level; selecting another roll mode exits it without ending the pitch takeoff. **GO AROUND** rolls wings level if banked more than 3°, otherwise holds the present heading, with the bank limited to 10°.

sections.title: Vertical modes
sections.summary: Vertical speed, altitude hold and capture, speed on pitch, turbulence, takeoff and go-around pitch, and the MD-10's level change and PROF.

blocks.content: Every vertical mode is flown as a commanded vertical speed (see [Control laws](#control-laws)). What differs is where the command comes from, and that decides who controls the speed. In vertical speed and altitude modes the autopilot controls the flight path and the speed is the throttles' job, by hand or autothrottle. In the speed-on-pitch modes (IAS and MACH HOLD on the DC-10, level change and PROF climb on the MD-10) the elevator holds the speed and the thrust decides whether the aircraft climbs or descends.

**VERT SPD** is the basic pitch mode. It is selected by rolling the **vertical speed wheel** off its center detent, from any mode, and holds the rate on the wheel: 100 ft/min per detent, from 8,000 ft/min down to 4,000 ft/min up. Pitch is limited to 22° nose up and 10° nose down. When the wheel is not itself the selection and an autopilot is flying, the wheel is driven to follow the commanded vertical speed, so rolling it starts from the rate the aircraft already has.

**ALT HOLD** is selected by clicking the wheel into its center **ALT HLD** detent, and is the other basic pitch mode. The aircraft levels off and holds the altitude it arrives at; it does not climb or descend back to the altitude at the moment of selection. Engaged from a 2,000 ft/min climb the arrest takes up to about 200 ft. ALT HOLD is also where the altitude preselect ends.

**Altitude preselect.** Set the altitude in the **ALT** window with the ALT knob and **pull** the knob to arm: ALT appears in the ARM window, alone or as a suffix (RAD ALT, ILS ALT). Arming starts no climb or descent; the aircraft goes on doing what its pitch mode says. Choose VERT SPD, IAS or MACH to go toward the altitude, and the capture happens on the way. While armed, turning the knob moves the altitude that will be captured.

The capture starts where the altitude law's command meets the vertical speed the aircraft already has, so the pitch does not step: **ALT CAP** in the pitch window, the ARM window goes blank, and the captured altitude is fixed at that moment. From then on the knob is the crew's again and turning it moves nothing. Within about 250 ft the mode becomes **ALT HOLD**. An altitude armed while holding another one waits until a pitch mode moves the aircraft, and an aircraft climbing or descending away from the armed altitude does not capture it back. The **RESET** button cancels the preselect and resets the altitude advisory (see [Warning Systems](warning-systems)). Takeoff, go-around and a captured glideslope outrank the preselect.

**IAS HOLD** and **MACH HOLD** are selected with the IAS and MACH pushbuttons and hold the airspeed or Mach that existed at the press, by pitch. The law trades height for speed at the thrust the crew have set: with more thrust the aircraft climbs at the selected speed, with less it descends. It reads the speed's own rate of change, so it answers a throttle movement within seconds rather than waiting for the speed to drift (time constant about 10 seconds). These are the climb and descent modes of the DC-10: set the thrust with the N1 mode or by hand, hold the speed on the elevator, and let the preselect capture the level.

Do not hold the speed with IAS or MACH HOLD while the autothrottle is in SPD. Two loops would then control the same speed, one with the elevator and one with the thrust, and fight each other. On the aircraft the SPD mode inhibits IAS and MACH HOLD; the simulation does not model that interlock, so the crew must keep the two apart: use N1 or manual thrust with IAS/MACH HOLD, and SPD with VERT SPD or ALT HOLD.

**TURB.** Either pilot's **TURB** pushbar reverts the autopilot from CMD to CWS (the lever drops to CWS), turns the autothrottles off, and removes the command bars from both ADIs; the fast/slow indicators stay in view. The pitch window shows TURB and the roll window goes blank. With the autothrottle off the thrust stays where the crew set it, so the aircraft is not chasing gusts with the throttles; the autopilot holds altitude in pitch while the crew keep the wheel. Trimming in TURB disconnects the autopilot. To leave TURB, release the pushbar, re-engage CMD and reselect the modes.

**TAKE OFF** (TO/GA on the ground) puts speed guidance on the pitch bar after lift-off, limited to 22° nose up. It is a flight director mode only. **G/A** puts speed guidance on pitch with a 15° limit, and an engaged autopilot flies it. Both are described with the [takeoff and go-around](#go-around).

blocks.title: Pitch mode summary
rows: Rolling the wheel off the detent
Another pitch mode, the preselect capture
Wheel to the ALT HLD detent; end of a capture
ALT HOLD within about 250 ft; another pitch mode
Elevator (thrust set by crew or N1 mode)
Another pitch mode, the preselect capture
Another pitch mode; an AP lever to CMD in the air
Another pitch mode; the preselect capture

blocks.content:
**V/S and FPA.** Rolling the **pitch wheel** engages V/S (or FPA, chosen with the V/S-FPA button) from any mode except a land mode, a dual-director approach below 1,500 ft, or takeoff and go-around below 400 ft. Out of altitude hold the first detent selects ±100 ft/min the way the wheel was rolled; out of any other mode it starts from the present vertical speed. Each detent is 100 ft/min or 0.1°; the range is 8,000 ft/min down to 4,000 ft/min up, and ±9.9° of flight path. The autothrottle holds speed (THRUST).

**Altitude capture and HOLD.** The FCCs always control to the FCP altitude window unless PROF is engaged. The capture begins on its own at the point where an arc flown at 0.05 g would level the aircraft exactly at the window altitude, and the FMA reads HOLD with the target from the start of the capture. **Pushing** the ALT knob engages hold at the present altitude, with a small adjustment for a smooth level-off. Changing the window during a capture cancels it, restores the previous mode and re-arms the capture.

**LEVEL CHANGE.** **Pulling** the ALT knob engages flight level change: the elevator holds the speed (PITCH in the speed window) and the autothrottle sets climb thrust going up (CLB THRUST) or idle going down (IDLE CLAMP). The aircraft climbs or descends directly to the window altitude and captures it. (For level changes of 5,000 ft or less the aircraft computes a reduced thrust; the simulation flies the full limit and idle.)

**Speed.** Turn the IAS/MACH knob to preselect, **pull** to select (the aircraft accelerates or decelerates to it, by pitch or thrust as the vertical mode decides), **push** to hold the present speed. **FMS SPD** makes the FMS speed the reference: the window shows dashes and the speed legend turns magenta. Selecting an FCP speed cancels it, and pushing FMS SPD within 10 s of preselecting a speed edits the FMS speed instead. The reference changes between IAS and Mach automatically at 26,000 ft (or at the preselected Mach or IAS).

**PROF** couples the FMS vertical profile: the FMS sets the targets and the FCCs and autothrottle fly them, climbing at climb thrust with speed on pitch, leveling at FMS altitudes, and descending on the path with speed on thrust (or at idle with speed on pitch when above the path). The FCP altitude window is always the absolute ceiling or floor: PROF never flies through it, and when the profile wants to leave a level the window is holding, the FMA shows **VERT ALERT** until the crew reset the window. PROF does not engage below 400 ft after takeoff (armed on the ground, it engages there) and is cancelled by the pitch wheel, a push or pull of the ALT knob, a go-around or a glideslope capture. See [Flight Management](flight-management).

**Speed envelope protection.** Every speed the autothrottle or the elevator flies is held between **VMIN + 5 kt** and **VMAX − 5 kt** (VMAX is Vmo/Mmo or the flap placard). VMIN is the FMS's (1.3 Vs of the configuration, bank-compensated), so protection needs FMS weight data. If the speed reaches a limit, the autothrottle engages itself (if available) on speed, FMS SPD and PROF hand back to the AFS, and level change reverts to V/S at the present rate, flashing; the speed window shows **LO SPEED** or **HI SPEED** alternating with **PROTECTION** inside a white flashing ATS OFF box. If the speed falls to VMIN − 10 kt in an altitude mode with an engine out, the aircraft leaves the altitude at maximum continuous thrust to hold VMIN.

**TAKEOFF** pitch: on the ground the FD takeoff mode engages automatically with a director on and V2 confirmed on the FMS TAKEOFF page. The pitch bar shows about 0° below 80 kt, about 6° at 80 kt and about 15° at rotation, then holds V2 + 10 kt; if an engine fails, the target is the speed at the failure, between V2 and V2 + 10 kt. Thrust reduces to climb thrust at the FMS CLB THRUST altitude (default 1,500 ft AGL).

**Altitude alert (MD-10).** On the MD-10 the altitude alert is an FCC function. The PFD altitude box turns steady amber 1,000 ft from the FCP window altitude, and on the first approach to it also turns amber with a tone if more than 0.12 g would be needed to capture it. Once the altitude has been acquired, a deviation of 150 ft or more flashes the box amber with the tone, until the aircraft returns or a new altitude is selected. The alert is inhibited only in the glideslope mode and is not affected by the AFS OVRD OFF levers.

sections.title: Autothrottle and speed control
sections.summary: One servo, three clutches, two computers: how the thrust levers are driven, the modes, and the speed guidance behind the fast/slow indicators.

blocks.content: The autothrottle positions the three thrust levers to hold either a speed or a thrust limit. On every aircraft in the family the levers are driven by **one duplex servo**: its output shaft carries a **servo brake** (on aircraft that have one) and reaches the three levers through **three drive clutches**. The levers therefore move together as a unit. A pilot who holds one lever simply slips its clutch; the servo drives on with the other two.

blocks.alt: Schematic of the autothrottle. Left: AT/SC computer 1 (DC BUS 1) and AT/SC computer 2 (DC BUS 3) on the DC-10/KC-10, or the ATS channels in FCC 1 and FCC 2 on the MD-10, both feeding one duplex servo. The servo output shaft carries the servo brake, then splits through three clutches to thrust levers 1, 2 and 3. Inputs to the computers: CADC airspeed and Mach, the thrust rating computer's N1 (or EPR) limit and error, flap and slat position, gross weight, radio altitude, the SPD window, and the TO/GA button. A side panel shows the speed control system's output to the ADI fast/slow indicators and the flight director pitch bar.
blocks.title: Autothrottle architecture
blocks.caption: Two computers drive one servo. The clutches let a pilot hold one lever without disconnecting anything.

blocks.content: **Override and the balancer.** Holding all three levers stops the servo moving them; once they are let go, the autothrottle brings them back close to where it had them. A single lever held back and then released stays offset from the other two by the same amount, and the offset lasts until the crew move that lever or the automatic retard closes all three. In the simulation the crew's own levers (a hardware quadrant cannot be moved by the aircraft) carry exactly what the clutches carry: the distance between the levers. While the autothrottle drives, the engine with the highest crew lever gets the servo's position and each lower lever takes a proportionally smaller share, so a stagger is kept and all three still close together. Three levers at idle and three at the firewall command the same thing. When the autothrottle is engaged, the servo picks up from where the crew's levers are, so nothing steps.

A failure of the autothrottle duplex servo can cause an uncommanded throttle advance, past the thrust limit. Monitor the thrust levers and the engine instruments whenever the autothrottle is engaged, in any mode.

Two independent **Automatic Throttle / Speed Control (AT/SC)** computers, No. 1 on DC BUS 1 and No. 2 on DC BUS 3, are each armed by an **ATS** lever on the glareshield. Either or both may be engaged; both drive the same servo. A lever does not stay at ON unless its computer accepts it: with its computer unpowered or failed, the lever springs back to OFF.

blocks.title: Autothrottle modes
rows: Nothing: engaged but not moving the levers. On the -30, -40 and KC-10 the servo brake is set.
ATS lever ON on the ground with no thrust mode selected; on the -30, -40 and KC-10, 20 s after the nose strut compresses; at 80 kt on a takeoff in N1 mode.
Driven until the highest engine reaches the thrust rating computer's limit, then held within about 0.5 % N1.
N1 pushbutton (available on the ground: this is how takeoff thrust is set); TO/GA in flight.
Driven to hold the speed in the SPD window, never above the rating limit.
ATS lever ON in flight; SPD knob pulled (in flight only).
SPD, holding the alpha speed instead because the selected speed is below it.
Closing toward idle for the landing, then to the idle stop at main gear spin-up.
Descending through 50 ft radio altitude with slats extended; with FLARE in an autoland.

blocks.content:
**The ground and the takeoff.** The SPD mode cannot be engaged on the ground; a SPD selection made there is remembered and granted once airborne. With the ATS levers ON before takeoff the FMA reads CLAMP. Pushing **N1** releases the brake, the FMA reads N1 and the levers advance to the takeoff limit on the thrust rating computer. At **80 kt** the servo brake clamps the shaft and the FMA reads **CLAMP**: the levers stay where they are through rotation and the initial climb. To take the thrust by hand, disengage the autothrottle. (If the FMA does not change from N1 to CLAMP at 80 kt, the PM calls "No Clamp".) In flight the brake is released by pushing N1, pulling the SPD knob, or a go-around.

The DC-10-10 and -15 have no servo brake: the FMA still reads CLAMP on the ground, but there is no 20-second set and no 80-knot clamp. FedEx does not authorize the autothrottle for takeoff on any DC-10-10 (see [Limitations](limitations)).

**The rating as a ceiling.** In SPD the thrust rating computer's limit is a ceiling: if the selected speed needs more thrust than the limit, the levers stop at the limit with the speed error uncleared. **Nothing annunciates** when the N1 limit or the flap placard speed is holding the levers back, so a climb in VERT SPD at a rate the thrust cannot sustain will lose speed with SPD still showing. The speed loop runs the servo at full rate for a speed error of 50 kt or more, and uses the aircraft's acceleration as a lead so it stops advancing once the aircraft is already accelerating toward the target. A full lever travel takes about 5 seconds. With the engines at flight idle, the servo crosses the idle range at full rate when thrust is needed again, so the engines respond promptly.

The rating mode, and the thrust it works to, are the thrust rating computer's (see [Engines](engines)). If the computer fails with the autothrottle in N1, the autothrottle disengages and a flag covers the N1 LIM readout. SPD remains available with a backup ceiling of about 90 % N1 on the CF6 aircraft; the crew should set the N1 limit bugs by hand. The DC-10-40 has no equivalent backup ceiling. On aircraft with the digital engine instrument display, a limit dialed on the display's command counter in MAN replaces the computer's.

blocks.title: Alpha speed: the safe stall margin

blocks.content: The **alpha speed** is a computed minimum safe speed: a stall margin from the table above, multiplied by the stall speed of the present configuration at the present weight. Each margin multiplies the stall speed of its own flap setting, so the same 1.30 gives a higher speed at 35° than at 50°. In SPD the autothrottle holds the higher of the selected speed and the alpha speed, and annunciates ALPHA SPD while the alpha speed governs. The same speed is the target of the TAKE OFF and G/A pitch guidance. In N1, CLAMP and RETD the alpha speed is computed but does not act.

**Retard.** Outside an autoland, RETD arms when the aircraft descends through 50 ft radio altitude with the slats extended. In an autoland it comes with the FLARE. The levers close at a programmed rate (roughly 6 % of lever travel per second), and at main gear spin-up they go to the idle stop at full servo rate. A go-around disarms the retard and keeps it disarmed until the go-around is over.

**Go-around.** TO/GA in flight with the flaps out puts the autothrottle into N1 and the thrust rating computer into the G/A limit; the levers advance to go-around thrust if either ATS lever is ON. An autothrottle engaged during the go-around comes up directly in N1. The speed control's go-around mode ends when the crew select SPD (pull the SPD knob, normally once the altitude capture shows in the FMA), or on the ground below 80 kt.

blocks.title: Disengagement and warning lights
rows: ATS disengage button on throttle 1 or 3
Both channels disengage, levers to OFF, red ATS lights flash. A second push resets the red lights.
Autothrottle disengages and cannot be re-engaged while TURB is in.
Thrust rating computer fails in N1 mode
Loss of a computer's power or a computer failure
That channel disengages; the lever drops to OFF.

blocks.content: Each pilot's panel carries **ATS 1** and **ATS 2** warning lights, each with a red upper and an amber lower half. The **red** light flashes when the autothrottle disengages and no channel remains engaged. The **amber** light comes on steady when one channel disengages while the other stays engaged; it is inhibited below 100 ft in DUAL LAND. Pushing a light, or the disengage button with nothing engaged, resets them. A disengaged channel's lever must be cycled to OFF before it will engage again.

children.title: Speed control system and fast/slow indicators (DC-10 and KC-10)

blocks.content:
The AT/SC computers are also the **speed control system**, which runs whether or not an autothrottle is engaged. It computes one speed error and sends it three ways: to the autothrottle servo, to the **fast/slow indicator** on each ADI, and, in TAKE OFF and G/A, to the flight director pitch bar as speed guidance.

In SPD the fast/slow pointer shows the error from the SPD window speed (or the alpha speed, if higher); full deflection is about 10 kt. In TAKE OFF (after lift-off) and G/A it shows the error from the computed takeoff or go-around speed. It is biased out of view in N1 (outside TAKE OFF and G/A) and in RETD, and a SPD flag covers it when the computer has no valid airspeed. Flown by hand, centering the fast/slow with the throttles is exactly what the autothrottle does.

**SPEED CONT TEST.** The overhead SPEED CONT TEST selector (SLO / FAST, spring-loaded to center) replaces the speed error with half the fast/slow scale while held: both fast/slow pointers move one dot toward SLO or FAST. It works only on the ground with both ground sensing relays made. With an autothrottle engaged the test releases the servo brake, engages SPD (shown in the FMA) and the levers move: slowly forward on SLO, aft on FAST. Released, the brake sets again. The test is part of the flight engineer's preflight.

**Stall warning.** The stall warning (stick shaker) circuits live in the AT/SC computers but work independently of the autothrottle: two channels, one per computer and angle-of-attack vane, either of which shakes both columns. They are inhibited on the ground and for 5 seconds after nosewheel lift-off. The overhead STALL TEST selector (L / R) tests each channel on the ground; the shakers start after about 5 seconds. See [Flight Controls](flight-controls).

**Performance management.** On the line aircraft the Performance Management System can command pitch through the FGS and thrust through the autothrottle. In the simulation the PMS is advisory: it computes and displays targets, and the crew fly them with the FGS and autothrottle modes above. See [Flight Management](flight-management).

Each FCC contains one autothrottle channel; the two drive separate sections of the same duplex servo, which gives two monitored channels. Both engage when the **AUTO FLIGHT** switch is pushed (on the ground it engages the autothrottles only), and also when PROF is pushed. The autothrottle is designed for the whole flight: it can be engaged on the ground and stays engaged until reverse thrust is selected on the landing roll. It engages by itself to protect the speed envelope (see [Vertical modes](#vertical-md10)).

blocks.title: MD-10 autothrottle modes
rows: Holds the FCP or FMS speed on the throttles, between VMIN + 5 kt and VMAX − 5 kt.
T/O THRUST, CLB THRUST, MCT THRUST, GA/THRUST (altitude window)
Drives to the FMS thrust limit while pitch holds the speed.
Throttles to flight idle and held there (level change and PROF descents).
Engaged in takeoff, servos unable to move the throttles: on the ground with thrust below about 70 % of the takeoff setting, and from 80 kt. Full manual control remains.
Throttles to idle when the AP enters FLARE, or below 50 ft radio altitude with flaps beyond 28.5°.

blocks.content: The thrust limit comes from the FMS (takeoff, go-around, climb, maximum continuous, cruise). The autothrottle is disengaged by either **ATS disconnect switch** on throttles 1 and 3, by any throttle in reverse, by an **AFS OVRD OFF** lever, or by a failure. Every disengagement except reverse thrust raises the red flashing **ATS OFF** box; a push of an ATS disconnect switch makes it steady white (or amber if the autothrottle cannot be re-engaged). Retard ends with reverse thrust or a go-around.

sections.title: Approach and autoland
sections.summary: Localizer and glideslope capture and tracking, the LAND modes, align, flare, retard and rollout.

blocks.content: All three aircraft fly coupled ILS approaches with the autopilot or the flight director. The DC-10 and the MD-10 can also land automatically; the KC-10 cannot. The approach logic is the same idea on both systems: arm, capture the localizer, capture the glideslope, track both, and then either continue to a manual landing (approach only) or let the land modes take the aircraft to the runway.

blocks.alt: Side-view profile diagram of a DC-10 DUAL LAND autoland on a 3° glideslope, distance on the horizontal axis and radio altitude on the vertical, with FMA strips drawn above each event: localizer capture (SPD | LAND→ILS | LOC CAP | ALT HOLD), glideslope capture (SPD | ILS | LOC TRK | G/S CAP), G/S TRK 20 s later with the preland test, DUAL LAND (SPD | DUAL LAND | LOC TRK | G/S TRK), 1,000 ft stable call, 200 ft ALGN (rudder decrab, upwind wing low), about 60 ft FLARE with RETD in the ATS window, main gear spin-up ROLL OUT with the pitch window blank, nose lowering, and the rollout on the centerline. A second, smaller strip shows the MD-10 equivalents (LOC / G/S DUAL LAND, ALIGN, FLARE DUAL LAND, ROLLOUT ROLLOUT, RETARD).
blocks.title: Autoland sequence
blocks.caption: The heights are those the simulation uses; the source documents give ALGN between 140 and 200 ft and the flare at about 50 to 60 ft.

blocks.content: **Arming.** The **ILS** pushbutton on the directional control panel arms the localizer and the glideslope: ILS (or ILS ALT) in the ARM window. The coupled autopilot flies **its own side's ILS receiver** (receiver 1 for AP 1, receiver 2 for AP 2), so that receiver must be tuned to the ILS. With a flight director only, the approach captures and tracks for the director exactly as it would for the autopilot. Pressing ILS again gives the arm up; retuning the receiver, or losing the localizer for more than about 2 seconds, gives it up too until the glideslope has been captured, and the button must be pressed again. To fly the localizer without the glideslope, use the RAD/INS (RAD/FMS) button with the HSI on the localizer (see [Lateral modes](#lateral-dc-kc)).

**Localizer.** LOC CAP is annunciated as the aircraft enters the capture, inside about two dots, and LOC TRK when it is established on the centerline; LOC TRK will not engage above 2,500 ft radio altitude. The ARM window keeps ILS through the localizer capture, because the glideslope is still to come. Intercept in HDG SEL with ILS armed. On the localizer the bank limit falls with radio altitude, from 28° to 5° near the runway, and below 1,000 ft the beam-error gain is reduced in proportion to the beam's increasing sensitivity as the aircraft nears the antenna.

**Glideslope.** The glideslope can be captured from above or below. The capture point is not a fixed deviation: the faster the aircraft is closing the beam, the farther out the capture begins, so that the pitch-over arrives on the beam without overshooting. With no closure at all it captures inside about one dot, and never with the needle near its stop. The capture starts from the vertical speed the aircraft already has, so there is no pitch step. G/S CAP is followed by **G/S TRK** after 20 seconds. Maximum speed for an automatic glideslope capture is 250 kt (FedEx).

**Gain programming.** A glideslope converges toward the transmitter, so a dot of deviation means fewer feet the lower the aircraft is. Below about 2,000 ft radio altitude the pitch computer reduces the beam-error gain in proportion to height, reaching zero near 60 ft, which is where the flare takes over. Before G/S TRK the beam error is not integrated (an integrator charged during the capture would hold its output when the error reached zero and cause a slow oscillation); in G/S TRK an integrator removes any steady offset. A glideslope lost briefly is ridden through for up to about 5 seconds on the aircraft's own vertical path.

**What leaves the glideslope.** Before the glideslope is captured any pitch mode may be used (descend to the beam in VERT SPD or ALT HOLD with ILS armed). Once captured, rolling the vertical speed wheel, or selecting IAS or MACH, disengages the glideslope and leaves the localizer tracking; the glideslope comes back only with a fresh approach. In SNGL or DUAL LAND those selections do nothing (see below).

**Approach only.** When both beams are captured without LAND selected, the ARM window changes from ILS to **APPR ONLY** on the DC-10. The KC-10's ARM window has no APPR ONLY legend: the ILS arm stays through G/S CAP and goes blank at G/S TRK. The autopilot will track the beams to the minimums but will not flare: disconnect and land by hand. FedEx minimum height for the autopilot on a coupled approach without autoland is 72 ft AGL (see [Limitations](limitations)).

Monitor AP OUT OF TRIM while tracking the glideslope. If the light stays on for more than 3 seconds, disconnect the autopilot and fly by hand (FedEx limitation): the stabilizer is not keeping up with the elevator, and a disconnect at a lower height would leave a larger out-of-trim force.

**Arming LAND.** With one autopilot in CMD, the **LAND** pushbutton arms the approach by itself: no ILS press is needed first. The ARM window shows ILS while the beams are being captured, and the same localizer and glideslope captures follow as for an ILS approach. For **DUAL LAND**, move the second AP lever to CMD after LAND is selected (only in LAND may both levers stand in CMD). Both ILS receivers must be tuned to the same ILS; on aircraft with a single ILS control head this is automatic.

After the glideslope capture the guidance runs a **preland test** of both systems. The ARM window then reads **DUAL LAND** (both autopilots engaged and both systems good: fail-operational), **SNGL LAND** (one autopilot engaged, or one of two failed the test: fail-passive; the failed one stays engaged with its amber AP light on) or **APPR ONLY** (a single autopilot failed the test). In the simulation the preland test takes a few seconds after the capture; on the aircraft it runs for about 30 to 40 seconds from G/S TRK and must finish by 300 ft.

**The autoland pitch lock.** Once SNGL LAND or DUAL LAND shows, the vertical speed wheel, IAS and MACH do nothing: the approach can be left in pitch only with **TO/GA**, and every autoland go-around is a TO/GA go-around.

blocks.title: DC-10 autoland sequence
rows: LOC CAP, then LOC TRK below 2,500 ft
Captures and tracks the localizer; ILS stays in the ARM window.
G/S CAP; ARM shows ILS until the preland test answers
Pitches onto the glideslope from the present vertical speed.
DUAL LAND, SNGL LAND or APPR ONLY
Pitch selections locked out in SNGL/DUAL LAND.
Glideslope gain falling with height; localizer gain falling below 1,000 ft.
Rudder yaws the nose onto the runway heading; the roll channel lowers the upwind wing to hold the centerline (forward slip).
Glideslope gain zero; the flare law takes the sink rate from about 12 ft/s to about 3 ft/s at touchdown; thrust levers close.
Levers to idle; nose lowered smoothly to the runway, then the elevator streamlined; rudder and nosewheel steering hold the localizer.
Continues until the crew move the AP levers to OFF.

blocks.content:
**Align.** On the approach the autopilot flies a crab into any crosswind, with wings level. Near 200 ft it removes the crab with a **forward slip**: the yaw channel, now in the parallel mode with up to about ±23° of rudder authority (felt in the pedals), turns the nose onto the runway heading at a limited rate, and the roll channel opposes the resulting turn with limited cross-control aileron, lowering the upwind wing to hold the localizer. A synchronizer remembers the crab angle at engagement so the rudder and aileron offsets build smoothly. The bank allowed is about 9° at the start, reducing to 5° near the runway. FedEx limits the autoland crosswind to 10 kt including gusts.

**Flare.** At about 60 ft the glideslope's gain is zero and the flare circuits control the elevator. The flare commands a sink rate that is a function of radio altitude, about 12 ft/s at 60 ft reducing to about 3 ft/s at touchdown, with a growing nose-up term in the last few feet; the nose-down authority is reduced as the runway nears. The autothrottle switches to RETD at the same moment and the levers close at the programmed rate.

**Rollout.** At main gear spin-up the roll channel switches from ALGN to **ROLL OUT**: localizer deviation, damped by yaw rate, drives the rudder, and once the nose gear is on the runway nosewheel steering joins it. The pitch windows go blank, but the pitch computers still fly the elevator: they lower the nose from the flare attitude to the nosewheel touchdown and then reduce every command to neutral within about a second. ROLL OUT continues until the crew move the AP levers to OFF. Disconnect before turning off the runway.

**Failures in DUAL LAND.** If one autopilot drops out, the other completes the landing in SNGL LAND, and the amber light of the one that dropped comes on (the amber lights are inhibited below 100 ft). An overpower in DUAL LAND drops AP 1 to CWS and AP 2 to OFF. The PAFAM watches the whole approach and, on the DC-10, commands TAKEOVER when it predicts an unsafe landing (see [PAFAM](#pafam)).

**CAT II and CAT III.** FedEx flies CAT III approaches coupled in DUAL LAND using the monitored-approach concept, with rollout guidance where available; CAT II approaches are coupled and either autolanded or landed by hand. The decision regime runs from 500 ft radio altitude to the ground. On a CAT III approach the captain calls "Approaching alert height, I have the airplane" at 200 ft, the first officer calls "Alert height" at 100 ft, and the second officer monitors the systems and calls abnormalities ("No align", "Approach only", "No flare", "No rollout"). A minimum threshold crossing height of 47 ft is required for every autoland, and the maximum speed in SNGL or DUAL LAND is 235 kt. See [Limitations](limitations) and [Normal Procedures](normal-procedures).

The KC-10's LAND switch is placarded **INOP** and selects nothing; the aircraft has no ALGN, FLARE, ROLL OUT or PAFAM. Fly the ILS with the ILS pushbutton (or the localizer alone with RAD/FMS and the EHSI on the localizer), and disconnect the autopilot for a manual landing at or above the applicable minimums. Because no LAND mode can engage, the vertical speed wheel works throughout the approach, and the ARM window goes blank at G/S TRK.

**Arming.** Push **APPR/LAND** with an ILS tuned and the AP or FD in any mode except takeoff or go-around: LAND ARMED appears above the roll window. At localizer capture the roll window shows **LOC**, LAND ARMED moves above the altitude window, and the bank limit becomes 30°; at localizer track it reduces to 10°, and to 5° below 200 ft. At glideslope capture the altitude window shows **G/S** under LAND ARMED. Selecting any other pitch or roll mode before a land mode engages cancels the approach. The localizer can be intercepted at up to 90°, but high speed or intercepts beyond 30 to 40° may overshoot.

**Flight director only.** A director-only approach is limited to CAT I and II. LOC and G/S are white, and at glideslope capture the altitude window reads **G/S APPR ONLY** and LAND ARMED is removed. Below 1,500 ft a dual-director approach can only be left with the GA switch.

**Land modes.** With an AP engaged, tracking both beams, DUAL LAND engages after the aircraft has been below 1,500 ft radio altitude for 10 seconds: both APs engage, the FMA roll and altitude windows turn green and read **LOC** and **G/S DUAL LAND**, and the AP legend changes to **AP**. If DUAL LAND is not available (second AP unavailable, autothrottle not engaged, or the second ILS not usable), **SINGLE LAND** engages instead (white). The system keeps trying for DUAL LAND down to 400 ft; if no land mode has engaged by then, it reverts to **APPR ONLY**, the AP continues to track the beams, and it disconnects automatically at 100 ft for a manual landing. A reversion from DUAL to SINGLE LAND, or from SINGLE LAND to APPR ONLY, flashes the altitude window five times; reversions are inhibited below 100 ft. With a land mode engaged every other mode except go-around is inhibited.

To fly an approach to an MDA instead, set the FCP altitude window to the MDA before a land mode engages: the system goes to APPR ONLY and levels off at the window altitude.

**Align, flare, rollout.** In SINGLE or DUAL LAND the roll window shows **ALIGN** for the forward-slip decrab (the FCOM gives 150 ft; the simulation's shared laws begin it at about 200 ft). At about 50 to 60 ft the AP flares (**FLARE DUAL LAND** or **FLARE SINGLE LAND**) and the autothrottle retards (**RETARD**). At main wheel spin-up both windows read **ROLLOUT**: the nose is lowered to the runway and the rudder holds the localizer centerline. Reverse thrust disengages the autothrottle without a warning. Disconnect the AP at the end of the rollout, before turning off. The GA switch is the only way out of DUAL LAND, SINGLE LAND or a dual-director APPR ONLY below 1,500 ft.

The MD-10 limitations prohibit automatic landings above 8,000 ft MSL, limit the wind components to 25 kt headwind, 10 kt tailwind and 15 kt crosswind, and limit the speed to 200 KIAS with SINGLE or DUAL LAND engaged; see [Limitations](limitations).

sections.title: Takeoff and go-around guidance
sections.summary: The TO/GA button on the ground and in the air, and the MD-10's windshear guidance.

blocks.content: The **TO/GA** button is on the No. 2 thrust lever. (In the simulation it also answers the simulator's autothrottle TO/GA binding.) What a press selects depends on where the aircraft is:

rows: Flight director TAKE OFF in roll and pitch.
In flight with the flaps out of the full-up position
Go-around: FD and autopilot G/A, thrust rating computer to G/A, autothrottle to N1 at G/A thrust, speed control to G/A.
In flight with the flaps up

blocks.content: **TAKE OFF.** The roll bar commands wings level throughout (a HDG SEL pull takes the roll). After lift-off the pitch bar commands **speed guidance**: the attitude that holds the computed takeoff speed, limited to **22°** nose up. The fast/slow indicator is valid only after lift-off. In the simulation the speed flown is the speed control system's alpha speed for the configuration and weight (see [Autothrottle](#ats-dc-kc)), standing in for V2 + 10 kt; the engine-out schedule (V2 to V2 + 10 kt) is not modeled. TAKE OFF is a flight director mode only: an AP lever moved to CMD in the air ends it, and the autopilot starts in HDG HOLD and VERT SPD at the present climb. It also ends when both FD switches go OFF or another mode is selected. FedEx does not permit the takeoff mode at weights below the VMCG-limited weight with derated thrust.

**Go-around.** The press puts G/A in the roll and pitch windows and N1 in the autothrottle window, and releases the approach, LAND and NAV arms; an armed altitude preselect stays armed. The pitch commands speed guidance (the alpha speed in the simulation, standing in for V2 + 10 kt on three engines) with a **15°** limit; if 15° is not enough to hold the speed, the fast/slow shows FAST with the bars centerd. The roll levels the wings and holds the heading. If both autopilots were in CMD for an autoland, **AP 2 drops** at the press. The retard is disarmed for the go-around, so a go-around begun near the ground does not close the levers as the aircraft sinks through 50 ft.

The usual flow: TO/GA, rotate to the go-around attitude and confirm go-around thrust, flaps 22, positive rate gear up, set and arm the missed approach altitude (FMA reads N1 | ALT | G/A | G/A), climb power and IAS HOLD at 1,500 ft as the procedure requires, and at altitude capture select SPD on the autothrottle. FedEx does not permit the autopilot for a go-around with an engine failed. Above the minimum altitude on a non-autoland approach, FedEx also flies an autopilot go-around with the vertical speed wheel (about 1,500 ft/min climb). See [Normal Procedures](normal-procedures).

**Takeoff.** On the ground the FD takeoff mode engages by itself with a director on and V2 confirmed on the FMS TAKEOFF page (until V2 is confirmed the pitch bar is removed). AUTO FLIGHT on the ground engages the autothrottles only; the autothrottle shows T/O THRUST and then **T/O CLAMP** from 80 kt. Above 100 ft AUTO FLIGHT engages the AP in its takeoff mode. Below 400 ft in takeoff the altitude capture is disarmed, the pitch wheel does nothing and no other pitch mode can be selected; above 400 ft any other pitch mode ends the pitch takeoff, and an altitude capture ends it automatically. The thrust reduces to climb at the FMS CLB THRUST altitude.

**Go-around.** The **GA switch** on the center thrust lever works in approach conditions: below 2,500 ft radio altitude with the flaps or slats extended. A push exits the present modes (including a land mode), brings both directors into view even if selected off, and the AP (if engaged) follows them: wings level if banked more than 3°, otherwise the heading held, with the bank limited to 10°. The autothrottle goes to the go-around thrust limit, the speed window shows the reference speed and PITCH, and the altitude window GO AROUND. The reference speed is the higher of the present speed and the FMS go-around minimum (the alpha speed stands in for it in the simulation); FMS SPD is cancelled. An AP go-around survives a momentary touchdown if pressed before main gear spin-up; a press after spin-up disconnects the AP. The FD go-around can be engaged up to 20 seconds after nose gear compression.

The MD-10's windshear alert and guidance system (WAGS) is part of the AFS. It is available on takeoff from 80 kt to 1,500 ft radio altitude, and on approach from 1,500 ft to 50 ft. It detects a performance-decreasing shear (a growing tailwind or a downdraft) and shows a red **WINDSHEAR** at the top left of the PFD, or a performance-increasing shear (a growing headwind or an updraft) shown in amber; the legend flashes three times and then stays steady, and red has priority.

**Guidance** commands a 1° flight path until the target speed is reached, then holds that speed: V2 + 30 kt on takeoff, 1.3 Vs + 20 kt (or higher, within the flap placard) on a go-around. Above 450 ft a level or slightly descending path is accepted; below 450 ft, if a climbing path is not possible, the guidance flies toward the stick shaker angle of attack and accepts the height loss needed to avoid a stall. In a decreasing shear the bank is limited to 5° and the roll and altitude windows flash. Guidance continues until the aircraft is above 1,000 ft, climbing at 750 ft/min or more, and at V2 + 10 (takeoff) or VREF (go-around) for 15 seconds. Selecting another pitch mode ends the pitch guidance; the GA switch resumes it.

items: **On takeoff** guidance engages after lift-off (it does not command the rotation); the autothrottle stays clamped and shows the maximum takeoff rating even after a flex takeoff, and the crew must set that thrust by hand. Before V1 a windshear warning means reject.

**On approach** guidance engages when the GA switch is pushed or the thrust reaches 95 % of the go-around rating; the thrust rating changes to go-around, the speed reference rises to at least 1.3 Vs + 20 kt, and the autothrottle advances to go-around thrust.
After a go-around is begun, a detected shear starts guidance automatically.

sections.title: PAFAM landing monitor
sections.summary: The Performance And Failure Assessment Monitor: a predicted touchdown point on a CRT, and the arbiter of autopilot disconnects in the landing.

blocks.content: The **Performance And Failure Assessment Monitor (PAFAM)** supervises the automatic landing. It has two functions of different kinds. The first is **performance prediction**: it runs simplified models of the aircraft and autopilot in accelerated time to predict where the aircraft will touch down, and draws that prediction on a small five-color CRT on each pilot's front panel, so the crew can judge before the runway is in sight whether the landing will be good. The second is **reversion inhibit**: it decides whether an in-line monitor's failure signal may actually disconnect an autopilot channel during the landing.

blocks.alt: DC-10-30 captain's PAFAM display on short final, prediction mode: a yellow perspective runway raster expanding from a vanishing point above the screen, the runway threshold as the lowest horizontal line, a green rectangle inside it for the touchdown zone, and an orange cross whose intersection sits slightly left of center and long within the green zone, with the left arm longer than the right. A small inset beside it shows the TEST pattern (yellow rasters, green cross, large yellow TEST).
blocks.title: PAFAM display, prediction mode

blocks.content: **The display.** A yellow runway raster expands toward the bottom of the screen as the aircraft closes the runway, at the rate the real runway would appear to expand through the windscreen, about a fixed vanishing point; it does not tilt with attitude. It barely moves until about 200 ft (3,000 ft range) and then moves faster. The lowest horizontal line is the threshold. A **green** area is the touchdown zone: ±60 ft laterally and ±1,000 ft longitudinally about the nominal touchdown point, on the centerline about 500 ft beyond the glideslope transmitter. An **orange cross** shows the prediction: its **intersection** is the predicted touchdown point, and the length of each arm is the uncertainty in that direction, so a long left arm says the landing could end up farther left than predicted. The arms are 0.010 inch per foot laterally and per 20 ft longitudinally, up to 1 inch and 0.5 inch. For an acceptable landing the whole cross should stay in the green.

blocks.alt: Three DC-10 PAFAM display states side by side: TAKEOVER in large red letters with the yellow arrow figure in the upper left corner above the T; NO TRACK in large red letters on a blank tube; and the live prediction raster with NO ILS in small red letters along the bottom.
blocks.title: PAFAM TAKEOVER, NO TRACK and NO ILS

blocks.content:
**When it runs.** Selecting LAND (or ILS) powers the PAFAM into standby; it becomes operational when the localizer and glideslope are both in TRACK. In **ILS mode** (the ILS pushbutton without LAND) the same pictures appear, the test is about 10 s, and the displays blank at 100 ft radio altitude because no automatic landing will follow. In LAND the displays run to touchdown.

**Only the intersection commands TAKEOVER.** The arms show uncertainty and may extend beyond the green zone while the predicted point is still inside it; that alone is not a TAKEOVER. The arrow points to the pilot with the better information; with equivalent information, the left (captain's) arrow is chosen.

**Reversion inhibit.** Each sensor the PAFAM watches supplies a validity signal and a control signal, and the PAFAM can judge a third factor itself: the aircraft's **response**. It inhibits an autopilot disconnect until two of the three are recognized as improper. A monitor trip that is not confirmed and does not persist is ignored and the landing continues; a genuine failure has its inhibit removed and the channel (or pair of channels) disconnects. The rudder is the exception: two servos share each rudder actuator, so a yaw failure reverts both rudders from parallel to series operation together rather than disconnecting them. In LAND the inhibit function is removed at 115 ft radio altitude; the display carries on.

**Self-test.** The PAFAM tests itself twice a second. A failure removes all display information **and** all reversion-inhibit voltage together, shutting the unit down, and latches a fault indicator on the failed unit. With the PAFAM failed the autoland channels' own monitors disconnect without arbitration.

sections.title: Yaw dampers
sections.summary: Why a swept-wing trijet needs artificial yaw damping, and how four channels on two rudders provide it.

blocks.content:
**Why they are needed.** A swept-wing transport has a lightly damped lateral-directional oscillation, the **Dutch roll**: a disturbance in yaw makes one wing advance, its sweep gives it more lift, the aircraft rolls, the roll produces sideslip the other way, and the aircraft swings back and forth in a coupled yaw and roll with a period of a few seconds. Sweep makes the rolling response to sideslip (dihedral effect) strong, and the fin's natural damping comes from the air it moves, so it falls as density falls. The oscillation is therefore least damped at high altitude and high weight, which is where an airliner spends its cruise. Left alone, the DC-10's Dutch roll would be uncomfortable at best and, at the extremes of the envelope, a handling hazard.

The yaw damper adds the damping the airframe lacks. A yaw rate gyro senses the yaw rate and the damper moves the rudder against it, in proportion. Rate feedback of this kind removes energy from the oscillation every cycle, exactly as a shock absorber does.

blocks.alt: Schematic of the yaw damper. Two yaw computers: computer 1 (lower rudder, left emergency buses) and computer 2 (upper rudder, right emergency buses). Each computer has a yaw rate gyro feeding a washout filter, a Mach-scheduled gain (from the CADC, with a fixed maximum-gain bias at flaps 35° or more), a structural filter, and two identical channels A and B. Each channel drives a transfer valve and a mod piston limited to ±2.5° of rudder; the two pistons are mechanically summed into one rudder actuator, ±5° total, in series with the pilot's pedal input. A comparator watches the two pistons and lights UPPER or LOWER YAW DAMP INOP. Each channel's engage chain is drawn: switch, 115 V AC excitation, AC power relay, 28 V DC engage solenoid. The parallel autoland servo (up to ±23°) is shown dashed on each actuator.
blocks.title: Yaw damper, functional schematic

blocks.content:
**Architecture.** There are two yaw computers: **computer 1 drives the lower rudder, computer 2 the upper**. Each has two identical channels, **A** and **B**, fed from the same yaw rate gyro through the same signal chain. Each channel drives a transfer valve and a **mod piston**; the two pistons of a computer are mechanically summed to drive that rudder's actuator. Each piston is limited to ±2.5° of rudder, so two channels give ±5° on each rudder. This is **series** operation: the damper's rudder movement adds to the pilot's pedal input without moving the pedals, and the pilot does not feel it and cannot override it by holding the pedals.

Because the stop is on each piston, one channel engaged gives half the authority (±2.5°), and a channel failed hard over in one direction is opposed by its healthy partner, leaving that rudder close to neutral rather than hard over. That is why the crew's isolation procedure judges the aircraft's handling, not a light.

**Signal chain.** The yaw rate passes through a **washout** (high-pass) filter, which removes the steady yaw rate of a turn so that the damper does not oppose a turn the pilot is making, and a **structural filter**, which removes the high-frequency yaw rates from fuselage bending. The gain is scheduled with **Mach number** from the CADC: as Mach rises the rudder becomes more effective and less rudder is needed, so the gain falls. With the flaps at 35° or more, or if the CADC input fails, the Mach input is replaced by a fixed bias equal to about 0.25 Mach, which gives the maximum gain. Before engagement an integrator nulls any residual signal so the rudder does not jump when the channel engages; the stored bias then washes out slowly.

**Engagement.** Each channel's switch energizes its 115 V AC excitation, an AC power relay, and through that relay its 28 V DC engage solenoid. The relay is in series ahead of the solenoid on purpose: if the 115 V AC supply is lost, the solenoid loses its DC too and the channel disengages with the rudder centerd, rather than staying engaged without a valid signal. The switches are not electrically held.

**Monitoring.** In each computer a comparator watches the two mod pistons. If they disagree, the **UPPER** or **LOWER YAW DAMP INOP** light comes on (DC-10/KC-10, on the pilots' overhead annunciator panel), but nothing is disengaged automatically: in series mode the crew decide. Switching either switch of the affected subsystem OFF disarms its comparator and puts the light out. Two faults are quiet: a dead computer or a dead rate gyro leaves both channels agreeing perfectly about nothing, so no light comes on and half the aircraft's yaw damping is gone. Only the ground self-test, and the aircraft's handling, reveal them.

**Turn coordination.** On the aircraft the series channels also provide turn coordination: a high-passed bank angle signal gives rudder during roll-in and roll-out, and a low-passed yaw rate holds the steady rudder of a turn. The simulation's yaw damper provides damping only; turns are coordinated by the aerodynamics and the crew.

**Parallel mode.** For the autoland the yaw computers also drive the rudders in **parallel** mode, up to about ±23° of the rudder's 24°, felt in the pedals: this is the ALGN decrab and the ROLL OUT steering (see [Autoland](#autoland-dc10)). Parallel operation needs the series yaw damper hardware to be usable.

**Controls (DC-10 and KC-10).** The **YAW DAMP** panel on the pilots' overhead carries four switches, **UPPER A, UPPER B, LOWER A, LOWER B** (OFF / ON), the **YAW DAMP TEST** switch-light, and two amber **YAW DAMP TEST FAIL** lights. The panel is on the pilots' overhead; the flight engineer normally works it.

**Self-test.** On the ground, with hydraulic pressure on both rudder systems and all four switches ON, pushing the TEST switch-light starts a test of about 20 seconds: the TEST light, both TEST FAIL lights, both YAW DAMP INOP lights and the MASTER CAUTION lights come on, and on the surface position indicator the rudders move left half an increment, return slowly, move slightly right and return. At the end every light goes out. A TEST FAIL light that stays on shows that subsystem failed the test. If any condition is not met (airborne, no hydraulics, a switch off) the test does not start, and there is no light to say so.

blocks.alt: DC-10-30 pilots' overhead panel, automatic flight area: the YAW DAMP panel with UPPER A and B and LOWER A and B switches all ON, the YAW DAMP TEST switch-light and the two amber YAW DAMP TEST FAIL lights extinguished; beside it the SPEED CONT TEST selector (SLO / FAST), the STALL TEST selector (L / R) and the FD CMD selector at NORM (BOTH ON 1 / NORM / BOTH ON 2); and the UPPER YAW DAMP INOP and LOWER YAW DAMP INOP legends on the annunciator panel, extinguished. All legends legible.
blocks.title: Overhead automatic flight controls (DC-10 and KC-10)

blocks.content: **Controls (MD-10).** The MD-10's yaw dampers are controlled from the AFS panel on the forward overhead: four switch-lights, **UPPER A, UPPER B, LOWER A, LOWER B**, each with a **FAIL** and an **OFF** legend. If a channel malfunctions its FAIL light comes on; pushing the switch-light turns that channel off, OFF comes on and FAIL goes out. There is no test button and no summary INOP light. See [Flight Controls](flight-controls) for the AFS panel's other functions.

blocks.alt: MD-10-30 forward overhead AFS panel, yaw damper section: four square switch-lights labeled UPPER A, UPPER B, LOWER A and LOWER B, each with a FAIL upper half and an OFF lower half; LOWER B shown with OFF illuminated amber, the others dark. Legends legible.
blocks.title: MD-10 yaw damper switch-lights

blocks.content: A minimum of two yaw damper channels must be operative for takeoff (see [Limitations](limitations)). With one channel per rudder the authority is halved; with both channels of one rudder off, the other rudder alone damps the Dutch roll. In flight, the KC-10 T.O. imposes no limitation with all yaw dampers inoperative: smooth flying prevents an inadvertent Dutch roll.

sections.title: Operation
sections.summary: The automatic flight system through a normal flight, deck by deck.

blocks.content: This section shows how the modes fit together on a normal flight. The checklists themselves are in [Normal Procedures](normal-procedures); the limits are in [Limitations](limitations).

children.title: DC-10 and KC-10 through a flight

blocks.content: **Preflight.** The flight engineer turns all four YAW DAMP switches ON (YAW DAMP INOP, TEST and TEST FAIL lights out) and runs the yaw damper self-test with hydraulic pressure available. The STALL TEST selector is held at L and then R: both stick shakers run after about 5 seconds each time. The SPEED CONT TEST selector is held at SLO and then FAST: both fast/slow indicators move to half scale. The pilots test the annunciators with ANNUN LT TEST (the FMA strips show T-E-S-T), select the FD switches to FD, and check the director: turning the HDG knob either way moves the roll bars that way, and the bank angle selector changes how far they move; the vertical speed wheel moves the pitch bars. AP levers OFF, ATS levers OFF, the SPD window set, the ALT window set to the cleared altitude, the bank angle selector as required.

**Takeoff (autothrottle takeoff, -30, -40 and KC-10).** ATS levers ON before takeoff: CLAMP. TO/GA on the runway: TAKE OFF | TAKE OFF in the roll and pitch windows. Push N1: the FMA reads N1 and the levers advance to the takeoff limit; check the N1 against the limit. At 80 kt check CLAMP ("No Clamp" if not). Rotate to the pitch bar; after lift-off it commands the takeoff speed with a 22° limit and the roll bar wings level. Pull the ALT knob to arm the cleared altitude (ALT in the ARM window).

On the -10 and -15 the autothrottle is not used for takeoff (FedEx): set thrust by hand and engage the autothrottle in the climb.

**Climb.** At or above the minimum engagement height (FedEx: 500 ft AGL), move an AP lever to CMD: TAKE OFF ends and the autopilot starts in HDG HOLD and VERT SPD at the climb rate it finds. Set climb thrust (N1 mode with CLIMB selected on the thrust rating computer, or by hand) and press IAS to climb at a constant speed on pitch, or keep VERT SPD with the autothrottle in SPD and watch the speed. Pull HDG for HDG SEL, or press RAD/INS (RAD/FMS) with the HSI on the navigation unit for FMS. At the cleared altitude ALT CAP and then ALT HOLD appear; select SPD on the autothrottle (pull the SPD knob) so the throttles hold the speed in level flight.

**Cruise.** ALT HOLD (or MACH HOLD on a cruise climb with N1 thrust), SPD or N1 on the autothrottle as the operator prefers, FMS TRK or RAD TRK in roll. The yaw dampers damp the Dutch roll throughout. In turbulence, push TURB.

**Descent.** Set the new altitude and pull the ALT knob. Start down with the vertical speed wheel (with the autothrottle in SPD) or with IAS HOLD and reduced thrust by hand or in N1 (not both IAS HOLD and SPD). The preselect captures the new level.

**Approach.** Tune the ILS on both receivers and set the courses, set the approach speed in the SPD window (the alpha speed will hold the autothrottle above the safe margin), the bank angle selector to 15° for the intercept as FedEx does, and the missed approach heading. Fly the intercept in HDG SEL, then press **LAND** (DC-10, for an autoland) or **ILS** (for an approach to minimums). For DUAL LAND, move the second AP lever to CMD once LAND is selected. Watch for LOC CAP, LOC TRK, G/S CAP, G/S TRK, then the land status; set the missed approach altitude once on the glideslope. On the DC-10, the PAFAM shows the TEST pattern and then its prediction.

**Landing.** In SNGL or DUAL LAND: ALGN near 200 ft, FLARE and RETD near 60 ft, ROLL OUT at spin-up, reverse thrust (which disengages the autothrottle), and AP levers OFF before turning off the runway. On an approach-only approach, disconnect the autopilot at or above the minimum height (FedEx: 72 ft AGL) and land by hand; the autothrottle retards through 50 ft if left in SPD. Push the flashing red lights to reset them.

**Air refueling (KC-10 receiver and tanker).** Do not use the autopilot's navigation modes during air refueling. See [Air Refueling](air-refueling).

**Before takeoff.** Confirm V2 on the FMS TAKEOFF page so the FD takeoff mode can engage, set the FCP altitude window to the cleared altitude and the speed window as required, arm NAV once the engines are running if the departure is flown on the flight plan, and arm PROF if the operator does. Push **AUTO FLIGHT**: on the ground it engages both autothrottles only.

**Takeoff.** Advance the throttles; the autothrottle sets T/O THRUST and clamps (T/O CLAMP) from 80 kt. Follow the pitch bar: about 6° at 80 kt, about 15° at rotation, then V2 + 10 kt. NAV guidance comes in at 100 ft for the directors; above 100 ft AUTO FLIGHT engages the AP in its takeoff mode, and AP NAV couples from 400 ft. At the thrust reduction altitude the autothrottle changes to CLB THRUST; PROF (if armed) engages at 400 ft.

**Climb, cruise and descent.** With PROF and FMS SPD the FMS flies the vertical profile and the speeds (magenta), within the FCP altitude window: raise the window to climb further, lower it before the top of descent (VERT ALERT reminds you). Without PROF, pull the ALT knob for a level change, push it to hold, or roll the pitch wheel for V/S. The speed reference changes to Mach at 26,000 ft. The speed envelope protection keeps the speed between VMIN + 5 and VMAX − 5.

**Approach and landing.** Tune the ILS, set the approach speed (or FMS SPD), and push **APPR/LAND**. LOC, G/S, then DUAL LAND after 10 seconds below 1,500 ft with the FMA turning green; ALIGN, FLARE and RETARD, ROLLOUT. Reverse thrust disengages the autothrottle; disconnect the AP at the end of the rollout and acknowledge AP OFF with a second push. On an APPR ONLY approach, disconnect before 100 ft and land by hand.

sections.title: Failures and non-normal operation
sections.summary: What fails, how it shows, and what the crew do about it. Procedures are in Sections 2 and 3.

blocks.content: The automatic flight system is designed so that most failures disconnect or degrade one channel and announce it, leaving the crew with the other system or with manual control. The dangerous failures are the quiet ones: a mode that is still annunciated but no longer achievable, a servo that drives without a command, a damper that has stopped damping without a light. The crew's defense is the FMA, the flight instruments and their own hands on the controls. The procedures are in [Abnormal Procedures](abnormal-procedures) and [Emergency Procedures](emergency-procedures).
