blocks.content: If the autopilot makes an uncommanded pitch or roll maneuver, hold the control wheel firmly and disconnect it with the AP release (disconnect) button. Do not try to correct an autopilot fault by trimming or by pushing other mode buttons first.

sections.title: Simulation notes
sections.summary: What is modeled, what is simplified, and what is not there.

blocks.content: **Modeled in depth.** The aircraft is flown by its own autopilot control laws, not the simulator's default autopilot: every pitch mode through one vertical speed cascade on the elevator, with auto pitch trim on the stabilizer; every lateral mode through a bank command and a roll rate loop; gain schedules with airspeed; altitude, localizer and glideslope captures planned on the aircraft's own rates; glideslope and localizer gain programming; the DC-10's preland test, DUAL and SNGL LAND, the forward-slip align with the parallel rudder, the flare, retard, nose lowering and rollout on rudder and nosewheel. The autothrottle is one servo, three clutches and a balancer, with CLAMP, N1/EPR, SPD, ALPHA SPD and RETD modes and the thrust rating computer as the ceiling. The yaw damper is four channels on two rudders with the washout, Mach gain, structural filter, engage chain, comparator and self-test. The PAFAM predicts, displays and arbitrates disconnects. The MD-10 has its own FCC mode logic, FCP, FMA, PROF coupling, speed protection, windshear guidance and altitude alert on the same laws and servo.

items: **Hardware throttles.** A hardware quadrant cannot be moved by the aircraft. While the autothrottle is engaged your levers set only the split between the engines; the 3D levers show the servo's position. Leave your levers together for normal flight.

**Control wheel steering** is simplified: in CWS the roll is fully manual (no bank hold on release) and the pitch is held in the standing vertical mode except while the column is displaced. The aircraft's force-sensing CWS, with its overpower thresholds in pounds, is approximated by column and wheel displacement.
**MD-10 roll CWS (RCWS)** is not modeled; an overpower disconnects the AP.
**TAKE OFF and G/A pitch** fly the speed control system's alpha speed for the configuration and weight in place of V2 + 10 kt (DC-10/KC-10); the engine-out V2 schedule is not modeled on those decks.
**IAS/MACH HOLD with autothrottle SPD**: the interlock that prevents both controlling speed at once is not modeled. Do not combine them.

**Autopilot power** on the DC-10 and KC-10 comes from the AT/SC circuit breakers; the separate flight guidance breakers are not modeled. An autopilot's engagement is not affected by the loss of its hydraulic system (on the aircraft an autopilot in LAND disconnects when its hydraulic system fails), and the KC-10's AP 2 is not affected by the hydraulic system 3 elevator shutoff valve.

**Yaw dampers do not gate autopilot engagement.** Turn coordination is not modeled. The MD-10's parallel rudder in takeoff and go-around (engine-failure compensation) is not modeled; parallel rudder is used only in ALIGN and ROLLOUT.

**FMA legends.** The DC-10 decks show the KC-10's RAD and FMS legends (RAD CAP, FMS TRK) where some DC-10 tapes read VOR and INS. With LAND selected, the ARM window shows ILS until the preland test answers (there is no LAND arm legend), and DUAL LAND is amber like every ARM legend. An armed altitude preselect stays armed through the glideslope.

**Preland test** takes a few seconds after the glideslope capture rather than the aircraft's 30 to 40 seconds, and DUAL LAND does not require the autothrottle, a bus split or matching course knobs on the DC-10. The MD-10's ALIGN begins at about 200 ft (the FCOM gives 150 ft) and the MD-10 uses one ILS receiver for both FCCs.
**Back course** (B/CRS) modes are not available; the BACK CRS switch is inoperative.

**Aural warnings.** The DC-10/KC-10 autopilot disconnect aural in LAND is not sounded. The MD-10's AP OFF aural sounds through the central aural warning system as a tone, without the voice; the windshear aural is not sounded.
**ADI rudder (decrab) indicator** stays out of view.

**One set of guidance.** The DC-10 and KC-10 compute one set of roll and pitch modes for both directors, so the two pilots' bars never disagree and the bias-out of a conflicting director does not arise. The FD CMD selector lights the ADI FD lights when off NORM but does not change the bars' source.

**MD-10 WAGS**: the detection threshold is a typical industry value, not the aircraft's own; the pitch limit indicator and the GPWS and TCAS inhibits are not modeled. The level change's reduced-thrust taper for small level changes is not modeled.
**Pausing or slewing** the simulator suspends auto pitch trim.

blocks.content:
**Failures you can inject from the EFB.** In the AUTO FLIGHT group: *Yaw damper inoperative* (upper or lower: a channel hardover, which lights the INOP light and exercises the isolation procedure) and *Stall warning or auto slat fault*. In INSTRUMENTS, *Loss of primary attitude* removes the autopilots' attitude references. On the DC-10 and KC-10, pulling an AT/SC circuit breaker removes that autothrottle and, in the simulation, that autopilot. See [EFB](efb).

**Simulator key bindings.** The simulator's own autopilot keys and buttons work the cockpit controls as a hand would: autopilot master and disconnect move the AP levers (DC-10/KC-10) or work AUTO FLIGHT and the wheel disconnect (MD-10); heading hold pulls the HDG knob; altitude hold centers the vertical speed wheel (DC-10/KC-10) or pushes the ALT knob (MD-10); the autothrottle disconnect key is the throttle disengage button; the TO/GA key is the TO/GA (GA) button. A mode the panel has no gesture for is not answered.

parts.title: Navigation
parts.summary: Radio navigation and the inertial navigation and reference systems.

blocks.content: The navigation systems tell the crew where the aeroplane is and how to get where it is going. They fall into two families that complement each other. The **radio aids** measure the aeroplane's position relative to a ground station: a bearing (VOR, ADF, TACAN), a deviation from a beam (localizer and glideslope), a slant range (DME) or a moment of passage (marker beacon). They are accurate near the station and useless out of its range. The **self-contained systems** measure the aeroplane's own accelerations and rotations and integrate them into a position (inertial navigation), or blend radio fixes with heading and airspeed (area navigation). They work anywhere, but an inertial position slowly drifts and must be checked against, or updated from, the radio aids.

This part covers the radio receivers and their control heads, the switching that decides which receiver each instrument shows, the theory of inertial navigation, and each long-range unit fitted to the family: the Litton AINS-70, the Delco Carousel IV-A, the Collins INS-61B and ANS-70 on the DC-10, the KC-10's inertial navigation units, and the MD-10's air data inertial reference units with its navigation display. Route planning on GPS and FMS boxes (the HT-9100, the KC-10 FMS and the MD-10's Pegasus FMS) is in [Flight management](flight-management). Attitude and heading instruments are in [Flight instruments](flight-instruments), the autopilot's navigation modes in [Automatic flight](automatic-flight), and weather radar, TCAS, GPWS and the transponders in [Surveillance](surveillance).

**Architecture.** Every installation has three layers. **Sensors** produce raw measurements: two VOR receivers, two ILS receivers, two DME interrogators, a marker beacon receiver, two ADF receivers (and on the KC-10 two TACAN sets), and three inertial platforms. **Computers** turn measurements into a position and steering: the inertial navigation units, the AINS-70's navigation computers, or the FMS. **Presentation and switching** route the result to the crew and the autopilot: on the DC-10 the RAD/INS switching unit, the RMIs, HSIs and ADIs; on the KC-10 the display control panels, EHSIs and RMIs; on the MD-10 the electronic instrument system and the ND.

**Redundancy.** Every radio receiver except the marker beacon is duplicated, and each of a pair is fed from a different side of the electrical system. The inertial platforms are triplicated on three separate circuits. The design goal is that a single failure costs each pilot at most one instrument, never both of one pilot's instruments, and that a failed unit can be identified by comparison with the other two. The crossed ILS feeds to the DC-10's ADIs (described under [ILS](#ils)) are the clearest example of that philosophy.

On the KC-10 the glareshield VHF NAV control heads tune VOR and ILS together, and the FMS CDUs command the TACANs, the ADFs and the inertial units: the aeroplane has no dedicated TACAN or ADF control head.

On the MD-10 the flight management system tunes the VOR, DME, ILS and ADF receivers automatically, and the crew tune manually through the MCDU. The three ADIRUs provide attitude, heading and inertial position to the displays and the FMS.

children.title: Navigation equipment fits
children.summary: Which long-range navigation unit each aircraft carries, and what changes with it.

blocks.content: The radio receivers are the same hardware on every DC-10 and KC-10. What differs is the **long-range navigation unit**: the box that holds a route, computes a present position independently of ground stations and steers the aeroplane along great-circle legs. The DC-10 was delivered with several different units over its life, and the simulation offers the principal ones as alternative fits. The KC-10 carries one configuration, and the MD-10's flight management system replaced the whole category.

blocks.content: The fit is part of the aircraft's equipment configuration, chosen in Infinity Manager or on the EFB Configuration app's Aircraft Configuration page. Some units are available only with some product editions. Changing the fit while the simulation is running replaces the box, and the new unit starts with an empty route (on the AINS-70 and ANS-70, an empty core). A Carousel IV-A or INS-61B fitted while the aeroplane is airborne or has an engine running comes up already aligned and navigating. On the AINS-70, ANS-70 and HT-9100 fits the three platforms are not replaced: they keep their alignment only if the new fit's mode selectors are at NAV. The KDC-10 is simulated as a DC-10-30 and is offered the same fits.

Every DC-10 fit except VOR only carries three inertial mode selectors on the overhead, and on every one of those fits the three platforms behind them also supply attitude and heading to the glass instrument options (MFD and FPDS). Turning a mode selector off on any fit can therefore cost a pilot's glass attitude display, not only navigation. See [Flight instruments](flight-instruments#inertial-attitude).

sections.title: Radio navigation
sections.summary: The short-range receivers, their theory of operation, and how their outputs reach the instruments.

blocks.content: The radio navigation system is the aeroplane's set of **dependent** position-determining aids: every one of them measures something relative to a transmitter on the ground (or, for TACAN air-to-air, another aircraft). The receivers do not compute beam geometry for themselves in any meaningful sense: they report what the signal says, and they report when it says nothing. Most of the system's design is about that second part: deciding which receiver is live, whether its output is valid, and which instrument it reaches.

On the MD-10, tuning is the FMS's job: the on-side flight management computer autotunes the VOR/DME and ILS receivers for the route and the approach, and either MCDU's NAV RADIO page tunes any radio manually (see [Flight management](flight-management)). This section describes what the receivers measure; the MD-10's presentation is in [MD-10 navigation display](#md-10-nd).

children.title: VOR
children.summary: VHF omnidirectional range: magnetic bearing from a ground station by phase comparison.

blocks.content: **Principle.** A VOR ground station radiates two 30 Hz signals. The **reference phase** is frequency-modulated onto a 9,960 Hz subcarrier and radiated equally in every direction, so its phase is the same wherever it is received. The **variable phase** comes from a directional pattern rotated electronically at 1,800 revolutions per minute (30 per second), so its phase at the receiver depends on the receiver's azimuth from the station. The receiver demodulates both and measures the phase difference, which is the magnetic bearing of the aeroplane from the station: the **radial**. Because the radial is a property of the aeroplane's position and not of its heading, a VOR tells the crew where they are, not where they are pointing.

The receiver uses the radial in two ways. Compared with a course the crew have selected, it gives a **course deviation** (how far off the selected radial the aeroplane is, as an angle) and a **TO/FROM** sense (whether flying the selected course would take the aeroplane toward or away from the station). Compared with the aeroplane's magnetic heading from the compass system, it gives the **bearing to the station** shown by an RMI pointer. Deviation is angular, so a dot represents fewer miles close to the station than far from it, and directly overhead the geometry breaks down: in the **cone of silence** above the station the radial changes rapidly and is unreliable until the aeroplane is clear of it.

**Frequencies.** The VHF NAV band runs from 108.00 to 117.95 MHz in 50 kHz steps. Frequencies from 112.00 to 117.95 MHz are VORs only. Between 108.00 and 111.95 MHz the band is shared: even tenths of a megahertz (108.20, 108.45…) are VORs, odd tenths (108.10, 108.15, 109.30…) are localizers. The odd-tenth rule gives exactly forty localizer channels.

**Receivers.** Two VOR receivers sit on the main radio rack. VHF NAV 1 drives the captain's HSI and VHF NAV 2 the first officer's HSI (fed straight, side to side), and both drive the RMI bearing pointers. A receiver is in **standby** whenever its control head holds a frequency of the other kind: **the VOR receiver when its head is set to a localizer frequency, the ILS receiver when its head is set to a VOR frequency**. Nobody selects standby; the frequency decides it.

**Validity.** A receiver delivers a radial only when it is powered, tuned to a VOR frequency, not failed, and receiving a usable signal from the station. Otherwise the HSI's NAV flag comes into view (the striped flag on the Biman HSI, the CRS flag lamp on the KSSU HSI), the deviation bar centers (Biman) or is removed (KSSU), the TO/FROM indication disappears, and the RMI pointer for that receiver flags. A centerd bar with the flag out of view is "on course"; a centerd bar with the flag in view means nothing at all.
On the MD-10 the two VOR receivers feed the NDs and supply their bearing data to the FMS. The ND's VOR mode shows a course deviation indicator at 5° a dot (see [MD-10 navigation display](#md-10-nd)).

children.title: ILS
children.summary: Localizer and glideslope: two beams, two receivers, and two ways of tuning them.

blocks.content: **Principle.** The localizer transmitter radiates two overlapping lobes along the extended runway centerline, the left one (seen from the approach) modulated predominantly at 90 Hz and the right one at 150 Hz. On the centerline the two modulations are equal; to one side one of them dominates. The receiver measures the difference in depth of modulation and turns it into a deflection toward the course: an aeroplane right of course sees more 150 Hz and the bar deflects left, telling the pilot to fly left. The glideslope works the same way in the vertical plane on a UHF carrier between 329.3 and 335.0 MHz, with the 90 Hz lobe above and the 150 Hz lobe below a path normally 2.5° to 3° above the horizontal.

Because the deviation is a ratio of two signals and not a bearing, ILS sensitivity is fixed in angle and becomes finer in distance as the aeroplane approaches the runway. Full-scale deflection close in represents only a few tens of feet, which is why a stable approach and a correctly tuned, identified and course-set receiver matter more on an ILS than on any other aid.

**Receivers.** Two ILS receivers are installed. Each has a **localizer section** (108.10 to 111.95 MHz, forty channels) and a **glideslope section** (329.3 to 335.0 MHz, forty channels). There is no glideslope frequency control anywhere in the aeroplane: tuning a localizer selects its paired glideslope automatically. The two sections can fail independently. A failed glideslope section with a good localizer leaves a **localizer-only** approach, annunciated by the GS flag alone, and the localizer can still be flown.

**Flags.** With a localizer tuned on an instrument's receiver and that instrument selected to ILS, a failed or unpowered receiver, or an absent signal, puts the GS flag in view and withdraws the glideslope pointer (glideslope section), and puts the NAV flag in view and removes the localizer deviation (localizer section). With nothing tuned, or a VOR frequency tuned, the ADI simply shows no ILS symbology and no flag: there is nothing to annunciate because no approach has been asked for. The HSI is stricter: its NAV flag is in view whenever the selected source delivers no lateral deviation, tuned or not.
Two arrangements exist in the fleet, and which one an aeroplane has depends on the airframe and, on the DC-10, on the fitted long-range unit.

blocks.content: **Why the ADI feeds are crossed.** On the pedestal arrangement both ILS receivers are tuned to the same localizer from one head. Feeding each pilot's ADI from the opposite receiver, while each HSI is fed from its own, means that one receiver failure costs each pilot a different instrument instead of costing one pilot both. Each pilot keeps one good ILS display, and a disagreement between a pilot's ADI and HSI is itself the clue that one receiver is wrong. On a healthy aeroplane the crossing is invisible; it shows itself only when a receiver fails, which is exactly when it is needed. The approach coupler of the flight guidance system reads the receivers straight.

**The DME on the pedestal arrangement.** The DME interrogators follow the glareshield heads, not the pedestal head. To read the ILS's paired DME on an approach, set the localizer frequency on the glareshield head as well; the VOR receiver on that side then goes to standby, and the DME channels on the localizer's pairing.

**Glass HSIs.** On the electronic HSIs (the DC-10's MFD and FPDS options and the KC-10's EHSI) the course arrow in ILS is drawn at the localizer's published front course automatically, whatever the knob is set to. The electromechanical HSIs' course arrow is geared to its knob or counter and must be set by the crew.

The marker beacon receiver is fixed-tuned to 75 MHz and lights a lamp, with an aural tone, as the aeroplane passes over a marker transmitter's vertical fan. It discriminates between markers by their modulation tone. One receiver drives two sets of three lights, one set on each pilot's instrument panel, wired in parallel.

blocks.title: Marker lights
rows: Airway marker (and the inner marker, which shares its tone)

blocks.content: The receiver has **no ON/OFF switch**: it runs whenever DC bus 3 and its MARKER BEACON circuit breaker are powered, and it always operates at high sensitivity, which gives an early indication of an approaching marker. Each light lens is its own press-to-test and lights only that lamp, while the MKR BCN button on the overhead RADIO NAV TEST panel tests the receiver itself (see [Radio navigation tests](#radio-nav-tests)).

children.title: DME
children.summary: Distance measuring equipment: slant range by interrogation and reply.

blocks.content: **Principle.** The airborne interrogator transmits pairs of pulses on a UHF channel paired with the VOR or localizer frequency. The ground transponder replies after a fixed delay. The interrogator measures the round-trip time, subtracts the delay and converts the remainder to distance at the speed of light, about 12.4 microseconds of round trip per nautical mile. To pick its own replies out of those addressed to every other aeroplane using the station, the interrogator jitters its pulse timing and looks for replies that keep a constant delay after its own interrogations. Until it has found them it is **searching**; once it has, it is **tracking** (locked on), and only then is a distance shown.

DME measures **slant range**, the straight-line distance to the station, not the distance over the ground. The difference is negligible at long range but large close in: directly over a station at 36,000 ft the DME reads about 6 NM. A fix or a ground speed computed from slant range near the station is correspondingly wrong, which is why the area navigation computers reduce slant range to ground range before using it.

**Installation.** Two interrogators, DME 1 on AC bus 1 and DME 2 on AC bus 3. Neither has a frequency control of its own: each follows the frequency of its own side's glareshield VHF NAV head, so tuning a VORTAC or VOR/DME tunes its DME, and an automatic retune of the VOR by the long-range unit retunes the DME with it. On the KC-10 the dual DME indicator's two windows read DME 1 and DME 2, paired with the two glareshield heads; TACAN range is shown on the EHSIs.

**The DME selector.** On the CIV-A, INS-61B and VOR-only fits the right-hand switch beside each glareshield head is the DME selector, STBY / DME NORM / OVRD. STBY holds the interrogator out of search; it is **not** a power switch, and the interrogator stays energized and warm in STBY as long as its circuit breaker is in. NORM starts the search and tracking. On the AINS-70, ANS-70 and HT-9100 fits the switch in that place is OFF / AUTO TUNE instead, and the DME interrogates continuously with no selection needed.

**Display.** A DME window has three states. A **shutter** (striped bar) covers it when the interrogator is unpowered or failed; **dashes** show while it is powered but has no distance (searching, held in STBY, or with no station tuned); **digits** appear only on lock-on. After a retune the dashes are visibly in view for a moment, about two seconds, while the new station is found. The DC-10's distance windows appear on the HSI (the onside DME), on the RMI or the ALT/DME indicator (both DMEs, by equipment fit), and on the digital DME indicator option.

children.title: ADF
children.summary: Automatic direction finder: relative bearing to an NDB or broadcast station.

blocks.content: **Principle.** The ADF receives low and medium frequency transmissions between 190 and 1,750 kHz on two antennas. The **loop** antenna is directional: its output depends on the angle between the loop and the arriving wave, with a sharp null when the loop is edge-on to it. The **sense** antenna is non-directional and resolves the loop's 180° ambiguity. Together they give the **relative bearing** of the station from the aeroplane's nose. On an RMI the pointer rides on the compass card, so read against the card it shows the **magnetic bearing to the station**: the aeroplane's magnetic heading plus the relative bearing.

Low-frequency bearings are less trustworthy than VOR radials. The airframe itself distorts the arriving wave (quadrantal error); sky waves at dawn and dusk mix with the ground wave and make the pointer wander (night effect); waves crossing a coastline bend toward the shore (coastal refraction); and thunderstorms attract the pointer toward the lightning. A steady pointer and a positive identification are the crew's checks.

**ANT and ADF.** With the function at **ANT** the loop is out of circuit and the set is a plain receiver, used for identifying a station, tuning or listening to a broadcast. It gives no bearing. At **ADF** the loop is in circuit and the pointer seeks the station. BFO (beat frequency oscillator) and the AI/NORM tone selections are aural aids for identifying unmodulated or weak carriers; they do not affect the bearing or the receiver's power.

**DC-10.** Two ADF receivers, ADF 1 on DC bus 1 and ADF 2 on DC bus 3, tuned from two tuner units on the center console. Two styles of tuner unit are fitted by equipment option (analog or digital); both are described in [ADF control panels](#adf-panels). In ANT the bearing pointer stops where it was and its flag comes into view. Bearings are shown on the RMIs (the dual RMI's pointers through their VOR/ADF knobs) and, on the KSSU HSI, on two ADF pointers of its own.

**KC-10.** The two ADF receivers have no control head. They are tuned, switched between ADF and ANT, powered and tested from the FMS CDUs (the ADF CONTROL and NAV STATUS pages), and they accept the whole 190 to 1,750 kHz band. In ANT the RMI and EHSI bearing pointers move to the 9 o'clock position (270° relative). The ADF TEST drives the pointers to 45° left of the lubber line (315° relative) for 10 seconds.

**MD-10.** The ADFs are tuned by the FMS or manually on the MCDU, and their bearings appear on the NDs as the No. 1 (single) and No. 2 (double) bearing pointers. ADF bearings are never used for FMS radio position updating.

children.title: TACAN
children.summary: The KC-10A's two military TACAN sets: bearing and range from ground beacons and air-to-air.

blocks.content: TACAN is the military equivalent of a VOR/DME combined in one UHF channel: the ground beacon's rotating antenna pattern gives a bearing, and a DME-type interrogation gives range. TACAN-1 and TACAN-2 feed their respective TACAN RMI pointers and, when selected, the EHSIs, which show the TACAN slant range. Each pilot's EHSI uses its own set (pilot TACAN-1, copilot TACAN-2), and the autopilot's radio modes can fly a TACAN radial. The sets are controlled entirely from the FMS CDUs; there is no TACAN control head.

blocks.title: TACAN characteristics
rows: 390 NM (bearing and range are both lost beyond it)
TR, R, AA, BCN; MODE TYPE NORM or INVERSE
ON/OFF on the FMS POWER page; both ON at power-up

blocks.content: **Modes.** In **R** (receive) the set gives bearing, course deviation, TO/FROM and aural identification, but no range. In **TR** (transmit/receive) it also interrogates the beacon for slant range. The air-to-air modes measure bearing and range to a cooperating aircraft for rendezvous. A channel the set cannot tune is shown in amber on the CDU.

**Flags.** The EHSI's TCN source flags whenever the set delivers no bearing: beyond range, searching, warming up, failed, switched off or during the barred phase of its self-test. The FMS NAV STATUS page reports the set GO or NGO, which is a statement about the equipment, not about the signal.

**Self-test.** From the TACAN STATUS page on the ground: for about 7 seconds the TACAN RMI pointers point to 270°, the EHSI distance shows 0.0 and the EHSI bearing pointer and CDI are removed; then, to 15 seconds, the pointers read 180°, the course deviation bar centers with a TO indication at a 180° course, and the distance reads 0.0 NM in a ranging mode (TR). After the test the flags return unless a usable signal is present.
Do not run a TACAN self-test in flight with the autopilot coupled to a TACAN radial. If the ground-only inhibit fails, the test bearings can cause an abrupt maneuver.

children.title: Source selection and RAD/INS switching
children.summary: What each HSI and ADI is looking at, and how the crew choose it.

blocks.content: Each DC-10 pilot has a source switch beside their glareshield VHF NAV head, the **HSI switch** of the RAD/INS switching unit. With a long-range unit fitted it has three positions, **VOR**, **ILS** and **INS** (placarded **HSI NAV** on the HT-9100 fit); on the VOR-only fit it has two. The captain's switch selects for the captain's instruments and the first officer's for the first officer's. The HSI annunciates its source: the Biman HSI's window shows a RAD or ILS flag over a printed INS, with the seat's number beneath; the KSSU HSI's drum reads VOR TO, VOR FROM, ILS or INS.

blocks.title: HSI switch logic (DC-10)
rows: Long-range unit's vertical deviation, where it computes one
Not shown (glideslope pointer shows the unit's vertical deviation where it computes one)

blocks.content: Each seat's switch acts on its own instruments only. One pilot can fly an ILS while the other monitors the INS track: the captain at ILS and the first officer at INS is a legitimate configuration. The ADI shows a localizer and glideslope only when its own seat's switch is at ILS, so **both pilots must select ILS to see the approach on both ADIs**.

**Cross-track scale at INS.** At INS the deviation bar shows the long-range unit's cross-track distance in miles, not an angle. Its scale is the unit's: 3.75 NM a dot for the Carousel IV-A and the INS-61B; for the AINS-70 and ANS-70, 1 NM a dot at 250 kt ground speed rising to 3.75 NM a dot at 500 kt; for the HT-9100, a full scale that follows its flight phase (see [Flight management](flight-management)).

**The right-hand switch.** On the AINS-70, ANS-70 and HT-9100 fits it is **OFF / AUTO TUNE**: at AUTO TUNE the long-range unit may retune that side's VOR receiver (and therefore its DME) to the navaid it has selected for radio updating. The HT-9100 does not autotune; the switch moves, but nothing is retuned. On the CIV-A, INS-61B and VOR-only fits the switch is the DME selector, STBY / DME NORM / OVRD (see [DME](#dme)).

The KC-10 has no HSI source switch or right-hand switch on the glareshield. Each pilot's **display control panel** selects the EHSI's navigation source on its NAV knob: **FMS** (the pilot's FMS side), **VOR** (the VHF NAV receiver, which shows a localizer automatically when a localizer frequency is tuned) or **TCN** (the seat's own TACAN). With VOR selected, the tuned band decides: a VOR frequency shows the VOR, a localizer frequency the ILS. The ADIs read their own receivers straight. The BRG button steps the EHSI bearing pointer through OFF, FMS 1, FMS 2, VOR 1, VOR 2, TCN 1, TCN 2, ADF 1 and ADF 2. The DME on the KC-10 always interrogates.

blocks.alt: Diagram of the DC-10 RAD/INS switching unit: for each seat, the three-position HSI switch (VOR, ILS, INS) selecting between VOR receiver, ILS receiver and long-range unit for the HSI; arrows showing the ADI localizer and glideslope fed from the opposite ILS receiver on the pedestal arrangement, and from the same side on the HT-9100 fit; the CRS knob and pedestal course counter feeding the HSI course arrow.

children.title: RMI and HSI presentation
children.summary: Reading bearing, deviation and distance on the electromechanical instruments.

blocks.content: The **RMI** (radio magnetic indicator) has a compass card driven by a compass system and two bearing pointers. Each pointer shows the magnetic bearing to its station read at the head of the pointer, and the bearing from the station (the radial the aeroplane is on) at the tail. An RMI answers "where is the station?" at a glance, independent of any course the crew have set. Its OFF flag covers the lubber line when the heading input is unusable, and each pointer has its own flag for an invalid bearing.

The **HSI** (horizontal situation indicator) answers "where am I relative to the course I want?". A compass card rotates under a fixed aeroplane symbol and lubber line. The **course arrow** shows the selected course and carries the **course deviation bar**, which moves across a four-dot scale painted on the rotating center: because the bar and scale turn with the course, the display is a plan view of the aeroplane and the selected track. TO/FROM arrows ride on the bar. A **glideslope pointer** runs on a vertical four-dot scale on the right; it shows above center when the aeroplane is below the glidepath. The **heading bug** is set from the flight guidance panel's HDG knob.

blocks.content: **DC-10 instrument fits.** Which bearing and situation instruments are installed is part of the equipment configuration. The DME display option selects the RMI type: a dual RMI with a VOR/ADF knob for each pointer, a single RMI, or a KSSU RMI with DME windows. On the single and KSSU RMIs, pointer 1 follows VOR 1 and pointer 2 follows VOR 2. The bottom display option fits a KSSU HSI (which also carries two ADF pointers), a Biman HSI, or a glass MFD. The Biman HSI's source window has INS printed with RAD and ILS flags sliding over it and the seat's number beneath. The glass HSIs are described in [Flight instruments](flight-instruments#dc10-mfd).

**KC-10 instruments.** Each pilot has a TACAN RMI (both TACAN pointers on the pilot's own compass card), a VOR/ADF RMI (each pointer selectable between VOR and ADF on its NAVSELECT knob, on the other seat's compass system so that each pilot has one card from each compass), and the dual DME indicator. The EHSIs and EADIs are electronic displays driven through the display control panels (see [Flight instruments](flight-instruments#kc10-eadi-ehsi)).

sections.title: Inertial navigation: theory of operation
sections.summary: How inertial units sense motion, why alignment takes time, how errors grow and how they are updated.

blocks.content: The principles below apply to every inertial unit in the fleet. The individual units differ in their controls, their timings and their updating, which are described unit by unit in the sections that follow.

An inertial navigator is a dead-reckoning computer that measures its own motion instead of being told it. Three **accelerometers** on mutually perpendicular axes measure specific force: the acceleration of the aeroplane plus the reaction to gravity. If the computer knows exactly which way each accelerometer is pointing, it can subtract gravity, integrate the remaining acceleration once to get velocity over the earth, and integrate again to get distance traveled, hence latitude and longitude. Everything therefore depends on knowing the accelerometers' orientation, and that is the job of the **gyroscopes**, which hold or measure orientation relative to inertial space.

A **gimballed stable platform** mounts the accelerometers on a table isolated from the airframe by gimbals. Gyros on the table sense any rotation and drive torque motors that keep the table level and pointing in a known direction while the aeroplane maneuvers around it. Because the earth rotates and the aeroplane moves over a curved surface, the computer must also torque the platform continuously so that it stays level with the local horizontal as the aeroplane travels. Pitch and roll are read directly off the gimbal angles, which is why every inertial unit is also an attitude reference. The AINS-70's inertial sensor systems, the Carousel IV-A and the INS-61B are platform systems.

The **Carousel** refinement rotates the Delco platform continuously about its vertical axis. A gyro's residual bias is fixed relative to the gyro, so as the platform turns the bias sweeps through every horizontal direction once per revolution and its effect on the level axes averages toward zero. It is a mechanical way of cancelling the error source that most limits a platform's long-term accuracy.

A **strapdown** system dispenses with the gimbals: the sensors are fixed to the airframe and the computer keeps track of their orientation mathematically from the measured rotation rates, transforming each accelerometer sample into the local level frame in software. Ring-laser gyros, which have no spinning parts, made strapdown practical. The KC-10's LTN-101 inertial navigation units and the MD-10's ADIRUs belong to this later generation.

A level platform carried over a curved earth must tilt relative to inertial space at exactly the rate the aeroplane's velocity carries it around the earth, or it will no longer be level. The computer does this by feeding its computed velocity back as a torque command. That feedback loop has a remarkable property, first described by Max Schuler: it behaves like a pendulum whose length is the radius of the earth, and its natural period is 2π√(R/g), about **84.4 minutes**. A platform tuned to this period is insensitive to the aeroplane's own accelerations: when the aeroplane accelerates, the platform does not tilt, because its "pendulum" is pivoted at the center of the earth.

The price is that errors oscillate. A small tilt or velocity error does not grow without bound; it swings back and forth with the 84-minute Schuler period. A gyro drift, which keeps disturbing the loop, produces a position error that grows along a mean line with an 84-minute ripple on top, and a much slower 24-hour oscillation from the earth's rotation turns the direction of the error over the course of a day. This is why inertial errors are quoted as an average rate (nautical miles per hour) rather than as a fixed number.

The simulation applies this shape to every inertial unit in the fleet. Each unit drifts at its own mean rate, on its own bearing, so that no two units agree exactly. The error starts at zero rate on entry to NAV, is only about a tenth of the mean line ten minutes later, reaches the mean line about 42 minutes (half a Schuler period) in, and runs a little ahead of it at the hour. A unit in NAV cannot tell that the aeroplane is parked, so a platform left navigating at the gate drifts exactly as it would in flight.

blocks.alt: Graph of inertial position error against time over three hours: a straight dashed mean line at about 1 NM per hour, and the actual error curve starting flat at zero, crossing the mean line at about 42 minutes and every Schuler half period after, with an 84-minute ripple. Second curve for a platform that was manually updated at 90 minutes, dropping to near zero and growing again. Axes labeled.
blocks.title: Inertial error growth
blocks.caption: The Schuler loop bounds the oscillating part of the error; gyro drift sets the mean rate.

blocks.content: Before it can navigate, an inertial unit must find the local vertical and true north for itself, with the aeroplane stationary. It does this in two stages. **Leveling** comes first: the accelerometers sense the direction of gravity, and the platform (or, in a strapdown unit, the computed reference frame) is driven until the horizontal accelerometers read zero. Leveling is fast, and on the platform systems attitude data become valid once it is complete, long before navigation is possible.

**Gyrocompassing** finds north. The earth turns at 15.04° per hour about its polar axis. At latitude λ the component of that rotation about the local vertical is Ω sin λ and the horizontal component, pointing north, is Ω cos λ. A level platform aligned exactly north senses the horizontal component only about its north axis. If it is misaligned in azimuth, its east axis picks up part of the earth rate and the platform begins to tilt about that axis. The unit detects the tilt with its accelerometers and turns the platform until the tilting stops: the platform has then found north. Because the signal is the earth's rotation, a few degrees an hour, it is tiny, and the unit must average it over minutes to reject noise and vibration. That is the fundamental reason an alignment takes ten to fifteen minutes.

**Latitude matters in two ways.** First, the north-seeking signal is proportional to cos λ: at 60° it is half its equatorial value and near the poles it vanishes, so alignment takes longer or becomes less accurate the further from the equator, and above a unit's limit (76.5° for the AINS-70, with warnings of degraded alignment above 77° for the INS-61B and 80° for the Carousel) it cannot be done properly. Second, the ratio of the vertical to the horizontal components of earth rate is tan λ, so a gyrocompassing unit measures its own latitude. It compares that with the latitude the crew inserted and rejects an alignment whose inserted latitude disagrees. **Longitude has no physical signature**: the earth looks the same at every longitude, so a wrong longitude is accepted silently and carried as a constant position error for the whole flight. Insert the present position carefully, and cross-check the longitude in particular.

**The aeroplane must not move.** During alignment the unit cannot distinguish the aeroplane's motion from the earth's rotation or from a tilt of the platform. Taxiing or towing ruins the alignment; each unit detects it and either restarts or refuses to complete. Normal loading, servicing and light gusty winds are tolerated. An inertial unit cannot be aligned in flight; once navigation is lost in the air it can provide attitude only (ATT or ATT REF) until the next ground alignment.

blocks.title: Alignment timelines
INS alignment: Instant / Realistic
blocks.content: The EFB's Settings app has an **INS alignment** row under AIRCRAFT with two choices. **Realistic** (the default) runs every alignment for its real duration. **Instant** removes only the waiting: every inertial unit on every aircraft (the AINS-70's platforms, the Carousel IV-A, the INS-61B, the KC-10's INUs and the MD-10's ADIRUs) completes its timed phases at once, and the AINS-70's DATA SEARCH takes no time of its own. Everything else still applies: the mode selectors must be set, the present position must be inserted (and is still checked), the aeroplane must be stationary, and the INS-61B still needs its 26 V AC. The choice is saved with the aircraft. See [EFB](efb).

Inertial errors come from four main sources, and each grows differently. An **initial position error** (a wrong present position inserted) is carried unchanged for the whole flight. An **azimuth alignment error** makes the computed track slightly wrong, so its position error grows in proportion to distance flown. **Accelerometer bias** produces a tilt that the Schuler loop bounds and oscillates. **Gyro drift** keeps disturbing the loop and produces an error that grows steadily with time: it dominates on long flights and is the figure usually quoted.

A navigation-grade unit of the DC-10 era drifts about 1 NM per hour. Certification required a 95 % probability of staying within 2 NM per hour, and some units' monitoring logic deliberately assumes that pessimistic figure. In the simulation each platform has its own mean drift rate of roughly 1 NM per hour and its own direction, so the three units of an installation slowly disagree. That disagreement is useful: with three independent units, the one that has drifted furthest from the other two is the suspect.

Inertial error does not depend on what the aeroplane does, only on how long it has been navigating. Time spent in NAV on the ground before take-off counts exactly as flight time does, which is one reason to align close to departure on a long ground delay, and one reason the post-flight comparison of the final position against the gate coordinates is a meaningful health check of a unit.
Because an inertial position degrades with time and a radio fix does not, the two are combined. The methods used in the fleet are:

items: **Manual update.** The crew freeze the displayed position as the aeroplane passes over a known point (a navaid or a visual fix), then insert the point's coordinates. The unit applies the difference as a correction. The correction is always measured at the moment of the freeze, not at the moment of insertion, so the time taken to type it does not matter.

**DME updating.** A DME range places the aeroplane on a circle around the station. Two ranges from well-separated stations intersect at two points, one of which the unit's own position resolves; the geometry is best when the stations are 30° to 150° apart as seen from the aeroplane. A single range corrects only the component of position along the line to the station, which is why some units restrict single-station updating to stations off to one side of track.
**VOR/DME updating.** A radial and a range from one station fix the position completely (rho-theta), at the cost of the VOR's angular error growing with distance.

**Triple mixing.** With three independent platforms, the Carousel IV-A can steer each toward the median latitude and median longitude of the three. A median rejects a single unit that has gone badly wrong instead of averaging it in.

**Filtering.** The radio data are noisy and occasionally wrong (a station tuned in error, a reflection, a slant range close in). The update logic therefore blends a fix in gradually, tests it for reasonableness against the inertial position before accepting it, and rejects fixes that disagree by more than the expected error. The INS-61B's DME update is a Kalman filter that weighs each range against an estimate of its own uncertainty.

blocks.content: Most units keep two positions: the **pure inertial** position from the platform alone, and the **corrected** position that includes the updates. Keeping them separate allows a bad update to be removed, lets the crew see how far the platform has drifted, and gives the reasonableness tests an unbiased reference.

The shortest path between two points on a sphere is the arc of a **great circle**. Except along a meridian or the equator, a great circle's track is not constant: it changes continuously along the leg, by many degrees on a long oceanic leg. An inertial navigator flies great circles by computing, at every instant, the **desired track** (the great-circle track at the point abeam the aeroplane), the **cross-track distance** (the aeroplane's perpendicular distance from the great circle, left or right) and the **track angle error** (the difference between actual and desired track). Ground speed, drift angle and wind follow from the same solution.

The steering signal to the flight director and autopilot is a bank command built from cross-track distance and track angle error: far off track the unit commands a cut toward the leg, limited in angle so that it does not turn across it, and close in it commands a smooth capture. The INS-61B's law, for example, limits bank to 30° and roll rate to 2° per second, cuts toward the leg at 10° per nautical mile of cross-track up to a 45° intercept (90° while capturing a new leg).

At the end of a leg the unit must turn onto the next one. Flying to the waypoint and then turning would overshoot the new leg, so units **anticipate** the turn, starting it early by a distance that grows with ground speed and with the size of the track change. An **ALERT** precedes each waypoint by a set time (two minutes on the Carousel IV-A, about three minutes on the INS-61B, 15 seconds on the AINS-70's HSI alert). In AUTO the unit switches legs itself; in MANUAL it flies on along the old leg's great circle past the waypoint, flashing the alert, until the crew insert the next leg.

sections.title: AINS-70 area navigation system
sections.summary: The Litton AINS-70: three inertial sensor systems and two radio-updating navigation computers.

blocks.content: The AINS-70 is the DC-10's default long-range fit. It combines inertial and radio navigation in one system: over land it fixes position continuously from VOR/DME stations it selects and tunes itself, and over water it navigates on its platforms alone. Its tape data base and route assembly make it a forerunner of the flight management system rather than a plain INS. The crew interface follows the DC-10 Area Navigation Flight Crew Handbook (MDC-J4400-1).

The AINS-70 is not three separate navigators but one area navigation system with redundant parts. Three **inertial sensor systems** (ISS) supply inertial position, velocity, attitude and heading. Two **navigation computer units** (NCU) each blend all available inertial, radio, air data and compass inputs into a single best position, autoselect and tune VOR/DME stations, hold the data base and the flight plan, and compute steering. Two **control display units** (CDU) on the pedestal give the crew access to the computers; two **flight data storage units** (FDSU), one for each computer, hold the tape data base; one **inertial sensor display unit** (ISDU) reads and initializes the platforms; and three **mode selector units** (MSU) on the overhead switch the platforms. Each ISS has its own **battery unit**.

blocks.title: AINS-70 components
rows: Inertial platform: position, velocity, attitude, heading. Each on its own circuit (ISS 1 on AC generator bus 1, ISS 2 and 3 on the right emergency 28 V AC system), with its own cooling fan and battery unit
Blends sensors, selects and tunes navaids, holds data base and flight plan, computes steering. NCU 1 on the L EMER AC bus, NCU 2 on the R EMER AC bus
Crew interface, one per NCU, on the pedestal
Tape cartridge data base for its NCU: navaids, airways, terminal procedures, company routes. Each system has its own guarded IPL button
Reads any one ISS and initializes its position by trim
OFF / NAV / ATT for each ISS, with four annunciators

blocks.content: **Master and slave.** With both NCUs healthy and their **crosstalk** link working, NCU 1 is master: it selects the navaids and crosstalks its selections to NCU 2, and the two computers keep their data bases and flight plans in step entry by entry, so an entry made on either CDU reaches both. If crosstalk fails but the master is valid, NCU 2 selects independently, and every entry must then be made on both CDUs. If one NCU fails, the other takes over the selection and tuning of both VOR/DME receivers; the failed side's CDU shows a steady FAULT and that pilot's HSI loses its area navigation data. A compass or air data failure on one side is covered by the opposite side's input while crosstalk works.

**Comparators.** The two NCUs continuously compare their outputs and annunciate a disagreement: cross-track 1.0 NM, vertical deviation 325 ft, distance 1.0 NM, latitude or longitude 1.0 minute (XCHEK); magnetic heading 10° and true heading 2° (COMP). The three platforms' positions are compared against a limit of (2 + 4T) NM, where T is the average time in hours since alignment, so a platform drifting well beyond its class is identified.

blocks.alt: Block diagram of the AINS-70: three ISS boxes with their MSUs and battery units, the ISDU switching between them; two NCUs linked by crosstalk, each with its CDU and FDSU; VOR/DME receivers 1 and 2 with the AUTO TUNE path from the NCUs; compass and CADC inputs; outputs to each pilot's HSI (cross-track, vertical deviation, ALERT) and to the flight guidance system. Bus supplies annotated.
blocks.title: AINS-70 block diagram

blocks.content: Each ISS has a mode selector on the overhead with three positions and four lenses. There is no separate ALIGN position: turning the selector from OFF to NAV starts the alignment, and the platform enters navigation by itself when the alignment is complete. The ISS needs 115 V AC to start. Once running, its battery carries it through a loss of aircraft power, but it never starts on the battery.
