blocks.content: The battery is good for about 30 minutes when fully charged (5 minutes is the certified minimum). It charges only while its ISS runs on aircraft power, and each minute it carries the unit takes about ten minutes on aircraft power to put back. The MSU lamps are on the battery direct bus, so they can annunciate with the main battery switch off.

blocks.alt: DC-10 overhead, AINS-70 fit: the three ISS mode selector units side by side (No. 1 left, No. 3 center, No. 2 right), each selector at NAV, with the four lenses ALIGN MODE, BAT OPER, BAT WARN, ISS WARN; ALIGN MODE lit on all three during alignment. Placards legible.
blocks.title: AINS-70 mode selector units

blocks.content: The ISDU is a single readout shared by the three platforms. It shows what one selected ISS believes, and it is the crew's backup way of giving a platform its present position. The readouts work in flight, but trimming is inhibited. Leave SYS SEL at OFF when not reading it.

blocks.title: ISDU
rows: Selects the ISS to read or set (the order matches the MSUs on the overhead). OFF blanks the display
Selected ISS present position: latitude left, longitude right
Ground speed (kt) left, true track right; true heading on the ground
Latitude or longitude alone, ready to be trimmed
F M S (S/W) – OFF – S M F (N/E)
Spring-loaded to OFF. Slews the displayed coordinate south/west or north/east at slow, medium or fast rate
All digits show 8 (the right readout's leading half-digit shows 1)
Blank when no reliable data are available or the unit has failed. Brightness is controlled by a photocell

blocks.content: **Initializing with the ISDU.** Select the ISS on SYS SEL, select LONG and trim to the ramp longitude, then select LAT and trim the latitude, then check POS. The latitude must be slewed for every ISS being initialized, even if the correct value is already displayed, because the slew is the insertion. Check the trimmed latitude very carefully: a small latitude error fails the alignment, and the system cannot detect a longitude error at all.

blocks.alt: AINS-70 ISDU close-up: SYS SEL knob at 1, DISP SEL at POS, TRIM knob at OFF, readouts showing N 33°55.9 and W 118°25.8, PRESS TO TEST on the brightness knob. Labels legible.
blocks.title: ISDU

blocks.content: Turning the MSUs to NAV starts **coarse alignment**: the gyros spin up and the platforms level while they wait for a present position. **Fine alignment** begins the moment the present position is inserted, normally on the CDU during route definition (or by ISDU trim), and takes **13 minutes**. Attitude outputs become valid about five minutes after the MSU is turned on; heading and navigation only when the alignment completes. Alignment is possible only between 76.5° N and 76.5° S, with the aeroplane stationary.

items: If no position is inserted within 3 minutes of selecting NAV, ISS WARN blinks until one is.

About two minutes into fine alignment the platform has found its own latitude well enough to judge the inserted one. An inserted latitude in error fails the alignment (malfunction 13, UPDATE EXCESSIVE): ISS WARN blinks. Re-insert the correct position. A second attempt with a gross latitude error locks up the ISS and it needs maintenance.
Moving the aeroplane while ALIGN MODE is lit fails the alignment (malfunction 14, VELOCITY EXCESSIVE); doing it again gives malfunction 34. Only switching that MSU to OFF clears it; then realign.
An overheated platform (its cooling fan failed) cuts out and loses its alignment. It cannot be realigned in flight.

blocks.content: The LRU STATUS page shows each platform's alignment progress as a two-digit code with an action digit: 90 briefly at turn-on, then 1-80 while it waits for the crew to insert the position, then 70, 60, 40, 10 through fine alignment, and 02 when complete. A dash beside a code is normal.

Each NCU continuously decides which inputs it can trust and annunciates a **navigation mode** on the CDU. The mode tells the crew what the position is based on and therefore what it is good for. There are six:

blocks.title: AINS-70 navigation modes
rows: At least one VOR/DME or DME, an ISS in NAV, air data
Normal mode over land. Meets RNAV accuracy (AC 90-45) and sole-means requirements
As R/I, but radio data insufficient for RNAV accuracy (one ambiguity-qualified DME, or a VOR only)
Inertial navigation with partial radio updating
An ISS in NAV; nothing else required
Basic mode over water with no VOR/DME
VOR/DME or two DMEs, compass, air data; no ISS in NAV
Reversionary mode when no platform is navigating. Meets RNAV accuracy
One ambiguity-qualified DME, or a VOR only if recently in R; compass, air data
Last resort: true airspeed along heading plus the last measured wind

blocks.content: When several modes qualify at once, the NCU uses the best: R/I is retained as long as its estimated accuracy is adequate for RNAV; below that it down-modes to SR/I, and with no usable radio to I. R and SR are used only when no platform is navigating. Only R/I and R are gated on accuracy: the NCU keeps an **accuracy estimate** that improves toward a floor while radio fixes are accepted and grows when they are not (the estimate assumes an inertial drift of 2 NM per hour, less when more than one ISS is navigating, and 25 NM per hour in dead reckoning). R/I or R is annunciated only while the estimate is within 1.5 NM above 300 kt TAS, or 0.6 NM below.

**Downmode alert.** A drop of the annunciated mode onto SR/I, SR, I or D/R makes the mode blink on PROGRESS and lights the CDU's ALERT light, 8 seconds after the downmode below 300 kt TAS or 60 seconds above it. Line key 6 on PROGRESS acknowledges it; a further downmode alerts again; an up-mode puts the alert out at once without a press. The climb through the modes during an alignment and the first mode after power-up do not alert.

**Polar navigation.** Above 85° latitude the NCUs change their navigation reference: the blended position converges on the new reference at 0.5 % of the difference per second (about eight minutes), and heading, ground speed and track switch at once to the nearest good ISS, re-determined every 200 milliseconds. THDG and COMP faults are to be expected within about 50 NM of the pole. Manual updates and deleting an ISS should be avoided in the polar region. (The polar reference change is not simulated; see [Simulation notes](#simulation-notes).)

The NCUs fix position from the two VOR/DME receivers. The navaids they can use are those **in core**: the stations the FDSU loaded along the assembled route during the data search. With no route assembled, there is nothing in core to fix on and the system navigates in I (or D/R). Radio updating therefore starts only once a route has been assembled.

**Autoselection.** Every 5 to 10 seconds the master NCU ranks the in-range navaids in core: pilot-selected stations first, then VOR/DMEs, DME-only stations and VOR-only stations, each by range. From the five best it chooses a pair, preferring two DMEs whose bearings from the aeroplane are 30° to 150° apart (the best geometry for a DME/DME fix), then a VOR/DME, then DME-only, then the shortest range. The best station goes to side 1 and the second to side 2 unless a receiver failure dictates otherwise. Below 300 kt TAS with a terminal navaid in range the NCU uses terminal-area logic. A station already tuned is kept on its side when possible, so that both receivers are not retuned at once.

**AUTO TUNE.** With a seat's right-hand glareshield switch at AUTO TUNE, the NCU retunes that side's VOR/DME receiver to its selection. With the switch at OFF the NCU displays the station it wants on the PROGRESS page with TUNE, and the ALERT light blinks to ask the crew to tune it by hand (line key 5 with an empty scratchpad suppresses the light). A failed station goes on a **failed navaid list** and is not reselected until the crew select it, a route is assembled, or the aeroplane first slows below 300 kt TAS.

blocks.title: Radio acceptance criteria (each fix is tested before use)
rows: Each navaid has a programmed range of 40, 70, 130 or 250 NM; beyond it the station is not used
Two DMEs are ambiguous within 5 NM of the baseline between them, or when their bearings are within 10°
A single DME is not used while the aeroplane passes close to the station
A DME is inhibited when its slant range is less than (ground speed in kt)² ÷ 28,800 NM, where the range is changing too fast near the station
A VOR is not used inside a 90° cone above the station
A fix is rejected if it differs from the computed position by more than a limit that grows with time since the last update (at most 15.6 NM for a DME, 60° for a VOR)
A VOR-only update is allowed only within a range that grows from 20 NM at 33, 40 or 57 NM per hour for three, two or one ISS

blocks.content: Accepted fixes are blended into the position gradually, never snapped, so that the position does not jump every second and the comparators do not trip on a healthy system. With a platform navigating, the blended position cannot worsen faster than the platforms drift.

Each CDU has a monochrome CRT of 13 lines of 16 characters: six pairs of a small label line over a large data line, and a scratchpad line beneath them. There is no title line: a page names itself in its first label line. Six **line keys** on the left select the line pair beside them. Three **lever switches** on the right move between pages (upper), slew a page line by line (lower) and, on the present-position page, trim latitude (middle) and longitude (lower). An entry is typed into the scratchpad and inserted by pressing the line key where it belongs. **There is no ENTER key.**

blocks.title: AINS-70 CDU keys and lights
rows: Insert the scratchpad at that line, or select the item beside it
Brings new pages into view laterally (PROGRESS ↔ FLIGHT PLAN ↔ PERFORMANCE)
Lower: slews a page vertically line by line. On the present-position page, middle trims LAT and lower trims LONG
PAGE INDEX: PERFORMANCE DATA, LRU STATUS, ROUTE DEFINITION
Clears the scratchpad or a standing message on this CDU
Scratchpad entry. N, S, E, W are the hemisphere keys; L and R the offset sides
Steady: NCU or CDU failure, system inoperative. Blinking: an LRU or input failure
Blinks for CHECK NEXT, a mode downgrade, a BAROSET request or a manual tuning request. Press PROG to see the message

blocks.title: Principal pages
rows: FROM waypoint, actual time over and altitude; TO waypoint, ETA and altitude; the next leg's course and distance (or BAROSET); NEXT waypoint; the two VOR/DMEs in use (A autoselected, C pilot-selected, TUNE when one must be tuned by hand); offset, GMT and the navigation MODE. Line 6 shows faults and alerts to acknowledge

One line pair per waypoint: the VIA (airway or DIR), the ident and the altitude constraint. Up to 59 waypoints, six visible at a time, including up to 15 pilot-defined (LAT/LONG or place/bearing/distance). [ENTER] marks the end of the plan; STORAGE LIMIT AFTER marks the last waypoint whose data are in core
Wind, heading, track, drift, cross-track, ground speed, distance, present position (with any manual update made on it), DIST TO and MODE
Reached from a flight plan waypoint: SID, available airways from it, DEFINE HOLD at it, SELECT STAR, company route after it, DEFINE NEW ROUTE BY FROM VIA TO, and the waypoint's coordinates
Route assembly from the tape (see below)
ISS alignment and action codes, DELETE or RESTORE ISS, the fault list and the platforms' malfunction codes

blocks.alt: AINS-70 CDU on the DC-10 pedestal showing the PROGRESS page: FROM SXC with time and FL350, TO HNDSN with ETA, next leg course and distance, VOR/DME line reading A SXC / A LAX, MODE R/I on line 6. Line keys left, three lever switches and the amber FAULT and white ALERT lights right, keyboard below with PROG, FLT PLN, IDX, DIR, CLR. Text legible.
blocks.title: AINS-70 CDU, PROGRESS page

blocks.content: The FDSU tape holds the airline's data base: navaids, airways, terminal procedures and **company routes**. Before flight the crew **assemble** a route: the NCUs read the route's waypoints and a swath of data along it (navaids within 200 NM, airways and waypoints within 150 NM, and the departure, destination and alternate terminal data) into their working memory, **core**. In the simulation the tape's data are the simulator's current navigation data cycle; TAPE IDENT and EFFECTIVE PERIOD show its AIRAC identity and validity.

items: IDX, then line key 6 (ROUTE DEFINITION). CONFIRM blinks; press line key 6 again. (On the ground only: with either air data TAS above 130 kt the entry gives ERROR, so that a ground assembly cannot dump the data base in flight.)
DATA SEARCH shows for about 40 seconds while the computers prepare.

ROUTE DEFINITION shows TAPE IDENT and EFFECTIVE PERIOD. Enter GMT (ENTER TIME) if required. Then either type a company route number at ENTER CO ROUTE, or define the route by FROM-VIA-TO (airports, LAT/LONG or gateways).
A second route can be added, or postponed, on the next page.
After about 10 seconds the box shows what was requested. A name the tape does not hold shows NOT STORED, and the box will not continue until it is corrected.

About 15 seconds later it asks for the aircraft's position. With no ramp data, the airport reference point is offered: adjust it to the aircraft's actual position by typing over it or trimming with the middle (LAT) and lower (LONG) levers, then press line keys 4 and 6 to insert LAT and LONG. **This starts the 13-minute fine alignment of every waiting ISS** and seeds both NCUs.
The data search proper runs for a few minutes; other duties can be done meanwhile. SEARCH COMPLETE ends it, and the flight plan is in core.

blocks.content: **EFB route imports.** A flight plan sent from the EFB (for example from SimBrief) is never pushed straight into the AINS-70. It is **filed on the tape as a company route** under a five-digit number between 00001 and 00999, and the crew assemble it the normal way by typing that number at ENTER CO ROUTE. A long plan is filed as several numbered company routes, to be joined in flight. The tape directory holds nine imported routes; filing another drops the oldest. See [EFB](efb).

**Standing messages.** DEFINE ROUTE, DATA SEARCH, SEARCH COMPLETE, STORAGE LIMIT, INITIATE SEARCH, DATA SEARCH FAIL and NO DATA FOUND blink in the scratchpad on every page; CLR clears one on its own CDU, and DATA SEARCH clears itself. When the route runs beyond the data in core, STORAGE LIMIT AFTER marks the last covered waypoint; press its line key (or respond to INITIATE SEARCH within 15 minutes) to load the next swath. In flight a route is changed through REVISE (company route after a waypoint, or DEFINE NEW ROUTE BY FROM VIA TO).

blocks.title: Flight plan entries
rows: Inserts the waypoint at that line. Place/bearing/distance up to 400 NM; bearings magnetic
Strings the airway from that waypoint to the fix
Intermediate point on the vertical profile

blocks.title: DIRECT TO
rows: Line key opposite a flight plan waypoint
Waypoint ident or LAT/LONG, inserted at line 2
Direct to a waypoint in or out of the plan
To a point 15.5 NM along magnetic track 270 from the insertion point (up to 400 NM)

blocks.content: A direct-to synthesizes a turn point (T-P) at the current switching point carrying the insertion altitude, so the new leg starts where the aeroplane actually turns. On PROGRESS, line key 6 accepts a parallel **offset** (L21, R21; 0 deletes it) and a GMT (/HHMM). Line key 3 accepts a BAROSET (four digits, millibars or inches) when the box requests one.

**Navaid selection on PROGRESS.** Line key 5 takes a navaid ident: SXC selects it on the NAV-1 side, /SXC on the NAV-2 side, -SXC deletes it from autoselection (a later pilot selection restores it). A selected station beyond its programmed range appears momentarily and disappears, and autoselection resumes.

**Manual position update (PERFORMANCE page).** As the aeroplane passes over a known point, press line key 5 with the scratchpad empty to freeze the position. Type the point's ident or LAT/LONG and press line key 5: the NCU's position moves by the difference between the known point and the frozen position. Pressing line key 5 again with an empty scratchpad unfreezes without updating, and a - entered at line 5 reverts the position to its pre-update value carried forward. Place/bearing/distance is not accepted, and an update is refused in a radio mode. Line key 6 on PERFORMANCE with an ident or LAT/LONG shows the distance and track to that point (DIST TO) for ten seconds.

Whenever the FAULT or ALERT light blinks, select PROGRESS. Line pair 6 shows up to two items to acknowledge, in priority order, with the first word of each on the label line and the second on the data line (for example CHECK FAULT MODE over NEXT HDG2 R/I). Line key 6 with an empty scratchpad acknowledges them and resets the lights.

blocks.title: CDU alerts
rows: Turn of more than 90° to capture the next leg; next leg shorter than 1 NM, or longer than 700 NM in an inertial mode or 350 NM in a radio mode; a possible discontinuity; or no next waypoint
Check the flight plan; acknowledge with line key 6
Downmode to SR/I, SR, I or D/R
Check the radio updating; acknowledge with line key 6
A barometric setting is required for the vertical profile
Enter it at PROGRESS line key 3
AUTO TUNE at OFF and the NCU wants a station tuned
Tune the station shown, or press line key 5 to suppress the light
An LRU or input has failed (for example ISS, ISC or XTALK; the priority order of the 33 possible items is fixed)
Read the fault on line 6 and LRU STATUS
NCU or CDU failure: that system is inoperative

blocks.content: **ISS faults and deletion.** A failed platform annunciates on FAULT and its MSU's ISS WARN is steady. On LRU STATUS a platform can be removed from the NCUs' blend with DELETE ISS and put back with RESTORE ISS. The ISS action codes beside the alignment codes read: 1 insert present position; 2 switch the MSU to OFF and realign; 3 switch to ATT; 4 replace the unit; 5 remove the attitude slew test connector.

**Initial program load (IPL).** Each system's guarded IPL button reloads its NCU's program from its FDSU tape. It is normally needed only when a new tape is installed, for troubleshooting, or to clear a locked-up NCU; it is never started from the CDU. The sequence is a computer test of about 1.5 minutes, a system self-test of about 1.3 minutes, an optional manual display test (each key and lever is exercised, and two VERIFICATION OF SIGNALS TO HSI pages drive the NCU's own HSI and flight director to test indications), the crosstalk check, a data search of about two minutes, and the PAGE INDEX. All route data are lost in an IPL unless the opposite system holds a route, which is then crosstalked over while both CDUs freeze for about 30 seconds. Core otherwise survives a power interruption, so a cold aeroplane needs no IPL; GMT is lost and must be re-entered.

With a pilot's HSI switch at INS, the NCU on that side drives the HSI: the deviation bar shows cross-track distance at 1 NM a dot at 250 kt ground speed, rising to 3.75 NM a dot at 500 kt, and the glideslope pointer shows deviation from the vertical profile toward the TO waypoint's altitude constraint (a TO waypoint with no altitude flags it). Turn anticipation is a function of ground speed and track change, never more than 10 NM. Fifteen seconds before each leg switch the TO waypoint blinks on the CDU and the HSI ALERT is commanded on until the switch.
The flight guidance system couples to the AINS-70 through the RAD/INS pushbutton with the HSI switch at INS: see [Automatic flight](automatic-flight). The CDU shows angles in the magnetic reference.

sections.title: ANS-70 area navigation
sections.summary: The early DC-10-10s' radio area navigation computer, single or dual.

blocks.content: The Collins ANS-70 is offered on the DC-10-10 Early, DC-10-10 Late and DC-10-10F Late as a single (ANS-70S) or dual (ANS-70D) installation. It is an area navigation computer **without an inertial platform of its own**: it navigates by statistically combining DME and VOR fixes with magnetic heading and air data, autotunes its VOR/DME receivers according to range and geometry, and dead-reckons on true airspeed, heading and its last measured wind when out of radio coverage.

No ANS-70 operating manual exists in the sources available for this simulation. Its architecture, as described in the public record of the ANS-70A (a navigation computer, a tape data storage unit, a tuning adapter and a CDU), is the AINS-70's without the inertial sensors, so the simulation builds the ANS-70 as the **AINS-70's crew interface running on navigation computers that have no platform**. Everything in [AINS-70](#ains-70) about the CDU, route definition, the tape data base, the flight plan, direct-to, holds, the manual update, navaid selection and AUTO TUNE applies, with these differences:

blocks.title: ANS-70 compared with the AINS-70
rows: One (NCU 1 and CDU 1, on the L EMER AC bus); it feeds both pilots' HSIs
Two, one on each emergency AC bus
R, SR and D/R only (no inertial modes)
Grows at 25 NM per hour (dead reckoning)

blocks.content: The three mode selectors on the overhead (OFF / NAV / ATT, with the AINS-70's four lamps) are still fitted and still switch three inertial platforms, but on this fit those platforms serve only the attitude and heading of the glass instrument options; the ANS-70 does not use them for navigation. They take their alignment position automatically. Radio updating, as on the AINS-70, waits for an assembled route, so before route assembly and out of coverage the computers dead-reckon: the position holds while the wind holds and walks off when the wind changes.

sections.title: Carousel IV-A inertial navigation system
sections.summary: The Delco Carousel IV-A: three independent carouselling inertial navigators with DME updating and triple mixing.

blocks.content: The Carousel IV-A (CIV-A) is the classic airline INS of the 1970s: a self-contained inertial navigator with nine coordinate waypoints, nine DME station slots and no data base. Its platform rotates continuously in azimuth to average out gyro bias (see [Accelerometers, gyroscopes and platforms](#inertial-sensors)). The procedures follow the Delco Carousel IV-A operations manual.

Three complete inertial navigation systems are installed. Each consists of a **navigation unit** (the platform and its computer) and a **battery unit** in the electronics bay, a **mode selector unit** (MSU) on the overhead and a **control/display unit** (C/DU) on the pedestal. Each box operates independently and depends only on its own instruments for position and velocity. There is no master and no shared solution, and a failure in one box does not stop the others navigating.

Three things cross between the boxes: the positions used for **triple mixing**, keyboard entries made with **REMOTE** lit, and **DME data**. The DC-10 has two DME interrogators, so box 1 uses DME 1 and box 2 uses DME 2, and box 3, which has no receiver of its own, updates on the data the other two share over the link. The HOLD function is never transmitted between boxes. The tape loaded in the simulated boxes is CIV-A-21, which displays an Accuracy Index.

**Power.** A box can be turned on only with both its primary power (its INS circuit) and its battery unit available; once running it operates on either. The standard battery carries a box for about 15 minutes. Below about 19 V the box shuts itself down, and it does so only while it is running on the battery: a flat battery with primary power present does not stop a running box. Each navigation unit is cooled by a blower and has heaters for a fast warm-up. An overtemperature shuts the box down in STBY or ALIGN, but only warns in NAV or ATT. Loss of cooling air can damage the unit.

blocks.title: CIV-A mode selector unit
rows: Power on, fast warm-up, gyros run up, platform caged to the airframe (computer mode 9). Also the position a box downmodes to: it keeps its attitude outputs if the platform was already level, but loses its azimuth alignment
Leveling and gyrocompassing (modes 8 to 0). NAV may be selected from mode 5
Navigation. Selected from OFF or STBY, the box aligns first and enters NAV by itself at mode 5
Attitude only. The computer and C/DU shut down, the alignment is lost, and NAV cannot be re-entered without a ground realignment
The desired alignment status has been reached (mode 5). Stays lit until NAV is selected. With NAV already selected the box enters navigation at mode 5 and the light does not come on
The box has shut down automatically because of low battery voltage

blocks.content: The STS display (data selector at DSRTK/STS) shows what the box is actually doing, which is not necessarily what the selector says: moved straight from STBY to NAV, the first STS digit stays 0 until the alignment is complete and then becomes 1.

The C/DU's displays are lamp arrays: a left data display (five digits with a hemisphere, degree sign and decimal point), a right data display (six digits) and a two-digit FROM-TO display. Data are loaded in two stages: keys put the data into the display, the crew verify it, and INSERT puts it into the computer. CLEAR cancels a load in progress and returns the display to the computer.

blocks.title: CIV-A C/DU controls
rows: Selects what the two data displays show (table below). POS, WAY PT and DSRTK/STS also accept data
Selects the waypoint, or DME station slot, displayed or loaded at WAY PT
AUTO: legs switch automatically at each waypoint. MAN: the crew insert each new leg

Data entry. N on 2, S on 8, W on 4, E on 6 (a compass rose around 5); FRQ on 3, L/L on 7, DME on 9. Keys 7+9 together, or 7 then 9 within one second, open the DME position display; 3+9 (or 3 then 9) the DME altitude and frequency display
Inserts the displayed data. Lit while a load is in progress, and lit at ALIGN until the present position is in
Cancels the load being typed. During a present-position entry, a second press cancels a half already inserted; waypoint and DME halves are stored by their own INSERT
Freezes the POS display for a position update. At WAY PT, shows the pure inertial position
Waypoint, DME station and position-update entries made on this C/DU are sent to every other box whose REMOTE is lit
Starts a leg change: the next two keys are FROM and TO, then INSERT. With a DME display up, the next key designates the DME station in use
At DSRTK/STS: press and release to walk the action and malfunction codes. Elsewhere: lamp test (all 8s, FROM-TO 8 8, every lamp)
Brightness of the displays and lit keys
The box is running on its battery; also lit for 12.8 seconds during the mode 8 battery test, which is normal

blocks.title: Data selector positions
rows: Track angle error, L or R
Desired track (the tape identifier until the present position is loaded)

blocks.content: Below 75 kt the box shows heading in place of track, zero drift angle, and desired track minus heading in place of track angle error, because there is no meaningful ground track at low speed. Below 10 kt TIME reads 999.9. With true airspeed unusable or below about 190 kt, both wind displays read zero.

blocks.title: Status word (DSRTK/STS, right display)
rows: 1 in NAV; 0 in ALIGN or STBY
Action or malfunction code; blank when none
Computer mode number in ALIGN; Accuracy Index in NAV
Desired performance index (PI): 5 in ALIGN and not changeable; the selected PI in NAV

blocks.alt: Delco Carousel IV-A control/display unit on the DC-10 pedestal with its mode selector unit: C/DU data selector at POS, left display N 33°56.1, right display W 118°24.3, FROM-TO 1 2, waypoint selector at 1, AUTO/MAN at AUTO, keyboard with N, S, E, W, L/L, FRQ, DME legends, lit keys HOLD, REMOTE, INSERT, WY PT CHG, CLEAR, lamps ALERT, BAT, WARN, TEST switch and DIM knob. MSU selector at NAV with READY NAV and BAT lamps. Legends legible.
blocks.title: Carousel IV-A C/DU and MSU

blocks.content: The whole alignment is a countdown of **computer mode numbers**, shown in the fifth digit of the status word. Every alignment time the box has falls out of it:

blocks.title: Carousel IV-A computer modes
rows: STBY: fast warm-up, gyros spin up, platform caged
Coarse leveling to the local horizontal; 12.8-second battery test (C/DU BAT lit). Attitude becomes valid
Azimuth alignment by gyrocompassing. Waits for the present position to be inserted
Gyrocompassing continues; the loaded latitude is compared with the computed one
READY NAV: alignment adequate. NAV may be selected
About 3.4 minutes each; 0 is reached 17 minutes after 5

blocks.content: From room temperature the box takes about **15 minutes from OFF to NAV**; a realignment that skips the warm-up (for example during a transit stop, with the box left in STBY) takes about **10 minutes**. Turning the box OFF restarts the warm-up. Above 80° latitude the alignment is degraded and takes longer. With NAV selected directly the box still aligns, and enters NAV at mode 5 by itself.

items: A present position more than 76 NM from the position the box stored at shutdown sets malfunction 41 and lights WARN. Check and reinsert the position; clear the code with TEST at DSRTK/STS.

Towing or taxiing during the alignment sets malfunction 57 and abandons the alignment, including the loaded position. The box restarts the alignment by itself and waits again for the present position: reinsert it.
Selecting ATT destroys the alignment.
Moving the selector from NAV back to ALIGN keeps the box aligned and asks for no new position. Any new alignment from STBY or OFF asks for a new present position.

blocks.content: The box holds **nine waypoints** by number and has no data base: every waypoint is a latitude and longitude typed in by the crew (or loaded from an EFB route import, which fills waypoints 1 onward in every box that is aligning or navigating, puts each on leg 1 2, and cuts a long route into cards of nine waypoints). Waypoints, DME stations and the leg survive switching a box off. Waypoint 0 is reserved: it receives the ramp position, and the present position whenever a leg is started from 0. An unloaded waypoint reads 0000.0 N 00000.0 E.

**Legs.** The box flies the great circle from the FROM waypoint to the TO waypoint, shown in the FROM-TO display; at ALIGN it starts at 1 2. In AUTO it switches legs at each waypoint in the sequence 1 2, 2 3 … 9 1, and each new leg must be flown for 25.6 seconds before another automatic switch. To change the leg, press WY PT CHG, then the FROM and TO numbers (they appear in the FROM-TO display as typed), and INSERT. Before inserting, the new leg's distance and time can be read at DIS/TIME. A leg from 0 to any waypoint flies **direct** from present position.

**ALERT lamp.** The amber ALERT lights two minutes before the TO waypoint (not below 250 kt ground speed). In AUTO it goes out when the leg switches. In MAN it flashes once the waypoint is passed, while the box flies on along the old leg, until the crew insert a new leg; it also flashes in AUTO on a leg shorter than 25.6 seconds.

**Steering.** With the HSI switch at INS the deviation bar shows cross-track at 3.75 NM a dot. The box sends track angle error, cross-track and a steering signal to the flight guidance system, which couples through the RAD/INS pushbutton (see [Automatic flight](automatic-flight)).

children.title: Position updating, DME, mixing and accuracy

blocks.content: The box keeps two positions: the **inertial** position from its platform alone, and a **correction** from manual updates, DME updating and triple mixing. POS shows inertial plus correction; WAY PT with HOLD lit shows the inertial position alone. How the correction is used is set by the **desired performance index (PI)**, a digit keyed at DSRTK/STS in NAV and inserted:

blocks.title: Desired PI
rows: Aided inertial: DME updating when a station is in use, triple mixing otherwise
Unaided inertial; corrections already made are kept
Erase every correction; the display returns to 5

blocks.content: **Accuracy Index.** In NAV the fifth status digit shows an estimate of position error in nautical miles. It is forced to 0 on entering NAV, grows as three times the hours of unaided flight (reaching its ceiling of 9 after three hours), and falls while DME updating is in use, faster with two stations than one; triple mixing draws it toward 4. DME updating needs valid altitude, so without it the index does not fall.

**Manual position update.** At POS, press HOLD as the aeroplane passes over the checkpoint: the displayed position freezes. Key the checkpoint's latitude and longitude (INSERT stays lit until both halves are in) and insert. The correction is measured against the inertial position at the moment of HOLD, and HOLD goes out when the update is accepted. An update larger than 33 NM is accepted but records malfunction 49 and lights WARN. One larger than about 60 NM is rejected: WARN lights (malfunction 49), HOLD stays lit and the display shows the reference position. Pressing HOLD again forces the update; corrections beyond about 180 NM are only partly accepted. With REMOTE lit an update reaches only those boxes whose own HOLD was pressed.

**DME stations.** Nine DME station slots are loaded at WAY PT. Select the slot on the waypoint selector, open the DME position display (keys 7 and 9) and insert the station's latitude and longitude separately; open the altitude and frequency display (keys 3 and 9), key 2 or 8 and the altitude in thousands of feet (0 to 15), INSERT, then key 4 or 6 and the frequency (108.00 to 135.95 MHz, shown in the longitude format, 11 75.0 for 117.50), INSERT. A station is usable only when all three are loaded. Move the data selector to any position other than WAY PT and DIS/TIME to leave the DME displays.

**DME updating.** With a DME display up, press WY PT CHG and the slot number to designate that station: the FROM side blanks and the TO side flashes the station number. Select PI 4, and tune the aeroplane's DME (that side's glareshield VHF NAV head) to the station. A range counts only while the receiver is tuned to the designated station's stored frequency. The box tests the ranges continuously against its own position; a station that fails the range-rate test within 2.5 minutes, or the delta-range test within 2.5 minutes (5 minutes when two stations are in use, and only inside 250 NM), is dropped and the station designator returns to 0. Stations at least 15 NM off the desired track give the best result. DME updating needs valid altitude. Designate 0 to stop DME updating.

**Triple mixing.** With all three boxes in NAV, no box with WARN lit, PI 4 selected on a box and no DME updating in progress on it (its own or shared), that box steers its correction toward the **median** latitude and the **median** longitude of the three boxes. The median, unlike an average, rejects a box that has drifted badly. The transition is eased on, and the correction built up is kept when PI 4 is deselected.

**REMOTE.** Pressing REMOTE on one C/DU makes its waypoint coordinates, DME station data and manual position updates go at once to every other box whose REMOTE is lit; leg changes, the desired PI and DME designations are not carried. The present position at alignment is **not** carried by REMOTE and must be inserted on each C/DU, and HOLD must be pressed on each box. Before relying on the boxes, check that all three are flying the same leg.

When WARN lights, set the data selector to DSRTK/STS and press and release TEST. The status word first shows the **action code** for the worst condition recorded; successive presses walk through the **malfunction codes**, then the display blanks (or returns to the action code if a condition is still present). A walk clears codes for conditions that have ended. Codes 22 to 27 (analog output feedback) do not light WARN, and on the ground they must persist for 6 seconds before they are recorded. While WARN is lit the box's navigation outputs are flagged invalid and it takes no part in triple mixing, until a TEST walk clears the code.

sections.title: INS-61B inertial navigation system
sections.summary: The Collins INS-61B: three independent inertial navigators with DME position updating.

blocks.content: The Collins INS-61B is a contemporary of the Carousel IV-A with a different philosophy of control: sequence keys (L/L DEF, NAV DEF, UD) rather than lit function keys, a nine-position data selector with a STATUS position, and a status code in place of the Carousel's mode countdown. It is not a carouselling platform. The procedures follow the Collins INS-61B operations manual.

Three independent systems are installed, each an inertial navigation unit (INU) and a battery unit in the electronics bay, a CDU on the pedestal and a mode selector unit (MSU) on the overhead. The only connection between systems is the data link used for remote waypoint loading; there is no position mixing between them. Each INU needs its primary 115 V AC, its heater supply and a 26 V AC attitude excitation (all from its INS circuit in the simulation), and its battery unit. A system starts only with both primary power and battery available, runs on either once started, and carries on the battery for about half an hour. The alignment does not progress while a box runs on its battery alone, and because the 26 V AC goes with the primary supply, a box on its battery loses its attitude outputs (STATUS 0070).

The simulated boxes run program -012, a DME program: the position-update function uses a DME station instead of a manual checkpoint. Box 1 updates on DME 1 and box 2 on DME 2; box 3 has no DME receiver and does not update.

blocks.title: INS-61B mode selector unit
rows: Warm up, cage, and align to the inserted present position
Navigate. Selected before the alignment is complete, NAV is entered automatically when it completes (not with a WARN condition, a latitude disagreement, or the heater or cooling air lost)
Roll and pitch attitude and platform heading only. From OFF, at least 1 minute to valid attitude. After ATT the system must be realigned on the ground
26 V AC attitude excitation missing during the alignment
Alignment complete; NAV may be selected
Battery or charger malfunction; with primary power lost, the INU shuts down

blocks.content: The 916K-2 CDU has a left data display of five digits and a right one of six, a two-digit FR TO display, a one-digit WPT display, a nine-position data selector, a four-position function switch, a ten-key keyboard and four lit sequence keys. Invalid or unavailable data are shown by the **(=)** symbol at the left of a window. There is **no CLEAR key**: to abandon a sequence, momentarily turn the data selector to another position and back, then start again.

rows: TK/GS, HDG/DA, XTK/TKE, POS, WPT, DIS/TIME, WIND, DSRTK/SXTK (desired track and selected cross-track offset), STATUS
T: test sequences 09, 19, 29. M: manual operations (all keyboard entry, manual leg change). A: automatic leg sequencing. R: load waypoints from another system
Data entry. Secondary legends: 2 N, 8 S, 4 W, 6 E; 1 L and 3 R (offset side); 7 DSTK; 9 SXTK; 0 CMPT

Starts a latitude/longitude entry: present position (aligning), a waypoint (at WPT), a DME station (at POS in NAV, function M), or a remote load (function R). The first key after it is a hemisphere key, which also says which display is being loaded; L/L DEF again moves to the other display
Starts a navigation definition: two digits into FR TO, then INSERT. A leg; 77 angle navigation; 99 selected offset; 00 computer access; at function T, the test codes

blocks.content: **Entering coordinates.** Digits go in from the most significant; leading zeros must be entered and trailing zeros may be omitted: W090°00.0' can be entered as W09. Latitude and longitude may be entered in either order, and an unloaded waypoint reads (=), so both halves must be keyed before INSERT will accept it.

MSU knob at NAV with ALIGN, READY and BATT WARN lamps. Legends legible.
blocks.title: INS-61B CDU and MSU

blocks.content: Turn the MSU to ALIGN with the data selector at POS. The alignment runs through the phases below, shown as a STATUS number in the left display at STATUS. It does not proceed unless 26 V AC is present for the first minute, and it stops at 0090 until the present position has been inserted (L/L DEF, the coordinates, INSERT).

blocks.title: INS-61B alignment phases
rows: Caging and gyro spin-up, then platform temperature stabilization
64 s, or as long as the platform takes to reach temperature (½ to 3 min, longer in a cold equipment bay)
Platform leveling (attitude valid at its end)
Fine alignment, one count each 10 s; then the READY light

blocks.content: The whole sequence is about **15 minutes** (906 s at best, about 17 minutes from a cold-soaked bay), plus any wait for the present position. A present position re-entered at STATUS 0050 or lower sends the alignment back to 0050 and costs about **10 more minutes**. A realignment from NAV or ATT skips the caging and needs at least **14 minutes** stationary. Above 77° latitude the alignment is degraded.

items: After heading determination the INU knows its own latitude. If the inserted latitude disagrees, WARN flashes (steady once the alignment completes) with the ALIGN lamp lit. Reinsert the correct present position.
A box turned off and on again within 2.5 minutes shows (=) until 2.5 minutes after turn-on. Leave it on.
Moving the aeroplane after heading approximation has begun (STATUS 0080 to 0000) sends the alignment back to 0090, and the present position must be reinserted.
Returning the MSU from NAV to ALIGN reverts the alignment to 0090 and the present position must be reinserted.

blocks.content: **Waypoints.** Nine waypoints can be loaded from the keyboard (WPT, the waypoint number, L/L DEF, coordinates, INSERT). Waypoint 0 cannot be loaded from the keyboard: it receives the present position when a leg from 0 is defined or angle navigation is selected. At power-on the FR TO display is blank and no leg is defined; until one is, XTK/TKE, DIS/TIME and DSRTK/SXTK read (=).

**Legs.** NAV DEF, the FROM and TO numbers, INSERT. A leg is valid only if both waypoints are loaded and they are between 1 and 3,999 NM apart. Defining an invalid leg does not leave the old one in force: the NAV DEF lamp flashes, FR TO blanks and the HSI cross-track flag comes into view until a valid leg is inserted. A leg from 0 flies direct from present position. In **A** the box sequences automatically: the ALERT lamp lights inside the alert circle (187 seconds to go), the FR TO display steps to the next leg at the capture circle (117 seconds), and the steering changes to the new leg at the turn point, which depends on the intercept angle and ground speed. In **M** the box flies on past the waypoint, the ALERT lamp flashes, and distance and time are measured from the waypoint just overflown until the crew define a new leg; the lamp stops flashing once the aeroplane is more than the alert-circle time beyond it. Past waypoint 9 sequencing wraps to 1.

blocks.title: Other navigation definitions (NAV DEF)
rows: Angle navigation: fly a great circle from present position on an entered initial track (waypoint 0 is written)
Selected offset: fly parallel to the leg at an entered cross-track distance, L (key 1) or R (key 3)
Computer access: distance and time between any two loaded waypoints, without changing the leg

blocks.content: **Steering.** The roll command is limited to 30° of bank and 2° per second of roll rate. Off track, the box cuts toward the leg at 10° per nautical mile of cross-track, up to a 45° intercept, and up to 90° while capturing a new leg, a direct-to, an offset or an angle problem, until within 4.5 NM. Turn anticipation follows from a 30° bank turn through the change of course. With the HSI switch at INS the deviation bar shows cross-track at 3.75 NM a dot.

**DME position update (program -012).** Tune that side's DME to the station. With the function switch at M and the data selector at POS in NAV, press L/L DEF (WPT shows H), key the **station's** coordinates and INSERT. The left display then shows an **update-status number**, the box's estimate of its radial position error, starting at 1.3 plus the hours of flight; the right display shows the angle from the aeroplane's track to the station, and WPT shows E. As the box processes ranges the number falls; when it reaches 1.5, press UD and INSERT. WPT shows U and the displays show the updated position. To remove an update, M, UD, INSERT.

A single DME range tells the box nothing across the line of sight to the station, so the across-track error shrinks only as that line turns while the aeroplane flies past. The update is therefore not available within 15 NM of the station below 10,000 ft (30 NM above), outside a box extending 130 NM along and across the track from the insertion point, or with the station less than 20° or more than 160° from track. Below 50 kt ground speed the left display shows present position instead of the update-status number, and no update is accepted while the ALERT lamp is lit.

**Remote loading.** With the function switch at R, press L/L DEF, key the source system's logic number and INSERT: on box 1, 1 is INS 2 and 2 is INS 3; on box 2, 1 is INS 1 and 2 is INS 3; on box 3, 1 is INS 1 and 2 is INS 2. The source must be aligning or navigating. Its loaded waypoints are copied for as long as the switch stays at R; leaving R clears the leg.

With the function switch at T, NAV DEF and a test code run the tests: **09** (in NAV only), **19** (preset readouts on every data selector position and a test picture on the HSI: distance 10, TO, cross-track L 3.7, desired track 90, after the cross-track flag shows for 1 second) and **29** (the analog outputs; the cross-track flag stays in view for the whole test). In NAV, sequence 09 also clears the WARN for STATUS codes 0020 and 0050; the code remains displayed.

sections.title: Inertial reference on the HT-9100 fit
sections.summary: The three IRS mode selectors that remain when the GPS-based HT-9100 is fitted.

blocks.content: With the HT-9100 fitted, navigation is by GPS and the HT-9100's own dead reckoning (see [Flight management](flight-management)). The three inertial platforms remain, as attitude and heading references for the glass instrument options, under three five-position mode selectors of the LTN-92 pattern. They take their alignment position automatically and align in about 13 minutes from ALIGN or NAV; their heading is valid only in NAV.

sections.title: KC-10 inertial navigation units
sections.summary: The KC-10A's three LTN-101 INUs, controlled through their mode selectors and the FMS CDUs.

blocks.content: Three independent LTN-101 inertial navigation systems are installed, each a mode selector unit (MSU) on the overhead and an inertial navigation unit (INU) in the avionics compartment. The INUs are navigation **sensors** for the FMS: they supply position and velocity, and the FMS performs all navigation computation, blending them with the GPS receivers into its navigation solutions. They also supply attitude to the ADIs, the autothrottle and the weather radar, and azimuth stabilization to the compass systems. The FMS CDUs provide all functional control of the INUs; there is no INS control display unit. The CDU pages involved (START INIT, NAV STATUS, INU UPDATE) are described in [Flight management](flight-management).

blocks.title: KC-10 mode selector unit
rows: Normal operating mode. From OFF, the INU aligns and then enters NAVIGATE automatically
Pitch, roll and platform heading only; no navigation solution. Pull the knob to select. Selected in flight, navigation is cancelled until another ground alignment

blocks.content: **Alignment.** With aircraft power and the CDUs on, set the MSUs to NAV. Each INU receives its present position automatically from GPS 1 and GPS 2 as soon as they have one, aligns for **10 minutes** and enters NAVIGATE by itself. The START INIT 3/3 page shows each INU's alignment status and TIME TO NAV (>6 MIN, then whole minutes). If an INU has no position, the CDU annunciates INU 1 (2, 3) NO INIT: enter an INIT POS on START INIT 2/3, then press INIT INU on START INIT 3/3. Moving the aircraft during the alignment annunciates EXCESS INU MOTION and pauses the alignment, which continues when the motion stops. Alignment is possible only on the ground; normal loading, servicing and light gusty winds do not disturb it.

**In flight.** If an INU loses its navigation capability in the air (for example after an interruption of its power), it switches to ATT automatically, and it cannot navigate again until it has been aligned on the ground. An INU failure is shown NGO on the NAV STATUS page, and the side's FMS solution falls back to its next sensor.

blocks.title: FMS navigation solutions involving the INUs

blocks.content: The designated solution defaults to INU 1 with GPS for the pilot and INU 2 with GPS for the copilot. While its GPS is tracking, a hybrid solution follows the GPS and the INU's drift is washed out; if the GPS is lost, the hybrid coasts on its INU, carrying only the drift accumulated since the GPS last aided it. A pure INU solution carries the INU's full drift. An **INU UPDATE** moves an INU's position to a designated solution, a manual position or a navaid at the moment of FREEZE; the INU carries that correction until its next alignment. INU updates should not be made in flight, and if one is required, use the most accurate data available.
**INS selector.** The overhead INS selector, at CAPT ON AUX or F/O ON AUX, makes the instruments and systems that normally take their attitude from INU 1 (or INU 2) take it from INU 3.
Do not move the aircraft after the alignment has started. If it is moved, turn the INU off and start the alignment again.

blocks.alt: KC-10A overhead: the three INU mode selector units (OFF, NAV, ATT) at NAV, with the INS selector and CADC selector nearby; adjacent FMS CDU showing START INIT 3/3 with INU 1, 2, 3 alignment status and TIME TO NAV 4 MIN. Placards legible.
blocks.title: KC-10 INU mode selectors and START INIT page

sections.title: MD-10 air data inertial reference system
sections.summary: The three ADIRUs: alignment from the MCDU, the NAV OFF lights and source transfer.

blocks.content: Three air data inertial reference units, **ADIRU 1**, **ADIRU 2** and **ADIRU AUX**, continuously compute latitude and longitude, track, attitude, magnetic and true heading, vertical speed and ground speed for the display units, the FMS and the automatic flight system. Normally the captain's display units use ADIRU 1 and the first officer's ADIRU 2; ADIRU AUX is a hot spare. Each unit runs on 115 V AC and has a dedicated battery good for about 15 minutes. During navigation, steering is done by the flight management computers; the ADIRUs accept no pilot inputs once they are navigating, and they cannot be realigned in flight.

blocks.title: IRS control panel (forward overhead, left side)
rows: Normal position. The ADIRU powers up, aligns for about 10 minutes and enters the nav mode automatically
The unit is off or aligning, or it has detected a primary failure of attitude, heading, angular rate or acceleration
No present position received within 10 minutes of turn-on, or the entered position failed the comparison test (about 1° of latitude and/or longitude against the stored or computed position)

blocks.content: **Alignment.** Set the three selectors to NAV: the NAV OFF lights come on steady and NO TAXI appears on each PFD speed tape. Give the units their position from the MCDU's F-PLN INIT page: ALIGN POS fills from the loaded route's origin, or a position can be typed at 3L/3R, and **INITIALIZE IRS** (4R) transmits it. The units then align for about ten minutes and enter nav by themselves, when the NAV OFF lights and NO TAXI go out. An entry refused by the comparison test makes NAV OFF flash; sending the same position again overrides the refusal. The aircraft must not be moved during alignment; movement restarts it.

**Source transfer.** Each pilot's source input select panel (SISP) carries an IRS switch. Pushing it puts that pilot's displays on ADIRU AUX; pushing it again returns them to the onside unit. On the aircraft the switch lights CAPT ON AUX or F/O ON AUX and the ND annunciates IRS AUX; the simulation shows neither (see [Simulation notes](#simulation-notes)). The flight instrument side of the transfer is in [Flight instruments](flight-instruments#switching-md10).

A unit that loses its navigation function but keeps its attitude (IRU NAV FAIL) remains usable for attitude. Near the poles the units switch to true heading north of 73° N or south of 60.5° S, and back south of 72.5° N or north of 59.5° S. Each unit's drift, between about 0.6 and 1.1 NM per hour, can be read on the FMS IRS status page. The units' attitude and heading outputs, and the alerts they raise, are described in [Flight instruments](flight-instruments#adirs).

sections.title: MD-10 navigation display
sections.summary: ND modes and how raw radio and inertial data appear on them.

blocks.content: Each pilot has a navigation display, normally on display units 2 and 5, controlled from that pilot's EIS control panel (ECP) on the glareshield. The ND shows the aeroplane's position, the flight plan, waypoints, navaids, airports, weather, ground speed and true airspeed, wind, distance and time to the next waypoint and the clock. This section covers its use for navigation; the flight plan and FMS functions are in [Flight management](flight-management), and the weather and traffic overlays in [Surveillance](surveillance).

blocks.content: A receivable station is not needed for the VOR or ILS test, but the receiver must be powered, serviceable and tuned to a frequency in its own band (a VOR test with a VOR frequency, an ILS test with a localizer). The tests act inside the receivers, so every instrument the receiver feeds shows the test, including the crossed ADI. The VOR and ILS tests are inhibited while the flight guidance system has a beam captured (LOC TRK, GS TRK and the modes after them). The DME test needs the interrogator powered and interrogating (not STBY). On the KC-10 there are no DME test buttons: the TACANs are tested from the FMS.

blocks.content: Each long-range unit's mode selectors, CDU and displays are described with the unit: [AINS-70](#ains-70) (mode selectors, ISDU, CDU), [ANS-70](#ans-70), [Carousel IV-A](#carousel-iv-a) (MSU and C/DU), [INS-61B](#ins-61b) (MSU and CDU), and [the HT-9100 fit's IRS selectors](#ht-9100-irs).
The KC-10's INU mode selectors are described in [KC-10 inertial navigation units](#kc-10-inu); the CDU pages in [Flight management](flight-management).

The MD-10's IRS control panel and SISP IRS switches are described in [MD-10 air data inertial reference system](#md-10-adirs), and the ECP's navigation controls in [MD-10 navigation display](#md-10-nd). Radio tuning on the MCDU is in [Flight management](flight-management).

sections.title: Operation
sections.summary: Normal use from alignment to shutdown.

blocks.content: Navigation operation follows the same pattern on every aircraft: align the inertial units on the ground with an accurate present position, set up and test the radios, load and check the route, fly it while cross-checking the units against each other and against the radio aids, and check the units' accuracy at the end of the flight.

Align the inertial units early in the preflight, as soon as AC power is established, so that the alignment is complete before engine start, and do not move the aeroplane until it is. The procedures below give the system steps; the full preflight is in [Normal procedures](normal-procedures).

items.action: ADJUST TO RAMP, INSERT (line keys 4 and 6)

blocks.content: Insert the position within three minutes of selecting NAV, or ISS WARN blinks until it is. If the CDUs are not available, initialize each ISS with the ISDU (see [Inertial sensor display unit](#ains-70-isdu)). Before engine start the mode on PROGRESS normally reads I; R/I comes up once the aeroplane is within range of in-core navaids and the radio fixes are accepted.

From cold the box reaches READY NAV in about 15 minutes. Insert the present position on each C/DU: REMOTE does not carry it. Load the waypoints on one C/DU with REMOTE lit on every box, then check them on each box, and check that all three are on the same leg (1 2).

items.item: Waypoints (WPT, number, L/L DEF, coordinates, INSERT)

items.action: T: TESTS 19, 29 AS REQUIRED, THEN M

blocks.content: **HT-9100 and ANS-70 fits.** Turn the three mode selectors to NAV. The platforms take their position automatically and align in about 13 minutes; on the HT-9100 fit the ALIGN lights go out when they are aligned with NAV selected. The HT-9100's own initialization is in [Flight management](flight-management); the ANS-70 is initialized by route definition on its CDU as for the AINS-70.

items.item: START INIT 2/3: designated solution present position

items.action: IF SHOWN: INIT POS, INIT INU

blocks.content: With GPS available the INUs initialize themselves and navigate after 10 minutes. If the aeroplane is moved, EXCESS INU MOTION appears and the alignment waits until it stops.

items.item: F-PLN INIT: ALIGN POS (or LAT/LONG at 3L/3R)
NAV OFF lights and NO TAXI (after about 10 minutes)

items.action: HOLD: CDI CENTERD, TO, RMI POINTERS 180°

items.item: Localizer frequency (pedestal head, or glareshield heads)

items.action: UP/L, THEN DN/R: ONE DOT EACH WAY
TUNE, IDENTIFY IN ANT, THEN ADF

blocks.content: A receivable station is not needed for the self-tests, only a frequency in the right band on a powered receiver. Release each test button and observe that the instruments return to their pre-test indications. On the KC-10, the ADF and TACAN tests are run from the FMS NAV STATUS and TACAN STATUS pages; allow 90 seconds for a TACAN to warm up after it is first powered.

**Departure.** Each pilot sets their HSI switch for the departure: VOR for a radial departure, INS for a long-range unit departure. With the AINS-70 or ANS-70, AUTO TUNE lets the computers keep both VOR/DMEs on the stations they want; with AUTO TUNE off, tune the stations shown on PROGRESS when TUNE appears. Coupling the flight guidance system to the long-range unit uses the RAD/INS pushbutton with the HSI switch at INS (see [Automatic flight](automatic-flight)).

**Monitoring an inertial installation.** Three independent boxes (CIV-A, INS-61B) should agree; a box whose position, ground speed or wind departs from the other two is the suspect. Over a navaid or a known fix, compare the boxes' positions with it. On the CIV-A, PI 4 with a DME station designated, or triple mixing, keeps the boxes corrected over land; watch the Accuracy Index rise over water and fall when updating resumes. On the INS-61B, update boxes 1 and 2 by DME when a suitable station is available. On the AINS-70, watch the MODE on PROGRESS: R/I over land, I over water. A downmode alert over land means the radio updating has stopped; check the stations and the AUTO TUNE switches.

**Waypoint checks.** Before each waypoint, check the next leg: on the CIV-A and INS-61B, the next waypoint's coordinates and the FROM-TO display; on the AINS-70, the flight plan and any CHECK NEXT alert. In MAN the leg must be changed by hand at each waypoint, and the ALERT lamp flashing past a waypoint is the reminder.

**KC-10.** The FMS normally flies hybrid INU/GPS solutions and the INUs' drift is washed out while the GPS is tracking. Select FMS on the display control panel NAV knob for FMS navigation, VOR or TCN for a radial. The autopilot's RAD modes fly a VOR or TACAN radial; its FMS modes fly the FMS steering. See [Flight management](flight-management) and [Automatic flight](automatic-flight).
**MD-10.** Navigation and radio tuning are automatic. Monitor the ND in MAP; select VOR or APPR to cross-check raw data, and the bearing pointers for navaid bearings.

blocks.title: ILS setup, pedestal arrangement (all fits except the HT-9100)
ILS setup, glareshield arrangement (KC-10, DC-10 with HT-9100)

blocks.content: On the pedestal arrangement each pilot's ADI reads the opposite ILS receiver. If a pilot's ADI and HSI disagree on the localizer or glideslope, one of the two receivers is in error: compare with the other pilot's instruments to identify it.
On the MD-10 the FMS autotunes the ILS for the selected approach. Select APPR on the ECP to monitor the raw localizer and glideslope on the ND.

At the gate, compare each inertial unit's present position with the gate coordinates before switching it off. The difference divided by the time in NAV is the unit's drift rate, the best indication of its health: about 1 NM per hour or less is normal, and a unit well outside the 2 NM per hour class figure should be reported. Then set the mode selectors to OFF. On the DC-10 and KC-10, the platforms draw power and cooling air while they run, and should not be left running without aircraft power on the ground.

The AINS-70 keeps its data base and flight plan in core through a power-off; only an IPL clears them. The CIV-A and INS-61B remember their last position at shutdown, against which the next alignment's inserted position is checked.

sections.title: Failures and non-normal operation
sections.summary: What fails, how it shows, and what the crew do.

blocks.content: Navigation failures rarely announce themselves loudly. A flag, a blinking light or a disagreement between two instruments is usually all there is. The duplicated radios and triplicated platforms exist so that a failure can be identified by comparison: two instruments that disagree mean one is wrong, and a third source decides which. Make the comparison before acting on any single indication.

On emergency power the remaining navigation is VOR 1 and 2, ILS 2, NCUs 1 and 2 and platforms 2 and 3. See [Electrical](electrical).

blocks.content: Procedures for these failures are in [Abnormal procedures](abnormal-procedures) and, for loss of primary attitude, [Emergency procedures](emergency-procedures).

**Modeled in depth.** The receivers' tuning, band logic and standby rule, their power supplies, validity, search and lock-on, failures and self-tests are modeled, together with the RAD/INS switching and the crossed ADI feeds of the pedestal ILS arrangement. Each long-range unit is a full model of its own manual: the AINS-70's platforms, navigation modes, accuracy estimate, navaid autoselection, radio acceptance criteria, crosstalk, comparators and its whole CDU and route-definition procedure; the Carousel IV-A's mode countdown, C/DU grammar, DME updating, triple mixing and malfunction codes; the INS-61B's alignment phases, sequence keys, DME Kalman update and STATUS codes; the KC-10 INUs' alignment and solutions; and the MD-10 ADIRUs' alignment and source transfer. Every inertial unit drifts at its own rate along the Schuler-shaped curve described in [Schuler tuning](#schuler-tuning). The drift and every alignment clock stop during an active pause, and a slew is treated as a reposition that carries the unit's existing error with it.

**Spawning.** An aeroplane loaded with engines running, on the runway or in flight, has its mode selectors at NAV and its inertial units already aligned and navigating, as if the crew had aligned them at the gate. The AINS-70's and ANS-70's core is still empty, and ROUTE DEFINITION is refused in flight, so after an airborne load a route has to be built through the flight plan's REVISE page. A cold-and-dark load starts with every selector OFF.

**Radio measurements.** The beam geometry (radial, deviation, slant range, bearing) comes from the simulator's own radios: NAV 1 and NAV 2 for the glareshield heads and NAV 3 for the DC-10's pedestal ILS head, kept in step with the control heads in both directions. A frequency set from the EFB, an external program or a hardware radio panel is adopted into the control head's window. Stations are identified by frequency against the navigation data. The DME's OVRD position behaves as NORM, a lost DME signal returns to search without coasting, and the simulator's own beacon coverage decides when a marker lamp lights. The marker beacon HI/LO sensitivity switch on the pedestal is inoperative: the receiver always operates at HI.

**DC-10 specifics.** The ADF tuner units tune 190 to 999 kHz only (they have three digits). With AUTO TUNE active, the frequency window keeps showing the crew's frequency while the long-range unit retunes the receiver behind it. On the electromechanical HSIs the card is always magnetic (the INS-era TRU presentation is not modeled), the course arrow stays on the CRS knob at INS rather than showing desired track, the distance window shows the onside DME at every source, and the HSI ALERT annunciator does not light. The INS selector transfers attitude and heading to platform 3 but does not change which long-range box drives a pilot's HSI. Each pilot's RMI card follows that pilot's own compass system; on the aircraft the RMI cards are crossed (compass system 1 drives the first officer's RMI and system 2 the captain's), so that each pilot has one card from each compass. The ADF panels' AI/NORM and OFF/BFO switches have no effect, and the MKR BCN test lights the lamps without sounding the tones. The INS FLOW OFF lights are not fitted to the cockpit: a failed platform fan is modeled (the platform heats and eventually cuts out) but shows only at cut-out.

**AINS-70.** The tape data base is the simulator's current navigation data cycle (MSFS or Navigraph, as chosen under Navigation data in the EFB's Settings), so the stations in core and the routes that can be assembled come from it. The data search durations described only as "a few minutes" in the handbook are about two minutes. The time to valid attitude during alignment is estimated. The 76.5° alignment latitude limit and the polar navigation reference change above 85° are not simulated. The NAV HDG MAG/TRU switch is not on the model, so the CDU always shows magnetic angles. The MSU lamp test is not available, and some fault sources (VOR, DME, HDG, CADC, THDG, ASC, FDSU, NAVPOS) are not yet annunciated on the CDU. Of the comparators, only the latitude/longitude cross-check (XCHEK) and the platform position comparison can trip; the cross-track, vertical deviation, distance and heading comparisons never do, and the platform comparison's time runs from the moment the aeroplane was loaded rather than from alignment.

**Carousel IV-A and INS-61B.** The CIV-A's MSU lamps (READY NAV, BAT) are computed but do not light on the current 3D model: read the status display instead. The CIV-A's DME MIXING IN PROGRESS lamp, its TEST switch's HSI test picture, the semi-permanent fault recall (HOLD and TEST) and the ADEU card reader are not modeled, and its waypoints are not cleared when a box is turned on. The INS-61B's lamps work but have no lamp test, and its BATT WARN cannot light because no battery failure can be injected. The INS-61B's (=) symbol is drawn as a single bar, and its L/R and P/H/E/U indications are not drawn. On these two fits the glass instrument options take attitude and heading from three platforms that follow the AINS-70's alignment timing (attitude about five minutes and heading about 13 minutes after ALIGN or NAV is selected; STBY does not count), not from the boxes themselves, so the glass heading can come valid at a different moment from a box's READY indication. The ANS-70 has no manual in the sources and is built as described in [ANS-70](#ans-70).

**KC-10.** The simulated installation is the later one with LTN-101 INUs controlled from the FMS. Earlier revisions of the KC-10 flight manual describe LTN-72 units with STBY, ALIGN, NAV and ATT REF positions, READY NAV and BATT lamps and a position entered before ALIGN; those are not modeled. The INU batteries are not simulated: any interruption of an INU's power drops it, and in flight it returns in ATT and cannot navigate again until a ground alignment. The INU/GPS blending filter is not modeled; a hybrid solution with its GPS tracking follows the GPS. The TACANs' air-to-air and BCN modes never lock on (there are no other TACAN-equipped aircraft), the antenna select and automatic gain control switches have no effect, and a TACAN self-test always passes; the self-test is refused in the air and stops at lift-off. The dual DME indicator shows the two VHF NAV DMEs (on the real aircraft it is the TACAN DME indicator); TACAN slant range is shown on the EHSIs.

**MD-10.** The VOR, ILS, DME and ADF receivers are the simulator's own and cannot be failed individually. Of the SISP source switches, only the IRS switch is functional for navigation, and it lights no switch-light and puts no IRS AUX annunciation on the ND; the VOR and APPR source switches are inoperative. The ADIRUs' air data half is represented by the air data computers. A refused INITIALIZE IRS position is accepted when sent a second time, so that a relocated aeroplane can always be aligned.

The **INS alignment** setting (Realistic or Instant) in the EFB's Settings applies to every inertial unit and to the AINS-70's data search; see [Alignment by gyrocompassing](#gyrocompass-alignment).

parts.title: Flight Management
parts.summary: Flight management, GPS navigation and performance management computers: the HT9100 and PMS on the DC-10, the KC-10's FMS and the MD-10's Pegasus.

sections.title: Introduction
sections.summary: Which flight management and performance computers each aircraft carries, and the principles they share.

blocks.content: Flight management on this family is not one system but four, from different generations. The DC-10 was designed in the late 1960s for a crew of three: long-range navigation was by inertial navigation systems or the AINS-70 area navigation system, and speeds and thrust settings came from the performance manual. Two computers were added later. The **Performance Management System (PMS)** of the 1980s took over the vertical half on the DC-10-30 and -40, computing economy speeds, thrust targets and a vertical profile to the bottom of descent. The **HT9100 GPS/FMS** of the late 1990s replaced the inertial long-range units with satellite navigation and a flight management keyboard on retrofitted DC-10s. The KC-10A received its own military **Flight Management System** with GPS and new inertial units, and the FedEx MD-10 conversion took the MD-11's **Honeywell Pegasus FMS** with full lateral and vertical guidance.

This part describes those four computers: what each one is, its control display unit and every page a crew uses, how to initialize it and build a route, how it navigates laterally and vertically, what performance it computes, how it couples to the autopilot and autothrottle, its databases and data entry rules, its messages, and a walk through a typical flight. The inertial units, the AINS-70, the CIV-A and INS-61B, the ANS-70 and the VOR/DME/ILS receivers are described in [Navigation](navigation); the autopilot and autothrottle modes the computers feed are in [Automatic Flight](automatic-flight).

DC-10 with HT9100: three independent HT9100 units (NPU, GPS antenna, MCDU), each feeding its side's HSI and the autopilot NAV coupler through the HSI NAV switch position, with the FMS MODE switch selecting which unit each seat reads. DC-10-30/-40 with PMS: the PMS CDU and PMCU taking CADC, INS, engine N1/fuel flow, thrust rating indicator mode and ALT SEL, with a dashed (not connected) line to the FGS and ATS. KC-10A: three CDUs (CDU1 hosting FMS1, CDU2 hosting FMS2, CDU3 a third head), the 1553 bus, three INUs, three GPS receivers, TACAN/ADF radios, feeding the EHSIs and the autopilot through the display control panel NAV knob at FMS. MD-10: FMF1 and FMF2 with crosstalk, three MCDUs, three IRUs, two GNS, VOR/DME autotuning, feeding the FCCs (roll, pitch, speed and thrust targets) and the NDs. Labels legible.
