blocks.content: **One long-range unit at a time.** On a DC-10 the Navigation Systems category is a radio group: the aircraft carries exactly one of AINS-70, CIV-A, INS-61B, HT9100, or (DC-10-10 Early, Late and -10F Late only) ANS-70S, ANS-70D or VOR ONLY. AINS-70 is the default. A change of unit rebuilds the unit from cold, in flight as on the ground, so any route it held is lost. The PMS is a separate category and can be fitted with any long-range unit.

Fitting the PMS removes the AUTO BRAKE panel from the pedestal, because both units use the same panel position. A DC-10 with the PMS fitted has no autobrake selector. See [Landing Gear](landing-gear) for the autobrake system.

children.title: Principles of area navigation and flight management
children.summary: The ideas every unit in this part is built on: position estimation, the flight plan as legs, steering, vertical paths and the edit transaction.

blocks.content: Every computer in this part answers the same three questions continuously: where is the aircraft, where should it be, and what should the autopilot do about the difference. They differ in what sensors they trust, how much of the route they can describe, and whether they also answer the vertical and speed questions. The ideas below are common to all of them; each unit's own section then says how it applies them.

No single sensor is both accurate and continuously available. An **inertial unit** integrates accelerations twice, so its position is smooth and independent of anything outside the aircraft, but its error grows with time: the platform's gyro drift and accelerometer bias feed a Schuler oscillation of 84.4 minutes period whose amplitude ratchets up through the flight, on the order of one to two nautical miles per hour for the units on this family (see [Navigation](navigation)). **Radio fixes** from two DME stations, or one VOR/DME, are accurate near the stations and useless far from them. **GPS** is accurate everywhere the satellites are in view, but needs a minimum geometry and can be degraded or lost without warning unless the receiver checks itself.

A flight management computer therefore blends. The HT9100 trusts GPS alone and falls back to dead reckoning on heading, true airspeed and the last computed wind. The KC-10 FMS keeps several candidate solutions (each INU alone, each INU aided by a GPS) and lets the crew designate one per side. The Pegasus forms a weighted average of three inertial units, rejects any unit that wanders more than 36 NM from the average, and corrects the result with GPS and DME/DME radio fixes. The quality of the blend is reported as **actual navigation performance (ANP)** or estimated position uncertainty, a radius within which the true position lies with 95 % probability, and is compared with the **required navigation performance (RNP)** for the phase of flight: typically 2.0 NM en route, 1.0 NM in the terminal area and 0.3 NM on an approach.

**Integrity** is a separate question from accuracy. A GPS receiver with five or more satellites in view can check each range against the others (receiver autonomous integrity monitoring, RAIM) and compute a protection limit, the largest position error that could go undetected. With fewer satellites, or poor geometry, it can no longer prove its own answer is right even when the answer happens to be accurate. That is why the HT9100 annunciates UNABLE RNP when either accuracy or integrity falls short.

children.title: The flight plan as a string of legs

blocks.content: A route in a modern box is not a list of points but a list of **legs**, each defined by a path and a terminator in the ARINC 424 sense: track to a fix, direct to a fix, course to an altitude, heading to a radial intercept, a holding pattern ending at a manual termination, an arc of constant radius, and so on. Half of the leg types in a departure procedure end at an altitude, a radial or a crew action rather than at a fix. The computer has to construct the path in flight from the aircraft's own performance, which is why a departure can look different on the map before and after takeoff.

Where two parts of a route do not join (a procedure whose first fix is not on the route, a waypoint inserted with nothing after it) the box inserts a **route discontinuity**. A discontinuity is a deliberate stop: the computer will not invent a path across it. Reaching one ends lateral guidance and the autopilot reverts to a heading mode, so every route must be checked for discontinuities before departure and each one closed or accepted.

For the active leg the computer derives two numbers: **cross-track error (XTK)**, the perpendicular distance from the desired path, and **track angle error (TKE)**, the difference between the aircraft's ground track and the desired track. These are what an inertial navigation system has always sent the DC-10's roll computers, and what the autopilot's FMS modes fly: a bank command proportional to the track change needed to close the cross-track error at a controlled angle, limited to the coupler's maximum intercept. Because both numbers are taken in the navigation unit's own frame (true north), a compass card that has drifted cannot move the aircraft off the route.

**Leg sequencing** is the moment the TO waypoint becomes the FROM waypoint. For a fly-by waypoint the computer anticipates the turn: it starts the turn early, at a distance that depends on ground speed, bank limit and the course change, so the aircraft rolls out on the next leg rather than overshooting it. A fly-over waypoint is crossed first and the turn made afterwards. Each box also has rules for **direct-to** (a new leg from present position), **intercept course** (fly the present heading until a chosen course to a fix is captured), **parallel offsets** and **holding patterns**, described in each unit's section.

There are two ways to build a descent. A **geometric path** joins altitude constraints with straight lines at a chosen angle (typically 3°) back from the end of descent; it is simple, repeatable and independent of the aircraft, which is why the HT9100 and the KC-10 FMS use it for their advisory paths. A **performance path** assumes flight idle thrust and the planned descent speed, so it follows the aircraft's own drag and wind: it is steeper at high altitude, where the true airspeed is high, and shallower below the speed limit altitude. The Pegasus and the PMS build performance paths backward from the bottom of descent, and the Pegasus flies its path with the elevator while the autothrottle holds speed.

**Economy speed** trades fuel against time. With fuel cost alone the best cruise speed is the maximum-range speed, the speed at which fuel burned per nautical mile is least; any time-related cost (crew, maintenance, schedule) pushes the best speed higher. The **cost index** expresses that ratio as one number: zero gives maximum range, a high value approaches the maximum cruise speed. The PMS accepts 0 to 255 and the Pegasus 0 to 999.

A computer that is steering the aircraft cannot let a half-typed change take effect. Every unit with a keyboard in this part therefore separates the plan being flown from the plan being edited. A change to the active route first creates a **modified** copy: the page title shows MOD, the change can be reviewed on the map and the pages, and only the EXEC key (or, on the Pegasus, the asterisked INSERT prompt) makes it active. ERASE or CANCEL MOD throws it away. Each box also keeps at least one **inactive** plan (RTE 2 on the HT9100, SEC FPLN on the KC-10, SEC F-PLN on the MD-10) for building a re-route or the next flight without disturbing the one being flown.

sections.title: Navigation data and flight plan loading
sections.summary: Where the navigation database comes from, how a box looks an identifier up, and how a planned route reaches each unit.

blocks.content: Every unit in this part reads one navigation database, shared with the other navigation systems on board. Two sources are available, and the crew choose between them. **Navigraph** is the aircraft's own navigation database, an AIRAC cycle supplied with the aircraft, and it is the default. **MSFS** is the simulator's own facility database. The selection is made on the EFB (Settings, Aircraft, **Navigation data**: MSFS or Navigraph) and, on the MD-10, also on the MCDU (MENU, NAV DATA). It is saved with the aircraft and restored on the next flight. If the selected source cannot be opened the aircraft falls back to the other one and says so: the EFB setting shows the source actually in use, and the MD-10's NAV DATA page shows it in amber.

blocks.title: What each navigation data source contains
rows: Runways (and runway waypoints such as RW27L)
SIDs, STARs, approaches and their transitions
Airport communications, localizers, terminal waypoints (KC-10 DATABASE pages)

blocks.content: Leave the source at Navigraph for normal operation. With the MSFS source the DEP/ARR, SID and STAR pages of every unit are empty, runways cannot be entered, airways cannot be typed into a route and the KC-10's airport data lists are blank. Routes imported from SimBrief still load, because the import carries every fix.

**A lookup takes time.** When the crew type an identifier the box does not already hold, it sends a query to the database and continues working; the answer arrives a frame or more later. While it waits, each box says so in its own words: STANDBY ONE on the HT9100, SEARCH IN PROGRESS on the KC-10 FMS. An identifier the database does not hold is answered NOT IN DATA BASE (HT9100, Pegasus) or NOT IN DATABASE (KC-10); an identifier that names more than one place opens the box's duplicate page (SELECT DESIRED WPT, SELECT WPT or DUPLICATE NAMES), listed nearest first, for the crew to choose.

**The cycle shown on the box** is the aircraft's database cycle. The HT9100 shows its active and inactive database on IDENT, the KC-10 FMS on START INIT 1/3, the Pegasus on A/C STATUS. NAV DATA OUT OF DATE (HT9100), DB EXPIRED (KC-10) and CHECK DATA BASE CYCLE (Pegasus) compare the cycle's dates with the date the box believes it is.

A route can always be typed in on the unit's own keyboard. It can also be loaded from the EFB's **Route** app, either from the crew's latest SimBrief flight plan or from the simulator's own planned route ([EFB, Route](efb#route-app)). The EFB only asks; the aircraft resolves each fix against the selected database and delivers the route the way the real unit would receive one: straight into the active route on the HT9100, into the secondary flight plan on the KC-10 FMS, and as an ACARS route uplink on the Pegasus.

blocks.title: What each flight management unit does with an imported route
rows: The active route of every powered unit, through the box's own ACTIVATE and EXEC. Forecast winds and any pending modification are erased; the flight number and cruise altitude are filled in
Review the LEGS pages, close discontinuities, complete PERF INIT

INDEX, SEC FPLN, ACTIVATE (5R), then EXEC. At least CDU 1 or CDU 2 must be switched on, or the load is refused
Both FMFs, as ACARS ROUTE DATA. While the FMS is dark or showing PLEASE WAIT the uplink is held and delivered when it can be

blocks.content: **In the air** an imported route starts at the leg the aircraft is on: everything before the FROM waypoint of the nearest leg is trimmed off. If the aircraft is more than 100 NM from every leg nothing is trimmed and the whole route loads. A Pegasus route longer than 100 waypoints is sent whole, but the FCOM advises against more than 100 and the EFB says so.

sections.title: HT9100 GPS/FMS
sections.summary: The DC-10's satellite navigation and flight management retrofit: three independent units, each with its own MCDU.

blocks.content: The **HT9100 GNSS Navigation Management System** (Honeywell/Trimble) is a lightweight GPS flight management system. It meets the TSO C129 and AC 20-138 standards for en-route, terminal and non-precision approach navigation, and the requirements for a primary means of navigation in oceanic and remote airspace. On the DC-10 it replaces the inertial long-range units: there is no inertial platform behind it, and its only position sensor is its own GPS receiver, backed by dead reckoning. It is fitted as a Professional equipment option in the Navigation Systems category.

Each unit has three components: the **navigation processor unit (NPU)**, which holds the receiver, the navigation database and the flight management software; the **GPS antenna**; and the **multipurpose control display unit (MCDU)** on the center pedestal. The DC-10 installation follows the Gemini Air Cargo fit: **three complete units**, GPS 1, GPS 2 and GPS 3, each with its own NPU, antenna and MCDU. The simulated units run the later software standard described in the 007F pilot's guide, which adds a vertical navigation path, a user database, along-track and place-bearing/place-bearing waypoints, abeam points and the DATA branch to the June 1996 load.

**Three independent boxes.** The three units are deliberately separate: each navigates on its own satellites, holds its own two routes and shows its own pages. They share only two things. A **position comparator** watches the three solutions and raises VERIFY POSITION on every unit if any two of them drift apart. A **crossload bus** lets the crew copy the user database from one unit to the others on the ground (MAINTENANCE, NDB CROSSLOAD). Nothing else crosses: a route typed into GPS 1 is not in GPS 2 unless the crew put it there.

**Which unit drives which seat** is chosen with the **FMS MODE** switch on the overhead panel, which is present only with the HT9100 fitted. In NORM each pilot's instruments read their own side's unit: GPS 1 for the Captain, GPS 2 for the First Officer. CAPT ON 2 puts the Captain's instruments on GPS 2; F/O ON 1 puts the First Officer's on GPS 1. “Instruments” means everything the seat takes from the unit: the HSI course deviation, the vertical deviation pointer, the EHSI route on the MFD, and the autopilot coupling when that seat's channel is in command. Each MCDU stays on its own unit whatever the switch says. GPS 3 is never selected to the instruments: it is a third, independent navigator and the crew's cross-check.

blocks.alt: DC-10-30 center pedestal with the HT9100 fit, daylight: the three HT9100 MCDUs in their pedestal positions, each screen lit on a different page (unit 1 ACT RTE 1 LEGS, unit 2 PROGRESS, unit 3 POS REF), the green EXEC light above each EXEC key visible. Inset: the overhead FMS MODE switch in NORM with its CAPT ON 2 and F/O ON 1 legends legible.
blocks.title: HT9100 MCDUs on the center pedestal, and the FMS MODE switch

blocks.content: **Power.** Each unit is supplied by its own DC bus. The NPU's power supply rides through an interruption of a fraction of a second, such as a bus transfer, without the screen blanking or the steering flagging. Past that the unit goes dark, but an internal battery keeps everything the crew entered (both routes, the active route selection, an open modification, PERF INIT, winds, the flight number) for about half a minute; a unit powered again inside that time comes back on IDENT with all of it. After a longer loss the active route is deactivated and the entries are cleared, as the pilot's guide describes. When changing from ground power to the APU, or the APU to the engines, make the change promptly.

The receiver solves for latitude, longitude, altitude and its own clock error from the pseudoranges to the satellites in view, so it needs at least four. The accuracy of that solution depends on the satellites' geometry, expressed as a dilution of precision: satellites spread across the sky give a small DOP and a tight position; satellites bunched together give a large one. The HT9100 computes its accuracy from the geometry it actually has and shows it as the **ACTUAL** figure beside the RNP on POS REF, with the number of satellites in the solution as **SV USED**.

**Integrity** is checked by RAIM: with more than four satellites (or four and the barometric altitude, which enters the solution as an extra vertical measurement) the receiver can test each range against the others and compute a protection limit. With six or more measurements (six satellites, or five and the barometric altitude) it can also identify and exclude a faulty satellite (fault detection and exclusion). If the protection limit exceeds the allowance for the phase of flight, RAIM LIMIT EXCEEDS appears with the value; if accuracy or integrity no longer meets the RNP, UNABLE RNP appears, and RNP AVAILABLE is shown once when it recovers.

**Dead reckoning.** With too few satellites to navigate, the unit annunciates DEAD RECKONING and continues on heading and true airspeed from the aircraft's sensors and the last wind it computed; POS REF's 4L prompt changes from <HDG/TAS OVERRIDE to <DR. The DR position degrades with every minute of wind error, so treat it as a short-term bridge and cross-check with radio navaids. Loss of the heading or true airspeed input is reported as HDG INPUT FAIL or TAS INPUT FAIL.

children.title: Flight phase and required navigation performance

blocks.content: The unit decides its own flight phase from the active route and its position, and the phase sets the RNP it must meet, the full-scale deflection of the HSI course bar, and the lead of the waypoint alert. The crew can enter a different RNP on POS REF (3L); an entry less stringent than the phase requires raises VERIFY RNP ENTRY, and a phase change to a more stringent RNP than the crew's entry raises VERIFY RNP-POS REF. The unit never selects the oceanic phase itself: for an oceanic or remote crossing the crew enter the RNP on POS REF.

blocks.title: HT9100 flight phases
rows: Default, and whenever there is no route or no position
Within 30 NM of the destination or the origin; after a missed approach is executed
From 2 NM before the final approach fix, flying to it, until the runway or the missed approach
Not selected automatically: the crew enter the RNP (10 NM for oceanic/remote airspace) on POS REF, and the unit stays in its en route phase

blocks.content: On the approach, UNABLE APPROACH appears if RAIM is not available at approach RNP or the unit's own destination prediction has failed. At 30 NM from the destination the unit runs its destination RAIM prediction automatically and raises CHECK DEST RAIM-POS REF if it fails. The EHSI on an MFD-equipped DC-10 uses its own full-scale values (5.0, 1.0 and 0.3 NM) for the same phases.

blocks.alt: One HT9100 MCDU, face on, lit, showing ACT RTE 1 LEGS: the 14-line by 24-character color LCD with the cyan title and page number, magenta active waypoint row, white waypoints with course and distance labels, the dashed separator and green <RTE 2 LEGS / RTE DATA> prompts, and a scratchpad entry. Around it, all 66 keys legible: six line select keys each side; function keys RTE, LEGS, DEP/ARR, HOLD, PROG, VNAV, ATC; special keys BRT/DIM, CLR, /, PREV, NEXT, MENU, DATA, EXEC with its green light above; the alphabetic and numeric keys, SP, the decimal point and +/-.
blocks.title: HT9100 MCDU

blocks.content: **The display** is a color LCD of 14 lines by 24 characters. The top line is the page title and page number; then six pairs of a small-font label line and a data line, each data line beside a line select key (LSK 1L to 6R); and the bottom line is the **scratchpad**. The colors carry meaning: **white** for data and entry error messages, **magenta** for the active leg, **yellow** for alerting messages, **cyan** for titles, page numbers and labels, and **green** for action prompts such as ACTIVATE> or <POS REPORT. Large characters are data the crew entered or verified; small characters are predicted, default or computed values. Box prompts mark an entry required for minimum operation, dash prompts an optional one. On a modified page the word MOD in the title is drawn in black on a cyan block.

blocks.content: **The scratchpad belongs to the MCDU, not the page.** What the crew type stays there as they change pages, which is how an identifier typed on one page is entered on another. A system message covers the scratchpad without consuming the entry beneath it: typing pushes the message into the background, and it returns when the entry is cleared. Entry error messages (white) can only be removed with CLR; alerting (yellow) and advisory (white) messages are also removed when their condition ends.

blocks.title: IDENT page

blocks.content: **IDENT** is the first page at power-up. It shows the aircraft model, the active navigation database (2L) with its effective dates (2R), the inactive database below it, and the software part number. The only change allowed here is the active database: copy the inactive one to the scratchpad with 3R and enter it at 2R. That is possible on the ground only and **erases any flight plan already entered**, so select the database before building the route. A database shown in yellow is corrupt. 6R goes to POS REF.

blocks.alt: HT9100 POS REF page on the ground: POS (GPS) N32°53.80 W097°02.50 at 1L; UTC(GPS) 1509.8z at 2L and GS 0KT at 2R; RNP/ACTUAL 1.00/0.24 at 3L and SV USED 7 at 3R; green <HDG/TAS OVERRIDE at 4L; INTEGRITY PREDICTION center label over green <ACT RTE at 5L and DEST RAIM> at 5R; dashed separator; green ROUTE> at 6R.
blocks.title: POS REF page

blocks.content: **POS REF** shows the GPS position (1L, which can be copied to the scratchpad for a position check), UTC from the GPS and ground speed, the RNP and the actual navigation performance (3L, where an RNP can also be entered), the satellites in the solution, the dead-reckoning prompt at 4L (<HDG/TAS OVERRIDE, or <DR in dead reckoning), the two integrity predictions (<ACT RTE at 5L for the active route, DEST RAIM> at 5R) and ROUTE> at 6R.

**DEST RAIM** predicts whether approach RNP (0.30) will be available at the destination for seven times at five-minute steps, from 15 minutes before the arrival time to 15 minutes after. The destination and arrival time default to the active route's and its ETA, and either may be entered. A NOT OK row is drawn in yellow.

Inset: RTE 1 page 2/2 with VIA/TO rows J87 IAH, DIRECT SBI, A766 EDGAR and the dashed entry row, ACTIVATE> at 6R.

Entering an airway and its exit fix strings every fix of the airway between. The last row is always an empty pair of dash prompts for the next segment.

**DEP/ARR INDEX** lists both routes' origin (<DEP and ARR>) and destination (ARR>) airports, and an OTHER line where any airport can be entered for review. **DEPARTURES** shows two independent lists for the origin: SIDs on the left, runways on the right. Choosing a SID moves it to 1L with <SEL>, shows its enroute transitions under a TRANS label and removes the other choices; pressing it again deselects it. **ARRIVALS** lists STARs on the left and, on the right, approaches above runways; choosing an approach chooses its runway, and its transitions are then listed for selection. On the active route each choice is a modification (ERASE undoes it); after EXEC the page lists everything again with <ACT beside the choices. Procedures for an OTHER airport are for review only.

blocks.title: ACT RTE LEGS page

blocks.content: **LEGS** lists the route waypoint by waypoint, five to a page, each under a label line with the course and distance of the leg to it. On an active route the first row is the **active waypoint**, drawn magenta; as it is passed the list scrolls up. The right column shows each waypoint's altitude constraint (and, with VNAV, the path angle and predicted altitude), with flight levels above the transition altitude.

Its right keys open the **WIND** page for that waypoint: up to four altitudes (entered at 1L) with a direction and speed for each (entered at the right keys), and the initial cruise altitude and temperature at 5R. Winds are kept by waypoint name, so inserting a waypoint does not move them, and an entered wind applies along the route until the next waypoint with its own entry. blocks.content: The pattern is recomputed at every passage of the fix: the turn radius from the holding true airspeed plus the wind at 25° of bank, limited to 30° for patterns and entries, and the leg length from the wind along the inbound course. The size is computed for no more than the FAA maximum holding speed for the altitude (200 KIAS to 6,000 ft, 230 KIAS to 14,000 ft, 265 KIAS above); a faster aircraft gets HIGH HOLDING SPEED as the fix approaches.

The HT9100 does not generate published holding patterns automatically unless the hold is part of a terminal procedure. Check every hold's inbound course, turn direction and leg length against the chart.

blocks.content: **DESCENT** shows, after the top of descent, how far the aircraft is LONG or SHORT of the path along its own angle, the vertical track error (to the nearest 10 ft) and the present vertical speed. Below are the active vertical waypoint (the top of descent before it is reached, then the next point where the path changes), the one after it and the end of descent, each with altitude, distance to go and vertical speed required. 5L takes any waypoint and altitude for a vertical bearing (VB) from present position, with the aircraft's flight path angle beside it. 6R switches the vertical deviation output to the instruments ON or OFF.

blocks.title: PROGRESS page 1

blocks.content: **PROGRESS 1/2**, titled with the flight number, shows the last waypoint with its altitude, actual time and fuel; the TO waypoint (magenta) with its direct distance and ETA; the next waypoint and the destination with distance along the route and ETA; and at 5R, within 200 NM of it, the time and distance to the top of descent. **PROGRESS 2/2** shows true airspeed and ground speed, wind, heading and track, drift angle, cross-track error, track angle error, the vertical track error once past the top of descent, SAT, fuel used in total and per engine (numbered left to right), and the calculated fuel quantity (takeoff fuel less fuel used). True airspeed and heading are magenta if entered by hand and yellow if failed. **POS REPORT** (PROGRESS 6L) gathers the last waypoint, altitude, speed, TO and next waypoints with times, destination ETA, temperature and wind for a voice position report.

children.title: DATA pages and the user database

blocks.title: DATA INDEX
rows: REF NAV DATA: a database fix's type, position, elevation, magnetic variation and frequency
NEAREST INDEX, then the nearest airports, VOR/DMEs, NDBs or waypoints with course and distance, nearest first
FIX INFO: bearing and distance from a database fix to the aircraft (the radial the aircraft is on); <ERASE FIX at 6L
USER WPT LIST and USER WPT
MESSAGE RECALL (every message since power-up), NDB CROSSLOAD, and maintenance pages

blocks.content: **The user database** holds up to 128 routes and 256 waypoints in non-volatile memory. Each unit has its own, and each is kept with the aircraft between sessions. A **user waypoint** is defined on USER WPT by an identifier of up to five characters and a latitude/longitude or a place/bearing/distance or place-bearing/place-bearing (SAVE USER WPT> at 5R); once saved, its name can be entered anywhere a fix is accepted. A **user route** is saved from RTE page 1 (SAVE RTE# at 5R) and recalled from USER ROUTES (RTE 4R) or at CO ROUTE, into an inactive route, as flown or inverted.

**NDB CROSSLOAD** (MAINTENANCE INDEX 5L, on the ground only) copies the user database between a unit and its cross-side unit: units 1 and 2 with each other, unit 3 with unit 1. On either unit of the pair select <TRANSMIT to send its database or RECEIVE> to take the other's, then <USER DB (3L) and BEGIN TRANSFER> (3R); the page counts the transfer in per cent, with ABORT> while it runs, and the received database replaces the receiving unit's own. COMM FAIL TRANSFER ABORTED means the cross-side unit is not powered. Because routes are not crossloaded directly in this installation, the user database is the way to copy a typed route into the other units: save it on unit 1, crossload, and load it from USER ROUTES on units 2 and 3.

Each unit holds two routes, **RTE 1** and **RTE 2**, each of up to 200 legs (ROUTE FULL refuses anything more). A route that is not active is edited in place. A route becomes active in two steps: ACTIVATE> on its RTE page, then EXEC. ACTIVATE> is offered only once the PERF INIT entries are complete (gross weight or ZFW, fuel, reserves and cruise altitude); until then 6R reads PERF INIT>. From then on every change to it is a **modification**: the title shows MOD, <ERASE appears at 6L and the EXEC light comes on, and nothing changes in the steering until EXEC is pressed. ERASE restores the unmodified route. The inactive route is the place to build a re-route in flight; to fly it, enter the next fix at its LEGS 1L, ACTIVATE and EXEC.

A route can also be loaded from the EFB, which places it in the active route of every powered unit (see [Loading a planned route](#fm-route-loading)). Either way, review the LEGS pages against the flight plan and chart, waypoint names, magnetic courses and distances, and close every discontinuity before departure.

**Sequencing.** The unit sequences fly-by waypoints early by its turn anticipation and flies the turn; a waypoint passed wide is sequenced only within 20 NM abeam of it. Reaching a discontinuity, or the end of the route, ends guidance and the autopilot reverts to heading.

**Direct-to.** Enter the fix at 1L of ACT RTE LEGS page 1 (a fix already in the route can be downselected from its own row). The modification shows the new leg from present position. Two options are offered before EXEC, one or the other: **INTC CRS** at 6R flies the present track until it meets a chosen inbound course to the fix (the original course is offered with a chevron for a route fix; type a course for any other), with NOT ON INTERCEPT HDG and the EXEC light out while the present track cannot meet the course short of the fix; **ABEAM PTS** at 4R projects the bypassed waypoints onto the new direct path (those within 700 NM, taking the winds entered within 100 NM of each) so that reporting points and winds are kept. RTE COPY at 5R puts the route as it was into the other slot.

**Holding.** Press HOLD. With no hold in the route, LEGS opens with a HOLD AT prompt: enter a route fix at 6L for a hold after it, or line-select PPOS at 6R for a hold at present position on the present track (its course cannot be changed). An off-route fix typed into HOLD AT appears as HOLD AT XXX in the scratchpad and is placed at the LEGS row before which it is to go, with a discontinuity after it (NO EXIT DISCONTINUITY) until the crew join the route. Each is a modification: review the HOLD page and EXEC. The hold is a leg of its own after its fix and can be deleted without leaving a gap. EXIT HOLD arms the exit and the aircraft leaves at the next passage of the fix (EXIT HOLD ARMED a minute out); a direct-to out of the hold also ends it. MOD HOLD PENDING warns of an unexecuted hold modification as its fix approaches.

**Parallel offset.** On the active RTE page, enter L or R and a distance of 1 to 99 NM at OFFSET (6R), for example L25, and EXEC; airborne and outside a SID only. The unit flies the offset and cancels it at the end of the route segment where it cannot continue, with END OF OFFSET up to two minutes before. DELETE at 6R and EXEC cancels it.

**Approaches and the missed approach.** An approach chosen on ARRIVALS replaces the destination leg; its missed approach is held in the route after the runway and is not flown until the crew start it. LEGS lists the held missed approach under a separator with a green <EXECUTE MISSED APPROACH prompt: pressing it arms the missed approach as a modification and EXEC starts it. Pressing **TO/GA** on the center throttle in the air does the same at once, without EXEC. The leg to the missed approach point stays active, so an early go-around still flies to that point first; executing the missed approach takes the unit out of approach mode immediately. A new approach chosen during the missed approach replaces it and goes direct to its first fix.

The HT9100 gives **lateral steering only**; its vertical path is advisory, for the crew to fly with the autopilot's pitch modes. The path is geometric. It is built backward from the **end of descent (E/D)**, the last at-constraint below the cruise altitude, at the PERF INIT descent angle (or a procedure's own angle into its leg). An at-constraint pins the path; at-or-above, at-or-below and window constraints move it only where a straight line would break them. At the speed transition altitude the path includes a deceleration segment, level and about 10 NM long in this installation; a constraint above that altitude removes the segment. A path that would rise toward E/D, or that misses a constraint, is reported as ACT DESCENT PATH INVALID; a modification that leaves no path at all shows DESCENT PATH DELETED.

**The vertical deviation** is output from 30 seconds before the top of descent to E/D, with VDEV ON on the DESCENT page. It drives both glideslope pointers, on the HSI and the ADI, of a seat whose nav source switch is at HSI NAV, at a full scale of 500 ft en route and in the terminal area and 150 ft on the approach; the HSI's vertical deviation window then shows the navigation computer's deviation, not ILS. The MFD's EHSI shows the same deviation on its FMS vertical scale (500 ft terminal, 200 ft approach), with digits beyond full scale. The output is removed in a discontinuity, an offset, a crew hold, the missed approach and with UNABLE RNP. VERT TRK CHANGE ALERT precedes each change of vertical track and END OF DESCENT the last constrained leg.

The vertical deviation looks like a glideslope but is not one. It is a computed path referenced to barometric altitude, and the HT9100 provides no vertical guidance to the autopilot. Fly it with V/S or the altitude modes, observing the published minimum altitudes.

The HT9100's performance function is light. PERF INIT's cruise altitude and descent angle shape the descent path and its top of descent; its weights, fuel and reserves complete the page so that a route can be activated, and CHECK FUEL-VNAV is raised when the fuel on board falls below the reserves. Fuel used is integrated from the engines' fuel flows, per engine and in total, on PROGRESS 2/2. The leg times on RTE DATA are computed at the present ground speed, and the top of descent on PROGRESS 1/2 is given with its distance and an ETA at the present ground speed. The wind on PROGRESS 2/2 is the one the unit computes from heading, true airspeed and GPS ground velocity. The unit does not compute takeoff or landing speeds.

Each seat's long-range data comes from the unit the FMS MODE switch gives it. With that pilot's nav source switch at **HSI NAV**, the HSI course bar shows the unit's cross-track deviation at the phase's full scale and the TO/FROM, and the glideslope pointers show the vertical deviation when it is output. On a DC-10 with the electronic flight instruments, the EHSI draws the unit's route and active leg.

**Autopilot.** With the nav source switch of the seat in command at HSI NAV, the RAD/INS pushbutton arms the autopilot's FMS mode: FMS on the arm line of the flight mode annunciator, FMS CAP during the intercept and FMS TRK once established. The coupler flies the unit's cross-track error and track angle error, re-captures at each leg change, and feeds forward the bank of a holding turn or arc. During an INTC CRS it holds the present track until the course is captured. If the unit has nothing to steer (a discontinuity, the end of the route, a unit not yet navigating) the mode drops back to armed and the heading modes take over. The autothrottle and the autopilot's pitch modes take nothing from the HT9100. See [Automatic Flight](automatic-flight) for the modes and their annunciations.

Messages appear in the scratchpad in three classes. **Alerting** messages (yellow) and **advisory** messages (white) are conditions: they stand while the condition exists, can be removed with CLR, and are removed automatically when the condition is corrected; if the condition returns, the message returns. **Entry error** messages (white) answer a keystroke and are removed only with CLR. MESSAGE RECALL (DATA, MAINTENANCE) lists every message since power-up.

children.summary: Preparing the HT9100 for departure, flying the route, and the common in-flight changes.

blocks.content: The steps below are done on the unit that will drive each seat: GPS 1 by the Captain and GPS 2 by the First Officer, with GPS 3 as the cross-check. If the route is loaded from the EFB it is already active in every powered unit, and the steps reduce to checking it and completing PERF INIT.

GPS position within 1 NM of the gate, UTC correct
Airways (VIA) and fixes (TO) from the flight plan
Check names, courses and distances; close discontinuities

items.item: PERF INIT (RTE 6R PERF INIT>, or VNAV)

From the load sheet; GR WT computed

Forecast winds at the cruise levels for waypoints where they change

blocks.content: **Copying the route to the other units** (on the ground). Save the finished route on unit 1 (RTE page 1, SAVE RTE# 5R). Crossload the user database (DATA, MAINTENANCE>, <NDB CROSSLOAD): on unit 1 select <TRANSMIT, which sends to unit 2, and on unit 3 select RECEIVE>, which takes unit 1's; on each, <USER DB and BEGIN TRANSFER>. Then on units 2 and 3 load the route from USER RTES (RTE 4R) into RTE 1, complete PERF INIT, and ACTIVATE and EXEC. Alternatively enter the route on each unit by hand, or load it from the EFB, which fills every powered unit at once.

items.action: As required for the departure (HSI NAV for an RNAV departure)
Set to the first leg's track
Active waypoint is the first fix of the departure

blocks.content: **After takeoff**, with the nav source switch at HSI NAV, push RAD/INS to arm the FMS capture; FMS CAP and then FMS TRK follow. Monitor sequencing on LEGS. Re-enter CRZ ALT on PERF INIT when cleared to a new cruise level.

items: **Direct to a fix:** LEGS, downselect or type the fix, line-select it to 1L, check the MOD page, EXEC.
**Intercept a course to a fix:** as direct-to, then type the inbound course at INTC CRS (6R) if it is not offered, EXEC. Keep the heading until the course is captured.
**Close a discontinuity:** downselect the waypoint after the ROUTE DISCONTINUITY banner and line-select it into the THEN boxes, EXEC.
**Delete a waypoint:** CLR on an empty scratchpad to show DELETE, line-select the waypoint, EXEC (or move the following waypoint up to it).
**Change destination:** RTE page 1, new airport at DEST 1R, complete the route on RTE or LEGS, EXEC.
**Major re-route:** build it in RTE 2 (RTE COPY first if most of the route stays); when cleared, enter the next fix at RTE 2 LEGS 1L, ACTIVATE, EXEC.
**Hold:** HOLD, line-select the fix into HOLD AT (or PPOS), review the HOLD page, EXEC. To leave: HOLD, EXIT HOLD, EXEC.
**Offset:** RTE page 1, type L or R and the distance (L25) at OFFSET 6R, EXEC. To cancel: DELETE to 6R, EXEC.

**Arrival:** DEP/ARR, ARR>, select STAR, transition and approach; LEGS to clean up discontinuities; EXEC. For a GPS approach check DEST RAIM, set the nav source switch to HSI NAV and keep the FMS mode engaged; the unit enters approach mode 2 NM before the final approach fix.
**Go-around:** TO/GA, or <EXECUTE MISSED APPROACH on LEGS and EXEC; push RAD/INS to fly the missed approach procedure.

sections.title: Performance Management System
sections.summary: The DC-10-30 and -40's vertical performance computer: economy speeds, thrust targets, optimum altitudes and a profile to the bottom of descent.

blocks.content: The **Performance Management System (PMS)** was designed to take the vertical half of the flight off the crew's hands at a time when fuel had suddenly become the largest cost of operating a widebody. It continuously computes an optimum vertical profile from present position to the **bottom of descent (BOD)**: the climb, the cruise with any step climbs, and the idle descent, with the speeds and thrust settings that minimize cost for the entered cost index. In the aircraft as built it was integrated with the flight guidance system and the autothrottle, and when the crew engaged **PERF** it flew that profile itself, commanding pitch through the autopilot and thrust through the autothrottle, with PERF annunciated in both the autothrottle and pitch windows of the flight mode annunciator.

The PMS is fitted to the **DC-10-30** (CF6-50C2, rated in N1) and the **DC-10-40** (JT9D-59A, rated in EPR), including their freighter and tanker variants and the KDC-10. It is a freeware option in the PMS category of Aircraft Configuration, OFF by default. (The option is also offered on the DC-10-10 and -15, for which no PMS is simulated: there, selecting it removes the AUTO BRAKE panel and fits a unit that does nothing.) The computation is called the **Performance Optimization Algorithm (POA)**; in the simulation it is built from the simulated aircraft's own drag, thrust, fuel flow and thrust rating tables, so that its predictions match the aircraft being flown.

blocks.title: Advisory in this simulation
blocks.content: The PMS computes and displays everything described here, but the switching unit that would put its commands on the autopilot and autothrottle is not simulated: PERF cannot be engaged. The crew fly the PMS speeds and thrust targets with the autothrottle and autopilot modes on the glareshield. The CLB, CRZ and DES lamps show the mode PERF would engage into, and the CDU MESSAGE lamps stay dark.

**Three units.** The **control display unit (CDU)** is on the center pedestal, in the position the AUTO BRAKE panel occupies on an aircraft without the PMS. The **performance management computer unit (PMCU)** and the **switching unit** are in the avionics compartment. The CDU and the PMCU are fed separately from 115 V AC, so a dark CDU does not mean a dead computer: the PMCU carries on computing and its data is there when the CDU returns. All essential data is retained through a loss and return of power in flight; the profile is simply recomputed.

blocks.title: What the PMCU reads
rows: Baro-corrected altitude, vertical speed, CAS, Mach, TAS, SAT
Present state; CADC FAIL disengages PERF in the aircraft and is reported
Position, ground speed, true track and heading
Counting down the trip and BOD distances; a BOD defined by latitude/longitude
N1, fuel flow, bleed and shaft loads
Counting down gross weight and fuel; engine-out detection; installed thrust limits
Which thrust limit the PMS computes
The armed altitude, mode prediction, ARM ALT? reminders
Minimum speed band, ADD DRAG / REMOVE DRAG, ground-only rules

blocks.content: The PMS does not read gross weight or fuel from the aircraft. The crew enter both on the PLAN page and the PMS counts them down by the engines' fuel flow from that moment, which is why every prediction of weight and fuel is a prediction from now rather than from the gate.

**The speed band.** No PMS speed is ever outside **VMIN** to **VMAX**. VMIN is the higher of the 1.3 g low-speed buffet speed and 1.5 times the clean stall speed, or 1.5 times the stall speed with slats extended; the buffet margin is applied on top of the load factor of the present bank angle, so VMIN rises in a turn. VMAX is the lower of the 1.3 g high-speed buffet speed and VMO/MMO, and the PMS keeps 5 kt below it. An edited speed outside the band is refused with VMAX or VMIN and the limiting value.

**Economy speeds.** In cruise the POA finds the Mach that minimizes cost per nautical mile, fuel flow plus a time cost proportional to the cost index, divided by ground speed. At cost index 0 that is the maximum-range Mach; a higher index moves it toward the top of the band. The economy climb is close to the maximum rate of climb speed and is flown at the climb thrust limit; the descent is at idle, on the descent speed schedule (M.82/300 kt as set in the shop, the NON OPT default) or the optimum descent speed.

**Altitudes.** The **maximum altitude** is the lowest of 42,000 ft, the altitude at which 300 ft/min of climb remains on cruise thrust at the economy Mach, and the 1.3 g buffet altitude at that Mach. The **optimum altitude** is the one with the least cost per mile at the economy Mach, never above the maximum; on a short trip it is capped where climb and descent still leave cruise to fly. Both are shown on every PERF page's title line as OPT/MAX (for example FL310/332). With an engine out the title shows instead the **2-engine maximum altitude**, the altitude at which 100 ft/min of climb remains on two engines at maximum continuous thrust.

**The profile.** From present position to the BOD: a climb at the climb limit on the climb schedule, including the 10,000 ft speed change and the level-off at an armed altitude below the planned one; a cruise in 50 NM steps with a **step climb** wherever the aircraft has become light enough for the next planned altitude; and an idle descent built backward from the BOD through up to two **crosspoints** (crew-defined altitude/distance points). Each event carries its distance and time from present position, gross weight and, when fuel was entered, fuel on board. A full solution takes about two seconds and is repeated continuously; while one is being computed the BOD weights show ---.- and the slew arrows flash.

**Thrust limits.** The PMS computes engine limits in the same way as, but independently of, the thrust rating computer, from the mode selected on the thrust rating indicator: CL gives the climb limit (CL), ALTN CL on the -40 the alternate climb limit (ALCL), CR or MCR on the -30 the cruise limit (CR), and any other mode the maximum continuous limit (MCT). If speed cannot be held on the cruise limit, as in a high-altitude turn, the PMS selects CL automatically; after an engine loss it selects MCT. On the -30 the limits and targets are in N1; on the -40 in EPR.

blocks.title: PMS control display unit

blocks.content: **The display** is a four-line, 24-character amber LED matrix with no colors and no second character size. The top line does two jobs: characters 1 to 12 are the **page title**, characters 13 to 24 are the **scratchpad**, which normally shows page content (the OPT/MAX altitudes on the PERF pages) until the crew type into it or a message appears. A long entry, such as a latitude and longitude, grows leftward into the title. The other three lines are data lines, each acted on by the **line select key** beside it, drawn (1), (2) and (3) on the left of the display. There is no label line and no right-hand key: a line select key acts on its whole line. Arrows in the top right corner show which way the slew switch has more to offer.

blocks.content: **Entering data.** A line with several fields is addressed with slashes: 270/310/350 loads three cruise altitudes, /350 only the second, //390 only the third. To clear one field, press CLEAR to put the word CLEAR in the scratchpad, add slashes before it to address the field (/CLEAR, //CLEAR), and press the line's key. Flight levels are typed as their digits (310), Mach numbers as their fraction (.82), and a negative wind with the alternate function key and 7. Before a gross weight is entered only the PLAN and STS pages can be called up.
The simulated PMS is pinned for metric weight display: gross weight and fuel are entered and shown in tonnes (234.5T), not thousands of pounds. One tonne is 2,204.6 lb.

Fuel on board. Enables all fuel predictions; BOD fuel computed on the right
Trip distance, NM, which activates the profile (minimum 50 NM on the ground). In the air this line becomes the BOD line: BOD ALT and distance, loadable as ALT/DIS, ALT or /DIS

blocks.content: The default **BOD** is 30 NM short of the remaining trip distance, at 10,000 ft and 250 kt; with no other definition the PMS counts the distance down on the INS ground speed once airborne. The BOD can be redefined on the expanded BOD page (PLAN, then (3) with the scratchpad empty) by latitude and longitude or by a VOR frequency, radial and distance; within 200 NM a latitude/longitude BOD is measured from the INS position. **REPLAN** (PLAN, CLEAR, (3), then confirm) returns the PMS to NON OPT modes, keeps GWT and FUEL counting down, and clears all other profile data.

**PLAN-CRZ** (slew up from PLAN) is optional; with nothing on it the POA flies an unconstrained optimum profile with zero wind and a standard day. Line (1) takes up to three planned cruise altitudes (270/310/350), which the PMS sorts and uses for step climbs. Line (2) takes the average wind component for the cruise, plus for a tailwind and minus for a headwind, up to 250 kt. Line (3) on the ground takes the temperature, or the deviation from standard after a slash, at the initial cruise level (CHECK TEMPERATURE beyond 40 °C from standard); in the air it shows the 2-engine maximum altitude with its distance and time. **PLN CRZ W/V** refines the cruise wind by altitude: three lines, defaulting to 4,000 ft above and below the cruise level, with the measured wind on the middle line; a wind shear of more than 20 kt per 1,000 ft is refused (CHK WND PROFILE). **PLN DES W/V** takes a descent wind as altitude/direction/speed (150/80/45).

Each function key calls up its mode's page, and each mode has sub-modes on pages the slew switch reaches in a ring. All share one layout: the title with the sub-mode and OPT/MAX altitudes; line (1) the speed and the thrust target (N1 on the -30, EPR on the -40); line (2) the thrust limit in force (CL LIM, CR LIM, ALCL LIM or MCT LIM); and line (3) the next vertical event with its altitude, distance and time, or the crew's inquiry. When a page offers a sub-mode the crew have not selected, SEL and SPD alternate on line (1) and pressing (1) selects it.

blocks.alt: PMS CLB OPT page on the LED display: CLB OPT FL310/332 with slew arrows; SPD[250] and N1 103.2; CL LIM 103.2; 308KT 10000 / 12NM 0:03.

PERF sub-modes

The higher of 1.5 Vs clean and the 1.3 g low-speed buffet speed (maximum angle)

The economy speed at the flight level shown

(2) calls the page, (2) again selects it at 1,000 ft/min; V/S edits 200 to 6,000 ft/min (MAX RATE if idle cannot achieve it); CLEAR into (1) lets the speed vary at idle
After an engine loss above the 2-engine maximum altitude

blocks.content: **Line (3) inquiries.** On CLB, CRZ, DES and WPTS, an altitude entered at (3) shows the distance and time to reach it, a /distance the altitude there, and ALT/DIS creates a **crosspoint** (up to two) that the descent must meet. A climb inquiry is valid only to the next top of climb, and CHECK ENTRY answers an altitude below the aircraft (or above 42,000 ft) in the climb, or above it in the descent. CLEAR, (3) removes an inquiry.

blocks.alt: PMS DES [NON OPT] page on the LED display: DES[NON OPT] FL350/362; SPD[M.820/300] FLT IDLE; DES[V/S]NOW? SHORT 1.5NM; 250KT 10000 / 55NM 0:12.
blocks.title: DES page

blocks.content: **Starting the descent.** Within five minutes of the top of descent, with a lower altitude set in ALT SEL, line (1) lights with SEL and SPD flashing: pressing (1) enables the descent for automatic entry at the top of descent. Without a lower altitude armed, ARM ALT? appears. SELECT DES is shown within 3 NM of the top of descent if the descent is not enabled, and PAST TOD 3 NM after it. Once descending, line (2) shows how far the aircraft is **LONG** or **SHORT** of making the BOD at idle, and the non-clearable ADD DRAG or REMOVE DRAG advises the speed brakes.

**WPTS** lists the vertical events ahead, each with altitude, distance and time: a speed change at 10,000 ft (for example 308KT 10000), ARM* for a level-off at an armed altitude, TOC*, STEP*, TOD* (shown with the fuel on board), X-PT* for each crosspoint and BOD*. Slewing reaches the expanded pages: **PPOS**, with position, TAS, wind, SAT, ground speed, track, heading and drift; one **WPT X-PT** page per crosspoint (and an empty one while there is room for another), where a crosspoint is defined by ALT/DIS and optionally placed by latitude/longitude or VOR frequency/radial/distance, with its speed; and **WPT BOD**, with the BOD's speed and wind and its geographic definition.

blocks.title: STS page
rows: STS, airframe and engine (DC10-30 -50C2 or DC10-40 -59A), software -005
FAULT STATUS ?: the current faults, three to a page
KD/KF: drag and fuel flow factors, -9.9 to +9.9 %, default 0
DES: the default descent schedule (M.82/300KT); changed on the ground only, and kept as the new default

blocks.content: The cost index and the two factors all move the optimum speeds and every prediction: KD scales the aircraft's drag, KF its fuel flow, to match an individual airframe.

**Mode logic.** The PMS's own mode follows the aircraft's state against ALT SEL, each new state having to persist for 1.2 seconds before it is taken. More than 512 ft below ALT SEL and climbing or level is CLB; within ±512 ft of ALT SEL is CRZ; descending more than 240 ft/min towards a lower ALT SEL is DES; with no ALT SEL the vertical speed alone decides. In this simulation that mode drives the CLB, CRZ and DES lamps and the advisories, and the crew's speed and thrust selections on each page decide the profile the POA computes.

**Flying the PMS targets.** With PERF unavailable, use the PMS as a performance computer: set the autothrottle speed or the thrust rating mode and the autopilot's IAS/MACH or V/S modes to the speed and thrust on the active PERF page. In the climb the thrust target equals the climb limit; in cruise it is the N1 or EPR that holds the economy speed level at the flight level shown; in the descent it is idle (FLT IDLE), or the N1 needed to hold the DES [V/S] speed and rate. The speeds change through the flight as the weight falls, so check the PERF page at each event.

**Engine failure.** The PMS detects an engine loss from a lost N1 signal or an N1 well below the other two, selects the MCT limit at once (SELECT MCT LIMIT reminds the crew to select it on the thrust rating indicator) and replaces OPT/MAX with the 2-engine maximum altitude. Below that altitude it keeps computing a three-engine profile until the crew confirm: CONFIRM ENGINE FAILURE alternates with the 2-engine line on PLAN-CRZ, and (3) confirms it, after which the profiles are computed for two engines. Above the 2-engine maximum the failure is confirmed automatically and the PMS enters **DRIFTDOWN**, a descent sub-mode annunciated by the DES lamp, with the minimum drag speed at MCT down to the 2-engine level. Planned cruise altitudes cannot be entered in DRIFTDOWN (NO ENTRY).

Several messages may compete for the scratchpad. In order of priority: refusals of a data entry; clearable fault messages; other clearable advisories; non-clearable advisories; non-clearable fault messages. Each CLEAR clears one clearable message; a non-clearable one is only overwritten by CLEAR and returns, and several non-clearables alternate. A message also clears itself when its condition ends. A refused entry is held behind its message: the first CLEAR brings it back for correction.

children.title: How to: using the PMS through a flight

items.action: Cruise altitudes, wind component, temperature or deviation

items.item: PLN CRZ W/V, PLN DES W/V

items.action: COST index and KD/KF as required

items.item: MAX LAND WT?, CHK BOD FUEL

items: **Climb.** After takeoff press CLB. CLB OPT shows the speed (250 kt bracketed below 10,000 ft) and the N1 or EPR target, equal to the climb limit. Set the clearance altitude in ALT SEL (ARM ALT? reminds you). When the restriction no longer applies, press CLEAR then (1) twice to show the unrestricted optimum speed. Use CLB MAX for a maximum-angle climb, or enter a speed for CLB [NON OPT].

**Cruise.** Press CRZ. Fly the CRZ OPT Mach; the N1 target is the setting that holds it level. Line (3) shows the next event (STEP* or TOD*). STEP CLB? appears five minutes before a step point: obtain the clearance and set the higher altitude in ALT SEL. Use HOLD/ENDUR for holding speed.

**Descent.** Within five minutes of TOD set the cleared lower altitude in ALT SEL, press DES and press (1) when SEL/SPD flash. At TOD reduce to idle and descend at the DES speed; watch LONG/SHORT on line (2) and ADD DRAG or REMOVE DRAG. Define crosspoints with ALT/DIS at line (3) for crossing restrictions. Use DES [V/S] ((2) twice) for a constant-rate descent.
**Engine failure.** Select MCT on the thrust rating indicator, confirm the failure on PLAN-CRZ with (3) if asked, and follow DRIFTDOWN to the 2-engine level if above it.
**Re-plan.** For a diversion or a new trip: PLAN, CLEAR, (3), confirm REPLAN, then enter the new BOD altitude and distance on line (3).

sections.title: KC-10 Flight Management System
sections.summary: The tanker's GPS/inertial FMS: three CDUs that are themselves the computers, one shared data set, and the mission, radio and IFF pages.

blocks.content: The KC-10A's **Flight Management System** is a military navigation and mission computer built around three **control display units (CDUs)** on the center pedestal. Unlike an airliner FMS with separate computers behind the keyboards, the CDUs are the computers: CDU 1 hosts **FMS1**, CDU 2 hosts **FMS2**, and CDU 3 is a third head working on FMS1's side. They share a MIL-STD-1553B data bus with three **LTN-101 inertial navigation units (INUs)**, three **GPS receivers** (GPS1 and GPS2 civil, GPS3 military with precise positioning), the bus interface units, the air data computers and the radios.

Beyond navigation and flight planning, the FMS replaces several control heads: it tunes and controls the two **TACAN** sets and two **ADF** receivers (the KC-10A has no TACAN or ADF control head), initializes and monitors the INUs, carries the **air refueling mission patterns** (racetracks, orbits, rendezvous and intercepts), and on this aircraft, with TCTO 1308 incorporated, controls the **IFF** and the TCAS and hosts the **data link** pages. This section concentrates on navigation, flight planning and performance; the radios are described in [Navigation](navigation), the IFF in [Surveillance](surveillance), data link in [Communications](communications), and the refueling procedures in [Air Refueling](air-refueling).

blocks.alt: One KC-10A FMS CDU, face on, lit, showing ACT LEGS 1/4: cyan title, cyan FROM waypoint PEABO with SEQUENCE AUTO/INHIBIT at 1R (AUTO green), the active leg 079° 115NM and TO waypoint BUM in magenta with ---/FL290 at 2R, following waypoints in white, the divider and LEG WIND> at 6R, the scratchpad between cyan brackets and the annunciation line at the bottom. Around the screen all 75 keys legible: six line keys each side; IDX, MSN, COM, NAV, IFF, M3, MSG on the upper row; DIR, FPLN, LEGS, DEP/ARR, PERF, PREV, NEXT, EXEC on the lower row; BRT and DIM; CLR DEL, +/-, /, DATA, INAV, PROG, STAT, MARK; the alphanumeric keys with SP and the decimal point.
blocks.title: KC-10 FMS CDU

blocks.content: **One data set, three heads.** While the bus is joined, the two FMS sides work on one shared data set: an entry made on any CDU goes into the same flight plans, and every CDU shows the result. What belongs to each CDU is only its display: the page it shows, its scratchpad and which annunciations its crew member has viewed. Each CDU can therefore be used independently and simultaneously by the pilot, copilot and flight engineer. (The aircraft's FMS BUS SPLIT function, which separates the two sides with their own copies of the data, is not available in the simulation: the bus is always joined.)

**Power.** Each CDU is switched by its own toggle on the right side of the **aft overhead panel** (CDU 1, CDU 2 and CDU 3) and protected by its own circuit breaker. The switches cold-start OFF; on an aircraft started with engines running they are found ON. If a CDU's supply is lost while it is switched on, the INU batteries carry it for 30 seconds (its status reads DGR); a CDU switched OFF goes dark at once. While either CDU 1 or CDU 2 runs, the data set is kept. If both go dark, the flight plans and the initialization entries are lost; the PILOT WPT LIST, the data cartridge and the mark points survive.

blocks.alt: KC-10A flight deck: the center pedestal with the three FMS CDUs (CDU1 left, CDU2 right, CDU3 aft) and the two display control panels between the radar control and the CDUs; inset of the aft overhead panel's right side showing the three CDU power toggle switches labeled CDU 1, CDU 2, CDU 3, all ON.
blocks.title: CDUs and CDU power switches

blocks.content: Each FMS side computes several **navigation solutions** from the sensors: each INU on its own (INU1, INU2, INU3), each INU blended with a civil GPS (CIV1 from INU1/GPS1, CIV2 from INU2/GPS2), and each blended with the military GPS3 (MIL1, MIL2). Each side flies one **designated solution**, normally CIV1 for FMS1 and CIV2 for FMS2, chosen on INAV SELECT. In civil operating mode the quality is shown as **ANP** (actual navigation performance); in military mode as **EPU** (estimated position uncertainty). A GPS-aided solution washes INU drift out continuously; an INU-only solution coasts on the platform and carries whatever error it has. CHK FMS1-FMS2 POS appears when the two sides' positions differ by more than the active RNP, and CHK FMS1 GPS (or FMS2) when a side's solution has lost its GPS.

**INU alignment.** The INUs align on the ground in about **10 minutes** from a known position. Normally the GPS position initializes the FMS and the INUs automatically; otherwise the crew enter the position on START INIT 2/3 and command INIT INU on 3/3. Moving the aircraft during alignment interrupts it (EXCESS INU MOTION) until the motion stops. An INU that loses navigation in flight reverts to attitude only (ATT) and cannot be realigned until on the ground. The INU mode selectors and the inertial theory are described in [Navigation](navigation).

blocks.title: Flight modes and RNP
rows: Default (crew-selectable to OCEANIC on FMS INAV)
Airborne within 31 NM of the destination; the FLIGHT MODE key is then disabled
From 2 NM before a database approach's final approach fix, flying to it

blocks.content: A crew RNP between 0.15 and 4.00 NM may be entered on FMS INAV; one larger than the base RNP is shown in amber. The ANP or EPU turns amber when it exceeds the RNP, with CHK FMS1 ANP (civil) or CHK FMS1 NAV ERR (military). TO/GA, a direct-to (other than to the final approach fix) or the missed approach returns the APPROACH mode to TERMINAL.

**The screen** has 15 lines of up to 24 characters: a title line, six pairs of a label line and a data line, the **scratchpad** framed by cyan brackets, and at the bottom the **FMS annunciation line**, which shows the highest-priority annunciation, the MSG cue at its left and EXEC when a modification is pending. The CDU has no separate annunciator lamps; the MSG and EXEC key legends light with their cues. Colors: **cyan** for titles, labels, the scratchpad brackets, dividers and the FROM waypoint; **magenta** for the TO waypoint and active leg (the color of the flight plan on the EHSI); **green** for a selected mode or toggle position; **white** for data; **amber** for an out-of-date, failed or out-of-limits item. Large characters are crew entries, small characters computed values.

NAV RADIO CONTROL: TACAN and ADF

blocks.content: **Scratchpad rules.** A scratchpad message replaces the entry until it is cleared; keys typed over a message are ignored until CLR DEL is pressed. A line key pressed under a message does nothing, except under INVALID ENTRY, where it tries the text beneath again. A line key that refuses an entry answers with its reason (NO ENTRY ALLOWED, NOT ON GROUND, FUNCTION UNAVAILABLE and so on).

blocks.title: KC-10 FMS entry formats
rows: Hemisphere first; four digits of latitude and five of longitude; whole degrees need no minutes. /NAME may be added
Five characters: N = north/west, E = north/east, S = south/east, W = south/west; the letter in third place for longitude of 100° or more
Three-digit bearing (magnetic, or true with T), 0.1 to 199.9 NM; /NAME may be added
Becomes a place/bearing/distance waypoint on the first base; NO INTERSECTION if the bearings never cross
Searched in the database and the PILOT WPT LIST; SELECT WPT for duplicates
A at or above, B at or below, S a step climb altitude (one altitude field per waypoint)
Speed 105 to 370 KIAS; altitude -2,000 to 65,000 ft or FL000 to FL650
IDENT/0 on that waypoint's own row
0.1 to 99.9 NM; L or minus left, R or plus right

blocks.content: A waypoint entered into a plan with a /NAME is stored in the PILOT WPT LIST first (DUPLICATE PILOT WPT if the name is taken, PLT WPT LIST FULL at 200). Along-track entries (IDENT/DIST) and Mach constraints are answered FUNCTION UNAVAILABLE.

rows: NAV DATA (navigation database name) and RFL DATA (refueling database), the ACTIVE and SEC database effective dates (amber when out of date), UTC and DATE; NDB and RFL status while a database is being loaded
DES SOL PPOS (the designated solution's position, copy only), AIRPORT (enter the departure airport to show its reference position), PILOT/REF WPT, and INIT POS at 5R (ground only)

INIT GPS >COMMAND (FUNCTION UNAVAILABLE in the simulation: the GPS receivers initialize themselves); INU1, INU2 and INU3 MODE (ALIGN amber, NAVIGATE green) with TIME TO NAV; INIT INU >COMMAND at 5L, which sends INIT POS to the aligning INUs; ATT HDG at 6L for an attitude-only alignment

blocks.content: START INIT 1/3 is the first page at a cold start. The AIRPORT and INIT POS entries are accepted on the ground only (NOT ON GROUND in the air), and INIT INU without an INIT POS answers ENTER PARAMETERS.

blocks.alt: KC-10 ACT FPLN 1/3 in the air: ORIGIN KCID, DIST 811, DEST KJFK on the first data line; ROUTE KCIDKJFK and ALTN KLGA; VIA/TO rows DIRECT KPIT and DIRECT KIAD; divider; >COPY ACTIVE at 5L, OFFSET ---.- at 6R, <SEC FPLN at 6L. Inset: SEC FPLN 1/4 with ORIG RWY, <ROUTE LIST at 5L, ACTIVATE< at 5R, <SEC LEGS and SEC PERF>.
blocks.title: ACT FPLN and SEC FPLN

blocks.content: **FPLN** shows the plan as a route: ORIGIN, the total DIST and DEST on the first line, the ROUTE name and ALTN on the second, then VIA/TO pairs (page 1 carries one pair on the ground, with ORIG RWY at 3R, and two in the air; later pages five). The title says which plan is shown: **ACT FPLN** (the plan being flown), **MOD FPLN** (a pending modification of it, with MOD in white) or **SEC FPLN** (the secondary plan). On ACT and MOD the rows start at the active leg. A hold has its own HOLD AT row, a discontinuity a DISCONTINUITY row with box prompts, and the last row is always ----- ----- for the next TO.

blocks.title: FPLN fields
rows: ICAO airports. The origin cannot be changed or deleted in the air
The plan's name; on ACT or MOD FPLN, a stored route of that name on the selected card becomes the MOD FPLN (EXEC to fly it)
Alternate airport, for the ALTN predictions
DIRECT and the next fix. An airway entered in VIA answers FUNCTION UNAVAILABLE in this simulation; airways in an imported route are already expanded
Copies ACT into SEC (COPY N/A where not possible)
Makes SEC the MOD FPLN; EXEC flies it
The stored routes on the data cartridge
CANCEL MOD (6L on a MOD page)

blocks.content: **LEGS** lists the plan waypoint by waypoint, five to a page: the FROM waypoint (cyan) at 1L with **SEQUENCE AUTO/INHIBIT** at 1R, then the TO waypoint (magenta) and the following waypoints (white), each under the course and distance of the leg to it, with the speed/altitude constraint or step altitude at the right keys. 6R leads to **LEG WIND**, **LEG DATA**, **LEG INFO** and **LEG FUEL**, which show each waypoint's entered winds and ISA deviation, predicted times and altitudes, fuel flow and fuel adjustments, with the values above each waypoint's identifier. The RTA (required time of arrival) is entered on the line above the waypoint it applies to.

blocks.title: What a LEGS line key does
rows: Copies the waypoint (COPY N/A for the FROM, a discontinuity or a hold)
Deletes the waypoint, closes a discontinuity or removes a hold (the FROM cannot be deleted: INVALID DELETE)
Inserts a discontinuity before the waypoint
An identifier, on the magenta TO row (ACT/MOD)
An identifier already further down the plan
A constraint or step altitude, at a right key
Sets that waypoint's speed/altitude constraint or step climb altitude (advisory)

blocks.content: **DIRECT-TO** (DIR) lists a blank line at the top for any waypoint and the next four plan waypoints below. A direct-to opens a MOD FPLN to be executed, and cancels any parallel offset. If a MOD FPLN already exists, MOD IS ACTIVE appears: execute or cancel it first. The intercept course prompt (INTC CRS) drawn on MOD LEGS after a direct-to answers FUNCTION UNAVAILABLE, and the VNAV direct-to prompts on the right are not available.

The DEP/ARR key opens the **DEPART** page for the origin when a plan exists, SEC is not displayed and the aircraft is on the ground, or airborne within 50 NM of the origin or less than halfway; it opens the **ARRIVAL** page for the destination when airborne beyond that. With no plan, or a second press, it opens the **DEP/ARR INDEX**. DEPART lists runways and SIDs in alphabetical and numerical order; ARRIVAL lists STARs on the left and, on the right, approaches from the most precise (ILS) down to visual approaches, then runways. Pressing a choice declutters the lists to what is compatible with it and shows its transitions (VECTORS heads an approach's transitions); pressing it again takes it back. Each choice strings its segment into the MOD FPLN at once (EXEC, or >CANCEL MOD at 6L). Reached afresh, the page lists the selected items first in green. Pages for other airports are for display only.

blocks.alt: KC-10 FMS1 PROGRESS 2/4: TO CID05 (magenta) with ETE 0:05:38; TAS 291KT and BRG/DTG 026°/23.5NM; WIND 013T/15 with HEAD 6 and LEFT 8 components; GS 296KT, SAT +15°C, DTK/TRK 025°/022°; TKE L2.5°, XTK R15.0NM, MVAR E1.0; FMS2 PROG 2> at 6R.

rows: LAST, TO, NEXT, DEST and ALTN with distance and ETA

The TO waypoint with ETE, TAS, bearing and distance, wind with head/tail and cross components, ground speed, SAT, desired track and track, track angle error, cross-track error, magnetic variation. FMS1 from CDU 1 and 3, FMS2 from CDU 2; FMS2 PROG 2> switches
TO waypoint, its predicted altitude and the target altitude; distance and time to the top of descent
Time navigation: speed target, RTA and ETA at the RTA waypoint, IAS/Mach, FAST/SLOW and EARLY/LATE, the arrival window, SPD TGT RESET (not available)

blocks.alt: KC-10 MOD PERF INIT 1/3: OP WT 240000LB, CRZ ALT FL270; PASS/WT 12/170LB, ALTN CRZ ALT 17000; CARGO 1200LB, = ZFW 243240LB; MANUAL FUEL 116000LB, = GWT 359240LB; FUEL FLOW 18000LB/HR, FUEL MODE SENSED/CALC with CALC green; divider; >CANCEL MOD at 6L, VNAV SETUP> at 6R. MOD in white in the cyan title.
blocks.title: PERF INIT page 1

blocks.content: **PERF MENU** (PERF key) offers PERF INIT and SEC PERF, VNAV SETUP and SEC VNAV, RTA LIMITS and T/O WINDOW. The FMS provides basic predictive performance: from gross weight, fuel, cruise altitude and fuel flow it predicts each leg's fuel and ETA, the top of climb and descent, and the arrival at the destination and alternate. It does not compute any speeds (takeoff, approach or go-around), and its VNAV is advisory only: it cannot be coupled to the autopilot.

blocks.title: PERF INIT and VNAV SETUP
rows: OP WT, PASS/WT, CARGO, MANUAL FUEL (PLAN FUEL on SEC), FUEL FLOW (CALC mode only) and FUEL MODE SENSED/CALC on the left; CRZ ALT, ALTN CRZ ALT, ZFW (computed, or entered) and GWT (ZFW plus fuel) on the right
ISA DEV, and CLIMB, CRUISE and DESCENT winds
RESERVES, TAXI FUEL, ETD, WARP; DEST and ALTN ETE, ETA and FUEL (amber below the reserves)
Target speed (default 290/.70), TRANS ALT, two SPD/ALT LIMIT lines (default 160/10000)
Target speed (300/.74), CRZ ALT (the same field as PERF INIT's)
Target speed (.74/290), TRANS FL (the same field as TRANS ALT), two SPD/ALT LIMIT lines, VPA 1.00 to 6.0° (default 3.0°)
Low and high speed limits for climb, cruise and descent (200/.60 to 350/.90), used to meet an RTA
Earliest, desired and latest takeoff times for a valid RTA, referenced to ORIGIN, PPOS, DEST or LAST

blocks.content: Several defaults on these pages are the box's generic values, not KC-10 values: FUEL FLOW 350 LB/HR and SPD/ALT LIMIT 160/10000 among them. Enter real values, including sensible RTA LIMITS for the gross weight, or the predictions will be meaningless.

ACT edits open the MOD FPLN and need EXEC; SEC edits are saved at once. In SENSED mode the fuel field shows the aircraft's total fuel and the fuel flow is the engines' own. The climb time and fuel come from the KC-10A performance manual's three-engine climb data, the climb distance from the VNAV CLIMB target speed; the descent is the latest constant-angle path at the VPA to the destination elevation, with arrival constraints as ceilings.
