children.title: Mission patterns
children.summary: Racetracks, closed random patterns, intercepts, refueling tracks and anchors, and tactical approaches, flown through the autopilot.

blocks.content: The MSN key opens **FPLN MISSION**, whose prompts build the tanker's special patterns: <RCF, <CRP, <INTERCEPT, <REFUEL, TACT APPR> and HOLD>. A pattern is attached to a waypoint of the plan (INSERT XXX BEFORE? or ATTACH XXX AT? asks for the line key of that waypoint), shows on LEGS as a row of its own under its fix, and is **flown**: when the aircraft reaches the fix the FMS activates the pattern, stops sequencing the plan, and steers the autopilot around the pattern while the EHSI map draws it in magenta. A pattern is left only by a **direct-to** out of it; course edits on LEGS are refused while one is flown. A plan can carry a limited number of patterns and intercepts (MAX PTRNS IN FPLN, MAX INTERS IN FPLN).

blocks.title: Mission patterns
rows: Racetrack, circle or figure-eight of set length, width and turn direction on a fix and inbound course, with ICAO hold-type entries and a 10-second turn alert; RACETRACK ACTIVE while an RTK is flown
Closed random pattern: the fix and a set of waypoints flown in a loop, REV to reverse; INHIBIT overflies the fix
A moving intercept of another aircraft: the minimum-time solution in the air mass, or the point of closest approach (PCA INTERCEPT, NO INTR SOLUTION)

A published refueling **track** or **anchor** from the refueling database (RFL DATA, the AP/1B tracks and anchors of North and South America), or one defined by the crew: AR IDENT, entry, altitude block, initial, control and exit points, offset, orbit length (14 NM default), turn direction, orbit entry, ORBIT ETD, and on 4/4 the roll-out range (LEAD or TRAIL, 3.0 NM default), receiver TAS and ORBIT MODE (ORBIT, RDVZ, TRACK or DISABLED)
A tactical approach: final approach fix and a missed approach point at the touchdown zone plus 50 ft on a set glidepath; REMOVE restores the destination

blocks.content: **The refueling orbit.** With ORBIT MODE enabled and the control point active, the FMS flies the orbit at the computed offset, so that the final turn at constant bank rolls out on the inbound course with the wind accounted for, and shows the **turn relative bearing** and **turn range** at which the receiver should be seen to begin the turn. ORBIT ACTIVE or ANCHOR ACTIVE is annunciated, and REFUEL BNDRY EXCEED if the aircraft leaves the published airspace. A control point with ORBIT MODE disabled is treated as an ordinary waypoint. The procedures are in [Air Refueling](air-refueling) and the equipment in [Air Refueling Systems](air-refueling-systems).

blocks.alt: Four KC-10 CDU pages side by side: REFUEL 1/4 with AR IDENT AR105-NE, ENTRY IP/CP, TYPE TRACK/ANCHOR (TRACK green), ALTITUDE FL190AFL330B and CATALOG>; REFUEL 2/4 with INITIAL POINT, CONTROL POINT, EXIT POINT and <TRACK CHKPTS; REFUEL 3/4 with OFFSET, ORBIT LENGTH 14.3NM, MODE IND, ORBIT ETD, INB CRS/DIR and ORBIT ENTRY AUTO/OUTB/INB/FIX; REFUEL 4/4 with ROR MODE LEAD/TRAIL 3.0NM, RCVR TAS, TURN REL BRG and RANGE, ORBIT MODE ORBIT/RDVZ/TRACK/DISABLD.
blocks.title: REFUEL pages

children.title: ACT, MOD and SEC flight plans

blocks.content: The FMS holds three flight plans of up to 200 waypoints each (FPLN FULL beyond), with up to six holds and a history of the last 39 waypoints flown. **Every edit to the ACT FPLN opens a MOD FPLN**: the title reads MOD, EXEC is annunciated, and the change takes effect only on EXEC (>CANCEL MOD discards it). If a MOD stands unedited for 60 seconds, EXEC MOD FPLN is annunciated on all three CDUs. **SEC FPLN** edits take effect at once, which makes it the place to build the next route, a re-route or an alternate plan. ACTIVATE on SEC FPLN turns it into the MOD FPLN; EXEC makes it the ACT FPLN. COPY ACTIVE puts the ACT FPLN into SEC.

A route can be built by hand on SEC or ACT FPLN, recalled from the data cartridge (ROUTE LIST, or its name at ROUTE), or imported from the EFB into SEC FPLN (see [Loading a planned route](#fm-route-loading)). Routes are saved to the cartridge from SEC FPLN (LOAD/SAVE).

**Sequencing** runs on the designated solution while SEQUENCE is AUTO; INHIBIT stops it and holds the active leg (SEQ INHIBITED). Reaching a discontinuity raises DISCONTINUITY; the last waypoint, LAST WAYPOINT; a plan with nothing to fly, NO FPLN.

**Holds.** MSN, HOLD> opens ACT LEGS with a HOLD AT prompt if the plan has no hold, the ACT FPLN HOLD page if it has one, and the ACT HOLD LIST if it has more (left column ACT/MOD, right column SEC). For a plan waypoint, press the key of the HOLD AT boxes with the waypoint in the scratchpad; the page becomes MOD FPLN HOLD, where the inbound course, turn direction and either leg time or leg distance (not both) can be set, then EXEC. An off-plan fix entered at HOLD AT shows HOLD AT IDENT in the scratchpad and goes before the waypoint whose key is pressed next. The default hold is inbound on the leg's course with right turns and 1.0-minute legs. Once a hold is the active leg its direction and inbound course cannot be changed. <EXIT HOLD (6L on LEGS or the FPLN HOLD page), then EXEC, arms the exit (EXIT ARMED), and the aircraft leaves at the next fix crossing. A present-position hold and holds in SEC are not available (FUNCTION UNAVAILABLE).

**Parallel offset.** With a fixed-track active leg to a fixed waypoint, enter the offset at OFFSET on ACT FPLN and EXEC. The offset ends automatically at a turn of more than 100°, with OFFSET WILL END two minutes before and OFFSET TERMINATED when it ends; entering zero or DELETE at OFFSET (then EXEC), or a direct-to, cancels it. INVALID LEG TYPE answers an offset on a pattern or procedure that does not allow one.

**Missed approach.** The missed approach is part of the plan but the FMS does not fly it by itself: at the missed approach point, airborne, it selects INHIBIT (SEQ INHIBITED) and the runway track flies on. Pressing **TO/GA** for about a second, or selecting AUTO at LEGS 1R, starts the missed approach on ACT and any open MOD, giving coupled missed approach guidance to the flight director and autopilot. TO/GA pressed earlier lets the approach run through the missed approach point into the missed approach without stopping. After a landing with no go-around the plan stays inhibited until the crew select AUTO.

The VNAV SETUP pages and the LEGS constraints exist to calculate ETAs, the RTA and fuel; nothing in the FMS steers vertically. The predictions run continuously for the ACT (or MOD) and SEC plans: each leg's ETA and fuel, the top of climb and descent, the destination and alternate, the RTA solution and the takeoff window. A step altitude (S) on LEGS becomes the new cruise altitude when its waypoint is crossed. The annunciations CHK FUEL AT DEST and CHK FUEL AT ALTN (arrival fuel below the reserves), UNABLE RTA, CHK SPEED (IAS off the RTA speed target by more than the CONFIG SPD ALERT) and UNABLE CRZ ALT are raised from the plan in force.

**Vertical deviation.** From 30 seconds before the top of descent to the destination, the FMS outputs the aircraft's deviation from its own predicted descent path to the EHSI and EADI scales, in feet, and in APPROACH also as an angle with a target altitude for the EADI. The path respects every constraint ahead and stays level at a step-down until the line ahead comes down through it. The output is removed on the ground, in a hold, in a mission pattern and once the missed approach is started. It is advisory: fly it with the autopilot's pitch modes.

Each pilot's EHSI and EADI take the FMS data when the **NAV** knob on that pilot's **display control panel** (center pedestal) is at **FMS**: the route and active leg on the map, the course deviation at the flight mode's full scale, the vertical deviation, the TO waypoint data and the waypoint alert, which flashes the TO/FROM triangle the CONFIG WPT ALERT time before the waypoint (10 seconds in terminal and approach). The pilot's side uses FMS1 and the copilot's FMS2. PUSH-DIRECT on the display control panel flies direct to the active waypoint at once, without EXEC.

**Autopilot.** With the EHSI navigation source at FMS, the RAD FMS pushbutton arms the FMS capture: FMS on the arm line of the flight mode annunciator, FMS CAP during the intercept, then FMS TRK. The coupler flies the designated solution's cross-track and track angle error, and in a mission pattern the pattern's own steering with its turns fed forward. If the FMS has nothing to steer, the FMAs change from FMS TRK to HDG HOLD. DP/MASTER DISAGREE (amber) means the autopilot's side is not the FMS bus controller. See [Automatic Flight](automatic-flight).

While MODEL AIRCRAFT is running (SIM ACTIVE annunciated) the model's position, track and speed replace the navigation solution, and the EHSI and an engaged, coupled autopilot follow the model, not the aircraft. Use MODEL AIRCRAFT on the ground only, and stop it before flight.

**Annunciations** are conditions. They stand while their condition is true, appear on the annunciation line in priority order, and are listed on the MESSAGES page (MSG key) as NEW until viewed there and OLD afterwards. A clearable annunciation is cleared when the MESSAGES page is left; a non-clearable one stays in the OLD list until its condition ends. Whether an annunciation has been viewed is kept per CDU. **Scratchpad messages** answer one keystroke and are reset with CLR DEL.

items: **After takeoff:** with the EHSI source at FMS, push RAD FMS to arm; FMS CAP, then FMS TRK. Monitor PROGRESS 2/4 for cross-track and track error.
**Direct to:** DIR, enter the fix at the top line (or press a listed waypoint), EXEC. Or type the fix over the magenta TO waypoint on LEGS, EXEC.
**Change of route:** build it on SEC FPLN (COPY ACTIVE first if most of the route stays), then ACTIVATE and EXEC when cleared.
**Hold:** MSN, HOLD>, put the fix into the HOLD AT boxes, set the hold on MOD FPLN HOLD, EXEC. To leave, <EXIT HOLD, then EXEC.
**Offset:** ACT FPLN, enter L or R and the distance at OFFSET, EXEC. To cancel, enter 0 (or DELETE) at OFFSET and EXEC.

**Refueling rendezvous:** MSN, <REFUEL, AR IDENT (or CATALOG), check the points on 2/4, set offset, orbit length, turn direction and entry on 3/4, roll-out range, receiver TAS and ORBIT MODE on 4/4 (it starts DISABLED), then answer INSERT REFUEL BEFORE? with the LEGS line key of the waypoint the refueling segment is to precede, and EXEC. The orbit is flown once the control point is the active waypoint with ORBIT MODE enabled.
**Arrival:** DEP/ARR (twice, or the INDEX, if DEPART opens), ARR>, choose the approach, an optional transition and STAR, EXEC; check LEGS for the discontinuity a VECTORS transition leaves.
**Go-around:** TO/GA for about a second sequences the FMS from INHIBIT to AUTO; push RAD FMS for coupled missed approach guidance.

sections.title: MD-10 Flight Management System
sections.summary: The Honeywell Pegasus FMS of the FedEx conversion: dual flight management functions, three MCDUs, and lateral, vertical and speed guidance through the flight control computers.

blocks.content: The MD-10's **flight management system (FMS)** is the MD-11's Honeywell Pegasus, fitted when FedEx converted the DC-10 to a two-crew glass flight deck. It is used for flight planning, navigation, performance management, guidance and flight progress monitoring. It consists of two **flight management functions**, **FMF1** and **FMF2**, hosted in the aircraft's avionics computers, and the **multifunction control and display units (MCDUs)** on the forward pedestal: the Captain's on the left, the First Officer's on the right, and a third MCDU that also provides standby navigation. The crew select flight modes on the glareshield **flight control panel (FCP)** and enter plans and data on the MCDUs; progress is monitored on the MCDUs and the navigation displays.

Once initialized, the FMFs build a flight profile from origin to destination and guide the aircraft along it by sending roll, pitch, speed and thrust commands to the two **flight control computers (FCCs)**. Three FMS functions can be used separately or together: **NAV** (lateral guidance along the route), **PROF** (the vertical profile) and **FMS SPD** (the speed target). Takeoff and go-around references, minimum and maximum speeds and the thrust limits also come from the FMS. The FCC modes and their annunciations are described in [Automatic Flight](automatic-flight).

blocks.alt: MD-10 Pegasus MCDU, face on, lit, showing ACT F-PLN 1/2 before takeoff: title ACT F-PLN 1/2 with the next-page arrow, labels FROM, ETE, SPD, ALT; rows RW22R 0000 133/ 10, H222° to 410, CYN5 CYN 03 220/5000, J37 ENO 11 200/15000, J37 MOSSI 19 .74/FL250, J37 MARBY 21 .78/FL275, the slew arrows. Around the screen: six line select keys each side; function keys DIR INTC, NAV RAD, PERF, INIT, TO/APPR, F-PLN, PROG, FIX, SEC F-PLN, REF, ENG OUT, MENU, PAGE, the up and down slew keys; numeric keys 1-9, /, 0, decimal point; letters A-Z, minus, plus, SP and CLR; the BRT knob and light sensors; the MSG, OFST, DSPY and FAIL annunciators.
blocks.title: MD-10 MCDU

blocks.content: **Dual operation.** The normal mode is **DUAL**: the two FMFs talk over a private intersystem bus so that an entry on either MCDU is made in both FMFs at once and leg sequencing happens in both together, while each computes its own aircraft position, gross weight and active thrust limit. The FMF on the side of the FCC in control is the **master**, and both flight directors follow its steering. Button pushes are processed in the order received (simultaneous pushes favor the master's own MCDU), and only one flight plan modification is processed at a time. The two FMFs compare their results and report a disagreement: FMF POSITION MISMATCH (more than 5 NM, or twice the RNP), GROSS WEIGHT MISMATCH (more than 15,000 lb), THRUST LIMIT MISMATCH (more than 1 % N1).

**Degraded modes.** After a power interruption of more than four seconds an FMF resynchronizes with the other, showing PLEASE WAIT and refusing keystrokes from either MCDU for the few seconds this takes. If crosstalk cannot be established both FMFs run **INDEPENDENT** (INDEPENDENT OPERATION), each with its own plan; RESET FMF on SENSOR STATUS tries to restore DUAL, resynchronizing the FMF selected from the other. If an FMF fails completely, the MCDU drops to its MENU page; the MCDU can then run **STANDBY** navigation from its own copy of the flight plan (see [Standby operation](#pegasus-standby)). Without valid performance data the FMS runs with NO FMS SPD/PROF on A/C STATUS: navigation only, with no FMS speed, profile, fuel predictions or thrust limits.

blocks.alt: MD-10 forward pedestal: the Captain's MCDU on the left and the First Officer's on the right, each lit (left on F-PLN INIT 1/3, right on PROGRESS), with the third MCDU position visible; the glareshield FCP partly in view above with its FMS SPD, NAV, PROF and AUTO FLIGHT buttons legible.
blocks.title: MD-10 MCDUs on the forward pedestal

blocks.content: Each FMF forms the aircraft position from the three **IRUs** (the MD-10's air data inertial reference units), the two **GNS** receivers and the VOR/DME receivers. The inertial position is a weighted average of the three IRUs computed five times a second; an IRU that lies 36 NM or more from the last computed average, or whose velocity is more than 20 kt from it, is left out of the average until it comes back inside 36 NM. If any IRU fails that test or is not in normal operation, each FMF uses a single IRU (IRU1 failed: FMF1 uses IRU3 and FMF2 IRU2; IRU2 failed: FMF1 IRU1, FMF2 IRU3; IRU3 failed: FMF1 IRU1, FMF2 IRU2), with SENSOR FAIL.

The radio position is normally from two DME stations, and from a single VOR/DME when no pair crosses at between 30° and 150°. The FMF **autotunes** the VOR/DME receivers to the stations that will give the best fix, using each station's class and figure of merit from the database (figure of merit 0, 1, 2 and 3 for 40, 70, 130 and 250 NM). A manually tuned radio is not autotuned again until its frequency is cleared, and a station can be excluded on the NAVAID page. When the radio and inertial positions differ by 12 NM or more and a different pair of stations does not resolve it, VERIFY A/C POSITION appears and updating reverts to inertial; IRS ONLY NAVIGATION is shown after a period without radio or GNS updating, RADIO ONLY NAVIGATION if all IRU inputs are lost, and A/C POSITION INVALID if no position can be computed for two minutes.

**IRU alignment** is started on the IRS panel (see [Navigation](navigation)) and needs the present position from the FMS: F-PLN INIT shows INITIALIZE IRS* at 4R while an IRU is waiting for it, and pushing 4R sends the displayed latitude and longitude. ALIGN IRS reminds the crew if the F-PLN INIT page is not displayed. POS REF and IRS STATUS then show the IRUs' positions and status.

blocks.content: The phase decides which PERF page is active, what the TO/APPR key shows, and which INIT fields lock once airborne. At flight complete the active flight plan and the pilot-defined waypoints not used by the secondary flight plan are deleted.

**The display** has 14 lines of 26 characters: the page title (with the page number and a next-page arrow when the page has more), six pairs of a small-font label line and a data line beside the line select keys, and the **scratchpad (SP)** at the bottom. Large characters are crew entries or data that define the plan; small characters are predicted, default or computed values, which change to large when the crew overwrite them. **Box prompts** mark a mandatory entry, **brackets** an optional one, and **dashes** a field that cannot be entered or is still being computed. An **asterisk** beside a line select key means that pushing it will affect the active flight plan or situation. A triangle beside a waypoint means it must be overflown; an arrow, the required turn direction.

blocks.content: **Data entry.** Type into the scratchpad from left to right, following the format the field shows, and push the line select key. With an empty scratchpad, a line select key copies the field into the scratchpad, or selects a page, procedure or mode. With CLR in the scratchpad it deletes the field. Altitudes are taken as flight levels if two or three digits are typed (or with FL), and as feet if four or five (500 ft is typed 0500). A runway waypoint is typed as the airport and runway (KORD27L) and shown as RW27L. A waypoint can be a database identifier, a latitude/longitude or a place/bearing/distance; the last two create a pilot-defined waypoint, one of up to 40.

**Messages** are of two types. A **type I** message appears at once, overwriting the entry (which reappears when the message is cleared), and is cleared by the next key push. A **type II** message lights MSG and shows MCDU MSG on the ND; it waits until the scratchpad is empty, is stored (up to five) and cleared one at a time with CLR, and most clear themselves when no longer true. CLR on one MCDU does not clear the other's messages. PLEASE WAIT cannot be cleared.

blocks.content: **ROUTE SELECTION** appears after a FROM/TO (or ALTN) entry and shows each stored company route between the two airports, one per page (PAGE for the next); *INSERT puts it in the plan, RETURN TO leaves without it. A company route with a procedure the aircraft may not fly strings a discontinuity in its place (INVALID CO RTE PROC).

children.title: F-PLN, LAT REV and VERT REV

blocks.content: **ACT F-PLN 1/2** lists the plan from the FROM waypoint at the top: each waypoint with the airway or procedure leading to it on the label line, the predicted time (ETE before takeoff, ETO after), and the predicted speed and altitude, constraints in large font. Pseudo waypoints, (T/C), (S/C) and (T/D), are shown in brackets for reference. **ACT F-PLN 2/2** shows the same rows with distance, temperature and wind. The slew keys scroll the plan; both pages scroll together.

blocks.title: What the F-PLN keys do
rows: Inserts it there, pushing the rest down
Right key, a speed or altitude
Enters or changes that waypoint's constraint (/SFLnnn: a cruise-level constraint, one of the INIT cruise levels)
EXIT AT FIX or RESUME HOLD for a hold

blocks.alt: MD-10 LAT REV FROM KJFK page: title with the waypoint and its position N4038.0/W07346.4; <SID at 1L, STAR> at 1R, <AIRWAYS at 2L, HOLD> at 2R, PROCEDURE TURN> at 3R; NEXT WPT *[ ] at 4L, NEW CO RTE [ ]* at 4R; OFFSET *[ ] at 5L, NEW DEST [ ]* at 5R; ENABLE ALTN * TO KJAX at 6L, RETURN TO ACT F-PLN> at 6R.
blocks.title: LAT REV page

blocks.content: **LAT REV** offers every lateral revision allowed at the waypoint in its title. At the origin (before takeoff) it offers <SID; elsewhere STAR>, HOLD> and PROCEDURE TURN>. <AIRWAYS (2L), NEXT WPT (4L), NEW CO RTE from here (4R), NEW DEST (5R), a parallel OFFSET (5L, only at the FROM waypoint on a great-circle leg to a fixed waypoint) and ENABLE ALTN (6L, divert to the alternate along the active plan). Entries marked with an asterisk affect the active plan.

**SID** lists the origin's SIDs and runways, the transitions of a selected SID, and the engine-out SID the FMS selects automatically for the runway; **STAR** lists the arrivals and the approaches the aircraft is certified for, then transitions, with **APPR TRANS** offered when an approach transition is not selected automatically. A non-precision approach is not strung until a MIN PROF altitude is entered at 2R; in PROF the aircraft will not descend below it, and PROF disengages when altitude hold is reached there. **AIRWAYS** takes VIA and TO pairs; entering a second airway in VIA computes the intersection (named after the airway with an X if it is not a database fix). In each, *INSERT puts the selection into the plan and RETURN TO cancels it.

blocks.title: VERT REV
rows: EFOB at the waypoint and EXTRA at destination; SPD, AT OR ABOVE, AT ALT and AT OR BELOW constraints (then *CLB or DES* to confirm the phase); PROGRESS> at 2R under an RTA label; the climb or descent SPD LIM at 5R (default VCL/10000); RETURN TO
VERT REV 2/2 (PAGE, or right keys of cruise waypoints on F-PLN 2/2)

Up to four altitude/wind entries per waypoint, sorted descending (altitudes carry to all waypoints, winds are per waypoint; others are computed in small font), ALT/TEMP at 1R, PREV>/NEXT> between waypoints, *INSERT to apply

blocks.content: **DIR INTC** shows a page titled ACT F-PLN with DIR TO at 1L and INTC FIX/CRS at 1R above the plan. Select a plan waypoint with its left key, or type any defined waypoint into 1L (a latitude/longitude or place/bearing/distance creates a pilot waypoint); the fix then shows with an asterisk, and pushing 1L flies the direct-to from present position. For an intercept, enter the inbound course at 1R (the fix and course together, or the course after selecting the fix); once the course is in, 1R shows its asterisk and pushing it starts the intercept: if the present heading crosses the course before the fix, heading is held to the intercept; otherwise the plan is unchanged and NOT ON INTC HEADING appears. With the fix in 1L, *WITH ABEAM POINTS at 2L keeps the bypassed waypoints as abeam points. Pseudo waypoints, markers and non-fixed waypoints cannot be selected.

**HOLD** (LAT REV 2R) inserts or modifies a holding pattern with a pilot-controlled exit at any waypoint, or at the FROM waypoint for a present-position hold (the hold fix is then called T-P). The title shows HOLD AT (crew-defined), DATABASE HOLD AT (published) or STANDARD HOLD AT (FMS defaults). INB CRS defaults to the published or plan inbound course (current track at present position); TURN defaults to right; TIME/DIST to 1.0 minute at or below 14,000 ft and 1.5 above (time or distance, not both). The page also shows trip fuel, reserves and alternate fuel from the fix, and after insertion the LIMIT UTC/FUEL: the time at which the fuel on board falls to trip plus reserve plus alternate plus final. The default holding speed is maximum endurance, limited to 230 KIAS up to 14,000 ft, 240 KIAS to 20,000 ft, 265 KIAS to 34,000 ft and M.83 above. A change takes effect at the next crossing of the fix (at once on the active leg before entry). Capturing a localizer or VOR during a hold to a manual termination selects EXIT AT FIX automatically.

**PROC TURN** (LAT REV 3R) defines a procedure turn at the waypoint: the aircraft turns to the outbound course from the fix, flies the inbound distance, turns and rolls out on the inbound course back over the fix. Database procedure turns appear on F-PLN automatically.
The crew are responsible for keeping the aircraft within the holding airspace.

blocks.alt: MD-10 EDIT CLB 1/3 page: PRED TO FL 250 at 1R; ECON 280/.780 at 2L; MAX CLB 210 with UTC 0029 and DIST 22 at 3L; EDIT 260/MMO with UTC 0030 and DIST 26 at 4L; CLIMB FORECAST> at 5R; TRANS 18000 and OPT/MAXFL 341/398 at 6L, THRUST LIMITS> at 6R.
blocks.title: PERF page in climb

blocks.content: The PERF key shows the **active** PERF page for the phase, titled with the active speed mode and phase (ECON CLB, EDIT CLB, ECON CRZ, ECON DES and so on). It lists the speed modes available in that phase, the active one in large font and the others in small font with an asterisk for activation, with time and distance predictions to the PRED TO altitude (the FCP altitude in small font, or a crew entry). The NEXT PAGE chain leads from CLB to **PRESELECT CRZ** and **PRESELECT DES**, where the crew can preselect the speed mode for the coming phase. The left of the title line can show ??? when the aircraft is between the FMS target altitude and a conflicting FCP altitude, or TIME when a time constraint is adjusting the ECON speed.

blocks.title: FMS speed modes
rows: The economy speed for the cost index (not editable)
ECON with a crew-chosen CAS, set on PRESELECT DES on the ground; CLR returns to ECON
A crew CAS and/or Mach (a CAS alone takes MMO as its Mach, a Mach alone VMO as its CAS)
Best angle of climb speed (not editable)

blocks.content: ECON is the default only at power-up on the ground; otherwise the last mode stays active, and a mode preselected for cruise becomes active when the cruise page does. An EDIT speed in cruise does not carry into the descent. From the FCP: pushing **FMS SPD** within 10 seconds of preselecting a speed on the FCP activates EDIT at that speed; pushing it at any other time activates ECON; pushing or pulling the speed knob returns the FMS speed mode to ECON. The cruise page shows the time and distance to the next step climb point (STEP NOW once it is passed and the FCP altitude has not been raised; TO T/D within 200 NM of the top of descent). The descent page shows the PATH ERROR, vertical (feet) and horizontal (NM), on a ±1,000 ft scale.

blocks.alt: MD-10 AUTO THRUST LIMITS page before takeoff with a flex temperature entered: title AUTO THRUST LIMITS; column headings N1, TAT, FLEX; T/O 110.2 at 1L with TAT 20° and FLEX 50 at 1R; FLX DERATE label over ->T/O 108.7 at 2L (active, large); MCT 102.5 at 3L with SELECT ALT* at 3R; CLB 100.8 at 4L with OVERRIDE [ ]* at 4R; CRZ 99.9 at 6L; RETURN TO TAKEOFF> at 6R.
blocks.title: AUTO THRUST LIMITS page

blocks.content: **THRUST LIMITS** (from TAKEOFF, the active PERF page or GO AROUND) shows and selects the FMS's thrust limits, the limit the FCCs control the throttles to in the aircraft (in the simulation the FCCs sequence their limit themselves: see [Simulation notes](#simulation-notes)). One limit is always **active**, shown on the left with an arrow and its N1 in large font. In **AUTO** mode (the default at power-up and in preflight) the FMF makes every transition itself: takeoff, then climb at the thrust reduction altitude (when the takeoff limits are replaced by G/A), cruise, MCT after an engine failure or in low-speed protection, and back. Selecting any limit shown in large font puts the page in **MANUAL** mode, where only the crew change the limit, except for engine failure, windshear and low-speed protection; SELECT AUTO* returns to AUTO. CLB, MCT and CRZ are always armed. Entering a **FLEX** temperature (1R, or TAKEOFF 1L) from the present TAT up to 50 °C (MD-10-10) or 60 °C (MD-10-30) makes FLX T/O the active takeoff limit; clearing it restores T/O. In windshear the flex rating is replaced by the full takeoff or go-around rating until the windshear has ended and the aircraft is above the thrust reduction altitude. Selections on this page set limits only; the thrust used is the autothrottle's.

blocks.alt: MD-10 TAKEOFF KORD RW32L page: FLEX empty at 1L, TOCG/TOGW 25.3/585.0 and THRUST LIMITS> at 1R; PACKS OFF and N1 108.7 at 2L, SLOPE/WIND +1.0/+15 at 2R; FLAP boxes and STAB at 3L, OAT 15C at 3R; V1, VR, V2 dashes at 4L-6L with VFR, VSR/V3 235 and VCL 275; CLB THRUST 2150, ACCEL 3650 and EO ACCEL 1450 at 4R-6R.
blocks.title: TAKEOFF page
TAKEOFF (TO/APPR key on the ground)
rows: Assumed temperature, TAT to 50 °C (-10) or 60 °C (-30); also sets THRUST LIMITS; clear for full thrust. A flex takeoff is not simulated: the entry is accepted but the thrust stays at the full takeoff rating
From WEIGHT INIT (changing one changes the other)
PACKS is a non-functional display; the takeoff N1
Runway slope and wind component, each with + or - (or U/D, H/T); + is uphill and headwind
Takeoff flap, 10° to 25°; the stabilizer setting is computed
Mandatory; with C or F; push 3R with an empty SP to convert. Not from the TAT display
Entered by the crew (large font); CHECK/CONFIRM VSPDS until all three are entered or the message is cleared; can be overwritten until the throttles are set for takeoff
Flap retract, slat retract and clean climb speeds, computed (VFR once V1, VR and V2 are in)
Thrust reduction, acceleration and engine-out acceleration altitudes; computed and editable in preflight

blocks.content: The TAKEOFF page is available before and during the takeoff; once left after takeoff it cannot be recalled. In the air TO/APPR shows **APPROACH** (not available with no destination): the clean, slat-extended and flap minimum maneuvering speeds, the landing configuration (the alternative at 6L can be swapped in with its key), **VREF** (1.3 times the stall speed for that configuration, not editable) and **VAPP** (VREF + 5 kt, editable for wind), the landing weight, the runway length and elevation, and a TIMER (up to 59:59) that starts the EIS countdown timer. **GO AROUND** (APPROACH 6R in cruise, descent or approach, and automatically when the G/A button on the center throttle is pushed) shows VFR, VSR and the clean minimum speed, and the CLB THRUST (default 1,500 ft AGL), ACCEL (default 3,000 ft AGL, above CLB THRUST) and EO ACCEL (default 800 ft AGL) altitudes, minimum 1,000 ft AGL.

The FMS does not compute V1, VR and V2 in this aircraft: they stay dashed until entered. The EFB Performance app's **Send to Avionics** button (under Set Bugs on its Takeoff page) enters V1, VR, V2, flap, FLEX, OAT and acceleration altitude on TAKEOFF, TOGW and TOCG on WEIGHT INIT, and flight number, cruise level, cost index and alternate on F-PLN INIT, through the same pages and checks as typing them.

children.title: PROGRESS, NAV RADIO, FIX and the reference pages

rows: Titled with the flight number: FROM with actual time and altitude, TO with predicted time and altitude, NEXT; temperature, wind, usable fuel; destination and alternate ETA, distance to go and estimated fuel on board. A waypoint entered at 6L is monitored like the destination, without changing the plan

VOR 1 and 2 by identifier or frequency with course (VOR ARM* for the FMS VOR mode, not above 18,000 ft), ADF 1 and 2, the ILS with its course (derived from the runway) and LOC ONLY*, and preselect fields at 6L/6R. Autotuned entries are in small font
Two pages: a reference fix with radial and distance to the aircraft, up to three radials from it with the predicted crossing time, distance and altitude on the plan, and the abeam point
The four nearest airports with bearing and distance (in the simulation, airports with a runway of at least 4,500 ft), and one of the crew's choosing at 5L
DEFINED WAYPOINT (the 40 pilot waypoints), WAYPOINT, NAVAID, CLOSEST AIRPORTS, ACARS, POS REF, DOC DATA, A/C STATUS, MAINT (preflight or after flight only), SENSOR STATUS, MEMORY READOUT

FMC position (freeze with 1L, or enter a position for an UPDATE*), IRS mixed position, RNP/ACTUAL; IRS/GNS POS with each IRU's and GNS's position and status; IRS STATUS with drift rates and status codes after flight
The navaids in use for bearing pointers, position computation and ILS DME, with class, frequency, elevation, declination and figure of merit; DESELECT at 4R stops one being autotuned for the flight
SEC F-PLN INIT, SEC F-PLN, SEC PROGRESS
Up to three altitude/wind entries for the climb or descent, the airport's wind and temperature, anti-ice for the descent path; *INSERT to apply
Route and takeoff data requests and review; an uplinked route is inserted into the secondary plan
Failed sensors only; RESET FMF when independent
Subsystems (FMF-1 or FMF-2 when transferred), STANDBY NAV/RAD*, and <NAV DATA (the simulator's navigation data source)

blocks.content: The FMS holds the **active** flight plan (with its alternate) and a **secondary** flight plan. Changes to the active plan made on the F-PLN, LAT REV, VERT REV and procedure pages take effect when inserted (the asterisked prompts). The secondary plan is for planning: SEC F-PLN INIT builds it from a company route or FROM/TO, COPY ACTIVE (3L) copies the active plan into it for evaluating a change, and CLEAR SEC (4L) empties it. **ACTIVATE SEC*** (4R) makes it the active plan, and the old active plan becomes the secondary. With NAV engaged, ACTIVATE SEC is offered only when the secondary plan's first leg is the leg being flown, so that no lateral maneuver results. A cruise level in the secondary plan lower than the aircraft is not transferred; a higher one becomes the new cruise level, but no climb starts until the FCP altitude is raised. Predictions appear on SEC F-PLN only when it was made by copying the active plan.

An imported route from the EFB arrives as **ACARS ROUTE DATA**: review it on ACARS ROUTE (REF INDEX, ACARS, REVIEW at 1R), INSERT it into the secondary plan (which also fills the flight number), and activate it with ACTIVATE SEC on SEC F-PLN INIT (see [Loading a planned route](#fm-route-loading)). Do not enter more than 100 waypoints.

children.title: Guidance: NAV, PROF and FMS SPD

blocks.content: **NAV** can be armed on the ground with all three engines running; it engages at 100 ft in flight director and can be coupled to the autopilot from 400 ft. It compares the aircraft's position with the active leg and sends steering commands to the autopilot and flight directors, sequencing the legs automatically.

**PROF** controls the vertical profile, with the FCP altitude always the absolute ceiling or floor. It may be armed on the ground and engages automatically at 400 ft; the reduction from takeoff to climb thrust at the thrust reduction altitude is automatic once PROF (or a level change) is engaged. In the climb the autothrottle holds the climb limit and the elevator the FMS speed, leveling at each altitude constraint and at the FCP altitude. In cruise PROF holds the level and FMS SPD the speed. **Step climbs:** the FMS computes the optimum step point; set the new level in the FCP and the climb begins there. **Descent:** lower the FCP altitude before the top of descent and, in PROF and FMS SPD, the descent starts automatically at T/D. On the descent path PROF steers pitch to the path, like an ILS glideslope, while the autothrottle holds the speed target, with some throttle activity; if the aircraft accelerates on the path the crew use the speed brakes. An early or en-route descent is started with level change or V/S, and in cruise the new cruise level is then re-entered on F-PLN INIT. NAV and PROF end when the localizer and glideslope are captured; in a missed approach they can be engaged again to fly the missed approach procedure.

**The descent path** is computed backward from the destination: from the point where the slats and flaps are expected to be extended, through the altitude and speed constraints, at idle above the descent speed limit altitude and slightly above idle below it, up to the cruise level, where it defines the T/D. It takes the speed mode and the forecast winds into account. The approach decelerates through each configuration's minimum speed to VAPP. Constraints that cannot be met are reported (ALT ERROR AT, SPD ERROR AT, SPD LIM EXCEEDED), and climb or cruise constraints still unsequenced when the descent starts are deleted (CLB ALT CSTRS DELETED, CRZ ALT CSTRS DELETED).

**FMS SPD** supplies the speed target for the active mode (ECON, EDIT, MAX, POLICY) limited by speed and altitude constraints, the speed limit, and the FCCs' envelope of VMIN + 5 to VMAX - 5 kt. A speed outside the envelope hands FMS SPD and PROF back to the FCCs, which engage speed protection.

**Parallel offset.** At LAT REV for the FROM waypoint, enter the offset in NM (L or R) at 5L. It becomes active at once; the aircraft intercepts the parallel track at up to 45° and the OFST light comes on. The FMS cancels the offset itself when the next leg cannot be offset, such as a hold entry, showing CANCELLING OFFSET, and rejoins the plan at up to 45°.

children.title: The flight plan on the navigation display

blocks.alt: MD-10 Captain's ND in MAP mode, 80 NM range, heading up: the white aircraft symbol at the bottom with the curved green trend vector, the active flight plan as a solid magenta line through waypoints MOSSI (magenta, the TO waypoint) and MARBY, GVE, SANNY (white, with identifiers), the TO waypoint data box top right with ident, distance and time, ground speed and TAS and the wind arrow top left, VOR and airport symbols from the ARPT and VOR/NDB selections in the background, and a tuned VOR circled in magenta. Range arc and heading scale legible.
blocks.title: Navigation display, MAP mode

blocks.content: In MAP mode each pilot's ND draws that side's active flight plan as a **solid magenta line** through the plan's waypoints, the TO waypoint in magenta and the others in white with their identifiers, with a gap wherever the plan has a discontinuity. The TO waypoint's identifier, distance and time are shown in the upper right corner. The airports, navaids and waypoints selected with the ARPT, VOR/NDB and WPT switches on the EIS control panel (ECP) are drawn from the same navigation database, within the selected range, and tuned navaids are circled. The ND modes, ranges and symbols are described in [Flight Instruments](flight-instruments).

When the FCC detects an engine failure, or the crew push ENG OUT, the PERF page shows *CONFIRM ENG OUT and CLEAR* at line 6. Confirming (6L) computes the engine-out maximum altitude (the altitude at which two engines at MCT give 100 ft/min of climb) and new MAX CLB, MAX END and ECON targets, and selects the MCT limit (the thrust limits stay in MCT until AUTO is selected after the engine-out state is cleared). CRZ FL ABOVE MAX FL appears if the cruise level is above the new maximum. Engine-out mode cancels time constraints and multiple cruise levels. If the failure occurs on a SID with an engine-out SID in the database, the flight plan page appears with *CONFIRM EOSID CLEAR*. In the takeoff the speed target is the speed at the failure (between V2 and V2 + 10) up to the EO ACCEL altitude, then V3, and takeoff thrust is kept until V3, clean configuration and the all-engine ACCEL altitude are all reached. To return to the three-engine state, push ENG OUT again and select CLEAR.

**Driftdown.** Above the engine-out maximum altitude, after confirming, lower the FCP altitude: the FMS enters the driftdown descent, shown on the **D/D ENG OUT DES** page with the driftdown speed at 1L, at MCT with the speed on pitch. The aircraft will not leave the FCP altitude in FMS modes until it is lowered; if the speed decays to VMIN the FMS modes drop out and the FCCs' speed protection takes over.

Each MCDU keeps its own copy of the active flight plan (up to 118 waypoints) and of the onside radio tuning, updated continuously. If its FMF stops answering within three seconds, the MCDU shows MENU and keeps the radios on their last frequencies. **STANDBY NAV/RAD*** on MENU gives the **STANDBY NAV RADIO** page (onside VOR, ADF and ILS by frequency, with preselect); on the third MCDU the prompt is F-PLN* and gives **STANDBY F-PLN** and **STANDBY PROGRESS**, with present position and ground speed from the IRUs and lateral guidance along the stored plan. In standby the navigation database is not available: waypoints are entered as an identifier and latitude/longitude (or a latitude/longitude, named like N51W050) with the left keys only, and only waypoints, tracks and distances are kept, so discontinuities may appear where data was lost. If the FMF has completed an automatic reset before standby is selected, the standby plan and tuning are cleared.

blocks.content: In this version only the Captain's MCDU keyboard is connected (see [Simulation notes](#simulation-notes)). Make every entry below on the Captain's MCDU; the crew column shows the usual division of work between the pilots.

items.action: Model, engine and database effectivity checked; database swapped if needed (4L, CONFIRM)
CO ROUTE or FROM/TO; route selected; ALTN; FLT NO
INITIALIZE IRS* (4R) with the gate position
ACARS REVIEW, INSERT into SEC, ACTIVATE SEC, or build on F-PLN with LAT REV
LAT REV at the origin, <SID: runway, SID, transition, *INSERT
Checked against the flight plan; discontinuities resolved; constraints checked
BLOCK, TOGW or ZFW, TOCG, ZFWCG, reserves
Ballast and fuel type as required
Flap, slope/wind, OAT, V1, VR, V2; CLB THRUST and ACCEL altitudes (no FLEX: flex takeoff is not simulated)
Speed modes (ECON); PRESELECT CRZ and DES as required
Autotuning checked; navaids for the departure set

items: **Before takeoff:** with all engines running, arm NAV and PROF on the FCP (NAV ARMED, PROF ARMED), FMS SPD as required. Set the FCP altitude to the clearance altitude.

**Takeoff and climb:** NAV engages at 100 ft, PROF at 400 ft; at the thrust reduction altitude the limit changes to climb, and the FMS accelerates at the ACCEL altitude. Couple the autopilot from 400 ft. Raise the FCP altitude as cleared; PROF levels at constraints and the FCP altitude.
**Cruise:** check the step climb prediction on the CRZ page; when cleared, set the new level in the FCP and the climb starts at the step point. Enter forecast winds on VERT REV 2/2 as required.

**Descent preparation:** set up the arrival with LAT REV, STAR> (STAR, approach, transitions, MIN PROF for a non-precision approach) and *INSERT; check APPROACH (VREF, VAPP, configuration); enter descent winds on DESCENT FORECAST.

**Descent:** before T/D lower the FCP altitude to the clearance; in PROF and FMS SPD the descent starts at T/D. Monitor PATH ERROR on the DES page; use speed brakes if the aircraft gains speed on the path.
**Direct to:** DIR INTC, select a plan waypoint or type the fix into 1L, then push 1L* (or *WITH ABEAM POINTS at 2L). For an intercept, enter the course at 1R, then push 1R*.
**Hold:** LAT REV at the fix, HOLD>, check or change INB CRS, TURN and TIME/DIST, *INSERT. To leave, EXIT AT FIX at F-PLN 1R.
**Approach:** arm the approach on the FCP; NAV and PROF end at localizer and glideslope capture.
**Go-around:** push G/A; the GO AROUND page appears. Engage NAV and PROF again to fly the missed approach procedure.
**After landing:** at engine shutdown the FMS completes the flight and clears the active plan; a plan in the secondary flight plan is kept for the next leg.

sections.title: Failures and non-normal operation
sections.summary: What fails in each flight management computer, how it shows, and what the crew do.

blocks.content: A flight management failure rarely leaves the aircraft without navigation: each fit has a second unit, a second computer or a standby mode, and the radio aids remain. The first actions are always the same: keep the aircraft under control on heading and altitude, identify which unit or sensor has failed, transfer the affected seat's instruments to a good source, and re-engage the autopilot's navigation mode on it. Checklists are in [Abnormal Procedures](abnormal-procedures).

blocks.content: **Navigation data.** All units read the selected navigation data source (EFB Settings, Aircraft, Navigation data). The aircraft's own Navigraph cycle is complete; the MSFS source provides airports, navaids, waypoints and nearest searches but no runways, procedures, airways or published holds, so the procedure pages are empty with it. Lookups are asynchronous, which is why an identifier can take a moment to be accepted.

**GPS.** The GPS receivers of the HT9100, the KC-10 FMS and the MD-10 are fed a fixed, healthy satellite picture rather than a moving constellation: the satellite counts do not change, RAIM is always available, and the destination and approach RAIM predictions (DEST RAIM, APPR P-RAIM) always read OK. The GPS position is the simulator's own position. GPS losses and the resulting dead reckoning or coasting can be produced with the EFB failure **GPS failure** (GPS 1 or 2). **Nav CDU failure** (CDU 1 or 2) fails the fitted long-range unit's CDU or the MD-10's MCDU, and **Inertial nav unit failure** an inertial unit or IRU.

**HT9100.** Each unit is modeled as a separate box with its own GPS solution, two routes, its own user database, the later-load page set, holds, offsets, intercepts, abeam points, the missed approach with TO/GA, the geometric descent path and the vertical deviation to the analog and electronic instruments. Each unit is powered from its own DC bus in the simulation (unit 1 the left emergency DC bus, unit 2 the right emergency DC bus, unit 3 DC bus 3); the operator's circuit breakers are not modeled. Not available: route crossload between units (copy routes through the user database instead), the navigation database half of NDB CROSSLOAD, and the pages behind <HDG/TAS OVERRIDE (or <DR) and <ACT RTE on POS REF and behind CONFIGURATION, BITE HISTORY, RETURN TO SERVICE and INTERFACE CHECK on MAINTENANCE INDEX (each shows NOT IMPLEMENTED); NAT latitude/longitude names and latitude/longitude crossing entries on the RTE pages; the ATC key (inoperative in the aircraft too). The MCDU's MSG annunciator and the GPS STATUS annunciators (APPR, RNP ALERT, WPT, OFSET) are not present on the simulated flight deck; read the messages in the scratchpad. The AUTO TUNE position of the nav mode switch does nothing with the HT9100 fitted.

The HT9100's predictions are limited in the simulation: PROGRESS 1/2's LAST, TO, NEXT and DEST rows, the cross-track and track angle error on PROGRESS 2/2 and the waypoint fields of POS REPORT show dashes; the leg times on RTE DATA use the present ground speed; forecast winds are stored but not used; there is no top of climb. The messages DISCONTINUITY, END OF ROUTE, UNABLE CRUISE ALT and RAIM LIMIT EXCEEDS are not generated, and GPS ANTENNA FAIL, TIMEOUT-RESELECT and SOFTWARE CONFIG INVALID cannot occur. The EFB's Nav CDU failure blanks a unit's MCDU while its NPU goes on navigating and steering. Holding CLR does not clear the whole scratchpad: clear it a character at a time.

**PMS.** The PMCU's computations, every page, the data entry rules, the advisories and the engine-out logic are modeled, against the simulated aircraft's own drag, thrust, fuel flow and thrust rating tables. PERF coupling to the autopilot and autothrottle is not: the PMS is advisory, the CLB/CRZ/DES lamps show the predicted mode and the CDU MESSAGE lamps stay dark. The handbook does not publish the cost index law, the engine-out detection thresholds or the descent optimum speed law; the simulation uses reasonable laws for them, so treat the effect of cost index on OPT speeds as indicative. Because the simulated aircraft's high-speed drag depends on Mach but not on lift coefficient, OPT often equals MAX at weights below about 500,000 lb. Weights are displayed in tonnes. NAV AID and DIR are inoperative (INS waypoint control), the TESTS sub-pages are not provided, per-INS positions on INS STS/POS are not shown, and a BOD defined by a VOR is counted down rather than updated by DME. The line select key lamps are not lit; the flashing SEL/SPD is the cue. Holding CLEAR acts as a single tap: the two-second clear of a field is not available, so clear a field with the CLEAR word and its line key. The PMS option is also offered on the DC-10-10 and -15, which have no simulated PMS; selecting it there removes the AUTO BRAKE panel.

**KC-10 FMS.** The three CDUs, the shared data set, ACT/MOD/SEC with EXEC, every INDEX and DATA page, PERF and VNAV predictions, the radios, the mission patterns (flown through the autopilot), INAV and STATUS, the IFF and the data link pages are modeled. The FMS BUS SPLIT function and the FMS HEADING TRUE/MAG switch are not on the simulated flight deck (the bus is always joined and courses are magnetic). The INU batteries are not simulated, so INU ON BATTERY never appears. These answer FUNCTION UNAVAILABLE: airway entry by the crew (imports carry their airways), along-track waypoints, Mach constraints, editing the FROM waypoint on LEGS, INTC CRS after a direct-to, present-position holds and SEC holds, SPD TGT RESET, INIT GPS and manual UTC/DATE entry on START INIT (the GPS receivers initialize themselves and give the time). Also not available: VNAV direct-to, holding time in predictions, en-route constraint and constant-speed predictions, loiter fuel for a refueling ETD, and the second end of two-ended anchors. The data link has no ground station: downlinks are acknowledged at link level and nothing ever answers. DATA LOADER 2 runs its load ritual with the same databases coming back. The refueling database is the AP/1B tracks and anchors of North and South America; REFUEL MISMATCH is never raised.

**MD-10 FMS.** Both FMFs with crosstalk, the full FCOM page tree, the generated performance database (from the DC-10 Flight Manual, CF6-6D for the MD-10-10 and CF6-50C2 for the MD-10-30), NAV, PROF and FMS SPD through the FCCs, thrust limits, engine-out mode, standby and the ACARS route uplink are modeled. The IRUs are the simulated ADIRUs, which align and drift; the GNS position is the simulator's own. In this version **only the Captain's MCDU keyboard is operative**: the First Officer's and the third MCDU display the FMS pages but their keys are not yet connected (so the third MCDU's STANDBY F-PLN cannot be reached), and the MCDU annunciators (MSG, OFST, DSPY, FAIL) are not shown. The FMS transfer switches (CAPT ON 2, F/O ON 1) are not present; both MCDUs stay onside. V1, VR and V2 are not computed (enter them, or use Send to Avionics). The FCCs sequence the autothrottle's thrust limit themselves (takeoff, climb at the thrust reduction altitude, cruise, MCT, go-around), as the AUTO mode would; a MANUAL selection on THRUST LIMITS changes only the page. A flex takeoff is not simulated: a FLEX temperature is accepted and FLX T/O becomes the active limit on the page, with its N1 dashed, but the takeoff is flown at the full takeoff rating. The derated ratings show dashes. The DECEL prompt is not provided. The navigation databases carry no engine-out SIDs, so no EOSID is listed on the SID page or offered after an engine failure. The ND draws the active flight plan, its waypoints and the TO waypoint data; pseudo waypoints (T/C, T/D), constraint labels, the secondary plan, holding patterns and the vertical deviation indicator are not drawn on the ND. The forecast winds entered on the FORECAST pages do not yet change the climb and descent predictions. The weight and balance system is not fitted, so CHECK WEIGHTS does not appear.

parts.title: Weather Radar and Surveillance
parts.summary: Weather radar, ground proximity warning, TCAS and the ATC transponders.

sections.title: Introduction
sections.summary: Four systems that watch the world outside the aircraft: weather, terrain, traffic and the ground controller's radar.

blocks.content: This part covers the four systems that look outward from the aircraft and warn the crew about what they find. The **weather radar** paints precipitation and ground returns ahead of the aircraft. The **ground proximity warning system (GPWS)** watches the flight path against the terrain below and calls out when the two are converging. The **traffic alert and collision avoidance system (TCAS)** interrogates other aircraft's transponders and advises the crew how to maneuver vertically when a collision threat develops. The **ATC transponders** answer the ground controller's secondary radar and the TCAS of other aircraft, and give this aircraft's own TCAS its link to the outside world.

The four are independent boxes with independent power, but they are not unaware of each other. The GPWS takes precedence over the TCAS: while the GPWS is speaking, the TCAS falls back to traffic advisories only and stays silent. On the DC-10 the keypad transponder head is also the TCAS control panel. And the weather radar and TCAS share the same family of displays on the aircraft that carry glass navigation displays. The architecture and the reasoning behind each system are described below, followed by the controls panel by panel, normal operation, and failures.

blocks.alt: Functional block diagram of the surveillance systems. Left column: the weather radar (two receiver/transmitters, one split-axis antenna in the nose radome, the pedestal control panel, two indicators on the side consoles; stabilization input from the vertical gyros on the DC-10 and MD-10 and from the INS on the KC-10). Center: the GPWS computer with its inputs (radio altimeters, CADC 1 barometric rate and airspeed, ILS deviations, gear and flap position, roll attitude) and outputs (glareshield GPWS, BELOW G/S and WINDSHEAR legends, voice to the cockpit speaker, terrain picture to the navigation displays). Right: the TCAS processor with upper and lower antennas, the Mode S transponder link, CADC altitude, radio altitude and gear lever inputs, the two TVSIs, and the control source per deck (transponder keypad head on the DC-10, FMS CDU on the KC-10). Bottom: the two ATC transponders and the control head, with the link to the simulator's transponder. Arrows show the GPWS-to-TCAS precedence line.

Two things in that table are worth noticing. First, the radar's two systems are on opposite generator buses, so the loss of one AC bus costs one radar system and one indicator, never both. Second, the GPWS voice and the GPWS computer are on different circuits: a computer can be working and speaking into a dead speaker, in which case it still claims precedence over the TCAS even though nobody hears it.

sections.title: Weather radar
sections.summary: A dual-system X-band radar with one stabilized antenna, two indicators, and the theory needed to read it.

blocks.content: The weather radar is a Bendix RDR-1FB class airborne radar: two complete receiver/transmitters (**R/T 1** and **R/T 2**, selected as **SYS 1** and **SYS 2**), one antenna in the nose radome, one control panel on the pedestal and, on the DC-10 and KC-10, two independent color indicators on the side consoles. It detects precipitation and displays it in three calibrated levels, maps the ground for navigation, and on the KC-10 interrogates radar beacons. The same radar is modeled on all three aircraft; what differs is the control head, the source of the antenna's stabilization signal, the tilt range, and the KC-10's fault lights.

The design follows a simple redundancy rule: anything that radiates or processes is duplicated, and the mechanical parts that cannot sensibly be duplicated are shared. Both R/Ts are energized whenever the radar is out of OFF. The selected one transmits and drives the antenna; the other stays warm in standby, ready to take over. The antenna and its waveguide are single, so an antenna drive failure takes the whole radar, while an R/T failure is cured by selecting the other system.

rows: Generate the X-band pulses, receive the echoes, apply gain and sensitivity-time control, and quantize the video into three levels. Each has its own 3-minute transmitter time delay.

A 30-inch-class antenna on a split-axis gimbal: azimuth scan of ±90°, an elevation axis carrying tilt and pitch compensation, and an outer roll gimbal. A ferrite beam shaper forms either a pencil beam about 3° wide or a vertically spread fan beam for mapping.

children.title: How an airborne weather radar sees
children.summary: Pulses, reflectivity, beam geometry and attenuation: what the picture means and what it cannot show.

blocks.content: A pulse radar measures range by time. The transmitter sends a pulse of microwave energy a fraction of a microsecond long, and the receiver listens for echoes. Radio energy travels about one nautical mile in 6.18 µs, so an echo from a target 1 NM away returns after about 12.36 µs (the *radar mile*), and the indicator places each echo along the sweep line at a distance proportional to its delay. Bearing comes from the antenna: the beam is narrow, so whatever echoes is on the line the antenna is pointing along at that instant. Sweeping the antenna from side to side and painting each line builds the plan-position picture on the indicator.

The radar operates in the X band, around 9.3 GHz, with a wavelength of about 3.2 cm. That choice is a compromise. A shorter wavelength gives a narrower beam from a dish small enough to fit in a nose, and raindrops scatter it strongly, which is what a weather radar wants. The price is attenuation: the same drops that make rain visible also absorb and scatter the energy on its way through, a problem discussed below.

Raindrops are small compared with 3.2 cm, so they scatter in the Rayleigh regime, where each drop's echo grows with the sixth power of its diameter. A few large drops therefore return far more energy than many small ones. Meteorologists express this as the **reflectivity factor**, Z, the sum of the sixth powers of the drop diameters in a unit volume, usually quoted in dBZ. Because big drops fall fast and mean heavy rain, Z correlates with rainfall rate, R, through an empirical **Z-R relationship**; the standard one, Z = 200 R^1.6 (Marshall and Palmer), is the one this radar's calibration follows.
With the receiver at its calibrated gain (AUTO), the radar quantizes the echo into three levels, each painted in its own color:

blocks.title: Calibrated weather levels (gain AUTO)
rows: Light to moderate rain; usually little turbulence
Moderate to heavy rain; convective cells likely
Heavy rain; thunderstorm cores, possible hail and severe turbulence
Nothing detected, or nothing the beam reached

blocks.content: Two consequences follow from the physics. First, **the radar sees water, not turbulence**. Turbulence is associated with strong gradients of reflectivity and with convective cores, so the picture is an indirect guide to it, not a measure of it. Second, **ice is a poor reflector**. The dielectric property that governs scattering is about five times weaker for ice than for liquid water, so dry hail, ice crystals and snow paint far more weakly than rain of the same mass. The top of a towering cumulonimbus, above the freezing level, can look harmless while the core below is violent. Scanning the part of the storm below the freezing level, where the water is liquid, gives the truest picture of its strength.

The absence of color is not the absence of weather. Dry hail, clear-air turbulence, the anvil and the upper part of a storm can return little or nothing. Avoid thunderstorm cells by a wide margin regardless of how they paint, and remember that turbulence can extend several thousand feet above a storm and 20 NM or more beyond its visible echo.

children.title: Beam width, tilt and the curvature of the earth

blocks.content: The pencil beam is about 3° wide between its half-power points. That sounds narrow, but the beam spreads with distance: its diameter grows by about 318 ft for every nautical mile of range. At 50 NM it is about 16,000 ft across, and at 150 NM nearly 48,000 ft, deeper than most storms are tall. A storm is only painted at its true strength while it fills the beam. Far away, the beam is larger than the cell, the echo is averaged with empty air, and the storm paints weaker and larger than it is. This **beam-filling** effect, together with the falloff of echo strength with range, is why distant weather should be re-evaluated on a shorter range as it comes closer.

**Tilt** is the angle of the beam's center line above or below the horizontal. A small angle has a large effect at range: each degree of tilt raises or lowers the beam center by about 106 ft per nautical mile. At 50 NM, one degree is 5,300 ft. Fine tilt adjustments of a quarter or half a degree are therefore meaningful, and the indicator should be allowed at least one complete antenna scan after each change before the new picture is judged.

The earth curves away below the horizontal. Radio waves bend slightly downward in the standard atmosphere, which radar engineers model by drawing the earth with four-thirds of its real radius; on that model the ground drops below a horizontal line from the antenna by about 0.66 ft times the square of the range in nautical miles (the right-hand column above). The same model gives the **radar horizon**, the farthest range at which the beam can graze the earth: about 1.23 times the square root of the height in feet, in nautical miles. From 10,000 ft that is about 123 NM; from 35,000 ft, about 230 NM. Beyond the horizon the beam passes over the ground, so weather there is seen only by its upper parts.

blocks.alt: Schematic side view of the radar beam from an aircraft at 35,000 ft. The 3° pencil beam is drawn with its center line at 2° down tilt, expanding with range; range marks at 25, 50, 100 and 150 NM with the beam diameter labeled at each. The earth's surface is drawn as a curve dropping below the horizontal, with the ground intercept of the beam's lower edge marked and the radar horizon at 230 NM. A thunderstorm with its freezing level marked shows the beam passing through its wet core at 50 NM and over its top at 150 NM.
blocks.title: Beam geometry and tilt
blocks.caption: A thunderstorm 50 NM ahead is cut through its core; the same storm at 150 NM would be seen only in its upper, icy part, or overflown entirely.

blocks.content: Tilt management follows from this geometry. On the ground before takeoff, tilt down until ground returns appear, then sweep up slowly through the level beam to find weather on the departure path. In climb, raise the tilt gradually so the beam stays on the weather of interest and ground returns stay at the outer edge of the picture. In cruise, select the shortest range of interest and tilt down until ground returns just appear at the edge of the display, then step out through the longer ranges, repeating the check after every course change of about 45° or more. In descent, the classic rule is to tilt up about one degree for every 10,000 ft lost to keep ground clutter from swamping the picture, and about one degree every 5,000 ft below roughly 15,000 ft over high or built-up terrain.

children.title: Gain, sensitivity-time control and target clarity

blocks.content: **Gain** sets the receiver's sensitivity and therefore the rainfall rates at which each color begins. In **AUTO** the receiver runs at its calibrated gain, which is also its maximum: the thresholds are the 1, 4 and 12 mm/h of the table above. Moving the GAIN control out of AUTO can only reduce sensitivity. Because Z grows with R to the power 1.6, every 16 dB of gain reduction raises each threshold tenfold in rainfall rate, so a modest reduction strips the green away and leaves only the strongest cores. Reduced gain is useful for examining the structure of a large area of returns, to find the cores and the gaps between them, and for ground mapping. It must be returned to AUTO before weather is judged by color.
With GAIN out of AUTO the colors no longer mean the calibrated rainfall rates. A cell that paints yellow at reduced gain may be red at AUTO.

The echo from rain that fills the beam falls off with the square of range, so without correction the same storm would paint weaker every mile further away. **Sensitivity-time control (STC)** compensates by holding the receiver's gain down for echoes arriving soon after the pulse and raising it as the delay grows. The radar normalizes storm returns in this way out to about 80 NM: within that range, equal storms paint equally regardless of distance. Beyond 80 NM the compensation stops and distant returns weaken with range again. STC is active in the weather modes and in the KC-10's MAP 2; it is inhibited in MAP (DC-10, MD-10) and MAP 1 (KC-10), where a strong, unsmoothed picture of near terrain is wanted.

**Target clarity (TGT CLAR)** on each indicator fine-tunes the first level only: green in the weather modes, blue in MAP. It moves the threshold of that level a few decibels either side of calibration, to clean background noise off the picture or to bring out weak returns. Turning it counterclockwise lowers the threshold (more green, and eventually receiver noise speckling the screen); clockwise raises it. Its mid position is the calibrated setting, and it does not affect the yellow or red levels.

children.title: Attenuation, shadowing and the limits of the picture

blocks.content: At X band, heavy rain absorbs and scatters a significant fraction of the energy passing through it. The amount grows with rainfall rate. A beam that penetrates an intense cell returns from the cells behind it weakened, so they paint smaller and weaker than they are, and a strong cell can completely hide a second, larger one behind it. The tell-tale is a **radar shadow**: an area with no returns, not even ground returns, directly behind an intense echo. Never plan to fly into a shadow or through the far side of a cell that the beam could not penetrate.

Some echo shapes are known indicators of hail and severe weather: U shapes, thin protruding fingers, scalloped edges and hook-shaped appendages, which change rapidly from scan to scan. A narrow band of green and yellow between the red core and the edge of an echo means a steep reflectivity gradient, which is usually associated with more severe turbulence than a wide, gentle gradient.
The simulation does not model attenuation or radar shadowing: a cell behind another paints at its true strength. Fly as if it did. See [Simulation notes](#simulation-notes).

The antenna scans ±90° either side of the nose at eight complete cycles a minute: one cycle, left to right and back, takes 7.5 s, and each single pass across the 180° sector about 3.75 s. The scan is a nearly constant rate of about 50° per second with a short turnaround at each stop, so the sweep line moves evenly across the picture and the image does not bloom at the edges.

Without stabilization, a beam tilted 2° down would point 10° down at the left of the scan in a 10° right bank and 6° up at the right, painting ground on one side and empty sky on the other. The antenna therefore uses a **split-axis** mount. The outer roll gimbal turns opposite to the aircraft's bank, up to 43.5° either way. Inside it, the elevation axis carries the selected tilt plus a pitch correction that varies with azimuth: full correction straight ahead, none at the 90° stops, where a pitch change does not move the beam up or down. Pitch compensation extends to 25° nose up or down. The result is a beam whose tilt is referenced to the horizon, not to the aircraft's floor, throughout normal maneuvering.

The servos stabilize on the **sensed** attitude, from the vertical gyro (DC-10, MD-10) or the inertial platform (KC-10) feeding each system. If that source is wrong, the antenna faithfully stabilizes to the wrong horizon and the beam points where the aircraft is not looking: a toppled or erecting gyro tilts the whole picture, painting ground on one side of the screen. That is the purpose of the MD-10's STAB button, which takes a faulty signal out and lets the antenna follow the aircraft's axes. On the DC-10 the radar follows the vertical gyro the seat's VERT GYRO switch has selected, so switching that seat to the auxiliary gyro moves the radar with the ADI. A source that loses power removes the signal altogether, and the antenna then simply follows the aircraft's body axes.

Beyond the stabilization limits (more than 43.5° of bank or 25° of pitch) the gimbals reach their stops and the picture is no longer level. Even inside them, the resolver law used to apportion pitch correction leaves a small second-order error, a degree and a half or so at large pitch angles, which is inherent in this type of antenna.

blocks.title: OFF while moving (DC-10, KC-10)
blocks.content: Moving the function switch to OFF while the aircraft is in motion can damage the antenna: without power, the unstabilized antenna is free to bang against its mechanical stops. Select STBY for taxi and select OFF only when stopped. In the simulation, doing so latches an antenna failure that lasts for the rest of the flight. The MD-10's pushbutton head has no STBY position and is exempt.
Every control head selects from the same set of radar modes, but each head engraves them differently. The table lists what each mode does to the transmitter, the antenna, the beam and the receiver.

blocks.title: Radar modes
rows: No; both R/Ts warm up, antenna does not scan

blocks.content: **Weather** (NORM, WX) is the primary mode: pencil beam, STC active, three calibrated levels. Significant weather is shown out to 300 NM, with STC normalization inside 80 NM. Ground returns also appear, and over 100 NM the weather mode makes a better long-range ground map than the map modes.

**Contour** (CONT, DC-10 only) is the weather mode with the contour circuit added: wherever the echo exceeds the heavy threshold, the display is blanked to black instead of red. A red core becomes a black hole surrounded by yellow and green. The convention dates from monochrome radars, where it was the only way to show intensity, and it carries an obvious trap: a black area inside an echo is the most intense part of the storm, not a gap.
In CONT, a black hole ringed by yellow is a heavy rain core. Do not mistake it for a clear path through the weather.

**Map** modes switch the beam to a **fan**: the ferrite shaper spreads the energy downward in a cosecant-squared pattern, so the beam illuminates the ground evenly from near the aircraft out to the horizon instead of in a narrow band. Returns are painted blue (weak), yellow and red (strong). Smooth water reflects the beam away and paints black; fields and farmland paint blue; hills, towns and coastlines yellow; mountains and large cities red. The fan's center sits a little below the pencil's, so about 2° more up tilt is needed for the same picture when changing from PENCIL to FAN. On the DC-10 and MD-10, MAP forces the fan; the KC-10's PEN/FAN switch selects either in MAP 1 and MAP 2 (pencil gives better point-target definition and is used for air-to-air skin painting).

**MAP 1** (KC-10) is medium-range mapping with STC inhibited; **MAP 2** enables STC to stop nearby returns smearing during low-level mapping. **BCN** (KC-10) forces the fan, transmits interrogations to airborne and ground radar beacons, and paints their coded replies in green; it is the tanker's rendezvous mode. **WX/T** (MD-10) selects weather with turbulence detection on the real FedEx radar; this radar has no turbulence-detecting receiver, so WX/T behaves as WX.

**Test** switches the transmitter into a dummy load, so no energy leaves the antenna and the test is safe on a ramp, and generates a test pattern on the indicators. The antenna scans and is driven by a synthetic pitch and roll signal, so the test exercises the drive and the stabilization servos as well as the receiver and the display.
The pattern is described under [Test pattern](#wxr-test-pattern).

The transmitter tube needs time to warm before high voltage is applied, so each R/T has a **3-minute time delay** that starts when it is first powered, whatever mode is selected. Both R/Ts are powered together whenever the radar is out of OFF, so a radar that has been in STBY for three minutes has both systems ready. Selecting the other system (SYS 1 to SYS 2 or back) starts a **transfer delay of about 90 s** on the newly selected R/T; if its 3-minute warm-up is still running, the longer of the two applies.

blocks.content: A momentary power interruption shorter than about half a second, such as a bus transfer, does not restart the delays; the R/Ts ride through it, transmission and scan stop for the moment, and the picture returns. A longer interruption resets the delays.

Each indicator is a self-contained color display with its own control strip along the top. Both show the video from the selected R/T, but each pilot chooses their own range, intensity, target clarity and marker, and can freeze their own picture with HOLD. The KC-10 carries the same indicator as the DC-10.

blocks.alt: DC-10 captain's weather radar indicator in NORM (WX legend), 150/30 range, gain AUTO. Upper left: mode legend WX in blue. Upper right: range 150/30 and the color bar with red, yellow, green cells and H and L letters. Blue azimuth lines at 0°, 30° and 60° either side and five blue range arcs. A squall line at 60-90 NM with red cores, yellow and green edges, and ground returns at the outer edge. Control strip legible: RANGE knob (OFF 5 25 50 150 300), TGT CLAR, INT, NOR/MKR/DLY selector, HOLD button, SLEW switch.
blocks.title: Radar indicator, weather picture

blocks.content: The picture is a 180° sector, heading up, with the aircraft at the apex. Azimuth lines mark the nose and 30° and 60° either side. Five equally spaced range arcs divide the selected range; the range and the mark spacing are lettered at upper right (for example 150/30). The mode is lettered at upper left. The **color bar** at upper right shows the three colors in use with H (high) and L (low) at its ends; a color missing from the bar is a color the radar has lost (an R/T or indicator fault). The symbology is blue in the weather, test and beacon modes and green in the map modes, so it never competes with a return of the same color.

A **question mark** in place of the mode legend means the selected R/T has failed or lost its power, or the antenna drive has failed, and the picture cannot be trusted. Select the other system, or use the other indicator, as appropriate.

**HOLD** freezes the indicator's picture so the crew can study it or compare it with the next scan; the antenna keeps scanning. While held, the mode legend alternates with the word HOLD about once a second. A second press returns to the live picture, and an indicator always comes up live when powered.

The **marker** (MKR) is a yellow range arc that the SLEW switch moves in and out; its range is lettered at upper right. It moves in 0.1 NM steps from 0.3 to 5 NM on the 5 NM range and in 1 NM steps from 5 to 300 NM on the others; held, the SLEW switch steps slowly at first and then fast. **Delay** (DLY) starts the sweep at the marker's range instead of at the aircraft, so the full selected range is spent on the area beyond it: with the marker at 25 NM and the 5 NM range selected, the display shows 25 to 30 NM in fine detail. The marker itself is not drawn in DLY, and the range lettered is the delay range. Delay is used to examine a distant cell or a beacon code closely.

blocks.alt: Two KC-10 radar indicator pictures side by side. Left: MKR selected, 50/10 range, a yellow variable range marker arc at 25 NM with 25 lettered at upper right and MKR at upper left. Right: DLY selected, 5/1 range, the sweep starting at 25 NM, showing the expanded area 25-30 NM with a beacon return in green; DLY at upper left and 25 at upper right.
blocks.title: Marker and delay

blocks.content: On every flight load the captain's RANGE selector sits at 50 NM and the first officer's at OFF, so the first officer's indicator stays dark until a range is selected.

In TEST the R/T generates a range-locked pattern that checks the whole chain from receiver to screen. Five concentric color bands fill the lower third of the display: green, yellow, red, yellow and green, from about 0 to 48 NM. Beyond them, a band of graduated green noise from 50 to 80 NM shows the STC working (its density rises with range as the gain rises), and a band of coarse green noise from 80 to 100 NM shows the receiver's noise floor. Rotating TGT CLAR visibly changes the noise in that band.

blocks.alt: KC-10 radar indicator in TEST at 150/30: TEST legend upper left in blue, color bar red/yellow/green with H and L. Five concentric bands in the lower third: green, yellow, red, yellow, green out to about 48 NM; graduated green noise from 50 to 80 NM increasing with range; coarse green noise from 80 to 100 NM; blue azimuth lines and range marks.
