blocks.content: On the DC-10 the pattern appears about 20 s after TEST is selected. On the KC-10 it cannot be read until the 3-minute transmitter delay has run. A test is complete once the antenna has carried the valid pattern across one whole pass of the screen, stop to stop: from a cold radar on the DC-10 that is about 26 s after selecting TEST, and from a radar already warm in STBY, between 4 and 8 s. Each system is tested in turn by moving the SYS switch.

children.title: Weather on the glass navigation displays

blocks.content: DC-10s fitted with the MFD electronic HSI or the FPDS paint the same radar picture on those displays as well. The MFD EHSI shows weather automatically on its map formats whenever the radar is transmitting; the FPDS navigation display shows it when its WXR button is selected. Both draw the returns within 60° either side of the picture's up direction, and both take the receiver's calibrated thresholds rather than either indicator's TGT CLAR setting. Their legends show the radar's mode and the tilt selected on the control panel. See [Flight instruments](flight-instruments).
The KC-10's EHSI does not paint weather; its TERR/WXR selection shows the EGPWS terrain picture only. The radar picture is on the two indicators.

On the real MD-10 the radar picture is drawn on the navigation display, selected by pushing the WX BRT knob on each ECP. In the simulation the MD-10's radar runs (its head, R/Ts, antenna, delays and electrical loads are all modeled), but the ND does not yet draw its picture or its annunciations. See [Simulation notes](#simulation-notes).

sections.title: Ground proximity warning system
sections.summary: The computer that compares the flight path with the ground below, its six warning modes, its voice, and the terrain picture.

blocks.content: Controlled flight into terrain, a serviceable aircraft flown into the ground by a crew unaware of the danger, was the leading cause of airliner hull losses when the DC-10 entered service. The ground proximity warning system is the answer to it. Its principle is simple: the computer knows the aircraft's height above the ground from the radio altimeter, its rate of descent from the air data computer, its configuration from the gear and flaps, and its position relative to the glideslope from the ILS. From those it recognizes a set of hazardous combinations, the **modes**, and warns with a light and a voice before the situation becomes unrecoverable.

The original GPWS looks only straight down: it can tell that the ground is rising fast beneath the aircraft, but not that a mountain lies ahead of level flight. The **enhanced GPWS (EGPWS)** adds a worldwide terrain database and a navigation position, so it can draw the terrain around the aircraft on the navigation displays, colored by its height relative to the aircraft, and look ahead along the flight path. The basic modes are kept unchanged underneath. The simulation models the computer's health monitor, Modes 1 to 6 with their voice and lights, the self-tests, the panel switches, and the EGPWS terrain picture. The look-ahead terrain alerts and the windshear detection (Mode 7) are not modeled; see [Simulation notes](#simulation-notes).
Each aircraft carries a different generation of the computer. They share the modes and most of the numbers but differ in what they say, what they light, and how they are tested.

blocks.title: GPWS fits
rows: BELOW G/S light only, below 800 ft
Below 1,000 ft, with G/S INHIBIT legend

blocks.content: The DC-10 is delivered with the basic computer, as the airlines first fitted it: a health monitor, a lamp self-test and the BELOW G/S light, with no voice and no warnings from Modes 1 to 4. Two options turn it into the enhanced computer that later operators retrofitted. The **voice** option runs all the warning modes with the EGPWS's messages, adds the GLIDESLOPE voice to the BELOW G/S light and gives the self-test its enhanced sequence; Mode 5 keeps the basic computer's 800 ft ceiling. The **terrain** option adds the terrain database behind the terrain picture on the MFD EHSI and the FPDS. The two are independent, and both are off on a new aircraft (see [Simulation notes](#simulation-notes) for how they are set). The separate terrain display, a professional equipment option of its own, does not depend on either.

rows: Captain's radio altimeter (basic computer); either altimeter (EGPWS)
Captain's ILS receiver, front course only (the MD-10 uses the simulator's NAV 1)
Nose and both main gear down-locks
The captain's radio altimeter decision-height setting (MD-10: the captain's EIS control panel minimums, with RA selected)
FLAP OVRD, STEEP APPR, TERR OVRD, glideslope cancel, TEST

blocks.content: The computer cannot warn without a radio height and a barometric descent rate. If either is lost for longer than the confirmation time, the computer declares itself failed and stops warning; it recovers by itself when the input returns. A radio altimeter held in its self-test counts as lost, which is how the maintenance books fail the computer deliberately. An unpowered computer also reads as failed. For the first few seconds after power-up the warning modes are held off while the computer initializes, and a computer that first comes to life in the air does not mistake that moment for a takeoff.

The computer runs on AC BUS 1, its legends on DC BUS 1, and its voice through a speaker on a third circuit. A failed computer annunciates nothing but its FAIL (where the aircraft has a FAIL indication). On the DC-10 there is no GPWS FAIL light: in the simulation a failed or unpowered computer, and the self-test, light only the pilots' MASTER CAUTION, with no lamp on any panel to say why. The self-test is the way to confirm the computer is serviceable.

Each mode watches its own envelope, a boundary in a two-dimensional space such as radio height against descent rate, and asks the voice for its message when the aircraft crosses into it. Inside an envelope a mode repeats its message only if the penetration gets about 20% deeper, so a steady condition is announced and then left alone while a worsening one is announced again.

blocks.alt: Four small envelope charts in a 2 by 2 grid, each with radio altitude (ft) on the vertical axis. Mode 1: barometric descent rate on the horizontal axis, outer SINK RATE line and inner PULL UP line from near the ground up to 2,450 ft. Mode 2: terrain closure rate on the horizontal axis, the 2A boundary up to 1,650 ft expanding to 2,450 ft with airspeed and the 2B boundary capped at 789 ft. Mode 3: altitude loss on the horizontal axis, DON'T SINK region up to the end of the takeoff phase. Mode 4: airspeed on the horizontal axis, TOO LOW GEAR below 500 ft and 190 kt, TOO LOW FLAPS below 245 ft and 160 kt, and the TOO LOW TERRAIN boundary rising to 1,000 ft at 250 kt.
blocks.title: GPWS Modes 1 to 4, envelope shapes
blocks.caption: Shapes for orientation; the numbers are in the text.

blocks.content: Mode 1 compares the barometric descent rate with the radio height. It runs below 2,450 ft radio altitude and has two boundaries, both allowing less descent the nearer the aircraft is to the ground. Crossing the outer one produces two SINK RATE messages and lights the GPWS legend; crossing the inner one produces a continuous PULL UP. As a rough guide the outer boundary lies near 4,300 fpm at 2,000 ft and falls to about 1,500 fpm close to the ground. The mode does not care about configuration: it protects against a high sink rate on any approach, and against an unnoticed descent in cruise over low terrain.

Above a valid front-course glideslope the outer boundary is made less sensitive, so that a crew capturing the glideslope from above is not nagged. On the KC-10, the **STEEP APPR** switch moves both boundaries to higher descent rates for approaches steeper than the normal 3°.

Mode 2 warns of rising terrain. The computer derives a **closure rate**, how fast the ground is coming up to meet the aircraft, by combining the radio altitude's rate of change with the barometric vertical speed in a complementary filter. The radio altitude rate alone would react instantly to every building and cliff edge, and the barometric rate alone cannot see terrain at all; blended, the filter follows real terrain trends while one sharp edge does not read as a mountain.

**Mode 2A** applies with the flaps not in the landing range. Its upper boundary is about 1,650 ft radio altitude at low speed, expanding to 2,450 ft as airspeed increases from 220 to 310 kt to give more warning at higher speed. Entering it produces TERRAIN, TERRAIN and then a continuous PULL UP. After the aircraft leaves the PULL UP area, TERRAIN repeats while the closure continues, and the GPWS legend stays lit until the aircraft has gained 300 ft of barometric altitude, 45 s have passed, or FLAP OVRD is selected.

**Mode 2B** applies with the flaps in the landing range, on an ILS approach with both localizer and glideslope within two dots, and for the first 60 s after takeoff. It is less sensitive, so that a normal approach over rising terrain does not trigger it: the upper boundary is 789 ft, and with landing flaps the lower boundary lies between 200 ft (at a high descent rate) and 600 ft (with little or no descent), so that the last stage of a normal approach over rising ground is quiet. FLAP OVRD also selects Mode 2B, for a landing with less than the normal landing flap.

Mode 3 protects the climb-out. After takeoff, or after a go-around started below 245 ft, the computer watches for any loss of barometric altitude. The loss it tolerates grows with the height above the ground, so a small sag close to the ground warns while a larger one higher up is accepted. A loss beyond the allowance lights the GPWS legend and produces DON'T SINK. The protection lasts until the computer judges that the aircraft has climbed clear of the takeoff phase, at about 1,500 ft radio altitude.
Mode 4 warns when the aircraft is close to the ground in the wrong configuration or at too high a speed for the height. Its sub-modes depend on the gear and flaps:

rows: Gear up, not in the takeoff phase
Below 500 ft at less than 190 kt
Below a boundary rising from 500 ft at 190 kt to 1,000 ft at 250 kt
Gear down, flaps not in the landing range
Below 245 ft at less than 160 kt
Gear down, flaps not in landing range, faster
Below a boundary rising from 245 ft at 160 kt to 1,000 ft at 250 kt
Takeoff phase, gear or flaps not in landing configuration

blocks.content: Mode 4C uses a **terrain clearance floor** that grows with the climb. The floor is 75% of the aircraft's average radio height over the last 15 s, limited to 500 ft at 190 kt and below and rising linearly to 1,000 ft at 250 kt and above. A climb that levels off and then sinks back toward rising ground descends through the floor and warns, even though the descent rate is too small for Mode 1 and the closure too gentle for Mode 2. FLAP OVRD silences TOO LOW FLAPS for a landing with less than normal landing flap; it does not silence TOO LOW TERRAIN.

Mode 5 warns of a descent below the glideslope on a front-course ILS. It runs with the localizer within two dots, above 50 ft radio altitude and below 1,000 ft (800 ft on the DC-10, with or without the voice option). Between 1,000 and 500 ft the KC-10 and MD-10 computers also require a descent of at least 500 fpm, so a level segment below the beam is not warned. When the aircraft is more than 1.3 dots below the glideslope, the amber BELOW G/S legends light and the voice says GLIDESLOPE twice, at reduced volume (the **soft** alert); two more follow each time the deviation grows by about 20%. Below 300 ft with more than 2 dots, the **hard** alert repeats GLIDESLOPE continuously (on the real aircraft also at full volume).

A crew deliberately below the glideslope, for example on a visual approach or following a published offset, can cancel the alert. The cancel removes both the light and the voice and lasts until the aircraft leaves the band in which it can be set: below 30 ft, or above the band's ceiling.

blocks.title: Glideslope cancel
rows: The BELOW G/S switch-light; the G/S INHIBIT legend lights while the cancel is in effect

blocks.content: In the simulation the DC-10's and KC-10's glareshield caps cannot yet be pressed, so the glideslope cancel is available on the MD-10 only.

Mode 6 is advisory. On the approach it calls the radio height at FIVE HUNDRED, ONE HUNDRED, FIFTY, FORTY, THIRTY, TWENTY and TEN feet, each once per approach, re-arming on landing or after a climb above 2,500 ft. It calls MINIMUMS when the aircraft descends through the decision height set on the captain's radio altimeter, provided it is set between 10 and 1,000 ft. On the MD-10 that is the radio minimums set on the captain's EIS control panel with its MINIMUMS selector at RA; with BARO minimums selected there is no MINIMUMS callout. MINIMUMS takes priority over a height callout due at the same moment, and a callout that cannot be spoken within about a second is dropped rather than said late: FIFTY at thirty feet would be worse than nothing.

**BANK ANGLE** warns of excessive roll close to the ground. Above 150 ft radio altitude it calls BANK ANGLE, BANK ANGLE at 40° of roll. Below 150 ft the limit reduces progressively to 10° at 30 ft, stays at 10° below 30 ft, and is inhibited below 5 ft. The callout repeats once if the roll increases by a further 20%, and continuously if it reaches 40% beyond the angle of the first callout.

The computer has one voice and never talks over itself. When two modes want to speak at once, the more urgent message goes first and interrupts a less urgent one already in progress. The order is the computer family's own:

PULL UP (and its TERRAIN or OBSTACLE, PULL UP forms)
TERRAIN, TERRAIN

blocks.content: While the computer is speaking, the TCAS gives way: it reverts to traffic advisories only and silences its own voice (see [TCAS](#tcas)). This holds even when the GPWS speaker itself is unpowered, because the precedence is the computer's, not the speaker's.

rows: KC-10 (guarded switch-light); MD-10 (GPWS switch at FLAP OVRD)

Tells the computer the aircraft is in the landing configuration when it is not: silences TOO LOW FLAPS, selects Mode 2B, and ends Mode 2's held lights. Used for a landing with less than normal landing flap.
Desensitizes both Mode 1 boundaries for a steeper-than-normal approach.
Inhibits the enhanced terrain functions to avoid nuisance alerts (for example at an airfield missing from the database). The basic Modes 1 to 6 continue normally. It does not light TERR FAIL.

blocks.content: An override left selected removes protection. Check FLAP OVRD, STEEP APPR and TERR OVRD off (and FLAP OVRD guarded on the KC-10) on every preflight.

An EGPWS computer with its terrain database draws the terrain around the aircraft on the navigation displays. Each piece of ground is colored by its height **relative to the aircraft**, not by its absolute elevation, so the picture answers the pilot's real question: which ground is above me, which is close below me, and which is safely beneath. The colors are drawn as speckled dot patterns of different densities, fixed to the ground and laid on the map north-up, so they stand diagonally on the screen at a heading of 045° and do not shimmer as the picture is redrawn.

blocks.title: Terrain colors
rows: 500 ft below to 1,000 ft above (250 ft below with the gear down)
Green, solid (50% when red or yellow terrain is also in view)

blocks.content: When the aircraft is safely above all terrain in view, so that everything would be black, the display shades the highest ground in view in green so that the shape of the land stays visible. The yellow band reaching to 250 ft below the aircraft with the gear down keeps the approach terrain conspicuous on final.

blocks.alt: KC-10 captain's EHSI in MAP format, 40 NM range, TERR selected on the display control panel, descending at 6,000 ft toward mountainous terrain: speckled red and amber areas ahead on the right, 25% amber close to the track, green to the left, cyan sea along a coastline, black low ground at lower left. The terrain cells visibly diagonal to the heading-up card. Legends readable.

Where the terrain picture is shown

blocks.content: **TERR FAIL** is the computer's own answer to the question whether its terrain functions can work. It lights (amber, with MASTER CAUTION on the KC-10) when the terrain function has failed, when the computer itself has failed, or when the navigation system cannot supply a valid position and altitude of sufficient accuracy. On the KC-10, a present position not yet entered in the inertial units is enough to light it, and after a loss of GPS the navigation accuracy degrades until TERR FAIL lights, typically 15 to 30 minutes later. Selecting TERR OVRD inhibits the terrain functions but does not light TERR FAIL. The MD-10 splits the same information into two alerts on the engine and alert display: TERRAIN FAIL (the function has failed) and TERRAIN NOT AVAIL (no usable position).

Every computer tests itself on demand, lighting each legend in turn and, where it has a voice, saying a representative set of messages through the speaker. The test runs only on the ground, and is refused with the flaps in the landing range. The MD-10's test also needs ADIRU 1 aligned and navigating, since the computer takes its inertial data from it.

blocks.title: Self-test sequences
rows: FAIL indications on (KC-10: GPWS, W/S FAIL and TERR FAIL lights)
WINDSHEAR legends on: siren and WINDSHEAR, WINDSHEAR, WINDSHEAR; then the caution step, silent (not on the MD-10)
GPWS on, TERRAIN, TERRAIN, PULL UP

blocks.content: The enhanced computers have a second, longer test. A momentary press of the test switch starts **Level I**, the short test above. Holding the switch for two seconds or more turns it into **Level II**, which says the computer's whole vocabulary in order, from SINK RATE through the obstacle messages; a further two-second hold during Level II terminates it. Both levels begin identically up to and including GLIDESLOPE, because until the switch has been held for two seconds the computer cannot know which test it is running. The KC-10's Level I takes about 16 s.
On the MD-10 the GPWS switch springs back from TEST by itself after about a second. A click runs Level I; holding TEST for about half a second or longer is treated as a hold and runs Level II.

sections.title: Traffic alert and collision avoidance system
sections.summary: TCAS II on the DC-10 and the enhanced ETCAS on the KC-10: how threats are judged in time, not distance, and what the crew must do.

blocks.content: TCAS is an airborne collision avoidance system that works independently of ground radar. It interrogates the transponders of aircraft around it, measures their range and bearing from the replies, reads their reported altitude, and tracks them. From the tracks it predicts each intruder's **closest point of approach (CPA)** and, if the predicted miss is too small, warns the crew: first with a **traffic advisory (TA)** to help them see the traffic, then, if the threat persists, with a **resolution advisory (RA)**, a vertical maneuver that restores safe separation. TCAS II gives vertical advice only; it never commands a turn, because its bearing measurement is far too coarse to base a lateral escape on.

The DC-10 carries a standard TCAS II processor; the KC-10 carries the **ETCAS**, the same TCAS II logic with enhancements for formation flying: an extended vertical surveillance envelope and tagging of formation members. The MD-10 has no TCAS in this simulation.

TCAS sees only aircraft with an operating transponder. An aircraft with no transponder, or with its transponder off, is invisible to it. TCAS is a backup to air traffic control separation and to see-and-avoid, not a replacement for either.

This part describes how the TCAS is designed to work. In the simulation no other aircraft reach the TCAS yet: the traffic displays stay empty (apart from the DC-10 TVSIs' self-test pattern), no TA or RA is ever issued, and the TCAS voice is not heard. See [Simulation notes](#simulation-notes).

rows: Surveillance, tracking, threat evaluation and resolution logic. Powered from AC BUS 1.
Interrogate and receive; the directional pattern gives bearing. With the gear lever down the lower antenna is switched to a non-directional mode, because the nose gear would distort its pattern.
The processor's own transponder: on the DC-10 the selected set under the keypad head, on the KC-10 the APX-119 IFF. Without it the processor cannot operate.
Combined vertical speed and traffic displays on each pilot's panel. The vertical speed needle comes from the air data computer; the traffic picture and the RA arcs from the processor.
Glass displays (DC-10 MFD and FPDS fits, KC-10 EHSI)
Traffic symbols on the map formats.
The voice, through the combined GPWS/TCAS speaker.

blocks.content: The processor's other inputs are own altitude, as the quantized 100-ft altitude word the transponder reports (so own and intruder altitudes are compared on the same basis), the radio altitude for the low-altitude inhibits, the gear lever position for the antenna switching, and the GPWS's voice for its precedence.

The TVSI is really two instruments behind one glass, and its two failure areas show it. A failed air data computer stops the vertical speed needle and flags it while the traffic picture carries on; a failed or unpowered TCAS processor blanks the traffic and the arcs and shows TCAS FAIL while the needle keeps flying. The KC-10 carries TVSIs as standard. On the DC-10 they are an equipment option; a DC-10 with the KSSU or digital VSI has no TCAS display unless its MFD or FPDS glass shows the traffic.

**DC-10 control.** The TCAS is operated from the Gables G7490-07 keypad transponder head: its MODE knob selects TA or TA/RA, its BLW/N/ABV switch the vertical envelope, and its TEST button runs the TCAS self-test. The original drum transponder head has Mode A/C sets that cannot support TCAS, so with that head fitted the TCAS stays in standby. See [ATC transponders](#transponders).

**KC-10 control.** The ETCAS is operated from the FMS CDU: the TCAS 3/4 page selects TCAS MODE (STBY, TA, TA+RA), ENVELOPE (ABV, NORM, BLW), ETCAS on or off and the tagging pages. The IFF must be on and its MASTER at NORM with Mode 3/A on, and the COM TRANSMIT page's IFF selection must be ON; with IFF OFF on that page (its power-up default) the TCAS is held in standby. See [Flight management](flight-management).

TCAS judges threats in **time**, not distance. For each intruder it computes **range tau**, the range divided by the closure rate: the time in seconds to closest approach if nothing changes. Two aircraft a mile apart and diverging are no threat; two aircraft ten miles apart closing head-on at 900 kt are 40 s from collision. It computes a **vertical tau** the same way, the relative altitude divided by the relative vertical speed, and an intruder becomes a threat only when both the horizontal and the vertical taus fall below the thresholds. A diverging intruder has no closest approach ahead of it and no tau at all.

Tau alone fails at short range and low closure: an aircraft a quarter of a mile away, co-altitude and overtaking slowly, has a long tau but is plainly dangerous. TCAS therefore adds a minimum range (and a minimum vertical separation) inside which an intruder is a threat whatever its tau. The thresholds are not fixed: TCAS selects a **sensitivity level** from own altitude, giving the least warning time close to the ground, where traffic is dense and aircraft are slow and expected to be near each other, and the most at high altitude, where closure rates are highest.

blocks.title: Threat classes
rows: Beyond 6 NM or more than ±1,200 ft
Within 6 NM and ±1,200 ft, not a threat
Predicted CPA within the TA thresholds: 20 to 48 s ahead depending on altitude; vertical within ±850 ft (±1,200 ft above FL300)
Predicted CPA within the RA thresholds: 15 to 35 s ahead depending on altitude

blocks.content: A TA normally comes 10 to 15 s before an RA, which gives the crew time to look for the traffic and prepare. An intruder whose transponder does not report altitude can still raise a TA on its range and closure, but never an RA, because without altitude there is no vertical solution; such traffic is not displayed at all above 14,500 ft. Each symbol carries the intruder's altitude relative to own aircraft in hundreds of feet, with a plus sign above the symbol when the intruder is above and a minus sign below it when the intruder is below, and an arrow beside it when the intruder is climbing or descending at 500 fpm or more.

The vertical extent of the traffic picture is selectable. **NORM** shows traffic within 2,700 ft above and below. **ABV** extends the view upward for the climb and **BLW** downward for the descent, to 9,000 ft on the DC-10's TCAS II and to 12,700 ft on the KC-10's ETCAS with ETCAS on (9,000 ft with it off), keeping 2,700 ft on the other side. The selection changes what is displayed, not the threat logic.

Side view: the ±850/±1,200 ft TA band and the NORM ±2,700 ft display envelope, with the ABV and BLW extensions to 9,000 ft (TCAS II) and 12,700 ft (ETCAS).
blocks.title: TCAS warning volumes
blocks.caption: The warning areas are time-based: they grow with closure rate, so a fast head-on intruder is warned much further out than a slow one.

blocks.content: An RA solves one problem: make the vertical miss distance at CPA larger than a safe minimum. TCAS chooses the **sense**, climb or descend, that gives the larger miss, and then the least **strength** of maneuver that achieves it. Once chosen, the sense is held; it is reversed only if the projected miss under it fails by a margin, so that the crew is not given a climb and a descend alternately on measurement noise.

A **corrective RA** calls for a change of vertical speed: the TVSI shows a red arc over the forbidden vertical speeds and a green arc over the target, and the pilot flies the needle out of the red and into the green. A **preventive RA** asks only that the present vertical speed not be changed into a forbidden range: it shows a red arc and no green, and the needle is already outside the red. An RA can later **strengthen** (INCREASE CLIMB, INCREASE DESCENT), **weaken** to a gentler requirement once separation is assured, or **reverse** if the intruder maneuvers. When the conflict is resolved, CLEAR OF CONFLICT is announced and the arcs disappear.

blocks.title: Advisory voice messages

blocks.content: TCAS assumes a crew response within about 5 s of an initial RA, with a pitch change smooth and positive enough to need roughly 0.25 g, and within about 2.5 s for a strengthening or reversal, with up to about 0.35 g. From level flight a correctly flown RA typically costs 300 to 500 ft of altitude. Between two TCAS-equipped aircraft the systems coordinate through their Mode S transponders so that their RAs are complementary.
Close to the ground some advisories would be dangerous, and TCAS withholds them:

rows: Below 900 ft radio altitude descending, or 1,100 ft climbing
All RAs inhibited: TCAS reverts to TA ONLY, and all TCAS voice messages are silenced
Treated as low: RAs and INCREASE DESCENT inhibited (the safe direction)
TCAS reverts to TA ONLY and its voice is silenced

blocks.content: TA ONLY is annunciated on the TVSI whenever RAs are inhibited, whatever the cause. The priority order across the warning systems is windshear first, then the GPWS, then TCAS: an aircraft about to hit the ground does not need a descend advisory.

blocks.content: While the processor is in standby the traffic area shows only the vertical speed scale and the TCAS legend. The range buttons on the TVSI bezel select the display range; in the simulation the display stays on its default 10 NM range (see [Simulation notes](#simulation-notes)).

Formation flying and air refueling put aircraft deliberately close together, a situation in which standard TCAS would generate a stream of advisories. The ETCAS adds two functions for it. With ETCAS on, the ABV and BLW envelopes extend to 12,700 ft so that a rendezvousing receiver can be seen climbing or descending toward the tanker from far above or below. **Tagging** lets the crew enter up to 30 formation members by their Mode 3/A codes on the CDU's tagging pages; a tagged member's symbol is drawn inside a box, and when a member idents its symbol blinks for 15 s. Tagging does not apply to an intruder that has generated an RA.
During formation flight and air refueling TA mode is normally selected, so that the deliberately close traffic does not produce RAs, and TA ONLY is then annunciated.

The self-test displays a fixed pattern on both TVSIs for about 8 s: TEST in the mode area, one traffic symbol of each class at a known range and bearing, and both a red and a green arc. If the processor detects a fault during the test, the test ends with a failure indication instead of a pass. On the DC-10 the test is started by the keypad transponder head's TEST button, which also runs the control head's own test.

sections.title: ATC transponders
sections.summary: Two transponders under one control head on the DC-10 and MD-10, the IFF on the KC-10, and how each reaches the simulator's air traffic control.

blocks.content: A transponder makes the aircraft visible to **secondary surveillance radar (SSR)**. The ground radar transmits interrogation pulse pairs on 1030 MHz; the spacing of the pair asks a question. **Mode A** (also written Mode 3/A) asks for identity, and the transponder replies on 1090 MHz with a four-digit octal code set by the crew, one of 4,096. **Mode C** asks for altitude, and the transponder replies with the pressure altitude, referenced to 29.92 inHg and coded in 100-ft steps, from the air data computer. The controller's screen shows the code and the altitude beside the aircraft's position. **Mode S** adds a unique 24-bit aircraft address, selective interrogation of one aircraft at a time, and a data link that TCAS uses to coordinate resolution advisories between aircraft.

**IDENT** adds a special identification pulse to the replies for a short time after it is pressed, which makes the aircraft's target bloom or flash on the controller's screen. Reserved codes carry their own meaning: 7700 emergency, 7600 radio failure, 7500 unlawful interference. Because Mode C altitude is uncorrected pressure altitude in 100-ft steps, it is the same number every TCAS in the sky compares with its own.

children.title: DC-10: two transponders, two possible heads

blocks.content: The DC-10 carries two ATC transponders, ATC 1 on AC BUS 1 and ATC 2 on AC BUS 3, sharing one dual control head on the aft pedestal. Both sets are powered whenever their buses are; the control head selects which one replies, and the other stands by with its receiver alive and its transmitter silent. A failure of one set is cured by selecting the other.

The control head is an equipment choice made on the EFB: the **original drum head**, the standard fit, or the **Gables G7490-07 keypad head**, a professional option. Both heads drive the same two transponders and tune the same code. Only the keypad head operates the TCAS.

The original head shows the code on four drums, one digit each, with a knob under each drum. Each knob steps its own digit from 0 to 7 and back to 0; there is no carry from one digit to the next, so setting 1200 means turning the first knob to 1, the second to 2, and leaving the others at 0. A MODE knob selects **STBY** (both sets powered, neither replying), **A** (the selected set replies to Mode A with the code, and to Mode C with altitude if ALT RPTS is ON) or **B** (the selected set replies only to Mode B interrogations). The ATC 1/2 switch selects the replying set. IDENT adds the identification pulse for about 15 s. TEST, held, lights the test lamp beside it while the selected set is powered and serviceable.

Mode B is a legacy interrogation mode used by some ground radars outside North America. A Mode A/C radar, which is what the simulator's air traffic control and the online networks use, receives no identity reply from a set at B, so the simulator treats B as standby. The drum head's sets do not support Mode S and therefore cannot serve a TCAS; with the drum head fitted the TCAS stays in standby.
The keypad head combines the transponder control, the Mode S flight identification and the TCAS control in one panel with an eight-character display. Its MODE knob has five positions:
A separate **BLW / N / ABV** switch selects the TCAS display envelope, and the **XPNDR** selector picks transponder 1 or 2.

**Entering a code.** In ATC mode, key the four digits on the keypad (0 to 7; an 8 or a 9 shows INVALID). The new code is transmitted 5 s after the fourth digit, or at once if IDENT is pressed before then, which also starts an ident. An incomplete entry reverts to the previous code after 5 s, and IDENT does not transmit it. CLR deletes the last digit; held for 2 s it clears the whole entry.

**Flight identification.** The ATC/FID key switches the display to the Mode S flight identification. Letters are entered by multi-tap: each key carries its digit and up to three letters (1 ABC, 2 DEF and so on, 9 YZ), and repeated presses within 1.5 s step through them; after 1.5 s, or when a different key is pressed, the cursor moves on. The airline's call-sign letters are kept when a new flight number is typed. ENT accepts the identification, and the FID light flashes until it has been accepted. In the simulation the flight identification is kept by the panel but is not passed to the simulator's own ATC identity.

**Test.** TEST lights every display segment and indicator for about 3 s, then shows CP1 PASS and CP2 PASS (the selected side first), or CPn OFF for a side whose control-panel supply is missing, and at the same time starts the TCAS self-test. The code and the flight identification are kept through a power interruption.

The KC-10A modeled here carries the AN/APX-119 IFF transponder (with TCTO 1308), which supports the military Mark XIIA modes (1, 2, 3/A, C, 4 and 5), Mode S and ADS-B Out, and serves the ETCAS. It has no control head of its own: every IFF function is operated through the FMS CDUs. The essentials:

items: The IFF is switched on on the CDU's POWER page, and is powered from the LEFT EMER DC bus through the IFF XPNDR circuit breaker.
The COM TRANSMIT page's IFF selection must be ON for the transponder to reply at all. It defaults to OFF at power-up, which inhibits every reply (emission control) and holds the TCAS in standby.
IFF 1/4 selects MASTER (STBY, the default, or NORM) and the modes. Mode 3/A and altitude reporting switch on automatically once the aircraft is airborne.
A Mode 3/A code is entered by typing it into the scratchpad and pressing the M3 function key; pressing M3 with an empty scratchpad starts an IDENT.
Codes and modes are kept in the IFF's own memory across power-down; the other selections return to their defaults.

blocks.content: The IFF pages, Mode 4 and Mode 5 are described in [Flight management](flight-management).

The MD-10 has two Mode S transponders and a single Gables G6990-09 control panel on the left side of the aft pedestal. The panel has an octal keypad (0 to 7) with CLR, a code indicator showing the selected transponder and the code (for example ATC1 1200), an IDNT button, a function selector (STBY, XPDR, TA, RA/TA), a TEST button, an ALT RPT switch and an XPDR 1/2 selector.

items: **STBY** powers the transponders but inhibits replies. **XPDR** lets the selected transponder reply; it sends altitude when ALT RPT is on.
**TA** and **RA/TA** select the TCAS modes on an aircraft fitted with TCAS. The MD-10 in this simulation has no TCAS, so they behave as XPDR.

A new four-digit code becomes the transmitted code 5 s after its last digit. CLR abandons an entry and blanks the indicator, and a second CLR shows the transmitted code again; the transmitted code itself never changes on a CLR. A partial entry left alone lapses about 3 s after its last digit.
**IDNT** adds the identification pulse for about 20 s and lights its legend while it does.
**TEST**, held, shows PASS (or F for a fault) in the code indicator.

blocks.content: A transponder failure is announced on the engine and alert display as ATC XPDR 1 FAIL or ATC XPDR 2 FAIL.

The simulator has its own transponder, which is what its air traffic control and the online networks see. The aircraft keeps it in step with the panel. The **code** goes both ways: a code set on the panel is sent to the simulator, and a code set outside the cockpit (by the simulator's ATC window and its automatic squawk assistance, an EFB, a hardware panel, or a key binding) is adopted by the panel, so the drums roll or the display changes to show it. On the KC-10 an outside code is entered into the IFF as if the crew had typed it on a CDU. The **state** (standby, on, altitude reporting) is the panel's alone: if something outside the cockpit changes it, the panel puts it back. The simulator's IDENT key bindings press the fitted head's IDENT.

sections.title: Operation
sections.summary: Using the radar, GPWS, TCAS and transponders through a flight, and how they interact.

blocks.content: The checklists in [Normal procedures](normal-procedures) give the actions in order; this section explains how each system is used and why. Responses to GPWS and TCAS warnings are also in [Emergency procedures](emergency-procedures).

**Before transmitting.** A radar that radiates on the ground can harm people close to the antenna and interfere with other equipment. Do not select a transmitting mode (NORM, CONT, MAP on the DC-10; WX, MAP 1, MAP 2, BCN on the KC-10; WX, WX/T, MAP on the MD-10) unless the area ahead of the nose is clear of people, and never during refueling or with the beam directed at buildings, other aircraft or refueling areas. TEST radiates into a dummy load and is safe.

**Preflight test.** Select STBY, SYS 1, gain AUTO, tilt full up, INT and TGT CLAR at mid-range and 150 NM on the indicator, then select TEST and check the pattern: five bands, the STC noise from 50 to 80 NM and the coarse noise from 80 to 100 NM, with TGT CLAR varying the noise. Repeat on SYS 2, then return to STBY. On the KC-10 allow the 3-minute delay before reading the pattern.

**Preflight test.** The MD-10 has no STBY: TEST powers the radar. Since the navigation display does not yet draw the radar picture in the simulation, the test pattern cannot be checked; select OFF after the test or leave the radar in TEST until a weather mode is wanted.

items: **Taxi**: STBY (the MD-10, which has no STBY, stays OFF or in TEST). The DC-10 and KC-10 must not be switched OFF while moving.

**Before takeoff**, where weather is a factor: WX (NORM), gain AUTO, NOR, a suitable range. Tilt down to paint ground, then sweep slowly up to full UP and back to about 0°, looking for weather on the departure path, and settle on the tilt that shows it best.
**Climb**: raise the tilt progressively so the beam stays on the weather and ground clutter stays at the outer edge.

**Cruise**: select the shortest range of interest and tilt down until ground returns just appear at the outer edge; step out through the longer ranges. Repeat after any course change of about 45° or more.
**Descent**: note the tilt at top of descent and raise it about 1° per 10,000 ft lost (about 1° per 5,000 ft below 15,000 ft over high or built-up ground).
**After landing**: STBY (OFF on the MD-10). **Parking**: OFF, once stopped.

blocks.content: **Avoiding weather.** Evaluate cells early and at the shortest range that contains them, where resolution is best. Deviate upwind of storms where possible, since hail and turbulence are carried downwind under the anvil. Give red cells and cells with steep gradients or hail-shaped echoes a wide berth: 20 NM is a common minimum from severe storms. Do not fly into a gap between cells that the beam may not have penetrated, and treat an area with no ground returns behind a strong cell as unknown, not clear. Re-evaluate continuously: a storm can grow faster than an aircraft at 450 kt can go round it.

On a flight that starts in the air, the radar is already in weather mode (NORM on the DC-10, WX on the KC-10 and MD-10) and warm. On the ground with engines running the DC-10 and KC-10 radar starts in STBY, warmed up; the MD-10's, which has no STBY, starts OFF. From a cold and dark start it is OFF.

**Air refueling.** The tanker's radar is used for rendezvous: BCN to find the receiver's beacon, MAP 1 with FAN and about 5° up tilt to skin-paint a receiver at short range. Return it to STBY before closing to formation, and do not transmit near the other aircraft or during refueling. See [Air refueling](air-refueling).

**Preflight.** On the ground with the flaps not in the landing range, run the self-test and confirm each legend and message in turn; on the KC-10 check that STEEP APPR, TERR OVRD and FLAP OVRD are off and FLAP OVRD is guarded, and that TERR FAIL goes out at the end of the test (a present position must be entered in the inertial units first). On the MD-10, align the ADIRUs before testing.

**PULL UP and TERRAIN warnings.** When a warning sounds and the crew cannot immediately see that the aircraft is clear of terrain, treat it as real and fly the escape maneuver without delay; do not spend time trying to confirm the warning. The escape: disconnect the autopilot and autothrottle, apply maximum thrust, level the wings and retract the speedbrakes, and rotate smoothly (about 3° per second) toward 20° nose up, increasing pitch to the stick shaker if necessary to avoid the ground. Leave the configuration alone until clear. The pilot monitoring watches airspeed; on the DC-10 and KC-10 the flight engineer calls the radio altitude. When the warning stops and the terrain is clear, climb to a safe altitude, then reconfigure. The full procedure is in [Emergency procedures](emergency-procedures).

**Caution messages** call for correcting the condition: SINK RATE, reduce the descent rate; DON'T SINK, stop the altitude loss; TOO LOW GEAR or TOO LOW FLAPS, check the configuration (go around if it cannot be corrected); GLIDESLOPE, return to the glideslope or, if below it intentionally and in visual conditions, cancel the alert; BANK ANGLE, reduce the bank.

The GPWS is not a collision avoidance system, but another aircraft passing close beneath the tanker can trigger it. During air refueling or formation flight, an indiscriminate climb in response to a GPWS warning can endanger the other aircraft: use every source available, radio altimeter and radio included, to judge the situation before maneuvering.

items: **Before takeoff**: select TA/RA (DC-10: keypad head MODE TA/RA; KC-10: TCAS 3/4 TCAS MODE TA+RA, with COM TRANSMIT IFF ON and IFF MASTER NORM) and the ABV envelope for the climb.
**Cruise**: NORM envelope. **Descent**: BLW.
**After landing**, clear of the runway: STBY (or TA, as the operator requires).
Within 2,000 ft of an assigned level, reduce the vertical speed to about 1,500 fpm (1,000 fpm in RVSM airspace near other traffic) to avoid needless RAs from traffic leveling above or below.

blocks.content: **Traffic advisory.** Look for the traffic, using the symbol's bearing and relative altitude; the pilot monitoring calls it out. Do not maneuver on a TA alone: a TA carries no information about which way to go. Modest changes of vertical speed during a climb or descent are not evasive maneuvers and are acceptable.

**Resolution advisory.** Respond immediately and smoothly. Disconnect the autopilot and set the flight director aside, and fly the vertical speed needle out of the red arc and into the green within about 5 s, using a pitch change of the order of 2° at cruise Mach, 4° at 250 kt and 5° or more at approach speeds. Fly an INCREASE or a reversal within about 2.5 s with a firmer input. Never maneuver opposite to an RA: the other aircraft may be following a coordinated RA of its own. Do not exceed the stick shaker. A climb RA with the aircraft in the landing configuration is flown as a go-around. Tell ATC as soon as practical (for example, “Center, Gold 21, TCAS climb”), and after CLEAR OF CONFLICT return promptly to the clearance and say so.

**TA mode.** Select TA where RAs would be unhelpful or unsafe: closely spaced parallel approaches, formation flight and air refueling (KC-10), and with an engine inoperative, when the aircraft may not be able to achieve the climb rates an RA assumes. Return to TA/RA as soon as the reason has passed.

In the simulation the TCAS does not yet receive any traffic, so TAs and RAs do not occur in flight. Set the modes as described so the procedures are practiced; see [Simulation notes](#simulation-notes).

Set the assigned code and select the replying transponder before taxi. Select the reporting mode (A with ALT RPTS ON on the drum head, XPNDR or a TCAS mode on the keypad head, XPDR with ALT RPT on the MD-10) when ATC or the operator requires it, and in any case before takeoff. Press IDENT only when ATC asks for it. In an emergency, 7700 may be set if ATC has not already assigned a code; on the KC-10, an emergency selection on the IFF sets 7700 automatically. Return to STBY at the gate.
If the selected transponder fails, select the other one. On the MD-10 a failure is announced as ATC XPDR 1 FAIL or ATC XPDR 2 FAIL.
After every FMS cold start check the COM TRANSMIT page: its IFF selection defaults to OFF, which silences the transponder and holds the TCAS in standby until it is selected ON (or MASTER ON).

rows: Radar R/T 1 and the captain's indicator on AC BUS 1, R/T 2 and the first officer's indicator on AC BUS 3; the radar's load follows its mode (nothing in OFF, reduced in STBY). GPWS computer AC BUS 1; TCAS processor AC BUS 1; TVSIs on the emergency AC buses.
Antenna stabilization. A gyro or platform error mis-points the beam; an unpowered source leaves the antenna unstabilized.
GPWS (all modes), TCAS (low-altitude inhibits). A radio altimeter held in its test fails the GPWS.
GPWS barometric rate, altitude and airspeed; the transponders' and TCAS's altitude; the TVSI needle.
GPWS Modes 2 and 4 (down-locks, flap position); TCAS lower antenna (gear lever).
EGPWS terrain function position and accuracy (TERR FAIL); KC-10 radar stabilization; MD-10 GPWS self-test interlock.
A GPWS voice message puts the TCAS in TA ONLY and silences it.
The DC-10's keypad head is the TCAS control; the KC-10's IFF selections gate the ETCAS.
Transponder code and state follow the panel; outside code changes are adopted.

blocks.content: **Weather radar, modeled in depth.** Both R/Ts with their 3-minute, 20 s, 90 s and indicator delays and their ride-through of short power interruptions; the scan; the split-axis stabilization on the sensed attitude while the beam points by the true attitude (so a bad gyro really mis-points it); every mode, beam, gain, STC and TGT CLAR threshold; the contour circuit; the test pattern and its completed sweep; the indicators' range, marker, delay and hold; the electrical loads; the faults in the table above; and the antenna damage from OFF while moving (DC-10, KC-10).

**Weather radar, simplified.** Precipitation comes from the simulator's own weather through its weather-radar view, which shows rain out to about 135 NM: on the 150 and 300 NM ranges more distant weather does not appear. Ground returns are computed from the beam geometry (height, tilt, bank) over the simulator's terrain, with water painted black. HOLD freezes the indicator's ground returns and noise, but the precipitation drawn by the simulator may keep updating. If the picture ever sweeps all the way round in one direction instead of back and forth, turn the RANGE selector OFF and back on. The KC-10 uses the DC-10's supply split (R/T 2 and the first officer's indicator on AC BUS 3), although the KC-10 flight manual puts the whole radar on AC BUS 1.

**Weather radar, not modeled.** Attenuation and radar shadowing; beacon and aircraft targets (BCN and air-to-air skin painting show nothing); turbulence detection (WX/T is WX); the MD-10's predictive windshear and ground clutter suppression (its IDNT button does nothing); radome icing; the R/T altitude limits. On the MD-10 the radar runs but the navigation display does not yet draw its picture or its annunciations, and the antenna's stabilization comes from the same vertical-gyro attitude source as on the DC-10 rather than from the ADIRUs.

**GPWS.** The health monitor, Modes 1 to 6, the voice (from the aircraft's own recordings, with the computer family's priority order), the self-tests, the override switches, the glideslope cancel (MD-10 only, since the DC-10 and KC-10 caps cannot yet be pressed), TERR FAIL and the terrain picture are modeled. Not modeled: windshear detection (Mode 7; its legends and voice appear only in the self-test), the look-ahead terrain and obstacle alerts (CAUTION TERRAIN, TERRAIN, PULL UP from the database), and the louder hard GLIDESLOPE. The Mode 1 to 3 envelope curves are close approximations; the Mode 4 and 5 numbers are the published ones. The MD-10 uses the KC-10's bank-angle law, and its EGPWS speaks the altitude callouts and MINIMUMS in the KC-10's voice (on the real aircraft the central aural warning system makes them), with MINIMUMS taken from the captain's radio minimums. The DC-10's voice option keeps the basic computer's 800 ft Mode 5 ceiling.

**DC-10 GPWS options.** The voice and terrain options are stored with the aircraft and are off by default. They are not yet offered on the EFB; until they are, the DC-10 flies with the basic computer.

**Terrain picture.** The terrain database is served by the Infinity Manager application. With the Manager not running, or its terrain database not downloaded, the terrain displays paint the whole area magenta (unmapped). The MD-10's navigation display does not yet draw the terrain picture.

**TCAS.** The processor, its tracking, threat logic, RAs and inhibits, the TVSIs and the self-test are modeled, but no traffic from the simulator (AI or multiplayer aircraft) reaches the TCAS yet. What you will see today: the TVSI's vertical speed needle, the mode legends (TA ONLY, TCAS STBY, TCAS FAIL) and, on the DC-10, the self-test pattern. What you will not see: any traffic symbol on the TVSIs or the glass displays, any TA or RA, or the RA arcs outside the test. Its voice messages are not heard. The TVSI range buttons do not yet work, so the traffic display stays on 10 NM. The KC-10's TCAS self-test cannot be started from the cockpit. There is no RA coordination with other aircraft. The MD-10's TCAS is not modeled: its transponder panel's TA and RA/TA positions act as XPDR, and its navigation display draws no traffic.

**Transponders.** The code and state are linked to the simulator's transponder both ways, as described above. Mode B and the drum head's TEST lamp are modeled as the books describe, but the simulator's ATC only recognizes Mode A/C, so Mode B reaches it as standby. The keypad head's flight identification is not passed to the simulator. The KC-10's Mode 4 and Mode 5 are modeled only as far as the simulator can exercise them (nothing interrogates them).

**Failures.** The failures listed above are built into the systems, but they are not yet offered on the EFB Failures page. Pulling the circuit breakers in the power table produces the corresponding power failures.

parts.title: Communications
parts.summary: VHF, HF and UHF radios, audio and interphone, crew call and the cockpit voice recorder.

sections.title: Introduction
sections.summary: VHF, HF and UHF radios, the audio and interphone systems, crew call and the voice recorder.

blocks.content: The communications system connects the crew with air traffic control and their company, with each other, with the cabin and with the ground crew. It has four layers. The **radios** (VHF on every aircraft, HF on the DC-10 and KC-10, UHF on the KC-10) carry speech to and from the outside world. The **audio system** (audio control panels, interphones and the passenger address) routes microphones and receivers at each crew station. The **crew call system** signals between the flight deck, the cabin attendants and the ground crew with lights and chimes. The **cockpit voice recorder** records the flight deck for accident investigation.

The radios are built around redundancy by number rather than by switching: three independent VHF transceivers on the DC-10 and MD-10, each with its own antenna (and on the DC-10 its own control head), so the loss of any one leaves two. Their supplies are split between the left and right emergency DC buses, so a radio survives the loss of the main generators. Two of the radios are also connected to the simulator's own COM 1 and COM 2, which is how the aircraft talks to the simulator's air traffic control and to online networks.

Right: the crew call system linking the overhead call panel with the attendant stations and the nose wheel well horn; the cockpit voice recorder on AC BUS 1 with its four channels. sections.title: VHF communications
sections.summary: Line-of-sight voice radios: theory, the three styles of control head, and tuning.

blocks.content: VHF voice radio uses amplitude modulation in the band 118.000 to 136.975 MHz. At these frequencies radio waves travel in straight lines and pass through the ionosphere instead of being reflected by it, so VHF is a **line-of-sight** medium: it reaches as far as the radio horizon and no further, but within that range it is clear and free of the fading and noise that afflict HF. The usable range between an aircraft at height h1 and a station at height h2 (both in feet) is roughly 1.23 times the sum of their square roots, in nautical miles. An aircraft at 35,000 ft reaches a sea-level station at about 230 NM; at 5,000 ft, about 87 NM; on the ground, a few miles. This is why VHF range shrinks so dramatically on descent, and why oceanic flights need HF or satellite communications.

Channels in the civil band were traditionally 25 kHz apart. Congestion in Europe led to **8.33 kHz** spacing, three channels in each 25 kHz slot, identified by six-figure channel names (118.005, 118.010, 118.015, 118.030 and so on) that do not equal the actual carrier frequency. The DC-10's and MD-10's heads tune the 25 kHz channels only; the KC-10's military-band sets tune 8.33 kHz channel names between 118.000 and 137.000 MHz.

Each VHF set has two frequencies ready, an **active** one on which it transmits and receives, and a **standby** one that the crew can preset. Changing frequency is then a single switch action, and the previous frequency stays available to return to if the new one does not answer.

Three heads on the pedestal control VHF 1, VHF 2 and VHF 3. Each head has two frequency windows, FREQ 1 on the left and FREQ 2 on the right, each with its own concentric tuning knobs (outer knob MHz, inner knob kHz), and a transfer switch that selects which window is active. The MHz knob steps through 118 to 136 and wraps round; the kHz knob steps through the 25 kHz channels of the selected megahertz and wraps within it, without carrying into the megahertz digits, as on the real heads.

Two styles of head are available, selected on the EFB's Aircraft Configuration page. The **analog** head (standard) shows each frequency on mechanical drums, and an OFF flag drops across the window that is not active; with the radio unpowered both windows are flagged. It has a SQUELCH switch. The **digital** head (option) shows the frequencies in illuminated digits with a light beside the active window, and has a TEST switch: held up, it lights every segment of both displays and both window lights. Both styles drive the same radios, so a frequency set on one is there when the other is fitted.

blocks.alt: DC-10 center pedestal, two VHF control heads side by side. Left: the analog head with drum windows reading 121.900 (FREQ 1, active) and 135.650 (FREQ 2) with the OFF flag across FREQ 2, transfer switch, SQUELCH switch and the two concentric knob pairs. Right: the digital head with illuminated digits 118.700 and 124.350, the FREQ 1 active light lit, transfer switch and TEST switch.
blocks.title: DC-10 VHF control heads, analog and digital

blocks.content: The KC-10 has two VHF sets, VHF 1 and VHF 2, with digital heads on the aft pedestal. They cover 116.000 to 151.975 MHz, which includes the military VHF band above the civil one. Between 116.000 and 117.975 MHz they receive only; transmission is inhibited. Between 118.000 and 137.000 MHz they tune 8.33 kHz channel names as well as 25 kHz channels, and elsewhere 25 kHz channels. The head's layout is that of the DC-10's digital head: two windows with their knobs, a transfer switch, and a combined TEST / SQ DSBL switch whose momentary TEST position lights every segment and both window lights.

The MD-10 has three VHF sets controlled from three identical **communication radio panels (CRP)** on the aft pedestal. A CRP is not tied to one radio: its radio select buttons (VHF 1, VHF 2, VHF 3) choose which set it controls, and its ACTIVE and STBY windows then show that set's frequencies, with the radio's name above each (for example VHF 1). New frequencies are set in the STBY window with the concentric knobs (outer MHz, inner kHz) and moved to ACTIVE with the transfer button, which swaps the two. A set cannot transmit on its standby frequency. Each panel is normally left on its own radio (panel 1 on VHF 1 and so on); if two panels select the same radio, both show and tune it.

blocks.alt: MD-10 aft pedestal, the three communication radio panels: each with ACTIVE and STBY LCD windows in whitish lettering (VHF 1 121.900 / 124.350 on panel 1, VHF 2 and VHF 3 on the others), the transfer button between the windows, the concentric frequency knobs, and the row of radio select buttons VHF-1, VHF-2, VHF-3, HF-1, HF-2.

blocks.content: The real MD-10 also has two HF sets selectable from the CRPs. They are not fitted in the simulation, and the HF-1 and HF-2 select buttons do nothing.

sections.title: HF communications
sections.summary: Long-range radio by the ionosphere: theory, the DC-10's heads and the KC-10's ACS panels.

blocks.content: High-frequency radio, 2 to 30 MHz, reaches beyond the horizon. Part of the energy follows the earth's surface as a **ground wave**, useful for a few hundred miles at the low end of the band; the rest travels upward and is refracted back to earth by the ionized layers of the upper atmosphere, the **sky wave**, landing hundreds or thousands of miles away. Between the end of the ground wave and the first return of the sky wave lies a **skip zone** where nothing is heard. The ionosphere changes with the sun: by day it is dense and refracts high frequencies well, while its lower layer absorbs the low ones; at night the absorbing layer disappears and the refracting layers thin out. Hence the operator's rule of thumb: **high frequencies by day, low frequencies by night**, and the practice of publishing several frequencies for each oceanic station so the crew can pick the one that propagates best at the time.

Aeronautical HF voice uses **single sideband (SSB)**. An AM signal carries its information twice, in an upper and a lower sideband either side of a carrier that itself carries none. SSB suppresses the carrier and one sideband, putting all the transmitter's power into the one that remains and halving the bandwidth, which roughly quadruples the useful signal for the same power. **USB** (upper sideband) is the aeronautical standard; LSB and AM remain for compatibility with other stations.

Do not transmit on HF during refueling: the high RF voltages on the antenna and nearby structure can cause arcing. Do not transmit on HF on the ground with people near the antenna or working on the aircraft's skin, which can carry a dangerous induced voltage.

Two HF control heads on the overhead panel control HF 1 and HF 2. Each has a function selector, **OFF**, **USB**, **LSB** and **AM**, which also switches the set's power, and four frequency knobs: whole megahertz (2 to 29), hundreds of kilohertz, tens of kilohertz and kilohertz. The selected frequency appears on drums, for example 05.262 (5.262 MHz). The set covers 2.000 to 29.999 MHz in 1 kHz steps.

blocks.alt: DC-10 overhead panel, the two HF control heads: HF 1 drums reading 08.879 with the function selector at USB; HF 2 reading 05.616 at OFF; the four frequency knobs under each readout legible.

children.title: KC-10 HF with the Automatic Communications System

blocks.content: The KC-10's two HF sets are controlled by menu-driven **Automatic Communications System (ACS)** remote control panels on the overhead. The ACS was designed to take the guesswork out of HF: in its automatic mode it scans a list of channels, measures their link quality, and establishes a link with a called station's address by itself (automatic link establishment). It can also be operated as a conventional radio, and in the simulation that is how it works: the panel's fields, power, self-test and frequency selection are modeled, but not the automatic link establishment, the preset channel contents, data messages or frequency hopping (see [Simulation notes](#simulation-notes)).

blocks.content: Military aircraft talk to each other and to military controllers on UHF, 225.000 to 399.975 MHz in 25 kHz steps, with an international military distress (**guard**) frequency of 243.0 MHz. Like VHF it is line of sight. The KC-10 carries two sets: **UHF 1**, an ARC-164 with its panel on the forward pedestal, and **UHF 2**, an ARC-171 with its panel on the right aft pedestal. Both can run their main receiver and a separate guard receiver together.

sections.title: The radios and the simulator
sections.summary: Which radios drive the simulator's COM 1 and COM 2, and how tuning flows both ways.

blocks.content: The simulator has two COM radios; its air traffic control and online network clients (such as vPilot) work through them. The aircraft has more radios than that, so it connects two of them: **VHF 1 is always COM 1**, and **COM 2 is the radio selected as Primary COM2** on the EFB's Aircraft Setup page. The choices are each family's own radios:

items: **Panel to simulator.** Whenever the active or standby frequency of a connected radio changes, it is sent to the simulator's COM radio as set. The simulator's radios hold civil VHF only (118.000 to 136.990 MHz), so a UHF, HF or military VHF frequency is sent but not held; the EFB's Aircraft Setup page then shows that COM 2 is not on frequency.

**Simulator to panel.** A frequency changed outside the cockpit (by the simulator's ATC window, a network client, a hardware panel or a key binding) is adopted by the connected radio, snapped to its nearest legal channel. A UHF set adopts it only while it is on manual tuning, so that stored presets are never overwritten. If the crew turn a knob at the same moment, the crew win.
**Power.** The simulator's COM radio follows the connected radio's supply: an unpowered or failed VHF 1 also silences COM 1.

**Transmitting.** Which COM radio the simulator transmits on is the simulator's own selection (its ATC window or the COM 1 / COM 2 transmit-select key bindings). On the DC-10 and KC-10 those key bindings also push the captain's audio panel VHF 1 or VHF 2 microphone selector in, so the panel shows the selection.

blocks.alt: In-sim EFB, Configuration app, Aircraft Setup tab on a DC-10: the Primary COM2 row with VHF-2, VHF-3, HF-1, HF-2 choices (VHF-3 selected) and the status line showing the simulator's COM2 on frequency; the Brakes row below.

blocks.content: Online network clients read only the simulator's VHF COM radios. To use COM 2 on a network, select a VHF radio as Primary COM2.

sections.title: Audio control panels, interphone and passenger address
sections.summary: How microphones and receivers are routed at each crew station, and the interphone networks.

blocks.content: Every crew member can listen to many receivers at once but should transmit on only one. The **audio control panel (ACP)** at each station resolves that: a row of interlocked **microphone (transmit) selector** buttons chooses the single system the station's microphone keys, and a row of **receiver volume** controls sets how loudly each radio, navigation receiver and interphone is heard. Pushing one transmit selector releases whichever was in; pushing the one that is in releases it, leaving the station transmitting on nothing, which is a legitimate position. The microphone is keyed by the control wheel switch or the panel's own push-to-talk.

blocks.content: In the simulation the audio control panels move but do not route audio: what is heard and which radio transmits are the simulator's own audio settings and COM transmit selection. The captain's VHF 1 and VHF 2 transmit selectors follow the simulator's COM 1 and COM 2 transmit-select key bindings (see [The radios and the simulator](#sim-radios)).

The **flight interphone** connects the flight crew's stations to each other, and to jacks for the ground crew at the nose gear and the external power receptacle; it is selected with INT on the audio panels. The **service interphone** connects the flight deck handset with the attendant or courier stations and the maintenance jacks around the aircraft, and on the KC-10 it also carries the air refueling intercom to the receiver through the boom. Calls on the service interphone are signaled by the crew call system described below. On the MD-10 the MAINT INTPH button connects the maintenance interphone jacks to the service interphone.
No interphone carries voice in the simulation; the call lights, chimes and the MAINT INTPH light are modeled.

The passenger address carries announcements from the flight deck handset and the attendant stations to the cabin speakers, together with the chimes that accompany the passenger signs and the call system. On the DC-10 and KC-10 call panels, the PA switch-light connects the flight deck handset to the PA, and its ON legend lights while it is connected; pressing it again, or pressing any call button, disconnects it. The simulation has no PA audio; the PA ON light and the cabin chimes are modeled.

Selective calling saves the crew from listening to a noisy HF frequency for hours. Each aircraft has a four-letter SELCAL code; a ground station that wants to talk to it transmits that code as a sequence of audio tones, and the aircraft's decoder, monitoring the selected radio, recognizes its own code and alerts the crew with a chime and a light. The crew can then turn the HF volume down until called.

The DC-10 has a SELCAL panel on the pedestal in one of two styles, selected on the EFB. It is not operative in the simulation: no SELCAL calls are generated. The same panel's MARKER HI/LO switch, which on the real aircraft sets the marker beacon receiver's sensitivity, is not connected either: the receiver stays at HI (see [Navigation](navigation)).
On the KC-10, SELCAL is a mode of the HF ACS with alerts on a SELCAL annunciator panel. It is not modeled.
On the real MD-10 a SELCAL call lights the CALL light on the audio control panel and the central aural warning system sounds a chime. It is not modeled.

sections.title: Crew call system
sections.summary: Lights and chimes between the flight deck, the attendant stations and the ground crew.

blocks.content: The call system lets any station attract another's attention before talking on the service interphone. Its relays, lights and chimes run on the SERVICE INTERPHONE (CALL) circuit, DC BUS 1: a call made while that bus is dead is never made, and a call standing when it drops is lost.

items: **Cabin to flight deck.** An attendant presses PILOT at the attendant panel: a high chime sounds on the flight deck, and the blue CALLING half of that station's switch-light on the overhead call panel lights.

**Flight deck to cabin.** The crew press a station's switch-light while its CALLING is out: a high chime sounds in the cabin for that station (on the real aircraft a pink call light also comes on at the station).

**Answering.** Pressing a station's switch-light while its CALLING is lit answers the call: the light goes out and nothing rings. (A RESET button, or replacing the handset, does the same on aircraft that have one.)
**Mechanic.** The MECH button sounds a horn in the nose wheel well for as long as it is held, to call the ground crew to the interphone jack.

blocks.content: The chimes are the cabin's two-tone set: the **high** tone for calls in either direction, the **low** tone when a passenger sign comes on. Both are heard inside the aircraft.

The DC-10's overhead call panel has four station switch-lights, **FWD ATTND**, **MID ATTND**, **OVRWING ATTND** and **AFT ATTND**, one for each pair of doors from front to back, each with a CALLING lower half; **ALL STATION**, which calls every station at once; **MECH**; and **PA** with its ON legend. On the passenger aircraft each attendant panel can call every other station as well as the flight deck, and each has a RESET that withdraws its own calls. On the freighters and tankers there is one attendant station, at the forward door, so every call is FWD's.

blocks.alt: DC-10 overhead crew call panel close view: four switch-lights FWD, MID, OVRWING and AFT ATTND with the blue CALLING lower half of AFT ATTND lit; ALL STATION; MECH; PA with its ON lower half lit.
blocks.title: DC-10 overhead call panel

blocks.content: The KC-10's panel has three switch-lights: **FWD ATTND** (CALLING), **MECH** and **PA** (ON). The tanker has one attendant station, at the forward door. Its RESET button is not on the panel in the simulation, so FWD ATTND answers its own call, as on the DC-10.

blocks.content: The MD-10's panel on the forward overhead has four buttons. The **COURIER** switch-light shows CALL (blue) when the courier's station calls the flight deck; pressing it while lit puts the call out, and pressing it while dark calls the courier's station with a chime. **CALL RESET** puts out every CALL light. **MECH CALL** sounds the nose wheel well horn while selected, and its light shows it. **MAINT INTPH** connects the maintenance interphone jacks, its light showing ON.

sections.title: Cockpit voice recorder
sections.summary: The four-channel recorder, its test and its meter.

blocks.content: The cockpit voice recorder records whenever the aircraft has electrical power, with no switch. It has four channels: three for crew audio (radio and interphone, transmitted and received), which are the captain's, first officer's and flight engineer's audio panels on the DC-10 and KC-10, and the two pilots and the service interphone handset on the MD-10; and the cockpit area microphone on the fourth. It keeps the most recent 30 minutes or so on a continuous loop, overwriting the oldest, so that after an accident the investigators have the last stretch of the crew's words and the cockpit's sounds. The recorder itself, in its crash- and fire-protected case with an underwater locator beacon, is in the aft fuselage; the control unit is on the overhead panel. It is powered from AC BUS 1.

blocks.alt: Cockpit voice recorder control unit on the overhead panel (Fairchild type, as fitted to all three decks): the round area microphone grille, the test monitor meter with an ivory scale 0 to 10, a red band to about 7.4 and a green band from 8 with GOOD beneath, needle at 9 during a test; the TEST and ERASE push-buttons and the HEADSET jack.

sections.title: Operation
sections.summary: Using the radios and the call system through a flight.

items: **Preflight**: test the voice recorder (the needle stays in the green through the whole test). Set the radios; choose Primary COM2 on the EFB if a radio other than VHF 2 is wanted on the simulator's COM 2. On the KC-10, power the HF sets with PWR and run their INIT self-tests.

**Taxi and departure**: preset the next frequency in the standby window (MD-10: STBY) before it is needed, and transfer when instructed. The previous frequency remains in the other window to return to if the new one does not answer.

**En route**: a common division of the three VHF sets is VHF 1 for ATC, VHF 2 for ATIS, company and air-to-air, and VHF 3 for company operations or the emergency frequency 121.5. Beyond VHF range, HF carries position reports (on the DC-10 and KC-10). The KC-10 normally monitors UHF guard on one set with the mode selector at BOTH.

**Calls from the cabin**: a high chime and a lit CALLING (MD-10: CALL) mean an attendant or the courier wants the flight deck; answer on the service interphone and press the station's switch-light (MD-10: COURIER, or CALL RESET) to put the light out.

blocks.content: Do not transmit on HF during refueling or with people close to the HF antenna or working on the aircraft's skin.

**Losing VHF 1.** VHF 1 is the only radio connected to the simulator's COM 1, so with it lost (its LEFT EMER DC supply, its breaker, or a failure) COM 1 is silent. Continue on COM 2. On the DC-10 and MD-10, VHF 2 and VHF 3 share one breaker on the RIGHT EMER DC bus, so they fail together if that supply is lost.

**Modeled.** The tuning of every radio, with its band, channel spacing and wrap-around; power and failure of each set from its own circuit; the displays (drums and OFF flags, digital windows and test patterns, the MD-10 panels' LCD windows, the UHF and HF panel displays); the two-way link to the simulator's COM 1 and COM 2 and the Primary COM2 selection; the crew call lights and chimes; the voice recorder's test and meter.

**What you hear.** Radio audio is the simulator's own. Only the radios connected to COM 1 and COM 2 are heard, and only on frequencies the simulator's radios can hold (civil VHF). VHF 3 (unless selected as COM 2), HF propagation, the UHF guard receivers, squelch and the VHF TEST and squelch switches have no effect on what is heard.

**Not modeled.** The audio control panels' routing (their buttons and levers move; the captain's VHF 1 and VHF 2 transmit selectors follow the simulator's transmit-select keys); interphone and PA voice; SELCAL; ACARS and other data links on the DC-10 and MD-10; the HF ACS's automatic link establishment, preset channel contents, data messages and anti-jam hopping; the ARC-164's HAVE QUICK operation (the A position shows the anti-jam flag only); UHF direction finding; the KY-58 secure voice panel (KC-10); stuck-microphone protection; the nose wheel well horn's sound; the mechanic calling the flight deck; the voice recorder's ERASE and headset tones. The MD-10's HF radios and its audio control panels are not fitted.

**Cabin stations.** The attendant panels in the passenger cabins can call each other and the flight deck, as described above. Their EVAC switches drive an evacuation signal (lights and horn at every station, silenced station by station with EVAC RESET) built to a generic design, since no DC-10 book describing it was available.

**Failures.** VHF, HF, UHF and voice recorder failures are built into the system but not yet offered on the EFB Failures page; pulling the circuit breakers in the power table gives the corresponding power losses. The power table describes the simulation, which feeds each set from one bus; the KC-10 flight manual lists UHF 1 on the left emergency DC bus, UHF 2 on both right emergency buses, HF 1 on AC BUS 1, DC BUS 1 and the battery bus, and HF 2 on both right emergency buses and the battery bus.

parts.title: Warning and Recording Systems
parts.summary: Master warning and caution, the annunciator panels and the MD-10's EIS alerting, the aural warnings and the takeoff warning, the clocks, and the flight recorders and AIDS.

sections.title: Introduction
sections.summary: What the warning and recording systems do, how the two flight decks alert their crews, and what each aircraft carries.

blocks.content: The warning and recording systems do three jobs. They **alert**: they tell the crew that a system needs attention, how urgently, and which system it is. They **keep time**: the clocks give the crew Greenwich Mean Time, elapsed time and a stopwatch. And they **record**: the flight data recorder and the cockpit voice recorder keep a crash-survivable record of the flight, and on DC-10s so equipped the aircraft integrated data system (AIDS) records engine and airframe data for the airline's maintenance department.

Alerting uses three senses. **Visual** alerts are the master lights, the annunciator panels and, on the MD-10, the text alerts on the Engine and Alert Display. **Aural** alerts come from one central unit that decides what the cockpit speakers say. **Tactile** warning is the stick shaker, which shakes both control columns as the wing approaches the stall; it is described with the stall warning system in [Flight Controls](flight-controls#stall-warning). The ground proximity, windshear and traffic warnings come from their own computers and are described in [Surveillance](surveillance).

The three-crew and two-crew flight decks alert in fundamentally different ways, and the reason is the flight engineer. On the **DC-10 and KC-10** every system carries its own lights at its own controls, most of them on the flight engineer's panel, where the engineer monitors the detail. A light the pilots need to know about is repeated forward through a chain of attention-getters: a **cue light** on the overhead panel names the system, and a **MASTER CAUTION** or **MASTER WARNING** light on the glareshield says how urgent it is. The pilots are told that something needs attention and where to look, and the engineer is told what it is.

The **MD-10** has no flight engineer. Automatic system controllers do most of what the engineer did, and a central warning function in the Electronic Instrument System (EIS) watches every system, decides which fault is the root cause, and presents it as a leveled text alert: on the Engine and Alert Display (EAD), on the system's synoptic page of the System Display (SD), as a lit cue switch on the System Display Control Panel (SDCP), and on the glareshield MASTER lights. A computer does the monitoring and filtering that a third crew member did, so that two pilots see one message for one failure rather than a panel of consequential lights.

blocks.alt: Functional schematic, two panels side by side. Left, DC-10/KC-10: system lamps on the flight engineer's panel feed four cue lights (ELEC, FUEL, HYD, PNEU) and the summary lights on the pilots' overhead annunciator panel, which feed the pilots' MASTER CAUTION (through a 3 to 5 second delay) and MASTER WARNING lights and the flight engineer's own MASTER CAUTION and MASTER WARNING lights; a separate box labeled CENTRAL AURAL WARNING UNIT takes fire, overspeed, gear, takeoff, cabin pressure, autopilot, stabilizer and altitude inputs and drives two cockpit speakers through a priority logic. Right, MD-10: all system outputs feed a CENTRAL WARNING function in the EIS, which drives the EAD alert area, the SD synoptic alert and consequence areas, seven SDCP cue switches, the glareshield MASTER WARNING/MASTER CAUTION lights and the CAWS (tone and voice) speaker output.
