sections.title: Alerting philosophy
sections.summary: How the aircraft grade an alert, why the master lights work the way they do, and what each kind of alert asks of the crew.

blocks.content: An alerting system has to balance two failures of its own. If it says too little, a fault goes unnoticed. If it says too much, the crew stop listening, or are buried in consequential alerts and miss the cause. Both flight decks solve this the same way in principle, by **grading** every alert by urgency and **directing attention** to where the detail is, but they do it with different hardware.

On the three-crew aircraft a light's color is its urgency. A **red warning** light reports a condition that needs immediate attention and usually immediate action: a fire, a cabin altitude above limits, a pneumatic overheat, a lost emergency bus. An **amber caution** light reports a condition that needs attention but not instantly: a pump with low pressure, a failed channel. **Blue, white and green** lights are advisories and status: a valve open, a switch on, a gear down and locked.

A light is normally mounted on or next to the control or gauge it reports on, so the crew member who sees it has the remedy at hand. A system whose controls are spread over more than one panel reports instead on one of the two annunciator panels: the pilots' overhead panel and the flight engineer's upper panel No. 2. Not every amber light is a caution in the master-caution sense: some are advisory and deliberately do not light MASTER CAUTION, because they report a configuration the crew chose rather than a malfunction.

blocks.title: Instrument marking colors
rows: Warning, danger, maximum or minimum limit

blocks.content: The MD-10 grades every alert on a four-step scale inherited from the MD-11, Level 3 being the most urgent. The level fixes the alert's color and format, where it goes on the EAD, which master light it lights and which tone the CAWS sounds. Within a level there is no priority: the latest alert goes to the top of its group.

rows: Emergency condition: immediate awareness and immediate corrective or compensatory action

blocks.content: Two rules keep the list readable. Only the **root cause** is listed: alerts that follow from the first failure are inhibited, so a lost generator does not also list every bus it fed. And an alert held back during the takeoff and landing windows appears when the window closes, if its condition still stands (see [Alert inhibits](#alert-inhibits)).

A **dark cockpit** is one in which every light is out when everything is normal, so that any light is news. The MD-10 applies the idea rigorously. Its overhead switchlights show no legend in their normal positions, and the lighting switches that are normally on (NAV, BCN, HI-INT) carry only an OFF legend, which glows when the light is switched off.

The DC-10 and KC-10 apply it in part. The annunciator panels are dark in normal flight, and the landing gear lights go out when the gear is up and locked with the throttles above idle. But the flight engineer's panel is full of blue advisory and green status lights that report configuration, because on a three-crew flight deck the engineer's scan is the monitoring system.

The master lights and the cue lights share one mechanism, and understanding it explains every behavior in the cockpit. Each of them watches a list of lamps. It is lit while any lamp on its list is lit and has not been **acknowledged**. Pushing its cap acknowledges every lamp lit at that moment, puts the light out and **rearms** it. A lamp that goes out is forgotten; if it comes back, it is new.

Three things follow. First, pushing a master light does not hide a second failure: a lamp that lights after the push is unacknowledged and lights the master light again, even with the first fault still standing. Second, a fault that corrects itself puts the master light out without a push. Third, the individual lamp is never reset by the master light: it stays lit until its condition clears, so the record of what failed stays on the panel where it belongs.

The pilots' MASTER CAUTION and the cue lights wait about 4 seconds (the books give 3 to 5) after a caution lamp lights before they come on. The delay filters out nuisance flashes from transient cautions, a pump that drops its pressure for a moment as a valve moves, and it gives the flight engineer, who sees the lamp at once, the first look. MASTER WARNING has no delay.

The ear cannot be closed or turned away, so aural warnings are reserved for conditions that need attention now or that are about to become hazardous: fire, overspeed, an unsafe configuration for takeoff or landing, a cabin losing pressure, an unexpected autopilot disconnect, the stabilizer moving, and the approach to a selected altitude. Each has its own sound, so a trained crew identifies it without looking.

Only one warning sounds at a time. Two simultaneous sounds would mask each other and neither would be identified. The DC-10 and KC-10 unit picks the **highest-priority** warning and holds the rest waiting underneath; as each is corrected the next sounds. The MD-10's CAWS adds a spoken word to each tone and lets standing warnings **take turns**, the newest interrupting the one in progress, so that a lower warning is never silenced for long by a higher one. See [Aural warnings](#aural-warnings) for both units.
Stall warning is tactile only on the DC-10 and KC-10: the stick shaker, with no light and no sound. A pilot already pulling back on the column feels it before anything could be read or heard.

sections.title: Master lights and annunciator panels
sections.summary: The glareshield and flight engineer's master lights, the cue and summary lights, the two annunciator panels, and the lamp tests.

blocks.content: The visual alerting system of the three-crew aircraft is a set of relays and lamps rather than a computer. Each system lights its own lamps; the annunciator panels repeat the ones that need repeating; and four kinds of attention-getter, the master lights, the cue lights, the summary lights and the glareshield ENGINE FIRE light, tell each crew station that one of those lamps has something to say.

children.title: MASTER WARNING and MASTER CAUTION lights

blocks.content: Each pilot has a red **MASTER WARN** and an amber **MASTER CAUTION** push-to-reset light on the glareshield. The flight engineer has their own pair, a split switch-light labeled **MASTER WARNING** and **MASTER CAUTION** below the annunciator block on upper panel No. 2. The captain's glareshield also carries the red **ENGINE FIRE** light, which belongs to the fire detection system (see [Fire Protection](fire-protection)).

blocks.alt: DC-10-30 glareshield, captain's side, close view: the red ENGINE FIRE light (PRESS TO RESET), the red MASTER WARN light and the amber MASTER CAUTION light (both PRESS TO RESET) side by side, MASTER WARN and MASTER CAUTION illuminated; the first officer's identical MASTER WARN and MASTER CAUTION pair inset. Legends legible.
blocks.title: Glareshield master lights

blocks.content: Every master light follows the rule described in [The attention-getting chain](#attention-getters): lit while a lamp on its list is lit and unacknowledged; a push acknowledges everything lit at that moment and rearms the light; a lamp that goes out and returns is new. The four lights differ in whose lamps they watch, who can reset them and when they come on.

items: **The pilots' pair.** Either pilot's cap resets both pilots' lights of that color, because one relay drives both lamps. Pushing a pilot's light does not reset the flight engineer's.

**The flight engineer's pair.** Reset only from the flight engineer's station, by the engineer's own caps, and resetting them does not affect the pilots' lights. A cue light push never resets the flight engineer's MASTER CAUTION.

**Timing.** MASTER WARNING comes on at once at all three stations. The flight engineer's MASTER CAUTION comes on at once, together with the caution lamp on their panel. The pilots' MASTER CAUTION comes on about 4 seconds later.

**Lists.** All three MASTER WARNING lights watch the same red lamps. The flight engineer's MASTER CAUTION watches a subset of the pilots' list: the lamps at the engineer's own station and those that light every master caution. A forward-panel caution such as SELECT ELEV FEEL MAN lights the pilots' MASTER CAUTION only.

blocks.content: **Autoland inhibit.** During a DUAL LAND approach all master warning and caution lights are inhibited below 100 feet radio altitude, so that a non-critical fault cannot distract the crew in the flare. The inhibit masks the lights; the relays keep running underneath it, so anything that arrives in the flare is shown the moment the inhibit lifts.

**Power.** MASTER WARN LTS (overhead B-1) feeds every MASTER WARNING light and its relays, and MASTER CAUTION & CUE LTS (overhead B-2) feeds every MASTER CAUTION light and the four cue lights; both are on the battery bus, so the master lights survive the loss of every generator. Each feeding lamp counts only while it can light: a lamp whose own breaker is out cannot raise a master light. The relays forget their acknowledgements when they lose power, so any lamp still lit when power returns lights the master light again.

A cue light tells the pilots which system has a caution without saying what it is; the detail is on the engineer's panel. A cue light comes on about 4 seconds after one of its lamps, together with all three MASTER CAUTION lights.

Pushing a lit cue light puts it out, acknowledges the lamps of its system lit at that moment, and rearms it. The same push puts out the pilots' MASTER CAUTION lights if no other unacknowledged caution is holding them on; it does not affect the flight engineer's MASTER CAUTION. A further lamp of the same system lighting later relights the cue, and a corrected condition puts it out without a push.

blocks.content: The red summary lights on the bottom row of the overhead annunciator panel repeat the flight engineer's warning lights forward: **EMER BUS OFF**, **CABIN ALT**, **PNEU TEMP HI**, **PNEU MANFLD FAIL** and **APU FIRE**. A summary light cannot be reset. It stays lit as long as the condition exists, so that a warning the pilots have acknowledged on the master light still reminds them it is there. Each of these conditions also lights MASTER WARNING.

The pilots' overhead annunciator panel carries the caution and advisory legends of systems whose controls are not on the pilots' panels, the cue and summary lights, the **ANNUN LT TEST** cap and the **PRESS TO BRT/DIM** button. The KC-10's panel is the DC-10's with one legend added (FLOOD LT DOOR NOT CLOSED) and the military IFF MODE 4 cell blanked. A legend for equipment the aircraft does not carry, such as the center anti-skid legend on a Series 10, stays dark and lights only on test.

blocks.content: A lamp test is a test of the lamp and its circuit, not a power source. The test relays are powered through WARN LT DIMMING & TEST (DC bus 1), and each lamp lights on test through its own supply. With the aircraft dead, or DC bus 1 unpowered, no test switch lights anything. With one system's lamp breaker pulled, that system's lamps stay dark on test, which is exactly what the test is meant to reveal.

**PRESS TO BRT/DIM** buttons on the overhead panel and the flight engineer's panel switch the annunciator lamps at that station between bright and dim. They do not dim the master lights or the flight engineer's door lights, which must be seen in any cockpit lighting.

sections.title: EIS alerting
sections.summary: The MD-10's central warning function: the EAD alert list, the SD synoptic and text pages, the SDCP cue switches, the master lights, the inhibits and the essential items checklist.

blocks.content: The MD-10's alerting is a function of the Electronic Instrument System. A central warning function evaluates the state of every system against a catalog of alerts, each with a fixed level, message and cue switch, and raises an alert when its condition is met. Because it sees the whole aircraft at once, it can recognize that one failure explains several symptoms and list only the root cause. The alert then appears in four places: on the **EAD**, on the system's synoptic page of the **SD**, as a lit **cue switch** on the SDCP, and on the glareshield **MASTER WARNING** or **MASTER CAUTION** lights. Not every alert in the catalog is raised in the simulation yet (see [Simulation notes](#simulation-notes)).

The alert list needs AC power or emergency power, that is, at least one emergency AC bus powered. On the battery alone the list is not held, the MASTER lights and the CAWS are silent, and fire alerts do not display; this is why the battery-only fire test shows no master lights.

Each of the three alert columns in the lower third of the Engine and Alert Display takes messages of up to 17 characters. The left and center columns have six lines each; the right column has four, since its last two lines belong to the **reminder messages**. Level 3 alerts start at the top of the left column, followed by Level 2, then Level 1, the latest alert of each level at the top of its group. Level 0 alerts fill from the right column, above the reminder area.

When more than 16 alerts are due on the EAD, higher levels take priority and Level 0 alerts are displaced to make room. A displaced alert is not deleted: it reappears as space frees. The bottom of the center column is shared with the essential items checklist; when the checklist shows, it displaces any alert in that cell.

A **reminder message** is the cue switch's name (ENG, HYD, ELEC, AIR, FUEL, CONFIG, MISC) in a fixed place in the reminder area. It replaces Level 2 and Level 1 alerts that the crew have acknowledged with the cue switch: boxed amber for a Level 2, unboxed amber for a Level 1. It says that the system still has an acknowledged alert, which remains on its synoptic and on the STATUS page.

blocks.alt: MD-10 Engine and Alert Display, lower third close-up: three alert columns; left column a red boxed Level 3 alert with leading triangle at the top, then amber boxed Level 2 alerts; center column amber unboxed Level 1 alerts with the white boxed takeoff essential item STAB TRIM at its foot; right column cyan Level 0 alerts above two reminder lines showing a boxed amber HYD and an unboxed amber FUEL. All text legible.
blocks.title: EAD alert area

blocks.content: Each system synoptic page (ENG, HYD, ELEC, AIR, FUEL, CONFIG) shows the system's schematic in its upper two thirds and, in its lower third, the system's Level 3, 2 and 1 alerts in the left column with their **consequences** aligned in the right column. Consequences are short white statements of what the failure means or what the crew should do (WING A-ICE NOT AVAILABLE, DEPART ICING AREA). A page holds five alerts and five consequences; when there are more, PRESS (cue switch) AGAIN TO CONTINUE appears and the next push of the same switch shows the next page.

blocks.title: SD text pages
rows: Every alert on the system pages, grouped by system in cue switch order (ENG, HYD, ELEC, AIR, FUEL, CONFIG, MISC), each group headed by its label even when empty, then a MAINT group of Level 1 maintenance alerts. Up to 51 alerts a page
All consequences of the current failures beside their alerts, grouped by level. Up to 21 a page (see [Simulation notes](#simulation-notes))
Alerts and consequences of systems with no synoptic, as text. Up to 17 a page

blocks.alt: MD-10 System Display showing the HYD synoptic: hydraulic schematic in the upper two thirds; lower third with an amber boxed Level 2 alert HYD 1 PRES LO in the left column and white consequence lines in the right column; PRESS HYD AGAIN TO CONTINUE at the bottom. Legible.
blocks.title: Synoptic page with alerts and consequences

blocks.content: The System Display Control Panel on the aft pedestal has ten switches and the six display brightness knobs. Seven of the switches, **ENG**, **HYD**, **ELEC**, **AIR**, **FUEL**, **CONFIG** and **MISC**, are **cue switches**: each has a white light bar that comes on when an alert of its system appears. **STATUS** and **CONSEQ** select their pages only, and **ND** asks for a third navigation display.

The light goes out, the system's alerts are acknowledged, and its synoptic is shown. Level 2 and 1 alerts leave the EAD and become reminders; Level 3 alerts stay on the EAD

blocks.content: A lit cue switch is extinguished only by the crew's push, never by the fault clearing on its own, so an alert cannot disappear from the cue switches unseen. Turning a BRT knob fully counterclockwise through its detent switches that display unit off, and the displays reconfigure around it (see [Flight Instruments](flight-instruments)).

Each pilot's glareshield carries a red **MASTER WARNING** and an amber **MASTER CAUTION** push-light, beside BELOW G/S and ENGINE FAIL (see [Surveillance](surveillance) and [Engines](engines)). MASTER WARNING **flashes** while a Level 3 alert or the fire detection control unit's fire relay has something unanswered. MASTER CAUTION lights for unanswered Level 2 and Level 1 alerts, for a fire detection system fault, and while a fire test is running.

Pushing either pilot's MASTER WARNING puts out both lights and resets them for the next alert; MASTER CAUTION works the same way. The push answers for everything lit at that moment and acknowledges nothing: the alerts stay on the EAD and their cue switches stay lit, so the crew still have to look at the system. A new alert lights the light again. MASTER WARNING is also the fire bell cutout: pushing it silences the fire warning (pulling that fire handle also does).

blocks.alt: MD-10 glareshield, captain's side, close view: red MASTER WARNING (lit) and amber MASTER CAUTION push-lights, the amber BELOW G/S light with G/S INHIBIT beneath, and the ENGINE FAIL light. Legends legible.
blocks.title: MD-10 glareshield master lights

blocks.content: Between the start of the takeoff roll and the first safe altitude, and in the last part of the approach, a non-critical alert is more likely to cause a dangerous reaction than to help. The EIS therefore holds back new alerts in defined windows. An inhibit holds back an alert whose condition arises inside the window; an alert already displayed stays, and a held alert appears when the window closes if its condition still stands. Level 0 alerts are never inhibited.

Level 2 and 1 alerts and MASTER CAUTION
1,000 ft above the departure airport, or 120 s after liftoff

blocks.content: Exceptions: the engine fire alerts are never inhibited (their MASTER WARNING is held back from V1, though the fire detection unit's own relay still lights it), FUEL DUMP ON is never inhibited, and Level 3 alerts are not inhibited during landing. On the ground each takeoff window follows the throttles, so an abandoned takeoff hands the alerts back as the throttles come back.

The EIS checks the items that must be right for takeoff and for landing and shows the first one that is not, white and boxed, at the foot of the center alert column. Only the highest item not met is shown; when it is corrected the next unmet item appears, and when all are met a **green box** appears.

blocks.content: If the takeoff roll begins with an item outstanding, the box and message turn red, except SPOILERS, which stays white. A flap setting that disagrees with the TAKEOFF page keeps the green box away, and on the aircraft it also sounds the flap takeoff warning when the throttles are advanced (see [Takeoff warning](#takeoff-warning) and [Simulation notes](#simulation-notes)). A LANDING GEAR message with the gear handle down is settled by the primary gear lights: if they show the gear safe, it is down and locked.

sections.title: Aural warnings
sections.summary: The DC-10 and KC-10 central aural warning unit, the MD-10's central aural warning system, and what triggers each warning.

blocks.content: Every aural warning except the APU fire horn comes from one central unit, which receives the conditions from the systems and decides what the cockpit speakers sound. The DC-10 and KC-10 carry a tone generator with a strict priority order. The MD-10 carries the central aural warning system (CAWS), which pairs each tone with a spoken word and lets standing warnings take turns. The conditions that trigger them are largely the same, because the systems behind them are.

The central aural warning unit sits on the main radio rack and drives two speakers in the pilots' side consoles. It knows eight warnings and discriminates between them by **pitch, duration and repetition rate**: a bell, a clacker, a continuous horn, an intermittent horn, a wailer, a deep horn and a chord. Most of its inputs are combinations: of some 36 input signals, most warnings need several to coincide before they sound.

**Priority.** The unit sounds only the highest-priority warning present. A lower warning is not cancelled by a higher one: it waits underneath, and sounds the moment the higher one is corrected or silenced. A gear horn heard after the fire bell stops is therefore not a new fault; it was there all along.

**Fire and overspeed take turns.** Strict priority would bury an overspeed under a fire for as long as the fire burned, so these two alternate: about 2 seconds of bell, about 0.75 second of silence, about 2 seconds of clacker, silence, and round again, starting with the bell. The maintenance test of this sequence holds a fire test and an overspeed test together.

**Power.** The eight channels are on three breakers, so one bus failure silences only some warnings. ENG FIRE & OVSPD AURAL WARN (overhead panel) is on the battery bus, so the fire bell and the clacker survive the loss of all generators. TO/LDG CAB PRESS AURAL WARN (lower main panel C-11) is on AC bus 3, and ALT ALERT HOR STAB AUTOPILOT AURAL WARN (lower main panel B-11) on AC bus 2. A dead channel does not hold off a live lower one.

blocks.title: Aural warnings, DC-10 and KC-10, in priority order

GEAR HORN OFF (throttle condition only); extending the gear
Gear handle pulled out of DN on the ground
Correcting the configuration; retarding throttles 1 and 2
Intermittent horn, the same as takeoff
CABIN ALT WARN HORN button (horn only, lights stay on)
ALT ALERT HOR STAB AP (AC bus 2)
ALT ALERT HOR STAB AP (AC bus 2)
ALT ALERT HOR STAB AP (AC bus 2)
Selecting an altitude above field elevation and turning the baro set knob to bring it within 750 ft

blocks.content: The **APU fire horn** is not part of the unit. It is an exterior horn in the left main wheel well, on the battery bus, that warns ground personnel of an APU fire and is silenced from the APU ground control panel (see [Fire Protection](fire-protection)).

blocks.alt: Functional diagram of the DC-10 central aural warning unit: eight input lines on the left (fire, overspeed, landing gear, takeoff, cabin pressure, autopilot disconnect, stabilizer motion, altitude advisory), each passing through its breaker group (ENG FIRE & OVSPD on the battery bus, TO/LDG CAB PRESS on AC bus 3, ALT ALERT HOR STAB AP on AC bus 2), into a priority logic block with a fire/overspeed alternator (2 s on, 0.75 s off), and a single output to two speakers. Each input labeled with its tone.
blocks.title: Central aural warning unit priority logic

blocks.content: The MD-10's CAWS resides in its versatile integrated avionics (VIA) units. Each warning is a **cycle**: about one second of tone followed by about one second of voice, repeated for as long as the warning stands. A voice removes any doubt about which warning is sounding, which matters on a two-crew flight deck where nobody else is watching the panels.

**Sequencing.** When two or more warnings stand, the CAWS plays one cycle of each in turn. A warning that has just arisen interrupts the one in progress, and sequencing then continues with the new warning included. No standing warning is silenced by another for more than a few seconds.
**Power.** The CAWS, like the alert list and the master lights, needs AC or emergency power: on the battery alone it is silent.

blocks.title: CAWS warnings
rows: Any new engine or APU fire
Fire bell and six tritones, once
The fire is out, the MASTER WARNING light is pushed, or that fire handle is pulled
APU fire, with no engine fire
The fire is out, MASTER WARNING is pushed, or the APU fire handle is pulled
Lower cargo fire, main deck smoke
The detection clears or MASTER WARNING is pushed
Automatic cargo fire test (first ADIRU switched on)
One group of tritones per test
Slats retracted or speed below the limit
Configuration corrected, or GEAR HORN OFF (throttle condition)
Intermittent horn and one word per wrong item, in turn: “BRAKES”, “STABILIZER”, “FLAP”, “SLATS”, “SPOILER”
Each item corrected, or throttles 1 and 2 retarded
Three cycles; again after the altitude switch resets and trips
A wheel autopilot disconnect switch is pushed after one full cycle, or the autopilot is re-engaged

blocks.content: The **slat overspeed** limit is the takeoff slat placard: 260 KIAS on the MD-10-10 and 270 KIAS on the MD-10-30. The CAWS also sounds the windshear warning from the flight control computers and the radio altitude callouts; both are described with the ground proximity warning system in [Surveillance](surveillance).

Each system decides its own warning condition, including its own silencing switch where it has one, and hands the aural unit a single signal. Only the takeoff warning is assembled by the aural unit itself, because it combines switches from five systems (see [Takeoff warning](#takeoff-warning)).

The bell sounds while the engine fire detection system reports a fire and its bell has not been cut out. On the DC-10 and KC-10, pushing the glareshield ENGINE FIRE light silences the bell and rearms it, so a second engine fire rings it again. A lower cargo fire lights MASTER WARNING and its panel lights but is not one of this unit's aural warnings. On the MD-10, the fire warnings are the CAWS's, and the cargo fire has its own tritones. Detection logic and the loop test are in [Fire Protection](fire-protection).

Each central air data computer compares its computed airspeed with the maximum operating speed it computes for the current altitude, VMO below the crossover altitude and the speed equivalent to MMO above it, the same value that drives the maximum speed pointer on the airspeed indicators. When computed airspeed exceeds that value the computer's overspeed signal closes; it opens again 2 kt below the limit, so a speed hovering on the limit does not make the clacker chatter. Either computer's signal sounds the warning. A computer with invalid airspeed or limit data inhibits its signal rather than risk a false warning.

The **MAX SPD WARN TEST** switch on the pilots' overhead test panel, held at 1 or 2, drives that computer's overspeed signal directly. The test proves the computer, its output and the aural channel; a computer that is unpowered or still initializing fails it. On the MD-10, holding ANNUN LT TEST also sounds the overspeed warning.
Two conditions sound the gear warning, and they differ in one respect: whether the crew can silence it.

blocks.title: Landing gear warning logic
rows: Any gear not down and locked; any throttle at idle; airspeed below 215 KIAS
GEAR HORN OFF, while the flaps are short of the landing range (28.5°). The silence holds until the condition clears, so a new approach gets a new horn
Any gear not down and locked; flaps at 28.5° or more

blocks.content: The flap switch is in the left outboard flap position transmitter, so it reads the flap surface, not the handle. On the DC-10 and KC-10, “down and locked” also requires the gear handle at DOWN: pulling the handle straight out of its DN detent on the ground sounds the horn and turns every gear light red, which is the preflight test of the warning. The MD-10's warning reads the gear alone, so the same action turns the gear lights red and sounds nothing. With the center gear isolation switch at UP (Series 30 and 40, KC-10), the center gear is disconnected from the gear warning. Gear lights and their logic are in [Landing Gear](landing-gear).

The cabin altitude warning switch trips at about 10,000 ft cabin altitude. It lights CABIN ALT and MASTER WARNING and sounds the intermittent horn. On the DC-10 and KC-10, the flight engineer's **CABIN ALT WARN HORN** button silences the horn and leaves the lights on; the horn re-arms for the next trip of the switch. On the MD-10 the CAWS plays three cycles and stops, and plays again only after the switch resets and trips again. The same switch lights the passenger signs (see [Lighting](lighting)). Cabin pressure control is in [Air Conditioning](air-conditioning).

The stabilizer motion detector sounds the horn during each continuous movement of more than 1° at more than 0.08° per second under manual trim, and of more than 1° in one continuous run under automatic pitch trim. The automatic trim moves the stabilizer in runs, each followed by a stop, so small autopilot corrections stay silent; a long run that relieves a large out-of-trim load sounds it. The warning stops when the stabilizer stops. Its purpose is to make a runaway or unexpected trim movement audible before it becomes a control problem (see [Flight Controls](flight-controls)).

On the DC-10 and KC-10, approaching the altitude preselected on the flight guidance panel, the altitude advisory computer lights the altitude alert lights on the altimeters steady at about 750 ft to go and sounds a 2-second chord; the light goes out at about 250 ft to go. A later deviation of more than 250 ft from the captured altitude flashes the light silently. On the MD-10 the flight control computers provide the alert, and the CAWS sounds the C-chord and “ALTITUDE” once. Operation is described in [Flight Instruments](flight-instruments) and [Automatic Flight](automatic-flight).

On the MD-10, a disconnect signal from either flight control computer sounds the CAWS autopilot disconnect warning, which continues until a pilot pushes a wheel autopilot disconnect switch after one full cycle, or the autopilot is re-engaged. On the DC-10 and KC-10, the real unit's wailer sounds when the autopilots disengage in the land mode; see [Simulation notes](#simulation-notes).

sections.title: Takeoff warning
sections.summary: The configuration warning that sounds if a takeoff is begun with the aircraft not set for it, and how to test it.

blocks.content: Configuration-related takeoff accidents have typically begun with something the crew believed they had set: flaps or slats retracted, a stabilizer trimmed for landing, a spoiler handle out of its detent, a parking brake still on. The takeoff warning catches these at the last moment, when the throttles are advanced on the runway, and sounds while any of them is wrong.

**Arming.** The warning is armed when the ground shift mechanism is in **ground mode** and **throttle 1 or throttle 2** is advanced for takeoff, about a quarter of the way up its travel. Throttle 3 alone does not arm it. Ground mode is what makes the warning silent in flight, where none of these conditions is a takeoff hazard; it also means that a ground-sensing failure that leaves the system in ground mode arms the warning in the air.

blocks.title: Takeoff warning conditions (any one sounds it, once armed)
rows: Slats not at takeoff extend (the slat TAKEOFF light out)
Flaps in the landing range, 35° or more
Flaps not at a takeoff setting: retracted, or 26° or more: “FLAP”
Spoiler handle not fully forward (RET, armed or not, is forward)
Stabilizer trim not in the takeoff green band

blocks.content: On the DC-10 and KC-10 the takeoff warning does not detect flaps set to 0° with the slats extended, nor a takeoff flap setting other than the one planned: it watches only the slats and the landing flap range. Setting and checking the takeoff flap is a crew task the warning does not replace. The slat function of the takeoff warning must be operable for takeoff.

A warning that sounds as the throttles are advanced for takeoff means the configuration is wrong: reject the takeoff and correct the cause before trying again. On a go-around or touch-and-go after touchdown, with the aircraft in ground mode, the warning may sound briefly while the flaps, spoilers or stabilizer are still being reset.
On the MD-10, a flap setting that disagrees with the FMS TAKEOFF page also stops the green essential items box from appearing (see [Essential items checklist](#essential-items-checklist)).

blocks.alt: Logic diagram of the takeoff warning: GROUND MODE AND (THROTTLE 1 ADVANCED OR THROTTLE 2 ADVANCED) arms an AND gate; its other input is an OR of five conditions: SLATS NOT T.O. EXT, FLAPS IN LANDING RANGE (35° or more), SPOILER HANDLE NOT FORWARD, STAB NOT IN GREEN BAND, PARKING BRAKE NOT RELEASED. Output to the central aural warning unit, priority 4, intermittent horn. A second panel shows the MD-10 variant with each condition producing its own voice word.
blocks.title: Takeoff warning logic

blocks.content: On the DC-10 and KC-10 the test uses the slat condition: with everything else set for takeoff and the slats retracted, advancing throttle 1 or 2 must sound the warning. Who runs it differs by deck. On the DC-10 the captain does it in their cockpit preparation; on the KC-10 it is part of the flight engineer's interior inspection; on the MD-10 the first officer does it in the cockpit preparation, with the aircraft as it stands (flaps and slats retracted).

items.action: FULL FORWARD, horn sounds; then IDLE, horn silent
FULL FORWARD and back to IDLE (freedom of travel)

blocks.content: If the warning does not sound, maintenance action is required before takeoff. On the DC-10 and KC-10 the test must be done with the parking brake released, otherwise the brake term sounds the horn and the slat function is not proven. The test with the slats retracted does not check the stabilizer, flap or spoiler terms; those are checked by the configuration flows and the BEFORE TAKEOFF checklist.

sections.title: Clocks
sections.summary: The pilots' clocks, the DC-10 flight engineer's clock and the MD-10's navigation display clock.

blocks.content: Every clock in the aircraft is a crystal-controlled movement that keeps time on its own once set. The clocks are powered through one breaker, ELEC CLOCK (overhead A-18), on the battery direct bus, so they keep running in a cold aircraft as long as the battery is connected. A clock advances only while powered: with its breaker out for ten minutes it is ten minutes slow until reset, as a real clock is.

**Setting.** When the aircraft is loaded, each clock sets itself once to the simulator's Greenwich Mean Time (UTC) on its first powered moment and then runs freely. It is not slaved to the simulator's time afterwards, so it drifts only if its power is interrupted or the crew change it, and a clock the crew have set deliberately stays where they set it. Changing the simulator's time of day after loading does not move the clocks; reset them with their set controls.

Each pilot's instrument panel carries a digital and analog clock with three functions. A digital **GMT** window shows hours and minutes, set with the hour and minute set knobs. A digital **ELAPS** window shows long-term elapsed time in hours and minutes, run from the ELAPS button. An analog dial carries the **chronograph** (CHRO): a sweep second hand that turns once a minute and a minute marker, both started from zero by the CHRO button and returned to zero by the next push.

A second button for the chronograph, labeled **CLOCK**, is on each pilot's light control panel below the clearview window, where it can be reached without looking down at the instrument panel. It does exactly what the CHRO button does, on the same movement: a start on one button is returned to zero by a push on the other. The chronograph is used, for example, to time engine starts.

Inset: the CLOCK button on the captain's light control panel below the clearview window.

blocks.content: The MD-10 conversion replaced the pilots' panel clocks with a clock on each navigation display, at the top right: a circle with UTC hours and minutes above and a second line below. The UTC comes from that seat's clock movement, powered and set as described above; until the movement has been set from the simulator the UTC digits are blank.

The second line normally shows the **elapsed flight time** in cyan, counted by the EIS. It starts when the aircraft lifts off and stops 30 seconds after touchdown, so a touch-and-go keeps counting. It is reset when a V2 is entered on the FMS TAKEOFF page for the next flight, and lost if the EIS loses power.

Each pilot's **TIMER** selector, below the clearview window on the light control panel, runs a counter on that pilot's own navigation display: the first push starts it, the second stops it, the third resets it to 00:00. While running or stopped the timer replaces the elapsed flight time on the second line, in white, as minutes and seconds; after the reset the line returns to the elapsed flight time.

sections.title: Flight recorders
sections.summary: The flight data recorder and its FLT RECORDER OFF light, the cockpit voice recorder, and the aircraft integrated data system.

blocks.content: The flight data recorder (FDR) and the cockpit voice recorder (CVR) are the accident recorders: crash-protected units in the tail that preserve the last hours of flight parameters and cockpit audio for investigators. The aircraft integrated data system (AIDS), fitted to some DC-10s, is a maintenance recorder: it records engine and airframe data for the airline's engineering department and can print reports in flight.

The flight data recorder starts and stops automatically. It records whenever **any engine is operating** or the aircraft is **in flight** (the ground sensing relays in flight mode), provided the **parking brake is released**. The parking brake interlock keeps the recorder off during engine ground runs with the parking brake set, while making sure it runs from the moment the brake is released for taxi. On the aircraft a FLT RCDR switch on the flight engineer's panel can force the recorder on; in the simulation it is inoperative (see [Simulation notes](#simulation-notes)).

The amber **FLT RECORDER OFF** light on the flight engineer's annunciator block lights whenever the recorder is not recording: not running, unpowered, or failed. It is therefore on during a normal preflight with the parking brake set and the engines stopped, and goes out after engine start once the parking brake is released. The recorder is powered through FLT RCDR (avionics panel D-5, AC bus 3); the light through FLT RCDR OFF LT (avionics panel E-5, DC bus 3).

“Engine operating” is sensed by the engine's oil pressure being up. On a DC-10 with the AIDS fitted, the recorder's data arrive through the AIDS's flight data acquisition unit 1, so a failure of that unit stops the recorder too and lights FLT RECORDER OFF along with the AIDS FAULT light.

The cockpit voice recorder records whenever the aircraft has electrical power: the crew's audio panels (radio and interphone, transmitted and received) and the cockpit area microphone, four channels in all. Its control unit on the overhead panel carries the area microphone, a **TEST** button, a test monitor meter, an ERASE button and a headset jack. It is powered through COCKPIT VOICE RCDR (avionics panel B-5, AC bus 1).

Pushing **TEST** applies a test signal to each channel in turn over about 5 seconds. The meter shows each channel's recording level, and must stay in the green band (8 or more on its 0 to 10 scale) throughout; a channel that drops out of the green for its part of the cycle has failed. The test does not run with the recorder unpowered or failed. The crew check it during the cockpit preparation.

blocks.alt: Cockpit voice recorder control unit on the overhead panel, close-up: area microphone grille, TEST button, ERASE button, headset jack and the test monitor meter (0 to 10, green band from 8 up) with its needle in the green during a test.
blocks.title: Cockpit voice recorder control unit

blocks.content: The AIDS collects engine and airframe data, records it for analysis by a ground computer, monitors engine limits and certain flight events, and prints reports on board. It was an airline option on the DC-10, and on this aircraft it is an equipment option: select it in the EFB under Configuration, Aircraft Configuration, Engineer zone, AIDS Panel (see [EFB](efb)). It is not available on the fire tankers. With it fitted, the AIDS control panel (the flight data entry panel, FDEP) appears on the flight engineer's upper panel No. 3.

blocks.content: The DMU, the acquisition units, the FDEP and the printer are powered through AIDS DC PWR (lower main panel D-2, DC bus 1), and the DAR through AIDS DIGITAL RCDR (lower main panel H-2, AC ground service bus). The DMU takes its time from the flight engineer's clock.

Legends legible.
blocks.title: AIDS flight data entry panel

blocks.content: The FDEP has an **IDENT** window of five characters (four letters and an engine number) and a **VALUE** window of a sign and four digits, with leading zeros blank and the decimal point implied by the parameter (+ 868 is 86.8 % N1; +6630 is 663 °C EGT). The keypad has the digits 0 to 9 and the keys CLEAR, EVENT, INSERT and PRINT, and two switch-lights, **FAULT** and **LIMIT**. The **MODE** selector has three positions: STBY (no recording), AUTO (recording at the rate the program sets for each flight mode) and FAST (continuous recording).

Codes are keyed as letters, and the keypad carries the letter groups of a telephone keypad on its digit keys: 2 ABC, 3 DEF, 4 GHI, 5 JKL, 6 MNO, 7 PQRS, 8 TUV, 9 WXYZ. DATE is keyed 3-2-8-3. The DMU recognizes the code and spells it in the IDENT window when INSERT is pushed; an unrecognized code shows WHAT. Every operation except EVENT starts with CLEAR.

blocks.title: AIDS codes
rows: Day and month, e.g. 0407 for 4 July
Gross weight from the load sheet (loaded)
Hundreds of kg, e.g. 2055 for 205,470 kg
Fan and core speed, each engine

blocks.content: In AUTO the DMU works out where the aircraft is in its flight and records more often when more is happening: continuously through engine start, takeoff, climb and landing, and once every 400 seconds while taxiing and en route. The flight mode is sequential: each mode is entered from the one before, so a takeoff passing below 1,700 ft radio altitude is not mistaken for an approach.

blocks.title: AIDS flight modes
rows: On the ground, all engines below 20 % N2
Any start valve open (held 40 s after it closes)
Any engine above 40 % N2, below takeoff thrust
Radio altitude below 1,700 ft for 12 s, landing flaps, or the land mode armed
On the ground after landing, until 40 s after ground speed falls below 60 kt

blocks.content: FAST records continuously whatever the mode; select AUTO as soon as possible to save tape. STBY records nothing, and on the ground it also clears the values loaded for the flight. **EVENT** makes one recording and marks it, or only marks the tape where recording is continuous, so the crew can flag a moment for engineering. A limit exceedance always records. The DAR signals TLOW when three quarters of its tape is used.

The DMU monitors each engine's EGT, N1 and N2 against that engine's own limits for the current flight mode (the start limit in engine start, the takeoff limits with their time allowances in takeoff and initial climb, the continuous limits otherwise), and the APU's EGT. An exceedance lights the **LIMIT** light (not for the APU) and is queued; pushing CLEAR then LIMIT shows the parameter in IDENT and its present value in VALUE, updated every second, and pushing LIMIT again steps to the next exceedance.

blocks.title: Automatic printouts
rows: About 50 s after takeoff thrust is set; and on any engine EGT, N1 or N2 limit exceedance or APU EGT exceedance, a data block about every 2 s until the parameter is back within its limit, up to 16 blocks
Mean sink rate below 40 ft radio altitude greater than 10 ft/s
Vertical load factor above 2.0 g or below 0.0 g, in any mode but pre-flight
Actual gross weight above the maximum landing weight during the rollout (about 363,500 lb on the -10 and -15, about 403,000 lb on the -30 and -40)

blocks.content: The crew can also request an ENG, LOAD or FCTR (flight controls, control forces and hydraulic temperatures) printout: CLEAR, key the code, check it in IDENT, PRINT. One printout is produced per request. The printer works through its queue at its own speed and can hold about 24 printouts.

blocks.alt: Illustration of an AIDS LOAD printout strip from the printer: a heading block with date, flight number, GMT, flight mode 8 and the trigger OVERWEIGHT LANDING, followed by one data block of gross weight, center of gravity, vertical acceleration and sink rate values. Marked as an illustration of the real system.

blocks.caption: The format of the real system's overweight landing report. The aircraft records the printout and its trigger, but the cockpit has no printer to show the paper.

blocks.content: Every AIDS unit except the FDEP has built-in test equipment. A malfunction of an AIDS unit or of the flight data recorder lights the **FAULT** light (and FLT RECORDER OFF if the recorder is involved). Push CLEAR, then FAULT: the IDENT window shows the failed component. If FAULT stays lit, push it again until every failed component has been shown. A fault that has been displayed does not light FAULT again until the MODE selector is moved from STBY to AUTO on the ground before the next flight; SYNC may repeat.

sections.title: Operation
sections.summary: The warning and recording systems through a flight: the preflight tests, handling an alert, takeoff, approach and landing.

blocks.content: The cockpit preparation proves each alerting path before it is needed. The tests below are those of the warning and recording systems; the fire, stall, ground proximity and other system tests are in their own parts and in [Normal Procedures](normal-procedures).

blocks.title: Warning system preflight tests, DC-10 and KC-10
rows: Annunciator lights: ALL TEST, then AREA TEST at each selector position

All F/E lamps lit except the fire loop and cargo door lights (KC-10: and brake temperature); four cue lights, the summary lights except CABIN ALT and APU FIRE, CAB CARGO SMOKE and all master lights lit; all out on release. Reset master lights as required
On with the aircraft parked, whatever the test switches

See [AIDS procedures](#aids-procedures); FAULT out with MODE at AUTO

Gear warning system and SD CONFIG synoptic

blocks.content: On the three-crew aircraft a MASTER CAUTION or MASTER WARNING tells the pilots to look up; the cue or summary light tells them which system; the flight engineer, whose own master light came on first, identifies the specific light on their panel and calls it. Resetting the master light rearms it for the next fault, and should follow identifying the fault, not replace it: the individual light stays on until the condition clears. A cue light that relights after being reset means a second lamp of that system has come on.

On the MD-10 the pilot monitoring announces the alert and pushes its lit cue switch. The push resets the master light, shows the synoptic with the alert and its consequences, and (for Level 2 and 1) moves the alert into the reminder area. The synoptic shows the actual system configuration, so the crew can see what the automatic controller has done before they act. Level 1 alerts have no written procedures beyond the NO TAKEOFF list: their message, consequences or the nature of the alert define the response. A **flashing reminder** with no MASTER CAUTION means a Level 1 alert that appears only on the synoptic, usually an automatic controller's own action; push the cue switch when time permits.

Silence an aural warning with its own silencing control or by correcting the condition, never by pulling its breaker, except where a procedure says so: the gear-up landing and ditching procedures trip TO/LDG CAB PRESS AURAL WARN (lower main panel C-11) to stop the horn from sounding throughout the approach (see [Emergency Procedures](emergency-procedures)). A breaker pulled this way also silences the takeoff warning and the cabin altitude horn.

items: **Before takeoff.** On the MD-10 the takeoff essential items checklist runs from V2 entry and two engines running; the green box confirms the configuration. On all three, advancing throttle 1 or 2 arms the takeoff warning.

**Takeoff.** On the MD-10 Level 2 and 1 alerts are held from throttle advance and Level 3 alerts from V1, and released as described in [Alert inhibits](#alert-inhibits). On the DC-10 and KC-10 the flight data recorder has been running since the parking brake was released with an engine running; on the DC-10 the AIDS (if fitted) prints an ENG report about 50 seconds after takeoff thrust.
**Cruise.** The altitude advisory sounds once as each new cleared altitude is approached. MASTER CAUTION events are dealt with as above.

**Approach.** Retarding the throttles to idle with the gear up below 215 kt sounds the gear horn; GEAR HORN OFF silences it until the condition clears, but with the flaps at 28.5° or more the horn cannot be silenced until the gear is down. On a DC-10 or KC-10 DUAL LAND approach the master lights are inhibited below 100 ft. On the MD-10 the landing essential items checklist runs, and Level 2 and 1 alerts are held from 1,000 ft.

**After landing.** The MD-10's elapsed flight time stops 30 seconds after touchdown. On the DC-10 and KC-10 the flight data recorder stops when the parking brake is set at the gate, and FLT RECORDER OFF comes on.

sections.title: Failures and non-normal operation
sections.summary: How the warning and recording systems fail, what the crew see, and where the procedures are.

blocks.content: The warning systems are built so that one failure removes as little as possible: the master lights and the fire and overspeed warnings are on the battery bus, the aural channels are split across three breakers on different buses, and every lamp is on its own supply. The price is that a bus failure silences some warnings and not others, and the crew must know which.

blocks.content: After the ground sensing breakers are reset before touchdown in the ground-mode abnormal, the takeoff warning horn sounds continuously with the flaps in the landing range until the throttles are retarded. This is expected.

**Modeled in depth.** The DC-10 and KC-10 master lights, cue lights and lamp tests follow the real relay logic: acknowledgement by push, rearming, the pilots' caution delay, the flight engineer's separate pair and list, the DUAL LAND inhibit, and each lamp's own supply. The central aural warning unit's priority order, waiting warnings, fire and overspeed alternation and three breakers are modeled, as is every condition behind it. The MD-10's alert list, inhibits, essential items checklist, cue switches, reminder messages, master lights and CAWS turn-taking are modeled, with the CAWS cycles timed to recordings of the MD-11's system. The clocks are real movements that hold when unpowered. The flight data recorder's run logic, the cockpit voice recorder's test, and the AIDS (flight modes, recording, limits, BITE, keypad and printout triggers) are modeled.

items: **MD-10 alert coverage.** The simulation knows all 516 alerts in the MD-10's lists, but only about 350 of them are raised. The other 166 have no condition yet: for those faults no alert appears, no cue switch lights and no master light comes on, although the system itself has failed and its synoptic shows it. Among the alerts named in this manual that never appear are AIR SYS TEST, EMER LTS TST PASS and the emergency light battery alert. When a failure gives no alert, read the synoptic and the overhead panel.
**MD-10 consequences.** No consequence statements are provided: the consequence areas of the synoptic pages and the CONSEQ page are always empty.
**MD-10 preflight.** Because the AIR SYS TEST alert is not raised, release ANNUN LT TEST once the lights and the overspeed warning have been checked.

**MD-10 Level 1 presentation.** Every Level 1 alert is shown on the EAD and lights its cue switch and MASTER CAUTION. The aircraft's maintenance alerts that appear on the STATUS page only, and the synoptic-only alerts announced by a flashing reminder, are not yet distinguished.
**MD-10 synoptic call-up.** Any new alert (except an APU fault) returns the SD to the secondary engine page if another page is showing, not only the secondary engine parameter alerts.

**MD-10 speeds.** The gear warning uses 215 KIAS, as the DC-10 does (the MD-10 FCOM gives 210 kt), without the FCOM's 16-second delay for gear in transit with landing flaps. The slat overspeed uses the takeoff slat placards (260 KIAS Series 10, 270 KIAS Series 30); the FCOM's warning text gives 280 kt.
**Autopilot disconnect (DC-10, KC-10).** The wailer for an autopilot disengaged in the land mode is not modeled. The slats-extended half of the DC-10 overspeed warning is also not modeled.
**APU fire horn.** The exterior horn's logic is modeled in the fire protection system, but it makes no sound and its ground panel switch is not in the cockpit model.

**Flight data recorder.** The flight engineer's FLT RCDR switch (NORM, OVRD), which on the aircraft runs the recorder with the engines stopped or the parking brake set, is inoperative and rests at NORM. On the MD-10 the flight data recorder is not presented at all.
**KC-10 flight engineer's clock.** The KC-10's flight engineer's clock is not part of the simulated panel; only the pilots' clocks are fitted.

**DC-10 ground proximity failure.** The DC-10 has no ground proximity failure light. In the simulation a failed or unpowered DC-10 ground proximity computer can still light the pilots' MASTER CAUTION, with no light on any panel to say why.

**Pilots' clocks.** The ELAPS button runs start, stop, zero on three pushes; the books give it start and zero on two, as the CHRO button has. The chronograph's minute marker turns once an hour rather than once in 12 minutes.
**MD-10 timer.** The TIMER selector counts up only; the real selector's DN count-down from the APPROACH page time and its tone are not modeled.
**AIDS.** The printer has no paper in the cockpit model: printouts are queued, timed and reported as faults, but the text is not shown. CIP and EP are recognized but show no value.

**Takeoff warning.** The throttle switch closes at about a quarter of lever travel, and the stabilizer green band is taken as 2.0° to 10.0° nose up for every DC-10 series; the printed bands vary with weight and center of gravity. On the MD-10 the FLAP term reads the flap angle only (retracted, or 26° or more): a takeoff flap that disagrees with the FMS TAKEOFF page holds back the green essential items box but does not sound the warning.

blocks.content: **EFB.** The AIDS is fitted from the EFB's Configuration app, Aircraft Configuration, Engineer zone (not on the fire tankers or the KC-10). The EFB Failures app has no entries for the recorders or the AIDS, but bus failures and pulled breakers (from the cockpit panels, shown and reset in the Failures app) exercise every power path described here. The captain's and first officer's ADI and HSI display failures listed in the Failures app are described in [Flight Instruments](flight-instruments).

parts.title: Landing Gear and Brakes
parts.summary: Gear extension and retraction, the center gear, nosewheel steering, brakes, anti-skid, autobrakes, parking brake and brake temperature.

sections.title: Introduction
sections.summary: What the landing gear does, how it is powered, and how the fit differs between airframes.

blocks.content:
The landing gear carries the aircraft on the ground, absorbs the energy of each touchdown, steers the aircraft while taxiing and stops it. On the DC-10 family it is a tricycle arrangement: two main gears, each with a four-wheel truck, a steerable two-wheel nose gear and, on the long-range airframes, a two-wheel **center gear** on the fuselage centerline. Every main-gear and center-gear wheel carries a multi-disc hydraulic brake; the nose wheels are unbraked.

The part is built around four subsystems that share hydraulic power but are otherwise independent: **extension and retraction** (hydraulic, with a mechanical free-fall back-up), **nosewheel steering** (hydromechanical, from a tiller and the rudder pedals), **brakes** (two complete brake systems on two hydraulic systems, each with its own accumulators and anti-skid), and the **position indication and warning** system that tells the crew where every leg is.

The architecture follows two rules that explain most of its detail. First, the failure that removes the means of lowering the gear must never prevent the gear from coming down. Hydraulic system 3 alone raises and lowers the gear, and the design accepts that single source because the gear can always be released mechanically and fall by gravity onto spring-loaded locks. System 3 is itself backed by the reversible motor pumps, which can repressurize it from system 1 or system 2 as long as it keeps its fluid.

Second, losing one hydraulic system must not cost landing braking. Each brake has two separate groups of pistons in alternate cavities of the same housing, one group fed by brake system 1 (hydraulic system 1) and the other by brake system 2 (hydraulic system 3). Either group alone can stop the aircraft from any normal landing. Hydraulic system 2, which powers flight controls, has no part in the gear or the brakes.
