blocks.content: The KDC-10 flies as a DC-10-30 and has the -30's center gear and autobrake. The DC-10-30 Tanker (firefighting) gives up its center gear, although the cockpit still carries the switch and the center-gear indications, which then do nothing. The DC-10-40 Omega keeps its center gear.

sections.title: Gear arrangement and structure
sections.summary: Main, nose and center gear, the shock struts, and the ground sensing mechanism that tells the aircraft it is on the ground.

blocks.alt: Two plan views of the aircraft from below, side by side. Left: DC-10-10 with nose gear and two main gear trucks only. Right: DC-10-30 with the two-wheel center gear on the centerline between the main trucks. Each wheel numbered as on the brake temperature panel: 1 and 2 left truck forward axle, 3 and 4 right truck forward axle, 5 and 6 left truck aft axle, 7 and 8 right truck aft axle, 9 and 10 center gear. Label the anti-skid wheel pairs L OUTBD, L INBD, R INBD, R OUTBD and CTR, and show the wheel wells and door outlines.
blocks.title: Gear arrangement, plan view
blocks.caption: Without center gear (DC-10-10, -15, MD-10-10) and with it (DC-10-30, -40, KC-10, MD-10-30). The brake numbers are the ones the brake temperature panel uses.

blocks.alt: Side exterior view of a DC-10-30 on the ground, gear down, with the nose gear, the left main gear truck and the center gear visible. Overlay the retraction paths: nose gear swinging into the forward fuselage well, main gear swinging inboard into the fuselage wheel well, center gear retracting into its well between the main wells.
blocks.title: Gear arrangement, side view

blocks.content:
Each main gear is an oleo-pneumatic shock strut hinged at its top to a trunnion fitting in the wing root, with a truck beam at its lower end carrying two axles, four wheels and four brakes. The gear swings inboard to retract into a wheel well in the lower fuselage. A folding side brace takes the side loads, and a pair of lock links holds the brace straight: with the links pushed over center by springs and a hydraulic downlock cylinder, the side brace cannot fold and the gear is **down and locked**. To retract, the downlock cylinder first pulls the links out of their over-center position.

A hydraulic **truck beam trim cylinder** connects each truck to its strut. It is pressurized on both sides from system 3, which positions the truck perpendicular to the strut so that it stows correctly in the well, and damps the fore-and-aft pitching of the truck during taxi, touchdown and braking. A trim cylinder interlock blocks the gear handle from being moved to UP if a trim cylinder line ruptures, because a truck that is not held square cannot be stowed.

Each main gear has two kinds of doors. The **strut doors** are linked to the gear and move with it. The large **inboard (wheel well) doors** have their own hydraulic cylinders and latches. They open at the start of each gear cycle and close again at its end, so they are closed both with the gear down and with it up. A follow-up cable from the side brace repositions the door control valves as the gear travels, closing the doors in the last few degrees of travel. With the gear up the doors also carry the gear: the main gear is held up by system 3 pressure in its retract cylinder, and if that pressure is lost the gear settles onto its latched doors.

A visual downlock indicator, a button that rises through the upper wing surface when the gear is down and locked, can be seen from the cabin windows over the wing.

The nose gear is a steerable dual-wheel oleo strut in the forward lower fuselage. A single retract cylinder moves it, and a separate **unlock cylinder** drives its lock links: over center with the gear down, unlocked for travel, and over center again at the top, so that the nose gear is held retracted by its own locked linkage rather than by hydraulic pressure. That is why a loss of system 3 leaves the nose gear up until something upsets the links, and why the alternate extension system includes a cable and roller that do exactly that.

The nose gear forward doors are driven by links from the drag brace: they open while the gear is in transit and are closed at both ends of its travel. The aft doors are linked to the strut and simply follow it. Two steering cylinders straddle the strut (see [Nosewheel steering](#nosewheel-steering)). On retraction the steering is mechanically bypassed and the wheels centerd, so the nose wheels cannot be turned in the well.

The long-range airframes carry a third main gear on the fuselage centerline between the two main trucks: a shock strut with a single axle and two braked wheels, retracting into its own well behind four doors that are moved mechanically by the gear. It is not steerable. It came with the -30 and -40, whose maximum weights are far beyond the -10's, and it does two jobs. It takes a share of the weight off the wing gears, which keeps the main gear loads and the pavement loading within limits. And it adds two brakes, a quarter more heat sink than the eight main brakes alone, which matters most in a high-energy rejected takeoff.

The center gear is braked from both brake systems and has its own anti-skid valves. It retracts and extends with the main and nose gear on system 3 through its own control valve. When retracted it is held up by an over-center lock, like the nose gear, so it does not fall by itself when system 3 is lost and it has a separate alternate extension handle (see [Alternate extension](#alternate-extension)).

Because it carries part of the weight, operating with the center gear retracted is a limited configuration. It is normally extended for every takeoff and landing. With it retracted, the landing weight is limited (363,500 lb on the FedEx DC-10-30; 400,000 lb on the KC-10 against 436,000 lb with it down), FedEx adds 450 ft to the landing distance, and special performance data apply. The [Limitations](limitations) section has the figures. The crew can keep it retracted with the **CTR GEAR isolation switch** (see [Center gear control](#centre-gear-control)).

Every leg uses an oleo-pneumatic shock strut: dry nitrogen in the upper chamber and hydraulic fluid below, separated by a floating piston, with a metering pin passing through an orifice in the piston head. The strut does two different things with the energy of a touchdown. The **gas spring** stores it: as the strut shortens, the gas volume falls and its pressure rises roughly as P·V^n = constant, with n near 1.35 for a fast compression. The **orifice** dissipates it: fluid forced through the metering orifice drops pressure in proportion to the square of its velocity, so the damping force rises steeply with sink rate. The metering pin's taper varies the orifice area along the stroke, giving heavy damping where the energy must be absorbed and free flow near full extension.

The proportion matters. A strut that only stored energy would bounce the aircraft back into the air; one that only dissipated it would have no static support. The oleo absorbs most of the touchdown energy as heat in the fluid and then settles on its gas spring at the static position. Main struts are serviced to 238 ±12 psi of nitrogen and the nose strut to 100 ±5 psi, both fully extended; each main strut holds about 11.5 US gal of fluid.

The gear is designed for a 10 ft/s (600 ft/min) sink rate at maximum landing weight, and the KC-10 T.O. requires a hard landing inspection after any touchdown above 600 ft/min. An emergency landing above maximum landing weight should not exceed 360 ft/min. Each strut also carries a compression switch, and the nose strut drives the ground sensing mechanism described next.
A mechanical **ground sensing mechanism** on the nose gear follows the extension and compression of the nose strut. It has three outputs:

items: It mechanically **disables rudder pedal steering** when the strut extends.
It moves the **anti-retraction lock** clear of the gear handle when the strut extends.

It cams two switches that energize the **ground control relays**, which put a long list of systems into their ground or flight mode. The FedEx and KC-10 books call this the **ground shift**: GROUND mode with the nose strut compressed, FLIGHT mode with it extended.

blocks.content: Keying it to the nose strut rather than to the main gear is deliberate. The nose strut extends at rotation, seconds before the main gear leaves the runway, so the gear handle is free to move the moment the aircraft flies, and flight idle is already selected when it is needed. On landing the nose strut compresses only after the nose wheel is down, by which time the main gear has been on the runway for a few seconds; the systems that need the earliest possible ground signal (the anti-skid and the automatic ground spoilers) take it from main wheel spin-up instead.

blocks.title: What the ground shift switches
rows: Anti-retraction lock in place: the handle cannot be moved to UP
Flight idle, selected at rotation; after landing it is held for a few seconds so reverse thrust spools from flight idle
Can be pulled to GROUND SPOILER
Ground proximity warning and flight recorder

blocks.content: The relays are powered through two breakers, L GND SENS and R GND SENS (upper main panel P-1 and S-1 on the DC-10). Opening them forces the relays into flight mode, which is how the crew recovers the flight-mode systems when the mechanism stays in ground mode after takeoff. It does not move the mechanical anti-retraction lock, which is what the GEAR HANDLE REL button is for. See [Failures](#failures).

sections.title: Extension and retraction
sections.summary: The gear handle, its interlocks, the selector valve and the sequence of a normal gear cycle.

blocks.content:
Gear extension and retraction combine a mechanical control path with hydraulic actuation. The gear handle drives push-pull cables and a dual cable run to the **landing gear selector valve** in the right main wheel well. That valve is six valves in one housing: the gear control valve, a **bypass valve**, two main gear door control valves and two door manual-open valves used by maintenance. The selector valve ports system 3 pressure to the retract, downlock, unlock, door and door latch cylinders in the order the gear needs, while restrictors in the up and down lines meter the flow so that the doors have time to move and the legs do not slam into their stops. Metering pins in the main gear retract cylinders snub the end of the retract stroke and the start of the extend stroke.

Nothing electrical sits in the main control path. The gear handle moves the valve; the indication system watches the result. The one electrically driven valve is the center gear's, whose actuator the CTR GEAR isolation switch can drive (see [Center gear control](#centre-gear-control)).

blocks.alt: Timeline diagram of a DC-10-30 gear cycle in two rows. Retraction: handle UP; main gear doors unlatch and open; downlock and unlock cylinders break the lock links; main, nose and center gear travel up; follow-up cable closes the main doors in the last degrees; legs reach the up position; doors latched; red lights go out. Extension: handle DOWN; door latches release and doors open while the legs leave their up position; legs travel down under hydraulic power and gravity; lock links go over center; doors close by follow-up; green lights. Show the red light lit throughout transit and the approximate durations from the maintenance manual: main retraction within about 10 s, main extension 16 to 20 s.
blocks.title: Retraction and extension sequence

children.title: The gear handle and its interlocks

blocks.content:
The GEAR handle has two positions, UP and DOWN, with a detent at each. A spring holds it in its detent; to move it the pilot pulls it out (aft) first. Pulling it out of the DOWN detent, even without raising it, operates a switch that tells the warning system the handle is not down, which is how the gear horn is tested on the ground. On the DC-10 and KC-10 the handle and its position lights are on the first officer's instrument panel; on the MD-10 they are on the center instrument panel.

Two interlocks can hold the handle at DOWN:

items: **The anti-retraction lock.** A spring-loaded lock crank blocks the handle at DOWN. A cable from the ground sensing mechanism pulls the crank clear when the nose strut extends, so the handle is free from rotation onward. The **GEAR HANDLE REL** button beside the handle moves the crank clear by hand. It is for one failure only, a ground sensing mechanism that stays in ground mode after takeoff, and must never be used on the ground.

**The trim cylinder interlock.** System 3 pressure to the truck beam trim cylinders also extends a small interlock cylinder that keeps a crank clear of the selector valve's input. If a trim cylinder line ruptures, a fuse closes to save the system 3 fluid, the interlock loses pressure, and the crank blocks the handle from UP. The gear stays down, which is the safe outcome for a truck that can no longer be stowed.

blocks.content: A third protection is physical rather than designed: a leg carrying the weight of the aircraft cannot be retracted. Even with the GEAR HANDLE REL button held on the ground, the retract cylinders are sized to swing a hanging leg through its arc, not to lift the aircraft off its wheels. Up to 150 lb of force may be applied to the handle without damage (160 lb on the MD-10).

rows: The selector valve ports system 3 pressure to the gear system. The main gear door valves go to OPEN and the door latch cylinders push the door rollers off their hooks; the inboard doors open.
The main gear downlock cylinders pull the lock links out of their over-center position against the downlock springs. The nose gear unlock cylinder does the same for the nose lock links.

The retract cylinders swing the main gear inboard and the nose gear into its well; the center gear retracts on its own valve unless isolated. The trim cylinders hold each truck square to its strut. Every red light is on while a leg is in transit.

As the main gear rises, the follow-up cable moves the door valves back toward CLOSED; the doors start to close in the last few degrees and latch behind the gear. The nose forward doors close with the drag brace and the aft doors with the strut.

The nose and center gear lock links go over center at the top. The main gear is held up by system 3 pressure, with its latched doors under it. The proximity sensors at the locks and door latches report up and locked and the red lights go out, provided no throttle is at idle.

blocks.content:
The maintenance standard is that the main gear retracts within 10 seconds of the handle reaching UP, measured to doors closed, and the nose gear within 10 seconds to up and locked. The legs need not move in unison.

Brake heat goes into the wheel wells with the gear. With the gear retracted a flush ram-air inlet ahead of each main wheel well ducts cooling air over the brakes, but a hot brake still cools faster in the free stream with the gear down, which is why the abnormal brake procedure can call for the gear to be left extended after takeoff.

When the handle moves to DOWN, a direct link from the selector valve drum puts the main gear door valves to OPEN at once, and pressure reaches the door latch cylinders, downlock and unlock cylinders and the retract cylinders together. The latch rams release the doors first, and the main gear leaves its up position while its doors are still opening. The legs extend under hydraulic power with gravity helping, the lock links snap over center under their springs and downlock cylinders, and in the last few degrees of main gear travel the follow-up cable starts the doors closing. The center gear extends with the others when its isolation switch is at NORM.

The maintenance standard for the main gear is 16 to 20 seconds from the handle reaching DOWN to down and locked, not counting door closing. As each leg locks, its red light goes out and its green light comes on.

rows: Continuous system 3 pressure in the retract cylinder. If pressure is lost, the gear rests on its latched inboard doors.
Side brace locked by over-center lock links, downlock springs and the downlock cylinder.
Strut doors linked to the gear. Inboard doors hydraulic, latched, closed with the gear up and with it down.
Over-center lock links, locked at the top by the unlock cylinder.
Forward doors driven by the drag brace (open only in transit). Aft doors linked to the strut.
Four doors moved mechanically by the gear.

blocks.content: The difference between the main gear and the other two is the key to the alternate extension system. A main gear held up by pressure only needs its door latches released and its trapped pressure vented to fall. The nose and center gears are locked up mechanically and need their links upset first. The main gear door **maintenance safety hook**, installed to let mechanics stand on an inboard door, is the one condition that lights both the red and the green light of that main gear at once.

sections.title: Center gear control
sections.summary: The CTR GEAR isolation switch: keeping the center gear up while the other gear extends.

blocks.content: The center gear's hydraulic control valve has an **electric motor actuator** with two limit positions, NORMAL and UP. The crew command it with the **CTR GEAR isolation switch** next to the gear handle.

items: **NORM.** The actuator sits at its normal limit and the center gear control valve follows the gear handle: the center gear extends and retracts with the other gear.

**UP.** The actuator drives the valve to UP. The center gear retracts (if it was down, system 3 is available and it is not carrying weight) and stays retracted whatever the gear handle does. Its position lights are inhibited, and its input to the gear warning system is removed, so a retracted center gear does not keep the warning alive when everything else is down and locked.

blocks.content: Returning the switch to NORM with the handle DOWN lets the center gear extend: its red light comes on while it travels and its green light when it locks.

blocks.title: Center gear logic
rows: Stays retracted; retracts if it was down and is not carrying weight

blocks.content:
The actuator is powered through the CENTER GEAR CONTROL breaker on DC bus 1. Because it is a motor, losing that supply freezes the valve where it is: the switch can be moved but nothing follows it, which is the meaning of “center gear control” in the KC-10's list of effects of losing DC bus 1. Nothing in this path is gated by the ground sensing mechanism. The switch does not pass through the gear handle, so the anti-retraction lock does not stop it; only the weight on the center leg does.

On the DC-10-30, DC-10-40 and KC-10 the switch is a two-position toggle (UP, NORM) beside the gear handle, with a lock pin that secures it in either position; the KC-10 assigns it to the copilot. On the MD-10-30 the conversion replaced it with a blue lighted push-push switch, **CTR GEAR NORM/UP**, on the center instrument panel; when it is lit the center gear stays retracted.

blocks.alt: Close-up of the DC-10-30 first officer's instrument panel beside the landing gear handle: the CTR GEAR isolation toggle with UP and NORM legends and its lock pin, the four gear position lights NOSE, LEFT, CTR, RIGHT, the GEAR HANDLE REL button and the GEAR LT TEST button. Switch shown at NORM.
blocks.title: CTR GEAR isolation switch (DC-10-30, -40, KC-10)

blocks.content: **When the crew use it.** The center gear is normally used for every takeoff and landing. Isolation is for:

items: a center gear that will not extend, or whose indication cannot be made safe: selecting UP clears its red light and its contribution to the horn;
operations where performance and landing weight permit it to stay retracted, for example a ferry or a functional check flight (it reduces drag);
a procedure that calls for it, such as GEAR UNSAFE with the handle down on a -30, where the gear is cycled with the center gear isolated to see whether the main and nose gear then lock.

blocks.content: With the center gear isolated, land within the reduced landing weight and add the landing distance penalty from [Limitations](limitations).

Selecting UP with the center gear down and system 3 pressurized retracts it, in flight or on any leg that is not carrying weight. Check the switch position against the intended configuration before the gear handle is moved.

sections.title: Alternate extension
sections.summary: Free-fall extension of the main and nose gear by the floor lever, and of the center gear by its own handle.

blocks.content: If system 3 cannot extend the gear (no fluid, both its pumps and the reversible motor pumps unable to pressurize it, or a gear handle jammed at UP), the main and nose gear are released mechanically and fall. The **alternate gear extension lever** is in a floor well to the right of the pedestal, under a hinged cover placarded ALTERNATE LANDING GEAR EXTENSION, ALTERNATE OUTBOARD AILERON UNLOCK, PULL UP FORCIBLY FULL STROKE. Lifting it to its latched position does four things through two cable runs:

items: Releases the main gear door latches and upsets the nose gear lock links. **It does not release the center gear.**

Moves the bypass valve in the selector valve to BYPASS. System 3 pressure is blocked downstream of the selector, and the trapped up-pressure in the main gear and door cylinders is vented to return, so nothing hydraulic holds the gear up.
Shuts off system 3 pressure to the nosewheel steering, which then works from system 1 alone and is limited to about 25° to the right with the tiller.
Unlocks the outboard ailerons if they were locked out (see [Flight controls](flight-controls)).

blocks.content:
Once released, each leg swings down under its own weight and the airstream, the cylinders' restrictors slowing it, and the downlock springs push the lock links over center. The maintenance check allows 14 to 18 seconds for the nose gear to free-fall and lock. Allow time before expecting three green lights. The gear position lights work normally during an alternate extension: a leg that is down and locked shows green whatever the handle position, and with the handle still at UP it also shows red, because the leg does not agree with the handle.

The lever is preloaded when raised with the flaps retracted; restrain it when stowing. Stowing it with system 3 operative restores the selector valve and steering, and **retracts the gear if the handle is at UP**. That is why the procedures for a handle jammed at UP keep the lever raised for the rest of the flight.

Reduce to 230 KIAS before an alternate extension, and do not exceed 260 KIAS with the gear extended by the alternate system (Mach 0.70 in both cases). With the outboard ailerons mechanically unlocked, the airspeed is limited to 260 KIAS.

**Center gear (DC-10-30, -40, KC-10, MD-10-30).** The center gear has its own **CENTER GEAR ALTERNATE EXTENSION** handle under a cover plate in the floor forward of the lower main circuit breaker panel, placarded PULL UP AFTER MAIN GEAR ALTERNATE EXTENSION. Pulling it releases the center gear's uplock mechanically and the gear falls and locks. It only works once system 3 pressure is off the gear system, either because the main lever has put the selector valve to bypass or because system 3 is dead, and the crew wait until the main gear is down before pulling it: the delay lets the bypass take effect and avoids a temporary hydraulic lock of the handle. A moderate force is needed, and the center gear may take about a minute to show down and locked.

The same handle checks whether the center gear is up and locked, since there is no other way of seeing it: pulled gently until resistance is felt, a red band on the cable stopping at floor level means up and locked; if the cable travels on (about 12 in) the gear is not locked. In the simulation this handle cannot be operated; see [Simulation notes](#simulation-notes).

blocks.alt: Two floor-level views of the DC-10-30 flight deck. Left: the alternate gear extension lever to the right of the pedestal with its access cover open, the placard ALTERNATE LANDING GEAR EXTENSION / ALTERNATE OUTBOARD AILERON UNLOCK / PULL UP FORCIBLY FULL STROKE legible, the lever stowed and a ghosted outline of it raised and latched, the lever release pushrod knob on its outboard side. Right: the center gear alternate extension cover plate forward of the lower main circuit breaker panel, placard CENTER GEAR ALTERNATE EXTENSION / PULL UP AFTER MAIN GEAR ALTERNATE EXTENSION / LIFT COVER FOR ACCESS legible.
blocks.title: Alternate extension controls

blocks.content: **Mechanical checks.** If neither indicating system can be believed, the gear can be checked directly. Each main gear pushes a visual downlock button up through the top of the wing when it is down and locked, visible from the overwing windows. Viewing tubes in the forward cabin floor show the nose gear lock links, whose painted marks align when the gear is locked up or down. A viewing window in the cabin floor shows the main gear door uplock indicators, a red stud and stripe aligned when a door is closed and latched. Cargo can cover these on a freighter.

sections.title: Position indication and warning
sections.summary: The two gear indicating systems, the red light law and the gear warning horn.

blocks.content: Magnetic proximity sensors at every lock and at the main gear door latches report each leg's state to two independent indicating systems. On the DC-10 and KC-10 one system drives the pilots' lights beside the gear handle and the other drives the flight engineer's lights on their upper panel; on the MD-10 the second system feeds the gear symbols on the SD CONFIGURATION page. Each gear has a green (safe) light and a red (unsafe) light: NOSE, LEFT, RIGHT and, on center-gear airframes, CTR. A green light on either system is sufficient proof that the gear is down and locked; an unsafe indication on one system only does not require a visual check.

blocks.title: Gear position lights
rows: Gear down and locked, handle DOWN
Gear still up and locked with the handle at DOWN (it has not left its uplock)
Gear down and locked with the handle at UP (alternate extension) or with the handle pulled out of the DOWN detent
Gear up and locked, handle UP, inboard doors closed, all throttles above idle
Gear up and locked, **any** throttle retarded to idle
Gear up, an inboard main gear door not closed
Main gear door maintenance safety hook installed
Center gear isolated (CTR GEAR at UP)

blocks.content: The red light law has four terms, two of them belonging to the whole aircraft rather than to one leg: a red light comes on when that gear is in transit, when it does not agree with the handle, when an inboard door is not closed with the gear up, or when **any throttle is at idle with the gear up**. The last term surprises crews: a descent at idle thrust with the gear up shows three (or four) red lights at any altitude and any speed. That is intended. Idle thrust is the aircraft's best evidence that a landing is coming, and the lights warn of an unsafe landing configuration silently, long before the horn is allowed to sound. A single throttle at idle is enough. The lights go out as soon as all throttles are above idle again.

blocks.title: Gear warning horn
rows: Any gear not down and locked (or the handle not down) **and** any throttle at idle **and** below 215 KIAS
Silences it. The silence lasts until the condition clears, so the next approach gets a new horn. The red lights stay on.
Any gear not down and locked **and** flaps extended beyond the approach range (28.5° of flap or more)
No effect. This horn cannot be silenced.

blocks.content:
The flap term comes from a switch in the left outboard flap position transmitter, so it follows the flap surface, not the flap handle. Above 215 KIAS the throttle condition lights the red lights but does not sound the horn. A center gear isolated with the CTR GEAR switch is left out of both conditions. The horn itself and its priority among the other aural warnings are described in [Warning systems](warning-systems).

On the ground the whole chain is tested by pulling the gear handle out of its DOWN detent without raising it: every gear light turns red and the horn sounds; GEAR HORN OFF silences the horn and the red lights stay; releasing the handle back into the detent restores the greens. Each light lens can be pressed to test both of its lamps, and on the DC-10 and KC-10 a GEAR LT TEST button tests the pilots' set together. The flight engineer's lights have their own lenses and answer only the engineer's test.

blocks.alt: DC-10-30 first officer's instrument panel, landing gear area, cockpit view: GEAR handle at DOWN with its UP and DOWN legends and the LIMIT SPD placard (EXT 260 KIAS .70M, DOWN 300 KIAS .70M, RET 230 KIAS .70M), the GEAR HANDLE REL button, the four gear position lights NOSE, LEFT, CTR, RIGHT all green, the GEAR LT TEST button and the CTR GEAR isolation switch at NORM. All legends legible.
blocks.title: Gear handle and position lights (DC-10, KC-10)

blocks.content: **MD-10.** The primary lights beside the GEAR handle on the center instrument panel read NOSE, LEFT, RIGHT and CNTR. The secondary system draws each gear on the SD CONFIGURATION page: white when up and locked, green when down and locked, red when unsafe or in disagreement with the handle, and green with red together when a main gear door safety hook is installed or a locked leg disagrees with the handle. The gear aural warning is part of the central aural warning system: it sounds for any gear not down and locked with any throttle at idle below 215 KIAS (silenceable with GEAR HORN OFF on the forward pedestal) and for any gear not down and locked with the flaps in the landing range (not silenceable). On the MD-10 the aural reads the legs only, so pulling the handle out of its detent turns the gear lights red without sounding anything.

sections.title: Nosewheel steering
sections.summary: A hydromechanical servo: tiller and rudder pedals on one cable run, powered by systems 1 and 3.

blocks.content: The nose wheels are steered by a mechanically controlled, hydraulically powered system. The captain's **nose gear steering wheel** (the tiller, on the left console) and both pilots' **rudder pedals** drive one closed cable run down to the nose gear, where the two inputs are summed and fed to a **steering control valve**. The valve meters system pressure to two steering cylinders that straddle the strut. A **follow-up sector** on the strut feeds the actual wheel angle back into the same linkage, so the valve opens in proportion to the difference between commanded and actual angle and closes as the wheels arrive: a classic hydromechanical position servo.

blocks.title: Steering authority
rows: Nose strut compressed and hydraulic pressure available. Overrides the pedals.
10° either side of center at full pedal
Ground sensing mechanism in ground mode. Disconnected mechanically when the nose strut extends.

blocks.content:
The split of authority follows from what each input is for. The pedals give fine directional control on the takeoff and landing roll, where a few degrees of nose wheel are all the aircraft can use and more would make the steering twitchy; the tiller gives the large angles needed to turn a 180-ft-long aircraft at walking pace. Because both inputs share one cable run, moving the pedals on the ground also moves the tiller, and a tiller held against the pedals wins.

**Hydraulic supply.** System 1 feeds the steering valve directly. System 3 reaches it through the nose gear down line, downstream of the gear selector valve, so it is available only with the gear selected down normally. The supplies are independent: if either system 1 or system 3 fails completely, tiller steering is limited to about 25° in the direction of the failed system, while pedal steering is barely affected. Raising the alternate gear extension lever removes system 3 from the steering in the same way, leaving about 25° to the right.

**Bypass and shimmy damping.** A steering bypass valve can cross-connect the two cylinders, letting the wheels castor. It goes to bypass mechanically when the nose gear retracts (and the wheels are centerd), so the wheels cannot be steered into the side of the well. With the cylinders in their normal neutral position the fluid trapped between them acts as a **shimmy damper**, so there is no separate damper. Relief valves protect the cylinders against external torque, such as a tug turning the wheels.

**Towing.** Before the aircraft is towed or pushed, the ground crew insert a steering **bypass pin** at the nose gear. With it in, the cylinders are cross-ported, the tow bar sets the wheel angle, and the tiller and pedals steer nothing. The pin must be out before taxi. The simulation's tug and its pin are described in [Ground operations](ground-operations).

Check the tiller is centerd before trying to raise a gear handle that will not move to UP: a tiller that is not centerd can mean a nose strut that has not extended, and the nose wheel may be damaged. Do not try to move a tiller that is not centerd in flight.

blocks.alt: DC-10 captain's left console: the nose gear steering wheel (tiller) in its centerd position, with the console edge, the captain's rudder pedals partly visible below. Show the tiller's travel arc with 68° left and right marked. Cockpit view from the captain's seat.
blocks.title: Nose gear steering wheel

blocks.content: **Rollout.** After an automatic landing the autopilot's yaw channel steers the runway centerline by moving the rudder pedals, and through them the nose wheel's 10° of pedal steering. See [Automatic flight](automatic-flight).

sections.title: Brakes
sections.summary: Multi-disc brakes on every main and center wheel, two independent brake systems, accumulators and pressure indication.

blocks.content: Every main-gear and center-gear wheel has a hydraulic multi-disc brake: eight brakes on the -10, -15 and MD-10-10, ten on the airframes with a center gear. The nose wheels are unbraked. The pilots' toe pedals meter brake pressure through cables to two **dual brake control valves**, one in each main wheel well; both pilots' pedals are joined by torque tubes, so either pilot brakes all wheels. Pedal forces are very light, and a pedal can be pushed to its stop even with the system working normally: full pedal gives about 3,000 psi at the brakes, released pedals about 60 psi of return pressure.

blocks.alt: Schematic of the DC-10-30 brake and anti-skid system, ground mode. From the captain's and first officer's brake pedals, cables to the two dual brake control valves. Hydraulic system 1 feeding brake system 1 and hydraulic system 3 feeding brake system 2, each through a brake manifold with check valve and restrictor, two accumulators, the dual brake control valve, the anti-skid manifolds with one anti-skid control valve and one fluid quantity limiter per wheel, to one piston group in each of brakes 1 to 10. Parking brake valve in each anti-skid return line. Wheel speed transducer in each main and center axle wired to the anti-skid control box. Brake pressure transmitters to the captain's SYS 1 / SYS 2 brake pressure indicator. Brake temperature sensors to the F/E's BRAKE TEMP panel. System 1 and system 3 color-coded.
blocks.title: Brakes and anti-skid: schematic

blocks.content:
Each brake is a stack of discs on a torque tube bolted to the axle flange. **Rotating discs**, faced with friction pads, are keyed to the wheel; **stationary discs**, faced with wear pads, are keyed to the torque tube, with a pressure plate at one end and a back plate at the other. Pistons in the brake housing push the pressure plate, clamping the stack. The housing has two separate hydraulic circuits connecting **alternate piston cavities**: half the pistons belong to brake system 1, half to brake system 2. Self-adjusting retraction mechanisms keep the running clearance constant as the stack wears, so the fluid volume of an application does not grow with wear, and a **wear indicator pin** shows how much lining is left.

The brake is a heat sink. Its torque is the clamping force times the lining friction coefficient times the effective radius times the number of friction faces, and every foot-pound of work it does ends up as heat in the discs. Stopping a 450,000 lb aircraft from 160 kt puts about 510 million ft·lb into ten brakes, roughly 51 million ft·lb each, in under a minute. What limits a brake is therefore not its torque but its capacity to absorb that heat; see [Brake temperature and energy](#brake-temperature).

**Steel or carbon.** The DC-10s and the KC-10 have tri-metallic steel brakes; the DC-10-10's absorb less energy each than those of the later airframes, as its brake cooling charts show. The FedEx MD-10 conversions have carbon brakes. Carbon stores more heat per kilogram than steel and keeps its friction and its strength at temperatures where a steel stack starts to fade, which makes it lighter for the same energy. A steel stack holds its friction through its normal working range and loses it progressively when driven well beyond its rated energy; a second rejected takeoff on unrested brakes is exactly that case.

**Wheels and fuse plugs.** Each wheel carries three fusible plugs in its inboard half, 120° apart, which melt at 224 ±2 °C (430 ±10 °F) and let the tire deflate rather than burst when heat from the brake soaks into the wheel. A bolt-on heat shield sits between brake and wheel. A **brake inoperative jumper kit** in the right main wheel well lets maintenance block one faulty brake for dispatch under the MEL.

**Brake system 1** is powered by hydraulic system 1 and **brake system 2** by hydraulic system 3. Each provides pressure to every main and center brake independently of the other. Each system consists of a brake manifold (with a check valve and a one-way restrictor in its inlet), accumulators, a dual brake control valve, an anti-skid control valve and a **fluid quantity limiter** for each wheel, a parking brake valve in the anti-skid return line, and a pressure transmitter feeding the flight deck indicator.

The fluid quantity limiters are hydraulic fuses. Each passes the small volume an application needs; if a brake line ruptures, the limiter closes after its rated volume and stays closed until its inlet pressure falls to a few psi, so one broken hose cannot drain a hydraulic system.

**Why one system is enough.** With one system gone, each brake still has half its pistons. The brakes are sized so that half their clamping force can still drive the tires to the limit of runway friction at normal landing weights, which is why both manuals say adequate braking for all landing conditions is available with only one brake system.
The DC-10's autobrake uses the same fact: its landing mode works through brake system 1 alone, so even MAX is a half-piston brake (see [Automatic brake system](#autobrakes)).

Each brake system has its own bank of bladder **accumulators** (two per system on the DC-10 and KC-10), precharged with dry nitrogen to 1,000 ±50 psi. A check valve upstream of the bank traps their charge when the hydraulic system stops, and the manifold's restrictor lets the system refill them in a few seconds when it restarts. The accumulators do three things: they supplement normal pressure during a brake application, they maintain parking brake pressure, and they give reserve braking after a hydraulic system has failed.

The reserve is finite and predictable. Each full application moves a fixed volume of fluid into the brake pistons, and because the nitrogen expands polytropically, the pressure falls by a smaller step each time. Fully charged accumulators give about **six normal manual applications**: on a ten-brake aircraft with a dead hydraulic system, the first full application leaves roughly 2,400 psi, the sixth about 1,400 psi. Releasing and reapplying throws away a fill each time, which is why the procedures say to avoid cycling the pedals on accumulator pressure and to use one steady application.

**MD-10.** FedEx's MD-10 manual gives two accumulators per brake system and about ten manual applications from a full charge; the simulated MD-10s carry a slightly larger bank (see [Simulation notes](#simulation-notes)). The MD-10 can also back up brake system 2 with an electric auxiliary hydraulic pump on system 3.

rows: Normal: the hydraulic system is supplying the brake system.
Brakes available. With the hydraulic system off, this is accumulator pressure.
Enough pressure to hold the parking brake.
Both needles at 1,000 psi or less
No significant braking. The accumulator precharge is never displayed.

blocks.content: Each needle shows the higher of its hydraulic system pressure and its own accumulator pressure. On the DC-10 and KC-10 the two needles share one indicator on the captain's instrument panel, labeled SYS 1 (HYD SYS 1) and SYS 2 (HYD SYS 3), in psi × 1,000. On the MD-10 they are two indicators on the forward pedestal's anti-skid panel. The flight engineer checks both during their preflight and before landing.
