sections.title: Anti-skid
sections.summary: Skid detection from wheel deceleration, the pressure modulator, locked-wheel and touchdown protection, monitoring and failure behavior.

blocks.content: A fully automatic, pressure-modulating anti-skid system is installed in each brake system. Every main and center wheel has a **wheel speed transducer** in its axle, driven through the hubcap, that produces a signal at 45 cycles per wheel revolution; every brake has an **anti-skid control valve** on each brake system, a two-stage servo valve that can divert part of the applied pressure to return. An **anti-skid control box** holds one wheel card per wheel plus test and monitoring cards. The system only ever reduces pressure: it meters whatever the pedals or the autobrake ask for down to what each tire can use, wheel by wheel.

A braked tire develops friction by slipping: its surface turns a little slower than the ground passes under it. Friction rises with slip to a peak, typically at 10-20 % slip, then falls as the tire approaches a lock, where it is sliding and both its braking and its sideways grip collapse. A locked tire also flat-spots and can burst within a few hundred feet. Maximum deceleration, and directional control, both live just on the near side of that peak, and no pilot's foot can hold eight or ten wheels there at once on a changing surface.

The DC-10's system does not measure slip directly; it would need a ground speed reference it does not have. It watches each wheel's **deceleration**. An aircraft cannot decelerate at anything like 20 ft/s² (0.6 g), so a wheel that slows faster than that must be falling off the friction peak into a skid. The control box sends an immediate dump signal to that wheel's valve when the wheel decelerates at more than **20 ft/s²**, or when its speed drops by more than **8 mph** below where it was.

Releasing the brake lets the wheel spin back up within a fraction of a second. The **modulator** then decides where to reapply. It remembers how long the skid signal lasted and leaves a matching bias on the valve, so pressure comes back slightly below the level that caused the skid, then lets the bias decay slowly, so pressure creeps up until the next incipient skid. The result is a saw-tooth pressure trace hunting just below the friction peak, with only small pressure changes needed once the modulator has found the level. With the pedals held fully down the modulator, not the pilot, sets the usable pressure at each wheel.

That is why the system works best with the pedals bottomed, or at least held steady: pumping the pedals keeps resetting the level the modulator is converging on.

blocks.alt: Diagram with three stacked time traces over about 3 seconds of maximum braking: aircraft speed and one wheel's speed (the wheel dipping below aircraft speed at each incipient skid and recovering), the skid detector's dump signal, and the brake pressure at that wheel showing a saw-tooth: commanded pressure at the top, a dump at each skid, reapplication slightly below the previous skid level, slow climb to the next skid. Label the 20 ft/s² deceleration and 8 mph velocity departure triggers and the modulator reapply level.
blocks.title: Anti-skid cycle

blocks.content:
A wheel that is already stopped, on ice or after a severe skid, cannot show the deceleration the skid detector looks for. The **locked-wheel detector** covers that case by comparing each wheel with its partner on the other side of the aircraft. When the paired wheel across the aircraft is turning faster than **29 mph**, the locked-wheel arming circuit is energized, and any wheel turning slower than **11 mph** has its brake pressure dumped.

The arming circuit is also energized in the air, through the ground sensing switches. That is **touchdown protection**: with the anti-skid armed after the gear is down, the aft main wheels' brakes are held released, so the aircraft cannot be landed on locked wheels even with the pedals depressed. The aft wheels spin up first at touchdown, and through the pairing logic that protects the forward wheels too. Braking can start as soon as the wheels spin up; the system does not wait for the ground shift. On the ground, a shift from ground to flight mode releases the aft wheels at low speed and leaves normal braking on the forward wheels.

Below about **10 kt** (main gear) and **3-4 kt** (center gear) the anti-skid becomes inactive and the brakes revert to manual power braking, with the ANTI-SKID FAIL lights staying out. Taxi braking and the last few knots of every stop are unmodulated, and a hard stop from that speed is felt as a lurch: the reason the procedures disconnect an autobrake above about 10 kt.

Electrical power is removed from the anti-skid control box with the gear retracted; the box comes alive when the gear is extended, and its integrity is proved by a test, not assumed.

Four amber **ANTI-SKID FAIL** lights, one per fore-and-aft wheel pair, are on the pilots' overhead annunciator panel: L OUTBD, L INBD, R INBD, R OUTBD, plus CTR on the airframes with a center gear. On most airframes repeater legends are also on the flight engineer's panel. The **ANTI-SKID** switch (ARM / OFF) and the **TEST** button are on the overhead panel.

blocks.title: ANTI-SKID FAIL lights
rows: Both AC power supplies to the control boxes lost
Either parking brake valve fails to open with the parking brake released
Parking brake released: the valves take about half a second to open
All on for about 0.5 s, then out
A fault detected in one wheel circuit (by the self-test or the monitor)
The light for that wheel pair

blocks.content:
The parking brake valves are monitored only while the parking brake is released: setting the brake lights nothing, but releasing it flashes every FAIL light for the half second the valve motors take to open, and a valve that fails to open leaves them all on. A single FAIL light does not say which component has failed, only that a fault exists in that wheel pair.

**The test.** With the ANTI-SKID switch at ARM and the gear handle down, pushing TEST injects a false skid signal into every wheel card and checks each valve's response; all FAIL lights come on while it is held and must all go out when it is released. A light that fails to come on, or stays on, marks a fault in one or both wheels of that pair. The test works with the parking brake on or off and at taxi speeds below 30 kt. In the simulation the TEST button is not operative; see [Simulation notes](#simulation-notes).

blocks.alt: DC-10-30 overhead panel, anti-skid area: the ANTI-SKID switch at ARM with its OFF position marked, the TEST button, and on the overhead annunciator panel the five amber legends ANTI-SKID L OUTBD FAIL, L INBD FAIL, R INBD FAIL, R OUTBD FAIL and CTR FAIL, plus PARK BRAKE ON and AUTO BRAKE, all unlit. Legends legible.
blocks.title: Anti-skid controls and FAIL lights (DC-10, KC-10)

blocks.content: **MD-10.** The ANTI-SKID switch (ARM / OFF) and TEST button are on the forward pedestal's anti-skid panel, beside the brake pressure indicators. Anti-skid faults appear as EIS alerts with the CONFIG cue: **ANTI-SKID FAIL** (the whole system, level 2), **ANTI-SKID L FAIL**, **ANTI-SKID R FAIL** and, on the -30, **ANTI-SKID C FAIL** (protection lost on wheels of that gear, level 2), and **ANTI-SKID OFF** (switch at OFF, level 1). The alerts are monitored with the gear handle down, and the half-second valve transition on a parking brake release raises nothing.

With the anti-skid off or failed, the brakes become **manual power brakes**: pressure is proportional to pedal deflection, all the way to locking the wheels. Skids are hard to feel through the pedals. Build pedal pressure slowly until the aircraft is decelerating moderately, get the spoilers out straight away, use reverse thrust, and spread the stop over most of the runway. Should a skid develop while system pressure is normal, let the brakes off and reapply them the same way; on accumulator pressure alone, do not pump the pedals. Excessive pedal can blow tires and, on the center-gear airframes, overload the center gear's lower drag link.

The landing distance increases significantly, and the maximum landing weight falls (411,000 lb on the KC-10 against 436,000 lb). FedEx does not dispatch with the anti-skid inoperative. The autobrake cannot be armed without the anti-skid. The procedures are under ANTI-SKID FAIL LT(S) ON in [Abnormal procedures](abnormal-procedures); figures are in [Limitations](limitations).

With the ANTI-SKID switch at OFF braking is proportional to pedal pressure and there is no skid or locked-wheel protection. Leave the switch at ARM with a FAIL light on unless the procedure says otherwise: protection may remain on the wheels that are not affected.

sections.title: Automatic brake system
sections.summary: Landing and takeoff modes, arming and activation, the 45 kt and 60 kt thresholds, disarming and the rejected takeoff.

blocks.content:
The automatic brake system (**ABS**) applies the brakes for the crew after landing and in a rejected takeoff. It was a retrofit kit on the real fleet, installed on some DC-10-30s only; in this simulation every DC-10 variant has it. The KC-10 has no autobrake.

The system consists of the AUTO BRAKE panel on the pedestal, an amber **ABS** light on each side of the glareshield, an amber **AUTO BRAKE** light on the overhead annunciator panel, an auto brake control unit, and two manifolds. The **landing manifold** feeds brake system 1 through a metered servo valve, so the control unit can regulate its pressure; the **takeoff manifold** feeds both brake systems through dual shuttle valves at full pressure, with no regulation. The control unit takes discrete inputs from the ground spoilers, the throttles (levers 1 and 3), all four brake pedals, the flap handle and the gear handle, plus wheel spin-up, deceleration from the flight guidance linear accelerometer, and the anti-skid's status.

blocks.alt: DC-10-30 pedestal AUTO BRAKE panel close-up: the AUTO BRAKE deceleration selector with detents T.O., OFF, MIN, MED, MAX (a LAND bracket over MIN, MED and MAX), selector at OFF; the ARM-DISARM switch at DISARM. Inset: one glareshield ABS light and the overhead AUTO BRAKE annunciator, both unlit. Legends legible.
blocks.title: AUTO BRAKE panel and lights
AUTO BRAKE controls
rows: Takeoff mode: maximum pressure from both brake systems when the ground spoilers deploy in a rejected takeoff with the ABS armed.
Landing mode: a deceleration level, applied from brake system 1 only once the spoilers deploy after touchdown with the ABS armed.
Arms the system. Held in ARM by a magnet, which lets go on any disarm: the switch drops to DISARM by itself.

blocks.content: Selecting a detent does nothing on its own: the ARM-DISARM switch is the arming action, and it stays up only while every arming condition is met. If a condition is missing the switch simply will not stay in ARM; nothing lights. The selector itself never moves by itself: the crew turn it to OFF after takeoff and after landing.

**Arming.** With the gear handle down, select MIN, MED or MAX and move the ARM-DISARM switch to ARM. The system arms only if it is serviceable, the anti-skid is armed and working, and the linear accelerometer is valid. The Before Landing check confirms the ABS and AUTO BRAKE lights are out, the selector is at the planned level and the switch is at ARM.

**Activation.** Automatic braking starts when the ground spoilers deploy, automatically or by hand, with throttles 1 and 3 retarded and the brake pedals released. In the simulation the activation also waits for the main wheels to reach **45 kt** of wheel speed, so spoilers deployed during a taxi never start it; once started, braking continues through 45 kt to the stop. After deployment the system waits about **4 seconds** in MIN or MED, and about **2 seconds** in MAX, so that the nose wheel is on the runway before the brakes come on.

blocks.title: Landing mode levels
rows: System 1 through the metered servo valve
System 1 through the metered servo valve
Open loop: full brake system 1 pressure, limited only by the anti-skid
About 10 ft/s² on a dry runway, more or less with conditions

blocks.content:
In MIN and MED the control unit compares the measured deceleration with the selected level and trims brake pressure to hold it constant, whatever the reverse thrust, spoilers and wind are contributing. More reverse means less brake, and less brake heat. MAX does not regulate: it applies full brake system 1 pressure and lets the anti-skid limit it. Because the landing mode uses brake system 1 alone, MAX is half of each brake's pistons; it is a firm stop, but softer than both pilots' pedals bottomed.

A constant deceleration gives a stopping distance of V²/2a from brake application. FedEx's own example, MED at 148 kt, gives 5,740 ft; the table below shows the same relation at other speeds, dry, with no slope. These figures explain the levels; they are not performance data, which are in [Mission planning](mission-planning).

blocks.title: Approximate distance from brake application to stop, dry runway

blocks.content: **On the runway.** Stowing the ground spoilers releases the brakes **without** disarming the system: the ABS lights stay out and braking returns if the spoilers are redeployed (after the activation delay, and in the simulation only above 45 kt). Raising the flaps to less than 30° above 60 kt disarms the landing mode and lights the ABS lights; below 60 kt braking continues whatever the flaps. To avoid an abrupt stop, take over above the anti-skid's cutout of about 10 kt: press the pedals gradually and hold them until the ARM-DISARM switch drops and the ABS lights come on, then brake to a smooth stop. On a CAT III approach FedEx requires the autobrakes when they are available.

children.title: Takeoff mode and the rejected takeoff

blocks.content:
**Arming.** Select T.O. and move the ARM-DISARM switch to ARM. In addition to the general conditions, the ground spoilers must be armed and the flaps set to less than 30°. Takeoff power does not disarm it: in takeoff mode the pedal and throttle takeovers count only once automatic braking has actually started, so the arm survives the throttles being advanced for takeoff and any braking during taxi.

**The rejected takeoff.** The crew close the throttles; the armed automatic ground spoilers deploy as the throttles reach idle (or the crew deploy them by hand); the ABS activates **immediately**, with no delay, and applies maximum pressure from **both** brake systems, limited only by the anti-skid. That is the maximum braking the aircraft has: every piston of every brake.

The **60 kt split** decides which mode the system runs. An abort initiated above 60 kt is a full dual-system stop. Initiated at or below 60 kt, the ABS reverts to landing mode operation and applies MIN braking, through brake system 1, after the landing mode's delay. The test is taken at the moment of initiation and latched: an abort begun at 80 kt stays a maximum-effort stop as the aircraft slows through 60 kt. In the simulation an abort below 45 kt of wheel speed does not start the autobrake at all; brake with the pedals.

Once braking has started, the crew can take over by pressing the pedals beyond 40 % of their travel or by advancing throttle 1 or 3. The FedEx Rejected Takeoff procedure calls for **maximum manual anti-skid braking** regardless; the autobrake disarms as soon as the pedals pass 40 %, and its value is in the seconds before the pilot's feet arrive.

**A normal takeoff.** The T.O. arm holds through liftoff. Moving the gear handle to UP disarms the system: the switch drops without lighting the ABS lights. The selector stays at T.O. until the After Takeoff checklist turns it to OFF.

rows: Either pilot presses a brake pedal beyond about 40 % of travel
Landing mode at any time; takeoff mode once braking
Throttle 1 or 3 advanced beyond 15° on the ground (throttle 2 is not wired)
Landing mode at any time; takeoff mode once braking
ARM-DISARM switch moved to DISARM with the selector at T.O. or a LAND detent
Arm again with the gear down
ABS malfunction (control unit, or the linear accelerometer)
Selector to OFF and back to a detent, then ARM (if the fault has cleared)

blocks.content:
Every disarm drops the magnetically held ARM-DISARM switch to DISARM. A malfunction latches: putting the switch back to ARM does nothing until the selector has been cycled through OFF, which is the system's way of making the crew acknowledge the fault. A pilot takeover does not latch; the switch alone rearms. Stowing the spoilers is not on the list. Throttle 1 or 3 left above 15° does not disarm an arm made at approach power; it only withholds the brakes until the throttles are retarded.

An armed autobrake needs the anti-skid. With the ANTI-SKID switch at OFF, a failed anti-skid control box on brake system 1, or the AUTOBRAKE SYS breaker open, the ARM-DISARM switch will not stay in ARM.

sections.title: Parking brake
sections.summary: Pawls that hold the pedals applied, valves that trap the pressure, and automatic repressurization.

blocks.content: The parking brake combines three separate mechanisms:

items: **The pawls.** The PARK BRAKE handle on the left side of the center pedestal turns a torque tube carrying locking pawls. Setting the brake is a gesture: apply full braking with the toe pedals, pull the handle fully aft, then release the pedals. As the feet come off, the pawls catch the brake cable arms in the applied position and hold both dual brake control valves open.

**The parking brake valves.** The handle also operates a switch that drives a motorized valve in each brake system's anti-skid return line to CLOSED, so brake pressure cannot leak back through the anti-skid valves. The valves are on AC bus 2 and take about half a second to travel. If their power is lost they stay where they are: a set brake stays set.

**The trapped pressure.** The fluid shut in behind the closed valves, backed by the accumulators, keeps the brakes applied. With the hydraulic systems shut down the pressure bleeds away slowly, and after several hours there may be none at the brakes. While the brake pressure indicators show pressure, the brakes have it; the white band is enough to hold the aircraft.

blocks.content:
Because the pawls hold the control valves applied, a parking brake that has bled down is **repressurized automatically** as soon as either hydraulic system is pressurized again, without touching the handle. Two amber lights show that the handle is set: PARK on the pedestal and PARK BRAKE ON on the overhead annunciator panel (on the MD-10, the PARK light and a PARK BRAKE ON alert).

On the aircraft the parking brake is released by pressing the toe pedals fully and letting them up, which lets the spring-loaded pawls fall clear; the valves then reopen and every ANTI-SKID FAIL light flashes for the half second they take. In the simulation the parking brake is released by moving the handle forward, or with the simulator's parking brake key.

The takeoff warning (an intermittent horn on the DC-10 and KC-10, a tone and a voice on the MD-10) sounds if throttle 1 or 2 is advanced for takeoff with the ground shift in ground mode and the parking brake not released, whether because the pawls are still in or because pressure is still trapped behind a closed valve.

Do not set the parking brake on hot brakes (brake temperature in the caution or danger zone, or an OVHT light on). Clamping a very hot stack can fuse its discs and holds the heat against the wheel. Chock the wheels instead.

blocks.alt: DC-10-30 center pedestal, left side: the PARK BRAKE handle in the set (aft) position, the amber PARK light illuminated beside it, and the GEAR HORN OFF button. Legends legible.
blocks.title: Parking brake handle and PARK light

sections.title: Brake temperature and brake energy
sections.summary: Brake temperature monitoring, the energy zones, fuse plugs and cooling.

blocks.content: A temperature sensor in each brake housing reports the heat-sink temperature. On the DC-10 and KC-10 the readings go to the flight engineer's BRAKE TEMP panel; on the MD-10 they are shown on the SD CONFIGURATION page. The real fleets had brake temperature monitoring on some aircraft only; every aircraft in this manual has it.

The panel, on the flight engineer's upper panel, has one **OVHT** switch-light per brake, laid out like the gear in plan view (1 and 2 on the left truck's forward axle, 3 and 4 on the right truck's forward axle, 5 to 8 on the aft axles, 9 and 10 on the center gear), a **BRAKE TEMP** indicator reading °C × 100 from 0 to 5, a **DIFF TEMP** light and a **TEST** button.

items: With no switch-light pressed the indicator shows the **hottest** brake.
Pressing one OVHT switch-light shows that brake's temperature. Pressing two or more at once gives an erroneous reading.
An OVHT light comes on when its brake reaches **400 °C**.
DIFF TEMP comes on when any brake is far above or far below the average of the others. A hot brake suggests one that is dragging; a cold one suggests one that is not working.
Holding TEST lights every OVHT light and DIFF TEMP and puts the needle in the white band; releasing it returns the panel to its pretest indication.

blocks.alt: DC-10-30 flight engineer's upper panel, BRAKE TEMP section: ten OVHT switch-lights numbered 1 to 10 in the plan-view layout (1 2 and 3 4 forward, 5 6 and 7 8 aft, 9 10 center), the round BRAKE TEMP indicator scaled 0 to 5 in °C × 100 with its white test band, the amber DIFF TEMP light and the TEST button. One OVHT light illuminated, needle near 4. Legends legible.
blocks.title: BRAKE TEMP panel (flight engineer)

blocks.content: The SD CONFIGURATION page shows each brake's temperature as white digits in °C beside its wheel. A brake above 400 °C turns its digits amber and boxes them, and raises the **BRAKE OVERHEAT** alert (level 2). A large difference between brakes raises **BRAKE DIFF TEMP** (level 1). A blank reading means no data for that brake. In the simulation the same page also shows each tire's pressure; see [Wheels and tires](#tires-and-wheels).

blocks.alt: MD-10-30 System Display, CONFIGURATION page: plan view of the aircraft from behind with control surface boxes, flap and slat indications, stabilizer trim, and the gear at the bottom: nose gear, both four-wheel main trucks and the two-wheel center gear, each wheel outline with its tire pressure inside and its brake temperature in °C beside it. Gear symbols green (down and locked). One brake reading boxed in amber above 400 °C. Labels legible.
blocks.title: SD CONFIGURATION page (MD-10)

blocks.content:
A stop converts the aircraft's kinetic energy, ½mv², into heat. Thrust at idle adds to it; aerodynamic drag, the spoilers and reverse thrust take some away, and the brake energy charts conservatively ignore reverse thrust. The energy grows with the square of speed: a 450,000 lb aircraft carries about 510 million ft·lb at 160 kt, and 800 million at 200 kt. Spread over ten brakes, a maximum-weight abort near V1 asks each one to absorb tens of millions of foot-pounds in under a minute.

The KC-10 manual defines three zones, read from the brake temperature indication or, with the indication inoperative, from the brake energy chart:

blocks.title: Brake temperature and energy zones (KC-10 T.O.)
rows: Check the cooling time before the next takeoff.
400 °C or more, or an OVHT light on
Do not set the parking brake. Fuse plugs may melt. Maintenance inspection before the next flight.
Clear the runway, do not set the parking brake, prepare to evacuate. Fire is possible within 30 minutes.

blocks.content:
**Where the heat goes.** The heat is made at the friction faces and then spreads: through the stack to the temperature sensor in the housing, and through the heat shield into the wheel. That is why brake temperatures can keep rising for **15 to 25 minutes** after the aircraft stops, and why the fuse plugs, which melt at 224 °C in the wheel, let go minutes later rather than during the stop: a brake held at 400 °C for more than five minutes may melt them. A tire deflated by its fuse plugs after a high-energy stop is the system working, not failing.

**Cooling.** Brakes cool slowly when parked, in the order of an hour and a half to cool most of the way from a heavy stop, and faster in moving air. The FedEx cooling charts give the minimum ground time before the next takeoff from weight, altitude and brakes-on speed (for example, a DC-10-30 at 450,000 lb at sea level needs about 149 minutes after a maximum-effort stop from 160 kt, and a stop from 180 kt is in the fuse plug melt zone), with 1.4 minutes added for every 6 °C above 10 °C. In flight, extending the gear cools a hot brake far faster than the ram-air duct in the closed wheel well.

A second rejected takeoff without adequate cooling may cause brake failure and an inability to stop; published takeoff weight limits are then invalid. After a high-energy stop, approach the tires only from the front or rear, and not before 45 minutes. See the REJECTED TAKEOFF and ABNORMAL BRAKE procedures in [Emergency procedures](emergency-procedures) and [Abnormal procedures](abnormal-procedures), and the brake limits in [Limitations](limitations).

sections.title: Wheels and tires
sections.summary: Over-pressure and over-temperature protection, inflation, tire speed and hydroplaning.

blocks.content:
The wheels are split forged aluminum halves bolted together around a tubeless tire, interchangeable among all main and center positions. Each wheel, nose wheels included, has a **frangible disk** that releases the tire's pressure at 350 ±5 psi so that over-inflation can never burst a tire. Each main and center wheel also has the three **fuse plugs** described under [Brake temperature](#brake-energy), which release it at 224 °C.

Tire pressure distribution matters, especially at heavy weights. An underinflated tire flexes more and heats much faster during taxi, and the two tires on an axle must be inflated to specification so that one does not carry more than its share of the load: FedEx limits the difference between the two tires on an axle to 15 psi. Minimum inflation pressures depend on weight and ambient temperature and are in the maintenance manual and [Limitations](limitations).

**Tire speed.** The tires are rated to a maximum ground speed: 195 kt on the FedEx DC-10-10 and 204 kt on the DC-10-30 and KC-10. The limit matters for high-altitude, hot-day and flapless takeoffs and landings.

**Wet runways and hydroplaning.** On a dry runway tire wear does not change braking friction. On a wet runway braking falls to roughly a third of its dry value, and a badly worn tire is much worse. On standing water a rolling tire can ride up on a wedge of water and lose contact entirely: dynamic hydroplaning begins at about 9√p kt, where p is the tire pressure in psi (about 125 kt for a 200 psi main tire). A hydroplaning wheel spins down; the locked-wheel protection releases its brake as long as its partner across the aircraft is still turning, but it cannot help if both are on water.

**Tire pressure indication (MD-10).** The FedEx MD-10 has no tire pressure indication in the cockpit; tire failures are found from vibration and outside cues. The simulated SD CONFIGURATION page, drawn after the MD-11's, does show each tire's pressure inside its wheel outline, and a tire well below its nominal pressure, or one differing markedly from its axle partner, turns amber.

**Tire failure.** A failed tire shows as vibration, a pull toward the failed side and reduced braking on that wheel; its axle partner takes the load. FedEx does not recommend rejecting a takeoff for a tire failure above V1 minus 20 kt. After a tire failure on takeoff, leave the gear down, reduce weight, turn the autobrake selector OFF and plan a flaps 35 landing to reduce the risk of flap damage from debris. See TIRE FAILURE DURING TAKEOFF ROLL in [Abnormal procedures](abnormal-procedures).

sections.title: Controls and indicators
sections.summary: Every landing gear, brake and steering control, panel by panel.

blocks.content: Most controls are common to the three flight decks: the rudder pedals and toe brakes, the steering tiller on the captain's console, the parking brake handle on the pedestal and the alternate gear extension lever in the floor. The gear handle, the gear lights, the anti-skid controls and the brake indications are where each deck puts them: the first officer's panel, the overhead and the flight engineer's panel on the DC-10 and KC-10, the center instrument panel, the forward pedestal and the System Display on the MD-10.

rows: Nosewheel steering up to 10° either side on the ground, through the ground sensing mechanism.
Meter brake pressure in both brake systems through the dual brake control valves; full pedal about 3,000 psi. Pressing either pedal beyond 40 % of travel takes over from the autobrake (DC-10).
Nose gear steering wheel (tiller), captain's left console
Nosewheel steering up to 68° either side; overrides the pedals. Springs back to center when released.
PARK BRAKE handle, left side of the center pedestal
Set: apply full toe brakes, pull the handle aft, release the pedals. Closes the parking brake valves and holds the brakes applied.
The PARK BRAKE handle is set.
Silences the gear warning horn for the throttle condition. No effect on the flap condition or on the red lights.
Alternate gear extension lever, floor right of the pedestal (under a cover)

Releases the main gear door latches and the nose gear lock links, puts the selector valve to bypass, removes system 3 from the steering, unlocks the outboard ailerons. The main and nose gear free-fall. Does not release the center gear.
Restores system 3 to the gear and steering. Retracts the gear if the handle is at UP. Restrain the lever: it is preloaded.
CENTER GEAR ALTERNATE EXTENSION handle, floor forward of the lower main circuit breaker panel (-30, -40, KC-10, MD-10-30)
Releases the center gear after the main gear has been extended by the alternate lever. Also checks the center gear up and locked. Not operable in the simulation.

blocks.title: First officer's instrument panel
rows: Positions the landing gear selector valve. Pull aft out of the detent to move it. Held at DOWN on the ground by the anti-retraction lock.
Pulled out of DOWN, not raised
Signals handle not down: every gear light red and the horn (the ground test).
Gear position lights: NOSE, LEFT, RIGHT, CTR (CTR on -30, -40, KC-10)
That gear is down and locked.
That gear is in transit, disagrees with the handle, or (all lights) any throttle is at idle or an inboard door is open with the gear up.
Gear up and locked, doors closed, throttles above idle; or the center gear isolated.
Tests both lamps of that light.
Tests the pilots' gear lights together.
Moves the anti-retraction lock clear so the handle can be raised if the ground sensing mechanism is stuck in ground mode. Never on the ground. A leg carrying weight still cannot retract.
CTR GEAR isolation switch (-30, -40, KC-10), with lock pin
Center gear extends and retracts with the GEAR handle.
Center gear driven up and kept retracted whatever the handle; its lights and warning input inhibited.

blocks.title: Captain's panel, glareshield and overhead
rows: Brake pressure indicator, captain's instrument panel
Pressure in each brake system. Above the red band: brakes available. White band: enough to hold the parking brake.
ABS lights (amber), glareshield, one each side (DC-10)
The autobrake has been disarmed by a malfunction or by a pilot takeover (pedals, throttle 1 or 3, or the ARM-DISARM switch). Not lit by turning the selector to OFF.
Anti-skid off: full manual control of brake pressure, all ANTI-SKID FAIL lights on. The autobrake cannot be armed.
ANTI-SKID FAIL lights (amber), overhead annunciator panel: L OUTBD, L INBD, R INBD, R OUTBD, CTR
Switch OFF, power to the control boxes lost, or a parking brake valve not open (a 0.5 s flash on every parking brake release is normal).
A fault in that wheel pair.
PARK BRAKE ON light (amber), overhead annunciator panel
The PARK BRAKE handle is set.
AUTO BRAKE light (amber), overhead annunciator panel (DC-10)
Autobrake malfunction. The system has disarmed; MASTER CAUTION comes on with it.
Selects the takeoff mode, off, or a landing mode level. Turned by hand only; it never returns to OFF by itself.
Arms the selected mode. Magnetically held in ARM; drops to DISARM on any disarm or if an arming condition is missing.

blocks.content: The full logic is in [Automatic brake system](#autobrakes). The simulator's own autobrake key commands turn this selector (low, medium and high go to MIN, MED and MAX) and the autobrake disarm command drops the ARM-DISARM switch, exactly as a hand would.

rows: Gear position lights: NOSE, LEFT, RIGHT, CTR
The second indicating system: same law as the pilots' lights. Each lens tests only its own lamps.
OVHT switch-lights 1 to 8 (1 to 10 with center gear)
That brake is at 400 °C or more.
The BRAKE TEMP indicator shows that brake. Do not press two at once: the reading is wrong.
The hottest brake, or the selected one.
A brake far hotter (dragging) or colder (not working) than the rest.
All OVHT lights and DIFF TEMP on; needle in the white band.
Same conditions as the pilots' overhead legends.

blocks.title: Center instrument panel and forward pedestal
rows: As on the DC-10: pull aft out of the detent to move it; held at DOWN on the ground by the anti-retraction lock.
GEAR lights: NOSE, LEFT, RIGHT, CTR (CTR on the -30)
Down and locked / unsafe or disagreeing with the handle / up and locked with the handle up.
Releases the anti-retraction lock if the ground sensing mechanism malfunctions.
Keeps the center gear retracted whatever the handle. Not operable in the simulation: the center gear always follows the handle.
GEAR HORN OFF button, forward pedestal
Silences the gear aural warning for the throttle condition.

blocks.title: Forward pedestal anti-skid panel and glareshield
rows: As on the DC-10. OFF raises the ANTI-SKID OFF alert.
BRAKE HYD PRESS indicators SYS 1 (HYD SYS 1), SYS 2 (HYD SYS 3)
The higher of each hydraulic system's pressure and its brake accumulator's.
The PARK BRAKE handle is set. The PARK BRAKE ON alert appears on the EAD.

blocks.content: Some FedEx MD-10-30s had an automatic brake system; the simulated MD-10s do not. The AUTO BRAKE selector and ARM switch drawn on the forward pedestal are inoperative, the glareshield ABS DISARM lights are blank, and no AUTO BRAKE alert is ever raised.

blocks.title: Landing gear and brake alerts (MD-10)
rows: Anti-skid protection lost on one or more wheels of that main gear.
Anti-skid protection lost on the center gear wheels.
The ANTI-SKID switch is at OFF.
A significant difference between brake temperatures.

blocks.alt: MD-10-30 forward pedestal: the ANTI-SKID panel with the ANTI-SKID ARM/OFF switch (guarded at ARM), the TEST button, the two BRAKE HYD PRESS indicators SYS 1 (HYD SYS 1) and SYS 2 (HYD SYS 3) at 3,000 psi, the AUX HYD PUMP switchlight, the AUTO BRAKE selector and ARM-DISARM switch, and the PARK BRAKE handle with the amber PARK light. Legends legible.
blocks.title: Forward pedestal brake controls (MD-10)

sections.title: Operation
sections.summary: The gear, brakes and steering through a flight, and how they interact with the other systems.

blocks.content: This section follows one flight from the system's point of view. The checklists themselves, with their crew assignments, are in [Normal procedures](normal-procedures).

Before any hydraulic system is pressurized, the gear handle must be DOWN and in its detent and the main gear doors closed (or maintenance cleared): pressurizing system 3 with a handle that is not down, or with doors open, can move the gear or the doors. If both the red and green lights of a main gear are on together, a door safety hook is installed; consult maintenance before applying hydraulic power. On the -30, -40 and KC-10 the CTR GEAR switch is checked at NORM. The parking brake is checked; if it is set, it is not released until the aircraft is chocked or attached to a tug.

On the DC-10-30 the center gear must be free to move as the struts compress and extend during loading and fueling, so it is never chocked, and FedEx does not load or fuel a -30 with the parking brake set.

items: **Gear lights and warning.** Handle DOWN and in, three or four green. Press GEAR LT TEST or the lenses. Pull the handle out of the DOWN detent without raising it: all lights red and the horn sounds (throttles at idle). GEAR HORN OFF silences the horn. Release the handle: greens return.

**Brakes.** With the aircraft chocked, set the parking brake and check the PARK and PARK BRAKE ON lights. Release it and watch all ANTI-SKID FAIL lights flash for about half a second as the parking brake valves open. Set or release as required and check both brake pressures in the white band.
**Anti-skid.** ANTI-SKID switch ARM. Its integrity is proved after the gear is next extended.
**Brake temperature** (flight engineer, DC-10 and KC-10). Hold TEST: all OVHT lights and DIFF TEMP on, needle in the white band; release, everything returns to the pretest indication.
**Exterior.** Gear pins and the steering bypass pin removed and stowed, tires and brake wear pins checked, struts showing normal extension, no hydraulic leaks at the brakes or the steering cylinders.

blocks.content:
Use the tiller for turns and the rudder pedals for small corrections on straight segments; the pedals' 10° of steering is too little for a turn onto a taxiway, and a tiller held against the pedals wins. Turn with gentle tiller inputs: the nose wheels are well ahead of the main gear, and the main trucks track inside the nose wheel's path. Taxi braking is unmodulated by the anti-skid below about 10 kt, so brake smoothly; the light pedal forces make it easy to over-brake.

Brakes heat up in a long taxi, more so at heavy weight and with frequent braking, and a dragging brake shows as a rising temperature and a DIFF TEMP light long before it can be felt. On the DC-10 and KC-10 the flight engineer checks the BRAKE TEMP indication before takeoff; on the MD-10 the CONFIG page shows it.

Before takeoff the anti-skid is armed, the parking brake released (otherwise a takeoff throttle sounds the takeoff warning) and, on the DC-10 if the autobrake is used, the selector at T.O. and the switch at ARM with the spoilers armed.

At rotation the nose strut extends and the ground sensing mechanism goes to flight mode: rudder pedal steering disconnects, the anti-retraction lock withdraws from the gear handle, and the ground control relays switch the engines to flight idle and the other systems to their flight logic. With a positive rate of climb, select the gear UP (230 KIAS / Mach 0.70 maximum for retraction). On the DC-10 the gear handle moving to UP disarms a T.O. autobrake without lighting anything; the After Takeoff checklist then turns the selector to OFF. The red lights go out when every leg is up and locked and the inboard doors are closed, as long as no throttle is at idle.

In descent, red gear lights with the throttles at idle and the gear up are normal; they go out as soon as a throttle is advanced. Below 215 KIAS the same condition also sounds the horn, which GEAR HORN OFF silences.

Select the gear DOWN at or below 260 KIAS (Mach 0.70); with it down the limit is 300 KIAS. The gear takes about 20 seconds to show three or four green. With the gear down, the anti-skid control box is powered and the Before Landing checklist confirms it: on the DC-10 and KC-10 the anti-skid test, on the MD-10 the absence of anti-skid alerts. On the DC-10, set the autobrake level and arm it, and check the ABS and AUTO BRAKE lights out.

**Touchdown.** Keep your feet off the brakes. The main wheels spin up; the automatic ground spoilers deploy; on the DC-10 the armed autobrake waits its 2 or 4 seconds for the nose wheel and then brakes; the anti-skid modulates every wheel. As the nose strut compresses the ground shift returns to ground mode: the engines return to ground idle after a short hold that lets reverse thrust spool from flight idle, and the engine 2 reverser interlock releases. Lower the nose promptly: it puts weight on the main gear and brings pedal steering in.

With manual braking, apply firm, steady pedal pressure and let the anti-skid do the modulating. With the autobrake, take over above about 10 kt by pressing the pedals smoothly past 40 % until the ARM-DISARM switch drops and the ABS lights come on, then brake to a stop and taxi clear.

Clear of the runway the autobrake selector goes to OFF (DC-10) and the flight engineer checks the brake temperatures, the OVHT and DIFF TEMP lights. Remember that brake temperatures may keep rising for 15 to 25 minutes after the stop. If brake temperature is in the caution or danger zone, do not set the parking brake: stop where the aircraft can be chocked, and follow ABNORMAL BRAKE. The parking brake is set at the gate once the aircraft has stopped; it holds on accumulator pressure after the engines are shut down and repressurizes automatically when hydraulic power returns.

rows: System 3 powers the gear; systems 1 and 3 the brakes and steering. Gear retraction and the brakes' refill are demands on those systems. The reversible motor pumps back up system 3.
The anti-skid boxes need AC buses 1 and 3; the gear warning DC bus 2; the center gear control DC bus 1; the autobrake DC bus 3 (DC-10); the parking brake valves AC bus 2.

Ground spoiler deployment is the autobrake's activation signal and the automatic ground spoilers and the autobrake share the 45 kt wheel-speed floor. The alternate gear extension lever also unlocks the outboard ailerons.

The ground shift selects flight or ground idle and controls the engine 2 in-flight reverse interlock and the engine failure detector. Throttles 1 and 3 are autobrake takeover inputs; any throttle at idle feeds the gear warning.
Sounds the gear warning and the takeoff warning, including the parking brake term.
After an automatic landing the yaw channel steers the rollout through the rudder pedals and the nose wheel.
The wing and antenna anti-ice valves are held closed while the ground shift is in ground mode.

sections.title: Failures and non-normal operation
sections.summary: What fails, how it shows, and which procedure handles it.

blocks.content: The gear's failures fall into three groups: a leg that will not go where the handle sends it, a handle that cannot be moved, and losses of braking, anti-skid or steering. The tables give the effect, the indications and the crew response; the checklists are in [Emergency procedures](emergency-procedures) and [Abnormal procedures](abnormal-procedures), under the names shown in capitals.

rows: Leg fails to extend (uplock will not release)
Its red light on from the moment the handle reaches DOWN, no green; gear horn when a throttle is at idle or the flaps reach landing.
GEAR UNSAFE LT(S) ON WITH GEAR HANDLE DOWN: confirm on both panels, alternate extension. If it still will not come down, prepare for LANDING WITH ABNORMAL LANDING GEAR CONFIGURATION.
The leg reaches down but its brace is not locked; it can collapse when the aircraft lands on it.
Red stays on, no green, on one or both panels.
Confirm the handle fully DOWN and in. A green on either panel is a locked gear. Otherwise alternate extension at 230 KIAS or below, then recycle per the checklist; check the mechanical indicators.
Leg unsafe with the handle UP
Either the leg is on its up stop but not locked, or its uplock sensor is wrong.
Its red light stays on with the handle UP and the throttles above idle.
GEAR UNSAFE LT(S) ON WITH GEAR HANDLE UP: compare both panels; if confirmed, gear down and limit the speed to 260 KIAS, or continue if the gear is seen to be up and locked.
Gear handle will not move to UP
Ground sensing mechanism stuck in ground mode, or trim cylinder system failed.
Handle held at DOWN after takeoff. With the ground sensing stuck, the flight-mode systems stay in ground mode (see below).
GEAR HANDLE WILL NOT MOVE TO UP POSITION: check the tiller centerd, 230 KIAS or below, hold GEAR HANDLE REL and select UP. If it is the trim interlock, leave the gear down (300 KIAS maximum).
Ground sensing mechanism stays in ground mode after takeoff
The ground control relays stay in ground mode.

Takeoff warning armed, stall warning and stick shakers inhibited, engine 2 in-flight reverse interlock released, engine failure detector armed, wing and antenna anti-ice inoperative, engines held at ground idle.
Open the ground sensing breakers (L and R GND SENS) to restore flight mode; reset them just before touchdown, or the engines stay at flight idle and the engine 2 reverser is limited.
Gear handle will not move to DOWN
The handle is jammed at UP.

GEAR HANDLE WILL NOT MOVE TO DOWN POSITION: 230 KIAS or below, alternate extension lever raised and latched, then the center gear handle. Keep the lever raised for landing: stowing it would retract the gear. Tiller steering is limited to about 25° right.
No normal gear operation unless the reversible motor pumps restore pressure. Brake system 2 on its accumulators. Steering on system 1.
System 3 pressure low; brake SYS 2 falling to accumulator pressure.
The hydraulic procedure in [Abnormal procedures](abnormal-procedures) or [Emergency procedures](emergency-procedures): alternate extension, then the center gear handle.
Center gear will not extend, or isolated
Landing on the main and nose gear only.
CTR red light (or dark with the switch at UP).
CTR GEAR switch UP to clear the light and the warning input. Landing weight limited (363,500 lb DC-10-30, 400,000 lb KC-10) and 450 ft added to the landing distance (FedEx).
CENTER GEAR CONTROL power lost (DC bus 1)
The center gear control valve stays where it is.
The CTR GEAR switch has no effect.
Note it among the effects of the DC bus 1 loss; the center gear keeps following the handle if it was at NORM.
Pilots' gear warning power lost (LANDING GEAR WARN, DC bus 2)
Pilots' gear lights and horn inoperative.
Use the flight engineer's lights; a green on either panel is a locked gear.

blocks.content: **Reasoning about an unsafe light.** The two indicating systems are independent, so an unsafe light on one panel with a green on the other is almost always an indication fault, and the gear is down and locked. A red light on both panels with the handle down is a real problem until proved otherwise. Use the mechanical indicators where you can see them. Before recycling a gear on a center-gear airframe, remember that the CTR GEAR switch can keep the center gear out of the cycle.

children.title: Brake, anti-skid, steering and tire failures

rows: One brake system lost (hydraulic system 1 or 3)
Half the pistons of every brake. Braking is adequate for every landing. On the DC-10, without hydraulic system 1 the autobrake landing mode has no supply.
That brake pressure falling; hydraulic system indications.
Brake normally with the remaining system; the hydraulic procedure covers the rest. Do not use the autobrake without system 1.
Accumulator braking only: about six applications.
Both brake pressures at accumulator level and falling with each application. At 1,000 psi or less no significant braking.
One steady application, no cycling. Maximum reverse thrust. Follow the accumulator braking guidance in the hydraulic procedure.
Anti-skid fault in one wheel pair
Reduced protection on the affected wheels.
One FAIL light (DC-10, KC-10) or ANTI-SKID L, R or C FAIL (MD-10).
ANTI-SKID FAIL LT(S) ON: verify the parking brake released, switch OFF then ARM, test. If the fault remains, leave the switch at ARM, autobrake OFF, manual braking technique, longer landing distance.
Anti-skid control box failure, or anti-skid inoperative
Protection degraded or lost; with the system inoperative the brakes are manual power brakes and wheels can lock. The DC-10 autobrake will not arm.
All FAIL lights (DC-10, KC-10) or ANTI-SKID FAIL (MD-10).
As above. Reduce weight, use full reverse and the whole runway; maximum landing weight reduced.
A set brake cannot be released by the valves; a released one cannot be set.
If stuck closed, all ANTI-SKID FAIL lights stay on after the parking brake is released.
Maintenance. Brake pressure may remain trapped.
AUTO BRAKE and both ABS lights, MASTER CAUTION, ARM-DISARM switch at DISARM.
Selector OFF; brake manually. To try again, selector OFF and back to a detent, then ARM.
Dragging brake, or brakes hot after heavy use
Heat building in one or more brakes; a dragging brake also pulls the aircraft to its side.
Rising BRAKE TEMP, DIFF TEMP, OVHT lights (MD-10: BRAKE DIFF TEMP, BRAKE OVERHEAT).
ABNORMAL BRAKE (MD-10: BRAKE OVERHEAT): after takeoff with OVHT on or above 400 °C, extend the gear (260 KIAS maximum) until below 360 °C; on the ground determine the zone and act on it.
Brake temperature in the caution or danger zone after a stop
Fuse plugs may melt; fire is possible in the danger zone.
OVHT lights, BRAKE TEMP 400-500 °C or above.
ABNORMAL BRAKE: do not set the parking brake, clear the runway, keep personnel away; in the danger zone prepare to evacuate. Do not take off again until cooled.
Vibration, pull to one side, debris.
Felt and heard; possibly reported by the tower.
TIRE FAILURE DURING TAKEOFF ROLL: reject only well below V1 (not above V1 − 20 kt). If continuing, do not retract the gear, reduce weight, autobrake OFF, flaps 35 landing.
No response to the tiller or pedals.
Steer with differential braking and asymmetric thrust; stop and request a tow.

sections.title: Simulation notes
sections.summary: What the simulation models, what it simplifies, and how the gear meets the simulator.

blocks.content: **Modeled in depth.** Each leg runs through its own door, unlock, travel and lock sequence on hydraulic system 3, with real flow demand on the hydraulic system; free-fall extension; the anti-retraction lock and GEAR HANDLE REL; the CTR GEAR isolation switch with its motor actuator and breaker; the gear position lights, door terms and both horn conditions; oleo struts that stroke and settle under load; nosewheel steering as a hydraulic servo; two brake systems with accumulators, restrictor refill and leakage; per-wheel anti-skid with skid and locked-wheel detection and a modulator; the DC-10 autobrake as described above; the parking brake's pawls, valves and trapped pressure; brake heating and cooling per brake, fuse plugs, tire pressure and tread; and the ground shift that other systems read.

children.title: How the gear meets the simulator

items: **Gear handle.** The G key, a hardware gear lever and the 3D handle all move the same handle. On the ground the anti-retraction lock refuses an UP selection unless GEAR HANDLE REL is held, and even then a leg carrying weight does not retract. An aircraft loaded on the ground always starts gear down.

**What you see and what the simulator flies.** The drawn gear and doors follow the gear sequence described in this part. The simulator's contact points and gear drag follow the gear handle and move within a few seconds of it. A leg that fails to extend is drawn up with its red light on, but the simulator still lands on that wheel; a collapsed leg is drawn folded. During an alternate extension the simulator's gear is held down from the moment the lever is raised.

**Brakes.** The toe brakes act through the simulator's own brakes. Maximum manual braking is set about a quarter softer than the aircraft's flight-test maximum. The simulation reduces your braking when its brakes would deliver less (anti-skid release, fade, a deflated tire), and it adds braking for the autobrake, for a dragging brake and while the chocks are in. The brake key applies full braking and counts as pedals beyond 40 % for the autobrake.

**Steering.** Moving the tiller (drag it in the cockpit, or bind a hardware tiller to the steering axis) steers the nose wheel through the simulated steering system, with its hydraulic supply and rate. Rudder pedal steering is the simulator's own: at walking pace full pedal turns the nose wheel much further than the aircraft's 10°, reducing to about 20° above about 15 kt, and it does not depend on hydraulic pressure. During an automatic rollout and during a tow the simulation places the nose wheel itself.

**Parking brake and chocks.** The 3D handle and the simulator's parking brake key move the same handle. The ground crew's chocks (EFB Ground Ops) hold the aircraft with or without the parking brake; they put no heat in the brakes. A cold-and-dark aircraft loaded on the ground starts with the parking brake released, the brakes unpressurized and the chocks in. See [Ground operations](ground-operations) and the [EFB](efb).

**Gear collapse.** A touchdown at roughly 1,500 ft/min or more collapses the gear. Nothing in the cockpit flags a landing above the 600 ft/min hard-landing threshold; the EFB's flight log records each landing's sink rate.
**Center gear alternate extension handle**: not operable. On the -30, -40 and KC-10, a center gear that cannot extend on system 3 stays up; select CTR GEAR UP and land with it retracted.

**Free fall without the lever**: with system 3 lost and the handle at DOWN, the main and nose gear fall by themselves in the simulation; on the aircraft they wait for the alternate extension lever. The lever works as described. After a free fall the main gear doors close; on the aircraft they stay open.

**Timing**: the main gear takes about 14 s to retract and about 20 s to extend, the nose gear about 10 s and 15 s, the center gear about 14 s and 18 s, and a free fall about 25 s (the center gear about a minute).
**Trim cylinder interlock**: not simulated; the gear handle is never blocked by it.
**Steering**: losing system 1 or 3 slows the steering instead of limiting it to 25° toward the failed system, and the alternate extension lever does not limit right turns.

**Brake supply**: braking effectiveness does not yet depend on hydraulic pressure. The brake pressure indications, the accumulators and the parking brake do; the stopping power does not drop when both brake systems are lost. Fly the procedures as written.

**Brake pressure needles (DC-10, KC-10)**: the pilots' needles show hydraulic systems 1 and 3 directly, not the higher of system and accumulator, so they fall to zero after shutdown while the accumulators still hold the parking brake. The MD-10's pedestal indicators show the higher of the two.

**Anti-skid**: the ANTI-SKID TEST button is inoperative; the FAIL lights are proved by the annunciator light tests. Touchdown protection covers every braked wheel in the air and ends at touchdown rather than at wheel spin-up, so do not land with the brakes applied: a wheel braked through the touchdown can stay locked. The center gear's anti-skid cuts out at the same 10 kt as the main gear's. One failed anti-skid control box lights the failure indications and stops the autobrake arming, but skid protection continues on every wheel; only with both boxes failed (or the switch OFF) do the brakes become manual.
**Runway friction**: wet and contaminated runway friction is the simulator's; the simulated tires do not hydroplane.
**Brake temperature**: the indicated temperature peaks when braking stops instead of 15-25 minutes later; the fuse plugs still melt minutes after a high-energy stop.
**Parking brake**: released by moving the handle forward, not by pressing the pedals.
**Autobrake**: an activation needs 45 kt of main wheel speed, so an abort below 45 kt does not start it. Fitted to every DC-10 variant.
**Gear indication**: the pilots' and the flight engineer's gear lights share one source, so losing the LANDING GEAR WARN supply (DC bus 2) darkens both. The main gear door lights are not drawn.
**Ground sensing**: pressurization and probe heating take the simulator's own on-ground signal, so a ground sensing mechanism stuck in ground mode does not affect them.

**MD-10**: the CTR GEAR NORM/UP switch, the AUTO BRAKE controls and the pedestal AUX HYD PUMP switch are inoperative (use the overhead hydraulic panel for the auxiliary pumps). The gear lights use the DC-10 law, including the throttle-idle term the MD-10 manual does not list. The gear aural uses 215 KIAS and 28.5° of flap with no radio altitude term, where the MD-10 manual gives 210 kt, 1,200 ft radio altitude and 30° of flap. Brake temperatures are shown on both MD-10s. The SD CONFIGURATION page shows tire pressures, which the FedEx MD-10 does not have. Each brake system has three accumulators; the MD-10 manual itself gives three in its hydraulics chapter and two in its landing gear chapter.

**Not simulated**: the center gear's up-and-locked cable check, the maintenance gear handle in the right wheel well, the gear lock pins, the anti-skid's automatic test on gear extension (MD-10), and any tail skid or tail-strike indication.

parts.title: Pneumatics
parts.summary: Engine and APU bleed air, its regulation, distribution and protection.

blocks.content: The pneumatic system collects compressed air from the engines, the APU or a ground air cart, brings it to a usable pressure and temperature, and distributes it to everything on the aircraft that runs on air: the three air conditioning packs (and through them cabin pressurization and trim air), wing anti-ice, the engine starters, lower cargo compartment ventilation and heating, and potable water tank pressurization. Engine cowl anti-ice is taken from the engine side of the same plumbing.

The system is built as **three independent pneumatic systems**, numbered for the engines that normally feed them. Each engine has its own bleed installation (two compressor ports, a high-stage valve, a precooler, an overpressure valve and a pressure regulating and shutoff valve, managed by its own controller) discharging into its own section of the pneumatic manifold. Two motor-driven **isolation valves**, the 1-2 and the 1-3, can join system 1 to system 2 and system 1 to system 3. Normally they are closed and each engine feeds only its own users; the valves are opened to start engines from the APU or a ground cart, to let one engine supply the users of a system whose engine is out, and to isolate a failed manifold.

The design follows from two requirements that pull in opposite directions. The users want a steady supply at roughly 45 psig and no hotter than about 470 °F (243 °C) under every condition from ground idle to takeoff power and from sea level to FL420, while the engine compressor delivers air whose pressure varies by a factor of ten, and whose temperature by several hundred degrees, over the same envelope. Two compressor ports, a pressure regulator and a heat exchanger are how the system bridges that range. The three-way split exists for failure isolation: a burst duct, a runaway valve or a failed engine takes out one system, and the isolation valves let the crew decide how much of the remaining air to share.

blocks.content: Throughout this part, **system 1, 2 or 3** means the engine's bleed installation together with the manifold section it feeds. Manifold section 1 runs along the left side of the fuselage and into the left wing, section 3 the right, and section 2 serves the center of the aircraft, the aft fuselage and the APU. Pressures are gauge pressures (psig) unless stated otherwise.

sections.title: Bleed air sources
sections.summary: Engine compressor bleed, the APU's load compressor and ground air.

blocks.content: Air reaches the manifold from three kinds of source. In flight it comes from the engines. On the ground, before the engines are running, it comes from the APU or from an air cart connected to one or both ground connectors. Every source joins the manifold through a check valve, so a stronger source can never push air back into a weaker one: a stopped engine, a stopped APU or a disconnected cart is simply a closed door.

Each engine has two bleed ports on its high-pressure compressor. The **low-stage port** taps an intermediate stage and is the normal source of air: it is cooler, and taking air there costs the engine less work, because the air has only been compressed part of the way. The **high-stage port** taps at or near the compressor discharge and is used only when the low stage cannot hold the duct up: at low power, in an idle descent, and when anti-ice demands extra pressure and heat.

blocks.title: Bleed ports by engine
rows: Intermediate HPC stage (8th on the MD-10 FCOM)

blocks.content: **Why two stages.** Compressor delivery pressure rises roughly with the square of core speed and falls with altitude, because the engine starts from a lower inlet pressure. At takeoff power the low-stage port alone delivers well over 100 psig, far more than the system needs; at flight idle in a descent from altitude the same port may deliver less than the manifold is being asked to hold. A single port sized for idle would deliver dangerously hot, high-pressure air at takeoff; one sized for takeoff would starve the users at idle. Two ports, with a valve that opens the high stage only when needed, keep the system on the coolest air that will do the job.

**Why the air is so hot.** Compression heats air. For an ideal compression the temperature ratio is the pressure ratio raised to the power (γ − 1)/γ, about 0.29 for air, and a real compressor adds its losses on top. A compressor discharge at a pressure ratio near 30 sends air out above 500 °C at takeoff power on a warm day, and even the low-stage port delivers several hundred degrees. No aluminum duct in a wing or fuselage tunnel could carry that, which is why every engine's air is cooled in a precooler before it leaves the engine pylon, and why the duct temperature is watched as closely as its pressure.

blocks.alt: Schematic of one CF6 engine bleed installation in the pylon: low-stage port with check valve and high-stage port with high-stage valve joining an intermediate duct; overpressure valve venting overboard from the intermediate duct; the precooler with fan air supply from the fan duct through the fan air valve and its exhaust overboard; the pressure regulating and shutoff valve with its check function; duct temperature probe at the precooler outlet; pressure transmitter downstream of the regulator; the cowl anti-ice tap upstream of the regulator. The pneumatic system controller shown with electrical lines to the high-stage valve torque motor, the regulator torque motor and the fan air valve.
blocks.title: Engine bleed installation
blocks.caption: One system's valves, from the compressor to the manifold. The controller works on the intermediate duct (high-stage valve), the manifold (regulator) and the precooler discharge (fan air valve).

blocks.content: **Bleed is not free.** Every pound of air taken from the compressor has been compressed by the turbine's work and then leaves without producing thrust. To hold the same thrust the engine must run hotter: EGT and fuel flow rise and, at a fixed throttle, N1 and thrust fall slightly. Anti-ice raises the cost further, because it pushes the controller onto its high-flow schedule and draws large flows. This is the reason for bleed-off and packs-off takeoffs, for the bleed load limits per engine at takeoff power (see [Operation](#operation)), and for the effect of anti-ice on performance.

The APU has its own load compressor, rated at about 385 lb/min, enough to run all three packs on the ground or to start an engine. Its air reaches manifold section 2 through the APU **load control valve**, which regulates the manifold to about 44 psig, then through the **APU/ISOL valve** (a motor-driven gate the crew opens and closes) and a check valve. The check valve stops engine air flowing back into a stopped APU.

On the DC-10 and KC-10 the flight engineer's APU/ISOL VALVE switch both opens the gate and tells the APU to open its load control valve; with the 1-2 and 1-3 ISOL VALVE switches in NORM it also opens both isolation valves, so APU air reaches all three manifold sections. On the MD-10 the APU BLEED switchlight on the overhead AIR panel commands the same gate and valve, and the isolation valves are opened separately with their own switchlights. The APU's speed and load response are described in [APU](apu).

The APU's demand signal is what the manifold asks for. Packs switched on, a starter turning or a manifold below its set point all raise it, and the APU's control opens its load valve in response; with nothing drawing air the valve settles almost shut and simply holds pressure. On the DC-10 and KC-10, with the APU/ISOL VALVE switch at OPEN and the ENG IGNITION selector out of OFF, the APU runs at its higher engine-start speed for extra air (see [APU](apu)).

The APU is a ground and low-altitude source. It does not supply enough air, or air hot enough, for wing anti-ice, and in flight its air should be replaced with engine air as soon as the engines can supply it. On the three-crew aircraft the USE ENG PNEU SUPPLY light is the reminder.

Two ground pneumatic connectors, each behind its own check valve, accept a high-pressure air start unit. The first connector feeds manifold section 1 and the second section 3. A cart on one connector can supply the whole aircraft once the isolation valves are open: on the DC-10 and KC-10, by setting the APU/ISOL VALVE switch to OPEN with the ISOL VALVE switches in NORM (both valves follow it), or by opening the valves individually.

The air start unit is called, connected and controlled from the EFB's Ground Ops page: one or two hoses, a delivery pressure of 20 to 60 psig, and start and stop air. A new setting takes a couple of seconds to settle. The cart's hose pressure sags as the aircraft draws on it, as a real cart's does under a starter's load. Every cart disconnects and leaves if the aircraft moves. See [Ground Operations](ground-operations).

sections.title: Engine bleed regulation
sections.summary: The high-stage valve, pressure regulator, precooler and overpressure valve, and the controller that runs them.

blocks.content: Each engine's bleed air passes through a fixed sequence of devices before it reaches the manifold. The low-stage port feeds an **intermediate duct** through a check valve; the high-stage valve can add high-stage air to the same duct. The air then passes through the precooler, and finally through the pressure regulating and shutoff valve into the manifold. An overpressure valve on the intermediate duct protects everything downstream. The pneumatic system controller for that engine commands the high-stage valve, the regulator and the precooler's fan air valve, and holds the protective latches.

All the valves are pneumatically actuated and electrically controlled: duct air moves them, and torque motors or solenoids decide where. The consequence, used throughout the failure logic, is that each valve has a defined position when it loses its electrical control (see [Failures](#failures)).

The **high-stage valve** is a modulating butterfly between the high-stage port and the intermediate duct. It regulates the intermediate duct to about **58 ± 7 psig**: when the low stage alone cannot hold that pressure the valve opens just enough high-stage air to make up the difference, and when the duct is above its band it closes. It is spring-closed and opened by a torque motor, so without its control current it shuts and the engine supplies low-stage air only.

In practice the valve is open at idle and low power and closed at climb and takeoff power, and the handover happens on its own as thrust changes. The point at which the low stage takes over moves with altitude: because the compressor's delivery pressure falls as the aircraft climbs, the high stage stays open to a higher N2 at altitude than on the ground. In a descent at idle the high stage carries the duct. Holding patterns and autothrottle activity in turbulence can sit an engine near the handover point, so the duct pressure and temperature move as the valve opens and closes; selecting HI on the ENG PNEU SUPPLY selector steadies the supply (see [Controls and indicators](#controls-and-indicators)).

blocks.content: The **pressure regulating and shutoff valve** (pressure regulator) is the last valve before the manifold and the one that sets manifold pressure. Under controller authority it holds its manifold section at about **46 psig**. It has a pneumatic reference of its own as well: with its electrical control lost it stays open and regulates on that reference, at a slightly higher **48 psig**. It also acts as a check valve, passing air only into the manifold, so an APU-charged manifold cannot drain backwards into an idling engine's duct.

The regulator is also the system's shutoff valve. It closes when the ENG PNEU SUPPLY selector is set to OFF, when the engine fire handle is pulled, when the thermal shutoff trips and when a manifold failure lockout is set. Nothing else closes it: a stopped engine leaves its regulator commanded open, and it is the check valves that keep manifold air out of a stopped compressor.

**Theory of operation.** The regulator's controller is a proportional-plus-integral loop on the sensed manifold pressure. The integral part carries the standing opening the system needs at its present load, so there is no steady error: the manifold sits on 46 psig whether one pack or three are drawing. The proportional part provides damping, so that when a pack comes on line or the throttles are advanced quickly the valve does not overshoot. The regulator is the slower of the two valves in series and the high-stage valve the faster, which is what keeps the pair from fighting each other.

When the engine cannot supply 46 psig (at ground idle an engine typically holds 20 to 30 psig against its users) the regulator simply sits wide open and the manifold settles where supply and demand balance. With two sources on one joined manifold, the stronger one holds the pressure and the check valves keep the weaker one from contributing until the pressure falls to its level.

The **precooler** is a crossflow air-to-air heat exchanger in the engine pylon. Bleed air passes through one side; cool air from the engine's fan duct passes through the other and is dumped overboard. The **fan air valve** in the cooling stream is modulated by the controller to hold the precooler outlet at **470 °F (243 °C)**, or at **445 °F (229 °C)** whenever anti-ice is drawing on that system.

**Why the set point drops for anti-ice.** Wing and cowl anti-ice need heat rather than pressure, so with anti-ice on the controller moves to its high-flow schedule and uses more high-stage air. High-stage air arrives much hotter, so the precooler has more heat to reject at a given flow; the lower set point keeps the manifold and the wing ducting inside their temperature rating while the flow is high.

The heat the precooler can reject depends on how much fan air flows through it, which depends on fan speed and the valve opening, and on how much bleed air is passing. At high power with the packs on, a healthy precooler regulates with the fan air valve only a few per cent open; at idle it needs little cooling at all. A fouled matrix loses that margin: the valve drives to full open and the outlet temperature rises past its set point, first at the high-flow conditions of a climb. The fan air valve is spring-loaded open, so if the controller loses authority or its temperature sensor fails it gives maximum cooling and the duct runs cool rather than hot.

The duct temperature probe sits at the precooler outlet. Its reading drives the fan air valve, the overtemperature warning, the TEMP gauge on the flight engineer's panel and the bleed temperature on the MD-10's synoptic. With no air flowing (a shut-down system) the probe sees the still air in the duct, and the reading falls slowly as the duct cools.

The **overpressure valve** vents the intermediate duct overboard. It is spring-loaded open and closed by compressor pressure: as the engine's high-stage pressure rises from about 35 psig toward 90 psig the valve closes, and once closed it stays seated until that pressure falls back below about 51 psig. A separate relief function opens it at 210 psig and recloses at 175 psig, which is the protection against a runaway high-stage valve putting compressor discharge pressure into the duct. Placing the valve upstream of the regulator puts the relief where the dangerous pressures can occur.

Check valves decide which way air can flow through the plumbing. There is one at each engine's low-stage port, the regulator acts as one, and there is one at the APU tie-in and one behind each ground connector. Together they let any combination of sources share a joined manifold safely: each source contributes only while its pressure exceeds the manifold's, and none can be back-driven. A stopped engine needs no special handling, because its ports sit at ambient pressure behind closed check valves.

Each engine's bleed system has its own **pneumatic system controller**. It selects a mode from the selector position and the aircraft condition, commands the high-stage valve, the regulator and the fan air valve, and runs the protection logic. It works on **sensed** values: the same pressure transmitter and temperature probe words that drive the flight engineer's gauges and the MD-10's synoptic. A failed transmitter therefore misleads the controller and the crew alike, while the air itself behaves as physics dictates.

blocks.content: The controller and its valves draw on several separate circuits. Controller logic, monitoring, the high-stage valve solenoid, the regulator supply, the temperature indication and each lamp have their own breakers, and the regulator supplies are deliberately cross-wired: engine 1's regulator is on DC bus 2, engine 2's on DC bus 3 and engine 3's on DC bus 1. Losing one DC bus therefore degrades one regulator on a different engine rather than taking down a whole system. Losing the controller entirely drops the system onto its pneumatic fallbacks: regulator open and regulating at 48 psig, high-stage valve shut, fan air valve open. The system keeps supplying low-stage air but loses its electrical protection and indication; see [Electrical](electrical) for the buses.

The pneumatic manifold is three sections of ducting, one per system. Each engine's regulator discharges into its own section, and each section carries its own users. Two isolation valves join the sections, and their placards say exactly what they join: the **1-2 isolation valve** connects sections 1 and 2, and the **1-3 isolation valve** connects sections 1 and 3. Section 1 is the hub of the arrangement. There is no direct connection between sections 2 and 3: air from the APU, which enters section 2, reaches section 3 only through section 1 with both valves open.
