blocks.content: Manifold volume is small compared with the flows through it: a section turns over its whole contents several times a second at cruise demand. That is why manifold pressure responds within a second or two to a pack switching on or a starter valve opening, and why it falls quickly when its source is shut off and a user is still drawing. With everything shut the manifold still bleeds down slowly through valve seats and joints, over a minute or two.

Both isolation valves are motor-driven butterflies. The 1-2 valve's motor is powered from the right emergency AC bus and the 1-3 valve's from the left emergency AC bus, so losing one emergency bus freezes one valve and leaves the other usable. A motor-driven valve has no spring: without power it **stays where it is**. The ISOL VALVE DISAGREE lights have a third supply, DC bus 2.

Each valve has a three-position switch on the flight engineer's panel. OPEN and CLOSE drive it directly. **NORM** hands the valve to the APU/ISOL VALVE switch: with that switch at CLOSE both isolation valves in NORM are closed and each engine supplies only its own system; with it at OPEN both are open, so the APU or a ground cart reaches all three sections. This is why the normal ground configuration with the APU running (APU/ISOL VALVE OPEN, both ISOL VALVE switches NORM) joins the whole manifold, and the after-start action of closing the APU/ISOL VALVE switch splits it again without touching the isolation switches.

blocks.title: Isolation valve logic (DC-10, KC-10)
rows: Closed and held while a manifold failure trip is latched (see [Leak and overheat detection](#leak-and-overheat-detection))

blocks.content: The DISAGREE light compares the valve's position with the crew's selection, not with what the valve has been driven to. It is lit whenever the valve is not at the selected end of its travel, **including while it is moving**: a short flash as a valve strokes is normal and is the confirmation that it moved. A light that stays on means the valve did not get there (a jam, an unpowered motor, or a manifold failure trip holding it shut against the switch).

On the MD-10 each isolation valve has a single push-on, push-off switchlight on the overhead AIR panel. There is no NORM: un-pressed the valve is shut, pressed it is open, and the ON legend shows that the valve has opened. The MD-10 procedures open both valves for engine start and close them after start.

The APU/ISOL valve is the gate between the APU's load control valve and manifold section 2. It is powered from DC bus 1 and, unlike the two manifold isolation valves, it **closes** when it loses power, so a dead aircraft isolates its APU tie-in. On a cold and dark aircraft it is therefore closed even if the switch was left at OPEN; it opens when power returns.

The switch, not the valve, drives the two amber lights associated with it. APU/ISOL VALVE OPEN on the flight engineer's status block reports the switch at OPEN. **USE ENG PNEU SUPPLY** comes on when the switch is still at OPEN after the aircraft is airborne and the cabin is pressurizing (more than about 0.5 psi differential), with the MASTER CAUTION and the PNEU cue light. It is a reminder to move the pneumatic supply from the APU to the engines, and it applies whether or not the APU is running.

Opening an isolation valve joins two sections into one, and two regulators then try to hold one pressure. They cannot both win: the one set marginally higher, or with the stronger engine behind it, carries the load while the other's check function keeps it out. One engine then supplies two systems' users, with twice the flow through its precooler, and its duct can run hot. That is why the procedures forbid joining two **active engine supplies** in flight except for short transitions (moving from APU air to engine air, or a cross-bleed engine start), and why the -1 notes that high duct temperatures can follow the high flows of crossfeeding.

The legitimate uses of the isolation valves are therefore: joining the whole manifold to one ground source (APU or cart) for engine start and ground air conditioning; supplying the users of a system whose engine or bleed system is out from a remaining system, with the dead system's ENG PNEU SUPPLY selector at OFF; cross-bleed engine starts; and splitting a failed section away from the rest.

Users draw air in two different ways, and the difference explains much of what the gauges do. **Flow-controlled users** (the packs, wing and cowl anti-ice, cargo ventilation) have a valve that meters a scheduled flow whatever the supply pressure, as long as there is enough pressure to do so; below roughly 30 psig they progressively lose authority and their flow falls with the pressure. **Nozzle users** (the air turbine starters) exhaust overboard through a choked nozzle, so their draw depends on the absolute supply pressure and does not back off as the manifold falls. A single starter on a healthy APU-fed manifold pulls it down about 5 psi; three starters at once can drag it down to around 10 psig, which is why engines are started one at a time.

blocks.content: The DC-10's hydraulic reservoirs are not pneumatic users: they are bootstrap reservoirs, pressurized by hydraulic system pressure acting on a piston (see [Hydraulics](hydraulics)). The thrust reversers on the CF6 engines are driven by engine air, which is why a deployed reverser puts its engine's bleed controller on a separate schedule.

sections.title: Leak and overheat detection
sections.summary: MANFLD FAIL, PNEU TEMP HI, PNEU ABNORMAL and the automatic isolation that follows a duct failure.

blocks.content: A burst bleed duct is one of the more dangerous failures on the aircraft. Air at several hundred degrees escaping into a wing, a fuselage tunnel or a pylon can damage wiring, control cables, fuel lines and structure within minutes, and the regulator will keep feeding it as fast as the engine can supply. The system watches for this in two ways: continuous detection loops in the compartments the ducts run through, and the controller's own duct temperature and pressure monitoring.

Continuous **detection loops** run along each manifold section's route. A loop is a sensing element that reacts to the temperature of the air around the duct, anywhere along its length, so it does not detect a leak directly: the escaping air has to heat the compartment first. A large rupture trips its loop within seconds; a small seep may take minutes, or may never heat a well-ventilated bay enough to trip it. Section 1's run (the left forward fuselage tunnel area) carries **two** loops, sections 2 and 3 one each; either loop of the pair can trip the warning.

A tripped loop lights its red **MANFLD FAIL** light, the PNEU MANFLD FAIL summary light on the pilots' overhead annunciator panel and the MASTER WARNING lights. On the MD-10 it raises the AIR MANF n FAIL alert and the MANF legend. The detection system then acts on its own, without waiting for the crew:

blocks.title: Automatic actions on a manifold failure
rows: Engine 1 supply shut off and locked out

Engine 2 supply shut off and locked out (no engine 2 supply on the KC-10)

blocks.content: Both the supply shutoff and the valve trips **latch**, so a light that goes out (because the compartment has cooled once the flow stopped) does not restore the supply. A latched supply lockout is released only by rotating that system's ENG PNEU SUPPLY selector to OFF and back. A latched 1-3 trip is released by removing the condition that allowed it, all PNEU SUPPLY selectors back out of OFF; a latched 1-2 and APU/ISOL trip by setting the APU/ISOL VALVE switch to CLOSE. While a trip holds a valve shut against its switch the ISOL VALVE DISAGREE light stays on, which is how the crew sees it. A condition that is still present relatches through the reset immediately.

**Press to test.** Pressing a MANFLD FAIL light tests the **detection loops** behind it, not the bulb. The test injects a signal at the loop, so a healthy system lights the light (and the summary and master warning) exactly as a real overheat would, and runs the same automatic actions: the supply lockout and the isolation valve trips. A zone with a broken loop stays dark under the finger; on system 1, both loops must be healthy for the light to come on. The flight engineer's checks use exactly this. In the cockpit preparation check, with one outboard supply at AUTO, the other at OFF and the 1-3 ISOL VALVE switch at OPEN, pressing light 1 or 3 brings on the 1-3 ISOL VALVE DISAGREE light, which stays on after release until both selectors are back at AUTO. In the before-takeoff supply lockout check, with the engines running, pressing a light shuts that system down: its pressure falls to zero and stays there after release, until the selector is rotated to OFF and back to AUTO.
Do not re-pressurize a system that has been shut down by a manifold failure except for engine starting. The light may go out once the duct is no longer flowing, but the leak is still there.

children.title: Duct overtemperature (PNEU TEMP HI) and thermal shutoff

blocks.content: The red **PNEU TEMP HI** light reports that one system's own installation is over temperature: either the controller's duct temperature probe at the precooler outlet has passed **500 °F (260 °C)**, the red line on the TEMP gauge, or the detection loop around that engine's pylon and precooler has tripped. It brings on the PNEU TEMP HI summary light on the overhead annunciator panel and the MASTER WARNING. The light clears once the duct temperature has fallen about 30 °F below the warning value. It is deactivated with that system's ENG PNEU SUPPLY selector at OFF, which is also the first action of the procedure, so the light going out confirms the right system was shut down.

The warning does not close anything; it annunciates. A separate **thermal shutoff** at about **480 °C (896 °F)** closes the regulator and latches. Two thresholds give an escalation: the warning first, leaving the crew to reduce the load or shut the system down, and the hard shutoff only if the duct keeps heating. A thermal shutoff is reset by rotating the selector to OFF.

Common causes are a fouled precooler or a fan air valve stuck closed, which show first at high flow (a climb with packs and anti-ice on); high flow from crossfeeding two systems' users onto one engine; and a leak upstream of the regulator, which heats the pylon compartment. If pressure stays above about 10 psi with the system's supply shut off, the air is coming from somewhere else (an open isolation valve or a failed valve), and the procedure treats it as a secondary failure.

The amber **PNEU ABNORMAL** light, one per system, reports abnormal pressure, temperature or controller operation in that system. It is inhibited whenever the system is not being asked to regulate its own manifold to its own schedule: with the ENG PNEU SUPPLY selector at LO or OFF, and with the APU/ISOL VALVE switch at OPEN (APU or cart air in the manifold is not that engine's regulation to judge).

blocks.content: Because a stopped engine supplies nothing, the PNEU ABNORMAL lights come on if the aircraft is powered with the engines stopped, the supplies at AUTO and the APU/ISOL VALVE switch at CLOSE. They go out when the switch goes to OPEN or the supplies to OFF, and each goes out on its own once its engine is running and holding pressure.

On the DC-10 and KC-10 the pneumatic system is the flight engineer's: its controls and gauges are on the PNEU & AIR COND SYS panel of Upper Panel No. 2, with the summary lights on the pilots' overhead annunciator panel. On the MD-10 the same valves are commanded from switchlights on the overhead AIR panel, and the system is monitored on the AIR synoptic page and through alerts.

blocks.content: Small movements of pressure and temperature as the high-stage valve hands over to the low stage during a climb, or back during a descent, are normal. A pressure that does not respond when the throttle is moved through the handover range, or that settles well below normal for the power set, points to a valve problem.

The pneumatic system needs little attention once it is configured: the controllers schedule the high stage, regulate the manifold and cool the duct on their own. The crew's work is at the transitions, from ground air to engine air, into and out of a bleeds-off takeoff, and after a failure, and in keeping the bleed load on each engine inside its limits. The detailed checklists are in [Normal Procedures](normal-procedures).

items: **Cockpit preparation.** With the APU running (or an air cart connected), set the APU/ISOL VALVE switch to OPEN with both ISOL VALVE switches at NORM. Both isolation valves open (their DISAGREE lights come on briefly as they travel) and APU air pressurizes all three manifold sections to about 44 psig. The engine supplies are left at OFF until the engines are running; with the supplies at OFF and the APU/ISOL VALVE switch at OPEN the PNEU ABNORMAL lights are inhibited. Run the MANFLD FAIL test for each system.
**Before start.** Packs are normally off for engine start, so the APU can give the starters its full output.

**Engine start.** With the ENG IGNITION selector at START the APU runs at its higher start speed. Check at least 25 psi on the PRESS gauges before opening a start valve (35 psi gives assurance below −18 °C; a start can be made down to 15 psi, more slowly). Expect the pressure to drop about 5 psi as the start valve opens. Start one engine at a time.

**After start.** Set the ENG PNEU SUPPLY selectors to AUTO and the APU/ISOL VALVE switch to CLOSE. The isolation valves in NORM close, and each engine now supplies only its own system. The PRESS gauges show each engine's own idle supply, typically 20 to 30 psig. Packs to AUTO.

**Before takeoff.** Run the MANFLD FAIL and supply lockout check (KC-10). Set the pneumatic configuration the takeoff data calls for: packs on (normal), packs off, or bleeds off. Confirm the APU/ISOL VALVE switch is at CLOSE unless the APU is to run the packs for the takeoff.

**Climb.** As climb power is set the high-stage valves close and each system runs on its low-stage port; the PRESS gauges settle at about 46 psig and the TEMP gauges near 240 °C. After a bleeds-off takeoff, return the supplies to AUTO one at a time once climb power is set; if the APU was used, close the APU/ISOL VALVE switch, or the USE ENG PNEU SUPPLY light will remind you as the cabin begins to pressurize.
**Cruise.** The system runs on low-stage air. If anti-ice is selected, the systems supplying it move to the high-flow schedule and the duct temperature settles near 230 °C.

**Descent and holding.** At idle the high-stage valves carry the ducts. If an engine's supply fluctuates enough to disturb the air conditioning (the high stage cycling at the handover point in turbulence or on autothrottle), set that ENG PNEU SUPPLY selector to HI; return it to AUTO when thrust or altitude changes. Wing anti-ice needs about 35 psi; at idle in a descent, and particularly with one engine supplying both wings, the throttle may have to be advanced to hold it.

**After landing and shutdown.** Thrust reverser deployment puts each engine's bleed controller on its reverser schedule for the duration. At the gate the APU/ISOL VALVE switch is set as required to run the packs from the APU, the ISOL VALVE switches are left at NORM, and the APU/ISOL VALVE switch goes to CLOSE as the first step of shutting the APU down (see [APU](apu)).

blocks.content: When the Virtual Crew flies the flight engineer's seat it runs this sequence from the checklists, reading the takeoff data card to decide between a packs-on and a packs-off or bleeds-off takeoff; see [Virtual Crew](virtual-crew).

items: **Before start.** APU BLEED out (APU air on), 1-2 and 1-3 ISOL pushed in (ON lit), PACK switchlights OFF and BLEED AIR switchlights OFF. APU air pressurizes all three systems; check the bleed pressures on the AIR synoptic.
**Engine start.** Start one engine at a time from APU air; the bleed pressure readout drops a few psi as each starter valve opens.

**After start.** Push APU BLEED in (USE ENG AIR lit), release both ISOL switchlights (ON out), BLEED AIR switchlights on (OFF out), and PACK switchlights on. Each engine now supplies its own system; the AIR 1-2 and 1-3 ISOL ON memos clear.

**Takeoff.** For a packs-off takeoff the packs stay off with the bleeds on (PACKS ALL OFF memo); for a bleeds-off takeoff the bleeds are off as well (BLEEDS ALL OFF memo). Restore bleeds, then packs, after takeoff.
**Climb, cruise and descent.** The bleed systems schedule the high stage automatically. There is no LO or HI selection on the MD-10.

blocks.content: One engine's bleed system is sized to carry its own system's users, not the whole aircraft's. When isolation valves put two systems' users on one engine, or an engine is lost, keep the load on each remaining engine supply within the recommended maximum. The figures below are in addition to the lavatory and galley vent (and, on the MD-10, cargo heat and vent); the governing figures are in [Limitations](limitations).

blocks.content: In flight, do not interconnect two active engine pneumatic supplies except for short periods during the transition from APU air or during an engine cross-bleed start. Two regulators on one manifold do not share the load, and the duct of the engine carrying it can overheat.
Engine anti-ice draws from the engine side of its own regulator and does not count against these figures.

With an engine shut down its bleed system supplies nothing, and if its ENG PNEU SUPPLY selector is left at AUTO the PNEU ABNORMAL light for that system will come on with the low manifold pressure. The users of the dead system can be supplied from a remaining engine through an isolation valve, provided the dead system's supply is OFF (so two active supplies are not joined) and the remaining engine's load stays within its limits. Because section 1 is the hub, engine 1 can supply either neighbor, while engines 2 and 3 can each reach only section 1.

blocks.content: On the KC-10, with only two engine supplies, losing one leaves a **single pneumatic system** for the whole aircraft. The -1's single-system procedure opens the 1-3 valve so the remaining engine supplies both packs, selects AVIONIC FLOW to OVRD to cut cabin leakage, and limits the packs at high power; if wing anti-ice is needed, one pack goes off to make room for it. The APU can still be used as a source, but not joined to an active engine supply: if system 1 is the one left, the APU (which enters through section 2 and the 1-2 valve) may not be used for pneumatic power.

On the MD-10 the same principles apply with the switchlights: push the dead system's BLEED AIR switchlight to OFF and push the isolation valve that joins it to a live system. AIR SYS n OFF and BLEED AIR n OFF tell you whether the dead system is isolated or is being supplied from elsewhere.

Pneumatic failures fall into three groups: duct failures (leaks and ruptures), which are emergencies because of the heat they release; valve and controller failures, which cost one system's supply or make it run hot or high; and source losses (an engine, the APU), which are handled by reconfiguring through the isolation valves. The procedures are in [Emergency Procedures](emergency-procedures) (manifold failure, PNEU TEMP HI, decompression) and [Abnormal Procedures](abnormal-procedures) (PNEU ABNORMAL, ISOL VALVE DISAGREE, single-system operation, fluctuating pressure).

blocks.content: A bleed leak upstream of the regulator, in the engine pylon, cannot be stopped by the ENG PNEU SUPPLY selector, because the engine still feeds the intermediate duct. If a manifold failure or overtemperature persists with the supply off and the pressure or temperature stays high, the procedures direct shutting down the engine to remove the source.

**Modeled in depth.** Every pressure and flow in the pneumatic system is solved, not scripted: the ducts, valves, check valves and users form a network that is solved every frame, and the manifold pressure is whatever the sources and users balance at. Bleed port pressure and temperature are derived continuously from the engine's own compressor state, so they follow N2, altitude and outside temperature, and the air each engine gives up is fed back to it as a real extraction: EGT, fuel flow and thrust respond. In the simulation, at FL200 and 80 % throttle on a DC-10-30, three packs cost about 5 °C of EGT and a quarter of a per cent of thrust; with every anti-ice valve open as well, about 13 °C and 0.6 %.

Each valve has a real actuator with travel time and its own failure modes (stuck open, stuck closed, lying position feedback). The controllers regulate on sensed values with sensor lags, so a failed transmitter misleads both the controller and the gauge. The precooler is a heat exchanger driven by fan air, the duct walls have heat capacity (a shut-down duct stays hot for a while), detection loops heat only when hot air actually reaches them, and the manifold bleeds down slowly after its sources are shut. Effects such as a stopped engine's ports sitting behind closed check valves, an idling engine overpowered by the APU, or three starters dragging the manifold down to around 10 psig are outcomes of that network, not special cases.

**Simplified.** All CF6-powered airframes currently share one CF6 bleed port schedule, so the differences between the CF6-6D's and CF6-50's bleed pressures are not represented. On the DC-10-40 the JT9D's low-stage port cannot hold the manifold in the climb, so the high-stage valve carries the duct from takeoff to high altitude. Several valve sizes, the detection loops' trip temperature and the normal duct leak rate are estimates. Both lower cargo ventilation taps are on system 2; on the aircraft the forward compartment's is on system 1. The simulation's ground connectors feed systems 1 and 3; FedEx's schematic shows them on systems 1 and 2. The thrust reversers do not draw air from the system, and the antenna anti-ice valve draws a negligible amount.

**Detection.** The MANFLD FAIL lights watch the three manifold runs. The wing leading-edge sensors and the center accessory compartment detection (which on the aircraft shuts down all supplies) are not modeled, and a pressure-decay leak check exists in the model but has no display. On the flight engineer's equipment panel the MANIFOLD FAIL DETECT LOOP SELECT switch and the ENG 1-2 and 1-3 ISOL VALVE SELECT (primary and secondary motor) switches are not modeled, so the procedure steps that use them cannot be flown.

**Indication differences.** The three MANFLD FAIL lights on the flight engineer's panel do not yet illuminate in the 3D cockpit; the press-to-test function works, and the PNEU MANFLD FAIL summary, MASTER WARNING and ISOL VALVE DISAGREE lights respond normally. Some DC-10 operators' panels carry a green HI STAGE OPEN light, reporting the high-stage valve open, where the simulation has the KC-10's PNEU ABNORMAL function. The PNEU cue light and the master caution respond to USE ENG PNEU SUPPLY; the other amber pneumatic lights on the flight engineer's panel do not raise the master caution in the simulation.

**MD-10.** The MANF switchlight acts as a latching detection loop test: press once to start the test, again to end it. The APU BLEED switchlight's USE ENG AIR legend reports the switch pushed in (APU air off), and there is no reminder if APU air is left selected in flight. The alerts HI STAGE n FAULT, START AIR PRES LO, SEL APU AIR OFF, CAC MANF FAIL, AIR MANF TST FAIL and AIR SYS TEST FAIL are not raised.

parts.title: Air Conditioning and Pressurization
parts.summary: The air cycle packs, temperature control, ventilation and cabin pressurization.

blocks.content: The air conditioning system turns hot, high-pressure bleed air into cool, dry, breathable air, delivers it to the flight deck and cabin zones at the temperature each zone asks for, and in doing so supplies the mass flow that pressurizes the fuselage. Pressurization is the other half of the same air: the cabin pressure controller holds the cabin at a comfortable altitude by throttling how fast that air is allowed to leave through the outflow valve.

Three **air conditioning packs** (two on the KC-10) each cool the air from one pneumatic system in an air cycle machine. Their outputs join in a common **conditioned air manifold** under the floor, from which ducts run to each temperature zone. The packs are run cold enough for the zone that needs the most cooling; **trim air**, hot bleed air that has bypassed the packs, is mixed back into each zone's duct to warm the others to their selected temperatures. The air leaves the cabin through floor vents into the utility tunnels, warming the lower cargo compartments on its way, and finally goes overboard through the outflow valve, the avionics cooling venturi and the airframe's own leakage.

Pressurization is a mass balance. The packs push a nearly fixed flow of air into the fuselage, and the cabin pressure rises until the outflow through the outflow valve and the leaks equals it. Closing the valve raises the cabin pressure (the cabin descends); opening it lowers the pressure (the cabin climbs). The cabin pressure controller moves the valve to follow a schedule of cabin altitude against aircraft altitude, limits the rate at which the cabin climbs or descends, and never lets the differential pressure across the hull exceed the structural limit.

blocks.alt: Functional schematic of the DC-10 air conditioning system: bleed air from pneumatic systems 1, 2 and 3 through the three pack flow control valves into packs 1, 2 (left air conditioning compartment) and 3 (right compartment); each pack with heat exchangers, air cycle machine (compressor, turbine, fan), turbine bypass valve, water separator and ram air inlet and exhaust. Pack outlets through check valves into the conditioned air manifold, with ground conditioned air connectors. Trim air taken downstream of the pack 1 and pack 3 flow control valves through two trim air pressure regulating valves into the trim air manifold, then through one trim air valve per zone into the zone ducts: cockpit, forward cabin, center cabin, aft cabin. Zone duct temperature sensors and overheat switches, zone temperature sensors. Cabin air through floor grilles to the utility tunnels, cargo compartments and the outflow valve. Color key for hot, cold and conditioned air.

blocks.content: The packs are three identical refrigeration units that run automatically and independently. Packs 1 and 2 are in the left air conditioning compartment and pack 3 is in the right; each is supplied by the pneumatic system of the same number. The KC-10 has packs 1 and 3 only, because it has no number 2 pneumatic supply. Each pack consists of flow regulation, an air cycle machine with its heat exchangers, water separation, temperature control and its own protection.

blocks.alt: Schematic of one DC-10 air conditioning pack: the venturi flow control valve at the inlet; primary heat exchanger; air cycle machine with compressor, turbine and fan on one shaft; secondary (main) heat exchanger between compressor and turbine; water separator downstream of the turbine; the turbine bypass valve bridging from upstream of the heat exchangers to the turbine discharge; ram air inlet scoop and ram air exhaust door with the fan drawing through the heat exchangers on the ground; pack discharge temperature sensor and the check valve into the conditioned air manifold. Station temperatures annotated as typical cruise values.
blocks.title: Air conditioning pack

children.title: Air cycle machine and the bootstrap cycle

blocks.content: Bleed air arrives at the pack at around 45 psig and up to about 470 °F. Cooling it against outside air alone cannot bring it below outside air temperature, and on a hot day at the gate that is not cold enough to cool a cabin. The **air cycle machine** gets below ambient by expanding the air through a turbine, which extracts work from it and drops its temperature far below where it entered. The pack is a reversed Brayton cycle, with the bleed pressure as its source of energy.

The DC-10's machine is a three-wheel **bootstrap** unit: a compressor, a turbine and a fan on one shaft. The air first passes through the **primary heat exchanger**, rejecting heat to ram air. It then enters the ACM's compressor, which raises its pressure and with it its temperature. The hotter air passes through the **secondary heat exchanger**, where the larger temperature difference against ram air lets it reject much more heat than it could have before compression. It then expands through the turbine, which drives the compressor and the fan, and leaves at a temperature well below ambient. The word bootstrap describes this: the turbine's work pays for the compression that makes the cooling possible.

Expansion through the turbine cools the air below its dew point, and moisture condenses as fog. The **water separator** downstream collects the droplets and drains them, and the pack holds its discharge just above freezing so the separator does not ice. Ram air for the heat exchangers comes in through a ram air inlet and leaves through an exhaust door that is modulated with the temperature control; on the ground, with no ram pressure, the ACM's fan draws cooling air through the heat exchangers. A pack whose machine has seized has no fan and no turbine: it can cool only with what little the exchangers manage and heats up quickly.

A healthy pack on engine air at full cold on the ground discharges at about 40 to 50 °F on a warm day, reaching the separator floor on cooler days. The colder the outside air and the higher the airspeed, the more cooling margin it has; in cruise the packs can make far more cold than the cabin needs, and the temperature control throws most of it away by bypassing.

Each pack's inlet has a **flow control valve**, a normally closed venturi-type valve. It opens when its pack is selected on (AUTO or MAN on the DC-10 and KC-10, the PACK switchlight on for the MD-10) and its shutoff solenoid has power, and then meters a scheduled flow, about 115 lb/min, whatever the supply pressure, as long as the manifold has the pressure to push it. It needs at least 15 psig; below about 30 psig it progressively loses authority and the pack flow falls with the pressure. The shutoff solenoids share a battery bus circuit with the PACK OFF lights.

Pack flow is what pressurizes the aircraft, and its stability is what makes cabin pressure control possible: because each pack delivers nearly the same flow at any manifold pressure above its knee, the outflow valve sees a steady inflow to regulate against. Each pack's flow is shown on its FLOW gauge on the flight engineer's panel, where rated flow sits in the upper half of the dial rather than at its top.

The pack's discharge temperature is set by the **turbine bypass valve**, which blends hot air from upstream of the heat exchangers around the turbine into its cold discharge. Closed, the pack delivers all the cold it can make; open, it delivers warm air. The ram air doors are driven with it, open at the cold end and closed at the hot end. The flight engineer's PACK TEMP VALVE POS gauge shows the position, C at the cold end and H at the hot end.

In AUTO the pack temperature controller drives the bypass valve to deliver the discharge temperature the zone controllers ask for (see [Temperature control](#temperature-control)); it moves the valve through its full range in about 10 seconds. In MAN the crew drive the valve directly with the selector's MAN COLD and MAN HOT positions, much more slowly, about 35 seconds end to end. The controller never schedules a discharge hotter than about 180 °F: heating the cabin is trim air's job, and a pack asked for very hot air on a cold-soaked aircraft would otherwise trip itself. A pack that is switched off parks its bypass valve at full cold, so that when it comes back on line its discharge rises to its commanded value from below rather than arriving hot.

A pack overheat closes the pack's flow control valve and latches: the pack shuts down and its PACK OFF light comes on with the selector still at AUTO. The trip acts at about 200 °F of pack discharge temperature, after a short dwell so a single hot moment does not trip a healthy pack. The latch is reset by selecting the pack OFF and back on, which should wait until the pack has cooled and the cause is understood: an ACM failure, a bypass valve driven or stuck hot, or a pack run in manual too far toward HOT.

The KC-10's gauge markings give the crew's limits: a limit mark at 250 °F on the turbine inlet temperature gauge and at 190 °F on the pack discharge temperature gauge. In manual operation, keep the discharge below the mark, and watch it closely during descent, when the falling power and changing bleed temperature can push a manually set pack hot.

Each temperature zone has its own selector, controller, zone temperature sensor, duct temperature sensor, duct overheat switch and trim air valve. The zone controller compares the zone's sensed temperature with the selection and produces two outputs: a command to its own trim air valve, and a cooling demand to the pack temperature control.

**The coldest zone sets the packs.** A pack can make only one temperature, and every zone takes its air from the same manifold, so the only arrangement that satisfies every zone is to make the air cold enough for the zone with the greatest cooling demand and add heat everywhere else. The pack temperature control therefore takes the coldest requirement among the zones and commands the packs to it; each zone controller then opens its trim air valve as far as needed to bring its own duct air back up. This is why the trim air valves modulate continuously in normal operation rather than sitting shut, and why a single hot zone (a sunny flight deck, a crowded cabin section) drives the whole aircraft's pack discharge colder.

blocks.title: Zones
rows: COCKPIT, FWD CABIN, CTR CABIN, AFT CABIN
Four selectors on the flight engineer's panel. The lower galley rides with the cabin

The ARO STA zone feeds the aft cabin and cargo area and the ARO compartment; its sensor is in the ARO compartment, so keep the compartment door closed. The boom operator's COMPT TEMP knob trims its target by up to ±3.8 °F in AUTO
Three knobs on the overhead AIR panel

blocks.content: Each zone is a volume of air with its own heat loads (people and equipment) and its own heat loss through the skin, fed by its share of the conditioned air at its duct temperature. The zones are open to each other, so air mixes between neighbors. A zone answers a change of selection over several minutes: the duct temperature moves within seconds and the zone air follows over minutes.

Trim air is bleed air taken **downstream of the pack 1 and pack 3 flow control valves**, before the packs, so it is available only while pack 1 or pack 3 is on; the missing pack 2 on the KC-10 takes nothing away from it. Two **trim air pressure regulating valves**, one each side, feed a common trim air manifold and hold it at about 4 ± 1 psi above cabin pressure. From the manifold, one **trim air valve** per zone meters hot air into that zone's duct. The two regulators are on different DC buses, so losing one bus degrades one side.

The TRIM AIR switch on the flight engineer's panel (TRIM AIR button on the MD-10) opens and closes both regulators together. They also close, together and automatically, if any zone inlet duct or the avionics compartment overheats. One duct overheat shuts off trim air to the whole aircraft: that is how the aircraft is wired, because the most likely cause of a duct or avionics bay overheat is trim air that is too hot or a leaking trim air manifold. The shutoff **latches**. It is reset by switching TRIM AIR off and back on, and relatches at once if the overheat is still present.

blocks.title: Trim air protection
rows: Both trim air regulators closed and latched; DUCT AVIONIC COMPT OVERHEAT light (MD-10: TRIM AIR AVNCS OVHT legend, TRIM AIR OFF alert)
AIR COND TRIM AIR PRESS HI light: a regulator is no longer regulating

blocks.content: **With trim air off** there is no local reheat, and the packs become the aircraft's only temperature control. The pack temperature control then switches to a closed loop on the average of the zones' demands, weighted by each zone's share of the air, and is allowed to heat as well as cool. Every zone now gets the same air, so the zones drift apart: a warm flight deck and a cool cabin cannot both be satisfied. Moving zone selectors still changes the average the packs aim at.

In **AUTO** the zone selector sets a temperature between 65 and 85 °F; the middle of the range is 75 °F (24 °C). The controller runs its trim air valve to hold the zone there and contributes its demand to the pack temperature control. In **MAN** the controller is out of the loop: the crew drive the zone's trim air valve directly toward COLD or HOT, watching the VALVE POS indicator and the DUCT and COMPT temperatures, and the valve stays where it is left (the STOP position). Manual control is the back-up for a zone controller or sensor failure.

A zone controller works on its zone's sensed temperature. A failed zone sensor leaves the controller regulating on a frozen reading, so the zone drifts away from its selection with nothing to show it but the COMPT gauge's indication disagreeing with how the zone feels and with its neighbors; a failed duct sensor also blinds that duct's overheat protection. In both cases MAN takes the faulty sensor out of the loop.

children.title: Cabin temperature with the Virtual Crew

blocks.content: When the Virtual Crew flight engineer is on AUTO and a pack is delivering air, they keep each cabin zone between **65 and 75 °F** with its zone selector. The engineer reads the temperature the panel shows and moves a zone that is outside the band one detent (5 °F) at a time: cooler if it is warmer than 75 °F, warmer if it is colder than 65 °F. Because a zone takes minutes to answer, they wait two minutes before their first move and at least two minutes between moves on the same zone. The engineer leaves the cockpit selector to the pilots and does not touch a zone selector that has been set to MAN or STOP.

On APU air alone the packs may not reach the selection on a hot day; the flight engineer then keeps stepping colder, down to the 65 °F detent, which asks the packs for all the cooling they have. See [Virtual Crew](virtual-crew).

The pack outlets join the **conditioned air manifold** through check valves, so a pack that is off cannot draw air backwards out of the manifold. From the manifold, risers carry air to each zone in fixed proportions; trim air joins each zone's duct downstream of the split. Ground connectors on the manifold accept preconditioned air from a ground cart, which then supplies the zones exactly as the packs would, without loading the bleed system.

Air leaves the cabin through grilles near the floor into the **utility tunnels** that run the length of the fuselage beside the lower cargo compartments, warming the compartment walls as it passes, and from there is drawn aft to the outflow valve. This through-flow, rather than the electric or jet-pump heating, is what keeps the lower compartments warm in flight on a healthy aircraft.

The preconditioned air cart is called and set from the EFB's Ground Ops page: one or two connections, a flow of 50 to 400 lb/min per connection, and a temperature of 35 to 90 °F. Delivered air comes up and down over a couple of seconds. Airborne, the connections deliver nothing; the cart disconnects and leaves if the aircraft moves. See [Ground Operations](ground-operations).

The avionics compartment under the flight deck is cooled by cabin air drawn through the equipment racks. In flight the cabin differential pressure does the work: rack exhaust is dumped overboard through a **venturi** whose valve is open in flight, so the cooling flow is a small, deliberate cabin leak. On the ground and at low differential there is no pressure to drive the venturi, and cooling **fans** carry the racks instead (on the aircraft they run whenever the differential is below about 1.3 psid). The venturi valve is closed on the ground to stop inflow.

The AVIONIC FLOW switch (NORM, OVRD) gives the crew an override: OVRD closes the venturi valve and turns the cooling fans on. It is used when cabin inflow is short (operating on one pack) to stop the venturi's share of the outflow, and when the AVIONICS FLOW OFF light reports low cooling flow. A fan that has failed may keep the light on even in OVRD. The **center accessory compartment**, which houses electrical equipment, has its own fan drawing tunnel air through it and a CTR ACCESS COMPT FLOW OFF light; in flight the outflow valve's suction keeps it ventilated even with the fan failed.

The MD-10's equivalent is the AVNCS FAN switchlight on the AIR panel: pushed, it closes the venturi valve and turns on the exhaust fan (OVRD legend, AVNCS FAN OVRD alert); its FLOW legend comes on when avionics cooling flow is low. All avionics fans failed with no flow gives AVNCS AIR FLO OFF, and a center accessory compartment fan failure CAC AIR FLO OFF.

The avionics compartment overheat switch closes both trim air regulators. It is set high enough to act only on a real overheat, such as a trim air manifold leak in the bay, and shows as the DUCT AVIONIC COMPT OVERHEAT light (MD-10: AVNCS OVHT and AVNCS COMPT OVHT).

The KC-10's ARO compartment equipment rack has its own three-phase cooling fan and flow switch. Above about 1.5 psid the cabin differential cools the rack and the fan stops; at low differential the fan runs. Low flow lights AR AVIONIC FLOW OFF on the flight engineer's panel and AVIONIC FLOW OFF at the ARO station.

The forward and aft lower cargo compartments each have a pneumatic **jet pump** that drives a circulation of air around the compartment, and a temperature control valve that meters hot air into it. On the aircraft the center compartment is also heated by jet-pump air from pneumatic system 2; in the simulation it has no supply of its own and is warmed only by the cabin air in the utility tunnels. On the DC-10 the GALLEY VENT switch (the lavatory/galley vent and cargo heat switch) on the flight engineer's panel turns the jet-pump supply on and off.

On the DC-10 cargo panel, the FWD CARGO TEMP selector regulates the forward compartment at LO or runs it HIGH (valve fully open), and the AFT CARGO TEMP selector sets the aft compartment between 40 and 90 °F or HIGH; on either, MAN HOT and MAN COLD drive the valve directly and STOP holds it. Three CARGO COMPT TEMP gauges show the forward, center and aft compartment temperatures. A cargo fire shuts the affected compartment's ventilation automatically to starve the fire of air; see [Fire Protection](fire-protection).
On the MD-10 cargo heat and ventilation run automatically, and the compartment temperatures are shown on the AIR synoptic page.

The flight deck, cabin, lower cargo compartments, avionics compartment and center accessory compartment form one pressure vessel, pressurized by the conditioned air from the packs. Pressure is controlled by regulating the outflow: a single **outflow valve** group in the aft fuselage, positioned by one of the means of control, sets how fast the air leaves.

**The physics.** The cabin's air mass changes at the rate inflow minus outflow. The packs deliver a nearly constant mass flow; the outflow through the valve and the leaks rises with the differential pressure and with the valve's opening, and above a modest differential the flow through the valve is choked and depends only on cabin pressure and valve area. For any valve position there is therefore one cabin pressure at which outflow equals inflow, and the cabin settles there. A cabin of the DC-10's size holds well over a thousand pounds of air and its pressure time constant is measured in minutes, so the controller does not need to move the valve quickly: it trims the valve's position to make the cabin's rate of change follow its command, and the cabin altitude follows the rate.

**What the schedule balances.** A low cabin altitude is comfortable and keeps the passengers' oxygen pressure up; a high differential stresses the fuselage on every flight and shortens its fatigue life. The controller keeps the cabin at the departure field for the takeoff and initial climb, climbs it on a programmed schedule as the aircraft climbs, and lets its scheduled maximum of **8.6 psid** set the cabin altitude at high cruise (the safety valves relieve at 9.1 psi; see [Limitations](limitations#air-conditioning-pressurization)): at FL420, 8.6 psid is a cabin altitude of about 7,600 ft. Rates of change are limited for comfort (500 fpm up, 300 fpm down normally), because ears are more sensitive to a descending cabin than a climbing one.

blocks.alt: Functional diagram of DC-10 cabin pressure control: pack inflow into the pressurized fuselage (flight deck, cabin, cargo compartments, avionics bay); outflow paths through the aft outflow valve group (ram air shield, outflow butterfly valve, thrust recovery valve in sequence), the avionics venturi and airframe leakage; three positive pressure relief valves; the automatic controller (AUTO and SEMI-AUTO), the standby controller and the manual cable wheel driving the outflow valve through a common gearbox and sequencer; the independent cabin altitude warning switch; the indicators: cabin altitude and differential pressure, cabin rate, outflow valve position.
blocks.title: Cabin pressure control

blocks.content: The outflow valve is a group of three moving surfaces driven through one sequencer, so it has one position: the **ram air shield**, which deflects the airstream to create low pressure over the valve during takeoff and landing; the **outflow butterfly valve**, which handles the flow at low altitude and low differential; and the **thrust recovery valve**, which handles it at moderate to high differential and recovers some thrust from the exhausting air. Two electric actuators drive a shared gearbox, one for the automatic controller and one for the standby controller, each interlocked so that only one can drive at a time; full travel takes about 5.5 seconds. A cable from the manual wheel on the flight engineer's panel drives the same sequencer mechanically.

At cruise the valve operates nearly closed, because choked flow at cruise cabin pressure passes a great deal of air through a small opening. On the ground it is sized to pass the full flow of all three packs at almost no differential, so the doors can be opened at the gate. The OUTFLOW VALVE position indicator on the flight engineer's panel (OUTFLO on the MD-10 synoptic) shows the valve in every mode.

Three **positive pressure relief valves** protect the structure if the controller fails to limit the differential. They start to open at about 8.85 psid and are fully open at 9.1 psid, which is the maximum relief valve differential. Because the controller's own limit is 8.6 psid, a healthy aircraft never reaches them, and the CAB PRESS RELIEF OPEN light (MD-10: CABIN PRES RELIEF) always means something has gone wrong with pressure control. On the aircraft a flapper door at each relief valve's exhaust is held slightly open after the valve has lifted, an indication for the ground crew; its edge is painted red.

**Negative pressure** (outside pressure higher than cabin pressure, as in a fast descent with the cabin above the aircraft) is relieved at a small negative differential, so the fuselage is never loaded in the direction it is not built for.

In **AUTO** the automatic cabin pressure controller schedules the cabin through three flight phases, using the aircraft's pressure altitude, the landing field elevation set on the ALT SET scale and corrected by the LDG BARO setting, and the rate limits set on the RATE LIMIT selector.

blocks.title: Automatic schedule
rows: Weight on wheels, below takeoff thrust
Outflow valve fully open; no differential. After touchdown the cabin returns to field pressure
Held at the departure field elevation (zero cabin rate) until the aircraft has climbed 5,000 ft above the field
The higher of two targets: the dwell shelf (2,700 or 4,500 ft, at half the selected rate) or the programmed altitude for the present aircraft altitude, never below the 8.6 psid limit
The aircraft descends 1,000 ft below its highest altitude

Dwell and half rate cancelled. The cabin goes at the full rate limit to 300 ft below the selected landing altitude, following the programmed schedule if it meets it first. A climb back returns to the climb and cruise logic

blocks.content: **Two laws in the climb.** The dwell logic moves the cabin at half rate to a shelf matched to the destination, 2,700 ft for a low landing field and 4,500 ft for a high one, and holds it there, so that on a short flight the cabin makes one gentle climb and one gentle descent instead of following every change of aircraft altitude. The programmed altitude function raises the cabin with aircraft altitude along a schedule that keeps the differential just inside its limit at each altitude. Whichever target is higher wins, so the cabin sits on the shelf until the programmed schedule overtakes it, and then follows the schedule. The rate of change is the smaller of the programmed rate and the selected rate limit.

**The structural limit outranks the rate limit.** If the aircraft climbs faster than the cabin can follow at its rate limit, the differential would rise past 8.6 psid. When that happens the controller lets the cabin climb faster to stay on the differential limit; comfort gives way to structure. The rate limit selector is set to its index (500 fpm up, 300 fpm down) for normal AUTO operation.

blocks.alt: Graph of the DC-10 automatic pressurization schedule: aircraft altitude 0 to 42,000 ft on the horizontal axis, cabin altitude 0 to 8,000 ft on the vertical axis. Curves: the 8.6 psid maximum differential line reaching about 7,600 ft cabin at 42,000 ft; the programmed altitude schedule just above it; the dwell shelves at 2,700 and 4,500 ft; the takeoff hold at field elevation to 5,000 ft above the field; a descent leg to 300 ft below the landing field. Sample flight profile overlaid.
blocks.title: Automatic pressurization schedule
Typical cruise cabin altitude in AUTO

blocks.content: **Landing.** Set the destination field elevation on ALT SET and the destination altimeter setting on LDG BARO before descent; the controller uses the two together as the field's pressure altitude. The cabin is brought to 300 ft below that, so the aircraft lands very slightly pressurized and the cabin is never above the field at touchdown. At touchdown the controller drives the outflow valve fully open and the small remaining differential bleeds off. The maximum differential for takeoff and landing is 0.5 psi.
For touch-and-go landings select SEMI-AUTO: in AUTO each touchdown returns the controller to its ground logic and opens the outflow valve.

**SEMI-AUTO** is a mode of the same automatic controller. The ALT SET scale becomes the commanded cabin altitude rather than the landing field, and the RATE LIMIT selector sets the rate at which the cabin goes there: from 100 fpm up or 60 fpm down at its counterclockwise stop, through 500 up and 300 down at the index, to 2,000 up and 1,200 down at the clockwise stop. The takeoff hold, dwell shelves and half-rate logic are cancelled, but the 8.6 psid limit still applies: if the selected cabin altitude would need more differential than that, the controller holds the limit instead.

SEMI-AUTO is used when AUTO is not following its schedule properly, for touch-and-go landings, and whenever the crew want to fly the cabin to a particular altitude. The SEMI-AUTO ON light shows that the semi-automatic mode has the outflow valve. Because SEMI-AUTO depends on the automatic controller, a failure of that controller takes both AUTO and SEMI-AUTO away.

The **standby controller** is a separate box with its own actuator and its own power supply, a back-up for the automatic controller. It is a pure **rate** controller: there is no altitude target anywhere in it. With STANDBY selected (the STBY ON switchlight), the CABIN ALT RATE knob commands the cabin's rate of climb or descent: centerd, the cabin holds the altitude it is at; turned toward UP or DOWN, the cabin climbs or descends at a rate proportional to the knob's deflection, up to the rates set on the RATE LIMIT selector. The crew fly the cabin by rate, watching the cabin altitude and rate indicators.
The KC-10 has no standby controller; its back-up to the automatic controller is manual control.

**Manual** control is a cable from the CAB ALT control wheel on the flight engineer's panel to the outflow valve's sequencer, engaged by moving the CAB PRESS MAN/AUTO handle to MAN. It needs no electrical power at all, which makes it the last resort: it works with both electric actuators dead and both controllers failed. In the electric modes the wheel and the OUTFLOW VALVE indicator follow the valve; in MAN the wheel sets the valve's position and the valve travels there, more slowly than under electric drive. Opening the valve raises the cabin altitude; closing it lowers it. The crew control the cabin by small wheel movements, watching the cabin rate indicator, and must open the valve fully after landing to depressurize the aircraft.

In manual, avoid a wide-open outflow valve in flight: more than about two-thirds open can draw the cabin below outside pressure and is noisy. For unpressurized flight the outflow valve is set between half and two-thirds open (see [Limitations](limitations)).

Only one means of control drives the outflow valve at a time, and which one is decided by the crew's selection. If the selected channel has lost its power or failed, it does not hand over to another: it becomes **inoperative** and the valve stays where it was. The cabin then drifts as the aircraft climbs or descends, and the crew must select another mode. The SEMI-AUTO ON and STANDBY ON lights report the channel actually driving the valve, so a selection that has not taken shows dark.

blocks.title: Pressurization control channels
rows: AC (CABIN PRESS AUTO CONT, AC bus 1)
AC (CABIN PRESS STBY CONT, AC bus 2)
Overrides all others. Works with the actuators dead

blocks.content: The switches are independent on the panel and are resolved in order of authority: MANUAL (the CAB PRESS MAN/AUTO handle at MAN) overrides everything, then STANDBY, then the AUTO/SEMI-AUTO mode switch.

The cabin altitude warning comes from an **independent pressure switch** with its own sensing, not from the pressure controller. That independence is the point: a controller flying the cabin to the wrong altitude because of a failed sensor is exactly when the crew need a warning that does not share the failure. The switch closes at about **10,000 ft** cabin altitude and opens again at about **8,000 ft**.

On the DC-10 and KC-10 it sounds the cabin altitude horn in both pilots' consoles and lights the red CABIN ALT lights on the flight engineer's panel and the pilots' overhead annunciator panel, with the MASTER WARNING. The CABIN ALT WARN HORN button silences the horn; the lights stay on until the cabin has descended below about 8,000 ft, so a silenced warning is not forgotten. On the MD-10 it raises the CABIN ALTITUDE alert and the cabin ALT readout turns red. See [Warning Systems](warning-systems), [Oxygen](oxygen) for the masks, and [Emergency Procedures](emergency-procedures) for decompression and emergency descent.

The FedEx MD-10 conversion fitted two digital cabin pressure controllers with automatic channel changeover and an electric manual mode, controlled from a CABIN PRESS panel on the overhead and fed with the landing field elevation by the flight management system. **In the simulation the MD-10 is pressurized by the same automatic controller as the DC-10**, with the three-phase schedule, the dwell shelves and the 500 fpm up and 300 fpm down rate limits described above, and it runs in AUTO for the whole flight.

The overhead CABIN PRESS panel is not functional in the simulation, and the landing field elevation stays at its default of sea level. Landing at a field well above sea level, the cabin is therefore still below the field elevation at touchdown and the aircraft lands with some differential, which bleeds off quickly when the outflow valve opens on the ground. The AIR synoptic page shows cabin altitude, differential, rate, landing altitude and outflow valve position (see [Controls and indicators](#controls-and-indicators)).

On the DC-10 and KC-10 the air conditioning controls share the flight engineer's PNEU & AIR COND SYS panel (Upper Panel No. 2) with the pneumatic controls, and the pressurization controls and indicators are grouped beside it, with the manual outflow wheel on the lower panel. The DC-10's cargo temperature controls are on the cargo panel. On the MD-10 the air conditioning is controlled from the overhead AIR panel and monitored on the AIR synoptic page.

blocks.content: In normal operation the packs, the zone controllers and the automatic pressure controller run the cabin with no crew input beyond setting the zone temperatures and the destination on ALT SET and LDG BARO. The crew's work is at the transitions (ground air to engine air, takeoff, landing) and in reconfiguring after a failure. The full checklists are in [Normal Procedures](normal-procedures).

items: **On the ground.** Conditioned air comes from the packs running on APU or ground cart air (see [Pneumatics](pneumatics)), or from a preconditioned air cart on the conditioned air manifold. With the pack selectors and zone selectors at AUTO and TRIM AIR on, the cabin settles at its selections in five to ten minutes. On a hot day the APU's air may not let the packs reach a cold selection. (The APU delivers more air at its engine-start speed, which it runs at whenever the APU/ISOL VALVE switch is at OPEN and the ENG IGNITION selector is out of OFF; see [APU](apu).) The CAB PRESS MAN/AUTO handle is at AUTO; in AUTO on the ground the outflow valve is fully open.
**Engine start.** The packs are selected to PACK OFF so the APU's air goes to the starters, and back to AUTO after start once the engines are supplying the pneumatic systems.

**Takeoff.** Set the packs as the takeoff data requires: on for a normal takeoff, or off for a packs-off takeoff (see [Pneumatics](pneumatics) for bleeds-off takeoffs). As takeoff thrust is set the pressure controller holds the cabin at the departure field elevation.

**Climb.** Once 5,000 ft above the field the cabin begins to climb on schedule. Check the cabin rate and altitude and that the differential stays below the white arc. After a packs-off takeoff, return the packs to AUTO one at a time once climb power is set and the engine supplies are on.

**Cruise.** The cabin sits on its schedule, with the differential approaching 8.6 psid at the higher cruise levels. Adjust zone temperatures as needed; the packs settle cold and the trim air valves modulate.

**Before descent.** Check the destination field elevation on ALT SET and set the destination altimeter setting on LDG BARO. The controller begins its descent schedule when the aircraft has descended 1,000 ft.
**Landing.** The cabin arrives about 300 ft below the field elevation and the outflow valve opens at touchdown. For touch-and-go landings select SEMI-AUTO.
**After landing and shutdown.** Packs as required for ground conditioning; at shutdown TRIM AIR goes OFF.

blocks.content: When the Virtual Crew flies the flight engineer's seat, the packs are run through these transitions from the checklists, and the cabin zone temperatures are kept between 65 and 75 °F (see [Cabin temperature with the Virtual Crew](#virtual-crew-cabin-temperature)). ALT SET and LDG BARO remain checklist items for the crew to confirm.

Before start the PACK switchlights are pushed off so the APU's air goes to the starters; after start, with the bleeds on, the packs are switched back on. For a packs-off takeoff the packs stay off until after takeoff (PACKS ALL OFF memo). Zone temperatures are set with the three knobs and the rest is automatic, including the pressurization, which needs no crew input in the simulation.

children.title: Reduced pack operation and unpressurized flight

blocks.content: One pack supplies enough air to pressurize the aircraft even at its maximum altitude, because the outflow valve simply closes further to hold the cabin with less inflow. The margin goes to the leaks: with less inflow the valve runs nearer its closed stop, and any extra leakage shows as a cabin that can no longer hold its schedule. On the DC-10 and KC-10, when operating on one pack select AVIONIC FLOW to OVRD, which closes the avionics venturi and removes its share of the outflow.

With all packs off the cabin cannot be held: the outflow valve closes completely and the cabin climbs as the air leaks away. Unpressurized flight is conducted with the cabin pressure control in MANUAL and the outflow valve between half and two-thirds open (see [Limitations](limitations)).

**Pack load on the bleed system.** Each pack is a large load on its engine's bleed system, and the number of packs one engine supply can carry at high power is limited (one pack plus wing anti-ice at takeoff, go-around or maximum continuous power; two packs, or one pack plus wing anti-ice, below that). See [Bleed load per engine](pneumatics#bleed-load-limits).

To run a pack in manual, select it on the PACK IND SEL so the condition gauges show it, then drive the pack selector to MAN COLD or MAN HOT in short movements, watching the PACK TEMP VALVE POS and PACK DISCH TEMP gauges, and release it to STOP. When starting a pack in manual, position the valve between nine and twelve o'clock first; once flow is established adjust it in small steps. Expect a large change in the pneumatic supply when takeoff power is applied or reduced, and monitor the pack closely in descent, when it can overheat.

To run a zone in manual, turn its selector out of the AUTO arc and hold MAN COLD or MAN HOT while watching its VALVE POS indicator and COMPT/DUCT gauge, then release to STOP. If the valve does not move or the temperatures do not change, set TRIM AIR to OFF and let the packs alone control the temperature.

blocks.content: Air conditioning failures are rarely urgent on their own: a lost pack costs comfort and margin, and the aircraft can be pressurized on one. Pressurization failures range from a controller that has stopped following its schedule, which the crew take over with another mode, to a decompression, which is an emergency. The procedures are in [Emergency Procedures](emergency-procedures) (cabin altitude warning, rapid depressurization and emergency descent, smoke) and [Abnormal Procedures](abnormal-procedures) (PACK OFF light, trim air, avionics flow, automatic pressurization failure, standby, semi-auto and manual pressurization, CAB PRESS RELIEF OPEN).

blocks.content: During initial pressurization after takeoff, if the normal cabin schedule cannot be held in AUTO or manual and the OUTFLOW VALVE indicator shows fully closed, the cabin is losing air faster than the packs can supply it. Stop the climb and begin a descent immediately (see [Emergency Procedures](emergency-procedures)).

A selected pressurization mode that has lost its controller does not hand over to another one. If the cabin rate departs from what the schedule should give, check which mode light is on and select the next mode yourself.

**One cabin, one pressure.** The simulation treats the whole pressurized fuselage as a single vessel. The flight deck, cabin zones, lower cargo compartments, avionics compartment and center accessory compartment always share one pressure, so there are no differences between compartments and no compartment relief or decompression panels acting separately. Cabin pressure comes from a real mass balance: the packs' delivered flow (and ground conditioned air) goes in; the outflow valve, the airframe's leakage, the avionics venturi, any open door or hole and the relief valves let it out. Cabin altitude, differential and rate therefore respond to pack flow, valve position and leaks as they would in the aircraft (switch off a pack in cruise and the outflow valve closes further; switch them all off and the cabin climbs), and a decompression empties the whole hull at a rate set by the size of the hole. The temperature zones are separate thermal volumes inside that single pressure.

**Packs.** Each pack is modeled by its behavior (discharge temperature, the range its temperature control can reach, its flow and its trip) rather than as a chain of compressor, exchanger and turbine stations: the turbine inlet temperature, bypass valve position and discharge temperature on the gauges are real model values. Cooling depends on the bleed temperature it is given, outside air temperature and airspeed, and on the ground on the ACM's fan. The pack overheat trip is sensed at the pack discharge, about 200 °F; on the aircraft it is sensed in the machine. The temperature control commands one discharge temperature to every pack from the coldest zone, where the aircraft's lowest numbered pack follows all zones and the others the cabin zones only; the difference shows only when the flight deck is the coldest demand.

**Pressurization.** The automatic controller's phases, dwell shelves, rate limits, differential limit and landing logic follow the maintenance manual; the interior of the programmed cabin schedule is an estimate laid between its known end points, so cabin altitudes at intermediate cruise levels are approximate. The airframe's leak rate is sized to pass the aircraft's own leak check (differential falling from 7 to 6 psid in no less than 182 seconds). When a flight starts in the air, the cabin starts pressurized on the controller's schedule with the zones at their selected temperatures.

**Not modeled.** Recirculation and individual (gasper) air are not modeled. The cabin air shutoff handle, the ram air ventilation valve handle, the air conditioning compartment doors light and the pack 3 controlled-leak line are not modeled, and the -1 steps that use them cannot be flown. The avionics cooling fans run continuously; their automatic shutdown at high differential is not modeled (the KC-10's ARO rack fan does stop above about 1.5 psid). The lower cargo electric heaters have no switch and stay off, and there are no FWD or AFT CARGO VENT switches or CARGO FLOW OFF lights; compartment heat comes from cabin air and the jet-pump circulation, and the center compartment's own jet-pump heating is not modeled. The FWD CARGO TEMP selector's HIGH position runs the valve fully open, where FedEx's LO-HI selector regulates the compartment between about 40 and 65 °F. The KC-10's chemical defense equipment has no crew controls.

**MD-10.** The overhead CABIN PRESS panel is not functional: the MD-10 runs the DC-10's automatic controller for the whole flight, with the landing field elevation at its default of sea level, so it lands at high-elevation fields with some differential (which bleeds off quickly when the outflow valve opens). The CABIN AIR switchlight, the ECON switch, the auxiliary panel's CARGO HEAT and manual trim air valve switches, and the right observer's station pack gauges and manual pack controls are not modeled. The alerts CABIN RATE, CABIN INFLO LO, CPC FAULT, LDG ALTITUDE MAN, SET LDG ALTITUDE, OPEN OUTFLO VALVE, PACK n FLO DISAG, AVNCS EXH FLO OFF, CAB AIR NOT OFF, CABIN AIR OFF, LWR CARGO TEMP LO and the cargo heat alerts are not raised. Cargo set temperatures are not shown on the synoptic.

**Other differences.** On the DC-10 and KC-10, a pack's flow control valve does not close when its supply pressure is lost: a pack with no air shows zero on its FLOW gauge without a PACK OFF light. With its shutoff solenoid unpowered the valve closes, where FedEx's opens. The amber air conditioning lights on the flight engineer's panel do not raise the master caution in the simulation. STANDBY is engaged by pushing the STBY ON switchlight (and released by pushing it again) rather than by pulling the rate knob, as on some aircraft.

parts.title: Ice and Rain Protection
parts.summary: Bleed-air anti-icing of the outboard slats and engine inlets, electric heat for the air data sensors and windshields, rain removal, and the ice zones the aircraft leaves unprotected.

sections.title: Introduction
sections.summary: What is protected, what is not, and the two kinds of energy that do the protecting.

blocks.content: The ice and rain protection system keeps ice off the parts of the aircraft where it would do the most harm, and keeps the forward windshields clear. It uses two sources of energy. **Hot compressor bleed air** heats the five outboard leading-edge slats on each wing and the inlet lip (nose cowl) of each engine; on the DC-10 and KC-10 the same kind of air also heats the upper VHF antenna, whose ice would otherwise be shed straight into the No. 2 engine. **Electric heaters** warm the pitot tubes, static ports, angle-of-attack vanes and total air temperature probe, the outer ply of both forward windshields, the inner plies of the windshields and clearview windows, and, on the KC-10, the boom operator's aft and lower windows. Two independent electric wipers clear rain from the windshields.

Much of the airframe is deliberately left without protection. The inboard slats, the fan blades and spinners, the radome, the wiper arms and the whole tail (horizontal and vertical stabilizer) have no ice protection on any aircraft of the family. There is no ice detector either. The crew recognize **icing conditions** from total air temperature and visible moisture, and confirm ice by looking at the wiper arms and the window frames, which are unheated and sit in plain view.

Every bleed-air and electric system here is an **anti-icing** system rather than a de-icing system: it is designed to keep a surface warm enough that ice never forms on it, so it must be switched on before ice builds, not used to remove ice afterwards. A cowl lip or slat that has already collected a load of ice may shed it in pieces when heat is applied, and on an engine those pieces go into the fan.

blocks.title: Ice zones and how each is protected
blocks.caption: The zone layout the rest of this part walks through. Every aircraft in the family has the same zones, except that only the KC-10 has heated boom operator's windows.

blocks.content: Cloud and fog droplets do not freeze just because the air is below 0 °C. Freezing needs a nucleus to start on, and small, clean droplets can stay liquid down to about −40 °C. Such **supercooled** water is unstable: the moment a droplet strikes a surface, the surface provides the nucleus and the droplet freezes, wholly or in part. Airframe icing is therefore the meeting of three things: liquid water in the air (the **liquid water content**, in grams per cubic meter), a surface moving through it, and a surface temperature at or below freezing.

How fast ice grows on a given surface is, to a good approximation, the product of four terms: the **collection efficiency** of the surface, the liquid water content, the true airspeed, and the **freezing fraction**. Each term means something different, and together they explain almost everything a crew sees in icing.

**Collection efficiency** is the share of the droplets in the surface's path that actually hit it. It depends on the size of the body compared with the droplets' inertia. A body with a small leading-edge radius (a pitot mast, a thin vane, a wiper arm, the thin sections of the tail) cannot push the air aside far enough ahead of itself to deflect the droplets, so it catches nearly all of them. A large, blunt body such as the radome bends the airflow well upstream and the droplets are carried around it. This is why a pitot tube can ice over in minutes while the radome beside it is barely marked, and why an unprotected stabilizer collects more ice per foot of span than the wing does.

**True airspeed** sweeps more cloud per second through the surface's path, so a fast aircraft ices faster than a slow one in the same cloud.

The **freezing fraction** is set by the surface temperature. Well below freezing, colder than roughly −10 °C at the surface, every droplet freezes where it lands. The result is **rime ice**: white, opaque, porous, growing forward into the airflow in a shape that roughly follows the leading edge. Closer to 0 °C, only part of each droplet freezes on impact and the rest runs aft before freezing. The result is **clear (glaze) ice**: dense, transparent, hard to see, and prone to growing the double-horn shapes that destroy a leading edge's aerodynamics. Large drops, such as freezing drizzle and freezing rain, run back even further, beyond any heated area, and form ridges where the aircraft has no protection at all. That is why flight in freezing rain or severe icing is to be avoided.

rows: Small droplets, surface well below freezing
Roughness and added drag; follows the leading edge, sheds relatively easily
Horn shapes and runback; hard to see; heavy and strongly bonded
Surface below the frost point (often on the ground)

blocks.content:
**Why the criterion is total air temperature.** A leading edge does not sit at the static air temperature. Air brought to rest at the stagnation line is heated by compression, by roughly V²/2cₚ, which is about 11 °C at 300 kt true airspeed and about 6 °C at 220 kt. A leading edge in air at −8 °C static can therefore sit just above freezing in fast cruise and below it at holding speed in the same cloud. The aircraft's own probes measure total air temperature (TAT), which includes that rise, so the operating criterion is written on TAT: in flight, icing conditions exist when TAT is 6 °C or below and visible moisture in any form is present. On the ground the same 6 °C applies to outside air temperature, with visible moisture or a temperature-dewpoint spread of 3 °C or less, or with snow, ice, slush or standing water on the surfaces the engines can ingest from. The [limitations](limitations) section carries the exact wording.

Severity rises toward the warm end of that band: warmer clouds hold more liquid water, and the worst encounters are found between about 0 and −20 °C TAT. Colder clouds are increasingly made of ice crystals, which bounce off a cold airframe instead of sticking.

**What thermal anti-icing has to do.** To stay clear, a heated surface must stay above freezing wherever water strikes it. The heat it needs is set by the convective loss to the cold air flowing over it, plus the heat needed to warm the impinging water and, if it is to stay dry, to evaporate it. Water that is warmed but not evaporated runs back past the heated area and can freeze again behind it as **runback ice**. That loss grows with airspeed and liquid water content, which is why the pneumatic system schedules hotter, higher-pressure air whenever wing anti-ice is in use, and why a heated surface can, in an extreme encounter, collect ice even with its protection working correctly.

On the ground the hazard is different. Nothing is moving through cloud, so leading-edge accretion is not the problem; contamination that settles or grows on the upper surfaces is. **Snow** and ice pellets settle at the rate they fall on a skin at or below freezing. **Freezing rain and drizzle** freeze where they land and form clear ice. **Frost** grows directly from water vapour wherever the skin is colder than the air's frost point, even under a clear sky. **Freezing fog** drifts across a parked wing and rimes its windward surfaces.

The skin over an integral fuel tank follows the fuel, not the air. An aircraft that has spent hours at altitude lands with fuel far below freezing, and the wing skin it wets can collect frost and clear ice in air well above 0 °C: the **cold-soaked fuel** case. A full tank wets the whole upper skin; a tank drained to a third or less leaves an air gap and the skin follows the air again.

None of the aircraft's anti-icing heats the wing upper surfaces: the wing anti-ice heats only the outboard slats' leading edges, and it is inhibited on the ground in any case. The only removal is a de-icing crew's fluid. Under the **clean aircraft concept**, no frost, snow or ice may be adhering to the wings, tail or control surfaces at takeoff. Hot Type I fluid strips the contamination; a thickened Type IV coat applied as the second step of a two-step procedure protects the wing afterwards for longer. The fluid absorbs what falls on it until it is diluted past its freezing point; the time that takes is the **holdover time**, which shortens as precipitation gets heavier. The fluid is designed to shear off during the takeoff roll.

Even a thin layer of frost on the upper wing surface roughens the boundary layer enough to raise stall speed and reduce climb performance significantly. Snow cannot be relied on to blow away during the takeoff roll, and ice may be bonded underneath it.

Procedures for cold-weather preflight, de-icing and anti-icing, engine start and taxi are in [Adverse weather](adverse-weather). The EFB's ground services offer de-icing with Type I fluid alone or a two-step Type I then Type IV application, and GSX de-icing trucks are recognized as well (see [Ground operations](ground-operations)).

sections.title: Ice zones
sections.summary: Every place ice can form on the aircraft, protected or not, and what each zone is doing.

blocks.content: The clearest way to understand this system is as a list of **ice zones**: every surface where ice can form, whether or not anything protects it. The unprotected zones matter as much as the protected ones, because they are what the crew's procedures are about: keeping the slats retracted in slush, running the fans up to shed ice, avoiding freezing rain because the tail has no protection. The EFB's ICE page draws each zone where it is on the airframe, with its state and the ice it is carrying (see [EFB ice and rain page](#ci-efb)).
