blocks.content: The upper VHF antenna on the DC-10 and KC-10 is protected by bleed air too, but the simulation does not track ice on it as a zone; its valve and its DISAGREE light are fully modeled (see [Upper VHF antenna anti-ice](#antenna-anti-ice)).

**Leading edges.** Each wing has eight leading-edge slats. The five outermost (4 to 8) are anti-iced; the three inboard slats are not. The outboard wing has the thinnest section, so it collects ice fastest, and it carries the outboard ailerons; keeping its leading edge clean preserves lift and roll control at high angles of attack. The inboard slats have no protection, so they can carry ice into the approach. If ice has been encountered, the crew de-ice the outboard leading edges with wing anti-ice before extending the slats.

**Engines.** The cowl lip is the only part of the engine inlet that is heated. The fan blades and the spinner are not: ice that grows there is thrown off by centrifugal force, which is why the procedures periodically raise N1 in prolonged icing. Shed fan ice can strike the acoustic panels in the fan case and causes a short rise in N1 vibration as it goes.

**Air data probes and vanes.** These are the smallest bodies on the aircraft and so the fastest to ice. A pitot tube or static port that ices up corrupts every instrument and computer that uses it, which is why every probe has its own heater on its own circuit, spread across buses so that a single electrical failure costs only some of them. See [Air data sensor heat](#air-data-heat).

**Windows and wipers.** The forward windshields are heated on their outer ply. The wiper arms parked along the lower frame are not, and they are the one piece of the airframe the crew can actually watch icing in flight.

**Tail and radome.** The tail surfaces carry no ice protection at all, a positive design decision that runs through all the aircraft's documentation: an iced tail is avoided by avoiding prolonged severe icing and freezing rain, not by heating it. The radome's blunt shape keeps its collection low.

sections.title: Wing anti-ice
sections.summary: Hot pneumatic-system air through the five outboard slats of each wing, held off on the ground.

blocks.content: Wing anti-ice heats the leading edges of the five outboard slats (4 to 8) on each wing with hot air from the pneumatic manifold. The left wing is supplied from pneumatic system 1 and the right wing from pneumatic system 3; each side has its own shutoff valve, and one control (the FE's WING ANTI-ICE switch on the DC-10 and KC-10, the WING switchlight on the MD-10) commands both valves together. The inboard slats are not heated.

blocks.alt: Functional schematic of DC-10 wing anti-ice, both wings. Pneumatic manifold sections 1 and 3 each feed a wing anti-ice shutoff valve in the wing leading edge. From each valve a duct runs spanwise through the fixed leading edge to slat 3, drops into a telescoping slip-tube duct, and feeds piccolo tubes running through slats 4 to 8. Show the piccolo holes discharging into the slat nose cavity, the double-skin passage and the overboard exit at the slat's lower trailing edge. Show the valve solenoid powered through the WING ANTI-ICE switch and the ground-sensing relays, and the two valve position switches wired to the L and R WING ANTI-ICE DISAGREE lights. Inboard slats 1 to 3 shown unheated.
blocks.title: Wing anti-ice system

blocks.content: Each wing has eight leading-edge slats. A duct leaves the wing anti-ice shutoff valve, runs outboard through the fixed leading edge as far as slat 3, and then drops into a **telescoping duct**: a trombone-type slip tube with sealed bushings and a slip elbow at each end, so the duct keeps its integrity while the slats travel between retracted and fully extended. From there **piccolo tubes** run through slats 4 to 8. A piccolo tube is a duct pierced with many small holes; the holes meter the flow and spread it evenly along the span, aiming the hot air at the inside of the slat nose. The air then passes aft through the slat's double-skin passages, giving up its heat to the skin, and is discharged overboard at the slat's lower trailing edge. Because the telescoping duct works at any slat position, wing anti-ice is available in every configuration.

The air comes from the engine bleed system through the pneumatic manifold. Whenever a pneumatic system is supplying anti-ice air its pressure controller works in its high-flow mode and lowers its duct temperature set point slightly, trading a little temperature for the much larger flow the slats need; the system then delivers air at up to about 45 psig and roughly 230 °C. Each wing draws a flow comparable to an air-conditioning pack's, which is why wing anti-ice affects pneumatic pressure, engine bleed extraction and, through them, EGT and fuel burn (see [Effects on the pneumatic system and engines](#wing-anti-ice-bleed) and [Pneumatics](pneumatics)).

**The shutoff valve** is spring- and pressure-loaded closed, pneumatically operated and electrically controlled. Energizing its solenoid lets pneumatic pressure act on the actuator piston against the spring and the valve opens; it stays open only while the solenoid is energized **and** pressure is present. Loss of electrical power therefore closes the valve, and wing anti-ice is not available without power: the opposite of the engine cowl valves, which open when power is lost. Each valve carries two position switches that drive its DISAGREE light, and a visual position indicator for ground checks. A full stroke takes a few seconds.

Hot pneumatic air with no airflow over the slats would overheat and damage them in seconds. Ground-sensing relays therefore override the switch: with the aircraft on the ground both valves are commanded closed whatever the switch says. Selecting wing anti-ice ON before takeoff **arms** the system, and the valves open when the ground-sensing system changes to flight mode at liftoff. If wing anti-ice is still on at landing, both valves close automatically at touchdown (on the DC-10 and KC-10, when the nose strut compresses), and the DISAGREE lights flash on and off as the valves travel.

blocks.title: Wing anti-ice valve command
rows: Opened for the ground test (real aircraft; see below)

blocks.content:
**The DISAGREE lights** compare each valve with where it has been told to be. A light comes on while its valve is traveling, so it flashes for the few seconds of every selection; that flash is the crew's confirmation that the valve actually moved. It stays on if the valve does not reach the commanded position: failing to open in flight, failing to close, or, on the ground, remaining open with the switch in either OFF or ON. A light that stays on after the valve should have finished traveling is a valve failure, and that steady disagreement is what raises the pilots' MASTER CAUTION; a normal stroke does not.

On the MD-10 the same comparison drives the DISAG legend in the WING switchlight, and a valve that stays in disagreement produces the WNG A-ICE L or R DISAG alert.

**The ground test (DC-10, KC-10).** The switch's TEST position is spring-loaded back to OFF. On the real aircraft, holding it bypasses the ground-sensing relays and opens both valves on the ground so the crew can watch them cycle: both DISAGREE lights come on during the stroke and go out when the valves are open, and come on and go out again as the valves close when the switch is released. In the simulation the TEST position lights both DISAGREE lights and nothing else: it does not open the valves on the ground, and in flight it closes them as OFF does (see [Simulation notes](#simulation-notes)).

There is no overheat protection in TEST. On the ground do not hold the WING ANTI-ICE switch in TEST for more than 15 seconds: the slats can be seriously damaged by hot air with no airflow to carry the heat away. On the MD-10, the slats may be damaged if wing anti-ice operates for more than 30 seconds on the ground.

The upper VHF antenna stands on top of the fuselage, ahead of and in line with the No. 2 engine's inlet in the tail. Ice shed from it would go straight into that engine, so it is anti-iced with pneumatic system 3 air through its own shutoff valve inside the pressurized fuselage. The valve body is the wing valve's (the two are physically interchangeable but not functionally, because the antenna unit is vented overboard) and it works the same way: spring- and pressure-loaded closed, opened by its solenoid only when pneumatic pressure is present, closed on loss of electrical power or of pressure.

The antenna has no switch of its own. The **ENG 2 & ANT** anti-ice switch on the pilots' overhead commands both the No. 2 engine's cowl valve and the antenna valve, and both valves take their power from the same ENG 2 & ANT ANTI-ICE VALVE breaker on DC bus 2. The antenna valve's solenoid circuit runs through the ground-control relays, so it is dead on the ground: selecting ENG 2 & ANT ON before takeoff arms the antenna anti-ice, which comes on at rotation, and the relays close it again at landing.

The **ANT ANTI-ICE DISAGREE** light reports the valve, but the two aircraft wire it differently:

**DC-10.** The light is referenced to the switch. With the switch ON in flight it is on while the valve opens and stays on if the valve does not open. With the switch OFF it is on until the valve is closed, on the ground as well: a valve that sticks open shows as soon as the switch goes OFF. At landing the ground relays close the valve and remove the light's ON-side circuit together, so the light does **not** flash as the valve closes.

**KC-10.** The light is referenced to what the valve has been commanded to do (switch ON and airborne). It comes on whenever the valve is traveling, in either direction, so it **does** flash at touchdown as the relays close the valve, and on the ground an open valve lights it with the switch in either position.

On both aircraft a light that stays on beyond the valve's stroke raises the pilots' MASTER CAUTION. The light is also expected with pneumatic system 3 pressure low, since the valve cannot open without air.

children.title: Effects on the pneumatic system and engines

blocks.content: Wing anti-ice is the largest single bleed user the aircraft has after the air-conditioning packs. With it on, the pneumatic systems feeding the wings work in their high-flow mode, more air is extracted from the engines, and EGT and fuel flow rise for a given N1. On every CF6-powered aircraft (all but the DC-10-40) the thrust rating computer corrects its N1 limits for the anti-ice bleed. Takeoff is the exception to the usual direction: with wing anti-ice on, the takeoff and flexible takeoff N1 limits are **raised** (by about 1 %), so that rated takeoff thrust is still delivered while the slats draw air. Engine anti-ice above 8 °C trims the takeoff limits down slightly, and for go-around engine anti-ice, or engine and wing anti-ice, lowers the limit by about 0.5 to 1 % (see [Engines](engines)).

items: The APU is not used for wing anti-ice. It cannot supply air hot enough or in sufficient quantity to keep the slats clear.

On the MD-10, a pneumatic system that cannot keep at least about 35 psig and 170 °C while carrying wing anti-ice gives a BLEED AIR 1, 2 or 3 FAULT alert (the procedures call for 200 °C in takeoff, climb and holding).
For planning, FedEx increases destination fuel by about 1.3 % with engine anti-ice on, and by about 3.5 % (DC-10-10) or 2.7 % (DC-10-30) with engine and wing anti-ice on.

sections.title: Engine cowl anti-ice
sections.summary: Each engine heats its own inlet lip from a dedicated bleed port; the fan and spinner are not protected.

blocks.content: Each engine's nose cowl lip is anti-iced by hot air taken from **a dedicated bleed port on the engine's own high-pressure compressor**, separate from and isolated from the normal pneumatic system. Because the port is high on the compressor, the air is hot enough for ice protection at every power setting, including flight idle, and the cowl anti-ice of each engine is independent of the others and of the pneumatic manifolds. On the wing engines the air is ducted forward to the inlet lip and discharged through a nozzle that sets up a swirling flow around the lip's circumferential chamber (the D-duct). On the No. 2 engine the duct runs up through the vertical stabilizer to the inlet, and the air passes from the D-duct through a double-skin passage before being vented overboard.

blocks.alt: Functional schematic of engine cowl anti-ice for all three engines. For each wing engine: a high-pressure compressor bleed port, the cowl anti-ice valve on the right side of the engine, the duct to the inlet lip and the swirl nozzle in the D-duct. For the No. 2 engine: the duct rising through the vertical stabilizer to the inlet, the pressure regulator valve (KC-10, MD-10) with its downstream high-pressure switch, and the leak detection thermal switch below the duct inside the fin beside a hole in the duct shroud. Wiring from each valve's position switches to the ENG ANTI-ICE DISAGREE lights, from the three switches to the ENG ANTI-ICE SW ON light, the pressure switch to ENG 2 ANTI-ICE COWL PRESS HI and the thermal switch to ENG 2 ANTI-ICE COWL DUCT FAIL. Note on each valve: solenoid energized = closed.
blocks.title: Engine cowl anti-ice system

blocks.content: Each cowl valve is a spring-loaded-closed butterfly, opened by the engine's own bleed pressure and controlled by a solenoid. The logic is inverted compared with the wing valves: **energizing** the solenoid vents the actuator and the spring closes the valve; **de-energizing** it lets bleed pressure open the valve. The switch's OFF position is therefore the one that powers the solenoid. If electrical power is lost the solenoids drop out and all three cowl valves open, whatever the switches say, as long as the engines are running. The designers' reasoning is that losing ice protection on an engine is far worse than an unwanted bleed.

Each valve has two position switches feeding its **ENG ANTI-ICE DISAGREE** light, which comes on while the valve is traveling and stays on if the valve does not reach the commanded position. On the real aircraft the light flashes for about a second at each selection; a light that remains on steady is a valve failure, and that is what raises the pilots' MASTER CAUTION. A blue **ENG ANTI-ICE SW ON** light comes on whenever any of the three switches is ON; it reads the switches, not the valves, and is an advisory that raises no caution. The DC-10-40 has no such light.

children.title: No. 2 engine: pressure regulator and duct leak detection

blocks.content:
The No. 2 engine's duct is longer and runs through the fin, so its system has two extra protections.

**Pressure regulator.** On the KC-10 and MD-10 the No. 2 cowl valve is a pressure regulator rather than a plain shutoff valve, holding the duct at a controlled pressure however hard the engine is running, and a high-pressure switch downstream of it lights **ENG 2 ANTI-ICE COWL PRESS HI** (MD-10: ENG 2 A-ICE PRES) if the regulator lets through more than normal pressure. The light may come on momentarily when the ENG 2 & ANT switch is moved to ON, while the regulator catches up with the full bleed pressure; if it remains on, the regulator has failed high. The cowl is still anti-iced, only with more duct pressure than intended. The DC-10-40's regulator has no PRESS HI light, and the DC-10-10, -15 and -30 are simulated with a plain shutoff valve on engine 2 (see [Simulation notes](#simulation-notes)).

**Duct leak detection.** A thermal switch sits below the cowl anti-ice duct inside the vertical stabilizer, beside a hole in the duct's shroud. Hot air from a leak escapes through that hole onto the switch. When the air around the switch reaches 260 °F (127 °C) the switch closes and lights **ENG 2 ANTI-ICE COWL DUCT FAIL** (MD-10: ENG 2 A-ICE DUCT); when the temperature falls below 260 °F it opens and the light goes out. Because the leak is downstream of the valve, it only blows hot air while engine 2 anti-ice is on, and harder at higher power, so the light follows the leak for as long as the anti-ice is selected. There is no automatic reaction and the valve does not close; the secondary shroud lets protection continue. Where the route allows, the crew keep out of icing so that the system runs with a leak for as short a time as possible.

ENG 2 ANTI-ICE COWL DUCT FAIL light
ENG 2 ANTI-ICE COWL DUCT FAIL light
ENG 2 ANTI-ICE COWL DUCT FAIL light

Yes, on the real aircraft (not simulated)

blocks.content: Cowl anti-ice protects the inlet lip only, not the fan blades or the spinner. In moderate to severe icing ice builds on both, and since nothing heats them it is removed only by centrifugal force: as N1 rises, the load on the ice grows with the square of the rotational speed until pieces break off. Ice usually sheds unevenly, leaving the fan briefly out of balance, so shedding shows as a short rise in N1 vibration as thrust is applied. Shed fan ice can damage the acoustic panels in the fan case.

Operating above about 70 % N1 keeps the fan clear most effectively. When icing has to be flown at lower power (holding, descent), the procedures run each engine up in turn at regular intervals to shed what has built up, and on the ground in icing conditions each engine is run up briefly at regular intervals during long taxi or holding. The steps are in [Adverse weather](adverse-weather). If ice does build on a cowl lip because the anti-ice has failed, operate at the minimum practical power until it has been ingested, to limit compressor damage.

Cowl anti-ice air is compressor work the engine has paid for and does not get back as thrust. To hold the same N1 with the extra extraction the fuel control must burn more fuel at a higher turbine temperature, so EGT and fuel flow rise and the EGT margin at high power shrinks. On every CF6-powered aircraft the thrust rating computer applies a correction to its limits for engine anti-ice (on the CF6-50C2 and -50C2F, a small takeoff N1 penalty when engine anti-ice is on with TAT above 8 °C; the DC-10-40's JT9D computer has none); the KC-10 T.O. notes that with the computer setting N1 no further correction is needed for climb, cruise or maximum continuous thrust. Engine and airfoil protection both work at flight idle, so there is no need to carry extra power for ice protection in flight.

On the real DC-10-30, turning on engine 1 or engine 3 anti-ice also raises the minimum idle of all three engines to flight idle, which keeps compressor speed, and with it bleed pressure, up at low power. The DC-10-40 is not affected. The simulation does not model this idle change (see [Simulation notes](#simulation-notes)).

sections.title: Air data sensor heat
sections.summary: Electric heaters in the pitot tubes, static ports, TAT probe and angle-of-attack vanes, each on its own circuit.

blocks.content: Every external air data sensor has its own electric heater. The three pitot tubes (captain's, first officer's and auxiliary) sit just off the lower fuselage centerline aft of the radome; each has two heating elements. The total air temperature probe is on the bottom centerline forward of the nose gear well; it has a single element, and its one probe head feeds both central air data computers, so its heat matters to both. The two angle-of-attack vanes, one on each side below and forward of the forward passenger doors, have one element each. On each side a heated plate surrounds the primary static port cluster, and a separate heater surrounds the alternate static port; each static heater is regulated by its own thermostat and protected by a fuse.

blocks.alt: Exterior views of a DC-10-30 forward fuselage, left side and underside, with callouts: the three pitot tubes just off the lower centerline aft of the radome (CAPT, F/O, AUX), the TAT probe on the bottom centerline forward of the nose gear well, the left angle-of-attack vane below and forward of door 1L, and the left static plate (primary port cluster) with the alternate static port beside it, below and forward of the wing leading edge. A small inset shows the same items on the right side.
blocks.title: Heated air data sensors

blocks.content: The heaters are deliberately spread across the electrical system so that one bus failure costs only some of them. The captain's and first officer's pitot heaters are on the two emergency AC buses and keep heating when the aircraft is down to emergency power; the auxiliary pitot and TAT heaters are on AC bus 2; the left static plate and left vane are on AC bus 1 and the right ones on AC bus 3. The heater controller and monitor, the PITOT HEAT INOP light and the panel lighting are 28 V DC.

blocks.title: Air data heaters
rows: PITOT HEAT INOP (MD-10: PITOT HEAT CAPT)
PITOT HEAT INOP (MD-10: PITOT HEAT FO)
PITOT HEAT INOP (MD-10: PITOT HEAT AUX)
PITOT HEAT INOP in flight (MD-10: TAT PROBE HEAT)
115 V AC, scheduled with outside temperature
HTR CUR zero only (MD-10: AOA HEAT L or R FAIL)
L and R static plates, L and R alternate static ports

blocks.content: The KC-10 has an additional 28 V DC heater circuit for the right angle-of-attack vane, on DC bus 3, alongside the AC circuits.

On the three-crew aircraft all the air data heaters are controlled and monitored by one unit on the pilots' overhead panel: a heater controller, the **HTR CUR** meter and an eleven-position rotary selector placarded **METER SEL & HEAT**. The selector does two jobs. Turning it to **any position other than OFF** energizes every air data heater on the aircraft; the position chosen then decides only which heater the HTR CUR meter is reading. There is no separate probe heat switch. Returning the selector to OFF removes power from every heater.

The procedures leave the selector at TAT in normal operation. On the real aircraft a PITOT HEATER SELECT switch for each pitot tube, on the flight engineer's equipment panel, lets the crew choose element No. 1 or No. 2 after an element failure; that switch is not part of the simulated cockpit.

The MD-10 has no air data heat switch. The miscellaneous systems controller turns on every air data heater except the TAT probe's as soon as any engine FUEL switch is moved ON, and turns them off when all three FUEL switches are OFF. The TAT heater is allowed on only when the ground-sensing system senses flight. The ground and flight heat levels are the same as on the DC-10. Failures are reported by EIS alerts (see [MD-10 alerts](#ci-md10-alerts)). Maintenance personnel can override the controller from switches on the maintenance panel; these are not used in flight and are not part of the simulated cockpit.

A probe heater is sized to keep its probe clear at high speed in very cold air, where the airflow carries heat away very fast. In still air on the ramp the same heater would overheat the probe and shorten its life. The ground-sensing relays therefore change the heat level when the aircraft is on the ground:

**Pitot tubes.** In flight one element in each tube is energized. On the ground both elements are connected in series across the same supply, which roughly halves the current and the heat.

**TAT probe.** Not heated on the ground at all; the right ground-sensing relay removes its power. (A heated TAT probe in still air also reads high, from the heater's own warmth.)

**Angle-of-attack vanes.** Supplied with 28 V AC on the ground and 115 V AC in flight, the flight supply being scheduled against outside air temperature.

**Static ports.** Regulated by their thermostats at all times; a plate is held near 24 °C (75 °F), and its thermal switch opens if it reaches about 82 °C (180 °F) and does not re-close until the plate has cooled again.
Even with the ground schedule, pitot heater life is best served by keeping air data heat off on the ground except when needed for the checks and when icing conditions exist.

The HTR CUR meter shows the relative current drawn by whichever heater the METER SEL & HEAT selector is pointing at. Its scale, 0 to 5, is in arbitrary **units**, not amperes, and it is not linear in current: a pitot tube on the ground draws about half the current it draws in flight, yet its ground reading is only a few tenths of a unit lower (at least 0.4 units). What matters is whether the reading falls within the normal band for that heater, and above all whether it is **zero**.

The static port and angle-of-attack heaters have **no failure light** on the three-crew aircraft. A failed element in one of them is shown only by a reading of zero on the HTR CUR meter when that heater is selected. That is why the flight engineer walks the selector through every position during the checks: it is the only way to find a dead static or vane heater.

blocks.title: Normal HTR CUR readings
rows: L ALT STATIC, R ALT STATIC (thermostat closed)
Any position, heater unpowered or failed

blocks.content: Because the two primary static ports on each side share one plate heater, a single reading covers the whole cluster; if any element covered by a position has failed, that position reads zero. A static reading in the low thermostat-open band means the plate is warm enough that its thermostat has cut out, which is normal only on a hot plate.

The amber **PITOT HEAT INOP** light on the overhead annunciator panel watches the three pitot heaters and the TAT heater. It comes on when the METER SEL & HEAT selector is at OFF, and when any pitot heater, or the TAT heater in flight, is not drawing current: a failed element, a tripped breaker or a dead bus. On the ground the TAT heater is unpowered by design and is ignored. The light also turns on both pilots' MASTER CAUTION lights.

That behavior is used as a check: with the aircraft powered and the selector at OFF, the light and both MASTER CAUTION lights should be on, proving the monitor works; moving the selector to CAPT should put the light out. Static port and vane heaters do not affect this light.

children.title: What an iced sensor does to the instruments

blocks.content: An iced sensor rarely announces itself with a flag. Most of the failures it causes leave the signal electrically valid and simply wrong, which is why the heaters and their monitoring matter. In the simulation the ice on each sensor is carried through to the air data system, so these effects appear on the instruments (see [Flight instruments](flight-instruments)):

items: **Pitot inlet partly iced:** the pressure line responds sluggishly and airspeed lags.
**Pitot inlet blocked, drain open:** the trapped total pressure bleeds away through the drain and indicated airspeed decays toward zero.

**Pitot inlet and drain both blocked:** total pressure is trapped. In a climb the static pressure falls beneath it and indicated airspeed **increases**; in a descent it decreases. The airspeed indicator behaves as an altimeter.
**Static ports iced:** altitude and vertical speed freeze, and airspeed errs in the opposite sense to a blocked pitot.
**TAT probe iced, unheated:** the element sits in melting ice and its reading drifts toward 0 °C while staying valid, corrupting static air temperature and true airspeed on both air data computers.
**Angle-of-attack vane iced, unheated:** the vane freezes at its last angle and keeps reporting it as valid, so stall warning and any system using angle of attack are working from a stale value.

sections.title: Windshield and window heat
sections.summary: Electrically heated windshield outer plies, defogging of the windshields and clearview windows, and the KC-10 boom operator's windows.

blocks.content: The two forward windshields carry two heating systems each: **anti-ice**, which heats the outer glass ply to keep ice off the outside, and **defog**, which heats the inner ply to keep the inside clear of mist and frost. The two sliding clearview windows have defog heat only. Each windshield's anti-ice has its own controller and its own selector, so a failure on one side leaves the other side clear.

children.title: Windshield construction, and why it is heated

blocks.content: Each windshield is a laminate of glass and vinyl: glass, vinyl, glass, vinyl, glass. The anti-ice heater is a thin, transparent tin oxide coating on the inner face of the outer pane, where it meets the vinyl; current through the coating warms that pane from within. The defog coating sits on the outer face of the innermost pane. Temperature sensors are sealed into the outer ply, one in use and one spare. Each windshield has a primary and a secondary heated area, and in some icing conditions the secondary area may not clear completely. Every flight deck windshield and window will hold full cabin pressurization with one glass pane cracked.

blocks.alt: Cross-section diagram through a DC-10 forward windshield, outside on the left. Labeled layers from outside in: outer glass ply, anti-ice heating film on its inboard face, vinyl interlayer, middle glass ply, vinyl interlayer, inner glass ply with the defog film on its outboard face. Show the embedded temperature sensor in the outer ply, the bus bars along the edges feeding the films, and the mounting frame. Annotate: outer ply = anti-ice; inner ply = defog; inner plies and interlayers carry the pressure load.
blocks.title: Windshield construction

blocks.content: Heat does more than remove ice. A laminated windshield's strength in an impact depends heavily on its vinyl interlayers, which hold a broken pane together and absorb energy; vinyl is tough and pliable when warm and much more brittle when cold-soaked, and heated windshields are generally qualified for bird impact with their heat on. Keeping the glass warm also keeps the temperature difference across the laminate small, which reduces thermal stress, and defog heat keeps the inner surface above the cockpit's dew point. For these reasons defog is normally on for all flight, and windshield anti-ice is selected to NORM for flight whenever icing is imminent.

Each windshield's controller, in the avionics compartment, reads the outer-ply sensor and regulates the heater current by switching between output taps of an autotransformer. On initial turn-on it ramps the power up in steps over about 3 to 4 minutes, so that a cold windshield is not cracked by thermal shock; after that it holds the glass at its anti-icing temperature. On the real aircraft NORM controls the glass to about 27 °C (80 °F), for light icing, and HIGH to about 43 °C (110 °F), for moderate to heavy icing. Either can be selected directly from OFF without thermal shock. The left windshield is powered from AC bus 1 and the right from AC bus 3.

A monitor in the controller compares heat demand with heater current. Demand with no current flowing, current with no demand, an overheat, or an open or shorted sensor makes the controller remove power from the heater and turn on that side's **WINDSHIELD ANTI-ICE INOP** light (MD-10: WSHLD HEAT L or R FAIL). The trip is latched: the light stays on, and the heat stays off, until the selector is turned to **OFF**. Turning it back to NORM resets a controller whose fault has cleared; a fault that persists trips it again.

The selector's **SYS TEST** position tests the controller and monitor, the sensor circuits, the overheat detection and the INOP light itself: the INOP light comes on if all of them are working. SYS TEST is a test, not the OFF position, so it does not reset a tripped controller. The INOP lights also turn on the pilots' MASTER CAUTION.

Selector at SYS TEST, controller unpowered or failed

blocks.content: Windshield anti-ice off or inoperative carries no airspeed restriction. Select NORM for flight once icing is expected, and keep HIGH for the time spent in moderate or heavy icing.

Defog heats the inner ply of both windshields and both clearview windows. A single defog switch powers four separate controllers, one per window; they work like the anti-ice controllers, with the same stepped warm-up (about 4 minutes) and overheat protection, and a fault removes power from the affected window only. Conditioned air from diffusers above each clearview window also helps. The defog system is normally on at all times.
There is no annunciation of defog status on the three-crew aircraft.
On the MD-10 the WINDSHIELD DEFOG switchlight shows OFF when defog is switched off, and the EIS shows the WSHLD DEFOG OFF alert.

The boom operator's aft (rear view) window and lower window are electrically heated, from the 115 V AC ARO bus, under one **WINDOW HEAT** selector on the boom operator's overhead panel: SYS TEST, OFF, NORM and HIGH. NORM holds the windows in the normal range for light icing; HIGH applies more heat for moderate to heavy icing, and is worth considering whenever the ARO compartment is below 0 °C (32 °F). NORM can also be used for defogging and to help warm the compartment.

Although there is one selector and one light, each window has its own control system: the aft window's on its ARO WINDOW HEAT breakers (two power, one control) and the lower window's on its single LOWER WINDOW HEAT breaker. A malfunction in either turns off that window's heat and lights the amber **WINDOW HEAT INOP** light, which stays on until the selector is turned to OFF. An overheat trip clears when the window has cooled and the selector is cycled OFF then NORM; a failed controller does not clear, and its light returns as soon as heat is selected again. At SYS TEST the light comes on only if every overheat-prevention circuit in both windows is working. Pulling a window's breaker removes its heat without lighting the INOP light.

WINDOW HEAT INOP is a boom operator's light, part of the ARO station's caution group and its lamp test; it does not reach the flight deck MASTER CAUTION.

sections.title: Rain removal
sections.summary: Two independent two-speed wipers; rain repellent where fitted.

blocks.content: Each forward windshield has its own wiper system: an arm and blade, a two-speed 28 V DC permanent-magnet motor-converter at the base of the windshield, two control relays, its breakers and a three-position selector on the overhead (OFF, SLO, FAST on the DC-10 and KC-10; OFF, SLOW, FAST on the MD-10). The left wiper is powered from DC bus 1 and the right from DC bus 3, so one bus failure stops only one wiper. SLO runs the motor through a series resistor bank at about 165 strokes a minute; FAST runs it on the full 28 V at about 250.

Selecting OFF energizes a park relay that reverses the motor and drives the blade back down to its park position at slow speed, where a limit switch opens and a brake holds the arm out of the field of view. A wiper that loses power mid-sweep stops where it is.
Do not operate the wipers on a dry windshield, and do not operate them at high speed for more than 30 minutes.

**Rain repellent.** Where fitted, a single pressurized container behind the first officer's seat, with a pressure gauge and a quantity float behind a viewing door, supplies a nozzle at the base of each windshield through a timed solenoid valve. Each pilot has a RAIN REPLNT button: a press applies one measured quantity, which the wiper spreads; the button must be released and pressed again for another. Repellent is applied only in heavy rain, never to a dry windshield (it impairs visibility, and the wipers must then not be used), and not to the second windshield until it has proved effective on the first. The system is deactivated on FedEx DC-10s and removed from the KC-10, and it is not operative in the simulation.

sections.title: Drain mast heat and ice detection

blocks.content: **Drain masts.** Water drained from the aircraft's sinks leaves through two drain masts under the fuselage, forward and aft, each with an electric heater in its fairing. The heaters run all the time under the full control of the ground-sensing relays: low heat on the ground, higher heat in flight. There is no crew control. A mast that loses its heat in freezing air ices shut within minutes and the water behind it can no longer drain. On the real DC-10 a WTR DRAIN HEAT LOW light on the flight engineer's panel, active only on the ground, reports a failed mast heater.
Other small heaters keep water service panels, cargo door sill drains and cargo door latch actuators free of ice; they are automatic, need no crew action, and are not simulated.

**Ice detection.** No aircraft in the family has an ice detector. The crew decide that icing conditions exist from TAT, visible moisture and the temperature-dewpoint spread, and they detect ice that has formed by looking at the airframe: the windshield wiper arms parked along the windshield frame, the window frames and the unheated edges of the windshields. The wiper arms are particularly useful because they are thin, unheated and right in front of the crew, so they ice early and obviously while the heated glass behind them stays clear.

sections.title: Controls and indicators

blocks.content: On the DC-10 and KC-10 the controls are split between two crew stations. The pilots' overhead panel carries the engine and antenna anti-ice switches, the windshield, defog and wiper controls and the air data heat controller; its annunciator panel carries most of the lights. Wing anti-ice belongs to the flight engineer, on Upper Panel No. 2 beside the pneumatic controls it depends on. On the MD-10 everything is on the forward overhead panel as switchlights, and air data heat has no control at all.

blocks.content: The EFB's Systems app has an ICE page that shows the whole system at a glance (see [EFB](efb)). It draws a plan of the aircraft with every ice zone where it is on the airframe. A protected zone is shown as a pill in the color of its state; an unprotected zone as a plain label, because having no protection is the design and never a fault. Ice on a zone is drawn as a bar against that zone's own scale: two millimeters blocks a pitot tube and is nothing on a slat. The page also shows whether icing conditions exist, the HTR CUR reading on the three-crew aircraft, and the contamination on each wing's upper surface with the de-icing fluid's remaining holdover. The zone states are listed under [Ice zones](#ice-zones).

sections.title: Operation
sections.summary: Checks on the ground, when and how to use each system through a flight, the logic behind the lights, and how the system works with the others.

blocks.content: This section explains how the system is used and why. The procedures themselves (cold-weather preflight, de-icing, taxi, flight in icing conditions) are in [Adverse weather](adverse-weather), the checklist items in [Normal procedures](normal-procedures), and the governing figures in [Limitations](limitations).

**Exterior.** Pitot tubes, static ports, angle-of-attack vanes and the TAT probe clear of ice, snow and covers. Engine inlets clear of ice and snow inside and out, and each fan free to turn. Wings, tail and control surfaces free of frost, snow and ice, and the top of the fuselage clear ahead of the No. 2 engine, which would ingest anything shed from it. When in doubt, call for de-icing.

**Air data heat (FE).** With electrical power on and METER SEL & HEAT at OFF, check that PITOT HEAT INOP and both pilots' MASTER CAUTION lights are on: this proves the fault detection works. Turn the selector to PITOT CAPT: PITOT HEAT INOP goes out. Step through each position and check the HTR CUR reading against its ground band; the TAT position reads zero on the ground. Any other position reading zero is a failed heater, and for a static port or vane it is the only indication there will be. Return the selector to OFF unless air data heat is needed on the ground.

**Windshields.** Turn each windshield selector to SYS TEST and check its WINDSHIELD ANTI-ICE INOP light comes on; then to NORM and check the light is out. **Wing anti-ice.** Check the switch is OFF. The ground TEST is used only when called for, and never for more than 15 seconds. **Engine anti-ice** switches OFF unless icing conditions exist on the ground. **Wipers** OFF; do not run them on a dry windshield.

Air data heat comes on by itself with the first FUEL switch at engine start; check that no PITOT HEAT, TAT PROBE HEAT or AOA HEAT alert is displayed. When windshield anti-ice is selected on, check that no WSHLD HEAT FAIL alert follows, and that the DEFOG switchlight does not show OFF.

children.title: Engine start, taxi and takeoff in icing conditions

blocks.content:
When icing conditions exist on the ground, engine anti-ice goes on as soon as practicable after each engine is started and stays on until icing conditions no longer exist; if icing conditions exist after landing, it stays on until shutdown. Cowl anti-ice works at ground idle because its air comes from a high compressor stage.

During long ground operation in icing conditions with engine anti-ice on, each engine is run up to 60 % N1 for 30 seconds every 30 minutes to shed fan ice, with a final run-up in the takeoff position; the surfaces around the aircraft must be clear before running up. Keep the flaps and slats retracted while taxiing through slush or snow, so that it is not thrown up into the gaps, and set them for takeoff before entering the runway.

Wing anti-ice cannot be used on the ground; the ground-sensing relays hold its valves closed. When it is needed for takeoff it is selected ON before takeoff, which arms it, and the valves open at liftoff. Takeoff performance is computed with the anti-ice selection that will be used; on every aircraft but the DC-10-40 the thrust rating computer also applies its own correction for the extra bleed. Windshield anti-ice is in NORM for takeoff in icing conditions.
Because these are anti-icing systems, they go on when icing conditions are expected or met, not when ice is seen.

blocks.title: When to use ice protection
rows: In flight whenever TAT is 6 °C or below with visible moisture in any form; on the ground with OAT 6 °C or below and visible moisture, a temperature-dewpoint spread of 3 °C or less, or contamination the engines can ingest.

Whenever icing conditions are expected or encountered (FedEx: engine and wing anti-ice whenever OAT/TAT is 6 °C or below with visible moisture). Before extending the slats if ice has been encountered, to clear the leading edges first.
NORM for flight when icing is imminent. HIGH only for the duration of moderate to heavy icing.
On for all flight (DC-10, KC-10: METER SEL & HEAT out of OFF; MD-10: automatic).

blocks.content: Engine and airfoil anti-ice both work at flight idle, so holding and descent at low power need no extra thrust for protection. The fans and spinners are not protected, however: in moderate to severe icing below about 70 % N1 the procedures run each engine up in turn at intervals to shed fan ice, expecting a brief rise in N1 vibration as it goes. Monitor EGT with anti-ice on, especially at high power, and on the MD-10 watch for BLEED AIR FAULT, which means a wing's pneumatic supply is too weak to keep its slats clear.
When engine anti-ice (alone or with wing anti-ice) is needed, the crew also select engine ignition OVRD, and keep it selected until the aircraft is clear of icing.

The tail, inboard slats, fans and radome are never protected, so the defense against prolonged or severe icing is to leave it. Avoid flight in freezing rain and severe icing. Watch the wiper arms and window frames for ice, and use the EFB ICE page to see which zones are collecting.

If wing anti-ice is on at touchdown its valves close automatically as the ground-sensing system changes to ground mode, and the wing DISAGREE lights (MD-10: DISAG legend) flash as they travel. On the DC-10 and KC-10 the antenna valve closes at the same moment; on the KC-10 the ANT ANTI-ICE DISAGREE light flashes as it does, on the DC-10 it stays dark (see [System logic](#op-logic)). The TAT heater drops out, and the pitot heaters change to their reduced ground level.

If icing conditions exist on the ground, engine anti-ice stays on until shutdown. After shutdown the windshield heat is turned OFF and, on the DC-10 and KC-10, METER SEL & HEAT is returned to OFF.

blocks.content: **What lights the MASTER CAUTION.** The pilots' MASTER CAUTION lights follow the malfunction lights, never the advisories: a wing, cowl or antenna valve that stays in disagreement beyond its stroke, ENG 2 ANTI-ICE COWL DUCT FAIL, an ENG 2 ANTI-ICE COWL PRESS HI that remains on, either WINDSHIELD ANTI-ICE INOP light, or PITOT HEAT INOP. A wing valve that is open but receiving too little pneumatic pressure to heat its slats also raises it. The normal flash of a DISAGREE light during a valve stroke, the momentary PRESS HI on selection, the blue SW ON lights and a static or vane heater failure do not.

**Pneumatics.** Wing anti-ice draws from pneumatic systems 1 and 3, and the antenna from system 3. A system supplying anti-ice air runs in its high-flow mode with a slightly lower duct temperature set point. The cowls draw from each engine's own bleed air rather than from the manifold, so a shut-down engine has no cowl anti-ice. See [Pneumatics](pneumatics).

**Engines.** Anti-ice bleed raises EGT and fuel flow for a given N1, the thrust rating computer corrects its limits for it on every CF6-powered aircraft (all but the DC-10-40), and fan ice shows as N1 vibration when it sheds. See [Engines](engines).

**Air data.** Ice on an unheated probe is carried through to the air data computers and the instruments (see [What an iced sensor does to the instruments](#iced-probes) and [Flight instruments](flight-instruments)).

**Ground sensing.** The ground-sensing relays hold the wing and antenna valves closed, remove TAT heat, switch the pitot heaters to series and the vanes to 28 V AC, and lower the drain mast heat whenever the aircraft is on the ground.

sections.title: Failures and non-normal operation
sections.summary: How each failure shows, what it does, and what the crew does about it.

blocks.content: The non-normal checklists for these failures are in [Abnormal procedures](abnormal-procedures). The table summarizes what each failure does and how it shows.

blocks.content: A wing anti-ice valve open on the ground, or the TEST position held, puts hot air into slats with no airflow to cool them. Damage can occur within 15 seconds.

**Modeled in depth.** Ice grows on every zone separately, as a thickness, from the zone's collection efficiency, the liquid water in the air, true airspeed and the surface's own temperature, so small probes ice fast, the radome slowly, and a warm surface not at all. Cloud water follows the shape of the certification icing envelope (most water just below freezing, thinning with altitude) and precipitation adds water from the simulator's rain rate; frozen precipitation sticks less than rain. Icing conditions are the aircraft's own criterion: TAT 6 °C or below with cloud or precipitation. Heated surfaces shed their ice once warm. The ice is drawn on the airframe: slats, cowls, fans and spinners, tail, radome, windshields, wiper arms and the wing upper surfaces (the probes are too small to draw).

Valve strokes and DISAGREE flashes, the ground-sensing inhibits, the No. 2 regulator's momentary PRESS HI and its failure, the duct leak detector's temperature, the different DC-10 and KC-10 antenna light logic, the probe heaters' ground and flight levels, the static thermostats, the HTR CUR readings (including zero for a dead heater), the windshield controllers' latch and SYS TEST, the KC-10's boom operator's windows and the wipers' real stroke rates and parking are all modeled. Ground contamination is modeled too: frost (including the cold-soaked fuel case), snow, freezing rain and freezing fog on the wing upper surfaces, and de-icing fluid whose holdover shortens with precipitation and which shears off at rotation. Anti-ice bleed is a real load on the pneumatic system and the engines.

**MSFS's own icing.** The simulator keeps an icing model of its own, and its structural ice is what its flight model penalizes when the Icing effect assistance option is on. The aircraft drives the simulator's anti-ice switches from its own systems so that the two never fight: the simulator's structural de-ice follows wing anti-ice actually delivering air, each engine's anti-ice follows that cowl valve delivering, and windshield de-ice follows either windshield heating. The simulator's pitot heat is held on permanently, so pitot icing comes only from this aircraft's model. The aerodynamic effect of airframe ice therefore comes from the simulator's model (if the assistance option is on), while the ice drawn on the aircraft, the probe effects and every indication come from this aircraft's model. Ground contamination on the wing upper surfaces is tracked and drawn but does not by itself change the flight model.

**Simulator key bindings** work the cockpit controls as a crew member would: the anti-ice keys move the ENG anti-ice switches (all three, or one engine at a time); the windshield de-ice keys move both windshield selectors between OFF and NORM (never to SYS TEST, and leaving HIGH alone) or press both MD-10 windshield switchlights; the structural de-ice key works the FE's WING ANTI-ICE switch between OFF and ON (on the MD-10, the WING and TAIL switchlights together); and the pitot heat keys turn METER SEL & HEAT between OFF and its last heating position (TAT by default). The MD-10 has no pitot heat control for those keys to move.

**Simplified.** The windshield controllers warm the glass smoothly rather than in steps, and their controlled temperatures are approximate. A cowl valve stroke shows a DISAGREE flash of about two seconds rather than one. All the wing and cowl valve solenoids are powered from DC bus 1 (on the aircraft they are spread across buses; the antenna valve's DC bus 2 supply is modeled). The windshield SYS TEST position stays where it is put rather than springing back to OFF, so turn the selector back yourself. On the three-crew aircraft an under-supplied wing valve raises the MASTER CAUTION with no legend of its own. Each alternate static port heater shares its side's plate circuit, so one breaker removes both. With no electrical power at all the cowl valves rest open, their fail-safe position; this has no effect until bleed air is available.

items: **Not modeled:** the wing anti-ice ground TEST (TEST lights the DISAGREE lights only; in flight it closes the valves as OFF does).
**Not modeled:** defog on the DC-10 and KC-10 (the WINDSHLD DEFOG switch moves but is not connected); misting of the glass on any aircraft.
**Not modeled:** rain repellent; the RAIN REPLNT buttons do nothing.
**Not modeled:** the PITOT HEATER SELECT switches; the MD-10's maintenance-panel air data heat override, and the A-ICE SENSOR FAIL, AIR DATA HTR ON, ENG DUCT TST FAIL and PITOT HEAT OFF alerts.
**Not modeled:** the DC-10-40's inlet guide vane anti-ice and APU inlet screen anti-ice, and the DC-10-30's change to flight idle with engine 1 or 3 anti-ice on.

**Different from FedEx's DC-10s:** the DC-10-10, -15 and -30 are simulated with a plain shutoff valve on engine 2, so the ENG 2 ANTI-ICE COWL PRESS HI light never comes on; the FedEx CFM describes a pressure regulator and the PRESS HI light on its aircraft.
**Not modeled:** the KC-10's pressure-switch logic for the ENG 2 ANTI-ICE DISAGREE light; it reports valve position as on the other engines.
**MD-10 TAIL switchlight:** it lights when pressed but there is no tail anti-ice to switch, so nothing is heated.

**Not modeled:** thrust rating computer corrections for anti-ice bleed on the DC-10-40, whose JT9D computer carries none. The -15 uses the CF6-50C2's corrections, and the CF6-6D aircraft (DC-10-10, MD-10-10) have their own, from the FedEx -10 tables.
**Not modeled:** the WTR DRAIN HEAT LOW light (the drain mast heaters themselves work automatically), and the small cargo door and service panel heaters.
The upper VHF antenna's valve and light are modeled, but ice on the antenna itself is not tracked.
Ice drawn on the windshield glass may not be visible from inside the cockpit in the current release.

blocks.title: DC-10 engine anti-ice switches
blocks.content: In the current release the three ENG anti-ice toggles on the DC-10 pilots' overhead do not move on screen (a cockpit model fault; the KC-10's are unaffected). Each switch still works: a click, or the simulator's anti-ice key bindings described above, sets it and the system responds. The ENG ANTI-ICE SW ON light and each DISAGREE flash confirm the selection, so judge the switch by them rather than by the toggle.

**EFB.** The Systems app's ICE page shows every zone, its state and its ice (see [EFB ice and rain page](#ci-efb)). The Failures app offers engine and wing anti-ice valve disagree, the No. 2 cowl duct failure, antenna anti-ice valve disagree (not on the MD-10), pitot heat failure on each tube, windshield anti-ice failure on each side, and a cracked windshield or window (which only brings up its procedure: it has no effect on the aircraft). The ground services include de-icing with Type I fluid, or Type I followed by Type IV, and GSX's de-icing trucks are recognized.

parts.title: Oxygen
parts.summary: Diluter-demand crew oxygen from high-pressure cylinders, chemical-generator oxygen for passengers and supernumeraries, and portable equipment.

sections.title: Introduction
sections.summary: Two independent systems: stored gaseous oxygen for the crew, chemical oxygen generators for everyone else.

blocks.content: The aircraft carries two independent oxygen systems. The **crew oxygen system** stores gaseous oxygen at high pressure in cylinders in the avionics compartment, reduces it to a low line pressure, and delivers it on demand through a diluter-demand regulator at each crew station. The **passenger oxygen system** (on freighters and the tanker, the supernumerary and courier oxygen) has no stored gas at all: each group of masks is fed by its own chemical oxygen generator, which, once started, produces oxygen for a fixed time. The passenger masks drop automatically when the cabin altitude climbs through about 14,000 ft, or when the crew release them. Portable oxygen cylinders and smoke protection equipment complete the installation.

The two systems are designed for different jobs. The crew must stay fully capable through a decompression, a smoke or fumes event and the descent that follows, for as long as it takes, so they get a regulated supply that adapts to cabin altitude, can be switched to pure oxygen and to positive pressure, and lasts hours. Passengers and supernumeraries need only enough oxygen to stay conscious while the aircraft descends to a breathable altitude, so they get a simple, light, maintenance-free source that lasts a quarter of an hour or so. That fixed duration is what sets the pace of an emergency descent.

The crew oxygen system has no warning or caution light of its own on any aircraft of the family; its state is read from gauges. The crew's cue to use oxygen is the cabin altitude warning (see [Air conditioning and pressurization](air-conditioning)), smoke or fumes, or the procedures.

blocks.title: Crew oxygen system

blocks.content: Air is about 21 % oxygen at every altitude the aircraft can reach. What falls with altitude is total pressure, and with it the **partial pressure** of oxygen, which is what drives oxygen across the lungs into the blood. At sea level the oxygen partial pressure in the lungs is about 100 mmHg, after water vapour and carbon dioxide have taken their share. At a cabin altitude of 10,000 ft it is about 60 mmHg, which sits at the knee of the blood's oxygen saturation curve: up to that point saturation falls only slowly, beyond it steeply. That is why 10,000 ft is the conventional cabin altitude limit and why cabin altitude warnings are set there.

Supplemental oxygen restores the partial pressure by raising the oxygen fraction of what is breathed. A little added oxygen is enough at moderate cabin altitudes, and pure oxygen breathed at about 34,000 ft gives roughly the same lung oxygen pressure as air at sea level. Above about 40,000 ft even pure oxygen at ambient pressure gives less than air at 10,000 ft, and the only remedy is to deliver it under positive pressure, **pressure breathing**, which forces more gas into the lungs at some cost in effort.

That physiology is what the crew regulators implement. In their normal mode they dilute oxygen with cabin air, adding just enough oxygen for the cabin altitude, which saves a great deal of oxygen at low cabin altitudes. As the cabin climbs they add more until, at about 27,000 to 29,000 ft cabin altitude, they deliver pure oxygen. Above that they add a small positive pressure, and above about 40,000 ft they pressure-breathe. Selecting 100 % gives pure oxygen at any altitude, which also keeps smoke and fumes out of the breathing gas; selecting EMERGENCY adds positive pressure at any altitude, so that any leak at the mask seal blows outward and contaminated air cannot get in.

blocks.title: Time of useful consciousness (typical, seated, at rest)

blocks.content: The time of useful consciousness is the time a person can still act effectively after the oxygen supply is lost, not the time to unconsciousness. A rapid decompression, physical activity and individual differences can roughly halve it. Hypoxia also hides its own onset: the victim's judgment goes before any sense of distress arrives. Hence the rule that the crew don masks first, immediately and without waiting to diagnose the problem.

sections.title: Crew oxygen
sections.summary: High-pressure cylinders, a reducing regulator, and a diluter-demand regulator at each crew station.

blocks.content: Crew oxygen is delivered on demand, diluted automatically, and pressurized when needed. Each regulator can give the wearer three kinds of supply: oxygen mixed with cabin air in a proportion set by cabin altitude, undiluted oxygen at cabin pressure, and undiluted oxygen at a pressure slightly above cabin pressure.

The oxygen is stored in a high-pressure cylinder mounted upright in the avionics compartment, left of center, where it can be reached in flight. On the DC-10 described by the maintenance manual there is one cylinder of 115 cu ft usable capacity, weighing about 45 lb; FedEx DC-10s carry two cylinders of 111 cu ft, interconnected through their regulators and selected for quantity reading by an OXY QTY switch (SYS 1, SYS 2). The MD-10 has two cylinders, or four with the rigid cargo barrier and its courier seats. The KC-10 has three cylinders, manifolded together so that they drain together; the tanker's duration chart is drawn against the average pressure of all three.

A full cylinder is charged to 1,850 psi at 70 °F. Because the gas is sealed in a fixed volume its pressure follows its absolute temperature, by about 3½ psi per °F: a cylinder charged in a warm hangar reads noticeably less on a cold-soaked aircraft without having lost any oxygen, which is why duration tables are entered with pressure corrected to 70 °F.

The cylinder's **shutoff valve** carries a direct-reading pressure gauge and a **blowout disc**. If the cylinder pressure exceeds about 2,650 psi the disc ruptures and the whole contents of the cylinder are dumped overboard through a discharge port on the lower left side of the nose, blowing out a green indicator disc there. A missing green disc on the walk-around means a cylinder has discharged.

Mounted on the shutoff valve, the **regulator/refill valve** reduces cylinder pressure to a line pressure of about 70 psi (70 ± 8 psi). It also contains the refill port, with an automatic cutoff that closes at about 2,000 psi during servicing; a **line relief valve** that opens between 120 and 140 psi; and a **pressure transducer** that sends cylinder pressure to the quantity indicator on the flight deck. The two reliefs behave very differently: the line relief vents only until line pressure is back in range, while the cylinder's blowout disc empties the cylinder.

The reducing regulator is a spring and diaphragm. Like any such regulator it **droops**: the more oxygen flows, the further line pressure falls below its no-flow setting. The line pressure gauge shows this with two bands, a wide band for the normal operating range and a narrow band for the acceptable range when oxygen is being used under high-flow conditions, such as every crew member on 100 % or EMERGENCY.

Low-pressure distribution lines run from the regulator to a quick-disconnect receptacle at each crew station. Oxygen at low pressure is safer and lighter to plumb through the flight deck than oxygen at 1,850 psi, and keeping high-pressure oxygen confined to the cylinder and its valve, away from oil, grease and ignition sources, limits the fire risk that pure oxygen always carries.

**ARO/ADDITIONAL O2 SHUTOFF.** Every crew station aft of the flight deck (the three in the ARO compartment and those at the additional crew seats) is fed through one valve, mounted in the ceiling over the flight engineer and normally left open. Shutting it cuts off all of those stations while the flight deck keeps its supply, which protects the flight crew's oxygen if a line aft of the cockpit is damaged or leaking.

Each crew station has a quick-donning mask in a stowage box or bag, with the regulator built into the mask. FedEx DC-10s use full-face masks that protect against both hypoxia and smoke; the MD-10 uses an oronasal mask with separate smoke goggles and a vent valve to purge smoke from the goggles. The harness is pneumatic: squeezing the red inflation tabs on the regulator inflates it so that it can be slipped over the head with one hand, and releasing them lets it deflate and grip. A microphone in the mask connects to the audio system.

blocks.alt: Close-up of a DC-10 crew quick-donning oxygen mask and its mask-mounted diluter-demand regulator, out of its stowage bag. Legible: the red harness inflation tabs; the dilution control lever with its N (normal/dilute) and 100% positions; the EMERGENCY pressure control knob with NORMAL and EMERGENCY marks; the supply hose and microphone lead. The mask's face seal and the inflatable harness visible.
blocks.title: Crew mask and mask-mounted regulator

blocks.content: The regulator has two controls. The **dilution control** selects normal (DILUTE) or **100 %**. In DILUTE the regulator mixes oxygen with cabin air in proportion to cabin altitude up to about 27,000 ft cabin altitude, and above that delivers pure oxygen under positive pressure automatically. At 100 % it closes its air inlet and delivers pure oxygen on demand at any altitude. The **EMERGENCY pressure control** delivers pure oxygen under positive pressure at altitudes where positive pressure would not otherwise be supplied: pushing it gives a momentary flow (used to test the regulator and to clear the goggles), and rotating it to EMERGENCY locks the flow on. For EMERGENCY to deliver pure oxygen the dilution control must be at 100 %. The preflight and stowed setting is 100 %, so that a mask donned in smoke delivers pure oxygen at once.

If line pressure falls to about 25 psi while a regulator is in DILUTE, a warning device in the regulator closes its air inlet. Breathing becomes noticeably harder, telling the wearer that the supply is inadequate for the demand. On the MD-10 each stowage box also has a flow-indicating blinker, an OXY ON flag and a PRESS TO TEST AND RESET lever.

On the KC-10 the regulator is not on the mask. Each crew station has a lighted regulator panel mounted to the structure beside it, with every control on the panel and a hose to the mask. There are fourteen: five on the flight deck (pilot's, copilot's, flight engineer's, boom operator's and observer's), three in the ARO compartment (for the boom operator, instructor and observer seated there), and six at the additional crew seats. Only six additional crew seats may be installed forward of the cargo compartment because of the limited long-term oxygen supply. The four crew bunks have a portable 11 cu ft bottle each instead.

blocks.alt: Close-up of a KC-10 flight crew oxygen regulator panel, lit. Legible: the SUPPLY ON/OFF toggle at ON (right); the NORMAL OXYGEN / 100% OXYGEN toggle at 100% OXYGEN (center); the EMERGENCY / NORMAL / TEST MASK toggle at NORMAL (left); the FLOW indicator window showing white; the OXYGEN SUPPLY PRESSURE gauge reading about 70 psi.
blocks.title: KC-10 crew oxygen regulator panel

blocks.content:
The **SUPPLY** toggle (ON/OFF) is ON for all operations needing oxygen at that station and OFF when the station is unoccupied. The center toggle selects **NORMAL OXYGEN**, a mixture whose air content falls as cabin altitude rises until pure oxygen is delivered at about 29,000 ft, or **100% OXYGEN**, pure oxygen at any altitude in the quantity the wearer inhales. The left toggle selects NORMAL, **EMERGENCY**, which starts a constant flow at a positive pressure equal to 3.5 inches of water at any altitude, or **TEST MASK**, a momentary position spring-loaded to NORMAL that gives 11 inches of water to check the mask's seal.

The regulator also adds pressure automatically: between 29,000 and 39,500 ft cabin altitude a safety pressure of 0.1 to 2.0 inches of water, and at 40,000 ft and above pressure breathing at 2 to 15 inches of water, rising with cabin altitude.

The **FLOW** indicator shows white while oxygen is flowing through the regulator and black when it is not. With a demand regulator gas moves only during inhalation, so the indicator alternates white and black with the wearer's breathing; a continuous flow (EMERGENCY, or a leaking mask) holds it white. The **OXYGEN SUPPLY PRESSURE** gauge reads the pressure at the regulator's inlet, about 70 psi; it needs no electrical power and reads with the SUPPLY toggle off. The panel lighting is powered from the 28 V AC ground service lighting supply.

How long the crew oxygen lasts depends on cylinder pressure, the number of people breathing, the regulator setting and the cabin altitude, and the altitude effect is not what intuition suggests. A demand regulator delivers a volume of gas set by the wearer's breathing at cabin pressure. In normal (diluted) mode two things change as the cabin climbs: the share of oxygen in that volume rises, while the density of the gas falls. The first dominates up to the altitude where the regulator reaches 100 %, so consumption per person **rises** with cabin altitude to a peak at roughly 25,000 to 27,000 ft and then falls. On 100 % the oxygen share is fixed, only the density term is left, and consumption falls steadily with altitude, so 100 % costs most at low cabin altitude: at sea level it uses about five times the oxygen of normal mode. Positive pressure, and EMERGENCY in particular, adds a continuous leak at the mask and is expensive at any altitude.

Duration tables give **man-hours** of oxygen against cylinder pressure (corrected to 70 °F) and cabin altitude; dividing by the number of people on oxygen gives the duration. The figures below are from FedEx's table for its two-cylinder installation used down to 50 psig.

blocks.title: Crew oxygen duration, FedEx DC-10 (two 111 cu ft cylinders, man-hours)

blocks.content: FedEx also states that a fully charged system supplies five people at maximum (100 %) demand for about two hours, and at normal demand for about eight. The KC-10's chart works the same way from the average pressure of its three cylinders; its own worked example gives three crew members on normal oxygen at a 25,000 ft cabin altitude 6.1 hours from 1,000 psi.

sections.title: Passenger and supernumerary oxygen
sections.summary: Chemical generators behind drop-out doors, released automatically by cabin altitude or by the crew.

blocks.content: Passengers, supernumeraries and cabin attendants are supplied by self-contained **oxygen generating and dispensing units**: a chemical oxygen generator, two or more masks with reservoir bags, and the hoses between them, in a compartment closed by an electrically latched door. The compartments are in seat backs, overhead positions, partitions, lavatories and attendant stations. On a passenger DC-10 they are throughout the cabin; on the freighters they serve the supernumerary seats and lavatory forward; on the KC-10 the fourteen permanent seats have their masks in seven ceiling containers.

blocks.alt: Passenger cabin of a DC-10-30 after a decompression: an overhead oxygen compartment door hanging open, three yellow continuous-flow masks with transparent reservoir bags hanging on their lanyards, one mask pulled down. Inset cut-away of the chemical generator in the compartment: sodium chlorate core, insulation, filter, primer and firing pin, the firing-pin lanyard leading to the masks, and the small green flow indicator in a reservoir bag inflated.
blocks.title: Passenger oxygen unit

blocks.content:
A generator stores its oxygen chemically, in a core of sodium chlorate. A lanyard links its firing pin to the masks: pulling the first mask down toward the face pulls the pin, which strikes a primer and ignites an enriched starting cone at one end of the core. The core then burns slowly along its length, decomposing into salt and releasing pure oxygen, which passes through a filter to the masks. Every mask attached to that generator then flows, whether or not anyone is using it.

The reaction cannot be stopped, and using fewer masks does not make it last longer: a DC-10 or MD-10 generator produces oxygen for about 15 minutes, a KC-10 generator for at most 22 minutes. A spent generator is replaced on the ground.

The masks are continuous-flow, with no shutoff valve. Oxygen collects in each mask's reservoir bag between breaths; the wearer breathes the bag's contents first and then cabin air through an ambient valve for the rest of the breath. Because the flow is low the bags may not inflate fully between breaths. A small green compartment in each reservoir bag inflates when oxygen starts to flow, showing the mask is working; how fast it fills depends on cabin altitude and on how long the generator has been burning.

While it is producing oxygen a generator's case can reach about 500 °F (260 °C) and will burn whoever handles it, so leave it in its compartment. One that has come out while active is moved by its mask hoses only and set down in something metal, a lavatory sink for example. The scorched-fabric smell of a burning generator is expected; it neither contaminates the oxygen nor signals a fire.

The chemical approach suits this job. It needs no plumbing through the cabin and no stored high-pressure oxygen near passengers, it is light, and the generators keep for years without servicing. Its cost is the fixed duration, which turns a decompression into a race: the aircraft must be down to a cabin altitude where people can breathe unaided before the generators are spent.

Each compartment door is held shut by an electric latch. Two independent paths can release the latches:

**Automatic.** An aneroid switch in the cabin senses cabin pressure. When the cabin altitude climbs through about 14,000 ft (KC-10: 14,150 ± 350 ft) its contacts close, and they stay closed while the cabin altitude stays at or above that value. The switch energizes an eject relay that powers every door latch open. The relay incorporates a timer that removes power from the latches about 5 seconds after it closes; the latch mechanisms can be damaged if they stay energized longer, which is also why the manual switch must not be held at EJECT for more than 5 seconds.

**Manual.** A guarded, safety-wired **OXY MASK** switch (MD-10: the MASKS switchlight) bypasses the aneroid and the relay and releases the doors directly. It is a backup for an aneroid or relay that fails, and lets the crew present the masks at any cabin altitude, for example for smoke. The switch is held at EJECT for 3 to 5 seconds; holding it for more than 5 seconds can damage the door latch mechanisms.

The two release paths take their power from different AC buses, so a power failure that stops the automatic release in part of the cabin may leave the manual path able to do it. After any interruption of electrical power the crew therefore select EJECT again once power is back. As a last resort, each door can be opened by hand through a small access hole or finger hole.

blocks.title: Release circuits

blocks.content: On a passenger DC-10 the doors are grouped into forward, mid and aft cabin zones, and a release can succeed in one zone and fail in another.

Portable oxygen cylinders let crew members move about the aircraft on oxygen, fight a fire or give first aid. Each is a small cylinder, typically 11 cu ft, with a pressure gauge, a shutoff valve and a demand or pressure-demand regulator feeding a mask.

items: **DC-10 (FedEx):** two portable cylinders with full-face smoke masks on the flight deck, giving about 15 minutes of 100 % oxygen on demand from a full cylinder, plus two emergency escape breathing devices.

**KC-10:** thirteen portable 11 cu ft cylinders, each about 10 lb, on the flight deck, in the cargo compartment, lavatory, ARO compartment and at the additional crew seats, and one at each crew bunk. Support personnel also have an emergency passenger oxygen system (EPOS) hood at each seat: a self-contained hood with its own small oxygen cylinder, giving about 5 minutes under heavy workload and up to an hour sitting quietly.
**MD-10:** an 11 cu ft portable cylinder on the flight deck.

blocks.content: Portable oxygen equipment is not simulated as items the crew can use.

blocks.content: Crew oxygen is used at each crew station, through that station's mask and regulator. Quantity is monitored by the flight engineer on the DC-10 and KC-10, and on an indicator beside the first officer's mask on the MD-10. The passenger masks have one manual control, the guarded mask release switch. Which of these items are operable in the simulated cockpits is summarized in [Simulation notes](#simulation-notes).

sections.title: Operation
sections.summary: Preflight checks, normal use, decompression and smoke.

blocks.content: The emergency checklists that use oxygen (rapid decompression and emergency descent, smoke and fumes) are in [Emergency procedures](emergency-procedures); the checks are in [Normal procedures](normal-procedures). This section explains how the system behaves in each case.

**Quantity.** Check the cylinder pressure against the requirement for the number of crew and the planned flight (the duration tables are in man-hours, so the requirement grows with the number of people who might need oxygen). On the DC-10 the flight engineer reads OXY QTY and checks OXY LINE PRESS in the broad band; on the KC-10 the OXY QTY switch is moved through each cylinder; on the MD-10 the indicator beside the first officer's mask is read.

**Masks.** At each station check the mask and regulator are stowed, connected and set to 100 %, and that the supply flows when tested. The FLOW indicator is the test of a demand regulator: breathing normally through the mask for at least three breaths, it should alternate black and white; holding the breath, a white indicator means the mask is leaking. (A full-face mask with a continuous vent purge shows white even when it fits properly.)

In the simulation the DC-10 and MD-10 crew masks cannot be used, and the DC-10's OXY QTY and OXY LINE PRESS gauges and the MD-10's oxygen indicator do not read. Check the crew oxygen quantity on the [EFB Oxygen page](#ci-efb) instead; the mask checks cannot be performed.

On the KC-10 each occupied station's regulator is checked with SUPPLY ON and 100% OXYGEN, then EMERGENCY and TEST MASK, and the OXYGEN SUPPLY PRESSURE gauge should read about 70 psi. Regulators at the additional crew stations are left at NORMAL, 100% OXYGEN and SUPPLY OFF, their gauges reading about 70 psi with the SUPPLY toggle off.

In the simulation the flight deck and ARO regulators can be checked this way except for TEST MASK, which is not available; the OXY QTY indicator does not read (use the [EFB Oxygen page](#ci-efb)), and the additional crew regulators cannot be used.

In normal flight the masks stay stowed, ready to don, with the regulators set to 100 % so that a mask put on in smoke delivers pure oxygen immediately. Normal (diluted) oxygen is the economical setting when oxygen is needed for a long time and the air in the cabin is clean.
On the KC-10 each occupied station's SUPPLY toggle is ON for all operations; at an unoccupied station it is OFF, which also stops a free-flowing regulator from wasting the shared supply.

At the cabin altitude warning the crew don their masks first, before diagnosing anything: at 35,000 ft the time of useful consciousness is under a minute, and less after a rapid decompression. With the masks on and on 100 % (EMERGENCY if needed for positive pressure, or if there is any doubt about fumes), communication is re-established through the mask microphones and the emergency descent begins.
In the simulation the DC-10 and MD-10 crew masks cannot be donned, and the flight crew are not affected by hypoxia; fly the procedure for its timing and its descent.

The passenger and supernumerary masks drop automatically as the cabin altitude passes about 14,000 ft. If they do not, the crew hold the OXY MASK switch (MD-10: MASKS) at EJECT for 3 to 5 seconds, and if electrical power has been interrupted they recycle it to EJECT once power is restored. (In the simulation this backup is not available: the DC-10 and KC-10 cockpits have no OXY MASK switch, and the MD-10's MASKS switchlight releases nothing.) From the moment the masks drop the generators run for a fixed time, about 15 minutes on the DC-10 and MD-10 and at most 22 minutes on the KC-10, so the descent must bring the cabin to a breathable altitude within that time. The KC-10's procedures, for example, call for reaching 13,000 ft within 22 minutes of mask deployment.
Do not hold the OXY MASK switch at EJECT for more than 5 seconds. The door latch mechanisms can be damaged, and doors that did not open the first time may then not open at all.

For smoke or fumes the crew don masks and smoke goggles with the regulators at 100 %, so that no cabin air is drawn in. A momentary push of the EMERGENCY control, or a short period at EMERGENCY, clears smoke or misting from the goggles; on the KC-10 the EMERGENCY position does the same. Positive pressure keeps contaminated air out of a mask that does not seal perfectly, at the cost of a continuous flow. Once the smoke has cleared, returning the emergency selector to NORMAL extends the oxygen remaining. (DC-10 and MD-10: the crew masks cannot be used in the simulation; on the KC-10 the flight deck and ARO regulators work as described.)
The oxygen systems have no failure annunciation of their own on the DC-10 and KC-10; failures are found from the gauges, the FLOW indicators and the masks themselves.
