blocks.content: **Modeled in depth.** The crew cylinder bank (one cylinder on the DC-10 and MD-10, three manifolded cylinders on the KC-10), its reducing regulator with the droop the line gauge's two bands describe, the line relief and the cylinder's blowout disc. Oxygen use follows the regulator physics: the oxygen share rises with cabin altitude in normal mode while the gas density falls, so consumption peaks near the 100 % point, which is set per aircraft (27,000 ft on the DC-10 and MD-10, 29,000 ft on the KC-10). 100 %, EMERGENCY, the automatic safety pressure and pressure breathing are all modeled, and on the KC-10 the result has been checked against the T.O.'s duration chart. Each station draws only while it is in use, which on the KC-10 means its SUPPLY toggle is ON.

On the passenger side the aneroid, the automatic and manual release paths on their separate supplies, the three release zones, the latch damage from holding EJECT too long and the generators (their fixed burn time and their heat) are modeled. The aneroid responds to the cabin altitude **crossing** its trip altitude: a flight started in the air with the cabin already above it does not drop the masks until the cabin has come down below the trip altitude, while a real decompression after that still deploys them. On a passenger DC-10 with simulated passengers, passengers left without oxygen at high cabin altitude lose consciousness according to the time of useful consciousness; once the masks drop and their zone's generators are burning they put the masks on after a short delay and recover, and when the generators are spent they are breathing cabin air again.

items: **Simplified:** a zone's generators start as soon as its doors open, rather than when a mask is pulled.
**Simplified:** on the KC-10 the 5-second timer is treated as a delay; the masks drop about 5 seconds after the cabin passes the trip altitude.

**Different from the real aircraft:** the DC-10 and MD-10 crew cylinder holds less oxygen in the simulation than the real 115 cu ft cylinder, so crew oxygen would run out sooner than the real duration tables show; FedEx DC-10s and the MD-10 also carry two cylinders where the simulation has one. The simulated MD-10 has four crew stations.
Every flight begins with the crew cylinders at about 95 % of a full charge. There is no oxygen servicing control in the cockpit or the EFB.

blocks.content: **Not operable in the simulated cockpits.** These items are described above because they are part of the aircraft, but in the current release they cannot be used:

items: DC-10 and MD-10: the crew masks and mask-mounted regulators. No crew oxygen is consumed on these aircraft.
DC-10: the OXY QTY indicator and OXY LINE PRESS gauge on the flight engineer's panel are not driven. MD-10: the crew oxygen indicator is not modeled.

KC-10: the OXY QTY indicator and its switch are not driven; the ARO/ADDITIONAL O2 SHUTOFF valve cannot be operated; the six additional crew seat regulators cannot be used; the regulators' TEST MASK position is not available (the emergency toggle has NORMAL and EMERGENCY only). The five flight deck and three ARO regulators are fully operable.
DC-10 and KC-10: there is no OXY MASK switch in the cockpit, so the passenger masks can be released only automatically.
MD-10: the MASKS switchlight can be pressed but does not release the masks; only the automatic release works.
Portable oxygen cylinders, smoke hoods and escape breathing devices; FedEx's DON O2 MASK light.
Flight crew hypoxia is not simulated.

blocks.content: **EFB.** The Systems app's Oxygen page shows the bank's pressure and quantity, the line pressure, the endurance at the present draw, the stations in use, the aneroid's comparison and the zones (see [EFB oxygen page](#ci-efb)); on the DC-10 and KC-10 it is the practical way to read the crew oxygen quantity. The Failures app offers a rapid decompression (under pressurization), which exercises the passenger system; it has no oxygen system failures of its own.

parts.title: Lighting
parts.summary: Exterior, flight deck, cabin and emergency lighting, and the passenger signs.

sections.title: Introduction
sections.summary: What the lighting systems are, how they are built, and what each aircraft carries.

blocks.content: The aircraft's lighting divides into four systems: **exterior lighting**, for seeing and being seen; **flight deck lighting**, for reading the instruments and panels in any light; **cabin lighting** with the passenger signs; and **emergency lighting**, which lights the way out when everything else has failed.

Almost all of it is simple in principle: a switch or dimmer, a breaker, and a lamp on an electrical bus. A light is lit when it is selected, its breaker is in and its bus is powered, so the lighting fails exactly as the electrical system does, bus by bus, and the bus assignments in this part tell the crew which lights they will lose with each bus. Three parts of the system are mechanisms with behavior of their own: the **retractable wing landing lights**, which take several seconds to extend and light only when fully out; the KC-10's **receptacle floodlight doors**; and the **emergency lighting**, a logic unit with battery packs that switches itself on.

sections.title: Exterior lighting
sections.summary: Landing, taxi and turnoff lights, position and anti-collision lights, the scan and logo lights, and the KC-10's air refueling lights.

blocks.content: The exterior lights do two different jobs. Some let the crew **see**: the landing, taxi, runway turnoff and wing scan lights. Others let the aircraft **be seen**: the position lights, the anti-collision beacons, the high-intensity strobes and the logo lights. The distinction decides when each is used and why the second group is wired to survive more failures: the position lights and the turnoff, scan and logo lights are fed from the AC ground service bus, which can be powered from ground power with no generator running, so the aircraft can be lit on the ramp.

blocks.content: The two wing landing lights retract flush into the fuselage fillets when not in use and swing out about 80° on an electric drive to shine forward. Stowing them removes their drag and noise in cruise and protects the lens. Each has a three-position switch: **RET** drives the housing in and puts the lamp out; **EXT OFF** drives it out with the lamp off; **EXT ON** drives it out and lights the lamp.

The lamp is fed through the housing's extend limit switch, so it lights only when the housing is fully out. Selecting EXT ON on a stowed light gives about five and a half seconds of travel, then light. The EXT OFF position lets the crew extend early and light late, or keep the lights out but dark. The drive motor and the lamp are on separate breakers on the same bus (left on AC bus 1, right on AC bus 3). The motor stops where it stands if its power fails, and resumes when power returns; a housing stopped short of the limit stays dark.
With a housing extended the airflow over it is audible on the flight deck, a useful cue that a light has been left out after takeoff.

children.title: Nose gear lights and runway turnoff lights

blocks.content: The two lamps on the nose gear carry a taxi filament and a landing filament. The nose light switch has three positions: **OFF**; **TAXI**, which lights the taxi filaments at reduced intensity for ground operation; and **LAND**, which adds the landing filaments for full intensity. The nose lights are interlocked with the nose gear: they light only when the nose gear is down and locked, so they cannot burn inside a closed wheel well.

The two **runway turnoff lights** in the wing fillets light the ground ahead and to each side, supplementing the nose lights in turns and on high-speed turnoffs, and serve as ground floodlights for servicing. On the DC-10 and KC-10 each has its own switch. On the MD-10 the two WING & RUNWAY TURNOFF switchlights, LEFT and RIGHT, each light that side's turnoff light and wing scan light together.

The **position lights** follow the international convention that lets an observer judge another aircraft's heading at night: red on the left wingtip and green on the right, both facing forward, and white facing aft. The DC-10 family carries its aft white lights on the trailing edge of each wingtip rather than on the tail, which still gives the standard left, right and aft sectors. They are fed on two circuits from the AC ground service bus. On the KC-10 the NAV control is a dimmer, so the position lights can be turned down, for example for formation flying at night.

The two red **anti-collision beacons**, on top and underneath the fuselage, each flash about once a second. Switching them on signals to ground crew that engines are about to start or the aircraft is about to move, which is why the beacon is the first exterior light on in the starting sequence and the last off at the gate. They are fed from AC bus 1 with a standby feed from AC bus 2, so the loss of one bus does not put them out.

The **high-intensity strobes**, three white lights on each wingtip, make the aircraft conspicuous in the air and on the runway. Each flashes twice, pauses about a second, and repeats. On the ground they are used as the operator's procedures require, because their brilliance can dazzle other crews and ground staff. They are powered from AC bus 3.
The **logo lights** in the horizontal stabilizer floodlight the fin. Besides displaying the operator's markings they make the aircraft easier to see in the traffic pattern and on the ground at night.

**KC-10 beacons.** The tanker's beacons are anti-collision and rendezvous lights in one: each mast carries a red and a white light. The BEACON LT MASTER selector chooses BOTH, OFF, UPPER or LOWER, and the color selector RED, WHITE, RED-WHITE or SEQ. In SEQ the beacons flash a coded white, red, white sequence that a receiver can identify during a rendezvous. For air refueling the beacons are normally set to UPPER and RED; if any aircraft is flying visual wing formation the beacons are turned off, and the outside aircraft of the formation keeps its anti-collision lights on.

The two **wing scan lights**, on the fuselage sides forward of the wing, illuminate the wing leading edge and upper surface and the engine 1 and 3 nacelles, so that the crew can inspect them for ice at night (see [Ice and Rain Protection](ice-and-rain)) and check the wing for fluid leaks or damage. On the DC-10 the WING switch has OFF, a single-side position for ground servicing, and both lights. On the KC-10 a knob dims both lights. The MD-10 has no separate wing switch: each wing scan light follows its side's WING & RUNWAY TURNOFF switch.

The tanker carries floodlights that light the aircraft for the receiver pilots. Two **upper fuselage lights** in the fin crown, controlled by the UPPER FUSELAGE knob on the flight engineer's panel, light the top of the fuselage and the wings for a receiver formating above and behind. The boom operator's station has four EXTERIOR LIGHTING knobs for the forward and aft fuselage lights, the wing flood lights and the horizontal stabilizer lights; all four dim their lights from off to bright.

The tanker's own air refueling receptacle (UARRSI) has floodlights behind mirrored doors on either side of it, controlled by the AR RECP FLOOD & DOOR CONT knob: past CLOSED it opens the doors and the rheostat sets the brightness; at CLOSED the floods go out and the doors close. **FLOOD LT DOOR NOT CLOSED** on the overhead annunciator panel lights while the control is at CLOSED and the doors have not reached their closed limit, for the few seconds of their travel, or longer if they stop short. The doors are on AC bus 3 and stop where they are if it fails. The control is not fitted in the simulated cockpit, so the doors stay closed (see [Simulation notes](#simulation-notes)).
The boom, drogue and pod signal lights and the pilot director lights are described in [Air Refueling Systems](air-refueling-systems).

sections.title: Flight deck lighting
sections.summary: Integral panel lighting, floodlights, the thunderstorm lights, and the supplementary lights.

blocks.content: Flight deck lighting is layered so that the crew can read every instrument in any ambient light, from direct sunlight to a dark night, without glare, and so that no single failure leaves the instruments unreadable. Three systems overlap: **integral lighting** inside the instruments and behind the panel legend plates; **floodlights** that wash the panels from above; and the **thunderstorm** circuit that drives the floods to full brightness. Supplementary lights serve the crew's own work areas.

Integral lighting is the primary system: lamps inside each instrument and behind each engraved legend plate light the markings themselves, so the lighting is even and makes no reflections in the glass. Each panel's integral lighting has its own dimmer, from off to full, and its own circuits, so dimming one panel to match the darkness outside does not change another.

blocks.title: Integral lighting dimmers
rows: Captain's and first officer's instrument panels
PNL & FMA knobs on each pilot's light control panel
INSTR & PED PNL knob (forward overhead), all three instrument panels

blocks.content: The MD-10's six display units have their own brightness knobs on the System Display Control Panel; each display also adjusts itself to the ambient light (see [Flight Instruments](flight-instruments)).

Floodlights are the secondary system. On the DC-10 and KC-10 the main instrument panels have fluorescent and incandescent floods, controlled by dual concentric knobs: the outer knob switches and dims the fluorescent lamps, the inner knob the incandescent ones. Fluorescent light is even and economical; incandescent light dims smoothly to a very low level for night adaptation. The overhead panel, the pedestal and the flight engineer's panels have incandescent floods, each with its own knob, and the glareshield's flight guidance panel has its own flood (FGC FLOOD).

On the MD-10 one INSTR & PED FLOOD knob controls the floodlights of the three instrument panels and the pedestal, the OVHD FLOOD knob (inner ring) the overhead floods, and the inner ring of the FGS PNL & FLOOD rheostat on each side the flight guidance panel floods.
The cockpit **dome lights** give general illumination, switched by the DOME switch (DC-10 and KC-10: the dome light buttons on the overhead).

A nearby lightning flash can leave a dark-adapted crew unable to read their instruments for several seconds, just when turbulence makes reading them most important. The **THNDRSTRM** switch drives all instrument and panel floodlights and the dome lights to full brightness, overriding their individual knobs, so that the eye stays adapted to a bright cockpit and a flash does not blind it. It does not affect the integral panel lighting or the standby compass light. The override works through a control relay on its own breaker, COCKPIT THUNDERSTORM LT CONT (DC bus 1); each forced light still needs its own breaker and bus. The smoke and fumes procedures also call for the thunderstorm lights: in a darkened cockpit, bright light helps find the source of the smoke.

sections.title: Cabin lighting and passenger signs
sections.summary: The cabin lights, their decompression override, and the NO SMOKING and FASTEN SEAT BELTS signs.

blocks.content: Cabin lighting is controlled from the attendant panels at the doors rather than from the flight deck. On the freighters, the MD-10 and the KC-10 the main deck is lit by ceiling lights in bays, with entry lights at the doors and reading lights for the couriers or passengers, all selected on the panel at door 1L. On the passenger DC-10s, the open cabins built from them and the fire tankers, attendant panels at each door control the ceiling, sidewall, entry, aisle-crossing, lavatory entry and reading lights zone by zone. The panels and their switches are described in [Doors and Cabin](doors-and-cabin); the KC-10's boom operator's compartment lighting in [Air Refueling Systems](air-refueling-systems).

**Decompression override.** If the cabin altitude rises above about 10,000 ft, the cabin ceiling lights come on at full brightness automatically, whatever the attendant panels are set to (see [Simulation notes](#simulation-notes) for the main-deck cabins), so that passengers and crew can find their oxygen masks and the exits. The override is driven by the same cabin altitude switch that lights CABIN ALT, through a relay on its own breaker (DC bus 2).

The cabin's **NO SMOKING** and **FASTEN SEAT BELTS** signs (and RETURN TO CABIN in the lavatories) are switched from the flight deck. A low chime sounds in the cabin each time a sign comes on. The signs are powered through WARN SIGNS CONT (lower main panel D-11, DC bus 1).

sections.title: Emergency lighting
sections.summary: The battery-backed lights that light the cabin and exits if normal lighting fails, how they arm, and how they are tested.

blocks.content: The emergency lighting system lights the way out after a crash or a total electrical failure. It consists of cabin ceiling lights, exit signs, door lights and cockpit lights, and it comes on in three ways: **automatically** when normal lighting power fails with the system armed, when a pilot selects it **ON**, or when a cabin attendant selects it on at the forward left door.

**Power.** A logic unit selects the supply in priority order: the right emergency AC bus, then the left emergency DC bus, then the emergency battery packs. The packs carry the lights only when both emergency buses are lost, so their charge is kept for the case that needs it. Each pack feeds its own circuit, so one failed pack darkens only its share of the lights. The packs are kept charged from the right emergency AC bus.

blocks.title: Emergency lighting battery packs
rows: Passenger DC-10s, open cabins, fire tankers
Two (a third only with the 55-passenger kit)

blocks.content: **Arming and the automatic turn-on.** With the cockpit EMER LT switch at **ARM**, the logic unit watches the AC ground service bus. If it loses power, the emergency lights come on by themselves. Once on automatically they **latch**: normal power must be restored before the lights can be switched off at OFF. Neither alone releases them: power returning with the switch still at ARM leaves them on, and OFF on a dead bus does nothing. This is why the switch is left at OFF until AC power is established during the cockpit preparation and returned to OFF before the aircraft is shut down: a switch left at ARM on a battery-only aircraft turns the emergency lights on and drains the packs.

blocks.content: **Test.** Holding the **EMER LT TEST** button lights the emergency lights from the battery packs, testing them under load. On the KC-10, after 3 to 5 seconds held, the green **EMER LT TEST** light comes on if every pack's voltage is normal. A pack that is nearly flat, or has failed, keeps the light out. The test runs through EMER LT BATTERY TEST (DC bus 3).

blocks.content: **Modeled.** Every exterior and interior light is a switched circuit on its own breaker and bus, so pulled breakers and bus failures put out exactly the lights described above, and the lights' electrical loads appear on their buses. The wing landing lights' extend drive, its limit switch and its stop on power loss are modeled; the nose lights are interlocked with the nose gear downlock. The strobes and beacons flash; the KC-10's sequenced beacon runs its coded pattern. The emergency lighting logic unit, its supply priority, the automatic turn-on and latch, the battery packs' charge and endurance, and the test are modeled, as are the passenger signs with AUTO, the decompression term and the cabin chime, and the passenger cabin lighting with its decompression override.

items: **Landing light travel.** The wing landing lights extend in about 5.5 seconds; the FedEx manual gives about 10 seconds. The extend limit switch does not cut the motor's own load.
**Nose light interlock.** The nose lights follow the nose gear's downlock; the books describe the interlock as the gear handle at DOWN, which gives the same result except while the gear is moving.
**DC-10 wing switch.** The single-side position lights the left scan light only; FedEx aircraft placard it R ONLY.
**Thunderstorm lights.** Besides the floods and dome lights, the override also drives the map, briefcase and floor lights to full.
**Standby lighting.** The real aircraft's standby system, which lights selected floodlights from the battery when DC power fails, is not modeled.

**Emergency lights.** The emergency light switch, test and logic work on every deck, but only the KC-10's overhead has the DISARMED and EMER LT TEST lights: on the DC-10 there is no indication that the switch is not at ARM, and the test is judged by the emergency lights coming on. On the MD-10 the EMER LTS DISARM alert is displayed, but the EMER LTS TST PASS and EMER LT BAT 1 LO alerts are never raised, so the MD-10 test too is judged by the lights alone. The MD-10 uses the DC-10 freighter's two packs of at least 10 minutes; the MD-10 FCOM describes one battery of at least 15 minutes. On the main-deck cabins the exit signs light; the passenger cabins also show the emergency ceiling lights. The attendant's EMER LIGHTS switch works on the freighters, the MD-10 and the KC-10; the passenger cabins' attendant panels do not have it.

**KC-10.** The AR RECP FLOOD & DOOR CONT control is not in the cockpit model, so the receptacle flood doors stay closed and FLOOD LT DOOR NOT CLOSED never lights. The formation lights and the pilot director lights are not modeled.
**Main deck cabin.** The decompression override of the cabin lights is modeled on the passenger cabins only.

blocks.content: **Simulator keys.** The simulator's own light commands (strobes, navigation, beacon, logo, wing, landing and taxi lights, and the all-lights toggle) move the cockpit switches, as a crew member's hand would, and the panel lights command turns the panel lighting dimmers. They do not open the KC-10's receptacle flood doors or turn on its air refueling lights. Because the switch moves, a light whose bus or breaker is dead stays dark whatever the key. Landing lights selected by key extend and then light; taxi lights by key select TAXI.

parts.title: Doors, Cargo and Cabin
parts.summary: Doors and escape slides, cargo compartments and handling, cabin, galleys, water and waste.

sections.title: Introduction
sections.summary: What this part covers, how the fuselage is divided, and which doors and compartments each aircraft carries.

blocks.content:
This part describes everything in the fuselage behind the flight deck that the crew opens, closes, loads, serves or monitors: the cabin and cargo doors and their warning system, the escape slides and emergency exits, the cargo compartments and their handling, the passenger cabin and its crew, the galleys, and the potable water and waste systems.

The fuselage is a pressure vessel of semimonocoque construction, divided lengthwise by the main floor into a main deck and a lower deck. Everything inside the vessel is pressurized: the flight deck, the main deck, the three lower holds and the avionics compartment. The nose radome, the wheel wells, the wing center section, the air-conditioning pack bays and the tail cone are not. That boundary decides how every door is built. A door that opens into a pressurized compartment is either a **plug door**, larger than its opening and held shut by cabin pressure, or an outward-opening door held by latches and locked, with a vent that makes a door that is not locked impossible to pressurize. A door that opens into an unpressurized bay is a plain latched panel.

The simulation tracks twenty-seven doors, of four basic kinds:

- **Cabin doors** (eight positions, 1L to 4R): plug doors that move inboard and up into the ceiling, driven by an electric actuator in normal use or a nitrogen-powered air motor in an emergency, each with an evacuation slide whose arming lever also controls whether the electric drive works at all.
- **Lower cargo doors** (forward, center and aft): outward-opening doors hinged at the top, with an electric latch actuator, an electric door actuator and a hand-worked locking handle, interlocked by limit switches so that the sequence cannot be done out of order.
- **The main-deck cargo door** (freighters, MD-10 and KC-10): a very large door on its own independent hydraulic system, with two mechanical hold-open hooks and a hand-worked vent door that gates the whole locking sequence.
- **Service doors**: latched access panels to the avionics compartment, the air-conditioning bays, the accessory compartments, the tail cone, the lower galley and the radome, plus the KC-10's boom operator sighting door and refueling receptacle door.

A door warning system watches most of them through switches in the doors and jambs and lights amber annunciators for the flight engineer (on the MD-10, alerts on the engine and alert display).

blocks.content: Within the DC-10 button, the variants differ in what their main deck carries. The passenger aircraft (DC-10-10, -15, -30 and -40) have the full passenger cabin, four galleys and the lower galley. The freighters (-10F, -30F, -40F) have the main-deck cargo hall and a crew galley. The KDC-10 and the DC-10-40 Omega have an open cabin with rider seats forward and two galleys; the KDC-10 also carries the KC-10's boom and its sighting door. The fire tankers (-10 Tanker, -30 Tanker) have an empty main deck, no cargo and no main-deck cargo door. The MD-10 is a FedEx freighter conversion of the DC-10-10 and -30 and carries the freighter's doors and holds. The KC-10's main deck is a 463L pallet deck with a small crew and support-personnel area forward.

Related parts: cargo compartment heating and ventilation are in [Air Conditioning](air-conditioning), cargo smoke detection and extinguishing in [Fire Protection](fire-protection), the galley buses in [Electrical](electrical), the passenger signs and emergency lighting in [Lighting](lighting), the attendant call system in [Communications](communications), and the cabin oxygen in [Oxygen](oxygen).

sections.title: Cabin doors
sections.summary: Plug doors that move inboard and up into the ceiling, in three operating modes, with the slide arming lever as the interlock that decides which mode is available.

blocks.content:
Eight cabin door positions are provided, four on each side, numbered 1 to 4 from the front: 1 is the forward pair, 2 the mid pair, 3 the overwing pair and 4 the aft pair. The warning lamps name them by station (L FWD, R MID, L OVERWING and so on); crews and placards use the numbers. The forward doors are narrower than the other six. With its slide pack installed a forward door weighs about 245 lb and a mid door about 350 lb.

Every door is a plug door. It opens by moving inboard off its stops and then rolling up on tracks into the space above the ceiling, and it closes by coming down the tracks and being pushed outboard into the frame. Each door has interior and exterior controls; on the aircraft in the simulation the crew uses the interior ones.

A plug door is larger than its opening. Stops on the door edges bear against matching stops on the frame, so cabin pressure pushes the door outward onto the structure rather than trying to push it out of the hole. The load is large: a mid door of roughly 42 by 76 in has about 3,200 sq in of area, so at a cruise differential of 8 psi the frame carries some 25,000 lb through the stops. Because that load holds the door shut, nothing the crew can do opens a plug door against more than a very small residual differential, and the door's own latching only has to hold it against gravity and gusts on the ground. The penalty is mechanical: the door must first move inboard, into the cabin, before it can clear the frame, which is why it then travels up into the ceiling rather than swinging outward.

Each door is a frame of beams and intercostals with an aluminum skin, a viewing window, a seal that is a weather seal on the ground and a pressure seal in flight, insulation and a lining that also covers the slide pack on the lower inner face.

Cranks on the door ride on bogies in tracks on the forward and aft frames. Cam followers at the top of the door run on cams on the upper jamb to guide it in and out of the closed position, and bumpers at the top meet stops in the overhead when the door is driven fully open in an emergency. A **closer mechanism** of torque tubes and flexible shafts rotates the cranks when the lower bogies reach the bottom of the tracks, moving the door outboard into its frame. A sliding ceiling panel just inboard of each door moves aside as the door rises so that it can enter the overhead.

The door is driven from an **actuating mechanism** above the upper jamb: an electric actuator and an air motor, chained to a torque tube that turns two cable drums. Cables from the drums lift and lower the door. An **open/close lock** (a collar on the torque tube and a spring-loaded pawl) holds the door at either end of its travel, and a **close lock** at the upper forward corner captures a fitting on the door whenever the controls are in neutral. Both locks release when a control handle is moved off neutral.

Cabin door drive components
rows: Rotary actuator with a three-phase 115 V AC motor, reduction gearbox, clutch, magnetic brake and a self-resetting thermal protector that removes power after about 5 seconds of stall. The brake holds the door wherever power is removed.
Driven by nitrogen released from the door's own reservoir when a control handle is moved to EMERGENCY. Drives the same torque tube as the electric actuator, which is declutched.

blocks.content:
A cabin door has three operating modes, and the reason it has three is that each one covers a different loss.

**Normal (electric).** The door is driven by its electric actuator while the crew holds an OPEN or CLOSE control, and stops where the control is released, held by the magnetic brake. It needs the door's 115 V AC drive circuit and its 28 V DC control circuit, normally from the ground service buses, and it works only with the slide disarmed. A full opening takes about 13 seconds. The open and close limit switches stop the actuator at each end.

**Emergency (pneumatic).** Moving a control handle to EMERGENCY declutches the electric actuator, releases the close lock and opens the reservoir valve. The air motor drives the door up against its stops in no more than 10 seconds (about 8 in the simulation), with the open lock ratcheting behind it. If the slide is armed it deploys as the door reaches the top. Once the air motor has fired the opening cannot be stopped: the door runs to its stops whatever happens to the handle afterwards. A plug door held shut by cabin pressure cannot be opened this way, which is one reason the aircraft is fully depressurized before an evacuation.

**Manual lift.** If the reservoir is empty, the door can still be lifted by hand with the handle in EMERGENCY: pull the door inboard and upward with the lift bar, then push it up to the open position. Two people may be needed; a mid door weighs 350 lb, less the slide once the slide has dropped out of its pack.

**Auxiliary.** From outside, pulling the auxiliary handle declutches the actuator so the door descends under its own weight, governed by the air motor; releasing the handle stops and holds it. Door 1L alone can also be cranked open from outside through its manual drive. The auxiliary mode is a maintenance and ground-crew facility, used to close a door with no power or to open 1L on a dead aircraft.

children.title: Slide arming and the power interlock

blocks.content:
Each slide is packed on the lower inner face of the door. Its girt (the fabric apron at its top) is held by a **girt bar**. With the slide disarmed the girt bar sits in brackets on the door, so the slide rises with the door and stays packed. Arming the slide rotates the arming shafts in the jambs, which lock the girt bar into fittings in the floor; if the door is then opened, the girt stays on the floor and the rising door pulls the pack open and fires its inflation bottle. ARMED placards on the ends of the arming shafts show through small windows in the lower corners of the door lining when the slide is armed.

The arming lever does more than arm the slide, and that is the design's central idea. Two switches ride on the same arming shaft. The **power interlock** switch closes the circuits to the door's electric power switches only when the slide is disarmed, so **an armed door cannot be opened electrically at all**: the only way to open it is the emergency mode, which deploys the slide. The **girt bar** switch closes the slide circuit of the warning system when the slide is disarmed, so the door's warning lamp says either that the door is not secured or that its slide is not armed.

blocks.title: Slide arming lever: what each position does
rows: Opens the door pneumatically; slide stays packed
Opens the door pneumatically and deploys the slide

blocks.content:
An interlock in the jamb holds the arming mechanism in the disarmed position while the door is open, so a slide can be armed only once its door is closed. On the KC-10 a sliding mechanical safety latch on the arming lever holds it at DISARMED; it must be slid to the unlatched position before the lever can reach SLIDE ARMED. On every aircraft the order of work is therefore fixed: close the door, then arm; disarm, then open.

The interlock is also why a parked aircraft with its slides disarmed for boarding has every cabin door lamp lit, even with all doors shut. That is correct, and on the KC-10 and the freighters' forward doors it is what the DOOR DISARMED light beside each door switch exists to explain.

blocks.title: Door disarmed light on with the lever armed
blocks.content: The DOOR DISARMED light shows that the door control switch has power, not where the lever is. If it stays on with the arming lever at SLIDE ARMED, the power interlock has failed closed: moving the door control switch to OPEN will drive the door open with the slide armed and deploy it. Leave the switch alone and have the door inspected.

Each door carrying a slide also has a **SLIDE INFLATION CYLINDER LOW PRESSURE** light (the TEST lens on the door lining, over the slide pack). It comes on when the slide's own inflation bottle is too low to inflate the slide. The light runs from its own battery in the door, not from the aircraft, so it works on a dead aircraft; pressing the lens tests the bulb and its circuit. The slide's inflation bottle and the door's air reservoir are two different bottles: one inflates the slide, the other lifts the door.

blocks.content: The KC-10's 3L, 3R and 4L are deactivated: the doors are present and shut, but have no controls, slide, air bottle or warning lamp, and cannot be opened. The other five use the same mechanism as the DC-10's. On the real KC-10, doors 2L and 2R carry slide/rafts only in the support-personnel configuration, and door 4R has a ground escape rope instead of a slide.

The passenger cabin has the pushbutton door operating system: beside each door an OPEN (UP) and a CLOSE (DN) pushbutton run the electric drive while held. Its arming lever and red EMERGENCY handle are the same as on every DC-10. The open cabins of the KDC-10, the Omega and the fire tankers use the passenger cabin's door stations.

**Freighters and MD-10.** The FedEx DC-10 freighters and MD-10s use only the two forward cabin doors (four on some aircraft). The simulation fits all eight as working doors, each with a slide, an air bottle and (on the DC-10 freighters) a CABIN DOOR lamp, but only 1L and 1R have crew controls in the cabin. Doors 2L to 4R are opened, closed, armed and disarmed only from the EFB's Doors page. A flight started with the engines running loads with every slide armed; a cold and dark start, with every slide disarmed.

sections.title: Lower cargo doors
sections.summary: Three outward-opening doors whose latch actuator, door actuator and locking handle are interlocked by limit switches, with a vent door that keeps an unlocked door from being pressurized.

blocks.content: Three doors give access to the lower holds. The **forward** and **center** doors are on the lower right side of the fuselage and take containers, pallets or bulk cargo. The **aft** door, on the lower left, serves the bulk hold and takes loose cargo only. The doors differ in size but work identically. Each is hinged along its top edge and opens outward and up. Each is operated electrically from a control panel in the fuselage just forward of it, and can be worked by hand with drive tools when there is no power.

blocks.title: Lower cargo door openings
rows: 104 × 66 in without the lower galley (freighters, MD-10, KDC-10); 70 × 66 in with it (passenger aircraft)
LD-3 and LD-11 containers; the 88 × 125 in crosswise units only through the 104 in door

blocks.content: The KC-10's lower holds carry its forward and aft body fuel tanks, and its three lower cargo doors are welded shut. They have no controls and no warning lamps. All KC-10 cargo goes through the main-deck cargo door.

Four assemblies make up each door, and the interlock between them is the whole of its safety.

- **The latching mechanism.** Latches along the lower edge of the door hook over spools in brackets on the sill. Each latch is worked by a link from a crank on a torque tube that runs along the door. A **latch actuator**, an electromechanical linear actuator with a 28 V DC motor, magnetic brake and self-resetting thermal protector, rotates the torque tube to open or close all the latches together.
- **The door actuator.** An electromechanical rotary actuator with a three-phase 115 V AC motor swings the leaf open and shut, with its own brake (it holds the door at any position) and thermal protector. A gas-spring **counterbalance** assists opening and snubs the door as it closes.
- **The locking mechanism.** A handle on the outside of the door, released by a trigger, drives through rods and cranks to a **locktube** carrying **lockpins**. With the locktube locked, the lockpins sit behind flanges on the torque-tube cranks, so the torque tube, and with it every latch, cannot turn. The locktube cannot move to locked unless every latch is fully closed.
- **The vent door.** A small door in the cargo door, on the same linkage as the handle. With the handle off its locked position the vent door is open, and the hold is open to the outside through it.

blocks.alt: Schematic of a DC-10 lower cargo door seen from inside the hold, looking outboard. Show the leaf hinged at the top with the rotary door actuator and counterbalance at the upper edge; along the lower edge the torque tube with its cranks, links and latch hooks engaging spools on the sill, and the linear latch actuator; the locktube with lockpins behind the crank flanges; the exterior handle with its trigger connected by rods to the vent door and the locktube; the lockpin viewing port; and the five switches labeled: lock limit (at the locktube), proximity switch (at a lockpin), latch retract limit, latch extend limit, door open limit, door close limit. Inset: a crank-and-link pair just past dead center against its stop.
blocks.title: Lower cargo door latching and locking

blocks.content: The sequence is not scripted anywhere; it falls out of limit switches handing power from one actuator to the next. The rule that makes the door safe is that **with the locktube locked, the door actuator can never be powered**, and the latches can only be driven closed.

blocks.content: The exterior control panel has a guarded **POWER & LTS** switch, a **DOOR** switch spring-loaded to STOP with OPEN and CLOSE positions, a green **READY TO LOCK** light and a panel light. The guard over the power switch will not let the panel's access door close unless the switch is OFF, so a closed-up aircraft always has its cargo door panels unpowered. Releasing the DOOR switch at any point stops whatever was moving; the actuator brakes hold the latches and the leaf where they are.

Press the trigger and rotate the handle out

The door swings shut. At the close limit power transfers to the latch actuator, the latches close over their spools, and READY TO LOCK comes on.

blocks.content:
A viewing port near the bottom of each door lets the ground crew see that the lockpins are engaged. An **emergency call switch** inside each door lets someone shut in the hold light that door's SYS A lamp on the flight engineer's panel. The doors' seal heaters run whenever the aircraft is powered.

The doors may be operated in winds up to 40 kt and will withstand winds up to 52 kt when fully open. In the simulation the doors are worked from outside by the ground crew, through the EFB's Doors page or for GSX; see [Operation](#operation).
Ground equipment must be at least 28 in below the door opening before the door is closed. A loader left docked at the sill is struck by the closing door.

children.title: Why the interlocks matter: the over-center latch

blocks.content:
A lower cargo door opens outward, so cabin pressure pushes it open, and the only things holding it shut are its latches. At 8 psi a door of about 70 by 66 in carries roughly 37,000 lb, half of it along the latched lower edge. The latches survive that load through geometry. Each crank-and-link pair is rigged as a toggle that finishes just past its dead-center line against a stop. Past dead center, the door's own load drives the crank harder onto the stop, and the more pressure there is, the more firmly the latch holds. Short of dead center the same load drives the crank the other way, back-driving the latch actuator through its brake, and the latch hooks walk off their spools.

Everything else in the mechanism exists to guarantee that the latches really are over center before the hold is pressurized. The locktube cannot lock unless every latch is fully home. The lockpins, once in, physically stop the torque tube turning. The vent door rides on the handle, so a handle that is not home leaves a hole in the hull that no pack can pressurize past. And two independent sensors on two different buses watch the locktube and a lockpin, not the handle.

The arrangement is the product of experience. In June 1972 a DC-10's aft cargo door blew out climbing through about 11,750 ft near Windsor, Ontario, and in March 1974 another, near Paris, did the same at about 11,500 ft with the loss of the aircraft. In both cases a handle had been forced home over latches that had not reached over-center, and the linkage of the day let the vent door close regardless. The fixes that followed added the lockpin viewing ports, reworked the mechanism and introduced a closed-loop locking mechanism that ties the handle and the vent door to the real position of the lockpins.

The simulation models this failure physically. If the latches stall short of over-center and the handle is forced home, the vent door closes and the hold seals, but the locktube is held off by the cranks: on this aircraft both SYS A and SYS B stay lit, because they watch the locktube and a lockpin. Ignore them, and somewhere in the climb the cabin's own load back-drives the latches and throws the door open.
Never take off with a cargo door SYS A or SYS B lamp lit, or with a lockpin that cannot be seen engaged through its viewing port.

sections.title: Main-deck cargo door
sections.summary: The freighters', MD-10's and KC-10's large forward left door: an independent hydraulic system, over-center latches with lockpins, a hand-worked vent door, and hooks that hold it open at 85 and 165 degrees.

blocks.content: The main-deck cargo door is on the left side of the forward fuselage, aft of door 1L, with a clear opening of 140 by 102 in. It is fitted to the DC-10 freighters (-10F, -30F, -40F), the MD-10 and the KC-10; the passenger DC-10s, the KDC-10, the Omega and the fire tankers have none. The door is hinged along its top edge and opens upward and outward. It is controlled by hand from a hydraulic control panel behind a floor-level access door beside the door, and moved hydraulically, by a system completely separate from the aircraft's three hydraulic systems: an electric motor pump normally, or a hand pump when there is no electrical power. As a last resort the door can be unlatched by hand and lifted with a crane.

blocks.alt: Exterior three-quarter view of an MD-10-30 (or DC-10-30F) forward left fuselage with the main-deck cargo door raised on its 165 degree hook. Inset 1: the door's lower edge from inside, showing the latch hooks, lockpin tube, latch actuating cylinder and the vent door near the lower edge, with its handle. Inset 2: the main cargo door hydraulic control panel: the control handle (stowed down in its clip), the OPEN/CLOSE rotation markings, the CARGO DOOR LIGHTS switch, the hand pump socket and the instruction placard reading that the door latches at 85 and 165 degrees only. Labels legible.
blocks.title: Main-deck cargo door and its hydraulic control panel

children.title: Latches, lockpins and the vent door

blocks.content:
Latches along the lower edge hold the door shut. A hydraulic cylinder drives them open and closed, an over-center mechanism holds them closed, and **lockpins** on a lockpin tube, spring-loaded to the locked position and withdrawn by their own cylinder, lock them there. Because the pins are spring-loaded home, losing hydraulic pressure lets them snap back in rather than leaving them out.

An outward-opening **vent door** near the lower edge is the key to the whole locking sequence, and it is worked by hand from inside or outside:

- The cargo door cannot be unlocked or unlatched until the vent door has been opened.
- The vent door cannot be closed and locked until the latches are over center and the lockpin tube is locked.
- While the vent door is open the cabin cannot be pressurized beyond about 1 psi; it simply leaks away through the vent.

So the vent door is the first thing opened and the last thing closed, and a vent door that will not close is the crew's proof that the door behind it is not locked.

Two warning lamps watch the door. **CARGO DOOR SYS B** goes out when the door is closed and locked. **CARGO DOOR SYS A** goes out only when the door and the vent door are both closed and locked. (On the KC-10 this is the arrangement on aircraft 79-1710 and subsequent; the simulation models it on every aircraft with the door.) The lamps come on as soon as the lockpins retract and stay on while the door is open or unlatched.

The door can be stopped anywhere, but it can be **latched open** at only two angles: about 85° (the mid latch) and about 165° (full open). At each, a hook catches a roller and holds the door with no hydraulic pressure at all. The hooks only catch on the way down: to seat the door on one, raise it a few degrees above the hook, then lower it onto it. To come off a hook the door must first be raised clear of it again, which is why closing always begins by driving the door up.

The control handle is spring-loaded down into its clip. It is pulled up to operate and rotated to OPEN or CLOSE. Pulling it up also holds the hooks clear, which is what lets a door raised off a hook be driven straight down past it to close. Conversely, to seat on the 85° hook, the handle is rotated to CLOSE **without** being pulled up, so the hook can catch.

blocks.title: Main-deck cargo door: opening and closing
rows: Open the vent door (handle to UNLOCKED, door OPEN).
Lift the control handle out of its clip and pull it up and hold.
Lift the control handle out of its clip, pull it up and hold.
If the door is on a hook, rotate to OPEN until it rises clear of the hook.
Rotate to OPEN and hold. The lockpins withdraw, the latches open and the door rises.
Rotate directly to CLOSE and hold until the door is down and latched.
Hold until the door is a few degrees above the 85° or 165° hook, then release.
Release the handle and stow it in its clip.
To seat on the 85° hook, rotate to CLOSE without pulling the handle up, until the door rests on the hook. Release and stow.
Close and lock the vent door. Check both CARGO DOOR SYS lamps out.

blocks.content: The door may be operated in winds up to 40 kt and withstands 52 kt from any direction when seated on a hook. With winds of 40 to 65 kt expected, open it only to 85° and only with the aircraft parked so the wind is on its right side; do not use the 165° position.

On the electric pump the door takes the better part of a minute to reach full open; on the hand pump it takes many minutes. The **CARGO DOOR LIGHTS** switch on the same panel turns on floodlights on the inside face of the door. Before flight the exterior lockpin handle must be flush with the fuselage and the latch lockpin visible past its cam, as placarded.

sections.title: Service and access doors
sections.summary: Latched access panels to the compartments outside the cabin, the doors that have warning lamps, and the doors the simulation does not model.

blocks.content: Service doors give the ground crew access to the equipment compartments. They are latched panels with no actuator of their own, opened and closed by hand from outside. Those on pressurized compartments are plug doors like the cabin doors; those on unpressurized bays are plain panels. Several have a warning lamp, because an unlatched access door in flight is either a pressure leak or a panel that can depart the aircraft.

blocks.content: The **ARO sighting door** is the one service door with an actuator. It covers the boom operator's viewing window and is opened and closed electrically with the SIGHTING DOOR switch on the boom operator's overhead panel. The switch must be held until the door reaches its limit; released early, the door stops where it is. Its use is not limited by airspeed or altitude. The receptacle (UARRSI) door belongs to the KC-10's receiver system. Both are described in [Air Refueling Systems](air-refueling-systems).
The APU compartment doors are part of the APU and are described in [APU](apu). The lavatory doors are ordinary hinged doors with a sliding bolt lock and a VACANT/OCCUPIED sign.

**Flight deck door and crew entry.** The crew boards through door 1L by stairs or a jet bridge, or on the real KC-10 by a stowable ground entry ladder at 1L (not simulated). Door 1L can be opened from outside on a dead aircraft with its manual drive. The flight deck door has a viewer, ventilation and a pressure-relief panel that swings open in a rapid decompression of the flight deck, and a removable lower panel that is a crew escape route into the cabin if the door jams. FedEx aircraft carry an intrusion-resistant door with a keypad and an electric lock (28 V DC bus 2); the KC-10's lock is released electrically from the overhead and the MD-10's from the pedestal. The simulation draws the flight deck door but does not model its locking system.

sections.title: Door warning system
sections.summary: Two independent warning subsystems on two DC buses, a dual sensor system on every cargo door, and the cargo door indication test.

blocks.content:
Switches in the doors and jambs light an amber annunciator when a door is not properly closed and secured, or when a cabin door's slide is not armed. The system is built as **two independent subsystems**:

- The **passenger door subsystem**, with cargo **SYS B**, on 28 V DC bus 1.
- The **lower compartment subsystem**, covering the air-conditioning, avionics, center accessory, lower galley and AR sighting doors, with cargo **SYS A**, on 28 V DC bus 2.

Every cargo door has a **dual warning system**: two lamps, SYS A and SYS B, driven by different sensors on different buses. On a lower cargo door SYS A is the limit switches (door closed and locktube locked) and SYS B is the proximity switch at a lockpin; on the main-deck door SYS A is the door and its vent door closed and locked and SYS B the door alone. Two sensors that can disagree are the point: a single failure of a switch, a wire or a bus cannot make an unlocked door read locked, and a single lamp lit on its own, with its partner out, is most likely an indication failure rather than an unlocked door.

The cabin door and lower compartment lamps light the MASTER CAUTION lights at the flight engineer's station and the pilots'. The cargo door lamps are not dimmable and do not trigger MASTER CAUTION, and the flight engineer's annunciator lamp test does not light them: they have their own test.

A lamp goes dark when its bus is lost, whatever the door is doing. A dark door panel on a dead DC bus is not a panel of closed doors; check the buses before trusting it.

blocks.content: The momentary **CARGO DOOR INDICATION** switch, beside the cargo door lamps on the flight engineer's upper panel, tests the cargo door warning circuits. The DC-10 and the KC-10 have two different devices under the same name, and the difference matters when interpreting the result.

blocks.content: The test is the first step of the in-flight procedure for a single cargo door lamp: if the opposite system's lamp for the same door lights normally on test and goes out on release, the lit lamp is an indication fault and the door is locked. See [Failures](#failures).

The MD-10 has no flight engineer's panel. Its miscellaneous systems controller (MSC) reads the same SYS A and SYS B sensors on every cargo door and raises boxed amber level 2 alerts on the engine and alert display (EAD): CARGO DOOR FWD A, FWD B, CTR A, CTR B, AFT A, AFT B, UPR A and UPR B. UPR is the main-deck door; its A alert includes the vent door. The CARGO DOOR TEST switch on the forward overhead panel starts the MSC's test of the door circuits, which also runs automatically on the ground when a fuel lever is turned on; the CARGO DOOR TEST advisory shows while it runs, and CRG DOOR TEST FAIL if the test fails.

In the real aircraft an open or unlocked door also gives a DOOR OPEN alert, the cabin and compartment doors have alerts of their own (CABIN DOOR FWD L, CAC DOOR, AIR COND DOOR and so on), and the cyan CABIN DOORS OPEN shows when the cabin door slides are disarmed.

blocks.title: MD-10 cargo door alerts on the EAD

blocks.content: In the simulation the MD-10 raises the eight CARGO DOOR alerts. It does not yet raise DOOR OPEN, CABIN DOORS OPEN or the cabin and compartment door alerts, and the CARGO DOOR TEST switch has no effect, so the MD-10 has no cockpit indication of a cabin door. Check the cabin doors on the EFB's Doors page.

sections.title: Emergency exits, slides and evacuation
sections.summary: The cabin doors as emergency exits, the escape slides, the flight crew's own exits, the emergency equipment, and the passenger cabin's evacuation signal.

blocks.content: The cabin doors are the aircraft's emergency exits; there are no separate overwing hatches. Every exit has the backup the [operating modes](#cabin-door-modes) provide: if electric power is gone the door opens pneumatically from its own bottle, and if the bottle is empty it can be lifted by hand. From inside, an emergency opening of a door whose slide is armed deploys the slide automatically. The flight crew has two further exits of its own.

Each slide (on many aircraft a **slide/raft**, which doubles as a life raft in a ditching) is packed on the lower inner face of its door. It deploys when its door is opened in the emergency mode with the slide armed: the girt bar, locked into the floor fittings, holds the girt while the rising door pulls the pack open, and a lanyard fires the slide's inflation bottle. If automatic inflation fails, a manual inflation handle, visible once the slide has dropped, inflates it. Slides carry their own battery lights, handholds at the foot for the first evacuees to steady the slide, and, on slide/rafts, a quick-release handle and a mooring line.

The slide's inflation bottle is monitored by the SLIDE INFLATION CYLINDER LOW PRESSURE light on the door. A slide armed over a low bottle will not inflate when it deploys. In the simulation the passengers do not use a door whose slide has deployed.

blocks.alt: Interior view of door 1L in the passenger DC-10 cabin, closed, looking outboard. Show the slide arming lever beside the door at ARMED with its placard, the red EMERGENCY door control handle, the OPEN (UP) and CLOSE (DN) pushbuttons, the SLIDE INFLATION CYLINDER LOW PRESSURE test lens on the door lining over the slide pack, the slide mode verification windows in the lower corners of the lining showing the ARMED flags, and the air reservoir pressure gauge viewing port in the ceiling above the door. Labels legible.
blocks.title: Cabin door station, passenger cabin

blocks.alt: Interior view of door 1L in the main-deck cabin of an MD-10 (same arrangement on the DC-10F and, at five doors, the KC-10), closed. Show the slide arming lever at SLIDE ARMED with the KC-10's sliding safety latch (on the KC-10 view), the red EMERGENCY handle, the three-position DOOR CONTROL switch (OPEN, center off, CLOSE) and its DOOR DISARMED light beside it (out), and the SLIDE INFLATION CYLINDER LOW PRESSURE test lens on the door. Labels legible.
blocks.title: Cabin door station, main-deck cabin

blocks.content:
The flight crew's primary exits are the forward cabin doors and their slides. The alternate routes are the two sliding **clearview windows** beside the windshield, each with an **escape rope** in a compartment above it, and, if the flight deck door jams, its removable lower panel into the cabin. To leave by the window, the seat goes fully aft and outboard, the window is unlocked and wound fully open, and the rope, checked attached to the aircraft, is thrown out; the crewmember goes out head and shoulders first, keeping tension on the rope, and lowers themselves down the side of the fuselage. On the KC-10 the boom operator's seat must face forward before the pilot's window will open.

The clearview windows, escape ropes and the door's escape panel are not simulated.

blocks.title: Reference only
blocks.content: The portable emergency equipment is not simulated. This summary is from the operators' manuals, for orientation; the crew oxygen system and the emergency lights, which are simulated, are described in [Oxygen](oxygen) and [Lighting](lighting).

blocks.title: Typical emergency equipment
rows: Portable oxygen cylinders with full-face smoke masks
4 Halon: one on the flight deck, three on the main cargo deck
11 in the cabin, nine of them Halon, plus disposable units in the lavatories
At the clearview windows and above door 4R

blocks.content:
The passenger cabin's attendant panels carry a guarded **EVAC** switch at doors 1L and 2L, and an **EVAC RESET** button at each attendant station except 1R. Either EVAC switch ON commands the evacuation signal: EVAC lights and a horn at every attendant station, for as long as a switch stays ON. A station's EVAC RESET silences that station's horn until the signal is next commanded; it does not put out the lights. The signal runs from the attendant call system's supply (see [Communications](communications)).

The flight crew orders an evacuation on the PA and the interphone. The evacuation procedure itself is in [Evacuation](emergency-landing#evacuation). Its door-related items are worth understanding here: the aircraft must be fully depressurized (the outflow valve opened) before landing, because no plug door can be opened against residual pressure; the slides must be armed; and each exit is checked through its window for fire or obstruction before it is opened.

sections.title: Cargo compartments and handling
sections.summary: The holds and main decks each aircraft carries, their positions and limits, the unit load devices, the handling system, and loading through the EFB and GSX.

blocks.content:
Cargo travels in up to four compartments: the **main deck** on the freighters, the MD-10 and the KC-10, and three **lower holds** (forward, center and aft bulk) on every DC-10 and MD-10. The forward and center holds are separated by the wing center section. The KC-10's lower holds carry body fuel tanks instead of cargo. Every compartment is inside the pressure vessel and is heated and ventilated by the air-conditioning system (see [Air Conditioning](air-conditioning)); cargo smoke detection and fire extinguishing are described in [Fire Protection](fire-protection).

Cargo is carried in **unit load devices** (ULDs): containers and pallets built to standard base sizes that lock into rails and roller trays in the floor. A position on a deck is a footprint that takes certain devices, up to a height and a weight. The loading system moves each unit from the door to its position and locks it there.

blocks.title: Compartments by aircraft
rows: FS 879-1099, behind the lower galley: 6 LD-3 or 3 LD-11
FS 879-1099, behind the lower galley: 6 LD-3 or 3 LD-11
FS 595-1099: 16 LD-3, 8 LD-11, or 5 crosswise 88 × 125 in
As the -30F; the MD-10-10 without HUD as the -10F
As the -30F; the MD-10-10 without HUD as the -10F

blocks.content: The fire tankers carry no cargo. The passenger aircraft lose the front of the forward hold to the lower galley (FS 595-879), and their forward door is the narrow one; removing the galley, as the freighter conversion does, gives the full-length hold and the wide door that takes 88 × 125 in units crosswise. The -10 and -10F have the shorter center hold, and so the longer bulk hold.

The lower holds are 66 in high and take devices up to 64 in, across a floor about 164 in wide. Containers stand in rows: either two LD-3s side by side (the half-width container with a contoured outboard top) or one full-width LD-11 or LD-6 across the row. In the full-length forward hold, five crosswise positions take 88 × 125 in units (the 64 in AAK, the LD-7 pallet and the LD-9 and LD-26 containers) turned across the hold, in place of the rows they cover. A row and the crosswise position over it cannot both be loaded.

The bulk hold takes loose bags and parcels behind a restraint curtain and is loaded by hand through its small door.

rows: A row: one LD-11 or two LD-3

blocks.title: Lower hold positions

blocks.content:
The freighters' and MD-10's main deck is a cargo hall from a barrier net behind the crew area (about FS 498) to the aft bulkhead (about FS 1922), loaded through the main-deck door at rows 2 and 3. Ball mats at the door let a unit be turned and rolled across the sill; roller tracks and guides carry it aft. The hall is laid out in **14 rows**, each with a left and a right position marked by guide posts and a centerline guide; rows 2 to 14 can instead take one wide unit turned across the row (the M-1 container or the horse stall). Row 1, under the tapering crown, takes only the 64 in AAK. Published operator layouts for the DC-10-30F give 23 positions (eleven pairs and one aft); the simulation uses the 28 side positions the hall's guide posts mark.

The side positions take containers on the 88 × 125 in A base and the 96 × 125 in M base up to about 96 in high, the Demi container, the A-2 and the animal pens. A position's limit depends on where it is: about 7,100 lb a side at the ends of the hall rising to about 11,800 lb over the wing, and a row up to about 23,650 lb.

blocks.alt: Top-down schematic to scale, nose left, fuselage stations marked: DC-10-30F / MD-10 main deck with the crew area and forward barrier at FS 498, the main-deck cargo door on the left at rows 2 and 3 with its ball mat, 14 rows of left and right positions (M01L/R to M14L/R) between guide posts and a centerline guide, the crosswise positions M02P to M14P shown dashed, and the aft barrier at FS 1922. Annotate the heaviest positions over the wing.
blocks.title: Freighter main deck positions

blocks.content:
The KC-10's cargo floor is a 463L system: it takes the USAF HCU-6/E master pallet (88 × 108 in) and nothing else. Pallets stand in two longitudinal rows at a 109 in pitch, positions 2 to 12 left and right and 13 on the left only, where the boom operator's compartment hatch in the right floor takes the place of 13R. The crew and support-personnel compartment's bulkhead at FS 593.5 takes position 1, leaving 23 pallet positions. (The KC-10 loading manual's published layouts are 25 and 27 pallets.) In rows 2 to 12 two pallets can instead be coupled side by side along their 108 in edges into a 177 × 108 in pair for a long load.

All cargo except baggage goes on pallets through the main-deck door. The door area has powered lateral rollers that move a pallet across the sill at about 45 ft/min; along the deck, pallets are pushed by hand on the rollers.

blocks.title: KC-10 main deck limits (pallet included)
rows: Twice the lower of its two positions

blocks.content: The limits are the flight limits and include the pallet's own weight; the ground limit is 10,000 lb on any position. Loads approaching the height limits must be contoured to the fuselage, narrower toward the outboard edge. The loading manual also limits the cumulative load forward and aft of each station according to the body tank fuel; that is a loadsheet check, not enforced by the loading system.

blocks.alt: Top-down schematic to scale of the KC-10 main deck, nose left, fuselage stations marked: the crew and support-personnel compartment with its bulkhead at FS 593.5, the main-deck cargo door on the left with its powered lateral rollers, pallet positions 2L to 13L and 2R to 12R (88 by 108 in pallets at a 109 in pitch), the coupled pair positions 2P to 12P dashed across each row, and the boom operator's compartment hatch in the right floor at STA 1830 to 1869 where 13R would be. Flight limits shown per position: 6,500 lb or 10,000 lb.

blocks.content:
The lower holds have powered drive units in the floor, longitudinal and lateral, that move containers from the door to their rows at about 60 ft/min and are worked by the loading crew at each door. Their power comes through the aircraft's cargo loading circuits. In the simulation the freighter main deck is loaded under power at the same rate. The KC-10 is pushed by hand along the deck, with powered lateral rollers at the door only. The bulk hold is loaded by hand from a belt loader.

A unit is loaded far to near: the positions furthest from the door fill first, so nothing has to pass over a unit already locked in its path. Unloading is near to far. Each unit is raised by the loader to the sill, crosses into the aircraft, rolls along the deck to its position and is locked by the floor locks.

**Tail tipping.** With the aircraft on the ground, loading the aft part of a deck before the forward part can move the center of gravity behind the main gear. The ground CG must be kept forward of FS 1430 (40 % MAC); the tipping axis is at FS 1442 (44 % MAC). The loading system holds the next unit whenever it would take the ground CG past that limit, until weight forward of it allows the load to go on.

blocks.title: Conditions that stop cargo handling
rows: No loading; a job in progress freezes where it stands

Plan errors in a compartment (overweight, too tall, conflicting positions)

blocks.content: The weight of everything aboard reaches the flight model and the weight and balance through the aircraft's payload stations, so a load changes the gross weight, the CG and the trim the crew sees. Weight and balance planning is in [Mission Planning](mission-planning).

Cargo is planned and loaded from the EFB's **Cargo** app (see [EFB](efb)). Both decks are drawn to scale; press a position, choose a device from those that fit it, set its weight and, if it is not general cargo, what it carries. Plan issues (a position overweight, a device too tall, two units on the same floor) show in red. **Save Cargo** keeps a plan under a name and **Load Cargo** brings back a saved plan or a preset (Full Load and Half Load, built from the aircraft's own layout; Full Load on a freighter is 53 units and 116,200 lb, on the KC-10 23 pallets and 92,000 lb).

How the units reach the aircraft follows the GSX choice on the Ground Ops page:

- **GSX in use.** Start load calls GSX's loaders, which bring the units to each door. GSX waits for each cargo door it serves (forward, center and main deck) to be open; the ground crew open it, and the units roll into place as GSX's progress allows. GSX takes no stop command, so Stop is not offered.
- **GSX not in use.** The ground crew roll each unit in from the door, one at a time. Stop load keeps the units already locked and drops one still rolling; Start load carries on with the rest.
- **Load now and Unload now** put every planned unit aboard, or take everything off, at once.

The bulk hold always loads and unloads at once. In the simulation the holds can be loaded with their doors shut unless GSX is serving them.

blocks.alt: EFB Cargo app in portrait on an MD-10-30: main deck and lower deck drawn side by side to scale, nose up; several positions blue (planned), two amber (moving), the rest green (aboard); the panel on the right showing PLANNED / MOVING / ABOARD totals, the Loading section with Start load and Stop load, and a selected position's picker with device tabs, a weight stepper and contents tabs (General, Perishable, Pharma, Live animals). Text legible.
blocks.title: EFB Cargo app

blocks.content: A unit can be marked as carrying perishables, pharmaceuticals or live animals. Each has a temperature band it must be kept in, and the unit's own temperature follows its compartment's air with a lag set by its contents. Outside the band its condition falls, and live animals also suffer when the compartment is not ventilated, so the cargo heat and ventilation selections on the flight deck matter on those flights. The Cargo app's CARGO CARE list shows each sensitive unit's temperature and condition, and on a freighter the flight's review is scored on the cargo's condition.

**Cargo shift.** If the floor locks fail in flight, the units roll on their rollers with the deck: aft in a climb, forward in a descent or under braking, until they meet the next unit or the end of the compartment. The center of gravity moves with them and the aircraft trims differently. A full deck barely moves; a part-loaded one can shift a long way. The [Loose cargo](emergency-flight-path#loose-cargo) procedure secures the cargo, determines the CG and keeps changes of deck angle small. In the simulation the cargo cannot be re-secured in flight, so it moves again whenever the deck tilts.

sections.title: Cabin and passengers
sections.summary: Who rides on each aircraft, the seat maps, the passenger signs, the cabin crew and their service, boarding with or without GSX, and how the passengers judge the flight.

blocks.content: The seat maps are measured from the 3D cabins, seat by seat, so every passenger sits where a seat is drawn. Row 13 is skipped and seat letters skip I. The passenger cabin has four galleys (FWD and FWD B at the front, MID by door 2, AFT behind door 4), lavatories forward, mid and aft, and an attendant's jump seat at each door.

blocks.title: Passenger cabin layout

blocks.content: The NO SMOKING and FASTEN SEAT BELT signs are switched from the flight deck. Each switch has an AUTO setting on most decks. At **AUTO**, NO SMOKING lights with the landing gear handle down, and SEAT BELTS lights with the flap handle out of UP or the gear handle down. Whatever the switches say, both signs light when the cabin altitude passes about 10,000 ft, from the same pressure switch that lights CABIN ALT. A low chime sounds in the cabin each time a sign comes on. The signs are powered from 28 V DC bus 1.

rows: Push switchlight: ON or OFF, no AUTO

blocks.content: Passengers stay seated with the belt sign on, and grow restless if it stays on for a long time in smooth air. The cabin crew sit down whenever it is lit. The sign lighting itself is described in [Lighting](lighting).

children.title: Cabin crew and the cabin service

blocks.content:
The passenger cabin has seven flight attendants: two forward, two mid and three aft, with jump seats at 1L and 1R, 2L and 2R, 4L and 4R, and 3L. They sit in their jump seats with the seat belt sign on, throughout taxi, and in rough air. On the ground with the sign off they prepare the cabin. In flight they run a service sized to the flight's length: drinks only on a short flight, a meal service on a longer one, and a second round on a long one. The flight time comes from the SimBrief plan loaded in the EFB, or is assumed to be two hours.

The service is physical. Meals are loaded into the galley ovens and are hot only when the oven has heated them, which takes about 20 minutes for a full oven; coffee exists only once a water heater has brewed it; carts are fetched from a galley before each pass; and a meal that waits too long on a cart arrives cold. The crew stop working when the seat belt sign comes on in flight or the ride turns uncomfortable, and resume when it is safe. They answer passengers' call buttons, look after the airsick, and in an emergency go to passengers who have passed out from lack of oxygen or are suffering from heat or cold.

With the flight attendants on **AUTO** (the default, in Virtual Crew), they run the cabin themselves. With them **OFF**, the Passengers app's Service tab becomes the purser's station: tap an attendant and give them a task (drinks, meals, coffee or collecting trays in a zone; work an oven or the coffee makers; answer calls; give aid; prepare the cabin) from a selection wheel. The service can also be turned off altogether in Virtual Crew. See [Virtual Crew](virtual-crew) and [EFB](efb).

Passengers and riders are boarded from the EFB's **Passengers** app. Set the number in each class (or Empty, Half, Typical, Full) and the boarding order (random, back to front, or window seats first), then press **Board**; **Board now** seats everyone at once. Deboarding works the same way.

Passengers walk through the real doors. A door is usable when it is fully open, its slide has not deployed, and something is at it: without GSX that means the stairs the Ground Ops page brings to 1L and 1R; with GSX, its own stairs or jet bridges. Each passenger walks to the nearest usable door's cross-aisle, down an aisle to the row, stows a bag if they have one (most do, and stowing takes anything from a few seconds to twenty), and sits, waiting for any seated neighbor between their seat and the aisle to stand. One stair door admits about 15 passengers a minute and a jet bridge door about 20, and a full passenger cabin through two stair doors takes something over ten minutes. A shut door holds the boarding until it is opened.

**With GSX** (chosen on the Ground Ops page and running), Board and Deboard call GSX's own boarding and deboarding. The aircraft tells GSX how many passengers to bring, and the cabin follows GSX's count. GSX does not wait for cabin doors, so open 1L (or the door GSX is serving) yourself; the Passengers app's DOORS hint says when one is needed. The KC-10 is a cargo aircraft to GSX, so its riders always board with the EFB's ground crew.

Each passenger weighs about 190 lb with personal items and carry-on. Their weight reaches the flight model through six payload stations along the cabin, so a boarding moves the CG as the seats fill.

blocks.alt: EFB Passengers app, Boarding tab, on a passenger DC-10-30 during boarding: the seat map with seats gray (empty), blue (someone coming) and green (seated), passengers walking as amber dots in the aisles, doors 1L and 1R green (usable); the CABIN panel showing BY THE GROUND CREW, TO BOARD / ABOARD / STANDING counts, weight and time left, Stop and Board now buttons; the PLAN with passengers per class and the boarding order. Text legible.
blocks.title: EFB Passengers app

children.title: Comfort, complaints and the flight review

blocks.content:
With **Simulate passengers** on (the default, in the EFB's Settings), the passengers are more than weight. Each cabin zone (forward, mid and aft, split at doors 2 and 3) feels the air the air-conditioning system delivers to it: a cabin between 63 and 75 °F is comfortable, and outside that band a growing share of passengers are unhappy. They feel the ride, through filtered accelerations in each axis, including the low-frequency motion that makes people airsick. They feel cabin pressure changes in their ears when the cabin climbs faster than about 800 ft/min or descends faster than about 600 ft/min, and a cabin above 8,000 ft. They notice steep bank and pitch, hard braking and a firm landing. A cabin left too cold or too hot for long enough, or a high cabin altitude, can make individual passengers ill.

Discomfort becomes complaints, which appear in the Passengers app, and some passengers press their call buttons. At the end of the flight the passengers' review scores it, factor by factor. With the simulation off, the passengers are weight only: boarding, deboarding and the CG still work.
Passengers also use the lavatories during the flight, drawing water and filling the waste tanks; see [Water and waste](#water-and-waste).

sections.title: Galleys
sections.summary: The crew galley of the freighters, MD-10 and KC-10, and the passenger cabin's four galleys, appliance by appliance.

blocks.content: Each aircraft carries either the main-deck **crew galley** (the freighters, the MD-10 and the KC-10) or the **passenger galleys** (the passenger DC-10s, and two of them in the open cabins of the KDC-10, the Omega and the fire tankers), never both. Every appliance is simulated as a body that heats or chills: an oven cavity under its thermostat, a water vessel, a refrigerated compartment. Each has its own circuit breaker, so a pulled breaker or a shed galley bus kills it and its lamps, and each puts its real load on the electrical system.

The crew galley stands inboard of and just forward of door 1L. Its control panel carries the breakers for each appliance and the controls below. It is powered from the AC ground service bus through the GALLEY PWR breaker, which is the breaker the smoke and fumes procedures pull. The galley's OVHT lamp is on the battery bus.
On the DC-10 this galley is fitted to the freighters only.

The passenger cabin has four galleys. The FWD and FWD B galleys are at the front, the MID galley by door 2 and the AFT galley behind door 4. The open cabins keep the FWD and AFT galleys only. The galleys are fed from the **galley buses** (three on the -30 and -40 flight deck, four on the -10 and -15), each normally supplied by its generator bus through the galley load control: the MID galley from galley bus 1, the AFT galley from galley bus 2, and the FWD and FWD B galleys from galley bus 3. A galley bus is shed as a whole, and the flight engineer's GALLEY BUS switches and GALLEY PWR OFF lights control and monitor them (see [Electrical](electrical)).

blocks.content: An oven warms to LOW, MED or HIGH in about 3, 4 or 5 minutes and holds there under its thermostat while its timer runs. A full oven takes 32 meals, which take about 20 minutes to heat from the chiller at MED; while it works the cavity sags, and once the timer stops the meals stay hot for a long time behind the closed door. A water heater brews a pot of coffee in about 4 minutes. The cabin crew work these appliances themselves during the service, and the switches move under their hands; anything you move yourself is yours until the crew come back to that appliance.
