blocks.content: **The lower galley.** On the passenger aircraft the front of the forward lower hold, FS 595 to 879, is a galley area with its own left and right service doors and a GALLEY DOORS warning lamp. The simulation models its doors and the shortened forward hold behind it; it does not model the lower galley's equipment or lifts. The freighter conversion and the KDC-10 remove it, giving the full-length forward hold.

sections.title: Water and waste
sections.summary: Pressurized potable water tanks fed from the pneumatic system or a compressor, the line drain, freeze protection, and the lavatory waste tanks and drain masts.

blocks.content: Potable water is stored in one, two or three **63 US gal** tanks in the left forward utility compartment, each the heart of a separate water system. The tanks are filled and drained only at an exterior servicing panel. Each tank is pressurized with air, and that pressure pushes water to the galleys and the lavatory washbasins. Waste water from the basins and galleys drains overboard through two heated **drain masts**; the toilets flush into waste tanks that the lavatory service truck empties on the ground.

Each tank is pressurized with bleed air from pneumatic manifold 1 or 2 (manifold 3 feeds no water system) through a pressure regulator. The regulator is a spring and diaphragm, a proportional device: it holds about 43.5 psi with no water flowing and lets the tank droop toward 38 psi at the heaviest draw, because a diaphragm regulator can only pass more air by opening further, and it can only open further when the pressure it senses is lower. That droop is normal and is not a fault.

When the supply air falls below about 26 psi (engines and APU shut down, or the pneumatic supply off), an electric **compressor** takes over, provided there is electrical power. It is run by a pressure switch with built-in hysteresis rather than a control loop: it starts when the tank falls to the bottom of the band, about 38 psi, and stops when it is back at about 43.5 psi, so a compressor-fed tank cycles across the same band a bleed-fed one droops across. A system is pressurized only with its PRESS/DEPRESS switch at PRESS and the LINE DRAIN switch CLOSED.

Each system has a **WTR SYS PRESS LO** light. It is set to come on above the pressure at which water stops flowing, so some water is still available for a while after it lights, and below the regulated band, so a healthy system at full draw does not trip it. Setting a system's switch to **DEPRESS** vents its tank overboard and lets the water in its supply lines drain back into its own tank; it is the first action for a water leak, and its PRESS LO light then confirms the system is depressurized.

**Distribution.** On the DC-10-30, system 2 feeds the forward galley and lavatories, and systems 1 and 3 the aft. The two-system aircraft feed the forward galley and lavatories from system 1 and the aft from systems 1 and 3, and supply the mid galley and lavatory through an automatic switch-over valve that selects whichever of systems 1 and 3 holds more water once the two differ by about 10 %, and stays there until a change is needed.
**Distribution.** The single water system feeds the galley and the lavatories directly.

Water left standing in an unheated aircraft freezes, lines first. Setting the **LINE DRAIN** switch to OPEN depressurizes every tank and, after a 90 second delay, opens the drain valves so the supply lines empty overboard. The tanks are not drained by it; that is done at the servicing panel. The **LINE DRAIN DISAGREE** light is on for the whole delay and whenever any drain valve is not where the switch has commanded it, so a light that stays on after the delay means a stuck valve.

The lines and the tanks freeze at very different rates. With the aircraft cold-soaked at -30 °F, the lines can freeze in about an hour, while a full tank takes about ten. The difference is the tank's mass and insulation: before water can freeze it must give up its latent heat, about 144 BTU per pound, on top of the heat of cooling to the freezing point, and a 63 gallon tank holds over 500 lb of water behind insulation while a line holds a few pounds in bare tubing. When an aircraft is to be left in freezing conditions without heat, have all water systems drained.

The two drain masts are heated at all times. Ground sensing relays control their heaters: low power on the ground, where the mast is cooled only by still air, and higher power in flight, where the slipstream would otherwise freeze the outlet. A drain mast heater that fails goes unnoticed on the ground and freezes its mast shut in flight.

Each lavatory has a water heater under its basin (the two left aft lavatories share one), with an amber power-on light. A heater that overheats switches itself off and lights a red light; it can be reset with a button under its top cover once it has cooled.

On the passenger aircraft the forward and mid lavatories each have their own waste tank and flush pump. The aft lavatories share one tank with three flush pumps, normally one per flush, with a backup mode that fires all three. The flush levers in the cabin work the simulated flush pumps, and passengers flush them as they use the lavatories in flight. On the KC-10 the forward and Z lavatories are recirculating toilets with integral tanks. The lavatory service on the EFB's Ground Ops page empties every waste tank.

blocks.content: The doors are watched from the flight deck and worked from the cabin and from outside. The flight engineer has the door annunciators, the cargo door indication test and the potable water panel; the MD-10's pilots have alerts. Cabin doors are opened and closed at their own door stations or from the EFB. Cargo doors are worked from their exterior panels by the ground crew, whom the EFB and GSX direct.

sections.title: Operation
sections.summary: The doors, cargo, cabin and water through a turn and a flight: what is checked, who works what, and what the aircraft does by itself.

blocks.content: The normal procedures in [Normal Procedures](normal-procedures) give the checklist items in order. This section explains what lies behind them. On the DC-10 and KC-10 the doors and water are the flight engineer's; on the MD-10 the crew rely on the alerts and the EFB.

A cabin door's electric drive needs its 115 V AC drive circuit and its 28 V DC control circuit; on the aircraft these come from the ground service buses, so the doors work on ground power or the APU without the main buses being fully set up. A lower cargo door needs its three-phase 115 V AC door actuator circuit, the 28 V DC latch actuator circuit and its control circuit; the main-deck door needs power for its motor pump (or a crew member on the hand pump). On a dead aircraft no door moves electrically. The emergency mode, being pneumatic, needs no power at all.

The door warning lamps need 28 V DC buses 1 and 2. A door panel that is dark on a dead bus says nothing about the doors.

**Arrival and preparation.** At the gate the slides are disarmed before any door is opened, and with them disarmed every cabin door lamp on the flight engineer's panel (DC-10, KC-10) is lit: that is the normal parked picture, not a fault. With power on, open door 1L (and 1R if needed) from the door station or the EFB's Doors page; on the Ground Ops page's Services tab, call stairs or a catering truck to the forward doors and the belt loader to the bulk door. Opening an armed cabin door from the EFB takes two presses: the first disarms it, the second opens it.

**Cargo.** Plan the load in the Cargo app and start it. With GSX in use, the ground crew open each cargo door as GSX's loaders arrive and shut it when GSX has finished; without GSX, open the cargo doors from the Doors page if you want them open, and the crew roll the units in. Watch the CG on the Cargo app and the flight engineer's weight and balance: the loading system holds a unit that would tip the aircraft, but the CG for flight is the crew's.

**Passengers.** Board from the Passengers app once a door is open with stairs or a bridge at it. Catering stocks the galleys, and the cabin crew prepare the cabin. The lavatory service empties the waste tanks.

**Flight engineer's checks.** The flight engineer checks the door annunciators and tests the cargo door lamps (the Before Start checklist's cargo door lights item):

1. Hold the CARGO DOOR INDICATION switch at TEST. On the DC-10 every cargo door lamp comes on; on the KC-10 both CARGO DOOR lamps come on if, and only if, the door is closed and locked.
2. Release it. The lamps of any door that is closed and locked go out; those of open doors stay lit.

On the potable water panel, check the quantities adequate for the flight, each PRESS/DEPRESS switch at PRESS and each WTR SYS PRESS LO light out (the tanks pressurize from the pneumatic manifolds with the APU running, or from the compressor on electrical power).

**Before start.** When loading and boarding are done, close every door. The ground crew close, latch and lock each cargo door, close its vent door and switch its panel off; the CARGO DOOR lamps go out. Close the cabin doors from their stations or the EFB, then arm every slide (the EFB's Arm all waits until every cabin door is shut). On the DC-10 freighters, doors 2L to 4R have no controls in the cabin: arm their slides with the EFB's Arm all, or their CABIN DOOR lamps stay lit. With the doors closed and the slides armed, every door lamp is out. The slides stay armed from before the aircraft leaves the ramp until it reaches its final parking place.

**Before start.** When loading is done, have the cargo doors closed and locked: the CARGO DOOR alerts on the EAD go out. Close doors 1L and 1R and arm their slides, from the door stations or the EFB; doors 2L to 4R are worked from the EFB only (Arm all arms every door). The MD-10 gives no cockpit indication of a cabin door in the simulation, so confirm the cabin doors closed and armed on the EFB's Doors page.

blocks.content:
Once the cabin is pressurized, every plug door is pressed into its frame and cannot be opened; an accidental pull of an EMERGENCY handle does nothing while the differential holds. In the simulation the handle stays at EMERGENCY until it is stowed, and a door whose handle is left there opens, deploying an armed slide, as soon as the differential falls away: stow it. The cargo doors are held by their latches and lockpins and watched by their two sensors. A lamp that lights in flight is dealt with by the procedures in [Abnormal Procedures](abnormal-procedures); see [Failures](#failures) for the reasoning.

The cabin crew sit with the seat belt sign on and work the service with it off. Water is drawn by the galleys and the lavatories; watch for an unusual fall in a system's quantity, which suggests a leak.

Taxi in with the doors closed and the slides armed. At the gate, with the parking brake set and the aircraft fully depressurized, disarm every slide before any door is opened, and check that the cabin door lamps (and on the KC-10 and the freighters' forward doors, the DOOR DISARMED lights) come on. Then open the doors. An armed door will not open electrically; an armed door opened with its EMERGENCY handle deploys its slide onto the ramp.

If the aircraft is to be left cold in freezing weather without heat, drain the water lines with LINE DRAIN and have the tanks drained at the servicing panel.
Disarm a cabin door's slide before opening the door. An armed slide deploying at the gate can injure anyone below the door.

sections.title: Failures and non-normal operation
sections.summary: How the doors, cargo and water systems fail, what the crew sees, and where the procedures are.

blocks.content: Most door failures show as a lamp that is on when it should be out, or out when it should be on, and the first question is always whether the door or the indication has failed. The design answers it. A cabin door in flight is a plug held shut by the cabin, so a lit cabin door lamp with normal pressurization is not a door about to open. A cargo door has two sensors on two buses, so one lamp alone, with its partner out and testing normally, is an indication fault; both lamps together are a door that may not be locked. The procedures are in [Abnormal Procedures](abnormal-procedures) and [Emergency Procedures](emergency-procedures).

rows: A CABIN DOOR lamp, or AVIONIC COMPT EXT DOOR, AVIONIC COMPT WHL WELL DOOR or CTR ACCESS COMPT DOOR
These are plug doors: with the cabin pressurizing normally, the door cannot open. Likely a switch or a slide disarmed.

Pressurize on schedule. If the cabin holds, continue at the captain's discretion. If it will not pressurize, take manual control of the outflow valve, establish two-pack operation and land at the nearest suitable airport.
An unlatched panel on an unpressurized bay: cabin pressure does not hold it, and it can depart the aircraft.
Land at the nearest suitable airport.
One CARGO DOOR lamp (SYS A or SYS B)
Probably an indication fault: a failed sensor, or someone in the hold pressing the emergency call switch (SYS A only).
Hold the CARGO DOOR INDICATION switch at TEST. If the other system's lamp for the same door lights normally and goes out on release, disregard the lamp and continue.
Both CARGO DOOR lamps for one door, or a single lamp that fails the test
The door may not be locked.

Lower cargo door: descend to an altitude where no more than about 2 psi differential is held and land at the nearest suitable airport. Main-deck door: descend to where pressurization is not needed, depressurize and land at the nearest suitable airport.

children.title: A cargo door alert in flight

With a single CARGO DOOR alert (A or B) the QRH has the crew perform the cargo door test; if the other sensor on that door tests correctly on the miscellaneous systems display, the alert is an indication fault, logged for maintenance, and the flight continues. With both alerts for one door, or a failed test, set the cabin pressure system to manual, descend to 15,000 ft or the minimum safe altitude, whichever is higher, reduce the cabin differential to 2 psi or less (about 9,500 ft cabin at 15,000 ft) and land at the nearest suitable airport.

The cargo door test does not work in the simulation, so a single alert cannot be confirmed as an indication fault from the flight deck: treat it as unconfirmed. (The failure the EFB injects, CARGO DOOR FWD B alone, is an indication fault.)

blocks.content: If the cargo's locks fail in flight, units roll with the deck until they fetch up against the next unit or the end of their compartment, and the CG moves with them. The crew feels it as a trim change. Follow [Loose cargo](emergency-flight-path#loose-cargo) in Emergency Procedures: secure the cargo, determine the CG and keep changes of deck angle small. In the simulation nobody can re-secure the cargo in flight, so it moves again whenever the deck tilts.

**Modeled in depth.** Every door's mechanism is simulated through its own switches: the cabin doors' three modes, the slide arming lever and its power interlock and girt bar switches, the nitrogen reservoir that each emergency opening draws down, the plug doors' refusal to open against cabin pressure; the lower cargo doors' latch and door actuators, locktube, lockpins and vent door, handing power on from limit switch to limit switch, including what cabin pressure does to latches that are not over center; the main-deck door's hydraulic latches, spring-loaded lockpins, vent door and hold-open hooks. Each door's circuits are real loads on the electrical system. An open door, an unsealed cargo door or a leaking seal is a real leak in the cabin pressure model, and an open main-deck vent door caps the cabin at about 1 psi. The warning lamps are evaluated from the switches, through the test switch, and through their own buses last, so a lost bus darkens its lamps rather than showing doors closed.

The cargo holds, positions and limits come from operator and loading manual data; the cargo's weight and the passengers' weight reach the flight model through payload stations. The galleys' appliances and the water systems' pressure, quantity, freezing and waste are simulated physically.

**Simplified.** Only the pneumatic opening's 10 second maximum is published; the other door times are estimates. The exterior door controls (handles, cargo door panels, auxiliary handle and 1L's manual drive) are not in the cockpit: the EFB and GSX ground crews work the cargo doors, so the auxiliary mode, 1L's manual drive and the manual lift are not available to you. Service doors cannot be opened in the simulation, so their lamps light only on test. A slide arming lever can be set to ARMED with its door open (the jamb interlock is not modeled); that door then cannot be closed electrically until its slide is disarmed. A pulled EMERGENCY handle stays pulled: in flight it does nothing while the cabin holds pressure, but unless it is stowed the door opens, deploying an armed slide, as soon as the differential falls below about 0.2 psi. On the real aircraft the bottle discharges at once and bleeds away within seconds, and the door stays shut. Cargo can be loaded with the hold doors shut unless GSX is serving them. The wind limits for the cargo doors are not enforced on the doors themselves, though cargo handling stops above 52 kt.

**Different from the real aircraft.** The real FedEx DC-10 freighters and MD-10 use two cabin doors (four on some aircraft); the simulation fits all eight, each a working door with a slide (and, on the DC-10 freighters, a CABIN DOOR lamp). Only 1L and 1R have crew controls in the cabin; 2L to 4R are opened, closed, armed and disarmed from the EFB's Doors page. On the real KC-10, door 4R has an escape rope rather than a slide; the simulation gives it a slide. The freighters' main deck is laid out in 14 rows from its guide posts, where operators publish 23 positions; the KC-10 has 23 pallet positions, its bulkhead taking position 1. The six lower cargo door lamps on the DC-10 flight engineer's panel carry STBY A and STBY B legends in the 3D cockpit; they are the FWD, CTR and AFT CARGO DOOR SYS A and SYS B lamps. The passenger DC-10's GALLEY DOORS lamp is not drawn. The DC-10 freighters keep the passenger aircraft's water systems and lavatories.

**Not modeled.** The flight deck door's lock, the lavatory doors, the clearview windows and escape ropes, the portable emergency equipment, the slides beyond arming and deployment, the lower galley's equipment, and the crew galley's coffee brewer. The passenger cabin's evacuation signal is simulated, but no EVAC light or horn is drawn or heard yet. On the MD-10, the DOOR OPEN, CABIN DOORS OPEN and cabin and compartment door alerts and the CARGO DOOR TEST switch do not work, so there is no cockpit indication of a cabin door, and the water panel is not modeled; neither is the DC-10-40's water panel. The galleys' water system selectors move but do not change which system feeds the galley, and the lavatory heater reset buttons and the aft toilets' backup mode switch are not in the cabin model. The potable water tanks start each flight about 85 % full and cannot be refilled in the simulation.

**Failures you can practice from the EFB.** Cargo door unsafe in flight: on the DC-10 and MD-10 the forward lower door's proximity switch fails (SYS B lamp alone; the test shows it is an indication fault); on the KC-10 the main-deck door's vent door jams open (CARGO DOOR SYS A on, the cabin limited to about 1 psi). Cargo shifts in flight: every unit's locks fail and the load rolls with the deck. The circuit breakers of the doors, water systems and galleys can be pulled like any other, with their real effects.

**EFB settings that change this part.** Simulate passengers (Settings): passengers with comfort, complaints and a review, or weight only. GSX (Ground Ops): whether GSX's vehicles or the EFB's ground crew serve the doors, cargo and passengers. Flight attendants AUTO or OFF, and the cabin service on or off (Virtual Crew).

parts.title: Air Refueling Systems
parts.summary: The flying boom, the centerline hose and reel, the wing pods, the offload fuel system and the receiver system.

blocks.content: The air refueling systems pass fuel from this aircraft to another in flight, and, on the KC-10A, take fuel from another tanker. Three delivery methods exist in the family. The **flying boom** is a rigid, telescoping fuel tube that the boom operator flies into a receptacle on the receiver: it moves fuel fastest and suits large receivers. The **centerline hose and drogue** trails a flexible hose from a reel in the aft fuselage for probe-equipped receivers. The **wing air refueling pods** (WARP) put a smaller hose and drogue under each wingtip, so two probe receivers can refuel at once. The **receiver system** (UARRSI) is the KC-10A's own receptacle on top of the fuselage.

Every delivery method is built from the same four elements: a **delivery device** that the receiver connects to (boom nozzle, drogue coupling); a **mechanism** that positions it (the boom's flight controls and telescope, a hose reel); a **fuel supply** that holds the right pressure at the delivery point whatever the receiver takes; and a **signal path** that tells both crews what the other is doing (the boom's signal coils and lights, the hose's position switches and signal lights). The parts below take each device in turn, then the fuel supply, the receiver system, the controls, and how the whole works in flight.

blocks.alt: KC-10A in level flight seen from behind and slightly below, boom lowered to the refuel trail position (about 30° down, telescope partly extended), centerline hose trailed from the chute right of the boom, and both wing pod hoses trailed at full trail. Drogue canopies inflated. Daylight, clear sky.

blocks.title: Which DC-10s have air refueling equipment
blocks.content: Under the DC-10 button only two variants carry refueling equipment: the **KDC-10**, which has the boom and the boom operator's station, and the **DC-10-40 Omega**, which has the wing pods. Every other DC-10 (passenger, freighter, and the -10 and -30 fire tankers) has none, and this part does not apply to it.

blocks.alt: Functional schematic of the KC-10A air refueling systems. Left: the three body tanks (FWD, CTR WING, AFT), each with two hydraulically driven AR pumps labeled with their hydraulic system (FWD L sys 1, FWD R sys 3, CTR L sys 1, CTR R sys 3, AFT L sys 3, AFT R sys 2), feeding the AR manifold. From the manifold: BOOM VALVE to the boom (with the two bypass valves back to the AFT tank), DROGUE VALVE to the centerline hose reel, ALTN TRANS and ISOL valves to the wing crossfeed manifold and the two WING DROGUE VALVES to the pods. The FPCU drawn with its four pressure stations (nozzle, drogue venturi, crossfeed, AR manifold). Top: UARRSI receptacle and AR MASTER valve into the receive manifold. Bottom: hydraulic system 2 and the AR alternate supply through HYD SEL to boom or reel; system 3 to the hoist. Electrical: ARO AC bus from GEN BUS 3, ARO DC bus from DC BUS 3 with alternate from DC BUS 1.
blocks.title: KC-10A air refueling systems, functional schematic

blocks.content: On the KC-10A the offload fuel lives in three body tanks below the cabin floor, apart from the engine-feed fuel in the wing tanks, so the tanker can carry a different fuel grade for its receivers. Six hydraulically driven AR pumps, two in each body tank, feed a common AR manifold. A two-channel fuel pressure control unit (FPCU) varies their speed to hold 50 ±5 psi at whichever delivery point is open. Each pair of pumps in a tank is split across two hydraulic systems and the two FPCU channels, so no single hydraulic, electrical or controller failure stops an offload. See [Fuel](fuel) for the body tanks and their plumbing.

The boom and the centerline reel share one hydraulic source, selected by the boom operator's HYD SEL lever: hydraulic system 2 backed by the **AR alternate supply** (an auxiliary reservoir, accumulator and the 2-3 reversible motor pump), which keeps the boom flying if system 2 loses its pumps or its fluid. The hoist that raises and lowers the boom runs on system 3. The ARO station has its own AC and DC buses, fed from generator bus 3 and DC bus 3, with an automatic change-over of the DC bus to DC bus 1. See [Hydraulics](hydraulics) and [Electrical](electrical).

The wing pods are self-contained except for electrical power: each has a ram air turbine driving its own fuel pump and hose reel, and needs only a pressurized inlet line from the wing crossfeed manifold. That is why the same pods could be fitted to the Omega DC-10-40, which has no AR pumps.

The KDC-10 is simulated as a DC-10-30 (center gear, pack 3, the DC-10-30 flight deck, its four-tank fuel system) carrying the KC-10A's boom and the KC-10A's complete boom operator's station in the tail. The boom is identical in geometry and behavior to the KC-10A's. What differs is what powers it:

items: **Electrics.** The boom's circuits are the KC-10A's by name, fed from the buses the KC-10A's ARO buses are fed from: DC BUS 3, AC BUS 3, the 115 V AC and 28 V DC ground-service buses, and the battery bus. There are no ARO buses, so the station's AR BUS ISOL, GND SVC BUS ISOL and AR DC BUS ALTN switches do nothing.

**Hydraulics.** There is no AR alternate supply. HYD SEL at BOOM puts hydraulic system 2 directly on the boom, and the boom's flow demand lands on system 2. The hoist runs on system 3, as on the KC-10A.
**Fuel.** There is no fuel side. The boom is a mechanism only: the FUEL FLOW and FUEL PRESS indicators on the boom operator's panel rest at zero.

**The rest of the station** (its oxygen regulators, window heat, compartment temperature and avionics-rack cooling) belongs to KC-10A systems the DC-10-30 does not have, and is inert. The sighting door, the lamps and the station's lamp test work.
The drogue control panel on the station has no hose behind it, and there are no wing pods.

blocks.content: The Omega is a DC-10-40 tanker carrying the KC-10A's wing pods on its long-span wing. It has no boom, no centerline hose, no AR pumps and no boom operator's station. Both of the KC-10A's pod panels are mounted on its flight engineer's panel: the pod control panels (POD POWER, HOSE TRAIL/REWIND, HOSE JTSN, BITE, COUNTER RESET, SIG/FLOOD and their lights) and the WING AERIAL REFUEL panel (WING VALVE, POD VALVE, RESET and their lights). The pods are therefore worked by the flight engineer.

Each pod is fed from its wing's crossfeed manifold through its WING DROGUE VALVE. With no AR pumps, that manifold is pressurized by the engine tanks' boost pumps through the X-FEED valves, so a pod is dry until the flight engineer opens the X-FEED valves as well as the WING DROGUE VALVE. Pod power and controls ride the DC-10-40's own buses. See [Wing pod fuel supply](#pod-fuel-supply).

The **boom operator** (BO) flies the boom and works the hose reels from the aerial refueling operator's (ARO) station in the tail. The **flight engineer** (FE) sets up the offload fuel system, monitors the hydraulic supply and the offload, and on the Omega works the pods. The **pilots** fly a steady platform: the tanker's autopilot is normally engaged during refueling, and the pilots monitor the BOOM/DROGUE ENGAGED lights and the receiver's position as the boom operator reports it.

sections.title: Flying boom
sections.summary: KC-10A and KDC-10.

blocks.content: The flying boom is a faired, telescoping fuel tube hung from a gimbal under the tail cone. Small aerodynamic surfaces near its end let the boom operator fly it, like a tethered glider, to a position just above and behind the receiver's receptacle; the telescope then pushes the nozzle into the receptacle, the receiver's toggle latches grip it, and fuel flows. Because the boom is rigid and its own aerodynamics carry it, it can move several times more fuel per minute than a hose and puts the precision of the contact in the boom operator's hands rather than the receiver pilot's.

The KC-10A's boom is a fly-by-wire design. A digital boom control unit (BCU) stands between the boom operator's flight control stick and the surfaces, closes position and rate loops on the boom's own sensors, schedules its gains on the boom's own airspeed sensor, and runs the signal system that sequences a contact and its disconnect. The sections below describe the structure, the flight controls and their control law, the telescope, the hoist that stows the boom, the limits, the signal system and disconnect logic, the independent disconnect, and the power supplies.

blocks.alt: Side and rear views of the KC-10A boom. Side view: tail cone with the gimbal and its roll axis drawn inclined 5° to the waterline; outer faired tube; telescoping inner tube with the nozzle; elevator near the end of the outer tube with a fin and rudder at each elevator tip; hoist cable from the tail cone fairlead to the boom's mid-point; boom latch and chock at the stowed position; elevation scale from the STOW mark (15° above horizontal) through 0°, the refuel trail (about 30°) to the 45° down stop. Rear view: the boom rolled about its roll axis, swinging on an arc, roll scale to 32.5° each side.
blocks.title: Boom anatomy and its two axes

blocks.content: The boom is two aerodynamically faired tubes, one telescoping inside the other on rollers. A fixed fuel tube inside the telescoping tube, with a sliding seal, carries fuel without leaking as the telescope moves. At the forward end a fuel line swivel and a flexible line take the fuel across the boom's pitch and roll axes; an inflated surge boot damps fuel pressure surges during coupled flight and at disconnect. The nozzle at the end of the telescoping tube carries the signal coil, the two fuel pressure transducers the FPCU regulates on, the nozzle load sensors, and the independent disconnect actuator.

The boom weighs 1,914 lb dry, 2,138 lb full of fuel with the telescope retracted and 2,298 lb full and extended. About a third of the dry mass is in the telescoping part, so running the telescope out moves the boom's center of gravity aft by several feet and makes it noticeably heavier in pitch at the end of its stroke.

The gimbal gives two degrees of freedom. **Elevation** is the boom's angle below the tanker's horizontal reference, read on the boom operator's ELEVATION indicator: the stowed boom sits 15° above that reference, at the indicator's STOW mark, and the down stop is 45° below it. **Roll** is rotation about the roll axis, read on the ROLL indicator: the roll trunnion turns 32.5° each way. The roll axis is not horizontal but inclined about 5° to the tanker's waterline, a choice the designers made for stability and control.

blocks.content: Where the KC-135's boom steers with two ruddevators set in a V, the KC-10A's has an all-moving **elevator** across the boom near the end of the outer tube, with a **fin and rudder** at each elevator tip, the fins canted outward about 25°. Each surface has its own hydraulic actuator. The elevator moves the boom in elevation; the two rudders, moving together, roll it; differences between them trim the boom. The surfaces are positioned only through the BCU: there is no mechanical link from the stick.

With FLT CONT off, the surfaces float. The boom then trails like a weathervane at an elevation where its weight, the elevator's airload and the cable (if the hoist holds it) balance. With FLT CONT on and boom hydraulic pressure available, the BCU flies the boom to the trail position the BOOM ELEVATION POSN switch selects and holds it there against gusts, the tanker's maneuvers and the boom's own weight.

children.title: Theory: why the boom rolls instead of yawing

blocks.content: The boom does not swing sideways about a vertical hinge. It **rolls**: the whole boom rotates about its near-longitudinal roll axis, so its nozzle travels sideways on an arc and rises slightly as it goes. The geometry has three consequences a boom operator feels.

items: **Weight is a restoring pendulum.** A boom rolled to one side has lifted its center of gravity, and its weight pulls it back toward the bottom of the arc. Lateral control is therefore a balance between rudder side force and a spring-like gravity term, and the boom returns toward 0° roll by itself when the rudders center.

**Roll authority depends on elevation.** A rudder's side force rolls the boom through the boom's offset from its roll axis. At high elevations (boom well below the tail) that offset is large and the rudders are powerful. Near the roll axis, with the boom close to level and lying almost along it, the lever arm vanishes and the rudders can do little; the structural roll limit is only 5° with the boom above 0° elevation for that reason. This is also why contact is not attempted beyond 10° roll: the boom's lateral stiffness falls off the further it is rolled.

**Dynamic pressure sets the forces.** The surfaces' authority grows with dynamic pressure. At low speed the boom's weight dominates and it hangs lower and responds more slowly; at high speed the airload dominates and the boom is pushed up toward the airstream. The BCU's gain schedule (below) compensates for most of this, but not all.

children.title: Boom control unit and control laws

blocks.content: The BCU is a digital computer in the ARO compartment. It reads the boom operator's two hand controllers, the boom's elevation and roll transducers (dual rotary transducers on the gimbal), its rates, its own dynamic-pressure (Qc) sensor, and its normal and lateral accelerometers. It commands the elevator, the two rudders and the telescope servo, runs the signal system, monitors itself, and stores faults for maintenance.

**The flight control stick is a position command.** Centerd, it asks for the trail position the ELEVATION POSN switch selects (0° at STOW, about 30° at REFUEL). Moved, it asks for a boom position offset from that trail: full forward is 50°, full aft 15° above horizontal, full left or right 30° of roll. The boom operator faces aft, so moving the stick left swings the boom to the operator's left, which is the tanker's right. Because stick position is boom position, a released stick always brings the boom back to trail, and a boom operator can fly the nozzle to a point in space rather than managing rates.

Each axis runs two nested loops. The outer loop turns the error between commanded and measured position into a demanded rate, limited so the boom never moves faster than it safely can. The inner loop turns the rate error into a surface command. An integrator in each axis carries the trim: the steady elevator angle that holds the boom's weight against its airload, the rudder offset a failed rudder or a sideslip demands. Without that integral action a proportional law would need a fixed bias to hold the trail, and the trail would wander with airspeed and weight.

**Gains are scheduled on the boom's own Qc sensor.** Surface effectiveness rises with dynamic pressure, so the BCU lowers its gains as Qc rises and raises them as it falls, between fixed limits. Below about 200 KIAS the schedule reaches its upper limit and can no longer fully compensate: the boom's response is slightly reduced, more noticeably during rapid up commands above 30° elevation, damping falls, and overshoots of 2° to 3° follow rapid or evasive commands.

blocks.alt: Block diagram of one boom control axis. Stick position plus trail position (from ELEV POSN switch) plus BOOM TRIM offset gives the commanded position; minus the measured position from the gimbal transducer gives position error; a gain and rate limiter give the demanded rate; minus the measured rate gives rate error; a gain scheduled on the boom Qc sensor plus an integrator feed the surface actuator (elevator or rudders); the boom dynamics block returns position and rate. Side inputs: hoist ownership switch (BCU follows the boom in RAISE/HOLD), FLT CONT switch, servo monitor latching the FAIL light.

blocks.content: **BOOM TRIM.** If the boom does not trail at 0° roll and 30° elevation with the stick centerd, the boom operator moves the BOOM TRIM switch UP, DOWN, LEFT or RIGHT to move the trail the stick is centerd on. Trim is a slow correction of a few degrees, not a flying control. A boom that will not trim to 0° roll and 30° elevation is a mandatory maintenance write-up.

**While the hoist holds the boom, the BCU follows it.** With the hoist lever at RAISE or HOLD the winch, not the elevator, owns the boom's elevation, so the BCU tracks the boom rather than fight the cable, and the stick adds only an offset. In LOWER the BCU walks its command down toward the STOW trail more slowly than the drum can pay out, which is why the boom stops descending at about 0° until the boom operator selects FREE WHEEL. The integrator stays live in LOWER: a DOWN command held on the stick there makes the elevator pull against a cable that can pay out no faster than its flow limiter allows, and can break it.

children.title: Coupled mode, ALAS and the stick shaker

blocks.content: Once the nozzle is latched in a receptacle, the boom is no longer a free body: it is pinned at one end to the tanker and at the other to the receiver, and every relative movement of the two aircraft loads the nozzle. Two functions reduce those loads. The **coupled flight control law**, active whenever the flight control system is COUPLED, uses boom position to back-drive the flight control stick so that it follows the boom as the boom follows the receiver. The **automatic load alleviation system** (ALAS), active when the ALAS switch-light shows ENABLE and the system is COUPLED, senses radial loads on the nozzle and back-drives the stick to align the boom with the receiver, holding the loads low without the boom operator's help. The boom operator can override ALAS.

One second after contact the control laws move from FREE FLIGHT to COUPLED. At that moment ALAS engages, the stick forces go to their highest setting, the stick shaker becomes armed and COUPLED lights. Moving the stick away from its commanded position then shakes it, a deterrent against a large input while the boom is pinned. A sustained radial nozzle load above 500 lb lights HI NOZZLE LOAD and also couples the flight controls, but without ALAS. After a disconnect, COUPLED and ALAS hold for the selected receiver disconnect delay, then the stick forces return to the STICK FORCE selections and the control law blends back to FREE FLIGHT over about a second.

ALAS works in two independent axes. A failure in one lights ROLL ALAS INOP or ELEVATION ALAS INOP; tracking and the stick shaker continue in the other. A failed flight control stick in an axis is shown by its ALAS INOP light, a five-second tone in the boom operator's headset and a stick gone limp in that axis; the back-drive and ALAS are then lost there.

Boom controls are extremely sensitive in COUPLED. Large or abrupt stick inputs can take the boom past a structural limit or into the tanker or the receiver. Guard the flight control stick whenever the system is COUPLED, including when it is coupled by the CONTACT MADE TEST.

items: **FLT CONT on without boom hydraulics.** If FLT CONT is moved to ON with HYD SEL at OFF or DROGUE, the ELEV FAIL and both RUD FAIL lights come on with the aural warning. They stay on until HYD SEL is set to BOOM and FLT CONT is cycled OFF and back ON.
**Servo monitor.** A surface that stays well off its command latches its FAIL light (ELEV, L RUD, R RUD), and the telescope servo latches TLSCP FAIL.
**Momentary DC interruption.** The two flight control status lights that are not on come on and go off, the one that is on goes off and back on, and the stick shows a small transient.

**Momentary AC interruption.** The position instruments start toward their unpowered position, both ALAS INOP lights and all four FAIL lights blink, and every lit status light and annunciator goes off and back on.

**Longer interruption: BCU shutdown.** The four FAIL lights and the aural warning come on and the stick goes limp. After a DC shutdown the AR SIG SYS status lights go out; after an AC shutdown the position instruments go to their unpowered position (elevation at the STOW mark, roll 0°, telescope 0 ft) and both ALAS INOP lights come on. To restart, set FLT CONT to OFF and cycle AR MASTER PWR with both supplies back.
**Accelerometer failure.** FLT CONT DEGRADED: the boom still flies normally in COUPLED, but in FREE FLIGHT its sensitivity and response are degraded and precise control is harder.
**Stored faults.** MAINT REQD lights with the ELEVATION POSN switch at STOW when a failure is stored in the BCU's maintenance memory. Flight control performance is not affected.

blocks.content: The telescoping tube travels 22 ft on a closed-loop chain-cable drive turned by a hydraulic servo motor. Three linear transducers (LVDTs) measure its extension; all three are required. The telescope control stick (at the boom operator's and the instructor's positions, the instructor's overriding) is a **position command**: its travel is the extension. The servo retracts at up to 10 ft/s and extends somewhat more slowly. In STOW the BCU retracts the telescope automatically, and the telescope answers its control only in REFUEL.

In the coupled mode the telescope also controls the axial push and pull between the aircraft, which limits axial nozzle loads automatically. Two **dual bypass valves** let the fuel the retracting tube displaces flow back into the aft body tank instead of building pressure in the boom; they are spring-loaded closed, opened by hydraulic system 2 through the HYD SEL, and powered open whenever FLT CONT is on with the CONTACT light off or a retract is commanded. The boom valve will not open unless both bypass valves are closed (KC-10A). A disagreement between a bypass valve and its command lights its BYPASS DISAGR light on the F/E's fuel panel.
In the coupled mode the telescope also controls the axial push and pull between the aircraft, which limits axial nozzle loads automatically.

**TLSCP AT DISC.** With the TLSCP AT DISC switch-light at AUTO, a disconnect retracts the telescope at its maximum rate, 10 ft/s, until fully retracted, whatever the telescope control is asking for; the telescope control must then be brought back to the retracted position before it commands the telescope again. MAN leaves the telescope where it is at a disconnect; it is used with receivers such as the C-130 and fighters, when manual boom latching is in use, or when normal disconnect capability is lost.

**Emergency retraction.** If the telescope servo fails (TLSCP FAIL), the telescope can still be retracted by pulling the telescope control fully to retract: an emergency path on the battery bus retracts it slowly. The LTS & EMER TLSCP INOP light shows that battery power for this path, and for the four FAIL lights, is lost. Driving the telescope against its stops with the emergency retraction is a mandatory maintenance write-up.

A hydraulic hoist winch on **system 3** raises the boom on a cable attached near its mid-point and lets it down under gravity. A rechargeable shock absorber cushions the boom against the airframe in the stowed position, and a mechanical **latch** at the chock holds it there. The BOOM HOIST lever and the BOOM LATCH lever on the boom operator's overhead panel control them.

blocks.title: BOOM HOIST lever
rows: The hoist motor winds the cable in and raises the boom.
The hoist motor is hydraulically locked. With system 3 depressurized the lock is lost, and an unlatched boom falls.
The motor turns backwards as gravity lowers the boom; a flow limiter prevents it lowering too fast. The drum turns only while the boom's weight pulls the cable.

The clutch actuator disengages the hoist motor, and the cable tension motor keeps a constant pull on the cable so it cannot go slack while the boom maneuvers. A detent prevents the lever moving to HOLD inadvertently.

blocks.content: The **clutch actuator** is electric: its motor runs on the 115 V AC ground-service supply and its control on the 28 V DC ground-service supply. Electrical power is needed to re-engage the hoist when the lever moves from FREE WHEEL back to RAISE. The **cable tension motor** runs on the boom hydraulic supply through HYD SEL at BOOM.

The **latch** is a hook worked through a cable and lever linkage from the BOOM LATCH lever (LOCK, UNLOCK). It closes only on a boom seated in its chock: a LOCK selection on a boom that is not seated leaves the hook open, and the lever must be cycled to UNLOCK and back once the boom is seated. BOOM/DROGUE DEPLOYED lights whenever the boom is not stowed and latched, and BOOM/DROGUE NOT STOWED when that is true with the landing gear handle down.

Do not apply a DOWN command on the flight control stick with the hoist lever at LWR: the elevator's pull on a cable that can pay out only as fast as its flow limiter allows may break the cable.

Do not move HYD SEL from BOOM to OFF with the boom deployed and the hoist lever at FREE WHEEL: it removes pressure from the cable tension motor, and the slack cable or the motor can be damaged. If it happens, set the hoist lever to RAISE to take the slack out before returning HYD SEL to BOOM.

**A broken hoist cable** leaves the boom with no means of being winched into its chock. It can still be stowed by flying it there with its own elevator, holding it in the chock with the stick and locking the latch. That needs dynamic pressure: increase speed to 300 KIAS or more. The boom may not fly to the stowed position above 20,000 ft, because for a given indicated airspeed the surfaces' lift falls slightly with altitude as compressibility grows, or in a turn, where the load factor makes the boom heavier.

children.title: Structural limits and the disconnect envelope

blocks.content: Two sets of limits surround the boom. The **structural limits** are where the boom itself would be damaged. The **disconnect envelope**, set well inside them, is where the BCU automatically disconnects a receiver, so that the nozzle is out of the receptacle before the structure is at risk. The receiver's own envelope, published for each receiver type, decides how the boom operator sets the adjustable limits.
The structural elevation limit is 42°. Exceeding a structural limit is a mandatory maintenance write-up. See [Limitations](limitations) for the boom's airspeed and altitude envelope.

blocks.title: Disconnect envelope
rows: Knob on the ELEVATION indicator, 1° steps
Two knobs on the ROLL indicator, each its own side

blocks.content: Each adjustable limit is a mechanical cursor on its indicator's bezel: the cursor stands where its knob put it, powered or not, and the BCU's limit logic reads the cursor itself. The roll limits are applied side by side, so a boom rolled right is judged against the right limit only. The roll limits are always armed. The elevation and telescope limits are armed by the BOOM ENV LIMITS ELEVATION and TLSCP switches at ACTIVE. In READY the limits are deactivated and only show; in CONTACT any armed limit crossed, or about to be crossed, disconnects.

blocks.alt: Diagram of the KC-10A boom envelope seen from behind the boom. Elevation on the vertical axis from 0° to 45° down, roll on the horizontal axis from 30° left to 30° right. Outer stepped boundary: the structural roll limits (5° above 0°, 18° from 0 to 18°, 27° from 18 to 40°, 24° below 40°) and the 42° elevation limit. Inner shaded box: the disconnect envelope with the upper elevation limit drawn as a band from 20° to 27°, the fixed 40° lower limit, and the left and right roll limits as bands from 11° to 25°. Inset: telescope scale 0 to 22 ft with the fixed 6 ft and 21 ft disconnect limits and a typical 12 ft contact extension.
blocks.title: Boom structural limits and disconnect envelope

blocks.content: A failed boom position instrument does not disable its disconnect limits, but that part of the envelope may shrink to its smallest adjustable size. Discontinue boom refueling after a position instrument failure except in an emergency.

The **air refueling signal system** is the electrical conversation between the tanker and the receiver. An induction coil in the boom nozzle mates with a similar coil in the receiver's receptacle; through them pass the receiver's contact-made signal, either side's disconnect signal, and the boom interphone. The tanker's half, the signal amplifier, is controlled by the BCU and cycles through three states: **READY**, **CONTACT** and **DISCONNECT**. The upper halves of the three status lights on the boom operator's instrument panel show the signal system's state; their lower halves show the flight control system's (FREE FLIGHT, COUPLED, FREE FLIGHT), which exists only with FLT CONT on.

blocks.alt: State diagram of the boom signal system. Three boxes: READY / FREE FLIGHT, CONTACT / COUPLED, DISC / FREE FLIGHT. Arrows: READY to CONTACT on receiver contact signal (NORM), CONTACT MADE TEST (NORM) or EMER CONTACT MADE (NORM or OVRD); CONTACT to DISC on the DISC trigger, the receiver's disconnect through the coil, or the BCU's automatic disconnect at an armed envelope limit (actual or anticipated); READY to DISC on the DISC trigger; DISC and CONTACT to READY on RESET TO READY. Side notes: COUPLED one second after CONTACT (not in STOW); COUPLED holds for RCVR DISC DELAY after DISC; TLSCP AT DISC AUTO retracts at 10 ft/s; tones 1 beep CONTACT, 3 beeps DISC, 4 beeps DISC from READY in NORM.

The pilot director lights stay on and follow the boom until reset. Three beeps (four from READY in NORM).

blocks.content: **NORM and OVRD.** The AR SIG SYS OVRD switch-light normally shows NORM. OVRD bypasses the signal amplifier: the boom operator then makes CONTACT manually with the EMER CONTACT MADE trigger as soon as the nozzle is seated, and all normal boom functions follow. OVRD is used when the amplifier fails, for receivers with Boeing-type receptacles, and for manual boom latching. Pressing the switch-light again restores NORM if the boom signal coil tests GOOD. In OVRD the tanker's disconnect does not reach the receiver's toggles: the receiver pilot must initiate the disconnects, or the boom operator uses the independent disconnect.

**Receiver disconnect delay and anticipation.** A receiver takes a finite time to release its toggles after a disconnect signal, and a boom approaching a limit keeps moving during that time. The RCVR DISC DELAY selector (0.25 to 2.0 s in eight steps) tells the BCU how long that release takes for the receiver type. While coupled, the BCU projects the boom's position ahead by the boom's rate times that delay, and commands the disconnect early enough that the nozzle is free before the limit itself is reached. The same delay is how long COUPLED and ALAS hold after the disconnect. A limit reached at high rate can still jam the nozzle in the receptacle, above all with the receiver rolled well over and the boom at low elevation.

**BOOM COIL TEST.** The test button measures the resistance of the nozzle's signal coil and shows OPEN, GOOD or SHORTED on its indicator. With an open or shorted coil the normal signal system cannot be used: the tanker can disconnect only through the independent disconnect system, and there is no interphone with the receiver. Pressing BOOM COIL TEST in CONTACT advances the receiver's signal system to disconnect.
**Aural tones.** A tone generator in the ARO headsets supplements the lights: one beep for CONTACT, three for DISCONNECT, and four if DISC is selected from READY in NORM (three in OVRD).

The independent disconnect system (IDS) releases the nozzle without the receiver's cooperation and without the signal coils. It is electrically controlled and pneumatically actuated: a compressed-air bottle on the telescoping tube drives the nozzle's toggle latches flush, so the boom can be pulled out of a receptacle whose own toggles are still latched. Pressing the flight control stick's disconnect trigger through its second detent fires it. A holding circuit keeps the nozzle's toggles retracted, and the INDEP DISC light on, until RESET TO READY is pushed.

The INDEP DISC gauge on the boom operator's instrument panel is a direct pressure reading of the bottle (dial PSI × 100). The bottle is serviced to 2,000 psi; the preflight minimum is 1,500 psi. Its green band, 1,000 to 2,000 psi, means one or more disconnects remain; below 1,000 psi (red) the system cannot be depended on. Each shot spends part of the charge, so receiver-initiated disconnects, when feasible, conserve IDS capability for when it is needed.

**Theory: why the gauge falls in the cruise.** The bottle is a sealed gas charge, so its pressure is proportional to its absolute temperature. A bottle serviced to 2,000 psi in a warm hangar and cold-soaked to −30 °C at altitude reads close to 1,650 psi with no air lost. That is physics, not a leak: a leak shows as a steady fall at constant temperature.

The boom's surfaces, telescope, bypass valves and cable tension motor run on the boom hydraulic supply selected by the HYD SEL lever (DROGUE, OFF, BOOM). On the KC-10A that supply is hydraulic system 2 backed by the AR alternate supply: normally system 2's engine-driven pumps and the alternate supply together; with the number 2 engine pumps failed, the 2-3 reversible motor pump powers both; with system 2's fluid lost, a low-level switch closes the shutoff on system 2's side of the 2-3 pump and isolates the pump and the auxiliary reservoir for the boom or drogue alone. If the auxiliary reservoir runs low, the 2-3 pump stops and the boom hydraulics are lost. The hoist runs on system 3 throughout. See [Hydraulics](hydraulics).

On the KDC-10 there is no alternate supply: HYD SEL at BOOM connects hydraulic system 2 directly to the boom, and the boom's flow demand is drawn from system 2. A loss of system 2 is therefore a loss of the boom's flight controls and telescope. The hoist runs on system 3. See [Hydraulics](hydraulics).

The surfaces need pressure to fly the boom. The boom operator's BOOM HYD PRESS LOW light comes on as the boom supply falls through about 1,700 psi and goes out above about 2,100 psi; MAIN HYD PRESS LOW shows the main system feeding it. With FLT CONT on and no boom pressure, the BCU latches the ELEV and RUD FAIL lights.

Boom flight control surface flutter may follow a failure of hydraulic system 2 if the flight control actuator reservoirs are not pressurized. Move HYD SEL to BOOM for about 2 minutes (system 2 pressurized) before takeoff and every 8 hours thereafter. The computer check during preflight and boom use during refueling satisfy the requirement within the 8-hour limit.
