The guarded AR BUS ISOL switch locks out the ARO AC and DC buses; GND SVC BUS ISOL locks out the ARO ground-service buses; the sprung AR DC BUS ALTN PWR switch (GND TEST) tests the change-over relay on the ground. See [Electrical](electrical).

children.title: Pilot director lights and boom lighting

blocks.content: The **pilot director lights** are two rows of lights under the forward fuselage, ahead of the wing root, that tell the receiver pilot where the receiver is in the boom envelope. The left row gives elevation: one green, two amber and two red triangular panels with a white **U** (up) at its forward end and **D** (down) at its aft end. The right row gives telescope extension: one green, two amber, two red and four white rectangular panels with a white **A** (aft) forward and **F** (forward) aft. The BCU drives them from the boom's position, scaled automatically to the envelope the boom operator has selected, and lights the appropriate panel slightly ahead of the boom's movement to give the receiver pilot more time to respond. The boom operator can light the red panel and letter at either end of a row with the coaching switch to direct a large (steady) or small (flashing) correction. They come on at CONTACT, stay on and follow the boom after a disconnect until the system is reset, and are not active in READY/COUPLED.

blocks.alt: KC-10A forward lower fuselage seen from below and behind, as a receiver pilot sees it in the contact position: the two pilot director light rows ahead of the wing root. Left row: green, two amber, two red triangles with U at the front and D at the back. Right row: green, two amber, two red and four white rectangles with A at the front and F at the back. White centerline stripe on the fuselage underside visible.
blocks.title: Pilot director lights
blocks.caption: The simulation does not drive the pilot director lights; see Simulation notes.

blocks.content: Other boom lighting: two fluorescent **boom marking** lights on the tail cone light the extension markings on the telescoping tube; two **nozzle lights** light the nozzle and the receptacle area, with a dimmer and a foot switch that brings them to full bright; a **receiver flood light** lights the receiver. The boom operator also controls the tanker's own exterior lighting stations that a receiver formates on: the forward and aft fuselage underbody lights, the horizontal stabilizer lights and the wing flood lights. See [Lighting](lighting).

sections.title: Boom operator's station
sections.summary: KC-10A and KDC-10.

blocks.content: The aerial refueling operator's (ARO) compartment is at the rear of the aircraft, below the cabin floor, reached through a hatch in the right rear of the cabin floor and a ladder. It seats the boom operator, an instructor and an observer, each with an oxygen regulator and an audio panel. A window looks aft and down at the refueling area; side mirrors show the formation off the wingtips. The boom operator sits facing aft, so the operator's left is the tanker's right.

blocks.alt: KC-10A ARO compartment from behind the boom operator's seat, looking aft: the sighting window with the sighting door open and the boom trailed outside; the boom operator's instrument panel below the window (ELEVATION, ROLL and TELESCOPE indicators, FUEL FLOW, FUEL PRESS, INDEP DISC gauge, three signal system status lights); the overhead panel above; the boom control panel on the aft left side panel and the drogue control and hose reel monitor panels on the right; the two WARP panels; the flight control stick at the right hand and the telescope control stick at the left. Station lights on.
blocks.title: Boom operator's station

items: **Overhead panel:** AR MASTER PWR, the sighting door switch, BOOM HOIST and BOOM LATCH levers, HYD SEL, FLT CONT, BOOM ELEVATION POSN, the BOOM ENV LIMITS switches, BOOM COIL TEST, BOOM AUDIO, the station's bus switches, ANNUN PWR, the lighting controls, window heat and compartment temperature.

**Instrument panel:** the ELEVATION, ROLL and TELESCOPE indicators with their limit cursors and knobs, FUEL FLOW with the FUEL OFFLOAD counter, FUEL PRESS, the INDEP DISC gauge, the three signal system status lights and the boom's annunciators.

**Aft side panels:** the boom control panel on the left (ALAS, AR SIG SYS OVRD, TLSCP AT DISC switch-lights, RCVR DISC DELAY); on the KC-10A, the drogue control panel and hose reel monitor panel on the right, and the two WARP panels.

**Hand controllers:** the flight control stick, with the disconnect trigger (DISC, and IDS through the second detent) and an interphone switch; the telescope control stick, with RESET TO READY, the EMER CONTACT MADE trigger and the BREAKAWAY SIG switch. The instructor has a second telescope control stick that overrides the boom operator's.
**STATUS/TEST panel:** a two-line display through which the boom operator runs the BCU's preflight self-test, recalls stored faults and reads sensor values.

blocks.content: **Sighting door.** An electric actuator opens and closes the door over the viewing window. The sighting door switch must be held at OPEN or CLOSE until the door reaches its limit: released early, the door stops where it is. A crank drives the door if power fails. There is no airspeed or altitude restriction on operating it.
Do not transmit on HF while in contact with, or close to, the boom. HF transmissions may cause uncommanded boom movement.

The centerline hose and drogue refuels probe-equipped receivers. A hydraulic hose reel in the aft fuselage, offset to the right of the ARO viewing tunnel so that the hose clears the boom, pays 80 ft of hose out of a short exit chute to a paradrogue. About 69 ft of hose is outside the chute at full trail. The system has five subsystems: the hose and drogue, the reel actuation, the position indicating, the guillotine, and the lighting. The boom operator works it from the drogue control panel and the hose reel monitor panel on the operator's right aft side panel; it takes its hydraulics from the same HYD SEL lever as the boom.

blocks.alt: KC-10A tail seen from behind and below at refueling speed: the boom stowed, the centerline hose trailed from its chute right of the ARO window to full trail, the paradrogue canopy inflated. The hose's markings legible: black hose, 12-inch white bands every 10 ft, 5-ft bands through the refueling range, and the three 24-inch bands at the fuel flow initiation point, the recommended refueling position and the inner limit.
blocks.title: Centerline hose and drogue at full trail

blocks.content: The hose is black, marked with 12-inch white bands every 10 ft and every 5 ft through the refueling range, and with 24-inch bands at the fuel flow initiation position, the recommended refueling position and the inner limit. The refueling range runs from about 5 ft to 40 ft forward of full trail.

The **paradrogue** is a ring and arms carrying a nylon canopy. It collapses inside the exit chute and inflates once in the airstream, giving the receiver a stable, cone-shaped target that guides its probe into the coupling. Its ball-shaped housing holds a pressure regulator and a surge suppressor that protect the receiver's fuel system. Four lights powered by an air-driven generator in the drogue mark it at night.

**Theory: how the hose flies.** A trailed hose is a catenary in a stream of air. Its own weight pulls it down, cross-flow drag on each length of hose and the drogue's drag pull it aft, and the tension that results increases from the drogue toward the reel. The faster the tanker flies, the more the drag dominates and the flatter and higher the hose trails; slower, it sags lower behind the tanker. A sideslip swings it to one side. The tension at the reel, which the response system must match, therefore depends on airspeed and air density: it rises roughly with dynamic pressure.

The reel is hydraulically driven from the boom and drogue hydraulic supply with HYD SEL at DROGUE. A reel lock holds the drum stowed; it releases only with the drive behind it (DROGUE MASTER PWR on, HYD SEL at DROGUE and pressure available) and the HOSE switch at TRAIL. With no pressure, an unlocked reel turns freely and the drogue's drag pulls the hose out to its stop.

items: **TRAIL.** The lock releases and the drogue's drag pulls the hose out against a payout brake that limits its speed, slowing over the last few feet to the full-trail stop. Switch to full trail takes no more than about 17 s at 270 KIAS and 25,000 ft.
**Full trail.** The trail-limit switch sets the full-trail relay, which locks in the reference tension for the response system (below). READY comes on about 5 s after full trail.

**REWIND.** The reel winds the hose in, slowing over the last few feet, until the drogue stop switch stops it at the stowed position and the reel locks. Switch to stowed takes no more than about 16 s at 270 KIAS and 25,000 ft. REWIND clears the full-trail relay.

blocks.title: Reel switches
rows: Sets the full-trail relay, which locks in the reference pressure for hose tension.
Stops the reel with the drogue at the stowed position during a rewind.
Puts out HOSE REEL NOT LOCKED when the reel is locked.
Defines the refueling range, 5 ft to 40 ft forward of full trail. See below.
Flashes the external amber READY light when the forward limit of the range is exceeded.

blocks.content: When a receiver's probe pushes the drogue forward, the drag that held the hose taut no longer does: without help the hose would go slack, form a loop and whip, which can break the hose or damage the receiver. The **response system** prevents this by making the reel a constant-tension winch. At full trail it records the tension the hose is carrying in that flight condition as its reference; from then on it pulls with a constant fraction of that reference. As the receiver pushes in, the reel winds the slack hose in; as the receiver drops back, the drogue's drag overcomes the reel and pulls hose out again. The hose stays taut across the whole refueling range.

The reference is only right for the speed and altitude it was set at. If the tanker slows after the reference was set, the hose's drag falls below the reel's pull and the reel winds hose in by itself; if it speeds up, the hose is under-tensioned and responds sluggishly. **REEL RESP RESET** re-references the response system to the present flight condition: READY goes out when it is pushed and comes back about 5 s after release, and the external red signal light goes out. Reset the reel response after establishing the refueling altitude, attitude and airspeed, and before each contact; do not push it with a receiver in contact.

**The 55-knot check.** The same physics gives a simple test that the response system works. Set the reference at 325 KIAS, then slow at about 1 kt per second: as drag falls below the reel's pull, the reel starts to rewind the hose. A healthy system starts rewinding within a 55-kt reduction. As hose winds on, the drum's effective radius grows and its pull at the hose falls, so a response rewind stalls short of stowing the drogue; that is also why a hose that will not rewind normally may need a deceleration of up to 80 kt before the response winds it home.

**Hose reel monitor.** With the HOSE REEL MONITOR switch ON, the monitor continuously compares the response setting with the present flight condition. If they disagree, RESP INOP lights (and the external red signal light comes on, inhibiting the external READY light); the condition holds until reset. With the hose stowed, HOSE REEL TEST at MON tests the monitor: RESP INOP comes on for about one second and goes out. With the hose trailed and READY on, HOSE REEL TEST at SYS tests the response system itself: the hose rewinds to the forward limit of the range and redeploys to full trail, READY returns about 5 s later, and RESP INOP stays out. RESP INOP may flicker as a receiver first engages, or as it moves the hose between the aft limit and full trail; that is normal. Pushing and holding REEL RESP RESET for at least 2 s clears it.

children.title: Fuel range position switch and its logic

blocks.content: A single fuel range position switch on the reel decides when fuel may flow. It is read behind the full-trail relay: the range is measured forward of full trail, so a hose trailing out (whose first 29 ft lie forward of the range) and a hose rewinding do not count.

blocks.title: Refueling range logic
rows: Pushed in 5 ft to 40 ft (in range)

blocks.content: The drogue valve and the hose reel bleed valve are interlocked through this switch: the bleed valve relieves the hose's trapped pressure whenever the hose is outside the range, because a pressurized hose can stop a receiver's probe from making a contact. If the normal bleed does not relieve it, opening the drogue valve and scavenging the AR manifold below 10 psi will; REEL RESP RESET must be held in RESET to open the drogue valve with the hose at full trail. Closing the drogue valve before the receiver disconnects avoids trapping pressure for the next contact.

The guillotine on the reel lets the boom operator jettison the hose and drogue in an emergency. The hose runs through its aperture; when fired by two cartridges on a 28 V signal (if only one fires electrically, the other fires sympathetically), its blade severs the hose and clamps both cut ends shut, so no fuel is spilled. The drum end stays on the reel; the whole length outside, with the drogue, falls away. The HOSE JTSN switch is under a guard, and DROGUE MASTER PWR is not in the circuit: the guillotine fires with the hose stowed or trailed. After a jettison DROGUE POSN shows the barber pole and BOOM/DROGUE DEPLOYED stays on, because there is no drogue at the stop switch.

rows: STOW or TRAIL for those positions; a barber pole with the hose between them, with DROGUE MASTER PWR off, or after a jettison. After a response rewind or a receiver's push-in it keeps showing TRAIL until DROGUE MASTER PWR is switched off.
Hose at full trail with the reel response set; comes on about 5 s after full trail. Out when the receiver pushes the hose in about 5 ft.
RESP INOP (amber, hose reel monitor panel)
Hose stowed: the monitor is inoperative. Hose deployed: the reel response is improperly set for the present flight condition.
HOSE REEL NOT LOCKED (amber, boom annunciators)
DROGUE MASTER PWR off and the reel not locked.
The boom not stowed and latched, or the drogue not at its stop with the reel locked.
The same, with the landing gear handle down.

blocks.content: Three **external signal lights** on the aft fuselage tell the receiver pilot the system's state. **Red** is steady when reel pressure is too low or RESP INOP is on, and flashes when the boom operator signals a breakaway with BREAKAWAY SIG. **Amber** is steady at full trail with the response set, goes out when the receiver pushes in about 5 ft, and flashes beyond the forward limit. **Green** is on while fuel is being transferred. A floodlight lights the hose markings; the boom operator controls the signal lights' and floodlight's intensity.

sections.title: Wing air refueling pods (WARP)
sections.summary: KC-10A and DC-10-40 Omega.

blocks.content: A wing air refueling pod (WARP) hangs on a pylon under each wing near its tip. Each is a complete hose-and-drogue refueling system in its own right: a ram air turbine (RAT) drives a fuel pump; the pump's pressure drives the hose reel and delivers fuel to the receiver; a digital refueling control unit (DRCU) runs the pod. Only electrical power for control and signals, and a pressurized fuel line from the wing crossfeed manifold, come from the aircraft. Two probe receivers can refuel at the same time, one on each pod.

blocks.alt: Right wing air refueling pod under the outer wing, seen from behind and below in flight: the pylon, the two-bladed ram air turbine at the pod's nose turning, the hose trailed to full trail from the pod's tail with the paradrogue inflated, white and orange hose bands visible, the red guide lines painted on the wing underside either side of the pod and on the pod's belly, and the pod's paired red, amber and green signal lights under its tail cone.
blocks.title: Wing air refueling pod

items: **Hose and reel.** The hose is 2.0 in inside diameter and 79 ft long, 5 ft of which stays inside the pod, so 74 ft trails. It is black with white and orange bands marking significant lengths. A buffer spring around its outer end throws the coupling and drogue into the airstream at the start of a trail and absorbs the shock at the end of a rewind. The grooved drum is chain-driven by a **vane pump** powered by fuel pressure, so the reel is driven and braked by fuel, not hydraulics.

**Reception coupling and paradrogue.** An MA-4 coupling at the end of the hose provides dual secondary pressure regulation and surge protection for the receiver. The paradrogue on the coupling supplies the drag that pulls the hose out, stabilizes the hose end, and guides the receiver's probe. Four lights on an air-driven generator mark it at night.

**Ram air turbine and fuel pump.** A two-bladed, 25-in RAT whose pitch an electric motor varies drives the pod's fuel pump. The pump provides delivery pressure and the pressure that trails and rewinds the hose.
**Fuel control valve (FCV) and pod fuel valve.** The FCV ports fuel through the vane pump one way to brake a trail and the other to rewind. The pod fuel valve controls delivery to the receiver.
**Signal lights.** Paired red, amber and green lights under the pod's tail cone. Red guide lines on the wing underside on each side of the pod, and one on the pod's belly, help the receiver align.

blocks.content: In cruise the RAT is feathered and turns slowly, 600 to 1,200 rpm, enough to lubricate the pump with minimum drag. When the DRCU needs pump pressure, to trail or rewind the hose or to deliver fuel, it drives the blades toward fine pitch and governs the RAT's speed. The RAT is limited to 6,900 rpm. Above 7,000 rpm for 5 seconds, or above 7,500 rpm at once, the pod trips: the FCV closes, the fuel spill vent opens, FUEL PRESS HIGH and FUEL PRESS LOW flash together, the red signal light comes on steady, and a deployed hose creeps out to full trail in the passive mode. With the hose stowed, HOSE STOWED flashes if the RAT exceeds 2,000 rpm. RAT speed, and the pump's fuel temperature that follows it, come down as airspeed is reduced.

**Theory: why the pump heats.** A pump turning at speed churns its fuel; with fuel flowing through it to a receiver or circulating back to the tank, the heat is carried away. With nothing circulating, the pump's fuel temperature climbs. FUEL TEMP HIGH comes on above 120 °C; the spill valve then dumps the hot fuel into No. 1 main tank (left pod) or No. 3 main tank (right pod), and the light goes out once the fuel cools below 50 °C. Circulation stops when the hose is jettisoned or POD POWER is off.

children.title: Digital refueling control unit and hose modes

blocks.title: Hose modes
rows: Hose wound in, parking brake set
POD POWER on, HOSE TRAIL/REWIND to TRAIL

After a 5-second delay the motor-operated parking brake releases (HOSE STOWED stays on meanwhile), the buffer spring throws the drogue into the airstream, and drag pulls the hose out with the vane pump braking it to about 5 ft/s, slowing to about 2 ft/s as full trail nears. From about 46 ft the tensator springs wind on, preloading the take-up. READY comes on at 69 ft. At 74 ft a mechanical brake stops the reel and a microswitch enables the jettison.
HOSE TRAIL/REWIND to REWIND at full trail

The FCV drives the vane pump in reverse, winding the hose in at up to 8 ft/s. HOSE TRANSIT flashes each 2 ft of travel. The parking brake engages as the hose reaches 12 ft; within about a foot of stowed the panel shows HOSE STOWED. The switch may be returned to TRAIL at any time to re-trail.
A FAIL, a RAT overspeed, or a breakaway signal

The FCV gives more resistance than in an active trail, and the hose creeps out to full trail at about 2 ft/s. The red signal light stays on. At full trail the pod returns to normal if the fault has cleared.
BREAKAWAY SIG (on the centerline drogue panel, or the boom telescope control stick)

At full trail the red pod signal lights flash for 10 seconds and READY goes out. With the hose pushed into the refuel range they flash until it reaches full trail. A hose short of full trail goes passive and creeps out. Nothing happens with the hose stowed.

blocks.content: Once TRAIL is selected, do not select REWIND until the hose reaches full trail: reversing early can damage the parking brake. A rewind selected within the first 12 ft is not acted on until the hose is past 12 ft. If trail is started below 230 KIAS the drogue may not have enough drag to overcome the tensators and the hose may stall short of full trail: READY does not come on, fuel cannot be transferred and the jettison is not enabled. Increase speed to 230 KIAS or more (not above 300 KIAS) to pull it to full trail; once there, the tanker may slow for the refueling.

The pod's equivalent of the centerline response system is its **tensators**: constant-force spring reels that wind on from about 46 ft of trail. When a receiver pushes the drogue forward, the tensators take the slack hose up; when it drops back, the drogue's drag pulls the hose out against them. The take-up works only from about 46 ft to full trail. Pushed inside about 46 ft, the tensators stop and the hose goes dead: a loop forms that can damage the receiver.

blocks.title: Hose positions, pushed in from full trail
rows: READY (internal blue and external amber) on. Pod fuel valve closed.
Refuel range entered: amber and READY out, pod fuel valve opens if armed, pilots' L or R DROGUE ENGAGED on.
Amber and READY flash: the inner limit is being approached. Back beyond 57 ft, they stop flashing.
Pod fuel valve closes, green FUEL FLOW signal light out, fuel transfer stops. Back beyond about 49 ft, transfer resumes.

blocks.content: The range is measured in from full trail. A hose trailing out through 69 to 49 ft does not open the pod fuel valve: the valve opens only once the hose has been at full trail and is then pushed back into the range.

Each pod is fed from its wing's crossfeed manifold through an electrically operated **WING DROGUE VALVE** in the wing's outboard section, opened and closed by the flight engineer. Beyond that valve, the pod's own **pod fuel valve** controls delivery to the receiver: armed by the F/E's POD FUEL VALVE switch, it opens automatically when the hose is in the refuel range and closes outside it, or when the pod fails and shuts down. The pod's pump regulates 50 ±5 psi at the coupling at every flow from zero to its maximum of about 420 GPM, provided the inlet has at least 10 psi; below that the RAT slows delivery to stay within what the inlet can supply.

**The inlet must be pressurized before the hose is deployed.** A shut WING DROGUE VALVE traps whatever pressure was in the line beyond it; on a cold aircraft that is none. Below 10 psi the F/E's FUEL INLET PRESSURE LOW light comes on; below 6 psi the pod's FUEL PRESS LOW comes on, the hose cannot be rewound, and if the condition lasts 10 seconds the pod fails. A pod with a hose deployed and FUEL PRESS LOW on therefore cannot be stowed until the pressure is restored.

**KC-10A.** The normal source is the AR pumps in a body tank, routed through that tank's alternate transfer (ALTN TRANS) and isolation (ISOL) valves into the wing crossfeed manifold. With an ALTN TRANS valve, an ISOL valve and at least one WING DROGUE VALVE open, and the boom valve closed, the FPCU regulates on the crossfeed transducers and holds 50 ±5 psi at the middle of the manifold. Opening the centerline drogue valve with both ALTN TRANS valves closed returns control to the drogue transducers. The engine-feed and transfer pumps in the wing and body tanks are an alternate source. The AR pumps alone, without the ALTN TRANS path, do not pressurize the crossfeed manifold, and neither do the boost pumps with the crossfeed valves shut. With the AR pumps feeding the pods, the engine crossfeed valves are normally left closed. See [Fuel](fuel).

**DC-10-40 Omega.** There are no AR pumps and no body tanks. Each pod's crossfeed manifold is pressurized by the engine tanks' boost pumps through the X-FEED valves, so a dry pod on the Omega is first an X-FEED question and then a WING DROGUE VALVE one: open the X-FEED valves and the WING DROGUE VALVE, and confirm FUEL INLET PRESSURE LOW is out, before trailing the hose. See [Fuel](fuel).
Keep the wing pod fuel system, including the hose, full of fuel. A full system reduces the risk of lightning-strike damage and lubricates the pod's fuel pump.

Each pod's control panel has a four-digit display. Normally it shows the fuel the pod has offloaded in units of 100 lb (150 is 15,000 lb). FAIL means the pod's control has failed (for example the fuel control valve, the RAT blade control or the data bus); the hose then goes passive. A blank display means the pod's processor has failed, and the lights may all be out with it.

items: BITE pressed for less than 2 seconds shows the RAT's speed in hundreds of rpm, prefixed r (r-65 is 6,500 rpm). Pressed again, the pump's fuel temperature in °C, prefixed t (t-9 is 9 °C).
COUNTER RESET returns the display to the offload and zeroes it. Held, it shows 8888 as a display test.
BITE held for 2 to 7 seconds on the ground starts the pod's built-in test, a sequence of numbered steps the boom operator and flight engineer follow on the display.
Cycling POD POWER off and on also zeroes the counter.

blocks.content: A hose that cannot be rewound can be jettisoned with the pod's guarded HOSE JTSN switch, which fires an electromechanical disconnect at the reel. The hose must be at full trail: the full-trail microswitch enables the jettison. All pod power is removed while the switch is held, and it must be held no longer than half a second or the jettison solenoid is damaged. If the hose does not separate immediately, it may separate later with no further action.

sections.title: Offload fuel system
sections.summary: The AR pumps, the fuel pressure control unit and the delivery valves.

blocks.content: Fuel for receivers comes from the forward, center wing and aft body tanks, and the air refueling (AR) fuel system delivers it to the boom, the centerline drogue or the wing pods. Its parts are six hydraulically driven AR pumps, the fuel pressure control unit (FPCU), a boom shutoff valve, a drogue shutoff valve, two hydraulically operated bypass valves at the boom, a pressure relief valve and a WING DROGUE VALVE in each wing. The main tank transfer pumps and the crossfeed manifold can move wing tank fuel into the body tanks. The body tanks, their fill and isolation valves, and the main tank system are described in [Fuel](fuel).
Equalize the fuel in the body tanks by offloading selectively rather than by transferring fuel between the body tanks or between the body tanks and the main tanks.
In the simulation the pumps and valves can be set up as described, but with no receiver nothing is offloaded: see [There is no receiver](#sim-no-receiver).

Each body tank has two AR pumps, a left and a right, each turned by a hydraulic motor. The pumps in a tank are driven by different hydraulic systems, so a hydraulic failure costs at most one pump per tank. The FPCU's left channel controls the three left pumps and its right channel the three right pumps, one in each tank.

Select AR pumps for an offload in this order of priority: from hydraulic system 3, R FWD, R CTR, L AFT; from system 1, L FWD, L CTR; from system 2, R AFT. If possible, limit the pumps drawn from system 3 to two. A pump is armed by its AR PUMP switch on the F/E's fuel panel with either the boom's AR MASTER PWR or DROGUE MASTER PWR at PWR; if there is fuel in its tank, the tank's low-level float switch is closed and the pump's LOW light comes on, showing that it is able to run. For boom refueling the pumps start when the signal system reaches CONTACT. For drogue refueling, internal transfer or dumping, AR PUMP OVRD starts the armed pumps directly. In the center wing tank the pumps will not run with the AR ISOL VALVE closed.

**Start sequence.** One pump on each channel may start at a time. A pump takes about six seconds to start: at two seconds its blue hydraulic pressurization light comes on (the HYD PRSRZ lights beside the fuel panel), at four seconds the servo valve current begins, at six seconds the motor is at breakout torque. If the pump has not raised more than 10 psi (its LOW light out) within 17 seconds, the FPCU shuts it down, and it stays down until its switch is cycled OFF and ON. The next pump on a channel starts when control pressure is reached, but no sooner than 17 seconds and no later than 34 seconds after the previous one. Pumps selected before contact start in the order aft, center, forward; with BOOM/DROGUE ENGAGED or AR PUMP OVRD, the first pump selected starts first, then the aftmost, then the rest.

**Deactivation.** When a tank reaches its low level, its float switch shuts both its pumps down and their LOW lights come on; turn the switches off. The FPCU also shuts a channel's three pumps down on an overpressure, or when the two transducers it compares disagree. A failed boom or hose reel transducer shuts down its channel's pumps, but only during the refueling phases that use that transducer. A pump whose hydraulic system has lost pressure turns slowly, never makes its 10 psi and is shut down; do not reset a pump that shut down for low hydraulic pressure. Fuel pumps should be turned off when their LOW lights come on.

The FPCU is a two-channel microprocessor that controls the AR pumps' activation, speed and shutdown. It does not regulate flow. It regulates **pressure at the delivery point**, by varying the pumps' speed, and leaves the flow to the receiver: whatever the receiver's fuel system will accept at that pressure is what flows. Each station has two pressure transducers, each controlling one channel and so one pump in each tank. The FPCU also uses one transducer to watch for excessive pressure and the other to check that one: if they disagree, it shuts the channel down.

blocks.title: FPCU control stations
rows: Boom nozzle (two transducers in the nozzle)
The boom shutoff valve is open
Centerline drogue (venturi throat in the hose reel system)
The drogue shutoff valve is open
An ALTN TRANS valve and an ISOL valve in the forward or aft body tank, and a WING DROGUE VALVE, are open
Pumps running with both the boom and drogue valves closed: fuel dump, internal transfer, reverse refueling

blocks.content: **Theory: why pressure, not flow.** Regulating delivery pressure gives the receiver's own fuel system, which knows how much it can accept, control of the flow, and gives the tanker a pressure its receivers are designed for. The centerline's venturi is shaped to reproduce the pressure drop along the hose, so a pressure held at its throat is close to the pressure at the coupling 80 ft away. A pressure loop also stays well-behaved when the receiver's demand changes suddenly, as at a disconnect, where a flow loop would drive the pumps toward full speed against a closed valve.

items: **Boom valve.** Controlled automatically during refueling when the F/E's BOOM VALVE switch is armed: it opens in contact and is powered closed in READY/FREE FLIGHT and DISC/FREE FLIGHT, and whenever a retract is commanded. It will not open unless both boom bypass valves are closed. With the boom's FLT CONT switch off, its operation is independent of the signal system.

**Drogue valve.** Interlocked through the fuel range position switch: armed by the F/E's DROGUE VALVE switch, it opens when the hose is pushed in about 5 ft and closes outside the refueling range. With the drogue stowed it may be operated directly by its switch; with the hose at full trail, REEL RESP RESET must be held to open it.
**Boom bypass valves.** Route the fuel displaced by a retracting telescope into the aft body tank. See [Telescope](#boom-telescope).
**WING DROGUE VALVES.** Shutoff valves in each wing's crossfeed manifold feeding that wing's pod. See [Wing pod fuel supply](#pod-fuel-supply).

blocks.content: Each boom and drogue valve takes its power through its system's master switch on the boom operator's panels, and can be opened by hand in the aircraft by disconnecting its connector and moving its manual override handle.

Identical offload fuel flow indicators on the F/E's fuel panel and the boom operator's instrument panel show the offload rate and, on a resettable counter, the total offloaded through the boom or the centerline drogue. The wing pods count their own offload on their own displays. The boom operator's FUEL PRESS indicator shows the pressure in the boom or drogue when its valve is open, or in the AR manifold when both are closed; the F/E has an AR FUEL PRESS gauge.

blocks.title: Refueling flow figures
rows: No maximum is published: the FPCU holds 50 ±5 psi at the nozzle and the receiver's acceptance sets the flow
Up to about 420 GPM per pod at 50 ±5 psi coupling pressure
Onload through the UARRSI (KC-10A as receiver)
Up to 1,200 GPM, about 7,800 lb/min, with all valves open
300 GPM maximum, about 2,000 lb/min; one AR pump gives the limiting rate

blocks.content: After refueling, the tanker's offload manifold, the boom, and the receiving manifold from the UARRSI to the front spar can be drained, which reduces unusable fuel and the spill hazard in a crash landing. The F/E's MANF SCAV selector chooses what is drained: **RCVR** drains the receiving manifold into No. 2 main tank; **BOOM** drains the boom's line alone; **TANKER** drains the AR manifold and the boom into the aft body tank and No. 2 main tank. When MANF SCAV PRESS LOW comes on steady the job is done: return the selector to OFF. It should take no more than 10 minutes; the light may flicker without a fault.
Keep the boom full of fuel whenever the flight path may take the aircraft near lightning, as a precaution against fuel vapour ignition by a strike.

The KC-10A can itself be refueled by a boom tanker through the **Universal Air Refueling Receptacle Slipway Installation** (UARRSI), a receptacle on top of the fuselage above the flight engineer's station. Fuel passes from the tanker's nozzle through the receptacle, the AR master fuel valve and a receiving manifold to the refuel isolation valve, and from there through the crossfeed manifolds and each tank's refuel valve into any or all tanks. The receptacle's poppet valve is spring-loaded closed and shuts as the nozzle is withdrawn.

blocks.title: In the simulation
blocks.content: There is no tanker to connect to, and the receptacle door crank, AR RESET, the AR RECP LATCH test and the UARRSI hydraulic shutoff valve are not connected, so the receiver system cannot reach READY. AR MASTER, AMPL OVRD and the lights work. See [Receiver system](#sim-receiver-status).

blocks.alt: Top of the KC-10A forward fuselage behind the flight deck, seen from above and behind as a tanker's boom operator would see it: the UARRSI slipway door open (hinged at its forward edge, its aft end lowered to form the slipway), the receptacle and its toggle latches visible at the bottom of the slipway, the slipway lights and the floodlights either side, red lead-in stripes on the fuselage.
blocks.title: UARRSI receptacle, slipway door open

blocks.content: A hydraulically actuated door, hinged along its forward edge, normally covers the receptacle. Opened, its aft end moves down to expose the receptacle and the door becomes the boom's slipway. The door is spring-loaded open and hydraulically closed, and is worked by a crank handle on the F/E's table: cranked OPEN it springs open with or without hydraulic pressure; cranked CLOSED it needs pressure. The door and the receptacle's toggle latches are powered by hydraulic system 1 through a manual shutoff valve under the cabin floor just forward of the left cabin door. The UARRSI hydraulics are kept unpressurized except while in use, to avoid leaks in the flight deck overhead; the shutoff valve must remain closed for all flight operations except when required for refueling. With system 1 lost, the toggles are inoperative.

The receiver's signal system works with the tanker's to set up the automatic READY, LATCHED and DISCONNECT sequence. Its signal amplifier is turned on by the F/E's **AR MASTER** switch, the same switch that opens the AR master fuel valve. An induction coil in the receptacle mates with the coil in the tanker's nozzle; through them pass the contact-made signal, the disconnect signals and the boom interphone.

blocks.title: Receiver signal system states
rows: AR MASTER on and the slipway door open

The nozzle seated: its switch energizes the latch control valve solenoid, system 1 drives the latch cylinder, the toggles engage the nozzle, and a contact-made signal goes to the tanker. READY goes out at contact.
LATCHED, once the toggles have latched

A disconnect signal from the receiver pilots (A/R DISC, the ATS disconnect buttons on the throttles) or from the tanker through the coils, or the contact signal lost while latched: the solenoid de-energizes and the toggles release the nozzle. Holds until AR RESET.
Amplifier Override at OVRD: the amplifier bypassed and the signal system's power moved from DC bus 1 to DC bus 3
AMPL OVERRIDE, with the other three

blocks.content: After a disconnect, the system is returned to READY by pressing AR RESET once the boom is clear of the receptacle; pressed with the nozzle still in, it would latch again. The four status lights are on the F/E's panel and the pilots' windshield panel. A test switch, AR RECP LATCH, on the F/E's equipment panel sends a simulated contact-made signal without a nozzle: while it is held the toggles latch and LATCHED comes on; on release DISCONNECT comes on. If both autothrottle and speed control circuit breakers are open, the ATS disconnect buttons will not give an A/R disconnect.
With the Amplifier Override at OVRD (manual boom latching), the tanker's disconnect signal does not reach the toggles. The receiver must initiate all disconnects.

Lighting for night refueling: slipway lights (four modules of three lamps, exposed when the door is open) and two floodlights each side of the receptacle reflected by the door's mirrored inner surface, each with its control on the F/E's panel. The boom operator of the tanker decides their setting. The UARRSI audio system connects the tanker's boom interphone to the flight interphone.

The boom and the centerline hose are worked from the boom operator's station; the wing pods from the station's two WARP panels on the KC-10A, and from the flight engineer's panel on the Omega. The flight engineer sets up the offload fuel system on the fuel panel and monitors the AR hydraulic and status lights. The pilots have the ENGAGED lights and the receiver lights on the windshield panel.

blocks.content: In the simulation the flight control stick, the telescope control and BOOM TRIM are your own joystick, throttle and trim, handed to the boom by the EFB. The disconnect trigger, RESET TO READY, EMER CONTACT MADE and the CONTACT MADE TEST exist only as bindable inputs for external control-binding utilities, and the telescope stick's BREAKAWAY SIG is not available. See [Flying the boom and the stick switches](#sim-flying-the-boom).

This section follows each system through a refueling as a sequence of actions and responses. The checklists themselves, with crew duties, are in [Air Refueling](air-refueling).

Notify the pilot. HOIST RAISE, LATCH UNLOCK, HOIST LWR
The hoist takes the boom's weight off the hook, the latch opens, and the boom lowers under gravity until it stops at about 0°, where the BCU holds the STOW trail.

Confirms control throughout the envelope at refueling speed.

The receiver's toggles latch; its contact signal advances the signal system.
CONTACT, one beep; COUPLED about 1 s later. Pilots' BOOM/DROGUE ENGAGED on. AR pumps start (if armed); fuel flow and pressure.

ALAS (if enabled) and the coupled law keep the nozzle loads low; the BCU watches the envelope.
Disconnect trigger, or the receiver's disconnect, or an armed limit
Toggles release; COUPLED holds for the RCVR DISC DELAY; the telescope retracts at 10 ft/s if TLSCP AT DISC is AUTO; pumps stop.
DISC, three beeps; FREE FLT. Pilots' BOOM/DROGUE ENGAGED out.
RESET TO READY once the nozzle is clear
The signal system returns to READY for the next contact.
The telescope retracts; the BCU flies the boom up to about 0°.

ELEVATION at the STOW mark (15° above) with no movement on LWR. BOOM/DROGUE DEPLOYED out.
FLT CONT OFF, HYD SEL OFF, BOOM AUDIO OFF, sighting door CLOSE (hold)

If the ELEVATION indicator shows movement with the hoist at LWR after LOCK, the latch has not closed: unlock and repeat the stow.

System 2 and the AR alternate supply (KC-10A), or system 2 alone (KDC-10), power the boom and the centerline reel through HYD SEL. System 3 powers the hoist. The AR pumps' hydraulic motors draw from systems 1, 2 and 3, and an offload loads the engine-driven pumps; a hydraulic failure stops the pumps it drives. The FE runs the hydraulic pumps and the 2-3 motor pump to suit. See [Hydraulics](hydraulics).

The KC-10A's ARO AC and DC buses come from generator bus 3 and DC bus 3 (change-over to DC bus 1); the KDC-10's boom circuits from AC BUS 3 and DC BUS 3. A long enough interruption shuts the BCU down. The pods take power from AC generator bus 1 (KC-10A) or the DC-10-40's own buses (Omega). See [Electrical](electrical).

Offload comes from the body tanks through the AR pumps (KC-10A), or from the wing crossfeed manifold (pods). The CG moves as fuel is offloaded: check it before and during the offload. See [Fuel](fuel).

The tanker's autopilot is normally engaged during refueling, without its navigation modes. In the simulation the boom's control intercept requires the autopilot in command. See [Automatic flight](automatic-flight).
The KC-10A's FMS flies refueling orbits and rendezvous patterns and computes the turn range and offset. See [Flight management](flight-management) and [Rendezvous procedures](ar-rendezvous).

A trailed boom and hoses add drag. The minimum refueling speed with wing pods installed is 5 kt higher than without.

blocks.content: Most air refueling failures end the use of the failed device; few threaten the tanker. The exceptions are a boom that moves on its own, which must be shut down at once, a boom or hose that cannot be stowed, which changes the landing, and anything that disturbs the formation, which calls for a breakaway. The procedures are in [Emergency and abnormal procedures](ar-emergency-abnormal).

blocks.content: On recognizing uncommanded, uncontrollable or unresponsive boom movement, move FLT CONT to OFF immediately and do not move it back to ON.

The simulation models the air refueling systems as mechanisms, in depth. The boom is a flying body: it trails, swings in roll like a pendulum, sags at low speed and rises at high speed, under its weight, each element's airload, the hoist cable and its stops, and it rests on and slides along the ramp on the ground. The boom control unit flies it with scheduled gains, integral trim and the hoist hand-over; the signal system runs its full logic, including the disconnect anticipation, the receiver disconnect delay, automatic telescope retraction and the tones; the IDS bottle's pressure follows its temperature. The centerline hose and each pod hose are flying chains of masses under weight and drag, drawn as they fly, on reels with their real logic: the response system and the 55-knot check, the hose reel monitor, the tensators, the RAT and the pump's temperature, the DRCU's modes, counters and BITE, and the guillotines.

There is no other aircraft in the simulation, so nothing ever plugs into the boom, a drogue, or the KC-10A's receptacle. A boom contact can be made only with the CONTACT MADE TEST or EMER CONTACT MADE, which advance the signal system and couple the flight controls; nothing pushes on the nozzle except the ground. No fuel is offloaded through the boom, the centerline drogue or the pods, and the offload flow indicators and counters stay at zero. The refuel-range logic on the hoses still answers the hose's own position: slowing down with the centerline response set, for example, winds the hose into its range and puts READY out.

The coupled control law's stick back-drive, ALAS's actual load alleviation, the stick shaker and the stick force changes are not modeled; COUPLED and ALAS drive their lights, the disconnect hold and the anticipation. The STICK FORCE selectors are not modeled.

children.title: Flying the boom and the stick switches

blocks.content: The boom is flown with your own joystick, throttle and trim through the EFB's Air Refuel app: its **ARO Input** switch hands them from the aircraft to the boom, provided the autopilot is in command. The stick flies the boom, any throttle lever is the telescope, and your trim inputs are the BOOM TRIM switch. See [Flying air refueling in the simulation](ar-in-the-simulation) and [EFB](efb).

The switches on the boom operator's hand controllers are not on the 3D station: the disconnect trigger (DISC, and IDS through its second detent), RESET TO READY, EMER CONTACT MADE and the CONTACT MADE TEST are provided as bindable inputs for external control-binding utilities. The BREAKAWAY SIG switch on the telescope control stick and the pilot director light coaching switch are not available; the drogue panel's BREAKAWAY SIG is, on the KC-10A.

The roll and elevation limit knobs move their cursors one degree a click, where the real roll selectors have 2° detents. The BOOM COIL TEST indicator has no needle in the 3D model. The BCU's preflight self-test and the STATUS/TEST panel, the boom interphone (BOOM AUDIO is read but carries nothing), the side viewing doors and the sighting door's hand crank are not modeled. HF transmissions do not disturb the boom.

children.title: Lighting and other items not modeled

items: The pilot director lights, the boom marking, nozzle and receiver flood lights, the centerline drogue's and the pods' external signal lights and floodlights, and the drogue lights are not driven. The boom operator's FWD FUSELAGE, AFT FUSELAGE, HORIZ STAB and WING FLOOD lighting knobs work.
HOSE REEL TEST at SYS is not modeled. In the 3D model the TEST switch has two positions; ON performs the MON test with the hose stowed.

A drogue separating from its hose, a hose fracturing, the hose whip that follows, gusts along the hose, and pod or hose icing are not modeled. A jettisoned hose is drawn falling away for about 10 seconds in flight; on the ground it lies where it fell until the aircraft is reloaded.
The fuel spill from a pod hose rewound through the refuel range with its valve armed is not modeled. The hose-trailed temperature limits are not enforced.
The F/E's offload flow indicator is scaled in US gallons per minute and the boom operator's in pounds per minute × 1000.

blocks.content: The receiver signal system is modeled in full, but only its AR MASTER and AMPL OVRD switches are connected in the cockpit, together with its four lights on the windshield panel and their twins on the F/E's panel. The UARRSI door crank, AR RESET, the AR RECP LATCH test switch, the UARRSI hydraulic shutoff valve and the A/R DISC function of the ATS disconnect buttons are not connected, so the system cannot reach READY. AMPL OVERRIDE lights with AR MASTER on and the override selected.

The real KDC-10 conversion operated its boom by remote video from the flight deck. The simulation, like the 3D model, gives it the KC-10A's boom operator's station in the tail, powered from the DC-10-30's own buses and hydraulic system 2. Its boom circuit breakers are not on the DC-10-30's breaker panels and cannot be pulled.

The Omega's pods are the KC-10A's installation carried over: their behavior, limits and controls are the KC-10A's, mounted on the flight engineer's panel and fed by the boost pumps through the X-FEED valves. Its pod panel's lights answer the F/E's AREA TEST at UPPER PNL 3, and the WING AERIAL REFUEL half the LOWER panel test. With no centerline drogue panel, no breakaway signal reaches the Omega's pods.
Air refueling failures are not in the EFB's Failures app. They occur in the simulation as consequences, and many can be produced deliberately:

items: A hydraulic failure scheduled from the EFB (system 2, system 3, or the engine pumps) acts on the boom, the hoist and the centerline reel as described above. With FLT CONT on and no boom pressure the FAIL lights latch.
Selecting FLT CONT with HYD SEL at OFF or DROGUE latches ELEV and both RUD FAIL with the aural warning.
Holding a DOWN command with the hoist at LWR can break the hoist cable. The broken-cable stow then works only at about 300 KIAS or more, low, and wings level, as the book says.
An electrical interruption long enough shuts the BCU down, and needs the restart.

A pod trailed with its WING DROGUE VALVE shut, or on the Omega with the X-FEED valves shut, shows FUEL PRESS LOW and fails after 10 seconds, and its hose cannot be rewound until the pressure is restored.
A pod hose trailed below 230 KIAS stalls short of full trail, and a hose rewound well above 280 KIAS may stall short of stowed.
The centerline's 55-knot check, a response rewind that stalls short, and a receiver-less RESP INOP from changing speed after a reset all behave as described.

blocks.content: The Virtual Crew does not run the air refueling checklists: the boom operator's, the flight engineer's and the pilots' refueling duties are yours. On the KC-10A the Virtual Crew's flight engineer does run the normal checklist's boom items, such as notifying the boom operator and the scramble checklist's AR MASTER PWR and HYD SEL to BOOM for two minutes. See [Virtual Crew](virtual-crew).

parts.title: Aerial Firefighting System
parts.summary: The air tankers' retardant pod: its tanks and doors, the constant-flow drop controller, the emergency drop, the panels, and how a drop is flown.

blocks.content:
The DC-10 air tanker is a **very large air tanker (VLAT)**: a transport aircraft converted to carry a load of fire retardant or water far larger than the classic piston and turboprop air tankers, and to lay it on the ground along a wildfire in one controlled release. The conversion described here is the 10 Tanker Air Carrier installation, approved under FAA Supplemental Type Certificate **ST01870LA** for the DC-10-10 and later amended to add the DC-10-30. In this manual it applies to two aircraft: the **DC-10-10 Tanker** and the **DC-10-30 Tanker**. No other DC-10, KC-10 or MD-10 variant carries it.

The firefighting equipment is mission equipment added to an otherwise standard airframe. The flight deck, engines, fuel, hydraulic and flight control systems are those of the DC-10-10 and DC-10-30 described in the rest of this section. What the conversion adds is a retardant pod under the fuselage, the hydraulic and electrical equipment that works its doors, a set of control panels at the flight engineer's station, and drop switches for the pilots.

blocks.alt: DC-10-30 Tanker exterior, left side view in flight or on the ramp, wheels down: the canoe-shaped retardant pod under the fuselage from just behind the nose gear to behind the wing, its forward and aft fairings, and the three pairs of drop doors (FWD, CTR, AFT) along its keel legible as separate panels. No center main landing gear. Callouts for FWD, CTR and AFT tanks.
blocks.title: The DC-10-30 Tanker
blocks.caption: The pod runs along the belly between the nose gear and the main gear. Each of the three tanks empties through its own pair of doors.

blocks.content: **Architecture in one paragraph.** Three tanks, FWD, CTR and AFT, hang in line in the pod and hold 9,400 US gallons between them. Each tank empties by gravity through a pair of doors that run along its bottom, opened and closed by a hydraulic actuator. Each tank has its own electro-hydraulic power pack, installed in what used to be the forward lower cargo compartment, so the three tanks are hydraulically independent of each other and of the aircraft's own hydraulic systems. A computer controller for each tank, coordinated by a master sequencer at the flight engineer's station, opens the doors just far enough to hold the flow the crew has selected, so the retardant reaches the ground at an even density along the whole line. A separate emergency system, with its own stored hydraulic energy in each tank's pallet and its control on the battery bus, opens every door at once and empties the pod in about two seconds.

blocks.alt: Functional schematic of the DC-10 tanker retardant system. Left to right: the three tanks (FWD 2,700, CTR 4,000, AFT 2,700 US gal) each with its door pair, vent and fill line; below each tank its hydraulic power pack (AC motor on GALLEY BUS 1/2/3, pump, pressure switch, accumulator, relief valve), its emergency accumulator charged through a check valve, the emergency dump valve and the three directional valves feeding the door actuator and latches. Above: the three tank controllers and the master sequencer on DC BUS 1/3/1, the quantity panel and the emergency relay on the BATTERY BUS, the pedestal NORMAL DROP and EMERGENCY DROP switches and the yoke buttons. Fill manifold with three 3-inch couplings at the bottom.

blocks.content:
A retardant sortie is short, low and heavy, and it repeats. The tanker loads at an air tanker base, takes off at up to about 380,000 lb, flies to the fire, drops its load in one or more passes at about 300 ft above the terrain, and returns to reload. Most of the system's design follows from four facts about that sortie:

- **The drop must lay an even line.** Retardant works only where it lands at the right density, so the tanks must release it at a controlled, steady rate rather than all at once. That is why the doors are computer-scheduled.
- **The drop is flown low and slow at heavy weight**, often over mountains and in smoke. If an engine fails or the terrain closes in, the crew must be able to shed the whole load at once, whatever has failed. That is why the emergency system has its own energy and its own power source.
- **The load is a large part of the aircraft's weight**, and it leaves in seconds. The aircraft pitches and climbs as it goes, and its center of gravity moves.
- **Turn times are minutes.** The tanks fill fast through large couplings and stop filling by themselves.

**A typical sortie**, as the operator's procedures describe it:

1. **Load and depart.** The base loads the tanks by weight, in about 8 to 10 minutes. Takeoff speeds are higher than the basic aircraft's and the cabin stays unpressurized while the tanks hold liquid.
2. **Transit.** Most flights to the fire are flown under visual rules. A close fire is flown at about 200 KIAS; a distant one is planned as a normal flight at a suitable altitude and speed, with fire-response cruise around 380 KTAS. The crew joins the fire's tactical frequency early and calls the air attack aircraft 30 to 40 nm out.
3. **Configure.** The aircraft is slowed to 15/EXT flaps and slats about 10 to 15 minutes out. Inside the fire traffic area the speed is about 150 KIAS.
4. **Orbit.** If the target is busy, the tanker holds in a left-hand orbit, usually 1,000 to 1,500 ft above the terrain with 22/EXT, while the crew studies the target, the run-in, the hazards and the escape route.
5. **Pattern and run-in.** The tanker joins the lead plane on downwind (15/EXT), flies a base leg (22/EXT) and turns final at 150 KIAS minimum with 35/EXT and the gear up, about 800 to 1,000 ft behind the lead plane.
6. **Drop.** At the release point the captain calls the drop, the drop switch is held, and the doors open at the selected flow. The flight engineer calls “Drop complete”.
7. **Escape.** On that call the crew retracts to 22/EXT, sets climb thrust and flies the briefed escape route.
8. **Return or re-attack.** With load left after a split drop, the crew repositions for another pass. Empty, it returns to the base, where a quick turn may load water or retardant and fuel at the same time with the No. 2 engine running.

blocks.alt: Plan and profile diagram of a typical DC-10 air tanker drop pattern: left-hand orbit at 1,000-1,500 ft AGL above the fire; join-up with the lead plane on downwind at 15/EXT; base leg at 22/EXT; final at 150 KIAS minimum, 35/EXT, gear up, 800-1,000 ft in trail of the lead plane, descending to 300 ft AGL; the release point and the drop line along the fire's edge; DROP COMPLETE and the escape climb at 22/EXT with climb thrust, turning away downhill from the terrain. Wind arrow and terrain contours shown.

blocks.content: The same installation is fitted to both tankers, at the same stations, because the DC-10-10 and DC-10-30 fuselages are the same length. They differ in the airframe underneath it.
The fire tankers are not the air-refueling tankers. The KDC-10 and the Omega DC-10-40 carry refueling equipment and no retardant system; see [Air Refueling Systems](air-refueling-systems).

The conversion's FAA-approved flight manual supplement and the operator's operations manual add limitations and corrections to those of the basic DC-10. The speed and performance corrections follow from the pod itself: it adds drag, and the bow wave of its forward fairing changes the pressure at the static ports with angle of attack. The table lists them; where it is silent, the basic aircraft's [Limitations](limitations) apply.

blocks.title: Minimum fuel with water or retardant aboard (DC-10-30 conversions)

blocks.content: The supplement sets the minimum fuel by tail number, for the full five-tank installation and for its alternate configuration with the fairing tanks inoperative (see [Tanks and pod](#tank-installation)). The simulated tankers carry the three drop tanks only.

sections.title: Retardant tank system
sections.summary: The pod and its tanks, the doors, the power packs, the emergency system, the electrical supply and the loading system.

blocks.content: The tanks sit in a canoe-shaped pod attached under the fuselage through internal reinforcement of the fuselage structure. On the aircraft the FAA evaluated, the pod is roughly 62 ft long and 78 in deep, narrowing from 80 in across at the fuselage to 15 in at the keel. The tanks are derived from the constant-flow tanks Erickson built for its Air-Crane helicopters. They release their load downward through doors in their floor, under gravity alone: nothing pumps the retardant out of the aircraft.

Three tanks lie in line along the pod: **FWD**, **CTR** and **AFT**. Each is a hopper. Its sides slope inward from the fuselage to a narrow slot along the keel, which the doors close. The FWD and AFT tanks share one cross-section; the CTR tank has a wider one, which is how it holds 4,000 US gal in about the same length as its neighbors hold 2,700. The tank shell is a little larger than the approved load, so a full tank keeps an air space (the **ullage**) above the liquid, and each tank breathes through a vent at the top.

Transverse baffles divide each tank into bays. They exist to stop the load surging fore and aft when the aircraft accelerates, brakes or pitches, which would move the center of gravity and slosh liquid out of the vent. A baffle cannot reach down into the closed doors, because the doors must swing clear, so the bays stay connected through the trough the closed doors form. The baffles therefore blunt a surge, but in a sustained nose-up attitude the load still runs slowly aft through that trough until the surface is level again.

blocks.alt: Side-view installation drawing of the DC-10 tanker pod against the fuselage outline, nose to the left: FWD, CTR and AFT tanks with their baffle bays, approximate stations (about 63, 81 and 99 ft aft of the nose), vent on top of each tank, door pair along each keel, fill lines from a manifold with three 3-inch couplings on the pod side; the three hydraulic power pack pallets in the former forward lower cargo compartment; the manual emergency release handles on the cabin wall just aft of door R2; the wing's mean aerodynamic chord marked for reference, showing the pod's centroid ahead of the leading edge of the MAC.
blocks.title: Tank installation, side view

blocks.content: 9,400 US gal is the load the Interagency Airtanker Board approved for the DC-10. The load's centroid sits about 81 ft aft of the nose, some 8 to 9 ft ahead of the leading edge of the wing's mean aerodynamic chord. A full load therefore moves the aircraft's center of gravity well forward, and a drop moves it aft again; see [Handling in the drop](#handling-in-the-drop) and [Mission Planning](mission-planning).

blocks.title: The five-tank installation
blocks.content: The aircraft's own manuals describe a larger installation: three drop tanks plus a forward and an aft **fairing tank**, each fairing tank connected to the drop tank beside it and fitted with its own drop door. With the fairing tanks the system holds about 11,973 US gal of water (3,765 in each of the FWD and AFT tanks and 4,443 in the CTR); in the alternate configuration, with the fairing tanks deactivated, about 9,427. The simulation models the three drop tanks at the 9,400 US gal approved load.

The tanks carry either **long-term retardant** or **water**. A long-term retardant such as Phos-Chek LC-95A-Fx is mixed at the base from a liquid concentrate and water (5.5 parts water to one part concentrate for LC-95A-Fx). Its fire-retarding salts keep working after the water has evaporated, so it is laid as a line ahead of or along a fire's edge, where the fire will arrive later. It is colored so the line shows from the air. Water only cools and wets, and works only while it is wet, so it is dropped directly on the fire.

The two behave differently in the tanks:

rows: About a hundred times faster than retardant

blocks.content: Mixed retardants vary: depending on the product and how it is mixed, the operator's figures run from about 9.1 to 9.4 lb per gallon. The base loads by weight, so a lighter product loads more gallons for the same weight on its meter. The approved contents are water or other approved dispersants; no foam system is installed.

Each tank closes at the bottom with two doors that run the full length of the tank. Each door is hinged along its outboard edge, and the two meet on the centerline at the keel. Closed, each door leans about 47° from the vertical, so the pair forms a shallow V that is the bottom of the tank. Opening swings both doors down and outward together toward the vertical. Fully open, both doors hang vertical and leave a clear slot as wide as the hinge lines are apart, about 22 inches, along the whole tank: an opening of roughly 2.6 to 2.9 square meters (28 to 31 sq ft) per tank. The doors are geared to move together, so a tank's two doors act as one **gate**, and the gate's position is a single number: its stroke, from closed to fully open.

blocks.alt: Cross-section through a DC-10 tanker retardant tank, looking forward, in two halves: left half doors CLOSED and latched, right half doors FULLY OPEN. Shows the hopper walls sloping from the fuselage to the keel, the two doors hinged on their outboard edges and meeting at the centerline (about 47° from vertical when closed, vertical when open), the latch hooks and the latch-release cylinder, the door actuator and its linkage, a baffle with the trough under it, the liquid surface, the ullage above it and the vent. Dimension: slot width about 22 in when fully open.
blocks.title: Tank cross-section and doors

blocks.content:
**Latches.** Hooks hold each door shut. Before the gate can move, a small hydraulic cylinder on the opening side pulls the hooks clear. The hooks spring home when nothing holds them, and catch when the doors reach the closed position. A tank's two **GATE CLOSED** lights, one per door, mean closed **and** latched, so a hook that has released shows open before the door has moved. Because the latches need hydraulic pressure to clear, a tank with no pressure cannot open its doors, normally or otherwise.

**The actuator.** One hydraulic actuator drives each gate. Three identical directional valves feed it in parallel, so a single failed valve slows the gate rather than stopping it; with all three failed only the emergency system can move it. A position sensor on the actuator tells the controller where the gate actually is. The controller drives the gate to a commanded stroke and holds it there within a small band, starting the valves only when the gate is outside the band and letting them run until it lands on the target. A closed gate starts for any opening command at all, so even the smallest flow at a low coverage level opens it.

**The liquid works on the doors.** The weight of the load presses outward on the doors. That pressure helps them open and resists their closing, and it grows with the load factor. A loaded gate whose latches have cleared will fall open on its own if its hydraulic supply runs out mid-stroke. Closing against a full head of liquid in a pull-up, on a power pack whose pressure has sagged, a gate can stall partly open until the load has drained or the pressure recovers.

**Speed.** The certification criteria ask that doors reach within 10° of fully open in half a second, and that doors meant to open together start within 0.05 second of each other. The gates do both: a gate on a full power pack strokes in under half a second, and in a ganged drop the three gates start together.

children.title: Theory: gravity outflow, venting and slosh

blocks.content:
Liquid leaves an opening in the bottom of a tank at a speed set by the height of liquid above the opening, the **head**. The flow through the opening is the orifice law:

**Q = Cd · A · √(2 · g · N · H)**

where Q is the volume flow, A the open area, Cd a discharge coefficient (less than one, because the stream contracts as it leaves), g gravity, N the load factor along the aircraft's vertical axis and H the head. Three consequences shape everything the controller does:

- **Flow falls as the tank drains.** Through a fixed opening, flow is proportional to the square root of the head. In a hopper-shaped tank the surface is wide near the top and narrow near the doors, so the head falls slowly at first and quickly near the end. A fixed-opening tank therefore pours heavily at first and dribbles at the end.
- **Load factor matters.** In a 1.5 g pull-up a given opening passes about 22% more than at 1 g; in a push-over it passes less. A drop flown while pushing over the top of a ridge delivers less through the same opening.
- **The opening needed for a given flow grows as the head falls.** To hold a constant flow the gate must open wider and wider as the tank empties, until it is fully open. From then on the flow falls with the head, and nothing more can be done.

**Venting.** Every gallon that leaves through the doors must be replaced by a gallon of air, or the pressure in the ullage falls and the effective head falls with it. Air reaches the ullage through the vent and, when it can, by bubbling up through the doors against the outgoing stream. A wide-open gate passes plenty of air that way; a narrow opening carrying a fast stream passes almost none. A tank whose vent cannot keep up then gulps air in pulses, the flow surges and stalls, and the line on the ground is broken. This is called **coke-bottling**, and the certification criteria require a tank to give uninterrupted, reproducible and nearly linear flow even with the ullage pressure depressed. The vents are sized so that even an emergency dump, the most violent outflow the tanks see, keeps the ullage depression within about a quarter of a psi.

**Slosh.** The liquid surface stays square to the apparent gravity, so it tilts when the aircraft accelerates, brakes or pitches. Each bay's surface rocks with a natural period of about a second and a half when full, slower as it empties. The baffles damp these surges. A full tank keeps its ullage space above the liquid so that a normal taxi and takeoff do not push liquid up the vent; a hard stop, such as a rejected takeoff at full load, can spill some.

blocks.content:
**What the crew sees.** PUMP ON lights while the motor turns. LOW PSI lights when the pack's pressure is below its operating range. PUMP FAIL lights when the controller has called for the pump and it has not run for several seconds; the error stays latched until RUN PUMP is selected or the tank controller loses power. The motor heats in use, more so when it runs for long periods against a leak; PUMP OVTEMP on the quantity panel lights when it overheats.

**The galley bus connection.** Because the pumps are on the galley buses, the galley load control logic that sheds the galleys when generating capacity is reduced (on a single generator, for example) also sheds the pumps. The basic aircraft's galley load is removed on the tankers, so the galley buses carry the three pumps and nothing else. On the aircraft the pre-drop checklist sets the GALLEY BUS switches to OVERRIDE; see [Electrical](electrical) for the galley buses.

The air tanker certification criteria call for **a separate emergency dump that can empty the whole load in under six seconds**, with its energy stored apart from the normal tank system, an indication the crew can check to see it is ready, and electrical controls fed from a supply kept apart from the aircraft's normal buses. The DC-10 meets that with three parts:

- **An emergency accumulator for each tank**, on the tank's pallet. It is charged from the tank's own power pack through a check valve, so once charged it is isolated: a pack that fails or is switched off cannot drain it, and a running pack keeps it topped up. A healthy emergency accumulator holds its charge for many hours with the system off. Its **E-DUMP PSI** light on the master sequencer shows that its pressure is within operating limits.
- **A latching relay on the battery bus.** The guarded EMERGENCY DROP switch on the pedestal, moved forward momentarily, latches the relay through the Emergency Drop breaker. With the Emergency Drop Power breaker live, the relay opens every tank's dump valve, which ports the emergency accumulator to the door actuator through a shuttle valve ahead of the normal directional valves. The latches clear and every door swings fully open.
- **A manual emergency release handle for each tank**, on the cabin side wall just aft of door R2. Pulling a handle opens that tank's doors on its emergency accumulator with no electrical power at all.

An emergency drop **overrides the entire retardant system**: whatever the controllers were doing, they stop, and the doors open fully, unregulated. The whole load leaves in about two seconds, the CTR tank last. The emergency system needs only two things: charged emergency accumulators and, for the switch, a live battery bus. It does not need DROP SYS POWER, the controllers, the power packs or the aircraft's AC power.

**The relay holds only while it is powered.** If DC power to it is interrupted after the switch has been used, the relay opens, and the doors close on whatever pressure is left in the emergency accumulators. That is also how the system is reset: with the tank arming and hydraulic power switches off, the emergency drop breakers are pulled and reset. A handle, put back, closes its doors if the normal accumulator still has pressure.

If DC power is disrupted after the EMERGENCY DROP switch has been used, the emergency relay opens and the doors close on residual accumulator pressure, without warning. On the ground this is a hazard to anyone near the doors. To prevent it, pull the tank's manual emergency release handle and disarm the tank.

**Readiness at power-up.** Emergency accumulators that have never been charged, or have stood for a long time, hold little or nothing. The E-DUMP PSI lights come on only once the packs have run long enough to charge them, a couple of minutes from empty. Until a tank's light is on, an emergency drop may not open that tank's doors.

The system draws on three supplies, arranged so that the emergency system survives what disables the normal one: the pumps on the AC galley buses; the controllers, the arming and the drop command on DC buses 1 and 3; and the emergency drop and the quantity panel on the battery bus. In this manual Tank 1, 2 and 3 on the breaker placards are taken to be FWD, CTR and AFT.

blocks.title: Power and control architecture

blocks.content:
The tanks are filled from the ground through the pod, without electrical power. The loading crew connects one, two or three hoses from the base's loading pump to **3-inch cam-lock couplings**; the aircraft can be loaded from either side. The couplings feed a **fill manifold**, and from it a fill line runs to each tank, entering just above the door hinge line through a **shut-off valve** and a **float valve**. As a tank reaches its approved load the float closes and that tank stops taking liquid; the others carry on until their own floats close. The lines are sized in proportion to the tanks, so the three fill in step. When the pump stops, the tanks settle to equal levels through the manifold within seconds.

The base loads **by weight**. The loader watches the base's mass-flow meter and the aircraft's own gauges, and stops when either shows full. With three hoses a full load takes about 8 to 10 minutes; with one, much longer. The same couplings take a suction hose to off-load, which leaves only the small amount trapped in the closed doors' trough.

Ground crew member in high-visibility vest at the coupling.

sections.title: Drop control system
sections.summary: The controllers, the constant-flow law, coverage levels, drop quantities and the ways a load can be released.

blocks.content: The drop is controlled by a Trotter Controls FRDS GEN II system, upgraded in 2015 to meet the Interagency Airtanker Board's VLAT specification. It is a **master sequencer** and three **tank controllers**, one per tank, linked to each other. Each tank controller is a complete controller for its own tank: it reads the tank's quantity, computes the gate opening, drives the gate and watches the power pack. The master sequencer sits above them, turning one drop selected by the flight engineer into an order for each tank. If the master sequencer fails or loses contact with a tank, each tank can still be dropped from its own panel, one tank at a time.

Four switches stand between a dark system and a drop, and they are deliberately separate: DROP SYS POWER powers the system, MASTER HYD PWR wakes the tank controllers and lets their pumps run, MASTER ARMED lets the tanks arm, and each tank's own ARMED switch arms that tank. The logic below is what the panels' lights report.
