blocks.content:
**ONLINE and INOP.** After power-up the master sequencer shows the **Tank Status** page, which lists each tank as ONLINE or OFFLINE and as OK or INOP. A tank controller takes a few seconds to come ONLINE, and the crew cannot force it. A tank the crew marks **INOP** on that page is left out entirely: the master shows no errors for it, does not count its contents, and does not drop it. A tank marked OK that cannot drop shows its reason on the master's status line instead. The page returns to the main page by itself once every tank is ONLINE or INOP, unless the crew has been working it.

**Memory.** The controllers keep their settings, the INOP marks and what they have learned about the tanks through a power cycle.

children.title: The constant-flow principle and coverage level

blocks.content:
The quantity that matters on the ground is the **coverage level** (CL): US gallons of retardant per 100 square feet. Fire agencies specify it for each target, because a given fuel needs a given density of retardant to stop a fire, and anything less is wasted. A tanker flying at ground speed V and laying a pattern of effective width W sweeps W × V square feet per second. To lay coverage level CL it must release

**Q = CL × W × V / 100**

gallons per second. With the width and the ground speed fixed by the run, a constant coverage level means a **constant flow**. That is the whole case for constant-flow control: a tank that pours out through a fixed opening lays a heavy pattern at the start of the line and a thin one at the end, and only part of the line is at the coverage level asked for. The controller instead opens the gate just enough at the start and wider as the tank empties, holding the flow until the gate is fully open.

The same balance gives the length of the line a quantity G lays:

**Line length = G × 100 / (CL × W)**

so a higher coverage level gives a shorter, denser line and a lower one a longer, thinner line. The flight engineer chooses the trade by choosing the coverage level and the quantity.

The DC-10's controller commands **150 US gal/s per coverage level**: coverage level 8 is 1,200 US gal/s, as in the flight manual supplement's own example. That example also fixes the effective pattern width at about 61 ft, at the drop speed of about 150 kt. The table follows from those two numbers.

blocks.title: Coverage levels
columns: Line from a full 9,400 US gal load
Time to drop 9,400 US gal at that flow
Certification minimum, line per 100 US gal

blocks.content: The master sequencer offers coverage levels 1, 2, 3, 4, 6, 8 and 12; a tank control panel, used alone, offers 1 to 4. Broadly, the lighter the fuel the lower the coverage level it needs: grass takes the lowest levels, heavy brush and slash the highest. The fire's air attack or lead plane gives the coverage level and quantity for each drop.

blocks.alt: Plan-view diagram of drop footprints on the ground from the same 4,700 US gal (half) load at three coverage levels, drawn to a common scale: CL 2, a long thin strip about 3,840 ft long; CL 4, about 1,920 ft; CL 8, a short dense strip about 960 ft long; all about 61 ft wide. Shading density proportional to coverage. Below, a contrasting footprint from a fixed-opening tank: dense at the start, tapering to thin at the far end.
blocks.title: Coverage level and line length
blocks.caption: The same quantity laid at three coverage levels. Under constant-flow control the density is even along the line; a fixed opening lays it heavy at the start and thin at the end.

blocks.content: **Ground speed.** The controller holds a flow; it does not measure ground speed. The coverage actually laid is the flow divided by the area swept each second, so it falls as ground speed rises. The coverage levels assume about 150 kt over the ground. At 150 KIAS on a warm day over a fire at 5,000 ft the true airspeed is closer to 165 kt, and a tailwind adds to it: the line is then roughly 10 to 15% longer and lighter than the display says. A headwind does the opposite. This is one reason the drop is flown at a steady, briefed speed.

children.title: AUTO: how the controller holds the flow

blocks.content:
In AUTO, each tank controller runs its loop about 30 times a second:

1. From its estimate of what is left in the tank, it finds the head, using a table of the tank's height against volume.
2. From the commanded flow, the head and the load factor measured by its own accelerometer, it computes the open area the orifice law needs: A = Q / (Cd × √(2 · g · N · H)).
3. It converts that area to a gate stroke using a table of flow against stroke, and drives the gate there.
4. It reduces its estimate of the tank's contents by what the gate is passing at the stroke the position sensor reports.

The flow tables come from the tank and gate themselves, so AUTO is accurate at the reference condition of a level drop at about 150 kt, and drifts only by what really differs on the day: the head, the load factor, the air entering the vent.

**Stopping on quantity.** A gate cannot shut instantly, and liquid keeps flowing while it closes. So the controller starts closing early, when what is left of the quantity falls to a **lead**: the volume that will flow during the closing stroke, plus a correction it has learned. After each drop, once the doors have latched and the liquid has settled for a few seconds, the controller compares the drop its quantity reading shows with the drop it was asked for, and adjusts the correction for that coverage level. The first drops at a coverage level are the least accurate; later ones close in on the quantity asked.

**Dropping to empty.** With the quantity at ALL there is no lead: the gate holds the flow until the estimate reads empty, then opens fully for about a second to let the tail out, then closes.

**Saturation.** Late in a drop at a high coverage level the head may be too low for even a fully open gate to pass the commanded flow. The gate is then fully open and the flow falls with the head. At coverage level 8 a full ganged load takes a little over 8 seconds rather than the 7.8 the flow alone would give.

children.title: TIMER, MAN and the GATE switch

blocks.content:
**TIMER.** The gate opens to the fixed stroke that would pass the commanded flow at the reference condition, and stays there for the time the quantity would take at that flow. TIMER does not use the quantity reading, so it still works on a tank whose level sensing has failed. But a fixed opening passes less as the head falls, so a TIMER drop always delivers less than asked, and the shortfall grows the emptier the tank is. Successive TIMER drops from one tank come out progressively smaller.

**MAN.** The doors go from closed to fully open, without regulation, for as long as the drop switch is held, and close when it is released. MAN is a hard-wired path that bypasses the tank's computer: it works with the computer failed, provided the tank is armed and has hydraulic pressure. It is effectively a salvo of one tank.

TIMER and MAN work only on a tank selected alone with SWITCH ASSIGN. Under the master sequencer, a tank in TIMER or MAN is an error and takes no part in the drop.

**The GATE switch** opens or closes gates directly, in any mode, on the armed tanks of the controller SWITCH ASSIGN selects: at MASTER, every armed tank; at a tank, that tank. Like MAN, it bypasses the tank computers. It is the means of closing doors that will not close, and of opening them on the ground.

**Who wins at the gate.** If more than one thing is asking, the gate obeys them in this order: the emergency system, then the GATE switch, then MAN, then the tank computer. With none of them asking, the valves are centerd and the gate stays where it is.

children.title: Drop quantity and the maximum available

blocks.content: The quantity is selected as a fraction: **1/8, 1/4, 1/2, 3/4 or ALL**. The fraction is of the **maximum available**, which the controllers set after each refill as the aircraft becomes airborne: they follow the tanks' quantity readings on the ground and fix the maximum at lift-off. Every 1/8 is therefore meant to be the same number of gallons, on the eighth press as on the first (in the simulation the eighth takes whatever is left and can come out short). That is how the system meets the certification requirement that a tank of 4,000 US gal or more can make at least eight equal releases, equal meaning within 12% of their mean.

blocks.title: Drop quantities from a full load (maximum available 9,400 US gal)

blocks.content: The displays show the gallons the selection represents, worked out from the maximum available. Tanks marked INOP are left out of the master's maximum. Because the maximum is fixed at lift-off, the tanks must be loaded and their quantity readings live before takeoff.

Releasing the drop switch early ends any drop at once: the doors close, and the quantity released is whatever left before they latched. A partial drop called by the captain (“Drop” … “Stop drop”) is flown this way.

Under the master sequencer, the DUMP CNTRL switch decides how one drop is shared between the tanks.

**GANGED** is required for normal operation. All tanks in the drop open together. Each tank's share of the flow, and of the quantity, is its share of the load aboard: with full tanks the FWD and AFT tanks each take about 29% and the CTR about 43%. The tanks therefore empty together, the doors start within milliseconds of each other, and the load's own centroid hardly moves during the drop; the aircraft's center of gravity moves aft smoothly as the load leaves.

**SEQUENCED** is provisional. The tanks open one after another, FWD, then CTR, then AFT, each at the full commanded flow. The next tank opens when the one before has about half a second of flow left, so the hand-overs overlap and the line stays continuous, with a heavier spot at each hand-over. Because the forward tank empties first, the center of gravity moves aft faster at the start of the drop and the trim change comes in steps rather than smoothly.

blocks.content: The drop system is run from the flight engineer's station, where the **master sequencer main control panel** and the **fire retardant tank quantity panel** are. The pilots have the **drop control panel** on the center pedestal, a drop button on each control wheel, and the two **drop status lights** on the glareshield.

The panel is the **master sequencer** and three **tank control panels**, FWD, CTR and AFT, side by side. In normal operation everything is set on the master sequencer with SWITCH ASSIGN at MASTER, and the tank panels only report. Each tank panel comes into its own when that tank is selected alone. Most settings are made with the master's **datawheel**: turning it changes the highlighted setting, and pressing its center (a “click”) selects the other.

The tank could drop in AUTO: the MAN conditions, plus a working controller with a quantity reading and no gate fault. Normal operation needs both lights.
The tank is armed (with MASTER ARMED up). Must be up for the master sequencer to drop the tank.
The tank is not armed; the master shows NOT ARMED for it. Cycling the switch clears a GATE FAULT.
Normal. Constant-flow control; the tank takes the master sequencer's drop.
Doors open to a fixed opening for a set time. Only with SWITCH ASSIGN at this tank; an error on the master.
Doors go from closed to fully open, unregulated, while the drop switch is held. Only with SWITCH ASSIGN at this tank; an error on the master.
Enables the tank's power pack. Works only with MASTER HYD PWR on.
No hydraulic power to the tank.
Changes the tank's own coverage level (1 to 4). Does nothing with SWITCH ASSIGN at MASTER.

blocks.content:
The master sequencer and each tank control panel have a backlit LCD: dark characters on a yellow-green background. The setting the datawheel will change is shown inverted. A dark display means that controller has no power or has failed.

**Master display, main page.** The top row shows the **coverage level**, the **quantity** in all tanks marked OK (boxed), and the **drop quantity** as a fraction. The row beneath shows what the selection will do: the **flow** in gallons per second, the length of the **ground line** in feet, and the drop quantity in **gallons**. The status line runs along the bottom. Each time the coverage level or the quantity is changed, the master recalculates the flow, the ground line and the gallons, and passes the new settings to the tank controllers.

**Tank Status page.** Comes up when the master sequencer is powered, and from the main page with NO/MENU. It lists FWD, CTR and AFT, each as OK or INOP and as ONLINE or OFFLINE, with a box round the highlighted tank. It returns to the main page by itself once every tank is ONLINE or INOP, unless the crew has been working it; YES or NO/MENU returns to the main page at any time.

blocks.alt: Two DC-10 Tanker master sequencer LCD pages side by side, yellow-green background with dark characters. Left, the main page: top row coverage level 8 (inverted, selected), quantity 9400 in a box, 1/2; second row 1200, 960, 4700 with the legends GALS/SEC, FEET, GALLONS beneath; STATUS line READY below a rule; bezel legends COVERAGE LEVEL, QUANTITY (GALS), GALLONS TO DUMP and STATUS. Right, the Tank Status page: title 'Tank Status', rows FWD OK ONLINE, CTR INOP (boxed, highlighted) ONLINE, AFT OK ONLINE.
blocks.title: Master display: main page and Tank Status page

blocks.content: **Tank displays.** The top row shows the coverage level, the **tank's** quantity (boxed) and the drop quantity as a fraction; the middle row the flow, the gallons to drop and the ground line; the status line runs along the bottom. Under the master sequencer, a tank in AUTO and marked OK shows its own share of the master's drop: the master's coverage level, and its share of the gallons and of the flow. Assigned alone, it shows its own settings.

blocks.title: Status line messages
rows: Not armed (on the master: MASTER ARMED off).
Armed, pressurized and able to drop.
Doors closing at the end of a drop.
The tank, or every tank in the drop, is empty or nearly so.
Master only: MASTER ARMED is on but no tank marked OK is armed.
The tank controller is not online to the master.
The tank's ARMED switch is down, or its arming is unpowered.
The tank is not in AUTO, so it will not take the master's drop.
The tank has no quantity reading, so AUTO cannot work.
The gate did not close and latch within a few seconds. The tank will not drop again until its ARMED switch is cycled.
The pump was called for and did not run.
The tank's hydraulic pressure is low.

blocks.content: On the master's status line, an error is prefixed with the tank it belongs to, for example CTR LOW PSI. The master shows the first such error among the tanks marked OK.

The quantity panel is on the flight engineer's engine instrument panel. It has four red LED displays, one for each tank and one for the total, and it works from the battery bus alone, so it shows the load even with the rest of the drop system switched off. A tank's display lights whenever the battery bus is powered and that tank's ARMED switch is up.

blocks.alt: DC-10 Tanker fire retardant tank quantity panel on the flight engineer's engine instrument panel: three red seven-segment LED displays labeled TANK QUANTITY (gallons) for FWD, CTR and AFT reading 2700, 4000 and 2700, a fourth labeled COMBINED ONBOARD QUANTITY reading 9400; beside each tank display a green ARMED light (on) and an amber PUMP OVTEMP light (off); the master ARMED light and the LAMP TEST button. All legends legible.
blocks.title: Fire retardant tank quantity panel

rows: TANK QUANTITY displays, FWD, CTR, AFT
The tank's contents. Lit with the battery bus powered and the tank's ARMED switch up.
The total of the tanks displayed.
The tank's ARMED switch is up.
PUMP OVTEMP lights, one per tank (amber)
The tank's hydraulic pump motor is overheating. Drop the load as soon as possible and disarm the tank; see [Failures](#failures).
The MASTER ARMED switch is up.
Tests every light on the panel.

children.title: Drop control panel and yoke buttons

blocks.content: The **drop control panel** is on the center pedestal between the pilots. It carries the system's power switch and the two drop switches. A further drop button sits on the outboard handle of each control wheel, so the pilot flying can drop without taking a hand off the controls. In the simulation these buttons are wired in parallel with the pedestal's NORMAL DROP; on the aircraft they are emergency drop switches (see [Simulation notes](#simulation-notes)).

blocks.alt: Close-up of the DC-10 Tanker drop control panel on the center pedestal: the DROP SYS POWER toggle (ON), the spring-loaded NORMAL DROP push button, and behind it the EMERGENCY DROP toggle under its red guard (guard closed). Placards legible.
blocks.title: Drop control panel

rows: Powers the master sequencer and the tank controllers. OFF before engine start, ON after. The quantity panel and the emergency system do not need it.
The normal drop system is dark and nothing can be armed.
Starts the selected drop if a valid selection is made and the system is armed. Hold it for the whole drop: releasing it closes the doors at once.

Latches the emergency relay: every tank's doors open fully on its emergency accumulator and the whole load is jettisoned, overriding the rest of the system. Needs the battery bus and charged emergency accumulators.
Yoke drop buttons, one on each control wheel
In the simulation, a normal drop exactly as the pedestal's NORMAL DROP button. On the aircraft, an emergency drop.

blocks.content: Two lights mounted on top of the glareshield, in the middle where all three crew members can see them, give the pilots the state of the drop system during the run. Their logic is under [Drop status lights logic](#drop-status-logic).

blocks.alt: DC-10 Tanker flight deck from the captain's seat during a run-in: the glareshield's drop status lights, ARMED (on) and DROP COMPLETE (off), centerd on top of the glareshield; the captain's control wheel with the drop button on its outboard handle visible under the thumb; the center pedestal's drop control panel in the lower right of the frame.
blocks.title: Pilots' drop controls and status lights

The drop has finished: the doors have closed after a release or a partial drop, or a drop to empty has left less than 5% of the maximum available.

blocks.content: On the two fire tankers the EFB has a **Fire Support** app, which loads the tanks and chooses the product. It works only on the ground with the aircraft stopped, in the same conditions as the ground services: weight on the wheels, not moving, on a suitable surface. A load goes in as soon as **Load** is pressed. Nothing reaches the tanks before then.

blocks.alt: The in-sim EFB in portrait showing the Fire Support app on a DC-10-30 Tanker on the ramp: PRODUCT row with the Retardant / Water choice (Retardant selected, 'LC-95A-Fx, 9.01 lb/gal'); LOAD group with the Total row (Empty, Full and Distribute buttons and a TOTAL GAL field reading 9400); TANKS group with FWD, CTR and AFT rows, each with its current and maximum gallons, a slider and a TARGET GAL field; the LOAD, WEIGHT and GW readouts showing now > after; Reset and Load buttons.
blocks.title: EFB Fire Support app

Total, with Empty, Full and Distribute
A total quantity, spread over the three tanks in proportion to their capacities (so the load's center stays where a full load's is) by Distribute or by pressing Enter. Full and Empty set every tank.
Each tank's contents and capacity, and a target set with the slider (in tens of gallons) or typed exactly, up to the tank's capacity.
The gallons aboard, their weight and the gross weight, now and after the load.

Shown in amber when the simulator is not carrying the tanks' weight as it should.

sections.title: Operation
sections.summary: The drop system through a sortie: preflight, loading, the pre-drop checks, the drop, the post-drop checks, the return, and the aircraft's handling as the load leaves.

blocks.content: The checklists below are written for the simulated aircraft: every control they name is in its cockpit. Where the operator's checklists call for equipment the simulation does not have, the item is left out and the omission noted. The full normal checklists are in [Normal Procedures](normal-procedures).

**Exterior.** On the walk-round the flight engineer checks the drop tank area on both sides: the pod and its fairings for security and damage, the fuselage skin around the modification, the fill ports, the drop doors and the mounting points, and the hydraulic panels. Inside the former forward lower cargo compartment, the three hydraulic pallets are checked for leaks and general condition, for the 1,000 psi accumulator precharge and for reservoir quantity. In the cabin, the manual emergency release handles must be stowed.

**Cockpit.** With electrical power on the aircraft, the flight engineer runs the drop system's preliminary check. It proves the panels, the lights, the controllers and the power packs, and leaves the tanks armed at their own switches but the system safe at MASTER ARMED.

items.action: ON, PUMP ON then off, LOW PSI out

items.item: LAMP TEST (master sequencer and quantity panel)

items.action: ON (once the packs have charged them)

blocks.content: The company's normal checklist then has DROP SYS POWER **OFF** in the Before Start checklist and **ON** again in the After Start checklist, so the system is dark through engine start and live from then on. The quantity panel and the emergency system stay powered from the battery bus throughout. DUMP CNTRL must be checked at GANGED: GANGED is the only position approved for normal operation.

At an air tanker base the loading crew fills the tanks through the couplings by weight, as described under [Loading system](#loading-system), while the flight crew watches the quantity panel. In the simulation, open **Fire Support** on the EFB with the aircraft stopped on the ground:

1. Choose the **product**: Retardant or Water.
2. Set the **load**: Full, or a total and Distribute, or a target for each tank.
3. Check the gallons, their weight and the gross weight after the load.
4. Press **Load**. The tanks fill at once and the quantity panel shows the new contents.

A load, or a change of product, is taken only on the ground. Load before takeoff: the drop quantities are fractions of the maximum available, which the controllers fix as the aircraft lifts off, so a load added later could not be dropped in AUTO or TIMER. A partial load is spread in proportion to the tanks' capacities, which keeps its center where a full load's is.

Plan the load against the takeoff and drop-site performance. Full tanks and 40,000 lb of fuel make a gross weight of about 370,000 lb, comfortably inside the structural limit; it is performance, at a high airport on a hot day, that may call for less fuel or a smaller load. See [Mission Planning](mission-planning).

The takeoff is heavy, and the conversion's speed corrections apply: V1 3 kt and VR and V2 10 kt above the basic flight manual's. The cabin is not pressurized while the tanks hold liquid; fly with the cabin pressure controller in manual and the outflow valve well open, which keeps cabin altitude close to aircraft altitude. The conversion's maximum operating altitude is 28,000 ft.

The maximum available is fixed at lift-off from the tanks' quantity readings. With DROP SYS POWER on after start, or the quantity panel reading the armed tanks, those readings are live and the drop quantities will be right.

About 10 to 15 minutes from the fire the crew slows to 15/EXT, and runs the pre-drop checklist before arriving at the target area, so that the aircraft is ready to drop on arrival unless a delay is expected. The 210 KIAS flap limit for flaps 5 to 15 applies.

Run before arriving at the target area or entering the orbit, about 5 nm out as a guide. The flight engineer announces the number of tanks, the quantity and the coverage level, and the first officer checks the coverage level against the lead plane's instruction.

items.item: MASTER HYD PWR and tank HYD PWR
MASTER ARMED and tank ARMED switches
TANKS ARMED MAN and AUTO lights

blocks.content: On the aircraft, the pre-drop checklist also sets the GALLEY BUS switches to OVERRIDE, puts the GPWS switch to OFF or INHIBIT and the flap override switch to OVRD (silencing the flaps-35, gear-up warning), and may use the aural warning cancel button that silences the GPWS and landing configuration warnings until the flaps are raised above 28°. The simulated flight deck has none of these: leave the GALLEY BUS switches ON, and expect the ground proximity and landing gear warnings during a run flown low with 35/EXT and the gear up.

**Configuration.** Final is flown at no less than 150 KIAS with 35/EXT and the gear up. That configuration gives a steady platform at low speed and lets the aircraft turn a little tighter, at little cost in drag. The trade is acceleration: with that much flap at that weight, speed is slow to build and, on a run that tips over a ridge and down the far side, just as slow to shed. Speed is therefore set before the run begins, and on a steep descent the thrust is used to hold it. The FAA's training profile for the type descends to drop height at 1,500 to 2,000 ft/min.

**Height.** The normal drop height is 300 ft above the terrain, the minimum for safety; it may be higher for the terrain or for the fuel type, and higher still at high coverage levels. Fire agency standards set no less than 250 ft above the ground or the tree canopy. The FAA's evaluation of the DC-10-30 tanker flew partial, metered and emergency drops at maximum weight at 300 ft above the ground and 150 KIAS.

Plan every pattern so that base is at or below downwind, and every run-in level or downhill, never uphill. Stay at or above the lead plane on downwind and base. Arm the drop system before starting the run-in. A run-in that looks unsafe is not flown; the crew talks it over and sets up a different one.

**The release.** The run-in starts only once both pilots have identified the target. The release is the captain's call, “Stand by … Drop”, and the drop switch is held from “Drop” until the drop is complete; a partial drop ends on the captain's “Stop drop”, when the switch is let go. The nose-down trim goes in as the load starts to leave. Through the drop the height above the terrain is held constant, so that the retardant falls the same distance all along the line, with the wings level unless the line is deliberately laid in a turn.

**The escape.** It begins on the flight engineer's “Drop complete”, or sooner if the terrain requires: “Flaps 22” from the pilot flying, 22/EXT and CLIMB on the thrust rating computer from the pilot monitoring, then the briefed escape route. When further passes are planned, the captain may stay at 35/EXT to maneuver.

items.action: 300 ft AGL or as briefed, held constant
HOLD until drop complete or “STOP DROP”
NOSE-DOWN TRIM as the drop starts; hold the height

blocks.content:
A split drop releases part of the load and keeps the rest for another pass, on the same target or another. Select the quantity (1/8 to 3/4) and press as for a full drop: the doors close by themselves when the quantity has gone and DROP COMPLETE lights. The next press puts DROP COMPLETE out and starts the next drop. Each 1/8 is an eighth of the load at lift-off, so the same selection gives the same gallons every time. The controller corrects each drop for what it learned from the last, so successive drops at one coverage level match closely.

Between passes the system stays armed. The coverage level and quantity can be changed for the next pass on the master datawheel; the displays show at once the flow, line length and gallons the new selection gives.

items.item: MASTER ARMED and tank ARMED switches

blocks.content: Disarming the tanks puts out the ARMED lights, and switching MASTER ARMED off puts out DROP COMPLETE. On the aircraft the post-drop checklist also returns the flap override and GPWS switches to normal (with the flaps checked at 22° or more first) and the GALLEY BUS switches from OVERRIDE; none of those are on the simulated flight deck. If the aircraft is to return, reload and go again, the operator's quick-turn checklists are used.

A tanker lands empty: it does not land loaded unless the drop system has failed. The descent and before landing checklists are the normal ones, with VREF not less than 140 KIAS. Before landing, check that every GATE CLOSED light is on: a gate that is not closed hangs below the pod, and taxiing then calls for care.

After the last flight of the day the drop doors are left open where possible. To open them on the ground, with the tanks armed and pressurized, hold the GATE switch at OPEN GATE with SWITCH ASSIGN at MASTER; check first that nobody is under the pod.
Do not taxi, tow or jack the aircraft with the drop doors open unless it cannot be avoided, and then with extreme caution.

A drop removes up to 85,000 lb of retardant (78,400 lb of water) from an aircraft of about 370,000 lb, in as little as eight seconds at coverage level 8: more than 10,000 lb a second. Two things happen at once:

- **Weight falls.** The wing, still at the same angle of attack and speed, now produces more lift than the lighter aircraft needs, so the aircraft starts to climb.
- **The center of gravity moves aft.** The pod's centroid is ahead of the wing's mean aerodynamic chord, so the load holds the CG forward, and removing it moves the CG back. A full load moves the CG about 13% MAC forward on a 395,000 lb aircraft, and a full drop moves it back by as much. The FAA's differences training for the type simulates a full drop as a loss of about 100,000 lb with the CG moving aft from 15% to 26% MAC. A CG moving aft with the trim and elevator unchanged pitches the nose up.

The two add up to a marked nose-up pitch and climb as the load leaves, which crews meet with nose-down trim at the start of the drop and forward pressure through it. At low coverage levels the drop is slower and the change gentler; at high levels it is abrupt. A ganged drop moves the CG smoothly; a sequenced one, forward tank first, in steps. After the drop the aircraft is much lighter, accelerates and climbs well, and its escape performance is far better than its run-in performance.

**Engine failure in the run.** An engine lost on the takeoff or the drop run is handled with the normal engine-out technique first. The load is not the first thing to go; but when the terrain or the aircraft's climb is in doubt, it goes without hesitation, and the emergency drop empties the pod in about two seconds. At drop weight the climb on two engines may be poor, so every run is planned with an escape route that still works after a power loss.

See [Flight Characteristics](flight-characteristics) for the aircraft's handling at heavy weight and in the drop configuration, and [Mission Planning](mission-planning) for weight and balance.

rows: The pumps run from GALLEY BUS 1, 2 and 3, and are shed with the galleys when generating capacity falls; a GALLEY BUS switch OFF stops its tank's pump. The controllers and arming run from DC BUS 1 and 3; the quantity panel and the emergency system from the battery bus. See [Electrical](electrical).
None. Each tank has its own power pack; the aircraft's hydraulic systems neither feed nor depend on the drop system.
The load's weight and position are carried on the aircraft's payload stations, so gross weight and CG follow the tanks as they fill and empty. See [Mission Planning](mission-planning).
No pressurization while the tanks hold liquid. In heavy smoke, all three packs off. See [Air Conditioning](air-conditioning).
Low over the terrain with 35/EXT and the gear up, the ground proximity and landing gear warnings sound. See [Warning Systems](warning-systems).

On the aircraft, the forward fairing's bow wave affects the static ports; the air data computers are corrected for it and static source error correction switches are added beside the weather radar indicators. Indicated stall speeds on the normal static system are 4 kt higher.
Minimum fuel by tail number with water or retardant aboard; all fuel pumps on for the drop.

sections.title: Failures and non-normal operation
sections.summary: How the drop system fails, what the crew sees, and the drop tank system procedures.

blocks.content: The drop system is built so that no single failure leaves the crew unable to get rid of the load. Each tank has its own controller, power pack and emergency accumulator, so a failure in one tank's equipment leaves the other two working. Each tank's computer can be bypassed by MAN and the GATE switch. The master sequencer can be bypassed by selecting the tanks one at a time. Behind all of it, the emergency drop needs nothing but charged emergency accumulators and the battery bus.

blocks.title: Failures
rows: The pump motor is running hot
Drop the load as soon as possible; disarm the tank. [PUMP OVTEMP](#pump-ovtemp-procedure)
Pump does not run (motor, its breaker, or its galley bus)
The accumulator is not recharged; pressure falls with each gate movement
PUMP FAIL after a few seconds, then LOW PSI; PUMP ON out; ARMED MAN and AUTO out once pressure is low; master status “(tank) PUMP FAIL”
Usually the galley buses shed (reduced generating capacity, GALLEY BUS switches off)
PUMP FAIL and LOW PSI on all three tanks
Restore the galley buses; meanwhile as LOW PSI or PUMP FAIL
The pack stores almost nothing; the pump starts and stops every few seconds; a gate stroke may stall
PUMP ON cycling every few seconds
As LOW PSI or PUMP FAIL; have the precharge serviced
GATE CLOSED stay on after the drop switch is pressed
Doors will not close and latch
The tank keeps draining while open; the tank will not drop again until reset
GATE CLOSED out after the drop; status GATE FAULT
That door never reads latched; the doors still hold, but weep slightly; every drop ends in a gate fault
One GATE CLOSED light out; GATE FAULT after each drop
Cycle the tank's ARMED switch after each drop
Slow door movement; possibly GATE FAULT
None in flight; have it repaired
The gate stays where it is; the emergency system cannot move it either
Doors stuck; GATE FAULT if open
If stuck open, the tank drains; plan the landing for open doors
The tank must breathe through its doors; small openings choke and pulse
Drops at low coverage levels erratic and short
No specific action; wide openings are the least affected
Status NO QUANTITY; quantity dashes; ARMED AUTO out
Select the tank alone and drop it in TIMER or MAN
Display blank; AUTO and TIMER lost; the tank is OFFLINE to the master
Tank display dark; master status “(tank) OFFLINE”
Drop the other tanks under the master; drop the failed tank alone in MAN, or with the GATE switch, or by emergency drop
No master display; the master shares out no drop
Drop the tanks one at a time with SWITCH ASSIGN at each tank
An emergency drop will not open that tank's doors
That tank's E-DUMP PSI light out
Run the tank's pack to recharge it; if the light stays out, use the normal system or MAN for that tank
DC BUS 1 or DC BUS 3 lost
Loses the controllers and arming on that bus: FWD and AFT on DC BUS 1, CTR on DC BUS 3. DC BUS 1 also feeds the Normal Drop circuit
Affected tank displays and lights dark; OFFLINE on the master
Drop the remaining tanks; emergency drop for the rest if needed. With DC BUS 1 lost, only the emergency drop remains
Emergency drop unavailable; quantity panel dark; an emergency drop under way stops and the doors close
Quantity panel and E-DUMP PSI lights dark

blocks.content:
**Condition:** The load must be shed at once: an engine failure or a loss of performance in the run with the terrain or the aircraft's performance in question, or a tank that cannot be dropped normally, once clear of the fire area.

**Objective:** Empty all three tanks in seconds, independently of the normal drop system.

Every tank with a charged emergency accumulator opens fully; the whole load is gone in about two seconds and the aircraft pitches up and climbs as in a normal drop, only faster. In the simulation the DROP COMPLETE light does not come on after an emergency drop, which bypasses the controllers: confirm on the quantity panel. The doors stay open while the emergency relay is latched.

To restore the system, the operator's procedure is: tank ARMED and HYD PWR switches off, EMERGENCY DROP switch back to normal, then the Emergency Drop and Emergency Drop Power breakers pulled and reset. Once the relay opens, the doors may close on the residual pressure in the emergency accumulators.
After an emergency drop, any interruption of DC power to the emergency relay closes the doors on residual accumulator pressure. On the ground, keep people clear of the doors.
**Condition:** A PUMP OVTEMP light on the quantity panel: that tank's hydraulic pump motor is overheating.

items.action: DROP ALL as soon as possible

blocks.content: The cause of the overheat must be found and corrected before the tank is used again.

A motor overheats when it runs for long periods, typically because something is drawing on its pack continuously: a leaking accumulator, or a pack whose precharge has gone. Its cooling may also have degraded.

children.title: LOW PSI or PUMP FAIL light on

blocks.content: **Condition:** LOW PSI or PUMP FAIL on a tank control panel.

**If the affected tank's ARMED (MAN and AUTO) lights are still on:** the tank still has the pressure to drop. Proceed with the normal drop, and have the accumulator serviced after landing.

**If they are out:**

blocks.title: LOW PSI or PUMP FAIL, tank not armed

items.item: Affected tank, when clear of the fire area

blocks.content:
The affected tank's emergency accumulator was isolated from its pack by its check valve, so it keeps its charge after the pack fails: check its E-DUMP PSI light before relying on it. The emergency drop opens every tank, so use it only once the operating tanks have been dropped. On the aircraft the affected tank can also be emptied with its manual emergency release handle, before the normal drop if time allows.

RUN PUMP clears a PUMP FAIL and runs the pump by hand, which shows whether the pump will run at all. If all three tanks show PUMP FAIL together, the cause is almost certainly the galley buses rather than three pumps: the pumps run from GALLEY BUS 1, 2 and 3 and are shed with the galleys.

**Condition:** The drop switch is held with a valid selection and the system armed, and a tank's GATE CLOSED lights stay on.

On the aircraft the procedure starts by pulling and resetting the tank's power and control breakers (galley bus for the pump, upper main for the control). If the doors still do not open:

All tanks' doors open. Once the system is reset they may close again on the residual pressure in the accumulators. On the aircraft, the manual emergency release handle for the affected tank is the alternative; putting the handle back closes the doors if there is pressure in the normal accumulator.

The GATE switch at OPEN GATE, and MAN with the tank selected alone, bypass the tank's computer. If the fault is in the computer rather than the hydraulics, either may open doors that AUTO will not.

**Condition:** After a drop, a tank's GATE CLOSED lights stay out; its status shows GATE FAULT.

On the aircraft the procedure starts by pulling and resetting the tank's power and control breakers. If the EMERGENCY DROP switch was used, its power and control breakers must be reset after the switch is back at normal before the doors can close. Then:

items.item: MASTER ARMED and all three tank ARMED switches
items.action: ARMED (cycle the affected tank's switch to clear GATE FAULT)

blocks.content:
**If the doors still fail to close:** use care taxiing after landing; the doors hang below the pod. On the aircraft, also check that the manual emergency release handle for the tank is stowed, because a pulled handle holds the doors open.

A gate trying to close against its load is the hardest work its actuator does, and the load factor makes it harder. If a gate stalls part-open in a pull-up, it may close once the aircraft is back at 1 g or the tank has drained.

**Modeled in depth.** Each tank is simulated as a liquid in a hopper divided by baffles: its surface tilts and sloshes with the aircraft's accelerations, runs between bays, seeps through the door seals and can spill through the vent. Each gate's outflow follows the orifice law with the tank's head, the load factor and the air entering the vent, so flow really does fall as the tank empties and rise in a pull-up. The controllers fly the constant-flow law, learn from each drop, share drops ganged or sequenced, and report through every light and display described here. Each tank's power pack has its pump, pressure switch, accumulator, leakage and motor heating; the emergency accumulators charge through their check valves; the emergency relay drops with its power. The pumps, controllers and emergency system draw on the aircraft's galley, DC and battery buses.

The load's weight is carried on the simulator's payload stations, so gross weight and CG move with every gallon, and the aircraft pitches up as it drops. A visual drop curtain leaves each gate in proportion to its flow, red for retardant and white for water, above about 15 kt true airspeed.

**Different from the aircraft, or simplified.**

- The tanks are the three drop tanks at the 9,400 US gal approved load. The forward and aft fairing tanks of the full installation are not modeled.
- The **yoke buttons are normal drop buttons**. The aircraft's flight manual supplement and the FAA's Flight Standardization Board report describe them as emergency drop switches; in the simulation the only emergency drop switch is the pedestal's.
- The flow for each coverage level is fixed for a drop at about 150 kt over the ground; the controller does not take ground speed into account.
- The quantity readings are calibrated for retardant. A water load reads about 12% low on the cockpit displays (the EFB shows the true quantity), and the drop quantities and flows worked out from those readings are correspondingly less accurate with water.
- Eight successive 1/8 drops are equal to within a few percent, except the last, which takes whatever is left and can be noticeably smaller.
- The tank panels' datawheels turn but do not select: on a tank panel only the coverage level can be changed, and its drop quantity stays at ALL.
- The DUMP CNTRL switch is at SEQUENCED when the aircraft is loaded. Set it to GANGED.
- The wording of the displays' status line is the simulation's own.
- The pod's own structural weight is not added to the aircraft's empty weight.
- The exterior doors move through only a small angle: a fully open gate looks barely open from outside.
- The drop leaves no pattern on the ground and has no effect on fire in the simulator. The ground line and coverage figures are the controller's calculation.
- The Normal Drop circuit, which also powers the master sequencer and the glareshield drop status lights, is on DC BUS 1, so losing DC BUS 1 leaves only the emergency drop. The aircraft's documents do not say which bus feeds it.
- At the start of a session the power packs and emergency accumulators are empty. Run the packs for a couple of minutes before relying on an emergency drop.

**Not modeled.**

- The manual emergency release handles in the cabin.
- The retardant system's circuit breakers are not on the simulated breaker panels, so procedure steps that pull and reset them cannot be done. After an emergency drop the relay stays latched, and the doors stay open, until the battery bus loses power.
- The aural warning cancel button, the GPWS inhibit switch, the flap override switch and the OVERRIDE position of the GALLEY BUS switches. The ground proximity and landing gear warnings sound during a low run with 35/EXT and the gear up.
- The master sequencer's blue power light.
- The loading couplings and hoses: the tanks are loaded from the EFB's Fire Support app instead.
- The conversion's air data changes (the static source error correction and the modified airspeed indicators), and its 310 KIAS limit in the overspeed warning.
- The Virtual Crew does not operate the drop system: the flight engineer's drop-system items are yours.
- The drop system's own failures cannot yet be selected in the EFB's failures app. Electrical failures that shed the galley buses or remove a DC bus do affect it.

parts.title: Electronic Flight Bag
parts.summary: The in-sim tablet: flight planning, loading, performance, documents, ground services and settings.

sections.title: Introduction
sections.summary: A tablet that gives the crew the planning, loading, performance and ground tools a dispatcher, load controller and ramp would.

blocks.content: The **electronic flight bag** (EFB) is a tablet computer on the flight deck. It carries the tools a line crew would otherwise get from dispatch, load control, the ramp, the performance engineer and maintenance: the flight plan, the fuel and payload, the takeoff and landing data, the checklists, the ground services and the failures you want to practice. It is the simulation's own instrument, not a copy of any operator's equipment, and it is the same on every aircraft of the family. What it does, it does to the simulated aircraft through the same controls and systems a crew would use: a refuel from the EFB flows through the refuel panel's valves, a failure fails a real component, and a cargo plan is carried by the same weight and balance the flight model flies.

**One application, several screens.** The tablet on the flight deck is the **host**. It reads the aircraft's systems, keeps the lists that must exist once (the failures armed and active, the fuel plan's queue, the flight log), and publishes what it reads. Every other screen is a **mirror** of it. On the KC-10 and the KDC-10 a second tablet at the boom operator's station mirrors the flight deck's, and any number of real tablets or desktop browsers can be paired through Infinity Manager. A mirror shows what the host shows, and a press on a mirror is sent to the host and applied there (the boom operator's tablet, itself in the aircraft, writes cockpit controls directly). The open app, the notes, the checklist ticks and the settings are shared, so every screen agrees on where it is; zoom, scroll position and the Home page shown are each screen's own.

blocks.alt: The EFB Home screen on the flight deck tablet, held in landscape, on a DC-10-30 at the gate. Left column: the AIRCRAFT widget (DC-10-30, a KMEM to KLAX route line with the aircraft symbol at the start, PARKED badge, IAS, GS, ALT and HDG), the WEIGHTS widget (gross weight in klb with the fuel bar, FUEL and ZFW) and the LINK widget. Right: the four-column app grid with every app tile legible. The dock (Flight, Route, Ground Ops, Notes, Settings) along the bottom, page dots above it.
blocks.title: EFB Home screen
blocks.caption: The first Home page: the aircraft, weight and link widgets beside the app grid. Swipe left for the clocks, chronometer and notes.

blocks.content: The apps appear on the Home screen in the order of a flight's preparation. Some are for one kind of aircraft only, and an aircraft that has no use for an app does not show it. The table lists them all.

blocks.title: EFB apps
rows: The equipment fit of a DC-10 flight deck; the primary COM2 radio and brake choice
Phase of flight, block and flight times, progress against the plan, landings
Loads a SimBrief plan or the sim's planned route into the long-range navigation unit; the navigation log
Navigraph charts with the aircraft drawn on georeferenced sheets
The automated first officer and flight engineer, the cabin crew, the cruise CG target
Chocks and covers, ground power and air, servicing, fuel, doors, pushback
Plans and loads unit load devices position by position, on the decks to scale
Boards and deboards passengers, cabin comfort, the cabin service
Takeoff and landing data (TOLD card), climb, cruise, holding, descent and approach
The boom operator's autopilot control and receiver settings
Live system diagrams and monitor tables
Injects, schedules and clears failures; circuit breakers; aircraft reset
The aircraft's normal checklists, run with or without the Virtual Crew
Scratchpads with templates (CRAFT clearance, ATIS, holds, takeoff and landing data)
Brightness, keyboard, GSX, SimBrief, navigation data, INS alignment, passenger simulation

blocks.content: The EFB works in pounds and knots throughout. A SimBrief plan made in kilograms is converted when it is fetched. There is no unit setting.

sections.title: The tablet and its screens
sections.summary: Where the tablet is, how it turns, the boom operator's tablet, paired tablets, and how to type on it.

blocks.content: The flight deck tablet is a portrait screen of 800 by 1,100 pixels in its own mount. Click on it with the mouse as you would press it with a finger.

Each flight deck carries the tablet in a mount within reach of the crew. The tablet **turns on its mount** between portrait and landscape. When it turns, the screen follows the way a phone does: the new layout starts at the tablet's angle and swings upright as it grows. Every app has a layout for each orientation. The Home screen puts its widgets in a column on the left and the apps in four columns on the right in landscape; the Cargo and Doors pages turn their drawing of the aircraft nose-left; the Systems diagrams grow to fill the wider screen.

blocks.alt: DC-10-30 flight deck, cockpit view: the EFB tablet in its mount, screen on and showing the Home screen, with enough of the surrounding panels to locate it. A second inset or angle shows the tablet turned to landscape on the same mount.
blocks.title: EFB mount, DC-10 flight deck

blocks.alt: KC-10A flight deck, cockpit view: the EFB tablet in its mount, screen on and showing the Home screen, with the surrounding panels legible enough to locate it.
blocks.title: EFB mount, KC-10 flight deck

blocks.alt: MD-10-30 glass flight deck, cockpit view: the EFB tablet in its mount, screen on and showing the Home screen, with the surrounding panels legible enough to locate it.
blocks.title: EFB mount, MD-10 flight deck

blocks.content: The KC-10 and the KDC-10 carry a second EFB at the boom operator's station in the aft fuselage. It is a mirror of the flight deck's tablet: it shows the same app, the same notes and settings, and every reading the flight deck's tablet publishes. A press on it that changes something in the cockpit, such as an Air Refuel selection, goes straight to the aircraft; a press on something the flight deck's tablet keeps, such as the failure lists or the fuel plan, is sent to the flight deck and applied there. It turns between portrait and landscape on its own mount.
The boom operator's tablet gets its readings through Infinity Manager, as a paired tablet does. With the manager closed it shows no readings, though its presses that write to the cockpit still work.

blocks.alt: KC-10A boom operator's station, looking forward from the operator's position: the second EFB tablet in its mount beside the ARO panel, showing the Air Refuel app.
blocks.title: EFB at the boom operator's station

blocks.content: Infinity Manager serves the same EFB to any tablet or desktop browser on your network. Open the manager's EFB page, then scan its QR code with the tablet or enter its pairing code; the tablet remembers the pairing and reconnects by itself next time. A paired tablet is a mirror: it follows the flight deck's screen, and its presses are relayed to the flight deck's tablet, which applies them and posts the answer back. If the flight deck does not answer within about 8 seconds, the tablet says so.

blocks.title: What each screen can do
rows: Ground Ops, Route, Passengers, Failures, Virtual Crew presses
Applied, or relayed to the flight deck
Shows the plan; presses not available
Passengers' boarding only, relayed to the flight deck; Ground Ops' and Cargo's GSX requests and the GSX menu are not available
Yes, on the flight deck's session
Yes, on the flight deck's session
One shared setting dims both in-sim screens
Sets the in-sim screens'; the device keeps its own

blocks.content: Every control works from a mouse click or a touch. The simulator gives the tablet no scroll wheel, so long pages **drag-scroll**: press anywhere on the page and drag, and the page carries on with momentum when you let go. The Home screen's two pages swipe sideways the same way.

When a text box is selected, the EFB **holds the simulator's keyboard**, so what you type goes into the box and not to the aircraft's key bindings. Holding the keyboard also raises the simulator's own text prompt, which takes the next click made anywhere else; the EFB's buttons that work on a selected box act on the press rather than the release for that reason. On the flight deck tablet an **on-screen keyboard** docks under the screen while a box is selected (Settings can turn it off); numeric boxes get a number pad, and boxes for identifiers type in capitals. Enter moves to the next box.
A paired tablet raises its own keyboard, so the EFB's keyboard never appears there.

sections.title: Home screen and navigation
sections.summary: The Home screen's widgets and app grid, the dock, the system navigation and the messages that float over every app.

blocks.content: The Home screen has two pages over a dusk wallpaper. The **first page** carries three widgets and the app grid. The **second page**, a swipe to the left, carries the clocks, a chronometer and the newest note. The page dots above the dock show which page is open; press a dot to go to it.

blocks.title: Home screen widgets
rows: The aircraft loaded (for example DC-10-30, KC-10, MD-10-10); with a plan loaded through Route, the origin-to-destination line with the aircraft symbol at the share of the plan flown; the phase of flight as a badge; IAS, GS, ALT and HDG; with a plan, TO GO NM, ETE and ETA UTC
Gross weight in thousands of pounds, a bar showing fuel as a share of gross weight, FUEL and ZFW
The connection to Infinity Manager, and whether this screen is the flight deck panel or a mirror
UTC to the second, and local time
A chronometer shared by every screen: started on the flight deck, it runs on every paired tablet too
The newest note: its template, when it was started, and what it holds

blocks.content: The **dock** along the bottom holds the five apps used most: Flight, Route, Ground Ops, Notes and Settings. The **system navigation** floats at the foot of every app: **Back** returns to the previous screen (a screen inside the app first, such as an open note's list, then the app shown before, then Home), **Home** goes to the Home screen, and the **switcher** lists the apps to jump between them. Every app opens in a frame whose header band is the app's own color.

The EFB keeps its screens compact. **A button that cannot be pressed is not drawn**, and neither is a switch that cannot move, so what you see is what you can do now. When something is unavailable for a reason worth knowing, a single amber line says why: the aircraft is moving, a GSX request failed, the chocks-away countdown is running.
A few messages float in a bubble at the top of the screen, over whatever app is open, because they need the captain's answer:

items: **Checklist offers.** With a Virtual Crew seat on AUTO, the crew offer each checklist as the flight reaches it: “Start Before Start Checklist?”, with **Start** and **Not Now**. See [Virtual Crew](virtual-crew).

**Crew requests.** A crew member who needs the captain says so: “Call for ground power and ground air” when the APU will not supply, “Ground equipment still at the aircraft” before taxi, “Start No. 2 engine?” with **Yes** and **Not Now**, and the calls for the captain's handles after takeoff and before landing. A request about the ground carries a **Ground Ops** button that opens the app.

**Tow broken.** If a towbar breaks or the aircraft runs away from the tug, “Tow broken: the tug has gone” with what happened, until **OK**. See [Pushback and towing](ground-operations#pushback-and-towing).

blocks.content: While the view is in the tow tug's cab, every EFB screen, the flight deck's, the boom operator's and every paired tablet, shows only the tug's steering screen until the view returns to the flight deck. See [The tug cab view](ground-operations#tug-cab-view).

sections.title: Planning and navigation apps
sections.summary: Flight, Route, Charts / Data and Notes.

blocks.content: Four apps carry the flight plan and the crew's notes from the gate to the destination. **Route** is where a plan enters the aircraft; **Flight** and the Home screen then follow the aircraft against it; **Charts / Data** shows the airport and procedure charts; **Notes** holds the clearances, the ATIS and the crew's own takeoff and landing figures.

Flight is the log of the flight in progress. Top to bottom it shows the **phase of flight**, the **block and flight times**, the **destination** (origin to destination with distance to go, ETE and ETA), the **last landing**, and the current IAS, ground speed and heading. The flight deck's tablet keeps the log from the aircraft's own readings, so every screen shows the same times.

blocks.alt: The Flight app on the flight deck tablet, landscape, during cruise on a KMEM to KLAX flight: CRUISE phase badge, OUT, OFF times stamped with ON and IN blank, the DESTINATION card with distance to go, ETE and ETA, the LAST LANDING card from the previous flight with its sink rate, pitch and bank, and the IAS, GS and HDG readouts.
blocks.title: Flight app
Phases of flight
rows: Moving on the ground below 50 kt
On the takeoff roll, above 50 kt
Climbing at 300 ft/min or more, and level just after takeoff
After 15 seconds within 300 ft/min of level flight, at any height; only a climb or descent of 500 ft/min or more ends it
Descending at 300 ft/min or more, more than 3,000 ft above the ground
Descending at 300 ft/min or more below 3,000 ft above the ground, and level segments below that height
On the ground above 50 kt after a landing

blocks.content: **Block times.** **OUT** is stamped after 5 seconds of movement faster than 3 kt; **OFF** at liftoff; **ON** at touchdown; **IN** after 30 seconds at rest following a landing. Moving again clears IN, so a long hold short of the gate does not stand as the block-in time. Five minutes at rest after a landing closes the flight, and the next OUT starts a new log. Under the times, **Start** stamps whatever is missing at once (OUT, and OFF if airborne), for a flight that was loaded already moving; **Reset**, after a confirmation, clears the four times and keeps the landings.

**Landings.** Each landing is recorded with its sink rate, pitch and bank at touchdown, from the simulator's touchdown record (or, without one, the last vertical speed before the wheels touched). A liftoff within 5 seconds of a touchdown is a bounce, and a second touchdown within 15 seconds of it is the same landing. The app marks a landing **hard** against the limit descent velocities of the certification rules: 10 ft/s at maximum landing weight and 6 ft/s at maximum takeoff weight, interpolated between. That is a guide to how firm the landing was, not the maintenance manual's hard landing inspection criterion.

**Distance and times to go** follow the SimBrief plan loaded through Route: direct to the navigation unit's TO waypoint, then along the plan's legs to the destination (direct to the destination if the plan has no TO waypoint). ETE needs the aircraft airborne at 50 kt or more over the ground. Flight shows a plan only while the navigation unit holds one loaded through Route; with none loaded, its DESTINATION card points to Route. The log is not kept across a reload of the aircraft.

Route loads a flight plan into whichever long-range navigation unit the aircraft carries, and shows what the unit made of it. The plan comes from one of two places: the crew's latest **SimBrief** operational flight plan (OFP), fetched by the aircraft for the SimBrief username set in [Settings](#settings-app), or the simulator's own **planned route** from its world map. The EFB only sends the request and shows the result; the aircraft's navigation system does the work of resolving each fix against its database and loading it, exactly as its own data loader or ACARS would. The app has two pages, **Load** and **Navlog**.

blocks.alt: The Route app's Load page on a DC-10-30 with an AINS-70 fit, landscape: the route's two ends KMEM and KLAX, SIMBRIEF as its source and a LOADED badge; the Load from SimBrief, Load from Sim and Clear buttons; the accent line with the next step on the CDU (ROUTE DEFINITION); the unit's card with COMPANY ROUTE, waypoints and last kept; and below a section break, FLIGHT PLAN PARTS with two boxes, part 1 LOADED and part 2 NOT LOADED with its Load button. Send to Performance under the presses.
blocks.title: Route app, Load page

blocks.content: **The Load page** shows the route's two ends, where it came from and the state of the job as a badge; the presses **Load from SimBrief**, **Load from Sim** and **Clear** (on the MD-10, **Clear report**, because nothing outside the FMS clears its flight plan); the crew's next step on the unit, in an accent line; and what the unit holds of the route. Once a route is held, **Send to Performance** copies its airports, runways and levels into the [Performance](#performance-app) pages. A press the aircraft would refuse is not drawn: on a VOR ONLY fit there is no Load at all, and with no SimBrief username there is no Load from SimBrief, only a line and a Settings button.

blocks.title: What each navigation unit does with a loaded route
rows: 9 waypoints per card, into every box that is aligning or navigating
Nothing more: each box flies leg 1 to 2, or direct to waypoint 1. A box OFF or in ATT keeps what it had
Select the FUNCTION switch to A so the box changes legs by itself (a cold cockpit starts at T)
59 rows per company route, filed on the data tape with a five-digit route number
On the CDU: PAGE INDEX, ROUTE DEFINITION, the route number into line 5, then on the ground the present position. In flight a later part joins on the REVISE page, CO RTE AFTER
200 legs; goes straight into the active route through the box's own ACTIVATE and EXEC
Nothing more; winds and any pending change are erased by the load
200 waypoints, into SEC FPLN on every running FMS side
INDEX, SEC FPLN, ACTIVATE, then EXEC. A CDU must be switched on first
No fixed limit (the FCOM advises 100 waypoints); sent as an ACARS route uplink
On the MCDU: REF INDEX, ACARS, REVIEW, INSERT, then SEC F-PLN, ACTIVATE SEC

blocks.content: **Flight plan parts.** A route longer than the unit holds is cut into **parts** the unit can take whole: nine-waypoint cards on the CIV-A and INS-61B, 59-row company routes on the AINS-70. The first part loads with the import. The Load page then shows a box for each part with its two ends, LOADED or NOT LOADED, and its own **Load** (or **Reload** for the part the unit holds). Each later part starts at the last point of the part before, so the crew load the next part as the aircraft nears the end of the current one; on the AINS-70 the later part's list ends with its TO waypoint and the box says how to join it in flight. Only the current route is kept: a newer import replaces it and Clear forgets it.

**The Navlog page** is the SimBrief OFP as SimBrief wrote it, fetched by the EFB itself: the route string, flight number, cruise level, cost index, alternate, air distance, time en route, and block and trip fuel; then the log fix by fix, without SimBrief's top-of-climb and top-of-descent points. It has two views. **Log** lists waypoint, airway, flight level, track, distance, time and fuel on board in pounds. **Positions** lists each fix's latitude and longitude as an INS takes them (N47 27.0) and a navaid's frequency, for crews who type the route into a CIV-A or INS-61B by hand. The unit's TO waypoint is marked, and on a route in parts the log shows only the part the unit holds (“Part 2 of 3 in the unit: JMS to KORD”).

The AINS-70 needs its route assembled on the CDU before it flies it: the filing on the tape puts nothing in the navigation computers. See [Navigation](navigation) for the CDU procedure, and [Flight management](flight-management) for the KC-10 and MD-10 FMS pages.

Charts / Data shows an airport's charts from the chart sources linked in Infinity Manager (Navigraph). The **browse** screen has the airport bar (the loaded route's two ends, the airports last looked up, and a box for an ICAO identifier), the tabs **Pinned**, **Airport**, **Departure**, **Arrival**, **Approach** and **Reference**, a runway filter on tabs whose charts name runways, and the list of charts. Press a chart to open it in the **viewer**: drag to pan, double-press or use the plus and minus buttons to zoom, **Fit** to fit the page (a second press fits the width), **Turn** to rotate it a quarter turn, **Night** for a dark sheet, and **Previous sheet** and **Next sheet** to step through the tab. On a georeferenced chart the aircraft is drawn at its position and heading, and **Follow aircraft** keeps it centerd. A chart can be pinned to the Pinned tab.

blocks.alt: The Charts / Data app's viewer, landscape, showing an airport diagram at KLAX with the aircraft symbol on a taxiway at its true position and heading, the viewer tools (zoom, Fit, Turn, Follow aircraft, Night) and the pin, and the attribution line under the sheet.
blocks.title: Charts / Data, chart viewer

blocks.content: Charts are licensed content and exist only inside a running aircraft: Infinity Manager serves them only while the simulator runs, this aircraft is connected, and the flight deck's tablet has checked in within the last few seconds. A paired tablet rides on that session. When the session ends the chart is removed from every screen at once.
The open airport, tab, chart and night setting are shared, so the flight deck and a paired tablet show the same chart; zoom and pan are each screen's own.

Notes holds typed scratchpads. **New note** offers six templates: **Blank**, **CRAFT** (clearance limit, route, altitude, frequency, transponder), **ATIS**, **Hold Clearance**, **Takeoff Data** and **Landing Data**. Each template is a set of labeled boxes; Enter moves to the next box, and in a box of several lines Shift+Enter starts a new line. Press a note's title to rename it, and **Select** on the list to delete several at once. Notes are kept between sessions and shared with every paired screen.

**Pull data** on the ATIS, Takeoff Data and Landing Data templates fills the wind, visibility, ceiling, temperature and dew point, and altimeter setting from the simulator's current METAR for the airport in the APT box, the time on an ATIS, and the zero-fuel weight from the aircraft. With no airport typed, a takeoff note uses the loaded route's origin and a landing note its destination; a takeoff note on the ground falls back to the nearest reporting station. METAR wind is true.

blocks.alt: The Notes app, portrait, with a CRAFT clearance note open: the C, R, A, F and T boxes filled with a typical departure clearance, the on-screen keyboard docked at the foot of the screen.
blocks.title: Notes, a CRAFT clearance

blocks.content: The Virtual Crew app sets who works the aircraft beside you. **FLIGHT DECK** has a row for each automated seat (on the DC-10 the Flight Engineer/Second Officer and the First Officer; on the KC-10 the flight engineer and copilot; on the MD-10 the first officer), each **OFF**, **MANUAL** or **AUTO**. On MANUAL a seat works its own items of any checklist you start in [Documents](#documents-app), moving the real switches; on AUTO the crew also offer each checklist as the flight reaches it and check the captain's items as they are done. On the DC-10, **Target Cruise CG** sets a CG the second officer holds in the cruise by transferring fuel. **FLIGHT ATTENDANTS** sets the cabin crew to run the service themselves or under the purser's orders, and turns the cabin service on or off. The full description is in [Virtual Crew](virtual-crew).

blocks.alt: The Virtual Crew app on a DC-10-30, portrait: the FLIGHT DECK card with the Flight Engineer/Second Officer and First Officer rows, each with OFF, MANUAL and AUTO, and under them the Target Cruise CG row with Set (or minus, plus and Off) and the current CG; the FLIGHT ATTENDANTS card with the Cabin service and Attendants run it (AUTO) switches.
blocks.title: Virtual Crew app

sections.title: Ground, fuel, cargo and passengers
sections.summary: Ground Ops and its Fuel page, Cargo and Passengers: how the aircraft is serviced and loaded, and how the load reaches the flight model.

blocks.content: In the simulation, as on the real aircraft, the airplane's weight and balance is the sum of what is in its tanks, holds and seats. The EFB loads each of them **through the aircraft's own systems**: fuel through the fuel system's refuel panel and valves, cargo by a loading crew rolling each unit along the hold's rollers into its locks, passengers by walking them through the open doors to their seats. The aircraft's systems then hand the result to the flight model, which flies the weight and center of gravity they add up to. MSFS takes mass only in two places, its fuel tanks and its payload stations, so the aircraft writes its fuel to the simulator's tanks once a second and spreads each unit of cargo and every passenger over a fixed grid of payload stations along the fuselage. The weight and CG you see on the flight deck instruments and in the EFB therefore agree with what the flight model flies.

Do not edit the payload stations on the simulator's own weight and balance page while the EFB's cargo or passengers are in use. The aircraft takes an outside edit to a station as a sign that something else owns it and stops writing that part of the payload (the cargo, the passengers or the retardant tanks, whichever the station belongs to) for the rest of the session: the cargo or cabin you see then no longer weighs anything. Fuel loaded from the simulator's fuel page, its fuel truck or GSX's is accepted and taken into the fuel system.

Plan the load against the limits first: the structural weights, the CG envelope and the loading schedule are in [Limitations](limitations) and [Mission planning](mission-planning). The EFB enforces the hardware's own limits (a tank's capacity, a position's and a device's maximum weight, the floor two units would share) but does not check the aircraft's zero-fuel weight or CG envelope for you.
Ground Ops is the ramp: everything that is done to the aircraft at the stand, from the chocks to the pushback. Its five pages follow the order of a turnaround, under page buttons at the top:

rows: Chocks, pitot covers, engine covers and cones; ground power; the air-start and conditioned-air carts
[Ground operations: chocks, covers and cones](ground-operations#ramp-items) and [ground power and air](ground-operations#ground-power-and-air)
Stairs or a catering truck at each forward door, the belt loader, catering, lavatory, cleaning, de-icing
A block fuel spread over the tanks in the loading schedule, a target per tank, Refuel or Instant
Every door on an outline of the aircraft, opened, stopped, closed, armed and disarmed
GSX, the simulator's own tug, or AeroTow, the simulated tow tug

blocks.content: **Every page is grayed** while the aircraft is in the air, moving, or stopped off a paved surface, with a caution sign in the middle of the page saying which. Three things stay live so they can still be stopped or worked: doors 1L and 1R below 20 kt, a running refuel's progress and its Cancel, and the Pushback page while a tow is at the aircraft. While GSX is in use the app's header carries a **GSX menu** button that opens GSX's own menu, the one place a running GSX service can be stopped.

The Fuel page sets how much fuel each tank is to hold and then loads it, either progressively through the aircraft's refuel panel or at once. It shows only the tanks the aircraft has: tanks 1, 2 and 3 on every aircraft; the center auxiliary tank on the -15, -30, -40, MD-10-30 and KC-10, and on a DC-10-10 with the extended-range option; the aft auxiliary tank on a DC-10-30 with the extended-range option; and the forward and aft body tanks on the KC-10.

blocks.alt: Ground Ops' Fuel page, landscape, on a DC-10-30 at the gate: the PLAN group with the Block fuel row, its SimBrief and Distribute buttons and BLOCK LB box showing 165,000; the TANKS group with Tank 1, Tank 2, Tank 3 and Center aux, each with a slider and a TARGET LB box; the summary line FUEL, GW and CG after the load; the Reset, Refuel and Instant buttons; and the REFUELING group with its progress bar, rate in lb/min, pounds to go and Cancel refuel.
blocks.title: Ground Ops, Fuel page
Fuel page controls
rows: The total fuel wanted, typed in pounds
Fetches the latest SimBrief OFP's planned ramp fuel for the username in Settings and puts it in BLOCK LB
Sets every tank's target from the block fuel, in the aircraft's loading schedule (below). Enter in BLOCK LB does the same
A target per tank: drag the slider (it moves in whole hundreds of pounds, several hundred at a time on a big tank) or type the exact figure
The fuel aboard, the gross weight and the center of gravity in percent MAC that the targets would give
Loads the targets through the refuel panel, at the rate the fuel system delivers. Not offered while any tank is set below what it holds
Sets every tank to its target at once
While a refuel runs: its progress, the flow in lb/min, the pounds to go and the time left, or Waiting for ground service power
Stops the refuel where it stands. The targets are kept, so Refuel resumes it
**Call truck** asks GSX for its refueling service; Hose on while GSX's hose is connected

blocks.content: **The loading schedule.** Distribute does not share the fuel out by capacity, which no operator does; it follows each aircraft's own fuel loading schedule, which gives each tank's final quantity for a total. On the DC-10 and MD-10 (Series 10 and 30, and the -15 and -40 by the Series 30 rule) the three main tanks are filled equally until tanks 1 and 3 are full, then tank 2 until it is full, then the center auxiliary tank, then the aft auxiliary tank. The KC-10 follows its own seven steps: 5,000 lb in each main tank; 15,000 lb in the forward body tank; the mains equally until 1 and 3 are full; tank 2 until full; the center wing tank and both body tanks equally until the forward body tank is full; the center wing and aft body tanks equally until the aft is full; then the center wing tank until full. The reasoning is structural: fuel kept in the outboard wing relieves the wing's bending moment in flight, so the wing tanks are filled first and emptied last. See [Fuel](fuel) and [Mission planning](mission-planning).

**Refuel and Instant.** **Refuel** works the aircraft's refuel panel as a refueller would: it arms the panel and sets each tank's load-select target, and the fuel then flows through the modeled refuel adapters, fill valves and float valves at whatever rate the fuel system's network allows. It needs what the real panel needs, the aircraft on the ground with its ground service bus powered (see [Electrical](electrical)); until then the page reads Waiting for ground service power. Refuel only adds fuel. A failed fill valve stops its tank filling, exactly as on the aircraft. **Instant** is the simulator's quick load: the quantities change at the next moment, with no panel, valves or power. It is refused in the air.

The targets go to the fuel system one tank at a time, each once the last has been taken (the page says how many are still to go). A refuel is not stopped by the aircraft moving, so its progress and Cancel refuel stay live even when the rest of the page is grayed. The CG preview is a mass-weighted mean of the aircraft's present CG and each tank's arm, in the weight and balance manual's percent of MAC.

Cargo plans the load one position at a time, on drawings of the decks to scale, and then loads it. The **main deck** (on the freighters and the KC-10) and the **lower deck** are drawn side by side with the nose up in portrait, one above the other with the nose left in landscape, over the same span of fuselage stations so a main-deck row and the hold beneath it line up. Every position is drawn where the aircraft's layout puts it, and every weight limit and fit comes from the aircraft: the app holds no catalog of its own.

blocks.alt: The Cargo app on a DC-10-30F, portrait: the main deck and the lower deck drawn side by side to scale, nose up, with positions colored blue (planned), amber (moving) and green (aboard); a main-deck position selected and the panel beside it showing PLANNED, MOVING and ABOARD totals, the Loading section with Start load, and the pressed spot's options as tabs, the unit models that fit, a weight stepper and the contents tabs General, Perishable, Pharma, Live animals. Save Cargo and Load Cargo in the header.
blocks.title: Cargo app

blocks.content: **Planning.** Press a position on a deck to select it. The panel shows the position's options as tabs (a single position, a full row, a crosswise pallet, a coupled pair, where the layout has them), the unit models the aircraft says fit there, and once a unit is planned its gross weight with a stepper, **Change unit** and **Remove**. A wider position takes the press over every cell it covers, and a cell a planned unit rules out is grayed. Colors: blue planned, amber moving, green aboard, red a plan issue. With no position selected, the panel lists the holds, each with **Load now**, **Unload now** and **Clear**, and an **All holds** row with **Load all**, **Unload all** and **Clear**. A planned unit's contents can be set to **General**, **Perishable**, **Pharma** or **Live animals**.

**What the plan is checked against.** Every unit is checked as it is planned, and every issue is listed against its position: a position the aircraft does not have, a unit the position does not take, a weight below the unit's own tare or over the device's or the position's maximum, two units that would share floor, a compartment's total over its limit, a unit too tall for its position, and two **door rivals**, rows at a door where whichever went in first would shut the other out. The issues must be cleared before the hold will load.

blocks.title: Loading presses
rows: The crew roll each planned unit in from its door, one at a time, into its locks
Calls GSX's boarding: GSX's loaders bring each unit to its door and the crew roll it in as GSX's progress allows
Stops the roll: units already locked stay aboard, one still rolling is taken off, Start load resumes
Not offered: GSX has no stop
The crew roll every unit out
The hold loaded or emptied at once

blocks.content: The bulk hold loads and unloads at once either way.
