A hold refuses to load, and says why in a short line at the top (“Main Deck: Refused - Reason: Engine Running”), when the aircraft is airborne or moving, has neither the parking brake set nor the chocks in, has a tug connected, has the engine on the door's side running, or when the door cannot be worked, the wind is too strong for an open door, cargo already aboard is in the way, or there is nothing to load. **Once loading has started, the same conditions freeze it** where it stands, as a loading crew would stop: the aircraft moving, an engine starting on the door's side, the parking brake released with no chocks, a tug hitched or the wind rising past the door's limit. The units carry on by themselves once the condition has cleared. Lost handling power holds only the units that need it, and they resume by themselves.

**The tail-tip hold.** A freighter loaded from the front can sit on its tail if the aft holds fill before the forward ones. The loading crew therefore choose the order: units load from the far end of a hold toward the door and unload from the door end first, and a unit whose move would put the CG on the ground past the tipping limit is passed over for one that does not. When every unit that could move would, the work holds, and the panel says Holding: tail-tip risk. Loading the forward hold first, or keeping cargo near the door while other cargo moves (the KC-10 manual's own remedy), clears it.

**Save Cargo** keeps the plan under a name. **Load Cargo** lists the presets, **Full Load** and **Half Load**, worked out of the aircraft's layout at typical weights inside every limit (a DC-10 freighter's Full Load is 53 units and 116,200 lb; the KC-10's is 23 pallets and 92,000 lb), and the saved plans this aircraft can take, each with **Load** and **Delete**. Loading one replaces the plan: the old plan is cleared first, then the new units are sent once the aircraft reports it empty. Units whose floor or way in is held by cargo already aboard are left out, and a line says how many.

**Cargo care.** A unit carrying perishables, pharmaceuticals or live animals has a temperature and a condition. While one is aboard or was delivered this trip, a CARGO CARE list shows each such unit's position, contents, temperature and condition (green from 85 %, amber from 70 %, red below), and why it suffers: too warm, too cold, or no ventilation. Keep the cargo compartments' temperature and ventilation where the shipment needs them (see [Air conditioning](air-conditioning)). On a freighter, with the passenger simulation on, the flight's review is drawn here and judged on the cargo alone.
Cargo presses are made on the flight deck's tablet or the boom operator's. A paired tablet shows the plan and what fits each position, but cannot press.

Passengers boards and deboards the cabin and shows it happening, seat by seat. It appears only on aircraft with passenger seats: the passenger DC-10s, and the riders' seats on the KC-10, the KDC-10 and the DC-10-40 Omega. The cabin is drawn to scale beside three tabs: **Boarding**, **Rating** and **Service**.

blocks.alt: The Passengers app on a passenger DC-10-30, landscape, during boarding: the cabin seat map with gray empty seats, blue seats with someone coming for them, green seated passengers and amber dots walking the aisles; doors 1L and 2L green (usable); the Boarding tab's CABIN card with TO BOARD, ABOARD and STANDING counts, weight and time left, the Board, Stop and Board now buttons, and the PLAN card with per-class counts, Empty/Half/Typical/Full and the boarding order choice.
blocks.title: Passengers app

blocks.content: **Boarding tab.** CABIN shows the job and who is boarding (by the ground crew or by GSX), TO BOARD, ABOARD and STANDING in the cabin's colors, the weight aboard and the time left, with **Board** (or **Resume boarding**), **Deboard**, **Stop** (and **Cancel** while stopped), **Board now** and **Deboard now**. PLAN sets the passengers per class with steps of 1 and 10, the presets **Empty**, **Half**, **Typical** and **Full**, and the boarding order (**Random**, **Back to front**, **Window first**). DOORS lists only a door with something to say; with none usable it says how to fix it and offers Ground Ops. Board sends the plan shown with the press, so the cabin boards what the page shows.

Passengers walk in through the **usable doors**: a cabin door that is open with stairs or a jetway at it. Without GSX, set stairs at door 1L or 1R on the Services page and open the door on the Doors page. With GSX in use, GSX brings the stairs or jetway and Board calls GSX's own boarding, so only an open door is owed; a shut one holds the job and the DOORS hint says to open 1L. The KC-10's riders always board with the EFB's own ground crew.

**Rating tab.** With **Simulate passengers** on (here or in Settings), the passengers feel the flight. COMFORT shows each occupied zone's air in the words of the thermal comfort standard and the percentage unhappy (neutral and 5 % between 63 and 75 °F), and the ride; the cabin altitude and rate, with amber or red lines for ears, masks and airsickness. A review scores the flight and lists the passengers' comments, and COMPLAINTS lists each one with its seat and zone. A passenger taken ill (hypoxia, cold, heat) is listed under MEDICAL and drawn in their condition's color. With the simulation off, the passengers are weight only.

**Service tab.** Present only on a passenger cabin, with the passengers simulated, the cabin service on in Virtual Crew and the flight attendants off AUTO. It is the purser's station: tap an attendant on the cabin drawing and a wheel offers them tasks (drinks, meals, coffee, trays, the ovens and water heaters, answering calls, first aid, cabin preparation) and the zone to do them in. Galleys are stocked by catering from Ground Ops. See [Virtual Crew](virtual-crew).

sections.title: Performance
sections.summary: Takeoff and landing data and en-route performance from the aircraft's own performance manuals, computed the way the books work them.

blocks.content: Performance is the flight engineer's performance manual and TOLD card (takeoff and landing data) in the tablet. It has seven pages under tabs: **Takeoff**, **Climb**, **Cruise**, **Holding**, **Descent**, **Approach** and **Landing**. Each page computes for the airframe loaded, and an answer calculated for one airframe is not shown on another's page. The numbers are the manuals' own charts and tables, read cell by cell and curve by curve, and evaluated the way the manuals' worked examples evaluate them; where a book has no chart for an airframe, the page says how it fills the gap (below).

blocks.alt: The Performance app's Takeoff page, landscape, on a DC-10-30 after Calculate Performance: the Clear Data, Pull Aircraft Data and Calculate Performance buttons at the top; TAKEOFF CONDITIONS filled (APT KMEM, RWY 36L, GW 520.0, CG 26, OAT +20, PA +250, wind, RWY HDG, RWY AVAIL, slope, RCR, anti-ice Off, AC Off, reverse thrust Yes, TO THRUST Reduced, RETURN FLAP 35); TAKEOFF COMPUTATIONS (X-WIND, COMP, CALC, CL GR, EFL, 5 RALW, 25 CGLW, MTOGW, FLAP, ASSUMED TEMP, TSLW, VMCG, VCEF, VMBE, VR, VRMIN, V2, MAX BRAKE TEMP, BRAKE ZONE); the TOLD CARD with GW, FLAPS, N1 and ASSUMED TEMP, the six big SPEEDS (V1, VR, V2, VFR, VSR, 0/RET VMM), STAB and ACCEL HT; Set Bugs at the foot.
blocks.title: Performance, Takeoff page

blocks.content: The long-wing aircraft use the KC-10A's performance manual, T.O. 1C-10(K)A-1-1, written for the same wing and CF6-50C2 engines the DC-10-30 and MD-10-30 carry. The short-wing aircraft use the FedEx DC-10 Flight Manual's Series 10 performance chapter. Every chart was digitized from the manuals' own artwork and every table read from its text, to within about half a knot on a speed and a few feet on a distance of the printed lines. Each was then checked against the manuals' worked examples: some 360 charts and more than 1,300 checks, all passing. Where a chart runs off its printed frame the page clamps to the edge and flags the cell rather than extrapolating.

blocks.title: Data by airframe
rows: KC-10 manual at an equivalent condition
KC-10 manual, thrust carried to the JT9D
EPR, from the thrust rating computer's own tables
KC-10 manual at an equivalent condition; FedEx N1, stabilizer trim, 0/RET minimum maneuver speed and emergency return
FedEx Series 10, including its Quick Reference Landing Data
As the -10, on the CF6-50's thrust
FedEx Series 10 tables, the N1 carried to the CF6-50C2

blocks.title: DC-10-10, -15, -40 and MD-10-10 takeoff limits
blocks.content: No manual available to the simulation gives field lengths or takeoff limit weights for the short-wing aircraft or the DC-10-40. Their takeoff limits are therefore read from the KC-10's charts at an equivalent condition: speeds read at the same weight (the FedEx Series 10 speeds sit within 2 % of the KC-10's there), field-limited weight scaled by the square root of the thrust ratio, climb-limited weight by the thrust ratio (and on the short span by its poorer engine-out lift-to-drag), minimum control speeds by the root of the thrust ratio, and, on the aircraft without center gear, brake energy for eight brakes instead of ten. Treat those weights as approximate.

Thrust on the card agrees with the aircraft's **thrust rating computer** (TRC): the card's N1 carries the same bleed and anti-ice corrections the TRC applies (packs off, wing anti-ice, engine anti-ice above 8 °C), so the target the crew read on the card is the one the TRC drums show. On the DC-10-40 the card gives EPR from the TRC's own JT9D tables and offers **ALTN T.O.**, the TRC's alternate takeoff rating. See [Engines](engines) and [Automatic flight](automatic-flight).

Each page has three buttons at its top: **Clear Data** empties its boxes; **Pull Aircraft Data** fills every box the aircraft, the simulator and the route can answer, and says where each value came from; **Calculate Performance** works the page. The boxes a page cannot calculate without carry an accent outline. A blank GW, CG, OAT or PA box takes the aircraft's own reading and shows it. Choice boxes show a preset until one is chosen: anti-ice Off, air conditioning Off, reverse thrust Yes, reduced thrust, three engines, a 25° holding bank, 35/EXT, nothing failed. The Approach and Landing pages share one set of landing-condition boxes, so the destination's conditions are typed once.

blocks.title: What Pull Aircraft Data fills
rows: The aircraft's gross weight and center of gravity
OAT, PA, wind, dew point, field elevation, RCR

On the ground, the aircraft's own readings at the field (within 5 NM of the airport): outside air temperature, pressure altitude, wind, dew point from the humidity, elevation, and a runway condition reading from the surface
The anti-ice and pack switches as set, and the brake temperature gauge
The simulator's METAR for the airport in the APT box (else the route's origin or destination, else on the ground the nearest reporting station)
RWY HDG, RWY AVAIL or RWY LENGTH, SLOPE, ELEV

The runway typed, or the one the aircraft is lined up on, from the simulator's airport database. RWY AVAIL is the runway's full length, with no deduction for lining up: reduce it yourself as the manual requires. On Landing, RWY LENGTH starts past a displaced threshold

blocks.content: **Send to Performance** on Route's Load page fills, on every page at once, what the flight plan knows: the departure airport, runway and its data on Takeoff; the destination and arrival runway on Approach and Landing; the top-of-climb level, ISA deviation and climb wind on Climb; the cruise level and ISA deviation on Cruise; the top-of-descent level, destination elevation and descent wind on Descent. It never fills a weight or the day's conditions; those stay Pull Aircraft Data's. Typed values are kept with the aircraft, and answers are stored with each calculation.

The Takeoff page is the takeoff section of the KC-10's TOLD card worksheet and the TOLD card itself, worked in the manual's order. It answers four questions: how heavy the aircraft may be on this runway today, which flap gives the most weight, how much thrust it needs, and the speeds and trim to fly it.

blocks.title: TAKEOFF CONDITIONS
rows: Airport and runway (for Pull Aircraft Data and the card)
Gross weight in thousands of pounds; CG in percent MAC
Pressure altitude of the field, ft
Direction and speed, with gust (10G16) or VRB
Runway condition reading; standing water depth, inches
The controlling obstacle's height above the departure end of the runway and its distance from it
Packs on or off for takeoff
Yes, or No to use the no-reverse charts
Reduced or Max (DC-10-40: Reduced, ALTN T.O. or Max)
The brake temperature reading, for the brake zone

blocks.title: TAKEOFF COMPUTATIONS and the TOLD card
rows: Crosswind on the gust; head or tail component
The wind the charts are entered with: 150 % of a tailwind including gust, and no headwind credit
The gross climb gradient the obstacle demands, never less than 2.5 %
Equivalent field length: the runway available corrected for slope, wind, CG, runway condition (RCR) and air conditioning and anti-ice bleed, the length the charts are entered with
Runway available limit weight at 5° flaps and climb gradient limit weight at 25° flaps: the two ends of the flap trade
Maximum takeoff gross weight at the optimum flap, and that flap
ASSUMED RALW/TEMP, ASSUMED CGLW/TEMP, ASSUMED TEMP
For reduced thrust: the temperature at which each limit falls to the actual weight, and the lower of the two (never below the flat-rating temperature, else maximum thrust)
Tire speed limit weight (not limiting at 20° flaps and more)
Minimum control speed on the ground; critical engine failure speed; maximum brake energy speed
Maximum allowable weight when VMCG sets V1, on the full runway
Rotation speed and its minimum; takeoff safety speed

The maximum allowable brake temperature at brake release for this takeoff (with BTMS above it, the cooling time is noted); and the energy zone of a rejected-takeoff stop from V1, NORMAL, CAUTION or DANGER, from the BTMS reading (100 °C when none is entered)
GW, FLAPS, N1 (EPR on the -40) and ASSUMED TEMP (the value to set on the TRC; 3 °C lower with engine anti-ice)
V1, VR, V2, VFR (flap retraction), VSR (slat retraction) and the 0/RET minimum maneuver speed
A landing at this field at takeoff weight: distance, RCR, VAPP, TAS, the minimum maneuver speeds and VTH

blocks.content: **How the page works it.** First the wind: the head and tail components and the crosswind on the gust, a variable wind taken at its worst, and the calculation wind. Second the obstacle: the gross gradient it needs at the most limiting flap. Third the runway limit at 5° flaps and the climb limit at 25° flaps. The larger flap shortens the takeoff roll but costs climb gradient; the smaller flap climbs better but needs more runway. The page searches every flap from 5 to 25° for the setting where the lower of the two limits is highest, which is the **optimum flap** and **MTOGW**. If an obstacle limits and MTOGW is short of the gross weight, it applies the manual's optimized solution: it shortens the runway used in steps, which moves the obstacle further out relative to the liftoff point, while MTOGW rises.

**Reduced thrust.** With TO THRUST at Reduced, the page traces the runway and climb limits through the actual gross weight back to their temperatures. The lower of the two is the **assumed temperature**: the hottest day on which the aircraft could still meet both limits at this weight on full thrust. Setting that temperature on the TRC derates the engines to exactly the thrust that day would give, which preserves the limits while saving engine life. It is never set below the flat-rating break; if no reduction is possible, the card is a maximum-thrust card.

**V1.** The decision speed must satisfy three limits at once. It may not be below **VMCG**, or an engine failure before V1 could not be controlled on the ground; it should equal **VCEF**, the speed at which accelerating on to V2 and stopping take the same runway; and it may not exceed **VMBE**, or a stop from V1 would exceed the brakes' energy capacity. The page takes V1 as the higher of VCEF and VMCG, warns if that exceeds VMBE (with the weight to take off, about 3,500 lb a knot), and on a reduced-thrust card lowers the assumed temperature until VMBE is at least VCEF. When VMCG sets V1, it computes **MAW** and warns if the gross weight exceeds it. VR (never below VRMIN) carries its slope, CG and air conditioning corrections and V2 its slope and CG corrections; if V1 exceeds VR, VR is raised to V1. The brake figures assume the stop is made from V1.

**Set Bugs** at the foot of the page writes the card to the electromechanical airspeed indicators of both pilots: bug 1 V1, bug 2 VR, bug 3 VFR, bug 4 VSR, bug 5 the 0/RET minimum maneuver speed, and V2 into the glareshield SPEED select. On an aircraft whose TRC has a T/O FLEX selector (the KC-10, DC-10-30 and DC-10-15), a reduced-thrust card also dials its assumed temperature into the T/O FLEX thumbwheels; selecting the T/O FLEX mode remains the crew's press. A maximum-thrust card leaves the thumbwheels alone. The bugs are written once per press, so the crew can drag them afterwards.

**Send to Avionics** on the MD-10 sends the card to the Pegasus FMS, which types it into its own pages as the crew would: on the TAKEOFF page V1, VR and V2 as crew entries, the flap, OAT, acceleration height and FLEX temperature (a maximum-thrust card sends no FLEX); on WEIGHT INIT the takeoff gross weight and CG, with BLOCK from the fuel aboard (or ZFW, if the crew have typed one); on F-PLN INIT the flight number, cruise level, cost index and alternate from the SimBrief plan loaded through Route. A value a page refuses shows that page's own message on the MCDU. Each PFD then draws its own seat's FMS takeoff speeds.

Not computed: the worksheet's configuration changes (center gear retracted, a wheel brake or anti-skid inoperative), shown as N/A; the mission-accomplishment headwind credit, never taken on takeoff; drag index deviations; windshear takeoff speeds.
The en-route pages answer the dispatcher's questions for the flight plan, from the manuals' tables.

rows: Start GW, start and top-of-climb altitude, ISA deviation, wind; on the long wing also engines (3 or 2), schedule (normal or derated) and drag index, on the short wing the field elevation

Fuel, distance and time to climb from brake release (the takeoff allowance included) or from an altitude for a climb begun in flight, the weight at top of climb, the climb schedule and N1 (EPR on the -40); the service ceiling (long wing) or maximum recommended weight (short wing) and the optimum altitude
GW, cruise altitude, ISA deviation; CG on the long wing, the schedule (long-range cruise or Mach 0.82 to 0.85) and ice protection on the short wing

Long wing, at Mach 0.82 on three engines: N1, IAS, TAS, fuel flow per engine and total, nautical miles per 1,000 lb, maximum continuous thrust; optimum altitude and the next 4,000 ft step; buffet margin corrected for CG. Short wing: the same for the schedule chosen, with the cruise thrust limit, maximum recommended weight and 1.3 g buffet
GW, hold altitude, ISA deviation, engines, time and fuel available; on the long wing the turn bank and drag index, on the short wing the slats, ice protection and pattern
Holding speed (on the long wing for the legs and for the turns), fuel flow, endurance, and fuel for the time

Schedule (long range, en route or penetration on the long wing; low or high speed on the short wing), from altitude, to altitude (destination elevation on the short wing), wind; drag index on the long wing
Fuel, time, distance and rate of descent, and the speed schedule

blocks.content: The Approach and Landing pages finish the TOLD card for the destination. **Approach** gives the approach and minimum maneuver speeds, the threshold speeds for each flap setting, the wind components, the go-around N1 and the single-engine speeds. **Landing** gives the runway and configuration, the landing distance and the card. Both, and the Takeoff page's emergency return, compute through the same routine, so the same conditions give the same speeds and distances on all three. On the ground, OAT and PA come from the aircraft (an emergency return to this field); in flight they are the destination's, and PA can be worked from the field elevation and the altimeter setting.

blocks.alt: The Performance app's Landing page, landscape, after Calculate Performance for KLAX runway 25L at 380,000 lb: LANDING CONDITIONS, the RUNWAY and CONFIGURATION groups (flaps/slats 35/EXT, center gear, brakes, anti-skid, spoilers, wing reversers, dual hydraulic failure No), LANDING DISTANCE with FLARE, GROUND ROLL and LDG DIST, the RWY MARGIN, and the TOLD CARD - LANDING with VAPP, VTH and the minimum maneuver speeds; Set Bugs at the foot.
blocks.title: Performance, Landing page

blocks.content: **Approach speed.** VAPP is the threshold speed plus the full gust increment and half the steady wind above 20 kt, at most 20 kt added; TAS is VAPP corrected for density altitude. **Landing distance** is the flare distance plus the ground roll at 35 or 50° flaps, the roll corrected for the speed additive, the calculation wind, downhill slope and the stopping distance ratio at the runway condition. An abnormal configuration enters as an **equivalent RCR**: center gear retracted, a wheel brake, anti-skid or the spoilers inoperative each lower the effective runway condition, and several at once take the lowest. Other flap and slat settings go through the 50/EXT distance and the manual's correction charts; a dual hydraulic failure multiplies the 50/EXT roll; a deactivated wing reverser adds 10 % to the roll. Standing water over 0.10 inch lands at RCR 6, and a wet runway is taken at RCR 12 at best. The page checks the touchdown ground speed against the 204 kt tire limit and the maximum brake energy speed, and the landing weight against the maximum landing weight (436,000 lb on the KC-10, less with anti-skid inoperative or the center gear up). Headwind and uphill-slope credit are taken only with MISSION ACCOMPL. set to Yes.

**Short-wing aircraft.** The DC-10-10, -15 and MD-10-10 work Approach and Landing from the FedEx Series 10 tables instead: VREF and the minimum maneuver speeds by setting, VAPP the greater of VREF + 5 kt and VREF plus the wind additive (the larger of half the steady wind above 20 kt and the full gust, at most 20 kt), and the landing distance from the Quick Reference Landing Data at medium braking, dry or wet, at flaps 35 or 50. The maximum landing weight is 363,500 lb at flaps 35 and 375,000 lb at flaps 50.

**Set Bugs** on the Landing page sets bug 1 back to its rest position (60 kt) and bugs 2 to 5 to the threshold speed and the 22/EXT, 0/EXT and 0/RET minimum maneuver speeds, lowest first. The bugs cannot pass one another on the dial, so they are set in speed order. The SPEED select is left for the crew.

Set Bugs drives the speed bugs of the electromechanical airspeed indicators. Glass primary flight displays (the MD-10's PFDs and the DC-10's optional flat-panel displays) keep their speed references in their own systems: set them there.

sections.title: Mission apps
sections.summary: Air Refuel on the air refueling tankers and Fire Support on the air tankers.

blocks.content: Two apps belong to the mission aircraft and appear only on them. They never share an aircraft, so each takes the slot after Performance on the Home screen.

Air Refuel is on the KC-10 and the KDC-10. At its top is the **ARO Input** switch, which hands the boom operator control of the aircraft through the autopilot; under it are two pages, **Aircraft Control** and **Refueling Setup**. The top stays in view while a page scrolls. The air refueling systems and procedures themselves are in [Air refueling systems](air-refueling-systems) and [Air refueling](air-refueling).

blocks.alt: The Air Refuel app on the KC-10, landscape: the ARO Input card at the top showing the boom in control; the Aircraft Control page with the four FMA windows and the flight data under them, the SPEED, HEADING, ALTITUDE and V/S boxes with their knob buttons (Pull SPD, Pull SEL, Push HOLD, Pull ARM, ALT HOLD), the bank limit, the square mode keys and the AP levers and ATS.
blocks.title: Air Refuel app

rows: Gives the boom operator the aircraft through the autopilot, or takes it back. Shown as the aircraft reports it: off, the boom, refused (the autopilot was not in CMD; switch off and on again), or the autopilot lost

A copy of the glareshield autopilot panel: the four FMA windows with attitude, Mach and the flight data under them; SPEED, HEADING, ALTITUDE and V/S typed (Enter or leaving the box sends; an altitude under 1,000 is a flight level), with the aircraft's reading under each and their knob actions; the bank limit; the mode keys, green while the FMA shows their mode; the autopilot levers and the ATS

The receivers of the KC-10's air refueling tables, for the boom and on the KC-10 the drogue. Choosing a boom receiver sets the ARO panel at once: the three disconnect limit knobs and RCVR DISC DELAY. The page reads the panel back, says when it differs from the receiver, and offers **Set ARO**. Under it, the receiver's data, optimum refueling altitude first, and notes. A drogue receiver sets nothing

blocks.content: If the autopilot drops out while the boom operator has the controls, the stick stays with the boom: the ARO Input card turns red and a banner says so over every app. Nothing hands the controls back by itself. Press **Return controls to the cockpit** on the card (or **Return controls** on the banner) to give them back to the pilots.

Fire Support is on the DC-10-10 and DC-10-30 Tankers. It loads the three retardant tanks, forward, center and aft, of 2,700, 4,000 and 2,700 US gallons. The tanks and the drop system are described in [Aerial firefighting](aerial-firefighting).

rows: **Retardant** (LC-95A-Fx, 9.01 lb per US gallon) or **Water** (8.34 lb per US gallon), written at the press. On the ground the tanks are reloaded as the new product with their gallons kept

A target per tank, dragged in tens of gallons or typed, and a total, which **Distribute** or Enter spreads in proportion to the tanks' capacities so the load's center stays where a full load's is. **Full** and **Empty** set every target
Loads each changed tank at once. Nothing reaches the tanks before it. **Reset** drops the targets
The gallons, their weight and the gross weight, now and after the load; an amber line when the simulator's payload is not carrying the tanks' weight

blocks.content: Loading is on the ground only, gated like Ground Ops: grayed in the air, moving or off pavement, and the targets are dropped when the gate closes.

blocks.alt: The Fire Support app on a DC-10-10 Tanker, portrait: the Product choice (Retardant selected), the Load total with Distribute, Full and Empty, the three tank rows (FWD tank, CTR tank, AFT tank) with sliders and gallons, the Reset and Load buttons, and the readouts of gallons, weight and gross weight now and after the load.
blocks.title: Fire Support app

sections.title: Systems, Documents and Web
sections.summary: The live system diagrams, the checklists, and a web browser.

blocks.content: Systems shows the aircraft's systems as diagrams drawn live from the simulation, with monitor tables of the values behind them. It is a maintenance engineer's view rather than a flight deck instrument: it shows quantities no gauge on the panel shows (a pump's flow, a duct's temperature, a bus's current), so use it to understand what a system is doing, not as a replacement for the panel. A rail on the left lists twelve systems in five groups:

items: **Engines** and **APU**, drawn as cutaways. The engine page draws one engine (ENG 1, 2 or 3) with its gas path in the color of its own temperature, blue cold to red hot, as bright as its spools turn, and arrows of air moving down the core and the bypass; a second view shows the oil and gearbox side. In a compressor stall the arrows over the stalled stages stutter in amber; in a surge the core's arrows turn forward in red. The JT9D on the DC-10-40 is drawn with its own stage counts. The APU page draws the APU in section with its bleed valves and the flight engineer's APU lamps beneath.

**Electrical**, **Hydraulics**, **Pneumatics** and **Fuel**. The hydraulic page follows the hydraulic systems block diagram of the operator's manual (engines at the foot, the users in rows, the reversible motor pumps between systems); the electrical page follows the flight engineer's panel layout (generators at the foot, the AC tie bus across the middle, DC above).
**Air Conditioning**, **Water**, **Oxygen** and **Ice & Rain**. The ice page also shows the simulator's own structural ice where the aircraft is not keeping a surface clear.
**Landing Gear**.
**Air Data**, drawn as the pitot-static system diagram, with the instruments' readings.

blocks.content: Color means state and nothing else: green live, amber off-normal, red failed, gray at rest, blue armed or a level, and dashed gray with a dash where there is no data. A line's identity is written beside it, never coded by color. While Systems is open the aircraft sends the open page's data; an amber line says when nothing is arriving. The open system is shared with paired screens; the engine and view are each screen's own.

blocks.alt: The Systems app, portrait, on the Hydraulics page of a DC-10-30 with engines running: the rail of twelve systems on the left, the block diagram with the three engine-driven pump pairs at the foot, the three systems in green, the 1-3 and 2-3 reversible motor pumps, and the users in rows; under it the monitor tables of pressures, quantities, temperatures and flows.
blocks.title: Systems app, hydraulics page

blocks.content: Documents opens on two icons, **Checklist** and **Manual**, with a box headed **IMPORTED** beneath them for the crew's own documents. The Manual icon and the Imported box are reserved for later versions; Checklist is the aircraft's normal checklist.

**The checklist** is each family's normal checklist as its book prints it: on the DC-10 the FedEx normal checklist card, on the KC-10 the pilot's and flight engineer's abbreviated normal checklist, on the MD-10 the FCOM's normal checklists. Ahead of the book's checklists comes **PREFLIGHT**: the same books' preflight procedures from arriving at the aircraft to the first checklist, cut to the actions done to the aircraft, with the steps behind a vague CHECK or SET written out under the item. The DC-10 checklist adds the flight manual's STARTING ENGINES and PASSING 10,000 FT pages, the KC-10's BEFORE TAXI, and a LEAVING AIRCRAFT checklist. The full expanded procedures are in [Normal procedures](normal-procedures).

blocks.alt: The Documents app showing the DC-10's BEFORE START checklist, portrait: the checklist title with Start and Reset at the top, the run strip naming the item and who has it (S/O) with Stop, the items with their responses and crew letters, several ticked, the active item as a light green row, an item's dropdown open showing its steps, Takeoff Data with its Go to Performance button, and Previous and Next at the foot.
blocks.title: Documents, a checklist page
Checklist controls
rows: Opens a checklist. COMPLETE marks one with every item ticked
With a Virtual Crew seat on MANUAL or AUTO: starts the crew's run of the checklist and opens it
While a run is on: nothing more is begun or moved until Resume
The item in hand, who has it (S/O, F/O, CAPT; FE, CP, P on the KC-10), and a note if a step failed; Stop ends the run
Press to tick or untick. The item being worked, or watched, is a light green row
Unfolds the steps behind the item (or a walkaround area's points); does not tick it
On BEFORE START's Takeoff Data and IN RANGE's Airspeed Bugs (and the equivalent items on the other books): opens Performance at the takeoff or landing page
Clears every checklist's ticks, after a confirmation
Step through the checklists in order

blocks.content: Ticks are shared by every screen and kept with the aircraft, so they survive closing the app and restarting the simulator. Once Performance's Set Bugs has been pressed, the blanks it can answer are filled in: the gross weight on BEFORE START, the flaps and trim on BEFORE TAKEOFF, the landing flaps on BEFORE LANDING. Items below the line are shown apart under BELOW THE LINE, as the book prints them.

Web is a web browser for the flight deck tablet. The page is rendered by a real browser engine that Infinity Manager runs on your computer, and the tablet draws its pictures and sends your clicks back, so any site works as it does on the desktop. The toolbar has **Back**, **Forward**, **Reload** (Stop while a page loads), the address box (words are a search, anything with a dot is an address) and the keyboard. A click on the page is a click; a drag scrolls. When a text field on the page is selected, a field bar shows its label, a box for the physical keyboard, the on-screen keyboard and **Done**. **Clear Data** in the header clears cookies, the cache and the site's storage, after a confirmation.

The browser belongs to the flight deck's tablet. The page stays open while you use other apps, and reopening Web returns to it; a session left idle for 15 minutes is closed and the next opens at the last address. Sound is muted. Paired tablets and the boom operator's tablet show where the browser is instead. Web needs Infinity Manager running and a Chromium-based browser (Edge or Chrome) installed on the computer; without one it reports the browser unavailable after about 35 seconds.

sections.title: Failures
sections.summary: Inject, schedule and clear failures drawn from the emergency and abnormal checklists; pop and reset circuit breakers; repair the aircraft.

blocks.content: Failures is the instructor's station. Its failures are drawn from the emergency and abnormal checklists of the KC-10 flight manual, less air refueling and the equipment only the KC-10 carries, so every failure you inject is tied to a checklist; this manual's procedures are in [Emergency procedures](emergency-procedures) and [Abnormal procedures](abnormal-procedures). A failure fails a real component in the simulation, a pump, a valve, a bearing, a sensor, and the aircraft then shows it the way it would: the lights, the gauges, the behavior that follows. The app lists only what the aircraft loaded has: the center gear and the center auxiliary tank where fitted, the units only the KC-10 has or lacks, and on the MD-10 nothing that belongs to the flight engineer's panel.

A rail on the left, which opens on hover, lists the **Overview**, **Random Failures**, and a page for each system section. The Overview is available on every edition of the aircraft; the Random page and the system sections are part of the Professional edition and above. Below Professional the rail is not drawn.

blocks.alt: The Failures app's Overview, landscape: the side rail open with Overview, Random Failures and the twelve system sections (AC, ICE, ELEC, FIRE, FLT, FUEL, HYD, GEAR, PNEU, ENG, PRES, MISC); the ACTIONS card with Clear All, Reset Breakers and Reset Aircraft; SCHEDULED FAILURES listing Engine 2 failure armed at V1 142 kt with Fail now and Disarm; ACTIVE FAILURES with System 1 leak and Hide; POPPED BREAKERS with one popped and one pulled breaker.
blocks.title: Failures, Overview

rows: Clears every active and scheduled failure (after a confirmation). Clearing a failure removes its cause; damage it has already done, such as lost oil or a seized engine, stays until Reset Aircraft, and a breaker it popped stays out until it is reset
Pushes every circuit breaker that is out back in, including the ones the crew pulled (after a confirmation). A breaker whose failure is still active pops again

Repairs the aircraft's wear and damage at once (after a confirmation): engine bearing wear, a seized rotor, lost oil, hot-section damage and blade damage; APU oil and overspeed trips; CSDs reconnected and generator bearings; an overheated transformer-rectifier or inverter; brake heat and wear, tires and a collapsed gear leg; lost hydraulic fluid; spent fire bottles; oxygen bottles, dropped masks and spent generators; deployed slides; and on the KC-10 a parted boom hoist cable and jettisoned hoses. It leaves fuel, payload, water, battery charge, breakers and the active failures alone, so a failure still active goes on failing
Each armed failure with its trigger, **Fail now** and **Disarm**
Each failure in force. **Hide** draws the lists as black bars, for a surprise
Every circuit breaker that is out, marked Popped (by a failure or an overload) or Pulled (by the crew), with its own Hide

blocks.content: A short circuit behind a breaker pops it, and it pops again after every reset while the cause stands, as a real breaker would. An overload pops a breaker the same way. The lists are kept by the flight deck's tablet and are not kept across a reload of the aircraft.

Open a system section and press a failure to open its sheet. If the failure applies to one of several units (an engine, a generator, a hydraulic system, a side), pick the unit first. Then either press **Fail now**, or set a trigger under SCHEDULE and press **Arm**. On a failure already in force the sheet offers **Clear failure**; on an armed one, **Fail now** and **Disarm**.

blocks.title: Triggers
rows: Climbing or descending through an altitude
DIRECTION, ALTITUDE (feet, or a flight level)
Accelerating or slowing through an indicated airspeed
On the takeoff roll at V1
V1 (KT); blank takes the V1 of the last Performance takeoff card
At liftoff, approach, touchdown or cruise

blocks.content: The phases are read from the aircraft's motion: **liftoff** and **touchdown** when the aircraft leaves or meets the ground above 50 kt; **approach** when it is airborne, descending at 300 ft/min or more, through 3,000 ft above the ground; **cruise** after a minute within 300 ft/min of level flight at FL180 or above.

**Random Failures** sets up failures the aircraft chooses: the switch, START AFTER (MIN), EVERY (MIN) FROM and TO, MAX FAILURES, WHEN (any time, in flight, on the ground), and the sections covered, chosen with **Edit**.
The random failure setup is stored but does not yet fail anything. Schedule failures individually for now.

Once armed or in force, a failure with units is listed under a title naming its unit, for example Engine 2 failure or System 1 leak. On the MD-10, fly the equivalent MD-10 procedure in Sections 2 and 3. The Section column links to the chapter that holds the procedure; the app badges the emergency ones EMER. Most failures map one to one onto a component: a pump, a heater, a valve, a sensor. Some conditions have several possible causes, and the simulation fails the one the checklist is written around. Knowing which helps you read the indications:

columns: What fails, and how it shows
rows: Generator off line, loss of all generators
Loss of field excitation: the generator trips off line and its GEN OFF light comes on

The generator's main bearing fails. GEN FAIL lights and the machine stays on line on its auxiliary bearing; GEN FAIL RESET relights it at once, which is how the crew tell a real failure from a spurious one. After about five hours on the auxiliary bearing it seizes
Generator frequency high; CSD oil temperature high; CSD oil pressure low
CSD governor drift; a blocked CSD oil cooler; a CSD oil leak

A fire in the core bay: ENGINE FIRE, the handle and fuel lever lights, both loop lights and the bell. It burns while a firewall shutoff is open and smoulders for about 3 minutes after the handle has shut them. A fire under a minute old when the first bottle is fired takes one bottle; an older one re-flashes once and takes the second
APU FIRE, both APU loop lights, and the APU shuts itself down. On the DC-10 and KC-10 the fire goes out once the shutdown has cut its fuel
Fuel burning in the tailpipe of a stopped or starting engine: EGT rises with no fire warning; motoring with the fuel lever off purges it within about 30 seconds

Oil smoke in one bleed source's air reaches the cabin smoke detectors at the cabin's own air change rate, about 3 minutes. Shutting that source off clears the air over minutes, the light some minutes later
Flaps fail to move as selected, one side

That side's drive disconnects; the other runs on until the skew brake stops it just under 6° of asymmetry and FLAP DISAGREE lights. Returning the handle to the last symmetrical position brings them back into line
Flaps fail to move as selected, both sides
The flap control valve jams: the flaps hold and the command pointers follow the handle
Damaged front compressor blades: at cruise the engine surges, bangs and rolls back with EGT rising; idle clears it, and a slow advance brings it back
Oil pressure low; oil quantity abnormal
An oil leak: pressure falls as the tank empties, temperature climbs as less oil carries heat away, and a dry engine wears toward seizure. An external loss shows in quantity first
Oil jets restricted below the transmitter: the pressure rises at once and the starved bearing wears toward failure in about two hours at cruise unless the engine is shut down
Contaminated fuel loads the filter: FUEL FILTER PRESS DROP (ICING on the -40) in about 5 minutes at cruise, then the bypass opens and the engine runs on
The platform is lost. Clearing the failure does not restore it: the unit must realign from cold, so in the air it does not navigate again that flight
FLOW OFF only, the platform navigating on; the unit's thermal cutout takes it about 12 minutes later
The crew's input to all three axes is lost: the aircraft stops following the yoke and pedals, while the autopilot in CMD still flies
Gear handle will not move up
The nose gear's ground-sensing mechanism sticks in GROUND: the anti-retraction lock holds the handle until GEAR HANDLE REL, and the systems that read the ground shift stay in ground mode
Tank 1's fill float fails: a transfer into a full tank 1 runs on into the vent box, lighting TANK OVERFILLED; the FILL switch stops it
Every unit's locks fail: units roll with the deck until they meet the next or the compartment end, and the CG moves with them

sections.title: Configuration and Settings
sections.summary: The equipment fit, the aircraft setup choices, and the settings, including those that change how the aircraft behaves.

blocks.content: Configuration has three pages under tabs: **Keybinds**, **Aircraft Configuration** and **Aircraft Setup**. Keybinds is reserved for the crew's own control bindings in a later version.

**Aircraft Configuration** chooses the equipment fitted to a DC-10 flight deck, the same choices Infinity Manager's equipment page offers: which attitude and heading instruments, radar altimeter, DME and ADF displays, navigation systems, radios, transponders, engine instruments, fuel gauges and the rest. The choices are grouped by the flight deck's zones, **Glareshield**, **Pilots' Panels**, **Centre Panel**, **Pedestal** and **Engineer**, and a zone is chosen on a line drawing of the flight deck: press a zone's label or its panel, and its categories are listed, each as one row with its choice at the row's end. The flight engineer's station is behind the viewer, so its label sits at the drawing's lower right with an arrow toward it; the Engineer zone also holds the airframe's range options (the extended-range tank) and firefighting equipment. A selection waits for the aircraft to report the change (8 seconds at most), with the pressed option ringed meanwhile; a refusal is shown under the title.
The KC-10A and the MD-10s have fixed flight decks, so their Configuration app has no Aircraft Configuration page and opens on Aircraft Setup.

blocks.alt: The Configuration app's Aircraft Configuration page on a DC-10-30, landscape: the underlined tabs Keybinds, Aircraft Configuration and Aircraft Setup; the line drawing of the DC-10 flight deck with the Pedestal zone's lines lit white and the others dimmed, the Engineer label at lower right with its arrow; beside it the Pedestal zone's rows (Navigation Systems, PMS, VHF Radios, ADF Radios, Transponders, Selcal Options), each with its choice at the row's end.
blocks.title: Configuration, Aircraft Configuration
Aircraft Setup
rows: The family's radios other than VHF-1: VHF-2, VHF-3, HF-1, HF-2 (DC-10); VHF-2, UHF-1, UHF-2, HF-1, HF-2 (KC-10); VHF-2, VHF-3 (MD-10)

The simulator has two COM radios and the flight deck more. VHF-1 is always the simulator's COM1; this selects which of the aircraft's other radios the simulator's COM2 follows, for ATC and online networks. A radio this aircraft does not carry falls back to VHF-2. Shown as the aircraft resolved it. Not kept across a reload: a fresh load starts on VHF-2
Stored with the EFB for each family. No aircraft system reads it yet: the DC-10s and KC-10 are modeled with tri-metallic brakes and the MD-10s with carbon

blocks.content: Settings is a list of groups. A choice made on any screen reaches the flight deck, and the settings that belong to the aircraft are shown as the aircraft reports them, so a row never shows a press the aircraft did not take.

blocks.alt: The Settings app, portrait: BRIGHTNESS with the slider and Auto-Brightness on (Daylight outside.); APPEARANCE with the accent color swatches; TEXT ENTRY with the on-screen keyboard switch; LINK with Manager, This screen, Use GSX and the SimBrief username with its Edit button; AIRCRAFT with the aircraft name, Navigation data (MSFS, Navigraph), INS alignment (Realistic, Instant), Simulate passengers and Realism.
blocks.title: Settings
Settings
rows: Dims the screen with a dark veil over it

Follows the light outside on the same photocell the flight deck's displays dim on. The slider then sets the brightness for the light it is moved in, so a day and a night level are each kept: 100 % and 20 % out of the box
The keyboard docked under the screen while a box is selected (flight deck tablet only)

Ground services from GSX Pro's vehicles and crews instead of the EFB's: ground power, stairs, catering, lavatory, cleaning, de-icing, refueling, cargo and passenger boarding, and GSX's pushback. Takes a press only while GSX is running. Turning it off restarts GSX, so its vehicles, crews and anything GSX placed leave. See [GSX](ground-operations#gsx)
Used by Route's Load from SimBrief, the Navlog, the Fuel page's SimBrief and Performance. Press **Edit** to change it; Enter or **Save** keeps it, **Cancel** leaves it
The database the aircraft's map, navaids and flight plans use. If the one chosen is not available, the row says which is in use. On the MD-10 the MCDU's MENU, NAV DATA changes the same setting

Instant removes the waiting from every inertial alignment, the DC-10's INS and AINS platforms, the KC-10's INUs and the MD-10's ADIRUs, and from the AINS-70's DATA SEARCH. Everything else still counts: the mode selectors must be turned, the present position entered (and its latitude check passed), and the aircraft kept stationary
On, passengers feel the flight (comfort, complaints, illness, a review) and the cabin service runs. Off, passengers and cargo are weight only
Stored for a later version; no aircraft system reads it yet

blocks.content: **Settings that change the aircraft elsewhere.** The Virtual Crew seats (OFF, MANUAL, AUTO), the cruise CG target and the flight attendants' mode are set in the Virtual Crew app and kept with the aircraft; see [Virtual Crew](virtual-crew). The pushback provider chosen on Ground Ops' Pushback page is kept with the EFB.

blocks.title: INS alignment, Realistic
blocks.content: On Realistic an inertial platform takes its real time to align: some twelve to thirteen stationary minutes for a full alignment. Plan the cockpit preparation around it, or choose Instant. An aircraft loaded in the air, on a runway or with an engine running arrives with its platforms already aligned. See [Navigation](navigation).

sections.title: Using the EFB: procedures
sections.summary: Step by step: plan a flight, load fuel, cargo and passengers, compute takeoff data, run a checklist, call ground services, and practice a failure.

blocks.content: These procedures use the EFB from the flight deck's tablet. Any step can be done from a paired tablet instead, except the Cargo presses, Ground Ops' GSX requests and the GSX menu. The aircraft's own procedures, which these support, are in [Normal procedures](normal-procedures).
**Objective:** take a SimBrief flight plan from the gate to a calculated TOLD card, with the route, fuel and payload in the aircraft.

items: Prepare the OFP on SimBrief for this aircraft type and route.
**Settings**: check the SimBrief username, the navigation data (MSFS or Navigraph) and the INS alignment choice.

**Route**, Load page: press **Load from SimBrief**. Wait for the badge to read LOADED, then do the next step the accent line gives on the navigation unit (for example ROUTE DEFINITION on the AINS-70, ACTIVATE and EXEC on the KC-10 FMS, the ACARS uplink on the MD-10).
**Route**, Navlog page: review the route, levels and fuel against the OFP.
**Route**, Load page: press **Send to Performance** to put the airports, runways and levels into Performance.
Load the fuel ([Load fuel](#load-fuel)), the cargo ([Load cargo](#load-cargo)) and, on a passenger aircraft, the passengers ([Board passengers](#board-passengers)).
Check the gross weight and CG on the Home screen's WEIGHTS widget and the Fuel page against [Limitations](limitations).
Compute the takeoff data ([Compute takeoff data](#compute-takeoff-data)).
Open **Ground Ops**, **Fuel**. The aircraft must be stopped on a paved surface.
Enter the block fuel in BLOCK LB, or press **SimBrief** to fetch the plan's ramp fuel.
Press **Distribute** (or Enter). Each tank's target is set by the aircraft's loading schedule.
Adjust any tank by dragging its slider or typing its TARGET LB, if the plan needs it.
Check FUEL, GW and CG after the load.

For a refuel through the panel, make sure the aircraft's ground service bus is powered (ground power or the APU), then press **Refuel**. The REFUELING group shows progress, flow and time to go. To stop early, press **Cancel refuel**; Refuel resumes it.
For an immediate load, or to remove fuel, press **Instant**.

blocks.content: With GSX in use, **Call truck** on the Fuel page calls GSX's refueling instead; the fuel GSX's truck delivers is taken into the aircraft's tanks.

items: Set the parking brake or put the chocks in (Ground Ops, Ramp), with every engine shut down and no tug connected.
Open **Cargo**. Press **Load Cargo** and choose a preset or a saved plan, or plan unit by unit: press a position, choose the option and the unit model, set its weight and contents.
Clear every issue the panel lists.
Open the cargo doors the load needs (Ground Ops, Doors), and keep the aircraft powered (ground power or the APU): a hold whose handling loses power holds its powered units until power returns.
Press **Start load** for the crew to roll the units in, or **Load now** on a hold for an immediate load. With GSX in use, Start load calls GSX's loaders.

Watch the decks turn from blue to amber to green. If the work holds, read the hold's status line: a tail-tip hold, no handling power, an emergency stop for an interlock, or a blocked path. A refused press is said in one line at the top.
Close the cargo doors when loading is complete.

Without GSX: on **Ground Ops**, **Services**, set **Stairs** at door 1L (and 1R if wanted); on **Doors**, open the door. With GSX: request GSX's boarding with Board in step 4; GSX brings the stairs or jetway, and you open the door.
Open **Passengers**, Boarding tab. In PLAN, set the passengers per class (or a preset) and the boarding order.
Check DOORS: at least one usable door.
Press **Board**, or **Board now** to seat everyone at once.
When ABOARD equals the plan, close the doors and arm the slides (Doors page, **Arm all**, or the cabin's own handles).
Open **Performance**, **Takeoff**. If Route's Send to Performance was not used, enter APT and RWY.
Press **Pull Aircraft Data**. Check each value it filled, and the line telling where it came from.
Complete the boxes it could not fill: the obstacle, the anti-ice and packs for takeoff, reverse thrust, the thrust (Reduced or Max), the return flap. Outlined boxes are required.
Press **Calculate Performance**.
Check that MTOGW is at or above GW, that RWY REQ'D is within RWY AVAIL, that no warning is shown (for example a MAW below GW when VMCG sets V1), and that the BRAKE ZONE allows the takeoff.
Copy the card to Notes or the checklist as the crew practice requires.

DC-10 and KC-10: press **Set Bugs**. Check both airspeed indicators' bugs and the SPEED select; on a reduced-thrust card check the T/O FLEX thumbwheels on the TRC, then select its T/O FLEX mode. On the DC-10-10 and -40, whose TRCs have no assumed-temperature selector, set the card's N1 or EPR by hand.
MD-10: press **Send to Avionics**, then check the FMS TAKEOFF and WEIGHT INIT pages on the MCDU and the speeds on both PFDs.
Set the stabilizer trim to the card's STAB and the flaps to its FLAP before takeoff, as the BEFORE TAKEOFF checklist requires.
Open **Documents**, then **Checklist**. The index lists PREFLIGHT and the book's checklists, each with **View** (and **Start** when a Virtual Crew seat is on MANUAL or AUTO).

Without the Virtual Crew: press **View**, read each item, do it, and press its row to tick it. Unfold an item's dropdown to see the steps behind it. The checklist reads COMPLETE when every item is ticked; **Next** opens the following one.

With the Virtual Crew on MANUAL: press **Start**. The run strip shows which item is being worked and by whom; the crew move their own switches and tick their own items. Tick the captain's items yourself as you do them. **Pause** holds the run; **Stop** ends it.
With a seat on AUTO the crew offer each checklist in a bubble at the right point of the flight. Press **Start** to run it; the crew also tick the captain's items they can see done.

blocks.content: Ground power, the air carts, the stairs and trucks, and the cabin services are all called from Ground Ops. The step-by-step procedure for a whole turnaround, and for a pushback, is in [Ground operations](ground-operations#turnaround-procedure). In short: open **Ground Ops**, **Ramp**; press **Call** beside Ground power, wait for it to arrive (or press **Instant**), press **Connect**, then put the aircraft's EXT PWR on as the [Electrical](electrical) procedure describes.
**Example: engine failure at V1.**

items: Compute the takeoff data on Performance first, so the card's V1 is known.
Open **Failures**, open the rail and choose **Power Plant**.
Press **Engine failure**, pick the engine, set WHEN to **V1**, leave the V1 box blank to use the card's V1, and press **Arm**.
On the Overview, check SCHEDULED FAILURES lists it. Press **Hide** if you would rather not know which engine.
Take off. The failure fires at V1; fly the procedure in [Emergency procedures](emergency-procedures).
After the flight, press **Clear All**, then **Reset Breakers** and **Reset Aircraft** to put the aircraft back to serviceable.

blocks.content: Any failure can be failed at once with **Fail now**, or armed at a time, an altitude, a speed or a phase. Several can be armed at once.

**Modeled in depth.** The EFB acts on the aircraft through the aircraft's own systems: a refuel flows through the refuel panel, fill valves and float valves; cargo is rolled into its locks by a loading crew with real interlocks; passengers walk through usable doors to their seats; a failure fails a component and everything downstream of it. Weight and balance from fuel, cargo and passengers reach the flight model through its fuel tanks and payload stations.

**Simplified.** Instant fuel loads and the Load now and Board now presses skip the work they stand for. The performance takeoff limits of the DC-10-10, -15, -40 and MD-10-10 are scaled from the KC-10's charts, and the DC-10-15's engines take the CF6-50C2's thrust rather than their own rating. The Flight app's hard landing mark uses the certification descent velocities, not the maintenance manual's inspection criterion.

items: Not yet available: the Documents Manual and Imported box; the Keybinds page; the Realism and Brakes choices, which nothing reads; random failures, which are stored but fail nothing; and four failures that are listed but not modeled (cracked windshields and windows, electrical smoke of unknown origin, fuel fumes in the cabin, and tank 1 or 3 outboard transfer).
Not kept across a reload of the aircraft: the Flight log, the failure lists, and the Primary COM2 choice.
A paired tablet and the boom operator's tablet show readings only while Infinity Manager is running. A paired tablet cannot make Cargo presses.
GSX requests go to GSX's Remote API on its default port. If GSX's remote port has been changed, a request answers “no answer from GSX”.
Charts appear only while the aircraft is running and its flight deck tablet is connected to Infinity Manager.
Editing a payload station on the simulator's own weight and balance page stops the aircraft writing that part of its payload (cargo, passengers or retardant) for the session.
Set Bugs drives the electromechanical airspeed indicators only; glass speed tapes take their speeds from their own systems (on the MD-10, through Send to Avionics).

Performance: Pull Aircraft Data fills RWY AVAIL with the runway's full length, with no lining-up allowance; the KC-10 manual's corrections for the wing refueling pods (KC-10, DC-10-40 Omega) are not applied.

parts.title: Virtual Crew
parts.summary: The automated second officer, flight engineer, first officer and copilot: their modes, how they run the checklists with you, a whole flight with them on each deck, and their cruise duties.

blocks.content: The DC-10 and the KC-10 were designed to be flown by three: a captain, a first officer and a flight engineer at the systems panel behind them. The MD-10 conversion took the flight engineer out and gave the engineer's work to automatic systems controllers and to the first officer. The **Virtual Crew** lets one person fly any of them as the line crew would. It fills the seats you are not sitting in with automated crew members who work their own share of every normal checklist: they move the switches in the cockpit, run the tests, make the callouts that are theirs, ask you for what only you can do, and on AUTO follow the flight and offer each checklist when it falls due.

You always sit in the left seat as captain and pilot flying. The first officer is therefore always the pilot monitoring (FedEx's PM, the KC-10 book's PNF). On the DC-10 the systems seat belongs to the **second officer (S/O)**, FedEx's name for the flight engineer, and the EFB and this part use that name for the DC-10. On the KC-10 the same seat is the **flight engineer (FE)**, who also answers the boom operator's items. The MD-10 has no third seat: its virtual crew is the first officer alone.

The crew is driven entirely by the checklists. Real crews set the cockpit up by **flows**, each crew member working their own panels from memory, and then read the checklist to confirm the flows were done: FedEx's manual reminds its crews that a checklist is not a do-list. The Virtual Crew joins the two. A checklist is run item by item, in order; when the run reaches an item that belongs to a virtual seat, that crew member does the flow for it at a hand's pace and then answers it. An item that belongs to you waits until you do it and tick it, or, with a seat on AUTO, until the crew sees it done. The checklists are the aircraft's own books, the same ones you read in [Documents](efb#documents-app): FedEx's DC-10 card with the Flight Manual's preflight procedures, the KC-10 abbreviated checklist (T.O. 1C-10(K)A-1CL-2) with the -1's preflight inspections, and FedEx's MD-10 FCOM normal procedures.

children.title: What the crew does, and what it does not

blocks.content: The crew members are line crew working the normal checklists. They are not an autopilot, a failure monitor or a second captain. What they do, they do through the same switches you would use, so everything they move is visible on the panels and can be moved back by you.

rows: Work its own items of every normal checklist, PREFLIGHT included, moving the switches in the cockpit
Fly the aircraft, or move the flight-path controls in flight (autopilot, autothrottle, thrust levers, gear, flaps before landing)
Run the tests that are its own, held as long as a crew member would hold them (annunciator, fire loops, hydraulic and fuel checks, stall and overspeed warning, radar)

Call for your controls when they are due (“Positive rate. Gear up.”, “Gear down.”) and check your takeoff settings against the takeoff card
Scan the panels for malfunctions or call them out

On AUTO, offer each checklist as the flight reaches it, and tick your items as it sees them done
Speak: every callout is written in the EFB's crew bubble
In the cruise, hold a target CG with fuel transfers (DC-10 S/O) and keep the cabin between 65 and 75 °F (DC-10 and KC-10 flight engineer on AUTO)

sections.title: The crew members
sections.summary: Who sits where on each flight deck, and the share of the work each virtual crew member takes.

blocks.content: Each book divides the work by seat, and the Virtual Crew keeps that division exactly. On the three-crew decks the systems seat runs the electrical, hydraulic, fuel, pneumatic, air-conditioning and pressurization panels, the APU, the fire detection tests and the doors; the right seat works its own side of the cockpit, the pilots' tests the book gives it, the engine start where the book gives it that, and the pilot monitoring's duties in flight. On the MD-10 the systems controllers run the panels in AUTO and the first officer does what is left of the flight engineer's work.

children.title: DC-10: second officer and first officer

blocks.content: The **second officer** owns the systems panel from power-up to leaving the aircraft. The S/O makes the cockpit safe before power goes on, puts the battery on, starts the APU and puts its power on the buses (or asks for a ground power cart when it will not), checks the hydraulic, electrical, fuel and fire detection systems, sets the panel for engine start, takes the electrical load onto the engine generators after start, sets the pneumatics and packs for taxi and from the takeoff card for takeoff, arms and disarms the escape slides, runs the landing and nose lights passing 10,000 ft, starts the APU again after landing and shuts the panel down at the gate. In the cruise the S/O holds the CG you set and, on AUTO, the cabin temperature.

The **first officer** is the pilot monitoring. On the ground the F/O sets their own instruments (HSI, flight director, static source, DME), runs their tests (weather radar, stall warning, overspeed warning, speed control, ADI, landing gear warning), turns the window and probe heat as the preflight requires, starts the three engines, arms the spoilers and autobrakes and sets the lights and transponder for takeoff. In flight the F/O calls for the gear and flaps and answers the items when you have moved them, sets the thrust rating computer to GA before landing, and after landing cleans up: lights, flaps and slats, stabilizer trim, radar, transponder, spoilers.

blocks.content: The tanker's **flight engineer** does more than the DC-10's second officer, because the -1 gives the FE more. Before the pilots arrive they do the exterior/interior initial inspection (chocks, covers, battery, fire detection, APU and electrical power, hydraulic system, the manifold failure test, packs, CDUs and MSUs), the interior inspection, which on the KC-10 includes the stall, overspeed, speed control, GPWS, gear warning and emergency power tests, and the exterior inspection. They read every checklist, as the -1 says the flight engineer does. During the start they check the start pressure and start No. 2 if you say so; otherwise they start it during taxi at Before Takeoff. The FE parallels the generators and shuts the APU down on three engines, runs the manifold failure check before takeoff, checks the engine pumps after landing and asks whether to shut No. 2 down for the taxi in. The boom operator's checklist items (boom operator's preparation, cabin report, cabin doors) are answered from the FE's seat.

The **copilot** sets their oxygen regulator, compass and flight director, runs their weather radar test, sets the windshield anti-ice, defog, pitot heat and navigation lights, turns the beacon on for start, sets the engine anti-ice before taxi, calls for the gear and selects climb thrust after takeoff, selects GA on the thrust computer for the approach, calls for gear and flaps before landing, and after landing retracts the flaps and trims the stabilizer. You start engines 3 and 1 yourself, as the -1's start table has the pilot do; on AUTO the crew answers those items when it sees each engine running.

The MD-10 is flown by two, so its virtual crew is the **first officer** alone. The preflight power-up is the F/O's: the cockpit safety inspection before power (battery on last), external power if a cart is plugged in, the engine and APU fire test on battery and again on AC, and the APU start with APU PWR on the buses. The F/O does their cockpit preparation (annunciator test, air conditioning, IRS and the cargo fire test, ignition, emergency power and lights, GPWS, yaw dampers, gear and takeoff warning tests, the radar test on both systems, transponder), sets the FLAP T.O. selector from the takeoff card, starts all three engines, shuts the APU down after start, arms the spoilers, sets the lights, radar and transponder for takeoff, and calls for the gear and flaps as pilot not flying. After landing the F/O retracts the spoilers and flaps, trims, sets the lights and starts the APU; at the gate they work the parking checklist and power the aircraft down when you leave.

The overhead's systems controllers (hydraulic, fuel, air and electrical) are left in AUTO. Where the book's step is marked [MANUAL], it applies only with that panel's SYSTEM in MANUAL, and with the panel in AUTO the first officer leaves it to the controller. With the hydraulic SYSTEM in MANUAL the F/O runs the book's pump checks and works the RMPs; with the fuel SYSTEM in MANUAL they turn the tank pumps on before start and off at parking, but do not run the fuel panel check or set the transfers after takeoff.
Whatever Flight Engineer/Second Officer mode is stored, it has no effect on the MD-10: its systems seat is always empty, and the Virtual Crew app shows only the First Officer row.

sections.title: Crew modes
sections.summary: OFF, MANUAL and AUTO for each seat: who moves which switch, what AUTO adds, and how the choice is kept.

blocks.content: Each virtual seat has its own mode, set in the [Virtual Crew app](efb#virtual-crew-app) under FLIGHT DECK with a three-way selector: **OFF**, **MANUAL** or **AUTO**. The two seats are independent: the S/O can be on AUTO while the F/O is OFF, or the other way round.

blocks.title: What each mode means
rows: Nobody sits there: every item with this seat's letter waits for your tick, like your own
Done by the crew member when you start a checklist
None from this seat: you start every checklist yourself
DC-10 S/O: holds the cruise CG target, if one is set
Checked by the crew and ticked in turn when seen done; an item no switch shows waits for your tick
Each checklist offered as the flight reaches its point
DC-10 S/O: cruise CG. DC-10 and KC-10 flight engineer: cabin temperature

blocks.content: AUTO's flight-following belongs to the crew as a whole: with **either** seat on AUTO, the offers appear and your items are checked. Two behaviors belong to one seat only. The cabin temperature control needs the flight engineer's seat on AUTO (DC-10 and KC-10). And the two PASSING 10,000 FT checklists run themselves without an offer when the seat that reads them is on AUTO: the S/O on the DC-10, the FE on the KC-10, the first officer on the MD-10. Otherwise they are offered like the others.

Every item in the books names who answers it, by the letters the book uses, and those letters decide who does the work. The crew never takes an item that is not its seat's, and never leaves its own to you while its seat is on MANUAL or AUTO.

rows: You, by tick (on AUTO also by the crew's check)

blocks.content: An item with more than one responder is answered seat by seat in a fixed order: the systems seat first, then the right seat, then you. On the DC-10's BEFORE TAKEOFF, for example, Flaps & Slats belongs to the captain and to the F/O: the F/O checks your setting first, then the item waits for you. An item whose crew member has nothing to move for it, such as a reading, a document or a test whose only result is a light to look at, is answered by that crew member as soon as it is their turn, with nothing moved.
With a seat OFF, its items wait for you. The run strip then names the empty seat (S/O or F/O; FE or CP on the KC-10) as having the item, since it is that seat's item you are covering.

children.title: Changing modes, and how they are kept

items: A mode change takes effect from the next item the run reaches. An item a crew member has already begun is finished even if you set that crew member's seat to OFF meanwhile.
Turning AUTO off while the crew is watching one of your items returns that item to a plain wait for your tick.
The modes, and the cruise CG target, are kept with the aircraft between sessions. The first time an aircraft is flown both seats are OFF and no target is set.
The Virtual Crew app shows the mode as the aircraft read it back. A press is shown at once and confirmed a moment later.

sections.title: How a checklist run works
sections.summary: Starting a checklist, the crew's walk down it, your items, the crew's calls and questions, and what happens when an item cannot be done.

blocks.content: A **run** is the crew working one checklist with you. It begins when you press Start, walks the checklist from the first item to the last in the book's order, and ends when every item is answered or when you stop it. Only one run exists at a time. Apart from the flight engineer's cruise duties ([Cruise duties](#cruise-duties)), the run is the only way the crew acts on the aircraft: with no run, the crew moves nothing.

items: From the checklist index in Documents: press **Start** beside the checklist. Start is shown on every checklist while either seat is on MANUAL or AUTO, PREFLIGHT's included. The checklist opens and the run begins.
From an open checklist: press **Start** at the top of the page.
From AUTO's offer: press **Start** in the bubble. The run begins and Documents opens at that checklist.

blocks.content: Starting a checklist clears that checklist's ticks, so that nothing left from an earlier flight answers an item, and begins at its first item. Starting a checklist while another run is under way stops the first run: the item a crew member was working is abandoned where it stood.

Each Start also hands the crew the takeoff card from the [Performance app's takeoff page](efb#takeoff-page), if one has been calculated: the AC (packs) and anti-ice selections it was computed with, its FLAP and its STAB. The crew reads them when it sets the takeoff bleeds and anti-ice and when it checks your flaps and trim. The card handed over is the one stored when you pressed Start; a card recalculated afterwards reaches the crew with the next Start.

The takeoff page's AC selection starts at Off, and Pull Aircraft Data copies the packs as they are set at that moment. A card calculated without changing AC, or pulled after the crew has set the packs off for the engine start, is a packs-off card, and the crew will set the aircraft up for a packs-off (on the DC-10 and KC-10, bleeds-off) takeoff. Check that AC reads On before you calculate if you want a packs-on takeoff.

The run takes the items in order at a speaking pace: about a second before the first item, and about a second and a half between one item answered and the next called. On each item the seats it names answer in turn: the systems seat, then the right seat, then you. A crew member whose item it is does that item's flow, one switch at a time with a short pause between, holding a test as long as its lights take to read, and then answers. The DC-10 S/O's hydraulic check takes about half a minute and the fuel crossfeed check about forty seconds, as they would by hand. An item a crew member has nothing to move for is answered at once.

When the run reaches one of your items it stops and waits, however long you take. Tick the item on any EFB screen and the run goes on. The walk never skips ahead: the next item is not called until the current one is answered.

items: **Ticking ahead.** Once the run has started, you can tick your items before it reaches them, as a real crew completes its flows before the checklist is read. A ticked item is passed when the run arrives at it. Ticks made before you press Start are cleared by it.

**Ticking a crew item.** Ticking an item that belongs to a crew member answers it at once. If they have not begun it they never do; if they are working it they stop where they are. This is how you take an item over.
**Unticking.** An item the crew answered stays answered in the run even if you untick it on the page.

blocks.content: The crew's switch movements are a hand's: each switch is moved once, to the position the item wants, and then left. A crew member does not hold a switch against you, and does not come back to it unless a later item calls for it.

children.title: Your items on MANUAL and on AUTO

blocks.content: On MANUAL every item that is yours waits for your tick. On AUTO the crew also watches your items: when the run reaches one, the crew looks at the control it names and, if it is already where the item wants it, ticks it and moves on. If it is not, the run waits on that item, watching, and ticks it the moment you set it. The walk stays in order: an item you set early is ticked in its turn, not before. Your own tick still answers the item at once.

The crew can only check what a switch or the aircraft shows. Briefings, readings, clearances, radio and navigation set-ups, the DC-10's INS alignment and most tests leave no position to look at, and those items wait for your tick on AUTO too. A check sees only the final position: an item whose book answer includes a test (Yaw Dampers On & Test, Emergency Power Check & Off, Emergency Lights Test & Arm) is ticked once the switch is in place, whether or not you ran the test. A few items the book answers with either of two positions are ticked as soon as they are reached: the DC-10's BEFORE START Parking Brake and AFTER START Engine Anti-Ice, the KC-10's LEAVING AIRCRAFT Parking Brakes and the MD-10's BEFORE START PARK BRAKE.
The flow tables in [A flight with the Virtual Crew](#flight-flow) mark each of your items the crew checks on AUTO (“AUTO: seen ...”).

children.title: Items the crew answers without setting them

blocks.content: A crew member answers some of their items with nothing moved although the book's answer asks for a setting or a test. They are not saying it is done: these are things the Virtual Crew does not do. Set them yourself, before or after the crew reaches them. The visual checks, readings and documents the books list are answered the same way and are not repeated here.
