blocks.caption: Each item appears only when it has been called. The belt loader's door, and whether there is one, depends on the variant.

sections.title: The aircraft at load: cold and dark, or ready to fly
sections.summary: What the aircraft looks like when the simulator loads it, and what changes after a Ctrl+E, a slew or a rewind.

blocks.content: The simulator hands the aircraft over in one of two states, and the aircraft decides which from what the simulator gives it: whether it is on the ground, and whether any engine is lit. An aircraft **on the ground with no engine running** is taken to be as it was left parked: cold and dark, or at the gate with only the APU. An aircraft **in the air, or with an engine running** (on a runway, a taxiway or at a gate with engines lit) is taken to have been prepared at the gate before it moved, and arrives ready to fly.

columns: Parked (on the ground, no engine running)
Ready to fly (airborne or an engine running)
rows: Chocks in; pitot covers and engine covers on; traffic cones placed (none with GSX). Take them away on the walkaround
None at the aircraft: only the battery until ground power is called
Released, with no pressure stored in the brakes, so a tug can move the aircraft at once; the chocks hold it
As the simulator's flight state sets it
At rest: align them in the cockpit preparation (or set INS alignment to Instant)
Aligned and navigating; gyros erected; radar warmed
Cabin crew seated with the seat belt sign on (on a runway, a taxiway or in the air)

blocks.content: The panel itself is read, not rewritten, at a load: switches stand where the simulator's flight state put them. The one exception is a contradiction: an engine the simulator has running cannot have its fuel lever shut, so its lever is set to run.

blocks.alt: Exterior view of a DC-10-30 loaded cold and dark at a remote stand, three-quarter front left: chocks at the nose and main gear, the pitot covers with their streamers blowing in the wind, the engine inlet covers on all three engines with streamers, the traffic cones, no ground carts, doors closed.
blocks.title: A cold-and-dark load

blocks.content: **Ctrl+E.** The simulator's auto-start lights the engines, and the aircraft follows: each engine is taken up as running when the simulator has it lit, and its fuel lever is set to run. It puts no ground equipment on and takes none off, but the engine covers come off by themselves as each engine passes 10 % N2, and the pitot covers once the aircraft moves. The simulator's auto-shutdown sets the three fuel levers off and lets the engines spool down.

**Slew, map teleport, Back on Track.** These move the aircraft without its physics, so every gyro and platform integrates motion that never happened. When a slew ends, or the aircraft jumps further than it could fly in one moment, or the simulator's clock runs backwards, the compass system and vertical gyros are re-erected and synchronized as at a fresh load, if an engine is running. The inertial platforms' **position is not reset**: after a long slew or rewind, update the INS or FMS position as you would after a ground move. After a rewind the fuel is taken from the simulator's restored tanks. A hitched tow tug follows a slew with the aircraft; a tug parked on the ramp stays where it stood.

sections.title: The Ground Ops app
sections.summary: Five pages in the order of a turnaround, and the rules that gray them.

blocks.content: Ground Ops is on the EFB's dock. Its five pages, **Ramp**, **Services**, **Fuel**, **Doors** and **Pushback**, are chosen with buttons at the top and follow the order of a turnaround. Each shows what the aircraft reports, not the last press: a cart called reads On its way with its time to arrive until it is there. A button that cannot be pressed now is not drawn. Under the page buttons an amber line appears only when there is something to say: why the page is grayed, the chocks-away countdown, or GSX's link not being live. A GSX request that failed shows there too, in a box with a red GSX badge; press it to dismiss.

The Fuel page is described with the EFB, in [The Fuel page](efb#fuel-page). The other four are described below: Ramp in [Chocks, covers and cones](#ramp-items) and [Ground power and air](#ground-power-and-air), Services in [Servicing](#servicing), Doors in [The Doors page](#doors-page), Pushback in [Pushback and towing](#pushback-and-towing).

blocks.title: When the pages are grayed
rows: Moving faster than 1 kt for more than a second
Doors 1L and 1R below 20 kt; a running refuel and its Cancel; the Pushback page while a tow is at the aircraft
Stopped off a paved surface (grass, dirt)

blocks.content: A grayed page shows a caution sign, “Aircraft not suitable for ramp services”, with the reason. Ramp services need the aircraft stopped because nothing at a real aircraft follows it: a cart left plugged in when the aircraft moves tears out its cable.

sections.title: Chocks, covers and cones
sections.summary: The pre-flight items on the Ramp page: what each does to the aircraft, and when it comes off by itself.

blocks.content: The top of the Ramp page has four tiles, **Chocks**, **Pitot covers**, **Engine covers** and **Cones**, each with its state and a switch. An item goes on only with the aircraft stopped on the ground, and comes off from the page (the chocks and covers also by clicking them in the simulator's walkaround). Each also comes off **by itself** when the aircraft does something that would take it away on a real ramp, and a press that would come straight off again is refused rather than remembered.

blocks.alt: Ground Ops' Ramp page, portrait, on a DC-10-30 at the gate: the page buttons with Ramp selected; the four tiles Chocks (In), Pitot covers (On), Engine covers (On) and Cones (Placed) with their switches; the GROUND POWER group with Ground power Connected and its Disconnect and Dismiss buttons; the AIR CARTS group with Air start not at the aircraft and its Call button, and Conditioned air Connected, air on, with its Hoses choice at 2, Flow per hose and Temperature settings.
blocks.title: Ground Ops, Ramp page

rows: Hold the aircraft where it stands, parking brake set or not: the simulator's own chocks are set and the wheel brakes held while they are in
The aircraft moves (it has rolled past them) or leaves the ground
Block the ram inlet of all three pitot tubes, with the drain holes left clear: the pitot lines vent to static and every airspeed indicator reads nothing
The aircraft moves with an engine running, or leaves the ground. Towed with every engine shut down, they stay on
Inlet covers on all three engines, with streamers
Stopped, with every engine below 10 % N2
Traffic cones set out around the aircraft. Not available while GSX is in use
The aircraft moves or leaves the ground

blocks.content: **Why the chocks matter.** A DC-10 parked with the brakes released is held only by its chocks, and the airline books never leave a parked aircraft on its brakes alone: the second officer releases the parking brake during their safety check only once the chocks or a tug are in place, and the captain holds the brakes set at block-in until the ground crew report the chocks in. The simulation keeps that logic. The chocks hold the aircraft against wind, slope and an engine at idle; they also hold it against a tug, so the tug cannot move the aircraft until they are out. If the simulator refuses its own chocks, the Ramp page says so and the wheel brakes hold the aircraft instead.

**Taking the chocks away sends the ramp away.** Removing the chocks is the ramp's signal that the aircraft is about to leave. With anything at the aircraft, the amber line reads “Chocks removed: everything at the aircraft disconnects and leaves in 5 s”, counting down; when it runs out, every cart and truck disconnects and drives away, every cabin service stops, and the stairs, catering trucks and belt loader are cleared. Put the chocks back in within the 5 seconds to keep them. It is the removal that warns, not the absence of chocks: a cart called afterwards to an aircraft without chocks comes and stays. GSX's own vehicles belong to GSX and stay. Taking the chocks out is therefore the last ramp action before pushback.

**Pitot covers.** With the covers on, the airspeed indicators read nothing, because the pitot pressure has nowhere to come from. The simulation removes them by itself once the aircraft moves under its own power, so it never lets you take off with them, but take them off on the walkaround as the checklist requires. The covers stay on during a tow with the engines shut down, as they would on a maintenance tow.

**Covers and cones are drawn with their streamers.** Each streamer turns and lifts in the wind the aircraft feels, the wind less the aircraft's own motion over the ground, so a parked aircraft's streamers blow downwind and a moving one's stream aft. The DC-10-40's wing engine covers fit its JT9D nacelles.

blocks.alt: Close-up of the DC-10's forward fuselage, left side: the pitot tube covers on, with their ribbons and rope streaming downwind in a fresh breeze.
blocks.title: Pitot covers and streamers

blocks.content: The landing gear ground lock pins are not modeled; the checklist items that name them are answered by the chocks and ground equipment. Engine cowl opening is a ramp maintenance action and is not offered on the EFB.

sections.title: Ground power and air carts
sections.summary: The ground power unit, the air-start cart and the conditioned-air cart: how to call them and what each supplies to the aircraft.

blocks.content: Three carts serve the aircraft from the ramp: a **ground power unit** (GPU) for electrical power, an **air-start cart** (ASU) for pneumatic pressure to start the engines, and a **conditioned-air cart** (PCA) to heat or cool the cabin without the packs. The carts deliver into the aircraft's own systems through their real connections: the GPU into the external power receptacle, so EXT PWR AVAIL lights and the crew put EXT PWR on; the air-start cart into the pneumatic system's two ground connectors; the conditioned-air cart into the air-conditioning distribution. Nothing is at the aircraft when it is loaded.

Every cart lives the same life: **called**, it drives up from the equipment line in about 45 seconds and **parks** at the aircraft; it is **connected** and **disconnected** as often as the crew like; **dismissed**, it disconnects if it is still plugged in and drives away in about 20 seconds. While a cart is on its way its Call button reads **Instant**, which parks it at once. The row shows what the aircraft reports: Not at the aircraft, On its way with the time left, At the aircraft not connected, Connected, Leaving.

rows: The cart drives up and parks
Cable or hoses on the aircraft
The cart's air on or off. Connected, the hoses are on and nothing flows until Start air. The air comes up, and goes down, over about 2 seconds
Cable or hoses off; an air cart's air is cut at once

blocks.content: The carts can be called and connected only with the aircraft stopped on the ground. If it moves faster than 1 kt for more than a second, or leaves the ground, every cart disconnects and drives away at once, with no warning, and every service stops: nothing at a real aircraft follows it. A press made while the aircraft moves is refused, not remembered. The ramp order is therefore call, connect, start air; and in reverse, stop air, disconnect, dismiss.
The simulator's own request for ground power (its ground services menu) calls the EFB's ground power cart and connects it when it arrives, exactly as Call and Connect would.

The GPU plugs into the external power receptacle on the belly aft of the nose gear well and supplies the aircraft's external power bus at 115/200 V AC, 400 Hz. With it connected, the external power available light comes on and the crew can put EXT PWR on; without a cart connected the EXT PWR switch springs back off. The aircraft's side, the external power contactor and its interlocks with the generators and the APU, is described in [Electrical](electrical). The row reads Plugged in or Not plugged in, from whichever source supplies it.

With GSX in use the ground power is GSX's: the EFB's cart goes home, and the single button asks GSX for its GPU, which GSX's own menu then toggles. GSX's power is taken as connected while GSX reports its GPU service in progress.

Before the engines are started, the carts can stay. After engine start, dismiss ground power once the generators are on line; the chocks' removal sends anything left at the aircraft away 5 seconds later in any case.

The air-start cart supplies pressurized air to the pneumatic system through **one or two hoses**, for engine starting when the APU is unavailable or its air is not enough. **Hose 1** feeds the left side of the pneumatic manifold (the No. 1 engine's side) and **hose 2** the right side (No. 3's); the APU feeds the center. With one hose, the isolation valves carry the cart's air to the other engines' starters. The cart's **Pressure** is set from 20 to 60 psig, 35 psig at rest; a new setting is reached over about 2 seconds, and the pressure in the hose sags as the aircraft draws on it, most of all while a starter turns.

Start pressure matters. The FedEx manual cautions that a start below 20 psi risks a hot start and that a drop of about 5 psi when the start valve opens is normal; the KC-10 manual asks for at least 25 psi with the start valve closed, allows a start down to 15 psi when operations demand it with a slower acceleration to idle, and recommends 35 psi below 0 °F (-18 °C). Set the cart high enough that the duct pressure on the pneumatic gauges stays in that range with the start valve open. See [Pneumatics](pneumatics) and [Engines](engines).

The conditioned-air cart blows air at a set temperature into the air-conditioning distribution through **one or two ducts**; two give twice the flow and are the better choice for a wide-body cabin. **Flow per hose** is set from 50 to 400 lb/min (150 at rest) and **Temperature** from 35 to 90 °F (55 at rest): chilled for a summer turnaround, warm in winter. The packs can then stay off, saving the APU's bleed air and fuel. The air enters the cabin through the aircraft's own ducts, so the zone temperatures follow from the flow, the temperature and the heat load. See [Air conditioning](air-conditioning).
GSX has no air-start or conditioned-air vehicle, so both air carts are the EFB's whether GSX is in use or not.

sections.title: Servicing
sections.summary: The Services page: stairs and catering trucks at the forward doors, the belt loader, catering, lavatory, cleaning and de-icing; fuel and water.

blocks.content: The Services page has two groups. **AT THE DOORS** sets what stands at the forward doors and at the bulk cargo door. **SERVICES** runs the cabin services and de-icing. A timed service takes about 2 seconds to get going after **Start**, then runs for its time, and takes as long to wind down after **Cancel**; while it runs, its Start button reads **Instant**, which finishes it at once.

blocks.alt: Ground Ops' Services page, portrait, on a passenger DC-10-30: AT THE DOORS with Forward doors (1L stairs, 1R catering) and the Door 1L and Door 1R pickers (Clear, Stairs, Cater), and the Belt loader switch at the aft bulk door; SERVICES with Catering in progress and its time left, Instant and Cancel, Lavatory with the truck at the aircraft and its service Start, Cleaning done, De-icing with Start, and De-icing fluid set to Type I + IV.
blocks.title: Ground Ops, Services page
Services page
rows: Each forward door holds one thing: passenger stairs or a catering truck, never both. Stairs at a door make it usable for boarding. With GSX in use, one **Operate stairs** button asks GSX for its stairs

One belt loader at this aircraft's bulk cargo door (see [Ground equipment by aircraft](#ground-equipment-layout)). Not offered where there is no bulk door (the KC-10 and KDC-10), and hidden with GSX in use, which brings its own
About 15 minutes. A finished catering stocks the passenger galleys for the cabin service. The catering truck at a forward door makes its sound while the service works
**Call truck**, **Truck now**, **Dismiss truck**, and the service's **Start**, **Instant**, **Cancel** (GSX: **Call GSX**)

The lavatory truck is called like a cart and parks at the lavatory service panel. Its service, about 10 minutes, runs only while the truck is there with its hose connected, and empties every waste tank. Dismissing the truck mid-service stops it
About 15 minutes. A timer only: the cabin's cleanliness is not modeled
About 8 minutes: fluid onto both wings, the tail and the crown. The only thing that removes frost, snow or ice from the wing on the ground
The fluid both the EFB's and GSX's trucks spray. Type I + IV, the default, is the two-step treatment: heated Type I to remove the contamination, then Type IV to protect the wing for longer

blocks.content: While the aircraft stands in frost, snow or freezing precipitation, contamination settles on the wing's upper surfaces (see [Ice and rain protection](ice-and-rain)). Nothing aboard removes it on the ground: the wing anti-ice is for flight. The de-icing service sprays fluid while it works; the moment it finishes, the wing is clean under a fresh film of the chosen fluid, however much was on it. From then on the **holdover time** runs: the fluid absorbs precipitation until it is exhausted, and its capacity depends on the fluid type, so a Type IV film protects much longer than Type I alone. Plan the taxi and takeoff inside the holdover; see [Adverse weather](adverse-weather) for the procedures and holdover guidance.

A takeoff with a contaminated wing is a takeoff with a wing that stalls early and climbs poorly. De-ice as close to departure as the operation allows, and repeat it if the holdover runs out before takeoff.

Fuel is loaded from Ground Ops' **Fuel** page, through the aircraft's refuel panel or at once; see [The Fuel page](efb#fuel-page). With GSX in use, the Fuel page's **Call truck** brings GSX's fuel truck instead, and the fuel it delivers goes into the aircraft's tanks through the same refueling path, so a failed fill valve refuses it as it would refuse the panel. Fuel from the simulator's own fuel truck and its fuel page is accepted the same way.
Potable water is not a service: there is no water truck. The lavatory service empties the waste tanks.

sections.title: The Doors page
sections.summary: Every door on an outline of the aircraft: open, stop, close, arm and disarm, worked by the ground crew through each door's own controls.

blocks.content: The Doors page draws the aircraft's outline, nose up in portrait and nose left in landscape, with a button at each door the aircraft has, showing how far it is open. The cabin doors **1L** to **4R** sit beside the fuselage; the lower cargo doors on the right, **Lower front** and **Lower rear**, half-way out; the main-deck cargo door, where there is one, is **Upper cargo**, furthest out; and the aft door is always **Bulk cargo**. A door the aircraft does not have is not drawn: the KC-10's deactivated cabin doors and its sealed lower cargo doors do not appear.

**One press, three meanings.** A door's button sends a single PRESS, and the aircraft decides what it means from where the door is: a shut door opens; a moving door stops; a stopped door goes the way it can, open from shut, shut from open, and from part-way the opposite way to the one it was last sent. On an armed cabin door the press disarms the slide first, because the slide's power interlock keeps an armed door from opening under power. In the top corner a **Cabin doors** box has **Open all**, **Close all**, **Arm all** and **Disarm all**. Arm all waits until every cabin door is shut.

blocks.alt: Ground Ops' Doors page, portrait, on a DC-10-30F: the white outline of the aircraft nose up, with buttons at 1L and 1R (1L open 100 %, slide disarmed), the Upper cargo door button on the left (opening, 64 %), Lower front and Lower rear on the right (shut), Bulk cargo below 4L; the Cabin doors box in the top-left corner with Open all, Close all, Arm all and Disarm all.
blocks.title: Ground Ops, Doors page

blocks.content: **The ground crew work the real door.** Each press is carried out by a simulated crew member at the door's own controls, so the door's power, interlocks and timing decide: a lower cargo door needs its power and stops on its brakes, the main-deck door runs on its hydraulics, a plug-type cabin door is driven by its own motor and stops on its brake. Arming a door moves the cabin's own arm handle, so the levers drawn in the cabin agree with the slides. A door GSX is working belongs to GSX. A door cannot be opened in the air.

**Doors and motion.** As the aircraft begins to roll, every door except 1L and 1R is shut by the ground crew; those two shut from 20 kt. So doors 1L and 1R stay live on the page below 20 kt, for a late passenger or a pushback with the forward door still open. The doors themselves, their warning lights and the slides are described in [Doors and cabin](doors-and-cabin).

sections.title: Ground equipment by aircraft
sections.summary: Which equipment each variant takes, where it stands, and what it sounds like.

blocks.content: The ramp equipment is the same family-wide, with three differences that follow the airframe's exterior: where the bulk cargo door is, whether there is one, and which engine covers fit. The table lists them by variant.

**Where the equipment stands.** The ground power cart parks clear of the nose gear with its cable to the receptacle aft of the nose wheel well; the air-start and conditioned-air carts run their hoses and ducts to the connectors under the fuselage; the lavatory truck parks at its service position; stairs or a catering truck dock at each forward door; the belt loader docks at the bulk door. Everything that stands on the ground is placed from the landing gear, so it stays on the ground the tires stand on as the struts compress and extend with the load.

**Sounds.** Each piece of equipment sounds only while it is at the aircraft and working: the ground power unit while its cable is plugged in, each air cart while its hoses are on (louder as the aircraft draws harder on it, for instance during an engine start), the lavatory truck while it services, a catering truck while catering works at its door.

sections.title: GSX Pro
sections.summary: Using GSX Pro's vehicles instead of the EFB's: choosing it, what follows the choice, and how the aircraft works with GSX.

blocks.content: The aircraft works with FSDreamTeam's GSX Pro. The choice is **Use GSX** in the EFB's Settings, kept with the aircraft between flights. It is in effect only while GSX is actually **running**: GSX makes itself known only once its engine has started, so an installed GSX that has not started reads the same as none, and a GSX choice made on an earlier flight shows off and grayed until GSX runs, with a note saying it is waiting for GSX. A GSX started after the aircraft loads is noticed when it starts.

blocks.title: What follows the choice
rows: GSX's GPU. The EFB's cart goes home. The Ramp page's one button asks GSX for its GPU service; GSX's own menu toggles it
GSX's, at the doors GSX serves. The Services page's door pickers are replaced by one Operate stairs button
GSX's vehicles, called with Call GSX. When GSX reports a service completed, the aircraft takes it as done: the waste tanks are emptied, the galleys stocked
GSX's trucks spray, with the fluid chosen on the EFB's Services page
Call truck on the Fuel page requests GSX's refueling

Cargo's Start load and Unload call GSX's boarding and deboarding. GSX's loaders bring each unit to its door; the aircraft's own crew open the cargo doors for GSX and roll each unit into its locks as GSX's progress allows. The bulk hold loads at once

On the passenger DC-10s, the KDC-10 and the Omega, Passengers' Board and Deboard call GSX's services, with the plan's passenger count passed to GSX first. The KC-10's riders board with the EFB's crew: GSX treats the KC-10 as a cargo aircraft
GSX's pushback is offered on the Pushback page
None: the EFB's cones are withdrawn and GSX places none of its own
Air-start, conditioned-air carts, chocks, covers, AeroTow
Unchanged: the EFB's (GSX has no air carts)

blocks.content: **Doors.** GSX never opens a door; it waits for each door to be ready. For the cargo doors the aircraft's ground crew answer GSX's wait by working the real door, so a door without power keeps GSX waiting, and once GSX has finished and gone they shut it. For passengers GSX brings the stairs or jetway, and the crew owe only an open cabin door.

**The GSX menu.** While GSX is in use, Ground Ops' header carries a **GSX menu** button that opens GSX's own menu, which is where a GSX service is stopped (GSX offers no other way). A GSX request that fails shows under the page buttons in a box with a red GSX badge; press it to dismiss. Each GSX service shows GSX's own state and progress.

**Turning GSX off** sends away everything GSX has at the aircraft, cones included: the EFB restarts GSX, the same as GSX's own reset. A cargo job GSX was running stops with it. The EFB's own services take over.

The aircraft's GSX profiles place GSX's ground power unit about 2 m to the left of the real receptacle, so GSX's truck parks clear of the nose wheels, and its fuel truck at an estimated position on the right wing. GSX calls go from the flight deck's tablet (or the boom operator's) to GSX on the same computer; a paired tablet's Passengers boarding is relayed through the flight deck.

sections.title: Pushback and towing
sections.summary: The three ways to push back, the AeroTow tug and towbar, nose wheel steering under tow, driving the tug and its cab view, towing limits, and the ground crew's calls.

blocks.content: A DC-10 parked nose-in at a gate leaves backwards. Reverse thrust could back it off the stand, but on a ramp it blows debris at the terminal and the people around the aircraft and risks the engines ingesting it, so the aircraft is pushed. A **tug** pushes it back onto the taxiway, coupled to the nose gear by a **towbar**, while the crew start the engines. The same tug can also pull the aircraft forward into a stand or across the ramp with the engines shut down.

Ground Ops' **Pushback** page offers three providers, chosen with buttons at its top: **AeroTow**, the simulation's own tow tug, which you drive; **MSFS tug**, the simulator's built-in pushback; and **GSX**, GSX Pro's pushback, offered only while GSX is in use. The choice is kept between flights. The Pushback page stays live while a tow is at the aircraft, even with the aircraft moving, so the tow can always be stopped, steered and released.

blocks.alt: Ground Ops' Pushback page, portrait, with AeroTow chosen: the provider buttons (GSX, MSFS tug, AeroTow); the AEROTOW group with 1. Tug (Hitched, Dismiss), 2. Steering (2WS, 4WS, Crab with 2WS selected), 3. Drive (Driving the tug, 1.8 kt, Hand back), and View with the Tug view button; the note under it: Stick: the tug's speed, forward pushes back; center it to stop. Rudder: steering.
blocks.title: Ground Ops, Pushback page

blocks.content: AeroTow is a **towbar tractor** of the TLD TMX-550 class: a heavy, low four-wheel tug that faces the aircraft, so driving it forward pushes the aircraft back. The **towbar** is clamped to the nose gear axle at one end and pinned to the tug's hitch at the other. The tug is modeled as a vehicle of its own: its mass, its tires' grip on the ramp, its engine's tractive force and its service brake decide how fast it can move the aircraft and what it can hold. The aircraft, in turn, brings its own weight, its tires' rolling resistance and breakaway friction, the scrub of its bogies in a turn, the slope of the ramp, its engines' thrust and its brakes. The force in the towbar is the sum of all of them.

blocks.alt: Exterior view of the AeroTow tug hitched to a DC-10-30's nose gear on a ramp, from the side and slightly ahead: the low towbar tractor facing the aircraft, the towbar from its hitch to the nose gear axle, the nose wheels turned a few degrees, the cab with its driver's seat and steering wheel visible.
blocks.title: The AeroTow tug hitched to the nose gear
Tug and towbar data
rows: Towbar length, head pin to hitch pin
Towbar shear pin, DC-10-30, -40, KC-10, MD-10-30
Applies to the tug and to the towed nose gear alike
The simulated nose wheel's limit; the real nose gear's steering collar swings at least 71° each way with the bypass pin in
Changed only with the tug stopped

blocks.content: **The shear pin** is the towbar's fuse. It breaks at a set load so that an overload, a hard stop against the parking brake, the aircraft running onto the tug, a violent steering transient, breaks the bar and not the nose gear. The bar can only carry what the tug can react through its tires: past that, the tug's wheels skid instead. With this tug that has a consequence worth knowing. On the DC-10-10, -15 and MD-10-10 the lighter bar's pin fails before the tug's tires lose grip, so pushing hard against a set parking brake, or swinging the tug hard while moving, can shear it; on the larger aircraft the tug's tires spin first.

**Tug steering.** In **2WS** the tug steers on its front wheels, like a car. In **4WS** the rear wheels turn opposite to the front for a tighter turn. In **Crab** all four turn the same way, so the tug moves sideways at an angle without turning. A large steer folds the tug against the towbar even while it pulls: the hitch overhangs the front axle, so in a steady tight turn the bar swings toward the tug's bumper and rests there, and the turn holds at that angle until the steering is eased.

The nose wheel is normally steered hydraulically from the tiller and rudder pedals (see [Landing gear](landing-gear)). A towbar turning the wheel against those cylinders would fight the hydraulic pressure and could damage the steering. So before a tow the ground crew insert the **steering bypass pin**, which opens the bypass valve and cross-connects the two sides of the steering cylinders: the nose gear then **castors** freely, damped, and the towbar sets its angle. With the pin in, the tiller and pedals do not steer.

In the simulation the AeroTow tug **arrives hitched, with the bypass pin in**, and the pin comes out when the tug leaves after a release, or when a tow breaks. Under tow the nose wheel follows the bar exactly: the wheel drawn on the exterior and the bar always agree. The airline books add one rule the simulation keeps: the pin stays in until the tug is disconnected.
AeroTow is laid out as its steps. Calling the tug and sending it away never take the controls: the flow is call, release the parking brake in the cockpit, then take the tug's controls.

rows: No tug; Hitched. A call is refused with the aircraft moving, its motion not yet measured, in the air, or with the nose gear not down. After Dismiss: Leaving once the aircraft stops; Leaving once the parking brake is set or the chocks are in

blocks.content: **Driving.** With **Take the controls**, the aircraft's pitch and yaw controls drive the tug; roll and the throttles stay the aircraft's. The request waits, and takes the controls by itself, until the tug may drive: hitched, with the towbar seated on the nose wheel (it swings onto the wheel at about 20° per second after the call), on the ground. **Hand back** returns the controls to the aircraft and leaves the tug hitched and holding on its brake. **Dismiss** also hands the controls back at the press.

blocks.title: Tug controls
rows: Stick or yoke, fore and aft (axis)

The tug's **speed**: forward drives the tug toward the aircraft and pushes it back; aft pulls it forward; center is stop, and the tug holds on its service brake. A stick left deflected commands nothing until it has been brought to center or swept through it, so the tug never launches by surprise
Step the speed command a tenth of full at each press, and latch it there; step back to center to stop
The tug's **steering**, as its driver sees it: right rudder turns the tug to the driver's right, which is the aircraft's left
Step the steering a tenth of full at each press; rudder center (or center aileron and rudder) centers it

blocks.alt: Plan-view diagram of a pushback from a nose-in gate onto a taxiway behind: the DC-10's track in three positions as it is pushed straight back then swung tail-right onto the taxiway centerline, the tug and towbar at the nose in each position with the bar's angle shown, arrows for the tug's direction of travel and the aircraft's direction of motion, the main gear pivot marked, and the nose wheel's turn radius. Labels: push straight, tail right, straighten, stop, set brakes, disconnect.
blocks.title: A pushback onto the taxiway
blocks.caption: The aircraft turns about its main gear. To swing the tail to one side, the tug drives the nose the other way.

blocks.content: **How the aircraft turns.** A towed aircraft is a trailer pivoting about its main gear. The nose follows the towbar, and the tail swings the opposite way: to put the tail to the right as the aircraft goes back, the tug drives the nose to the left. Because the main gear are more than 70 ft behind the nose wheel, the tail sweeps a wide arc for a small movement of the nose, so start a turn early and gently, and straighten before the aircraft is lined up, as its yaw momentum carries it on. The tug answers its steering immediately; the aircraft answers the tug over many seconds.

children.title: Towing limits and what breaks the tow

blocks.content: **Speed.** The tug never moves faster than 5 mph, and neither does the towed nose gear: in a turn, where the tug articulates and the nose can move faster than the tug, the tug is slowed to keep the nose within the limit.

**Angle.** The towbar is held at the nose wheel's towing limit, about 68°; at the limit, the tug's further steering only folds it against the bar. On the real aircraft, over-steering past the gear's steering stops damages the steering collar.

**Engines.** The DC-10's engines are normally started during the pushback or after it stops. Idle thrust on the towbar is normal and expected. More thrust than idle pushes against the tug and loads the bar, and can shear it: keep the throttles at idle while the tug is attached.

**Brakes.** Do not brake while the tug is moving the aircraft, except to stop it in an emergency: the brakes stop the aircraft but not the tug, and the bar takes the difference. Setting the parking brake once the tow has stopped is the procedure, and the tug's release waits for it.

**Tug view** on the Pushback page puts the simulator's camera in the tug's cab, at the driver's eye, looking ahead onto the towbar and the aircraft's nose. The view rides the cab as it turns and articulates. Look around with the simulator's own camera controls: the pan keys or a hat step or sweep the look, a joystick axis bound to the camera sets it, and pan reset centers it. Mouse look does not turn the view in the cab. Entering the cab does not take the tug's controls, and leaving does not hand them back: Take the controls separately.

**MSFS tug** uses the simulator's built-in pushback. **Start / stop** starts and stops it (the same as the simulator's own pushback key); **Tail left**, **Straight** and **Tail right** steer it. Tail left turns the aircraft a quarter turn so the tail swings to the crew's left and the nose to the right, the turn that puts an aircraft pushed off a stand onto the taxiway behind it; Tail right the opposite; Straight holds the heading it has. The row shows the simulator's pushback state and the heading the tug is steering to. With GSX in use, **GSX** on the Pushback page offers **Request pushback**, which calls GSX's departure service. GSX then asks for the direction and handles the push in its own menu; its tug is GSX's, and the AeroTow tug stands aside while GSX pushes. Stop or change a GSX pushback from the GSX menu.

On the line, a pushback is a conversation on the interphone between the captain and the tug driver or headset operator, and the KC-10 manual has the aircraft commander brief the tow team first on the route, the emergency hand signals and when the bypass pin goes in and out. The simulation has no voice exchange with the ground crew: you are both the captain and the ground crew, and the EFB is the headset. sections.title: Procedures
sections.summary: A turnaround from block-in to pushback, a pushback with the AeroTow tug, the other pushback providers, a tow, and leaving the aircraft.

blocks.content: These procedures cover the ramp side of a turnaround. They sit beside the aircraft's normal checklists, which remain the authority for the flight deck's side: see [Normal procedures](normal-procedures). EFB presses are named as they appear on screen.
**Objective:** take the aircraft from block-in to ready for pushback, with the ramp services worked in the order a ramp would work them.

items: Stop on the stand and set the parking brake.
**Ground Ops, Ramp**: Chocks **In**. Release the parking brake only when the chocks are in, as the shutdown procedure directs.

Ground power: **Call**, then **Connect** when it is at the aircraft (or **Instant** while it drives up). When the external power available light comes on, put EXT PWR on and shut down the APU or the last engine as the shutdown procedure directs.
If the cabin needs cooling or heating without the packs: Conditioned air **Call**, **Connect**, choose **2** hoses, set the flow and temperature, then **Start air**.

**Doors**: disarm and open the cabin doors needed (the press disarms an armed door first), and the cargo doors.
**Services**: set **Stairs** or **Cater** at doors 1L and 1R; switch on the **Belt loader** if the bulk hold is to be worked.
**Passengers**: **Deboard**. **Cargo**: **Unload**.
Lavatory: **Call truck**, then the service's **Start** once it is at the aircraft. Catering and cleaning: **Start**.
**Fuel**: enter or fetch the block fuel, **Distribute**, then **Refuel** (with the ground service bus powered) or **Instant**. See [The Fuel page](efb#fuel-page).
**Cargo**: load the outbound plan. **Passengers**: board the outbound plan.
In frost, snow or freezing precipitation: choose the de-icing fluid and **Start** de-icing as late as the departure allows.
When the services are done: **Dismiss truck** (lavatory), clear the stairs and catering trucks at the forward doors, switch off the belt loader.
Remove the pitot covers, engine covers and cones (Ramp page; the covers also by clicking them on the walkaround).
Close the doors and arm the slides (**Doors**, **Close all**, then **Arm all**; Arm all waits until every cabin door is shut). Check the door warning lights out.

If the APU cannot supply start air: Air start **Call**, **Connect**, **2** hoses, set the pressure, **Start air**, and start the engines at the gate before the carts are dismissed. Otherwise start on the APU during or after the pushback.

Call the tug (below), then take the chocks away. Anything still at the aircraft is warned for 5 seconds and then sent away.

**Condition:** cleared to push back from a nose-in stand, engines to be started during or after the push.

**Objective:** push the aircraft back onto the taxiway, start the engines, and release the tug with the aircraft held.

blocks.content: Start the turn early and gently; straighten before the aircraft is aligned with the taxiway. Stop the push by centering the stick: the tug brakes the aircraft to a stop.

Keep the thrust at idle and do not use the wheel brakes while the tug is moving the aircraft, except to stop in an emergency. Either loads the towbar and can shear its pin or run the aircraft away from the tug.

**Amplification.** The tug's release waits for the aircraft to be stopped and held by the parking brake or the chocks; the Pushback page says what it is waiting for. Dismiss hands the controls back to the aircraft at the press, and the tug unhitches, removes the bypass pin and drives away once the aircraft is held. Do not taxi until the tug has gone. A pushback with the engines not to be started is the same, without the engine start; the pitot covers may stay on for a tow with every engine shut down.

blocks.content: **Modeled in depth.** The tow tug is a vehicle with mass, tire grip, tractive force and brakes, coupled to the nose gear by a towbar whose load is computed from the tug, the aircraft's weight, rolling and breakaway friction, bogie scrub, slope, thrust and brakes, with a shear pin and a tug that skids past its grip. The nose wheel castors under tow with the bypass pin in. The carts deliver into the aircraft's electrical, pneumatic and air-conditioning systems, with the cart's settings reached over time and the hose pressure sagging under the aircraft's demand. Chocks hold the aircraft without the parking brake. The pitot covers block the pitot inlets. De-icing fluid sets the holdover. The lavatory service empties the waste tanks and catering stocks the galleys.

**Simplified.** The carts' drive times, the cabin services' durations and the cleaning service are fixed timers. The tug's mass, grip and power are those of a typical tug of its class rather than a measured one; the towing speed limit and the shear pin loads are vendor figures. The simulated nose wheel's towing limit is the simulator's 68° rather than the real gear's 71°. Towing uses the simulator's gear geometry, whose wheelbase is about 3.5 ft longer than the real aircraft's. The towbar's own wheels do not turn.

items: Not modeled: the ground crew's voice calls and hand signals; the landing gear ground lock pins; static port covers; potable water servicing; the effect of engine covers and cones on anything but their drawing; a bypass pin forgotten by the ground crew.
Not on the EFB: opening the engine cowls.
The ground equipment is drawn only for your aircraft.

GSX's ground power is taken as connected while GSX reports its GPU service in progress. GSX's GPU plugs in about 2 m to the left of the real receptacle, and its fuel truck parks at an estimated position.
The tug cab view has not been tested in virtual reality.
After a slew, map teleport or rewind the inertial platforms keep their old position: update it before relying on the INS or FMS.

chapters.title: Emergency Procedures
chapters.summary: Time-critical procedures for fires, engine failures, smoke, decompression, loss of electrical or hydraulic power, and emergency landing, evacuation and ditching.

blocks.content: This section holds the procedures for conditions that threaten the aircraft or the people in it and that cannot wait: a fire, an engine failure at a critical moment, smoke in the aircraft, a loss of cabin pressure, the loss of all generators or of two hydraulic systems, and the procedures that end an emergency on a runway or in the water. Failures that need crew action but leave time to think are in [Abnormal Procedures](abnormal-procedures). The split follows the KC-10 flight manual (Sections II and IIA) and the MD-10 FCOM (chapters EP and AP); FedEx's DC-10 manual keeps both in one chapter and marks its emergencies.

Each procedure is written for a single failure, and assumes that the crew have tested the lights, checked the circuit breakers and positioned the switches correctly before it began. Real emergencies are rarely so tidy. When failures combine, the captain decides the order of work, and the procedures are a tool for that decision, not a substitute for it.

Three rules stand above every checklist in this section. **Fly the aircraft first**: one pilot flies, and nothing else matters until the flight path is under control. **Identify before you act**: a correct action on the wrong engine turns one failure into two. **Finish the job**: an emergency ends on the ground, and most of these procedures end with the words land at the nearest suitable airport.

children.title: How a procedure is laid out

blocks.content: Every procedure opens with its **Condition**, what triggers it and what the crew sees, and where it helps its **Objective**, what the procedure is trying to achieve. The checklist follows. Each line names the control or the item, the action or the state it must reach, and the crew member who does it.

items: **Memory items** are shown bold and boxed. They are done from memory, in order, as soon as the pilot calls for the procedure, and only then read back from the checklist. A procedure is never started by searching for it on the page.
**Decision points** are short lines such as *If the FIRE light remains on after 30 seconds:*. If the statement is true, do the steps that follow it; if not, skip to the next line after them.
**Consequence lines** in capitals, such as LAND AT NEAREST SUITABLE AIRPORT, tell the captain what the failure means for the rest of the flight. Start acting on them while the checklist continues.

**WARNING**, **CAUTION** and **NOTE** callouts mean what they mean throughout this manual: a warning protects people and the aircraft, a caution protects equipment, a note helps. During an emergency they are read aloud as part of the checklist unless the captain waives them or they do not apply.
**Practice** at the end of a procedure names the failure in the EFB that produces the condition, where one exists (see [Practicing emergencies](#practising-emergencies)).

blocks.title: Landing advisories
rows: Divert now to the nearest airport where a safe landing can be made, judged on runway length and surface, weather, approach aids and rescue facilities, not on distance alone
Extended flight is not advised. The captain chooses the airport and the timing, and a landing at destination or at a planned alternate may be acceptable
Plan the landing so that an evacuation can follow at once: brief the crew and passengers, depressurize, and stop on the runway if emergency services need access
The captain (the KC-10 flight manual's pilot)
The flight engineer, DC-10 and KC-10. FedEx calls the DC-10's flight engineer the second officer (S/O)
The pilot flying, whichever seat that is
The pilot monitoring. The KC-10 flight manual writes PNF, pilot not flying, for the same duty
Every crew member on the flight deck

blocks.content: The MD-10 has no flight engineer. Its procedures use CAPT, F/O, PF and PM, and the PM does the work the FE does on the three-crew aircraft.

The crew member who first sees an emergency announces it at once, clearly and without diagnosis: "Engine fire", not "Number two's on fire". The pilot flying keeps the aircraft under control. The captain decides what is wrong and calls for the procedure **by name**. On that call the crew members the checklist designates do their memory items. The FE then reads the checklist aloud from the top, memory items first: the FE reads each line and its response, the designated crew member confirms the control is in the stated position and answers with the response, and the FE moves on. Non-memory items are read, actioned by the designated crew member and answered when done. Notes and limitations are read aloud and acknowledged ("Crosswind limit 15 knots", "Understood, 15 knots"). At the end the FE announces the checklist complete.

The FE identifies the affected engine or system on their panel before anyone moves a control, and confirms the control the PM has a hand on. Five controls are never moved in an emergency until a second crew member has confirmed the hand is on the right one:

items: a throttle;
a fuel lever;
an engine fire handle;
a CSD disconnect button;
an engine hydraulic pump switch.

blocks.content: Each of these is irreversible in flight or close to it: a fuel lever shut on the wrong engine leaves the aircraft on one engine, a CSD once disconnected cannot be reconnected in the air, and a fire handle pulled on a good engine shuts off its fuel, hydraulics and bleed. If the captain is flying, they normally hand control to the first officer so that the captain and the FE can work the problem together, and the autopilot is used whenever it is available to reduce the flying workload.

The MD-10's emergencies come in two kinds. **Emergency alert procedures** are announced by a red level 3 alert on the engine and alert display (EAD) with an aural warning, and each procedure is titled with the exact wording of the alert. **Emergency non-alert procedures** cover conditions the alerting system cannot see, such as smoke of unknown origin, an all-engine flameout or unreliable airspeed, and the crew recognize them from the aircraft's behavior.

The crew member who sees the alert announces it and resets the alerting system by pushing the lit cue switch on the systems display control panel, which puts out the MASTER WARNING lights and calls the relevant synoptic page to the system display. An engine fire's aural warning is silenced only by a MASTER WARNING light or by pulling the fire handle. When there is no time for the synoptic, on short final for instance, either MASTER WARNING light resets the warning and the cue switch stays lit for later.

The PF flies and nothing else. Time permitting, the captain calls for the memory items and the checklist. The PM does the memory items with the PF confirming each one, then opens the QRH and works the checklist by **challenge, do, verify**: the PM reads the line, does it if it is the PM's to do or has the PF do it if it is the PF's, and checks the result. The PM reads the consequences aloud and gets the PF's acknowledgement, and announces "Checklist complete".

Much of what the flight engineer does by hand on the DC-10 is done on the MD-10 by the systems controllers: after an engine failure they reconfigure the hydraulic, electrical, pneumatic and fuel systems by themselves. Several procedures therefore begin by taking a controller out of the loop (HYD SYSTEM SELECT to MANUAL, for example) to see whether the alert is a controller fault or a real failure. The EAD shows only the most serious alert in a system when several failures overlap, so read the synoptic page as well as the alert.

Below a safe height the only actions are the ones that keep the aircraft flying. An engine fire after V1 is flown exactly like an engine failure after V1 until the aircraft is climbing away clean of obstacles: rotate at VR, climb at V2 to V2 + 10, gear up with a positive rate. Then:

columns: Earliest point for the memory items on takeoff
rows: Not before 400 ft above the ground for an engine fire or severe damage

Normally 1,000 ft above the field or the engine-out minimum flap retraction altitude, whichever is higher; there level off (ALT HOLD), retract the flaps on schedule, call for the checklist by name, do the memory items, retract the slats on schedule and continue the climb
No height is given: the PF flies the engine-out profile and the captain calls for the memory items and the checklist when time permits; autoflight may be engaged above 200 ft

blocks.content:
The captain may call for memory items sooner if waiting would itself put the flight at risk, but a fire handle pulled at 150 ft on a heavy aircraft takes a crew member's eyes and hands at the worst possible moment, and the fire will still be there at 400 ft. Once the procedure is complete, the normal checklists (After Takeoff, climb power) follow in their usual order, unless the captain judges that the emergency must come first.

In cruise there is time: identify the failure, call for the procedure, and work it. On final approach below about 1,000 ft, consider whether completing the landing is safer than starting a procedure; some procedures (second engine failure on final) are written for exactly that moment.

items: **Aural warnings and master lights.** Silence an aural warning and reset the MASTER WARNING and MASTER CAUTION lights as soon as their cause is recognized. This is normal crew action and is not listed in the procedures.
**Intermittent lights.** A warning or caution light that flickers or comes on momentarily is treated as if it were steady.

**Oxygen and interphone.** In any emergency calling for oxygen masks, select 100 % oxygen (and EMERGENCY, positive pressure, for smoke), select the mask microphone, set the interphone selectors so the crew can hear each other, and turn the cockpit speakers on. Return the regulator to NORMAL (diluted) when the cockpit is clear, to make the oxygen last.

**Circuit breakers.** A breaker tripped for no known reason is a warning that something is wrong in that circuit. In flight, reset a tripped breaker only when a procedure calls for it or the captain judges it necessary to complete the flight, once only, after about two minutes to cool. Never reset a fuel pump or auxiliary hydraulic pump breaker. See [Circuit breakers in the simulation](electrical#breakers-in-the-sim).
**Declaring the emergency.** Tell ATC as soon as the workload allows; squawk 7700 if there is no contact, and use 121.5 MHz if the normal frequencies fail. Tell the company when time permits.

**Choosing where to land.** The closest runway is not always the best. Weigh runway length and surface against the aircraft's condition (flap setting, braking, steering, reversers available), the weather and approach aids, the rescue services, and whether the aircraft will reach it.

blocks.content: These are FedEx's Phase One items. FedEx also expects the rejected takeoff to be flown from memory, so it is listed with them.

The KC-10 flight manual boxes only these items. Its APU fire, cabin cargo smoke, pneumatic manifold failure, reverser and hydraulic quantity procedures have none, it has no GPWS escape checklist, and its rejected takeoff is a crew flow in Section IV rather than a checklist. The procedures in this section follow that: where the KC-10 book boxes nothing, nothing is boxed.

The MD-10 FCOM boxes its recall items as the three-crew books do, but boxes fewer of them: in the engine fire procedure only the throttle, and none in the smoke, cabin smoke, APU fire or hydraulic procedures. The rejected takeoff and the GPWS escape are techniques in the FCOM's Procedures and Techniques chapter, to be flown at once but not boxed. This manual marks exactly the FCOM's boxed items.

blocks.content: The EFB's **Failures** app is an instructor's station built from the KC-10 flight manual's emergency and abnormal checklists: each failure it models produces the condition one of the procedures in this manual deals with, by failing a real component (a valve, a bearing, a detector, a duct) and letting the aircraft show it the way it would. A failure can be failed at once, or armed to fire at a time, an altitude, an airspeed, at V1 on the takeoff roll, at liftoff, on the approach, at touchdown or in cruise, and the lists can be hidden so that the crew do not know what is coming. See [Failures](efb#failures-app) and [Practice a failure](efb#practise-a-failure).

parts.title: Takeoff
parts.summary: The rejected takeoff, the continued takeoff after an engine failure at or after V1, and an engine fire on the ground.

blocks.content: V1 is the speed by which the decision to stop must have been made **and acted on**. The certified accelerate-stop distance assumes that the first stopping action (throttles closed, then brakes, spoilers and reverse) begins at V1 at the latest, with the stop made by maximum braking on the runway remaining. When the takeoff weight is limited by the runway, a reject begun after V1 cannot stop on the runway, and a continued takeoff after an engine failure before V1 may not clear the obstacles. V1 is therefore not a speed to reach and then think about: it is the end of the thinking.

The crew's callouts are built around that. From the start of the roll to 80 kt, anyone who sees any malfunction calls it, with just enough detail for the captain to decide; at low speed a reject costs little. From 80 kt to V1, only significant malfunctions are called. Approaching V1, the bar for stopping rises steeply: a stop near V1 is justified only by an engine failure, a fire, or a condition that leaves real doubt the aircraft will fly. The captain alone makes the decision and announces it: "Reject" or "Continue".

Experience in operations is that more accidents come from high-speed rejects than from continued takeoffs. In a borderline case close to V1, continue. Above V1, a reject is justified only if the captain judges the aircraft incapable of flight, and must then accept that it will probably not stop on the runway.

A wing engine failing on the roll yaws the aircraft toward the dead engine; the rudder and rudder pedal nosewheel steering hold it straight. A center engine failure gives no yaw at all and is usually first seen on the engine instruments (on the DC-10 and KC-10, the ENG FAIL light on the glareshield) or felt as a slower acceleration: the FE and the PM must watch for it.

**Condition:** A malfunction on the takeoff roll before V1 that the captain judges makes continuing unsafe: an engine failure, an engine fire or other fire warning, a configuration warning, or any condition that leaves doubt the aircraft will fly.

**Objective:** Stop on the runway with maximum use of every deceleration device, then deal with the cause.

items.action: MAXIMUM MANUAL ANTI-SKID BRAKING TO A COMPLETE STOP

items.item: Engine instruments, reverser lights, electrical panel

blocks.content: FedEx has the captain personally make every reject. The captain brings all three reverse levers up toward the reverse N1 limit without waiting to be told which reversers are available; in most rejects all three are, and the FE watches N1 so that no engine overspeeds in reverse. If the spoilers have not deployed, the FE pulls the handle aft, then out to engage the lock, and announces "Spoilers deployed". Tell the tower of the reject once the aircraft is under control.

items.action: SLIGHTLY FORWARD OF NEUTRAL; WINGS LEVEL
OBSERVE AFT; IF NOT, "NO SPOILERS", PULL AFT AND LIFT

blocks.content: The KC-10 flight manual gives the abort as a crew flow in its normal procedures, not as a boxed checklist: the pilot in command decides and announces, the pilot flying makes the stopping actions, the pilot not flying holds the nose down and calls the tower, and the FE monitors the engines and the spoilers. Runway conditions may call for less asymmetric reverse.
On the aircraft a reject deploys the armed spoilers when reverse thrust is selected. In the simulation they deploy as soon as two throttles are closed with the main wheels above 45 kt.

Keep braking, reverse thrust and the ground spoilers until a safe stop is certain. Brake hard and at once: the anti-skid system works best with the pedals fully depressed, and at high speed the brakes do most of the work. The commonest error in the simulator and in the aircraft is a late or soft brake application while attention is on the reversers. Hold the nose firmly down with slight forward column (never full forward, which unloads the main wheels), and expect the pitch-up from the spoilers and reverse thrust.

If directional control becomes difficult in reverse, especially on a slippery runway with a wing engine out, bring the reversers back to reverse idle (forward idle if necessary), regain control, and reapply reverse as the runway allows. Use symmetrical reverse thrust as far as the stopping distance permits.

**Autobrake.** With the AUTO BRAKE selector at T.O. and armed, the system applies full pressure from both brake systems the moment the throttles close in a reject above 60 kt, and that is the maximum braking the aircraft has. Its value is in the second before the captain's feet arrive: pressing the pedals past about 40 % of their travel disarms it, and the procedure is maximum manual braking regardless. An abort begun at or below 60 kt gets only minimum braking from the autobrake. See [Autobrake in takeoff mode](landing-gear#autobrake-takeoff).
The KC-10 has no autobrake, and the simulated MD-10 has none either: the stop is made entirely on the pedals.
**When the aircraft is stopped:**

items.action: DO NOT SET until the brake temperatures are known

blocks.content: On the MD-10 the PM reads the brake temperatures on the SD CONFIGURATION page; a brake above 400 °C turns amber and raises BRAKE OVERHEAT.

blocks.title: Brake temperature after the stop
rows: Check the brake cooling time before the next takeoff; complete the After Landing checklist
400 to 500 °C, or a brake overheat indication
Do not set the parking brake. A brake held above 400 °C for more than about five minutes may melt the wheel fuse plugs and deflate the tires. Maintenance inspection before the next flight

Clear the runway at once, do not set the parking brake, alert the fire services and be ready to evacuate: a fire is possible within 30 minutes. Keep everyone clear of the gear; after 45 minutes approach the tires only from the front or the rear

blocks.content: Brake temperatures go on rising for 15 to 25 minutes after a high-energy stop as the heat soaks from the friction faces into the housing and the wheel. After the aircraft is stopped, hold it with as little braking as possible. If an engine failure caused the reject, leave the hydraulic motor pumps on (DC-10, KC-10), so that braking and nosewheel steering are not lost.

**Practice:** EFB Failures, ENG, *Engine # failure*, armed with WHEN at Speed, accelerating through an IAS below V1 (100 kt, for instance). Expect the brakes to reach the caution or danger zone after a heavy reject near V1, and use **Reset Aircraft** to cool them before the next attempt. In the simulation the brake temperature indication peaks as the braking stops rather than 15 to 25 minutes later, although the fuse plugs can still melt minutes afterwards. See [Brake temperature and brake energy](landing-gear#brake-temperature).

**Condition:** An engine fails, or an engine fire warning comes on, at or after V1.

**Objective:** Continue the takeoff, fly the engine-out profile to a safe altitude clear of obstacles, and only then deal with the engine.

Takeoff performance is calculated for the loss of a wing engine at V1 (the most critical case, with the asymmetric thrust), and every one of the takeoff speeds is chosen around it: VR so that the aircraft reaches V2 by 35 ft on two engines, and V2 high enough above the minimum control speed in the air and the stall speed to give adequate control and climb. Flown accurately, the engine-out profile clears the obstacles in the departure path by a margin. Flown loosely (rotating early, holding the wrong speed, banking too much) it may not.

blocks.alt: Side-view profile diagram of a three-engine jet's takeoff with an engine failure at V1, left to right: the takeoff roll with the V1 point marked (Captain: "Continue"), rotation at VR, V2 at 35 ft, "Positive rate, gear up", the climb at V2 to V2 + 10 (bank limit 15°) to the engine-out acceleration altitude (1,000 ft above the field or the minimum flap retraction altitude for the DC-10, the acceleration height for the KC-10, the FMS EO ACCEL altitude, default 800 ft, for the MD-10), the level or shallow acceleration segment with flaps retracted on schedule, memory items and checklist called, slats retracted at the slat retraction speed, and the final climb at maximum continuous thrust at the clean minimum maneuver speed. Each segment labeled with its speed and its crew callout.
blocks.title: Engine failure on takeoff, profile

items.item: Engine fire or engine failure, and engine number

items.action: ROTATE SMOOTHLY TO ABOUT 15° (10° MINIMUM AT HIGH WEIGHT)

items.item: FE panel and forward engine instruments

items.action: V2 TO V2 + 10; BANK 15° MAXIMUM BELOW V2 + 10
AT 0°/RET MINIMUM MANEUVER SPEED TO A SAFE ALTITUDE

blocks.title: Engine fire or failure on takeoff (MD-10)

items.action: ABOUT 3° PER SECOND TO V2 AT 35 FT, INITIAL PITCH 12 TO 15°
PULL SPEED KNOB, SELECT V3 (or FMS PROF)
FOLLOW PITCH GUIDANCE TO A SAFE ALTITUDE
SELECT FOR MCT AT ACCELERATION ALTITUDE

blocks.content: **Speed to fly.** If the engine fails before V2, climb at V2. If it fails between V2 and V2 + 10, hold the speed it failed at. If the aircraft is already faster than V2 + 10, reduce to V2 + 10 when obstacle clearance matters and otherwise hold the speed. Never reduce below V2.

**Thrust.** The KC-10 manual and FedEx differ in emphasis. The KC-10 manual bases its reduced-thrust takeoffs on the loss of a wing engine and permits advancing the remaining engines to takeoff rated thrust only above 135 KIAS, because the minimum control speed on the ground was computed for the assumed temperature and more thrust earlier could exceed the rudder's authority. FedEx lets the pilot flying call for maximum power after a failure during a reduced-power takeoff, and for firewall power, throttles to the stops, if the flight is in doubt. In both, power beyond the rated thrust is the last resort: an engine pushed to its stops is the next engine at risk.

**FMS engine-out mode.** When the FMS detects the failure both MCDUs show the PERF page with *CONFIRM ENG OUT and CLEAR* prompts; the engine-out computations and guidance start only once CONFIRM is selected. With PROF engaged the aircraft then levels at EO ACCEL, accelerates to V3, and climbs again on schedule; through the all-engine acceleration altitude the thrust reduces to MCT once clean. See [FMS engine-out](flight-management#pegasus-engine-out).

**Technique.** Fly attitude first. In the takeoff mode the flight director's pitch bar initially commands more pitch than an engine-out climb can hold; following it at rotation produces an over-rotation and a pitch oscillation. Aim for the target attitude, hold it, and adjust for the speed: the airspeed indicator is the primary reference, and the bars soon settle. Hold the yaw with the rudder, not the ailerons: with the right rudder the control wheel is almost centerd and the slip ball is close to the middle, and a wheel held well over (raising spoilers on one wing) is the sign of too little rudder. Trim the rudder out once the pitch and speed are steady. Delay nothing in raising the gear once the climb is positive, and do not let the aircraft climb instead of accelerating while the flaps and slats come up.

items: Common errors: rotating when the engine fails rather than at VR; over-controlling the rudder; holding the wings level with aileron instead of rudder; missing a center engine failure; banking more than 15° below V2 + 10; letting the speed decay while retracting the flaps.
If an engine-out departure procedure is published for the runway, follow it if the failure occurs before its first turn point, and brief it before every takeoff.

If a second engine fails during the clean-up, the aircraft may be unable to hold altitude on one engine while the flaps, slats or gear are still out: set go-around thrust on the remaining engine, descend gently if necessary to reach the clean minimum maneuver speed, and clean up on schedule (see [Single engine operation](emergency-engines#single-engine-operation)).

blocks.content: In the simulation the TAKE OFF pitch mode of the DC-10 and KC-10 flies the speed control system's speed for the configuration and weight rather than the engine-out V2 schedule. After an engine failure, fly the speed by hand from the airspeed indicator.
The MD-10's parallel rudder engine-failure compensation in the takeoff and go-around modes is not simulated: the pilot flying holds the rudder, with or without the autopilot engaged.

**Practice:** EFB Failures, ENG, *Engine # failure*, with WHEN set to V1 and the V1 box left blank to take the Performance card's V1; press Hide to leave the engine a surprise. For a fire after V1, use FIRE, *Engine # fire*, armed at liftoff. See [Practice a failure](efb#practise-a-failure).

**Condition:** An engine fire warning during start, taxi, or a rejected takeoff, or a fire reported by ground personnel or the tower.

**Objective:** Shut off the fuel and extinguish the fire, then decide whether to evacuate.

On the ground there is no reason to wait for a safe height. Stop the aircraft, set the parking brake (unless the brakes are hot after a reject; then hold the aircraft on the pedals), and do the [Engine fire or severe damage](emergency-engines#engine-fire-severe-damage) memory items at once. Tell the tower and ask for the fire services.

items: If the fire warning goes out after the first bottle, shut down the remaining engines as the situation requires, keep the fire services informed, and decide with them whether to disembark normally or evacuate.
If the warning remains after the second bottle, or the fire is visibly not out, evacuate on the side away from the fire: see [Ground evacuation](emergency-landing#evacuation).

blocks.content: A fire in the tailpipe during a start, with EGT rising but no fire warning, is a tailpipe fire, not an engine fire: the fire detectors do not see it. Motor the engine with the fuel lever OFF to blow it out; do not discharge the fire bottles into an engine with a tailpipe fire, as the agent goes into the nacelle, not the tailpipe. The procedure is in [Abnormal Procedures](abnormal-procedures).
On the MD-10, pulling the engine fire handle also silences that engine's aural fire warning.

**Practice:** EFB Failures, FIRE, *Engine # fire*, failed with **Fail now** during taxi or armed at touchdown for an after-landing case. The Failures page's *Engine # tailpipe fire* produces the start-time tailpipe fire.

parts.title: Engines
parts.summary: Engine fire or severe damage, flight with one and with two engines inoperative, a second engine failure on final, the loss of all engines, and a thrust reverser deployed in flight.

blocks.content:
**Condition:** An engine fire warning: the fire bell (DC-10, KC-10) or aural warning (MD-10), the MASTER WARNING lights, that engine's fire handle light and fuel lever light, both of its LOOP lights, and the ENGINE FIRE light on the captain's glareshield (DC-10, KC-10) or the ENGINE 1, 2 or 3 FIRE alert (MD-10). Or **severe damage**: an explosion, a heavy rise in airframe vibration or buffet, repeated or uncontrollable stalls, or indications such as a loss of hydraulic fluid or oil quantity, or no N2.

**Objective:** Shut off everything that can feed the fire (fuel, hydraulic fluid, bleed air), put it out with the extinguishers, isolate the systems that engine served, and land.

The order of the memory items is the order of the fire's supplies. The throttle to idle first, so that the engine is not shut down from high power with a sudden yaw and an overspeed of the other engines' share; the fuel lever off, which cuts the fuel at the engine; the fire handle pulled fully, which closes the firewall fuel valves, the hydraulic shutoff, the bleed and the anti-ice and drops the generator; and only then the agent, which knocks the flame down for a few seconds. With the fuel still flowing the fire comes straight back, so the handle always comes before the agent. The 30-second wait lets the detectors cool and report.

The crew member who sees the warning announces "Engine fire" without a number. The FE identifies the engine on their panel and confirms the throttle, fuel lever and fire handle the PM has a hand on before each is moved. On takeoff, wait for the height the book gives before starting: FedEx 1,000 ft above the field or the minimum flap retraction altitude, the KC-10 manual at least 400 ft above the ground (see [When to start a procedure](emergency-procedures#when-to-act)).

blocks.title: Engine failure on takeoff or engine fire/severe damage (DC-10)

items.item: If fire or severe damage is indicated or suspected: engine fire handle / agent

blocks.content: FedEx's procedure covers any engine failure on takeoff as well as a fire: the throttle and fuel lever come first in every case, and the fire handle only when there is a fire warning or the signs of severe damage. The PM moves all three controls, each once the second officer has confirmed it is the right one.

Pull the handle straight down to its stop (FUEL & HYD OFF) without twisting, then rotate it firmly to AGENT 1, and check that the engine's AGT 1 LOW light comes on to confirm the discharge. A rotation during the pull can fire the bottle before the fuel is off, and the agent does not discharge unless the handle is held fully pulled against its spring while it is rotated. Silence the bell with the ENGINE FIRE light on the captain's glareshield; the handle light stays on as long as the fire does.

*If the fire handle light is still on after 30 seconds:* at the pilot's discretion, rotate the handle to AGENT 2 and check AGT 2 LOW. *If the fire warning still continues 30 seconds after the second bottle:* consider the engine still on fire and land as soon as possible.
Engine 2's two bottles are the APU's bottles as well. If both have been discharged into engine 2, there is no fire protection for the APU: do not start it.

items.item: Fuel tank pump switches, affected engine's tank
ENG HYD PUMP switches, affected engine
ENG PNEU SUPPLY selector, affected engine

items: **Tank pumps.** If the APU will be needed, leave one tank 2 aft pump (or the APU FUEL PUMP) on. Transfer fuel as needed to keep the lateral balance; if a fuel dump is in progress, turn the affected tank's pumps off when it ends.

**Pneumatics.** If the pneumatic temperature or pressure of the affected system is abnormal, close its ISOL VALVE switch: severe damage can break the pneumatic ducts. If that system's air is needed later, use the abnormal procedure for operation with a single pneumatic system. The KC-10 has no engine 2 bleed and no ENG 2 PNEU SUPPLY selector.

**Motor pumps.** Below 10,000 ft both motor pumps should be on (ARM or ON) as a backup source of pressure. The motor pump that supports the failed engine's system should be on; with engine 3 out, the 1-3 pump is preferred to the 2-3. A motor pump joining two operating engines' systems can be OFF for non-critical phases above 10,000 ft. With two engines out, both motor pumps go on, keeping all three systems, and never fewer than two, pressurized. At ARM both motor pumps start by themselves whenever an engine's N2 falls below 45 %.

**Vibration.** If continuous high airframe vibration is present, reduce speed and descend without delay to an altitude where it is acceptable. If it returns and further slowing or descent is not practical, a higher speed may reduce it.

blocks.content: **Consequence:** LAND AT NEAREST SUITABLE AIRPORT. Complete the After Takeoff checklist if it is still to do. If a second engine is also out, go to [Single engine operation](#single-engine-operation); otherwise review [Two engine operation](#two-engine-operation). In cruise at high weight, plan the driftdown to the two-engine altitude.

blocks.alt: Three-frame close-up of a DC-10-30 engine fire handle on the overhead panel during an engine 1 fire: frame 1, the red ENG 1 FIRE handle lit at NORM; frame 2, the handle pulled fully down to FUEL & HYD OFF; frame 3, the handle rotated to AGENT 1 with the AGT 1 LOW light beside it lit and AGT 2 LOW out. The placards NORM, GEN FIELD DISCONNECT, FUEL & HYD OFF, AGENT 1 and AGENT 2 legible in each frame.
blocks.title: Engine fire handle: pull, rotate

items.item: ENG FIRE handle / AGT LOW light

blocks.content:
**Consequences:** LAND AT NEAREST SUITABLE AIRPORT. On engine 2: 2 TO ENG, NO ENGINE AGENTS FOR APU.

Pull the ENG FIRE handle fully down and rotate it left or right to discharge a bottle; check that the AGT LOW light for that bottle comes on. Pulling the handle also silences that engine's aural fire warning.

*If the ENGINE FIRE alert remains after 30 seconds:* rotate the handle the opposite way to discharge the remaining bottle and check its AGT LOW light. Discharging both bottles into engine 2 leaves none for the APU.

Opening the ISOL valve lets a neighboring air system feed the dead engine's users. If the pressures or temperatures of that air system are abnormal (damage to the pneumatic components), turn the ISOL switch off again and do not repressurize that system for the rest of the flight.

*If continuous high airframe vibration is present:* without delay reduce airspeed and descend to a safe altitude where the vibration is acceptable; if it returns and further slowing and descent are not practical, increasing airspeed may reduce it.

Land at the nearest suitable airport. The systems controllers reconfigure the hydraulic, electrical and fuel systems for the lost engine by themselves; check the synoptic pages.

**In the simulation** an engine fire burns as long as its firewall fuel valve is open, and for about three minutes on its residue once the handle has shut it. A fire hit with the first bottle within its first minute goes out with that bottle, and the handle light goes out in about 15 seconds. A fire left burning longer comes back once after the first bottle, and the second bottle puts it out. Discharging with the fuel still on always lets it re-ignite. Both branches of the 30-second decision can therefore be practiced. See [Engine fire handles](fire-protection#fire-handles) and [Why the handle comes before the agent](fire-protection#agent-and-reflash).
**Practice:** EFB Failures, FIRE, *Engine # fire*; or ENG, *Engine # severe damage* (a failed gearbox and a fan imbalance: vibration, no fire warning).

**Condition:** One engine has been shut down or has failed and the engine procedure (fire or severe damage, or the in-flight shutdown in [Abnormal Procedures](abnormal-procedures)) is complete.

**Objective:** Settle the aircraft at an altitude and speed it can hold, plan the diversion, and fly the approach and landing on two engines.

items.item: Second engine fails on final checklist

blocks.content:
Below 14,000 ft go-around thrust may be used if required for a limited time (10 minutes in the KC-10 manual). Find the two-engine altitude and speed for the weight; descend to it if necessary and then hold the charted speed.

**Approach and landing.** Land with flaps 35°/EXT at VREF 35°/EXT + 10 kt, the extra speed giving a margin for the asymmetric go-around. Stabilize the approach early to minimize thrust changes: with a wing engine out every thrust change needs a rudder change, and with the center engine out a pitch and trim change. Configure flaps 22° and gear down at the final approach fix or 1½ dots below the glideslope, flaps 35° once the gear is down. Zero the rudder trim on the captain's command before touchdown, and use reverse on the operating engines with discretion. The KC-10 manual instead delays the flaps, slats and gear, and the descent through 2,000 ft above the ground, as long as practical, and adds 10 kt to the 22°/EXT minimum maneuver and 35°/EXT threshold speeds until the landing is assured.

Once configured for landing at a high weight and in extreme ambient conditions, the aircraft may have no go-around capability if another engine fails. With an outboard engine out the autopilot may not have the rudder authority for a go-around: fly an engine-out go-around by hand, with the autopilot disconnected, on the same profile as an engine failure on takeoff.
After landing, leave the hydraulic motor pumps on, so that full braking and nosewheel steering remain.

On the MD-10 there is no separate emergency procedure for one engine out: the engine procedure (ENGINE FIRE or the abnormal ENGINE SHUTDOWN IN FLIGHT) ends with the landing at the nearest suitable airport. The FMS's engine-out mode gives the two-engine maximum altitude and driftdown, and the approach is flown with flaps 35 and the landing speeds the FMS computes.
