Fly an engine-out go-around by hand if a wing engine is out, and keep the rudder trim zeroed before touchdown. See [FMS engine-out](flight-management#pegasus-engine-out).
**Practice:** EFB Failures, ENG, *Engine # failure* (the fuel to that engine cut off: a clean flameout, ready for a restart attempt).

**Condition:** A second engine fails or must be shut down, unless the aircraft is on final with the flaps, slats and gear down (then use [Second engine fails on final](#second-engine-fails-on-final)). If the flaps and slats are out but the gear is not yet down, use this procedure and go around if necessary.

**Objective:** Clean the aircraft up and hold the best speed, drift down to the altitude one engine can hold, reconfigure the systems for a long flight on one engine, and plan a landing with no go-around.

The aircraft may not hold level flight on one engine with the flaps, slats or gear extended. Retracting the flaps and the gear at the same time can overload the one remaining engine-driven hydraulic system: raise the gear after the flaps are up.

The flap handle at UP leaves the slats extended (0°/EXT); the slats come in once the speed allows. If driftdown is needed, or terrain clearance is a factor, hold altitude until the speed has fallen to about 240 KIAS (DC-10-10, -15) or 280 KIAS (DC-10-30, -40, KC-10), or the driftdown speed for the weight, then start the descent and hold the driftdown speed down to the level-off altitude.

items.item: AVIONIC FLOW switch (if engine 2 is operating)

items.action: ON (keep at least two systems pressurized)

items.item: ENG PNEU SUPPLY selectors, all (below 10,000 ft)

items: Above 10,000 ft one pack is kept running for pressurization: the KC-10 manual drives the other pack's temperature valve to full hot (PACK function selector held at MAN HOT, then PACK OFF), which closes its ram air doors and cuts their drag. With the cabin pressure MODE switch at SEMI-AUTO and the ALT SET scale at 10,000 ft, the cabin climbs gently so that the packs and bleeds can be shut off for the descent below 10,000 ft. The cabin altitude horn may sound with 10,000 ft set.
In icing conditions, leave the operating engine's ENG PNEU SUPPLY selector at AUTO and use the isolation valves for wing anti-ice.

The APU gives a backup electrical source and pneumatics, at the cost of range and go-around performance: leave it off if thrust or range is critical. If both of engine 2's bottles have been discharged, the APU has no fire protection.
At the bottom of the driftdown, hold altitude and let the aircraft accelerate as fuel burns off; the KC-10 manual then cruise-climbs at 270 KIAS.

blocks.content: **Choosing where to land.** The closest runway may not be the best: weigh the distance, the hydraulic systems remaining, the runway length and condition, the crosswind, the ceiling and visibility, and a precision approach. A single-engine approach commits the aircraft to land at 1,000 ft above the field.

blocks.title: Approach and landing on one engine (DC-10, KC-10)

items.item: GND PROX WARN FLAP OVRD switch (not in the DC-10 simulation)

items.action: UNTIL READY FOR THE FINAL DESCENT

items.item: At 1,000 ft (commit point): autopilot and autothrottles

blocks.content: Expect a higher than normal rate of descent and pitch attitude on the 0°/EXT approach. Cross the threshold at VREF, flare slightly to reduce the sink rate, close the throttle and fly the aircraft onto the runway: do not try for a smooth landing, which floats. Once the nose gear is down, raising all three reverse levers to the interlock also deploys the spoilers automatically, a backup to the manual deployment. The autobrake is not used. A landing over the maximum landing weight with the center gear up needs a maintenance inspection.

Do not attempt a single-engine missed approach below 1,000 ft above the field, below the 0°/EXT minimum maneuver speed, with the gear extended, or above the maximum weight for a two-engine-inoperative missed approach. Above 1,000 ft, a go-around is: autopilot off, go-around thrust, slats retract, continue descending while accelerating to the 0°/RET minimum maneuver speed, then climb at it.

The DC-10 has no ground proximity flap override switch in the simulation: with the GPWS voice option fitted, expect TOO LOW FLAPS warnings on a 0°/EXT approach, and disregard them once the configuration is confirmed.

Below 14,000 ft, 5 minutes of go-around thrust may be used if required. Delay the gear retraction until the flaps are up. Plan to land at the nearest suitable airport.

*If driftdown is required:* autothrottles OFF and thrust MCT. Check the driftdown speed schedule for the weight: continue level until the speed falls to the start-of-driftdown speed, then drift down to reach the one-engine maximum altitude at the bottom-of-driftdown speed. Determine the minimum safe altitude and range, consider a fuel dump to level off at a safe altitude while keeping the range, and select the driftdown altitude. Level at the maximum one-engine altitude, let the aircraft accelerate to 240 kt (Series 10) or 270 kt (Series 30) as fuel burns, and hold that speed for the cruise climb.

items.item: At or below 10,000 ft: pack switches (all)
If the hydraulic system is in MANUAL: 1-3 and 2-3 RMPs

blocks.content: With ENG IGN OVRD on, the inoperative engines' main tank pumps run; turning it off stops them. Above 10,000 ft keep one pack on for pressurization. Hold the clean configuration and the UP/RET VMIN + 30 speed until the maneuvering is done. **On final:** FLAP/SLAT handle 0/EXT and the 0/EXT approach speed, held until committed to land at 1,000 ft. **At 1,000 ft:** GEAR handle DOWN, three green (no autobrake); spoilers ARM; reach the 0/EXT threshold speed at or above 50 ft; zero the rudder trim before touchdown. Do not try for a smooth touchdown: at the threshold close the throttles and flare slightly; too much flare floats, uses runway and can strike the tail. Use reverse as required; raising all three reverser levers to the interlock extends the spoilers automatically.

Do not attempt a go-around below 1,000 ft above the ground, below the 0/EXT approach speed, with the landing gear extended, or above the maximum weight for a two-engines-inoperative missed approach. A missed approach above those limits: go-around thrust, FLAP/SLAT handle UP/RET, speed UP/RET VMIN + 30, holding the approach rate of descent while the slats retract until the UP/RET speed is reached, then climb.
The MD-10-30's center gear isolation switch, which the FCOM moves to UP at or below 10,000 ft, is not simulated: the center gear extends with the main gear.

**Practice:** EFB Failures, ENG, *Engines # fail* (1 and 2, 1 and 3, or 2 and 3). With engines 1 and 3 out, both wing engines are gone and the asymmetry is zero, but systems 1 and 3 lose their pumps; with a wing engine and engine 2 out, the asymmetry is at its worst.

**Condition:** On a two-engine approach with the gear down and the flaps and slats extended, a second engine fails.

**Objective:** Land. With the gear down and landing flaps on one engine, the aircraft cannot go around; reduce the drag to what one engine can carry to the runway.

items.item: GND PROX WARN FLAP OVRD switch (not in the DC-10 simulation)

blocks.content: Adjust the throttles to hold VAPP. The autobrake is inoperative.

blocks.title: Second engine fails on final approach (KC-10)

blocks.content: Use go-around power as required to continue the approach; the FE watches it and trims it to the N1 limit on the pilot's command. With the flaps at 22° the GPWS warns of the flap position: set the GND PROX WARN FLAP OVRD switch to OVRD to silence it.

On the MD-10 the FCOM's two-engines-inoperative procedure covers this case: if a second engine fails on final with the gear down, add power as required, set FLAPS 15, keep the speed at VREF + 5 for flaps 15 and continue the approach. Move the GPWS switch to FLAP OVRD, conditions permitting.
**Practice:** EFB Failures, ENG, *Engine # failure* active, then a second *Engine # failure* armed at Approach (the phase fires through 3,000 ft above the ground, descending).

sections.title: Loss of all engines (all engine flameout)

blocks.content:
**Condition:** All three engines flame out: EGT, N2 and fuel flow fall on all three, followed by N1, and the generators drop off one after another. On the DC-10 and KC-10 the aircraft then looks like a loss of all generators: every bus is dead except the battery bus, the flight and engine instrument flags are in view, and every bus OFF light is lit except BAT BUS OFF. Falling EGTs tell the two apart: if they are normal, it is the generators, not the engines (see [Loss of all generators](emergency-electrical#loss-of-all-generators)).

**Objective:** Restore power to the flight instruments and the flight controls at once, keep enough airspeed to windmill the engines and to fly, and relight.

Causes include fuel starvation or mismanagement, volcanic ash, and very heavy rain or hail at low power. Without engines, hydraulic power comes only from the windmilling engines' pumps and from the ADG driving auxiliary pump 1, and electrical power only from the battery and the ADG. Speed is everything: it windmills the engines toward the 10 % N2 a relight needs, it turns the ADG, and it keeps the aircraft above the minimum control speed with the little hydraulic power there is.

items.action: EXISTING CONFIGURATION, ABOUT 250 KIAS (10 % N2 FOR AIRSTART)

items.item: If all N2 gauges are below 45 %: ADG

blocks.content: If any engine is still above 45 % N2, the engines are running and the generators have failed: go to [Loss of all generators](emergency-electrical#loss-of-all-generators).

Refer to the captain's flight and engine instruments as their flags clear. Emergency power gives the captain's side, the A igniters and the engine instruments; the OVRD & AIR START switch gives continuous ignition on all engines. Do not use either autopilot on emergency power or the ADG. The ADG at HYD runs auxiliary pump 1 to pressurize system 3 for the flight controls (the motor pumps do not run in this mode). On the aircraft the pump starts by itself when the ADG deploys; in the simulation it does not, so select AUX PUMP 1 to START, after which it keeps running on emergency power while all three engines are below about 50 % N2. Trim with the long trim handles, sparingly and briefly, because the auxiliary pump's small output is easily overrun by the trim. Turning off engines 1 and 3's hydraulic pumps lets them windmill faster. Closing the outflow valve slows the cabin's climb.

blocks.title: Engine start envelope
rows: 240 KIAS to VMO/MMO (unrestricted); 220 to 240 KIAS (probable relight)

blocks.content:
Keep at least 10 % N2. An air start at altitude can accelerate to idle very slowly; if N2 is rising steadily and EGT is within limits, the start is progressing. Engine 2 may not relight until a tank boost pump has power again: it has no suction feed.

*If all engines remain inoperative after 45 seconds:* ENG 1 and 3 HYD PUMP switches all ON; ADG switch R EMER ELEC; TANK 2 L AFT pump ON; ENG 2 HYD PUMP switches OFF; motor pumps OFF; clock START, allow 45 seconds.

*If all engines still remain inoperative:* ADG switch HYD. Do not operate the flaps or slats. Extend the gear with the alternate gear extension lever when required, and move the gear handle to DOWN once the gear is down and locked. Maintain at least the speed in the table below for the configuration, and never less than 155 KIAS.

Keep at least 10 % N2, and do not operate the flaps or slats. *If engine 1 or 3 has not restarted within about 45 seconds,* turn at once to engine 2: ENG 1 and 3 HYD PUMP switches ON (one on each system); ENG 2 HYD PUMP switches both OFF; motor pump switches both OFF; ADG switch R EMER ELEC, which powers the TANK 2 L AFT pump and ignition system B; IGNITION selector CONT B.

*If no engine restarts,* keep trying, holding at least the minimum speed for control in the table below. When the landing is imminent: ADG switch HYD, ENG 2 L HYD PUMP switch ON, extend the gear with the alternate gear extension lever, and move the gear handle to DOWN once the gear is down and locked.

blocks.title: Minimum airspeed for control with all engines flamed out (KIAS)
Minimum airspeed for control with all engines flamed out (KIAS)

blocks.content: Flown at these speeds (and never below 155 KIAS) in any of these configurations, the glide descends at about 1,900 to 2,200 ft/min, and once trimmed for the configuration a flare to zero sink costs only about 150 ft (takeoff configuration) to 100 ft (cruise configuration).
FedEx gives tables for the DC-10-10 and -30 only. For the -15 use the -10 values, and for the -40 the -30 values, as the nearest.

*If an engine restarts:* outflow valve AUTO; that engine's hydraulic pump switches ON and AUTO; motor pumps as required; DC TIE 3 switch CLOSE (it powers DC bus 3 when the ADG goes to R EMER ELEC); ADG switch R EMER ELEC (this lets the motor pumps run); EMER PWR switch OFF; ignition as required; OVRD & AIR START switch OFF. Restart any engine still out with the in-flight engine start procedure in [Abnormal Procedures](abnormal-procedures). The ADG cannot be stowed in flight.

*If an engine restarts:* CAB PRESS MAN/AUTO handle AUTO (select the cabin altitude as required); that engine's hydraulic pump switches ON, and check its system's pressure in the white band; DC TIE 3 switch CLOSE (it powers DC bus 3 when the ADG goes to R EMER ELEC); ADG switch R EMER ELEC (this lets the motor pumps run); motor pump switches ARM; EMER PWR switch OFF; OVRD & AIR START switch OFF. Time permitting, restart the remaining engines, then complete the appropriate checklists. Below 18,000 ft, consider starting the APU for pneumatics, altitude and time permitting. The ADG cannot be retracted in flight and costs about 1 % in range.

The engine start envelope is the same as the DC-10's (above). The ENG IGN OVRD switch powers both ignition systems on all engines directly; the ADG is released with its handle on the pedestal. If time permits, the FCOM puts the cabin pressure system in MANUAL with the outflow valve closed to slow the cabin climb until an engine relights; that panel is not functional in the simulation.

*If an engine restarts:* ADG ELEC switch ON (the ADG then supplies both emergency AC buses), restart the remaining engines with the abnormal ENGINE RESTART IN FLIGHT procedure, verify the systems, and land at the nearest suitable airport.

*If no engine restarts:* throttles (all) IDLE, and keep the last flap and slat position; do not reconfigure. If ditching is required: gear UP and see [Ditching](emergency-landing#ditching). Otherwise extend the main gear with the alternate gear extension lever (the Series 30's center gear may be extended as desired), move the gear handle down, and do not stow the lever.

Fly at no less than the minimum speed for control in the configuration, and never below 155 KIAS: below it the windmilling engines' pumps and the ADG cannot give enough hydraulic power for the flight controls.

**In the simulation** the KC-10's start envelope (above) applies to every engine type, and at the envelope's speeds a windmilling core turns above the 10 % N2 a relight needs (about 15 % at 220 KIAS); well below them, a starter-assisted start with air from another source is needed. Turning off an engine's hydraulic pumps does not raise its windmilling speed in the simulation. The ADG is stationary below about 50 kt, gives useful power from about 120 kt and its full rating from about 180 kt. See [In-flight restart and windmilling](engines#inflight-restart) and [Air-driven generator](electrical#adg).

**Practice:** EFB Failures, ENG, *All engines flame out*. Clear the failure (or not) to choose whether a relight is possible: while it is active, the engines' fuel stays cut off and the procedure ends in a glide.

**Condition:** A reverser light in flight (REV UNLK, REV PRESS or REV THR on the DC-10 and KC-10; the U/L or REV indication, in red, on the MD-10), with or without buffet, a trim change or a loss of performance. A momentary or intermittent reverser light is treated as steady.

**Objective:** Remove the reverse thrust at once and keep control, then decide whether the engine can be used.

A reverser whose control valve fails to the deploy position drives its cowl out with no lever command. The in-flight interlock cannot stop it, because the interlock acts on the reverse lever, and reverse thrust then builds at whatever power that engine's throttle holds. On a wing engine the result is a yaw and roll toward that side and a loss of lift behind the reverser; on engine 2, a pitch change and a loss of thrust. Bringing the throttle to idle removes almost all of the effect, and shutting the engine down takes the air out of the drive, leaving the cowl where it stopped.

blocks.title: Thrust reverser deployed or any reverser light in flight (DC-10)

items.item: Aircraft behavior before the throttle was closed

blocks.content:
*If the aircraft behaved normally:* the light may be a sensing fault. On engine 1 or 3, keep that throttle at idle, leave the autothrottles off for the rest of the flight, and land at the nearest suitable airport. On engine 2, the throttle and autopilot may be used as desired. The procedure ends here.

*If there was buffet, a trim change or a loss of performance:* take whatever corrective action control requires, and move all the **reverse levers FULL DOWN** (forward idle). Watch the reverser lights and the aircraft.

*If all the reverser lights go out and the aircraft behaves normally:* the autopilot may be used, the autothrottles stay off for the rest of the flight. On engine 1 or 3, keep the throttle at idle; on engine 2, use the throttle as desired. Land at the nearest suitable airport.

*Otherwise:* affected engine's **fuel lever OFF**, autopilot and autothrottles as desired, and complete the in-flight engine shutdown procedure ([Abnormal Procedures](abnormal-procedures)).

The KC-10 manual has no memory items here: it starts from how the aircraft is behaving.

*If the aircraft is behaving normally:* autothrottles OFF (PF), and continued use of the affected engine is at the aircraft commander's discretion; autopilot as desired. The procedure ends here.

*If there is buffet, a trim change or a loss of performance:* take immediate corrective action as necessary to keep control, then:

blocks.title: Inadvertent thrust reversal or any reverser light on in flight (KC-10)

blocks.content:
*If the aircraft now behaves normally and all the lights are off:* continued use of the engine is at the aircraft commander's discretion; autopilot as desired.

*Otherwise:* shut the affected engine down (CAPT, F/O, FE) with the in-flight engine shutdown procedure in [Abnormal Procedures](abnormal-procedures); autopilot and autothrottles as required; reduce the gross weight as required, and land with flaps 35°.

In every case, do not use the autothrottles for the rest of the flight, and if a REV U/L or REV PRESS light comes on for engine 1 or 3, keep that throttle at idle and land as soon as practical.
If a REV UNLK light comes from known or suspected cowl damage, consider shutting the engine down unless it is needed for flight, and do not use that reverser on landing.

*If there is no buffet or trim change:* continue normal engine operation. The procedure ends here.

*If there is buffet or a trim change:* take immediate corrective action to keep control, then:

blocks.title: REVERSER DEPLOYED OR U/L OR REV DISPLAYED IN FLIGHT (MD-10)

blocks.content:
*If U/L or REV remains displayed, or the aircraft still behaves abnormally:* affected engine's FUEL lever OFF, and complete the abnormal ENGINE SHUTDOWN IN FLIGHT procedure; set the autopilot and autothrottles as desired, reduce the gross weight as required, and land with flaps 35°.

*Otherwise:* continued use of the engine is at the captain's discretion. Engage autoflight, then disengage the autothrottles immediately, and leave them off for the rest of the flight.
The MD-10's REV n FAULT and REV n PRESS FAULT alerts are not raised in the simulation; recognize the deployment by the red reverser legend on the EAD and by the aircraft's behavior.

**Practice:** EFB Failures, ENG, *Engine # reverser deploys in flight*. Try it at cruise power on a wing engine to feel the yaw and roll, and compare engine 2. See [Reverser failures](engines#reverser-failures).

parts.title: Fire, Smoke and Fumes
parts.summary: APU fire, smoke and fumes of unknown, air conditioning and electrical origin, main deck and lower cargo fires, fuel fumes, and removing smoke from the aircraft.

blocks.content: A fire in an aircraft in flight is the emergency that leaves the least time. Investigations of in-flight fires show the interval between the first sign of smoke and the loss of the aircraft can be as short as fifteen to thirty minutes, and that crews who spent that time on diagnosis rather than on getting to a runway did not survive it. Every smoke procedure in this part therefore has the same spine: **protect the crew** with oxygen and smoke goggles at once, **isolate** the source if it can be found quickly, and **land** at the nearest suitable airport while doing it. Diagnosis runs in parallel with the diversion, never in front of it.

items: Assume all smoke is toxic until its source is known. Burning wiring insulation and cargo produce carbon monoxide, hydrogen cyanide and acid gases that incapacitate in minutes.

100 % oxygen with positive pressure (EMERGENCY) keeps smoke out of a mask that does not seal perfectly, but uses oxygen much faster than the duration tables assume. Return the pressure selector from EMERGENCY to NORMAL as soon as conditions allow, and the dilution lever to NORMAL once the flight deck air is clear.

Smoke goggles go on over the mask if full-face masks are not fitted. Turn the cockpit speakers up: masks make the crew hard to hear. (In the simulation only the KC-10's crew oxygen regulators are modeled; see [Crew oxygen in the simulation](emergency-pressurization#decompression).)
Removing the source of ignition does not necessarily put a fire out: the material may go on burning on its own.

If the source cannot be found quickly or the situation becomes unmanageable, land immediately and prepare to evacuate: see [Preparation for emergency landing](emergency-landing#emergency-landing-preparation).

blocks.content:
**Condition:** An APU fire warning: the APU FIRE light on the FE's panel and the APU FIRE summary light on the pilots' overhead annunciator panel (DC-10, KC-10) or the APU FIRE alert with the aural warning (MD-10), both APU LOOP lights and the MASTER WARNING lights. The APU shuts itself down on the warning.

**Objective:** Make sure the APU is off and its fuel shut, extinguish the fire with engine 2's bottles, and rule out an air leak from engine 2's duct in the APU compartment.
Only engine 2's two fire bottles serve the APU. Every bottle discharged into the APU is lost to engine 2.

items.item: APU FIRE CONTROL switch (not fitted in the simulation)
APU FIRE CONTROL switch (not fitted in the simulation)

blocks.content:
The APU FIRE CONTROL switch makes sure the APU is shut down and arms the agent circuits. The simulated FE panel has no such switch: each APU FIRE AGENT control shuts the APU down, closes its fuel valves and removes its generator field, then fires that bottle into the APU compartment, so the first two items are one press here.

*If the APU FIRE light is still on after 30 seconds:* discharge APU FIRE AGENT CYL 2 and check engine 2's AGT 2 LOW light. Engine 2 then has no fire protection left.
Any crew member may do this procedure if the FE is not at their station. After the 30-second check, APU MASTER switch OFF, and land as soon as practical. Do not restart the APU.
**Consequence:** LAND AT NEAREST SUITABLE AIRPORT. Do not restart the APU.

items.item: APU FIRE handle / AGT LOW light

blocks.content:
**Consequences:** LAND AT NEAREST SUITABLE AIRPORT; ENG 2 AGENTS TO APU, NONE FOR ENG.

The APU warning may come from a fire or from a ruptured air manifold in the APU compartment. The APU shuts itself down and its bleed load valve closes; the FAIL light on the APU panel shows the automatic shutdown, and the START/STOP switch's ON light flashes until OFF is selected (which also puts out FAIL). Verify the discharge by engine 2's AGT LOW light beside its fire handle.

*If the fire warning continues after 30 seconds:* rotate the APU FIRE handle the other way to discharge the remaining agent and check the other AGT LOW light. All of engine 2's and the APU's agent is then gone. Land at the nearest suitable airport.

In the simulation the MD-10's APU FIRE control is turned, not pulled: turning it to AGT 1 or AGT 2 shuts the APU down, closes its fuel, removes the generator field and discharges that bottle in one movement, and it springs back to center.

**In the simulation** the APU shuts down by itself on the warning, which cuts the fire's fuel; the fire then burns on its residue for about three minutes, or goes out with a bottle discharged early. The APU fire horn for ground crew is not heard, and the FE's APU FIRE light does not latch. **Practice:** EFB Failures, FIRE, *APU fire*. See [APU fire protection](fire-protection#apu-fire).

sections.title: Smoke, fire or fumes of unknown origin

blocks.content:
**Condition:** Smoke, fire, fumes or an unusual odour on the flight deck or in the cabin whose source is not yet known.

**Objective:** Protect the crew, start toward a runway, and identify the type of smoke so that the right isolation procedure can follow.

blocks.title: Fire, smoke and fumes of unknown origin (DC-10)

items.item: Land at the nearest suitable airport

blocks.content:
Put on full-face masks, or masks and smoke goggles. Select the mask microphones, turn the cockpit speakers on, and set the interphone to flight interphone so that the whole crew and the couriers can talk. Keep the cockpit door shut to keep heavy smoke out, unless a greater emergency demands otherwise.

*If a descent is required:* autopilot as required, throttles IDLE, speed brakes FULL, airspeed as required, ATC notified (transponder 7700 if there is no contact), all fuel tank pumps ON, altimeters set. If structural damage is known or suspected, limit the speed; the gear and the speed brakes may be used for the descent.

Check the regulator's dilution at 100 %, and with goggles on make sure the mask vent valve is open; if there is no smoke or fumes on the flight deck, the vent valve may be closed. Return the regulator from EMERGENCY to NORMAL when it is no longer needed. Establish crew communication on the interphone, the boom operator included.

blocks.title: Determine the type of smoke, then go to its procedure
rows: Smoke coming from the air conditioning outlets
Smell of burning insulation, visible smoke from electrical components (circuit breaker panels, radios), abnormal electrical indications (fluctuating voltage or frequency, popped breakers)
Smoke detector lights on the FE's panel, smoke or fire seen on the main deck

blocks.content: On the KC-10 there are two more: a smell of fuel in the cabin goes to [Cabin fuel fumes](#cabin-fuel-fumes), and smoke or fuel fumes at the boom operator's station to [ARO compartment smoke or fuel fumes](#aro-compartment).

If the source of the smoke or fumes is not readily identifiable, or the situation becomes unmanageable, consider an immediate landing, and prepare for an emergency landing and evacuation. Consider stopping on the runway so that the fire services can reach the aircraft.
Once the fire is out or the source isolated, clear the air with [Smoke or fumes removal](#smoke-removal).

On the MD-10 one procedure covers smoke and fumes of electrical, air conditioning or unknown origin. It works through the **SMOKE ELEC/AIR selector**, which removes one generator channel and one air system at a time (NORM, 3/1 OFF, 2/3 OFF, 1/2 OFF) so that the source can be found by elimination. If the fumes are identified as fuel or oil and an engine's oil quantity is increasing, go to the abnormal ENGINE OIL QUANTITY INCREASE procedure instead.

Removing the source of ignition may not put the fire out. If conditions permit, delay any fuel dump until the smoke selector is in its final position: with the dump running during the selector changes, valves and pumps may not respond, and the dump may become uncontrollable.

blocks.title: SMOKE/FUMES OF ELECTRICAL, AIR CONDITIONING, OR UNKNOWN ORIGIN (MD-10)

items.item: Pause, and evaluate whether the smoke decreases

blocks.content:
CAB BUS OFF removes power from the cabin AC ground service bus and the cargo loading bus. Allow the air conditioning enough time to clear the contaminated air before judging.

*If the smoke or fumes decrease:* land at the nearest suitable airport. The procedure ends here.

Otherwise: EMER LT switch ARM; AP 1 if desired (verify AP 1 on the FMA); transponder 1 selected; VHF-1 or HF-1 for communication. Then **SMOKE ELEC/AIR selector to 3/1 OFF** (push and rotate) and ECON switch OFF. Generator channel 3 is now unpowered and BLEED AIR 1 and PACK 1 are off. Pause and evaluate.

*If the smoke decreases at 3/1 OFF:* leave the selector there for the rest of the flight. Verify ignition A selected, FLAP LIMIT selector to OVRD 1, select G/A on the MCDU THRUST LIMITS page, AUTO BRAKE selector OFF. Ignition B, the G/A switch, autobrakes, auto slats, the stick shaker, bleed air 1 and pack 1, the F/O's pitot heat, radio panel 2 and VHF-2 and HF-2 are lost; anti-skid works (leave it at ARM). If a go-around is needed, disconnect the autopilot and autothrottles. Land at the nearest suitable airport.

*Otherwise:* **selector to 2/3 OFF.** Channel 2, bleed air 3 and pack 3 are now off, and channel 3, bleed 1 and pack 1 are restored. If SEL FUEL SYS MAN is displayed, select the fuel system to MANUAL. At 2/3 OFF the reverser in-flight lockout is disabled: lifting reverser lever 1 or 3 would deploy that reverser. Pause and evaluate.

*If the smoke decreases at 2/3 OFF:* leave the selector there. The auxiliary and TAT probe heat, bleed air 3 and pack 3, engine 2's reverser, the stabilizer trim switches on the control wheels (use the LONG TRIM handles), the gear position lights (use the CONFIG synoptic), VHF-3 and the anti-skid test are lost. Land at the nearest suitable airport.

*Otherwise:* AP 2 if desired, transponder 2, VHF-2 or HF-2; **selector to 1/2 OFF.** Channel 1, bleed air 2 and pack 2 are off, channel 2 and air system 3 restored; return the fuel system to AUTO if it was put in MANUAL. Ignore the REV 1 and REV 3 PRESS FAULT alerts that appear about 10 seconds later: they come from the power loss, not from the reversers. If the autothrottles disconnect, re-engage them. Pause and evaluate.

*If the smoke decreases at 1/2 OFF:* leave the selector there. Verify ignition B, FLAP LIMIT selector OVRD 2, G/A thrust limit, AUTO BRAKE OFF. Ignition A, the G/A switch, auto slats, the stick shaker, auto ground spoilers, bleed air 2 and pack 2, the captain's pitot heat, reverse on engines 1 and 3, the GPWS, radio panel 1, VHF-1 and HF-1 and wing anti-ice are lost, and the autopilot fails when the IRU and IRU AUX lose power. Disconnect the autopilot and autothrottles for a go-around. Land at the nearest suitable airport.

*If none of the positions helped:* ECON ON, SMOKE ELEC/AIR selector NORM, and land at the nearest suitable airport.

In the simulation the SMOKE ELEC/AIR selector is read and raises SMOKE SW IN USE, but out of NORM it only splits the DC cross-tie: it does not yet unpower a generator channel or shut off a bleed and pack, and the ECON switch is not connected. The CAB BUS and EMER LT switches work. To isolate an air conditioning smoke source (the only smoke source the simulation produces), turn the BLEED AIR switches off one at a time, opening an ISOL valve and keeping a pack running from the remaining systems, and watch for the smoke to clear.
**Practice:** none directly: the EFB's *Electrical smoke, source unknown* produces nothing yet. Air conditioning smoke and cargo smoke (below) begin this procedure.

**Condition:** Smoke or an oil smell coming from the air conditioning outlets; possibly the main deck smoke detectors. Accomplish [Smoke, fire or fumes](#smoke-fire-fumes) first.

**Objective:** Find which bleed source or pack is contaminating the air by shutting them off one at a time, and continue on the clean ones.

The usual cause is engine oil leaking into the compressor air upstream of the bleed port (a seal failure), occasionally an overheated pack. The smoke reaches the cabin with the conditioned air and is carried out again only at the rate the cabin's air is changed, a few minutes, so each step of the isolation needs time before its result shows. If the smoke started while the APU was supplying the air, stop using APU air first.

items.item: If any pack's discharge temperature is above the red line, or its temperature valve reads full hot: that PACK function selector

blocks.content:
*If that stops the smoke:* land at the nearest suitable airport. The procedure ends here.

Otherwise, isolate the three systems and run them one at a time:

items.item: If it continues: ENG 2 PNEU SUPPLY and PACK 2
If it continues: ENG 1 PNEU SUPPLY and PACK 1

blocks.content:
*When the smoke stops:* continue on the system that is running, using the abnormal procedures for air conditioning with fewer than three pneumatic systems and, if needed, wing anti-ice with fewer than three systems. Land at the nearest suitable airport.

*If it never stops:* go back to [Smoke, fire or fumes](#smoke-fire-fumes) and determine the type of smoke again. If it is confirmed to be from the air conditioning and still has not stopped, consider unpressurized flight with all the pneumatic supplies and packs off. Land at the nearest suitable airport.

*If the smoke decreases:* engine 1 is the source. Continue with its supply off, using the abnormal procedure for operation with a single pneumatic system.

*Otherwise:* ENG 1 PNEU SUPPLY selector AUTO, ENG 3 PNEU SUPPLY selector OFF, cockpit door smoke screen as required (not simulated), and observe. *If the smoke decreases:* engine 3 is the source; continue with its supply off.

*If it still does not decrease,* both supplies are contaminated: at the pilot's discretion turn ENG 1 PNEU SUPPLY OFF as well, descend as required, and consider APU pneumatics and passenger oxygen.

On the MD-10, air conditioning smoke is handled by [Smoke, fire or fumes](#smoke-fire-fumes): the SMOKE ELEC/AIR selector shuts one bleed and pack off with each position. See the note there for the simulation.

**In the simulation** the source is oil smoke in one bleed source's air (engine 1, 2 or 3, or the APU). It builds up in the cabin until the smoke detectors see it, within a few minutes; shutting that source off clears the air over several minutes, and the smoke light goes out some minutes after that. Give each isolation step that long before moving on. **Practice:** EFB Failures, FIRE, *Air conditioning smoke, # bleed* (engine 2 not on the KC-10).

**Condition:** Electrical smoke or fire whose source cannot be found and removed at once. Accomplish [Smoke, fire or fumes](#smoke-fire-fumes) first. If the source can be found easily (a radio, a breaker panel), remove its power directly instead.

**Objective:** Remove power from the electrical systems one at a time, AC and DC together, until the smoke decreases, and continue the flight with the offending system isolated.

The DC-10's electrical system splits into three channels, each a generator bus feeding an AC bus and through a transformer-rectifier a DC bus. Isolating a channel completely therefore means opening its generator and APU generator connections, its AC bus tie and its DC tie. The order (3, 2, 1, then the battery buses) loses the least important equipment first, and the DC ties are arranged so that only one DC system is dead at a time. When power is removed from the source, the ventilation should clear the smoke noticeably; the pauses are for judging that.

Bright lighting makes a smoke source easier to find in a dark flight deck. All the tank pumps run so that each engine keeps at least one pump through the isolation. The autothrottles do not work during the bus isolation; autopilot 1 does (with system 3 isolated), but without auto pitch trim.

*If the smoke decreases with the bus ties isolated:* leave them in ISOL, do not connect external power after landing, and land at the nearest suitable airport. The procedure ends here.

items.item: DC TIE 1, DC X-TIE, DC TIE 3 switches
GEN 3 and APU GEN BUS 3 switches

blocks.content:
With system 3 dead, the first officer's flight instruments and flight guidance system 2, VHF and HF 2 are lost, and the standby lights come on with DC bus 3 off.

*If the smoke decreases:* continue with system 3 (and the galley buses) off. Trim the stabilizer by hand if autopilot 1 is in use; expect heavier than normal control forces when disconnecting it. Land at the nearest suitable airport.

*Otherwise:* GEN 3 (or APU GEN BUS 3) switch ON, DC TIE 3 switch CLOSE, then **GEN 2 and APU GEN BUS 2 switches OFF**, and observe. Most cabin systems are lost with system 2, and the emergency lights come on.

*If the smoke decreases:* continue with system 2 off and land at the nearest suitable airport.

*Otherwise:* GEN 2 (or APU GEN BUS 2) switch ON, DC TIE 1 switch OPEN, verify the first officer's instruments are normal, autopilot 1 OFF and autopilot 2 as required, then **GEN 1 and APU GEN BUS 1 switches OFF**, and observe. The captain's flight instruments and flight guidance, VHF and HF 1 and the flight interphone are lost with system 1.

*If the smoke decreases:* continue with system 1 off, trimming by hand if autopilot 2 is in use, and land at the nearest suitable airport.

*Otherwise:* GEN 1 (or APU GEN BUS 1) switch ON and DC TIE 1 switch CLOSE. The smoke is not from a generator channel; the battery buses remain.

items.item: GEN 3 and APU GEN BUS 3 switches
DC TIE 1 and DC X TIE switches

blocks.content:
The KC-10 manual isolates one system at a time with that system's own AC BUS TIE switch. Passenger oxygen comes from the EPOS and the guarded passenger OXY MASK switch, which is not simulated (the masks drop by themselves above about 14,000 ft cabin altitude). With system 3 dead the first officer's flight instruments and flight guidance system 2 are lost, and the standby lights come on.

*If the smoke decreases:* continue with electrical system 3 inoperative.

*Otherwise:* GEN 3 (or APU GEN BUS 3) switch ON, AC BUS TIE 3 NORM, DC TIE 3 CLOSE; then **AC BUS TIE 2 ISOL, GEN 2 and APU GEN BUS 2 switches OFF**, and observe. Most cabin systems are lost with system 2 and the emergency lights come on. *If the smoke decreases,* continue with system 2 inoperative.

*Otherwise:* GEN 2 (or APU GEN BUS 2) ON and AC BUS TIE 2 NORM; verify the first officer's flight instruments are normal; autopilot 2 as required; then **DC TIE 1 OPEN, AC BUS TIE 1 ISOL, GEN 1 and APU GEN BUS 1 switches OFF**, and observe. *If the smoke decreases,* continue with system 1 inoperative. *Otherwise* GEN 1 (or APU GEN BUS 1) ON, AC BUS TIE 1 NORM, DC TIE 1 CLOSE, and go on to the battery buses.
The next action disables the standby attitude indicator, the engine fire detection, the cargo fire extinguishing (DC-10), the master warning and caution system, and stops the APU.

Pull the three **BATTERY BUS FEED circuit breakers** (overhead panel A-13, A-14, A-15). *If the smoke decreases:* pull every circuit breaker on the battery bus, reset the three feed breakers, and watch. If the smoke returns, pull the feed breakers again and land at the nearest suitable airport with those vital systems lost; if not, find the faulty system by resetting the battery bus breakers one at a time, and land.

*If the smoke did not decrease:* reset the feed breakers and pull the **BAT DIR & L EMER DC FEED circuit breaker** (overhead panel, A-16). *If the smoke decreases:* pull every breaker on the battery direct bus except the three battery bus feeds, the emergency inverter power and the electric clock, and reset the feed breaker; if the smoke returns, pull it again (the battery direct bus, and with it the engine fire extinguishing, are lost) and land at the nearest suitable airport; if not, reset the battery direct bus breakers one at a time to find the faulty one, and land.

*If nothing decreased the smoke:* reset the feed breaker. The smoke or fire is not electrical: return the DC ties and the AC bus ties to their normal positions, go back to [Smoke, fire or fumes](#smoke-fire-fumes), determine the type again, and land at the nearest suitable airport, prepared to evacuate.

Pull all three **BATTERY BUS FEEDS circuit breakers**. *If the smoke decreases:* pull every breaker on the battery bus, reset the feed breakers, and watch; if the smoke recurs, pull the feeds again and land at the nearest suitable airfield; if not, restore the essential systems by resetting their breakers one at a time.

*If the smoke did not decrease:* reset the feeds and pull the **BAT DIR & LEFT EMER DC FEED circuit breaker**. *If the smoke decreases:* pull every breaker on the battery direct bus except the three battery bus feeds, the emergency inverter power and the electric clock, and reset the feed; if the smoke recurs, pull it again and land at the nearest suitable airfield; if not, reset the essential systems' breakers one at a time. *Otherwise* reset the feed and set the DC TIE and DC X TIE switches as required.

The KC-10 manual gives the battery bus feeds as A-11 to A-13 and the battery direct feed as A-14 on the overhead panel; the simulated panel has them at A-13 to A-15 and A-16, as on the DC-10.

Land immediately at the nearest suitable airport, even if the smoke is clearing, when the battery bus or the battery direct bus cannot be restored, or when nobody can confirm by sight that the fire is out.

**In the simulation** every switch and circuit breaker in this procedure works, and the effects of each isolation on the instruments and systems are those of the real electrical system. There is no electrical smoke source yet (the EFB's *Electrical smoke, source unknown* produces nothing), so the procedure can be rehearsed but the smoke never responds. Use **Reset Breakers** in the EFB afterwards to put every pulled breaker back. See [Electrical smoke](electrical#smoke-electrical) and [Circuit breakers](electrical#circuit-breakers).

**Condition:** Smoke detected on the main deck: the CAB CARGO SMOKE light and the smoke detector lights on the FE's panel (DC-10, KC-10) or the CABIN SMOKE alert with the aural warning (MD-10), or smoke or fire seen on the main deck. Light concentrations of smoke may not trigger the detectors.

**Objective:** Starve a main deck fire of air (the main deck has no built-in extinguishing), protect the crew, and land.

The main deck of a freighter (and of the KC-10) is a class E compartment: detection only, on the principle that a fire there can be controlled by cutting its air supply and descending until the aircraft can land. The procedure shuts down all but one pack, so that little fresh air reaches the main deck, and then raises the cabin altitude, which lowers the oxygen partial pressure the fire can use. The cabin is raised to about 25,000 ft, high enough to slow a fire, low enough that the crew's oxygen masks still work without pressure breathing. A fire inside a closed container soon uses up the oxygen in it; depressurizing denies it more.

items.item: Land at the nearest suitable airport

blocks.content:
Pull the CABIN AIR SHUTOFF handle only once all but one pack is off. *If landing is imminent:* use the CAB ALT wheel to let the cabin climb and hold about 0.5 psi of differential, never opening the outflow valve more than two-thirds (wider can unseat the doors and let air into the cabin). All tank pumps ON, altimeters set. Just before landing, outflow valve two-thirds open; immediately after touchdown, fully open so that the clearview windows and doors will open. Evacuate if required.

*Otherwise, above FL270:* with the CAB ALT wheel raise the cabin altitude to 25,000 ft at 1,000 to 2,000 ft/min. Evaluate all the possible sources, electrical indications and air outlets included. During the descent keep about 0.5 psi of differential, never more than two-thirds open. All tank pumps ON, altimeters set; outflow valve two-thirds open just before landing and fully open after touchdown. Evacuate if required.

*Otherwise, at or below FL270:* let the cabin climb with the CAB ALT wheel and hold 0.5 psi of differential, and continue as above.

The KC-10 manual has no memory items here; do [Smoke, fire or fumes](#smoke-fire-fumes) first. The boom operator leaves the ARO station, checks the cargo compartment and reports. If there is no smoke or fire, assume a detector malfunction; the procedure ends. Otherwise start the passenger oxygen if required (the masks drop by themselves in the simulation) and begin fighting the fire, then:

blocks.title: Cabin cargo smoke and/or light on (KC-10)

items.item: ARO/additional crew oxygen shutoff valve (all-cargo configuration; not simulated)

items.action: MAN; CONTROL CABIN PRESSURE AS REQUIRED

blocks.content: Close the oxygen shutoff valve and depressurize only once every crew member is back on the flight deck or on portable oxygen, and the passenger masks are out. *Above 27,000 ft:* raise the cabin to 25,000 ft at 1,000 to 2,000 ft/min. *Otherwise:* hold 0.5 psi of differential. Land as soon as practical. Just before landing, outflow valve two-thirds open (wider can unseat the doors); immediately after landing, fully open so that the clearview windows and doors will open. Then [Preparation for emergency landing](emergency-landing#emergency-landing-preparation), and if needed [Smoke or fumes removal](#smoke-removal).

No crew member should leave the flight deck to fight a fire unless it is known to be accessible and the measures already taken have not worked; anything beyond that is discretionary and must be closely coordinated. Do not open a dangerous goods container in flight when a fire inside it is known or suspected.

The CABIN AIR SHUTOFF handle, which stops conditioned air to the main deck (and must not be pulled with more than one pack running), and the cockpit air outlets are not simulated. With one pack running and the cabin depressurized, the procedure still has its main effect on the fire.

**Consequence:** LAND AT NEAREST SUITABLE AIRPORT.

*If CAB AIR NOT OFF is displayed* (the cabin air could not be shut off): turn the operating pack OFF, and descend as required to keep the cabin altitude at 25,000 ft, to starve the fire and avoid oxygen pressure breathing. When the aircraft is depressurized, set the outflow valve indicator to the 9:00 position (further, with no packs running, draws a negative pressure that unseats the doors). Move the oxygen dilution lever to NORMAL once the flight deck is clear. Land at the nearest suitable airport; after landing, before opening the clearview windows or doors, set the outflow valve full open.

*Otherwise:* at or above FL270, hold a 25,000 ft cabin until approaching FL250 in the descent; below 27,000 ft hold 0.5 psi of differential. Dilution lever to NORMAL once clear. Just before landing, rate selector CLIMB; when depressurized, outflow valve at 10:30 (no further with a pack running). Land at the nearest suitable airport; after landing, outflow valve full open before opening windows or doors.

In the simulation the MD-10's CABIN AIR switch, ECON switch and CABIN PRESS panel are not functional, and CAB AIR NOT OFF is not raised. Of this procedure's air controls only the PACK switches act: reduce to one pack, and descend.

**Practice:** EFB Failures, FIRE, *Main deck cargo smoke*. The smoke indication lingers long after the cause is gone, as on the aircraft. See [Cargo and cabin smoke protection](fire-protection#cargo-fire).

**Condition:** Smoke or heat in a lower cargo compartment: the FWD or AFT CARGO FIRE light with its detector lights and the MASTER WARNING (DC-10), or the CRG FIRE LWR FWD or AFT alert with the SMOKE or HEAT light on the cargo fire panel and the aural warning (MD-10).

**Objective:** Flood the compartment with Halon, cut its ventilation, keep the concentration up until the aircraft is on the ground, and land.

The lower holds are class C compartments with a built-in extinguishing system. Two bottles serve both holds: bottle 1 holds the main charge that knocks the fire down, bottle 2 a smaller charge kept back to restore the concentration as the agent leaks out of the compartment. The second shot is timed by the leakage rate, which is why the times below differ by compartment, by series and by whether the aircraft is pressurized. The KC-10 has no lower cargo fire protection.

blocks.title: Cargo FIRE light, forward or aft (DC-10)

blocks.content:
Arming the compartment completes the discharge circuit and, on the -30, shuts off that compartment's airflow. The discharge fills the compartment with agent and turns every smoke detector light in it on; they may stay on long after the fire is out.

*If AGENT 1 LOW has not come on after a minute:* trip and reset the cargo fire control agent 1 and 2 circuit breakers and select CYL 1 again. If AGENT 1 LOW still does not come on, pull the AGENT DISCH switch out and turn it to CYL 2, land at the nearest suitable airport and prepare to evacuate. The procedure ends here.

Otherwise turn the FWD and AFT CARGO VENT switches OFF, which stops the lower cargo ventilation and heat. The simulated FE panel has no separate cargo vent switches: its GALLEY VENT switch does their work.

Land at the nearest suitable airport and be prepared to evacuate. If the landing is expected before the time for cylinder 2, it can be fired before the approach to restore the concentration for the landing and the evacuation.

blocks.title: CRG FIRE LWR FWD or AFT (MD-10)

items.item: Flashing CARGO FIRE AGENT DISCH switch

blocks.content:
**Consequence:** LAND AT NEAREST SUITABLE AIRPORT.

The controller flashes FWD 1 or AFT 1 to show which bottle to fire, and the button goes on flashing until its LOW light comes on. If bottle 1's LOW was already lit from a low pressure, bottle 2's button flashes instead; if bottle 2's button is pushed by mistake, bottle 2 fires and bottle 1's goes on flashing. For a forward fire, some Series 30s also have a FWD FLOW switch to push OFF. CARGO HEAT OFF turns off all cargo heat.

*After about a minute, if the LOW light is on:* about 90 minutes after bottle 1, DISCH CARGO AGENT is displayed and bottle 2's button flashes: push it then. If MSC AUTO FAIL is displayed in the meantime, time the 90 minutes by hand. Land at the nearest suitable airport.

*If the LOW light is not on:* push the bottle 2 button below the flashing one at once, and land at the nearest suitable airport.

**In the simulation** the cargo bottles reach AGENT LOW within about a second rather than half a minute, a cargo shot reaches only the compartment it was directed into, and the smoke lingers after the fire is out. The MD-10's FWD FLOW switch is not connected and its CARGO HEAT switch is not modeled. **Practice:** EFB Failures, FIRE, *Forward lower hold smoke* or *Aft lower hold smoke*. See [Cargo and cabin smoke protection](fire-protection#cargo-fire).

**Condition:** A smell of fuel in the cabin, most likely from the body tanks or the air refueling plumbing in the lower fuselage. Accomplish [Smoke, fire or fumes](#smoke-fire-fumes) first.

**Objective:** Remove every source of ignition and fuel movement, keep the fumes moving out of the cabin, and land.

Stop all fuel transfer and air refueling. The boom operator stows the boom and drogues and leaves the ARO station. Do not use the AR pumps, and do not transfer fuel from the forward body tank unless it is needed to reach the destination. If an engine's oil quantity is changing, see the abnormal oil quantity procedure.

Do not let the cabin climb above 9,000 ft (that sets off the warning bell at the ARO station). Hold about 2.0 psi of differential in the descent and land with no more than 0.5 psi, so that the doors can be opened. Land as soon as practical, do not start the APU, and prepare for an emergency landing and evacuation.
The EFB's *Fuel fumes in the cabin* failure is listed but produces nothing in the aircraft yet.

**Condition:** Smoke or fumes remain in the aircraft after the source has been isolated or the fire put out. For smoke from the air conditioning or the main deck, complete those procedures first.

**Objective:** Flush the smoke out with the maximum airflow and, if necessary, by depressurizing and opening the outflow valve.

items.action: RAISE TO ABOUT 9,500 FT, 1,000 TO 2,000 FT/MIN UP
205 KIAS MAXIMUM (extend slats and flaps as needed)
OUTFLOW VALVE ½ TO ⅔ OPEN

blocks.content:
Every pack running gives the most airflow through the aircraft. Use SEMI-AUTO, STANDBY (DC-10) or the manual wheel to climb the cabin. Fly 205 KIAS or the minimum maneuvering speed for the configuration, whichever is lower, which is the clearview window speed. Do not open the outflow valve more than two-thirds: further draws a negative pressure in the cabin, makes noise, and pulls air in through the cargo doors.

*If the smoke is controlled on the flight deck:* land at the nearest suitable airport. The procedure ends here.

*Otherwise:* establish communication on headsets, and open either clearview window about 3 inches (the PM's, so that the PF's view stays clear), opening and closing it periodically as needed. If the cabin is found to be the source, pull the AVION COMPT FAN circuit breakers. Land at the nearest suitable airport.

**Unpressurized, packs off:** PACK function selectors OFF, communication established, 205 KIAS maximum, CAB PRESS MAN/AUTO handle MAN, outflow valve ½ to ⅔ open, clearview window about 3 inches as required, and land at the nearest suitable airport.

items.action: SYSTEM MANUAL, rate selector CLIMB (1,000 to 2,000 ft/min)

blocks.content: On the aircraft the CABIN ALTITUDE alert appears as the cabin climbs, and CABIN RATE above 1,500 ft/min (CABIN RATE is not raised in the simulation). *If the flight deck smoke is severe:* configure for 205 KIAS or the minimum maneuvering speed, whichever is lower, headsets on, and open the PM's clearview window 3 inches, closing and opening it as needed within the speed limit. Land at the nearest suitable airport.

In the simulation the clearview windows, the cockpit air outlets and the MD-10's CABIN PRESS panel are not functional. On the DC-10 and KC-10 the packs and the outflow valve do the work; on the MD-10, descend and keep the packs running.

sections.title: ARO compartment smoke or fuel fumes

blocks.content:
**Condition:** Electrical smoke or fumes, or fuel or fuel fumes, at the boom operator's station. Accomplish [Smoke, fire or fumes](#smoke-fire-fumes) first.

**Objective:** Remove power from the compartment's buses (for smoke) or every source of fuel and ignition (for fuel), and get the boom operator out.

blocks.title: Electrical smoke or fumes in the ARO compartment

blocks.content: Every light in the ARO compartment goes out, and the flight control warning lights and tone come on. When the smoke clears, and at the boom operator's discretion, return the AR BUS ISOL switch to NORM. *If the smoke returns:* discontinue the refueling, AR BUS ISOL back to ISOL, GND SVC BUS ISOL to NORM, and complete the post air refueling checklist. *If not:* the refueling may continue; with GND SVC BUS ISOL at ISOL the sighting door motor and the boom hoist actuator's control relay are unpowered (power is needed to reposition the hoist when the lever moves from free-wheel to raise), while the drogues are not affected.
With fuel or fuel fumes in the compartment, move only the switches needed to stow the boom or rewind the drogues: a switch operated in fuel vapour can ignite it.

**Fuel or fuel fumes:** the boom operator notifies the pilot and the FE turns the AR pumps off. The boom operator flies the boom to the stowed position and holds it until latched (or stows the hoses), turns off the boom's flight control and hydraulic power (or the drogues' power), leaves every other switch as set, reports "Boom (or drogues) stowed, leaving position", changes to a portable oxygen bottle and leaves the compartment.
These procedures have no EFB failure. The refueling procedures themselves are in [Air refueling](air-refueling) and the boom operator's station in [Air refueling systems](air-refueling-systems).

parts.title: Pressurization and Pneumatics
parts.summary: Cabin altitude warning and rapid decompression, the emergency descent, passenger oxygen, and pneumatic manifold failures and overheats.

sections.title: Cabin altitude warning or rapid decompression

blocks.content:
**Condition:** The cabin altitude warning (horn and CABIN ALT lights on the DC-10 and KC-10, the CABIN ALTITUDE alert on the MD-10) comes on as the cabin passes about 10,000 ft, or the cabin altitude is climbing rapidly. A rapid decompression shows itself unmistakably: a bang or a rush of air, fog as the air cools, dust and debris, cold, and the cabin altitude and rate indicators running up.

**Objective:** Protect the crew with oxygen first, try once to hold the pressure, and if the cabin cannot be controlled, descend at once to an altitude where nobody needs oxygen.

The time of useful consciousness, the time a person can still act sensibly without oxygen, is the reason the masks come first. At FL350 it is under a minute for a resting adult, and after a rapid decompression, when the lungs empty with the cabin, it can be half that. A crew member who stops to think before donning the mask may not get the chance to finish the thought. Not every pressurization problem is a decompression, though: a controller failure or a pack left off lets the cabin climb slowly, and that calls for the abnormal procedures, not a dive. The FE makes sure the pressurization system is correctly configured for the flight altitude before a descent is started for a slow climb.

blocks.title: Cabin altitude warning or rapid depressurization (DC-10)

blocks.content:
To close the outflow valve, move the CAB PRESS MAN/AUTO handle to MAN, push in the CAB ALT control wheel and turn it downward until the OUTFLOW VALVE indicator reads CLOSED. Check the oxygen regulators at 100 % and the microphone selectors at MASK, and turn the cockpit speakers on.

If the outflow valve is closed and the cabin still climbs, the valve is working and the aircraft has either a large leak or no pressurization air. Make no further attempt to close the valve.

*If the cabin altitude is controllable:* operate the pressurization system as required, using the abnormal procedures. The procedure ends here.

*If the cabin altitude cannot be controlled:* begin the [emergency descent](#emergency-descent) at once.

The outflow valve position is on the AIR synoptic page. If it is not closed, the FCOM calls for the CABIN PRESS SYSTEM SELECT switch to MANUAL and the manual rate selector to DESC. Pushing AVNCS FAN to OVRD (its OVRD legend lights) stops the avionics exhaust overboard, removing one leak from an aircraft already short of air.

*If the cabin altitude is controllable:* operate the cabin pressure system as required. The procedure ends here.

*If it is not:* perform the [emergency descent](#emergency-descent).

In the simulation the MD-10's CABIN PRESS panel and its manual mode are not functional, and the ECON switch is not connected; the MD-10 is pressurized by the automatic controller throughout. Skip those items, and if the cabin cannot be held, descend.

blocks.title: Crew oxygen in the simulation
blocks.content: The KC-10's crew oxygen regulators are simulated, with their 100 % and EMERGENCY selections and the oxygen they use. On the DC-10 and MD-10 the crew masks and regulators have no cockpit controls: donning them is a crew action the simulation does not see.

**Practice:** EFB Failures, PRES, *Rapid decompression*, armed in cruise. See [Pressurization](air-conditioning#pressurization), [Cabin altitude warning](air-conditioning#cabin-altitude-warning) and [Oxygen](oxygen).

**Condition:** The cabin cannot be kept below 10,000 ft (an uncontrollable decompression), or another emergency (a fire that cannot be put out, smoke that cannot be removed) demands the fastest possible descent.

**Objective:** Descend as fast as the structure and the passengers allow to 10,000 ft or the minimum safe altitude, whichever is higher, without overspeeding, without negative g, and without losing track of the terrain.

The descent is made with idle thrust and full flight spoilers, at high Mach and then high indicated airspeed. Drag rises with the square of the speed, so the fastest way down is the fastest safe speed, not a steep nose-down attitude: the profile is a 10° nose-down pitch at most, flown smoothly so that nobody is lifted out of a seat, with up to 30° of bank if a turn helps (off an airway, away from traffic or terrain). If structural damage is known or suspected, the speed must come down instead, and the gear can then add the drag the speed no longer gives.

blocks.alt: Side-view diagram of the emergency descent from FL370 to 10,000 ft: at the top, "Masks on, 100 %; crew communications; outflow valve closed"; the entry with autothrottles off, throttles idle, spoiler handle to SPD BRK FULL, pitch to no more than 10° nose down, up to 30° of bank; the descent leg at Mach 0.82 to 0.85 changing to 320 to 350 KIAS where the lines cross; side notes "7700 if no ATC contact", "altimeter setting, minimum safe altitude"; at 2,000 ft above the level-off altitude "reduce the rate of descent"; at 1,000 ft above "speed brakes as required"; the level-off at 10,000 ft or the minimum safe altitude, whichever is higher, with "speed brakes retracted, oxygen to NORMAL". A dashed alternative leg labeled "structural damage: limit speed, gear may be extended".
blocks.title: Emergency descent profile

items.action: MAXIMUM PITCH 10° NOSE DOWN, MAXIMUM BANK 30°

items.item: Passenger OXY MASK switch (not simulated: check the masks have dropped)

items.action: SET 10,000 FT OR MINIMUM SAFE ALTITUDE, ARM
TO 10,000 FT OR MINIMUM SAFE ALTITUDE, WHICHEVER IS HIGHER

items.item: NO SMOKE and SEAT BELTS switches

blocks.content: Preselecting the lower altitude and pulling the altitude select knob starts the descent in the pitch mode, so it can be flown on the autopilot. The NO SMOKING and SEAT BELTS alerts appear when their switches are on.

If structural damage is suspected or turbulence is present, FedEx limits the speed to the 0°/RET minimum maneuver speed, with the gear and the speed brakes used for drag as the damage allows. The KC-10 manual notes that known structural failures or turbulence may dictate other speed profiles and entry maneuvers.
If structural damage is suspected or turbulence is present, do not exceed Mach 0.85 or 287 KIAS (Series 10) or Mach 0.85 or 310 KIAS (Series 30).

The autopilot in CMD or CWS may fly the descent and is recommended; enter it with the vertical speed wheel at its maximum rate down and engage IAS or MACH hold when the target speed is reached. Do not disengage the autopilot to start the descent, and do not pull the spoiler handle past FULL into the ground spoiler range.

**Level-off.** Get the altimeter setting and check the minimum safe altitude on the way down. At 2,000 ft above the level-off altitude, reduce the rate of descent smoothly; at 1,000 ft above, retract the speed brakes as needed to control the speed and level off at 10,000 ft or the minimum safe altitude, whichever is higher. Then re-engage the autothrottles, select a long range cruise speed, set the oxygen regulators to NORMAL (if oxygen is still needed), consult the oxygen duration figures, and take the masks off once the cabin is at or below 10,000 ft. If the minimum safe altitude is above 10,000 ft, stay on oxygen and plan the route to descend further as the terrain allows.

The passenger and courier masks drop automatically when the cabin passes about 14,000 ft. The books back this up with a guarded passenger OXY MASK switch held at EJECT for 3 to 5 seconds; that switch is not simulated on the DC-10 and KC-10, so confirm the deployment with the cabin instead. On the KC-10, set IFF EMERGENCY on the CDU's IFF page; on the DC-10, set 7700 on the transponder.
Once started, the passenger oxygen supply lasts about 22 minutes whatever the rate of use. Plan the descent so that the cabin is at or below 13,000 ft within 22 minutes of the masks dropping.

Common errors: hurrying the entry (it should be deliberate and smooth); letting the speed fall back early and then overspeeding at low altitude; leaving the autothrottles engaged; forgetting the structural limits after a decompression caused by damage; and failing to call for the checklist and coordinate the crew.
**Practice:** EFB Failures, PRES, *Rapid decompression*, armed in cruise above FL300. In the simulation the passenger masks drop by themselves as the cabin passes about 14,000 ft.

**Condition:** The NO MASKS alert: the cabin altitude is above the deployment altitude and the oxygen mask compartments have not opened.

**Consequence:** MANUALLY DEPLOY OXYGEN MASKS.

On the aircraft, pushing the switch opens every oxygen compartment door in the cabin, and the alert goes when it has worked. Do not hold the switch longer than five seconds, which can damage the door latches.
In the simulation the NO MASKS alert is raised, but the NO MASKS switch releases nothing and its legend does not light: the masks drop only through the automatic release.

**Condition:** A manifold failure warning: on the DC-10 and KC-10 the red MANFLD FAIL light (and the PNEU MANFLD FAIL summary light and MASTER WARNING), on the MD-10 the AIR MANF 1, 2 or 3 FAIL alert. A detection loop along that manifold run has sensed the heat of escaping bleed air.

**Objective:** Shut off the air feeding the leak, keep the users that matter, and land.

Bleed air in the manifolds is at about 230 to 240 °C and some 45 psi. Leaking into the fuselage tunnel, the wing leading edge or the center accessory compartment, it can cook wiring, hydraulic and fuel lines and structure. The detection system acts on its own when a loop trips: that system's supply shuts off and the isolation valves next to it close. The crew's actions confirm the isolation, deal with the users that have lost their air, and find out by the pressure whether the leak is really stopped. A momentary or intermittent MANFLD FAIL light is treated as a steady one.

If an ISOL VALVE DISAGREE light stays on, turn the ENG PNEU SUPPLY selector of the system on the other side of that valve OFF as well. If the APU is supplying the manifold and MANFLD FAIL 2 is lit, move the APU/ISOL VALVE switch to CLOSE.

*If the affected system's pressure stays above 10 psi:* the leak is still being fed. Conditions permitting, bring the associated engine's throttle to IDLE (with more than one system affected, idle them one at a time to find which one feeds it) and land at the nearest suitable airport. With the throttle at idle the MANFLD FAIL light may not come on even though the leak remains.

blocks.title: Then, by the lights that are on
rows: WING ANTI-ICE switch OFF and leave icing conditions: wing anti-ice is not available. Continue with that ENG PNEU SUPPLY selector OFF; the antenna anti-ice is lost with system 3. Fly the abnormal procedure for air conditioning with fewer than three pneumatic systems
Continue with the engine 2 supply OFF; do not use the APU as a pneumatic source. If the pressure falls to 10 psi or less with the light still on, no engine shutdown or power reduction is needed

WING ANTI-ICE OFF, TRIM AIR OFF, cargo heat and galley vent OFF. When both lights go out, restore engine 1's supply and pack 1; if the lights return within 15 minutes, take them off again and try engine 2's supply and pack 2 instead. Continue on the system that stays quiet, with wing anti-ice unavailable, and restore the remaining users one at a time at 15-minute intervals, watching for the lights

WING ANTI-ICE OFF, AVIONIC FLOW OVRD, galley vent and cargo heat OFF, all PACK function selectors PACK OFF. Then do a pressure decay check: turn all ENG PNEU SUPPLY selectors to AUTO, let the pressures stabilize, turn them all OFF and compare how fast each system's pressure falls. Restore the one that holds its pressure best (AUTO) and its pack, and continue on it. If its light does not go out within about five minutes, recheck the decay rates. A system whose pressure stabilizes lower than normal for the power set is leaking: do not use it

blocks.content: Do not repressurize a manifold that has had a failure warning, and if system 2 is affected, do not use the APU as a pneumatic source: its air enters the manifold through system 2.

The KC-10 has no engine 2 bleed system, so it has no ENG 2 PNEU SUPPLY selector; its number 2 MANFLD FAIL light still watches the manifold section that carries APU air. Its manual boxes no items here and works by the light that is on.

Depart and avoid icing. *If the MANFLD FAIL light goes out,* continue with that supply OFF. *If not, and the system still shows pressure or a high temperature,* air is still leaking: consider shutting the engine down to remove the source. Otherwise the condition is unknown: land at the nearest suitable airport. (For system 1 the KC-10 manual first tries the MANIFOLD FAIL DETECT LOOP SELECT switch, which is not simulated.)

*Light 2 only:* close the APU/ISOL VALVE and the 1-2 ISOL VALVE, stop using APU air, and land at the nearest suitable airport.

*All three:* ENG PNEU SUPPLY selectors 1 and 3 OFF (the cabin then climbs at about 1,500 ft/min), AVIONIC FLOW OVRD, WING ANTI-ICE OFF, both PACK function selectors OFF, LAV/GALLEY VENT OFF, 1-3 ISOL VALVE CLOSE; avoid icing. When the lights go out, do a pressure decay check: each supply in turn to AUTO, let the pressure stabilize, back to OFF and note how fast it falls. Restore the supply with the slowest fall and its pack, LAV/GALLEY VENT ON and AVIONIC FLOW NORMAL, and continue on that system. A supply whose MANFLD FAIL light returns, or whose pressure stabilizes lower than normal for the power set, is not used again.

**Consequence:** LAND AT NEAREST SUITABLE AIRPORT.

The air system controller has already closed that system's bleed and isolated its manifold. With the throttle at idle the leak's pressure falls; when the alert goes, operate the engine at a thrust that keeps it from returning. Do not repressurize the affected air system.

**CAC MANF FAIL** is the MD-10's warning of a leak in the center accessory compartment. The FCOM procedure turns ECON OFF and AVNCS FAN to OVRD, then (in flight) does a pressure decay check with all three BLEED AIR switches on for five seconds and off again, restores the system with the slowest decay and its pack, and avoids icing conditions if system 1 or 3 stays off. The simulation does not model the center accessory compartment detection and does not raise CAC MANF FAIL.

In the simulation the three MANFLD FAIL lights on the FE's panel do not yet light in the 3D cockpit, although their press-to-test works: recognize the warning by the PNEU MANFLD FAIL summary light, the MASTER WARNING and the ISOL VALVE DISAGREE lights. The center accessory compartment detection (the all-three-lights case on the aircraft) is not modeled, and neither is the MANIFOLD FAIL DETECT LOOP SELECT switch the KC-10 manual uses for system 1.
**Practice:** EFB Failures, PNEU, *Pneumatic manifold # failure* (manifold 2 not on the KC-10). See [Manifold failure detection](pneumatics#manifold-fail).

**Condition:** A system's duct is over temperature: on the DC-10 and KC-10 the red PNEU TEMP HI light (with the summary light and MASTER WARNING) or the TEMP gauge above its red line (260 °C); on the MD-10 the BLD AIR 1, 2 or 3 TEMP HI alert.

**Objective:** Shut off the overheating source, find out whether it really shut, and restore what can be restored.

blocks.title: PNEU TEMP HI light on or temperature above red line (DC-10, KC-10)

blocks.content:
The TEMP HI light is deactivated with the selector at OFF, so the light going out confirms the right system was shut down. With no flow, the TEMP gauge falls only slowly.

*If the pressure is 10 psi or less and the affected system's ISOL valve was closed:* the regulator has shut. Open that ISOL VALVE switch so that the neighboring system feeds the affected system's users, and check that the ISOL VALVE DISAGREE light goes out and the pressure, temperature and PACK OFF light return to normal. Limit the one supply to two systems' demands. The procedure ends here.

*If the pressure is 10 psi or less and the ISOL valve was open:* the overheat may have come from high flow, with one engine feeding two systems' users. Close the ISOL VALVE switch. When the temperature is below the red line and the valve is confirmed closed, return the affected ENG PNEU SUPPLY selector to AUTO. If the TEMP HI light or the temperature returns, turn it OFF again and continue on the other systems; if not, continue with that supply carrying its own system's users only.

*If the pressure stays above 10 psi:* a secondary failure has occurred: the regulator has not fully closed, or air is reaching the duct from elsewhere. Watch the temperature. If it does not fall, turn the affected PACK function selector to PACK OFF to remove the flow. If it still does not fall, pull the affected system's PNEU SYS CONT circuit breaker: the pressure gauge goes to zero and the valves move to the position that lets the system cool.

In flight, do not connect two active engine pneumatic supplies, except briefly when changing over from APU air or during a crossbleed start. If the overheat happened above cruise thrust, a restoration may succeed once the power is reduced.

The BLEED AIR MANF/TEMP HI switch is wired in parallel with the BLEED AIR OFF switch and does the same thing. Wait 30 seconds.

*If the BLD AIR TEMP HI alert returns:* if flight conditions permit, slowly reduce thrust on that engine until the alert goes, and keep the engine at or below that thrust for the rest of the flight. The procedure ends here.

*If bleed air 1 or 2 is affected:* PACK 2 OFF, 1-2 ISOL ON, PACKS 1 and 3 ON. If only one bleed air source is available, also 1-3 ISOL ON, and select PACK 3 OFF when wing anti-ice is needed or the thrust is at MCT or more.

*If bleed air 3 is affected:* PACK 3 OFF, 1-3 ISOL ON, PACKS 1 and 2 ON. If only one bleed air source is available, also 1-2 ISOL ON, and select PACK 2 OFF when wing anti-ice is needed or the thrust is at MCT or more.

**Practice:** EFB Failures, PNEU, *Pneumatic system # temperature high*: a fouled precooler, which overheats first at high flow, in a climb with the packs and anti-ice on. See [Duct overheat](pneumatics#temp-hi).

parts.title: Electrical
parts.summary: The loss of all generators: emergency power, the generator resets, the ADG, engine 2's fuel, and flying on the emergency buses.

blocks.content:
**Condition:** Every generator bus is dead with the engines still running. On the DC-10 and KC-10 every AC and DC bus fed from the generators loses power at once: the flight and engine instrument flags come into view, every bus OFF light comes on except BAT BUS OFF (the battery takes the battery bus by itself), with EMER BUS OFF and the MASTER WARNING. On the MD-10, GEN ALL OFF is displayed, the autopilots and autothrottles disconnect and the FMA's red warning boxes flash.

**Objective:** Restore the flight instruments at once from the battery, try once to bring a generator back, and if that fails, restore the right side and engine 2's fuel with the ADG, conserve the battery, and land.

Engine 2 matters here more than anywhere else. It has no suction feed: its fuel is pushed to it by the tank 2 boost pumps, which are on the generator buses except the tank 2 left aft pump on the right emergency AC bus. With every generator lost it will flame out within a short time unless the ADG is put on the right emergency buses. The wing engines can draw fuel by suction, though not reliably at very high altitude (the MD-10 FCOM gives 38,000 ft as the limit for suction feed).

items.action: GEN RELAY / BUS TIE RELAY LOCKOUT RESET

items.item: Tank 2 pump switches (all) (DC-10; KC-10 after the ADG)

blocks.content:
Refer to the captain's flight and engine instruments as their flags clear: emergency power puts the left emergency AC and DC buses on the battery and static inverter. Do not use either autopilot on emergency power or the ADG. If the captain's attitude and heading come from an inertial unit, they become unreliable once the unit's own battery is exhausted. The OVRD & AIR START switch gives continuous ignition on all engines, in case a fuel or power interruption flames one out.

If the EGTs are falling below normal, the engines have flamed out: go to [Loss of all engines](emergency-engines#all-engine-flameout).

Isolating the bus ties and resetting each generator once separates a generator that has tripped for a reason of its own from a fault on the tie bus that took them all down. Do not reset a generator more than once for the same fault. When generator bus 1 comes back, turn EMER PWR OFF to save the battery.
*If all the generator buses stay unpowered* (KC-10: *if neither generator bus 1 nor 3 is operating*):

The ADG at R EMER ELEC carries the right emergency AC bus and, through TR 3, the right emergency DC bus: the first officer's instruments, VHF and HF 2, the B igniters and the tank 2 left aft boost pump, which keeps engine 2 fed. With the right side on the ADG, use emergency power only as required, to save the battery for the left side. Check the ADG on the VOLT/AMP/FREQ meter before relying on it. Pressurization is manual on the emergency buses.

*If engine 2 has flamed out:* restart it, within the start envelope, with the in-flight engine start procedure in [Abnormal Procedures](abnormal-procedures): number 2 throttle IDLE and fuel lever OFF, its hydraulic pump switches OFF, its tank pumps ON, the 2-3 motor pump ON, ENG 2 PNEU SUPPLY OFF, OVRD & AIR START ON. If its N2 is below 10 %, use a starter-assisted start with air from engine 1 or 3 through the ISOL valve (the 1-3 valve is on the left emergency AC bus, the 1-2 valve on the right), or increase speed. Allow 45 seconds for the light-up; engines are slow to accelerate at high altitude. After the start, GEN 2 switch RESET then ON, and return the pumps, pneumatics and packs to normal.

blocks.title: Then, by what came back
rows: EMER PWR switch OFF, CAB PRESS MAN/AUTO handle AUTO. Continue with all the AC BUS TIE switches at ISOL. Consider the APU as a backup source for the approach (APU GEN BUS switches ON if used). Land at the nearest suitable airport

At the captain's discretion, repower the dead buses through the tie bus (AC BUS TIE switches to NORM one at a time, watching the loads; consider leaving one of generator buses 1 and 3 isolated to protect the flight instruments) or from the APU. If every bus is repowered: EMER PWR OFF, CAB PRESS AUTO, DC TIE 3 CLOSE if required. Otherwise EMER PWR as required and all DC TIE switches CLOSE. Land at the nearest suitable airport, and use the abnormal procedure for a generator bus failure
EMER PWR OFF. Pressurization in AUTO or SEMI-AUTO
Generator bus 2 only, ADG on the right emergency buses
