The battery charger runs with EMER PWR OFF; use emergency power only as required. Pressurization in MANUAL (or STANDBY on the DC-10)
EMER PWR OFF, and ON only as required. Pressurization in MANUAL only
Plan a flaps 22°/EXT landing at the nearest suitable airport (the flap limiter may hold the flaps at 22°), and fly on the emergency buses (below)

blocks.content: The KC-10 manual then has the FE turn the tank 2 pumps on, restart engine 2 if it has stopped, and after the restart reset generator 2. *If no generator bus is restored,* use emergency power as required and land at the nearest suitable airfield. Otherwise EMER PWR switch OFF if not required, OVRD & AIR START switch OFF, and check the generator buses. *All restored:* tank 2 pumps as required, land as soon as practical. *Generator bus 1 and/or 3 restored:* all DC TIE switches CLOSE and evaluate the system; if bus 3 cannot be restored consider the ADG, if bus 1 cannot, consider the APU generator (battery fully charged first) and put the CAB PRESS MAN/AUTO handle to MAN; land as soon as practical. *Generator bus 2 only:* all DC TIE switches CLOSE, FUEL QTY IND PWR switch ALTN, CAB PRESS MAN/AUTO handle MAN, consider the ADG for the first officer's instruments, and land at the nearest suitable airfield. If the cause can be isolated, the other buses may be restored with the generator bus failure checklist.

With the EMER PWR switch ON the battery cannot be relied on for more than about 30 minutes, and an attempt to start the APU drains it further. When conditions allow, turn emergency power off and fly on the first officer's instruments (ADG) to keep the battery for the approach.

blocks.title: Flying on the emergency buses only
rows: Captain's on emergency power (battery, about 30 min), first officer's on the ADG; standby horizon on the battery bus (about 4 hours with BAT on and EMER PWR off)
Flight guidance, autopilots, autothrottles and stall warning inoperative
Stabilizer trim only through the long trim handles; elevator feel frozen at its force when power failed
Flaps may not extend beyond 22 to 28° (FedEx; the KC-10 manual: not into the landing range); flap and slat position indicators and gear lights inoperative
Anti-skid and thrust reversers inoperative, engines stay at flight idle after touchdown; ground spoilers by hand only

Pressurization manual only, cabin altitude warning inoperative; fuel dump, wing and windshield anti-ice, landing and navigation lights inoperative; hydraulics working but the hydraulic panel's indications lost
Engine 2 needs the ADG at R EMER ELEC for its fuel; A igniters on emergency power, B igniters on the ADG

blocks.content: The complete lists of what each emergency source powers are in [What stays powered](electrical#standby-configurations).

**Consequences:** LAND AT NEAREST SUITABLE AIRPORT; MANUAL CONTROL REQ, PRESSURIZATION; FLAP EXTENSION MAY BE LIMITED; WING ANTI-ICE, GPWS, AUTO SLAT EXTENSION, FUEL DUMP, LANDING GEAR INDICATIONS, ANTI-SKID, AUTO GROUND SPOILERS AND ALL ENGINE REVERSERS INOPERATIVE; on the Series 30 the upper and lower auxiliary tank fuel is trapped.

The EAD stays on the left emergency DC bus. Keep communication on VHF-1.
With all generators off, the HYD, AIR and FUEL panels' lights do not work: a switch pressed on those panels can change the system configuration without anything showing it.

*If the electrical system is in MANUAL:* push each GEN switch whose OFF light is lit, one reset attempt only. *If generator buses 1 and 3 are then powered* (AC 1 OFF, and AC 3 OFF or R EMER AC OFF, out): EMER PWR selector OFF, then ARM; restart engine 2 if required (the abnormal ENGINE RESTART IN FLIGHT; its tank 2 left aft pump is on the right emergency AC bus); land at the nearest suitable airport. The procedure ends here.

*Otherwise:*

With ADG ELEC ON (its ON light lit), the ADG supplies both emergency AC buses; the right emergency AC bus feeds the battery charger and TR 3, which feeds both emergency DC buses and the battery bus. Consequence messages can appear on the SD once the right emergency AC bus is powered. Stabilizer trim is available only through the LONG TRIM handles. Restart engine 2 if required. The gear position indications need DC bus 2 (instrument panel) or DC bus 3 (CONFIG page), the flap position needs AC bus 1 or 3, and flaps may not extend into the landing range on emergency power; windshield anti-ice and all exterior lights are lost, and the elevator feel stays at its pre-failure force.

The MD-10 FCOM files GEN ALL OFF with the abnormal procedures, as a level 2 alert. It is here because on the three-crew aircraft the same failure is an emergency. On the MD-10 the battery carries the captain's essential equipment for about 15 minutes until the ADG is deployed. With the EMER PWR selector at ARM the transfer to the battery is automatic. In the simulation the GEN buttons in MANUAL do not reset a tripped generator; in AUTO the controller makes its own reset attempts.

**In the simulation** the battery's endurance follows its actual charge and the actual emergency load rather than a fixed time, and a fully charged battery carries the emergency loads for more than 30 minutes on all three aircraft. The DC-10 and KC-10's EMER PWR switch has two positions, OFF and ON. The ADG deploys only from its handle, is stationary below about 50 kt, gives useful power from about 120 kt and its full rating of about 20 kVA from about 180 kt; asked for more than the air can give, its voltage and frequency sag. **Practice:** EFB Failures, ELEC, *Loss of all generators* (all three generators lose their field excitation and trip off; while the failure is active they trip again after each reset). See [Loss of all generators](electrical#loss-of-all-generators), [Emergency power](electrical#emergency-power-switch) and [Air-driven generator](electrical#adg).

parts.title: Hydraulics and Flight Controls
parts.summary: Hydraulic quantity loss, the three dual-system failures, the loss of all elevators and rudders, flying on a windmilling engine's pumps, the loss of all three systems, and the controllability check.

sections.title: Hydraulic quantity loss or HYD SYS 3 ELEV OFF

blocks.content:
**Condition:** A hydraulic system's quantity falling, or lost, with its pressure going; or the HYD SYS 3 ELEV OFF light (with the HYD cue and MASTER CAUTION): system 3 has fallen to about 4.75 US gal and the elevator shutoff valve has closed to isolate its lines into the tail.

**Objective:** Stop pumping fluid into a leak, keep at least one system alive, and find out which dual or single failure procedure applies.

blocks.title: Hydraulic quantity leak or loss, or HYD SYS 3 ELEV OFF light (DC-10)

items.item: ENG HYD PUMP switches, affected system

blocks.title: Hydraulic system quantity leak or loss (KC-10)

items.item: ENG HYD PUMP switches, affected system

blocks.content: The KC-10 manual files this as an abnormal procedure with no memory items. The FE first tells the boom operator to disconnect and stop refueling until the hydraulic state is known. Then fly the procedure for the system lost (system 1, 2 or 3 inoperative) in [Abnormal Procedures](abnormal-procedures), or [Dual hydraulic system failure](#dual-hydraulic-failure) if two are gone. The HYD SYS 3 ELEV OFF light has its own abnormal procedure in the KC-10 manual.

On the aircraft a failing system takes an autopilot with it without disconnecting it or saying so: system 1 or 3 lost fails autopilot 2, system 2 lost fails autopilot 1. Turning the motor pump off stops a healthy system's pressure being spent into the leaking one.
If all three systems are affected, leave the system 3 engine pump switches ON.
Fluid lost from system 2 can collect near the APU. Starting the APU after a system 2 loss may produce smoke.

*If HYD SYS 3 ELEV OFF is on and system 3 still holds 4 gal or more:* the valve has done its job. Return system 3's engine pump switches to ON and AUTO. Energizing the pumps or lowering the gear may drop the reading slightly below 4 gal; if it then stabilizes, carry on. *If system 3 keeps falling below 4 gal without stabilizing,* turn its engine pumps OFF again and go to the dual failure procedures (below) or [Loss of all hydraulic systems](#total-hydraulic-loss).

*Then, if systems 1 and 2 hold normal quantity:* motor pump selectors ARM, and monitor system 3. Autopilot 2 is inoperative without any annunciation, the 3-2 standby pump is lost, and the inboard elevators have no system 3 pressure. The procedure ends here.

If systems 1 and 2 are both inoperative and HYD SYS 3 ELEV OFF is on, every elevator is inoperative; pitch control is by stabilizer trim and thrust. Go to [Systems 1 and 2 lost with the system 3 elevator off](#sys-1-2-elev-off).
Otherwise go to the single system failure procedure in [Abnormal Procedures](abnormal-procedures) or to [Dual hydraulic system failure](#dual-hydraulic-failure).
The KC-10's HYD SYS 3 ELEV OFF light is not fitted in the simulated cockpit. The valve works, and its closure lights the HYD cue and MASTER CAUTION: read system 3's quantity to confirm it.
**Practice:** EFB Failures, HYD, *System # leak*, or *System 3 elevator off*. See [Elevator shutoff valve](hydraulics#elevator-shutoff-valve).

**Condition:** Two of the three hydraulic systems have failed (pressure and, usually, quantity lost): on the DC-10 and KC-10 the PRESS LO lights and gauges of two systems, on the MD-10 the HYD 1 AND 2 FAIL, HYD 1 AND 3 FAIL or HYD 2 AND 3 FAIL alert.

**Objective:** Isolate the failed systems, protect the survivor, and plan an early, long, stabilized approach in the configuration the surviving system can give, with the gear down by gravity.

Each surface on the DC-10 is powered by at least two systems, so the loss of any two leaves the aircraft controllable in all three axes. What changes with each pair is which high-lift devices, rudder, brakes and steering remain, and the procedures differ accordingly. Use one hydraulic control at a time where possible, so that the surviving system's pumps are not asked for two large flows at once. The effects of each pair are tabulated in [Loss of two systems](hydraulics#dual-system-loss).

items.item: ENG HYD PUMP switches, failed systems
ENG HYD PUMP switches, operative system

items: This is the KC-10 manual's sequence. FedEx files each pair as its own abnormal checklist, which starts with the surviving system's engine pumps ON, the autothrottles OFF and the rudder standby power; the actions come to the same. Do not air refuel with a dual hydraulic failure.
The autothrottles may be used, except for an approach and landing with less than 35° of flap.
With system 3 lost, the long trim handles do not move when the electric trim switches are used.
If the remaining system is powered only by a windmilling engine, use [Windmilling engine](#windmilling-engine-hydraulics).
**Consequence:** LAND AT NEAREST SUITABLE AIRPORT. Then fly the procedure for the pair that failed, below.

blocks.content: On the MD-10 each alert has its own procedure, below. Each begins by selecting the hydraulic system controller to MANUAL: if the alert goes away, the controller had misread the systems and the flight continues in MANUAL. The controller does not shut pumps off during taxi, takeoff and landing.

**Practice:** EFB Failures, HYD, *Hydraulic systems # fail* (1 and 2, 1 and 3, or 2 and 3): both engine pumps of each failed system, a line rupture and the fluid lost, so a motor pump has nothing to restore.

**Effects.** The upper rudder is lost; the lower rudder works through the 3-2 standby pump while system 3 lasts. The flaps are inoperative and stay where they are; the slats work on system 3 (retracted slats extend as the speed comes back), so plan a 0°/EXT landing if the flaps were up. The gear comes down by the alternate extension, keeping system 3 for the flight controls. Braking is on brake system 2 and the accumulators. Nosewheel steering works once the alternate extension lever is stowed after the gear is down.

**VMCA** with the upper rudder lost is 157 KIAS for the long-span aircraft with CF6-50 engines (DC-10-30, KC-10) and 145 KIAS for the DC-10-10; the books give no figure for the -15 and -40. Maximum crosswind 15 kt.

With less than 6 US gal left in system 3, lowering the gear may drop the quantity enough to close the system 3 elevator shutoff valve (HYD SYS 3 ELEV OFF), leaving pitch to thrust and stabilizer trim. If the valve closed as the gear came down, raising the gear may restore the elevators.

items: *If the RUD STBY PWR OFF light is on:* check the lower rudder with a gentle pedal input, wings held level with aileron. If it works, carry on (there will be no further warning if it fails). If it does not, turn the RUDDER STBY PWR switch OFF: both rudders are lost, directional control is by asymmetric thrust and lateral control, and after landing by differential braking, thrust and nosewheel steering. Plan a field with little or no crosswind.
Reduce the gross weight (dump) to the lowest practical before configuring: lower weight means lower speeds, and the 0°/EXT landing distance is long.

Plan to configure earlier than normal, and extend the slats only in stabilized flight. Review [Windmilling engine](#windmilling-engine-hydraulics) in case the system's engine fails: be ready to engage its starter on final as the speed comes back.
When ready to configure: pneumatic source established, OVRD & AIR START switch ON, the minimum maneuver speed for the existing configuration, AUX PUMP switches START.

*If the slats were retracted when the failure occurred:* FLAP/SLAT handle 0°/EXT (if necessary slow toward 1.3 VS clean to help them out). If they extend, fly the 0°/EXT landing at the 0°/EXT minimum maneuver speed; if not, return the handle to UP/RET, accelerate to the clean minimum maneuver speed and plan a no flap, no slat landing. *Otherwise* land in the existing configuration at its speeds, watching extended flaps for drift.
The inoperative systems may be reinstated for landing if they still show quantity.

blocks.content:
**Final.** Restrict the speed to 230 KIAS. Raise the alternate gear extension lever to its latch and wait for three green lights before anything else; then do not exceed 260 KIAS (the outboard ailerons are unlocked). On the -30, -40 and KC-10 the books then pull the center gear alternate extension handle for four green; in the simulation that handle cannot be operated, and the center gear stays up (a landing with it retracted is permitted below the weight limit for that case). Move the gear handle DOWN. After two minutes stow the alternate extension lever, which restores nosewheel steering. Flaps and slats at the planned setting; GND PROX WARN FLAP OVRD switch OVRD if required (not in the DC-10 simulation); spoilers ARM; anti-skid and brake pressure checked; bank angle selector 15°.

Make a normal approach, flare slightly at the threshold, close the throttles and fly the aircraft onto the runway; lower the nose firmly and select reverse at once. Do not reduce below VMCA until the landing is assured, and do not attempt a missed approach with both rudders lost and asymmetric thrust. If a go-around is needed, leave the gear down, or raise it only once clear of obstacles with the slats retracted.

**Consequences:** LAND AT NEAREST SUITABLE AIRPORT; CONSIDER FUEL DUMP TO < MAX LDG WT; FLAP EXTENSION/RETRACTION INOP; AUTOPILOT NOT AVAILABLE; PLAN LONG FINAL APPROACH; ALTERNATE GEAR EXTENSION REQUIRED; LEAVE GEAR DOWN FOR GO-AROUND; SPLRS DEPLOY WITH REV LEV; NOSEWHEEL STEERING RESTRICTED LEFT. Expect up to 15 % more fuel burn from control surface float.

*If the alert goes away in MANUAL,* the hydraulic system controller was at fault: continue in MANUAL and log it. The procedure ends here. Otherwise return HYD SYSTEM SELECT to AUTO.

*If HYD 3 ELEV OFF is also displayed:* all elevators and both rudders are lost: go to [Systems 1 and 2 lost with the system 3 elevator off](#sys-1-2-elev-off). *If RUDDER BOTH INOP is displayed:* directional control is by ailerons, spoilers and thrust, and with a wing engine shut down a missed approach should not be attempted.

blocks.title: Effects, HYD 1 AND 2 FAIL
rows: Both inoperative; autothrottles off before 50 ft unless the flaps are in a landing setting
Upper inoperative: VMCA 145 KIAS (Series 10), 157 KIAS (Series 30); lower rudder on the 3-2 pump unless HYD 3 ELEV OFF
Flaps inoperative (leave the handle where it is if they were out); slats work, but may not extend until the speed is reduced
One panel per wing; the drive may not pull the handle to the ground spoiler position
Steering 25° left, unrestricted right; system 1 accumulator and system 2 brakes, anti-skid working; no autobrake
Inboard elevators only (none with HYD 3 ELEV OFF); left outboard aileron lost, right outboard after slat extension

blocks.content: GPWS switch FLAP OVRD; maximum crosswind 15 kt; reduce weight as desired. **When ready for approach,** if the flaps are retracted: FLAP/SLAT handle 0/EXT (the slats may need the speed reduced first) and fly the 0/EXT speeds below. **When ready for the gear:** 230 KIAS maximum, alternate gear extension lever RAISED and latched, and after three green the Series 30's center gear alternate extension handle (not operable in the simulation); gear handle DOWN; stow the alternate lever after two minutes. Disconnect the autothrottles, cross the threshold at Vthreshold, close the throttles and fly a positive touchdown without holding the aircraft off (a tail strike is possible above 12° of pitch). Help the spoiler handle as it deploys. In a go-around, leave the gear down, or raise it only once clear of obstacles.

**Effects.** The slats are inoperative and stay where they are, possibly drifting (SLAT DISAGREE): slats in the takeoff position mean a 22°/EXT landing, in the land position 35°/EXT. The flaps work on system 2 (with the slats retracted, observe the flap placard speeds). The gear comes down by the alternate extension. Braking is on the accumulators only, without anti-skid. Nosewheel steering is inoperative. The upper rudder and stabilizer trim motor 2 depend on the 2-1 standby pump.

items: *If the RUD STBY PWR OFF light is on:* RUDDER STBY PWR switch OFF. The upper rudder is lost (VMCA as above, maximum crosswind 15 kt) and so is the stabilizer: plan a stabilizer-inoperative landing, ELEV FEEL selector MAN, and slew the feel down with the MAN SLEW control. Otherwise both rudders are available.
Reduce the gross weight; up to about 439,000 lb the speed can be reduced enough for normal flap operation.

Configure earlier than normal, extending the flaps only in stabilized flight. Review the windmilling engine procedure. Pneumatic source established and OVRD & AIR START ON when ready to configure; the existing configuration's minimum maneuver speed.

*If the slats were retracted when the failure occurred:* split the FLAP/SLAT handle (on the aircraft, loosen the interlock thumbscrew, swing the interlock clear, lift and hold the slat handle, then lift and pull the flap handle to the 0° detent) and plan a 22°/RET or 35°/RET landing, flap limit speeds permitting, with a lower than normal pitch attitude on final.

blocks.content: Braking is on the accumulators without anti-skid: increase the pedal force gradually, extend the spoilers at once, and avoid cycling the pedals. Skids, worn or blown tires and a center gear drag link failure are the risk. The 22°/RET distances are the worst case; a 35°/RET landing is shorter.

**Final.** Restrict the speed to 230 KIAS. Raise the alternate gear extension lever to its latch and wait for three green lights before anything else; then do not exceed 260 KIAS (the outboard ailerons are unlocked). On the -30, -40 and KC-10 the books then pull the center gear alternate extension handle for four green; in the simulation that handle cannot be operated, and the center gear stays up (a landing with it retracted is permitted below the weight limit for that case). Move the gear handle DOWN. Flaps and slats at the planned setting; GND PROX WARN FLAP OVRD switch OVRD if required (not in the DC-10 simulation); spoilers ARM; **ANTI-SKID switch OFF**; bank angle 15°; brake pressure checked. If the upper rudder is lost, do not slow below VMCA until the landing is assured, and avoid a high sink rate on final if the stabilizer is inoperative. After touchdown lower the nose firmly and select reverse at once.

**Consequences:** LAND AT NEAREST SUITABLE AIRPORT; CONSIDER FUEL DUMP TO < MAX LDG WT; SLAT EXTENSION/RETRACTION INOP; IF SLATS EXT/TO, MAX 22 FLAPS; IF SLATS EXT/LD, FLAPS AS SCHD; IF SLATS RET, 22 FLAPS OR 35; AUTOPILOT 2 NOT AVAILABLE; AUTO PITCH TRIM INOP; PLAN LONG FINAL APPROACH; ALTERNATE GEAR EXTENSION REQUIRED; BRAKES ON ACCUMULATORS ONLY; NOSEWHEEL STEERING INOPERATIVE.

If the alert goes away in MANUAL, continue in MANUAL and log it; otherwise return to AUTO. Autopilot 1 can be used, trimming by hand for speed and configuration changes. The rudder works through the 2-1 standby pump; if RUDDER UPR INOP is displayed, VMCA is 145 KIAS (Series 10) or 157 KIAS (Series 30), maximum crosswind 15 kt, and the stabilizer is inoperative too: fly the abnormal STABILIZER INOPERATIVE procedure, then continue. The flaps may not extend until the speed is reduced. Two spoiler panels per wing work. Braking is on the accumulators without anti-skid: manual braking, no pedal cycling, no autobrake. Stabilizer trim is at half rate with no auto trim.

**When ready for approach:** with the slats retracted, split the FLAP/SLAT handle (it can only be split at UP/RET, with both handles raised together first) and select flaps 22°; with the slats extended at TAKEOFF, select 22/EXT; with the slats at LAND, 35/EXT. Do not reduce below VMCA until the landing is assured. **For the gear:** 230 KIAS maximum, alternate extension lever RAISED and latched, after three green the Series 30 center gear handle (not operable in the simulation), gear handle DOWN, **ANTI-SKID switch OFF**, AUTO BRAKE OFF. GPWS switch FLAP OVRD for the 22° landings. Disconnect the autothrottles, cross at Vthreshold, close the throttles and raise the nose to at least level; do not hold it off, and help the spoiler handle as it deploys.

**Effects.** The lower rudder is lost; maximum crosswind 15 kt. The flaps and slats extend as selected on system 1: plan a 35°/EXT landing, and do not extend the flaps beyond 35° (the spoilers on the dead systems may float). The gear comes down by the alternate extension. Braking is on brake system 1 and the accumulators. Nosewheel steering is normal to the left and limited to 25° to the right.

blocks.title: VMCA with the lower rudder lost (KC-10, DC-10-30)

blocks.content:
Reduce the gross weight (up to about 439,000 lb allows normal flap and slat operation), configure earlier than normal with the slats extended in stabilized flight, review the windmilling engine procedure, and establish the pneumatic source with OVRD & AIR START ON when ready to configure.

**Final.** Restrict the speed to 230 KIAS. Raise the alternate gear extension lever to its latch and wait for three green lights before anything else; then do not exceed 260 KIAS (the outboard ailerons are unlocked). On the -30, -40 and KC-10 the books then pull the center gear alternate extension handle for four green; in the simulation that handle cannot be operated, and the center gear stays up (a landing with it retracted is permitted below the weight limit for that case). Move the gear handle DOWN. Flaps and slats 35°/EXT; spoilers ARM; anti-skid and brake pressure checked; bank angle 15°. Do not reduce below the charted VMCA until the landing is assured. After touchdown lower the nose firmly and select reverse at once.

**Consequences:** LAND AT NEAREST SUITABLE AIRPORT; CONSIDER FUEL DUMP TO < MAX LDG WT; AUTOPILOT NOT AVAILABLE; PLAN LONG FINAL APPROACH; ALTERNATE GEAR EXTENSION REQUIRED; NOSEWHEEL STEERING RESTRICTED RIGHT.

If the alert goes away in MANUAL, continue in MANUAL and log it; otherwise return to AUTO. Both autopilots are lost and the autothrottles must be off before 50 ft. The lower rudder is lost (RUDDER LWR INOP): VMCA 145 KIAS for the Series 10, and for the Series 30 the table above. The flaps and slats may not extend until the speed is reduced. Two spoiler panels per wing; steering 25° right, unrestricted left; system 1 brakes, system 2 accumulator, anti-skid working, no autobrake; three elevators; stabilizer trim at half rate. Do not attempt a go-around below VMCA.

**When ready for approach:** FLAP/SLAT handle 22/EXT. **For the gear:** alternate extension lever RAISED and latched, after three green the Series 30 center gear handle (not operable in the simulation), gear handle DOWN, AUTO BRAKE OFF. Then FLAP/SLAT handle 35/EXT: *if they reach 35/EXT,* plan a 35/EXT landing (the spoilers extend at wheel spin-up; help the handle at the end of its travel). *If not,* return to 22/EXT and plan a 22/EXT landing at the speeds below, GPWS switch FLAP OVRD. Disconnect the autothrottles, cross at Vthreshold, close the throttles and fly a positive touchdown.

sections.title: Systems 1 and 2 lost with the system 3 elevator off

blocks.content:
**Condition:** Systems 1 and 2 have failed and the system 3 elevator shutoff valve has closed (HYD SYS 3 ELEV OFF on the DC-10, HYD 3 ELEV OFF with HYD 1 AND 2 FAIL on the MD-10): the case of an uncontained engine 2 failure through the tail.

**Objective:** Fly the aircraft in pitch with stabilizer trim and wing engine thrust, in roll with the ailerons system 3 still powers, and land on a long runway with little crosswind.

blocks.title: What is lost and what remains
rows: Ailerons on system 3: both inboards; the right outboard once the flaps or slats are out or the alternate gear lever is raised
Stabilizer trim motor 2, the autopilots, the 3-2 standby pump
Stabilizer trim at half rate; pitch by thrust

blocks.title: Systems 1 and 2 inoperative, HYD SYS 3 ELEV OFF (DC-10, KC-10)

items.item: ENG HYD PUMP switches, systems 1 and 2

blocks.content: **Consequence:** LAND AT NEAREST SUITABLE AIRPORT, on the longest runway available, with little or no crosswind. Minimize the use of more than one hydraulic control at a time. Do not air refuel. Without rudders, directional control is by asymmetric thrust and lateral control: do not attempt a go-around if the thrust is asymmetric.

**Recommended technique.** Divide the work: one pilot flies pitch and speed with thrust and stabilizer trim, the other holds heading and wings level with the ailerons. Disengage the autothrottles. The aircraft will oscillate slowly in pitch (the phugoid): as the nose rises the speed falls, the lift falls and the nose drops, and the cycle repeats over a minute or so. The wing engines sit below the center of gravity, so more thrust pitches the nose up and less pitches it down. To damp the phugoid, add thrust as the nose starts down and take it off as the nose starts up; short, sharp changes (a jam acceleration, then a quick chop) work best, and thrust applied out of phase makes the oscillation worse. Thrust changes on all three engines together are fairly neutral in pitch; engine 2's line of thrust is close to the center of gravity. Make stabilizer changes in short inputs and anticipate the slow response by reversing the input before the attitude is reached. Lateral and longitudinal fuel transfer can help: balancing the wings lets both throttles be matched, and moving fuel aft lowers the trim speed.

items: Reduce the weight if needed, considering what it does to the controllability, slat extension and landing distance. Review the emergency landing preparation.

Begin the approach at least 4,000 ft above the field on an extended final (about 30 NM at 10,000 ft), and slow to the final approach speed before leaving the initial approach altitude. Plan a long, flat approach and use every approach aid.

Extend the slats with the speed at the clean minimum maneuver speed (slowing toward 1.3 VS if they do not move in about 10 seconds); expect a small nose-down moment, trimmed out. Extend the gear by the alternate system approaching the outer marker, about 5 to 7 NM out: expect a pitch-up and a drag increase.
By 500 ft have the speed and thrust stable so that no further thrust change is needed; move from stabilizer trim to thrust for the flight path in the last part of the approach.
At 100 ft ground effect gives a slight nose-down tendency: a small stabilizer input, or a burst of thrust. Aim toward the far end of the touchdown zone.

Flare with no more than 1° of nose-up stabilizer at the threshold (50 ft), close the throttles just before the main gear touches, and do not try for a smooth landing: reduce the sink rate and put it on.
On touchdown, full brakes and nose-down stabilizer; steer with the rudder pedal steering once the nose gear is down; reverse thrust as normal.

blocks.content: **Final (DC-10, KC-10).** When ready to configure: pneumatic source established, OVRD & AIR START ON, minimum maneuver speed for the configuration, AUX PUMP switches START; then the slats as for [systems 1 and 2 lost](#dual-hyd-1-2). Restrict the speed to 230 KIAS. Raise the alternate gear extension lever to its latch and wait for three green lights before anything else; then do not exceed 260 KIAS (the outboard ailerons are unlocked). On the -30, -40 and KC-10 the books then pull the center gear alternate extension handle for four green; in the simulation that handle cannot be operated, and the center gear stays up (a landing with it retracted is permitted below the weight limit for that case). Move the gear handle DOWN. If the slats are extended, stow the alternate lever after two minutes for nosewheel steering. If they are not, the books have the lever held about halfway raised until touchdown to keep the outboard ailerons unlocked; in the simulation the lever is either raised or stowed, so leave it raised until after touchdown, then stow it. GND PROX WARN FLAP OVRD switch OVRD if required (not in the DC-10 simulation); landing lights ON; spoilers ARM; anti-skid and brake pressure checked; bank angle 15°. The FE announces "Brace for landing" on the PA at 250 ft. After landing, be prepared to evacuate.

**MD-10.** Fly the HYD 1 AND 2 FAIL procedure for the configuration and the gear (the slats, the alternate extension, stowing the lever once the gear is down), with the technique above. Both pilots' wheel trim switches and the LONG TRIM handles (pushed firmly to at least the first soft detent) move the stabilizer. On touchdown apply full brakes and, as the nose comes down, reverse on the wing engines, watching brake system 2 pressure; deploy spoiler panel 3 at nose gear touchdown; use the restricted nosewheel steering until taxi speed.

A go-around is possible only by adding thrust and letting the nose come up, with no more thrust than a moderate climb needs: the thrust is not controlling the speed, and too much pitch brings the stick shaker or a stall. Keep any thrust asymmetry that was holding the wings level. If the approach is unstable and there is not the fuel for another, a stable touchdown near the runway may be better than a chase for the original aiming point.

**In the simulation** the elevator shutoff valve, the half-rate stabilizer trim and the thrust pitching moments are modeled, so the technique works as described. The loss of autopilot 2 pitch control when the valve closes is not modeled, and with systems 1 and 2 lost the simulation leaves no flight spoiler working on either wing (panel 3 still extends as a ground spoiler), where the books keep panel 3. **Practice:** EFB Failures, HYD, *Systems 1 and 2 lost, system 3 elevator off*.

sections.title: Single hydraulic system powered by a windmilling engine

blocks.content:
**Condition:** The only hydraulic system left is driven by the pumps of a failed, windmilling engine, after an all-engine flameout or a dual failure.

**Objective:** Keep the windmilling engine turning fast enough for its pumps to hold the system, reduce the demand on that system, and land without flaps or slats.

A windmilling core above about 5 % N2 turns its pumps fast enough for a small flow: enough to hold the system while little is asked of it, not enough for large surface movements, the gear or the high-lift devices. The procedure keeps the speed up, takes every other load off the system, and uses the starter to keep the core turning as the speed comes back for the landing.

blocks.title: Operation on a single system powered by a windmilling engine (DC-10, KC-10)

items.action: AT LEAST 5 % N2 ON THE WINDMILLING ENGINE, NOT BELOW 0°/RET MINIMUM MANEUVER

items.item: One of the two ENG HYD PUMP switches, windmilling engine
GND PROX WARN FLAP OVRD switch (not in the DC-10 simulation)

blocks.content:
The 0°/RET minimum maneuver speed runs from about 194 KIAS at 260,000 lb to 268 KIAS at 500,000 lb (KC-10). The autothrottles may be used except for an approach and landing with less than 35°. Rudder, aileron and stabilizer trim remain; make stabilizer trim changes in short inputs. Aileron effectiveness is reduced and the forces higher. The rudder is normal if engine 2 is the one supplying; use it for yaw control only. Disconnecting the windmilling engine's CSD takes its drive's drag off the core.

Plan a no flap, no slat approach and landing, and extend the gear by free fall (the alternate extension) when the landing is assured.

items.item: Pneumatic source to the windmilling engine

items.action: ENGAGE (to hold N2 as the speed falls)

blocks.content: Do not reengage a starter above 30 % N2: the starter may be damaged. Do not interconnect two active engine pneumatic supplies to set up the starter air.

**In the simulation** a pulled fire handle stops the engine but does not shut a hydraulic valve: a windmilling engine's pumps go on delivering either way, and turning its pumps off does not raise its windmilling speed. See [Loss of all three systems](hydraulics#total-hydraulic-loss).

**Condition:** All three systems have lost their fluid: no flight control surface can be moved; the surfaces float or trail with the airflow, and the stabilizer, flaps and slats stay where they were.

**Objective:** Fly the aircraft on the thrust of the wing engines alone to a landing site, and land with the lowest sink rate that can be achieved.

There is no checklist for this, only technique, learned from the DC-10 that reached Sioux City in 1989 after its number 2 engine's fan disk failed and cut all three systems in the tail. Immediately after the failure, use the controls normally for as long as any pressure remains; disconnect the autopilot and autothrottles and level the wings. Then:

items: **Roll and heading by differential thrust.** More thrust on the right wing engine rolls the aircraft left, and the reverse. To keep the descent rate down, the high throttle may need to stay near MCT and the low one as high as possible without upsetting the aircraft.

**Pitch by symmetric thrust,** damping the phugoid as described in [the elevator-off technique](#sys-1-2-elev-off): thrust on as the nose starts down, off as it starts up, in short sharp inputs, keeping any asymmetry that holds the wings level. The speed is set by the trim and the configuration, not by the thrust.
**Assess** the damage by any means (a chase aircraft, the view from the cabin) and the control available, with small turns, climbs and descents. Consider a practice approach at a safe height.

**Choose the landing site** on runway length and width, approach aids, weather, terrain, population and rescue services, and above all on how well the aircraft can be controlled. A distant, better site may be worth the flight if the aircraft can hold altitude to it with the gear down.
**Transfer fuel** laterally to balance the wings so both throttles can be matched, and from tank 2 or the auxiliary tanks to tanks 1 and 3 to move the center of gravity aft and lower the trim speed.

**Extend the gear** by the alternate extension well before the approach: it pitches the nose up and changes the phugoid, and needs time to settle; once settled the aircraft is steadier with the extra drag. The center gear (DC-10-30) adds braking and absorbs energy if it can be extended (not in the simulation).

**Approach** long and flat, reaching the outer marker, or 5 to 7 NM, at approach altitude, aligned and as stable as possible. Fly slightly below the glideslope (about half a dot, no flatter than 2½°): a steeper path means a higher sink rate near the ground. Watch for the engines accelerating unevenly from idle.

**Land.** Below about 100 ft ground effect tends to pitch the nose down and increase the sink rate: a sharp burst of thrust then a retard counters it. Move the aiming point toward the far end of the runway, and aim only to reduce the sink rate: a smooth touchdown is very unlikely. The PM calls radio altitude, sink rate and its trend from the outer marker in.

blocks.content: **In the simulation** all three systems can be emptied together by failing each one's leak in the EFB (HYD, *System # leak* for systems 1, 2 and 3). The thrust lines of the engines, the phugoid and ground effect come from the flight model, so the technique can be practiced; expect it to be very hard, as it was for the crew at Sioux City. See [Flight characteristics](flight-characteristics).

**Condition:** Structural damage, a flight control malfunction, or a fuel imbalance that cannot be corrected, leaving the crew unsure how slowly the aircraft can safely be flown.

**Objective:** Find, at a safe height, the configuration and the minimum speed at which the aircraft can still be controlled with a margin, before it has to be done near the ground.

items: Make a preliminary check for damage.
At 10,000 to 15,000 ft above the ground if possible, configure for the planned landing, with prudent judgment for each speed and configuration change.
Slow gradually, evaluating the control in turns and in simulated landing approaches; be alert for buffet, and do not go below the minimum maneuver speed for the configuration.
Determine the limiting configuration and the minimum safe speed: the speed at which a comfortable margin of control remains about every axis.
Fly the approach at that minimum safe speed plus 10 kt, all the way to touchdown, using the abnormal landing configuration procedures as appropriate.

blocks.content: Stop slowing well before any control needs full deflection: past that point there may be nothing left to recover with. If the response fades quickly, or the input needed in any axis nears its stop, go straight back to a configuration and speed already shown to be controllable.

With both rudders lost, the aircraft is steered with the ailerons and asymmetric thrust in the air, and with differential thrust, differential braking and nosewheel steering on the ground. Choose a runway with little or no crosswind, and with a wing engine out do not plan on a missed approach.

parts.title: Flight Path and Miscellaneous
parts.summary: The GPWS terrain escape, unreliable airspeed, upset recovery, loose cargo, a fuel dump running low, and pointers to the air refueling and air tanker emergencies.

blocks.content:
**Condition:** A ground proximity warning: the voice "PULL UP" or "TERRAIN TERRAIN, PULL UP" with the red GPWS lights (on the aircraft also "TERRAIN AHEAD, PULL UP" and a solid red terrain area on the navigation displays from the enhanced GPWS), or (MD-10) the red GROUND PROX message on the FMA, when the crew cannot immediately see that the terrain is clear (at night or in instrument conditions).

**Objective:** Climb away at the best rate the aircraft can give, at once, without first working out why.

There may be as little as 15 seconds between the warning and impact. The maneuver works only if it starts within a couple of seconds, which is why the pilot flying performs it at once, all items together as one movement (FedEx makes it a Phase One procedure; the MD-10 FCOM gives it as a technique to be flown immediately): the crews who have hit terrain after a warning were, in most cases, analyzing it. Do not ignore a short warning: act on it.

The KC-10 flight manual has no GPWS escape checklist and no memory items for it. Fly the escape maneuver described below: autopilot and autothrottles off, wings level and 20° nose up at about 3° per second with maximum thrust, speed brakes retracted, then tell ATC.

Roll the wings level and rotate at about 3° per second, a normal takeoff rotation, to 20° nose up, applying full power at the same time; a climb should be established within five seconds. If the terrain still threatens, go on raising the nose to the stick shaker, trading airspeed for height, and push the throttles to their stops (firewall power, the MD-10 FCOM's engine overboost; log any exceedance). Do not change the gear or flap configuration until terrain clearance is assured. Watch the radio altimeter for a steady or increasing clearance. When the warning stops and the terrain is clear, reduce to climb power and climb to the minimum safe altitude.
Do not hold an attitude that keeps the stick shaker going continuously: the aircraft is then at the edge of the stall, and a stall near the ground is not recoverable.

**Cautions are different.** "CAUTION TERRAIN", "TERRAIN", "SINK RATE", "DON'T SINK", "TOO LOW FLAPS", "TOO LOW GEAR", "TOO LOW TERRAIN", "GLIDESLOPE" and "BANK ANGLE" do not call for the escape maneuver: the pilot flying confirms the situation and corrects the flight path or configuration at once. If safe terrain clearance is in any doubt, fly the escape maneuver anyway.

The simulated DC-10 flies with the basic GPWS computer, which gives no voice and no warnings from modes 1 to 4: the voice option that would give them is modeled but not yet offered on the EFB. On the DC-10, fly the escape maneuver on your own judgment of the terrain. See [Surveillance](surveillance).

**In the simulation** the GPWS's basic modes are modeled, from the radio altitude, the barometric rate, the glideslope and the configuration; the look-ahead alerts from the terrain database (CAUTION TERRAIN, TERRAIN AHEAD) and windshear detection are not. Windshear recovery is in [Adverse Weather](adverse-weather). There is no EFB failure for this procedure: it is practiced by flying toward terrain.

**Condition:** Airspeed, Mach, vertical speed or altitude that do not agree with the pitch attitude and thrust for the phase of flight: a blocked or iced pitot or static system, volcanic ash, radome damage or poor maintenance. It may come with level 1 and 2 alerts (PITOT HEAT, WSHEAR DET FAIL, SEL ELEV FEEL MAN, SEL FLAP LIM OVRD), autopilot and autothrottle disconnects, IAS and ALT miscompares on the PFDs, pressurization problems, and overspeed or altitude aural warnings. On the takeoff roll it shows as a wrong reading at the 80 knots call.

**Objective:** Keep control with attitude and thrust, which are reliable, and only then find the faulty source.

The PFD attitude, the navigation display, the ground speed, N1 and the stick shaker can be trusted. Flight path angle, the pitch limit indicator, the vertical speed, the altimeter, altitude reporting and TCAS may or may not be, depending on the cause. The flight director's pitch bar, the autothrottle's speed protection and the overspeed warning cannot.

items.action: STABILIZE (normal pitch and thrust for the phase)

blocks.content:
Disregard the indicated airspeed, the pitch bar and the high speed warnings, and fly pitch attitude and thrust. If the stick shaker comes on, lower the nose to the horizon and add thrust, then return to the attitude and thrust for the phase. Disregard every alert and warning except the stick shaker until the aircraft is stable: they can be conflicting and disorienting. About 10° nose up with MCT is a safe initial climb if a climb is needed. If practical, get into visual conditions, and once stable make sure of the terrain clearance.

*If the unreliable source can be identified:* select the CADC on that side to the other side (the overspeed aural warning may go on, because the warning system does not know the CADC was switched). In the simulation the MD-10's CADC source switch is not connected, so this step changes nothing; fly the reliable side's instruments and the standby airspeed instead. *If the air data then returns to normal,* return the reliable side's AFS OVRD OFF switch to normal and use the autopilot and autothrottles on the reliable ADC; that side's FMS air data and its TAS and wind on the ND may still be wrong. Monitor pitch, thrust and airspeed. The procedure ends here.

*Otherwise,* fly the normal pitch attitude and thrust for each phase for the rest of the flight. The FCOM's tables of pitch and N1 by weight, altitude and configuration give the targets; the FMS's VNAV may be unavailable.

**For the approach and landing:** keep visual conditions if possible, establish the landing configuration early, check the speed against the IRS ground speed and the reported wind, use the radio altimeter, and choose a runway with an electronic or visual glideslope. On the DC-10 and KC-10 the equivalent procedure, for a damaged radome or suspect airspeed, is in [Abnormal Procedures](abnormal-procedures).
**Practice:** EFB Failures, MISC, *Nose radome damaged, airspeed unreliable* (all three pitot probes blocked).

**Condition:** The aircraft has unintentionally gone beyond 25° nose up, 10° nose down or 45° of bank, or is within those limits but at a speed wrong for the conditions (wake turbulence, a flight control malfunction, a mishandled autopilot disconnect, or the instruments misread).

**Objective:** Recover to level flight with the least altitude loss and without overstressing the aircraft.

These techniques assume the aircraft is not stalled. A stall can happen at any attitude, and shows as a continuous stick shaker with heavy buffet, a lack of pitch or roll authority, or a descent that cannot be stopped. If it is stalled, recover from the stall first: nose-down elevator, held until the stall recovery is complete and the shaker stops. The actions below are a logical progression; not all of them may be needed once the recovery is under way.

Excessive use of pitch trim or rudder can aggravate an upset, cause a loss of control or impose high structural loads. Use the trim sparingly, and the rudder only when the ailerons and spoilers cannot roll the aircraft and it is not stalled.

rows: Apply as much as full nose-down elevator, and nose-down stabilizer trim as needed
Roll the shortest way to wings level (unload and roll if the bank is beyond 90°)
Recover to level flight: nose-up elevator, nose-up trim if needed
Roll (up to about 60° of bank) to get a nose-down pitch rate
Adjust thrust and drag as required
Approaching the horizon, roll wings level, check the speed, set the thrust and the pitch attitude

blocks.content: There is no EFB failure for an upset. See [Flight characteristics](flight-characteristics) for the aircraft's handling at the edges of the envelope.

**Condition:** Cargo has broken free in flight: a trim change in pitch, noise from the cargo deck, or a report from the cabin.

**Objective:** Keep the cargo from moving further, keep the center of gravity within limits, and confirm the aircraft is controllable.

items.item: If out of limits: affected cargo
items.action: SHIFT TO BRING THE CG WITHIN LIMITS

blocks.content: Do not shift cargo in flight except when needed to keep control of the aircraft, and keep changes of deck angle to a minimum until the cargo is secure: a climb or descent sets it rolling again.

If the center of gravity cannot be kept within limits, or structural damage is suspected, do a [controllability check](emergency-hydraulics#controllability-check) before the approach. On the DC-10 freighters and the MD-10 the couriers (or the crew) do what the KC-10's boom operator does here.

**In the simulation** the cargo locks of every unit fail together: the units roll with the deck's slope until they meet the next unit or the end of their compartment, and the center of gravity moves with them. Nobody can go back and re-secure the cargo, so keep the deck angle small and fly the controllability check. **Practice:** EFB Failures, MISC, *Cargo shifts in flight*. See [Cargo shift](doors-and-cabin#cargo-shift-failure).

sections.title: Fuel quantity low during dump (TNK FUEL QTY LO)

blocks.content:
**Condition:** The TNK 1, 2 or 3 FUEL QTY LO alert during a fuel dump: the inboard compartment of tank 1 or 3, or tank 2, is below about 3,500 lb.

**Consequence:** STOP FUEL DUMP.

Open the guard and push the DUMP switch; its ON light goes out. *If the ON light does not go out,* push the guarded emergency stop switch (MANF STOP on the simulated panel; the FCOM's FUEL DUMP EMER STOP) and check that its STOP light comes on. Then reschedule the fuel distribution as required.

The simulation does not raise the TNK FUEL QTY LO alert. Watch the tank quantities during a dump and stop it yourself; on the aircraft (and in the simulation) the dump also stops at its own low-level cutoffs.

The air refueling emergencies of the KC-10 (and of the DC-10 tankers, the KDC-10 and the Omega) are in [Air Refueling](air-refueling): the **breakaway**, separating tanker and receiver at once on a "breakaway" call, in [Breakaway](ar-emergency-abnormal#breakaway); and two-engine refueling, towing fighters, pressure refueling and landing with the boom or a drogue in trail in the same part, [Emergency and abnormal procedures](ar-emergency-abnormal).
Smoke or fuel fumes at the boom operator's station are in [ARO compartment smoke or fuel fumes](emergency-fire-smoke#aro-compartment).

**Condition:** On a DC-10 air tanker, the retardant load must be shed at once: an engine failure or a loss of performance on the drop run with terrain or climb performance in doubt, or a tank that will not drop normally.

The EMERGENCY DROP switch opens every tank with a charged emergency accumulator, independently of the normal drop system, and empties the load in about two seconds. The procedure, and how to restore the system afterwards, is in [Emergency drop](aerial-firefighting#emergency-drop-procedure). After the drop, continue with the engine procedure that caused it.

parts.title: Emergency Landing, Evacuation and Ditching
parts.summary: Preparing the aircraft and the people on board for an emergency landing, the ground evacuation, and ditching.

blocks.content:
**Condition:** An emergency in flight that may damage the aircraft on landing, or call for an evacuation immediately after it: a fire, smoke, a structural or flight control problem, a hydraulic failure with poor braking or steering. For an unsafe landing gear indication, use the abnormal landing gear procedures instead.

**Objective:** Land as light, as slow and as well prepared as the time allows, with the aircraft depressurized, everyone strapped in and briefed, and the crew ready to evacuate the moment the aircraft stops.

blocks.title: Preparation for emergency landing and evacuation (DC-10, KC-10)

items.action: NOTIFY: cause, type of landing, time remaining, exits affected
BRIEF (boom operator or FE); cabin prepared
REDUCE (dump to maximum landing weight or less) if time permits
SEATED IN THE CABIN, TO HELP

blocks.content: The brief tells the people in the cabin what is happening, how long they have, the brace position and the signal for it, which exits to use and which not, and what to do after the aircraft stops. If smoke or fumes are or may be present, the cabin uses the smoke hoods for the evacuation. Extra crew members seated near the exits help the cabin crew or boom operator open them.

items.action: OUTFLOW VALVE FULL OPEN; DIFFERENTIAL PRESSURE ZERO
OFF, unless needed for electrical power

items.item: GND PROX WARN FLAP OVRD switch (final flaps 22° or less; not in the DC-10 simulation)

blocks.content: The cabin doors are plug doors and will not open against any remaining pressure. Make sure the aircraft is fully depressurized before landing: FedEx opens the outflow valve and turns the pneumatic supplies off below 5,000 ft.
Consider stopping on the runway, so that the fire services can reach the aircraft. After landing, use [Ground evacuation](#evacuation) if required.

On the MD-10, the captain alerts the couriers to the nature of the emergency, the time available and the brace signal; the crew reduce the weight as time allows, stow loose equipment, and brief the approach. The cabin must be depressurized at touchdown so that the doors will open. Announce the brace about 30 seconds before touchdown. After the stop, use [Ground evacuation](#evacuation) if required.

In the simulation the MD-10's cabin pressure stays under automatic control (its CABIN PRESS panel is not functional): the outflow valve opens fully on the ground, and any differential remaining at touchdown bleeds off within moments. Confirm zero differential on the AIR synoptic page before ordering the doors opened.

**Condition:** The aircraft is on the ground and must be abandoned at once: a fire that cannot be put out, smoke, fuel spilling near a fire, or structural damage, whether or not the landing was prepared for.

**Objective:** Stop everything that could feed a fire, then get everyone out through the exits that are safe to use.

The sequence below is a guideline, and the items may be done together or left out as the situation dictates. Each crew member does the shutdown items they are normally responsible for; after the aircraft stops, whatever is left is done by the captain or the last crew member able to function on the flight deck. Before any exit is opened, look through its window: an exit with fire or an obstruction outside is not used. If the fire is outside on one side, the captain tells the cabin not to open the doors on that side.

items.action: SHUT DOWN (APU FIRE AGENT button if required)
INITIATE: "EVACUATE, EVACUATE, EVACUATE" on the PA and interphone

items.item: Last crew member: EMER PWR switch

blocks.content: Emergency power keeps VHF 1 and the PA for the evacuation call. If the fire is not at the engines, consider keeping one of engine 2's bottles for the APU. Direct the evacuation to particular exits with the wind (which can lift the slides), the ground and any fire or damage in mind. The flight crew's primary way out is through the forward cabin doors and down their slides; the alternate is the flight deck's sliding windows with the escape ropes. Leave the flight deck door unlocked so that the people in the cabin can reach the windows.

blocks.title: Crew duties
rows: Directs and helps the evacuation, makes sure everyone is out; leaves by door 1L or 1R
Takes the first aid kit and goes to the ground to direct people away from the aircraft; 1L or 1R
Makes sure the forward doors are armed and their slides have deployed; 1L or 1R; helps the captain check everyone is out
Initiates the evacuation in the cabin on the captain's command and opens the exits away from any fire
Sit in a crew or courier seat for the landing and leave by the assigned exit

items.action: ALERT (nature of the emergency, time available, brace signal)

items.item: After the aircraft has stopped: outflow valve

blocks.alt: Plan-view diagram of the family's exits, three aircraft outlines side by side: the passenger DC-10 with its eight cabin doors (1L/1R to 4L/4R) each with its slide drawn deployed; a DC-10F or MD-10 freighter with the forward entry doors 1L and 1R (slides deployed) and the main deck cargo door marked not an exit; the KC-10 with its cabin doors and slides. On each, the flight deck's two sliding windows marked with escape ropes, an arrow for the wind with the slides on the windward side marked "check wind", and a fire symbol on one side with its doors crossed out "do not open on the fire side". On the passenger DC-10, the attendant EVAC switches at doors 1L and 2L marked.
blocks.title: Exits and evacuation routes

blocks.content: In the simulation the slides deploy when an armed door is opened in its emergency mode (arm them from the cabin door levers or the EFB's Doors page), and a deployed slide stays out until **Reset Aircraft**. The flight deck windows, escape ropes and portable emergency equipment are not simulated, and there is no evacuation signal on the flight deck: the flight crew order the evacuation on the PA. The passenger DC-10's attendant EVAC switches are in the cabin but have no visible or audible effect yet. See [Emergency exits](doors-and-cabin#emergency-exits) and [Escape slides](doors-and-cabin#escape-slides).
The passenger cabin's evacuation signal is described in [Evacuation signal](doors-and-cabin#evacuation-signal).

**Cargo loading evacuation (KC-10).** When an emergency arises during loading or ground work with no pilots or flight engineer on board, the boom operator takes charge: warns the loading crew and directs them out; tells the fire department by any means (the nature of the emergency, the tail number, the parking spot, the number of people on board); removes the fire source if it is accessible and fights the fire with the portable extinguishers if possible (offloading flammable or explosive cargo first, if possible); runs the APU fire procedure if it is an APU fire; then, conditions permitting, shuts down the APU, removes external power, turns the battery off, and counts the people. The ground evacuation checklist is then not needed.

**Condition:** A landing on water is unavoidable: no runway can be reached.

**Objective:** Touch down under control, as slowly as possible, wings level, on a closed and depressurized aircraft, with everyone strapped in and wearing life vests, and get everyone into the slide rafts.

A ditching is survivable when the aircraft meets the water at the lowest forward speed and sink rate it can manage, nose slightly up, with power still available to control the touchdown. The flaps are fully extended for the lowest speed; the gear is up so that it does not dig in and flip the aircraft; the aircraft is depressurized so that the structure is not loaded and the doors will open, and then closed up (outflow valve shut, pack ram air doors shut) to keep the water out for as long as possible. Empty fuel tanks help it float, but never ditch with the tanks dry: the engines are needed to the end.

items.action: MAYDAY: position, course, speed, altitude, situation, intention, ditching time and position, aircraft type, persons on board
DUMP TO THE MINIMUM FOR THE DITCHING PLAN

items.item: Cabin preparation, loose items, survival equipment
Below 10,000 ft: LDG CAB PRESS AURAL WARN circuit breaker (LM C-11 in the simulation; the KC-10 manual gives LM C-12)
GND PROXIMITY WARN circuit breaker (AV B-19 in the simulation; the KC-10 manual gives FO B-19)
PACK TEMP VALVE POS indicator (each pack, with PACK IND SEL)
NO SMOKING and SEAT BELTS signs
FE, observer and boom operator seats

blocks.content: Pulling the two breakers stops the gear horn sounding with the flaps out and the gear up, and the ground proximity warnings close to the water. Turning the pneumatic supplies off starts the depressurization; open the outflow valve fully with the wheel until the differential is zero, then wind it fully closed. With the packs held at MAN HOT until their temperature valves read H, the heat exchanger ram air doors, below the waterline, are mechanically closed.

**At touchdown and after (FedEx).** Hold the target speed and a medium nose-high attitude, with all operating engines. After the aircraft stops, command the evacuation. If time permits before leaving, pull the engine fire handles and discharge the bottles if required. The captain disconnects the slide raft (girt release loop) once boarded; the first officer takes the first aid kit; the FE opens the forward doors, makes sure the slides deploy and the rafts inflate, and takes the radio from the emergency equipment.

**At touchdown and after (KC-10).** Immediately before touchdown, on the pilot's command, the FE moves the fuel levers to OFF and pulls the engine fire handles and discharges the agents. Touch down about 10° nose up at the lowest speed and sink rate the thrust allows. After the stop the pilot directs the evacuation through doors 1L and 1R (and 2L and 2R where slide rafts are fitted), with the emergency equipment secured and the rafts launched.

items: **Where:** if practical, ditch near a ship. Plan the touchdown along the swell, on its back or windward side if possible; in a strong wind, into the wind. Touch down straight ahead, with no crab.
**How:** the slowest speed short of the stall buffet, flaps full and gear up, a shallow approach with a minimum sink rate, and never a stall from a steep approach.
**Brace** until the aircraft has come to rest: a second and a third impact are usual. Nobody releases a harness until it has stopped.
Inflate the life vests only after leaving the aircraft.

items.action: ADVISE (identification, ground speed, position, course, altitude, persons on board, fuel; nature of the emergency, intentions)

items.item: First aid, survival and loose equipment
NO SMOKE and SEAT BELTS switches
At or below 10,000 ft: PACK and BLEED switches

blocks.content: The left observer's seat must face forward so that the left sliding window can open. With the rate selector at CLIMB the outflow valve moves toward open; once the differential is below 0.5 psi, full DESC closes it fully. Expect continuous aural warnings with the gear up and the flaps out. Brief the brace 30 seconds before touchdown, and nobody releases a harness until the aircraft has stopped. If time permits before leaving, pull all the engine fire handles. If the flight deck door jams, leave by its smoke panel; if debris blocks the way to the cabin, use the windows.

The landing on water, flotation and the slide rafts are not simulated, and on the MD-10 the CABIN PRESS panel is not functional (turning the packs and bleeds off lets the cabin leak down instead). The procedure can be flown to the touchdown.

chapters.title: Abnormal Procedures
chapters.summary: Procedures for failures and other non-normal situations that aren't immediately dangerous.

blocks.content: An abnormal procedure deals with the failure of a system when the aircraft is not in immediate danger: a generator off line, a pump that has stopped, a valve stuck in the wrong place, a flap that will not move. The time-critical procedures, the ones that begin with memory items and protect the aircraft in the next minute, are in [Emergency Procedures](emergency-procedures). The split follows the KC-10 flight manual, whose Section IIA this section corresponds to; FedEx's DC-10 manual and the MD-10 manual draw the line in almost the same place, and where they differ, this manual follows the KC-10's for the three-crew aircraft and the MD-10's own for the MD-10.

The section is divided into parts by system, in the same order as the system parts of [Systems Description](system-description), and each part links back to its system so that the theory behind every procedure is one click away. Every part opens with **About these procedures**: what it covers, how the system's failures announce themselves, a table of the failures you can practice from the EFB with the procedure each one calls, and on the MD-10 the advisory alerts of that system. Every part closes with **Simulation notes**: how the injected failures behave and any step the simulation cannot fly.

Procedures for the three-crew aircraft and for the MD-10 are written separately, because the MD-10's systems controllers do much of what the flight engineer does by hand. Pick the aircraft at the top of the page and only its procedures are shown. Inside a part, procedures are grouped by sub-system.

When a failure appears, the crew member who sees it tells the Captain, and the pilot flying keeps flying the aircraft: no procedure is worth losing control or flight path for. The Captain decides when to start the procedure and, if several failures arrive together, in what order to deal with them. Each procedure assumes a single failure; with more than one, the Captain sets the priority.

On the DC-10 and KC-10 the flight engineer reads the checklist aloud, challenge and response, item by item; the crew member named on each step does it and calls out the result, and the flight engineer announces the checklist complete. On the MD-10 the pilot monitoring reads and does the steps in their area, coordinates the pilot flying's steps (thrust, flight path, flight controls), reads out the consequences, and announces “checklist complete”. Silencing aural warnings and resetting MASTER WARNING and MASTER CAUTION as soon as the cause is recognized is normal crew action and is not written into the procedures, nor are checking circuit breakers and testing lights where they are obviously relevant.

Do not reset a circuit breaker that tripped for an unknown reason unless a procedure tells you to, or unless the Captain judges that the flight depends on it: a breaker that has tripped is telling you something is wrong in the circuit. Allow about two minutes to cool and reset it once only. Pulling and resetting breakers at random can have unexpected effects because the systems depend on one another.
Never reset, or trip and reset, a fuel pump or auxiliary hydraulic pump circuit breaker.
Each checklist step names the crew member who does it.

rows: First Officer (the KC-10 manual's copilot, CP)
Flight engineer, DC-10 and KC-10. FedEx calls the DC-10's flight engineer the second officer (S/O).
Pilot monitoring (the books' pilot not flying, PNF)

blocks.content: The MD-10 has no flight engineer: its steps are the PM's, apart from thrust and flight path (PF) and decisions (CAPT). A step marked as a memory item is boxed and done without reading the checklist; abnormal procedures rarely have any.

Every procedure is laid out the same way. **Condition** says what has happened and what the crew see: the light, the alert, the gauge. **Objective**, where there is one, says what the procedure is trying to achieve, which is what lets a crew adapt sensibly when the situation does not quite fit. **Consequences**, where the source manual gives them, say what the failure costs, such as a landing at the nearest suitable airport. Then come the steps, each with its control as placarded, its action in capitals and its crew designator, and between them the notes that explain why.
**Decision points.** Where a procedure branches, it asks a yes-or-no question about something the crew can see, in bold, followed by what to do for each answer:

**Has the GEN OFF light gone out, with a normal AC load?**
YES: reparallel as required. End of procedure.
NO: GEN switch OFF. The generator cannot be restored. End of procedure.

Each answer either ends the procedure (**End of procedure.**), continues with the next step, or sends you to a named group of steps further down (*Generator off and disconnect* below) or to another procedure by link. Every branch visibly ends. The real manuals draw the same thing as a box with arrows; FedEx and the MD-10 manual put the YES actions directly under the box and draw the NO arrow past them, and the KC-10 manual prints YES and NO either side of the question box, with an arrow from each to the steps it leads to.

Effectivity inside a procedure is written in brackets: “(-30, -40, KC-10)” for the aircraft with a center gear, “Series 30” for the MD-10-30, and so on. A step or note that only one of the DC-10 and KC-10 has carries its own badge.

On the MD-10 an abnormal procedure is called by an alert on the engine and alert display. A **Level 2** alert (amber, boxed, with MASTER CAUTION and its system's cue switch lit) has a procedure, and the procedure's title is the alert's text exactly as displayed, with the system number filled in: GEN DRIVE 1/2/3 FAULT is the procedure for GEN DRIVE 1 FAULT, GEN DRIVE 2 FAULT and GEN DRIVE 3 FAULT. Pressing the lit cue switch resets MASTER CAUTION, shows the system's synoptic page with the alert's consequences, and usually replaces the alert with a reminder in the lower right of the display. On short final, MASTER CAUTION may simply be pressed and the alert left until there is time.

A **Level 1** alert is advisory: it has no written procedure, because what to do is in its own text, in its consequences on the synoptic, or is obvious, or because the system controller has already dealt with the fault. Each part lists the Level 1 alerts of its system with what they tell the crew. Some MD-10 failures have no alert at all, such as a gear handle that will not move or a stabilizer that will not trim; those have **non-alert procedures**, in sentence-case titles, alongside the alert procedures of their system.

The practical difference from the three-crew aircraft is where the work is done. On the DC-10 the flight engineer finds the failure on their panel and reconfigures the system by hand; on the MD-10 the controller has usually reconfigured it before the alert appears, and the crew's work is to confirm, accept and plan. Many MD-10 procedures therefore begin by asking whether the system is in AUTO, and act only if it is in MANUAL or the controller has given up.

The EFB's Failures app offers a failure for almost every condition in this section and in [Emergency Procedures](emergency-procedures), drawn from the KC-10 manual's checklists, and lists only what the loaded aircraft has. A failure fails a real component (a pump, a valve, a bearing, a sensor) and the aircraft then shows it as it would: the lights, the gauges, the behavior that follows. Failures can be triggered at once or scheduled, by time, altitude, airspeed or flight phase. Clearing a failure removes its cause but not the damage it has done; Reset Breakers pushes popped breakers back in, and Reset Aircraft repairs wear and damage. See [Failures](efb#failures-app).

Each part's **Failures you can practice** table names the EFB failure, the procedure it calls on each deck, and on the MD-10 the alert it raises. A few procedures cannot be practiced because nothing in the simulation produces their condition, and a few steps act on controls the simulation does not model; each part's Simulation notes says which.

parts.title: Engines
parts.summary: Abnormal starts, in-flight shutdown and restart, compressor stalls and exceedances, oil system faults, reversers, and engine protection in ash, rain and turbulence.

blocks.content: This part holds the abnormal procedures for the engines: starting problems and alternative starts, shutting an engine down and restarting it in flight, compressor stalls and limit exceedances, the oil system, a reverser that will not stow, and flight in volcanic ash, heavy rain and turbulence. Engine fire, severe damage, engine failure on takeoff, flight with one or two engines inoperative and a reverser deploying in flight are emergencies: see [Emergency Procedures](emergency-procedures). A tailpipe fire is with the fire protection procedures ([Tailpipe fire](abnormal-fire-protection#tailpipe-fire); MD-10: [Tailpipe fire](abnormal-fire-protection#md-tailpipe-fire)), and a clogging fuel filter with the [fuel](abnormal-fuel) procedures. The engines themselves are described in [Engines](engines).

On the DC-10 and KC-10 most engine problems show first on the instruments: the pilots' N1, EGT, N2 and fuel flow, and the flight engineer's oil pressure, temperature and quantity gauges and vibration indicators. Few have a light of their own. ENG OIL PRESS LO and ENG OIL STRAINER CLOG are amber legends on the pilots' overhead annunciator panel, and the oil pressure light also lights MASTER CAUTION. The START VALVE OPEN light in each START switch, the reverser lights and the DC-10's HIGH VIB lights complete the set. The flight engineer's scan of the engine panel, each engine compared with the other two and with its own reference bug, is the main detection system.

On the MD-10 the engines raise amber Level 2 alerts on the Engine and Alert Display: ENG 1/2/3 EGT HI, RPM HI, RPM LO, OIL PRESS LO, OIL TEMP HI and OIL FILTER, each with the ENG cue switch, MASTER CAUTION and a single chime. The ENG cue switch calls the secondary engine page with the oil readings and vibration. Conditions without an alert (a falling or rising oil quantity, a hot start, a stall that keeps EGT below the red line) are found on the displays, and their procedures are the FCOM's non-alert procedures, given here in sentence-case titles.

blocks.title: Failures you can practice
rows: ENG # EGT HI: [ENG 1/2/3 EGT HI](#md-eng-egt-hi), with [Engine compressor stall(s)](#md-compressor-stall)
No alert: [THRUST REVERSER FAILURE TO STOW](#reverser-fails-to-stow)
ENG # OIL PRESS LO, then ENG # OIL TEMP HI: [ENG 1/2/3 OIL PRESS LO](#md-eng-oil-press-lo)
No alert and no MD-10 procedure; watch the oil pressure on the secondary engine page
ENG # OIL TEMP HI: [ENG 1/2/3 OIL TEMP HI](#md-eng-oil-temp-hi)
No alert until the oil runs out: [Engine oil quantity low or decreasing](#md-oil-quantity-decreasing)
[Engine starter shaft failure](#starter-shaft-failure), then [STARTER VALVE MANUAL OPERATION](#starter-valve-manual)
No alert and no MD-10 procedure: FUEL lever OFF and ENG START switch in; see [Simulation notes](#simulation-notes)

blocks.content: The EFB's engine failure, two engines fail, all engines flame out and engine severe damage items are Section 2 emergencies. Their follow-up checklists, [ENG SHUTDOWN IN FLIGHT](#engine-shutdown-in-flight) and [ENGINE RESTART](#engine-restart-in-flight) (MD-10: [Engine shutdown in flight](#md-engine-shutdown-in-flight) and [Engine restart in flight](#md-engine-restart-in-flight)), are in this part, and on the MD-10 a flameout raises [ENG 1/2/3 RPM LO](#md-eng-rpm-lo). The EFB's list is in [EFB failures: engines](efb#failures-eng).
The engine Level 1 alerts the simulation raises (ENG n FUEL FILTER, FUEL CONTAMINATED, ENG n LOOP A or B, ENG FIRE AGENT LO) belong to the fuel and fire protection procedures.

sections.title: Starting
sections.summary: Hot, hung and no-light starts, starter and start valve faults, and starts on the battery, on a running engine's air and on a ground cart.

blocks.content: The start sequence, the starter's limits and the signature of each abnormal start are explained in [Starting and ignition](engines#starting-and-ignition). The engine does not protect itself during a start: no fuel control aborts a hot start, so every procedure here begins with the crew's own hand on the FUEL lever.

**Condition:** A ground start goes wrong in one of three ways. **Hot start:** EGT climbs fast toward or past the 750 °C start limit, often with N2 lagging. **Hung start:** the engine lights, then N2 stops climbing below ground idle with EGT high or rising. **No start:** fuel flow shows but EGT does not rise within 25 seconds of the FUEL lever going ON.

**Objective:** Stop the fuel, clear the unburnt fuel out of the engine with the starter, and decide whether another attempt is safe.

blocks.title: Start EGT
blocks.content: One start with EGT between 750 and 900 °C for less than 40 seconds is allowed: it may be continued and the flight completed, with a log entry. A start terminated after EGT passed 750 °C needs maintenance before another attempt; so does any start above 900 °C, or more than 40 seconds above 750 °C. These are the CF6 figures; the DC-10-40's JT9D-59A has its own starting limit, 505 °C turbine gas temperature (see [Limitations](limitations)).

**Has the ENG START switch already released?**
YES: let N2 fall before re-engaging the starter: 0 % is recommended, up to 20 % is normal, up to 30 % only in an emergency. Then continue with the next step.
NO: continue with the next step.
Do not select the other ignition system before the 30 seconds of motoring are complete. If fuel flow before light-off was above 700 pph, expect a second attempt to run hot as well.

Motoring with the fuel off turns the starter into a purge pump: compressor air sweeps the fuel that collected in the combustor and turbine out through the exhaust before it can burn, and it cools the hot section. If low duct pressure or a leaking check valve is suspected (a slow, hung or hot start), set all ENG PNEU SUPPLY selectors to OFF for the next attempt, so that no start air leaks away into the engines' bleed ducts.

**Did N2 fail to reach 15 % while motoring, or was a start EGT limit exceeded?**
YES: do not attempt another start; maintenance is required. If an EGT limit was exceeded, record the peak and the time above 750 °C. End of procedure.
NO: the start hung or did not light: continue with the next step.

blocks.title: Engines 1 and 3 on START A
blocks.content: On the aircraft, a failed start of engine 1 or 3 on START A is retried on START A with that engine's IGNITION EXCITER POWER TRANSFER switch (flight engineer's equipment panel) at TRANSFER, which makes the left emergency AC bus fire that engine's B ignitors instead of its A ignitors; START A must work on the wing engines for dispatch. The simulated cockpit has no transfer switches: make the second attempt on START B.

**Are the start indications normal?**
YES: the engine is serviceable for the flight; make a log entry. Where continuous ignition is needed later, select CONT A, or CONT B if system A has failed. End of procedure.
NO: continue with *Second attempt fails* below.

Make a log entry and call maintenance. If the first two attempts failed because of a configuration error rather than the engine, dry-motor it for 2 minutes before a third attempt; if the third fails, call maintenance. End of procedure.

**Condition:** The ENG START switch is pushed in for a normal start but N2 does not begin to rise, or rises and then decays. Either the starter's drive shaft has sheared at its shear section (designed to break before the accessory gearbox is damaged), or the start valve has not opened, or there is no start air.

**Is the START VALVE OPEN light on?**
YES: air is flowing to a starter that is not turning the engine: the shaft has failed. Go to *Shaft failed* below.
NO: the valve has not opened, or there is no air pressure behind it. Go to *No start air* below.
Call maintenance. End of procedure.

Duct pressure normally drops about 5 psi as a start valve opens; a gauge that did not move points to the valve rather than the air supply. Call maintenance. A valve that will not open electrically can be opened by hand at the engine: see [STARTER VALVE MANUAL OPERATION](#starter-valve-manual). End of procedure.

**Condition:** A wing engine's start valve will not open electrically and the engine must be started. A mechanic at the engine opens and closes the valve with its manual override handle, on the crew's command, while the crew run the rest of the start.

blocks.title: In the simulation
blocks.content: The ground crew cannot work the start valve by hand in the simulation. With the EFB's starter valve failure active, that engine cannot be started on the ground; in flight it can still be relit on its own windmill (N2 at 10 % or more). The procedure is given as the aircraft flies it.

Starter exhaust air and the valve's T-handle are hot enough to burn: the mechanic must wear hand and arm protection. Brief the ground crew in detail before starting, including the words used at each step.
Working the valve by hand with no pressure in the duct can damage its diaphragms. Pressurize the duct first.
Wait for the mechanic to confirm the valve is open.
