Wait for the mechanic to confirm the valve is closed, then check that the START VALVE OPEN light has gone out and monitor the rest of the start. The START switch still arms start ignition and still releases at cutout; only the air is in the mechanic's hands, which is why the 45 % call matters.

**Does the START VALVE OPEN light stay on?**
YES: tell the mechanic the valve is still open. If it cannot be closed, shut off that pneumatic system's supply and shut the engine down. End of procedure.
NO: end of procedure.

children.title: START VALVE OPEN light on with START switch released

blocks.content: **Condition:** The START VALVE OPEN light in an ENG START switch stays on, or comes on, after the switch has released: after a start or in flight. The start valve is open with the engine running. The overrunning clutch keeps the engine from driving the starter, but the starter turbine is now spinning on full duct pressure with no load, and a starter that overspeeds can fail violently.

**Does the START VALVE OPEN light go out?**
YES: the valve has closed. On the ground, the starter cutout failed to release the switch: go to [ENG START switch fails to release above 45 % N2](#start-switch-fails-to-release). In flight: end of procedure.
NO: the valve is stuck open: continue with the next step.
The KC-10 has no engine 2 bleed system and so no ENG 2 PNEU SUPPLY selector: for engine 2, closing the isolation valves isolates manifold 2.

**Is the aircraft on the ground?**
YES: go to *On the ground* below.
NO: go to *In flight* below.

items.item: APU/ISOL VALVE switch (if the APU supplied the start)
ENG PNEU SUPPLY selectors (if a cross bleed start was used)

blocks.content: Advise maintenance and make a log entry. End of procedure.

Do not repressurize the affected pneumatic system: with no air the starter turbine stops and the stuck valve is harmless. The engine may be kept running at the captain's discretion; watch EGT, N1, N2, fuel flow and the pneumatic pressure and temperature for signs of fire or severe damage, which would mean the starter has come apart. End of procedure.
With pneumatic system 1 or 3 shut off, wing anti-ice is not available. Avoid icing conditions.

children.title: ENG START switch fails to release above 45 % N2

blocks.content: **Condition:** During a ground start N2 passes about 45 % and the ENG START switch stays in, its START VALVE OPEN light still on. The speed switch in the N2 circuit has not dropped the holding coil. On the aircraft the same 45 % signal arms the hydraulic motor pumps, so that function is checked too.

**Does the 1-3/2-3 PUMP VALVE OPEN light come on?**
YES: the motor pumps would run continuously and could overheat their hydraulic systems. Use them ON only below 10,000 ft and OFF in every other phase of flight, and check the MEL for hydraulics (ATA 29) and starting (ATA 80) before dispatch. Continue with the next step.
NO: check the MEL for starting (ATA 80) for dispatch with the start switch cutout inoperative. Continue with the next step.

items.item: 1-3 PUMP and 2-3 PUMP selectors (before the AFTER START checklist)

blocks.content: Make a log entry. End of procedure.

**Condition:** The ENG START switch pops out before N2 reaches about 45 %, and the start valve closes with it. The usual cause is a brief interruption of the holding coil's power, for example a generator coming on line or external power being disconnected while the switch is in. Without the starter the engine may hang or run hot.
Re-engage the starter only at a suitable N2: 0 % recommended, up to 20 % normally, up to 30 % in an emergency.

**Did EGT exceed 750 °C (a hot start)?**
YES: notify maintenance and make a log entry. End of procedure.
NO: continue with the next step.

items.action: ACCOMPLISH, HOLDING THE START SWITCH IN IF REQUIRED

blocks.content:
**Does the 1-3/2-3 PUMP VALVE OPEN light come on?**
YES: the motor pumps would run continuously; use them ON only below 10,000 ft and OFF otherwise, and check the MEL (ATA 29 and ATA 80). Continue with the next step.
NO: check the MEL (ATA 80) for the start switch cutout circuit. Continue with the next step.

items.item: 1-3 PUMP and 2-3 PUMP selectors (before the AFTER START checklist)

blocks.content: Make a log entry. End of procedure.

A START switch that will not stay in at all usually means its holding coils have no power: check the ENG START & IGNITION CONT circuit breaker. With OVRD & AIR START on, the switches hold even with that breaker out.

**Condition:** No APU generator and no ground electrical power: the first engine is started on the aircraft battery, with an air cart for start air. The start controls run from the battery bus, and EMER PWR puts the battery and the static inverter onto the left emergency buses, which power ignition system A. That is why the start is made on START A, and why the battery's endurance sets the pace.
Chock the wheels or have the tug connected: with no engine running there may not be enough hydraulic pressure to hold the aircraft on its brakes during the start.

items.item: BEFORE START checklist (INS and TANK PUMP switches OFF)

blocks.content: EMER PWR IN USE comes on and the L EMER DC BUS OFF and L EMER AC BUS OFF lights go out. Do not try the start if the battery is below its minimum: it may not hold the start controls and the ignition through the start. The pneumatic pressure gauges do not read until their buses are powered.

**Is engine 3 to be started first?**
YES: set the 1-3 ISOL VALVE switch to OPEN (its valve is powered from the left emergency AC bus), then continue with the next step.
NO: continue with the next step; engine 1, on the cart's side of the manifold, is normally first.

items.item: ENG START switch (engine to be started)

blocks.content: Continue with a normal start without delay. Until the generator buses are powered the START VALVE OPEN light, the oil pressure gauge and the fuel flow indicator stay dark: watch the ENG OIL PRESS LO light.

**Did the engine start normally?**
YES: continue with *After the first engine* below.
NO: notify maintenance. End of procedure.

items.action: CHECK ON LINE (GEN OFF LIGHT OUT)

blocks.content: Make sure both brake systems are fully pressurized and the aircraft is chocked before turning off the running engine's hydraulic pumps.

items.item: Cockpit preflight and BEFORE START checklist

blocks.content: The hydraulic pumps come off so that the flight engineer's hydraulic preflight can be done as normal. Start the remaining engines either on the cart (APU/ISOL VALVE switch OPEN, which opens both isolation valves at NORM and lets the cart's air reach every starter; start; disconnect the cart; APU/ISOL VALVE switch CLOSE) or with [CROSS BLEED ENGINE START](#cross-bleed-start). End of procedure.

**Condition:** An engine is to be started on air from an engine already running, because neither the APU nor a cart can supply it. The supplying engine's throttle is advanced to raise its bleed pressure.

If starting in the blocks, set the parking brake or have the tug connected, and check the area behind the aircraft is clear before advancing the throttle. Advancing it too far switches the bleed to low stage, which lowers the pressure, and makes the jet blast more dangerous.
KC-10: engine 2 has no ENG PNEU SUPPLY selector; skip that step when engine 2 is the receiving engine.

Start the engine with the normal procedure. Every step before it serves the starter: the packs are off so that they do not take the air, the receiving engine's own supply is shut so that the air does not leak back through it, and the throttle is advanced only until the gauge shows 30 psi, because at idle the CF6 bleeds from its high stage and a larger advance hands the supply over to the lower-pressure low stage.
Complete the AFTER START checklist. End of procedure.

**Condition:** The engines are started on air from a ground cart because the APU cannot supply it. The EFB's air-start cart has two hoses: hose 1 feeds the left side of the manifold (engine 1's side), hose 2 the right side (see [Ground operations](ground-operations)).

With both hoses connected, set the APU/ISOL VALVE switch to OPEN so that the isolation valves open and the air reaches every starter. If system 1's pressure gauge does not work, the same switch position lets another system's gauge read the cart's pressure. Below 20 psi a start risks running hot.
Start any remaining engine with [CROSS BLEED ENGINE START](#cross-bleed-start). End of procedure.

children.title: Engine abnormal start (hot, hung or no start)

blocks.content:
**Condition:** During a ground start, EGT climbs fast toward the red start limit mark on the Engine and Alert Display (hot start), N2 stops climbing below idle after light-off (hung start), or EGT does not rise within 25 seconds of the FUEL lever going ON (no start). There is no alert for any of them: the crew sees them on the EAD.

**Objective:** Stop the fuel, purge the engine with the starter, and decide whether a second attempt on the other ignition system is worthwhile.

**Has the starter disengaged (ENG START switch in, light out)?**
YES: let N2 fall to 15 % or less, check that ENG IGN A or B is selected, and pull the ENG START switch (light on). Continue with the next step.
NO: continue with the next step.

**Was it a hot start?**
YES: record the peak EGT and the time EGT spent above 750 °C, and call maintenance. End of procedure.
NO: the start hung or did not light: continue with the next step.

**Was the failed start on engine 1 or 3, with ENG IGN A selected?**
YES: call maintenance. End of procedure.
NO: continue with *Second attempt* below.

items.item: ENG IGN (engine 1 or 3: A; engine 2: the other system)

blocks.content: Watch the starter air pressure, the starting fuel flow, the highest N2 reached and the peak EGT, which are what maintenance will want. If the engine still does not start, call maintenance. End of procedure.
The wing engines are always retried on system A: a failure with A already selected is a maintenance item whatever system B might do. The tail engine is simply retried on the other system.

children.title: Start valve light illuminated after start or in flight

blocks.content: **Condition:** The amber light in an ENG START switch stays on after the switch has popped in at the end of a start, or comes on in flight. The start valve is open with the engine running, so the starter turbine is being driven by duct air with nothing to load it.

**Is the ENG START switch still out?**
YES: push it in, then continue with the next step.
NO: continue with the next step.

**Has the light gone out?**
YES: no further action. End of procedure.
NO: the valve is stuck open: continue with the next step.

**Is the aircraft on the ground?**
YES: go to *On the ground* below.
NO: go to *In flight* below.

Make sure no air source can reach that starter: APU air off (the APU BLEED switchlight pushed in, USE ENG AIR lit) or the ground crew's cart shut off. Call maintenance. A later start needs the valve worked by hand, which the simulation does not offer. End of procedure.
Do not repressurize the affected pneumatic system unless it is needed, and avoid icing conditions: with manifold 1 or 3 unpressurized, that wing's anti-ice has no air. End of procedure.

sections.title: In-flight shutdown and restart
sections.summary: Shutting an engine down in flight, relighting it on its windmill or with the starter, and the MD-10's RPM LO alert.

blocks.content: Most procedures in this part that end with a shutdown end here, and so does the EFB's engine failure once the emergency actions are done. A failed engine windmills: ram air keeps both spools turning, the core at a few per cent N2 at approach speeds and in the mid-teens at cruise. At 10 % N2 or more the compressor delivers enough air for the combustor to relight on its own (a **windmill relight**); below that the starter must help, with air from another engine through the isolation valves (a **starter-assisted** start). See [In-flight restart and windmilling](engines#inflight-restart).

blocks.title: In-flight restart envelope
rows: 240 KIAS to VMO/MMO: unrestricted. 220 to 240 KIAS: probable relight

blocks.alt: Diagram of the in-flight engine restart envelope. Vertical axis pressure altitude 0 to 35,000 ft, horizontal axis indicated airspeed 150 to 380 KIAS with VMO and MMO drawn as a boundary on the right. Below 15,000 ft the whole speed range shaded green and labeled unrestricted. From 15,000 to 28,000 ft, green from 240 KIAS to VMO/MMO (unrestricted) and amber from 220 to 240 KIAS (probable relight). From 28,000 to 30,000 ft amber from 220 KIAS to MMO. Above 30,000 ft hatched gray, labeled relight may not occur. A dashed line at 220 KIAS from 15,000 to 30,000 ft labeled KC-10 flight manual limit. An inset note: windmill relight needs 10 % N2 or more; below that, starter assist with cross bleed air.
blocks.title: In-flight restart envelope

blocks.content:
**Condition:** An engine has failed, or a precautionary shutdown has been decided, by the crew or by another procedure. The checklist stops the engine and then deals with the three systems it was driving: its hydraulic system, its generator and its pneumatic supply.

**Consequences:** Land at the nearest suitable airport.

If there are signs of severe damage (airframe vibration, abnormal engine readings, a rapid loss of hydraulic pressure or quantity, or the sudden loss of the generator), use the ENGINE FIRE OR SEVERE DAMAGE procedure instead: see [Emergency Procedures](emergency-procedures).
When conditions allow, run the engine at idle for 3 minutes before shutting it down, so that the hot section cools evenly before the rotors stop.

**Did the fuel flow stop at once?**
YES: continue with the next step.
NO: pull the affected engine's fire handle, which also closes the fuel shutoff valve at the tank (the engine can take up to a minute to stop), then continue with the next step.

After the FUEL lever goes OFF, a fuel flow indicator can read zero for a moment and then show a false flow, which would also run up FUEL USED. If it does, pull that engine's FUEL FLOW IND circuit breaker. Fuel quantity that keeps falling after the shutdown can mean a leak between the tank and the engine.
Leave them on only if they are needed for fuel dumping, lateral balance or the fuel schedule; otherwise they are load the remaining generators do not need. Manage the fuel to keep the wings balanced.

items: The motor pump that links the failed engine's system to a live one: ON. With engine 3 failed, the 1-3 pump is preferred to the 2-3 pump.
A motor pump that links two operating systems: OFF in non-critical phases above 10,000 ft; ARM (FedEx: ON) for approach and landing and below 10,000 ft, as a backup source.
With two engines inoperative: both motor pumps ON. Keep all three systems pressurized if possible, and never fewer than two.

blocks.content: A windmilling engine still turns its pumps and gives its system some pressure, so they may be left on, but not after a fire or severe damage, or with the fire handle pulled.

A windmilling engine at 1.5 to 12 % N2 in a climb or slow cruise, with the nose more than 11° up (9.5° for the tail engine), can use its oil faster than normal. If those conditions cannot be avoided, keeping its hydraulic pumps on reduces the loss.
KC-10: there is no ENG 2 PNEU SUPPLY selector; for engine 2 skip that step.

Each step answers one consequence of the dead engine: its tank pumps have nothing to feed, the motor pump restores its hydraulic system, the isolation valves let the other bleeds carry its users, the APU replaces its generator, and TCAS stops asking for climbs the aircraft may not manage. Continue with the two-engine (or one-engine) operation, driftdown and approach procedures in [Emergency Procedures](emergency-procedures). End of procedure.

**Condition:** An engine that flamed out or was shut down is to be restarted in flight. If it failed or flamed out for no known reason, restart it only if it is needed for the safety of the flight; never restart an engine shut down for a fire or showing signs of damage.

items.item: ENG PNEU SUPPLY selector (affected engine; KC-10: engines 1 and 3 only)

blocks.content: Unloading the hydraulic pumps lets the core windmill faster. OVRD & AIR START fires both ignition systems on all three engines and powers the START switches for a starter assist. Check the aircraft is inside the restart envelope (table above).

**Is N2 10 % or more?**
YES: the engine can relight on its windmill alone: go to *Fuel on* below.
NO: continue with *Starter assist* below.

items.action: MAX ONE PER OPERATING PNEU SUPPLY (VERIFY)

items.item: ENG PNEU SUPPLY selector (engine supplying the air)

blocks.content: The 1-3 isolation valve is powered from the left emergency AC bus and the 1-2 valve from the right emergency AC bus. If a valve cannot be opened because its bus is dead, increase airspeed until N2 reaches at least 10 %.

**Does N2 stay below 10 % with the starter engaged?**
YES: pull the ENG START switch, set OVRD & AIR START to OFF, and complete [ENG SHUTDOWN IN FLIGHT](#engine-shutdown-in-flight). End of procedure.
NO: continue with *Fuel on* below.

Expect EGT to rise within 45 seconds of the FUEL lever going ON. An air start, especially at altitude, can accelerate to idle very slowly: while N2 keeps increasing and EGT is within limits the start is progressing, and should not be mistaken for a hung start. If a windmill start shows signs of running hot, a starter-assisted attempt is the better choice.

**Is the engine stabilized at idle with normal indications?**
YES: go to *Engine running* below.
NO (no EGT rise within 45 seconds, or an abnormal start): continue with *Failed start* below.
Further attempts may be made. If the engine cannot be restarted, complete [ENG SHUTDOWN IN FLIGHT](#engine-shutdown-in-flight). End of procedure.

Allow one minute's warm-up at idle before using power unless the safety of the flight needs it sooner, then return the hydraulic, electrical, pneumatic and air conditioning systems to normal. End of procedure.
The bleed steps serve the starter: the failed engine's own supply is shut so that the assisting air does not escape through it, and fewer packs and no wing anti-ice keep the manifold pressure up.

**Condition:** An engine flames out in flight with no fire or damage. The clearest sign is N2 falling below about 70 % with N1, EGT and fuel flow decreasing; its GEN OFF and PACK OFF lights may come on. Whoever sees it calls “engine flameout” without a number, and the failed engine is positively identified before any control is moved.

**Objective:** Relight the engine on its own windmill at once, while the core is still turning fast.
Do not use this procedure for a flameout on takeoff, a flameout with fire or severe damage, or when anything else rules out a restart.

**Is N2 below 10 %?**
YES: the core is too slow for a windmill relight: go to [ENGINE RESTART](#engine-restart-in-flight). End of procedure.
NO: continue with the next step.

**Did EGT rise within 45 seconds, and has the engine stabilized at idle with normal indications?**
YES: set OVRD & AIR START to OFF, allow one minute's warm-up unless the safety of the flight needs power sooner, and continue the flight monitoring the engine. End of procedure.
NO: continue with the next step.
Complete [ENG SHUTDOWN IN FLIGHT](#engine-shutdown-in-flight). End of procedure.

The FUEL lever stays ON until the relight has clearly failed: fuel is still being metered, so the moment both igniters fire on a core that is still turning fast, the engine relights and the governor brings it back to the throttle's setting. Every second of delay lets N2 decay toward the point where only the full restart will do. A slow acceleration at altitude is normal while N2 keeps increasing and EGT stays within limits.

**Condition:** Level 2 alert ENG 1, 2 or 3 RPM LO with the ENG cue switch, MASTER CAUTION and a single chime: that engine's N2 is below idle in flight with its FUEL lever ON. Normally a flameout or a failure. The alert also stands during an in-flight start until idle is reached, and it goes when the FUEL lever is moved to OFF.
Compare EGT, N1, N2 and fuel flow with the other engines, looking for a flameout or a failure.

**Are EGT and fuel flow normal?**
YES: the engine is running and the N2 signal is at fault: continue to operate the engine. End of procedure.
NO: continue with the next step.

N2 reading zero on an engine that is plainly still running, together with ENG OIL PRESS LO, is not an indication fault: the accessory gearbox has failed, taking the oil pumps and the N2 sensor with it, and the engine will seize. Use the ENGINE FIRE OR SEVERE DAMAGE procedure in [Emergency Procedures](emergency-procedures).

**Is a restart wanted?**
YES: go to [Engine restart in flight](#md-engine-restart-in-flight). End of procedure.
NO: go to [Engine shutdown in flight](#md-engine-shutdown-in-flight). End of procedure.

**Condition:** An engine is to be shut down in flight: after a failure, or as a precaution that another procedure calls for. With signs of severe damage, use the ENGINE FIRE OR SEVERE DAMAGE procedure in [Emergency Procedures](emergency-procedures) instead.
The OFF light comes on and AIR SYS 1, 2 or 3 OFF is displayed.

A windmilling engine at 1.5 to 12 % N2 in a climb or slow cruise, with the nose more than 11° up (9.5° for the tail engine), can use its oil faster than normal. If those conditions cannot be avoided, operating its hydraulic pumps reduces the loss.
Consider landing at the nearest suitable airport; for flight with an engine inoperative, see [Emergency Procedures](emergency-procedures). End of procedure.

The checklist is short because, in AUTO, the MD-10's hydraulic and fuel system controllers reconfigure their own systems for the dead engine, work the flight engineer does by hand on the DC-10. The crew's part is the air: the dead engine's bleed and its pack come off, and the isolation valve opens so that the remaining bleeds supply the whole manifold.
**Condition:** An engine that flamed out or was shut down is to be restarted in flight. Never restart one shut down for a fire or showing signs of damage.

**Is the hydraulic system in MANUAL?**
YES: push the affected system's L PUMP and R PUMP switchlights to OFF (OFF lights on), then continue with the next step.
NO: continue with the next step.

**Is the fuel system in MANUAL?**
YES: push the affected tank's PUMPS switchlight on (OFF light out), then continue with the next step.
NO: continue with the next step.
Air starts may be tried at any altitude and airspeed, but the FCOM's recommended envelope is the table above.

If ignition override does not work (no cyan lightning stroke on that engine's EGT display), the FCOM's alternative is to select ENG IGN A and B and that engine's anti-ice ON, which makes the controller fire the igniters for 60 seconds. The simulated controller has no automatic ignition, so in the simulation that alternative gives no spark.

**Is N2 below 10 %?**
YES: continue with *Starter assist* below.
NO: go to *Fuel on* below.

items.item: BLEED AIR switch (engine supplying the air)
FUEL lever (with N2 at 10 % or more)

blocks.content: Monitor N1, N2, EGT and fuel flow. EGT should rise within 30 seconds of the fuel going on.

**Is the start abnormal, or did the engine not start?**
YES: move the FUEL lever to OFF, push the ENG IGN OVRD switch OFF, and complete [Engine shutdown in flight](#md-engine-shutdown-in-flight). End of procedure.
NO: continue with *Engine running* below.
Allow a one-minute warm-up at idle and then return to normal thrust gradually, unless thrust is needed sooner for the safety of the flight.
Check that every system is in the mode and configuration wanted. End of procedure.

sections.title: Oil system
sections.summary: Low and high oil pressure, high oil temperature, abnormal oil quantity and a clogging scavenge filter.

blocks.content: Each engine's oil is watched in two independent ways: transmitters drive the pressure, temperature and quantity readings (the flight engineer's gauges; the MD-10's secondary engine page), and separate switches drive the low pressure and strainer lights or alerts. When a reading and its switch agree, believe them; when they disagree, suspect a sensor. Oil pressure follows N2, so a change only means something when it is compared at the same N2. The system and its failure modes are described in [Oil system](engines#oil-system) and [Oil system failures](engines#oil-failures).

blocks.title: Oil limits used in these procedures
rows: 30 to 90 psi; 15 psi or more at idle
135 °C at the oil inlet; 163 °C for 20 minutes
More than 10 psi at constant N2 may mean a pending failure

blocks.content: **Condition:** OIL PRESS low on the flight engineer's gauge, the amber ENG OIL PRESS LO legend on the pilots' overhead annunciator panel with MASTER CAUTION, or both. The light comes from a pressure switch (on at about 11 psi falling), the gauge from a separate transmitter.

items: **Oil pressure and the N2 reading lost together:** the lube pump has failed (the pump and the N2 sensor are both driven by the accessory gearbox). Running on can damage the engine.
**Pressure low or fluctuating while the quantity climbs at steady N2:** fuel leaking into the oil through the fuel/oil heat exchanger. Consider shutting the engine down.
**A drop of more than 10 psi at steady N2:** a restricted supply, a leak, or loss of oil tank pressurization.
**Low at altitude, recovering in the descent:** the oil tank has lost its pressurization, typically through a filler cap or remote fill port not properly closed.

items.item: Oil pressure and ENG OIL PRESS LO light

blocks.content:
**Is the aircraft in flight?**
YES: continue with the next step.
NO: go to *On the ground* below.

**Is oil pressure below the red line with the ENG OIL PRESS LO light on?**
YES: both sensors agree: shut the engine down with [ENG SHUTDOWN IN FLIGHT](#engine-shutdown-in-flight). End of procedure.
NO (pressure in the caution range, or only one of the two indications abnormal): continue with the next step.
Shut the engine down if the quantity falls abnormally, the oil temperature becomes excessive or vibration increases. End of procedure.

**Is oil pressure below the red line?**
YES: shut the engine down (FUEL lever OFF). End of procedure.
NO: continue normal operation. End of procedure.

Two independent sensors are the heart of this procedure. A real loss of oil shows on both, while a single abnormal indication is far more often a sensor than an engine. Once both agree, do not wait: with no oil pressure the bearings run dry, and beyond about 30 seconds they begin to wear, heat and seize.

**Condition:** Oil pressure more than 10 psi above its steady value at the same N2, or above the normal band. Contamination is narrowing passages downstream of the transmitter, so the pump is pushing against a higher resistance. The OIL STRAINER CLOG light may come on, but a restriction in some places raises the pressure with no light at all.

items.item: Oil quantity, oil temperature and engine vibration

blocks.content:
**Does oil temperature become excessive, or vibration abnormal?**
YES: shut the engine down with [ENG SHUTDOWN IN FLIGHT](#engine-shutdown-in-flight). End of procedure.
NO: keep monitoring. End of procedure.

A higher pressure sounds reassuring but means less oil reaching whatever lies beyond the restriction. The bearing it feeds slowly heats and wears, and the first signs are a rising oil temperature and vibration, on all four channels if it is a main bearing (see [Vibration monitoring](engines#vibration-monitoring)).

**Condition:** OIL TEMP in its caution range or climbing toward it. Operation in the caution range is allowed for 15 minutes; above the red line it is not allowed. With the oil quantity falling as well, suspect an external leak, a failing scavenge pump or high consumption. With the quantity normal, the fuel/oil heat exchanger's bypass valve has probably stuck open and the oil is no longer being cooled.

**Is thrust set at or below cruise thrust?**
YES: go to *Advance thrust* below.
NO: continue with the next step.
Reduce thrust as far as needed to keep the temperature from passing its limit.

**Is oil temperature within limits, or reducing?**
YES: keep operating the engine and monitor the temperature; log the maximum reached. End of procedure.
NO (it cannot be brought down, or it has passed 175 °C): go to *Shut down the engine* below.
More thrust sends more fuel through the fuel/oil heat exchanger, which may bring the oil temperature down.

**Is oil temperature within limits, or reducing?**
YES: keep operating the engine and monitor the temperature; log the maximum reached. End of procedure.
NO (it cannot be brought down, or it has passed 175 °C): continue with the next step.
Use [ENG SHUTDOWN IN FLIGHT](#engine-shutdown-in-flight). End of procedure.

The oil's cooler is the fuel on its way to the engine, so oil temperature is a balance between the heat the bearings and gears put in, which grows with power, and the fuel flow available to take it away, which also grows with power. Above cruise thrust the heat input is the side to attack, so the first remedy is less thrust; at cruise thrust or below, fuel flow is the scarcer side, and more thrust brings more cooling fuel. A cooler that is being bypassed gains nothing from more fuel flow; only less heat input helps it. The DC-10-40's JT9D has its own limits (table above).

**Condition:** OIL QTY moving away from its reference bug faster than normal consumption explains, either way. A small change is normal: oil is drawn into the sumps and gearboxes as power rises and returns as it falls, and a healthy engine uses a fraction of a quart an hour.

**Is the quantity decreasing?**
YES: go to *Quantity decrease* below.
NO (it is increasing): go to *Quantity increase* below.
Keep the engine running while pressure and temperature stay in their normal ranges. If either becomes abnormal, shut the engine down with [ENG SHUTDOWN IN FLIGHT](#engine-shutdown-in-flight).

An engine whose tank is empty can run for some time with normal pressure and temperature and then lose both quickly. If the quantity reads zero and the pressure begins to fluctuate, give serious thought to shutting the engine down even though the pressure is still in the normal range.

An external leak drains the tank while the pump keeps full pressure, because the pump draws from whatever is left; only when the tank is nearly dry do pressure and temperature move. Watching the quantity against the bug is what buys time to plan the shutdown. End of procedure.
Use this branch for a continuous increase, an increase with other abnormal indications, a quantity above 19 quarts, or fuel or oil fumes.

**Is oil pressure low or fluctuating at steady N2?**
YES: fuel is probably leaking into the oil through the fuel/oil heat exchanger, and diluted oil can damage the engine: consider a shutdown. Continue with the next step.
NO: keep the engine running while pressure and temperature stay normal. Continue with the next step.

**Are fuel or oil fumes detected?**
YES: set the affected engine's ENG PNEU SUPPLY selector to OFF (KC-10 engine 2: no selector) and see [Pneumatics](abnormal-pneumatics) for operation with that supply off. Continue with the next step.
NO: continue with the next step.
If oil pressure or temperature becomes abnormal, shut the engine down with [ENG SHUTDOWN IN FLIGHT](#engine-shutdown-in-flight). Log all the indications. End of procedure.

Fumes mean the contaminated oil is reaching the air: oil mist from the bearing sumps leaks into the compressor air that seals them, and from there into the bleed air and the cabin. Shutting that engine's supply keeps it out of the packs.

**Condition:** The amber ENG OIL STRAINER CLOG legend on the pilots' overhead annunciator panel, steady or flickering: the pressure drop across the scavenge filter has reached its switch setting (about 31 psid). Debris is loading the filter; beyond that point a bypass valve opens and unfiltered oil goes back to the engine with no further warning.

At idle the oil flow, and with it the pressure drop across the filter, is at its lowest. A light that goes out shows the filter is loading but the oil is still passing through it rather than around it.

**Does the light go out?**
YES: continue with *Light out at idle* below.
NO: oil is bypassing the filter: shut the engine down with [ENG SHUTDOWN IN FLIGHT](#engine-shutdown-in-flight). End of procedure.

items.action: ADVANCE SLOWLY UNTIL THE LIGHT COMES ON, THEN RETARD UNTIL IT GOES OUT

blocks.content: Operate the engine at or below that setting and watch it closely. Shut it down if the oil temperature rises, the pressure goes high or low, vibration increases, or the light comes on again. Log the oil pressure and temperature. End of procedure.

**Condition:** Level 2 alert ENG 1, 2 or 3 OIL PRESS LO with the ENG cue switch and MASTER CAUTION, or an oil pressure below the red line on the secondary engine page. The alert comes from the low oil pressure switch, the SD reading from a separate transmitter. The procedure is the same in either case.

**Is the SD pressure below the red line with ENG OIL PRESS LO displayed?**
YES: shut the engine down with [Engine shutdown in flight](#md-engine-shutdown-in-flight). End of procedure.
NO: continue with the next step.

items.item: Oil quantity, temperature and pressure (secondary engine page)

blocks.content: A pressure in the normal or caution range with the alert displayed, or below the red line with no alert, points to one failed sensor. End of procedure.

An oil leak usually brings ENG OIL TEMP HI soon after, as the starved oil stops carrying heat away; this procedure takes precedence. Oil pressure lost together with an N2 reading of zero on a running engine is a failed accessory gearbox: see [ENG 1/2/3 RPM LO](#md-eng-rpm-lo).

**Condition:** Level 2 alert ENG 1, 2 or 3 OIL TEMP HI with the ENG cue switch and MASTER CAUTION: oil temperature is above its continuous limit. OIL TEMP is amber and boxed on the secondary engine page, red above the red line.

Advancing the throttle increases the fuel flow through the fuel/oil heat exchanger and may lower the oil temperature. Operation in the caution range is allowed for 15 minutes; above the red line it is not allowed.

**Is oil temperature within limits?**
YES: continue operating the engine and monitor the oil temperature. End of procedure.
NO: shut the engine down with [Engine shutdown in flight](#md-engine-shutdown-in-flight). End of procedure.

Adjust means find the setting that brings the temperature down. With the oil quantity normal and no low pressure alert, a stuck-open heat exchanger bypass is the likely cause, and that responds to less thrust, not more. If ENG OIL PRESS LO came first, the oil is leaking away: follow [ENG 1/2/3 OIL PRESS LO](#md-eng-oil-press-lo).

**Condition:** Level 2 alert ENG 1, 2 or 3 OIL FILTER with the ENG cue switch and MASTER CAUTION: the scavenge oil filter is clogged or about to clog. The alert is inhibited with the oil below 35 °C, when thick oil would trip the switch harmlessly. Once the filter clogs, its bypass valve opens and unfiltered oil goes straight to the engine.
At idle the lower oil flow reduces the pressure drop across the filter, and the alert may go: that shows the oil is still passing through the filter, not around it.

**Does ENG OIL FILTER remain displayed at idle?**
YES: shut the engine down with [Engine shutdown in flight](#md-engine-shutdown-in-flight). End of procedure.
NO: advance the throttle to just below the point where the alert returns, and operate the engine at or below that thrust. End of procedure.

**Condition:** No alert. OIL QTY on the secondary engine page rises steadily above its cyan initial-quantity line, rises with other abnormal indications, or passes 19, or fuel or oil fumes are noticed. Fuel leaking into the oil inside the fuel/oil heat exchanger is the usual cause. A small change either way can be normal.

**Are fuel or oil fumes detected?**
YES: push the affected BLEED AIR switch (OFF light on) and the appropriate ISOL switch (ON light on), then continue with the next step. See [Operation with less than three bleed air sources](abnormal-pneumatics#md-less-than-three-bleeds).
NO: continue with the next step.
In icing conditions with only one bleed air source, observe the single-bleed limitations for the thrust required.

items.item: Engine oil pressure, quantity and temperature

blocks.content: If pressure or temperature becomes abnormal, the oil pressure or temperature procedure takes over. End of procedure.

children.title: Engine oil quantity low or decreasing

blocks.content: **Condition:** No alert. OIL QTY on the secondary engine page falls away from its cyan initial-quantity line faster than normal consumption, and turns amber and boxed below 4 quarts. Usually an external leak.
If oil pressure or temperature becomes abnormal, shut the engine down with [Engine shutdown in flight](#md-engine-shutdown-in-flight). End of procedure.

The pump keeps full pressure while there is oil to draw, so pressure and temperature stay normal until the tank is nearly dry, and then change quickly. The warning the quantity gives is the time to plan the shutdown.

sections.title: Thrust reversers
sections.summary: A reverser that will not stow after landing.

blocks.content: A reverser light in flight, or any sign that a reverser has deployed in flight, is an emergency: see [Emergency Procedures](emergency-procedures). How the reversers work, and why a failed reverser stays where it is, is in [Thrust reversers](engines#thrust-reversers) and [Reverser failures](engines#reverser-failures).

**Condition:** After landing, a reverser stays deployed when its reverse lever is brought down to forward idle: a reverser indication stays on with the throttles in the forward range (DC-10, KC-10: REV THR, or REV U/L with REV PRES; MD-10: REV or U/L in that engine's N1 dial). The reverser's stow drive has failed; the air and mechanical loads on the cowl hold a reverser where it is, so it stays out.
Do not cycle the reverser or try again to stow it: the attempt can damage the translating cowl's attachments. Leave it unstowed for maintenance.
With the cowl deployed, that engine's fan air is turned forward whatever the lever position: thrust set on it is reverse thrust. Keep its throttle at idle and taxi on the other engines.

**Do the reverser indications go out?**
YES: the reverser has stowed; no further action. End of procedure.
NO: continue with the next step.
With the lever back at reverse idle the reverser is commanded to where it already is, so it cannot be driven unexpectedly while maintenance people are working near it.

items.item: FUEL lever (affected engine, after 3 minutes at idle)

blocks.content: Both motor pumps on keep all three hydraulic systems pressurized with the engine shut down, so that full braking and nose wheel steering remain.

The MD-10 FCOM has no checklist for this failure; the steps above, from FedEx's DC-10 procedure, use controls the MD-10 shares. In the taxi phase the MD-10's hydraulic system controller runs both motor pumps whenever an engine is below 45 % N2, which keeps the shut-down engine's system pressurized.
Make a log entry. No takeoff until the reverser has been stowed and secured. End of procedure.

sections.title: Compressor stall, overspeed and overtemperature
sections.summary: Stalls and surges, EGT and rotor speed exceedances, and how vibration enters the decisions.

blocks.content: None of the manuals has a stand-alone procedure for high engine vibration. Vibration enters as a decision criterion instead: a rise after a compressor stall, with a high oil pressure or a clogging strainer, or with abnormal oil readings is a reason to shut the engine down, and airframe vibration with other signs of damage calls for the ENGINE FIRE OR SEVERE DAMAGE procedure in [Emergency Procedures](emergency-procedures). How to read the four channels (fan or core, one bearing or all) is in [Vibration monitoring](engines#vibration-monitoring). The DC-10's HIGH VIB lights come on above 4.0 units on any of an engine's channels; the KC-10 has no HIGH VIB lights; the MD-10 shows its COMP and TURB readings in amber when out of limits.

**Condition:** The airflow through the compressor breaks down. The signs, alone or together: one bang or a series, sluggish or no response to the throttle, N1 and N2 fluctuating or rolling back, and EGT high or rising fast because fuel is still being metered for air that is no longer arriving. The causes are aerodynamic: damaged blades, inlet distortion at extreme angles of attack or in a strong crosswind on the ground, and reverser efflux drawn back into the inlet at low speed.

**Was the throttle moving when the stall occurred?**
YES: the transient may have triggered it: continue with the next step.
NO: a stall at a steady setting points to damage. If the engine is needed, operate it at minimum thrust; if not, shut it down with [ENG SHUTDOWN IN FLIGHT](#engine-shutdown-in-flight). End of procedure.

**Has the stall cleared at idle?**
YES: continue with *Stall cleared* below.
NO: operate the engine at minimum thrust if it is needed; otherwise shut it down with [ENG SHUTDOWN IN FLIGHT](#engine-shutdown-in-flight). End of procedure.
Advance slowly to find out whether the stall comes back, checking that N1, N2 and EGT follow the throttle.

**Does the stall recur?**
YES: if the engine is needed, operate it at minimum thrust, below the setting where it stalls; if not, shut it down with [ENG SHUTDOWN IN FLIGHT](#engine-shutdown-in-flight). End of procedure.
NO: continue normal operation. End of procedure.

Run an engine that has shown a tendency to stall with great care. Shut it down if EGT is high or rises rapidly during the slow advance, or if vibration increases; with signs of damage, use the ENGINE FIRE OR SEVERE DAMAGE procedure in [Emergency Procedures](emergency-procedures).
After any compressor stall the engine cannot be dispatched until maintenance has inspected it. Record the TAT, altitude, airspeed, N1 and the weather at the time.

Idle moves the compressor's operating point well away from its surge line: less fuel, a lower pressure ratio, more margin. A stall set off by a transient, such as a rapid throttle movement or a gust of distorted inlet air, usually clears at idle and does not return. A damaged compressor has lost margin from part power upward, so it runs clean at idle and stalls again at some intermediate setting on the slow advance, which then becomes its ceiling. See [Compressor stall in service](engines#compressor-stall-failure).

**Condition:** N1, N2 or EGT has passed its red line. On the round dials the needle drags the max pointer past the red radial and leaves it there; on the tapes the warning light comes on; on the EIDS the ENG IND MAX light turns red, then blue. Every overspeed and overtemperature, with its peak and duration, goes in the log.

**Is the aircraft on the ground with the engine not started?**
YES: if the pointer moved during an electrical power transfer, reset it; no log entry is needed. Otherwise call maintenance and make a log entry. End of procedure.
NO: continue with the next step.

**Is the aircraft on the ground with the engine running?**
YES: continue with *On the ground* below.
NO: go to *In flight* below.

**Is EGT above 100 °C?**
YES: once N2 has fallen to 20 %, push the ENG START switch in and motor the engine until EGT is 100 °C or less, then pull it. Call maintenance and make a log entry. End of procedure.
NO: call maintenance and make a log entry. End of procedure.

Reduce thrust to try to regain normal indications.

**Are the engine indications abnormal at minimum thrust?**
YES: consider a precautionary shutdown with [ENG SHUTDOWN IN FLIGHT](#engine-shutdown-in-flight). Log the exceedance and land at the nearest suitable airport. End of procedure.
NO: continue with the next step.

**Did any parameter go above the range in the table?**
YES: reduce to flight idle and use more thrust only at the captain's discretion. Log the exceedance and land at the nearest suitable airport. End of procedure.
NO (the exceedance stayed within the range): normal operation may continue to the next landing. Log it. End of procedure.

The table is FedEx's and covers the CF6 engines only. A small excursion costs hot-section and rotor life; a large one may have damaged the engine, which is why the response steps up with the size of the exceedance. Motoring after a ground overtemperature carries the heat out of the turbine. See [Overspeed and overtemperature](engines#overspeed-overtemperature) and [EGT exceedances](engines#egt-exceedance).

**Condition:** Level 2 alert ENG 1, 2 or 3 EGT HI with the ENG cue switch and MASTER CAUTION: that engine's EGT is above its red line. The EGT digits on the EAD are red and boxed, and the highest value reached stays at the top of the scale until reset. A compressor stall is a common cause: if it came with bangs or a rollback, see also [Engine compressor stall(s)](#md-compressor-stall).

Retard it to a setting that keeps EGT acceptable.

**Does EGT remain above the red line?**
YES: shut the engine down with [Engine shutdown in flight](#md-engine-shutdown-in-flight). End of procedure.
NO: continue with the next step.

**Did EGT exceed 1,000 °C (MD-10-30) or 965 °C (MD-10-10)?**
YES: set the throttle to flight idle and use more thrust only at the captain's discretion. If any engine indication is abnormal at minimum thrust, consider a precautionary shutdown. End of procedure.
NO: operate the engine at a setting that keeps EGT below the red line. End of procedure.
**Condition:** Level 2 alert ENG 1, 2 or 3 RPM HI with the ENG cue switch and MASTER CAUTION: that engine's N1 or N2 is at or above its red line. The alert stays displayed for as long as it is.

Retard it until the speeds are within limits.

**Does the speed remain above the red line?**
YES: shut the engine down with [Engine shutdown in flight](#md-engine-shutdown-in-flight). End of procedure.
NO: continue with the next step.

**Did the speed exceed 116 % N1 or 103 % N2 (MD-10-10), or 125 % N1 or 111 % N2 (MD-10-30)?**
YES: set the throttle to flight idle and use more thrust only at the captain's discretion. If any engine indication is abnormal at minimum thrust, consider a precautionary shutdown. End of procedure.
NO: operate the engine at a setting that keeps N1 and N2 below their red lines. End of procedure.
**Condition:** No alert of its own; ENG EGT HI if EGT passes the red line. Bangs or a rumble, N1 and N2 fluctuating or rolling back, EGT high or rising fast, and sluggish response to the throttle.

**Is engine operation normal?**
YES: the stall was momentary and has cleared: continue operating the engine. End of procedure.
NO: continue with the next step.

items.item: ENG ANTI-ICE switch (affected engine) and WING ANTI-ICE switch

blocks.content: Ignition override relights the combustor if the stall has blown the flame out. Anti-ice is selected for its bleed: taking more air off the compressor lowers its operating line and widens the margin to surge.

**Is engine operation now normal?**
YES: continue with *Recovery* below.
NO: shut the engine down with [Engine shutdown in flight](#md-engine-shutdown-in-flight). End of procedure.
Run an engine that has shown a tendency to stall with great care. Shut it down if EGT is high or rises rapidly during the slow advance, or if vibration increases.

Advance slowly to find out whether the stall comes back, checking that N1, N2 and EGT follow the throttle. If it recurs, the captain may keep the engine at a reduced thrust at which it does not stall; if it does not, continue and monitor the engine. End of procedure.

sections.title: Volcanic ash, heavy rain and turbulence
sections.summary: Protecting the engines in a volcanic ash cloud, in heavy rain or hail and in severe turbulence.

blocks.content: What the three have in common is the engine's margin: ash erodes and chokes it, water cools the flame toward extinction, and turbulence distorts the inlet airflow. The answers are the same too: low thrust where possible, bleed air to widen the stall margin, and continuous ignition so that an engine that flames out relights while it is still turning fast.

On the DC-10 and KC-10, select continuous ignition (CONT A preferred) for heavy rain and severe turbulence; it has no time limit. Turbulence penetration speeds and technique are in [Adverse Weather](adverse-weather).

**Condition:** Flight into a volcanic ash cloud. N1, N2 and fuel flow decrease while EGT rises; engines may surge, torch from the tailpipe or flame out. Smoke or dust in the cockpit and a smell like electrical smoke are typical, and airspeed indications may become erratic or be lost altogether.

**Consequences:** Land at the nearest suitable airport.
Leave the ash by the shortest route. Consider an immediate descending 180° turn.

items.action: IDLE, OR AS LOW AS PRACTICABLE

items.item: WING ANTI-ICE switch, packs and pneumatic systems

blocks.content: The autopilot may be engaged again later at the captain's discretion.
Do not attempt an APU start after all engines have flamed out.

If ash has blocked the pitot system or damaged the air data computers, fly pitch and power as in [Suspect airspeed](abnormal-miscellaneous#suspect-airspeed). If an engine flames out or its EGT climbs beyond limits, use [ENG SHUTDOWN IN FLIGHT](#engine-shutdown-in-flight) and [ENGINE RESTART](#engine-restart-in-flight); several attempts may be needed, and a relight may only come once the aircraft is clear of the ash.
Land at the nearest suitable airport. End of procedure.

Ash melts in the combustion section, where the gas is hotter than the ash's melting point, and solidifies again on the cooler turbine nozzle guide vanes, choking the turbine: the engine runs hotter, loses surge margin and finally flames out. Idle thrust brings the combustor temperature down, which reduces the build-up and gives the most surge margin; the extra bleed of every air user widens it further. Continuous ignition relights an engine that flames out while it still windmills fast, and the APU and ADG are electrical insurance against losing more than one engine. Weather radar does not show ash.

**Condition:** Flight into a volcanic ash cloud (or ground operation in ash or dust). N1, N2 and fuel flow decrease while EGT rises; engines may surge, torch from the tailpipe or flame out. There may be smoke or dust in the cockpit, a smell like electrical smoke, St. Elmo's fire on the windshields at night, and landing lights that cast sharp shadows. Weather radar does not detect ash, and it may be invisible at night or in cloud.

**Objective:** Get out of the ash at the lowest practical thrust, with the most surge margin and the lowest EGT, so that as little ash as possible fuses onto the turbine.

Leave the ash by the shortest route. Consider a descending 180° turn. If airspeed indications are abnormal, see the airspeed lost, suspect or erratic procedure in [Emergency Procedures](emergency-procedures) for pitch guidance.

Do not use the windshield wipers: ash scratches the windshield, and the scratches glare at night. Avoid rapid throttle movements. Eroded compressor and turbine blades show as more fuel flow and EGT for the same thrust. Do the following as quickly as possible:

A lower EGT reduces the debris fused onto the turbine and hot section and much of the erosion of the compressor and blade tips.

**Has an engine flamed out or stalled, or is its EGT beyond limits or rising rapidly toward them?**
YES: continue with *Engine restart* below.
NO: go to *Landing* below.

**Is N2 below 20 %?**
YES: pull the ENG START switch, then continue with the next step.
NO: continue with the next step.

Monitor the start. At high altitude engines accelerate to idle very slowly, which can look like a hung start. If an engine fails to start, try again at once: a start may not succeed until the aircraft is out of the ash and within the normal speed and altitude range. Consider starting the APU, if available, to keep the electrical system powered if more engines are lost. Continue with *Landing* below.

Make a precautionary landing if the aircraft was damaged or an engine behaved abnormally in the ash. Expect sandblasted windshields and landing lights to reduce visibility on the approach. In prolonged exposure, put on crew oxygen (100 %) at the first smell of sulphur or sign of dust in the cockpit; do not deploy the passenger masks with the cabin pressurized, because they would only dilute contaminated cabin air. Report the ash cloud to ATC as soon as practical. End of procedure.

items: **On the ground in ash or dust:** switch bleed air off before using reverse and keep reverse to a minimum; taxi slowly on all engines with extra spacing, minimum thrust and light braking; avoid air conditioning (full cold if it must be used) and keep the APU for engine starting.
Before departure, check the windshield, pitot-static ports and inlets are clear. Do not take off into ash; let it settle, have the runway swept, and make a rolling takeoff with the packs off.

children.title: Severe turbulence and/or heavy rain ingestion

blocks.content:
**Condition:** Flight in severe turbulence, or in heavy rain or hail. Water and ice drawn into the engines take heat out of the flame and raise the fuel flow needed to keep it alight, worst at low thrust; turbulence distorts the inlet airflow and costs stall margin.

**Objective:** Keep every engine lit and every compressor clear of stall while flying attitude, not airspeed.
In turbulence, fly the FMS optimum altitude where possible for the best buffet margin, and descend if more margin is needed.

blocks.title: Turbulence penetration speeds
rows: 250 KIAS or climb speed, whichever is greater
250 KIAS or climb speed, whichever is greater

blocks.content: Move the throttles only to correct an excessive airspeed variation or to stay inside the red lines, and then slowly. Accept momentary changes in N1; do not chase airspeed.

Keep the autopilot engaged and watch it; disconnect it only if it does not hold an acceptable attitude. If it disconnects, fly attitude, giving up altitude to hold it, disregard the flight director pitch bar and do not trim; re-engage it once recovered.

Never apply force to the control wheel or column with the autopilot engaged. A sustained force makes it disconnect, and the surfaces it was holding then move abruptly; crews have over-controlled while trying to recover. If the autopilot is not doing what is wanted, disconnect it with a disconnect switch, not with force. After an unexpected disconnect, stabilize the attitude smoothly, relaxing the controls if necessary until the motion damps out.
The extra bleed demand increases the compressors' stall margin.

blocks.title: When clear of the turbulence and heavy rain

blocks.content: Leave the anti-ice on if icing conditions call for it. End of procedure.

The engines are full thermodynamic models with a hydromechanical fuel control, so the conditions in this part arise from their causes and respond to the crew's actions as described in [Engines](engines#simulation-notes). The EFB's engine failures behave as follows.

blocks.title: How the EFB's engine failures behave
rows: The front compressor blades are damaged. At cruise power the engine surges repeatedly: bangs, N1 rolling back several per cent, EGT climbing by more than 100 °C (MD-10: past the red line, ENG EGT HI) and vibration rising. Idle clears it, and a slow advance brings it back at some part-power setting.
The stow side of the reverser's control valve fails. Nothing shows in flight; the reverser deploys normally on the landing roll and then will not stow.

An oil leak downstream of the pump: pressure is gone within seconds and ENG OIL PRESS LO lights (MD-10: ENG OIL PRESS LO). The oil, no longer carrying heat away, passes 160 °C within about a minute and a half (MD-10: ENG OIL TEMP HI) while the quantity drains. After the 30-second dry-running allowance the bearings wear and vibration climbs, and an engine left running seizes within several minutes. A seized core does not windmill and cannot be restarted.

The oil jets are restricted downstream of the transmitter: pressure rises more than 10 psi at once. The starved bearing wears toward a failure, and an engine left running seizes after about two hours at cruise. The strainer light is not part of this failure.

The fuel/oil heat exchanger's bypass valve is stuck open: oil temperature climbs past 160 °C over a few minutes at high power, with pressure and quantity normal. Reducing thrust brings it back inside the limit; advancing the throttle does not help.

An external oil loss of about 20 quarts an hour: the quantity falls while pressure and temperature stay normal, until the tank runs dry (about 40 minutes from a cruise quantity) and the pressure goes with it.

Contamination loads the scavenge filter: OIL STRAINER CLOG (MD-10: ENG OIL FILTER) comes on first at high power, within about 15 minutes at cruise, and goes out at idle while the filter is only loading.
The fuel control over-fuels on its start schedule, giving a hot start. Every start of that engine runs hot while the failure is active.

The start valve will not open. The START switch still engages and arms start ignition, but the START VALVE OPEN light stays out and N2 does not move. The ground crew's manual valve operation is not available, so that engine cannot be started on the ground; in flight it can still be relit on its windmill at 10 % N2 or more, but not with the starter.

items: The EFB's engine failure items cut the engine's fuel: it flames out, windmills, and cannot be relit while the failure is active. On the MD-10 ENG RPM LO is raised and goes when the FUEL lever is moved to OFF. Engine severe damage shears the accessory gearbox: N2 reads zero, oil pressure is lost (MD-10: ENG RPM LO and ENG OIL PRESS LO) and vibration is high while the engine keeps running until it seizes.

The START switches move the opposite way to the aircraft's (see [Engines](engines#simulation-notes)): on the DC-10 and KC-10 the simulated switch is pulled out to engage the starter and drops back in at cutout, on the MD-10 it is pushed in to engage and pops back out. Where a procedure here says IN or PUSH to start and PULL to stop the starter (DC-10, KC-10), or PULL to start and PUSH to stop (MD-10), work the simulated switch the other way.
A START switch can be engaged only below 30 % N2.
DC-10 and KC-10: the START switches hold at any ENG IGNITION position, not only at START A or B; with the selector at OFF an engine cranks but cannot light.
The IGNITION EXCITER POWER TRANSFER switches are not fitted (see [ABNORMAL START](#abnormal-start)).

The hydraulic motor pumps' ARM function works on system pressure, not on the starter cutout's 45 % signal, so the motor pump checks in the two START switch procedures find the PUMP VALVE OPEN light out. No EFB failure sticks a start valve open or holds a START switch in.

BATTERY START: the KC-10 manual's alternative of starting on APU air, with the APU isolation valve and the 1-2 isolation valve opened by hand by the ground crew, cannot be done; use the air-start cart.
Turning a windmilling engine's hydraulic pumps off does not raise its windmilling speed, and a windmilling engine produces no thrust in the flight model, though its N1 and N2 are shown.
MD-10: there is no automatic continuous ignition, so the FCOM's alternative ignition for a restart (ENG IGN A and B with engine anti-ice) gives no spark; use OVRD.

Heavy rain and hail lower the flameout margin at low thrust and can make N1 wander; continuous ignition (MD-10: OVRD) relights a flameout while the core still turns fast. Volcanic ash is not modeled: its procedures are given for completeness.
Vibration is modeled on four channels per engine, with imbalance, bearing wear, stall damage and fan ice as causes, so the vibration criteria in these procedures work.

blocks.content: **Left out.** None of the books' engine procedures has been omitted. Within them, the cross bleed start's cargo heat switch step is dropped (the simulated DC-10 has no such switch), the transfer switch step is replaced as noted above, and the battery start's steps for talking to the ground crew on the maintenance interphone are left out. The EFB's **Reset Aircraft** repairs engine wear and damage but leaves active failures active; clear a failure in the EFB before expecting the engine to recover. See [EFB](efb).

parts.title: Auxiliary Power Unit
parts.summary: The APU generator's trip and bearing failure lights, the MD-10's GEN APU OFF alert, an automatic APU shutdown and the door after shutdown.

blocks.content: This part holds the abnormal procedures for the APU and its generator: the generator tripping off line, a generator bearing failure, an automatic shutdown of the APU, and its door after shutdown. An APU fire is an emergency: see [Emergency Procedures](emergency-procedures). A fault in an APU fire detection loop is with the [fire protection](abnormal-fire-protection) procedures. The APU itself is described in [Auxiliary Power Unit](apu), its generator's control and protection in [Electrical](electrical).

On the DC-10 and KC-10 the APU's lights are on the flight engineer's panels: APU GEN OFF and APU GEN FAIL in the APU generator block of the electrical panel, with the APU AC LOAD meter and the APU PWR AVAIL and APU PWR IN USE lights; APU OIL PRESS LO/TEMP HI and APU FUEL PRESS LO with the APU gauges. APU GEN OFF lights the ELEC cue light and MASTER CAUTION, but only once the APU is up to speed. An automatic shutdown has no light of its own: the gauges wind down and APU PWR AVAIL goes out.

On the MD-10 the APU panel on the aft overhead shows FAIL for an automatic shutdown and an amber OFF legend in the APU GEN RESET switchlight for a tripped generator. A tripped generator raises GEN APU OFF: a Level 2 alert with the ELEC cue switch and MASTER CAUTION when the electrical system is in MANUAL, a Level 1 alert in AUTO. APU FAIL (Level 1) reports an automatic shutdown. The APU's readings are in the APU box on the secondary engine page.

blocks.title: Failures you can practice
rows: [APU GEN OFF light on (AC LOAD zero)](#apu-gen-off)

blocks.content: The EFB's APU fire is a Section 2 emergency. See [EFB failures: electrical](efb#failures-elec) and [EFB failures: fire](efb#failures-fire).

blocks.title: MD-10 Level 1 APU alerts
rows: The APU has shut down automatically, or did not start (FAIL lit on the APU panel). Push START/STOP to stop it and clear the latch. Do not restart after a fire or an oil pressure or temperature fault; otherwise a second start may be tried once the shutdown cycle is complete and the OFF legend has gone out, about 3 minutes after STOP.
GEN APU OFF (electrical system in AUTO)
The electrical system has turned the APU generator off after a fault, or the APU FIRE control has been operated. See [GEN APU OFF](#md-gen-apu-off).

sections.title: APU generator
sections.summary: A protective trip, and a bearing failure.

children.title: APU GEN OFF light on (AC LOAD zero)

blocks.content:
**Condition:** The amber APU GEN OFF light with the ELEC cue light and MASTER CAUTION, the APU running and up to speed, APU PWR AVAIL and the APU PWR IN USE lights out and the APU AC LOAD meter at zero. The APU generator's control unit has sensed a fault, opened the generator's field contactor and locked it out. The APU keeps running and can still supply air; the generator buses it was carrying fall back to whatever other source can reach them.

**Objective:** Restore the generator once, with its voltage and frequency proved good before any bus is reconnected.

The simulated DC-10's electrical panel has no APU GEN RESET switch (the FedEx aircraft has one, used as on the KC-10 below), so the lockout cannot be cleared from the flight deck: the generator cannot be restored. Leave the APU GEN BUS switches OFF; the APU can still supply air. End of procedure.
Reset once only. A fault that trips the generator again after one reset is real, and reconnecting it repeatedly risks damage to the generator and to the buses it would feed.

**Is the APU GEN OFF light out, with normal volts and frequency?**
YES: continue with the next step.
NO: the generator cannot be restored; leave the APU GEN BUS switches OFF. End of procedure.

**Does the APU GEN OFF light stay out, with a normal AC load?**
YES: end of procedure.
NO: the generator cannot be restored: set the APU GEN BUS switches to OFF. End of procedure.

The bus switches come off first so that a restored generator is not connected to anything until its voltage and frequency have been seen on the meter. Reconnecting one bus at a time lets the flight engineer watch the load arrive in steps and catch a fault on a particular bus. If the APU generator was standing in for a lost engine generator, see [Electrical](abnormal-electrical) for operation with the generators that remain.

**Condition:** The amber APU GEN FAIL light in the APU generator block. It reports an impending or actual failure of the generator's main bearing, or a spurious signal. The generator is not tripped and goes on carrying its load, but a failed bearing ends in a seized generator.
On the ground, connect external power first if it is available, so that the buses have a source when the APU generator comes off.

**Does the APU GEN FAIL light stay out?**
YES: the light was caused by a spurious signal. End of procedure.
NO: the bearing is failing: continue with *APU shutdown* below.
FedEx's DC-10 procedure says not to attempt GEN FAIL RESET for the APU generator: go straight to *APU shutdown* below.
A later takeoff is made with the APU shut down or with the generator replaced. End of procedure.

An engine generator with this light is disconnected from its engine by its CSD disconnect, and the engine runs on. The APU generator has no CSD to disconnect: it is geared straight to the APU, so the only way to stop it turning on a failing bearing is to stop the APU.

**Condition:** Alert GEN APU OFF: Level 2, with the ELEC cue switch and MASTER CAUTION, when the electrical system is in MANUAL; Level 1 in AUTO. The APU is running, but its generator control unit has turned the generator off after a fault (or the APU FIRE control has been operated); the amber OFF legend in the APU GEN RESET switchlight on the APU panel shows the trip. The FCOM's GEN OFF procedure covers it, with the APU GEN RESET switchlight as the generator's reset.

**Consequences:** One reset attempt allowed.
Only one reset attempt is permitted.

**Does the OFF legend stay out, with GEN APU OFF gone?**
YES: the generator is back; the electrical power control unit reconnects it to any generator bus that has no engine generator, provided APU PWR is selected. End of procedure.
NO: continue the flight with the APU generator inoperative. End of procedure.

sections.title: APU operation
sections.summary: An automatic shutdown, and the door after shutdown.

blocks.content:
**Condition:** The APU stops without a crew command: N1, N2 and EGT run down, and APU PWR AVAIL and the APU PWR IN USE lights go out. Its electronic control unit has tripped one of its protections (see [Protection and automatic shutdowns](apu#protection)) and latched the shutdown. APU FIRE or APU OIL PRESS LO/TEMP HI stays lit if either caused it; APU FUEL PRESS LO points to fuel starvation.

**Objective:** Clear the latch, decide from the cause whether the APU may be started again, and if so restore its fuel first.
OFF removes the run command, which clears the latched shutdown; the doors close once the APU has run down.

**Did the APU shut down with APU FIRE or APU OIL PRESS LO/TEMP HI lit?**
YES: do not restart it. For APU FIRE, see [Emergency Procedures](emergency-procedures). End of procedure.
NO: continue with the next step.

**Is APU FUEL PRESS LO lit?**
YES: continue with *Restore APU fuel* below.
NO: go to *Restart* below.

items.item: Tank 2 pump switch in use, or APU FUEL PUMP switch

blocks.content: A start made before the shutdown cycle is complete and the door has closed (about 100 seconds on the aircraft) can hang and run hot. Observe the starter duty cycle and, in flight, the start envelope (normal mode up to 25,000 ft); see [Starting the APU](apu#starting-dc-kc). A repeated automatic shutdown is a maintenance item. End of procedure.

FedEx's next step for an APU that will not start or keeps shutting down in normal mode is a start in the standby control mode (CONT SYS switch at STBY), on the ground or, in flight, only in an emergency. Standby is not usable in the simulation: the APU cannot hold its speed in it and shuts itself down within seconds.

The cause decides the restart. A fire or an oil fault can only be made worse by another start. Fuel starvation leaves the machine undamaged once a pump is feeding it again; the APU sits above the fuel and cannot draw it up by suction, so it needs a pump running at all times.

children.title: APU DOOR OPEN light on after shutdown (on the ground)

blocks.content: **Condition:** On the ground, the blue APU DOOR OPEN light stays on after the APU has been shut down. The doors normally stay open for a time after the stop so that the APU keeps breathing while it runs down and cools: FedEx gives 60 seconds, and in the simulation they close about 90 seconds after the stop, once N1 has fallen below about 20 %. A light that stays on well beyond that means the inlet door has not closed.
Make a log entry; whether the aircraft can be dispatched with the door open is a question for the MEL (chapter 49). End of procedure.

blocks.title: How the EFB's APU failures behave
rows: The APU generator loses its field: its control unit trips it on under-voltage and locks it out. A reset (KC-10 APU GEN RESET switch, MD-10 APU GEN RESET switchlight) brings it back, and it trips again: the procedures' cannot-be-restored branch. The simulated DC-10 has no reset switch, so there the generator stays off.

The generator's main bearing fails: APU GEN FAIL lights and the generator stays on line, carried by its auxiliary bearing. GEN FAIL RESET puts the light out only for an instant, which is how a real failure is told from a spurious one. After about five hours on the auxiliary bearing the generator seizes. Not listed on the MD-10, which has no such light or alert.

items: DC-10 and KC-10: the APU GEN OFF light shows the generator's field contactor. It does not light during a normal APU start as it does on the aircraft; it lights after a protective trip, and it brings the ELEC cue light and MASTER CAUTION only with the APU up to speed.

MD-10: GEN APU OFF is Level 2 in MANUAL and Level 1 in AUTO. The APU GEN RESET switchlight resets the generator in either mode (on the aircraft it acts in MANUAL), and there is no automatic reset of the APU generator in AUTO.
An automatic shutdown latches until the APU MASTER is turned to OFF (MD-10: START/STOP pushed to stop). On the MD-10 the FAIL legend and the APU FAIL alert are the same latch.
The standby control mode is not usable: with STBY selected the APU cannot hold its governed speed and shuts down within about ten seconds. The MD-10's CONT SYS STBY switchlight is not connected.
The doors travel in about 12 seconds and close about 90 seconds after the stop. The aircraft's 90-second cooling run after APU air is shut off is not modeled: OFF (STOP) begins the shutdown at once.
The APU starter duty cycle is not enforced; observe it anyway.
Electrical load on the APU generator does not load the APU: its speed and EGT do not change with generator load.

blocks.content: **Left out.** FedEx's APU FAILS TO SHUT DOWN: its key step is the APU FIRE CONTROL switch (APU OFF/AGENT ARM), which is not fitted in the simulated DC-10 and KC-10 cockpits (each of the flight engineer's APU agent discharge controls does that switch's work but also discharges one of engine 2's bottles), and the simulation does not produce the failure. FedEx's APU FIRE WARNING HORN (OUTSIDE THE AIRCRAFT): it is worked by ground personnel at the external APU control panel, which is not simulated.

parts.title: Fire Protection
parts.summary: A fire detection loop alarming on its own, and tailpipe fires.

blocks.content: This part covers the fire protection abnormals that are not fires in the engine nacelles or the APU compartment: a detection loop alarming on its own, and a fire in an engine's tailpipe, which the detection system cannot see. Engine fire, APU fire, cargo fire and smoke are in [Emergency Procedures](emergency-procedures). How the detection and extinguishing systems work is in [Fire Protection](fire-protection).

Each engine and the APU are watched by two independent detection loops, A and B. With the LOOPS selector at BOTH, a fire warning needs both loops to alarm together, which protects the crew from shutting down a good engine for one faulty loop; a single loop in alarm lights only its LOOP light. The procedure for a lone LOOP light is therefore a diagnosis: prove the other loop works, and then trust it alone.

blocks.title: Failures you can practice
rows: Engine 1, 2, 3 or APU fire detection loop fault
ENG 1/2/3 LOOP A/B (Level 1): [procedure](#md-eng-loop); APU LOOP light: [procedure](#md-apu-loop)

blocks.content: The EFB's fire and smoke failures are listed in [EFB failures: fire and smoke](efb#failures-fire).

children.title: ENG/APU FIRE DETECT LOOP light on without fire warning

blocks.content:
**Condition:** One LOOP light (A or B) for an engine or the APU, with no fire warning: no bell, no ENGINE FIRE or APU FIRE light, no handle light. One loop is alarming and the other is not: almost always a false alarm in the lit loop, a contaminated or damaged sensing element.

**Objective:** Prove the unlit loop works, then select it alone so that a real fire still gives a warning.

items.action: NOTIFY: ONE LOOP LIGHT ON, AFFECTED ENGINE OR APU
SET TO THE LOOP NOT LIGHTED

blocks.content: A good loop gives a full fire warning on test. For an engine: the bell, the ENGINE FIRE light, that engine's fire handle light and fuel lever light, and the tested LOOP lights. For the APU: the APU FIRE lights, MASTER WARNING and the tested LOOP lights.

**Are the test indications satisfactory?**
YES: release the test switch and check the lights go out. Continue the flight with the LOOPS selector on the loop just tested. Detection is now on a single loop, but with full warning capability. End of procedure.
NO: the selected loop has failed too: set the LOOPS selector to the opposite loop (FE). If a fire warning then comes, use the engine fire or APU fire procedure in [Emergency Procedures](emergency-procedures). End of procedure.

Select the loop whose light is **out**, never the lit one. With the selector at A or B, any alarm on the selected loop is a fire warning, and for the APU an automatic shutdown: selecting the faulty loop turns a false LOOP light into a false fire warning.
**Condition:** ENG 1, 2 or 3 LOOP A or B (Level 1): one of that engine's detection loops is in alarm without a fire warning.

**Is the engine fire test satisfactory?**
YES: release the TEST switch and check the lights go out. Continue with the ENG LOOPS switch on the loop just tested. End of procedure.
NO: associated ENG LOOPS switch to the opposite loop (PM), and if a fire warning follows, use ENGINE FIRE OR SEVERE DAMAGE in [Emergency Procedures](emergency-procedures). End of procedure.

**Condition:** One APU detection loop in alarm without a fire warning: the FCOM's Level 2 alert APU LOOP A or B, and that loop's LOOP light on the APU fire panel. (The simulation shows the light but does not raise the alert; see [Simulation notes](#simulation-notes).)

**Is the APU fire test satisfactory?**
YES: release the TEST switch and check the lights go out. Continue with the APU LOOPS switch on the loop just tested. End of procedure.
NO: associated APU LOOPS switch to the opposite loop (PM), and use the APU FIRE procedure in [Emergency Procedures](emergency-procedures). End of procedure.

**Condition:** Fuel burning in an engine's tailpipe, usually during or just after a start or a shutdown, when fuel has pooled in the combustor or turbine and ignited there. The fire is inside the engine's gas path, downstream of the nacelle where the detection loops are, so there is no fire warning: the first sign is usually the EGT rising with the engine stopped or starting, or a report from the ground crew, the tower or another aircraft.

**Objective:** Starve the fire of fuel and blow it out by motoring the engine with the starter.

Discharging the engine fire extinguisher will not put out a tailpipe fire: the agent goes into the nacelle, not the gas path. If motoring does not put the fire out, or the engine cannot be motored, ground fire-fighting equipment may be needed.

**Is the starter engaged (the fire happened during a start)?**
YES: keep motoring with the starter. After the fire is reported out, ENG START switch PULL, light out (CAPT), and call maintenance. End of procedure.
NO: continue with the next step.

The starter is not engaged above about 20% N2 because the starter's clutch is designed to engage a slowly turning engine. The ignition selector is at START because on these aircraft it arms the start switch circuit; with the fuel lever OFF, no fuel reaches the igniters. Motoring drives a strong flow of air through the engine that both blows the burning fuel out of the tailpipe and cools it. After the fire is reported out, ENG START switch PULL, light out (CAPT). Maintenance is required. End of procedure.
**Condition:** Fuel burning in an engine's tailpipe, not shown in the cockpit: the first notice may come from outside the aircraft.
Discharging the engine fire agent will not extinguish a tailpipe fire. If motoring does not put it out, or the engine cannot be motored, ground fire-fighting equipment may be needed.

**Is the starter disengaged?**
YES: allow N2 to decrease to 20% or less, verify IGN A or B selected, and ENG START switch PULL (PM) to motor the engine.
NO: keep motoring.
After the fire is out, ENG START switch PUSH (PM), and call maintenance. End of procedure.

items: **Fire detection loop fault** puts one loop falsely into alarm: an engine detector's responder shorted closed, or the APU loop's cable contaminated into its alarm band. One LOOP light comes on with no warning, and the LOOPS selector and LOOP TEST switches work through the procedure as written.

**MD-10 loop test.** A zone whose LOOPS switch is at A or B is not tested by the LOOPS TEST switches in the simulation: only zones at BOTH are. Testing the unlit loop after selecting it, as the procedure says, therefore gives no test indication; treat the selected loop as good unless it alarms. The engine loop alerts are Level 1 in the simulation's alert list, and APU LOOP A/B is not raised at all: an APU loop fault shows only on the APU panel's LOOP lights.

**Tailpipe fire** is fuel burning in the tailpipe of a stopped or starting engine: the EGT rises with no fire warning, and motoring with the fuel lever OFF purges it within about 30 seconds. The simulated START switches move the opposite way to the aircraft's: on the DC-10 and KC-10 pull the switch out to motor the engine and push it in to stop; on the MD-10 push it in to motor and pull it to stop (see [Engines](abnormal-engines#simulation-notes)).
