**Not included.** FedEx's APU FIRE WARNING HORN (outside the aircraft) procedure: the APU fire horn and the external APU control panel are not simulated. APU procedures are in [Auxiliary Power Unit](abnormal-apu).

parts.title: Fuel
parts.summary: Pump, filter, fill valve and quantity failures, the KC-10's body tanks, fuel dump and fuel leaks.

blocks.content: This part covers fuel system failures: boost and transfer pumps, engine fuel filters, fill valves and transfer, quantity indication, the KC-10's body tanks, fuel dump and fuel leaks. How the system works is in [Fuel](fuel). The air refueling receiver and tanker fuel items are in [Air Refueling](abnormal-air-refueling).

On the DC-10 and KC-10 the flight engineer's fuel panel is the annunciation: an amber TANK PUMP PRESS LO light (LOW on the KC-10's switch-lights) for any main tank boost or transfer pump, and FUEL FILTER PRESS DROP for an engine filter, light the FUEL cue on the pilots' overhead annunciator panel and MASTER CAUTION; the auxiliary tank pump lights do not. The MD-10's fuel system controller runs the pumps and valves itself in AUTO and deals with most single failures without the crew: a pump alert is Level 1 while it is in AUTO, and becomes a Level 2 alert with a procedure when the system is in MANUAL and the crew must act.

Two warnings apply to every fuel procedure. **Never reset a tripped fuel pump circuit breaker**, and never trip and reset one: a pump breaker that has tripped may be protecting against a short inside a pump submerged in fuel. And remember that engine 2 and the APU cannot suction-feed: the center engine flames out without boost pump pressure, while engines 1 and 3 can draw fuel through their pumps' bypass at reduced altitude and thrust.

blocks.title: Failures you can practice
rows: TNK 1/2/3 FWD PMP LO or TNK 1/3, 2L/2R AFT PMP LO (Level 1 in AUTO): [forward](#md-fwd-pmp-lo), [aft](#md-aft-pmp-lo)
TNK 1/2/3 XFER PMP LO, with the pump commanded on: [procedure](#md-xfer-pmp-lo)
Centre aux upper tank pump pressure low

DC-10-30, -40: [UPR AUX TANK PUMP PRESS LO light on](#aux-tank-pump-press-lo) (-15: see [Simulation notes](#simulation-notes)). KC-10: [CTR WING pump LOW light on](#ctr-wing-pump-low), or with the pump selected [Transfer pump inoperative](#trans-pump-inop)
MD-10-30: AUX UPR L PUMP LO in MANUAL only (Level 1, no procedure)
Centre aux lower tank pump pressure low
DC-10-30: [LWR AUX TANK PUMP PRESS LO light on](#aux-tank-pump-press-lo). KC-10: as for the upper pump
MD-10-30: AUX LWR PUMPS LO, and AUX LWR L PMP LO in MANUAL (Level 1, no procedure)
ENG 1/2/3 FUEL FILTER; FUEL CONTAMINATED with two engines: [procedure](#md-eng-fuel-filter)
Alternate transfer valve fails closed (KC-10 only)
Main tank fill valves fail closed
[Tanks 1, 2 and 3 fill valves will not open](#main-fill-valves)
[Tank 1 or 3 fill valve will not open](#fill-valve-1-3)
FUEL QTY FAULT, with SEL FUEL SYS MAN and FUEL SYS MANUAL: [procedure](#md-fuel-qty-fault)

blocks.content: The EFB's fuel failures are listed in [EFB failures: fuel](efb#failures-fuel). The menu also lists an outboard compartment transfer failure (FUEL SCHED) that injects nothing yet (see [Simulation notes](#simulation-notes)). Electrical failures in the same app also take away the pumps on the failed buses.

blocks.title: MD-10 fuel Level 1 alerts
rows: TNK FWD/AFT/XFER PMP LO, TANK PUMPS LO (in AUTO)
A pump has low pressure and the controller is compensating. In MANUAL the same alerts are Level 2 with the procedures below.
AUX UPR L/R PUMP LO, AUX LWR L/R PMP LO (Series 30, in MANUAL)
That auxiliary tank pump has low pressure and should be considered inoperative; transfer from its compartment is slower.
AUX UPR PUMPS LO, AUX LWR PUMPS LO (Series 30)
The pumps commanded on in that compartment have low pressure: its fuel may not be transferable.
With the controller in AUTO and every boost pump and crossfeed for that engine off, the engine is feeding by suction alone. Monitor it.
That crossfeed valve has failed open or closed.
COLD FUEL RECIRC, FUEL TEMP LO
The controller is circulating fuel through tanks 1 and 3 to warm it. FUEL TEMP LO follows if the wing fuel comes within 3 °C of its freeze point: descend to warmer air.
About 4,000 lb or less in that tank.
SEL FUEL SYS MAN, FUEL SYS MANUAL
The controller has reverted to manual with the SYSTEM switch still in AUTO (push SYSTEM to acknowledge); the system is in MANUAL.
The auxiliary fill isolation valve (Series 30) or an outboard fill / manifold drain valve is inoperative. AUTO can still be used.

sections.title: Boost and transfer pumps
sections.summary: Main tank boost pumps, transfer pumps and the auxiliary tank pumps.

children.title: TANK PUMP PRESS LO light(s) on

blocks.content:
**Condition:** A TANK PUMP PRESS LO light (LOW on the KC-10) for a main tank boost pump that is switched on, with the FUEL cue and MASTER CAUTION. Either the pump has failed, or the tank is running out of fuel at that pump's inlet. The light compares the pump's output pressure with a threshold; it cannot tell the two causes apart, but the other pumps in the same tank can. Each main tank has two boost pumps (three in tank 2), any one of which can feed its engine at full thrust.

**Objective:** Find out whether a pump has failed or the tank is empty, then keep every engine fed.
Do not reset a tripped fuel pump circuit breaker, and do not trip and reset one.

items.item: TANK PUMP switch (remaining pump in the same tank)

blocks.content: If the check below shows a failed pump in tank 1 or 3, run that tank's transfer pump and open its crossfeed for takeoff, climb, approach and landing, so that the engine has a second pressurized supply when the fuel moves in the tank. Avoid relying on the forward pump alone. The tank 2 left aft pump is powered from the right emergency AC bus and has no control breaker: its three power breakers are pulled instead.

**Are the tank's PRESS LO lights out (the remaining pump's light came on briefly and went out)?**
YES: the tank still has fuel, so the pump has failed: pull the malfunctioning pump's control circuit breaker (FE) and do not use that pump again this flight. End of procedure.
NO: continue with the next step.

**Does the transfer pump run with its light out?**
YES: the tank still has fuel at the transfer pump, so both boost pumps have failed. Open the tank's crossfeed (X-FEED, OPEN) so its transfer pump feeds the engine through the manifold, and pull the failed pumps' control breakers (FE). If the failures are in tank 1 or 3, turn on a transfer pump from another tank as well for approach and landing. End of procedure.
NO (all of the tank's pump lights on or cycling): the tank is probably empty; continue with *Suspected empty tank* below.

items.item: TANK PUMP switches (tank with low fuel)

blocks.content: The transfer pumps' lights come on briefly and go out as they pressurize the manifold, and the engine is now fed by crossfeed from the other tanks. A quantity indicator that blanks during the test has failed: treat the tank as empty.

**Does the indicator respond normally to the test?**
YES: the indicating system is reliable and the tank is empty. Continue the crossfeed while watching the engine's fuel pressure, and transfer as required to regain the normal fuel schedule. End of procedure.
NO: the tank's indication cannot be trusted. Continue the crossfeed while watching the engine's fuel pressure, and calculate the fuel remaining from the departure fuel less the fuel used (allowing for any fuel taken on or offloaded); distribute the fuel using the indicators that are reliable. End of procedure.

While crossfeeding, watch for one tank going down while another, which should not be gaining, goes up: fuel is running between tanks through the manifold. Close the crossfeed valve; the affected tank's fuel can still be moved with its own transfer pump.

**Condition:** With a TRANS pump switched on, its PRESS LO light (LOW) comes on and stays on: the transfer pump has failed. On the KC-10 this includes a body tank TRANS pump and a center wing tank pump selected on; a center wing pump whose LOW light is on with its switch off is [CTR WING pump LOW light on](#ctr-wing-pump-low). The pump no longer pushes that tank's fuel into the manifold for transfer or dump. A main tank's engine is unaffected, since its boost pumps feed it, and those boost pumps, through the crossfeed, are the remaining way to move its fuel; a body or center wing tank's fuel must go by another route.

**Objective:** Isolate the failed pump and plan another route for the fuel that tank would have delivered.
Do not reset any tripped fuel pump circuit breaker.

items.item: Affected transfer pump control circuit breaker

blocks.content: Do not use the pump again this flight. If the light came on during a dump, keep the dump symmetrical by managing the other tanks.

**Is it a main tank's transfer pump?**
YES: when fuel must be moved out of that tank, use the crossfeed method: in the supplying tank, all boost pumps ON and its X-FEED OPEN; in the receiving tank, FILL VALVE OPEN (FE). The boost pumps then push fuel into the manifold and through the receiving tank's fill valve. End of procedure.
NO (a KC-10 body tank or center wing pump): transfer by another route when required, for example with the AR pumps or the remaining center wing transfer pump. End of procedure.
KC-10: opening a center wing upper pump's breaker also disables the lower pump on that side. If only the lower pump has failed, open only its own breaker.

children.title: UPR or LWR AUX TANK PUMP PRESS LO light on

blocks.content:
**Condition:** An upper or lower auxiliary tank pump's TANK PUMP PRESS LO light comes on and stays on with the pump selected (center auxiliary tank: upper and lower on the -30; upper only on the -40 and on the -10 with the center-wing tank). These lights do not light the FUEL cue. A steady light means a failed pump or an empty compartment; a **flashing** light means the compartment is running low, not a failed pump, and is not a reason for this procedure.

**Objective:** Tell a failed pump from an empty compartment by comparing it with the opposite side, then isolate a failed pump.
Do not reset, or trip and reset, a fuel pump circuit breaker.

**Is it a LWR light?**
YES: continue with *Lower pump* below.
NO: go to *Upper pump* below.

**Lower pump: is the opposite side's LWR light out?**
YES: the lower compartment still has fuel, so this pump has failed. PUMPS AUX TANKS selector (malfunctioning side) UPR, and trip that side's lower pump control breaker (FE). Do not reset it. End of procedure.
NO: the lower compartment is empty. PUMPS AUX TANKS selectors (both) UPR (FE). End of procedure.

**Upper pump: is the opposite side's UPR light out?**
YES: the upper compartment still has fuel, so this pump has failed. PUMPS AUX TANKS selector (malfunctioning side) OFF, and trip that side's upper and lower pump control breaker (FE). Do not use the pump again; do not reset the breaker. End of procedure.
NO: the upper compartment is empty. PUMPS AUX TANKS selectors (both) OFF (FE). End of procedure.

Each side has one breaker for its lower pump and one for its upper and lower pumps together. Tripping the upper-and-lower breaker for a failed lower pump disables the good upper pump on that side as well: for a lower pump, trip only the lower breaker. On the ground before takeoff, pull the breaker and call maintenance.

children.title: CTR WING pump LOW light on

blocks.content:
**Condition:** An upper or lower center wing tank pump's LOW light is on with its switch off. The pump, or its control, has failed. (A LOW light that stays on with the pump selected is [Transfer pump inoperative](#trans-pump-inop).)

**Objective:** Isolate the pump.

items.item: Affected pump's FUEL PUMP POWER circuit breaker

blocks.content: Do not use the pump for the rest of the flight. Its light may stay on after the breaker is pulled; no further action is needed. On the ground before takeoff, pull the breaker and call maintenance. End of procedure.

**Condition:** Level 2 alert TANK 1, 2 or 3 PUMPS LO with the FUEL cue and MASTER CAUTION, the system in MANUAL: every boost pump commanded on in that tank has low pressure, and the PUMPS button shows LOW. The engine is feeding by suction (engines 1 and 3) or is about to starve (engine 2).

**Objective:** Feed the engine from the manifold with the tank's transfer pump.

**Consequences:** TANK 2 PUMPS LO only: engine 2 may flame out.

The transfer pump now pressurizes the manifold and the open crossfeed feeds the engine from it. If the tank is in fact empty, its transfer pump's LOW legend lights too, and fuel must come from another tank's transfer pump through the manifold. End of procedure.

**Condition:** Level 2 alert TNK 1, 2 or 3 FWD PMP LO, the system in MANUAL: the tank's forward boost pump has low pressure. The aft pump keeps the engine fed. The forward pump matters at low fuel in a nose-down attitude, when fuel runs forward in the tank and away from the aft pump's inlet.

**At top of descent, is the tank's quantity less than 11,500 lb?**
YES: associated XFEED button ON, and the XFEED button of another tank whose pumps are running ON (PM), so that the engine also draws from the manifold through the descent. Crossfeed from another tank's forward pump is better than a transfer pump here: the transfer pump sits aft in its tank and can uncover as the attitude changes. End of procedure.
NO: no further crew action is required. End of procedure.

children.title: TNK 1/3 AFT PMP LO, TNK 2L/2R AFT PMP LO

blocks.content: **Condition:** Level 2 alert for an aft boost pump of tank 1, 2 or 3, the system in MANUAL. The forward pump still feeds the engine, but the aft pump is the one that keeps it fed in a nose-up climb.
The transfer pump backs up the failed aft pump through the manifold. End of procedure.
**Condition:** Level 2 alert TNK 1, 2 or 3 XFER PMP LO, the system in MANUAL: the tank's transfer pump is commanded on with low pressure, and its TRANS button shows LOW.
With the crossfeed open, the tank's boost pumps can deliver its fuel into the manifold in place of the transfer pump. End of procedure.

sections.title: Engine fuel feed
sections.summary: Engine fuel filters and low fuel temperature.

children.title: FUEL FILTER PRESS DROP light on

blocks.content:
**Condition:** An engine's FUEL FILTER PRESS DROP light (ICING on the DC-10-40) with the FUEL cue and MASTER CAUTION. The pressure drop across the engine's low-pressure fuel filter has risen: the filter is clogging, almost always with contamination (water, ice crystals or debris), and its bypass valve is about to open. Once it does, unfiltered fuel reaches the fuel control and the high-pressure pump.

**Objective:** Keep only filtered fuel reaching the fuel control where possible, and recognize contaminated fuel affecting more than one engine.

**Are all engines required (for example, in a climb at high weight or with another engine already inoperative)?**
YES: affected engine's throttle as required (PF). End of procedure.
NO: retard the affected engine's throttle until the light goes out (PF). End of procedure.

Why reducing thrust helps: the pressure drop across a clogging filter rises with the flow through it, so less fuel flow brings the drop back below the bypass point. With the light out, all the fuel reaching the fuel control has been filtered.
More than one FUEL FILTER PRESS DROP light is reason enough to suspect contaminated fuel: land at the nearest suitable airport.

**Condition:** The FUEL TEMP gauge (tank 3's outboard compartment) reads -35 °C or colder in a long cold-soaked cruise. Jet A freezes at -40 °C; as fuel approaches it, wax crystals form that can block filters and pump inlets. (If the fuel temperature gauge is inoperative, the TAT gauge gives a conservative guide.)

**Objective:** Warm the coldest fuel by circulating each wing tank's fuel through its outboard compartment, or descend.

The transfer pump lights come on and go out, and the FILL VALVE OPEN lights come on. Hold the fill valves open until the fuel temperature has risen 5 to 10 °C, then close them and turn the transfer pumps off. If the temperature cannot be held and the flight will continue for 30 minutes or more, consider descending to warmer air. End of procedure.

Why it works: the fuel in the thin outboard wing section, with the most surface for its volume, cools fastest, and that is where the tank 3 temperature probe sits. Each transfer pump draws the warmer fuel from its own tank's inboard compartment and the fill valve returns it through the outboard compartment, mixing it into the coldest fuel aboard.

**Condition:** Level 1 alert ENG 1, 2 or 3 FUEL FILTER: the engine's fuel filter is clogged and its fuel may be bypassing the filter. With two or more filters clogged, FUEL CONTAMINATED (Level 1) appears as well.

In flight, monitor the engine's operation; there is no checklist. Reducing that engine's thrust, where performance allows, lowers the flow through the filter and may stop the bypass. FUEL CONTAMINATED, with more than one engine affected, points to the fuel itself: land at the nearest suitable airport. On the ground the alert is a no-takeoff item. End of procedure.

sections.title: Transfer, fill valves and quantity
sections.summary: Fill valves that will not open, the outboard compartment schedule, overfill, and lost quantity indication.

children.title: Tanks 1, 2 and 3 fill valves will not open

blocks.content:
**Condition:** With the main tank FILL VALVE switches selected open, no FILL VALVE OPEN light comes on (on the KC-10, the flow line lights but the OPEN legend does not). The fill valves are solenoid-controlled and fuel-pressure operated; a fault in their common control power, or the valves themselves, can hold them all shut. Fuel can then no longer be transferred into the main tanks through them.

**Objective:** Try the valves on their alternate control power; if they stay shut, feed the engines directly from the other tanks, or fill tanks 1 and 3 slowly through the outboard fill valves.

items.item: BATTERY BUS SENSING circuit breaker (OH B-29)

blocks.content: Pulling the battery bus sensing breaker moves the fill valve control onto the battery direct bus. While it is out, battery bus sensing is lost and the BAT BUS OFF light is on.

**Do the FILL VALVE OPEN lights come on?**
YES: transfer (or, on the KC-10, onload) into the main tanks as required. When it is complete, close the FILL VALVE switches and reset the breaker (FE). End of procedure.
NO: continue with the next step.

**Is fuel to be onloaded (KC-10)?**
YES: go to *Onload with the main fill valves shut* below.
NO (a transfer): open the X-FEED valves and feed the engines directly from the auxiliary or body tanks through the manifold (FE). If desired, keep the outboard compartments of tanks 1 and 3 full by transferring into them through the MANIFOLD DRAIN & OUTBD FILL valves (switches to DRAIN/FILL), at about a quarter of the normal rate. That path has no automatic shutoff: stop about 3,000 lb below full so that fuel does not vent overboard, and return the switches to NORM. End of procedure.

blocks.title: Onload with the main fill valves shut

blocks.content: With the main tanks less than full, the gross weight must not exceed 556,000 lb and the zero fuel weight plus body tank fuel must not exceed 414,000 lb. These are wing bending limits: full wing tanks relieve the wing root of the fuselage's weight.

The outboard fill valves take fuel into tanks 1 and 3 only slowly; stop that onload about 3,000 lb below full. Into the body tanks alone the onload runs at about 3,200 lb per minute. When it is complete, set up the fuel management as required: keep tanks 1 and 3 about 3,000 lb below full through the outboard fill valves or by crossfeed, and return the MANIFOLD DRAIN & OUTBD FILL switches to NORM when that transfer is done (FE). End of procedure.

children.title: Tank 1 or 3 fill valve will not open

blocks.content:
**Condition:** With the tank 1 or 3 FILL VALVE switch selected open, its FILL VALVE OPEN light (OPEN legend) stays out. That wing tank cannot be filled through its fill valve, so a transfer into it would leave the wings out of balance.

**Objective:** Fill the tank another way, or balance the wings by feeding from the tank that will not fill.

**Is it a transfer into tank 1 or 3 (not an onload)?**
YES: open one or both MANIFOLD DRAIN & OUTBD FILL valves as required to keep the wings balanced (FE). Stop when the tank is about 3,000 lb below full. To use the body or auxiliary fuel faster, open the X-FEED valves and feed the engines from the manifold. When the transfer is complete, check the X-FEED valves closed and the MANIFOLD DRAIN & OUTBD FILL switches at NORM. End of procedure.
NO (KC-10 onload): close the tank 1 and 3 FILL VALVE switches, open both MANIFOLD DRAIN & OUTBD FILL valves (stop filling tanks 1 and 3 through them about 3,000 lb below full), set the tank 2 FILL VALVE as required, and onload into the body tanks, watching the center of gravity: with tanks 1 and 3 less than full it moves forward. The weight limits of [Tanks 1, 2 and 3 fill valves will not open](#main-fill-valves) apply. When the onload is complete, set up the fuel management, keep tanks 1 and 3 about 3,000 lb below full through the outboard fill valves or by crossfeed, and return the MANIFOLD DRAIN & OUTBD FILL switches to NORM when done (FE). End of procedure.

**Condition:** The FUEL SCHED light for tank 1 or 3. Each wing tank's outboard compartment is meant to stay full (it holds the wing tip's weight out where it relieves the wing bending moment) until the tank is down to about 10,500 lb, and then to empty into the inboard compartment. The light shows that the outboard compartment has emptied too early, or failed to empty on schedule. A nose-high attitude with 5,000 to 11,000 lb in the tank, or a transfer still running when the engine stops drawing on the tank, can light it for up to ten minutes without a fault.

**Objective:** Restore the schedule: move fuel back out to the outboard compartment, or get it out of the outboard compartment.

**Is the affected tank below 10,500 lb (11,000 lb in the FedEx procedure)?**
YES: the outboard compartment has failed to empty: its automatic transfer is inoperative. Continue with the next step.
NO: the outboard compartment has emptied too early. Go to *Refill the outboard compartment* below.

Count about 5,800 lb in the outboard compartment as trapped and unusable, and plan the rest of the flight without it. Watch the lateral balance and avoid sustained nose-high attitudes (more than 8°). Do not transfer fuel into the affected tank through its fill valve; if a transfer is needed, use crossfeed. As the main compartment nears empty its quantity may appear to rise and its pump lights come on: supply the engine from the other tanks by crossfeed (FE). End of procedure.

When tanks 1 and 3 read about 8,500 lb, TRANS PUMP OVRD switch PUSH/OVRD (FE): the wing-tip pumps move the outboard fuel inboard in about 6 minutes. When both TIP PUMP LOW PRESS lights are steady, TRANS PUMP OVRD switch PUSH/OFF (FE). End of procedure.

**Does the FILL VALVE OPEN light come on?**
YES: keep holding the switch; the FUEL SCHED light can take up to 5 minutes to go out. About 2 minutes after it goes out, FILL VALVE switch CLOSE and TRANS PUMP switch OFF (FE). If the light comes on again, repeat. End of procedure.
NO: FILL VALVE switch RELEASE TO CLOSE, and MANIFOLD DRAIN & OUTBD FILL switch (affected tank) DRAIN/FILL (FE); the FUEL SCHED light can take up to 20 minutes to go out. About 10 minutes after it goes out, MANIFOLD DRAIN & OUTBD FILL switch NORM and TRANS PUMP switch OFF (FE). End of procedure.
KC-10, FWD TANK FUEL SCHED light: usable fuel remains in the forward body tank with tank 1 or 3 already below about 4,000 lb. Transfer the remaining forward tank fuel to the main tanks.

**Condition:** The TANK OVERFILLED light during a transfer or refuel. Fuel is collecting in a wing vent box: a tank has been filled past its normal shutoff level, usually because a fill valve's high-level float has failed and the valve has not closed. If the vent box fills, fuel vents overboard through the wing vent outlet.

**Objective:** Stop filling the overfilled tank, find out whether fuel is being lost, and control the transfers by hand.

Stop filling the affected tank (its FILL VALVE switch closed) and control the transfers by hand to keep all tanks about 2,000 lb below full (FE). As the tank burns down, the vent box drains back into it and the light goes out. End of procedure.

**Is the aircraft on the ground?**
YES: stop the transfer or refuel and call maintenance. End of procedure.
NO: continue with the next step.

items.item: FILL VALVE and MANIFOLD DRAIN & OUTBD FILL switches
PUMPS AUX TANKS selectors (if transferring from the auxiliary tank)
TANK 2 TRANS pump switch (if transferring from tank 2 to tanks 1 and 3)

blocks.content: Let the affected tank burn down to about 3,000 lb below its maximum quantity. As it makes room, the vent box drains back into it.

**Does the TANK OVERFILLED light go out?**
YES: control any further transfer to keep the tank about 3,000 lb below its maximum; if the light comes on again, repeat this procedure. End of procedure.
NO: compare the quantity indicators, the FUEL USED counters and the known fuel (and look, if you can) to find out whether fuel is venting overboard, and continue with the next step.

**Is fuel venting overboard?**
YES: if the auxiliary tank was being transferred into the main tanks, do not transfer fuel between the main tanks; burn the auxiliary fuel by crossfeed instead, and do not let the auxiliary tank go below 2,000 lb before returning to tank-to-engine feed. If tank 2 was being transferred into tanks 1 and 3, do not transfer into the affected tank again: plan with the quantity it now shows. End of procedure.
NO: monitor the transfers to keep the tank about 3,000 lb below its maximum. End of procedure.

**Condition:** Every fuel quantity indicator blank, frozen or flagged at once. Something common to them all has failed: their power supply (normally AC BUS 1) or the quantity computer.

**Objective:** Restore the indicators on their alternate power, or manage the fuel by calculation.
At ALTN the indicators take their power from AC BUS 2 instead of AC BUS 1.

**Do the indicators work?**
YES: leave the switch at ALTN and log the fault. End of procedure.
NO: return the switch to NORM. Compute the fuel remaining from the departure fuel and the FUEL USED counters, and manage the transfers by time and fuel flow. Log the fault. End of procedure.

**Condition:** Level 2 alert FUEL QTY FAULT. The fuel quantity gauging system has detected bad data in one or more tanks. The FUEL synoptic shows which kind: a tank quantity in amber, a tank quantity covered by an amber X, or quantities that have frozen. With tank 1, 2 or 3 covered by an X the fuel system reverts to manual by itself; with every tank lost, as the EFB's quantity failure does, SEL FUEL SYS MAN and FUEL SYS MANUAL come with it.

**Objective:** Decide whether the indication can still be trusted, and if not, run the fuel by calculation.
**Amber tank quantity.** Two or more sensors in that tank have failed, but the quantity shown is still valid. Log the fault. End of procedure.
**Tank quantity covered by an X.** The gauging in that tank is inoperative: its quantity, the total fuel and the gross weight are lost.

**Is tank 1, 2 or 3 covered by an X, or does any tank hold ballast fuel?**
YES: SYSTEM button MANUAL (PM); hold the ballast fuel as required; calculate the affected tank's quantity as the departure fuel less the total fuel used and less the total of the working gauges. The FMS fuel on board and gross weight are now computed from fuel flow alone. End of procedure.
NO: no further crew action is required; the controller carries on in AUTO. End of procedure.

items.item: Calculated fuel on board (departure fuel less total used)

blocks.content:
**Can the tank 1 and 3 fill valves be latched at ARM?**
YES: continue with *Fill valves latched* below.
NO: go to *Fill valves will not latch* below.

items.item: AUX TANK L and R TRANS buttons (Series 30, when AUX UPR PUMPS LO is displayed)
All XFEED buttons (if a TNK1/2/3 FUEL QTY LO alert is displayed)

blocks.content: With the fill valves armed, each wing tank's own float holds it full while tank 2's transfer pump supplies it, so the wing stays loaded as the schedule intends without any quantity data. End of procedure.

items.item: AUX TANK L and R TRANS buttons (Series 30)
All XFEED buttons (if a TNK1/2/3 FUEL QTY LO alert is displayed)

blocks.content: End of procedure.

The FMS fuel on board and gross weight are not accurate during or after a dump while the quantity system is out. If a dump is needed, time it at 5,000 lb per minute, push the DUMP switch off when the time has elapsed, and subtract the fuel dumped from the FMS fuel on board.

**Condition:** Level 2 alert TNK WING OVERFILL: fuel is collecting in a wing vent box because a main tank has been filled past its shutoff level.

**Consequences:** Fuel may be venting overboard.

**Is the fuel system in AUTO?**
YES: continue with the next step.
NO: go to *Depressurize the manifold* below.

**Does the FUEL synoptic show the controller taking corrective action?**
YES: no further crew action is required. End of procedure.
NO: SYSTEM button MANUAL (PM), then continue with *Depressurize the manifold*.

**Depressurize the manifold.** Transfer pumps off and crossfeeds closed, so that nothing is pushing fuel into the fill valves (PM). Pressurize the manifold again only as needed to keep the main tanks 2,000 to 3,000 lb below full. End of procedure.

**Condition:** Level 2 alert DUMP VLV L or R DISAG: a dump valve has not reached its commanded position. On the aircraft both alerts also appear when a dump ends at the FMS dump-to gross weight; in this simulation the FMS value does not end a dump, so the alert always means a stuck valve.

**Consequences:** A valve stuck open dumps fuel whenever the manifold is pressurized; a valve stuck closed reduces the dump rate.

**Is the DUMP switch ON?**
YES: a valve has failed closed and the dump will take longer. End of procedure.
NO: a valve may be open with no dump selected. Do not pressurize the crossfeed manifold for the rest of the flight: verify all TRANS buttons OFF and all XFEED buttons OFF (PM), since any fuel pushed into the manifold would go overboard. End of procedure.

sections.title: KC-10 body tanks
sections.summary: Isolation, alternate transfer and fill valves of the forward, center wing and aft body tanks.

blocks.content:
**Condition:** A body tank's ISOL valve DISAGR light, steady: the isolation valve between that tank and the fill/transfer manifold has not followed its switch. Each isolation valve closes ten seconds after its switch is moved, and only after the tank's FILL VALVE switch has been closed.

**Objective:** Establish which way the valve has failed and route fuel around it.
If the MASTER FUEL ISOL switch is at ISOL, the light is normal: the master switch has locked the valves closed.

**Has the valve failed open?**
YES: continue the flight; there is no detrimental effect. With the manifold pressurized and the forward tank's valve open, fuel leaks into the forward tank at about 100 lb in a minute and a half. End of procedure.
NO (failed closed): if the center wing tank's valve has failed, no fuel can be put into that tank, but transfer out of it and offload are unaffected. If forward or aft tank transfer is needed, use the alternate path: the opposite body tank's ISOL valve OPEN and both ALT TRANS valves OPEN (FE). This cannot be done during an offload. End of procedure.

children.title: ALT TRANS VALVE DISAGREE light on

blocks.content: **Condition:** A forward or aft ALT TRANS valve's DISAGR light, steady. The alternate transfer valve, which connects a body tank's manifold to the aerial refueling manifold, has not followed its switch.

**Has the valve failed closed?**
YES: continue the flight, using the other ALT TRANS valve as required. If a dump is needed, the dump rate from that tank is reduced. End of procedure.
NO (failed open): fuel cannot be transferred into that tank during an offload. Transfer fills the AR manifold, and some of that fuel may become unusable until scavenged: scavenged AR manifold fuel goes to tank 2 and the aft tank. With the aft valve stuck open, only the fuel scavenged into tank 2 is usable; the fuel scavenged to the aft tank goes back into the AR manifold as soon as the aft tank's electric pump is turned on. End of procedure.

children.title: Body tank fill valves and isolation valves will not open

blocks.content:
**Condition:** With a body tank FILL VALVE switch selected open, the flow line lights but the OPEN legend does not, or the ISOL VALVE DISAGR light stays on. The combined fill and isolation valve control has failed.

**Objective:** Try the valves on their alternate control power; if they stay shut, onload and transfer into the main tanks only.

items.item: Desired body tank FILL VALVE switch(es)
BATTERY BUS SENSING circuit breaker (OH B-29)

blocks.content:
**Do the OPEN legends come on, with the ISOL VALVE DISAGR lights out?**
YES: transfer or onload as required; when complete, close the FILL VALVE switches and reset the breaker (FE). End of procedure.
NO: close the FILL VALVE switches, reset the breaker (FE), and transfer or onload into the main tanks only. Transfer from the center wing tank to the main tanks is still available. End of procedure.

**Condition:** The aircraft must land soon at a weight above the maximum landing weight, and there is time to reduce it. The dump system pumps fuel from the tanks through the fill/crossfeed manifold to two dump valves at the wing trailing edges, and a low-level float in each main tank stops that tank dumping at a reserve that cannot be dumped: about 11,000 lb in tanks 1 and 3 and 11,500 lb in tank 2 on the DC-10 (12,000 lb on the KC-10), so that about 33,000 to 40,000 lb always remains.

**Objective:** Dump to the required weight while keeping the fuel balanced and the center of gravity in limits.

DC-10-30 and KC-10 maximum speeds while dumping: 325 KIAS below 28,000 ft and Mach 0.82 above. Do not begin a dump for a takeoff emergency before the aircraft is at least at two-engine acceleration height. Monitor the fuel system closely during a dump when electrical malfunctions are present.

items.item: All TANK, TRANS (and PUMPS AUX TANKS) switches
L and R FUEL DUMP VALVE OPEN lights

blocks.content: The pump lights come on and go out as each pump starts, and the X-FEED DISAGREE lights as each valve travels. With all tank, transfer and auxiliary pumps running and the crossfeeds open, the average dump rate is about 5,000 lb per minute. Close any crossfeed selectively to correct a developing imbalance. When a main tank reaches its float, its transfer pump stops and that tank stops dumping; the pump lights of the last tanks dumping may come on while fuel is still going, so watch the quantities. If DC BUS 2 is lost, the automatic termination is inoperative and the dump must be stopped by hand.

**Must fuel be dumped from the body tanks?**
YES: continue with the next step.
NO: go to *Main tank dump (KC-10)* below.

items.item: FUEL DUMP switch / DUMP VALVE OPEN lights

blocks.content: Do not use the AR pumps for a dump with fewer than two hydraulic systems operating normally.

**Are the AR pumps available?**
YES: continue with the next step.
NO: go to *Main tank dump (KC-10)* below; the body tank transfer pumps go on dumping alongside the main tank pumps.

The AR pumps are used whenever possible so that the body tanks empty first: the hydraulic AR pumps run at a higher pressure than the electric pumps, so whatever else is selected their fuel takes the manifold. With them the rate is about 6,000 lb per minute, and about 5,000 lb per minute on the electric pumps alone; add about 5 minutes to the planned time when dumping below 90,000 lb total, because the rate falls as the tanks empty.

items.item: FWD and AFT ALT TRANS valves
AR pumps (one in each of the FWD, CTR WING and AFT tanks holding fuel)

blocks.content: With AR PUMP OVRD selected, the forward tank goes on dumping below 15,000 lb. If an AR pump stops on low hydraulic pressure, do not reset it. With an engine inoperative or a hydraulic system lost, observe the AR pump combinations permitted in [Limitations](limitations#ar-pumps-receiver).

blocks.title: When the body tank dump is complete or the AR pumps shut off on low level

blocks.content:
**Is the dump complete?**
YES: go to *When the dump is complete (KC-10)* below.
NO: continue with the next step.
With TRANS PUMP OVRD selected, the main tank pumps go on dumping until tank 2 is empty and tanks 1 and 3 are at about 4,000 lb each.
The structural limits that require full wing tanks above 556,000 lb gross weight or 414,000 lb zero fuel weight do not apply to a dump made for an emergency or abnormal condition.

items.item: All main tank pumps and main tank transfer pumps
FUEL DUMP switch / DUMP VALVE OPEN lights (if not already on)
X-FEED valves (when the dump is complete)
FUEL DUMP switch / DUMP VALVE OPEN lights

blocks.content: If a FUEL DUMP VALVE OPEN light stays on, opening a crossfeed valve or turning on a transfer pump dumps that tank's fuel overboard: leave them closed and off for the rest of the flight.
If time permits, transfer fuel to regain the normal fuel schedule before landing; once it is restored, the normal maximum operating speeds apply again. End of procedure.

**Condition:** The aircraft must land soon above its maximum landing weight. On the MD-10 the DUMP switch starts a dump sequence that runs the pumps and valves itself, in AUTO and MANUAL alike, at about 5,000 lb per minute, and stops at the low-level floats (about 11,000 lb in tanks 1 and 3, 11,500 to 12,000 lb in tank 2) or when the crew push the switch off. On the aircraft it can also stop at the FMS dump-to gross weight. In this simulation the FMS value does not stop it, and in MANUAL the dump runs only the pumps and crossfeeds whose buttons are in.
Series 30: maximum speeds while dumping are 325 KIAS below 28,000 ft and Mach 0.82 above.

FUEL DUMP ON is displayed while the switch is on. On the aircraft, DUMP VLV L DISAG and DUMP VLV R DISAG appear when the dump ends at the FMS dump-to weight. When the desired fuel or the calculated dump time is reached, DUMP switch OFF (PM).

**Is further dumping wanted?**
YES: DUMP switch ON again (PM), and OFF when the desired fuel or time is reached; then continue with the next step.
NO: continue with the next step.

**Does the DUMP switch's ON light fail to go out?**
YES: MANF STOP switch STOP (PM), the fuel dump emergency stop. End of procedure.
NO: no further crew action is required. End of procedure.

**Condition:** The fuel on board is less than the departure fuel minus the fuel used would predict, or a tank is going down faster than its engine is burning. The fuel is going somewhere other than the engines: overboard from a tank or a line, or from the engine's own fuel system.

**Objective:** Find whether the leak is in a tank or at an engine, and stop it at its source. Land at the nearest suitable airport if required.

items.item: All tank TRANS and FILL buttons

blocks.content: With every transfer stopped, each tank feeds only its own engine, so a tank whose quantity falls faster than its engine's fuel flow is the leaking one.

**Is a quantity decreasing abnormally from tank 1, 2 or 3?**
YES: continue with *Tank or engine* below.
NO: go to *Auxiliary tank (Series 30)* below. (Series 10: continue to monitor the fuel used and the quantities. End of procedure.)

items.item: TRANS button (auxiliary or a non-leaking main tank)

blocks.content: The suspect tank's engine is now fed from another tank through the manifold, and the suspect tank feeds nothing.

**Is the abnormal decrease now coming from the supplying tank?**
YES: the leak follows the engine, so it is in the engine's fuel system. Throttle (leaking engine) IDLE (PF), FUEL lever OFF (PM), ENG FIRE handle DOWN (PM); SYSTEM button as required; see [ENGINE SHUTDOWN IN FLIGHT](abnormal-engines#md-engine-shutdown-in-flight). End of procedure.
NO: the leak is in the tank. PUMPS button (leaking tank) ON, XFEED button (leaking tank) OFF, TRANS button (supplying tank) OFF (PM): use the leaking tank's fuel in its own engine until it is nearly empty, then supply the engine from another source. Do not transfer fuel into the leaking tank; consider moving its fuel to another tank. End of procedure.

items.item: AUX TANK L and R TRANS buttons

blocks.content:
**Is a quantity decreasing abnormally from the auxiliary tank?**
YES: all FILL buttons OFF, and handle a possible overfill as in [TNK WING OVERFILL](#md-wing-overfill). End of procedure.
NO: continue to monitor the fuel used and the quantities. End of procedure.

The fuel system is simulated as a hydraulic network: pumps make pressure, valves stroke, floats act on levels, and fuel goes only where the pressures send it, so pump failures, crossfeeds, suction feed and dump rates behave as the procedures expect. The points that change a procedure are these.

items: **Injected failures.** A boost or transfer pump failure stops that pump, and its PRESS LO light behaves as on the aircraft. The center auxiliary tank pump failures fail the left upper or left lower pump together with its pressure switch, which then reads low for good: on the KC-10 that pump's LOW light stays on even with its switch off, and on the MD-10-30 the individual pump alerts appear only in MANUAL. On the DC-10-15 the upper pump failure is offered, but the flight engineer's panel shows no auxiliary tank controls or lights, so nothing in the cockpit shows it. Fuel filter clogging loads the filter with contamination: PRESS DROP (on the MD-10, ENG FUEL FILTER) comes on after about five minutes at cruise, then the bypass opens and the engine runs on. The fill valve failures hold the valves shut whatever their control power, so the battery bus sensing breaker step does not open them and the procedures end on their NO branches. All fuel quantity indicators inoperative fails both quantity computers; on the MD-10 every tank is covered by an X and the controller reverts to manual. Tank overfilled is tank 1's high-level float failed: a transfer into a full tank 1 carries on into its vent box until the transfer is stopped, and the box drains back once the tank has room. The KC-10's ISOL and ALT TRANS valve failures stick the forward tank's valve closed.

**Battery bus sensing breaker (DC-10, KC-10).** The main tank FILL VALVE OPEN lights (the OPEN legends on the KC-10) and the TANK OVERFILLED light are powered through that breaker in the simulation, so they stay dark while it is pulled, whatever the valves do; BAT BUS OFF comes on as on the aircraft. Reset the breaker as soon as the check is done.

**Not modeled.** The FUEL QTY IND PWR switch (DC-10, KC-10): the quantity system stays powered while either AC BUS 1 or AC BUS 2 is, so the ALTN step has no effect. The tank 1 and 3 outboard compartment schedule monitor: the FUEL SCHED lights answer only the lamp test, and the EFB lists the outboard transfer failure as not modeled; it injects nothing. The KC-10's FWD TANK FUEL SCHED light likewise. On the KC-10, TRANS PUMP OVRD runs the wing-tip pumps and takes the main tank dump floats out of the loop, but does not release the forward tank below 15,000 lb: AR PUMP OVRD does that.

**Left out.** The KC-10's FWD TANK FILL VALVE WILL NOT OPEN, which sends the boom operator into the fuselage tank compartment to operate the valve by hand, and FUEL QUANTITY FLUCTUATION (a collapsed body tank bladder), because neither can happen in the simulation.

**Fill valves and the dump (DC-10, KC-10).** The FILL VALVE switches stay where they are set (the aircraft's magnetic hold is not modeled), and the FUEL DUMP switch does not close open fill valves: close them yourself before dumping, as the checklists above do. The dump works only in flight. When a tank reaches its float only its own crossfeed closes, with no DISAGREE or PRESS LO light; when all three main tanks have reached their floats the dump valves close by themselves. Losing DC BUS 2 puts out the DUMP VALVE OPEN lights but does not disable the low-level shutoff.

**Transfers into a part-full wing tank.** The main fill valves deliver into the inboard part of tanks 1 and 3, and the MANIFOLD DRAIN & OUTBD FILL valves only into the outboard compartment, which is normally already full while the tank holds more than about 10,000 lb. Once the part being filled is full, the rest of the transfer can be lost from the aircraft while the receiving tank's quantity stops rising. This affects every transfer these procedures call for (crossfeed transfers, the outboard fill path, refilling the outboard compartment): watch the receiving tank's quantity, stop the transfer when it stops rising, and compare the total fuel with the fuel used (see [Fuel](fuel#simulation-notes)).

**Fuel temperature.** Because the main fill valves do not deliver through the outboard compartment, the warming circulation in [Fuel temperature low](#fuel-temp-low) warms the tank 3 probe little, if at all: if the FUEL TEMP does not rise, descend or slow down.
**Suction feed** is not limited by altitude in the simulation; the MD-10 GEN ALL OFF procedure's 38,000 ft descent is still good practice.

**MD-10.** The controller does not switch off a failed pump, so the PMP OFF alerts are not shown. The pump alerts follow the FCOM's levels: Level 1 in AUTO, Level 2 in MANUAL; the individual auxiliary pump alerts appear only in MANUAL. A main tank fill valve failed closed raises no alert: its FILL legend and the synoptic's fill valve stay closed while the controller commands them open, and that tank no longer fills, so watch the lateral balance on the synoptic. The FMS dump-to gross weight does not stop a dump (the floats or the crew do), and in MANUAL the dump runs only the pumps and crossfeeds whose buttons are in. The MANF STOP switchlight is the dump emergency stop. The AUX TANKS L and R TRANS buttons and the MANF DRAIN switch are not functional, so the auxiliary tank steps of FUEL QTY FAULT and the fuel leak procedure act on nothing. The FSC AUTO FAIL, FUEL OFF SCHEDULE, LAT FUEL UNBAL, FUEL QTY/USED CHK, FUEL QTY ERROR, FUEL QTY ALERTS, FUEL SYS ALERTS, BALST FUEL DISAG, FUEL DUMP LEVEL, FMS DUMP DISABLED and TNK TIP FUEL LO alerts are not raised by the simulation and have no procedure here.

parts.title: Electrical
parts.summary: Generator, drive, bus and battery failures: what each light pattern means and how to restore or isolate the failed part.

blocks.content: This part holds the electrical abnormal procedures: generator and drive failures, AC and DC bus failures, the battery bus and the ground service buses. The loss of all generators is an emergency on the DC-10 and KC-10 and is in [Emergency Procedures](emergency-procedures); the MD-10 files the same condition, GEN ALL OFF, as a Level 2 alert, and its procedure is here. The APU generator's procedures are in [Auxiliary Power Unit](abnormal-apu). How the system works is in [Electrical](electrical).

On the DC-10 and KC-10 an electrical failure shows first on the flight engineer's upper panel: a GEN OFF, CSD OIL PRESS LO, AC BUS OFF or DC BUS OFF light brings on the amber ELEC cue light on the pilots' overhead annunciator panel and MASTER CAUTION; a red EMER AC or DC BUS OFF light brings on the EMER BUS OFF summary light and MASTER WARNING. The flight engineer reads the panel as a mimic diagram: which lights are on, in which column, tells the engineer which channel and which level of the system has failed, and the meters (selected to the affected generator or DC bus) confirm it. On the MD-10 the EPCU has already reconfigured the system by the time the crew see the amber Level 2 alert on the engine and alert display; the ELEC cue switch shows the ELEC synoptic with the alert's consequences, and the procedure is mostly about confirming, accepting and planning around what is lost.

Electrical procedures lean on two rules. First, a bus OFF light reports a sensing relay, not the bus: a tripped sensing breaker lights it over a live bus, so the checklists reset the sensing breaker before anything else. Second, a protective trip is reset **once**. A generator, a bus tie relay or a circuit breaker that trips again after one reset has told you the fault is real; leave it.

blocks.title: Failures you can practice
rows: GEN 1/2/3 OFF: Level 1 in AUTO (the EPCU makes the resets); Level 2 in MANUAL, [procedure](#md-gen-off)
GEN 1/2/3 OFF once the channel trips (Level 1 in AUTO; Level 2 in MANUAL, [procedure](#md-gen-off))
GEN OFF for the two lost (Level 1 in AUTO; Level 2 in MANUAL, [procedure](#md-gen-off))
GEN DRIVE 1/2/3 FAULT at the over-temperature switch: [procedure](#md-gen-drive-fault)
AC bus 1, 2, 3 failure; Left emergency AC bus failure
BUS AC 1/2/3 OFF (Level 1); BUS L EMER AC OFF: [procedure](#md-bus-l-emer-ac-off)
DC bus 1, 2, 3 failure; Left emergency DC bus failure
BUS DC 1/2/3 OFF (Level 1); BUS L EMER DC OFF: [procedure](#md-bus-l-emer-dc-off)
BUS R EMER AC OFF (Level 1; the right emergency DC bus and TR 3 behind it are not listed separately)
The BAT BUS OFF light; see [Simulation notes](#simulation-notes)
[DC GND SERVICE BUS OFF light on](#dc-gnd-service-bus-off)

blocks.content: The EFB's electrical failures are listed in [EFB failures: electrical](efb#failures-elec). Clearing a failure removes its cause; a breaker it tripped stays out until it is reset on the panel or with the EFB's Reset Breakers.

blocks.title: MD-10 electrical Level 1 alerts
rows: BUS AC 1/2/3 OFF, BUS DC 1/2/3 OFF, BUS AC GND OFF, BUS DC GND OFF
That bus is unpowered. The EPCU has done what it can; note the loads lost (the synoptic's consequences) and plan with them.
BUS R EMER AC OFF, BUS R EMER DC OFF
A right emergency bus is unpowered. With all generators lost, the ADG restores it.
AC TIE 1/2/3 OFF, AC TIE FAULT
A bus tie relay is open, or the tie bus has a fault and every channel runs isolated.
A DC tie relay is open.
A transformer-rectifier has failed; the EPCU closes the DC ties to cover its bus.
A drive has been disconnected. It cannot be reconnected in flight.
EMER PWR ON, EMER PWR SW OFF, BAT SWITCH OFF
The battery is carrying the left emergency buses, or a switch is out of its normal position.
BAT DISCHARGING, BAT LOW, BAT CHARGER INOP
The battery is supplying load, is low, or is not being charged.
ELEC SYS MANUAL, SEL ELEC SYS MAN, EPGS FAULT
The system is in MANUAL, or the EPCU wants the crew to take it to MANUAL (SELECT lit), or the EPCU has a fault.
The ADG ELEC switch is pushed with the ADG stowed.
SMOKE SW IN USE, CABIN BUS SW OFF
A switch is out of its normal position.

sections.title: Recognizing electrical failures
sections.summary: Which lights come on together for each kind of failure, and which procedure deals with them.

blocks.content: The flight engineer's electrical panel is laid out as the system is built: generators along the bottom, the generator and AC buses and their ties above them, the DC buses and their ties at the top. A failure lights a pattern, and the pattern names the failure. The KC-10 manual binds a diagram of these patterns into its electrical checklists; the table below is the same reasoning in words. The meters settle any doubt: the VOLT/AMP/FREQ selector's generator positions read the machine at its terminals, ahead of the generator relay, so a tripped generator reads dead while its bus may be perfectly healthy on the tie.

blocks.title: Light patterns and what they mean
rows: GEN OFF only; AC LOAD zero
The generator relay is open: a protective trip, a low-speed engine or the switch. Its bus is carried from the tie.
GEN OFF and CSD OIL PRESS LO
The drive is losing charge pressure, and the generator has dropped off line.
GEN FAIL only, AC LOAD normal
A generator bearing is failing; the generator is still on line.
That channel is off the tie: switch at ISOL, a bus tie relay locked out or failed to close, or the APU carrying the bus.
All three AC BUS TIE ISOL
Every channel is off the tie: probably a fault on the AC tie bus itself.
GEN OFF, AC BUS TIE ISOL, AC BUS OFF, and the channel's emergency and DC lights
A fault on the generator bus: differential protection has opened the generator relay and locked out the bus tie relay, so nothing can feed the faulted bus.
AC BUS OFF alone (or AC BUS 2 OFF with DC BUS 2 OFF)
The main AC bus behind its feed breakers, or only its sensing circuit.
L or R EMER AC BUS OFF alone
The emergency AC bus's feed or sensing circuit.
R EMER AC BUS OFF, R EMER DC BUS OFF and DC BUS 3 OFF together
The right emergency AC feed: with it go TR 3 and everything TR 3 feeds.
DC BUS OFF or EMER DC BUS OFF, the TR's DC LOAD at zero
A TR, its feeders, or the DC bus's sensing circuit.
The battery bus feeds, or its sensing circuit.
DC GND SERVICE BUS OFF (status light block)
TR 2B, its breakers, or the AC ground service bus.
[DC GND SERVICE BUS OFF light on](#dc-gnd-service-bus-off)

blocks.content: A partial actuation of an engine fire handle opens that engine's generator field and trips the generator. If a GEN OFF light comes on without an obvious cause, check that the fire handles are fully home.

sections.title: Generators and drives
sections.summary: Generator trips, bearing failures, frequency runaway, constant-speed drive failures, paralleling and single-generator operation.

children.title: ENG GEN OFF light on (AC load zero)

blocks.content:
**Condition:** A GEN OFF light on the flight engineer's panel with that generator's AC LOAD meter at zero, the ELEC cue light and MASTER CAUTION. The generator relay has opened. If the generators were paralleled, the generator bus is now carried from the AC tie bus and nothing else is lost; if they were not, the bus tie relay closes and does the same.

**Objective:** Find out whether the generator tripped on a real fault, restore it once if the fault has cleared, and disconnect the drive if the drive is the cause.

If the GEN OFF light is accompanied by CSD OIL PRESS LO, use [CSD OIL PRESS LO light on](#csd-oil-press-lo) instead. Check that the engine fire handle is fully in: a partly pulled handle trips the generator.

RESET re-closes the generator's field relay and clears its lockout; at OFF the generator is excited but not connected, so the meter now shows exactly what the machine is producing on its own, unloaded.

**Is the frequency above 420 Hz or below 380 Hz?**
YES: the drive is not holding speed; go to *Disconnect the drive* below.
NO: continue with the next step.

**Is the AC voltage within limits?**
YES: continue with the next step.
NO: the generator or its regulator has failed. Continue the flight with the GEN switch OFF and do not attempt another reset. End of procedure.

**Has the GEN OFF light gone out, with a normal AC load?**
YES: reparallel as required (PARALLEL GENS button, PUSH). End of procedure.
NO: the generator relay will not hold: GEN switch OFF. The generator cannot be restored. End of procedure.

items.action: GUARD OPEN, PUSH AND HOLD 3 SECONDS

blocks.content: Volts and frequency fall below the scale as the generator runs down. If they still show, the drive has not disconnected: keep the engine running with the generator off and monitor the drive. End of procedure.

Why one reset: the generator control unit trips the field for over- and under-voltage, over- and under-frequency, a feeder fault and a phase imbalance. Most of these clear when the transient that caused them does, which is why one reset is worth trying. A protection that trips again is reporting a fault that is still there; resetting it repeatedly only stresses the generator and the bus it is about to rejoin.

**Condition:** A GEN FAIL light for an engine generator, with the generator still on line and its AC LOAD normal. The light reports an impending or actual failure of the generator's main bearing, or a spurious signal. The generator keeps running on its auxiliary bearings, but only for a limited time; a bearing that seizes can shear the drive's input shaft. (APU GEN FAIL is in [APU GEN FAIL light on](abnormal-apu#apu-gen-fail).)

**Objective:** Tell a real bearing failure from a false light, and stop a failing generator before it seizes.

**Does the GEN FAIL light stay out?**
YES: the light was caused by a spurious signal. Continue normal operation and log it. End of procedure.
NO: the bearing is failing; continue with the next step.

items.action: GUARD OPEN, PUSH AND HOLD 3 SECONDS

blocks.content: If volts and frequency still show after the button is pushed, keep the engine running with the generator off and monitor it. The engine need not be shut down: if the generator seizes, the drive's input shaft shears. Once disconnected, the drive cannot be reconnected in flight; the next takeoff requires the drive disconnected or a serviceable generator fitted.

With one generator off, the remaining two carry the load through the tie. If a second generator is lost, see [SINGLE GENERATOR (ENG) OPERATION](#single-generator-operation). A bearing failure can go on to take the generator bus with it: if that channel's GEN OFF, AC BUS TIE ISOL and AC BUS OFF lights come on together, disconnect the drive and go to [Generator bus failure](#generator-bus-failure). End of procedure.

**Condition:** Generator frequency above the normal band on the FREQ meter, with paralleled generators all reading high together, or one channel high once unparalleled. A drive's governor has run away high. While the generators are paralleled the faulty drive pulls the whole tie up with it, because paralleled machines must turn in step; the meter then cannot show which one is at fault. Above 420 Hz the protection opens that channel's bus tie relay and then its generator relay by itself.

**Objective:** Separate the generators so the faulty one shows itself, then take it off and disconnect its drive.
Transient frequency excursions while an engine accelerates through about 70% N2 are normal and are not a reason for this procedure.
Moving each bus tie switch to ISOL and back unparallels the system: each generator then carries its own bus, and each frequency reads on its own.

**Is any generator's frequency still above 420 Hz?**
YES: continue with the next step.
NO: monitor the frequencies and continue with the generators unparalleled. End of procedure.

items.action: GUARD OPEN, PUSH AND HOLD 3 SECONDS

blocks.content: If volts and frequency still show after the button is pushed, keep the engine running with the generator off and monitor it. Reparallel the remaining generators as required. End of procedure.

children.title: CSD OIL PRESS LO light on

blocks.content:
**Condition:** A CSD OIL PRESS LO light on the flight engineer's electrical panel, with the ELEC cue light and MASTER CAUTION, with or without that generator's GEN OFF light. The drive's charge oil pressure is below its limit: a leak, a failed charge pump, or the drive running out of oil. The hydraulic speed control in the drive needs that pressure, and the oil also carries the drive's heat away; a drive that keeps running without it overheats, loses speed control and can seize.

**Objective:** Keep the generator while it still makes good power and the aircraft needs it; otherwise take it off line and disconnect the drive before it destroys itself.

**Are two engine-driven generators operating besides the affected one?**
YES: the aircraft does not need this generator; go to *Generator off and disconnect* below.
NO: continue with the next step.

items.item: AC BUS TIE switch (channel with CSD OIL PRESS LO)

blocks.content: The generators are now unparalleled and the affected generator carries only its own bus, so a drive that cannot hold speed can no longer drag the other generators' frequency with it. On the aircraft the AC BUS TIE ISOL light comes on; in the simulation it stays out in unparalleled operation (see [Simulation notes](#simulation-notes)).

**Are the generator's volts and frequency within the white or yellow bands, and steady?**
YES: monitor the generator indications and continue the flight with the generators unparalleled. End of procedure.
NO: continue with the next step.

items.action: GUARD OPEN, PUSH AND HOLD 3 SECONDS

blocks.content: With the GEN switch OFF the generator bus is taken over from the tie, and an AC BUS TIE ISOL light that was on goes out. Unstable frequency, frequency out of the bands, or CSD outlet or rise temperatures out of their normal range all count as a NO above.

If volts and frequency still show after the button is pushed, the drive has not disconnected: leave the generator off and keep the engine running. The engine need not be shut down even if the drive seizes, because the drive's input shaft is designed to shear first.

With one engine generator left, start the APU as soon as practical if that generator is unstable, and in any case before the approach, and continue with [SINGLE GENERATOR (ENG) OPERATION](#single-generator-operation). End of procedure.

**Condition:** A CSD TEMP indicator's outer (outlet) scale in the yellow band, 146-163 °C. The drive's oil is leaving it hotter than it should. Two different faults produce this, and the push-for-rise reading tells them apart. A high **rise** (the temperature gained across the drive, normally below 25 °C) means the drive itself is making too much heat: worn or overloaded. A normal rise on a high outlet means the oil is coming in hot: the oil cooler, which rejects the drive's heat to fan air, is not doing its job.

**Objective:** Unload the drive and watch the trend; disconnect it before it exceeds its limit.

items.item: CSD TEMP PUSH FOR RISE button / CSD TEMP indicator

blocks.content: The GEN OFF light comes on and the AC BUS TIE ISOL light goes out as the tie takes the bus. Hold the button and read the rise on the inner scale; release it and read the outlet temperature again. A drive that is no longer driving a loaded generator makes far less heat, so an outlet temperature driven by load should now settle.

**Is the temperature stable or decreasing in the yellow band?**
YES: monitor the drive and generator indications and continue the flight with the generator OFF. End of procedure.
NO (still rising in the yellow, or above the 163 °C red line): continue with the next step.

items.action: GUARD OPEN, PUSH AND HOLD 3 SECONDS

blocks.content: If volts and frequency still show after the button is pushed, keep the engine running with the generator off and monitor the drive. Its oil temperature may go beyond the red line; the engine still need not be shut down, because the input shaft shears if the drive or generator seizes.
End of procedure.

**Condition:** On the ground with all three engine generators running, pressing PARALLEL GENS does not bring the generators together: the AC LOAD meters stay apart and one or more channels stay off the tie. The automatic paralleling circuit compares each generator's frequency and phase with the tie bus and closes the bus tie relay only when they agree; a tripped AUTO PARALLEL CONT breaker, a bus tie switch at ISOL or another source still on the tie stops it.

**Objective:** Restore paralleling, or prove by the preferential-generator check that the system will still hand the tie bus to the right generator if one is lost.

This checklist is for use on the ground, after the normal after-start procedures and with generators 1, 2 and 3 operating. If all three AC BUS TIE ISOL lights are on, use [AC BUS TIE ISOL light(s) on](#ac-bus-tie-isol) instead.

items.item: AUTO PARALLEL CONT circuit breakers (LM A-15, B-15, C-15)

blocks.content: If a breaker was tripped, reset it and try PARALLEL GENS again. If the generators parallel, the procedure is complete. If not, carry out the preferential generator check below; it shows that the tie bus is passed from generator to generator in the 2-1-3 order as each one drops out, which is what the system relies on when it runs unparalleled.

blocks.title: What each step should show
rows: Bus ties 1 and 3 to ISOL and back
Generator 2, first in the order, holds the tie bus and its own generator bus.
Generator 1 takes the tie and carries generator buses 1 and 2.
Generator 3, last in the order, carries the tie and all three generator buses.
1 and 2 on, all GEN OFF lights out
Generators 1 and 2 come back on their own buses; generator 3 still holds the tie.
Generator 2 takes the tie again and carries buses 2 and 3.
Back to the starting state, generator 2 on the tie.

blocks.content: In the simulation the AC BUS TIE ISOL lights stay out in unparalleled operation, so the lights marked on in the table do not appear: follow the transfers on the AC LOAD meters instead, where the generator holding the tie carries the load of every bus on it. If the transfers follow the table, the preferential circuit works and the flight may continue unparalleled in accordance with the operator's minimum equipment rules; read the system's state from the load meters. If they do not, the system will not reliably cover a generator loss. End of procedure.

**Condition:** Only one engine-driven generator remains on line, after two have been lost by any of the procedures in this part. That generator carries all three generator buses through the AC tie bus, at up to its 90 kVA rating (AC LOAD 1.0).

**Objective:** Keep the remaining generator inside its rating and bring the APU generator in as a second source.
Shed what is not essential: auxiliary hydraulic pumps and boost pumps beyond those needed. Engine 2 needs two of its boost pumps on, because the center engine has no suction feed.

**Is the APU generator available?**
YES: continue with the next step.
NO: operate with all AC BUS TIE switches at NORM so the tie supplies every generator bus, and monitor the operating generator's AC LOAD meter. End of procedure.

The APU takes the generator buses whose own generators are off; the APU PWR IN USE lights for those buses come on and their AC BUS OFF and DC BUS OFF lights stay out. Leave the AC BUS TIE switches at NORM and monitor the AC LOAD meters. The APU generator never feeds the tie bus, so the engine generator and the APU each carry their own buses.

With only one engine generator on line, start the APU as soon as practical if that generator is unstable, and in any case no later than the APPROACH checklist, so that a second failure does not leave the aircraft on battery and ADG power. The APU in flight: see [Auxiliary Power Unit](apu).
End of procedure.

**Condition:** Level 2 alert GEN 1, 2 or 3 OFF with the ELEC cue switch and MASTER CAUTION; the GEN button's OFF legend lights and the generator turns amber on the ELEC synoptic. The electrical system is in MANUAL and the generator has tripped off line on a protective function; its generator bus is carried from the tie (or the APU). In AUTO the EPCU makes the reset itself, and a generator that stays off shows only as the Level 1 alert GEN n OFF, which has no procedure.

**Consequences:** One generator reset attempt allowed.
Only one reset attempt is permitted. A generator that trips again has a fault that is still there.

If the reset does not restore the generator, continue the flight with it inoperative. The remaining generators carry its bus through the tie; with only one generator left, consider starting the APU for a second source. End of procedure.

**Condition:** Level 2 alert GEN DRIVE 1, 2 or 3 FAULT with the ELEC cue switch and MASTER CAUTION. The FAULT legend of that DRIVE button lights, and FAULT shows beside the generator on the ELEC synoptic. The drive has a fault, low oil pressure or high oil temperature, that calls for disconnecting it.

**Consequences:** None.

**Is at least one other engine generator operating?**
YES: continue with the next step.
NO: do not disconnect the drive; go to *Last engine generator* below.

items.action: GUARD OPEN, PUSH AND HOLD 2 SECONDS

blocks.content: The DISC legend lights when the drive has disconnected, and the Level 1 alert GEN DRIVE DISC follows. It cannot be reconnected in flight. End of procedure.

items.item: APU (if available and flight conditions permit)

blocks.content: A drive with a fault still turns its generator, and the last engine generator is worth more running on a sick drive than disconnected. The generator stays on line with the alert displayed for as long as it makes good power; the APU gives a second source if the drive finally fails. If the APU is not available, monitor the generator's output on the synoptic. End of procedure.

**Condition:** Level 2 alert GEN ALL OFF. No engine generator is on line: every main AC and DC bus is lost. With the EMER PWR selector at ARM, the battery and static inverter have taken the left emergency buses automatically, so the Captain's displays and the standby instruments stay alive. The overhead HYD, AIR and FUEL panels lose their lighting.

**Objective:** Keep the engines fed, try one reset of each generator, and if the generator buses stay dead, deploy the ADG for the right emergency buses.

**Consequences:** Land at the nearest suitable airport. Pressurization needs manual control and flap extension may be limited. Wing anti-ice, GPWS, auto slat extension, fuel dump, the landing gear indications, anti-skid, autobrake (if installed), the auto ground spoilers and all reversers are inoperative; on the Series 30 the fuel in the upper and lower auxiliary tanks is trapped.
With all generators off, the HYD, AIR and FUEL panel legends are dark. Pushing switches on those panels changes the system configuration without any indication to the crew.

**Is the aircraft above 38,000 ft?**
YES: while continuing the procedure, begin a descent to 38,000 ft or below. With the boost pumps unpowered the wing engines feed by suction, which may not be sustained above that altitude.
NO: continue with the next step.

**Is the electrical system in MANUAL?**
YES: push each GEN button whose OFF legend is lit, once (only one reset attempt is permitted), and continue with the next step.
NO: the EPCU has already made its resets in AUTO; go to *Deploy the ADG* below.

**Are generator buses 1 and 3 powered?** (AC 1 OFF, AC 3 OFF and R EMER AC OFF lights out.)
YES: go to *Generator buses restored* below.
NO: continue with the next step.

The ADG now carries the right emergency buses. Only the LONG TRIM handles on the pedestal can then move the horizontal stabilizer. If required, restart engine 2 ([ENGINE RESTART IN FLIGHT](abnormal-engines#md-engine-restart-in-flight)). Landing gear position indications are lost while DC buses 2 and 3 are unpowered, and flap position on the PFD and configuration synoptic while AC buses 1 and 3 are unpowered.

**Is the airspeed at the time of the failure known?**
YES: the flap limiter has lost power and the flaps can only be extended to the limit that applied at that speed; take the maximum landing flap from the table below and use the matching reference speeds.
NO: land with flaps 15 (Series 10) or 20 (Series 30) and use the abnormal configuration reference speeds for that setting.
In both cases, land at the nearest suitable airport. End of procedure.

blocks.title: Maximum landing flap after loss of the flap limiter (Series 10 and 30)
columns: Airspeed at the time of failure

blocks.content: Generator bus 3 is powered when the AC 3 OFF and R EMER AC OFF lights are out. If required, start engine 2. Land at the nearest suitable airport. End of procedure.
On the DC-10 and KC-10 the same failure is handled as an emergency: see [Emergency Procedures](emergency-procedures).

sections.title: AC buses and ties
sections.summary: Bus tie isolation, generator bus failures, main and emergency AC bus failures.

children.title: AC BUS TIE ISOL light(s) on

blocks.content:
**Condition:** One or more AC BUS TIE ISOL lights on with the AC BUS TIE switches at NORM. The channel's bus tie relay is open: it has locked out after a fault, or has failed to close. A channel off the tie cannot share load or be rescued from the tie if its generator fails. All three lights together usually mean a fault on the AC tie bus itself, which the protection has isolated by opening every bus tie relay.

**Objective:** Clear a lockout that has served its purpose and reparallel; if the tie bus is faulty, run the channels isolated and use the APU, not the tie, to back up a lost generator.
The AC BUS TIE ISOL light is normally on when the APU generator is supplying that generator bus.

**Are all three AC BUS TIE ISOL lights on?**
YES: go to *All three channels isolated* below.
NO: go to *One or two channels isolated* below.

**Are all three AC BUS TIE ISOL lights still on?**
YES: there is a probable fault on the AC tie bus; go to *Tie bus fault* below.
NO: go to *One or two channels isolated* below.

items.item: If the APU generator is required: ELEC SYS RESET switch (affected channel)

blocks.content: With three ISOL lights on, attempt only one reset. The tie bus will not back up an inoperative generator: use the APU to supply a generator bus when one is lost. On the ground, use the APU or external power for the ground service bus, and do not connect external power to the AC tie bus.
End of procedure.

**Are any AC BUS TIE ISOL lights still on?**
YES: monitor the AC volt and frequency meters and continue the flight with the generators out of parallel. End of procedure.
NO: the generators are paralleled again. End of procedure.

Why the system isolates: the bus tie relays are the only path by which a fault on one channel can reach the others. Their protection opens them on a differential fault or an overload and keeps them open (locked out) until the crew clear the lockout, so that a fault cannot be reconnected automatically. The BUS FAULT reset is the crew's deliberate decision that the fault has gone; if the relay locks out again, it has not.

**Condition:** For one channel, GEN OFF, AC BUS TIE ISOL and AC BUS OFF come on together, with that channel's DC BUS OFF and, for channels 1 and 3, the emergency AC and DC bus OFF lights (red) and MASTER WARNING. GEN FAIL may also be on. A fault on the generator bus has tripped its differential protection: the generator relay has opened and the bus tie relay has locked out, so the faulted bus is deliberately left without a source. Everything on it is lost: the main AC bus, the TR and its DC bus (unless the DC tie is closed), the boost pumps on that bus and, for buses 1 and 3, the emergency AC bus.

**Objective:** Restore the instruments the crew need, protect the DC system, and then try to repower the generator bus from its own generator, the tie bus or the APU, once each.
The autothrottle levers may go back to ON once all BUS OFF lights are out. If the left emergency AC bus is lost, flags appear in the engine instruments and the Captain's flight instruments.

**Are the pilot's flight instruments abnormal in a critical phase of flight?**
YES: EMER PWR switch ON (PM). Use emergency power for as long as the phase of flight is critical; when it is no longer critical, or if the instruments are not restored, return it to OFF. With EMER PWR on, the battery cannot be relied on for more than 30 minutes.
NO: continue with the next step.

Closing the DC tie puts the dead DC bus on a working TR. If a DC tie was already closed for an earlier TR failure, it may be necessary to close all the DC tie and cross-tie switches. If the failure came from a loss of all generators, leave AC BUS TIE 1 or 3 at ISOL until the state of the tie bus is known.

**Is the GEN FAIL light on?**
YES: GEN switch OFF and CSD disconnect button PUSH AND HOLD 3 SECONDS (FE); then restore the bus from the tie or the APU (*From the AC tie bus* or *From the APU* below).
NO: continue with the sub-procedure for whatever supplied the generator bus before the failure: its own generator, the AC tie bus, or the APU.

**Are the generator's volts and frequency within the bands?**
YES: GEN switch ON (FE). If the GEN OFF light goes out and the AC load is normal, the generator bus is powered by its own generator: ELEC SYS RESET switch (affected) BUS FAULT, once, to clear the bus tie relay lockout; PARALLEL GENS, PUSH; DC tie switches OPEN as required; ATS levers and EMER PWR switch as required. End of procedure.
NO, or the GEN OFF light stays on: go to *From the AC tie bus* below.

**Has the AC BUS TIE ISOL light gone out?**
YES: the generator bus is powered from the AC tie bus. DC tie switches OPEN as required; ATS levers and EMER PWR switch as required. End of procedure.
NO: the fault is on the generator bus itself. Do not attempt another reset for that channel. Continue the flight with the affected circuits inoperative, EMER PWR as required. End of procedure.
If APU PWR AVAIL does not come on, the bus cannot be powered by the APU: go to *From the AC tie bus* above.

**Does APU PWR IN USE come on for the affected bus?**
YES: the generator bus is powered by the APU. Other APU GEN BUS switches ON as required, DC tie switches OPEN as required, ATS levers and EMER PWR switch as required. End of procedure.
NO: ELEC SYS RESET switch (affected) BUS FAULT, once only (FE), and continue with the next question.

**Has the affected AC BUS OFF light gone out?**
YES: the generator bus is powered by the APU. Other APU GEN BUS switches ON as required, DC tie switches OPEN as required, ATS levers and EMER PWR switch as required. End of procedure.
NO: there is probably a fault on the generator bus itself: affected APU GEN BUS switch OFF, do not attempt more resets for that channel, other APU GEN BUS switches ON as required, and continue with the affected circuits inoperative. End of procedure.

blocks.title: What a generator bus failure costs
rows: AC BUS 1, the left emergency AC bus and cabin bus 1. Automatic cabin pressure control, engine 1 automatic and high-stage pneumatic supply and the isolation valve 1-3 and pack manual controls (until the left emergency AC bus is restored); ground proximity warning and automatic ground spoilers; several boost pumps. INS 1 runs on its battery until it is exhausted.
The left emergency AC bus with EMER PWR (the battery is then off its charger). EMER PWR does not restore the Captain's attitude and compass instruments once INS 1's battery is exhausted.

AC BUS 2, DC BUS 2, the AC and DC ground service buses and the battery charger (cabin emergency lights come on; the battery remains available for emergency power). Cockpit automatic temperature control; the pilots' landing gear warning; engine 2 crossfeed control and its disagree light; control wheel trim switches; engine 2 reverser; engine 2 oil pressure and temperature indication (its low pressure light still works); the CSD 2 OIL PRESS LO light and outlet temperature.
On the ground, the ground service buses from the APU or external power.

AC BUS 3, the right emergency AC bus and cabin bus 3. The cabin pressure aural warning; engine 3 automatic and high-stage pneumatic supply, isolation valve 1-2 control and packs 1 and 3 automatic control (until the right emergency AC bus is restored); several boost pumps. INS 2 runs on its battery until it is exhausted.
The right emergency AC bus by deploying the ADG with its switch at R EMER ELEC (a drag penalty of about 1% in range).

blocks.content:
**Condition:** AC BUS 1 OFF or AC BUS 3 OFF, AC BUS 2 OFF with DC BUS 2 OFF, or L or R EMER AC BUS OFF, without the generator and bus tie lights of a generator bus failure.
