The generator bus is healthy; what has been lost is the bus beyond its feed breakers, or only the sensing circuit that drives the light. Sensing is taken from a single phase of each feed, so a feed that fails on another phase may give no light at all: then the only sign is equipment on that bus failing.

**Objective:** Prove whether the bus is really lost, restore it once from its feed breakers, and otherwise accept the loss.

**Are the pilot's flight instruments abnormal in a critical phase of flight?**
YES: EMER PWR switch ON (PM). Use emergency power only as long as the phase of flight is critical; the battery cannot be relied on for more than 30 minutes. If the left emergency AC bus feed breaker has tripped, do not use EMER PWR to restore that bus.
NO: continue with the next step.

**Has the light gone out, with the breakers staying in?**
YES: the bus is restored (or was never lost, if the sensing breaker was the cause). EMER PWR switch OFF (PM) if it was used; ATS levers as required. End of procedure.
NO: continue the flight with the affected circuits inoperative, using EMER PWR only while the phase of flight is critical. End of procedure.

blocks.title: Principal loads lost with each AC bus
rows: Captain's flight instruments and air data computer 1, VOR 1, the A ignitors, the lower yaw dampers, engine 1 N1, isolation valve 1-3 control.

Fuel quantity normal power, pneumatic manifold failure detection loop 1, left angle-of-attack and static port heat, left windshield anti-ice, left landing light, ground proximity warning, automatic ground spoilers, automatic cabin pressure control.

Manifold failure detection loop 2, TAT probe heat, nose landing and taxi light, the altitude alert and stabilizer aural warnings, engine 2 N1, primary stabilizer trim, crossfeed 2 light, engine 2 reverser control and lights, engine 2 anti-ice valve, engine 2 pressure regulator, the pilots' landing gear warning.

Manifold failure detection for pack 3, right angle-of-attack and static port heat, right windshield anti-ice, right landing light, the takeoff and landing cabin pressure aural warning, auto slat extension.

blocks.content: If AC BUS 1 cannot be restored, the automatic cabin pressure controller has lost its power: take pressurization to manual (CAB PRESS MAN/AUTO handle MAN). The autothrottles may be re-engaged once their thrust rating information is valid, or in speed mode with the N1 limit bugs set by hand. Other systems may be affected too; the bus's circuit breaker panel shows what else it feeds.

**Condition:** R EMER AC BUS OFF, R EMER DC BUS OFF and DC BUS 3 OFF together, with EMER BUS OFF and MASTER WARNING. The right emergency AC bus has lost its feed from generator bus 3, and because TR 3 is powered from that bus, the right emergency DC bus and DC BUS 3 have gone with it.

**Objective:** Put the DC buses back on a working TR, then try the AC feed once.

items.item: R EMER AC BUS feed circuit breaker (UM D-20)

blocks.content: Closing DC TIE 3 repowers DC BUS 3 and the right emergency DC bus from the DC tie, so the First Officer's radios and the upper yaw dampers come back at once. TR 3's input is pulled before the feed is reset, which keeps TR 3 out of the circuit in case it caused the trip; DC BUS 3 and the right emergency DC bus stay on the tie.

**Has the R EMER AC BUS OFF light gone out, with the feed breaker staying in?**
YES: the bus is restored. End of procedure.
NO: continue the flight with the affected circuits inoperative, and consider what they are. End of procedure.

The right emergency AC bus carries the First Officer's pitot heat, altimeter, vertical speed and HSI heading, air data computer 2, VOR 2 and ILS 2, HF 2, the B ignitors, engine 3 N1, isolation valve 1-2 control, INS 2 and, importantly, the tank 2 left aft boost pump. If it cannot be restored and the situation requires it, the ADG with its switch at R EMER ELEC powers it independently of the generators.

**Condition:** Level 2 alert GEN BUS 1, 2 or 3 FAULT with the ELEC cue switch and MASTER CAUTION. A fault on the generator bus has opened its generator relay and locked out its bus tie relay; the EPCU leaves the faulted bus unpowered, with the loads behind it.

**Consequences:** GEN BUS 1 FAULT: GPWS and auto ground spoilers inoperative. GEN BUS 2 FAULT: auxiliary pitot heat inoperative. GEN BUS 3 FAULT: auto slat extension inoperative. The ELEC synoptic lists the rest.

**Is the electrical system in MANUAL?**
YES: associated GEN button PUSH TO RESET (PM), once only, and continue with the next step.
NO: in AUTO the generator control unit makes the single bus fault reset automatically; go to the question *Is it GEN BUS 1 FAULT or GEN BUS 3 FAULT?* below.

**Is the generator bus powered?**
YES: if EMER PWR ON is displayed or its light is on, EMER PWR selector OFF, then ARM. Otherwise no further action is required. End of procedure.
NO: continue with the next step.

**Is it GEN BUS 1 FAULT or GEN BUS 3 FAULT?**
YES: continue with *Generator bus 1 or 3* below.
NO (GEN BUS 2 FAULT): go to *Generator bus 2* below.

A generator bus 1 fault can set off the First Officer's stick shaker, and a generator bus 3 fault the Captain's, because each stall warning computer loses part of its inputs. A false shaker can be silenced by pulling that pilot's STICK SHAKER circuit breaker on the overhead panel.
Continue with the affected circuits inoperative, review the consequences, and land at the nearest suitable airport. End of procedure.

**Generator bus 2.** The battery charger is not powered. In flight, if battery charging is wanted, consider deploying the ADG with the ADG ELEC button ON so that the charger is powered from the right emergency AC bus. Continue with the affected circuits inoperative, review the consequences, and land at the nearest suitable airport. End of procedure.

**Condition:** Level 2 alert BUS L EMER AC OFF and the L EMER AC OFF light on the ELEC panel. The left emergency AC bus, which feeds the Captain's air data, IRS and VOR side, has lost power, or only its sensing circuit has failed.

**Are MCDU 1 or VOR 1 operating?**
YES: the bus is powered and its sensing circuit has failed. If a later electrical failure calls for emergency power, rotate the EMER PWR selector to ARM or ON and deploy the ADG; the emergency power system is designed to last about 15 minutes until the ADG is deployed. No further crew action. End of procedure.
NO: the bus is lost; continue with the next step.

**Is the Level 1 alert ENG IGN NOT ARMED displayed?** (The simulation does not raise it: if ignition A is selected, treat the answer as YES.)
YES: ENG IGN switch SELECT B (PM): the A ignitors are on the lost bus.
NO: continue.
Land at the nearest suitable airport. If a later failure calls for emergency power, rotate the EMER PWR selector to ARM or ON and deploy the ADG. End of procedure.

Why EMER PWR goes to OFF first: with the selector at ARM, the loss of the left emergency bus makes the emergency power system put the battery (through the static inverter for AC) onto the emergency buses, and EMER PWR ON is displayed. Left there, the battery would be run down over the rest of the flight; it is the last source the aircraft has, and is kept, with the ADG, for a later failure that needs it.

sections.title: DC buses and battery
sections.summary: TR and DC bus failures, the battery bus and the ground service buses.

blocks.content:
**Condition:** DC BUS 1, 2 or 3 OFF (amber) or L or R EMER DC BUS OFF (red), without a generator bus failure. A transformer-rectifier has failed or lost its input, a DC feed has tripped, or only the sensing circuit has failed. The TR's DC LOAD meter tells which: at or near zero, the TR is not delivering; normal or high, the TR works and the fault is beyond it.

**Objective:** Restore the TR once, or carry its DC bus on another TR through the DC ties, without overloading the remaining TRs.

**Is the affected TR's DC LOAD meter at or near zero?**
YES: go to *TR not delivering* below.
NO: go to *Bus feed or sensing* below.

items.item: Affected TR output and input circuit breakers

blocks.content:
**Is the DC BUS OFF light out, with a normal DC load?**
YES: the TR is restored. End of procedure.
NO, the output breaker trips or the load rises above normal: the TR is overloading on a fault downstream. Pull its output breaker and continue with the affected circuits inoperative. Do not use EMER PWR to restore the left emergency DC bus, and do not close a DC tie to restore power: the tie would connect the fault to a healthy TR. End of procedure.
NO, the input breaker trips or the load stays at zero: the TR has failed. Pull its output and input breakers, then close DC TIE 1 (DC BUS 1 or 2) or DC TIE 3 (DC BUS 3) (FE).

**Is the DC bus restored through the tie?**
YES: monitor the DC LOAD meters. It may be necessary to close both DC TIE switches, or the DC X TIE, to share the load and avoid a high load on one TR. End of procedure.
NO: go to *Bus feed or sensing* below.

**Does the feed breaker stay in?**
YES: continue with the next question.
NO: do not reset it again; continue the flight with the affected circuits inoperative. End of procedure.

**Has the bus light gone out?**
YES: the bus is restored. End of procedure.
NO, and it is DC BUS 3: reset the DC BUS ISOL CONT and R EMER AC/DC BUS CONT breakers and close DC TIE 3 (FE). If DC BUS 3 OFF stays on, open DC TIE 3 again and continue with the affected circuits inoperative; do not reset a tripped breaker more than once. End of procedure.
NO, any other bus: continue the flight with the affected circuits inoperative. End of procedure.

blocks.title: Principal loads lost with each DC bus
rows: HF 1, ADF 1, Captain's stick shaker, flight guidance 1, auto pitch trim A, autothrottle 1, stabilizer trim rate control 1, elevator feel and flap limit 1, left fuel dump valve, crossfeed 1 light, engine 1 oil pressure and pneumatic gauges, engine 1 reverser control and lights, engine 1 fire agent discharge light, left ground sensing, manifold failure loop 1, engine 1 anti-ice valve, center gear control, slat position 1.

Primary stabilizer trim, crossfeed 2 light, engine 2 reverser control and lights, manifold failure loop 2, antenna anti-ice valve, landing gear warning, fuel dump valve indication and low-level shutoff.

First Officer's stick shaker, auto pitch trim B, autothrottle 2, stabilizer trim rate control 2, elevator feel and flap limit 2, right fuel dump valve, crossfeed 3 light, engine 3 reverser control and lights, engine 3 fire agent discharge light, ground sensing, manifold failure loop 3, engine 3 anti-ice valve, the flight engineer's landing gear warning, auto slat extend control, slat position 2.
VHF 1, VOR 1, UHF 1, transponder, engine 1 N1 sensor, the Captain's radio and navigation source switching, lower yaw dampers.
VHF 2, VOR 2, UHF 2, engine 3 N1 sensor, the First Officer's radio and navigation source switching, upper yaw dampers.

blocks.content: KC-10: losing the left or right emergency DC bus also takes that side's FMS CDU and EHSI. If it is the designated pilot's side, the autopilot may have to be switched to the side that still has valid navigation data.

**Condition:** The BAT BUS OFF light on with the battery switch at BAT. The battery bus is normally supplied from the DC tie segments through diodes, with the battery behind them; it has lost its supplies, or its sensing circuit has failed. The light itself is powered from the battery direct bus, so it can tell the crew the battery bus is dead. Much depends on that bus: fire detection, the warning and caution lights, engine start and ignition control, the APU, the standby horizon.

**Objective:** Prove whether the bus is really dead; if it is, restore its feeds once; if it cannot be restored, land.

items.item: BATTERY BUS SENSING circuit breaker (OH B-29)

blocks.content:
**Has the light gone out?**
YES: the sensing breaker was the cause. End of procedure.
NO: continue with the next step.

items.item: BATTERY BUS FEEDS circuit breakers (OH A-13, A-14, A-15)
items.action: PULL AND RESET, ONE AT A TIME

items.item: Tripped breakers on the BATTERY DIRECT BUS

blocks.content:
**Has the light gone out with the breakers staying in?**
YES: the bus is restored. End of procedure.
NO, the light stays on and a BATTERY BUS FEEDS breaker trips: there is a short on the battery bus. Do not reset again. Land at the nearest suitable airfield. End of procedure.
NO, the light stays on with the breakers in: continue with the next step.

items.item: DC TIE 1 switch (only if TR 3 is inoperative)

blocks.content:
**Has the light gone out?**
YES: End of procedure.
NO: test the bus: LOOPS A or B TEST switch (fire detection), TEST (FE).

**Is the loop test normal?**
YES: the battery bus is powered and only its sensing circuit has failed. Continue the flight, remembering that the light can no longer be trusted. End of procedure.
NO: the battery bus is unpowered. Land at the nearest suitable airfield. End of procedure.

The fire loop test is used here because the fire detection system lives on the battery bus: a normal test proves the bus is powered whatever its light says. With the battery bus lost, the crew have no fire detection or fire warning for the engines and APU, no master warning or caution lights, no engine start or ignition control, no CSD disconnect, no APU control, no standby horizon, and lose the engine hydraulic pump and motor pump controls and the fuel tank fill valves, among others.

children.title: DC GND SERVICE BUS OFF light on

blocks.content:
**Condition:** The DC GND SERVICE BUS OFF light in the flight engineer's status light block. The DC ground service bus, fed by TR 2B from the AC ground service bus, is unpowered, or the AC ground service bus is lost (its sensing breaker lights the same light). The TR 2B DC LOAD meter tells which: at or near zero, TR 2B is not delivering.

**Objective:** Restore TR 2B, or the bus through DC TIE 3, and confirm the AC ground service bus.
If other lights are on, use their procedures first. Before continuing, pull and reset the AC GND SERVICE TIE RELAY CONT, COCKPIT GROUND SERVICE BUS and DC GROUND SERVICE BUS breakers.

**Is the TR 2B DC LOAD meter at or near zero?**
YES: go to *TR 2B not delivering* below.
NO: go to *Bus sensing* below.

**Is the meter normal and the light out?**
YES: continue normal operation. End of procedure.
NO, the meter reads above normal or the output breaker trips: pull the TR 2B output breaker and continue with the affected circuits inoperative. End of procedure.
NO, the meter stays at zero with both breakers in, or the input breaker trips: pull both TR 2B breakers and close DC TIE 3 (FE).

**Has the DC GND SERVICE BUS OFF light gone out?**
YES: the DC ground service bus is restored through the tie. End of procedure.
NO: confirm the AC ground service bus by starting auxiliary hydraulic pump 1 (AUX PUMP 1 switch, START, then STOP). If the pump does not run, the AC ground service bus is lost as well: the battery charger and both auxiliary pumps are lost (pump 1 can still be powered from the ADG), with the navigation, runway turnoff and wing scan lights, the cabin lighting and the emergency light control. Continue with the affected circuits inoperative. End of procedure.

items.item: AC GND SERVICE BUS SENSING circuit breaker (LM G-14)
DC GROUND SERVICE BUS NORM circuit breaker (UM D-12)

blocks.content:
**Does the DC GROUND SERVICE BUS NORM breaker trip?**
YES: do not reset it again; continue the flight with the affected circuits inoperative. End of procedure.
NO: continue with the next question.

**Has the light gone out?**
YES: End of procedure.
NO: continue the flight with the affected circuits inoperative. End of procedure.

Lost with the DC ground service bus: the cabin door power and control, the runway turnoff and wing scan lights, the emergency light control and the cargo loading system; on the KC-10, the boom hoist and the ARO sighting door.

**Condition:** Level 2 alert BUS L EMER DC OFF and the L EMER DC OFF light. The left emergency DC bus, which powers the Captain's displays and the first VIA's main power supply, has lost power, or only its sensing circuit has failed.

**Are display units 1 or 3 operating?**
YES: the bus is powered and its sensing circuit has failed. If a later electrical failure calls for emergency power, rotate the EMER PWR selector to ARM or ON and deploy the ADG (about 15 minutes of emergency power until the ADG is deployed). No further crew action. End of procedure.
NO: the bus is lost; continue with the next step.
Land at the nearest suitable airport. If a later failure calls for emergency power, rotate the EMER PWR selector to ARM or ON and deploy the ADG. End of procedure.

The electrical system behind these procedures is simulated in depth: every relay, protective function, breaker and bus, with real voltages, frequencies and loads, so the light patterns and meter readings the checklists rely on appear as described. The differences that matter to the procedures are these.

items: **Reset controls (DC-10, KC-10).** The ELEC SYS RESET switches on the upper main circuit breaker panel work only in their BUS FAULT sense: each clears its channel's bus tie relay lockout. The KC-10 manual's second position, GEN RLY/BUS TIE RLY LOCKOUT, is not separate: the GEN switch's RESET position clears the generator's lockout. The procedures above are written for the panel as simulated.
**APU GEN RESET** is fitted on the KC-10 only. On the DC-10 an APU generator lockout cannot be reset from the flight deck.

**Left out.** The DC GND SERVICE BUS PWR selector (NORM and ALTN) is not in the cockpit, so the KC-10 checklist's ALTN steps are omitted and the bus always takes its normal feed from TR 2B. The Dual Land bus split, and with it FedEx's DUAL LAND PWR ON procedure, is not modeled.

**AC BUS TIE ISOL lights** are out in normal unparalleled operation: in the simulation ISOL lights only for a channel switched to ISOL, carried by the APU, or whose bus tie relay is locked out or will not close. So the ISOL light the KC-10 manual expects after ISOL, THEN NORM in CSD OIL PRESS LO and GEN FREQ HI stays out, and the preferential generator check cannot be read from the lights. Read paralleling from the load meters.
**CSD disconnect** needs the button held for about one second; three seconds works too. A disconnected drive is reconnected on the ground with the EFB's Reset Aircraft.

**Circuit breakers.** Every breaker named above exists at the position given, which is the simulated panel's (in a few cases one breaker stands for the two or three the KC-10 manual lists for one feed). A breaker tripped by a failure trips again after a reset while the failure stays active. Breakers popped by a failure or pulled by the crew are listed in the EFB.

**MD-10 resets.** In AUTO the EPCU makes up to three automatic generator resets rather than one. The GEN buttons in MANUAL do not reset a tripped generator in this build, and the GEN BUS FAULT RESET panel is not modeled, so the procedures' PUSH TO RESET steps have no effect.

**MD-10 source switches.** Of the source input select panel switches, only IRS is operative; the CADC, VOR and APPR switches and the EIS SOURCE selector called for in BUS L EMER AC OFF, BUS L EMER DC OFF and GEN ALL OFF do nothing yet.
**MD-10 ADG** carries only the right emergency buses, as on the DC-10; the battery charger is not repowered through it.

**MD-10 alerts not raised.** ELEC ALERTS (the MD-10's procedure for a battery bus failure with the electrical alerting lost) and GEN LOAD HI are not raised by the simulation, so they have no procedure here; nor is the Level 1 ENG IGN NOT ARMED that BUS L EMER AC OFF asks about. On the MD-10, the EFB's battery bus failure shows only as the BAT BUS OFF light and the loss of what the battery bus powers.

**Generator off line** is injected as a loss of field: the generator trips on under-voltage and trips again after its reset, so the procedures end with the generator off. **Generator fault** is a bearing failure: GEN FAIL lights, GEN FAIL RESET relights it at once, and the generator stays on line; left alone for about five hours on its auxiliary bearings, it seizes. **Generator frequency high** is a governor runaway climbing about 1 Hz a second until the protection opens the bus tie relay and then the generator. **Generator bus failure** is a feeder fault in both protection zones, so the bus can be repowered from nowhere. **AC bus tie isolated** is a bus tie relay stuck open: the BUS FAULT reset does not close it.

parts.title: Hydraulics
parts.summary: Pressure, pump, quantity and temperature failures of one hydraulic system, and what its loss means for the landing.

blocks.content: This part covers single hydraulic system failures: pressure low or high, pump failures, motor pump valves, quantity loss, the loss of one system and what it takes with it, and high fluid temperature. The loss of two systems, and operation on one system powered by a windmilling engine, are in [Emergency Procedures](emergency-procedures). How the three systems are built is in [Hydraulics](hydraulics).

The aircraft has three independent 3,000 psi systems, each with two pumps on its own engine, and no single system is essential: every primary control surface is powered by at least two systems, and the reversible motor pumps (1-3 and 2-3) can transfer power from a healthy system to a neighbor without exchanging fluid. That design shapes the procedures. A system that has lost pressure but kept its fluid can be repowered by its second pump or a motor pump; a system that has lost its fluid must be isolated, pumps off and motor pump off, so that nothing runs dry and a leak is not fed. The first question in almost every hydraulic procedure is therefore the quantity gauge.

On the DC-10 and KC-10 the flight engineer's hydraulic panel gives a pressure, quantity and temperature gauge for each system and a PRESS LO and TEMP HI light for each pump; a pump light brings on the HYD cue and MASTER CAUTION. On the MD-10 the hydraulic system controller manages the pumps and motor pumps in AUTO, and failures appear as amber Level 2 alerts with the HYD synoptic.

KC-10: with any hydraulic abnormal during air refueling, the flight engineer tells the boom operator to disconnect and discontinue refueling until the hydraulic status is known, because the boom, the drogue and the AR pumps depend on the hydraulic systems.

blocks.title: Failures you can practice
rows: HYD 1/2/3 PRES LO: Level 1 in AUTO; Level 2 in MANUAL, [procedure](#md-hyd-pres-lo)
HYD 1/2/3 QTY LO (Level 1 in AUTO, Level 2 in MANUAL), then HYD 1/2/3 FAIL: [QTY LO](#md-hyd-qty-lo), [FAIL](#md-hyd-1-fail)
HYD 1/2/3 TEMP HI: Level 1 in AUTO; Level 2 in MANUAL, [procedure](#md-hyd-temp-hi)
HYD PUMP 1L/2L/3L FAULT, Level 1 in AUTO and Level 2 in MANUAL (see the table below)
Hydraulic systems # fail; Systems 1 and 2 lost, system 3 elevator off
HYD 1 AND 2 FAIL and the others: [Emergency Procedures](emergency-procedures)

blocks.content: The EFB's hydraulic failures are listed in [EFB failures: hydraulic](efb#failures-hyd).

blocks.title: MD-10 hydraulic alerts without a procedure
rows: That engine pump is on but its outlet pressure is below 2,400 psi, or it is overheating; the pump's FAULT legend lights. The other pump and the motor pumps hold the system; if the system's pressure is lost, HYD PRES LO follows.
Both pumps of that system are off.
A pump has been turned off with its switchlight.
The system 3 elevator shutoff valve has closed: the reservoir has fallen to its low level, and system 3 now powers only what is upstream of the valve.
HYD 1-3 RMP DISAG, HYD 2-3 RMP DISAG
A reversible motor pump's valves are not where they were commanded.
RUDDER UPR INOP, RUDDER BOTH INOP, RUD STBY UPR/LWR OFF
A rudder has lost both its systems, or a rudder standby pump is off.
System 3 is isolated from the flight controls.
HYD SYS MANUAL, SEL HYD SYS MAN
The system is in MANUAL, or the controller has reverted and wants MANUAL selected.

sections.title: Pressure and pumps
sections.summary: Low or high system pressure, engine pump failures and motor pump valves.

blocks.content:
**Condition:** A system's HYD PRESS gauge reads low, usually with both of its PRESS LO lights on. The system has lost its pressure source: its pumps have failed or are not commanded on, or it has lost its fluid. With the right pump at AUTO, a low pressure with both PRESS LO lights on and the quantity normal points to a failure of the automatic circuit that should have brought the right pump in.

**Objective:** Separate a pump or control failure (fluid still there, system recoverable) from a leak (fluid going, system to be isolated).

The loss of a hydraulic system does not disconnect its autopilot or warn of an autopilot failure: the servo simply has no power. With system 1 lost, autopilot 1 may still be used if rudder standby power is available; with system 2 lost use autopilot 2; with system 3 lost use autopilot 1.

**Is the system's quantity low or decreasing?**
YES: the fluid is going. Affected ENG HYD PUMP switches OFF, and the motor pump selector of the affected pair OFF (FE); go to [HYDRAULIC SYSTEM QUANTITY LEAK OR LOSS](#hydraulic-quantity-leak).
NO: continue with the next step.

**Is the pressure normal again?**
YES: the automatic circuit had failed. Continue the flight with the R pump at ON and the L pump OFF (FE), and monitor the system. End of procedure.
NO: both engine pumps have failed. Motor pump selector of the affected pair as required (FE) and monitor the system. End of procedure.

The motor pumps should be OFF in non-critical phases of flight and at ON or ARM for approach and landing. A motor pump driving a failed system loads its donor system continuously, and in cruise the dead system's surfaces are already covered by the other systems; for landing, the flaps, slats, spoilers and brakes are worth the cost.

**Condition:** One engine pump's PRESS LO light on, with the HYD cue and MASTER CAUTION. That pump's own outlet is below 2,400 psi: it has failed, or the system behind it has lost pressure. Do not use this procedure if the light is accompanied by HYD TEMP HI lights; use [HYD TEMP HI](#hyd-temp-hi).

**Objective:** Find out whether one pump or the whole system has failed.

**Is the system's quantity low or decreasing?**
YES: affected ENG HYD PUMP switches OFF and the motor pump selector of the affected pair OFF (FE); go to [HYDRAULIC SYSTEM QUANTITY LEAK OR LOSS](#hydraulic-quantity-leak).
NO: continue with the next question.

**Is the system pressure low?**
YES: go to [HYDRAULIC PRESSURE LOW](#hyd-pressure-low).
NO: the other pump is holding the system and only the pump with the light has failed: ENG HYD PUMP L switch (failed pump) OFF (FE). If desired, the pump may be turned on again for landing. End of procedure.

Why the pump is turned off: a pump that has lost its output may be failing mechanically, and depressurizing it unloads it. Its depressurizing valve is held open by its control circuit, so the pump turns at no load until it is needed again. With the left pump off, the right pump at AUTO comes on by itself whenever the system pressure falls.

**Condition:** A system's HYD PRESS gauge reads above the normal band (above 3,500 psi). An engine pump's pressure compensator has failed, so the pump delivers full stroke regardless of demand and the system relief valve is limiting the pressure, or the gauge is wrong. A pump running against its relief valve turns most of its power into heat.

**Objective:** Find which pump is at fault by running the system on each pump in turn.

**What does the pressure read now?**
NORMAL: the L pump was at fault. Continue the flight with the R pump at AUTO; the L pump may be used in an emergency. End of procedure.
ZERO: the R pump's automatic circuit has failed: ENG HYD PUMP R selector ON (FE). If the pressure is then normal, continue the flight with the R pump at ON; the L pump may be used in an emergency. End of procedure. If not, continue with *Swap the pumps* below.
STILL HIGH: continue with *Swap the pumps* below.

**Is the pressure normal?**
YES: the R pump was at fault. Continue the flight with the R pump OFF; it may be used in an emergency. End of procedure.
NO (still in the high band with either pump): both pumps reading high is improbable; assume a gauge malfunction and return the R pump to AUTO (FE). End of procedure.

**Condition:** The blue 1-3/2-3 PUMP VALVE OPEN status light on with no reason for a motor pump to be running. Disregard it if a motor pump selector is at ON, or at ARM with any engine not running normally: the valves are then meant to be open. A reversible motor pump's shutoff valves are open: the unit is coupling the two systems, and a fault in one could draw on the other.

**Objective:** Close the valves, and if one has stuck open, accept it.

**Has the light gone out?**
YES: continue with the selectors OFF; they may be moved to ARM or ON for approach and landing. End of procedure.
NO: a valve has stuck open. Continue the flight with the selectors OFF, and watch both systems of the pair: with the valve open, the motor pump transfers power whenever the pressures of its two systems differ. End of procedure.

**Condition:** Level 2 alert HYD 1, 2 or 3 PRES LO with the HYD cue and MASTER CAUTION, with the hydraulic system in MANUAL (in AUTO the same condition is a Level 1 alert); the system's PRESS light on the HYD panel. The system's pressure is below 2,400 psi with its quantity still normal: its pumps are not delivering.

**Objective:** Unload the failed pumps and keep the system available for landing.

Repressurize the system for approach and landing (pumps on, motor pump as required). If it does not repressurize, go to [HYD 1 FAIL](#md-hyd-1-fail), [HYD 2 FAIL](#md-hyd-2-fail) or [HYD 3 FAIL](#md-hyd-3-fail) as appropriate. End of procedure.
**Condition:** Level 2 alert HYD 1, 2 or 3 PRES HI: the system pressure is above 3,500 psi. An engine pump's compensator has failed high, or the pressure sensor is wrong.

**Is the hydraulic system in MANUAL?**
YES: continue with the next step.
NO: in AUTO the controller turns off a pump with a high pressure (the simulated controller does not yet; see [Simulation notes](#simulation-notes)). Make a log entry; if the alert stays, the system pressure sensor has failed. End of procedure.

items.item: Associated HYD SYS L PUMP switchlight

blocks.content:
**Does the PRES HI alert stay displayed?**
YES: the left pump was not the cause. After 10 seconds, L PUMP switchlight ON again (PM) and make a log entry: if the alert remains, the pressure sensor has failed. End of procedure.
NO: the left pump was at fault; leave it off. End of procedure.

sections.title: Quantity loss and loss of one system
sections.summary: Leaks, the system 3 elevator shutoff valve, and what the loss of each system costs.

children.title: HYDRAULIC SYSTEM QUANTITY LEAK OR LOSS

blocks.content:
**Condition:** A system's HYD QTY gauge falling, or at zero, usually followed by its pressure and its PRESS LO lights. The system is losing fluid through a leak. Once the reservoir is dry the pumps cavitate and the system is gone, whatever is done with it.

**Objective:** Isolate the system at once so that its pumps are not damaged running dry and no motor pump pours another system's power into the leak; then prepare the landing around the surfaces that system powered.

Then go to the procedure for the system lost: [System 1 inoperative](#system-1-failure), [System 2 inoperative](#system-2-failure) or [System 3 inoperative](#system-3-failure). The inoperative system may be reinstated for landing if its gauge still shows quantity.

FedEx treats a hydraulic quantity leak or loss as a phase one procedure: autopilots OFF, the affected system's engine hydraulic pump switches OFF and its motor pump switches OFF, from memory, before the checklist is read.

**Condition:** Hydraulic system 1 has been lost and isolated by [HYDRAULIC SYSTEM QUANTITY LEAK OR LOSS](#hydraulic-quantity-leak).

**Objective:** Plan the approach around what system 1 took with it, and make sure the slats extend before committing to a configuration.

blocks.title: Effect of losing system 1
rows: Autopilot 1 may be used as required
Panels 2 and 4, left and right, inoperative
Left turns limited to 25°, right turns normal

If RUD STBY PWR OFF is lit: upper rudder inoperative, automatic stabilizer trim inoperative and stabilizer trim rate reduced; VMCA 157 KIAS and maximum crosswind component 15 kt. Otherwise both rudders work (the 1-3 standby pump powers the upper rudder from system 3)
FWD tank and CTR WING tank left AR pumps inoperative; UARRSI toggles inoperative

blocks.title: When ready to configure for landing

blocks.content:
**Have the slats extended?**
YES: further flap and slat extension should be normal. Fly the approach with the normal checklists and land with flaps 35°/EXT at most, to limit the effect of any spoiler float. If the flaps reach 35° but SLAT DISAGREE lights, return the handle to 22°/EXT, use the threshold speed for that configuration, and set the GND PROXIMITY WARN FLAP OVRD switch to OVRD/ON (KC-10; the simulated DC-10 has no such switch). End of procedure.
NO: flap/slat handle 15°/EXT (PM); once the flaps are out, slow gradually toward 1.3 VS for 15°/RET to help the slats. If they still do not extend, 22°/EXT if the flap placard speed permits, and slow toward 1.3 VS for 22°/RET. If the slats will not extend at all, go to [Asymmetric slats or no slat landing with flaps](abnormal-flight-controls#asymmetric-slats). End of procedure.

Why the 35° limit: with system 1 gone, two pairs of spoiler panels are held down by nothing but their actuators' trapped fluid and the airloads. At large flap angles the airflow over the wing can lift an unpowered panel (spoiler float), costing lift and roll control just when both matter most.

**Condition:** Hydraulic system 2 has been lost and isolated by [HYDRAULIC SYSTEM QUANTITY LEAK OR LOSS](#hydraulic-quantity-leak).

**Objective:** Know the rudder situation before the approach, and plan the crosswind and VMCA accordingly.

blocks.title: Effect of losing system 2
rows: Autopilot 2 may be used as required, unless the HYD SYS 3 ELEV OFF light is on, when it is inoperative
Panels 1 and 5, left and right, inoperative

If RUD STBY PWR OFF or HYD SYS 3 ELEV OFF is lit: lower rudder inoperative, maximum crosswind component 15 kt, and VMCA from the table below. Otherwise both rudders work (the 3-2 standby pump powers the lower rudder from system 3)
The boom and drogue hydraulic systems may be inoperative; AFT tank right AR pump inoperative. Refuel only if AR HYD RSVR PRESS LOW is out with the 2-3 motor pump ON

blocks.title: VMCA with the lower rudder inoperative (KC-10)

blocks.content: The inoperative system may be reinstated for landing if its gauge still shows quantity. Land with flaps 35° at most, to limit the effect of spoiler float. End of procedure.

Why VMCA rises: VMCA is the lowest speed at which full rudder can still hold the yaw of an engine failure at go-around thrust. With one rudder segment unpowered, less yawing moment is available at any speed, so the speed at which the remaining segment can balance the thrust asymmetry is higher. Do not attempt a go-around below it.

**Condition:** Hydraulic system 3 has been lost and isolated by [HYDRAULIC SYSTEM QUANTITY LEAK OR LOSS](#hydraulic-quantity-leak).

**Objective:** Plan the alternate gear extension and the slat extension before the approach.

blocks.title: Effect of losing system 3
rows: Autopilot 1 may be used as required
Trim rate reduced; the long trim handles do not move when the electric trim switches are used
Cannot be retracted, and must be extended with the alternate extension
Left turns normal, right turns limited to 25°
Boom hoist inoperative; FWD and CTR WING tank right AR pumps and AFT tank left AR pump inoperative

blocks.title: When ready to configure for landing

blocks.content: If the slats do not extend, use 15°/EXT and then 22°/EXT as for system 1, slowing toward 1.3 VS for the flaps-only configuration. If they will not extend at all, plan the landing with [Asymmetric slats or no slat landing with flaps](abnormal-flight-controls#asymmetric-slats), and extend the gear as below.

items.item: Center gear alternate extension handle (-30, -40, KC-10)

blocks.content: After the main gear alternate extension, wait for the three green lights before the next step; after an alternate extension do not exceed 260 KIAS.
The inoperative system may be reinstated for landing if its gauge still shows quantity. Complete the BEFORE LANDING checklist. End of procedure.

Why the gear must free-fall: system 3 alone powers the gear's retraction and normal extension actuators. Without it the gear can only fall under its own weight, which is what the alternate extension does: it releases the uplocks mechanically and lets gravity and the airflow swing the legs down into their locks. The 230 kt limit keeps the airloads low enough for gravity and the airflow to swing the legs down into their locks.

children.title: HYDRAULIC SYS 3 ELEV OFF light on

blocks.content:
**Condition:** The HYD SYS 3 ELEV OFF light (DC-10), with the HYD cue and MASTER CAUTION. System 3's elevator shutoff valve has closed. Two level switches in system 3's reservoir close it when the quantity falls to a low level, so that a leak in the long lines to the tail cannot empty system 3 completely: the valve sacrifices the elevators' system 3 supply to save the system for everything upstream of it. With the valve closed, each inboard elevator is powered by one system only, and the 3-2 standby pump that powers the lower rudder from system 3 is shut off too.

**Objective:** Find out whether system 3 is really losing fluid, and what the elevators and rudder have left.

**Is system 3's quantity at zero?**
YES: system 3 is lost. ENG 3 HYD PUMP switches BOTH OFF (FE), and complete [System 3 inoperative](#system-3-failure).
NO: the valve has closed on a system that still has fluid; continue with the next question.
In this configuration the inboard elevator is powered by a single hydraulic system. Autopilot 2 is inoperative, but it does not disconnect or announce its failure.

**Are hydraulic systems 1 and 2 quantities normal?**
YES: no further action. End of procedure.
NO: if system 1 is not operating, the right inboard elevator is inoperative; if system 2 is not operating, the left inboard elevator and the lower rudder are inoperative, RUD STBY PWR OFF is not lit, and both autopilots are inoperative. Complete [System 1 inoperative](#system-1-failure) or [System 2 inoperative](#system-2-failure) as appropriate. End of procedure.

**Condition:** Level 2 alert HYD 1, 2 or 3 QTY LO, with the hydraulic system in MANUAL: less than about 2.5 gallons remain in the reservoir (in AUTO the same condition is a Level 1 alert). A leak is the usual cause; HYD FAIL follows if the fluid is lost.

**Objective:** Stop pumping the remaining fluid into the leak, and keep the system for landing.
The system may be used for approach and landing. If the fluid is lost, go to [HYD 1 FAIL](#md-hyd-1-fail), [HYD 2 FAIL](#md-hyd-2-fail) or [HYD 3 FAIL](#md-hyd-3-fail). End of procedure.

**Condition:** Level 2 alert HYD 1 FAIL: system 1's fluid quantity is below about 1 gallon and the system is lost.

**Consequences:** Autopilot 2 not available; flap and slat extension may need a lower speed; 35° flaps maximum for landing; do not arm the autobrake (if installed); nosewheel steering restricted to the left.

**Is the HYD 3 ELEV OFF alert also displayed?**
YES: with system 3 also cut off from the elevators, the right inboard elevator has no power left: land at the nearest suitable airport. Continue with the next step.
NO: continue with the next step.
The 35° flap limit protects against the float of the spoiler panels system 1 no longer holds down. End of procedure.

**Condition:** Level 2 alert HYD 2 FAIL: system 2's fluid quantity is below about 1 gallon and the system is lost.

**Consequences:** Autopilot 1 not available; flap extension may need a lower speed; 35° flaps maximum for landing.

**Is the HYD 3 ELEV OFF alert also displayed?**
YES: the autopilots are not available and the lower rudder is inoperative. Land at the nearest suitable airport. VMCA is 145 KIAS on the Series 10; on the Series 30 take it from the table below. The recommended maximum crosswind component is 15 kt. Then continue with the next step.
NO: autopilot 2 may be used, and unless RUDDER LWR INOP is displayed the lower rudder stays available through the 3-2 non-reversible motor pump. Continue with the next step.
Plan a 35/EXT landing. Spoiler panels 1 and 5 are inoperative, and the flaps may not extend until the airspeed is reduced. End of procedure.
Do not attempt a go-around below VMCA.

**Condition:** Level 2 alert HYD 3 FAIL: system 3's fluid quantity is below about 1 gallon and the system is lost. System 3 powers the landing gear, so the gear must be extended with the alternate extension.

**Consequences:** Autopilot 2 and auto pitch trim inoperative; the 1-3 and 2-3 motor pumps inoperative; 35° flaps maximum for landing; slat extension may need a lower speed; alternate gear extension required; do not arm the autobrake (if installed); nosewheel steering restricted to the right.
Autoland is not approved. The autopilot must be disconnected by 100 ft AGL, and an autopilot go-around is not recommended.

items.item: When gear extension is required: airspeed
After three green lights: center gear alternate extension handle (Series 30)

blocks.content: End of procedure.
**Condition:** Level 2 alert RUDDER LWR INOP (Series 30 only): the lower rudder has lost both its hydraulic supplies. (The simulation lists this alert as Level 1.)

The maximum crosswind component is 15 kt. Determine VMCA from the Series 30 table in [HYD 2 FAIL](#md-hyd-2-fail): 201 KIAS at 260,000 lb landing weight, falling to 172 KIAS at 320,000 lb and above. End of procedure.

children.title: HYD TEMP HI light(s) on or HYD TEMP gauge high

blocks.content:
**Condition:** A pump's TEMP HI light (its case drain at 118 °C), or a system's HYD TEMP gauge in the yellow band (60 to 100 °C). A pump that is failing, or one forced to run against a blocked outlet, turns its input power into heat in the fluid. In system 2 there is a particular cause: a running 2-3 motor pump can deliver a pressure high enough to dead-head system 2's engine pumps, so that they churn the fluid without delivering it.

**Objective:** Remove the heat source while keeping the system available for landing.

Do not use this procedure during takeoff or landing with both TEMP HI lights of a system on: it may depressurize the system when it is needed most. If the safety of the flight requires it, use the system whatever its temperature. On the ground in hot weather, cycling the flight controls with the engine pumps running circulates and cools the fluid and may put the lights out; if not, maintenance is required.

**Is only one TEMP HI light on (with or without the HYD TEMP gauge high)?**
YES: continue with the next step.
NO (both TEMP HI lights of the system on, or the HYD TEMP gauge high): go to *Both pumps off* below.

**Is it system 2, with the 2-3 motor pump running (2-3 PUMP selector at ON, or at ARM with any engine shut down)?**
YES: go to *2-3 motor pump running* below.
NO: continue with the next step.

items.item: ENG HYD PUMP switch (associated with the light)
Other ENG HYD PUMP switch (same system)

blocks.content: That ends the KC-10 manual's procedure. FedEx adds a check: watch the system's temperature and TEMP HI light for 5 minutes. If the temperature does not come down or the light stays on, go to *Both pumps off* below; otherwise continue with the associated pump OFF. End of procedure.

items.item: ENG 2 HYD PUMP switch (associated with the light)
System 2 TEMP HI light and HYD TEMP gauge (after 5 minutes)

blocks.content:
**Is the light out, or the temperature decreasing?**
YES: the motor pump was the cause. Keep the 2-3 PUMP selector OFF in non-critical phases of flight and ON for approach and landing. End of procedure.
NO: continue with the next step.

Keep the motor pump selectors OFF in non-critical phases of flight and ON for approach and landing. With the system depressurized, choose the autopilot as in [HYDRAULIC PRESSURE LOW](#hyd-pressure-low). End of procedure.

**Condition:** Level 2 alert HYD 1, 2 or 3 TEMP HI, with the hydraulic system in MANUAL: the reservoir fluid is above 100 °C. In AUTO the controller should turn the system's pumps off itself and show HYD OFF, and the condition appears only as a Level 1 alert.

**Consequences:** Pressurize the system for approach and landing.

**Is the aircraft in flight?**
YES: if the phase of flight permits, affected HYD SYS PUMP switchlights and RMPs OFF (PM). The system should be on again for approach and landing. End of procedure.
NO: cycle the flight controls with the affected engine pumps running: the fluid circulates through the coolers and may cool enough for the alert to go out. If it stays, call maintenance. End of procedure.

Each hydraulic system is solved as a fluid network, with every pump, the motor pumps, the actuators and the leaks acting on pressure, so the gauges and lights respond to these procedures as they would on the aircraft. These are the differences that matter.

items: **Center gear.** The center gear alternate extension handle is not operable in the simulation. On the -30, -40 and KC-10, a center gear that cannot extend on system 3 stays up: select the CTR GEAR switch to UP and land with it retracted, allowing for the landing weight limits without the center gear. With system 3 lost and the gear handle at DOWN, the main and nose gear fall by themselves in the simulation even before the alternate extension lever is raised.

**Injected failures.** System pressure low fails the left engine pump and the automatic circuit, so the right pump at AUTO does not come in until it is selected ON: the HYDRAULIC PRESSURE LOW procedure's NO-leak branch restores the system. System pressure high fails the left pump's compensator high. System leak drains the reservoir at about half a quart a second, dry in about a minute. System temperature high is a failing engine pump heating the fluid while it runs; it drives the temperature gauge (and on the MD-10 the alert) but not the pump TEMP HI lights. Engine pump pressure low fails the left pump. Motor pump valve stuck open sticks both of that motor pump's valves. System 3 elevator off fails the shutoff valve's level switches low, so the valve closes on a full reservoir and the quantity check in that procedure leads to the NO branch.
**Motor pumps at ARM** open on low pressure in either system of the pair, so an armed motor pump cycles while it holds up a failed system. Use ON when a system depends on its motor pump.
**KC-10.** The flight engineer's HYD SYS 3 ELEV OFF light is not fitted in this cockpit: the valve's closure lights the HYD cue and MASTER CAUTION, and the system 3 quantity gauge tells the rest.

**Not modeled.** The loss of autopilot 2 pitch control when the elevator shutoff valve closes; the nosewheel steering angle limits with one system lost (steering is slower instead); the reservoir low-level switches that shut down the motor pumps; pump TEMP HI lights except for a pump overheat failure, which the EFB does not offer; fluid temperature rising from the pumps' own heat on a long flight.

**MD-10.** In AUTO the controller does not yet turn off a pump with a high pressure or a hot system, so a PRES HI stays until the crew select MANUAL and turn the pump off. HSC AUTO FAIL and HYD ALERTS are not raised by the simulation and have no procedure here.
**Dual failures.** With systems 1 and 2 lost, the simulation's spoiler mixers leave no flight spoilers; the aircraft manual expects panel 3 to keep working.

parts.title: Flight Controls
parts.summary: Flap and slat malfunctions and abnormal-configuration landings, flap limiter and stall warning faults, elevator feel and stabilizer failures, manual spoilers and loss of control.

blocks.content: This part covers flight control failures that leave the aircraft flyable: flaps and slats that will not move, or move unevenly; the flap limiter and the stall warning and auto slat system; the elevator feel system and the horizontal stabilizer; the automatic ground spoilers; and the loss of control through the normal pilot inputs. How the controls work is in [Flight Controls](flight-controls). Hydraulic failures that take flight controls with them are in [Hydraulics](abnormal-hydraulics).

Many of these procedures end in a landing with an abnormal configuration, and they share a pattern. First stop the problem growing: return the flap/slat handle to the last position where everything was symmetrical, because asymmetric lift is a rolling moment the ailerons must hold. Then reduce the weight, since every abnormal configuration lands faster than normal and the runway required grows with the square of the touchdown speed. Then fly a stabilized approach on a normal glide path at the speeds for the configuration you actually have, and resist the instinct to flare and hold the aircraft off: at these speeds that only floats it down the runway, and in a nose-high attitude risks the tail (on the KC-10, the boom).

On the DC-10 and KC-10 the indications are the flap/slat position indicator with its FLAP DISAGREE flag, the SLAT DISAGREE and SLAT TAKEOFF lights, and the SELECT ELEV FEEL MAN, SELECT FLAP LIMIT OVRD and AUTO SPOILER DO NOT USE lights with MASTER CAUTION. On the MD-10 they are Level 2 alerts with the CONFIG synoptic.

blocks.title: Failures you can practice
rows: Flaps fail to move: both sides, left side, right side
FLAP DISAG and SLAT DISAG: [NO FLAP/NO SLAT LANDING](#md-no-flap-no-slat-landing)
Slat disagree: left outboard, right outboard, inboard, sensor
With the autopilot engaged, STAB OUT OF TRIM ([procedure](#md-stab-out-of-trim)); then [STABILIZER INOPERATIVE](#md-stabilizer-inoperative), which has no alert
[AUTO SPOILER DO NOT USE light on](#auto-spoiler-do-not-use)
[LOSS OF CONTROL BY CONVENTIONAL PILOT INPUTS](#loss-of-control)
Stall warning or auto slat fault

blocks.content: The EFB's flight control failures are listed in [EFB failures: flight controls](efb#failures-flt). The yaw dampers are in [Flight Instruments and Automatic Flight](abnormal-flight-instruments).

blocks.title: MD-10 flight control alerts without a procedure
rows: The spoiler handle is armed when it should not be (for example with thrust advanced for takeoff). Disarm it.
Speedbrakes are extended with the flaps beyond the limit for speedbrake use. Retract them.

With the ELEV FEEL selector in MANUAL, the feel reference (ELF) speed is above 200 kt while the airspeed is below 200 kt, so the column is heavier than it should be: slew the ELF speed down to the airspeed (see [SEL ELEV FEEL MAN](#md-sel-elev-feel-man)).
The ELEV FEEL selector is out of AUTO (Level 1).

sections.title: Flaps, slats and the flap limiter
sections.summary: Flaps or slats that fail to move or move asymmetrically, the no-flap/no-slat landing, the flap limiter and the auto slat system.

blocks.alt: Summary diagram for the DC-10, KC-10 and MD-10 flap and slat malfunction landings, laid out as five columns, one per landing configuration: 50/EXT or 35/EXT (normal); 22/EXT (slats extended, flaps limited, the SLAT DISAGREE-during-extension case); 0/EXT (slats in the takeoff position, flaps failed retracted); 22/RET or 35/RET (slats retracted, flaps available, needing the split flap/slat handle); 0/RET (no flaps, no slats). Each column shows a side-view wing section sketch with the slat and flap positions drawn, the approach body attitude drawn on a small aircraft silhouette on a 2.75 degree glide path (about 8 degrees nose up at 0/EXT threshold speed, near level at 0/RET), the GPWS FLAP OVRD requirement (yes for 22 degrees or less), whether the main gear alternate extension is needed (0/RET only, to unlock the outboard ailerons), and an arrow scale under the columns showing approach speed and landing distance rising from left to right.
blocks.title: Flap and slat malfunction landing configurations
blocks.caption: From the most normal configuration on the left to the most demanding on the right. Speeds and distances rise toward the right; body attitude changes with slats more than with flaps.

blocks.content:
**Condition:** Either the flaps have split, shown by the inboard and outboard or left and right position tapes disagreeing with the FLAP DISAGREE flag in view and a rolling tendency, or the flap position tapes do not move when the handle is moved. Each wing's flaps are driven by hydraulic actuators through a mechanical interconnect; a disconnected drive leaves one side behind until a skew detector stops the other, and a jammed control valve holds both where they are.

**Objective:** Stop any asymmetry, try once to free a stuck valve, and land with the most extension that is symmetrical and agrees with the handle.

**Are the flaps asymmetric?**
YES: continue with *Asymmetric flaps* below.
NO (the tapes do not move as selected): go to *Flaps do not move as selected* below.

items.action: LAST POSITION WHERE FLAPS WERE SYMMETRICAL

items.item: AT/SC, flap indicator and horizontal stabilizer circuit breakers

blocks.content: With the autopilot engaged when the flaps split, the rolling tendency may be hidden until it is disconnected: be ready for it. Do not use the autothrottles or speed control: their speed schedule assumes symmetrical flaps. The flap position indicator is powered from two sources: asymmetric tapes with no FLAP DISAGREE flag and no roll may be a failed indication, and a visual inspection confirming normal flaps ends the procedure.

**Are the flaps symmetrical again?**
YES: if the asymmetry happened while retracting, further extension may be attempted, and the autopilot may be used again. If the flaps are in the landing range, continue with the normal checklists. End of procedure. Otherwise go to *Approach and landing* below.
NO: go to *Approach and landing* below.

blocks.title: Flaps do not move as selected

items.action: BELOW 221 KIAS, NOT BELOW 1.3 VS FOR 0°/EXT

blocks.content: 221 KIAS is the limit for the slats in the landing position. The handle loads are higher than normal. Moving the handle to full travel positions the override clapper mechanism in the flap control valve, which may force a sticking valve open; it may have to be repeated as more extension is needed.

**Do the flaps now extend as desired?**
YES: continue with the normal checklists. End of procedure.
NO: if the flaps stop at 20°, the flap limiter may have failed: see [SELECT FLAP LIMIT OVRD light on](#flap-limit-ovrd). Otherwise inspect the flaps visually (FE, BO). If they are where the handle says, disregard the faulty indicator and continue normally. End of procedure. If both inboard and outboard flaps have failed to extend, only the inboard flaps moved, or the position cannot be seen: flap/slat handle to the last position where the flaps were normal (PM); continue with the normal checklists if that is in the landing range, otherwise go to *Approach and landing*.

items.item: GPWS FLAP OVRD (if final flaps 22° or less; KC-10, the simulated DC-10 has no FLAP OVRD switch)

blocks.content: Land with the greatest flap/slat selection that gives equal extension of the inboard and outboard flaps and agrees with the handle. If the flaps stay asymmetric, find the most symmetrical configuration and fly the speeds for the smallest flap angle indicated. Do not use the autothrottles: they do not compute threshold speeds for anything but the normal landing flaps and would not let the aircraft slow below their minimum speed.

Plan a slightly wider pattern and a longer final. Slow to the approach speed (1.3 VS for the configuration) once stabilized on final, and fly a normal glide path, not a flat one. With less than the normal landing flaps the deck angle is higher than normal: at the 0°/EXT threshold speed on a 2.75° glide path it is about 8° nose up. At the threshold reduce the sink rate slightly without a flare, close the throttles and fly the aircraft onto the runway; lower the nose firmly to put weight on the wheels, and use reverse thrust at once, which also deploys the ground spoilers. End of procedure.
KC-10: with final flaps less than 35°, the boom can contact the runway at 13° body angle with the struts extended, or 11° with them compressed.

**Condition:** The SLAT DISAGREE light: at least one slat group is not where the handle has commanded. The slats are moved in groups by hydraulic actuators, each group's position reported by proximity sensors. A real disagreement may be symmetrical (all slats stopped short) or asymmetrical (one wing's outboard slats out, the other's in), and an asymmetry is felt as a trim change, buffet or roll. A misaligned sensor can light the lamp with every slat where it should be.

**Objective:** Get back to a symmetrical, known slat configuration, and plan the landing for the slats you actually have.

During takeoff or go-around, do not move the flap/slat handle until a safe altitude and airspeed are reached. If an asymmetry shows at any time as a trim change, buffet or roll, return the handle to the last position where the slats were symmetrical. Always keep a safe flying speed and correct an asymmetry at once.
**On the ground before takeoff:** if SLAT DISAGREE is on and SLAT TAKEOFF is off, recycle the handle and check SLAT TAKEOFF on and SLAT DISAGREE out. If the light stays on, do not take off.

V2 + 10 may be in the stick shaker range, but gives a margin to climb to acceleration height and the aileron authority to hold the wings level if the slats are asymmetric. Do not engage the autopilot or autothrottles. As the speed rises, the wheel needed to hold the wings level with asymmetric slats may increase, decrease or even reverse. The flaps may be brought to 15° before about 220 kt to respect their limit speed. During slat retraction with the light still on, do not exceed 270 KIAS or Mach 0.55, whichever is less.

If the aircraft behaves abnormally after takeoff (unusual deck angle, buffet, asymmetry), retract the slats at VSR; otherwise keep the configuration at a safe speed and bank angle until a visual inspection can be made. **Do the slats operate normally?**
YES: continue normal operations; another visual check may be needed when the slats are next extended. End of procedure.
NO: plan a 22°/RET or 35°/RET landing: see *Landing with slats retracted* below. End of procedure.
**In flight, other than during takeoff:**

items.action: LAST POSITION WHERE SLAT DISAGREE WAS OUT

blocks.content:
**Is the SLAT RESET light on?**
YES: the auto slat system has extended the slats: go to [Stall warning or auto slat malfunction](#stall-warning-auto-slat).
NO: determine where the handle was when the light came on, and continue below.

blocks.title: Landing configuration by case
rows: 22°/RET or 35°/RET (slats retracted): see *Landing with slats retracted*
Handle at 22°/EXT and 22°/EXT speeds. Do not split the handles. GPWS FLAP OVRD (KC-10)
22°/EXT if a visual inspection confirms all slats in the takeoff position; otherwise 22°/RET or 35°/RET
Handle at 22°/EXT and 22°/EXT speeds. Do not split the handles

blocks.content: Why 22°/EXT so often: the slats never retract beyond the position commanded, so returning the handle to 22°/EXT gives a known configuration whatever the slats did on the way. The 22°/EXT speeds are conservative, and if the slats are asymmetric their extra speed gives the ailerons more authority.

items.item: GPWS FLAP OVRD (if landing with 22°/RET; KC-10, the simulated DC-10 has no FLAP OVRD switch)

blocks.content: To split the handles, loosen the thumbscrew of the flap/slat handle interlock, swing the interlock out of the way and retighten it; lift and hold the slat handle, then lift and pull only the flap handle to the flap position wanted. Up to 360,000 lb landing weight use 35° flaps, because the 50°/RET approach speeds exceed the 50° flap placard; above 360,000 lb use 22°, because the 35°/RET speeds exceed the 35° placard (15°/RET speeds may be used while slowing to the 22°/RET approach speed). Consider the 204 kt tire speed limit.

This is the most demanding of the flap and slat landings. Fly a normal glide path, not a flat approach. The deck angle is nose down on the approach and close to the cruise attitude at touchdown: reduce thrust to stop it floating, and do not try for the normal nose-high landing attitude or hold the aircraft off. Expect 800 to 1,000 ft/min on the glide path at these speeds. With 35° flaps the spoilers deploy on wheel spin-up; with less, on reverse thrust selection. End of procedure.

**Landing with the slats in the takeoff position (0°/EXT or 22°/EXT):** fly a normal glide path using every guidance available. The deck angle is slightly higher than normal with 22° flaps and much higher without flaps: about 8° nose up at the 0°/EXT threshold speed on a 2.75° path. End of procedure.

**Condition:** Multiple malfunctions leave neither flaps nor slats for landing: both control valves jammed, or a dual hydraulic failure. (After a dual hydraulic failure, review that emergency procedure for the other effects on the systems and the handling.)

**Objective:** Land as slowly as a clean wing allows: lowest practical weight, the outboard ailerons unlocked for roll control, and a long stabilized final.

items.item: Minimum maneuvering and threshold speeds for 0°/RET
Center gear alternate extension handle (-30, -40, KC-10; not operable in the simulation, see Simulation notes)
GPWS FLAP OVRD (KC-10; the simulated DC-10 has no FLAP OVRD switch)

items.action: MIN MANEUVER AND THRESHOLD SPEEDS FOR 0°/RET

blocks.content: The main gear alternate extension lever is what unlocks the outboard ailerons, which are otherwise locked with the flaps and slats retracted; with the lever raised, nosewheel steering to the right is limited to 25°. After the main gear alternate extension, wait for three green lights before the next step, and do not exceed 260 KIAS. When dumping to the lowest weight, consider the 204 kt tire speed limit.

Fly minimum maneuvering speed until the turn onto base, slow 10 kt on base in level flight, and once established on final slow again in level flight to the approach speed. The clean wing decelerates slowly and accelerates quickly, so a level segment for slowing down is essential. Then fly a normal glide path; do not drag the aircraft in on a flat one, which only makes the touchdown point harder to judge. Near the runway, ground effect noticeably increases elevator effectiveness. At the threshold close the throttles and use a slight flare to check the sink rate; do not hold the aircraft off, which floats it, wastes runway and risks the tail. The auto slats may deploy in the flare.

**Is this the result of a dual failure of hydraulic systems 1 and 2?**
YES: when the landing is assured, release the alternate extension lever's spring latch and hold the lever aft of about 45° raised until touchdown, to keep the outboard ailerons unlocked. Restow it once firmly on the ground, to restore nosewheel steering for the rest of the rollout.
NO: continue.
On touchdown, lower the nose gear firmly to the runway and apply reverse thrust and brakes at once; full reverse may be used to a stop. Check that the spoilers extend to the ground spoiler position. After the rollout, stow the alternate extension lever. End of procedure.

children.title: SELECT FLAP LIMIT OVRD light on

blocks.content:
**Condition:** The SELECT FLAP LIMIT OVRD light with MASTER CAUTION. The flap limiter, which stops the flaps from extending beyond what the airspeed allows, has failed: its two channels disagree or have lost their airspeed. With the limiter failed in the safe sense the flaps stop at about 20°.

**Objective:** Select an override channel so the flaps can reach landing flap, and fly the flap placard speeds by hand.

If SELECT ELEV FEEL MAN is lit as well, the two central air data computers may be giving different airspeeds: see [Flight instrument malfunction](abnormal-flight-instruments#flight-instrument-failure).

**Does the FLAP LIMIT OVRD light come on (allow up to 20 seconds)?**
YES: do not exceed the flap limit placard speeds. End of procedure.
NO: FLAP LIMIT selector OVRD 2 (CAPT). If the FLAP LIMIT OVRD light then comes on, do not exceed the placard speeds. End of procedure. If it still does not, plan a 22°/EXT landing, with GPWS FLAP OVRD (FE; KC-10, the simulated DC-10 has no such switch). End of procedure.

Structural damage may result if the flap limit speeds are exceeded: with the limiter overridden, nothing but the crew protects the flaps. Do not use the autothrottles for a 22° landing. With less than 35° flaps the ground spoilers do not deploy on wheel spin-up; they deploy when the reverse levers are raised.

children.title: Stall warning or auto slat malfunction

blocks.content:
**Condition:** The slats extend by themselves with the handle at UP/RET (SLAT RESET light on), usually with the stick shaker running, at a speed and angle of attack where neither should happen. The auto slat system extends the outboard slats when a stall warning computer's angle-of-attack signal reaches its threshold, so a failed angle-of-attack vane or stall warning channel produces both symptoms together.

**Objective:** Find the faulty channel, silence it, and get the slats back in.

items.item: AT/SC STALL WARN 1 and 2 circuit breakers (AV B-13, AV D-13)
AUTO SLAT EXTEND CONT circuit breaker (UM K-8)

blocks.content: Pulling the stall warning breakers removes the false signal, and with it the autothrottles, speed control and stall warning. Cycling the auto slat control breaker and pushing SLAT RESET clears the latched extension command, and the slats retract.

**Do the SLAT RESET and SLAT DISAGREE lights stay on?**
YES: the outboard slats are still extended: do not exceed 270 KIAS or Mach 0.75, whichever is lower. Leave the AUTO SLAT EXTEND POWER breaker in and go to the RESET step below.
NO: continue with the next step.

items.item: AUTO SLAT EXTEND POWER circuit breaker (UM G-8)

blocks.content: With the auto slat power pulled, the auto slat system is disabled; resetting it is not recommended. Resetting the stall warning breakers may restore the autothrottles, speed control and stall warning. If the fault is still there the stick shaker runs again: pull the one AT/SC STALL WARN breaker that stops it. The two breakers serve the two independent channels of the dual system, so the one that silences the shaker identifies the faulty channel. End of procedure.

Pulling a stall warning breaker because the shaker ran may bring on the SLAT RESET light again, and the 1-3/2-3 PUMP VALVE OPEN light (the auto slat signal also opens the motor pump valves). Pull and reset the AUTO SLAT EXTEND CONT breaker to clear the signal. If the PUMP VALVE OPEN light will not go out, the 2-3 motor pump can dead-head system 2's engine pumps and heat its fluid: see [HYD TEMP HI](abnormal-hydraulics).

**Condition:** Level 2 alert FLAP DISAG: the flaps disagree with the handle, or with each other.

**Objective:** Match the handle to the flaps, try once to free a stuck valve, and land with a symmetrical, known configuration.

Place the flap/slat handle to match the flap position, and allow several seconds. If the alert remains, select the last symmetrical configuration. Use the abnormal configuration reference speed tables for the flap and slat setting you end up with.

**Were the flaps asymmetric?**
YES: land at the nearest suitable airport with the existing flap/slat setting. If the final flaps are less than 35°, GPWS switch FLAP OVRD; autobrakes (if installed) OFF; at 50 ft, autothrottles OFF. End of procedure.
NO: continue with the next question.

**Did the alert appear during an attempted retraction?**
YES: land at the nearest suitable airport. If the flaps are now less than 50°, further extension may be tried; if they then do not move as selected, match the handle to them. If the final flaps are less than 35°, GPWS FLAP OVRD, autobrakes OFF, and autothrottles OFF at 50 ft. End of procedure.
NO (during extension): continue with the next step.
The handle forces are higher than normal. Allow several seconds: driving the handle to the stop may let the flaps reset to normal operation.

**Do the flaps extend as desired?**
YES: no further crew action. End of procedure.
NO: return the handle to match the flaps. If the flaps are at 0°, go to [NO FLAP/SLAT EXTENDED LANDING](#md-no-flap-slat-extended). Otherwise land with the existing setting; if less than 35°, GPWS FLAP OVRD, autobrakes OFF, autothrottles OFF at 50 ft. End of procedure.
**Condition:** Level 2 alert SLAT DISAG: a slat group is not in the commanded position.

**Did the alert appear during climb-out, with the slats extended and the handle in a slat-extend position?**
YES: the stick shaker may operate briefly. If the flaps are beyond 15°, retract them to 15°; accelerate and retract the flaps and slats on schedule. Expect SLAT DISAG again on the next extension and use the *attempted extension* branch below then. End of procedure.
NO: continue.

Return the handle to the position where the alert was not displayed if it appeared while the handle was moving. If the alert is displayed with the handle in both a slat-retract and a slat-extend position, make a 22/RET landing.

**Did the alert appear during an attempted extension?**
YES: continue with the next question.
NO: plan a normal flap/slat landing. End of procedure.

**Is the flap/slat handle at 22/EXT or more?**
YES: flap/slat handle 22/EXT; do not split the handles; GPWS switch FLAP OVRD; plan a 22/EXT landing. End of procedure.
NO: continue with *22/RET landing* below.

Above 400,000 lb (Series 10) or 420,000 lb (Series 30), check the flap structural speed limits. The autothrottles do not retard by themselves at 50 ft with the flaps short of the landing range: disconnect them before 50 ft. Slow to cross the threshold at VTH, use a slight flare to check the sink rate and bring the nose to at least level, reduce thrust, and do not hold the aircraft off. At sea level the estimated landing distance is about 5,900 ft dry and 8,300 ft wet at 300,000 lb on the Series 10, and 7,900 ft dry and 11,700 ft wet at 400,000 lb on the Series 30. End of procedure.
A tail strike may occur at deck angles greater than 12°.
**Condition:** Level 2 alert SEL FLAP LIM OVRD: the flap limiter has failed. The FLAP LIMIT MANUAL light is on.

**Are SEL ELEV FEEL MAN or IAS COMPARATOR MONITOR displayed as well?**
YES: the airspeeds disagree: use the emergency procedure AIRSPEED: LOST, SUSPECT OR ERRATIC (see [Emergency Procedures](emergency-flight-path#unreliable-airspeed)). End of procedure.
NO: continue.

**After 20 seconds, is FLAP LIMIT DISAG displayed?**
YES: FLAP LIMIT selector OVRD 2 (PM). If after another 20 seconds FLAP LIMIT DISAG is still displayed, flap extension may be limited. End of procedure. If not, observe the placard flap limit speeds. End of procedure.
NO: observe the placard flap limit speeds. End of procedure.

**Condition:** Neither flaps nor slats are available for landing.

**Objective:** Land at the lowest practical weight with the outboard ailerons unlocked and a stabilized approach.

items.item: After three greens: center gear alternate extension handle (Series 30; not operable in the simulation)

blocks.content: The alternate gear extension lever is needed to unlock the outboard ailerons. With it raised, nosewheel steering to the right is limited to 25°. When dumping fuel, consider the tire speed limits: 195 kt (Series 10) and 204 kt (Series 30).

Once stabilized on the approach, slow in level flight to the approach speed. In this configuration the go-around switch sets go-around thrust limits only, with no autopilot, autothrottle or flight director guidance: fly the approach with the glareshield controls, with the autothrottles holding VAPP if available, on a normal glide slope. Disconnect the autothrottles and slow to cross the threshold at VTH; the throttles do not retard by themselves at 50 ft with the flaps short of the landing range. Close the throttles and fly no slower than VTH to touchdown with a slight flare; do not try for a smooth touchdown. On touchdown lower the nose gear firmly and apply full reverse and brakes at once; the spoilers extend when the reverse levers are raised, and full reverse may be used to a stop. End of procedure.
**Condition:** The flaps have failed at 0° with the slats extended (0/EXT).

Disconnect the autothrottles and slow to cross the threshold at VTH; reduce the sink rate slightly, close the throttles and fly to a positive touchdown. Do not try for a smooth one: an excessive flare floats the aircraft and uses runway. On touchdown lower the nose gear firmly and apply full reverse and brakes at once; full reverse may be used to a stop. End of procedure.
A tail strike may occur at pitch angles greater than 12°.

children.title: SELECT ELEV FEEL MAN light on

blocks.content:
**Condition:** The SELECT ELEV FEEL MAN light with MASTER CAUTION. The automatic elevator feel system is no longer holding its feel reference airspeed in step with the aircraft's airspeed. The feel unit makes the column force grow with speed, so that the pilot cannot overstress the aircraft at high speed with a light pull, nor find it heavy at low speed; with the feel stuck at the wrong speed the column is either too light (dangerously so at high speed) or too heavy (in the flare).

**Objective:** Take the feel to manual and keep it matched to the airspeed by hand.
If SELECT FLAP LIMIT OVRD is lit as well, the two central air data computers may disagree on airspeed: see [Flight instrument malfunction](abnormal-flight-instruments#flight-instrument-failure).

items.action: SET FEEL REFERENCE TO AIRCRAFT IAS

blocks.content: Rotate the slew selector until the elevator feel reference IAS pointer approximately matches the aircraft's IAS, and keep it matched as the speed changes through the rest of the flight, especially through the approach. End of procedure.

**Condition:** The horizontal stabilizer does not move with the control wheel trim switches, the ALTN trim switches or the long (longitudinal) trim handles. (If it will not trim nose up with the wheel switches but will with the long trim handles, continue the flight and log the fault.) Pitch is now trimmed only by holding the elevator, and the further the aircraft moves from the speed and configuration at which the stabilizer stopped, the more elevator, and the more column force, is needed.

**Objective:** Reduce the column forces, keep the configuration changes small, and land at a speed that leaves enough elevator authority for the flare.
**Consequence:** Land at the nearest suitable airport. Avoid turbulence as far as practical.

items.item: PRIMARY HORIZ STAB TRIM circuit breaker (UM J-5)
HOR STAB ALTN TRIM CONT circuit breaker (AV E-18)

blocks.content:
Once the stabilizer is known to be inoperative, do not keep trying the long trim handles: an intermittent drive can produce an unwanted trim change, and a stalled motor can overheat. **Are the flaps at 35°/EXT or 50°/EXT, with the aircraft in trim before the stabilizer failed?**
YES: land with the existing flap/slat setting. End of procedure.
NO: continue with the next step.

items.action: HOLD IN DECR UNTIL FEEL FORCE AS DESIRED

blocks.content: Control wheel steering reduces the column pressure needed against the out-of-trim condition, but disengages if the control forces become excessive, which needs prompt action. Disconnect the autopilot by the final approach fix at the latest and fly the landing by hand, ready for heavier than normal forces.

Make the approach and landing with flap/slat handle 35°/EXT; if the flaps are at 50° and the aircraft is trimmed there, land with 50°. Transfer fuel to move the CG toward the value that gives the smallest speed additive, determine the additive from the table for the stabilizer setting and CG, and fly the 35° threshold speed plus the additive.

blocks.title: Stabilizer inoperative threshold speed additive (KIAS), Series 10
Stabilizer inoperative threshold speed additive (KIAS), Series 30

blocks.content: With the CG known, add the additive to the normal VAPP, but not beyond VREF + 25. With the CG not known, add 5 kt to VREF if the stabilizer failed during the approach phase, otherwise 25 kt, and fly VAPP at the new VREF + 5. In every case set the MAN SLEW to minimum feel before landing.

blocks.title: Stabilizer inoperative threshold speed additive (KIAS), KC-10

blocks.content: Avoid a high sink rate and keep thrust on until the flare is made. The elevator may already be partly deflected to hold trim, so its response is slower than normal: be ready to use full column force for the flare. In a go-around, use the normal procedure but do not let the speed fall below the 35° threshold speed plus the additive.

Why the CG matters: with the stabilizer frozen, the elevator alone must balance the change in pitching moment between the trimmed condition and the landing. A forward CG needs more nose-up elevator in the flare, and a stabilizer stuck nose down leaves less of it, so the speed additive is largest in the top left of the table: forward CG with a nose-down stabilizer. Moving the CG aft by fuel transfer is the one thing the crew can do to reduce it. End of procedure.
**Condition:** Level 2 alert SEL ELEV FEEL MAN: the automatic elevator feel has failed to keep its reference speed matched to the airspeed.

**Are SEL FLAP LIM OVRD or IAS COMPARATOR MONITOR displayed as well?**
YES: the airspeeds disagree: use AIRSPEED: LOST, SUSPECT OR ERRATIC (see [Emergency Procedures](emergency-flight-path#unreliable-airspeed)). End of procedure.
NO: continue.
With the ELEV FEEL selector in MANUAL, the feel reference (ELF) speed is shown on the CONFIG synoptic. Slew it to stay approximately matched to the indicated airspeed. End of procedure.
**Condition:** Level 2 alert STAB OUT OF TRIM: with the autopilot engaged, the stabilizer is not following the autopilot's trim demand.

Watch the stabilizer position on the CONFIG synoptic for an autotrim response. **After 5 seconds, is there still no trim response?**
YES: push the AUTOFLIGHT switch (PF), and continue with the next question.
NO: no further crew action. End of procedure.

**Does the stabilizer fail to move?**
YES: firmly hold the control wheel against any abrupt pitching as the autopilot lets go; autopilot DISCONNECT; trim with the control wheel trim switches or the pedestal LONG TRIM handles. If the stabilizer still fails to move, go to [STABILIZER INOPERATIVE](#md-stabilizer-inoperative). End of procedure.
NO: no further crew action. End of procedure.

**Condition:** The stabilizer will not move by any trim means. There is no alert of its own.

**Objective:** Reduce the column forces and land at a speed that leaves enough elevator for the flare.

**Is the aircraft in trim with the landing flaps set?**
YES: land with the existing flap/slat setting. End of procedure.
NO: continue.
Slew the elevator feel reference speed on the CONFIG page to the speed wanted, and update it as required.

**Are the slats available?**
YES: plan a 35/EXT landing, and add the stabilizer inoperative speed additive to the normal VAPP. Take it from the tables below, by series, stabilizer setting and CG.
