If the stabilizer setting or the CG is unknown, add 20 kt. The landing distance increases by about 1% for each knot added. Hold the adjusted VAPP to touchdown.
NO: plan a 22/RET approach and landing with the slats-retracted abnormal configuration speeds, and GPWS switch FLAP OVRD. End of procedure.

blocks.title: Stabilizer inoperative threshold speed additive (KIAS), Series 10
Stabilizer inoperative threshold speed additive (KIAS), Series 30

blocks.content: Disconnect the autopilot no later than the final approach fix, ready for higher than normal forces. Avoid a high sink rate and keep thrust on until the flare. The elevator may be partly displaced and respond slower than normal: be ready for maximum control force in the flare. In a go-around, do not let the speed fall below VAPP.

children.title: AUTO SPOILER DO NOT USE light on / auto spoilers inoperative

blocks.content:
**Condition:** The AUTO SPOILER DO NOT USE light is on, or has been on at any time in the flight; or the spoiler handle will not arm; or the spoilers are to be extended by hand on landing for any other reason. The automatic ground spoiler control unit has a fault. Without the ground spoilers deployed at touchdown, the wing keeps much of its lift, little weight goes onto the wheels, and the brakes cannot do their work: the landing roll lengthens.

**Objective:** Land with the handle stowed and deploy the ground spoilers by hand as soon as the nose gear is down.

Increase the landing field length for the lost automatic extension. After the nose gear touches down, the pilot calls “ground spoilers” and the flight engineer moves the spoiler handle fully aft and up. With the automatic system inoperative, the in-flight lockout gate stops the handle moving aft until the nosewheel is on the ground. End of procedure.
**Condition:** Level 2 alert USE MAN SPOILERS: the automatic ground spoilers will not deploy by themselves.

blocks.title: Estimated landing distance with manual spoilers, sea level, 35/EXT (ft)

blocks.content: Standard day, no wind, zero slope, three engines at maximum reverse to 80 KIAS, reverse idle to 60 KIAS, then forward idle to a stop, air distance included. The QRH gives the full tables for 35/EXT and 50/EXT up to 10,000 ft with temperature, slope and wind corrections. End of procedure.

sections.title: Loss of control by conventional inputs

children.title: LOSS OF CONTROL BY CONVENTIONAL PILOT INPUTS

blocks.content:
**Condition:** The aircraft does not respond to the control wheel, column or pedals: the mechanical path from the pilots' controls to the surface actuators has been damaged or jammed. The autopilot may still work, because its servos act directly on valves mounted at the primary surface actuators, downstream of the damaged cables.

**Objective:** Fly the aircraft through the autopilot's modes to a landing.

The autopilot rolls the wings level and holds the existing heading and vertical speed. If its lever will not stay at CMD, or control is not regained, move the other autopilot lever to CMD. Hydraulic system 2 must be working for autopilot 1, systems 1 and 3 for autopilot 2, and system 1 or 2 for the automatic pitch trim.

Steer with the heading select (pull the heading knob for HDG SEL) and change altitude with the vertical speed wheel (VERT SPD or ALT HOLD in the pitch FMA). Speed is held by the autothrottle on the speed control knob.

items.item: At the final approach descent point: vertical speed wheel

blocks.content: About 50 ft above the runway, reduce the descent with the vertical speed wheel to give the landing attitude. After the main gear touches down, wind in a descent to lower the nose gear. After the nose gear is down, push the autopilot release button twice (to disengage and silence the flashing AP fail lights), keep the runway alignment by hand, and select reverse thrust; the autothrottle levers drop to OFF, and the autothrottle disengage button puts out the flashing ATS fail lights. End of procedure.

A coupled ILS approach may be flown: set the ILS frequency and course and push the ILS mode switch on a localizer intercept heading. Rotating the vertical speed wheel to flare at about 50 ft disengages the ILS mode (the FMAs show HDG HOLD and VERT SPD).

Every flight control surface's actuators, supplies and rates are modeled, and a surface that loses its power, or a control link that is failed, takes over that axis of the flight model, so the failures in this part are felt in the handling. These points affect the procedures.

items: **Center gear.** The center gear alternate extension handle is not operable in the simulation. On the -30, -40 and KC-10, a center gear that cannot extend on system 3 stays up: select the CTR GEAR switch to UP and land with it retracted, allowing for the landing weight limits without the center gear. With system 3 lost and the gear handle at DOWN, the main and nose gear fall by themselves in the simulation even before the alternate extension lever is raised.

**Flaps fail to move, both sides** jams the flap control valve: the tapes hold and the command pointer follows the handle. The momentary 50°/EXT that may free a sticking valve is not modeled, so the procedure always ends on its NO branch. **One side** disconnects that side's drive: the other runs on until the skew brake stops it just under 6° of skew and FLAP DISAGREE comes into view. The brake always lets the flaps move back toward symmetry, so returning the handle to the last symmetrical position works, and a cleared failure brings the flaps back into line.

**Flaps and slats fail retracted** jams both control valves where they are: arm it before the flaps come out if you want the no-flap/no-slat case. The auto slat system still extends the outboard slats, and the outboard ailerons stay locked until the main gear alternate extension lever is raised.
**Slat disagree** jams an outboard slat group (a real asymmetry), the inboard group (the light only), or misaligns a proximity sensor (a false light, nothing moves).

**Flap limit failure** fails both limiter channels: the flaps stop at 20° and SELECT FLAP LIMIT OVRD lights; OVRD still takes the flaps on. On the DC-10 and KC-10 the light does not come on merely for the FLAP LIMIT selector being out of AUTO. On the MD-10 the FLAP LIMIT MANUAL lamp lights only with an override selected, and FLAP LIMIT DISAG is not modeled, so the OVRD steps of SEL FLAP LIM OVRD do not show it. The flap limiter uses the KC-10's placard schedule on every aircraft; on the DC-10 and MD-10 fly the placard speeds yourself in the lower flap range.

**Elevator feel failure** fails both feel channels: AUTO is lost and MAN slew still drives the feel. Without force-feedback hardware the column force cannot be felt. On the MD-10 the ELEV FEEL knob has no pulled position: any position other than AUTO is manual and keeps slewing while it is held there.

**Stabilizer trim inoperative** jams the stabilizer against the wheel switches, ALTN trim, the long trim handles and the autopilot. The PRIMARY HORIZ STAB TRIM and AUTO PITCH TRIM breakers in the DC-10 checklist have no effect in the simulation; HOR STAB ALTN TRIM CONT does. The MD-10 STAB OUT OF TRIM alert is raised.

**Auto ground spoilers inoperative** fails the control unit: AUTO SPOILER DO NOT USE (MD-10: USE MAN SPOILERS, and DISARM SPOILERS if armed). The GROUND SPOILER handle position can be reached only on the ground, which matches the procedure.

**Flight controls unresponsive** cuts the crew's link to all three axes: the aircraft stops following the yoke and pedals, while the autopilot at CMD still flies it. Control wheel steering goes with the link. The MD-10 has the same failure and the same autopilot capability, but its manual has no procedure for it.

**Stall warning or auto slat fault** fails the Captain's angle-of-attack vane to full scale while still reading valid: both stick shakers run and the auto slats extend. The AT/SC STALL WARN and AUTO SLAT EXTEND breakers act as the procedure expects. The auto slat extension takes the outboard slats to the takeoff position rather than a separate smaller angle, and the flight engineer's AUTO SLAT EXTEND test switch is not modeled. On the MD-10 the stall warning is the simulator's own, with no FCC logic and no STALL WARN FAIL alert, so this failure has no MD-10 procedure.

**GPWS FLAP OVRD.** The simulated DC-10 has no FLAP OVRD switch (the KC-10 and MD-10 have one), so on the DC-10 the GPWS flap warning cannot be overridden for a landing with less than the landing flaps: expect it, and disregard it once the configuration is confirmed.

**Not modeled:** the MD-10's FCC DATA FAULT, AUTO SLAT FAIL, AUTO TRIM FAIL and SLATS INHIBITED alerts; primary surface jams, a stabilizer runaway and spoiler panel jams. FedEx's jammed flap/slat handle, jammed spoiler handle, unresponsive rudder pedal and OVRD LIGHTS BOTH procedures are left out because nothing in the simulation produces those conditions.

parts.title: Flight Instruments and Automatic Flight
parts.summary: Air data, attitude source and display failures, and yaw damper faults.

blocks.content: This part covers failures of the air data (pitot, static and the central air data computers), the attitude sources and the attitude and heading displays, and the yaw dampers. Unreliable airspeed of unknown cause and a damaged nose radome are in [Miscellaneous](abnormal-miscellaneous#suspect-airspeed) for the DC-10 and KC-10, and are an emergency on the MD-10 ([Airspeed lost, suspect or erratic](emergency-flight-path#unreliable-airspeed)). How the instruments work is in [Flight Instruments](flight-instruments) and [Automatic Flight](automatic-flight).

The instruments are built in two independent sides: the Captain's on CADC 1 and inertial platform (or vertical gyro) 1, the First Officer's on CADC 2 and platform 2, with a third source of each as the alternate and the standby instruments as the last resort. Each side normally reads only its own sources, so that comparing the two sides detects a failure. The procedures follow from that: identify the failed source by comparison (the side that disagrees with the standby instruments and with physics is the failed one), switch the affected side onto a good source with the source selectors, and couple the autopilot and autothrottle to the side that is still good, because a channel follows the air data of its own side.

blocks.title: Failures you can practice
rows: Captain's or first officer's airspeed indication failure
Captain's or first officer's static system blocked
Captain's or first officer's attitude display failure
Captain's or first officer's HSI display failure
Upper or lower yaw damper inoperative
YAW DMP CHAN FAIL (channel A only; no procedure). [YAW DAMP ALL FAIL](#md-yaw-damp-all-fail) needs every channel failed or off

blocks.content: The EFB's instrument and auto flight failures are listed in [EFB failures: flight controls](efb#failures-flt).

blocks.title: MD-10 instrument and auto flight Level 1 alerts
rows: YAW DAMP ALL OFF, YAW DMP UPR/LWR A/B OFF
Yaw damper channels are switched off.
GPWS FAIL, GPWS FAULT, TERRAIN FAIL, TERRAIN NOT AVAIL
The ground proximity or terrain function is lost or degraded.
A transponder has failed; select the other.

blocks.content:
**Condition:** One pilot's airspeed, altimeter or vertical speed disagrees with the other's and with the standby instruments, or shows its warning flags. The cause is one of three: the CADC itself has failed (all three of that side's air data instruments flag together); that side's pitot system is blocked or leaking (airspeed wrong, altimeter and vertical speed normal); or that side's static system is blocked (altimeter frozen, vertical speed at zero, airspeed wrong in a characteristic way). SELECT FLAP LIMIT OVRD and SELECT ELEV FEEL MAN may come on together, because the flap limiter and the feel system compare the two CADCs' airspeeds.

**Objective:** Identify which of the three it is, and put both sides and the automatics on good air data.

Do not use this procedure if the left or right emergency AC bus is unpowered: losing the left one fails the Captain's instruments, and the right one the First Officer's. The standby airspeed and altimeter remain. If PITOT HEAT INOP is lit, see [PITOT HEAT INOP light on](abnormal-ice-and-rain).

**Are that side's airspeed, vertical speed and altimeter warning flags all in view?**
YES: the CADC has failed; go to *CADC failure* below.
NO: continue with the next question.

**Is only the airspeed wrong, with the altimeter and vertical speed normal?**
YES: pitot malfunction; go to *Pitot malfunction* below.
NO (altimeter frozen, vertical speed zero, or both wrong): static malfunction; go to *Static malfunction* below.

items.item: CADC circuit breaker (CADC 1 OH F-6, CADC 2 OH F-21)

items.action: BOTH ON 2 (CADC 1 FAILED) OR BOTH ON 1 (CADC 2 FAILED)
BOTH ON 2 OR BOTH ON 1 (THE GOOD SIDE)

blocks.content: Check the transponder's altitude reporting with ATC, since it may come from the failed CADC. With both sides on one CADC, the airspeed pointers and altimeters work (the good side's barometric knob sets both) but the failed side's vertical speed indicator stays inoperative and its ADI speed flag remains. A failed thrust rating computer leaves the N1 limits at about 90%: if the autothrottle is wanted, compute the N1 limit and set the bugs by hand; with CADC 1 failed the autothrottle is available in speed mode only. The KC-10's FMS loses true airspeed and altitude from the failed CADC, and its boom flight controls are degraded. A trip and reset of the failed CADC's breaker may restore it; if so, return the CADC selector to NORM. Two-CADC aircraft with one CADC operative are limited to CAT I approaches. End of procedure.

items.action: BOTH ON 2 (CAPTAIN'S BAD) OR BOTH ON 1 (F/O'S BAD)

blocks.content: A completely blocked pitot traps its pressure: as long as the static port is clear, the airspeed then **increases** in a climb and **decreases** in a descent, the reverse of reality, because the instrument now reads the falling static pressure against a fixed total pressure. If the airspeeds cannot be trusted at all, go to [Airspeed lost, suspect or erratic](abnormal-miscellaneous#suspect-airspeed). Switching the CADC selector does not change which air data the overspeed warning, autothrottle or autopilot use; a false overspeed warning from the bad side can be silenced by pulling that CADC's breaker (which takes its CADC with it). If the SELECT FLAP LIMIT OVRD and SELECT ELEV FEEL MAN lights came on and the airspeeds are restored, pull and reset the four ELEV LOAD FEEL & FLAP LIMIT breakers to reset those warnings. End of procedure.

With a static system blocked, the altimeter and vertical speed show level flight whatever the aircraft does, and the airspeed **decreases** in a climb and **increases** in a descent. With a leak, both read wrongly.

**Do the instruments return to normal on the alternate static source?**
YES: End of procedure.
NO: the alternate source is blocked as well. Use the CADC and flight director selectors BOTH ON the good side to restore normal indications, and use the autopilot and autothrottle of the good side only: the Captain's source blocked, autopilot 2 and autothrottle 2; the First Officer's blocked, autopilot 1 and autothrottle 1. Do not trust the FMS true airspeed or ETAs from the bad CADC. If icing is the likely cause and the probe heat has failed, leave the icing conditions and find warmer air. End of procedure.

**Condition:** One pilot's airspeed or altitude disagrees with the other's and with the standby instruments; on the PFD the comparison monitor flags the disagreement. The MD-10 has no Level 2 alert or abnormal procedure of its own for a single air data source: an unreliable airspeed is handled with the emergency procedure AIRSPEED: LOST, SUSPECT OR ERRATIC (see [Airspeed lost, suspect or erratic](emergency-flight-path#unreliable-airspeed)), and SEL FLAP LIM OVRD or SEL ELEV FEEL MAN with an airspeed disagreement send the crew there too.

The physics of the failure are the same as on the DC-10: a blocked pitot makes the airspeed rise in a climb and fall in a descent; a blocked static port freezes the altimeter and the vertical speed, and makes the airspeed fall in a climb and rise in a descent. Fly pitch and thrust, compare the three sources, and use the side that agrees with the standby instruments. End of procedure.

**Condition:** Both pilots' primary attitude indications fail (ADI flags, or the attitude displays lose their attitude), because the primary sources behind them, the inertial platforms or vertical gyros 1 and 2, have failed. The standby horizon, with its own gyro on the battery bus, remains.

**Objective:** Fly on the standby instruments while restoring attitude from any platform that is still good.

**Has the third source (unit 3, or the auxiliary gyro) failed as well?** (KC-10: the CDU shows the INU annunciation for all three units.)
YES: continue the flight on the standby instruments. Mode selectors OFF (PM). End of procedure.
NO (units 1 and 2 failed, unit 3 good): INS selector CAPT ON AUX (CAPT): the Captain's attitude and heading now come from unit 3. Mode selectors 1 and 2 OFF (PM). End of procedure.

Once a mode selector leaves NAV, that unit's navigation cannot be recovered in flight. On units with an ATT REF position, ATT REF may be selected for the final approach; after selecting it, hold the wings level and the speed constant for at least 5 minutes while the gyros settle. With CAPT ON AUX selected, everything that normally takes unit 1's signals takes unit 3's instead.

**Condition:** One pilot's attitude indicator (ADI or EADI) or horizontal situation indicator (HSI or EHSI) fails: an electromechanical instrument shows its flags and freezes; an electronic one goes dark. The source behind it (the CADC, the platform, the compass) is still working and still feeds the other pilot and the autopilot.

**Objective:** Confirm it is the display and not its source, restore it if a breaker has tripped, and fly from the other pilot's side.

items.action: TRANSFER TO THE PILOT WITH THE GOOD DISPLAY IF APPROPRIATE

blocks.content: KC-10: the EADIs are MFD 1 (pilot) and MFD 3 (copilot), the EHSIs MFD 2 and MFD 4 on the DISP STATUS page. An EADI failure also takes that side's CADC data to its CDU, the INUs and the GPSs, its terrain display on the EHSI, and the miscompare function with the other EADI: set the CADC switch BOTH ON 1 or BOTH ON 2 as required, but switching it more than once affects the boom. An EHSI failure loses that side's Direct-To on the display control panel and some bearing pointers on the other side's EHSI; the display control panel's ADI/PFD button can put a composite display on the remaining screen. End of procedure.

DC-10: fly from the other pilot's instruments, with the standby horizon as the cross-check. Couple the autopilot to the side whose display is working, and use the other side's HSI for navigation. End of procedure.
**Condition:** A primary flight display or navigation display unit fails: it shows a red X, or goes dark. The ADIRU, air data and FMS data behind it are still good.

The display panel reconfigures automatically: the formats are reallocated among the units still working, keeping the PFDs and the engine and alert display in preference to the NDs and the systems display. A failed PFD unit (DU 1 or DU 6) therefore moves that pilot's PFD onto the adjacent ND unit, and a failed ND unit simply loses the map on that side. Monitor the reconfigured displays and cross-check with the standby instruments. If both of one pilot's units fail, fly from the other pilot's side. End of procedure.

children.title: UPPER/LOWER YAW DAMP INOP light(s) on

blocks.content:
**Condition:** An UPPER or LOWER YAW DAMP INOP light: a yaw damper, which damps the aircraft's Dutch roll through its rudder segment, has failed its self-monitor. Each damper has two channels, A and B, and a comparator that latches the damper INOP when the channels disagree, so a single channel failure (a hardover, for example) takes the damper out until the good channel is found.

**Objective:** Restore the damper on whichever channel is good.

**Is aircraft control normal?**
YES: continue on channel A. End of procedure.
NO: switch A OFF and switch B ON (CAPT). If the behavior is then normal, continue on channel B. End of procedure. If not, switch B OFF and continue with that damper inoperative. End of procedure.

There is no limitation with all yaw dampers inoperative: smooth flying prevents an inadvertent Dutch roll. Any one yaw damper switch ON with its damper working allows either autopilot to be engaged in CWS or CMD.

Why one channel at a time: with the comparator latched there is no way to tell from the light which channel failed. Running each channel alone, and watching for the yaw kick or rudder offset that a bad channel produces, finds the good one; the damper then works without its comparator's protection, so it is watched.

**Condition:** Level 2 alert YAW DAMP ALL FAIL: every yaw damper channel has failed. (YAW DMP CHAN FAIL, also Level 2, means one channel has failed and the others carry on; it needs no action beyond noting it.)

**Does its FAIL light come on?**
YES: that channel has failed: push it OFF.
NO: that channel is restored.
Try to restore the remaining channels the same way, one at a time, pushing OFF any switch whose FAIL light comes on before pushing the next. End of procedure.

The pitot-static systems are simulated as pressures, so a blocked pitot reads high in a climb and a blocked static freezes the altimeter, and the air data, attitude sources and displays are modeled separately, so a display failure leaves its source working. The differences that matter:

items: **Injected failures.** Airspeed indication failure blocks that side's pitot; static system blocked blocks both of that side's static ports (the alternate static source is clear, so the ALT position restores the instruments). Loss of primary attitude fails both pilots' primary sources (vertical gyros, inertial platforms and ADIRUs 1 and 2); the standby is what is left, and an autopilot channel drops with its attitude reference. Attitude display failure and HSI display failure fail the display only: a steam ADI stops with every flag in view, an electronic display goes dark (the KC-10's DISP STATUS shows the MFD NGO), the MD-10 PFD or ND shows a red X and the panel reconfigures. Yaw damper inoperative is channel A hard over: the comparator latches INOP, and the one-channel-at-a-time procedure finds it.
**Pitot heater select.** The PITOT HEATER SELECT switches are not modeled, so the KC-10 checklist's step of selecting the other heater system in the pitot malfunction branch is omitted.

**FD CMD selector.** On the DC-10 the FD CMD selector lights the ADI's FD light but does not move the command bars to the other side's flight director; on the KC-10 it is not operative. The KC-10's transponder CADC selector and FMS sensor-aid steps are not included.

**MD-10 source switches.** Of the source input select panel switches, only IRS is operative: the CADC switch and the EIS SOURCE selector do nothing, so an MD-10 air data failure cannot be switched away from the flight deck.

**Not included.** The KC-10's FMS bus, data link and BSIU procedures (CNS/ATM equipment not fitted to the simulated aircraft) and FedEx's glideslope alert procedure (a GPWS mode handled in [Weather Radar and Surveillance](surveillance)).

parts.title: Navigation and Communications
parts.summary: Inertial unit, CDU and GPS failures, divergence between units, and the MD-10's IRU and FMS failures.

blocks.content: This part covers the long-range navigation equipment: the inertial units and their control and display units, GPS, divergence between units, and the MD-10's inertial reference units and flight management computers. Each variant carries its own long-range fit (the DC-10s the AINS-70, the Carousel IV-A, the INS-61B or the HT9100; the KC-10 its FMS with LTN-101 inertial units; the MD-10 its ADIRUs and FMS), described in [Navigation](navigation) and [Flight Management](flight-management). The procedures here are written for the logic all of them share; the unit's own section of Section 1 explains its displays.

Inertial navigation fails gracefully, which makes its failures easy to miss. A unit that is drifting still shows a position, and only comparison with another unit, or with a radio fix, reveals the drift. The procedures therefore rest on cross-checking: with three units, the odd one out is the faulty one; with two that disagree, ground speed, radio aids and the flight plan decide which to believe. Communications have no abnormal procedures of their own in these manuals beyond ELT activation; a lost radio is handled by selecting another set, and the radios are described in [Communications](communications).
The EFB's navigation failures are listed in [EFB failures: flight controls](efb#failures-flt).

blocks.title: MD-10 navigation Level 1 alerts
rows: The IRU's navigation function has failed; its attitude may still be good.
The IRU did not complete its alignment.
The IRU is running on its battery.
That transponder has failed: select the other.

blocks.content:
**Condition:** An inertial unit has failed: its CDU warning light (WARN) or status page reports a failure, its attitude and heading flags appear on the instruments it feeds, or its position and ground speed have become unreasonable. On the KC-10 the INU status is on the NAV STATUS page.

**Objective:** Fly on another source, and give the affected pilot's instruments the third unit.
Do not use this procedure if the abnormalities come from an electrical power failure: restore the power first, using the electrical procedures.

Heading select or hold first, because an autopilot coupled to a failed unit's navigation may follow it. **Which unit has failed?**
UNIT 3: units 1 and 2 still feed the instruments and the navigation; no further action. End of procedure.
UNIT 1: INS selector CAPT ON AUX (PM). End of procedure.
UNIT 2: INS selector F/O ON AUX (PM). End of procedure.

With the INS selector at CAPT ON AUX (or F/O ON AUX), every instrument and system that normally takes attitude and heading from unit 1 (or unit 2) takes it from unit 3. On the KC-10, unit 3's messages then appear under unit 1's (or unit 2's) name, and an INU ON BACKUP PWR annunciation may flash briefly as the power transfers; the failure of INU 2 also costs its mixed navigation solution. If navigation must be continued with two units, see [Single INS failure](#single-ins-failure).

**Condition:** A navigation control and display unit fails: it goes blank, freezes or locks with FAULT lit (AINS-70). The computer behind it may still be navigating, and on the separate-box installations it is.

**Objective:** Keep navigating on the other unit and couple the autopilot to it.

**CDU 1 or CDU 2 failed:** use the autopilot of the other side (CDU 1 failed, autopilot 2; CDU 2 failed, autopilot 1), because only that side can still be coupled to long-range navigation. Re-enter route changes on the working CDU. End of procedure.

**Both CDU 1 and CDU 2 failed:** long-range navigation is lost; only VOR (and on the KC-10 TACAN and ADF, left on the stations they were tuned to) remain. Navigate by radio and tell ATC. End of procedure.

KC-10: CDU 1 failure takes FMS 1's navigation from CDU 2 and the pilot's EADI and EHSI, with INU 1's self test and GPS 1 selection; CDU 2 failure the same for side 2. Either may show NO ATC COMM, needing a new data link log-on. A CDU 3 failure leaves navigation intact but takes GPS 3, the fuel totalizer input and the altitude pre-select input to the FMS.

**Condition:** A GPS receiver fails (HT9100: GPS RECEIVER FAIL; KC-10 FMS: GPS NGO on the status page). The navigation reverts to the inertial units, updated by radio where the system can, and begins to drift.

**Objective:** Use the best navigation solution left.

KC-10: **Is GPS 1 or GPS 2 still available?**
YES: navigation solution CIV 1 or CIV 2 as required (PM). A single GPS failure in flight reverts automatically to the surviving GPS, and the failed one is not used again even if it recovers. End of procedure.
NO, but GPS 3 is: MIL 1 or MIL 2 as required (PM); the MIL solution is not approved in every airspace. End of procedure.
NO GPS at all: CIV 1 or CIV 2 as required (PM): even without GPS, the CIV solutions navigate more accurately than an inertial-only solution. End of procedure.

DC-10 (HT9100): with the GPS failed the unit continues by dead reckoning on its inertial and air data inputs. Cross-check the position with radio aids, tell ATC of any reduced navigation capability, and expect the position to drift with time. End of procedure.

**Condition:** Two inertial units' cross-track, distance-to-go or ETA readouts disagree and the disagreement is growing. (Not needed while any two operating units are within 12 nm of each other.) With two units, keep the unit not used for guidance displaying cross-track and track error, and compare distance and ETA periodically, so that divergence is caught early.

**Objective:** Decide which unit is right, or steer between them safely.

A lit WARN light identifies the faulty unit (see its malfunction codes in Section 1). If one unit is clearly at fault, use the other and continue with [Single INS failure](#single-ins-failure). Otherwise: **Is the divergence over 25 nm?**
YES: monitor the computer flight plan; steering its magnetic headings and ETEs is usually the best choice, updated with the latest wind data if the plan was already in error. A sudden divergence shows in the ground speed readouts: an abnormal jump marks the faulty unit. Use the weather radar for mapping. If the faulty unit cannot be found, see [Failure of all INS units](#all-ins-failure). End of procedure.
NO: continue with *Divergence of 25 nm or less* below.

items.action: CHECK WITH GROUND AIDS AND RADAR

blocks.content: If one unit is shown to be the more accurate, navigate on it. Until then, split the cross-track difference and steer the middle, and for along-track divergence base the ETAs on the average distance and ground speed. Tell ATC the navigation is unreliable, and ask other aircraft for wind data and, on an organized track, look for their contrails. End of procedure.

Why the ground speed is the tell-tale: an inertial unit's position error grows from its accelerometer and gyro errors, and it shows first as a velocity error. A platform whose gyro has failed suddenly shows a ground speed that jumps or wanders away from the other units' and from the flight plan's, long before its position is far off.
**Condition:** Operating on two inertial units, one fails. (With three units and one failure, no action is needed.)

items.item: Position, time and navigation data of the remaining unit

items.action: ADVISE OF PARTIAL LOSS OF LONG RANGE NAVIGATION

blocks.content: Check the remaining unit against every aid available: VOR/DME, NDB and broadcast station bearings, the weather radar's ground mapping. Oceanic and remote airspace usually requires two working long-range systems for entry: tell ATC, who may re-route or restrict the flight. End of procedure.
**Condition:** No inertial unit can be trusted for navigation.

Navigate by the computer flight plan's magnetic headings and times, corrected with the latest winds, and by every radio aid and radar fix available; tell ATC at once, since the aircraft can no longer meet long-range navigation requirements. Attitude may still be available from units that have failed only in navigation; see [LOSS OF ALL ATTITUDE INDICATIONS](abnormal-flight-instruments#loss-of-attitude) if attitude is lost too. End of procedure.

**Condition:** The emergency locator transmitter is transmitting without an emergency: heard on 121.5 MHz, or reported by ATC.

On the ELT control panel, check the ARMED/ON switch at ARMED, then press and hold TEST/RESET until the LED acknowledges with two short blinks. Tell ATC, with the registration (the 406 MHz signal identifies the aircraft), so that a search is not begun. End of procedure.

The ELT is not modeled in the simulation.
**Condition:** Level 2 alert IRU 1, IRU 2 or IRU AUX FAIL: that inertial reference unit has failed. Its attitude, heading and navigation are lost to the displays and systems it feeds.

**Is IRU 1 off?**
YES: IRS switch on the Captain's source input select panel CAPT ON AUX (PM).
NO: continue.
**Is IRU 2 off?**
YES: IRS switch on the First Officer's panel F/O ON AUX (PM).
NO: continue.
An auxiliary IRU failure alone needs no switching. End of procedure.

**Condition:** An MCDU fails (FAIL, blank screen), or a GNSS receiver loses its satellites. With one MCDU and one FMS computer still working, the other side's MCDU and FMS carry the navigation; the FMS continues with radio and inertial position updating if GPS is lost. Both FMS computers failing is the FMS DUAL FAILURE procedure.

With a single MCDU or GPS failure, continue on the working side: make route changes on the working MCDU and monitor the FMS position against radio aids. With both FMS computers failed, the FMS DUAL FAILURE procedure applies: both MCDUs go to standby navigation, vertical navigation and the autothrottles are not available, approach speeds come from the QRH performance tables, low speed protection and the FMS STARs and approaches are lost, and only the SINGLE LAND and APPR ONLY ILS modes remain; climb at 330 KIAS and Mach 0.83 (Series 10) or 340 KIAS and Mach 0.82 (Series 30) for a high-speed climb. End of procedure.

items: **Inertial nav unit failure** fails that platform and the box the fitted unit uses: the AINS-70's inertial sensor system, the CIV-A box (malfunction code 33), the INS-61B box (STATUS 0000), the KC-10 INU (NO DATA), or the MD-10 ADIRU 1, 2 or AUX. A cleared failure does not give the reference back: the unit realigns from cold, so in the air it does not navigate again.

**Nav CDU failure** fails that box's CDU: the AINS-70 and ANS-70 CDU locks up with FAULT lit and the other reads FAULT CDUn; the CIV-A, INS-61B and HT9100 faces go dark; the KC-10 FMS CDU goes dark and reads NO DATA; on the MD-10 the MCDU shows FAIL with a blank screen. Where the computer is a separate box it navigates on.
**GPS failure** fails the HT9100's receiver (GPS RECEIVER FAIL, then dead reckoning), the KC-10 FMS's GPS (NGO) or the MD-10's GNSSU (no satellites).

**INS selector.** On the DC-10 the INS selector transfers attitude and heading to platform 3 but does not change which long-range box drives a pilot's HSI. On the KC-10 the INU batteries are not simulated: any power interruption drops an INU, and in the air it returns in ATT only.
**MD-10.** Only the IRS source switch is functional, and it lights no switch-light and shows no IRS AUX on the ND.
**ELT.** The emergency locator transmitter and its control panel are not modeled on any deck, so ELT UNINTENTIONAL ACTIVATION cannot arise.

**Not included.** The KC-10's FMS bus, data link and BSIU procedures, for CNS/ATM equipment not fitted to the simulated aircraft, and FedEx's INS action and malfunction message tables, which belong to the units' own descriptions in [Navigation](navigation).

parts.title: Landing Gear and Brakes
parts.summary: Gear handle and unsafe gear indications, landing with an abnormal gear configuration, anti-skid, autobrake and hot brakes, and ground sensing failures.

blocks.content: This part covers the landing gear and brakes: a gear handle that will not move, unsafe gear indications with the handle up or down, the landing with a gear leg that will not extend, anti-skid and autobrake failures, hot brakes, and a ground sensing system stuck in ground mode. How the gear works is in [Landing Gear and Brakes](landing-gear). Evacuation after a gear-up landing is in [Emergency Procedures](emergency-landing#evacuation).

The gear is extended and retracted by hydraulic system 3, and every leg can also free-fall: the main gear alternate extension lever releases the main and nose gear uplocks and doors mechanically, and on the -30, -40, KC-10 and MD-10-30 a separate handle releases the center gear. Gravity and the airflow then swing the legs down into their locks. Each leg's position is shown by a green (down and locked) or red (in transit, or not where the handle says) light; the DC-10 and KC-10 repeat the lights on the flight engineer's panel, and the MD-10 shows a second set on the CONFIG synoptic. A procedure is only started once both sets agree, because a single bulb or sensor fault is far more likely than a gear fault.

blocks.title: Failures you can practice
rows: Gear handle will not move down
[GEAR HANDLE WILL NOT MOVE TO DOWN POSITION](#handle-will-not-move-down)
Gear handle will not move up
[GEAR HANDLE WILL NOT MOVE TO UP POSITION](#handle-will-not-move-up)
Nose, left main, right main or center gear unsafe, handle down
[GEAR UNSAFE LT(S) ON WITH GEAR HANDLE DOWN](#gear-unsafe-handle-down)
[GEAR UNSAFE INDICATION WITH GEAR HANDLE DOWN](#md-gear-unsafe-handle-down)
Nose, left main, right main or center gear unsafe, handle up
[GEAR UNSAFE LT(S) ON WITH GEAR HANDLE UP](#gear-unsafe-handle-up)
[GEAR LIGHTS ILLUMINATE WITH GEAR HANDLE UP](#md-gear-lights-handle-up)
Nose, left main, right main or center gear fails to extend
[GEAR UNSAFE LT(S) ON WITH GEAR HANDLE DOWN](#gear-unsafe-handle-down), then [LANDING WITH ABNORMAL LANDING GEAR CONFIGURATION](#abnormal-gear-landing)
[GEAR UNSAFE INDICATION WITH GEAR HANDLE DOWN](#md-gear-unsafe-handle-down), then [LANDING WITH ABNORMAL LANDING GEAR CONFIGURATION](#md-abnormal-gear-landing)
BRAKE DIFF TEMP, then BRAKE OVERHEAT: [procedure](#md-brake-overheat)

blocks.content: The EFB's gear failures are listed in [EFB failures: landing gear](efb#failures-gear). The center gear entries are offered only on airframes that have a center gear.

children.title: GEAR HANDLE WILL NOT MOVE TO DOWN POSITION

blocks.content:
**Condition:** The gear handle cannot be moved from UP to DOWN. The handle's mechanism is jammed, or the selector valve behind it will not move.

**Objective:** Extend the gear by free fall.

items.item: Center gear alternate extension handle (-30, -40, KC-10; not operable in the simulation)

blocks.content: 230 KIAS is the free-fall speed: low enough for gravity and the airflow to swing the legs down into their locks. The main gear doors stay open and the outboard ailerons are unlocked mechanically. Wait for the three main and nose greens before pulling the center gear handle: the delay lets the gear hydraulic bypass take effect, and pulling early can be blocked by trapped fluid. With the lever raised, nosewheel steering to the right is limited to 25°. End of procedure.
Leave the main gear alternate extension lever raised: it keeps the gear from being retracted inadvertently. Do not exceed 260 KIAS.

children.title: GEAR HANDLE WILL NOT MOVE TO UP POSITION

blocks.content:
**Condition:** After takeoff the gear handle cannot be moved from DOWN to UP. Something is holding it: the anti-retraction lock, when the ground sensing mechanism has stayed in ground mode (the aircraft's systems still think it is on the ground), or the trim interlock, when the landing gear trim system, which positions the main gear trucks for retraction, has lost its hydraulic pressure. GEAR HANDLE REL frees the handle from the first but not the second, which is how the procedure tells them apart.

**Objective:** Find out why, without forcing a retraction that could damage the gear.

**Is the nose gear steering wheel centerd?**
YES: go to *Handle release* below.
NO: nose gear steering wheel CENTER, then RELEASE (CAPT), and continue with the next question.

**Does the steering wheel stay centerd, and does the TAT gauge show its probe heat?**
YES: go to *Handle release* below.
NO: do not try again to retract the gear. Gear handle and lights VERIFY DOWN, 4 GREEN (ALL); gear-down IAS 300 KIAS maximum (PF). If TAT heat is not normal, the ground sensing is in ground mode: see the note below. End of procedure.

If the steering wheel index and the console index are not aligned, or there is any reason to suspect nosewheel tire damage (vibration at liftoff, a report from the ground), make no further attempt to retract the gear: a nose gear that is not centerd, or carries a damaged tire, can jam in the wheel well.

**Does the gear handle move to UP?**
YES: release the GEAR HANDLE REL button and check the gear lights out as the gear retracts (F/O). The ground sensing mechanism has stayed in ground mode: see the note below for its effects. End of procedure.
NO: a landing gear trim failure is indicated. Gear handle DOWN, 4 GREEN (ALL), and observe the gear-down speed limit (PF). The failure should have no adverse effect on landing. End of procedure.

With the ground sensing stuck in ground mode, the cabin does not pressurize normally; pitot and angle-of-attack heat stay low and the TAT heater is off; the takeoff warning stays armed; engine 2's in-flight reverse interlock is released; the autothrottle speed mode and go-around mode cannot be engaged; the stall warning, stick shakers and auto slats are inhibited; and wing and antenna anti-ice are inoperative. Normal flight mode can be restored for everything except the auto slats by pulling the GROUND SENSING circuit breakers (UM P-1 left and S-1 right). Reset them before landing, to restore engine 2 reverse and automatic cabin depressurization.

children.title: GEAR UNSAFE LT(S) ON WITH GEAR HANDLE DOWN

blocks.content:
**Condition:** With the gear handle DOWN, a gear leg shows a red light instead of green, confirmed on both the pilots' and the flight engineer's panels. The leg has not reached its downlock: it is jammed in its uplock or partway down, or its lock is not made, or its sensor is wrong.

**Objective:** Get every leg locked down by recycling or free fall; if a leg will not lock, decide how to land.

**Four green lights?**
YES: use the normal landing procedures. End of procedure.
NO: continue with the next question.

**Do the nose and main gear indicate down and locked (only the center gear unsafe)?**
YES: go to *Center gear unsafe* below.
NO: continue with the next step.

The boom operator (on the DC-10, another crew member) checks the mechanical indicators: on each main gear a marker that rises above the top of the wing when the leg is down and locked, and for the nose gear the red markings seen through the downlock viewing tube in the forward cabin floor. There is no visual check for the center gear.

**Does the gear indicate safe?**
YES: use the normal landing procedures. The gear warning horn cannot be silenced once the flaps are in the landing range with an unsafe light, even with the gear seen to be locked: land with the horn at 35°/EXT, or at 22°/EXT if the landing distance allows. End of procedure.
NO: continue with the next step.

**Does the gear now indicate safe?**
YES: use the normal landing procedures. Do not exceed 260 KIAS; nosewheel steering to the right is limited to 25°. End of procedure.
NO: go to [LANDING WITH ABNORMAL LANDING GEAR CONFIGURATION](#abnormal-gear-landing). End of procedure.

**Center gear unsafe.** Is the center gear needed for landing (gross weight above 400,000 lb)?
YES: continue with the next step.
NO: consider retracting the gear, setting the CTR GEAR switch to UP so the center gear stays up, and lowering the gear again; complete the BEFORE LANDING checklist, taking the landing performance and limitations without the center gear into account. End of procedure.

items.item: Center gear alternate extension handle (not operable in the simulation)

blocks.content:
**Four green lights?**
YES: use the normal landing procedures. End of procedure.
NO: if possible, retract the center gear and isolate it (the main gear alternate extension lever must be stowed before the gear can be retracted). Consider the effect of landing with the center gear retracted on performance and limitations, and use the normal landing procedures. End of procedure.

children.title: GEAR UNSAFE LT(S) ON WITH GEAR HANDLE UP

blocks.content:
**Condition:** With the gear handle UP, a gear leg's red light stays on, confirmed on both panels. The leg has not reached its uplock: it may be resting on its up stop unlocked, or a door may be blocking it, or the indication may be wrong.

**Objective:** Avoid flying with a leg that could fall out at speed; retract it again if it is safe to try.

The main gear can be seen through the viewing ports in the aft cabin floor and the nose gear through the uplock viewing tube in the forward cabin floor: red markings in line mean up and locked. For the center gear, pulling its alternate extension handle shows its position: if the handle stops with any part of the red band on its cable level with the floor, the center gear is up and locked. 260 KIAS is the gear extended limit: a leg that is not locked up may fall into the airflow at any moment.

**Does the gear appear normal?**
YES: gear handle DOWN, 4 GREEN (ALL), and continue with the next step.
NO (a main gear blocked by its door, for example, or the gear cannot be seen): gear handle DOWN, 4 GREEN; do not attempt another retraction; do not exceed 260 KIAS; maintenance action is required; use the normal landing procedures. End of procedure.

**Are the gear lights out?**
YES: continue normal operation and log it. End of procedure.
NO: inspect the gear visually again (BO). If it is up and locked, continue normal operation and log it. If not: IAS 260 KIAS maximum, gear handle DOWN, 4 GREEN; do not exceed 260 KIAS; maintenance action is required; use the normal landing procedures. End of procedure.

children.title: Gear handle will not move to down position

blocks.content: **Condition:** The gear handle cannot be moved from UP to DOWN. There is no alert.

items.item: Center gear alternate extension handle (Series 30; not operable in the simulation)

blocks.content: On the Series 30 wait for the three greens before pulling the center gear handle. Nosewheel steering is restricted to 25° to the right. Leave the main gear lever raised, to prevent an inadvertent retraction. End of procedure.

children.title: Gear handle will not move to up position

blocks.content: **Condition:** After takeoff the gear handle will not move from DOWN to UP. There is no alert.

**Does the gear handle remain down?**
YES: the landing gear trim system has failed; this should have no adverse effect on landing. GEAR handle DOWN, GEAR lights 3 GREEN (Series 10) or 4 GREEN (Series 30), and 300 KIAS / Mach 0.70 maximum. End of procedure.
NO (the handle moved up): check the GEAR lights out. If the ground sensor is not in flight mode, shown by the autopilot and FCP functions not engaging, the takeoff warning sounding when the flaps or slats are retracted, or the automatic cabin pressurization not working, go to [GROUND SENSOR FAILURE](#md-ground-sensor-failure). End of procedure.

children.title: Gear primary or secondary light(s) illuminate with gear handle up

blocks.content: **Condition:** With the gear handle UP, a gear primary light (beside the handle) or secondary light (on the CONFIG synoptic) stays on. If either indication for a leg is out, that leg is up and locked.

**For each gear, does the primary or the secondary display show the gear up?**
YES: consider the gear up and locked. End of procedure.
NO: airspeed 230 KIAS maximum and gear handle DOWN (PF, PM); continue with the next question.

**For each gear, is a primary or secondary green light on?**
YES: gear handle UP again. If each gear then shows up on one of its displays, consider it up and locked. End of procedure. If not, and flight conditions and time allow, check the visual uplock markings: if they show up and locked, consider the gear up and locked; otherwise do not exceed the gear extended speed (260 KIAS / Mach 0.70), and divert if necessary. End of procedure.
NO: do not exceed the gear extended speed (260 KIAS / Mach 0.70); a diversion may be needed. When ready for landing, use [GEAR UNSAFE INDICATION WITH GEAR HANDLE DOWN](#md-gear-unsafe-handle-down). End of procedure.

children.title: Gear unsafe indication with gear handle down

blocks.content: **Condition:** With the gear handle DOWN, a gear leg shows no green on either its primary light or the CONFIG synoptic. While any primary light shows unsafe, the gear aural warning sounds until touchdown.

**For each gear, is a primary or secondary green light on?**
YES: consider the gear down and locked. End of procedure.
NO: continue with the next step.

**Series 30: are the left, right and nose gear green?**
YES: if the center gear is not green, wait until the main gear has extended and pull the center gear alternate extension handle. If the center gear is, or then becomes, green, the gear is down and locked; if not, consider the maximum landing weight with the center gear retracted. Nosewheel steering is restricted to 25° to the right. End of procedure.
NO: the center gear may be keeping a main leg from locking. Alternate gear extension lever UNLATCH and STOW, gear handle UP; once the gear is retracted, CTR GEAR isolation switch UP and gear handle DOWN. If the left, right and nose gear are then green, consider the maximum landing weight with the center gear retracted. End of procedure. If not, alternate gear extension lever RAISE and LATCH, and continue with the next question.
(In the simulation neither the center gear handle nor the CTR GEAR switch works on the MD-10.)

**All aircraft: are the left, right and nose gear green?**
YES: on the Series 30, consider the maximum landing weight with the center gear retracted. Nosewheel steering is restricted to 25° to the right. End of procedure.
NO: continue with the next question.

**Do flight conditions and time permit a visual downlock check?**
YES: check the visual downlock indicators (they rise above the top of the wing when the main gear is locked down; the nose gear's red markings align in the viewing tube in the forward cabin floor, unless cargo blocks it). If they show the gear locked, consider it down and locked; on the Series 30 consider the maximum landing weight with the center gear retracted. End of procedure.
NO, or the downlocks do not show locked: do not exceed the gear extension speed (260 KIAS / Mach 0.70), and go to [LANDING WITH ABNORMAL LANDING GEAR CONFIGURATION](#md-abnormal-gear-landing). End of procedure.

sections.title: Landing with an abnormal gear configuration

blocks.alt: Diagram of the five abnormal landing gear configurations for the DC-10, KC-10 and MD-10, each drawn as a front view and a side view of the aircraft at touchdown: nose gear retracted (main gear on the runway, nose held off with nose-up trim, then lowered onto the forward fuselage); nose gear down with both main gears retracted (nose wheel and aft fuselage and engine pods on the runway); one main gear retracted (aircraft rolling on the nose gear and one main gear, the unsupported wing held up with aileron until lateral control runs out, then the wing and engine pod on the runway); one main gear and the nose gear retracted; all gear retracted (aft fuselage and engine pods). Each panel is labeled with the spoiler handle setting (armed only for the nose gear case), whether reverse thrust may be used, and which fuel levers go to OFF and when.
blocks.title: Abnormal landing gear configurations

children.title: LANDING WITH ABNORMAL LANDING GEAR CONFIGURATION

blocks.content:
**Condition:** Every means of extending a gear leg has failed: the aircraft must land with one or more legs up or partly extended.

**Objective:** Prepare the aircraft and the cabin, and land so that the aircraft touches as gently as possible and stays straight as long as possible.

Land with the center gear retracted and as many other legs extended as possible: a center gear alone, or with only one main gear, does nothing for lateral stability and can make the aircraft pivot. Fly the approach with power on at the computed speed, keeping thrust on to touchdown if needed, so that the aircraft meets the runway as softly as it can. All slide rafts are usable whatever the gear configuration with the aircraft stopped.

**Is the center gear extended (-30, -40, KC-10)?**
YES: main gear alternate extension lever STOW, gear handle UP, CTR GEAR switch UP (F/O), gear handle DOWN, so the center gear stays up.
NO: continue.

items.item: If the nose gear is unsafe: GPWS circuit breaker

blocks.content: Why the cabin is depressurized: with the fuselage resting on the runway or the doors distorted, any differential pressure left in the cabin could hold the doors shut. Reducing fuel lowers the touchdown speed and the fire load. The APU, at the tail, is in the area that strikes the runway first when the main gear is up.

blocks.title: A. Nose gear partially or fully retracted

blocks.content: Fly a normal glide path and flare to touchdown. Trimming nose up at touchdown helps hold the nose off; lower it onto the runway while the elevator is still effective, rather than letting it fall. Do not use reverse thrust. After nose contact, keep straight with rudder and differential braking. After the aircraft stops, carry out the evacuation procedure if required. End of procedure.

blocks.title: B. Nose gear extended, both main gear partially or fully retracted

blocks.content: Fly a normal glide path and flare to touchdown. As the aircraft settles onto the runway hold the wings level, and keep directional control with rudder, nosewheel steering and thrust as long as possible. End of procedure.

blocks.title: C. One main gear partially or fully retracted

items.item: When the wing touches: fuel lever (side with the abnormal gear)

blocks.content: Do not use reverse thrust on engine 2 or on the side with the abnormal gear. Fly a normal glide path and flare. After touchdown hold a pitch attitude of 6 to 8° with the wings level until almost all the lateral control is used: that is the lowest practical speed at which to let the wing down, keeping the pitch attitude; then lower the nosewheel promptly. Once the wing (engine pod) is on the ground, extend the ground spoilers. Keep straight with the opposite engine's reverse thrust, brakes and nosewheel steering. End of procedure.

blocks.title: D. One main gear and the nose gear partially or fully retracted

items.item: As the engine pod touches: associated fuel lever

blocks.content: After touchdown hold 6 to 8° of pitch with the wings level until nearly all lateral control is used, then gently lower the wing and the nose to the runway before control is lost. Use brakes and rudder against the swerve. End of procedure.
The aircraft touches down on the aft fuselage and the engine pods. After it stops, carry out the evacuation procedure if required. End of procedure.

children.title: Landing with abnormal landing gear configuration

blocks.content:
**Condition:** Every means of extending a gear leg has failed.

**Objective:** Prepare the aircraft and couriers, and touch down gently and straight.

Series 10: land with as many gear extended as possible. Series 30: land with the center gear retracted and as many other gear extended as possible. With a main gear partly or fully retracted, consider the widest runway available.

items.item: GND PROXIMITY WARN COMPTR circuit breaker (right avionics panel)

blocks.content: Plan a 50/EXT landing with a normal approach and flare, flying a power-on approach at the computed speed and carrying power to touchdown if needed. Complete the normal approach and landing checklists, and prepare the crew and couriers for evacuation at the right time. Then use the technique for the configuration:

blocks.title: Technique by configuration
rows: Nose gear partly or fully retracted
Normal approach and touchdown. At touchdown trim the stabilizer nose up; lower the nose gently before elevator effectiveness is lost; then rudder and differential braking.
Nose gear extended, both main gear partly or fully retracted
Normal approach and flare. Wings level; directional control with rudder, nosewheel steering and thrust as long as possible.
One main gear partly or fully retracted
Do not arm; extend once the pod is on the runway
Normal approach and flare. Hold 6 to 8° pitch, wings level, until nearly all lateral control is used; lower the nosewheels promptly.
Not on engine 2 or the side of the abnormal gear; opposite engine's reverse for directional control
One main gear and nose gear partly or fully retracted
At touchdown trim nose up. Hold 6 to 8° pitch, wings level, until nearly all lateral control is used; gently lower the wing and nose before control is lost; brakes and rudder.
Associated OFF as the pod touches
All gear retracted or partly extended

blocks.content: End of procedure.

**Condition:** One or more ANTI-SKID FAIL lights with the gear down and the green lights on. The anti-skid system releases each wheel's brake whenever that wheel begins to decelerate faster than the aircraft (the start of a skid), and keeps the wheel turning at the slip that gives the most friction. Without it, a hard brake application locks the wheels: a locked tire skids on a film of melted rubber at a fraction of the friction, and blows within seconds.

**Objective:** Prove the failure, and if it is real, plan a landing with careful manual braking.
With the switch at OFF all the ANTI-SKID FAIL lights come on, and they go out when it returns to ARM; on test they come on and go out when the button is released.

**Is the test satisfactory (lights out)?**
YES: End of procedure.
NO, on the ground: maintenance is required. End of procedure.
NO, in flight: plan the landing with the anti-skid partly or wholly inoperative, below.

With the anti-skid inoperative the landing roll is significantly longer; compute the landing distance from the performance data. Use extreme caution braking with any ANTI-SKID FAIL light on: skids are hard to detect.

Consider reducing the weight. Leave the anti-skid ARMED (it still protects the wheels it can). Brake by feel: increase pedal force gradually until a moderate deceleration is felt, extend the spoilers at once, and spread the stop over most of the runway available. Excessive pedal pressure gives skids, worn or blown tires, and on the center gear a possible lower drag link failure. If a skid develops with normal brake pressure, release the brakes and reapply in the same way; with only accumulator pressure, avoid cycling the pedals. After the landing roll, ANTI-SKID switch OFF (FE). End of procedure.

**Condition:** After a rejected takeoff or other maximum effort stop, after any abnormally heavy or long use of the brakes (a dragging brake through a long taxi, for example), or whenever brake temperatures are unusually high: the BRAKE TEMP indication high, or the BRAKE OVHT light on. A stop from above 130 kt is a high energy stop.

**Objective:** Judge how much heat is in the brakes, and protect the aircraft, the people near it and the next takeoff from what that heat can do.

**Is the aircraft airborne (after takeoff)?**
YES: if a BRAKE TEMP OVHT light comes on or a brake temperature is above 400 °C, extend the gear when performance allows and leave it extended until the temperature is below 360 °C and the light is out. The wheel fuse plugs may melt and deflate the tires. The brakes, wheels and tires need a maintenance inspection before the next flight. End of procedure.
NO: determine the brake energy zone from the brake temperatures, or if the temperature monitor is inoperative from the brake energy chart, and continue below.

blocks.title: Brake energy zones
rows: 400 °C or more, but below 500 °C, or BRAKE OVHT on

blocks.content: **Normal zone.** Forecast the peak brake energy from the brake energy chart, using the brake temperature before the brakes were applied, and the cooling time from the cooling chart before the next takeoff. Brake temperatures may take 15 to 25 minutes to peak after braking has stopped. End of procedure.

**Caution zone.** Do not take off with a BRAKE TEMP OVHT light on. Move the aircraft clear of the active runway, or to the ramp, with care. Do not set the parking brake. Keep everyone clear of the main gear. With 400 °C for more than 5 minutes the fuse plugs may melt and deflate the tires. Inspect the brakes, wheels and tires before the next flight; replace them if a fuse plug has melted. End of procedure.

**Danger zone.** Clear the active runway at once. Do not set the parking brake. Be prepared to evacuate. A fire is possible within 30 minutes: alert the fire services to a possible hydraulic fluid, grease or tire fire, and keep everyone clear of the gear. After 30 minutes, fog or foam may be used to shorten the cooling. Approach inflated tires only from the front or rear, never from the side. Replace the brakes, wheels and tires, and inspect the bogie beams and axles for heat damage.

Why the parking brake stays off: clamping a brake that is near its temperature limit holds the hot discs against each other and against the piston housings, concentrating heat where the seals and the fluid are, and can weld the discs together. Why sideways approach is forbidden: a tire or wheel that fails from overheating splits radially and throws its pieces out to the side.

children.title: ANTI-SKID FAIL or ANTI-SKID L/R/C FAIL

blocks.content: **Condition:** Level 2 alert ANTI-SKID FAIL, or ANTI-SKID L, R or C FAIL for one gear's anti-skid.

**Does the alert stay out?**
YES: ANTISKID TEST button PUSH AND RELEASE (PM). If the alert still stays out, no further crew action. End of procedure. If it returns, continue below.
NO: continue below.

Use 50/EXT unless 35/EXT is required, and consider dumping fuel to reduce the weight. Use the full length of the runway, full reverse, and smooth, gradual braking. After the landing roll, turn the anti-skid off. The QRH gives the landing distances with the anti-skid inoperative, by series, flap setting, weight and airport altitude. End of procedure.
**Condition:** Level 2 alert AUTO BRAKE FAIL: the autobrake has failed.

**Is the aircraft in flight?**
YES: AUTO BRAKE selector OFF (PM). The anti-skid works normally; after landing, brake manually as the runway conditions require. End of procedure.
NO: AUTO BRAKE selector OFF. If the alert stays, takeoff is not permitted unless the minimum equipment procedure is satisfied: call maintenance. If it goes out, takeoff is permitted, and the autobrake's LAND mode may be used for the next landing; for a rejected takeoff, brake manually with anti-skid. End of procedure.
**Condition:** Level 2 alert BRAKE OVERHEAT; usually preceded by the Level 1 alert BRAKE DIFF TEMP when one brake is much hotter than the others.

**Is the aircraft on the ground?**
YES: do not take off. Tell the ground crew to stay clear of the main gear. If a temperature exceeds 450 °C, stop the aircraft and call the emergency services; do not set the parking brake. (Temperatures above 999 °C cannot be measured and the affected brake's display goes blank, returning as it cools if the sensor survives.) End of procedure.
NO: flight conditions permitting, extend the gear to cool the brakes until the alert goes out. Record the brake positions and maximum temperatures in the maintenance log. End of procedure.

**Condition:** After takeoff the ground shift mechanism has not shifted to flight mode: the autopilot and FCP functions will not engage, the takeoff warning sounds as the flaps or slats retract, automatic pressurization is inoperative, the TAT heater current is zero and the pitot and angle-of-attack heater currents do not increase, the stall warning is inhibited (stick shakers and auto slats inoperative), and wing anti-ice is inoperative.
With some forms of ground sensor failure the in-flight reverse interlocks of all three engines are released. Keep the reverse levers in the forward thrust position.

items.item: GROUND SENSING circuit breakers (left and right)

blocks.content: Pulling the breakers restores normal flight mode for all the systems. Land at the nearest suitable airport. Until the breakers are reset, engine 2 normal reverse above idle is not available, all engines stay at flight idle, and the cabin does not depressurize automatically.

blocks.title: After landing, as soon as practical

blocks.content: End of procedure.

Each leg runs through its own door, unlock, travel and lock sequence on hydraulic system 3, with free fall, the anti-retraction lock, GEAR HANDLE REL and the CTR GEAR switch modeled, and per-wheel anti-skid and brake temperature, so these procedures can be flown largely as written. The differences that matter:

items: **The center gear alternate extension handle is not operable.** On the -30, -40 and KC-10 a center gear that cannot extend on system 3 stays up: select CTR GEAR UP and land with it retracted. The handle's up-and-locked cable check is not simulated either. On the MD-10 the CTR GEAR NORM/UP switch is inoperative as well.

**Visual checks.** The cabin floor viewing ports, the nose gear viewing tube and the wing-top downlock markers cannot be looked through or seen in the simulation; treat any visual check as not possible and take the procedure's other branch.

**Free fall.** With system 3 lost and the handle at DOWN, the main and nose gear fall by themselves in the simulation; on the aircraft they wait for the alternate extension lever. After a free fall the main gear doors close.

**Injected failures.** Gear handle will not move down refuses a DOWN selection; the alternate extension lever free-falls the gear with the handle still up. Gear handle will not move up sticks the nose gear ground sensing mechanism in ground mode: the anti-retraction lock holds the handle until GEAR HANDLE REL, and the systems that read the ground shift stay in ground mode (the stall warning inhibited among them) until the GROUND SENSING breakers are pulled. Pressurization and probe heating take the simulator's own on-ground signal, so they are not affected. Gear unsafe, handle down fails that leg's downlock. Gear unsafe, handle up keeps that leg's uplock from closing: the leg rides its up stop unlocked, green with the handle down and red again on the next UP. Gear fails to extend seizes that leg's uplock, so even the alternate extension cannot release it. A leg that fails to extend is drawn up with its red light on, but the simulator still lands on that wheel.

**Brakes.** Anti-skid failure fails brake system 1's control box: all the ANTI-SKID FAIL indications come on and the DC-10 autobrake will not arm, but skid protection continues on every wheel; only with both boxes failed, or the switch OFF, is the braking unprotected. The ANTI-SKID TEST button is inoperative: prove the FAIL lights with the annunciator light test. Braking effectiveness does not yet depend on hydraulic pressure. The dragging brake (brake 1) heats through the taxi and pulls the aircraft slightly left; the indicated temperature peaks when braking stops rather than 15 to 25 minutes later, though the fuse plugs still melt minutes after a high-energy stop.
**Steering.** Losing system 1 or 3 slows the steering rather than limiting it to 25°, and the alternate extension lever does not limit right turns.

**Not simulated.** The landing gear trim cylinder interlock (the handle is never blocked by it), the gear lock pins and any tail-strike indication. On the MD-10 the AUTO BRAKE controls are inoperative, so AUTO BRAKE FAIL and the AUTO BRAKE OFF steps have no effect.

parts.title: Pneumatics
parts.summary: Bleed system faults, isolation valve disagreements, and operating with one or two bleed sources.

blocks.content: This part covers the loss or malfunction of an engine bleed system and the isolation valves between them. A ruptured manifold and a bleed overheat are emergencies: see [Pneumatic manifold failure](emergency-pressurization#manifold-failure) and [Pneumatic temperature high](emergency-pressurization#pneu-temp-hi). How the system works is in [Pneumatics](pneumatics).

Each engine feeds its own pneumatic system through a pressure-regulating valve, with a high-stage valve that opens when the low-stage port cannot hold the manifold (at low thrust). The three systems (two on the simulated KC-10, which has no system 2) normally run separately, joined only through the isolation valves when one must supply another. Two principles run through every procedure: never interconnect two active engine supplies in flight (except briefly when changing from APU air or after a crossbleed start), because a stronger source back-pressures the weaker and the controls fight; and never repressurize a system that was shut down for a manifold failure, except to start an engine.

The bleed systems feed the air conditioning packs, wing and cowl anti-ice, engine starting. Losing a system therefore means re-arranging those users onto the remaining ones, with care not to overload a single engine's bleed at high thrust.

blocks.title: Failures you can practice
rows: AIR SYS 1/2/3 PRES LO once isolated: [procedure](#md-air-sys-pres-lo)
[Operation with less than three bleed air sources](#md-less-than-three-bleeds)
Pneumatic manifold # failure; pneumatic system # temperature high
AIR MANF FAIL, BLD AIR TEMP HI: [manifold failure](emergency-pressurization#manifold-failure), [temperature high](emergency-pressurization#pneu-temp-hi)

blocks.content: The EFB's pneumatic failures are listed in [EFB failures: pneumatic](efb#failures-pneu). Air conditioning smoke from one bleed source is in the fire and smoke group.

blocks.title: MD-10 pneumatic Level 1 alerts
rows: That engine's bleed is selected off.
AIR 1-2 ISOL DISAG, AIR 1-3 ISOL DISAG
An isolation valve is not in its commanded position.

blocks.content:
**Condition:** A PNEU ABNORMAL light for one engine's pneumatic system. The system's pressure or temperature regulation is not behaving: a regulating or high-stage valve stuck, or a controller fault. The pneumatic pressure and temperature gauges may or may not show it.

**Objective:** Shut the system down, then decide whether it is needed and, if so, whether it can be trusted.

**Is the affected system required for air conditioning and pressurization, or for wing anti-ice?**
YES: continue with the next step to evaluate it.
NO: leave it off and run the aircraft on the remaining system(s); with one system left (on the KC-10, always), see [OPERATION WITH SINGLE PNEUMATIC SYSTEM](#single-pneumatic-system). End of procedure.

items.item: ISOL VALVE switch (connecting the affected system)

blocks.content: With the isolation valve at NORM (its ISOL VALVE DISAGREE light out), the system is evaluated on its own, not interconnected with an active neighbor.

**For air conditioning or pressurization:** PACK function selector (associated) AUTO (FE). If the pneumatic pressure or temperature goes high, ENG PNEU SUPPLY selector OFF and consider the APU as an air source. End of procedure. Otherwise vary that engine's throttle so that the high-stage valve cycles, and watch the pneumatic pressure gauge for a clear change as the throttle moves. If the pressure changes clearly, keep using the system and monitor its pressure and temperature. End of procedure. If not, ENG PNEU SUPPLY selector OFF and consider the APU. End of procedure.

**For ice protection:** WING ANTI-ICE switch ON (FE) and evaluate the system against the minimum supply pressures and temperatures in the table. If the system meets them, continue and monitor it. End of procedure. If not, ENG PNEU SUPPLY selector OFF and leave the icing area. End of procedure.

blocks.title: Minimum engine pneumatic supply for wing anti-ice

blocks.content: Why these minimums: the leading-edge anti-ice works by blowing hot air along the inside of the slats. Below this pressure the piccolo tubes do not deliver enough flow to cover the whole span, and below this temperature the air cannot carry enough heat to keep the surface above freezing in the cold, wet air that causes icing.

**Condition:** Only one engine pneumatic system is available, the others having been shut down for failures.

**Objective:** Supply what matters most from the one system without overloading it.
Do not pressurize a pneumatic system that was shut down for a manifold failure, except to start an engine.

**Is wing anti-ice required?**
YES: continue with *Wing anti-ice required* below.
NO: go to *Wing anti-ice not required* below.

The ISOL VALVE DISAGREE light comes on and goes out as the valve travels. In the descent, hold about 35 psi of pneumatic pressure by advancing the supplying engine's throttle. One pack is shut down to leave enough air for the wing: the anti-ice has priority because ice on the slats threatens the aircraft, while one pack still pressurizes it. End of procedure.
Do not run more than one pack with the supplying engine at or above maximum continuous thrust.

With only one pack running, select the AVIONIC FLOW switch to OVRD. The APU is available as an air or electrical source, but two active sources must not be interconnected: if system 1 is the one still operating, the APU cannot be used for air, because both feed the same side of the manifold. End of procedure.

children.title: PNEU ISOL VALVE DISAGREE light on

blocks.content:
**Condition:** An ISOL VALVE DISAGREE light stays on: a pneumatic isolation valve has not reached the position its switch commands. The light normally comes on briefly while the valve travels.

**Objective:** Drive the valve with its second motor.

items.item: ENG ISOL VALVE SELECT switch (appropriate valve, FE equipment panel)

blocks.content: Open the door on the flight engineer's equipment panel and move the switch for the affected valve to SECONDARY, which selects the valve's alternate drive motor. The light should go out. (The simulation does not model this switch: see Simulation notes.) Both motors share one circuit breaker, so a breaker trip disables both. If the light stays on, treat the valve as stuck where it is and plan the bleed configuration around it. End of procedure.

**Condition:** Level 2 alert AIR SYS 1, 2 or 3 PRES LO: that air system's pressure is low with its bleed selected on. Its regulating valve has failed closed, or its engine cannot hold the manifold.

**Consequences:** None.

The AIR SYS OFF alert confirms the bleed is off. Opening the isolation valve lets the neighboring system pressurize the dead system's manifold, so its users (anti-ice, starting) stay available; the pack on that side is shut down so that one engine is not asked to supply two packs as well as everything else. End of procedure.

**Condition:** Level 2 alert BLEED AIR 1, 2 or 3 FAULT: that system's bleed pressure or temperature is too low for wing anti-ice, typically at low thrust.

**Consequences:** Temperature or pressure too low for anti-ice.

**Does the BLEED AIR FAULT alert go out?**
YES: if safety of flight permits, operate that engine at or above the thrust needed to keep the alert away. End of procedure.
NO: return the throttle as needed and continue with the next step.

When wing anti-ice is no longer needed, the affected bleed may be reinstated for normal use.

**Is it bleed air 1 or 2?**
YES: PACK 2 OFF, 1-2 ISOL ON, PACKS 1 and 3 ON (PM). If only one bleed source is left, also 1-3 ISOL ON, and select PACK 3 OFF when wing anti-ice is needed or thrust is at MCT or above. End of procedure.
NO (bleed air 3): PACK 3 OFF, 1-3 ISOL ON, PACKS 1 and 2 ON (PM). If only one bleed source is left, also 1-2 ISOL ON, and select PACK 2 OFF when wing anti-ice is needed or thrust is at MCT or above. End of procedure.

**Condition:** Level 2 alert AIR SYS 1-2 OFF: a manifold failure in the left forward tunnel, where systems 1 and 2 run side by side. The controller has closed both systems' regulating valves; the crew must find which manifold failed. When the red manifold lines on the synoptic turn white, the alert is replaced by AIR SYS 1 OFF and AIR SYS 2 OFF (Level 1).

**Consequences:** None.

items.item: When manifolds 1 and 2 are no longer red on the synoptic: ECON switch

blocks.content:
**Is AIR SYS 1-2 OFF displayed again within 15 minutes?**
YES: system 2 is the leaking one. PACK 2 OFF; do not repressurize air system 2. When the manifolds are no longer red, BLEED AIR 1 ON and PACK 1 ON (PM). If the alert returns again within 15 minutes, PACK 1 OFF, do not repressurize system 1 or 2, and verify PACK 3 is operating. End of procedure. If not, verify PACKS 1 and 3 are operating. End of procedure.
NO: system 2 is sound and system 1 is the leaking one. PACK 1 OFF; do not repressurize air system 1; leave or avoid icing conditions. End of procedure.

Why one system at a time: a leak in a tunnel shared by two ducts heats the same detection loop whichever duct fails. Repressurizing one system and waiting long enough for a leak to heat the loop again identifies the guilty duct without ever running both into the same hole.

children.title: Operation with less than three bleed air sources

blocks.content: **Condition:** One or two engine bleeds are unavailable (no alert of its own).

In flight, except briefly when changing from APU air or during a crossbleed start, do not interconnect two or more active engine bleed systems. Do not pressurize a system shut down for a manifold failure, except to start an engine.

**Are bleed air 1 or 2 (or both) off?**
YES: PACK 2 OFF, 1-2 ISOL ON, PACKS 1 and 3 ON (PM). If only one bleed source is available, 1-3 ISOL ON too, and select PACK 3 OFF when wing anti-ice is needed or thrust is at MCT or above. End of procedure.
NO (bleed air 3 off): PACK 3 OFF, 1-3 ISOL ON, PACKS 1 and 2 ON (PM). If only one bleed source is available, 1-2 ISOL ON too, and select PACK 2 OFF when wing anti-ice is needed or thrust is at MCT or above. End of procedure.

The pneumatic system is solved as a network of ducts, valves and users, with bleed pressure and temperature taken from each engine's compressor state and the air it gives up fed back to the engine, so throttle changes, high-stage operation and cross-feeding behave as these procedures expect.

items: **Injected failures.** Pneumatic system abnormal sticks that system's regulating valve closed; on the MD-10, AIR SYS PRES LO appears once the system is isolated (cross-fed through open isolation valves it is not low). Two pneumatic systems lost sticks two regulators closed. Isolation valve disagree fails the 1-2 valve's position feedback, so the valve itself works and only its indication is wrong.

**ENG ISOL VALVE SELECT switches** (primary and secondary motor) on the flight engineer's equipment panel are not modeled, so the step in PNEU ISOL VALVE DISAGREE cannot be flown; with the injected failure the light stays on, and the valve still answers its switch.

**Indications (DC-10, KC-10).** The amber pneumatic lights on the flight engineer's panel, PNEU ABNORMAL among them, do not raise MASTER CAUTION in the simulation; the PNEU cue responds to USE ENG PNEU SUPPLY. The three MANFLD FAIL lights do not yet illuminate. Some DC-10 panels carry a HI STAGE OPEN light where the simulation has the KC-10's PNEU ABNORMAL function, so FedEx's HI STAGE OPEN procedure is not included.

**Simplified.** All CF6-powered airframes share one bleed port schedule, so the CF6-6D's and CF6-50's bleed pressures do not differ; on the DC-10-40 the JT9D's high-stage valve carries the duct from takeoff to high altitude.

**MD-10.** The ECON switch is not functional, so its steps have no effect. The HI STAGE FAULT, START AIR PRES LO, SEL APU AIR OFF and A-ICE SENSOR FAIL alerts are not raised, and their procedures are not included.

parts.title: Air Conditioning and Pressurization
