parts.summary: Pack, trim air and equipment cooling failures, ram air ventilation, and standby and manual cabin pressure control.

blocks.content: This part covers the air conditioning packs, trim air and zone temperature control, the cooling of the avionics, center accessory and inertial unit compartments, and the cabin pressure controller. Decompression and emergency descent, and smoke and fumes, are in [Emergency Procedures](emergency-procedures). How the systems work is in [Air Conditioning and Pressurization](air-conditioning).

The packs turn hot, high-pressure bleed air into cold air by expanding it through an air cycle machine; trim air, a little hot bleed air added downstream, brings each zone back up to its selected temperature. The pressure controller then regulates how fast that air leaves through the outflow valve. Air conditioning failures are rarely urgent in themselves: the cabin has a large thermal mass and leaks slowly. What makes them matter is what depends on the air: the avionics, which are cooled by cabin air drawn through their racks, and the cabin pressure, which falls if too few packs deliver.

blocks.title: Failures you can practice
rows: SEL PACK OFF, then PACK OFF (Level 1)
Trim air pressure high, left or right regulator
[AIR COND TRIM AIR PRESS HI light on](#trim-air-press-high)
None: the radio rack fan keeps running, and [AVNCS AIR FLO OFF](#md-avncs-air-flo-off) needs both fans lost
[CTR ACCESS COMPT FLOW OFF light on](#ctr-access-flow-off)

blocks.content: The EFB's air conditioning failures are listed in [EFB failures: air conditioning](efb#failures-ac); the cargo door warning is in [Doors](abnormal-doors).

blocks.title: MD-10 air conditioning and pressurization Level 1 alerts
rows: The pack has overheated and the controller asks for it to be selected off; select it off, and it can be reset once cool.
The center accessory compartment fans are inoperative; on the ground, possible avionics failure.
The avionics fan switchlight is at OVRD.
A pressure relief valve is open: the differential is above about 8.85 psi.
CAB PRES SYS MAN, SEL CAB PRES MAN
The pressure controller is in manual, or wants manual selected.
A zone temperature selector is in manual.

blocks.content:
**Condition:** A PACK OFF light with the pack's function selector not at PACK OFF. The pack's flow control valve has closed: the pack has shut itself down on an overheat (the air cycle machine's turbine inlet too hot, usually because the ram air through its heat exchangers is not removing enough heat), or its bleed supply has failed.

**Objective:** Find which, cool the pack with manual control, and restart it if it will reset.

**Is the pneumatic pressure normal?**
YES: continue with the next step.
NO: the supply is the problem: associated ENG PNEU SUPPLY selector OFF (FE) and go to [OPERATION WITH SINGLE PNEUMATIC SYSTEM](abnormal-pneumatics#single-pneumatic-system). End of procedure.

items.action: MAN HOT OR MAN COLD AS REQUIRED

items.item: When the pack temperature valve is at about eleven o'clock: PACK function selector

blocks.content: Positioning the pack's temperature control (bypass) valve by hand sets a moderate discharge temperature that does not ask the turbine for its full cooling. The pack will not reset until its turbine inlet temperature is back below the red line.

**Has the PACK OFF light gone out?**
YES: control the pack with MAN HOT and MAN COLD as required, and monitor its temperatures and flow. End of procedure.
NO: the pack's thermal fuse must be reset by maintenance; leave it off. End of procedure.

With a pack off, the others keep the aircraft pressurized. With only one pack running, set the AVIONIC FLOW switch to OVRD: it closes the overboard venturi valve and runs the cooling fans instead, which stops the avionics cooling air leaking overboard and leaves more of one pack's flow to hold the cabin pressure.

**Condition:** No pack can be run: all have failed, or after a driftdown with two engines inoperative the remaining engine's bleed must be shut off to meet the one-engine-operative climb gradient. The aircraft is ventilated with outside air through pack 1's ram air path, unpressurized.

**Objective:** Depressurize in a controlled way at a safe altitude, then open the ram air path.

items.item: ENG PNEU SUPPLY selectors (unless icing conditions)

blocks.content: If icing conditions exist or are expected, leave the appropriate engine's PNEU SUPPLY selector at AUTO for anti-ice.

With the packs off, normal cabin leakage depressurizes the cabin at an acceptable rate; the cabin altitude warning may sound, depending on the aircraft's altitude. Once the differential pressure is zero:

items.item: CAB ALT wheel (outflow valve position indicator)
Ram air ventilation valve tee handle (not modeled in the simulation)
PACK 1 temperature valve (PACK 1 function selector MAN HOT or COLD, then PACK OFF)
PACK 3 temperature valve (PACK 3 function selector MAN HOT if needed, then PACK OFF)

blocks.content: The tee handle is under the avionics compartment access door in the flight deck floor: pull it fully forward (about 5 inches), release it and close the door. There is no speed restriction. It locks the ram air ventilation valve fully open; pack 1 must not be given bleed air again until maintenance has reset the valve. Setting pack 1's temperature valve to one o'clock routes the ram air into the distribution; setting pack 3's to full hot closes its ram air doors and reduces drag. Watch the ram air supply temperature on the PACK 1 gauges: if it is too cold, modulate it with the PACK 1 function selector in MAN. End of procedure.

**Condition:** The DUCT AVIONIC COMPT OVERHEAT light. A conditioned air duct, or the avionics compartment, has overheated, and the trim air has shut itself off. A duct overheat is almost always a zone's trim air valve stuck open, pouring hot bleed air into that zone's duct; an avionics compartment overheat is a cooling failure.

**Objective:** Tell the two apart, and restore trim air only if the cause is a duct that can be controlled.

A cooling period of about a minute may be needed before trim air can be restored. **Has the light gone out?**
YES: it was a duct overheat; continue with the next step.
NO: the overheat is in the avionics compartment, and trim air cannot be reset: go to [TRIM AIR INOPERATIVE](#trim-air-inop). End of procedure.

items.item: Duct temperatures and valve position indicators

blocks.content:
The zone whose duct temperature is highest, or whose valve position indicator shows its trim valve open when it should not be, is the culprit. **Is that zone's duct temperature under control?**
YES: End of procedure.
NO: rotate its selector to MAN and hold it in COLD. If that controls it, End of procedure. If not, TRIM AIR switch OFF and go to [TRIM AIR INOPERATIVE](#trim-air-inop). End of procedure.

**Condition:** Trim air is off and cannot be restored, after an avionics compartment overheat or an uncontrollable duct overheat, or the trim air has shut off by itself. Every zone now receives the same pack discharge air, with no trim air to warm the zones that want it warmer.

**Objective:** Use the pack temperature itself to give the best compromise across the zones.

Without trim air, the zone selectors can no longer warm their own zones; the cockpit selector, which sets the pack discharge demand, now effectively sets the temperature for the whole aircraft. Adjust it for the best compromise between the flight deck and the rest of the aircraft. On the KC-10, set the ARO station selector to MAN, STOP and adjust the forward cabin selector for the best compromise between the forward cabin and the ARO station. End of procedure.

children.title: AIR COND TRIM AIR PRESS HI light on

blocks.content:
**Condition:** The AIR COND TRIM AIR PRESS HI light. One of the two trim air pressure regulators is no longer regulating, a fault the pneumatic gauges do not show. There is enough margin to keep operating until maintenance is available.

**Objective:** Find the faulty regulator by taking its power away: an unpowered regulator closes.

items.item: L TRIM AIR PRESS REGULATOR circuit breaker (UM P-12)

blocks.content:
**Has the light gone out?**
YES: the left regulator was faulty: continue with its breaker pulled. End of procedure.
NO: the right regulator is faulty: reset the left breaker and pull the R TRIM AIR PRESS REGULATOR circuit breaker (UM S-12) (FE); continue with it pulled. End of procedure.

**Condition:** The AVIONIC FLOW OFF light: the cooling airflow through the avionics compartment's racks is low. In flight the cabin's differential pressure drives the air out through an overboard venturi; at low differential (on the ground, early in the climb) fans do the work.

**Objective:** Restore the cooling flow, or limit the heat the avionics make.

**Is the aircraft in flight?**
YES: AVIONIC FLOW switch OVRD (FE). If the light stays on, the avionics fan has failed: return the switch to NORM; the compartment is cooled by the cabin differential through the overboard venturi. End of procedure.
NO: turn non-essential avionics off (P, CP, FE): the weather radar to standby before taxi, TACAN, IFF and the HF radios; all may be turned on after takeoff. Limit the operation of all avionics to 60 minutes. End of procedure.

children.title: CTR ACCESS COMPT FLOW OFF light on

blocks.content: **Condition:** The CTR ACCESS COMPT FLOW OFF light: the cooling flow through the center accessory compartment, which holds electronic equipment, is low.

**Is the aircraft in flight?**
YES: a fan draws conditioned air from the cabin through the compartment, and in flight the airflow is adequate even with the fan failed. No action. End of procedure.
NO: operate the air conditioning packs as required. If the cabin and cargo doors need not stay open, close them: with the doors closed the conditioned air is driven through the compartment far more effectively. If the light goes out, End of procedure.

blocks.title: Doors must stay open, or the light stays on

blocks.content: One radio altimeter may be turned on 5 minutes before takeoff, and everything may be used after takeoff. Limit the operation of all the equipment to 30 minutes. End of procedure.
**Condition:** An INS FLOW OFF light: the cooling fan of that inertial unit's compartment has failed.

No action is required: the inertial unit need not be shut down. Monitor its operation and its comparison with the other units (see [Navigation and Communications](abnormal-navigation)); the fan needs maintenance. End of procedure.

DC-10: FedEx adds a watch on that unit's WARN annunciator. If it lights, the unit's navigation is no longer reliable: INS selector CAPT ON AUX or F/O ON AUX as required, that unit's mode selector to ATT REF where fitted (then wings level and constant speed for at least 3 minutes) or OFF, and continue with [Single INS failure](abnormal-navigation#single-ins-failure). In the simulation an uncooled platform does fail after about 12 minutes (see Simulation notes).

**Condition:** Level 2 alert AVNCS AIR FLO OFF: all avionics fans are off and there is no avionics cooling flow.

**Consequences:** Possible avionics failure. Land at the nearest suitable airport.

**Is the aircraft on the ground?**
YES: call maintenance. End of procedure.
NO: continue.

Land at the nearest suitable airport. **Is the nearest suitable airport within 90 minutes?**
YES: no further crew action. End of procedure.
NO: reduce the avionics heat load: pull the VHF COMM 1 and 2, VOR 1 and 2, ATC 2 and ILS 2 circuit breakers on the overhead panel, to be reset within one hour of landing; and run the MCDUs one at a time, pulling MCDU 1's breaker, resetting it after an hour and checking it agrees with MCDU 2, then resting MCDU 2 for an hour, and so on until landing. End of procedure.

**Condition:** Level 2 alert AVNCS COMPT OVHT, with the TRIM AIR AVNCS OVHT light on the overhead panel (which may stay lit until maintenance resets it). The avionics compartment or a conditioned air duct has overheated.

**Consequences:** None.

When the alert has gone, PACK 1 ON. **Does the alert come back?**
YES: PACK 1 OFF, and it must stay off for the rest of the flight. When the alert has gone, PACK 3 ON; if the alert comes back again, PACK 3 OFF: packs 1 and 3 must both stay off. End of procedure.
NO: pack 3 is the one that must stay off for the rest of the flight. End of procedure.

Why one pack at a time: the overheat is usually one pack's discharge, or the trim air downstream of it, running hot. Pack 2 alone keeps the aircraft pressurized while packs 1 and 3 are brought back one by one; the one that brings the alert back is the culprit.
**Condition:** Level 2 alert TRIM AIR OFF: trim air is off, selected or after an overheat.
Select the cockpit zone and set its temperature at least 4 °F (2 °C) below the courier zone's set temperature. End of procedure.

**Condition:** The automatic cabin pressure controller is not holding its schedule: the cabin altitude or its rate of change wanders, or the controller has lost its power (AC BUS 1).

**Objective:** Take the outflow valve under standby, and if necessary manual, control.

**Is the cabin altitude above 10,000 ft?**
YES: oxygen masks ON, 100% (ALL), and establish crew communication; then continue.
NO: continue.

Standby holds the current cabin altitude; the rate knob drives the cabin up or down. **Is the cabin pressure controllable?**
YES: continue in standby, as in *Standby and manual pressurization* below. End of procedure.
NO: continue with the next step.

**Is the cabin pressure controllable?**
YES: continue in manual, as in *Standby and manual pressurization* below. End of procedure.
NO: descend to 10,000 ft if practical, and use the decompression procedure in [Emergency Procedures](emergency-pressurization#decompression) if required. End of procedure.

**Standby and manual pressurization.** Set the cabin altitude to the higher of the altitude schedule's value (for the airplane altitude at maximum differential) and the destination field elevation, and change it at a normal rate, about 300 ft/min. Keep the cabin barometric scale on the local altimeter setting until above the transition altitude, then 29.92, and the destination setting for the descent. In manual, the cabin rate needs constant watching; the maximum differential is 8.8 psi, and outflow valve movement from fully open may be restricted above 200 kt. Before landing, bring the cabin slightly above the destination field elevation so that the aircraft lands at zero differential; in manual, set the outflow valve 1/2 to 2/3 open just before landing and fully open after landing.

Do not land with the cabin pressurized. In manual the automatic depressurization on touchdown does not work; in standby the outflow valve drives fully open on touchdown and a pressurized cabin dumps at an excessive rate.

children.title: CAB PRESS RELIEF OPEN light on

blocks.content: **Condition:** The CAB PRESS RELIEF OPEN light: a cabin pressure relief valve has opened, because the differential has exceeded about 8.85 psi, or the valve has failed open. The relief valves protect the structure when the outflow valve is not letting enough air out.

**Is the differential pressure indication normal?**
YES: the valve or its switch has failed; log it. End of procedure.
NO: the controller is overpressurizing the cabin; continue with the next step.

Raise the cabin altitude until the differential returns to normal and the light goes out. If the cabin will not climb in standby (or on the KC-10), CAB PRESS MAN/AUTO handle MAN and drive the CAB ALT wheel up, watching the outflow valve open, until the differential is normal and the light out; then continue in manual. End of procedure.

The cabin is simulated as one pressure vessel with a real mass balance of pack flow, outflow and leakage, and the packs by their discharge temperature, flow and overheat trip. These are the differences that matter for these procedures.

items: **Injected failures.** Pack off is that pack's overheat trip; all packs off trips every pack. Trim air inoperative forces the trim air overheat shutoff. Trim air pressure high leaves one regulator unregulated, though it still closes when unpowered, so pulling its breaker finds it as the procedure expects. The avionics and center accessory fan failures stop those fans. The avionics duct overheat jams a zone trim valve fully hot past the controller's limit: the duct trips, trim air shuts itself off, and OFF then TRIM AIR restores it until the duct trips again; the light goes out about 2.5 seconds after the shutoff rather than after a minute. The INS cooling fan failure pops that fan's breaker: only its FLOW OFF light comes on and the platform navigates on, but the simulation's thermal cutout takes the platform about 12 minutes later in a normal bay, where the KC-10 manual says it need not be shut down.

**Not modeled.** The ram air ventilation valve tee handle, the cabin air shutoff handle, recirculation and gasper air: the RAM AIR VENTILATION steps that use the handle cannot be flown, and with all packs off the aircraft is unpressurized with no ram air ventilation. The avionics fans run continuously, so their automatic shutdown at high differential is not modeled.

**DC-10 and KC-10 indications.** A pack whose supply pressure has gone shows zero flow without a PACK OFF light, because its flow control valve does not close on loss of pressure. The amber air conditioning lights on the flight engineer's panel do not raise MASTER CAUTION. STANDBY is engaged by pushing the STBY ON switchlight rather than by pulling the rate knob.

**MD-10.** The overhead CABIN PRESS panel, the CABIN AIR switchlight and the ECON switch are not functional: the MD-10 runs the automatic controller for the whole flight with the landing field elevation at sea level, so it lands at high fields with some differential. The CABIN INFLO LO, AVNCS EXH FLO OFF and other pressurization alerts are not raised. The avionics compartment fan failure stops only the compartment fan; the radio rack fan runs on, so AVNCS AIR FLO OFF, which needs both, does not appear. On the MD-10 a pack overheat raises SEL PACK OFF and then PACK OFF as Level 1 alerts, with no Level 2 procedure.

parts.title: Ice and Rain Protection
parts.summary: Anti-ice valve disagreements, probe and windshield heat failures, and cracked or arcing windows.

blocks.content: This part covers the anti-ice valves of the wings, the engine cowls and (DC-10, KC-10) the upper VHF antenna, the pitot and other probe heaters, and the windshields and side windows. How the systems work is in [Ice and Rain Protection](ice-and-rain).

Thermal anti-ice uses bleed air: a motor-driven valve opens to feed hot air into the slat leading edges or the engine inlet lip. Each valve has a DISAGREE light that compares its position with its switch, so the same light can mean a valve that failed to open when ice protection is wanted, or a valve that failed to close and is blowing hot air where it is not wanted (on the ground, enough to damage the slats within seconds). Every anti-ice procedure therefore begins by asking which way the valve failed, and most end by leaving the icing conditions if a surface cannot be protected.

blocks.title: Failures you can practice
rows: [ENG 2 ANTI-ICE COWL DUCT FAIL light on](#eng-2-cowl-duct-fail)
Left or right wing anti-ice valve disagree
Captain's, first officer's or auxiliary pitot heat inoperative
Left or right windshield anti-ice inoperative

blocks.content: The EFB's ice protection failures are listed in [EFB failures: anti-ice](efb#failures-ice). The EFB also lists a cracked windshield or window failure, but it injects nothing into the aircraft, so it cannot be used to practice the cracked window procedures (see [Simulation notes](#simulation-notes)).

**Condition:** A WING ANTI-ICE DISAGREE light, steady (it flashes briefly as a valve travels). That side's wing anti-ice valve disagrees with the WING ANTI-ICE switch: it has failed to open, so that wing's slats are not protected, or failed to close, so hot air is flowing with the switch off.

**Objective:** Prove what the valve is doing from the pneumatic pressure, and protect the slats on the ground.
Running the wing anti-ice on the ground for more than 15 seconds can damage the slats: without the cooling airflow of flight, the hot air overheats the leading-edge structure.

**Is the aircraft on the ground?**
YES: appropriate ENG PNEU SUPPLY selector OFF and associated ISOL valve CLOSE (FE), so that no hot air can reach the valve. End of procedure.
NO: continue with the next question.

**Is the WING ANTI-ICE switch OFF?**
YES: assume the anti-ice is on (the valve has failed open). Just before landing, appropriate ENG PNEU SUPPLY selector OFF and associated ISOL valve CLOSE (FE), so that the valve is not blowing hot air into the slats on the ground. End of procedure.
NO: the valve may have failed to open; continue with the next step.
Selecting HIGH before the anti-ice switch steadies the supply, so that any dip in the pneumatic pressure gauge can only be the anti-ice valve opening and drawing air.

**Did the pressure drop and recover?**
YES: the valve is opening; the light is faulty. Appropriate ENG PNEU SUPPLY selector AUTO (FE). End of procedure.
NO (pressure steady): the valve has not opened, as the light said. Appropriate ENG PNEU SUPPLY selector AUTO and WING ANTI-ICE switch OFF (FE), and leave the icing area as soon as possible. End of procedure.

**Condition:** An ENG ANTI-ICE DISAGREE light, steady: that engine's cowl anti-ice valve disagrees with its switch. Failed closed, the inlet lip can ice and shed ice into the fan; failed open, it takes extra bleed and, on the -30, may affect the takeoff thrust settings.

**Objective:** Try once to free the valve; if it stays failed closed, keep the engine out of icing.

**Is the engine anti-ice switch OFF (valve failed open)?**
YES: consider selecting the engine anti-ice ON to match the valve; there are no temperature limits on engine anti-ice in flight. If the light is on before takeoff with the temperature above 8 °C, apply the takeoff performance corrections for anti-ice. End of procedure.
NO: continue with the next question.

**Is the aircraft on the ground?**
YES: with the engine running, do not dispatch into icing conditions: maintenance is required. With the engine shut down, the light is a normal indication. End of procedure.
NO: continue with the next step.

Changing the thrust changes the duct pressure acting on a sticking valve and may free it. **Does the light stay on?**
YES: leave the icing conditions as soon as possible, at cruise thrust as far as practical. If that is not possible, climb or descend to where the TAT is warmer than +6 °C or colder than -20 °C (below about -20 °C the cloud is mostly ice crystals that do not stick), or fly faster than 400 KTAS (where kinetic heating keeps the lip clear). End of procedure.
NO: continue normal operations. End of procedure.
DC-10: with one or more ENG ANTI-ICE DISAGREE lights on, leave the icing area as soon as possible. When the lights are out, check the ENG 2 ANTI-ICE COWL PRESS HI light out.

children.title: ENG 2 ANTI-ICE COWL DUCT FAIL light on

blocks.content: **Condition:** The ENG 2 ANTI-ICE COWL DUCT FAIL light: engine 2's cowl anti-ice duct, which runs up through the tail to the center engine inlet, is leaking hot air into the surrounding structure, and a temperature detector beside it has tripped.
If practical, avoid icing areas, to keep the time with the duct leaking (and the anti-ice on) as short as possible. There are no other actions. End of procedure.

**Condition:** The ANT ANTI-ICE DISAGREE light, steady: the valve that heats the upper VHF antenna with system 3 bleed air disagrees with its command. The antenna's anti-ice works with engine 2's anti-ice.

**Objective:** Determine whether the valve has stuck open or shut, and protect the antenna or the structure accordingly.

**Is engine 2 anti-ice OFF (antenna valve failed open)?**
YES: consider engine and antenna anti-ice ON; there are no temperature limits in flight. Just before landing, ENG 3 PNEU SUPPLY selector OFF, PNEU ISOL VALVE 1-3 CLOSE and PACK 3 OFF (FE), so that no hot air reaches the open valve on the ground. On the ground, do not pressurize pneumatic manifold 3 except for up to a minute to start an engine. Log it. End of procedure.
NO: the valve has failed closed; continue.

**Is the system 3 pneumatic pressure normal?**
YES: avoid icing areas in flight (the antenna can ice); on the ground, do not dispatch into icing conditions and call maintenance. End of procedure.
NO: restore system 3 pneumatic pressure. If the light then goes out, End of procedure. If not, avoid icing areas in flight, and on the ground do not dispatch into icing conditions and call maintenance. End of procedure.
**Condition:** Level 2 alert WNG A-ICE L or R DISAG: a wing anti-ice valve disagrees with its command.
Running the wing anti-ice on the ground for more than 15 seconds can damage the slats.

**Is the aircraft on the ground?**
YES: WING ANTI-ICE switch OFF; tell maintenance to remove external air if it is in use; associated BLEED AIR 1 or 3 switch OFF and associated ISOL switch(es) OFF (PM). End of procedure.
NO: continue.

**Is the WING ANTI-ICE switch OFF?**
YES: assume the wing anti-ice is on. After landing, associated BLEED AIR 1 or 3 switch OFF and ISOL switch(es) OFF, and do not pressurize that pneumatic system on the ground. End of procedure.
NO: WING ANTI-ICE switch OFF (PM) and leave the icing area. End of procedure.

children.title: ENG 1/2/3 A-ICE DISAG and ENG 2 A-ICE DUCT

blocks.content: **Condition:** Level 1 alert ENG 1, 2 or 3 A-ICE DISAG: that engine's cowl anti-ice valve disagrees with its commanded position. Or ENG 2 A-ICE DUCT: engine 2's cowl anti-ice duct is leaking. Level 1 alerts have no checklist of their own.

**Consequence:** may have to depart the icing area. With a valve failed closed, leave icing conditions as soon as practical; with the duct leaking, keep the time with engine 2 anti-ice on to a minimum. Both are no-takeoff items on the ground unless relieved by the minimum equipment list. End of procedure.

**Condition:** The PITOT HEAT INOP light: one of the heated probes (the Captain's, First Officer's or auxiliary pitot, or the TAT probe) is not drawing heater current. An unheated pitot in icing conditions blocks, and the instruments it feeds read wrongly.

**Objective:** Find the failed heater, restore it if a breaker has tripped, and protect the air data.

items.action: ROTATE THROUGH CAPT, F/O, AUX, TAT

blocks.content:
The heater current meter shows which probe is drawing no current. **Is it the TAT probe?**
YES: check and reset the TAT PROBE HEAT circuit breaker if required (FE). If it was not tripped or will not stay in, the heater cannot be restored; if the TAT then becomes erroneous, the thrust rating computer, the autothrottle N1 modes and the TAS and SAT readouts are affected. End of procedure.
NO: check and reset the appropriate pitot heat circuit breaker (CAPT, F/O or AUX) (FE).

**Has the light gone out?**
YES: End of procedure.
NO: (the KC-10 checklist first selects the other heater system with the PITOT HEATER SELECT switch on the flight engineer's equipment panel, which the simulation does not model) an additional reset of the breakers is allowed, because each heater element has two power sources. If the light stays on, the system cannot be restored: probably a short between the breaker and the probe heater. End of procedure.

If the failure leads to airspeed indications that cannot be restored, or to SELECT FLAP LIMIT OVRD and SELECT ELEV FEEL MAN lights, go to [Flight instrument malfunction](abnormal-flight-instruments#flight-instrument-failure).

**Condition:** A WINDSHIELD ANTI-ICE INOP light: that windshield's heat controller has shut down or failed. The windshield heat keeps the outer ply clear of ice and, just as importantly, keeps the glass warm and pliant against bird strike.

Turning the selector off may reset the controller; some windshield heat faults clear themselves. **Does the light stay on?**
YES: associated selector OFF (F/O), and leave or avoid icing areas. End of procedure.
NO: continue normal operations. End of procedure.

children.title: Windshield or window cracked or arcing

blocks.content:
**Condition:** A windshield or clearview window ply has cracked, or its heating film is arcing. The windshield is a laminate: the inner structural plies carry the pressure load, and the outer ply carries the heating film. A crack in the anti-ice or defog ply is not a structural failure, so there are no altitude or pressurization limits for it; arcing is an electrical fault in the film, which the heat must be removed from.

**Objective:** Remove the heat from the damaged pane.

**Is it a clearview (side) window?**
YES: pull the associated CLEARVIEW DEFOG circuit breaker (FE). End of procedure.
NO (windshield): continue.

Avoid icing areas. **Does the arcing continue?**
YES: pull the associated WINDSHIELD DEFOG circuit breaker (FE). End of procedure.
NO: associated windshield anti-ice selector as required (FE). End of procedure.

children.title: PITOT HEAT, WSHLD HEAT and other heater alerts

blocks.content: **Condition:** Level 1 alert PITOT HEAT CAPT, FO or AUX, AOA HEAT L or R FAIL, TAT PROBE HEAT, or WSHLD HEAT L or R FAIL: that heater has failed. On the MD-10 the air data heaters run automatically with the engines; there is no crew control to reset them.

There is no checklist. Avoid icing conditions where practical, and watch the instruments fed by the unheated probe: if airspeed or altitude become suspect, compare the sources and use the emergency procedure AIRSPEED: LOST, SUSPECT OR ERRATIC if required (see [Emergency Procedures](emergency-flight-path#unreliable-airspeed)). With a windshield heater failed, avoid icing; the glass also loses some of its bird-strike resilience when cold. End of procedure.

children.title: Windshield, clearview or aft window cracked or arcing

blocks.content: **Condition:** A windshield, clearview or aft window is cracked, or its heating film is arcing. No alert.

**Is a windshield arcing?**
YES: associated WINDSHIELD ANTI-ICE switch OFF (PM). If the arcing continues, WINDSHIELD DEFOG switch OFF, pull the associated WINDSHIELD DEFOG circuit breaker (left avionics panel), then WINDSHIELD DEFOG switch ON again (PM).
NO: continue.

**Is a clearview window arcing?**
YES: WINDSHIELD DEFOG switch OFF, pull the associated CLEARVIEW DEFOG circuit breaker (left avionics panel), then WINDSHIELD DEFOG switch ON again (PM).
NO: continue.
Monitor the damaged unit. End of procedure.

Ice is simulated zone by zone, and every anti-ice valve, probe heater and windshield controller is modeled with its DISAGREE logic, current readings and ground inhibits, so these procedures behave as described with the exceptions below.

items: **Injected failures.** The anti-ice valve failures stick that valve where it is (an engine, wing or antenna valve), so the DISAGREE light and the pressure check in the wing procedure tell the truth. Engine 2 cowl duct failure is a leak in the duct, sensed by its detector. Pitot heat and windshield heat failures kill that heater: the current meter reads zero and the INOP light (or Level 1 alert) comes on. The cracked windshield or window failure only brings up its procedure: the crack is not drawn and it has no effect on the aircraft.

**Not modeled.** The PITOT HEATER SELECT switches (so the step of selecting the other heater system is omitted); windshield and clearview defog on the DC-10 and KC-10 (the WINDSHLD DEFOG switch moves but is not connected, so the defog breaker pulls act on nothing); rain repellent; the wing anti-ice ground test.

**DC-10 engine anti-ice switches.** In the current release the three ENG anti-ice toggles on the DC-10 pilots' overhead do not move on screen, although a click (or the simulator's anti-ice key bindings) still sets them: judge each switch by its ENG ANTI-ICE lights, not by the toggle. The KC-10's work normally.
**Different from FedEx's DC-10s.** Engine 2 has a plain shutoff valve in the simulation, so the ENG 2 ANTI-ICE COWL PRESS HI light never comes on.
**MD-10.** The A-ICE SENSOR FAIL alert is not raised, and its procedure is not included. The TAIL switchlight has nothing to heat.

parts.title: Doors
parts.summary: Cargo door warnings in flight: confirming the sensor, or depressurizing.

blocks.content: This part covers a cargo door warning in flight. The DC-10's lower cargo doors open outward, against the cabin pressure, so they are held shut not by the pressure but by their latches: a row of hooks driven over center onto spools on the sill, then locked by a locktube whose lockpins can only pass when every latch is fully over center. A vent door in each cargo door closes only when the locktube has gone home, so a door that is not locked cannot be pressurized. Two independent sensing systems, A and B, watch each door; a light from one system alone may be a sensor, while lights from both, or a confirmed failure, mean the door itself. How the doors work is in [Doors, Cargo and Cabin](doors-and-cabin).

The procedures reduce the load on a doubtful door the only way the crew can: by reducing the cabin differential pressure, to about 2 psi for a lower cargo door and to nothing for the main deck door. That costs a descent, and on a long flight the fuel and the diversion that go with it, but an outward-opening door that fails under pressure takes floor structure and control runs with it.

blocks.title: Failures you can practice
rows: Forward lower cargo door unsafe in flight (DC-10, MD-10)
Main deck cargo door unsafe in flight (KC-10)

blocks.content: The failure is listed in the EFB's pressurization and miscellaneous group: [EFB failures: pressurization and miscellaneous](efb#failures-pres-misc). A rapid decompression is in [Emergency Procedures](emergency-pressurization#decompression).

**Condition:** One or more cargo door lights on the flight engineer's panel in flight (on the DC-10 the FWD, CTR or AFT CARGO DOOR SYS A or SYS B lights of the lower doors; on the KC-10 the main deck CARGO DOOR SYS A or SYS B light). A door's latches, locks or vent door are not confirmed closed and locked by that sensing system.

**Objective:** Find out whether one sensor has failed or the door is really not secure; if it may not be, take the pressure load off it.

**Consequences:** With both the SYS A and SYS B lights of a door on, land at the nearest suitable airport.

**Is only one light on (one system, one door)?**
YES: continue with the next step.
NO: go to *Door not confirmed secure* below.

**Does the other system's light for the same door test normally (it lights on test and goes out after)?**
YES: the other system is working and sees the door secure: the lit light is a sensor fault. Continue normal flight. End of procedure.
NO: the other system cannot confirm the door either; go to *Door not confirmed secure* below.

**Door not confirmed secure.** Is it the main deck cargo door (the KC-10's, or a DC-10 freighter's)?
YES: go to *Main deck cargo door* below.
NO (a DC-10 lower cargo door): go to *Lower cargo door* below.

items.action: DESCEND TO WHERE PRESSURIZATION IS NOT REQUIRED

blocks.content: Descend to an altitude where the cabin need not be pressurized, and raise the cabin altitude with the semi-automatic, standby or manual pressure control until the aircraft is depressurized. Land at the nearest suitable airport. End of procedure.

items.action: DESCEND TO WHERE 2 PSI DIFFERENTIAL OR LESS CAN BE HELD

items.item: Cabin altitude (semi-auto, standby or manual control)

blocks.content: A 2 psi differential at 15,000 ft gives a cabin altitude of about 9,500 ft, so the aircraft stays below the altitude where oxygen is needed while the load on the door is cut to about a quarter of its cruise value. A lower cargo door is held shut by its latches, not by the pressure, and keeping a small differential costs little; the main deck door, much larger, is depressurized completely. Land at the nearest suitable airport. End of procedure.

KC-10: the main deck door's vent door stays open if its locks are not home, which limits the cabin to a very small differential: the cabin will not hold its schedule, and the cabin altitude climbs with the aircraft. That is the door protecting itself.
**Condition:** Level 2 alert CARGO DOOR FWD, CTR, AFT or UPR with the sensing system A or B: that door is not confirmed closed and locked by that system.

**Is only a single alert displayed?**
YES: perform the cargo door test. If the other sensor on the faulted door tests correctly on the MISC system display, no further crew action: log the fault. End of procedure. If not, continue below.
NO: continue below.

items.action: DESCEND TO 15,000 FT OR MSA, WHICHEVER IS HIGHER

blocks.content: At 15,000 ft a 2 psi differential gives a cabin altitude of about 9,500 ft, so the couriers need no oxygen while the load on the door is cut to about a quarter of its cruise value. Land at the nearest suitable airport. End of procedure.

items: **Injected failure, DC-10 and MD-10.** The forward lower cargo door's proximity switch fails: the SYS B light (CARGO DOOR FWD B on the MD-10) comes on alone, and the test shows system A sees the door secure. It is an indication fault, and the procedure's first branch ends it.

**Injected failure, KC-10.** The main deck door's vent door jams open: CARGO DOOR SYS A comes on and the cabin is limited to about 1 psi, so the procedure's descent and depressurization branch is the one that applies.

**MD-10.** The CARGO DOOR TEST switch does not work, so a single alert cannot be confirmed as a sensor fault from the flight deck; treat it as unconfirmed. The overhead CABIN PRESS panel is not functional, so the manual pressurization steps have no effect: the automatic controller keeps control of the cabin, and descending reduces the differential in any case.

**Not included.** FedEx's air conditioning door light, cockpit door FDAS and main cargo door opening in flight procedures: the air conditioning compartment door light and the flight deck door lock are not modeled, and the main cargo door cannot open in flight.

parts.title: Air Refueling
parts.summary: Where the refueling abnormal procedures are, and the KC-10's AR isolation valve, master valve and boom hydraulic temperature items.

blocks.content: The abnormal procedures for the refueling equipment, the boom, the centerline hose and drogue, the wing pods and the KC-10's receiver system, are with the rest of the refueling procedures in [Air Refueling: emergency and abnormal procedures](ar-emergency-abnormal), so that the boom operator and the cockpit crew work from one place during a refueling. This part lists them, and holds the three refueling fuel and hydraulic items that the KC-10 manual files under its fuel and hydraulic abnormals. How the systems work is in [Air Refueling Systems](air-refueling-systems).

blocks.title: Where the refueling abnormal procedures are
rows: [Boom abnormal procedures](ar-emergency-abnormal#ar-abnormal-boom): brute force disconnect, boom FAIL light or stick failure, uncommanded boom, FLT CONT DEGRADED, ALAS INOP, telescope lights, boom hydraulic pressure low, AR signal system failure, manual latching, broken hoist cable, latch failure, landing with the boom in trail
[Fuel and receiver abnormal procedures](ar-emergency-abnormal#ar-abnormal-fuel): 2-3 pump valve verification, reverse flow refueling, receiver system does not advance to LATCHED
AR ISOL valve, AR MASTER valve, AR BOOM HYD TEMP HI

blocks.content: Refueling failures cannot be scheduled from the EFB's Failures app. Some arise from hydraulic and electrical failures, and the KC-10's hydraulic abnormal procedures begin by telling the boom operator to disconnect: see [Hydraulics](abnormal-hydraulics).

children.title: AIR REFUELING ISOL VALVE DISAGREE light on

blocks.content:
**Condition:** The AR ISOL valve's DISAGR light, steady. The aerial refueling isolation valve, which connects the center wing tank's AR pumps to the refueling manifold, has not followed its switch.

**Objective:** Decide whether the failure matters for the offload, and route the fuel around it if it does.

**Is the MASTER FUEL ISOL switch at ISOL?**
YES: the AR ISOL valve stays operable, but the center wing lower compartment pumps are inhibited. End of procedure.
NO: continue.

**Has the valve failed open?**
YES: continue; there is no detrimental effect. End of procedure.
NO (failed closed): the center wing tank's AR pumps cannot deliver to the manifold. If they are needed for the offload, the valve can be opened by hand with its manual override handle (under an access door in the main cabin floor, right side; blocked if cargo is loaded in the pallet position over it). Otherwise transfer the center wing tank's fuel to the forward or aft body tanks and offload from there (not if the upper center wing tank holds JP-7 and the wing tanks do not). End of procedure.

children.title: AIR REFUELING MASTER VALVE STUCK OPEN or CLOSED

blocks.content: **Condition:** The receiver's AR master valve does not move when the AR MASTER switch is selected. (The light in the switch does not show the selected position.)

**Is the valve stuck open?**
YES: continue; there is no detrimental effect, but fuel transfer will fill the refueling manifold, which must then be scavenged to make that fuel usable. If wanted, the valve can be closed with its manual override handle in the right main cabin wall. End of procedure.
NO (stuck closed): open it manually (FE, BO) with the override handle, or from the center accessory compartment, where the valve is on the forward side of the center tank bulkhead. If it stays closed, no air refueling onload is possible. End of procedure.

children.title: AR BOOM HYD TEMP HI light on

blocks.content: **Condition:** The AR BOOM HYD TEMP HI light. The boom and drogue hydraulic fluid is hot: from hydraulic system 2 running hot, or from the BOOM/DROGUE HYD selector left at BOOM or DROGUE for a long time. Do not use this procedure if a system 2 HYD TEMP HI light is on or the system 2 temperature gauge is high: use [HYD TEMP HI](abnormal-hydraulics#hyd-temp-hi).
The flight engineer tells the boom operator to disconnect (if in contact) and discontinue refueling until the hydraulic status is known.

Do not move the BOOM/DROGUE HYD selector out of DROGUE while the centerline drogue is partly stowed, or stowed but not locked: the hose can run out rapidly and separate from the aircraft. If the selector is at DROGUE because of a stow or lock problem and conditions allow, consider trailing the drogue and selecting the hydraulics OFF, repressurizing and stowing before landing; if that is not possible and hydraulic damage looks imminent, consider jettisoning the hose.
End of procedure.

The KC-10's refueling fuel system and the boom and drogue hydraulics are simulated, but no EFB failure acts on the AR ISOL or AR master valves or heats the boom hydraulics, and the manual override handles in the cabin and the center accessory compartment cannot be reached in the simulation. These three procedures are included because they belong with the KC-10's fuel and hydraulic abnormals; see [Air Refueling Systems](air-refueling-systems) for what can be practiced.

parts.title: Aerial Firefighting System
parts.summary: The retardant system's non-normal procedures, for the DC-10-10 and DC-10-30 air tankers.

blocks.content: The DC-10-10 and DC-10-30 air tankers carry a retardant system of three tanks under the fuselage, with their doors, pumps and drop controller. Its non-normal procedures are written with the system itself, where its controls and logic are explained, in [Aerial Firefighting System](aerial-firefighting#failures). They are listed here so that every abnormal procedure can be found from this section.

blocks.title: Retardant system procedures
rows: The load must be shed at once (an engine failure or loss of performance in the run, or a tank that cannot be dropped normally)
LOW PSI or PUMP FAIL light on

blocks.content: An engine failure with a load aboard is first an engine failure: fly the aircraft and use the engine failure procedures in [Emergency Procedures](emergency-procedures); the emergency drop is the quickest way to restore the performance margin. A DC BUS 1, DC BUS 3 or battery bus failure takes parts of the drop system with it, as the system's failure table explains; the bus procedures are in [Electrical](abnormal-electrical).

parts.title: Miscellaneous
parts.summary: Unreliable airspeed and a damaged nose radome, and the overweight landing.

blocks.content: This part holds what belongs to no single system: flying with unreliable airspeed or a damaged nose radome, and landing above the maximum landing weight. Landing configurations for flap and slat failures are in [Flight Controls](abnormal-flight-controls), a jammed stabilizer in [STABILIZER INOPERATIVE](abnormal-flight-controls#stabilizer-inoperative), abnormal gear landings in [Landing Gear and Brakes](abnormal-landing-gear), and landing with an engine inoperative in [Emergency Procedures](emergency-procedures). The source manuals give no ferry procedure with an engine inoperative for these aircraft.

blocks.title: Failures you can practice
rows: [Airspeed lost, suspect or erratic; damaged nose radome](#suspect-airspeed)

blocks.content: The EFB's miscellaneous failures are listed in [EFB failures: pressurization and miscellaneous](efb#failures-pres-misc).

children.title: Airspeed lost, suspect or erratic; damaged nose radome

blocks.content:
**Condition:** The airspeed, Mach, altitude or vertical speed cannot be trusted: they disagree with each other, with the standby instruments, or with the pitch attitude and thrust. Causes include pitot or static blockage (ice, insects, volcanic ash), a damaged or lost nose radome, which disrupts the airflow over the pitot probes, and maintenance errors; several sources can fail together, leaving nothing to compare. Signs include an airspeed that does not fit the attitude and thrust, an altitude different from the real one, PITOT HEAT INOP, SELECT FLAP LIMIT OVRD with SELECT ELEV FEEL MAN, speed and airspeed flags, and pressurization problems. A lost radome adds a loud noise and a low-frequency buffet that, unlike stall buffet, hardly changes with speed or attitude.

**Objective:** Keep control with pitch attitude and thrust, which remain reliable, then find a good air data source.
These remain reliable: the attitude indicators, the inertial ground speed, the engine N1 and the stick shaker.

Set a normal attitude and thrust for the phase of flight. Never set an unusually high or low pitch attitude to chase the airspeed indication. Disregard the indicated airspeed, the flight director pitch bar, the speed command indicator and the overspeed warnings; disregard every annunciation and warning except the stick shaker until the aircraft is stable. If the shaker fires, lower the nose to the horizon and add thrust, then return to the pitch and thrust reference. About 10° of pitch with maximum continuous thrust gives a safe initial climb if one is needed. Once stable, ensure terrain clearance and, if practical, head for visual conditions.

**Can an unreliable air data source be identified?**
YES: CADC selector BOTH ON 1 (if the First Officer's instruments are bad) or BOTH ON 2 (if the Captain's are) (PM), and, if fitted, that side's STATIC AIR selector ALT. If the air data then return to normal, keep monitoring pitch, thrust and airspeed, and use the autopilot and autothrottles as desired. See also [Flight instrument malfunction](abnormal-flight-instruments#flight-instrument-failure). End of procedure. If they do not, continue as for NO.
NO: fly the rest of the flight on pitch attitude and thrust, using the tables below, the inertial ground speed and ATC's ground speed readouts as cross-checks. End of procedure.

Hail that damages the radome may also damage the wing leading edges and the angle-of-attack vanes. Damaged leading edges raise the stall speed and can cause a stall before the stall warning; damaged vanes can invalidate the stall warning altogether. The speeds in the tables carry a margin for typical hail damage; use the final approach speeds when working out the landing distance.
The KC-10 tables below are for standard temperature and CF6-50C2 engines. Interpolate the target pitch attitude for the gross weight. Actual speeds may be limited by the airspeed and Mach limits.

blocks.title: Climb, 0°/RET, maximum climb thrust (KC-10, sea level)
Final approach, 3° glide slope, sea level (KC-10)

blocks.content: DC-10: the FedEx flight manual carries pitch and power tables for each series in its flight instruments chapter; the technique is the same. Fly the attitude and thrust you know for the phase of flight, and cross-check with the inertial ground speed.

Why pitch and power work: for a given weight, configuration and altitude, a stabilized aircraft at a given attitude and thrust flies at one speed. The airspeed indicator measures that speed through a fragile pressure system; the attitude indicator and the N1 gauges measure the inputs that produce it through entirely different sensors, which a blocked pitot cannot touch.

**Condition:** An emergency requires a landing above the maximum landing weight, with no time, or no means, to dump fuel down to it.

**Objective:** Land at the lowest practical sink rate, with flaps that will not be overstressed, and have the aircraft inspected afterwards.

In normal operation the maximum landing weight is a hard limit; only an emergency, or on the KC-10 operational necessity, justifies exceeding it. The landing gear and the wing structure are designed for the landing weight at a given sink rate; above it, the energy the gear must absorb grows with the weight and with the square of the sink rate, which is why the sink rate limit is lower for an overweight landing.

blocks.title: Overweight landing rules
rows: Emergency or operational necessity; not recommended when planned
360 ft/min (6 ft/s) maximum; any landing above 600 ft/min is a hard landing
Logbook entry with the landing weight; maintenance inspection before the next flight
Overweight landing inspection, and a flap overspeed/overweight inspection

blocks.content: Plan the landing distance for the actual weight: it is longer, and the brakes absorb more energy, so expect high brake temperatures and use [ABNORMAL BRAKE](abnormal-landing-gear#abnormal-brake) (MD-10: [BRAKE OVERHEAT](abnormal-landing-gear#md-brake-overheat)) after landing. Use the longest suitable runway, full reverse, and a firm, controlled touchdown rather than a prolonged float. On the KC-10, with the anti-skid inoperative or the center gear retracted, the maximum landing weights fall to 411,000 lb and 400,000 lb respectively. End of procedure.
Some MD-10 procedures (severe damage to the overhead structure, for example) call for an overweight landing in preference to a fuel dump; the same principles apply.

items: **Nose radome damaged, airspeed unreliable** blocks all three pitots (the Captain's, the First Officer's and the alternate), so there is no good airspeed to compare with: fly pitch and thrust. The pitot inlet is modeled on pressure, so the blocked airspeeds read high in a climb and low in a descent. The radome's noise and buffet are not simulated.

**Landing weight.** The simulation does not record a landing above the maximum landing weight as an overweight landing; the EFB's flight log records each landing's sink rate, and a touchdown at about 1,500 ft/min or more collapses the gear.

chapters.title: Limitations
chapters.summary: The operating limits of each airframe, its engines and its systems: weights and center of gravity, airspeeds, engine and APU limits, and the limits of every system, with what each limit protects.

sections.title: General
sections.summary: What a limitation is, which manual each airframe's limits come from, and how the instruments mark them.

blocks.content:
This section states the limits within which the aircraft, its engines and its systems must be operated. A limitation is not advice. It is the edge of the flight testing, structural analysis and systems substantiation on which the type certificate rests, or a restriction the operator has added on top of it. Inside the numbers the aircraft has been shown to behave as described in this manual; outside them it either has not been shown to, or has been shown not to.

The layout follows the airline and Air Force limitations chapters: the general envelope first, then weights, center of gravity, airspeeds, the engines and the APU, and then each system in turn. Every table names its effectivity. Where it helps a crew judge what a limit protects and how much margin is behind it, a short explanation follows the numbers.

**Sources.** Each airframe's limits are taken from the manual it was flown by. The DC-10-10 and DC-10-30 figures are those of the FedEx DC-10 company flight manual, which carries the FAA-approved airplane flight manual limitations together with the company's own; a limit marked **(FDX)** is a FedEx addition, stricter than or additional to the approved figure. The KC-10A's limits are those of its flight manual, T.O. 1C-10(K)A-1, Section III. The MD-10's come from the FedEx MD-10 flight crew operating manual and the MD-10-30 airplane flight manual; the FCOM mixes FAA-approved limitations with manufacturer recommendations, and both are given here.

Where none of these manuals gives a value for a variant, the table says **not published in the sources used**. That applies mostly to the DC-10-15 and the DC-10-40, which none of the manuals behind this chapter covers. For those two series only the engine type-certificate limits of the JT9D-59A are given. Do not carry a DC-10-10 or DC-10-30 figure across to them unless the table says it applies.

blocks.title: Airframes, engines and the source of their limitations
rows: Not published in the sources used, except where a table says otherwise
Long span; center gear (removed on the -30 Tanker)
Not published in the sources used; engine limits from the engine type certificate
Long span with wing refueling pods; center gear
MD-10 FCOM chapter L (Series 30) and the MD-10-30 AFM

blocks.content: The FedEx DC-10s were freighters, and their weights and center of gravity limits are those of the FedEx fleet, by tail number. A passenger DC-10-10 or DC-10-30 of another operator was certificated to its own weights, which may differ. For the simulation's passenger variants, use the FedEx limits for the same series.

children.title: Kinds of operation and minimum crew

blocks.content:
The DC-10 is certificated in the transport category (FAR Part 25) for day and night operation under VFR and IFR, in icing conditions, and on extended over-water flights, provided the equipment the regulations require for each is installed and working.

**Minimum flight crew:** two qualified pilots and a third crew member qualified and certificated to perform the duties of flight engineer. FedEx calls this crew member the second officer.

**Minimum flight crew:** pilot, copilot and flight engineer. The boom operator is a mission crew member and not part of the minimum crew for flight.

Section III of the T.O. is the controlling list: it takes precedence over any other limitation in the manual, and some limits that belong to a specialized phase of flight (air refueling, cargo) appear in their own sections as well. With equipment inoperative, the minimum equipment list applies.

The MD-10 is certificated in the transport category for day and night operation under VFR and IFR, in icing conditions and on extended over-water flights, when the required equipment is installed and approved.

**Minimum flight crew:** two qualified pilots. The conversion removed the flight engineer's station; its functions are done by the automatic systems controllers and the two pilots.
Round-dial engine and system instruments carry their limits as colored markings. The convention is the same on every DC-10 and KC-10 panel:

rows: Maximum or minimum limit. Do not operate beyond it.
Caution or precautionary range: permitted, often for a limited time; sustained operation in it is not recommended.
The VMO pointer: the current maximum operating speed, VMO or the speed equivalent to MMO, whichever is lower.
A follower that stays at the highest value reached and is reset by the crew; it records an exceedance for the logbook.

blocks.alt: DC-10-30 center instrument panel, engine instrument column for one engine, close up: the N1 indicator with its red radial at 118.5 %, the EGT indicator with the yellow arc from 910 to 960 °C and the red radial at 960 °C, and the N2 indicator with the red radial at 109.5 %. The maximum limit pointers visible beside each needle. Markings and numerals legible.
blocks.title: Engine instrument limit markings
blocks.caption: Red radials mark the limits, the yellow arc the time-limited range. The maximum limit pointers record the highest value reached.

blocks.content: The 120 marking on the N1 dial sits away from where the eye expects it and is easily misread. In an overspeed, read the digital counter before choosing the overspeed action.

The MD-10's engine and system limits are drawn on the electronic displays. A parameter is white in its normal range. On N1 and N2, the pointer and digits turn red, and the digits are boxed in red, when the redline is exceeded. EGT has an amber line below its redline: above it for more than 5 minutes, the EGT pointer and digits turn amber and the digits are boxed; just below the redline is a band with a 2-minute allowance, after which they turn red and boxed, as they do at once above the redline. Oil temperature turns amber and boxed as soon as it passes its amber line, and red after 15 minutes in the band below its redline or at once above it. The highest N1, N2 or EGT reached above a redline is held as an amber mark at the top of the scale until the ENG MAX POINTER RESET button on the forward overhead panel is pushed.

blocks.alt: MD-10-30 primary engine display, all three engines running at takeoff thrust: the N1 dials with the magenta thrust-rating V and the red redline tick, the EGT dials with the amber line and the redline, and the N2 dials. One EGT pointer and its digits shown amber and boxed to illustrate a timed exceedance. Scale numerals and digits legible.
blocks.title: Engine limits on the MD-10 display

sections.title: Operating envelope
sections.summary: Altitude and temperature, runway, wind, maneuvering load factors and RVSM.

blocks.content: The operating envelope is the set of conditions in which the aircraft was certificated: the altitudes and air temperatures in which the engines, systems and performance data were demonstrated, the runways from which the takeoff and landing data are valid, and the loads the structure will carry. Pressure altitude is used throughout; for takeoff and landing, airport elevation may be used instead.

blocks.title: Maximum altitudes (DC-10-10, DC-10-30)
rows: Maximum operating altitude with three packs operating (FDX)

blocks.content:
Temperature limits vary linearly between the altitudes shown. FedEx does not permit sustained operation with a cabin altitude above 40,000 ft (FDX): above that altitude even 100 % oxygen delivered at ambient pressure cannot keep the blood saturated, so the limit protects the crew rather than the aircraft.

The DC-10-15 was built for hot and high airports and the DC-10-40 is a long-span aircraft like the -30, but their altitude and temperature envelopes are not published in the sources used.
The KC-10A is certificated within the altitude and temperature envelope of its flight manual figure. Its limits, read from that figure:

blocks.title: Operating envelope (KC-10A)
rows: About −54 to +50 °C at sea level, decreasing linearly with altitude
Airfield pressure altitude up to 8,500 ft
Airfield pressure altitude up to 14,000 ft, approved for use with the performance manual (T.O. 1C-10(K)A-1-1)
Permitted at outside air temperatures up to 55 °C

blocks.content: The MD-10 FCOM gives the altitude and temperature limits as an environmental envelope chart for each series (CF6-6 engines for Series 10, CF6-50 engines for Series 30), with separate en route and takeoff-and-landing boundaries. Airport elevation may be used in place of airport pressure altitude. Runway slope is limited to ±2 %. Read from the charts:

blocks.title: Operating envelope (MD-10), read from the charts
rows: About −54 to +50 °C at sea level; about −82 to −33 °C at 42,000 ft
About −54 to +50 °C at sea level; about −82 to −33 °C at 42,000 ft
10,000 ft (MD-10-30 AFM); the FCOM chart draws 8,500 ft
About −54 to +50 °C up to about 2,500 ft, falling to about +38 °C at 8,500 ft
About −54 to +50 °C up to about 2,500 ft, falling to about +35 °C at 10,000 ft (AFM)

blocks.content: The MD-10-30's two books disagree on the takeoff and landing boundary: the AFM's envelope, like the FedEx DC-10-30's, goes to 10,000 ft, while the FCOM's Series 30 chart stops at 8,500 ft, the Series 10 value. The AFM is the approved document; an operator flying to the FCOM would simply be more restrictive.

blocks.alt: Chart: pressure altitude (−2,000 to 42,000 ft) against ambient temperature (−90 to +50 °C), DC-10-30. Solid lines bound the en route envelope (−54 to +50 °C at sea level, −82 to −33 °C at 42,000 ft); a dashed box bounds the takeoff and landing envelope to 10,000 ft (−54 to +35 °C at the top). The ISA standard temperature line drawn and labeled. Axis numerals and labels legible.
blocks.title: Altitude and temperature envelope
blocks.caption: The en route envelope and the smaller takeoff and landing envelope. Between the corners the temperature limits vary linearly with altitude.

blocks.content: The taxi speed limits protect the tires and the landing gear. A heavy aircraft in a tight turn scrubs its main tires sideways and loads the outer gear far beyond its straight-line load; heat builds in the tire carcass with every mile of taxi, and that heat is still there at the start of the takeoff roll.
The pressure difference between two tires on the same axle should not exceed 15 psi: the harder tire would carry most of the axle load.
On the KC-10A the maximum taxi and takeoff weights assume tires of 28 ply rating or higher on all main and center gear wheels.
For takeoff weights above 555,000 lb (MD-10-30), tires of 28 ply rating or higher must be fitted on all main and center gear wheels.
Tire speed limits are ground speeds and are listed with the airspeeds; see [Tire speed](#tire-speed).
Wind limits are components along and across the runway. For the actual takeoff or landing the reported wind, gusts included, governs (FDX).

blocks.title: Wind limits, DC-10-10 and DC-10-30
rows: Maximum crosswind with braking action reported poor (FDX)
Takeoff with a tailwind and clutter on the runway (FDX)
Prohibited with any wind more than 45° off the runway heading, or with a crosswind component above 23 kt

blocks.title: Category II and autoland wind limits, DC-10 (FDX)

blocks.content: The 31 kt crosswind is the demonstrated value, which FedEx adopts as a limit. A static-thrust takeoff, with takeoff thrust set against the brakes, is limited further: a strong crosswind at low speed upsets the flow into the wing engines' inlets and can make a CF6-50 surge before the aircraft has the speed to align it.

blocks.title: Wind limits, KC-10A
rows: Not stated as a limitation; the performance manual's takeoff crosswind chart applies
Maximum wind 25 kt including gusts; crosswind 15 kt; tailwind 10 kt

blocks.title: Wind limits, MD-10
rows: Maximum demonstrated crosswind, rolling takeoff or landing

blocks.content: These are **limit load factors**: the largest loads the structure is required to carry without permanent deformation. The ultimate loads, at which failure is allowed to begin, are 1.5 times higher, and that margin is meant for the unexpected, not for use. In a level turn the load factor is 1/cos(bank), so +2.5 g is reached at about 66° of bank and +2.0 g at 60°; the positive limits therefore cap both the bank in a sustained turn and the severity of a pull-up. With flaps or slats out the limit is lower because the high-lift surfaces, their tracks and the wing's load distribution are designed for the approach, and a negative load factor with them extended is not allowed at all.

Maximum takeoff and in-flight gross weight is reduced when fuel density is below 6.5 lb/US gal. Low-density fuel puts less weight in the wing tanks, so less of the aircraft's weight is carried where the lift is and more of it bends the wing root. The flight manual's chart lowers the maximum weight so that at least +2.4 g flaps up and +1.9 g flaps down remain available, a little less than the normal limits. See [Fuel](#fuel-limits).

items: Manual switching to the alternate static system, where fitted, is prohibited for RVSM operation (FDX).
The autopilot must be engaged in ALT HOLD for RVSM operation (FDX).

blocks.content: RVSM separates aircraft by 1,000 ft between FL290 and FL410, which only works if the altimetry error and the height-keeping error of every aircraft stay small. The alternate static source has its own, larger position error, and a hand-flown aircraft wanders more than one in ALT HOLD; both rules keep the aircraft inside the error budget the airspace was designed for.
No RVSM limitations are published in the KC-10A and MD-10 sources used. The same two principles apply in practice: fly on the normal static system with the autopilot holding altitude.

sections.title: Weights
sections.summary: Structural weight limits for each airframe, what each one protects, and the center gear and anti-skid configurations.

blocks.content: The structural weight limits are the heaviest weights at which the airframe has been shown strong enough for each phase of operation. They are maxima: on a given day the performance limits (runway length, climb gradients, obstacles, tire speed, brake energy, the landing field length) and the center of gravity envelope may each allow less, and the lowest of all of them governs. Each limit protects something different:

blocks.title: The structural weight limits
rows: The heaviest weight for ground maneuvering. In every table here it is the takeoff weight plus 3,000 lb of taxi fuel.
Landing gear, wheels and tires under ground loads, including the side loads of turns and the bumps of taxiways.
The heaviest weight at the start of the takeoff roll.
The wing, fuselage and gear under the flight and ground loads of a takeoff at that mass, including a rejected takeoff.
The heaviest weight at which the flaps may be extended beyond 25° (the landing flap settings).

The flaps, their tracks and actuators. A heavier aircraft approaches faster, so the air load on the extended flaps rises with weight. In the normal configuration it sits 3,000 lb above the maximum landing weight.
The heaviest weight for a normal landing.
The landing gear and the airframe at the design sink rate at touchdown, 10 ft/s (600 ft/min). The energy the gear must absorb grows with mass.
The heaviest weight of the aircraft with no usable fuel aboard: everything above it must be fuel.

The wing root. Fuel in the wing tanks hangs along the span, where the lift is generated, and adds little to the bending moment at the root. Weight in the fuselage (cargo, and on the KC-10 fuel in the body tanks) hangs from the root and bends it fully.

blocks.content: On the DC-10 and MD-10 the zero fuel weight also has a **performance limit**. After a takeoff the aircraft must be able to dump down and return, and dumping cannot take it below the zero fuel weight plus the fuel that cannot be dumped. The maximum zero fuel weight is therefore also limited to the lower of the approach-climb and landing-climb limited weights for the takeoff airport's conditions, less 42,300 lb of undumpable fuel. On a hot, high departure this can be the governing limit. The KC-10A's flight manual states no such limitation.

The FedEx DC-10s carried the airplane performance and loading computer (APLC), which applied the zero fuel weight performance limit automatically and flashed MAXIMUM ZFW when it governed. The simulated aircraft has no APLC; its takeoff and landing figures come from the EFB's performance pages. Check the zero fuel weight limit yourself when departing from a hot or high airport.

blocks.title: Maximum structural weights, DC-10-10 and DC-10-30 (FedEx)
rows: 363,500 lb at flaps 35; 375,000 lb at flaps 50
Not published in the sources used
Not published in the sources used

blocks.content:
**DC-10-10 landing weight.** Above 363,500 lb a normal landing must be made with flaps 50, up to 375,000 lb. This is a brake limit, not a structural one: flaps 50 lowers the approach speed, and the energy the brakes must absorb goes with the square of the touchdown speed.

**Which DC-10-30 row.** The FedEx fleet was certificated at three takeoff weights. The simulation's EFB performance pages plan every DC-10-30 to the 580,000 lb aircraft's weights. The KDC-10 is simulated as a DC-10-30 and takes the same weights. The DC-10-30 Tanker has its own, much lower limits: see [the tanker conversion's limitations](aerial-firefighting#tanker-limitations).

**Overweight landing (FDX).** A landing above the maximum landing weight is prohibited in normal operation. It is justified only by an emergency, and requires a maintenance log entry giving the landing weight; maintenance inspects the aircraft before its next flight. If one cannot be avoided, touch down as gently as possible: the gear was designed for 10 ft/s at the maximum landing weight, but only for about 6 ft/s at the maximum takeoff weight.

items: Maximum in-flight gross weight: 590,000 lb.
The maximum taxi and takeoff weights require tires of 28 ply rating or higher on all main and center gear wheels.
The maximum unrestricted landing weight, 436,000 lb, is set at the design rate of descent at touchdown of 10 ft/s (600 ft/min).
A landing above the maximum landing weight is an emergency overweight landing. Its rate of descent at touchdown must not exceed 6 ft/s (360 ft/min).
A touchdown above 600 ft/min at any weight is a hard landing. After a hard or an emergency overweight landing, an overweight/hard landing inspection is required (AFTO Form 781 entry).

Planned overweight landings are not recommended; they may be made when operational necessity dictates or in an emergency, with no more than 35° of flaps. A flap overspeed/overweight inspection is then also required.
On training approaches, flap settings greater than 25° are not permitted at in-flight weights above 439,000 lb.
An overweight landing can exceed the flap placard, the tire speed or the brake energy limits; check them when time permits.
With the gross weight above 556,000 lb, or the zero fuel weight plus the fuel in the body tanks above 414,000 lb, main tanks 1, 2 and 3 must be kept full: see [Fuel](#fuel-limits).

blocks.content: The last rule is the zero fuel weight principle applied to a tanker. Fuel in the KC-10's forward and aft body tanks sits in the fuselage and loads the wing root exactly as cargo does. When cargo plus body fuel exceeds the 414,000 lb the root was designed to carry, only full wing tanks provide enough bending relief, so at those weights the body tanks are drawn down first and the wing tanks last.

Landings at gross weights from 363,500 lb to 375,000 lb must be made with flaps 50. This is a brake performance limit: flaps 50 lowers the approach speed and with it the energy the brakes must absorb.

blocks.title: Maximum weights, MD-10-30, by certificated takeoff weight

items: For takeoff weights above 555,000 lb, tires of 28 ply rating or higher must be fitted on all main and center gear wheels.
Minimum flight weight: Series 10, 236,000 lb; Series 30, 254,000 lb.

The zero fuel weight performance limit applies (approach-climb and landing-climb limited weight less 42,300 lb). If the flaps 15 approach-climb chart is used to set it, flaps 15 must be used for the approach in an emergency return to the departure airport.
The simulation's EFB performance pages plan the MD-10-30 to the 580,000 lb aircraft's weights.

blocks.content: The minimum flight weight exists because the takeoff and landing data, and the minimum control speeds behind them, were established down to that weight only. A very light aircraft has a low stalling speed but the same rudder and the same engine-out yawing moment, so VMCA, not the stall, starts to govern its speeds.

children.title: Center gear and anti-skid
children.summary: Why the long-span aircraft lose so much weight with the center gear up, and why anti-skid matters to the weight tables.

blocks.content: The DC-10-30, DC-10-40, KC-10A and MD-10-30 carry a third, two-wheel main gear on the fuselage centerline. It came with the long-range aircraft, which take off some 140,000 lb heavier than the DC-10-10: it takes a share of the weight off the wing gears, spreads the load on the runway pavement, and adds two braked wheels. Without it the two wing gears carry the whole aircraft, and every weight limit falls to a value close to the short-range aircraft's.

blocks.title: Effect of the center gear on the maximum weights
Effect of the center gear on the maximum weights
Effect of the center gear on the maximum weights (MD-10-30)

items: The DC-10-30 is normally operated with the center gear extended for takeoff and landing (FDX). With it retracted, the center-gear-retracted weights and special performance data apply.
The DC-10-10 and DC-10-15 have no center gear; the center gear of the DC-10-30 Tanker is removed by the conversion, and its own limits apply.

blocks.content: The center gear must be extended for takeoff and landing unless the operation is based on the AFM's Center Gear Retracted appendix. If it is retracted or removed, the operation must be based on that appendix.

**Anti-skid inoperative.** Without anti-skid the brakes can lock a wheel, and a locked tire on a dry runway wears through and bursts in a few hundred feet; the crew must brake well short of the friction limit, so the stopping distances are much longer. The anti-skid-inoperative weights keep the rejected takeoff and landing energies within what the brakes and tires can absorb at that gentler braking, and special takeoff performance data apply.

items: FedEx did not permit dispatch for revenue operations with the anti-skid system inoperative (FDX).
Anti-skid must be operative for takeoff unless the operation is based on the AFM's Anti-Skid Inoperative appendix.

sections.title: Center of gravity
sections.summary: The center of gravity envelopes in percent MAC, by gross weight, and why they are shaped as they are.

blocks.content: The center of gravity is stated in percent of the **mean aerodynamic chord** (MAC): 0 % is the leading edge of the MAC and 100 % its trailing edge. Measuring it this way ties the CG to the wing, which is what matters aerodynamically, because the aircraft's neutral point (the point about which the change in lift with angle of attack acts) lies at a nearly fixed fraction of the MAC.
On the KC-10A the MAC is 295.8 in long and its leading edge (LEMAC) is at fuselage station 1312; 1 % MAC is therefore about 3 in.

**The forward limit.** The further forward the CG, the more download the horizontal tail must make to trim, and the more nose-up stabilizer and elevator it takes to rotate for takeoff and to flare. The forward limit is where the tail would run out of authority at the lowest speeds, or where the nose gear would be loaded beyond its design. It stays at 8 % MAC at light weights and moves aft (to 10 % to 17 % MAC) at heavy weights, where the takeoff and flare demand more of the tail and the nose gear carries more.

**The aft limit.** The further aft the CG, the closer it comes to the neutral point and the smaller the static margin: the aircraft becomes less stable in pitch and lighter on the controls. The aft limit keeps a positive margin, acceptable stick-force gradients and good stall behavior. On the ground an aft CG also unloads the nose gear, which steers. At heavy weights the aft limit moves forward because the main gear and the wing-to-body structure would otherwise carry more than their design loads.

**Fuel moves the CG.** As fuel is used the CG moves, by an amount that depends on which tanks it comes from. The manufacturer therefore publishes a second, narrower **zero fuel weight CG envelope**: an aircraft loaded with its zero fuel CG inside it, and fueled and burned in the approved schedule, stays inside the gross weight envelope throughout the flight. Where the takeoff fuel is limited, the zero fuel envelope widens, because less fuel can move the CG less. Each table below gives the gross weight envelope; interpolate linearly between the weights shown. The limits apply in flight, for takeoff and for landing.

A CG near the aft limit is also the efficient one. Less tail download means less lift to carry on the wing and less trim drag, so keeping the CG as far aft as the envelope allows saves fuel. The KC-10 flight manual makes it a loading objective for cargo and dual-role missions.

The envelope is drawn to 449,000 lb, the taxi weight of the 446,000 lb takeoff weight for which the chart was made; the FedEx aircraft are limited to 440,000 lb by the weight table. The DC-10-10's forward limit moves a long way aft at heavy weights (16.9 % at 440,000 lb), much further than the long-span aircraft's. The MD-10-10's chart adds zero fuel CG limits that relax when the takeoff fuel is 114,000 lb, 102,000 lb or 80,000 lb or less, and a keep-out area for gross weights above 423,000 lb.
The DC-10-15's CG limits are not published in the sources used.

blocks.title: CG limits, DC-10-30 and MD-10-30, 580,000 lb aircraft
CG limits, DC-10-30, 565,000 lb and 572,000 lb aircraft (FedEx)
rows: 568,000 lb (565,000 lb aircraft) / 575,000 lb (572,000 lb aircraft)

blocks.content: For the 565,000 lb and 572,000 lb MD-10-30s the MD-10-30 AFM's charts give a forward limit of 9.9 % at the maximum weights, an aft limit of 24.8 % at 565,000 lb (24.6 % at the 568,000 lb taxi weight) or 24.4 % at 572,000 lb (24.1 % at 575,000 lb), and an aft-limit break at 27.8 % and 518,000 lb. The rest of their boundaries are given only graphically.

The long-span aircraft's envelope narrows sharply at the top: at 583,000 lb only 9.9 % to 23.6 % MAC is available, against 8 % to 29 % at landing weights. The aft limit there is set by the main gear and the wing attachment, which carry the most load when the CG is furthest aft. The zero fuel CG limits on the MD-10-30 charts relax when the takeoff fuel is 100,000 lb or less.
The DC-10-40's CG limits are not published in the sources used. The KDC-10 is simulated as a DC-10-30 and takes its limits.

Loading cargo so that the zero fuel CG falls within the desirable zero fuel CG envelope for cargo and dual-role missions (roughly 18 % to 25 % MAC, drawn shaded on the flight manual's chart) is a mission objective, not a limitation: it keeps the CG aft for economy.
In the cargo configuration, a zero fuel CG forward of 23.8 % MAC allows all the forward body tank fuel to be transferred to the wing tanks.
