sections.title: Airspeeds
sections.summary: VMO and MMO, the design maneuvering speed, flap, slat and landing gear placards, tire, turbulence and fuel dump speeds.

blocks.content: All airspeeds in this section are indicated airspeeds (KIAS) unless stated otherwise; where a Mach number is given with a speed, the lower of the two governs. Tire speeds are ground speeds.

children.title: Maximum operating speeds, VMO and MMO

blocks.content:
**VMO** (an indicated airspeed) and **MMO** (a Mach number) are the maximum operating limit speeds. Neither may be exceeded deliberately in any phase of flight: climb, cruise or descent. They are set below the design dive speed and Mach (VD and MD), which the aircraft demonstrated in flight test, and the gap is there to absorb an upset, a gust or a moment's inattention, not to be flown in.

The two limits protect against different things. VMO is a dynamic-pressure limit: it bounds the air loads on the structure, the loads from gusts (which grow with speed), the margin from flutter, and the energy of a bird strike on the windshield. MMO is a compressibility limit: near it, shock waves on the wing begin to separate the flow behind them, bringing buffet, a nose-down pitching tendency (Mach tuck, which the Mach trim compensates for), and a loss of control effectiveness. Low down the indicated-airspeed limit is reached first; high up, where the speed of sound is lower and the air thinner, the Mach limit is. The altitude at which a constant VMO equals MMO is the **crossover altitude**.

blocks.title: VMO (KIAS) and MMO, DC-10-10 and DC-10-30
rows: Not published in the sources used
Not published in the sources used

blocks.content: The DC-10-10's limit is a constant 340 KIAS up to the crossover near 27,800 ft and M 0.85 above it; the indicated values at 35,000 ft and above in the table are simply M 0.85 expressed in knots. The DC-10-30's limit rises from 350 KIAS at sea level to 375 KIAS at 10,000 ft, holds there to about 25,000 ft, and then gives way to M 0.88. Wherever the speed equal to MMO is lower than the tabulated VMO, MMO governs. The 347 KIAS printed for 27,800 ft is a few knots below M 0.88 at that height; it is reproduced as the manual prints it, and the lower figure is the one to fly to.

blocks.title: Overspeed band on the MD-10 PFD

blocks.content:
Full application of the rudder or ailerons, and maneuvers that take the wing close to the stalling angle of attack, are confined to speeds below **VA**. Below VA the wing stalls before a full, sudden control input or pull-up can load the structure beyond its limit; above it, the same input can break something before the wing stalls. VA rises with altitude because compressibility raises the indicated stalling speed, then falls again at high altitude with the Mach limit.

VA protects against one full deflection in one direction. It does not cover rapid reversals: alternating full rudder inputs, even below VA, can build sideslip and fin loads well beyond the design case.
VA for the DC-10-15 and DC-10-40 is not published in the sources used.
The KC-10A's VA, read from the flight manual's chart, is about 310 KIAS at sea level, rising to about 343 KIAS at 25,000 ft and decreasing above that with the Mach limit.

The MD-10 FCOM limits full application of the elevator, and maneuvers near the stall, to speeds below VA, and gives VA as a chart. Read from it: Series 10, about 263 KIAS at sea level, rising to about 300 KIAS near 28,000 ft and decreasing above; Series 30, about 310 KIAS at sea level, rising to about 340 KIAS in the mid-twenties and decreasing above.

The flap and slat placard speeds (**VFE**) protect the high-lift surfaces, their tracks, carriages and actuators, which are designed for the air loads of the takeoff and approach speeds and no more. The flap speeds are given in bands of flap angle: a band such as 5.1° to 15° applies to any flap angle inside it, whether it was reached through a fixed detent or the takeoff flap selector. The fixed detents are 0°, 15°, 22°, 35° and 50°; takeoff flap angles between them are set on the FLAP T.O. SEL thumbwheel. The slats have two placard speeds, one for their takeoff (mid) position and a lower one for full extension.

The flap and slat placard speeds (**VFE**) protect the high-lift surfaces, their tracks, carriages and actuators, which are designed for the air loads of the takeoff and approach speeds and no more. The flap speeds are given in bands of flap angle, and apply to any angle in the band however it was reached. The slats have two placard speeds, one for their takeoff (mid) position and a lower one for full extension.

blocks.title: Slat placard speeds, MD-10
rows: 270 KIAS / M .51 (TOGW 572,000 lb and above); 260 KIAS / M .51 (below 572,000 lb)

blocks.content: **Autoslat.** With the flaps and slats retracted, the stall warning system partially extends the outboard slats at the onset of stall warning, together with the stick shaker, to buy angle-of-attack margin; the SLAT RESET light comes on. Extension does not happen above the autoslat speed or with the slats already out. The autoslat limit is the speed for flight with the outboard slats in that position. Its Mach figure, M 0.75, is far above the normal slat limit because the event can happen in the clean configuration at altitude, and if the slats cannot be reset the aircraft still has to be flown to a landing. Once clear of the stall, retract them with the SLAT RESET switch-light.

blocks.alt: Drawing in the style of a flight deck placard, not a photograph: a black placard with white lettering headed FLAP / SLAT / GEAR LIMIT SPEEDS for the DC-10-30, listing flaps 0-5: 260 KT/.51M, 5.1-15: 250 KT/.51M, 15.1-25: 210 KT/.51M, 35: 185 KT/.51M, 50: 170 KT/.51M; slats TAKEOFF 260 KT/.51M, LAND 214 KT/.51M; gear VLO RET 230 KT, VLO EXT 260 KT, VLE 300 KT, .70M. All lettering legible.
blocks.title: Flap, slat and gear speeds, DC-10-30
blocks.caption: The placard values for the DC-10-30 below 572,000 lb takeoff weight; the heavier aircraft's differences are in the tables.

blocks.content:
**VLO** is the highest speed at which the gear may be moved; **VLE** the highest at which it may be flown down and locked. Retraction is limited more than extension because the gear must be swung up against its own drag with the doors open, and the actuators and door hinges are sized for that at 230 KIAS. Once down and locked, with the doors closed again, the gear tolerates 300 KIAS, which is what makes it useful as a drag device in an emergency descent.

An alternate extension releases the uplocks and lets gravity and air loads drive the gear down, with nothing hydraulic to control it, and is limited to 230 KIAS. After it the main gear doors stay open, which is why the extended-gear limit is then 260 KIAS.
The alternate extension speed of 230 KIAS is a FedEx limit (FDX).
The MD-10 FCOM lists gear retraction, extension, extended and alternate-extended speeds as above, without a separate alternate extension speed.

blocks.title: Maximum tire speed (ground speed)
rows: Not published in the sources used

blocks.content: The tire speed limit is set by the tire's construction: the centrifugal load on the tread and the heat generated by flexing both grow with rotational speed. Because it is a ground speed, it bites at high airports, in hot weather, with a tailwind, and above all in a flapless or slatless landing at high weight, when the touchdown speed approaches it. It is one of the limits a heavy-weight or overweight landing must be checked against.

blocks.title: Turbulence penetration speeds
rows: 280 to 287 KIAS, or M 0.80 to 0.85 above 35,000 ft, whichever range is lower
290 to 310 KIAS, or M 0.80 to 0.85 above 35,000 ft, whichever range is lower
Not published in the sources used

blocks.title: Turbulence penetration speed
rows: 290 to 310 KIAS or M 0.80 to 0.85, whichever is lower

blocks.title: Turbulence penetration speeds
rows: The greater of 250 KIAS or the climb speed may be used

blocks.content: The penetration speed is a compromise between two dangers. Too slow, and the angle-of-attack excursions of a strong gust can reach the stall buffet, while upsets come more easily and thrust changes have more effect on trim. Too fast, and the same gust loads the structure harder, because the load from a vertical gust grows with airspeed. The band sits between the two with margin to both. At high altitude, where the band between low-speed and high-speed buffet narrows, the Mach number governs, and most high-altitude turbulence is not severe enough to need a reduction at all: from M 0.85 to M 0.82 at 35,000 ft saves only about 17 kt of true airspeed. Fly attitude, accept the airspeed and altitude excursions, and do not chase either; the procedure is in [Adverse Weather](adverse-weather).

Not published in the sources used

blocks.content: Dump rates, undumpable quantities and the electrical cautions for dumping are under [Fuel](#fuel-limits).

sections.title: Power plant
sections.summary: Rotor speed, EGT, oil and starter limits for each engine type, the overspeed and overtemperature actions, thrust setting and reverser limits.

blocks.content:
Each engine limit protects a particular failure mode. **N1** and **N2**, the fan and core rotor speeds, are limited by the centrifugal stress in the discs and blades: stress rises with the square of rotor speed, and a disc that bursts is beyond what the engine case is designed to contain. **EGT**, measured downstream of the high-pressure turbine, stands in for the turbine inlet temperature, which cannot be measured directly; turbine blades lose life by creep and oxidation at a rate that climbs steeply with temperature, so the hotter limits come with a time allowance. **Oil temperature** is limited by the oil's breakdown and by bearing cooling, and the **minimum oil pressure** is what the bearings need to stay lubricated.

The EGT allowances are cumulative. Operation above the maximum continuous EGT is limited to five minutes in total, and any time spent in the two-minute band counts against the five minutes.
The engine instruments' red radials and maximum limit pointers mark the limits in the tables below.

blocks.title: CF6-6D overspeed and overtemperature
rows: Reduce thrust below the redline and continue normal operation.
Reduce to idle. Use higher thrust only at the pilot's discretion.

items: The 5-minute takeoff rating may be extended to 10 minutes for an engine-out contingency; the maintenance requirements for that extension must then be met.
The certified time and temperature limits apply whenever the maximum continuous EGT is exceeded. The 2-minute acceleration transient may occur at any point in the takeoff.
Landings and unplanned go-arounds are permitted at outside air temperatures up to 55 °C.
Idle N1, N2 and EGT limits are maintenance values, not crew limits.
Any operation beyond the stated limits must be recorded (duration and extent) in the AFTO Form 781.

blocks.content: The MD-10 FCOM gives the CF6-50C2's maximum N1 as 119.5 %, a point higher than the 118.5 % of the KC-10 and FedEx DC-10 manuals for the same engine, and starts its overspeed band at 119.6 % to match. Fly the MD-10 to its own book's figure.

blocks.title: CF6-50C2 overspeed and overtemperature
rows: Reduce thrust below the redline and continue normal operation.
Reduce to idle. Use higher thrust only at the pilot's discretion.

blocks.title: CF6-50C2 overspeed and overtemperature, MD-10-30
rows: Reset thrust and continue normal engine operation to landing.
Reduce to idle. Use higher thrust only at the pilot's discretion.

items: The actions in the overspeed tables assume a brief excursion. If any engine indication is abnormal once the thrust lever is at minimum thrust, consider a precautionary shutdown.
Every overspeed or overtemperature must be recorded, with its magnitude and duration, and reported to maintenance. Note the value on the maximum limit pointer before resetting it.

Above the upper band the engine has gone beyond the range for which the manufacturer accepts continued normal use. Idle thrust minimizes further damage while the engine is still available if it is needed.

blocks.content: The DC-10-15's CF6-50C2F is a variant of the CF6-50C2 rated for hot and high airports. Its operating limits are not published in the sources used. The simulation gives it the CF6-50C2's limits and thrust; treat the CF6-50C2 table above as the working figure.

No DC-10-40 flight manual limitations are available in the sources used. The figures below are the engine's own certificated limits from its FAA type certificate data sheet. An airframe manual may be more restrictive, never less. The certificate states rotor speed limits in rpm and does not define the 100 % reference behind the cockpit's percentage scales, so the N1 and N2 redlines in percent, and the EPR limits, are not published in the sources used.

blocks.title: JT9D-59A type-certificate limits
rows: 5 minutes; up to 10 minutes only with an engine inoperative
Turbine gas temperature, starting (ground and in flight)
If exceeded on an in-flight start, record the maximum and its duration
In a cold start, above 60 psig limits the engine to idle until the oil warms

blocks.content: The temperatures are stated at the low-pressure turbine discharge, behind the whole turbine, whereas the CF6's EGT is sensed further upstream in its turbine. The gas has given up a great deal of its heat to the low-pressure turbine by then, which is why the JT9D's figures look so much lower than the CF6's: they are not comparable numbers. The JT9D is a two-spool turbofan like the CF6, so the same principles of rotor stress and turbine life apply.

blocks.title: Starter duty cycle
rows: 30 seconds for each minute of operation
Cool 10 minutes before each further 5-minute cycle
At the lowest practical N2: preferably 0 %, and not above 20 %
Re-engagement, emergency (for example an engine fire indication)

blocks.content: The pneumatic starter is a small air turbine driving the engine's accessory gearbox through a reduction gear and an overrunning clutch. Its duty cycle protects the turbine's bearings and oil from overheating. The re-engagement limits protect the clutch: engaging a stationary starter onto a gearbox that is still turning makes the clutch pick up the rotating engine in one shock (a **crash engagement**), and the shock grows with N2.

**Start EGT.** If EGT rises above 750 °C during a start, the start is acceptable on a one-time basis provided it did not exceed 900 °C and spent no more than 40 seconds above 750 °C; advise maintenance and make a maintenance log entry.

**Start EGT.** The normal starting limit is 750 °C and the maximum 900 °C; peaks between them are limited to 40 seconds, and any start above 750 °C needs an AFTO Form 781 entry. One start into the 800 to 900 °C range is allowed and the intended flight may be completed before maintenance action; tell maintenance the temperature reached and ask for a delayed inspection and maintenance availability at the next stop. The flight manual's starting EGT chart divides exceedances into three areas: area A, record and have maintenance act before the next start (the flight may be completed); area B, record, with repeated starts there a cause for corrective action; area C, discontinue the start and have maintenance correct the fault before another attempt.

**Start EGT.** A logbook entry is required whenever EGT exceeds 750 °C during a start. If EGT stays above 750 °C for more than 40 seconds, or climbs quickly past 750 °C and looks set to exceed 900 °C, terminate the start with the fuel lever. One start into the 800 to 900 °C range is allowed and the intended flight may be completed before maintenance action; report the temperature and duration to maintenance.

blocks.title: Engine oil limits, CF6-6D and CF6-50C2 (FedEx DC-10)
Engine oil limits, CF6-50C2 (KC-10A)
rows: Normal pressure at flight and ground idle
10 psi at stabilized idle; below 10 psi at idle requires an engine shutdown
A deviation of more than 10 psi at steady N2 may indicate a pending engine failure
Full-scale surges may occur in cold-soaked starts; above 90 psi at rated core speed is acceptable with cold oil and fuel, and takeoff is permitted without a warm-up

blocks.content: Below the minimum oil pressure the bearings are no longer assured of an oil film and can fail within minutes; in other conditions than idle, follow the low oil pressure procedure in [Abnormal Procedures](abnormal-procedures).

items: Takeoff performance assumes takeoff N1 is set before 80 KIAS. After 80 KIAS do not adjust the thrust levers except to prevent exceeding an engine limit (FDX).
Do not engage the autothrottle SPD or N1 mode after 80 KIAS until a thrust rating other than takeoff has been selected on the thrust rating computer (FDX).
A takeoff N1 set before 80 KIAS may not be used at altitudes more than 2,000 ft above the takeoff airport's pressure altitude (FDX).
Reduced-thrust takeoffs are not permitted from runways contaminated by water, ice, slush or snow.
Use continuous ignition in heavy rain or severe turbulence (FDX).

blocks.content: The first three rules keep the takeoff consistent with the data it was calculated from. The takeoff N1 is valid for the takeoff airport's conditions; set it once, early, and leave it, and do not let a speed mode start trimming thrust during the roll. Reduced thrust is not permitted on a contaminated runway: slush and standing water add drag during the acceleration and lengthen the stop, and the full thrust margin is needed.

items: Engine limitations are presented in the AFM performance sections; the engine limits and the thrust setting charts must be observed.

Use ignition OVRD for flameout protection in severe turbulence or heavy rain. It may be used at any time at the captain's discretion and has no time limit, although continuous use shortens igniter life.
Select ignition OVRD ON whenever conditions call for engine anti-ice or engine and airframe anti-ice, for the duration of the icing encounter.

blocks.content: Thrust ratings are listed with the CF6-50C2 limits above. In severe turbulence set the engine ignition selector to CONT A or CONT B; see [Adverse Weather](adverse-weather).

items: Reverse thrust is prohibited in flight.
Reverse thrust must not be used to back the aircraft on the ground.

blocks.content: A reverser deployed in flight destroys lift over part of the wing and produces a large asymmetric force that the flight controls may not be able to hold. On the ground at very low speed, reversed airflow throws debris and hot gas forward into the inlets, and braking an aircraft that is rolling backwards can rock it onto its tail.

**Airworthiness directive limits (aircraft without the TRAS lock).** On FedEx aircraft not modified with the thrust reverser actuating system lock, AD 2002-08-17 added temporary limits for the wing engines (1 and 3). If the REVERSER UNLOCK (REV U/L) or REVERSER VALVE OPEN (REV PRES) light of engine 1 or 3 comes on in flight, even with normal performance, reduce that engine to flight idle and land at the nearest suitable airport. Takeoff is not permitted, unless the affected reverser is deactivated, after such an event, with either light on or inoperative, or with a reverser that did not stow after the previous landing.

Takeoff or landing with both wing reversers deactivated was not authorized for FedEx operations. Where permitted by the AFM it is prohibited from a contaminated runway, and needs 5 % more takeoff runway when wet; landing distance rises by 22 % wet and 48 % contaminated on the DC-10-10F, and by 10 % wet or contaminated on the DC-10-30F.

sections.title: APU
sections.summary: APU temperature and speed limits, starter duty cycle, and the start and operating envelopes.

blocks.title: APU limits, DC-10
rows: Maximum rotor speed, N1 and N2
2 Hz within the normal operating band
Do not use APU bleed air for wing anti-ice
Two consecutive start attempts; after 10 minutes' cooling, two more; then cool for 1 hour
Recommended for ground use only; acceptable starting up to 10,000 ft
Electrical load in flight, normal mode (FDX)
Electrical load in flight, standby mode (FDX)

blocks.content: The standby control mode is a degraded mode, used in flight only when the normal mode has failed. The in-flight operating envelope limits the generator load the APU may carry as the air gets thinner and warmer, because the APU's turbine temperature, not its generator, runs out first:

blocks.title: APU in-flight operating envelope, static air temperature (FDX)
APU limits, KC-10A
rows: Maximum rotor speed, N1 and N2
1 minute on, then 5 minutes off to cool; no more than four start attempts in 20 minutes, then at least 1 hour of cooling
Up to 30,000 ft, from about −54 °C (sea level) to +50 °C (sea level), narrowing with altitude
The APU may shut down if generator load exceeds 67 %, or 50 % in the warmest corner of the envelope between about 24,000 and 30,000 ft; pneumatics not recommended above 18,000 ft
Generator load not recommended; pneumatics not recommended above 18,000 ft. Use only if the normal mode has failed
NORM mode ±2 Hz within the normal band; STBY mode ±20 Hz
Do not use the APU for wing anti-ice: its air is neither hot enough nor plentiful enough to keep the wings clear
Do not run the APU during any air refueling operation, or with a known fuel leak in the boom pivot area

blocks.title: APU limits, MD-10
rows: Maximum rotor speed, N1 and N2
Two consecutive start attempts; after 10 minutes' cooling, two more; then cool for 1 hour
Do not use the APU for wing anti-ice
The APU must be off for the takeoff roll, in flight and for landing, even though APU takeoff and in-flight procedures appear in the manual

blocks.content: The APU's starter is an electric motor working hard against a cold, stationary rotor; repeated attempts heat its windings faster than they can shed the heat, which is what the duty cycle prevents.

blocks.title: Cabin pressure limits, DC-10
rows: Maximum differential pressure for takeoff and landing
Maximum differential pressure with three packs operating
2, except on aircraft modified for three-pack operation (N317FE-N319FE), which may run 3; a placard on the second officer's panel identifies them

blocks.title: Cabin pressure limits, KC-10A
rows: Maximum differential pressure at takeoff and landing

blocks.title: Cabin pressure limits, MD-10
rows: Maximum differential pressure at takeoff and landing
Turn one pack off before selecting ECON to OFF

blocks.content: The fuselage is a pressure vessel whose skin, frames and doors are sized for a maximum pressure differential. The relief (safety) valves open at 9.1 psi to keep the differential below that, whatever the controller does; FedEx's 8.8 psi operating limit keeps the normal schedule clear of the valves. The 0.5 psi limit for takeoff and landing exists so that the aircraft is essentially unpressurized whenever an evacuation is likely: plug-type doors cannot be opened against even a small differential, and a pressure step at touchdown is uncomfortable and loads the doors.

**Unpressurized flight.** Fly with the cabin pressure control in MANUAL and the outflow valve between half and two-thirds open, so that the cabin is ventilated by the packs' flow without building a differential.

items: If installed, set the FWD CARGO VENT and AFT CARGO VENT switches to OFF for unpressurized flight.
FedEx did not permit dispatch for revenue operations with the pressurization system inoperative (FDX).

blocks.content: The air tanker may not be pressurized while its retardant tanks hold water or retardant; see [the tanker conversion's limitations](aerial-firefighting#tanker-limitations).

Do not interconnect two or more active engine pneumatic supply systems, except for short periods during an engine start (FedEx: an in-flight start) or, on the KC-10A and MD-10, while changing over from APU air. Two engines feeding one manifold at different pressures fight each other through their regulating valves, and a leak downstream can no longer be isolated to one supply.

blocks.title: Maximum recommended load on one engine pneumatic supply
rows: At or above maximum continuous thrust (takeoff, go-around, MCT)
One pack plus wing anti-ice (both wings)
Two packs, or one pack plus wing anti-ice (both wings)

blocks.content: For this purpose each pack counts as one subsystem and the wing anti-ice as one. Engine anti-ice is not counted: each engine's cowl is anti-iced by its own bleed, independently of the pneumatic manifold. Bleed air is air the engine has already spent work compressing. At high thrust, taking more of it raises the turbine temperature for the same thrust and costs takeoff performance; at low thrust, one engine's supply cannot deliver the flow of more than two consumers at a usable pressure.
The lavatory and galley vent is not counted against the supply.
The lavatory vent and the cargo heat and vent are not counted against the supply. With three packs operating, turn one pack off before selecting ECON to OFF.
For takeoff with various bleed configurations, the thrust and performance corrections apply (FDX).

sections.title: Automatic flight
sections.summary: Autopilot, autothrottle, flight director, autoland and flight management limits.

items: Do not use either autopilot when on emergency power.
Maximum speed for automatic glideslope capture: 250 kt.
Maximum vertical speed at autopilot engagement: +4,000 ft/min climbing, −8,000 ft/min descending (FDX).
If the AP OUT OF TRIM light stays on for more than 3 seconds while the autopilot is tracking the glideslope, disengage the autopilot.
Do not use the autopilot for a touch-and-go landing, or for a go-around with an engine failed.
Do not engage the autopilot's CWS function for takeoff or landing (FDX).
Disengage the autopilot when operating on emergency power.
Do not let the autopilot capture the glideslope automatically above 250 kt: at excessive speed the capture can become unstable in pitch.

If the AP OUT OF TRIM light stays on continuously for more than 3 seconds after the aircraft is stabilized and tracking the glideslope, disengage the autopilot and disable the autopilot pitch trim (APT). Before engaging the autopilot again without APT, trim the aircraft manually and be tracking the glideslope at the final approach speed.
Do not use the autopilot go-around mode with an engine failed, or during touch-and-go landings.

If an autopilot is deactivated for flight by removing its computers, both the pitch and roll computers on that side must be removed. The autopilot and flight director on that side, the VOR/ILS receiver and radio altimeter self-tests and the altitude advisory are then inoperative; if the yaw computer is removed too, that side's rate-of-turn indication and its yaw damper are lost as well.
The LAND function is placarded inoperative: the KC-10A has no automatic landing. Category II approaches are flown coupled, with all engines operating, within the wind limits in [Wind](#wind-limits).
For non-precision approaches, disengage the autopilot no lower than the applicable minimums minus 50 ft.
Do not exceed 200 KIAS with the autopilot engaged in SINGLE LAND or DUAL LAND.

blocks.content: **Why these limits.** On emergency power the autopilot cannot be relied on to have all its computers, servos and monitors powered. The AP OUT OF TRIM light means the autopilot is holding a sustained elevator force that the stabilizer trim has not relieved; if it disconnected, or were disconnected, in that state the aircraft would pitch abruptly by the amount of the stored force, which on the glideslope is close to the ground. The minimum engagement altitudes give the pilot the height to recover from a hard-over before reaching the ground, and they reflect how the autopilot's fault monitoring was demonstrated in certification.

items: Do not use the autothrottles for touch-and-go landings.
Autothrottles are not authorized for takeoff on any DC-10-10.

Do not use the flight director's takeoff mode at weights below WMC (the maximum weight at which minimum control speeds govern the takeoff speeds and field lengths) when using derated (standard) takeoff thrust.

A failure of the autothrottle duplex servo can cause uncommanded thrust lever advances. Monitor the thrust levers whenever the autothrottles are engaged, in any mode: an unmonitored advance can overspeed an engine.
Make sure the autothrottles are disconnected after touchdown on a touch-and-go landing.

With derated takeoff thrust and speeds limited by VMCG for maximum thrust, the flight director may command the wrong airspeed and pitch attitude if an engine fails and the remaining engines' thrust is increased. It may also command the wrong speed and attitude when V2 has been corrected for the center of gravity.

blocks.content: The flight director limits share one cause. Its takeoff guidance is built around the V2 it is given and the thrust it expects. When V2 was set by the minimum control speed at full thrust rather than by the stall margin at the actual weight, and the crew then restores thrust after an engine failure, the pitch command no longer corresponds to a safe speed for the situation, so the crew must fly speed rather than the bars.

blocks.title: Autoland limits, DC-10
rows: Maximum speed, SNGL LAND or DUAL LAND
Maximum crosswind, SNGL LAND or DUAL LAND (FDX)
Minimum threshold crossing height, all autoland approaches (FDX)
Headwind and tailwind, CAT II and CAT III (FDX)
Maximum glideslope angle; maximum airport elevation
Not published in the sources used

blocks.content: The minimum threshold crossing height ensures the beam brings the aircraft over the threshold high enough for the autoland's flare law, which starts at a fixed radio height, to complete the flare before touchdown and to keep the main gear, some way behind and below the glideslope antenna, clear of the threshold.

blocks.title: Autoland limits, MD-10
rows: Automatic landings prohibited above 8,000 ft MSL (FCOM). The later revision of the MD-10-30 AFM gives 8,500 ft MSL
Maximum speed, SINGLE LAND or DUAL LAND engaged
Not published in the sources used

blocks.content: The elevation limit is an MSL figure, the airport's elevation, not a pressure altitude. At a high airport the true airspeed and ground speed for the same indicated approach speed are higher, so the flare and rollout happen faster than the autoland was demonstrated for.

items: FMS instrument approaches flown in instrument conditions must be published procedures retrieved from the FMS database, which must be current.
Fly them in the FMS approach mode, with GPS integrity monitoring (RAIM) available at the final approach fix.
Fly GPS tactical approaches only in visual conditions.
During dead reckoning with GPS as the selected navigation solution, select another valid solution or do not use the FMS for navigation.
The FMS does not fly every SID and STAR leg; unsupported legs appear as a discontinuity, and the pilot must intervene at LEG DISCON to fly the procedure correctly.
Do not use the required time of arrival (RTA) function to comply with an ATC clearance that contains a time.
Verify any manually entered V1, VR and V2 against AFM data. Before takeoff, recompute and re-enter the V speeds after any change that affects them.
The FMS performance predictions have not been demonstrated accurate: range, fuel management and engine-out terrain clearance must not be based on them.
On an ILS or IGS approach with the glideslope inoperative, do not use FMS PROF or its vertical deviation for descent after the final approach fix.
Do not use FMS PROF in descent or approach below the MDA(H) or DA(H).
Do not use the amber VMIN foot to set approach or landing target speeds until the aircraft has passed the acceleration altitude on the TAKEOFF page.
With GPS not installed, deselected or inoperative, display the raw-data bearing pointer or course deviation for an NDB or VOR approach on at least one approach or VOR display.
Outside the US National Airspace System, disable GPS updating for approach and terminal operations if the navigation database and charts are not referenced to WGS-84 or NAD-83.
A modified database approach must still comply with the published procedure.
Do not use the DUMP TO GW and DUMP TIME functions on the fuel initialization page; they do not work (unless the aircraft has the service letter fix).

blocks.title: Electrical load limits, KC-10A
rows: 1.0 to 1.5 per generator for 5 minutes; above 1.5 for 5 seconds
NORM mode: ±2 Hz within the normal band; STBY mode: ±20 Hz

blocks.content: Any condition that holds an electrical indication outside its normal range should be corrected at the earliest opportunity. Do not cycle the inertial navigation mode selector out of OFF more than three times in three minutes: repeated cycling builds up heat in the inertial navigation unit.

The loadmeters read in fractions of rated load, so 1.0 is the generator's or transformer-rectifier's rating. Above it, the windings, and for a generator its constant speed drive, heat faster than they are cooled; the timed allowances let the system ride through a lost generator or the inrush of a large motor while the crew sheds load. On the DC-10 and KC-10 the flight engineer manages the loads.
No electrical limitations are published in the MD-10 sources used; the automatic electrical system controller manages the generators' loads.

items: **Yaw dampers:** at least two channels must be operative for takeoff.
**Elevator load feel:** the ELEV FEEL switch must be in AUTO, except in an abnormal condition.
**Spoilers:** use the spoilers as speed brakes only with the flaps at 0°, with or without the slats extended. Do not extend the ground spoilers in flight.
**Takeoff warning:** the slat function of the takeoff warning system must be operable for takeoff.
**Yaw damper:** any two channels must be operating before the start of the takeoff.
**Elevator load feel:** use of the elevator feel switch is limited to AUTO, except in an abnormal condition.
**Speed brakes:** use only with the flaps fully retracted, with or without the slats extended.
**Ground spoilers:** do not extend in flight.
**Takeoff warning:** the slat function of the takeoff warning system must be operative for takeoff.
**Yaw damper:** two yaw damper channels must be operative for takeoff, and both must come from the same flight control computer.
**Elevator load feel:** the ELEV FEEL switch must be in AUTO, except in an abnormal condition.
**In-flight speed brakes:** use only in the 0° flap configuration, with or without the slats extended.
**Auto ground spoilers:** must be operative for takeoff, unless the operation is based on the AFM's Auto Ground Spoilers Inoperative appendix.
**Ground spoilers:** do not extend in flight.

blocks.content:
**Yaw damper.** A swept-wing aircraft has a lightly damped lateral-directional oscillation, the Dutch roll, which is worst at high altitude and low speed. The yaw dampers suppress it; with two channels operating at the start of the takeoff, a single failure still leaves a working damper for the rest of the flight.

**Elevator feel.** The feel system schedules the column force with airspeed so that a given pull produces about the same load factor at any speed. In manual, a feel setting chosen for low speed makes the column far too light at high speed, inviting an overstress.

**Speed brakes with flaps.** Spoilers raised ahead of extended flaps break up the flow the flaps depend on, causing buffet, a large loss of lift and loads on the flaps that they were not designed for.

**Slat takeoff warning.** A takeoff without the slats extended leaves the wing without the leading-edge high lift the takeoff speeds assume, and the stall comes at a far lower angle of attack than the crew expects. The slat warning is the last defense against that configuration error.

sections.title: Fuel
sections.summary: Loading, capacities, management and imbalance, ballast, fuel density and temperature, fuel grades and fuel dumping.

blocks.content: The fuel limits serve three purposes. The loading and usage schedules keep the wing's bending relief and the center of gravity within what the structure and the CG envelope were designed for. The imbalance limits keep the lateral trim within the ailerons' authority and the wing loads symmetric. The density and temperature limits keep the fuel pumpable and the engines fed.

items: Load the three main tanks evenly until tanks 1 and 3 are full, then continue loading tank 2.
On the DC-10-30, add any further fuel to the upper auxiliary tank at the same time until it is full, then put the rest in the lower auxiliary tank.
The quantity in each tank must not exceed the structural and usable values below.

blocks.title: Usable fuel, lb at 6.7 lb/US gal (FedEx)
rows: Not published in the sources used

items: Fuel density must be between 6.0 and 7.1 lb/US gal. Below 6.5 lb/US gal the maximum takeoff and in-flight gross weight is reduced, as shown in the flight manual's chart (read it with either the fuel density or the full-tank reading of main tank 1 or 3).

Fuel may be loaded in any sequence except: when the gross weight after refueling will exceed 556,000 lb, or the zero fuel weight plus the fuel to be loaded in the body tanks will exceed 414,000 lb, main tanks 1, 2 and 3 must be filled before the weight reaches 556,000 lb.
The CG envelope must not be exceeded during fueling.
At the completion of fueling the lateral imbalance must not exceed 4,000 lb, reduced by 100 lb for every 10,000 lb of main-deck cargo.
At the completion of fueling, main tank 2 must hold no less than main tank 1 or 3.
The quantity in each tank must not exceed the structural and usable values in the AFM's fuel tank capacity table.
The fill schedule applies to the quantity in each tank at the completion of fueling.
When full wing tanks are not needed, load the three main tanks equally to the quantity required.

For greater loads, load the three main tanks equally until tanks 1 and 3 are full, then fill tank 2 (Series 10: to the quantity required). On the Series 30, then fill the upper auxiliary tank, then the lower auxiliary tank.
Before engine start, each tank's quantity may vary by ±5 % because of the fuel system test; after engine start the system transfers fuel to meet the programmed schedule.
Fuel density must be between 6.3 and 7.1 lb/US gal. Reduce the maximum takeoff weight by 2,500 lb for each 0.1 lb/US gal below 6.5 lb/US gal.

blocks.content: The outboard tanks are filled first because fuel far out on the wing gives the most bending relief, and the body and center tanks last because their fuel loads the wing root as cargo does. Low-density fuel reduces the weight that full wing tanks can carry, and with it the relief: that is the reason for the weight reduction below 6.5 lb/US gal.

items: On the DC-10-30, transfer the auxiliary tank fuel to the main tanks until the auxiliary tank is empty. Leave the auxiliary tank pumps ON no longer than 10 minutes after their PUMP PRESS LOW lights begin to blink.
Then transfer from tank 2 to the outboard tanks until all three are even, and use fuel equally from each tank.
At least one aft pump in tank 2 must be ON for engine 2 to run.
Maximum lateral fuel imbalance: 2,000 lb (FDX).
Do not reset, or trip and reset, any fuel pump circuit breaker.
With the gross weight above 556,000 lb, or the zero fuel weight plus the fuel in the body tanks above 414,000 lb, main tanks 1, 2 and 3 must be kept full, for structural reasons.
Maximum lateral fuel imbalance: 4,000 lb below 556,000 lb gross weight; 2,000 lb at 556,000 lb or more. The allowable imbalance is reduced by 100 lb for every 10,000 lb of main-deck cargo.
Main tank 2 should not hold less than main tank 1 or 3.
Empty the center wing lower compartment as soon as possible.
Keep the CG within limits.
When the CG requires balance fuel in the forward fuselage tank, keep that fuel there until main tank 1 or 3 holds 5,000 lb or less.
At least one aft pump of main tank 2 must be ON for engine 2. With JET B or JP-4 above 40 °C, two aft pumps in tank 2 must be ON for engine 2, and the aft pump in tanks 1 and 3 for the wing engines.
Fuel remaining in a tank when its indicator reads zero is unusable.

If the manifold scavenge valve circuit breaker trips, do not reset it until maintenance has confirmed the solenoid housing is intact and the coil is not shorted to the case. Do not reset any tripped fuel pump circuit breaker.

blocks.content: **Yaw oscillation.** With certain combinations of fuel in the forward and aft fuselage tanks, fuel sloshing in the forward tank can drive a 0.4 Hz yaw oscillation, usually above M 0.85. It is not dangerous to the aircraft. If it occurs, transfer fuel out of the forward fuselage tank, preferably to the aft fuselage tank, until it dies down to an acceptable amplitude or stops.

items: On the Series 30, fuel is transferred from the upper auxiliary tank to each main tank, keeping them full, while the lower auxiliary tank keeps the upper one full until the lower tank is empty.
When the upper auxiliary tank is empty, tank 2 transfers to tanks 1 and 3 until all three are equal; fuel is then used equally from each.
Maximum lateral fuel imbalance between tanks 1 and 3: 2,900 lb (Series 10); 2,500 lb (Series 30).
With the quantity indication working, fuel remaining when an indicator reads zero is not usable in flight.
Do not reset any tripped fuel pump circuit breaker.

blocks.content: **Why not reset a fuel pump breaker.** A fuel pump breaker that trips may have tripped on a short circuit inside a pump that sits in the fuel tank. Resetting it can put an arc inside a tank of fuel vapour.

Ballast fuel is fuel carried to hold the center of gravity, typically on a ferry flight with an empty freighter, and declared unusable. It is part of the zero fuel weight. Normal loading and management apply, with these changes:

items: All ballast fuel goes in the upper auxiliary tank (FDX).
About 45,000 lb of ballast fuel is needed to ferry an empty aircraft (FDX).

All or part of the upper auxiliary tank's fuel may be declared ballast. Ballast is unusable and is added to the zero fuel weight; it must stay in the upper auxiliary tank, so turn the auxiliary tank pumps OFF before the tank reaches the ballast level.
The auxiliary fuel quantity indicator must be operative.
If fuel is dumped, the auxiliary tank pumps must be OFF when the ballast level is reached.
An INOP sticker recording the amount of ballast fuel is placed on the second officer's panel.

blocks.content: Ballast fuel provisions apply to the DC-10-30 only.

items: Ballast fuel may be loaded only in main tank 2, or on the Series 30 in tank 2 or the upper auxiliary tank, and in only one tank at a time.
Maximum ballast fuel: tank 2, 25,000 lb; upper auxiliary tank, 75,000 lb.

blocks.content: JP-4 and Jet B are wide-cut substitutes for the normal kerosene-type jet fuel. When either is used, these limits apply:

items: Altitude is limited to 20,000 ft when the indicated fuel temperature at takeoff is above 44 °C; the aircraft may climb without restriction once the indication has fallen to 40 °C. The fuel temperature indicator must be operative for takeoff.
At least two aft tank pumps in tank 2 must be ON for engine 2 when using JP-4 or Jet B above 40 °C.
The aft tank pump in tanks 1 and 3 must be ON for the wing engines.

Some FedEx tails carried further climb restrictions with wide-cut fuel above 30 °C at takeoff: a climb above 20,000 ft at no more than 1,000 ft/min while watching the aft pump pressure, and a reduced cruise speed at 25,000 ft until the fuel had cooled (FDX).

blocks.content: Wide-cut fuels (JP-4, Jet B) contain light fractions with a high vapour pressure. Warm and at low ambient pressure they boil in the tanks and lines, the pumps cavitate, and an engine fed on vapour can flame out. The altitude limit and the extra pumps keep the fuel pressurized until it has cooled.

items: Fuel temperature for starting: −40 °C to +60 °C, with the aircraft boost pumps operating.
Fuel temperature for all other operations: from 3 °C above the fuel's freezing point to +49 °C without boost pumps, or +60 °C with boost pumps operating.
When tank 3 holds less than 12,000 lb, its temperature probe reads air, not fuel, and the indication is not subject to the AFM limit; use TAT as a guide to the fuel temperature.
JP-4 and Jet B may be used only when the operation is based on the AFM's JP-4/Jet B fuel appendix.
The listed jet fuels, or any mixture of them, are approved for unlimited use in the KC-10A's engines and need no fuel control adjustment when switching between them; JP-8 is primary.
Avoid altitudes at which the indicated fuel temperature falls to less than 6 °C above the fuel's freezing point. Before using commercial fuel, obtain its freezing point from the supplier.
Commercial fuels may lack the icing inhibitor that stops water in the fuel freezing below 0 °C; take that into account in planning.

Aviation gasoline is for emergency use only: no more than 3 flight hours at a time, from sea level to 20,000 ft, with a fuel tank temperature of 24 °C or less and the boost pumps on throughout. Hotter gasoline can make the engine fuel pumps cavitate. Total use is limited to 10 hours between hot section inspections, and every use must be logged.

blocks.content: A suction-feed (pumps off) altitude limit is not published in the sources used for any of the three aircraft.

blocks.title: Fuel dump (FedEx)
rows: Maximum dump rate, all tank, transfer and auxiliary pumps on, crossfeeds open (FDX)
Undumpable fuel, each of tanks 1 and 3

blocks.content: The automatic shutoff ends the dump from each main tank at its low-level float; the undumpable figures above, 40,000 lb in all, are what FedEx counts on remaining, with margin for the floats' tolerance (see the [Fuel](fuel) system part). Without DC bus 2, the DUMP VALVE OPEN lights and the automatic shutoff do not work: monitor the fuel quantity and terminate the dump manually. With electrical malfunctions present, watch the quantity closely throughout the dump.
The maximum fuel dump speed is 325 KIAS below 28,000 ft and M 0.82 above. The KC-10A manual states no dump-rate or residual-fuel limitations.
The Series 30's maximum fuel dump speed is 325 KIAS below 28,000 ft and M 0.82 above. The undumpable fuel used for the zero fuel weight limit is 42,300 lb.

The undumpable quantity is the reserve that remains when the dump stops, and the reason the zero fuel weight performance limit subtracts it: an aircraft that dumps to return can never be lighter than its zero fuel weight plus this fuel. See [Weights](#weights) and the [Fuel](fuel) system part.

items: Auxiliary pump test: the minimum acceptable pressure is 2,400 psi, less 3 psi for each 1 °C of hydraulic system temperature above 0 °C (FDX).
The number 1 auxiliary pump must hold the minimum pressure in system 3; the number 1 and number 2 auxiliary pumps together must hold it in systems 1 and 3 and in systems 2 and 3 (FDX).

No minimum pressure is required when all three systems are powered by one or both auxiliary pumps; the number 2 pump, if operative, is required only to keep pressure in all three systems, and the manufacturer gives no minimum for that case (FDX).
Do not reset a tripped auxiliary hydraulic pump circuit breaker.

blocks.content: The temperature allowance in the auxiliary pump test reflects the fluid: as it warms, it thins, more of it leaks past the pump's internal clearances, and the pressure a healthy pump can hold at a given flow falls.

items: The number 1 auxiliary pump switch must be operational for dispatch. Both auxiliary pumps have an interchangeable wiring harness; the minimum equipment list gives the procedure.
The boom's hydraulic requirement before takeoff is under [Air refueling](#air-refueling-limits).

blocks.content: Do not reset any tripped hydraulic auxiliary pump circuit breaker.
The auxiliary pumps are large electric motor pumps. A breaker that trips on one may have tripped on a motor fault, and resetting it can turn an electrical fault into a fire.

**Icing conditions** exist when the outside air temperature (OAT) on the ground and for takeoff, or the total air temperature (TAT) in flight, is 6 °C or below and visible moisture in any form is present. Visible moisture means any of the following, of light, moderate or heavy intensity: clouds; a ceiling below 1,500 ft AGL; drizzle; rain; snow; snow grains; ice crystals; ice pellets; hail; small hail or snow pellets; mist; fog; or any of these with a blowing, low drifting, showers or freezing descriptor (FDX).

Icing conditions also exist when the OAT on the ground and for takeoff is 6 °C or below on ramps, taxiways or runways where surface snow, ice, standing water or slush may be ingested by the engines or freeze on the engines or nacelles; and when the OAT or TAT is 6 °C or below with a temperature/dewpoint spread of less than 3 °C.

**Icing conditions** are temperatures below 6 °C (42 °F) with visible moisture in any form, such as clouds in flight, fog, rain, snow, sleet or ice crystals, or temperatures below 6 °C with a temperature/dewpoint spread of 3 °C (5 °F) or less. In flight, the temperature is the TAT.

**Icing conditions** exist when the OAT on the ground and for takeoff, or the TAT in flight, is 6 °C or below and visible moisture in any form is present (clouds, fog with visibility of one mile or less, rain, snow, sleet, ice crystals). They also exist when the OAT on the ground and for takeoff is 6 °C or below on ramps, taxiways or runways where snow, ice, standing water or slush may be ingested by the engines or freeze on the engines, nacelles or engine sensor probes.

The threshold is 6 °C and not 0 °C because the air cools as it accelerates into an engine inlet or over a wing: a few degrees above freezing outside can be below freezing at the surface. In flight TAT is used because it includes the ram rise, the temperature the airframe actually sees. A temperature/dewpoint spread under 3 °C means the air is near saturation, so the same cooling condenses and freezes moisture that is not visible as cloud.

items: **Engine anti-ice must be on** when the OAT on the ground is 6 °C or below on surfaces where snow, ice, standing water or slush may be ingested or freeze on the engines or nacelles; when the OAT or TAT is 6 °C or below with a temperature/dewpoint spread under 3 °C; and when the OAT or TAT is 6 °C or below with visible moisture.

If engine anti-ice was used for takeoff only because of the temperature/dewpoint spread, it may be switched off at 250 KIAS if no other icing conditions exist. When the destination ATIS reports temperature/dewpoint-spread icing conditions, turn engine anti-ice on when descending through 10,000 ft into the approach.
**Wing anti-ice:** use for takeoff, and in flight, with the OAT or TAT at 6 °C or below and visible moisture present.
**Engine and wing anti-ice together:** whenever the OAT or TAT is 6 °C or below with visible moisture.
**Wing anti-ice ground test:** no more than 15 seconds.

**Engine anti-ice** on the ground in icing conditions: turn it on immediately after engine start and use it continuously until icing conditions no longer exist. In flight: on whenever the TAT is below 6 °C and visible moisture is present.
**Wing anti-ice ground test:** do not hold the WING ANTI-ICE switch in TEST for more than 15 seconds.
Do not use the APU for wing anti-ice.

**ENG ANTI-ICE switches** must be on whenever icing conditions are expected or encountered, or when the TAT is below 6 °C (42 °F) and either moisture is visible or the temperature and dewpoint are within 3 °C (5 °F) of each other, on the ground and in flight.
Select ignition OVRD ON whenever engine or engine and airframe anti-ice is called for, for the duration of the icing encounter.
**Wing anti-ice** has no AFM limitations. It should be on in flight when icing conditions are expected or encountered.

blocks.content: Engine anti-ice is preventive: it keeps ice from forming on the inlet lip, which, once grown, breaks off in pieces that the fan and core swallow, damaging blades and possibly flaming out the engine. That is why it goes on before ice is seen, and why on the ground it goes on as soon as the engine is running. Wing anti-ice protects the slats and the lift and stall margin the wing depends on. The ground test is time-limited because without airflow the hot bleed air can overheat the slat structure.

items: No speed limitation applies with windshield anti-ice inoperative or off. With it inoperative, leave icing conditions.
Select windshield anti-ice to NORM when icing is imminent, and to HIGH only for the duration of moderate to heavy icing.
Windshield defog should be ON in all flight conditions.
Do not run the windshield wipers at high speed for more than 30 minutes, or on a dry windshield.

Rain repellent (deactivated on the FedEx fleet): apply only in rain; do not apply it to the second windshield until it is shown to work on the first; do not turn the wipers on if it has been applied to a dry windshield by mistake.
Windshield anti-ice selectors in NORM for flight when icing conditions are imminent; HIGH only for the duration of moderate to heavy icing.

Apply rain repellent only in heavy rain. Do not apply it to the second windshield until repellency is established on the first. Do not turn on the wipers if repellent has been applied to a dry windshield by mistake.
Operating the wipers on a dry windshield is not recommended.
No speed limitations are associated with windshield heat off.
Windshield anti-ice selectors in NORM when icing conditions are imminent; HIGH only for the duration of moderate to heavy icing.
Windshield defog should be operated in all flight conditions.
Do not operate the windshield wipers at high speed for more than 30 minutes, or on a dry windshield.

blocks.content: The windshield's heat is applied through a conductive film in a laminated, multi-layer glass. HIGH heats faster and harder, which raises the thermal stress across the layers; it is kept for when NORM cannot keep up. Defog keeps the inner surface warm and clear of condensation. Rain repellent on dry glass leaves a smear the wipers spread into an opaque film, and wipers on dry glass scratch it.

sections.title: Warning systems and weather radar
sections.summary: Ground proximity warning, TCAS, windshear and weather radar.

items: Pilots may deviate from their ATC clearance to the extent necessary to comply with an EGPWS warning. File a flight safety report after any such deviation (FDX).

For an airport or runway not in the EGPWS airport database, inhibit the terrain awareness alerting with the TERRAIN OVRD switch before takeoff, or within 15 NM of the approach and landing, to prevent unwanted alerts.
Navigation must not be based on the terrain display.
Where the database has no terrain data, terrain awareness alerting is not available; where it has no obstacle data, obstacle alerting is not available.

If the FMS position given to the EGPWS is not accurate enough, the terrain clearance floor, terrain awareness and obstacle alerting are inhibited automatically and the TERR FAIL light comes on. The basic modes 1 to 6 and the mode 7 windshear detection are unaffected. Without GPS in the navigation solution, the position can degrade enough to do this in about 15 to 30 minutes, depending on the INU drift. The EGPWS uses the pilot's navigation solution, and the copilot's as backup.

With TERR OVRD on, the EGPWS reverts to basic GPWS (modes 1 to 6), which may give little or no warning of flight towards precipitous terrain with few obstructions before it. In the landing configuration, in a stabilized normal descent, with no glideslope signal being received, it gives no terrain warning at all: only the mode 6 callouts and mode 7 windshear remain.
Within 15 NM of an airport not in the EGPWS airport database, select TERR OVRD ON to prevent nuisance alerts.
Terrain clearances or descent rates during radar vectoring that do not match the regulatory standards for ground proximity equipment may cause nuisance warnings.
The windshear caution and warning are reactive: they detect windshear the aircraft is already in from air mass and acceleration measurements, and cannot predict windshear ahead.

The GPWS alerting and terrain display need barometric altitude referenced to sea level (QNH). If QFE is set on either altimeter, inhibit terrain awareness alerting and display with the TERRAIN OVRD switch.
Inhibit the terrain awareness features with TERRAIN OVRD when the FMS is navigating on the IRS alone (IRS NAV on the ND) over land, to prevent false terrain alerts.
Navigation must not be based on the terrain awareness display.

blocks.content: The enhanced GPWS compares the aircraft's position with a terrain database. It is only as good as that position: with an inaccurate position or a wrong altimeter reference it can warn of terrain that is not there, or miss terrain that is. The basic GPWS modes, which use the radio altimeter and the air data alone, remain whatever happens to the position.

If the TA/RA VSI shows an RA fail message, follow the aural annunciation, MAINTAIN VERTICAL SPEED, MAINTAIN, until CLEAR OF CONFLICT is annunciated. In a simultaneous encounter with several aircraft, a preventive "don't climb, don't descend" resolution can trigger the fail message while the aural message and the traffic display remain correct.

items: Pilots may deviate from their ATC clearance to the extent necessary to comply with a TCAS resolution advisory (RA). When CLEAR OF CONFLICT is announced, return promptly to the previous clearance.
Do not maneuver on the traffic display or a traffic advisory (TA) alone without seeing the traffic: they are aids to finding it and lack the accuracy for avoidance maneuvers.

Comply with an RA unless doing so is considered unsafe. Maneuvering opposite to an RA, especially one involving an altitude crossing, is extremely hazardous and is prohibited unless visual contact shows it to be the only safe course.
A target may drift on the outer boundary of the display; TA and RA functions are not affected.
All RA and TA aural messages are inhibited below 1,100 ft radio altitude climbing and below 900 ft descending.

blocks.content: No TCAS limitations are listed in the KC-10A manual's Section III.

items: Do not operate the weather radar within 160 ft of personnel, inside a hangar, or within 50 ft of fueling operations or a fuel spill (FDX).
In sustained banks of more than 15°, the windshear detection and recovery guidance system is desensitized, and alerts from a windshear encounter are delayed.
The predictive windshear system, if installed and operable, must be ON for takeoff.
The accuracy of the weather radar's turbulence detection mode has not been evaluated by the FAA; flight is not to be based on it.

blocks.content: A weather radar transmits pulses of several kilowatts. Close to the antenna the microwave energy can harm people and can ignite fuel vapour, which is why the radar stays off or in standby on the ground near people and refueling.

items: Gear operating and extended speeds: [Landing gear speeds](#landing-gear-speeds).
Tire speeds: [Tire speed](#tire-speed). Minimum tire pressures and taxi speeds: [Runway, taxi and tires](#runway-and-taxi).
Center gear retracted and anti-skid inoperative weights: [Center gear and anti-skid](#centre-gear-and-anti-skid).
Overweight and hard landings: [Weights](#weights).

blocks.content: The brakes' energy limit is not a fixed number but a function of weight, speed, temperature and altitude, found in the performance data: it governs a heavy rejected takeoff and an overweight landing, and after either the brakes need time to cool before another takeoff.

The crew oxygen duration tables give **man-hours** of oxygen for a cylinder pressure at 70 °F, with the cylinders used down to 50 psig. Divide by the number of people using oxygen to get the duration in hours. Duration rises with cabin altitude because a regulator at ambient pressure delivers the same volume per breath, but that volume holds less gas in thinner air. In the **diluted** (normal) setting, the regulator mixes cabin air with the oxygen at lower cabin altitudes, so the supply lasts far longer; at 100 % it delivers pure oxygen at every altitude.

blocks.title: 100 % oxygen, one 111 cu ft crew cylinder (man-hours)
Diluted oxygen, one 111 cu ft crew cylinder (man-hours)
100 % oxygen, two 111 cu ft crew cylinders (man-hours)
Diluted oxygen, two 111 cu ft crew cylinders (man-hours)

blocks.content: The walk-around bottle tables are in hours for one person. In pressure demand the regulator holds a slight overpressure in the mask, which keeps smoke out but costs oxygen: the bottle lasts less long than in plain demand, by up to half at altitude.

The MD-10 FCOM gives oxygen duration as charts for one and for two 111, 114 or 115 cu ft crew cylinders, used down to 50 psig: duration for a crew of five on 100 % oxygen at cabin altitudes from sea level to 40,000 ft, and the unpressurized flight time available after an emergency descent to 10,000 ft for two crew and up to eight observers. The descent charts assume a 17-second delay after the decompression, a descent of 10 minutes or less to 10,000 ft, 100 % oxygen for everyone during the descent, and diluted oxygen for the crew only afterwards. Plan from those charts.

Section III of the KC-10A manual gives no crew oxygen duration limits. The portable oxygen bottle durations are in the [Oxygen](oxygen) system part. With the increased accommodation unit installed, the extra personnel's oxygen must be connected, and cabin crew members must have demand masks that fit the portable units' regulators.

items: **Main cargo door:** before flight, verify that the external lockpin handle is flush with the fuselage, and visually verify that the latch lockpin is past the cam, as the placard shows.
**Door arming:** the door arming handles must be at SLIDE ARMED before the aircraft leaves the ramp, and remain there until it reaches its final parking place. Verify that the girt bar is in place.
**Main deck cargo door:** before flight, verify that the external lockpin handle is flush and visually verify that the latch lockpin is past the cam, as the placard shows.
**Engine and APU fire test:** must be done before the first flight of the day.

blocks.content: The lockpin check is the last proof that the cargo door's latches are over center and locked. The main deck door opens outward, so cabin pressure works to open it; an unlocked door can blow open in flight, with an explosive decompression and structural damage around the opening.

items: **Cargo door:** in the mid or full open position it withstands wind up to 52 kt from any direction. Do not operate it in winds above 40 kt from any direction: structural damage could occur.
Install the cargo door barrier net if the door is to stay open without a platform beside it and no observer is watching the door area. Do not lean on the net.

**Cargo loading:** do not exceed the maximum gross weight, the compartment load limits, the ground CG limits or the zone load limits. For heavyweight departures, consider zone loading when placing cargo: near full aft body tank capacity, even light cargo can exceed a zone limit.

**Evacuation slides:** each door arming handle must be at SLIDE ARMED before the airstairs or ramp is removed, and stay there until the stand or ramp is in place at the unloading point. Once a door is armed, verify that its girt bar is locked.

At least two operable slide rafts are required on every mission. A one-time flight to a repair facility with one operable raft is allowed if it is not an extended over-water flight (beyond gliding distance of land with all engines out), the raft is at a forward door, and no more than 12 people are aboard; latch the cockpit door open for takeoff and landing, since the cockpit windows may become the primary exits.

blocks.title: Dry ice in the cargo compartment, KC-10A

blocks.content: Dry ice sublimes into carbon dioxide, which the packs' fresh air must dilute and carry overboard; the safe load therefore depends on how many packs are running and how much of the cabin is shared with the crew. If a pack is lost in flight with dry ice aboard, follow the smoke or fumes removal procedure (from Smoke or Fumes Associated with Air Conditioning), do not put the cabin pressure control in manual, increase the cabin airflow by partial depressurization, raising the cabin altitude (not above 10,000 ft unless no passengers are aboard and there is adequate crew oxygen), and land as soon as practical. During loading, run the APU and both packs, open passenger door 4 and the boom operator station's air inlets with its hatch closed, load the dry ice in the aft part of the compartment, and close the environmental curtain before flight.

sections.title: Air refueling
sections.summary: Boom, centerline hose and wing pod limits, receiver limits and the clean-configuration buffet.

blocks.content: No refueling limitations for the KDC-10 or the Omega DC-10-40 are published in the sources used. The KC-10A's, below, are the nearest reference for their boom and wing pods; the procedures are in [Air Refueling](air-refueling).
These are the KC-10A's air refueling limitations. The procedures that work within them are in [Air Refueling](air-refueling).

items: Do not move the boom beyond its structural limits: structural damage may result.

To keep the boom's flight control actuator reservoirs pressurized, select HYD SEL to BOOM for about 2 minutes (pressurizing it from hydraulic system 2) before takeoff and every 8 hours after. The computer check during preflight and boom use during refueling count, as long as 8 hours do not pass. Without reservoir pressure, the boom's control surfaces may flutter after a failure of hydraulic system 2.
If the aircraft oversteps its speed limits during boom refueling, disconnect at once (if in contact) and stow the boom.

blocks.title: Boom refueling envelope
rows: 180 KIAS from sea level to 20,000 ft, then increasing linearly to M 0.88 at 37,000 ft
350 KIAS or M 0.88, whichever is lower, up to 37,000 ft

blocks.content: Although the boom may be flown as slowly as 180 KIAS, below 200 KIAS its response to control inputs is slightly reduced, most noticeably on rapid up commands above 30° of elevation; its damping is also degraded, and it overshoots by 2° to 3° after rapid or evasive commands.

blocks.title: Hose and drogue refueling envelopes
rows: 200 KIAS from sea level to 20,000 ft, then increasing linearly to M 0.88 at 37,000 ft
280 KIAS or M 0.88, whichever is lower, up to 35,000 ft
230 KIAS from sea level to 33,000 ft, then increasing linearly to M 0.74 at 35,000 ft
Wing pods, hose extension and retraction

blocks.content: Do not deploy a wing pod hose from the stowed position, or retract it fully, with the flaps or slats extended: it can damage the lower wing surface. Do not use the centerline drogue at the same time as either wing pod drogue.

items: **Significant events** must be reported: a hose whip, sine wave or "dead hose" after contact, or a contact or attempted contact that damages the tanker, the receiver or the drogue basket. Discontinue hose refueling after a significant event unless there is an emergency: the hose's integrity is then unknown and it could fail at any time.

**Icing:** avoid using the wing pods in icing conditions except in a fuel emergency. If ice is seen, or reported by the receiver, on any part of the hose, drogue or pod, rewind the hose as soon as conditions allow and end the refueling unless operational necessity dictates otherwise. Do not trail the hose again for 5 minutes after rewinding it.

**Cold soak:** with a static air temperature between −47 °C and −58 °C, the hose may stay trailed no more than 15 minutes before fuel transfer begins, and must be rewound when the transfer is complete unless another is about to begin. Below −58 °C, do not trail it except in a fuel emergency.
**Lightning protection:** keep the wing pod fuel system, hose included, full of fuel, to reduce the risk of lightning damage and to lubricate the pod's fuel pump.

children.title: Refueling pumps, receptacle and reverse refueling

blocks.content: With one engine inoperative, or with fluid lost from one hydraulic system, do not refuel in more than light turbulence, and run only these air refueling pump combinations:

blocks.title: Air refueling pumps with an engine or hydraulic system lost
rows: Engine 1, or hydraulic system 1 fluid loss
Aft tank right pump (system 2), and one system 3 pump: forward tank right, center wing tank right, or aft tank left
Engine 2, or hydraulic system 2 fluid loss
One system 1 pump (forward tank left or center wing tank left), and one system 3 pump (forward tank right, center wing tank right, or aft tank left)
Engine 3, or hydraulic system 3 fluid loss
Aft tank right pump (system 2), and one system 1 pump: forward tank left or center wing tank left

blocks.content: The air refueling pumps are hydraulically driven. Each engine drives one hydraulic system's pumps, so losing an engine or a system takes away part of the pumping power; the permitted combinations draw on what is left without overloading it.

items: **Receptacle:** keep the UARRSI hydraulic shutoff valve closed in all flight except when needed for refueling.

**Reverse refueling** (receiver to tanker) is not a normal operation but is available when operationally necessary. The maximum reverse rate is 300 US gal/min (about 2,000 lb/min), which one air refueling pump achieves. More pumps give a higher flow and may cause unacceptable surge pressures if a tension disconnect occurs.
**APU:** do not run the APU during any air refueling, or with a known fuel leak in the boom pivot area.

blocks.title: Mandatory AFTO Form 781 entries (air refueling systems)
rows: Boom retracted against the stops by emergency retraction
Boom will not trim to 0° roll or 30° elevation
Manifold scavenge system inoperative (tanker or receiver)
Significant event on the centerline drogue or a wing pod

blocks.content:
Air refueling is flown slowly and heavy, close to the clean wing's buffet boundary. At the minimum air refueling speed in normal conditions, a bank of more than 25° can bring on moderate buffet. After a flight in which moderate to heavy buffet was met through an inadvertent loss of speed, a heavy buffet (clean configuration) inspection is required (AFTO Form 781 entry).

Buffet is the shaking of the airframe by separated flow on the wing. Banking raises the load factor, and with it the angle of attack needed at the same speed, so a turn at a speed that was buffet-free in level flight can reach it. The inspection exists because sustained heavy buffet loads the tail and wing structure cyclically, in a way the crew cannot judge from the cockpit.

The DC-10-10 Tanker and DC-10-30 Tanker carry the retardant conversion's own limitations in addition to, and in places instead of, those of the basic aircraft. They include a lower maximum airspeed, altitude and takeoff weight, no pressurization with water or retardant in the tanks, no flight into known icing, corrections to the takeoff, landing and stall speeds, and a minimum fuel by tail number. They are listed in full in [Limitations of the conversion](aerial-firefighting#tanker-limitations), which governs for the tankers wherever it differs from this chapter. The DC-10-30 Tanker has no center gear: the conversion removes it.

The simulation does not enforce most of these limits, and exceeding one does not always produce a warning or a failure. The absence of a warning is not permission: fly to the numbers in this chapter. Where the simulation's own warnings or displays use a different value, it is listed here.

items: **Overspeed warning.** The overspeed warning, and on the DC-10 and KC-10 the striped VMO pointer, follow one schedule on every airframe: 365 KIAS, or M 0.88 where that is lower. On the DC-10-10 and MD-10-10 the warning therefore comes 25 kt above the 340 KIAS VMO, and only above M 0.88 instead of M 0.85. On the DC-10-30 and MD-10-30 it sounds 10 kt early between about 10,000 and 25,000 ft and late near sea level; on the KC-10A it is late below about 23,000 ft, where the real VMO is lower than 365 KIAS.

**Flap placard.** The automatic flap limiting and the flap limit speeds the simulation displays use the KC-10A's placard (270, 250, 220, 185 and 170 KIAS) on every airframe. The DC-10's limit for 15.1° to 25° is 210 KIAS (220 KIAS for the 572,000 lb DC-10-30), and the MD-10's bands are different again. Observe your own aircraft's placard. The MD-10's slat overspeed warning is set at 260 KIAS (Series 10) and 270 KIAS (Series 30).

**Engine limits.** The CF6-50C2 is redlined at 118.5 % N1 on every airframe that has it, including the MD-10-30, whose own manual gives 119.5 %. The DC-10-15's CF6-50C2F uses the CF6-50C2's limits. The DC-10-40's EGT limits follow the JT9D-59A's type certificate (685 °C for takeoff, 650 °C maximum continuous), but its N1 and N2 exceedances are still judged against the CF6-50C2's percentages, and its EPR gauge carries no limit index.

**Weights.** The simulator's payload and fuel pages allow up to 455,000 lb on the short-span aircraft and 593,000 lb on the long-span ones; these are loading ceilings, not limits, and on most variants they are above the structural weights in this chapter. The EFB's performance pages plan the DC-10-15 to 455,000 lb and the DC-10-40 to 555,000 lb takeoff and 403,000 lb landing; those are estimates, not published limits. The optional AIDS's overweight-landing report uses 403,000 lb as the landing weight of the long-span DC-10s, below the DC-10-30's 424,000 to 436,000 lb.
**No APLC.** The FedEx loading and performance computer is not fitted. Use the EFB's performance pages, and check the zero fuel weight performance limit yourself.
**Autoland.** The DC-10's SNGL LAND and DUAL LAND are modeled; fly them within the FedEx limits above. The KC-10A's LAND switch is placarded INOP, as on the real aircraft, and does nothing.
**TCAS.** The simulated MD-10 has no TCAS; its TCAS limitations are listed for completeness.
**Oxygen.** The simulated DC-10 and MD-10 carry one crew oxygen cylinder (use the one-cylinder tables); the KC-10A carries three.

chapters.title: Normal Procedures
chapters.summary: A complete flight on each flight deck, from a cold and dark aircraft to securing it, as amplified procedures with their checklists.

blocks.content:
This section sets out the procedures for a complete normal flight: the sequence of events from the moment the crew reaches a cold, dark aircraft to the moment they leave it secured on the ramp. It follows the structure of the KC-10 flight manual's normal procedures and of the FedEx DC-10 and MD-10 operating manuals: each phase of flight is described as an amplified procedure (what each crewmember does, in what order, and why), and each phase ends with the checklist that confirms the work was done.

The procedures are written for the aircraft as simulated. Every control they name exists and works on the flight deck it is written for. Where the real aircraft has an item the simulation does not, the step is left out or the item is listed in the part's Simulation notes.

The three flight decks fly the same airframe family with different crews and different philosophies, so most parts carry separate subsections for the three-crew DC-10 and KC-10 and for the two-crew MD-10. Pick your aircraft with the buttons at the top of the page and the reader shows only what applies.

items: **DC-10.** Captain, first officer and second officer (the flight engineer). The procedures and checklist are FedEx's, which every DC-10 variant in the simulation uses: the -10, -15, -30 and -40, the freighters, the air tankers and the Omega.
**KC-10.** Pilot, copilot, flight engineer and boom operator. The procedures and checklist are the USAF technical order's.
**MD-10.** Captain and first officer on the glass flight deck, with the systems controllers doing the flight engineer's work. The procedures and checklist are FedEx's MD-10 operating manual's.

blocks.title: How this section is arranged
rows: Safety checks, first power and the APU, the flight engineer's (or MD-10 first officer's) panel preflight, and the walkaround.
The pilots' flows, navigation set-up, takeoff data, the takeoff briefing and the Cockpit Preparation checklist.
Before Start, pushback, the start sequence and crew duties, After Start.
Before Taxi, taxi, Before Takeoff, the takeoff roll, initial climb and clean-up, After Takeoff.
The climb profile, passing 10,000 ft and the transition altitude, cruise, and the flight engineer's cruise duties: fuel, CG and systems monitoring.
Descent planning, landing data, the descent and approach checklists, holding, and the precision, non-precision, visual and circling approaches.
Before Landing, the landing, the go-around, rejected and balked landings, and the local pattern.
After Landing, taxi-in on two engines, parking, shutdown and securing the aircraft.
The complete normal checklist cards for each flight deck, as the EFB presents them.
Standard callouts, use of automation, thrust management, takeoff and landing technique, taxiing and two-engine taxi.

blocks.content: Speeds, thrust settings and configurations in this section come from the operators' manuals. Speeds and thrust for a particular takeoff or landing come from the EFB's Performance app (see [Performance and mission planning](mission-planning)); the operating limits are in [Limitations](limitations), which always takes precedence over anything written here.

sections.title: Crew duties and division of labour

blocks.content: Every procedure in this section names the crewmember who does each step. A step with two designators is done in coordination: one acts, the other checks. The designators are:

blocks.title: Crew designators
rows: Captain, the pilot in the left seat and pilot in command
C (FedEx DC-10 and MD-10), P (KC-10 pilot)
First officer, the pilot in the right seat
Flight engineer, at the side-facing station behind the first officer. FedEx calls the DC-10's flight engineer the **second officer** (S/O); the two titles mean the same seat and the same job
Pilot flying: the pilot controlling the flight path, by hand or through the autopilot
PF; P on the MD-10 card
Pilot monitoring: the other pilot, who monitors the flight path, works the radios and the checklists, and backs up the PF
PM (FedEx DC-10), PNF, pilot not flying (KC-10, MD-10)
Every crewmember on the flight deck

blocks.content: The EFB's checklists keep each book's own letters, so on the EFB the DC-10's flight engineer is **S** and the KC-10's pilot is **P**. The cards printed in this manual use the designators above.

The DC-10 and KC-10 were designed around a flight engineer. The pilots fly, navigate and talk to ATC; the flight engineer runs the aircraft's systems from their own panel, which carries the controls the pilots do not need to fly: electrical, hydraulic, fuel, pneumatic and air conditioning, pressurization, and the engine secondary instruments. The arrangement divides the workload by kind rather than by phase. During a takeoff, for example, the PF flies, the PM calls the speeds and sets or checks thrust, and the flight engineer watches the engines and the systems panel and calls anything abnormal.

blocks.title: Division of duties, DC-10 and KC-10
