rows: Commands the flight and makes every operational decision, including the decision to reject a takeoff, for which the captain takes control. Calls for every checklist. Taxis the aircraft. Briefs the takeoff and, as PF, the approach.

Flies as PF on alternate legs. As PM: radio communications with ATC, the flight guidance panel inputs while the PF is flying by hand, the speed and altitude callouts, the gear and flaps on the PF's command. On the DC-10 the F/O reads the Before Start, After Start and Shut Down checklists.

Preflights the aircraft inside and out, powers it up and starts the APU. Runs the systems through the flight: fuel management and the CG, electrical and hydraulic configuration, pneumatics, air conditioning and pressurization. Monitors the engines, computes takeoff and landing data, and backs up the pilots on speeds, altitudes and configuration. On the KC-10 the FE reads every checklist; on the DC-10, all but the three the F/O reads.

KC-10 only. Prepares the cabin, the cargo and the air refueling station; computes the weight and balance with a cargo load; reports "Cabin ready" before takeoff. When no boom operator is carried, the FE takes the boom operator's weight-and-balance and cabin duties, and pressurizes the boom flight controls for 2 minutes before flight.

blocks.content:
**Who sets the thrust.** On the DC-10, with the captain flying, the captain advances the throttles to about takeoff power and calls for the power; the first officer, as PM, sets each engine's N1 exactly and calls "Power set" before 80 kt, and the flight engineer monitors and will trim a throttle back if an EGT is about to exceed its limit. On the KC-10 the flight engineer sets takeoff power to the target N1 on the PF's command, and refines go-around and touch-and-go thrust. Either way, after 80 kt nobody touches a throttle except to prevent exceeding an engine limit.

**In an emergency** the PF keeps flying the aircraft and the PM works the problem with the flight engineer, unless the captain directs otherwise. The flight engineer reads the checklists, and on the DC-10 reminds the captain of the fuel dump time after an engine failure on takeoff.

The MD-10 conversion removed the flight engineer's station. Its systems are run by automatic systems controllers (fuel, hydraulic, electrical and the cabin pressure controller), whose overhead panels the crew normally leave in AUTO; the AIR panel (packs, bleeds and isolation valves) is always operated by hand. The procedures assume every controller in automatic. When one has been put in MANUAL, the steps marked **[MANUAL]** for that panel are done as well.

Each pilot has an **area of primary responsibility** where they may act on their own in a normal procedure: broadly, the captain the left side and the center pedestal's flight controls, the first officer the overhead panel and the right side. Anything outside a pilot's area, and every non-normal procedure, is done at the captain's direction. Controls the two share (the flight controls, thrust levers, flight control panel and trim) are normally worked by the PF.

blocks.title: Division of duties, MD-10
rows: Commands the flight, calls for the checklists, taxis the aircraft and makes the rejected takeoff decision.
Reads every checklist on the ground, works the overhead panels (AIR, fuel, hydraulic, electrical, lights), starts the engines while the captain times the start, and obtains the ATC clearances.
Flies the aircraft and positions the flight control panel (FCP) when the autopilot is engaged.

Reads every checklist in flight, works the MCDU (any entry that changes the flight profile is agreed by both pilots before EXECUTE), positions the FCP at the PF's direction when the PF is hand flying, works the gear and flaps on command, and makes the callouts. Repeats each command of the PF to show it is understood.

blocks.content: A normal checklist is a **check**, not a list of things to do. The crew first set up the aircraft for the next phase from memory, each by their own flow pattern over their panels; then one crewmember reads the checklist and the others confirm that the critical items are in fact done. Flows are fast and complete; the checklist catches what the flow missed. The flows are given in each part, in the order the hands move.

items: The captain (or the PF) calls for each checklist by name.

The reader challenges each item; the crewmember responsible for it answers with the response printed on the card, after looking at the control or indication, not from memory. Items the reader can see directly may be confirmed silently.
A response of "As Required" is never spoken as such: state the actual configuration ("Ignition, OFF").
An item that is inoperative is answered "Inoperative"; an item the aircraft does not have, "Not Installed".
A checklist started but not finished is reported "In progress". If a checklist is due and has not been called for, the reader prompts: "Standing by on the ___ checklist."
A checklist interrupted is reviewed from its start and resumed where it stopped.
The reader announces completion: "___ checklist complete."

blocks.content:
**Below the line.** Several checklists are printed in two halves separated by a line. The first half is done as soon as the crew are ready and held "down to the line"; the rest is done when its moment comes: the DC-10's Before Start when the aircraft is ready to push back, the Before Takeoff checklists when cleared onto the runway, After Takeoff passing the transition altitude, the descent and approach checklists passing the transition level or with the final approach mode selected.

**Silent items and checklists.** The DC-10 card marks items the flight engineer accomplishes silently (► on the cards in this manual); only an item found not done is reported. The KC-10's After Takeoff/Climb and the MD-10's After Takeoff are entirely silent: the FE or PM reads them silently, confirms each action, and announces completion.

blocks.title: Who reads the checklists
rows: The letter in each checklist's heading: the F/O reads Before Start, After Start and Shut Down; the FE reads the rest.
The responder printed against each item. Silent items are the FE's.
The crewmember coded after an item takes the action; when the response is in quotation marks they also report it aloud.
The F/O on the ground, the PM in flight. After Takeoff is a silent checklist done by the PM.
The pilot whose area the item is in; both pilots answer items that change the aircraft's configuration.

blocks.content: **The checklists in the simulation.** The normal checklists live on the EFB, in **Documents**, **Checklist** (see [Open and run a checklist](efb#run-a-checklist)). Each flight deck has its own book, printed as the operator printed it, preceded by a **PREFLIGHT** group built from the book's preflight procedures. On the EFB a row is ticked by pressing it, and pressing **Next** opens the following checklist. The EFB adds a few checklists the printed cards leave to procedures (Starting Engines, Passing 10,000 ft in the climb and in the descent, and on the DC-10 Before Taxi and Leaving Aircraft); they are part of the normal sequence in this manual too.

The **Virtual Crew** can take the seats you are not sitting in: on the DC-10 the flight engineer (second officer) and the first officer, on the KC-10 the flight engineer and the copilot, on the MD-10 the first officer. Each seat is set on the EFB's Virtual Crew app to **OFF**, **MANUAL** or **AUTO**. You fly as captain. The full description is in [Virtual Crew](virtual-crew); this topic says how it fits the procedures in this section.

blocks.title: Virtual Crew modes
rows: Nothing. You do that crewmember's work, or it is not done.

When you press **Start** on a checklist in Documents, the crew walk it at a speaking pace. On each item a virtual seat answers, that crewmember does the item's actions, moving the real switches on their panel and holding tests long enough to read, and then ticks it. Some items they only answer, with nothing moved (see [Items the crew answers without setting them](virtual-crew#answered-items)). Your own items wait for your tick.

As MANUAL, and the crew also watch the flight and offer each checklist in a bubble when its moment comes ("Start Before Takeoff Checklist?", with Start and Not Now). They tick the captain's items they can see done: the parking brake set, the beacon on, the fuel levers off.

blocks.content:
**What stays yours.** The flight controls, thrust levers, flaps and slats, stabilizer trim, gear handle, parking brake and fuel levers are the captain's. The virtual crew call for them and check them ("Positive rate. Gear up.") but do not move them, with these exceptions: the preflight tests (the MD-10 first officer's takeoff warning test moves the throttles), the parking brake released on chocks during the preflight, the spoiler handle armed and disarmed by the first officer (KC-10: the flight engineer), the engine start (on the DC-10 and MD-10 the virtual first officer raises each fuel lever at 15% N2; on the KC-10 the pilot starts engines 3 and 1 and the flight engineer starts No. 2), and after landing the flaps and slats up and the stabilizer to 2° ANU. See [Who moves what](virtual-crew#who-moves-what).

**Questions.** Some items need the captain's decision. The crew ask in a bubble and wait: whether to start No. 2 now or taxi on two engines (DC-10, KC-10), and whether to shut No. 2 down for the taxi-in (KC-10, which then moves its fuel lever). On the DC-10 and KC-10 the crew also ask, with a Ground Ops button, for ground power and air when the APU will not start or will not come on line, for air when there is none for the start (KC-10), and for any ground equipment still at the aircraft to be removed. The MD-10's first officer asks nothing: a failed APU start halts the run.

**When an item cannot be done** the walk halts on it with a short plain message and waits for you to fix it and tick the item. The crew never tick an item they could not do.

blocks.title: When AUTO offers each checklist
rows: Parked, fewer than three engines running
After Start (DC-10, MD-10), Before Taxi (DC-10, KC-10), Taxi (MD-10)
Climbing through 1,500 ft above the runway
Passing 10,000 ft Descent, then Approach (DC-10, KC-10)
Descending through 2,500 ft above the runway
On the ground after the landing, below 40 kt
Parked after the flight, parking brake set
Shut Down or Parking, then Leaving Aircraft

blocks.content:
The offer always moves to the latest checklist the flight has reached, so a crew who turn AUTO on in the cruise are first offered Passing 10,000 ft Climb, not Before Start; starting or dismissing an offer passes it and everything before it. With the seat that reads them on AUTO, the two Passing 10,000 ft checklists start themselves without a bubble. On the ground nothing is offered while the checklist before it on the card is incomplete (see [Where the offers stop](virtual-crew#offers-stop)). The KC-10's local pattern checklists and its alert-force checklists are never offered: start them yourself.

**Cabin temperature.** On the DC-10 and KC-10, with their seat on AUTO and a pack running, the virtual flight engineer holds the forward, mid and aft cabin zones between about 65 and 75 °F, one detent of the zone temperature selector at a time.

On the DC-10, with a **TARGET CRUISE CG** set on the Virtual Crew app, the virtual flight engineer holds the CG near it in level cruise above 20,000 ft by transferring fuel between tank 2 and the wing tanks (see [Climb and cruise](normal-climb-and-cruise#fe-cg-management)).

The virtual crew work the checklists and procedures in this section, not the emergency or abnormal procedures. With a failure, run the non-normal checklist yourself; a normal checklist the crew are running can be paused with the Pause button at the top of its page, or stopped with Stop on the run strip.

sections.title: The flight at a glance
sections.summary: Each phase of a normal flight and the checklist that closes it, on each flight deck.

blocks.title: Phases and checklists, DC-10
rows: Interior Safety Check, Cockpit Inspection, Second Officer Pre-Flight
Before Start (down to the line, then below it)
Before Takeoff (to the line, then below it)
Clear of the runway, at the gate
After Landing (silent), Shut Down, Leaving Aircraft

blocks.title: Phases and checklists, KC-10
rows: FE's Exterior/Interior Initial Inspection, FE's Interior Inspection, FE's Exterior Inspection, Pilot's Interior Inspection
After Landing, Parking - Engine Shutdown, Leaving Aircraft
Full Stop Taxi Back, Downwind, Before Landing (local pattern)

blocks.title: Phases and checklists, MD-10
rows: Cockpit Safety Inspection, Preliminary Cockpit Preparation
Captain's, F/O and Final Cockpit Preparation, then Cockpit Preparation
Before Start, Starting Engines, After Start

items: The procedures are flyable on every variant of each flight deck. Where a DC-10 variant differs (the -10's autothrottle, the -40's EPR engines, the -30 and -40's center gear, the freighters' cargo items) the text says so.

The EFB's checklists are the operators' books as printed, with a PREFLIGHT group built from their preflight procedures and a few checklists added for the simulation. Paperwork, loose equipment and briefings are left out of the EFB's preflight items; this manual mentions them only where they shape a procedure.

Items a card asks about that this simulation does not fit (FDAS, ACARS, the KC-10's SATCOM, Iridium phone and crypto items) are answered "Not Installed" or not applicable; the parts list them where it matters.
Ground handling (chocks, power and air carts, pushback, fuel and cargo) is done from the EFB's Ground Ops app; see [Ground operations](ground-operations).

parts.title: Preflight and Exterior Inspection
parts.summary: From a cold and dark aircraft to power on, the APU running and the walkaround done: the safety checks, the flight engineer's panel preflight and the exterior inspection.

blocks.content: The preflight begins when the first crewmember reaches the aircraft and ends when the cockpit is ready for the pilots' flows. Its order is driven by safety. Nothing is powered until someone has made sure that applying electrical, hydraulic and pneumatic power cannot start, move or deploy anything: a flap that drives into a maintenance stand, a gear door that closes on a mechanic, a slide that fires into the cabin. Then power goes on, the APU is started so the aircraft has its own electricity and air, and the systems are tested in the order their dependencies allow: electrical first, because everything needs it; hydraulics before the flight controls are checked; air before the packs and the wing anti-ice test.

On the three-crew aircraft the flight engineer does almost all of this before the pilots arrive. On the MD-10 the captain (or a designee) walks around while the first officer powers the aircraft and works the overhead panel. Allow time: the FedEx DC-10 starts the APU no later than 20 minutes before engine start when ground power is available, and an inertial alignment takes several minutes more than any other item (see [Navigation](navigation)).

blocks.title: Preflight sequence
rows: FE: exterior safety check, then Interior Safety Check
FE: Exterior/Interior Initial Inspection, items 1 to 13
FE: Cockpit Inspection, APU start (first item of the S/O Pre-Flight)

blocks.content: **The aircraft at the gate.** Loaded on the ground with no engine running, the aircraft is as it was left parked: chocks in, pitot and engine covers on, no carts connected, the parking brake released with the chocks holding it, the inertial platforms and gyros at rest. Ground power, an air-start cart, a conditioned-air cart and the removal of chocks and covers are all called from the EFB's **Ground Ops** app (see [Ground operations](ground-operations#aircraft-states)).

**Condition:** the aircraft parked, unpowered or on battery only.

**Objective:** make sure that putting electrical, hydraulic and pneumatic power on the aircraft will not move a surface, a gear door or a door slide, nor start anything.

children.title: DC-10: exterior and interior safety checks

blocks.content: **Exterior safety check (FE).** On the way to the aircraft, look before anything is powered:

items: Wheel chocks in place, or a tug connected.

The flight control surface areas clear of people and equipment, and the flap and slat positions noted. If one flap has drooped, the area under both wings must be clear, because the first hydraulic pressure will drive both flaps to the handle's position.
The main gear doors closed. If a door is open or a control area is not clear, do not pressurize the hydraulic systems until maintenance clears it.
The APU exhaust and intake areas, and the area behind No. 2, clear.

blocks.content: **Interior safety check (FE).** In the cockpit, before switching on the battery:

items.action: Consistent With Existing Position of Surfaces

items: **Escape slide arming lever latches.** Disarmed and locked at both forward entry doors. A forward door stands either fully open or fully closed on the ground.
**Ignition, OVRD & AIRSTART, wipers.** Off, so that power cannot fire an igniter or run a wiper over a dry windshield.

**Landing gear lever.** DOWN and in its detent. If the aircraft is powered, three green lights (four on the -30 and -40). A gear that shows red and green together is a maintenance call before hydraulic power goes on.
**Center landing gear switch (-30, -40).** NORMAL, with its safety pin installed.
**Flap/slat handle.** Agreeing with the surfaces seen on the exterior safety check. A handle that disagrees would drive the surfaces as soon as hydraulic pressure arrives.
**Radar.** Off and TEST, the indicators unpowered, so that applying power cannot radiate the antenna over the ramp (see [Weather radar](surveillance#weather-radar)).
**Parking brake.** Released, the chocks holding the aircraft. (FedEx: if the brake is found set, leave it set and call maintenance; a DC-10-30 is never loaded or fueled with the parking brake set.)
**Circuit breakers.** Set. A breaker tripped for an unknown cause is reset only once, after a cooling period, and never a fuel pump or auxiliary hydraulic pump breaker.

children.title: KC-10: FE's exterior/interior initial inspection, items 1 to 13

blocks.content: The KC-10's initial inspection combines the safety walk and first power in one numbered checklist. Its first items are the safety checks: chocks in place, the gear doors agreeing with the gear handle, the flight control surfaces and the APU inlet and exhaust areas clear, the boom and the centerline drogue stowed, the pitot and inlet covers removed. In the cockpit, the battery switch to BAT and its voltage checked, the FUEL DUMP switch cover closed and safetied, the spoiler handle retracted and disarmed, the flap/slat handle agreeing with the surfaces, and the gear handle down. The full initial inspection, with the power-up items that follow, is under [First power and the APU](#power-up-kc10).

Before power goes on the aircraft, the first officer (in the simulation, the Virtual Crew's first officer if that seat is on) makes the cockpit safe. The checklist is short because the MD-10's systems controllers will configure most panels themselves once powered.

items.item: Fuel Dump and Manifold Drain Switches

items: **Weather radar.** OFF. The antenna is not radiated with people near the nose.
**Fuel levers.** OFF, so that powering the aircraft cannot open an engine's fuel shutoff valve.
**Parking brake.** As required; released only with the chocks in.
**Spoiler and FLAP/SLAT handles.** Spoiler handle in the retract detent and disarmed; FLAP/SLAT handle agreeing with the surfaces, the flap/slat interlock in position.
**Gear handle.** DOWN.
**Fuel dump and manifold drain switches.** Under their guards.
**EMER PWR selector.** OFF, so the battery is not discharged into the emergency buses.
**Battery switch.** ON: the battery now powers the battery bus for the fire tests and the APU start.

blocks.content: The aircraft is powered either by an external power cart or by its own APU, which also supplies air for the packs and for engine starting. The APU can be started on the battery alone. If it will not start, or will not come on line, the crew call for ground power and air rather than spend the battery on repeated attempts. Detailed APU operation and limits are in [APU](apu).
The electrical side of the power-up is described in [Electrical power-up](electrical#power-up).
The electrical side of the power-up is described in [Electrical power-up, MD-10](electrical#power-up-md10).

children.title: DC-10: cockpit inspection and APU start

blocks.content: The cockpit inspection is the second officer's first pass through the flight deck. In the simulation it is the EFB's COCKPIT INSPECTION: the items that act on the aircraft. Its electrical item puts the battery on (BAT, locked) and requires any APU or ground power to show 112-118 V and 396-404 Hz before it is connected to the buses; a source outside those bands is never put on line.

items.action: Push: Flow Heard on Speaker; Release
OFF: LOCK FAIL On; NORM: Out

items.item: · Manifold Fail Detect Loop Select Switch
· DC Gnd Service Bus Pwr Switch

blocks.content:
**Oil.** APU oil 6 qt minimum for a start (2 qt after); engine oil 12 qt (16 qt for an international leg). Maintenance services oil between 5 and 30 minutes after shutdown, so a low reading on arrival may be oil still draining back.

**Oxygen.** Each crew bottle at least 1,610 psi, less when cold (the FedEx minimum falls with bottle temperature to 1,275 psi at -23 °C); leave the quantity switch on the lowest bottle. The mask check proves flow at EMERGENCY pressure, flow through the mask, and the mask microphone.
**APU start (FE).** FedEx starts the APU no later than 20 minutes before engine start, earlier for crew comfort. The EFB places the start at the head of the SECOND OFFICER PRE-FLIGHT:

items.action: BAT & L EMER AC, 23.5 V DC minimum

items.item: APU/ISOL VALVE switch and No. 2 crossfeed

items.action: RUN: APU DOOR OPEN light on

items: The APU/ISOL valve stays closed for the start so the APU's load control valve is not opened against a demand before the APU is at speed. The No. 2 crossfeed is checked closed so that the fuel pump feeding the APU keeps its pressure, rather than losing it into the engine manifold.
The APU's own DC fuel pump feeds it until AC is on the buses; then tank 2's right aft pump takes over and the DC pump goes off. A tank 2 pump stays on whenever the APU runs.

An APU that has not reached idle within 3.5 minutes is shut down. If it will not start or will not come on line, call for ground power and air (Ground Ops, Ramp) and put external power on the buses with the EXT PWR switch.

Do not open the APU/ISOL valve until air is wanted for the packs, an engine start or the wing anti-ice test: opening it early opens the APU's load control valve, raises its speed and shortens its life.

blocks.content: After the safety items, the initial inspection checks the radios, tests the engine and APU fire detection, starts the APU (or connects external power), and sets the panels the boom operator and the pilots will need: pressurization in AUTO with the outflow valve open, the lighting, the FE's equipment panel, the hydraulic system, the pneumatic manifold-fail lockout and the air conditioning. It ends with the three CDUs powered, the three inertial units' MSUs to NAV and the FMS initialized, so the alignment runs while the rest of the preflight is done.

items: **APU (18).** The APU GEN BUS switches are OFF for the start; the APU draws fuel from tank 2's right aft pump if AC is available, otherwise from its own DC pump. MASTER to RUN, then START and release to RUN. When APU PWR AVAIL comes on, the APU GEN BUS switches go on one at a time and the APU PWR IN USE lights confirm each bus.

**Hydraulic system (25).** The check proves the reversible motor pumps and the auxiliary pumps. Each motor pump is armed and switched off to see its valve cycle; the two aux pumps then pressurize system 3; with the rudder standby power armed, the 2-3 and 1-3 motor pumps are armed in turn and must bring systems 2 and 1 into their white bands from system 3. The KC-10 then leaves all engine pump L switches OFF and the R switches in AUTO: its left pumps go on after each engine start.

**MANFLD FAIL/Supply Lockout (26).** Each pneumatic system's MANFLD FAIL light is pressed and released with the valves set to isolate that system. The test latches the engine supply valve shut (the lockout), and the valve is reset by turning that engine's PNEU SUPPLY selector to OFF and back to AUTO.

**Pneumatic and air conditioning (27).** With APU air: APU/ISOL valve OPEN and the packs in AUTO. With a ground air cart: the cart connected, gauge 1 normal, APU/ISOL valve OPEN. With a conditioned-air cart only: packs off.

**FMS (32).** The FMS heading switch to MAG, then the START INIT pages: date, time and databases current, the present position correct, and the INUs navigating. See [KC-10 FMS](flight-management#kc10-fms-start-init).

The fire test is done on AC power when it is available; on battery alone the test shows the lights but not the aural warning, and must be repeated once the AC buses are powered.

items: **External power.** Push EXT PWR: the EXT PWR ON light, the AC and DC bus OFF lights out, and the GEN 1, 2, 3 ARM lights on, meaning each generator will take its bus when its engine runs.

**APU start.** Push the APU START/STOP switch: its ON light flashes during the start and goes steady, and APU PWR AVAIL appears, when the APU is on speed. Push APU PWR if the APU is to carry the buses.

If the APU will not start, push START/STOP again: its OFF light comes on and goes out when the shutdown cycle is complete, about 3 minutes later. Do not try another start before then; call for ground power and air instead.

blocks.content: With the aircraft powered, the flight engineer works their panel in a fixed flow, top to bottom and left to right, testing each system and leaving it in its configuration for engine start. The flow is a scan: each panel area is looked at once, in order, and anything found abnormal is dealt with before moving on. The checklist that follows confirms only the essential items.

items: **Annunciator lights, ALL TEST.** Every S/O annunciator lights except the fire loop, cargo door warning and brake temperature lights, which have their own tests; the four cue lights on the forward overhead, both MASTER WARN and MASTER CAUTION lights and the summary lights come on too. The CAB ALT and APU FIRE summary lights do not light on ALL TEST. A dark lamp is reported, not changed.

**Outflow valve, AUTO and open.** MANUAL, wheel a third closed, then AUTO: the wheel must run back to full open. This proves the automatic controller can drive the valve before the doors are closed and the packs started.

**Hydraulic system.** The minimum acceptable pressure for the test is 2,400 psi, less 3 psi for each degree C of fluid temperature above 0 °C. With the RMP switches off, each RMP is armed and turned off again to watch the 1-3/2-3 PUMP VALVE OPEN light cycle. Aux pump 1 brings system 3 into its white band; aux pump 2 adds to it. With the rudder standby power armed (RUD STBY PWR OFF light out), arming the 2-3 RMP brings system 2 up from system 3, and arming the 1-3 RMP brings system 1 up. Each RMP therefore proves it can power its system from system 3, which is what it must do if an engine pump or engine is lost. Brake pressures in the normal band, temperatures below the yellow band, quantities at least to the chevron (3.75 US gal) in systems 1 and 2 and 6.7 US gal in system 3, and the quantity bugs set. Then both aux pumps off: the pressure falls to zero.
**Engine hydraulic pumps.** All left switches ON, all right switches AUTO, every PRESS LO light on (the engines are stopped). The RMPs stay armed for the pilots' panel checks.

**Generators.** CSD oil pressure low lights on and CSD temperatures normal with the engines stopped. Each GEN switch through RESET to ON; GEN OFF lights on, AC load zero. The AC BUS TIE ISOL (amber) lights are on with APU power, because the APU generator is never paralleled with the engine generators, and out with external power. Bus tie switches NORM.
**DC power.** The DC TIE and DC X-TIE switches OPEN, so the DC buses are split and a fault on one cannot take the others.

**Fuel quantity test.** With the quantity system on NORM, the tank readings agree with the totalizer. On the digital gauges the test button lights every segment (888880 on the totalizer, 188880 on the tanks), blanks the displays, shows 99900 in each main tank, then returns; the standard drum counters instead roll to zero and back. ALTN and back to NORM must not change the readings. Compare the fuel on board with the fuel service record.

**Crossfeeds.** Each tank and transfer pump ON: its PRESS LO light cycles. Opening the No. 2 crossfeed cycles its DISAGREE light; opening Nos. 1 and 3 puts pressure on the No. 1 and No. 3 fuel pressure gauges from tank 2's pump; closing them lets the pressure decay. That proves both that the valves move and that they seal. All pumps then off, except No. 2 right aft with the APU running.

**Manifold fail lights.** Each MANIFOLD FAIL light held: the light (and for No. 1 the No. 2 light too), the PNEU MANIFOLD FAIL summary light and every MASTER WARNING light come on, and go out when released. The test also latches that engine's supply valve shut, as a real manifold failure would; the After Start check, which takes each supply selector to OFF and back, resets it.

**Wing anti-ice test.** With air in the manifold, TEST for no more than 15 seconds. On the aircraft the valves open, and the WING ANTI-ICE DISAGREE lights cycle as they open and again as they close on release; a DISAGREE light still on after the test means a valve is open, so remove the air source. In the simulation TEST opens no valve: both DISAGREE lights stay lit while the switch is held and go out on release.

**Cargo smoke and fire detection.** Hold the test: every smoke detector light, CAB CARGO SMOKE, the FWD and AFT FIRE lights, the CARGO FIRE summary light and the master lights. The agent discharge test lights AGENT 1 and 2 LOW. A flashing detector light during the test marks a detector that is deteriorating but still working.

**Engine and APU fire detection.** Loop selectors BOTH, then both loop test switches together: every loop light, the APU FIRE light, the fire handles, the fuel lever lights and the bell. Released, all out and the bell silent.

**Pressurization.** The standby controller exercised (STANDBY ON, the manual wheel follows the knob), then back to zero and pushed in; SEMI-AUTO and back to AUTO; the rate limit knob at 2 o'clock; the departure altimeter setting on LDG BARO and the **destination** field elevation in the ALT SET window, which the controller needs to bring the cabin down to the landing field at the end of the flight.
**Engine instruments.** Oil quantity at least 12 qt (16 international) and the bugs set; oil temperature normal, oil pressure zero.

**Brake temperature (where fitted) and cargo door lights.** Each tested: the OVHT and DIFF TEMP lights on and the gauge in the white band, then back to the pre-test reading; every cargo door light on in TEST.

blocks.content: The FE's interior inspection is a scan of the whole flight deck, the pilots' panels included, before the pilots arrive: the KC-10's flight engineer tests the yaw dampers, anti-skid, emergency power, emergency lights, GPWS, stall and overspeed warnings, speed control, pitot heat, the annunciators, the gear warning, the longitudinal trim and the takeoff warning, and then sets their own panel. The pilots' later scan confirms the result rather than repeating the tests.

items: **Elevator feel (5).** AUTO with the reference IAS in the white band; MAN and the slew checked both ways; back to AUTO, the needle returning to the white band.
**Yaw dampers (7).** All four on, then the test: every light on and out again after about 20 seconds.
**Emergency power (15).** ON: EMER PWR IN USE on, no flags, AC volts in the white or yellow band and the battery discharging on BAT & L EMER AC; OFF: the battery charging again.
**Stall warning (23).** Each side held until the columns shake, which takes 5 to 8 seconds.

**Longitudinal trim (42).** Both halves of each trim switch together move the handles and the indicator, with the stabilizer-in-motion horn; either half alone moves nothing (the split switch guards against a single runaway contact). The alternate trim and the copilot's switches are checked the same way. In the simulation the wheel trim switches are not modeled, so only the long trim handles and the ALT LONG TRIM switches can be checked (see [Cockpit preparation, Simulation notes](normal-cockpit-preparation#simulation-notes)).

**Takeoff warning horn (45).** Parking brake released, stabilizer in the green band, spoiler handle in RET and the flap/slat handle UP/RET, so that only the slat condition is tested: throttle 1 full forward sounds the horn because the slats are not at takeoff, and idle silences it; then throttles 2 and 3 together. The horn is driven by throttles 1 and 2 only.
**Electrical (60).** As the DC-10's: generators reset and on, AC bus tie isolation lights on with APU power and off with external power, DC ties open, battery locked.

**Fuel (76).** The quantity test, the aft pump checks, the fuel used counters reset, the manifold scavenge off and the master fuel isolation valve in NORM and pinned; the gross weight indicator set to the zero fuel weight; the wing pod control panel checked with the boom operator.
**Hydraulic motor pumps and aux pumps (77, 78).** Off and stopped at the end: system pressures fall away.

blocks.content: The walkaround is the final check of the aircraft's general condition before each flight: panels closed and latched, no leaks, no damage, probes clear, the gear safe, the doors closed. It is flown clockwise from the nose. In the simulation the walkaround is visual; the items the simulation does model on the ramp are the chocks, the pitot and engine covers and the traffic cones, which are taken away from the EFB's Ground Ops app or by clicking them on the walkaround.
Keep clear of the engine inlets and exhausts whenever an engine or the APU could be running. The KC-10 manual gives a 20 ft radius intake danger area around each engine at idle.

The second officer walks around before every takeoff. Turn the NAV and WING lights on first so that the bulbs can be checked; logo lights, where fitted, are left on. The center gear items apply to the -30 and -40.

items: Systems tests that light lamps, sound the bells and horns and move needles are modeled: the annunciator and fire tests, the hydraulic, fuel quantity, crossfeed, manifold fail, wing anti-ice, cargo smoke, brake temperature, stall, overspeed and speed control tests, the yaw damper test and the emergency power check. The anti-skid TEST button does nothing (the FAIL lights are proved by the annunciator light test), and the wing anti-ice test only lights the DISAGREE lights.

Visual-only items (tires, leaks, oil servicing records, the flight deck's loose equipment) have nothing to find in the simulation. The EFB's preflight leaves the paperwork and loose equipment out entirely.

Items the simulated aircraft does not carry are answered as not installed: the DC-10's flight deck access system (FDAS), ACARS and courier oxygen; the KC-10's SATCOM, data link and crypto items. The KC-10's IFF has no control head: its checks are made on the FMS CDU pages.

With the Virtual Crew's flight engineer (or MD-10 first officer) on, the PREFLIGHT checklists are run for you in real time: switches moved one at a time, tests held long enough to read; some tests are only answered (see [Items the crew answers without setting them](virtual-crew#answered-items)). If the APU does not start, the DC-10's second officer asks you to call for ground power and air and waits until ground power is connected, then puts it on the buses; the KC-10's flight engineer halts on the APU item and, once you have ticked it, asks for ground power and air at the electrical power item; the MD-10's first officer halts on the APU item.

parts.title: Cockpit Preparation
parts.summary: The pilots' flows and tests, navigation set-up, takeoff data and the takeoff briefing, and the Cockpit Preparation checklist.

blocks.content:
Cockpit preparation is the pilots' half of the preflight. Each pilot works their own panels in a fixed flow, testing the warning systems and flight instruments they will rely on and setting the panel for departure; together they load the navigation system, compute and cross-check the takeoff data and brief the departure. It ends with the aircraft configured for the Before Start checklist.

The flows assume the flight engineer (or on the MD-10 the first officer's preliminary preparation) has powered the aircraft and that hydraulic pressure is available for the control checks. On the DC-10 the second officer leaves the RMPs armed for exactly that reason; the captain starts the aux hydraulic pumps for their checks and stops them afterwards.
Before any hydraulic pump is started, make sure the flight control surfaces, spoilers, flaps and slats are clear and the landing gear handle is down.

The captain's flow runs over the overhead panel (annunciators, hydraulic flight control panel, flight controls, yaw dampers, anti-skid, compass, start panel, emergency power and lights, exterior lights), then the glareshield flight guidance panel, their instrument panel and the pedestal. The first officer's flow covers the overhead tests on their side (ground proximity and radar, radio navigation, stall and speed warnings, window and probe heat), the glareshield, their instrument panel and the center panel (thrust rating computer, flap and surface position indicators). The two flows meet on the instruments both pilots must check (altimeters, ADIs, radio altimeters, HSIs) and on the flight plan, which the captain reads and the first officer verifies.

items: **Aux hydraulic pumps, START (CAPT).** The pumps give pressure for the yaw damper, anti-skid, brake and stabilizer trim checks; the RMPs, left armed by the second officer, carry it to all three systems. When the checks are done, STOP, and tell the second officer the RMPs may be switched off.

**Yaw dampers, ON and TEST.** All lights out with the switches on. The test lights the TEST FAIL, INOP and TEST lights and drives each rudder: half an increment left, back to neutral, slightly right, neutral. Do not trim or touch the brakes during the test. A TEST FAIL light means a damper channel failed; cycle the affected switches and retest one channel at a time (see [Yaw dampers](automatic-flight#yaw-dampers)).

**Brakes.** With the main wheels chocked or a tug attached: parking brake set (PARK and PARK BRAKE ON lights), released (the ANTI-SKID FAIL lights flicker as the parking brake valves open), then set or released as appropriate, and both brake pressures in the white band. Never load or fuel the aircraft with the parking brake set.

**Stab trim.** Trim nose down, then nose up (in the simulation with the simulator's trim input; see Simulation notes): the long trim handles and the trim indicator move together and the stabilizer-in-motion horn sounds after about 1° of travel. A single aux pump may not drive the stabilizer fast enough for the horn; confirm it after engine start. Finish with the trim in the middle of the green band.
**Compass.** DG and back to SLAVED, once, to fast-synchronize; the index aligned. Resynchronize again once the INS has aligned.

**Emergency power, check and off.** FD switches off first, so the pitch bars do not cycle. EMER PWR ON: EMER PWR IN USE on (in the simulation only the flight engineer's light works), no flags on the captain's altimeter and VSI, the emergency buses powered from the battery through the inverter (AC volts and frequency in the white or yellow band, DC discharging). OFF: the battery charges and the light goes out.

**Ground prox and radar (F/O).** Both radar indicators on with the radar in TEST, and the test pattern checked on each. Push the GPWS test button (on the ground, flaps not at landing): with the default basic computer the GPWS legend and then the BELOW G/S light come on, with no voice; a terrain picture exists only with the optional terrain display (see [GPWS](surveillance#gpws-fits)). Radar indicators off afterwards.

**Stall and speed tests (F/O).** STALL TEST L, then R: the columns shake after 5 to 8 seconds. MAX SPEED WARNING TEST 1, then 2: the overspeed clacker. SPEED CONTROL TEST SLOW, then FAST: both fast/slow pointers move half scale and return.

**Pitot heat, check and off.** Any position but OFF powers every air data heater; the position only chooses which one the HTR CUR meter reads. Walk the selector through every position: each heater shows its current, except TAT, whose probe is not heated on the ground. A static or vane heater has no failure light, so a zero reading here is the only way to find a dead one. The PITOT HEAT INOP light out; selector OFF (After Start sets TAT).

**Altimeters and the altitude advisory.** No flags, the current setting set, the bugs at field elevation; the primary altimeters within 75 ft of field elevation. With the altitude preselect 1,000 ft above the field, wind the captain's baro knob toward it: the advisory light and tone at about 750 ft to go, the light out within 250 ft; back the other way, the light flashes 250 ft off the selected altitude; RESET cancels it.

**Engine instruments.** The max pointers within limits (they may jump on a power transfer and may then be reset); the digital EGT's overtemp recall light not lit; analog and digital readings agreeing.
**Thrust rating computer (F/O).** No flags; T.O. selected, the limit index markers on the N1 gauges matching the computer's N1 limit (EPR on the -40).

**Takeoff warning and throttles (CAPT).** Parking brake released (a set brake also sets off the warning, and would hide the slat test). Each of throttles 1 and 2 to full forward sounds the horn, because the slats are not at takeoff; the SLAT DISAGREE light stays out; idle silences it. Throttle 3 is moved through its travel for freedom. Then fuel levers OFF.
**Transponder/TCAS.** STBY, altitude reporting on, the code set if known; on a fit with TCAS, its self-test.

**Autobrake.** Selector OFF and the ARM-DISARM switch at DISARM. The selector has T.O., OFF and three landing settings (MIN, MED, MAX); the anti-skid must be armed and powered before any of them can be armed.

**INS flight plan (C, F).** Present position verified in each INS; the waypoints loaded and cross-filled; the captain reads each waypoint's coordinates while the first officer checks them against the master flight plan; and INS 1's distance to destination agrees with the flight plan, a check for a gross position error.

blocks.content: The KC-10 pilots' interior inspection is a scan pattern. The flight engineer has already tested the overhead systems during their interior inspection, so the pilots concentrate on what they will fly with: their oxygen and audio, the radios, the weather radar, the electronic flight instruments, the IFF and ETCAS (run from the FMS CDU pages; there is no separate control head), the FMS and navigation radios, the flight director, the autothrottle and autopilot panels, and the altitude advisory system.

items: **EHSIs/EADIs (10).** The DU test shows the status page with nothing in red; a red item calls for the built-in test. Back to the normal display.

**FMS (2, 38, 39).** Load the GPS keys and data cartridges where the mission requires them; enter the performance data (cruise altitude, fuel) and the flight plan, with the departure and arrival, and the winds; EXECUTE. See [KC-10 FMS](flight-management#kc10-fms).
**ATS panel (30).** ATS levers OFF and the SPD select set to V2, the bugs agreeing.

**Heading and vertical speed (31, 32).** HDG SEL and HDG HOLD checked with the roll bars following; bank angle selector 15°; the vertical speed wheel checked up and down and back to the ALT HOLD detent.

**Altitude advisory (33).** As the DC-10's: field barometric pressure set, the preselect 1,000 ft above the field and armed, the light and tone at 750 ft to go and out at 250 ft, the flashing light at 250 ft away, RESET; then the reported altimeter setting.
**Radio navigation (36).** Both VOR test buttons: flags, then the CDI centerd, TO, 180° ± 3°. The ILS test switches, one dot up and left, then down and right. The marker beacon lamps.

blocks.content: **Cockpit Preparation checklist.** With the crew aboard, the flight engineer reads the Cockpit Preparation checklist. It confirms the takeoff data, the altimeters, the FMS loading, the oxygen and the systems the flight engineer set during their inspection.

items: **Takeoff data, N1 limit, V-bugs (P, CP, FE).** The flight engineer computes the takeoff data from the performance manual (in the simulation, the EFB's Performance app and Set Bugs). The pilots check the bugs and the SPD select; the flight engineer checks the N1 limit and, for a reduced thrust takeoff, the assumed temperature on the TRC.
**Oxygen system (ALL).** Each regulator ON and 100% whenever the seat is occupied in flight.
**Exterior lights (CP, FE).** As required for the time of day and the ramp; the beacon is the signal to the ground crew that engines are about to start, so it goes on with the Before Start checklist.
**Cabin cargo smoke switch, avionic flow, pressurization (FE).** ARMED, NORMAL and set (AUTO, the destination field elevation in ALT SET, the departure setting on LDG BARO).

blocks.content: The MD-10's preflight panel scan divides the flight deck between the two pilots. The captain checks their glareshield, oxygen mask, source input selector, displays, clock and IRS position, and their radio and audio panels. The first officer does the overhead panel (annunciator test, air conditioning, IRS and cargo fire test, the hydraulic, electrical, air and fuel panels, emergency lights, signs, exterior lights, GPWS, the flight control panel's limits, yaw dampers, the start panel, pressurization and anti-ice), then their own glareshield and instruments, the gear warning and configuration synoptic, anti-skid, standby instruments, the takeoff warning test, the status page, radar, transponder and trims. If one pilot is not there for the scan, the other does all of it.

On the FCP: IAS 250, the heading window on the aircraft's heading (cross-checked with the standby compass), bank angle AUTO, the AFS OVRD OFF levers up, 10,000 ft in the altitude window.

items: **Annunciator lights.** Hold ANNUN LT TEST: every light on, MASTER WARNING flashing and the overspeed aural. On the aircraft the air system tests itself while the button is held and the button is released when the AIR SYS TEST alert appears; the simulation runs no air system test and shows no such alert.

**Air conditioning.** For the ground: the isolation valves ON (pressed, blue ON legends), the packs on (OFF legends out), zone temperatures as required. The APU BLEED switchlight is left out, so the APU's air reaches the manifold; pressed, it shows USE ENG AIR and shuts the APU off from the manifold.

**IRS and cargo fire test.** The three IRS NAV/OFF selectors to NAV start the alignment and the automatic cargo fire test (CARGO FIRE TEST alert). If no test runs or it fails, hold the manual test switch.

**IRS initialization.** On the A/C STATUS page check the model, engines and navigation database; on F-PLN INIT enter the company route or the departure and destination and initialize the IRS. See [Flight management](flight-management).

**Hydraulic, fuel and electrical panels.** In AUTO, nothing to do but check the panel: SYS 1, 2, 3 PRESS lights on with the engines stopped. With a panel in MANUAL, its [MANUAL] steps check each pump.

**EMER PWR selector.** OFF to ARM. On the aircraft this runs a 30-second self-test with EMER PWR ON displayed. The simulation runs no self-test: with AC power on the buses nothing is displayed, and on battery alone ARM transfers the emergency buses and EMER PWR ON stays until the selector goes back to OFF.
**GPWS.** Terrain override not set; the GPWS test switch held momentarily: the test lights and aurals (see [GPWS](surveillance#gpws-self-test)). The simulated ND draws no terrain picture.
**AFSCP and yaw dampers.** FLAP LIMIT and ELEV FEEL in AUTO, all lights out; the four yaw damper switches on, their OFF and FAIL lights out.

**Gear warning and CONFIG synoptic.** Three green (four on the Series 30, with the center gear in its normal position). The gear handle out of its detent but not up: red lights on the panel and the synoptic; release it: green.
**Anti-skid.** ARM. The simulation has no anti-skid test, so the ANTI-SKID NO TEST alert of the aircraft does not appear.

**Takeoff warning.** Throttle 1 to full forward sounds the warning because the slats are not at takeoff; idle silences it; then throttles 2 and 3 together. In the simulation the warning is a beeper with a voice naming the fault (SLATS), and only throttles 1 and 2 trigger it.
**Weather radar.** Each system to TEST in turn, then OFF. (The simulated ND does not draw the radar picture.)
**Transponder.** Transponder 1 or 2, altitude reporting on, STBY. The simulated MD-10 has no TCAS, so there is no TCAS test.

blocks.content: With both pilots seated, check the fuel load against the plan, set up the FMS, set the takeoff flap on the FLAP T.O. SEL thumbwheel, and set the flight control panel for departure.

items: **Fuel quantity.** The fuel loaded added to the quantity before fueling should agree with the total indicated; a difference of 4,000 lb or more means the magnetic stick readings are taken as the fuel on board. On the aircraft (Series 30) the fuel system's automatic preflight test may leave fuel in the upper auxiliary tank before start; the simulation does not run that test.

**FMS.** In the simulation, the EFB's Performance app computes the takeoff data and **Send to Avionics** writes it to the FMS; check the TAKEOFF and WEIGHT INIT pages and the speeds on both PFDs. The FMS TAKEOFF page also carries the acceleration and thrust reduction altitudes.
**FLAP T.O. SEL.** The takeoff flap from the card; the thumbwheel sets the movable detent the flap handle will stop at.
**Flight control panel.** Speed 250 KIAS or VCL (the clean climb speed), whichever is higher; heading and altitude for the departure.
**IRS.** The amber NO TAXI on the PFD has gone: the IRS has aligned enough to move. The alignment continues to NAV.
**Anti-skid.** ARM.
**Autobrake.** Not installed in the simulated MD-10; the item is answered "Not Installed".

blocks.content: **Cockpit Preparation checklist.** The first officer reads it; both pilots answer the items in their areas, and both answer the configuration items.

Takeoff data is computed for the runway, the conditions and the weight, and nothing about the takeoff is improvised from it. The data gives the flap setting, the stabilizer trim, the thrust (maximum, or reduced through an assumed temperature), the speeds V1, VR and V2, the flap and slat retraction speeds, the clean minimum maneuvering speed and the acceleration height. On the DC-10 it also gives the fuel dump time and weight to get back to landing weight, which the second officer will remind the captain of after an engine failure.

In the simulation the data comes from the EFB's **Performance** app, **Takeoff** page: pull the aircraft data, complete what it could not fill (obstacle, anti-ice, packs, reverse thrust, the thrust, the return flap), calculate, and check that the takeoff weight is within MTOGW, the runway required within the runway available, and the brake zone acceptable. See [Compute takeoff data](efb#compute-takeoff-data) and [Performance and mission planning](mission-planning).

**Setting it on the flight deck.** Press **Set Bugs**: it sets the airspeed bugs to V1, VR and the flap, slat and clean speeds, V2 on the SPEED select, and for a reduced-thrust card dials the assumed temperature into the thumbwheels. Then on the thrust rating computer: for maximum thrust select T.O.; for reduced thrust read the card's assumed temperature back from the ASSUMED TEMP thumbwheels and select T.O. FLX. Check that the limit markers on each N1 gauge show the computer's limit. The assumed temperature must be above the OAT; the computer refuses one that is not. The DC-10-10 has no flex mode: for a reduced-thrust takeoff select G/A and set the card's N1 by hand. The DC-10-40 rates in EPR with no flex mode; its EPR limit bugs follow the computer's limit by themselves. Set the stabilizer trim and the flap takeoff selector (dial-a-flap) to the card's values before takeoff.

Check the computer's limit against the card: they should agree within 0.5% N1. A limit that reads high may be a TAT that reads high: with little air moving over the probe on a hot ramp in the sun, the TAT reads warmer than the air.

**Setting it on the flight deck.** Press **Send to Avionics**, then check the FMS TAKEOFF and WEIGHT INIT pages and the V-speeds on both PFDs. Set the FLAP T.O. SEL to the card's flap, and the stabilizer trim before takeoff.

blocks.title: Restrictions on reduced-thrust (standard thrust) takeoffs, FedEx DC-10
columns: Do not use reduced thrust when
rows: The runway is wet, or has snow, slush, standing water or ice on it
The OAT is within 5 °C of the maximum OAT for the takeoff

blocks.content: An assumed temperature set wrongly on the thumbwheels gives a T.O. FLX limit lower than the takeoff needs. Read the card's temperature back from the thumbwheels, and read the N1 limit against the card.

**Takeoff data briefing.** The FedEx captain briefs the card before start, the speeds called aloud from high to low as the bugs are checked: the runway the data is for, the ATIS, the stop margin, the flaps and the stab trim, the dump time and weight, the minimum flap retraction height if not 1,000 ft, the thrust (maximum N1, or standard N1 with the assumed temperature set), and the type of takeoff: TOGA, vertical speed or raw data. When the speeds are limited by VMCG and reduced thrust is used, the flight director's takeoff mode would compute an unacceptably low V2, so a vertical speed takeoff is flown instead (the card says so).

The PF briefs the takeoff with all crewmembers present, once the ATIS and the clearance have been received (if the clearance comes only at pushback or during taxi, brief the expected departure and brief the changes during the Before Takeoff checklist). The briefing assumes standard procedures, so it covers only what this takeoff needs: which pilot flies, the runway, the departure routing with its speed and altitude restrictions, the engine-out procedure, terrain, the transition altitude, a non-standard flap retraction height, and anything abnormal (anti-ice, deferred items, windshear).

**Standard procedures** include the standard callouts (see [Callouts](normal-techniques#callouts)) and the rejected takeoff policy. The captain alone decides to reject a takeoff, and takes control to do it. Below 80 kt the takeoff is rejected for any malfunction; between 80 kt and V1 only for a significant one (an engine failure or fire, the takeoff warning horn, or anything that leaves the aircraft unsafe or unable to fly); after V1 the takeoff is continued. As V1 approaches, the bar for rejecting rises: a borderline stop near V1 is more dangerous than continuing. In an emergency the PF flies the aircraft, the PM works with the flight engineer and handles ATC unless the captain directs otherwise. The rejected takeoff procedure itself is in [Emergency procedures](emergency-procedures).

FedEx adds: on a rejected takeoff the second officer backs up the ground spoiler deployment and reports reverse thrust by exception ("No reverse on 3"); after an engine failure past V1 the second officer reminds the captain, at a suitable time, of the dump time to landing weight and waits for the order; with two engines failed they start dumping on their own and say so. On aircraft authorized for autothrottle takeoffs and fitted with autobrakes, both are used unless the captain says otherwise.

items: Stabilizer trim. The aircraft's control wheel trim switches are not modeled: your simulator's trim input (keys, wheel or axis) drives the stabilizer at full rate through the same path as the pedestal long trim handles, and the ALTERNATE trim switch drives it at half rate. The split-switch check of the wheel switches cannot be done. The takeoff green band in the simulation is about 2 to 10° ANU.

The anti-skid TEST button is drawn on every flight deck but does nothing; the voice recorder test works on all three. On the DC-10 the ADI test works, the DH light push does not; the KC-10 and MD-10 have no ADI test.
With the Virtual Crew on, the captain's items wait for your tick; on AUTO the crew tick those they can see set. See [Items the crew answers without setting them](virtual-crew#answered-items).

The default basic GPWS has a single lamp test (the GPWS and BELOW G/S lights) and no voice; the EFB's preflight step describes the voice option's test sequence and a FLAP OVRD guard, which the DC-10 does not have.

The Virtual Crew's first officer, when on, runs the radar test, the stall and speed tests, the gear warning test and their ADI test, sets the heat and anti-ice switches, and answers their instrument and thrust rating computer items. The first officer does not run the GPWS test, the radio navigation tests or the pitot heat current check: do those yourself.

The IFF and ETCAS have no control head of their own; their checks are made on the FMS CDU pages (see [KC-10 IFF](surveillance#xpdr-kc10) and [ETCAS](surveillance#tcas-etcas)). The crypto, data link and SATCOM items have nothing to load and are passed.

With the Virtual Crew's copilot on: the stall, speed and other overhead tests belong to the flight engineer's interior inspection; the copilot runs their oxygen regulator check and radar test and answers their other items.

The FLEX temperature can be entered on the MCDU, but it does not yet reduce the thrust the flight control computers set; MD-10 takeoffs are flown at full takeoff thrust. The AIR panel's ECON, SYSTEM and CABIN AIR switchlights, the HYD PRESS TEST switch and the EIS source selector are not connected; ANNUN LT TEST runs no air system test, EMER PWR ARM runs no self-test, and there is no anti-skid test.
The cabin pressure controller has no landing elevation input; it runs in automatic to a landing field at sea level and 29.92 inHg.
The ND draws no terrain, weather radar or traffic picture, and there is no TCAS.

parts.title: Before Start, Pushback and Engine Start
parts.summary: The Before Start checklist, pushback, the start sequence and each crewmember's duties during the start, and the After Start checklist.

blocks.content: Before Start closes the aircraft up and configures it to start engines: the doors closed and the slides armed, the fuel pumps feeding, the packs off so that every pound of air in the manifold goes to the starters, the ignition armed and the beacon on to tell the ground crew that engines are about to turn. The engines are then started in the order 3, 1, 2. The center engine comes last because it is the one that may be left until the taxi: the aircraft taxis well on the two wing engines, and No. 2's blast, high in the tail, is the hardest to keep off the ramp. After Start then hands the aircraft from ground power and the APU to the engines: the generators paralleled, the APU shut down, the engine bleeds and packs on, the hydraulic pumps checked.

The engines' starting system, its limits and what a normal start looks like on the gauges are described in [Engines](engines#start-sequence). Abnormal starts (no light-off, a hot or hung start, no oil pressure, no N1) are in [Abnormal procedures](abnormal-procedures).

The captain calls for the Before Start checklist when the cockpit set-up is finished. The first officer reads it to the line, and it is held there until the aircraft is ready to push back; the items below the line are then completed before the aircraft moves. The first officer reports "Down to the line".

blocks.title: Flows below the line
rows: Ignition: START A or START B
Engine hydraulic pumps: L OFF, R AUTO
Aft fuel boost pumps: ON (all four)

items: **Fuel quantity.** The second officer states the fuel on board from the totalizer; the captain the fuel the aircraft was released with. Any fuel panel test is repeated whenever the total fuel changes.
**INS.** NAV. The aircraft must not move until the alignment lights are out; a platform disturbed during alignment must start again.
**Compass.** SLAVED, resynchronized after the INS alignment: SLAVED to DG and back gives a fast synchronization.
**Altimeters.** Each crewmember states the setting; stating it confirms the altimeters were checked in the preflight. Cross-check all three, the standby included.
**Oxygen.** Checked and set to 100%; the second officer reads the quantity.

**Gross weights.** The zero fuel weight is set on the gross weight indicator, which adds the fuel on board; the second officer states the gross weight it shows. (FedEx subtracts any ballast fuel from the ZFW before entering it, because the totalizer counts that fuel already.)
**Cabin doors and lights.** Armed and the lights out before the aircraft moves. At no time is one door armed and the other disarmed.
**Ignition.** Alternate START A and START B from one leg to the next, so that both systems are proven.
**Cargo doors and lights.** The ground crew confirm every cargo door closed and locked; "Checked" means the door lights have been tested, "Out" that they are out.

**S/O panel set for start.** Left engine hydraulic pumps OFF and the right ones AUTO, so that each left pump can be proved on its own after its engine starts; the aft boost pumps on in every tank, the pumps that sit lowest and scavenge best; the packs off.

blocks.content: The flight engineer reads the Before Start checklist when the crew are ready to start. Except in a scramble, every door is closed and its slide armed before an engine starts, so that the cabin can be evacuated from any exit.

items: **INUs (1).** NAV (alignment status 01) before the aircraft moves.
**Beacon (2).** BOTH on the BEACON LT MASTER selector.
**Parking brake (3).** SET, the brake pressure above the minimum.

**Fuel pumps (5).** The AFT PUMP switches of tanks 1, 2 and 3: each pressure LOW light comes on and goes off, and its flow light comes on. The aft pumps are used because they sit in the lowest part of the tank. Tank 2's right aft pump is normally on already, for the APU.

**Ignition (7).** OVRD & AIR START OFF, then START A on odd-numbered days, START B on even-numbered days. On the aircraft START A or B also arms the start switches and raises the APU to about 97% N1 for more air (see Simulation notes for the simulation's version).

**Pneumatic pressure (8).** The PRESS gauges 1 and 3 in the normal range, at least 25 psi with the start valve closed. If every gauge reads less, turn the ENG PNEU SUPPLY selectors to OFF so that no air leaks back through an engine's supply valve. Below 0 °F (-18 °C) 35 psi assures a good start. A start may be made with as little as 15 psi if operations require it, watching N2 rise steadily; expect a slower start.

**Boom operator's preparation (9), cargo and cabin door lights (10, 11).** The boom operator reports the cabin ready. The CARGO DOOR INDICATION switch to TEST lights SYS A and SYS B; released, both out. Every cabin door light out. A door light out does not prove a slide is fitted.

blocks.content: Before pushback or taxi, every courier and crewmember not working is seated. The first officer reads the Before Start checklist; the AIR panel is set for the start because the packs must not take air the starters need, and the isolation valves must be open to carry the APU's air from its manifold to all three engines.

items.action: Closed, slides armed, no door alerts; windows locked
ON if the pushback starts before engine start
SET, or released on the ground crew's word for the push
1-2 and 1-3 ISOL ON; PACKs OFF; BLEED AIR 1, 2, 3 OFF; APU BLEED out (APU air on)

blocks.content: **Why the bleeds are off.** With the engine bleeds off, the manifold is a single pool fed by the APU through the open isolation valves; a running engine's bleed is not fighting the APU for it, and no start valve is fed from a bleed that has not come up. For a start with an air cart instead of the APU, push the APU BLEED switchlight in (USE ENG AIR shows) so the cart's air is not lost into the APU.

A pushback is a coordinated operation between the captain and the tug driver. The aircraft must be closed up, the inertial systems in NAV, hydraulic pressure available for the brakes, the ground equipment gone and the chocks removed before the tug takes it. While the tug moves the aircraft the parking brake is off, the thrust is at idle and the brakes are not used except to stop in an emergency; either would load the towbar. The steering bypass pin keeps the nosewheel steering out of the tug's way, and stays in until the towbar is off.

In the simulation the tug, its driving and the ground crew's calls are on the EFB's Ground Ops app, **Pushback** page; the full procedure is [Pushback](ground-operations#pushback-procedure).

items: **Brakes and hydraulic pressure.** With no engine running, brake pressure comes from the auxiliary hydraulic pumps (DC-10 and KC-10: the flight engineer starts them; MD-10: AUX HYD PUMP 1).
**Beacon.** On before the push: it is the signal to the ground crew that engines are about to start.
**Engine start during the push.** Start air comes from the APU. An air cart is a start at the gate with the chocks in: the cart goes when the chocks are removed.

**After stopping.** Set the parking brake, then clear the tug to disconnect. Do not call for the After Start checklist, nor taxi, until the tug and the ground crew are clear and have given the all-clear.

blocks.content: Starting is done by interphone with the ground crew and, where required, with ATC's start clearance. The normal sequence is engine 3, then 1, then 2. A subsequent start may begin once the previous engine's EGT has peaked, or at the captain's discretion once its generator is on line, the captain then watching the previous EGT until it peaks. Keep cockpit talk to the standard calls during the start.

A fuel flow above about 700 lb/h before light-off may give a hot start; the normal flow before light-off is about 550 lb/h. Watch for the EGT rise within 25 seconds of the fuel lever going on, and expect the duct pressure to drop about 5 psi as a start valve opens.

blocks.title: Crew duties during start (FedEx)
rows: Obtains start clearance from the ground crew and ATC.

Reads the pressure in all three pneumatic systems: "Start pressure ___ psi". FedEx wants 20 psi or more, because a start on less may run hot (the EFB card asks for 25). If one gauge shows none, opens the isolation valve to it.
"Turning number ___." Engages the START switch: its light comes on.
Monitors that the pneumatic pressure stays at 15 psi or more through the start.
At 15% N2 minimum, fuel lever ON.
Calls "Oil pressure number ___" at the first indication; watches the fuel pressure, the hydraulic pressure rise, the right engine pump PRESS LO light and the CSD OIL PRESS LO light go out.
Watches fuel flow and the EGT rise within 25 s.
Watches fuel flow, EGT and N2 for a normal start.
At about 45% N2 the START switch releases and its light goes out: "Start valve closed."
Confirms the switch released; when the generator comes on line: "Number ___ generator on line."

Watches N1, EGT and N2 stabilize; the ENG OIL PRESS light out by stable idle; resets the max pointers if a power transfer moved them; engine anti-ice on if required (in the simulation the toggles do not move on screen: confirm by the lights; see [Ice and rain](ice-and-rain#simulation-notes)).
Checks oil quantity, pressure and temperature; the system hydraulic pressure at least 2,800 psi.

blocks.content:
The EFB's STARTING ENGINES checklist turns these duties into items. After the parking brake is set and the towbar is off, the captain tells the ground crew "Cleared to disconnect", and calls for the After Start checklist once the last engine's EGT has peaked.

In the simulation the START switch is pulled out to engage the starter; a holding coil keeps it out, and it drops back in by itself at starter cutout, about 45% N2. The Virtual Crew's first officer, when on, works each start (switch, fuel lever at 15% N2) and asks before No. 2 whether to start it now or leave it for the taxi.

blocks.title: Crew duties during start
rows: Confirms ground and tower clearance: "Ready to start number ___."
Reports "Before Start checklist complete", calls "Ready to start number ___" and checks the pneumatic pressure is 25 psi or more (a 5 psi drop as the valve opens is normal).
Engages the ENGINE START switch: its light comes on. Watches N2 for rotation.
At 15% N2, FUEL lever ON: "Fuel lever on."
Watches the fuel flow and the EGT rise within 25 s; calls "EGT".
Checks the EGT rise and peak within the start limits.
Watches the START switch release and its light go out.
Checks oil pressure, quantity and temperature.
Watches N2 stabilize at idle (about 65%), N1 (about 25%), EGT normal and the ENG OIL PRESS LO light out.
Watches the HYD PRESS gauges in the white band, switches the engine's left hydraulic pump ON and confirms one pump in each system gives at least 2,800 psi; sets the oil quantity bug.

items.action: OUT, LIGHT OFF AT ABOUT 45% N2

items: **Number 2 engine** is normally started by the flight engineer, from their own switch and fuel lever, or left until the taxi (its start is then item 9 of the Before Takeoff checklist). In a scramble engines 2 and 3 may be started together.
Before starting the wing engines, the crew make sure nobody is in the intake danger area. Take care with No. 2's blast near buildings more than one storey high.

If the start switch pops out every time it is engaged, hold it. If N2 shows no rotation, release it. If the EGT does not rise within 25 seconds, fuel lever OFF, motor for 30 seconds, then release the switch.

Terminate the start (fuel lever OFF, motor 30 s) if the EGT exceeds 750 °C for more than 40 seconds, or rises rapidly past 750 °C and looks likely to exceed 900 °C, or if N2 hangs below idle. With no oil pressure (10 psi) by idle, fuel lever OFF. See [Limitations](limitations) for the start limits.

In the simulation the START switch is pulled out to engage and drops back in by itself at about 45% N2. With the Virtual Crew's flight engineer on, you start engines 3 and 1; the flight engineer asks whether to start No. 2 now or during the taxi, and starts it.

blocks.title: Engine start
rows: Engages the ENG START switch: its legend shows the start valve open.
Watches fuel flow and the EGT rise within 25 s.
Stops the clock. Checks a normal EGT rise and a peak within the start limits.
The START switch releases and its legend goes out.
N2 and N1 stabilized at ground idle; EGT and oil quantity and pressure normal.

items.action: PULL: LIGHT ON, START VALVE OPEN
POPS IN AT 45-52% N2: LIGHT OUT

items: If there is no N1 rotation 30 seconds after N2 reaches idle, shut the engine down.

If the start switch will not stay engaged, select the other ignition system and try again. If it releases before 45% and the engine decelerates, let N2 decay below 20% and hold the switch engaged until 45%.

In the simulation the MD-10's START switches are push-buttons that latch in and release themselves at cutout. The IGN A and IGN B buttons select the igniter system; the igniters fire only during a start (system A if neither is selected), and there is no automatic ignition after the start. The Virtual Crew's first officer, when on, starts all three engines and will not start one with a throttle off idle.

blocks.content: When conditions allow, the crew may start only the wing engines for the taxi and leave No. 2 until later, saving fuel and keeping the center engine's blast off the ramp. The decision is the captain's. Consider the weight, the taxiways' slopes and condition, the distance to the runway and the warm-up time: every engine runs at idle or taxi power for at least 3 minutes before takeoff. The captain does not call for the Before Takeoff checklist until all three engines are running.

blocks.title: A two-engine taxi is not authorized when (FedEx)
rows: Engine anti-ice is required for the taxi
Jet blast is a known concern on the ramps or taxiways
The taxiways are wet or contaminated
The visibility is low (below 1,200 ft RVR)

blocks.content: **Starting No. 2 during the taxi (FedEx's Delayed Engine Start checklist).** At the captain's call: ignition START A or B (F/O); fuel panel set, the aft pumps on and the crossfeeds closed (FE); No. 1 pack off (No. 3 may stay on for air conditioning) and the 1-2 isolation valve open (FE); start pressure 25 psi minimum, advancing No. 1 if more is needed (FE); start No. 2 with the normal procedure and callouts (F/O, FE); then 1-2 isolation valve NORM and ignition OFF. The second officer then checks No. 2's hydraulic pumps and generator, parallels the generators, and sets the normal pneumatic configuration, as in After Start.

**Starting No. 2 during the taxi.** The flight engineer starts it as item 9 of the Before Takeoff checklist: the ignition at START A or B and the pneumatic pressure adequate, then the normal start, and the ignition OFF afterwards.

Above 40% N1 and below 15 kt ground speed the engines form an inlet vortex that can lift debris off the ground into them. On two engines a heavy aircraft needs more thrust to move; keep it below that, or start the third engine.

With the Virtual Crew on, the delayed start is part of the run: the first officer (DC-10) or flight engineer (KC-10) asks at the No. 2 start whether to start it now; answer no and the item is passed. No. 2 is then started in the Before Takeoff checklist (DC-10: its first item, by the first officer; KC-10: item 9, by the flight engineer), and the APU is shut down once all three generators carry the buses.

The captain clears the ground crew off the interphone once the parking brake is set and the towbar is disconnected, and calls for the After Start checklist after the last engine's EGT has peaked. All three crewmembers do their flows; the first officer reads the checklist and calls it complete after the captain has answered "Checked" to the S/O panel. The second officer does their items silently and reports anything abnormal. If No. 2 is to be started later, the second officer does their items for the engines and systems that are running and the rest after the No. 2 start.

items: **Pitot heat, TAT.** The selector's TAT position monitors the ground sensing: the heaters are off on the ground and the meter reads zero; airborne, a current reading shows the heaters came on.

**Engine anti-ice.** On when icing conditions exist (TAT below 6 °C with visible moisture). On a long wait at ground idle in icing, run each engine up to 60% N1 for 30 seconds at least every 30 minutes, to shed fan ice. In the simulation the DC-10's three ENG anti-ice toggles do not move on screen although a click still sets them: confirm by the ENG ANTI-ICE lights (see [Ice and rain](ice-and-rain#simulation-notes)).

**Ground equipment cleared.** The first officer makes sure the captain has cleared the ground crew off the headset, the ground crew have cleared the aircraft, and the captain is on ground control's frequency before asking for taxi.
**S/O panel (CAPT).** The captain looks across: hydraulic switches up and their lights out, electrical lights out, aft pumps on and crossfeeds closed, only the expected annunciators lit.

**Hydraulic panel (FE).** Temperatures normal and quantities about as before start; rudder standby power ARM. All left pumps ON, their PRESS LO lights out; all right pumps OFF (their lights on), each system holding at least 2,800 psi on its left pump alone; right pumps back to AUTO; the 1-3 and 2-3 RMPs ARM. A pump that will not give 2,800 psi is an abnormal procedure.

**Electrical panel (FE).** CSD oil pressure lights out, CSD temperatures below the yellow band, GEN FAIL and GEN OFF out, the loads below the yellow band; each generator checked on the meter selector, which is then left on BAT & L EMER AC. APU GEN BUS switches OFF and external power off (and disconnected). Then push and release **PARALLEL GENS**: every AC BUS TIE ISOL light goes out as the three engine generators are paralleled on the tie bus. A light that stays on is the Generators Will Not Parallel checklist.

**APU (FE).** APU master switch OFF, then the APU/ISOL valve closed; the 1-2 and 1-3 ISOL VALVE DISAGREE lights cycle as the valves move. On the aircraft the APU runs on for 90 seconds with its air shut off, to cool, before it stops; in the simulation the shutdown begins at once.

**Pneumatic selectors and packs (FE).** All pneumatic lights out, temperatures and pressures normal. Each supply selector and pack to AUTO: the flow gauges normal and the PACK OFF lights stay out. Each supply then to OFF to see its manifold pressure fall, proving the supply valve closes, and back. FedEx's freighters then fly one pack: supplies 2 and 3 AUTO, the 1-2 isolation valve OPEN and pack 1 AUTO. With No. 2 not yet started, supply 1 AUTO and supply 2 OFF.

blocks.content: With the Virtual Crew on, the second officer's normal pneumatic configuration is all three supplies AUTO, both isolation valves NORM and all three packs AUTO, rather than FedEx's single pack.

The KC-10 has no After Start checklist. The flight engineer puts each engine's left hydraulic pump on as it starts (the last item of the starting checklist), and the electrical changeover, the APU shutdown and the pneumatic set-up follow in the Before Taxi and Before Takeoff checklists (see [Taxi and takeoff](normal-taxi-and-takeoff)). Until No. 2 runs, the APU stays on: its generator carries bus 2.

With all three engines running and stable, the first officer sets the anti-ice, changes the air system over from the APU to the engines and shuts the APU down; the captain coordinates the removal of the ground equipment and gear pins. The first officer reads the After Start checklist and then asks for the taxi clearance.

items.action: Push: ON legend out, OFF on
AUTO (MANUAL: check each L and R pump)

items: **APU.** After START/STOP is pushed, the APU on the aircraft runs a 90-second cooling cycle before it shuts down (in the simulation the shutdown begins at once). Its OFF legend stays lit until it has stopped and its door has closed. The engine generators have the buses by then.

**HYD panel (MANUAL only).** With the hydraulic controller in MANUAL: the aux pumps and RMPs off, each system's L pump off in turn (the R pump must hold the system on its own), then the L pumps back on. Back in AUTO each R pump returns to standby about 20 seconds after its system recovers (in the simulation the standby shows as an A on the HYD synoptic, not as an ARM legend on the panel).
**Courier report.** The courier compartment is ready for taxi. (No couriers are simulated; the item is passed.)
