The starters, start valves, igniters, light-off, acceleration and the starter cutout at 45% N2 are modeled, with the start air from the APU, an air cart or a running engine through the manifold. A start with too little air is slow and runs hot.

The START switches move the opposite way to the aircraft's (see [Engines](engines)). DC-10 and KC-10: in the simulation the switch is pulled out to engage and drops back in at cutout; on the aircraft it is pushed in and pops out, and the EFB's checklist step still says "Push". MD-10: in the simulation the switch is pushed in and pops back out at cutout; on the aircraft it is pulled out and pops in.
The simulator's auto-start (Ctrl+E) bypasses the start procedure: each engine is taken as running as the simulator lights it.

DC-10 and KC-10: the APU's speed rise for engine starting comes with any ignition position other than OFF while the APU/ISOL valve is open, and the START switches work whatever the ignition selector shows; on the aircraft only START A or B raises the APU speed and arms the switches.
The 3-minute warm-up and the cool-down before a shutdown are crew disciplines: nothing in the simulation enforces them.
No couriers or cabin crew report on the MD-10 freighter; the courier items are passed.

parts.title: Taxi and Takeoff
parts.summary: Before Taxi, the taxi, the Before Takeoff checklist, the takeoff roll and rotation, the initial climb and clean-up, and the After Takeoff checklist.

blocks.content:
From the moment the aircraft moves under its own power to the after-takeoff clean-up the workload is highest and the checklists most critical: a takeoff with the flaps, slats, spoilers or trim wrong is a takeoff the aircraft may not survive. The crew therefore configure for takeoff while taxiing, clear of the ramp, and check the configuration twice: once in the Before Takeoff checklist and once more, for the items that matter most, when cleared onto the runway.

The takeoff itself is flown to a profile: thrust and speed set by numbers computed before start, rotation to an attitude, a noise abatement climb at V2 + 10 kt to the acceleration height, and the flaps and slats retracted on schedule as the aircraft accelerates. Each pilot's job through it is fixed by the standard callouts (see [Callouts](normal-techniques#callouts)).

FedEx's card has no taxi checklist: the DC-10's Before Takeoff checklist is done during the taxi. The EFB adds the KC-10's Before Taxi, with the first officer's items given to the DC-10's first officer and the flight engineer's to the second officer, so that the anti-ice, hydraulics and air are confirmed and the ground equipment is gone before the aircraft moves.

items: **Anti-ice.** Engine anti-ice as the takeoff data was computed, the ENG ANTI-ICE DISAGREE lights out (in the simulation the DC-10's ENG anti-ice toggles do not move on screen although a click still sets them, so confirm by the lights; see [Ice and rain](ice-and-rain#simulation-notes)). Wing anti-ice is not used on the ground: its valves stay closed on the ground whatever the switch says.
**Hydraulic system.** The 1-3 and 2-3 RMPs armed, so that if an engine is lost on the takeoff its system is powered from system 3.
**Pneumatics and air conditioning.** The pneumatic lights out, temperatures and pressures normal.
**Taxi lights.** Landing lights extended but not on, the nose light at TAXI, the runway turnoff lights on.
**Ground equipment and gear pins.** Removed and the ground crew's signal acknowledged; the gear pins stowed aboard. (The captain asks for anything still at the aircraft to be removed: Ground Ops.)

blocks.content: With engines 1 and 3 running (No. 2 may be left for the taxi), the flight engineer reads Before Taxi.

items: **Windows (1).** Closed, the carriage roller against the track bumper, the lock-latch handle fully down and locked.

**Anti-ice (2).** Below 6 °C TAT with visible moisture in any form, or below 6 °C with a temperature-dewpoint spread of 3 °C or less, engine anti-ice goes on as soon as the engines are started and stays on until the icing conditions end. ENG 2 & ANT on before takeoff also arms the antenna anti-ice to come on at rotation. Wing anti-ice selected ON on the ground opens no valve; it arms the system to open in flight. On a long wait in icing, run each engine up to 60% N1 for 30 seconds every 30 minutes.
**Hydraulic system (3).** The 2-3 motor pump to ARM, the left pumps on and the right pumps in AUTO.
**Pneumatics and air conditioning (4).** The engine supplies back to AUTO and the packs off their start setting; lights out, temperatures and pressures normal.

**Ground equipment and gear pins (5).** The pilot has the ground crew remove the equipment and acknowledges their signal; the flight engineer makes sure the gear pins are removed and stowed (this may be done on the exterior inspection).

blocks.content: The MD-10 has no Before Taxi checklist: After Start ends with the ground equipment and gear pins removed, and the first officer then obtains the taxi clearance. The Taxi checklist is done as the aircraft taxis.

Before calling for taxi, the first officer makes sure the captain has cleared the ground crew off the headset, the ground crew have cleared the aircraft, and the captain is listening on the ground frequency. Both pilots keep the airport diagram out and follow the taxi route.

The aircraft is heavy and its pilots sit high and far ahead of the wheels: the nose gear is about 21 ft behind the pilots and the main gear about 93 ft. About 40% N1 is enough to break away; wait for the aircraft to respond before adding more. Do not exceed 40% N1 in congested areas, use the brakes intermittently and never ride them, and never use reverse thrust to slow down or back up. Turn speeds, turning technique and the two-engine taxi are in [Taxiing](normal-techniques#taxiing).

The second officer faces fully forward from the start of the taxi until 10,000 ft and watches the taxi route too.

**Cleared to configure.** Once clear of ramp congestion, the captain says "Cleared to configure": the first officer sets the flaps and slats, arms the spoilers, sets the trim and the autobrake, and the two pilots check the flight controls. The captain then calls for the Before Takeoff checklist, which the second officer reads to the line during the taxi. The captain does not call for it until all three engines are running.

The flight engineer reads the Before Takeoff checklist to item 19 during the taxi, starting No. 2 at item 9 if it was left. The pilot sets the flaps, the copilot the stabilizer trim. Items 20 to 25 wait for the takeoff clearance.

The pilots set the flaps and slats, arm the spoilers, check the flight controls on the CONFIG synoptic and set the stabilizer trim during the taxi; the first officer then reads the Taxi checklist and makes sure the clearance has been received.

blocks.title: Before takeoff flows
rows: Flaps and slats, spoiler, trim, autobrake, flight controls (elevator, ailerons)
Monitors on the surface position indicator
Pneumatic selectors and packs, wing anti-ice

items: **No. 2 engine, APU.** The EFB opens the checklist with a delayed No. 2's start (its ignition then back OFF) and, once all three generators carry the buses, the APU off.

**Flaps and slats.** The captain answers with the card's flap, the flap position indicator's reading and "T/O" for the slats at takeoff; the first officer checks. If the setting is 15 or 22° the fixed detent may be used; any other setting is made with the flap takeoff selector.

**Flight instruments.** No flags; the attitude indicators level with the aircraft; headings compared on every attitude indicator, HSI, RMI and the standby compass in the turns. One INS stays on its DATA page for the taxi and takeoff, showing the ground speed.

**Thrust computer.** T.O. (maximum thrust) or T.O. FLX (reduced), its limit within 0.5% of the card, with the anti-ice switches and pneumatic supply selectors set as the card assumed. FedEx uses reduced thrust whenever the performance allows. On the DC-10-30 the autothrottle is used for takeoff unless the captain says otherwise; it is never used for takeoff on a DC-10-10.

**Spoilers.** The AUTO SPOILER DO NOT USE light out, the handle raised to ARM and staying there; the second officer confirms. A handle that will not stay up, or the light on, is a matter for the MEL before departure: the ground spoilers could not be relied on to deploy by themselves in a reject.
**Trim.** Aileron and rudder trim zero; the stabilizer at the card's setting, inside the green band.

**Autobrake.** T.O. selected and the ARM-DISARM switch at ARM, the AUTOBRAKE and ABS lights out. T.O. arms only with the anti-skid armed, the spoilers armed and the flaps below 30°. In a rejected takeoff above 60 kt wheel speed the brakes then come on at full pressure as the ground spoilers deploy; between 45 and 60 kt they apply at the MIN rate, and below 45 kt nothing starts.

**Flight controls.** Both pilots move the ailerons; the captain the rudder (holding the steering tiller still); the first officer the elevator. Watch for full travel on the surface position indicator. Move the controls at a moderate rate, about 2 seconds from neutral to one stop, 4 to the other and 2 back for the elevator and ailerons, 1 and 1 for the rudder: on the ground the surfaces move faster than any air load would let them in flight. The aileron check is valid only once the flaps and slats are out, because the outboard ailerons are locked out with the flaps up.

**Fuel panel (silent).** Within lateral limits, the crossfeeds closed, the aft pumps on, the lights out. With more than 40,000 lb in tank 2, its transfer pump on and the No. 1 and No. 3 fill valves open, so that tank 2 feeds the wing tanks and the wing tanks stay full for structural relief.
**Aux hyd pumps.** Off (their ON lights out).
**Ignition (below the line).** OFF, or CONT A or CONT B in severe turbulence or heavy rain.
**Radar, transponder.** On; the radar set to a useful range and tilt for the departure. Transponder 1 with the captain flying, 2 with the first officer.

**Flight guidance.** The flight directors in the takeoff mode: TOGA pushed on the ground, TAKEOFF in both the roll and pitch windows, and ALT armed with the departure altitude set. For a vertical speed takeoff, TOGA and the altitude armed, then once on the runway heading the vertical speed wheel to about 2,500 to 3,500 ft/min: HDG HOLD and VERT SPD in the FMA. Call "Flight guidance" only once lined up.
**Lights.** On for the runway: landing lights on, the nose light at its landing position, high intensity (strobe) lights on.

**Pneumatic selectors and packs (silent).** As the takeoff data was computed. A packs-on takeoff is flown only when the data was computed for it (the data holds for one, two or three packs), normally in FedEx's single-pack configuration: supplies 2 and 3 AUTO, the 1-2 isolation valve open, pack 1 AUTO. Otherwise the packs are off, so that no engine gives up bleed air to them during the takeoff. With wing anti-ice needed for the takeoff, the supplies stay on and only the packs go off.
**S/O panel (silent).** Scanned before 80 kt: every system normal.

blocks.content: Never take off with ALT HOLD engaged: the flight director's pitch bars would command a return to the takeoff altitude. When the speeds are limited by VMCG and reduced thrust is used, do not use the takeoff mode (its V2 guidance would be too slow); fly the vertical speed takeoff the card calls for.

items: **Flaps/slats (1).** The flap handle into its detent: SLAT TAKEOFF light on, SLAT DISAGREE out, the flap tapes at the preselected degrees. The takeoff warning does not warn of flaps left at zero. If DISAGREE comes on with TAKEOFF out, recycle the handle.

**Flight controls (2).** The copilot rolls the wheel full left and right (full wing deflection on the indicator, the spoilers fully up on the down-going wing) and the column full forward and aft; the pilot, holding the nose steering wheel still, the rudder pedals full left and right.
**Trim (3).** The copilot sets the stabilizer; all three check the stabilizer, aileron and rudder trim indicators.
**Spoilers (4).** The AUTO SPOILER DO NOT USE light out, then ARM. A light that is lit, or that has lit at any point, means the automatic spoilers stay unarmed and are deployed by hand in a reject.
**Thrust computer (7).** The mode for the takeoff; for T.O. FLX the assumed temperature set (with engine anti-ice, the temperature that gives the reduced N1 for that case).
**Number 2 engine (9).** Started now if it was not started earlier; ignition OFF afterwards.
**Hydraulic system (10).** Temperatures and quantities normal; RUDDER STBY PWR at ARM; the motor pumps 2-3 and 1-3 to ARM; the PUMP VALVE OPEN and AUX HYD PUMP ON lights out.

**Electrical system (11).** CSD and generator lights out and loads normal; external power off; one amber AC BUS TIE ISOL light out; push PARALLEL GENS and all go out. The generators cannot be paralleled with external power on the tie bus, an APU generator on any generator bus, or a bus tie switch at ISOL.

**APU (12).** If not required: the APU GEN BUS switches off, the APU/ISOL valve closed and the master switch OFF. On the aircraft the APU runs on for 90 seconds to cool; in the simulation it begins its shutdown at once.

**MANFLD FAIL/Supply Lockout (13).** Both supplies AUTO, the APU/ISOL valve closed, the isolation valves NORM; each system's MANFLD FAIL light pressed: the light on and the system's pressure decays and stays at zero after release, then the selector to OFF and back to AUTO restores it. This proves the supply valve shuts on a manifold failure.
**Fuel systems (16).** Normal usage on the counters; the crossfeed DISAGREE and flow lights out; the aft pumps' flow lights on.

**FGS/ALT preselect (17).** TO/GA pushed: TAKEOFF in the roll and pitch FMAs. The departure altitude set and armed. Bank angle 15°. A power transient during the start can reset the flight guidance to HDG HOLD and ALT HOLD, which is why TO/GA is pressed now.
**Brake temperatures (18).** OVHT and DIFF TEMP lights out, the gauge below the maximum for a takeoff from the brake cooling chart (400 °C or more is the abnormal brake procedure).

**Pneumatic system (20).** When cleared for takeoff: for a normal takeoff both supplies AUTO and both packs on. For a bleeds-off takeoff both supplies OFF (no wing anti-ice is then available). With wing anti-ice needed, packs OFF, supplies on and wing anti-ice ON; the thrust computer is not usable then and the autothrottle is not used, and the takeoff N1 comes from the charts. The APU/ISOL valve closed unless the APU is to run the packs.

**Radar, IFF/ETCAS, lights (21 to 23).** Radar to the desired mode; ETCAS TA+RA on the CDU's TCAS page, with the IFF on (TA only when operating close to other aircraft on purpose); high intensity and landing lights as required, the strobes off at night in cloud.
**Annunciator panels (24).** Checked. A REV U/L or REV PRESS light for engine 1 or 3, or one that does not work, grounds the aircraft until the reverser is fixed or locked out.

blocks.content: For takeoff, go-around or maximum continuous thrust, do not take more than one pack, both wing anti-ice systems and the lavatory and galley vent from any one engine's pneumatic supply.

**Taxi procedure.** FLAP T.O. SEL checked and the FLAP/SLAT handle to the takeoff setting, the flaps and slats checked on the PFD; spoilers armed; the flight controls checked on the CONFIG synoptic (the green aileron, spoiler, elevator and rudder boxes must show full deflection, the nosewheel steering held still for the rudder); the stabilizer trim set for takeoff; the runway and V-speeds confirmed and the acceleration and thrust reduction altitudes checked on the FMS TAKEOFF page; the PF's takeoff and departure briefing. Any flight control check that does not show the right green boxes needs maintenance.

**Before takeoff procedure.** The first officer obtains the takeoff clearance. Both pilots review the EAD for alerts, reminders and the green box before taking the runway. Then the lights for the runway, the radar and transponder, and the air system for the takeoff.

items.action: XPDR (the book's TCAS position; no TCAS is simulated)
Packs-on: PACKs and BLEEDs ON. Packs-off: PACKs and BLEEDs OFF

items: **Packs-off takeoff.** Push the operating PACK and BLEED AIR switches so their OFF legends light. On the aircraft the thrust is advanced within 20 seconds, before the AIR SYSTEM OFF alerts come up; in the simulation the AIR SYS OFF alerts appear as soon as the bleeds are off. If wing anti-ice is needed, take off with the bleeds on and the packs off.
**Autobrake.** Not installed in the simulated MD-10.

blocks.content: Every engine must have run at idle or taxi power for at least 3 minutes. Static and rolling takeoffs are both permitted; the rolling takeoff is recommended, because it gets the engines to takeoff thrust while the aircraft is already moving, so the wing engines are less exposed to debris and crosswind. Line up on the centerline (offset just enough not to roll on the centerline lights) using the nose steering, then steer with the rudder pedals and move the left hand to the control wheel. Hold the column slightly forward of neutral during the roll to keep the nosewheel firmly on the runway.

Set the computed takeoff thrust before 80 kt. After 80 kt do not adjust the throttles except to prevent exceeding an engine limit. Engines that do not reach the computed takeoff N1 are unacceptable for flight.

**Captain flying.** The captain completes the Before Takeoff checklist while taxiing into position, then smoothly advances the throttles to about takeoff power and calls "Set standard power" (or "Set maximum power"). The first officer follows the throttles and sets each N1 exactly, finishing before 80 kt, and calls "Standard power set". The second officer watches the engine instruments and the annunciators through the roll and the initial climb. The captain keeps a hand on the throttles until V1, ready to reject.

**First officer flying.** When cleared, the captain lines up and says "You have the airplane"; the first officer takes control ("I have the airplane") and calls for the power. The captain sets the thrust, keeps a hand on the throttles until V1 (the decision to reject is still the captain's, and the captain takes control to do it), and calls "Power set".

**With the autothrottle (DC-10-30, -40).** With the flight director in the takeoff mode, advance the throttles to about takeoff power, move both ATS levers ON (or push N1 if they are already on): the FMA shows N1 and the throttles drive to the thrust computer's limit. Do not push the throttles past the target, or the autothrottle will pull them back. At 80 kt the FMA changes from N1 to **CLAMP** and the throttles stay where they are. If it does not, the PM calls "No clamp" and the PF pushes the ATS disengage button twice and flies the takeoff on manual throttles. The DC-10-10 and -15 have no autothrottle servo brake, so their throttles are not held at 80 kt even if CLAMP shows; FedEx never uses the autothrottle for takeoff on the -10.

The CF6 shows a thermal **N1 bloom**: once takeoff thrust is set, N1 rises 1 to 2% through the roll with the EGT, and falls back after lift-off as the engine's temperatures settle. That is the engine, not a throttle creeping: do not pull the throttles back after 80 kt to regain the initial setting, because that reduces the thrust the performance assumed. If an EGT approaches the acceleration limit, the second officer says "Engine ___ approaching overtemp, adjusting throttle" and trims it back; the captain can overrule the second officer if the thrust is needed.

**Rotation.** At VR (the PF watches their own airspeed; the PM calls "Rotate"), bring the column back to neutral and rotate smoothly at 2.5 to 3° per second to about 15°, taking about six seconds. Lift-off comes at about 10° pitch, depending on the weight. Hold the initial attitude until the pitch bars come alive, then follow them without chasing the speed: the attitude gives about V2 + 10 kt on three engines (V2 on two), and with the trim set right the column force at V2 + 10 is about zero. The gear comes up when a positive rate of climb has been seen and called, not at a speed. A rapid or early rotation can strike the tail before the wing has built the lift to climb; a slow one uses runway. Using CWS for the takeoff is not a FedEx procedure.

If the takeoff warning horn sounds as the throttles are advanced, reject the takeoff unless the captain judges that continuing is safer. The horn sounds with throttle 1 or 2 near takeoff thrust when the flaps are in the landing range, the slats are not at takeoff, the spoiler handle is out of RET, the stabilizer is outside the green band, or the parking brake is set (a parking brake input that only some aircraft had; every DC-10 in the simulation has it).

blocks.title: Takeoff duties
rows: Releases the brakes, advances the throttles to about flight idle (40 to 45% N1) so the engines spool up together, then commands "Set takeoff power". Keeps a hand on the throttles until V1.
Monitors the engine instruments as the throttles come up. With the autothrottle to be used and the flight director in takeoff mode, moves both ATS levers ON: N1 in the ATS FMA.
On command sets takeoff power to the target N1 and monitors the engines. Starts the clock.
Keeps straight with the rudder pedals; cross-checks the airspeed.
Monitors the controls and the airspeed. Calls "80 knots", "V1", "Rotate" and "V2".
Scans the engine instruments continuously; adjusts the throttles before 80 kt; calls "Power set".
At VR rotates smoothly, taking about 4 seconds, to the attitude that holds V2 + 10 (all engines) or V2 (two engines), or to center the flight director's bars. The takeoff mode commands at most 22°.
Watches the engines and the winds on CDU 3; reports a wind change of 10 kt or more along the runway or a sudden shift of 20° or more.
Confirms lift-off and a positive climb on the TVSI, radio altimeter and altimeter: "Gear up."
Confirms the positive climb: "Positive rate of climb, gear up", and raises the gear.
Watches the gear lights go out, then disarms the spoilers.

items: Flight idle by the end of the line-up distance makes sure the computed takeoff performance is achieved.

If the takeoff warning horn sounds as the throttles come up, stop: check the flaps and slats in the takeoff range, the trim in the takeoff band, the spoiler handle in RET and the parking brake released.
Some loss of oil quantity at takeoff thrust is normal; it comes back as the thrust is reduced.
After lift-off with TAKEOFF in the pitch FMA and CLAMP in the ATS, do not pull the speed knob: the autothrottle would drive to the thrust computer's N1 and could overspeed the engines.

blocks.title: Takeoff
rows: Sets the throttles to about 70% N1, checks the thrust symmetrical, calls "Auto flight"; checks the autothrottles advance to T/O thrust: "Check thrust." Keeps a hand on the throttles until V1.
Pushes AUTO FLIGHT: "Auto flight." Checks T/O THRUST in the FMA's altitude window, the throttles advancing to the right N1; fine-tunes as needed: "Thrust set."
Checks the airspeed and T/O CLAMP in the FMA.
Checks T/O CLAMP: "80 knots." (If the throttles do not clamp: "No clamp"; the PF disengages the autothrottle and continues on manual throttles.)
Checks the speed and puts both hands on the control wheel.
Rotates at about 3° per second to reach V2 + 10 at 35 ft; normally no more than 22° nose up.
Checks the positive rate, raises the gear: "Gear up."

blocks.content: On the ground the AUTO FLIGHT switch engages the autothrottles only; the flight director's takeoff mode is already engaged with a director on and V2 confirmed on the FMS TAKEOFF page.

The standard departure is a noise abatement climb: takeoff thrust at V2 + 10 kt to 1,500 ft above the runway, climb thrust from there to 3,000 ft, then acceleration and the flap and slat retraction. Below the minimum maneuvering speed for the configuration the bank is limited to 15°; to bank more, keep the takeoff flaps until at that speed (if the flap retraction speed is 165 kt and the slat retraction speed 200 kt, hold the flaps until 200 kt for a turn beyond 15°). Do not turn below 400 ft above the runway unless a departure procedure or ATC requires it. The autopilot may be engaged from 500 ft (MD-10: 200 ft, or 400 ft with NAV armed).

blocks.alt: Side-view profile diagram of a DC-10/KC-10 noise abatement takeoff and climb, not to scale. Ground roll with callouts 80 kt, V1, Rotate; rotation to about 15°, positive rate, gear up; climb at V2 + 10 to 1,500 ft AGL: climb thrust (TRC CL, ATS N1); 3,000 ft AGL: vertical speed about 1,000 ft/min, accelerate, flaps up at the flap retraction speed (0/EXT), slats retract at the slat retraction speed (UP/RET), After Takeoff checklist, bank limit unlimited (25°), IAS HOLD at 250 kt or the clean minimum maneuvering speed; 10,000 ft MSL: landing lights off and retracted, accelerate to climb speed (DC-10-10 330 kt, DC-10-30 355 kt); 18,000 ft or the transition altitude: altimeters 29.92, turnoff lights off; crossover to Mach 0.83 around FL240-FL290. Configuration bars along the bottom: flaps T/O, 0/EXT, UP/RET; thrust T/O, CL. Labels legible.
blocks.title: Takeoff and climb profile, DC-10 and KC-10

blocks.alt: Side-view profile diagram of an MD-10 normal takeoff (ICAO A), not to scale, with numbered points: 1 aligned, throttles to 70% N1, AUTO FLIGHT, T/O THRUST; 2 80 kt T/O CLAMP; 3 V1; 4 VR, rotate about 3°/s to V2 + 10 at 35 ft; 5 positive rate, gear up; 6 200 ft (400 ft with NAV armed) AUTO FLIGHT engages the autopilot; 7 1,500 ft LEVEL CHANGE (or PROF above 400 ft), CLB THRUST; 8 acceleration altitude 3,000 ft, accelerate to VCL; 9 flaps up (0/EXT) at VFR; 10 slats retract (UP/RET) at VSR. FMA legends T/O CLAMP, T/O THRUST, CLB THRUST shown at the transitions. Labels legible.
blocks.title: Normal takeoff profile, MD-10

items: Climb at V2 + 10 kt (the initial climb attitude is usually 15 to 22°). Look through the pitch bars rather than at them, and keep the airspeed indicator as the primary speed reference.

**1,500 ft AGL.** The PF calls "Climb power". The PM selects CL on the thrust rating computer, engages the autothrottle if it was not engaged for takeoff and pushes N1. Continue at V2 + 10 to 3,000 ft. After a packs-off takeoff the second officer brings the supplies and one pack back on after the thrust reduction, letting the engines settle for 3 or 4 seconds first.

**3,000 ft AGL.** Set the vertical speed wheel to about 1,000 ft/min and accelerate. At the flap retraction speed (the card's FR): "Flaps up" (the PM sets 0/EXT). At the slat retraction speed (SR): "Slats retract, After Takeoff checklist" (the PM sets UP/RET). Accelerate to 250 kt or the clean minimum maneuvering speed, whichever is higher; "Unlimit bank" (bank angle selector to 25°) and "IAS hold". If a level-off comes before 3,000 ft, retract on schedule at the level-off.

Engage the autopilot (the PF's own) in CMD or CWS when wanted, above 500 ft. With the takeoff mode used, the autopilot comes in with VERT SPD in the pitch window: check the FMA and the vertical speed it holds, which may be more than the aircraft can sustain while accelerating.
**10,000 ft.** Landing lights off and retracted; vertical speed 500 to 1,000 ft/min and accelerate to the climb speed (see [Climb](normal-climb-and-cruise#climb)).

blocks.content:
**Close-in turns.** When a turn is needed soon after takeoff: IAS HOLD, unlimit the bank and HDG SEL; keep V2 + 10 and the takeoff flaps through the turn; then limit the bank again and continue the normal profile.

**Cancelling the takeoff mode.** Push IAS (the bars hold the present speed), roll the vertical speed wheel (VERT SPD), or engage an autopilot in CMD (VERT SPD or ALT HOLD, as the wheel stands). In each case the roll mode goes to HDG HOLD, or stays in HDG SEL if that was selected.

blocks.title: After takeoff duties
rows: 1,500 ft AGL (obstacles permitting): asks for climb thrust.
Pushes CL on the thrust computer; the N1 limit and the max limit indexes agree.
Sets climb power and pressurizes: ENG PNEU SUPPLY selectors AUTO, the PACK selectors to AUTO one at a time, flows normal and PACK OFF lights out.
3,000 ft AGL or clear of obstacles: rolls the vertical speed wheel to about 1,000 ft/min (500 ft/min heavy or hot) to accelerate.
At the flap retraction speed: "Flaps up."
Checks the indications; FLAP/SLAT handle to 0: the flap tapes move up symmetrically.
At the slat retraction speed: "Slats retract."
FLAP/SLAT handle to UP/RET: slat TAKEOFF light out.
Turns the FLAP T.O. selector to the 0° stop.
Holds the retraction attitude to 250 kt or the clean minimum maneuvering speed; "IAS hold" at the climb speed; bank angle 25°.
Pushes IAS (MACH at the crossover); sets the climb speed in the SPD window; ATS levers ON as desired; altitude preselect set and armed.
Sets climb thrust if the autothrottle is not used; seat belt switch and exterior lights set; completes the After Takeoff/Climb checklist.

blocks.content: Where noise abatement is not a factor, the minimum height for accelerating is 800 ft above the runway with three engines, 400 ft with one inoperative, or higher if an obstacle demands it. Manually rolling the vertical speed wheel, or engaging any other pitch mode, ends the flight director's takeoff mode.

Engaging the autothrottle straight after takeoff with the thrust computer still in T.O. can overboost the engines as the bleed configuration changes. It does not happen in GA. Failure of the autothrottle's servo can advance the throttles uncommanded: watch the throttles whenever the autothrottle is engaged.

blocks.title: Initial climb
rows: Continues to V2 + 10, or the maximum pitch of 25°.
At or above 200 ft (400 ft with NAV armed): "Auto flight." The autopilot engages in the existing speed, roll and pitch modes.
Pushes AUTO FLIGHT: "Auto flight" when engaged.

Below the CLB THRUST altitude, selects PROF or LEVEL CHANGE (both available above 400 ft): T/O CLAMP becomes T/O THRUST and the thrust will reduce automatically at the CLB THRUST altitude. PROF also engages FMS speed and accelerates on the FMS schedule; LEVEL CHANGE needs the speed selected at the acceleration altitude.
At or above the acceleration altitude and the flap retraction speed: "Flaps up."
Confirms the speed, FLAP/SLAT handle to 0/EXT: "Flaps up."
At or above VSR and accelerating: "Slats retract." (Delayed in a sustained turn or in moderate turbulence.)
Confirms the speed, handle to UP/RET: "Slats retract." Disarms the spoilers; FLAP T.O. SEL back to 0.
After a packs-off takeoff: BLEED AIR 1, 2, 3 on, then the PACKs on. Checks the EAD for alerts. Does the After Takeoff checklist down to the line.

blocks.content: The FMS defaults the acceleration altitude to 3,000 ft above the airport (or the initial level-off) and the CLB THRUST altitude to the thrust reduction height on the TAKEOFF page; check both in the taxi.

The second officer reads After Takeoff silently, checks each action has been done, and announces "After Takeoff checklist complete" once the items below the line are done too. The items above the line follow the flap and slat retraction; those below the line are done passing the transition altitude (18,000 ft in the United States) or at 18,000 ft.

items: **Flap T/O selector.** Rolled forward past 0 to its mechanical stop, so that the movable detent cannot catch the handle on the approach.
**Auto brakes.** OFF (and disarmed).
**Hydraulic panel.** Temperatures, pressures and quantities normal, the lights out.

**Cabin press and temp.** With the packs on for takeoff, the cabin altitude and rate on schedule and the differential pressure rising. After a packs-off takeoff, the second officer starts the pressurization after the thrust reduction at 1,500 ft: the normal pneumatic configuration, the PACK OFF lights going out after a short delay. In AUTO the controller holds the cabin where it is until the aircraft is 5,000 ft above it, then follows its schedule.
**Turnoff lights, seat belt sign (below the line).** Off at 18,000 ft, the seat belt sign left on if the weather calls for it.
**Ignition (below the line).** OFF, or CONT A or B.

blocks.content: After an engine failure on takeoff, do not turn the pneumatic supplies and packs back on until the second phase of the engine failure checklist is being done.

The flight engineer starts the After Takeoff/Climb checklist after the first power reduction, reads it silently, confirms each action and tells the pilot when it is complete. If a landing is to follow at once, the Downwind checklist replaces After Takeoff/Climb, Descent and Approach (see [Local pattern](normal-landing#local-pattern)).

items.item: 8. Boom Operator/Exterior Lights & Seat Belt Sw

items: **Landing gear (1).** Up, the lights out. During retraction system 3's pressure may dip below 2,000 psi for a moment and its PRESS LO lights flash.
**Thrust computer (2).** Set as required; the N1 max limit knobs at AUTO, the limit indexes agreeing with the computer.
**Pressurization (4).** After a bleeds-off takeoff, the supplies to AUTO one at a time; otherwise check the aircraft is pressurizing normally.
**Spoilers (5).** Pushed down to DISARMED with the flat of the hand.
**Flaps/slats (6).** UP/RET: no flap tape or disagree flag in view, the slat DISAGREE and TAKEOFF lights out.
**Flap takeoff selector (7).** To the 0° stop, if it was used for the takeoff flap.

**Boom operator, exterior lights and seat belt switch (8).** Above 10,000 ft MSL tell the boom operator; landing lights retracted and off, the other exterior lights as required; once the boom operator has inspected the cargo, the seat belt switch off with the commander's agreement. In the simulation this is the Passing 10,000 ft Climb checklist.

blocks.content: After Takeoff is the MD-10's one silent checklist: the PM does it to the line after the clean-up, and finishes it at 10,000 ft or the transition altitude, announcing "After Takeoff checklist complete". Items marked ** are also done downwind between approaches in the pattern.

items: **AIR panel.** Bleeds and packs on (after a packs-off takeoff, bleeds first).
**HYD panel (MANUAL only).** The 1-3 and 2-3 RMPs off.

**FUEL panel (MANUAL only).** Series 10: tank 2's transfer pump on and the 1 and 3 fill valves armed, until tank 2 equals tanks 1 and 3. Series 30: the auxiliary tanks' transfer pumps on and the fill valves armed until the AUX UPR PUMPS LO alert, then tank 2 as on the Series 10. In AUTO the fuel system controller does this itself. The simulated MD-10-30 has no auxiliary tank buttons: its controller always moves the auxiliary fuel.

**Seat belts, exterior lights, altimeter (below the line).** At 10,000 ft the PM sets the seat belt sign as required, retracts the landing lights, turns the nose light off and the wing and runway turnoff lights off; both pilots set standard at the transition altitude (pull the BAROSET knob).

The automatic brake system is fitted to every DC-10 in the simulation (FedEx's card allows for aircraft without it). The KC-10 and the simulated MD-10 have none: their Auto Brake items are answered "Not Installed".
Wing anti-ice valves stay closed on the ground whatever the switch says; the switch selected on before takeoff lets them open once the nose gear strut extends at rotation.

The automatic ground spoilers and the autobrake start only at 45 kt of wheel speed or more, so spoilers deployed during a taxi never start the brakes; a rejected takeoff gets full autobrake pressure only above 60 kt.

The thrust rating computer's T.O. FLX mode works on the DC-10-15, -30 and KC-10, from the assumed temperature on the thumbwheels; the DC-10-10 has no flex mode, and the -40 rates in EPR, its limit bugs following the computer. The MD-10's FMS accepts a FLEX temperature but its flight control computers still set full takeoff thrust.

With the Virtual Crew on, the first officer (KC-10 copilot) checks the flaps and trim you set rather than setting them, calls "Positive rate. Gear up." at 50 ft with a climb, and watches for the flaps and slats to come up on your schedule; the flight engineer does the packs and pneumatics for the takeoff as the Performance app's card was computed (its AC box OFF meaning a packs-off takeoff).

parts.title: Climb and Cruise
parts.summary: The climb speed schedule and technique, passing 10,000 ft and the transition altitude, level-off, and the cruise: the flight engineer's fuel, CG and systems duties, and the MD-10's monitoring.

blocks.content: Once clean, the aircraft climbs on a speed schedule to its cruise level, and the workload drops to monitoring. That is when the flight engineer's work is most visible: the engineer manages the fuel, holds the center of gravity, watches every system, keeps the engines within limits and answers the pilots' questions about fuel, weight and altitude. On the MD-10 the systems controllers do that work and the pilots supervise them through the Engine and Alert Display and the System Display.

Below 10,000 ft climb at 250 KIAS, or the clean minimum maneuvering speed if that is higher (a heavy aircraft may need more than 250 kt clean; ATC is told). At 10,000 ft accelerate to the climb speed, hold it to the Mach crossover, then climb at the climb Mach. The best rate of climb and the best angle are at lower speeds; use them when they are needed and the standard schedule otherwise.

blocks.title: Climb speeds above 10,000 ft
rows: FMS climb speed (VCL) and Mach, in PROF

blocks.content: The DC-10 figures are FedEx's, who flew the -10 and -30 only; for the -15 and -40 use the -30's as a guide. The KC-10 figures are its performance manual's. The performance app and [Performance and mission planning](mission-planning) are the authority for a particular climb. In turbulence, fly the rough air speed in [Adverse weather](adverse-weather).

The usual climb uses the autothrottle in **N1** against the thrust computer's CL limit (EPR on the DC-10-40), and the autopilot in **IAS HOLD**, so that the thrust is fixed and the pitch holds the speed. At the crossover (FL240 to FL290 on the standard schedule) push **MACH**: MACH HOLD. If the climb Mach is above the planned cruise Mach, keep climbing at it and slow down after the level-off. At high altitude the hold modes can hunt in pitch; the vertical speed wheel, used with an eye on the speed, is the alternative.

items: **Altitude changes of more than 2,000 ft.** Set and arm the new altitude, select CL on the thrust computer, autothrottle in N1, and use the vertical speed wheel to reach the climb speed and attitude; then IAS HOLD or MACH HOLD.

**Altitude changes of 2,000 ft or less.** Set and arm the altitude, autothrottle in SPD, and about 1,500 ft/min on the vertical speed wheel. The speed stays constant within what the autothrottle can give under the thrust computer's limit.

**Altitude alerting.** Set and arm every cleared altitude before leaving the present one. The pilot who did not set it confirms ALT in the ARM window and says the altitude aloud ("230, set and armed"). With the autopilot engaged the PF sets it; hand flying, the PM. The PM calls 1,000 ft before the level-off ("230 for 240").

**Engine monitoring (FE).** N1, EGT and N2 at least every 5,000 ft in the climb, the fuel flows normal for the phase. The PF keeps the N1s matched. If any gauge goes past its limit mark, adjust that throttle; the autothrottle lets one throttle be held back and keeps it there relative to the others.
**Passing 10,000 ft.** Landing lights off and retracted, the nose light off, the seat belt sign as required (the Passing 10,000 ft Climb checklist, below).

**18,000 ft or the transition altitude.** The runway turnoff lights off, the altimeters to 29.92 in (1013 hPa) and cross-checked, the seat belt sign off if the ride allows. One INS on its DATA page (on the KC-10, a CDU) shows the wind through the climb, which tells whether the flight plan's winds are right and whether a different level would be better.
**Cruise data (FE).** No later than 1,000 ft below the cruise level, the flight engineer works out the expected cruise thrust (N1, or EPR) for the initial cruise.

blocks.content: In VERT SPD the autopilot holds the rate whatever happens to the speed. With the speed knob and the vertical speed wheel both in use, it is possible to command a climb rate the thrust cannot sustain: the speed bleeds away and the aircraft can stall. The autothrottle gives no warning when the thrust limit stops it. Watch the airspeed whenever the climb is in VERT SPD.

Do not use the autopilot in climbs above 4,000 ft/min or descents above 8,000 ft/min (FedEx gives the same figures as the limits for engaging it). The KC-10 manual warns that the vertical speed wheel locks beyond those rates and no other pitch mode can then be selected; in the simulation they are simply the wheel's end stops. Any manual operation of the longitudinal trim with an autopilot in CMD drops the autopilot lever to OFF.

**Level-off.** Before the cruise level, with the autothrottle in N1 and the autopilot in IAS HOLD, MACH HOLD or VERT SPD and the cruise level armed: as ALT CAP is annunciated, set the speed bug to the cruise speed as an indicated airspeed (for Mach 0.82 at FL350, about 280 kt) and select SPD on the autothrottle, then push CR on the thrust rating computer for the cruise limit (the DC-10-40's computer has no CR mode: see [Thrust rating computer](engines#thrust-rating-computer)). If the climb speed is the cruise speed, do it early enough not to overshoot. At level-off, compare the aircraft's performance with the plan.

The MD-10 normally climbs in **PROF** with FMS speed: the flight management system flies its climb speed schedule (250 kt below 10,000 ft, then VCL and the climb Mach) against the CLB thrust limit, and levels at the FCP altitude. LEVEL CHANGE with a selected speed does the same with the crew choosing the speed. At 10,000 ft the PF checks the acceleration to the en route climb speed; the PM sets the seat belt sign, retracts the landing lights, turns the nose light off and the wing and runway turnoff lights off. Both pilots set standard at the transition altitude by pulling the BAROSET knob, and the PM completes the After Takeoff checklist.

Altitude clearances are set in the FCP altitude window by the PF when the autopilot is engaged, by the PM at the PF's direction when hand flying. Any MCDU entry that changes the vertical profile is confirmed by both pilots before it is inserted (*INSERT). See [Automatic flight](automatic-flight) for the vertical modes.
The cards leave the 10,000 ft items to the climb profile; the EFB gives them a silent checklist of their own. On the DC-10 and KC-10 they are the flight engineer's; on the MD-10, the PM's.

The landing lights are switched off and retracted to stop their drag and noise; the nose light off; the seat belt sign off if the ride allows. With the Virtual Crew on, the second officer does this as the aircraft climbs through 10,000 ft.

The -1 puts these items in the After Takeoff/Climb checklist: above 10,000 ft MSL tell the boom operator, landing lights to RET and OFF, the other exterior lights as required, and, after the boom operator's cargo inspection and with the commander's agreement, the seat belt switch off.
The landing lights to RET, the nose light OFF, the WING & RUNWAY TURNOFF lights off (on the MD-10 each wing light follows its runway turnoff switch), and the seat belt sign as required.

Cruise at the planned Mach (long-range cruise from the placard for the weight, or the flight plan's Mach) and the planned level. Use the autothrottle: it holds the speed with predictable fuel burn, though in light chop the throttles hunt; if they hunt by more than about 3% N1, fly the throttles by hand. Step up as the weight comes off and the optimum altitude rises, unless the wind at the lower level is worth more than the range lost by staying low.

items: Monitor the FMA at every mode change, and the autopilot's tracking. If the autopilot does anything you are unsure of, disengage it, stabilize, retrim, and re-engage the other one if wanted.

Engine and wing anti-ice are used whenever icing conditions exist or are expected: TAT below 6 °C with visible moisture in any form. The higher the temperature up to 6 °C, the worse the icing tends to be; below -20 °C it is usually light, but heavy icing has been met far colder. When in doubt, turn the ice protection on (see [Ice and rain](ice-and-rain#op-in-flight)).
Cross-check the navigation: the long-range navigation system against the radio aids whenever they are in range.

blocks.content: In the simulation the DC-10's three ENG anti-ice toggles do not move on screen although a click still sets them: confirm by the ENG ANTI-ICE lights (see [Ice and rain](ice-and-rain#simulation-notes)).

children.title: The flight engineer in the cruise

blocks.content: The flight engineer's cruise work is a continuous scan of their panel plus a set of tasks the scan triggers. The scan follows the climb information of the KC-10 manual, which is the same panel the DC-10's second officer works: engines, hydraulics, electrical and APU, fuel, pneumatics and air conditioning, oxygen and pressurization, the annunciators and the fire detection lights. Anything outside its normal range is reported to the captain and, where there is one, handled with the abnormal checklist.

blocks.title: The flight engineer's cruise scan
rows: N1, EGT, N2 matched and within limits; oil quantity, temperature and pressure normal; fuel flows consistent with each other

One engine's EGT or fuel flow stands out from the others at the same N1. Engine vibration (KC-10 figures) above 5.0 units at the N1 frequency on either pickup, above 6.0 at the aft pickup's N2 frequency below 80% N2 or 4.0 above it, or a jump of more than 2 units on the trend: write it up and watch it
Temperatures between about 0 and 60 °C, pressures and quantities normal, the TEMP HI and PRESS LO lights out
A temperature above 60 °C: write it up
VOLT/AMP/FREQ selector on BAT & L EMER AC; DC volts in the green band, the battery amps at zero or an occasional pulse of charge; the AC loads balanced and below the yellow band
A DC TIE or X-TIE CLOSED light with its switch at OPEN: buses running paralleled, write it up, no change to procedure
Quantities falling as planned; tanks 1 and 3 about equal; fuel used agreeing with the quantity gone; fuel pressures normal
Tanks 1 and 3 approaching the lateral balance limit; a fuel used readout that disagrees with the others or with the quantities; a FILL VALVE OPEN light that stays on
Duct temperatures and pressures normal, the compartment temperatures as wanted
A compartment not holding its temperature: adjust its selector. Flying on one pack: AVIONIC FLOW to OVRD
Oxygen quantity normal; cabin altitude and rate on schedule; differential pressure not above the normal range mark
The cabin not holding its schedule with the outflow valve fully closed, during the initial pressurization: descend and depressurize unless the mission demands otherwise
Every FE annunciator out; every fire detector light out
A detector loop light without a fire warning: the abnormal procedure

blocks.content: **Thrust.** The thrust rating computer on CR (MCR) gives the cruise limit (the DC-10-40's computer has no CR mode); the autothrottle's SPD mode holds the speed under it. If the computer fails with the autothrottle in N1, the autothrottle drops out and a flag covers the N1 limit: set the speed in the SPD window and re-engage SPD, and the flight engineer computes and sets the N1 limit bugs by hand.

Each engine normally feeds from its own main tank: tank 1 to engine 1, tank 2 to engine 2, tank 3 to engine 3. One boost pump easily carries an engine at takeoff power, so tanks 1 and 3 run on one pump each; tank 2 always has two running, because engine 2 sits high in the tail and the extra pump guards it against a flame-out if a pump fails. Crossfeeding is not a normal method of fuel management; it is for a failed pump, an engine shut down, or a transfer that must be faster.

items: **The schedule.** The auxiliary tanks (-15, -30, -40, and the Extended Range -10) into the mains first; then tank 2 into tanks 1 and 3, keeping the wing tanks full, until the three are even; then all three burning together. A transfer that starts on the ground (more than 40,000 lb in tank 2) is already running at takeoff.

**Balance.** Keep tanks 1 and 3 within the lateral limit (see [Limitations](limitations)); by the In Range checklist they should be within 2,000 lb of each other, so that no balancing is needed on the approach. Plan transfers so that nothing has to come out of tank 1 or 3 below about 11,000 lb, where the tank's outboard fuel starts to refill its main compartment (see [Fuel](fuel)).
**The fuel log.** Compare the fuel used with the fuel remaining and with the flight plan as the flight goes on, and keep the gross weight current for the pilots' speeds and the next step climb.
**Fuel temperature.** On a long cold flight, watch the fuel temperature against its limit (see [Fuel temperature](fuel#fuel-temperature-technique)).

**The body tanks.** The fuel in the forward, center wing and aft body tanks is, for the structure, cargo: what is not needed for an offload or for ballast is moved into the main tanks as soon as practical. Transfer first from the center wing tank's lower compartment to its upper, then from the body tanks as the CG allows, then from tank 2 until it equals tanks 1 and 3. Before takeoff, the flight engineer transfers to put the CG as far aft as practical for the weight (aft of 24% MAC gives the best performance), within the zone and main tank limits.
**Main tanks full.** Above 556,000 lb gross weight, or with the zero fuel weight plus the body tank fuel above 414,000 lb, the main tanks are kept full for structural reasons.
**Lateral balance.** At most 4,000 lb between tanks 1 and 3 below 556,000 lb gross weight, 2,000 lb at or above it.
**Ballast.** Balance fuel is not transferred until the main tanks are down to about 5,000 lb each; it then goes equally into all three.

**Fill valves and overfill.** A FILL VALVE OPEN light that stays on means a fill valve is open: do not open a crossfeed or run a transfer pump unless fuel going into that tank is acceptable. A TANK OVERFILLED light during a transfer: stop the transfer and manage it by hand to keep the tanks about 2,000 lb below full.
**The boom.** Keep the boom full of fuel when the route may take the aircraft near lightning, against vapour ignition.

blocks.content: The fuel system's description and the transfer procedures are in [Fuel](fuel#fe-normal-operation) and [Main tank transfer](fuel#main-tank-transfer-procedure).
The DC-10's auxiliary tank transfer is in [Auxiliary transfer](fuel#auxiliary-transfer-procedure).
The KC-10's tank management and offload are in [KC-10 fuel management](fuel#kc10-fuel-management).

Where the fuel is decides where the center of gravity is. The wing tanks lie aft of the CG's normal range and tank 2 (in the center wing) forward of it, so moving fuel from tank 2 into the wing tanks moves the CG aft, and the other way moves it forward. An aft CG needs less tail download, so less trim drag and less fuel burned; a forward CG gives more stability and a lighter elevator. The limits in [Limitations](limitations) bound both.

FedEx sets no cruise CG target of its own; the transfers follow the fuel schedule. The simulation offers one: on the EFB's Virtual Crew app, **Target Cruise CG** sets a CG in % MAC for the virtual second officer to hold loosely. With their seat on MANUAL or AUTO, no checklist running and the aircraft level at or above 20,000 ft for a minute, the second officer starts a transfer when the CG is more than 1% MAC off the target and stops it within 0.3%: tank 2 into tanks 1 and 3 when the CG is forward of the target, tanks 1 and 3 into tank 2 when it is aft, with the crossfeeds closed. They stop short of a full receiving tank, of tank 2 falling to the wing tanks' level, of a wing tank at about 11,000 lb, and of a lateral imbalance; they leave the panel alone while tank 2 holds more than 40,000 lb. See [CG management](fuel#cruise-cg-target).

The KC-10's flight engineer manages the CG with the body tank transfers, keeping it aft of 24% MAC where the loading allows, and respecting the forward and aft zone limits, the main tank structural limits and the tipping limits on the ground (an aft load with fuel moved can sit the aircraft on its tail: no transfers while cargo is moved, once the tipping requirements have been met).

With the systems controllers in AUTO, the MD-10's fuel, hydraulic, electrical and air conditioning are managed automatically: the fuel system controller runs the transfers for each flight phase, balances the tanks and manages the fuel temperature; the pilots monitor. The PM's cruise scan is the EAD (engine indications and alerts) and the System Display pages in turn: fuel quantities and the transfers in progress against the plan, the engine secondary page, the hydraulic, electrical and air synoptics, and the STATUS page. An alert is handled with its QRH checklist. See [Fuel](fuel#md10-fuel-system-controller) and [Warning systems](warning-systems#eis-alerting).

A controller that has failed or been put in MANUAL hands its panel to the crew: the [MANUAL] steps of the normal procedures then apply, and in the cruise the PM does the transfers the controller would have done (the Series 10's tank 2 into tanks 1 and 3 until they are equal; on the Series 30 the auxiliary tanks first).

items: Fuel burn, transfer, the CG's movement with the fuel, the engines' climb and cruise thrust, and the cabin pressure schedule are modeled. The CG the simulation uses follows the tanks.
Engine vibration is indicated on every aircraft: on the flight engineer's panel on the DC-10 and KC-10, on the SD engine page on the MD-10.
The KC-10's seat belt switch works, but the Virtual Crew's flight engineer cannot move it: set it yourself at 10,000 ft and in the descent.

The DC-10's Virtual Crew second officer holds a target cruise CG and, on AUTO with a pack running, the cabin zone temperatures (about 65 to 75 °F); the KC-10's flight engineer holds the cabin temperatures but no CG target.

parts.title: Descent and Approach
parts.summary: Preparing for descent, the landing data and arrival briefing, the descent profile and its checklists, holding, the configuration schedule, and the precision, non-precision, visual and circling approaches.

blocks.content: The workload builds steadily from the top of descent to the runway. Good practice front-loads it: the landing data computed, the arrival and approach briefed, the radios and navigation set and the descent checklist done before the aircraft leaves cruise, so that the busy last minutes are left for flying and watching. The approach is then flown to a profile in which the aircraft decelerates and configures on a schedule, so that it arrives on the final approach stabilized: in the landing configuration, on speed, on the path, with the thrust set and the sink rate normal.

blocks.alt: Side-view diagram of a typical DC-10/KC-10 descent, approach and landing profile, not to scale, with distance from touchdown along the bottom (30, 20, 15, 5 NM): cruise Mach to 290 KIAS (KC-10 320 KIAS) at idle thrust, 2,500 to 3,000 ft/min; 18,000 ft: runway turnoff lights and seat belt sign on, altimeters to local, In Range (Descent) checklist; 10,000 ft about 30 NM out: 250 KIAS, landing lights extended and on; decelerating toward 0/RET minimum maneuvering speed; slats extended (0/EXT) with the Approach checklist; flaps 15/EXT; flaps 22/EXT and gear down at about 1.5 dots below the glideslope with the Before Landing checklist; flaps 35 or 50 before the final approach fix; stabilized by 1,000 ft; touchdown target 1,500 to 1,800 ft beyond the threshold. Inset: the MD-10's equivalent with PROF and the FMS speeds. Labels legible.
blocks.title: Descent, approach and landing profile

blocks.content: Before the top of descent: get the destination weather (ATIS), choose the landing flaps, compute the landing data, set the bugs, brief the arrival and the approach, set up the navigation, and set the pressurization for the destination.

items: **Landing flaps.** Flaps 35 or 50 are the normal landing settings; the captain chooses. Flaps 35 suits a strong crosswind (above about 15 kt when the landing distance is not critical), possible windshear, and noise abatement. Flaps 50 suits a short, wet or contaminated runway, a tailwind, an early turn-off, low visibility, a high landing weight, or a marginal computed landing distance; it also lowers the deck angle by about 1°, which helps the pilot see the runway. A DC-10-10 landing above 363,500 lb must use flaps 50.

**Landing data.** For the landing weight (the zero fuel weight plus the fuel expected at arrival), the flaps and the conditions: VREF (the KC-10's threshold speed, VTH), the approach speed VAPP, the minimum maneuvering speeds for 22/EXT, 0/EXT and 0/RET, the go-around N1 and the landing distance. In the simulation, the EFB's Performance app, Approach and Landing pages; **Set Bugs** on the Landing page sets VREF and the minimum maneuvering speeds on the DC-10 and KC-10 airspeed indicators (see [Performance](efb#landing-pages)).

**Approach speed.** VAPP is the greater of VREF + 5 kt and VREF plus the wind additive. The wind additive is the larger of half the steady wind above 20 kt and the full gust value, never more than 20 kt; when both apply, use only the larger. (Steady wind 30 kt: 30 - 20 = 10, half is 5, so VREF + 5.) Fly that speed to the flare. For an autoland, FedEx uses VREF + 5 whatever the wind, and curtails autoland when the gust additive would exceed 10 kt or the steady additive 5 kt.

**Arrival and approach briefing (PF).** The arrival's name and chart, the altitude and speed restrictions; the approach chart and its date, the approach and runway, the minimums (DA, DH or MDA) and the time to the missed approach point on a non-precision approach, the missed approach, the minimum safe altitudes, any special procedures or crew duties, the planned runway turn-off and the taxi route. The PF says how the autopilot, autothrottle and autobrakes will be used. In low visibility, brief the runway and taxiway lighting and the possible turn-offs too.
**Radio altimeter and barometric bugs.** Set for the approach: the DH on the radio altimeter for a CAT II or III approach or an RA minimum, the DA or MDA on the barometric altimeter otherwise.
**Windshield anti-ice.** NORM (and HIGH only for moderate to heavy icing). Descending into humid air, the heat keeps the windshield from fogging.

blocks.content: **Pressurization (FE).** The destination field elevation in the ALT SET window and the destination altimeter setting on the LDG BARO scale; the cabin altitude and rate on schedule. The controller then brings the cabin down to the landing field. For touch-and-go work the KC-10 uses SEMI-AUTO.

**FMS (PM).** The destination, STAR and runway selected or confirmed; the landing flaps checked and VAPP edited if necessary. On the EIS control panel each pilot sets RA or BARO and the minimums for the approach. The seat belt sign goes on as the descent starts, and the PM begins the Descent/Approach checklist, doing it through SEAT BELTS.

Stay at the cruise level until the planned top of descent. Plan to arrive about 30 flying miles from touchdown at 10,000 ft and 250 KIAS; at idle thrust the aircraft decelerates about 10 kt per mile in level flight, and descends about 300 ft per mile at the descent speed. Clean descents are best: flaps and gear are speed-limited, noisy and expensive. Use the spoilers when the profile needs them: fully extended they add about 1,000 ft/min to the rate of descent, and they may be used with the slats out.

blocks.title: Descent speeds
rows: Cruise Mach to 290 KIAS, 290 KIAS to 10,000 ft
Enroute: Mach 0.82 to 320 KIAS (about 28,900 ft), 320 KIAS to 10,000 ft; about 3° (300 ft per NM)
Mach 0.82 to 250 KIAS (about 39,800 ft), 250 KIAS below; about 2.75° (275 ft per NM)
Cruise Mach to 320 KIAS, 320 KIAS until joining the normal profile

blocks.content: Start the descent with the vertical speed wheel, disengage the autothrottle and bring the throttles slowly to idle. When the descent Mach and attitude are established, push MACH (MACH HOLD); at the descent IAS, push IAS (IAS HOLD). The throttles can then be used to adjust the rate, with the autothrottle off. MACH HOLD is sometimes less stable than IAS HOLD: if it hunts, use the vertical speed wheel. Engage the autothrottle when the altitude alert tone sounds; engaging it before ALT CAP cancels IAS HOLD and lets the rate be adjusted with the wheel before the capture (that interlock is not modeled in the simulation). Moving the wheel during ALT CAP cancels the capture. Another technique is to fly the descent on the vertical speed wheel with the autothrottle holding the speed.

items: **Behind the profile.** Without a speed restriction, increase the speed; then use the spoilers. With one, use the spoilers.
**Drag devices, KC-10 planning figures.** Idle thrust about 300 ft per NM; the speed brakes, the landing gear and the slats each add about 150 ft per NM at a constant speed.

**Limits.** Slats extended no faster than 260 KIAS or Mach 0.51 (270 KIAS or Mach 0.55 on the KC-10 and the heaviest DC-10-30s); the gear extended at 260 KIAS (300 extended) or Mach 0.70. On the KC-10, with the flap handle at 5° or more the speed brake handle is mechanically locked out unless the speed brakes were already out (not modeled in the simulation); a SPEED BRAKE light flashes if the spoiler handle is out of RET when the flap handle is moved aft of 0. Use the spoiler handle smoothly. See [Limitations](limitations).

**Hydraulics and pneumatics (FE).** The motor pump switches in ARM and every gauge normal; if the pneumatic supply cycles between high and low stage noisily in the descent, the supply selector to HI, and back to AUTO when the thrust or altitude changes.

blocks.content: The MD-10 normally descends in **PROF** on the FMS descent path, with FMS speed, the autothrottle at idle and the FCP altitude set to the clearance. Set each new clearance in the altitude window before the aircraft reaches the current one. FMS PROF is not used below the final approach fix altitude on an approach. With LEVEL CHANGE or vertical speed the crew fly the speed and rate; the spoilers are used as on the DC-10. At the transition level both pilots set the altimeters with the BAROSET knob, the standby altimeter too, and cross-check all three.

The arrival briefing is done before the checklist. The PF calls for the In Range checklist passing 18,000 ft; the PM switches on the runway turnoff lights and the seat belt sign first. The second officer gets the ATIS, agrees the landing flaps with the captain and computes the landing data. The second officer reads the checklist, does their items silently, and says when it is down to the line; the altimeters below the line are set at the transition level. From 10,000 ft to the gate the second officer faces forward.

items: **Airspeed bugs.** As the landing data card: VREF, VAPP and the 22/EXT, 0/EXT and 0/RET minimum maneuvering speeds; the speed command bug at the target speed.
**Hydraulic panel (silent).** Lights out, temperatures, quantities and pressures normal, the RMPs in ARM.

**Fuel panel (silent).** Every tank pump on, so that each engine has a forward and an aft inlet whatever the attitude; the crossfeeds closed; tanks 1 and 3 within 2,000 lb of each other, the fuel pressures normal and the fuel used about equal.
**Cabin pressure (silent).** The ALT SET scale at the destination field elevation, the destination's barometric setting set, the cabin on schedule.

blocks.content: The Descent checklist may be done before the descent starts. The flight engineer computes the landing data (forecast data may be used, updated before landing) and the landing distance for the first landing, and again for an abnormal configuration, a weight above the maximum unrestricted landing weight, or a wet or contaminated runway.

items: **Landing data, V-bugs (1).** The white bugs on the minimum maneuvering speeds for 0/RET, 0/EXT and 22/EXT and on VTH for the landing flaps, set by each pilot and cross-checked. The salmon bug, set by or for the PF, is the target: VTH plus the wind additives (all of the gust and half the steady wind above 20 kt, at most 20 kt). It also commands the autothrottle and references the fast/slow. Example: VTH 130 kt, wind 30 gusting 40: 5 + 10 = 15, target 145 kt.
**Crew briefing (2).** The penetration and approach: the navaids, the minimum and emergency safe altitudes, the descent rates, the minimums and VDP, the missed approach and the airfield.
**Radio altimeters (4).** The bug on the height above touchdown for the approach. The radio altimeter is the decision height reference only on a published RA approach.
**HF radios (6).** Silent, and not in AUT: an HF transmission at certain subharmonics of the VOR/ILS frequencies can make the flight director and the navigation flags misbehave on the approach.
**Pressurization (7).** The destination field elevation on ALT SET, the destination setting on LDG BARO.

**Altimeters and FMS baroset (9, 10).** At the transition level the local setting, cross-checked by all three; the FMS baroset entered when the FMS prompts for it. With a QFE setting or cold temperature corrections, the FMS vertical guidance is invalid.

blocks.content: **Reference ground speed.** The pilot computes the expected ground speed on final; the flight engineer watches the wind and the ground speed and calls a change of 10 kt or more, or a sudden shift in direction of 20° or more. Below 500 ft, a ground speed more than 20 kt from the reference ends the approach (see [Adverse weather](adverse-weather)).

The PM begins the Descent/Approach checklist as the descent starts, through SEAT BELTS, and finishes it at the transition level, as early as possible so that both pilots can watch the approach. Items marked ** are also done downwind between approaches.

items: **Altimeters (below the line).** The local setting at the transition level, set on both EIS panels and the standby altimeter, cross-checked.
**HYD panel (MANUAL only).** The 1-3 and 2-3 RMPs on for the approach.
**Courier report.** Passed in the simulation.

blocks.content: Descending through 10,000 ft (FedEx: at 250 KIAS), the landing lights are extended and switched on, the nose light on and the seat belt sign on. Make sure all the lights wanted for the approach are on before passing 10,000 ft.

items.action: ON: LEFT ON AND RIGHT ON LIGHTS

blocks.content: LDG LT switches to EXT ON, the NOSE LT to LAND, the WING & RUNWAY TURNOFF switches pushed (the LEFT ON and RIGHT ON lights), and the HI-INT OFF light out.

Tune and identify the holding fix's navaid on the way. Start slowing to the holding speed within 3 minutes of the fix, and cross it at or below the maximum holding speed. Hold clean for the best endurance: a racetrack pattern costs about 4% more fuel than straight flight, and the slats (below about 15,000 ft) about another 10%. If the holding speed for the weight is above the maximum, ask ATC for the higher speed, or hold with the slats out at the 0/EXT minimum maneuvering speed. Avoid long holding in icing with the flaps out. A holding level of about 24,000 to 26,000 ft is a good compromise between endurance and the fuel needed to divert.

items: Turns in the entry and the pattern at 3° per second, 30° of bank, or 25° with the autopilot or flight director, whichever needs the least bank.
Outbound timing starts over or abeam the fix, whichever is later (or when the turn outbound is complete if abeam cannot be found). Adjust the outbound leg to make the inbound leg the right length.
Correct the outbound heading and time for the wind so that the inbound leg comes out at the right length.

With the autopilot: the holding speed in the speed window with the autothrottle in SPD; HDG SEL for the turns and the outbound leg, the course armed to capture inbound (DC-10, KC-10: press RAD/INS after the last heading selection, because a heading selection gives up the arm). Step down in the pattern by setting and arming the new altitude and rolling the vertical speed wheel (or, on the MD-10, the FMS hold and the FCP).
Arriving at a clearance limit with no holding instructions, hold as published, or on the inbound course with standard turns; keep the last assigned level and ask for further clearance.

blocks.alt: Plan-view diagram of a standard right-hand holding pattern on a fix with the three entry sectors: direct entry (180° sector), teardrop entry (70° sector, outbound on a heading 30° from the outbound track for 1 minute then turn to intercept inbound), parallel entry (110° sector, turn to parallel the outbound track for 1 minute then turn back to the fix or the inbound track). Inbound leg 1 minute at or below 14,000 ft, 1.5 minutes above; the 70° and 110° sector boundaries labeled. Legible.
blocks.title: Holding pattern entries

blocks.content: Arriving in the terminal area, slow to no less than the 0/RET minimum maneuvering speed. Delay the flaps and slats as long as the ATC speeds allow, to save fuel and flap life; if a quick deceleration is needed, use the spoilers, the slats or the gear rather than extending flaps at their limit speeds. Slow to about the minimum maneuvering speed for the present configuration before selecting the next, then let the speed fall to no less than the next lower speed bug. Full bank capability (30°) exists at each configuration's minimum maneuvering speed.

blocks.title: Configuration schedule
rows: Terminal area, about 10 NM before the final approach fix
Decelerating through the 0/RET minimum maneuvering speed
"Flaps 15" (2 to 3 NM before the final approach fix in the stabilized approach)
15/EXT, the usual maneuvering configuration; 22/EXT also used (the KC-10's normal maneuvering flap)
15/EXT minimum maneuvering speed (about the 22/EXT speed + 10 kt)
Approaching the glideslope (about 1.5 dots below), or about 3 NM before the FAF on a non-precision approach
VAPP (the speed command bug on the target speed)

blocks.content: **Stabilized approach.** A well-planned arrival puts the aircraft within 10 miles of the final approach fix decelerating through the 0/RET speed, initially stabilized 2 to 3 miles before the fix with the engines spooled up, flaps 15, on the minimum maneuvering speed. Final stabilization (the landing configuration, the target speed, a normal sink rate, the thrust set and the aircraft on the path) must be complete no lower than 1,000 ft above the field, on a visual or an instrument approach. A short period of instability as the landing flaps go out is normal. The PM calls "Stable" or "Not stable" at 1,000 ft (500 ft on a visual approach), and an approach that cannot be stabilized is flown as a go-around: the MD-10 goes around if not stabilized by 500 ft, the KC-10 by the DH, the MAP, or 300 ft on a visual or circling approach. Below 2,000 ft the descent rate should not normally exceed 2,000 ft/min, and below 1,000 ft about 1,000 ft/min.
Do not descend below a published altitude until established on the course and on a published segment of the approach: within one dot on an ILS or VOR, within 5° on an NDB.

Call for the Approach checklist on every approach, visual or instrument, but never above the transition level. It is started no later than flaps 15 or at the PF's command, after the approach briefing; the second officer calls it down to the line, and does not call it complete until the mode selector is in its final position for the approach.

items: **Altimeter bugs.** The barometric and radio altimeter bugs set for the approach.
**Radios, HSI switches.** Tuned and identified; each HSI switch on the right source (ILS for an ILS or localizer approach, VOR for a VOR approach).

**Mode selector.** ILS or LAND for an ILS; RAD/INS, with the HSI on the VOR or localizer, for a VOR or localizer approach (FedEx's aircraft had a V/L button for this). To avoid capturing the localizer before the clearance, do not arm ILS or LAND until cleared for the approach. The second officer checks both FMAs show the right modes.

blocks.content: If the glideslope is captured before the localizer, the aircraft starts down the glideslope while still outside the localizer's protected airspace, and may descend into terrain. Do not descend below the approach altitude until the localizer is captured.
The Approach checklist is normally done after passing 14,000 ft MSL. Items 1 to 4 are done at once; items 5 to 8 before starting the approach.

items: **Fuel panel (1).** All lights out, the aft pumps on and the crossfeeds closed; for a full stop landing all tank pumps on. Two pumps on in tank 2 keep engine 2's supply uninterrupted. With any main tank below 5,000 lb, check every forward pump on and keep the main tanks about level, so no crossfeed or transfer is needed on the approach. A missed approach is not recommended with 1,500 lb or less in any main tank.
**Boom operator, exterior lights (2), cabin signs (3).** The boom operator told as the aircraft passes 10,000 ft; the lights set before passing it; the seat belt sign ON.
**Thrust computer (4).** GA, below 14,000 ft pressure altitude only: the GA light on and the N1 limit indexes agreeing (set them by hand if they do not).

**CDUs, EHSIs and radio aids (5).** CDU 3 shows the wind and the head or tail component; the flight engineer watches it through the approach. The PF's EHSI in full HSI mode, the PNF's may be in MAP. The navigation source VOR, ILS or TCN for a radio approach, FMS for a GPS approach.
**Annunciator panels (7).** Checked.

blocks.content: Below about 2,000 lb in tank 2, crossfeeding or transferring may open the tank 2 manifold drain valve and let fuel run into tank 2; feeding engines 1 or 3 from it can starve engine 2.

The ILS may be flown coupled to the autopilot, on the flight director, or by hand on raw data; the raw localizer and glideslope are always monitored against the director's commands. The modes, the capture logic, the land modes and the go-around are described in [Approach and autoland](automatic-flight#approach-and-autoland). This topic is the crew's side of the approach.

blocks.alt: Side-view profile of a three-engine ILS approach for the DC-10 and KC-10, not to scale, with the plan view above: approach preparations (In Range or Descent checklist complete, briefing, FD on, autopilot in CMD, autothrottle on); 15/EXT on the intercept heading, speed bug 15/EXT minimum maneuvering speed; slats extended and the Approach checklist; cleared for the approach: ILS (or LAND) armed; localizer capture: LOC CAP then LOC TRK, bank limit 15°, missed approach heading set; approaching the glideslope: flaps 22, gear down, Before Landing checklist, flaps 35 or 50, speed bug VREF plus additives; glideslope capture: G/S CAP then G/S TRK, missed approach altitude set; outer marker; 1,000 ft RA "Stable"; 500 ft "Cleared to land"; 100 ft above DA "Approaching minimums"; DA "Minimums"; touchdown 1,500 to 1,800 ft beyond the threshold. A side box shows the two go-around methods: above 500 ft vertical speed 1,500 ft/min with the autopilot; below 500 ft TO/GA. Legible.
blocks.title: ILS approach profile, DC-10 and KC-10

blocks.alt: Side-view profile of an MD-10 ILS approach with AUTO FLIGHT engaged, not to scale, with numbered points: 1 flight directors on, flaps and slats UP/RET at Vmin + 5; 2 entering downwind, slats extended; 3 base leg, flaps 22; 4 on the intercept heading and cleared, APPR/LAND pushed, LAND ARMED; 5 LOC captured, missed approach heading preselected; 6 1.5 to 2 dots below the glideslope, gear down; 7 1 dot below, landing flaps, slow to VAPP, Before Landing checklist; 8 final approach fix, "Final fix ___ feet"; 9 glideslope captured, missed approach altitude preselected; 10 below 1,500 ft for 10 s, DUAL LAND (green); 11 150 ft ALIGN; 12 50 ft FLARE and RETARD; 13 touchdown ROLLOUT; 14 reverse thrust. FMA legends shown at each point. Legible.
blocks.title: ILS approach profile, MD-10

items: Tune the ILS on both receivers (the coupled autopilot flies its own side's receiver) and identify it; set the inbound course on both. On the KC-10 the EHSI navigation source to LOC 1 and LOC 2 before the capture.

Intercept on a heading in HDG SEL. To avoid capturing the glideslope when cleared only for the localizer, arm the localizer alone: RAD/INS (RAD/FMS on the KC-10) with the HSI or EHSI on the localizer, pressed after HDG SEL, because a heading selection gives up that arm. When cleared for the approach, push **ILS** (DC-10: or LAND for an autoland): ILS in the ARM window.

**Localizer capture.** LOC CAP, then LOC TRK on the centerline (not above 2,500 ft RA); set the missed approach heading and the bank limit to 15°. Do not follow the flight director's first command to keep turning toward the localizer during a normal intercept: hold the intercept heading and the bars will center and lead a smooth capture. After a high-rate intercept that overshoots, set an intercept of no more than 20° and wait for the bar to center.

**Approaching the glideslope.** Flaps 22, gear down, the Before Landing checklist; flaps 35 or 50 and the speed bug on the target speed. At the glideslope capture (G/S CAP, G/S TRK after 20 seconds) set the missed approach altitude.

Check the glideslope altitude at the outer marker against the chart. Monitor raw data, the FMA and the speed throughout. With the autopilot in CMD watch the AP OUT OF TRIM light: on for more than 3 seconds, disconnect and fly by hand.

**Minimums.** At DA the aircraft must be in a position to land with little maneuvering; by 100 ft the cockpit must be laterally inside the lines of the runway edges and heading to stay there; otherwise go around. Disconnect the autopilot for a manual landing no lower than the minimum for a coupled approach (see [Limitations](limitations)).

blocks.content: **Main gear clearance.** The glideslope antenna is in the nose, about 27 ft above the main gear in the approach attitude, and the pilots' eyes about 35 ft above it. An ILS whose glideslope crosses the threshold below 47 ft therefore gives too little gear clearance (20 ft is the minimum): on such an ILS, a shallow one, or one with a short touchdown distance, drift up to 1.5 to 2 dots high from 200 ft, which adds about 10 ft. Never stay below the glideslope. At minimums on an ILS the runway looks closer and lower than on a visual approach because it is; be on or slightly above the glideslope.

**Autoland (DC-10).** Push LAND with one autopilot in CMD, then the second AP lever to CMD for DUAL LAND; the preland test then shows DUAL LAND, SNGL LAND or APPR ONLY. Once SNGL or DUAL LAND shows, the vertical speed wheel, IAS and MACH are locked out and the only way out in pitch is TO/GA: every autoland go-around is a TO/GA go-around. Autobrakes are used on every CAT III approach. Leave the autopilot engaged through the rollout until the aircraft is under control on the runway, and disconnect before turning off. See [Autoland, DC-10](automatic-flight#autoland-dc10).

**No autoland (KC-10).** The KC-10's LAND switch is inoperative: fly the coupled ILS to the minimums and disconnect for a manual landing. The vertical speed wheel stays usable throughout.
