Category II approaches are flown coupled by the copilot, the pilot landing; all engines operating, the wind within 25 kt (crosswind 15, tailwind 10), and any deviation beyond the decision regime limits (speed +10/-5 kt, half a dot on the glideslope or localizer, any warning flag, a descent rate over 1,000 ft/min, any GPWS warning) between the "100 feet to DH" call and the runway is a go-around.

items: Flight directors on and AUTO FLIGHT engaged; checklists complete; clean at or above Vmin + 5. Both NDs on MAP at minimum range, or one on MAP and one on APPR.
Entering downwind (or the equivalent): slats extended, speed at or above Vmin + 5. Flaps 15 or 22 may be used to slow down or lower the deck angle.
On the base leg: flaps 22, speed at or above Vmin + 5.

On the intercept heading and cleared for the approach: push **APPR/LAND**: LAND ARMED above the roll window. Intercept close in at a speed near the final approach speed and at a shallow angle; high speeds and intercepts beyond 30° may overshoot.

At LOC capture, preselect the missed approach heading. At 1.5 to 2 dots below the glideslope, gear down. At 1 dot below, landing flaps and slow to VAPP; the Before Landing checklist. With VAPP captured the go-around level-off speed may be preselected.

Crossing the final approach fix the PM calls "Final fix, ___ feet" and any deviation from the published altitude; the PF answers "Altitude checked". At glideslope capture (G/S in the altitude window; PROF disengages) preselect the missed approach altitude.

Below 1,500 ft for 10 seconds with the dual land test passed: LOC and G/S DUAL LAND in green (or SINGLE LAND or APPR ONLY in white, with their restrictions). The FCP is then disabled to protect the autoland; the GA switch is the way out.

At about 150 ft (200 ft in the simulation) ALIGN (the decrab); at 50 ft FLARE and RETARD; at main gear touchdown ROLLOUT. In APPR ONLY the autopilot disconnects at 100 ft. At DH, continue the autoland or manual landing, or go around.

Apply reverse thrust (it disconnects the autothrottle) and adequate braking; leave the autopilot engaged until a safe stop is assured and the visibility allows the pilot to take over. A two-engine ILS is the same with landing flaps limited to 35.

blocks.content: With PROF engaged and an ILS selected from the FMS database, the aircraft will not descend below the FAF altitude if the glideslope is not captured, but will fly level to the missed approach point (not modeled in the simulation: do not rely on it). See [Autoland, MD-10](automatic-flight#autoland-md10).

A non-precision approach has no electronic glideslope: the aircraft descends to a minimum descent altitude (MDA) and holds it until it can land or reaches the missed approach point (MAP). The aircraft is in the landing configuration (gear down, flaps 35 or 50) from the final approach fix, and descends at about 1,000 ft/min, enough to reach the MDA early enough to see the runway and join a normal landing path before the MAP. The PM times the leg from the FAF and makes the altitude calls; the PM calls radio altitude and sink rate every 100 ft below the MDA. On deciding to leave the MDA, the PF says "Leaving MDA". The autothrottle is used in SPD.

**The visual descent point (VDP)** is the point from which a normal 3° descent from the MDA to the touchdown begins. Without a published VDP, divide the height above touchdown at the MDA by 300 to get its distance from the threshold in miles (450 ft: 1.5 NM), corrected for where the DME is. Leaving the MDA before the VDP puts the aircraft low; reaching the VDP still in cloud usually means the landing will not be made.

blocks.alt: Side-view profile of a three-engine VOR or localizer approach, not to scale: 15/EXT and the speed bug, slats extended and the Approach checklist; cleared for the approach, RAD/INS (VOR or localizer) armed and captured, bank limit 15°, missed approach heading set, next altitude or MDA set and armed (preselect to the next 100 ft above the published MDA); about 3 NM before the final approach fix: flaps 22, gear down, Before Landing checklist, flaps 35 or 50; at the FAF: timing started, the FAF called, about 1,000 ft/min down; level at the MDA with altitude hold; 1,000 ft "Stable"; 500 ft "Cleared to land"; 100 ft above the MDA "Approaching minimums"; MDA "Minimums"; 0.2 NM or 10 s before the VDP "Approaching VDP"; at the VDP "VDP", the vertical speed about 600 ft/min down, autopilot off, "Leaving MDA"; touchdown 1,500 to 1,800 ft. A side box: go-around at or above the MDA by vertical speed (1,500 ft/min, autopilot on); below the MDA, TO/GA by hand. Legible.
blocks.title: Non-precision approach profile

items: Use the altitude arming and capture at every step-down fix and at the MDA. If the altitude window cannot be set to the exact MDA, set the next 100 ft above and fine-tune the descent to the MDA with the vertical speed wheel. Set the barometric altitude bug on the MDA; a radio altimeter setting is optional.

VOR and localizer approaches are flown with RAD/INS (RAD/FMS on the KC-10) and the HSI on the VOR or localizer, HDG SEL for the maneuvering before the capture: select HDG SEL first and press RAD/INS after it, because a heading selection gives up the arm. Two dots on the HSI is 10° on a VOR. Over the station (the cone of confusion), or departing the radial quickly, the roll mode shows RAD CRS and holds the course. If the VOR is the FAF, consider HDG SEL over the fix to hold the published course, then press RAD/INS again.
An NDB approach: HDG SEL to intercept and track the bearings; consider tuning the other needle to an offset VOR.

A back course: the HDG SEL method with the autopilot in CMD on raw data and the front course set (the RAD mode would turn the wrong way). The BACK CRS mode (flight director only on the real aircraft) is inoperative in the simulation. The localizer is very sensitive close in: small, prompt corrections. On the real aircraft the GPWS glideslope warning is cancelled against false glideslope signals; the DC-10 and KC-10 cancel caps cannot be pressed in the simulation.
At the MDA, set and arm the missed approach altitude and preset the missed approach heading.
Disconnect the autopilot no later than 50 ft below the MDA.

blocks.content: **Monitored non-precision approach (FedEx).** Below 1,000 ft ceiling or 3 miles visibility, the approach is flown with one autopilot in CMD and every working flight director, the autopilot staying engaged until leaving the MDA. The first officer is the PF from no later than the final approach course; the captain, as PM, manages and monitors, and calls "Approaching minimums" 100 ft above the MDA with a hand below the throttles. The first officer calls "Minimums" at the MDA. When the captain has the runway environment and is ready, they say "I have the airplane". The first officer calls "Approaching VDP" (0.2 NM or 10 seconds before) and "VDP"; at the VDP the captain calls "Leaving MDA", sets about 600 ft/min down, disconnects the autopilot and lands, the first officer calling the height and sink rate every 100 ft. If the captain has not taken control by the MAP, the first officer calls "Going around" and goes around.

items: Complete the checklists inbound to the IAF. Slats extended, at or above Vmin + 5. Follow the course with HDG, TRK, NAV or VOR TRACK.
Leave the IAF (or enter the base leg) with flaps 22 at or above Vmin + 5.
Before the FAF: gear down, landing flaps, slow to VAPP. After leveling, preselect the MDA in the FCP altitude window.

Crossing the FAF the PM calls "Final fix, ___ feet"; the PF answers "Altitude checked". Leave the FAF at VAPP and descend by vertical speed (start the timing and set a rate that reaches the MDA before the MAP), by flight path angle (the pitch wheel to the approach's angle; push the V/S-FPA button to show FPA), or in PROF (the altitude window on the MDA).
At the MDA, preselect the missed approach altitude. With the runway in sight, disengage the autopilot and land; without it at the MAP, or if a safe landing cannot be made, go around.

blocks.content: To fly a VOR or RNAV approach in the FMS, a minimum profile altitude (MIN PROF) is entered on the STAR page; PROF reverts to altitude hold at it, and the vertical deviation indicator is not used below it. GPS and RNAV approaches are flown in NAV from the database, with the flight director on or the autopilot engaged. A two-engine non-precision approach uses flaps 35.

sections.title: Visual approach and the traffic pattern

blocks.content: Finish the descent and approach checklists before entering the airport traffic area, so that the crew's attention is outside. Use every radio aid to identify the runway, and the electronic and visual glideslopes where there are any. The aircraft must be stabilized on final by 500 ft (MD-10: by 1,000 ft, and go around if not stabilized by 500 ft).

items: **The path.** A 3° glidepath at the target speed needs about 700 ft/min with no wind (the ground speed times 5). A flat approach shows as more thrust, a lower sink rate and a higher deck angle; a steep one as less thrust, more sink and a lower deck angle, as long as speed and attitude are steady. Adjust the thrust smoothly in small steps: large thrust changes mean an unstable approach.

**The aiming point.** 1,500 to 1,800 ft beyond the threshold (about 1,700 ft on the MD-10), which crosses the threshold at 40 to 60 ft of wheel height and gives a no-flare touchdown about 1,000 ft in. Smaller aircraft aim at 1,000 ft; the DC-10's pilots sit about 35 ft above the wheels, and the habit of aiming short lands short.

**Illusions.** An upsloping runway or approach makes the aircraft look high; haze, smoke, glare and darkness make it look higher than it is; a wide runway makes it look low. Bright lights look close, dim ones far. Cross-check the instruments and each other.

**VASI.** On a three-bar VASI the DC-10 uses the upper glidepath (the middle and far bars), whose aiming point suits its eye height. Do not use a two-bar VASI for glidepath guidance below 500 ft: on its lower edge the main gear can touch down short. A PAPI is set for the most demanding type expected at the runway; at an unfamiliar airport, make sure it gives the DC-10 enough threshold clearance.

**Cross-checks.** The approach lights pass under the nose at about 200 ft; the threshold disappears under the nose soon after the radio altimeter shows 75 ft, before the GPWS "50" call. Any time the radio altitude is 75 ft or less and the runway's approach end is still in view, the aircraft is dangerously low.

blocks.alt: Plan-view diagram of a left-hand visual traffic pattern for the DC-10, KC-10 and MD-10 with the runway at the bottom, with the configuration and speed at each point: entering downwind at 1,500 ft AGL, slats extended (0/EXT), Approach checklist (KC-10: Downwind checklist), speed 0/EXT minimum maneuvering speed; mid-downwind flaps 15, speed 15/EXT minimum maneuvering speed; abeam the threshold or turning base: flaps 22, gear down, Before Landing checklist, begin a slight descent (200 to 400 ft/min), never below 1,500 ft AGL before the base turn on a circle; on final: flaps 35 or 50, speed VREF plus additives, bank limit 15°, stabilized on a 2.5 to 3° path by 500 ft (MD-10 1,000 ft); touchdown target 1,500 to 1,800 ft. A side-view inset shows the descent from downwind to the threshold with the callouts (500 ft "Stable", "Cleared to land"). Distances: downwind about 2 to 3 NM abeam, final at least 1.5 NM. Labels legible.
blocks.title: Visual traffic pattern

blocks.content: **The pattern.** Slats out entering the downwind (the Approach checklist, or on the KC-10 the Downwind checklist); flaps 15 on the downwind; turning base, flaps 22, gear down and the Before Landing checklist, starting a slight descent of 200 to 400 ft/min; on final the landing flaps and the target speed, the bank limited to 15°. On a visual or circling approach the flaps 35 selection may wait until the final turn and the flaps 50 selection until rolling out on final; with 50° watch the speed closely, because the aircraft answers the thrust more slowly. The KC-10's pattern work (touch-and-go landings, full stop taxi-backs and the local pattern checklists) is in [Local pattern](normal-landing#local-pattern).

A circling approach is an instrument approach that ends with a visual maneuver to a runway not aligned with the final course. It is not an instrument maneuver: the runway environment must stay in sight throughout. The aircraft is approach category D (category E if maneuvering at 166 kt or more), and the protected airspace for the circle is small: as little as 300 ft of obstacle clearance inside it, and none outside.

items: FedEx requires the weather at or above 1,000 ft and 3 miles, or the circling minimums if higher, to start the approach and throughout it; the altimeter bugs at the field elevation + 1,000 ft or the circling MDA, whichever is higher.

Be configured in the landing configuration (flaps 35, gear down) with the Before Landing checklist done by the FAF, and fly the circle at VAPP (MD-10: Vmin + 5 for flaps 35) using the autothrottle; the autopilot with HDG SEL may be used to maneuver.

With the airport in sight at no lower than 1,000 ft or the circling minimums, start the circle by the shortest path to the downwind or base; stay as close to 1,500 ft above the airport as the cloud allows until a normal 3° descent to the runway can begin. Do not descend below the circling minimum until in position for that descent. Select flaps 50, if wanted, once in position.
The PM calls altitude and sink rate every 100 ft from 500 ft.

If visual reference is lost during the circle, climb toward the landing runway and fly the published missed approach for the instrument approach just flown (unless ATC gives another). If there is any doubt that the aircraft can be maneuvered safely to the runway, go around.

blocks.content: On an ILS that ends in a circle, set the circling MDA on the minimums and, before DUAL or SINGLE LAND shows, in the FCP altitude window: after the glideslope capture the aircraft descends to the MDA, the FMA showing APPR ONLY, and levels there in heading and altitude hold.

items: The DC-10 and MD-10 autoland, with align, flare, retard and rollout, are modeled; the KC-10 has none. See [Automatic flight](automatic-flight#approach-and-autoland).

MD-10: the cabin pressure controller has no landing elevation input in the simulation; it schedules the cabin as if the destination were at sea level on 29.92 inHg, so expect the cabin to reach sea level pressure on a high-elevation landing.
MD-10: the ND draws no weather radar, terrain or traffic picture, and there is no TCAS.
DC-10: the basic GPWS gives the BELOW G/S light without a voice unless the voice option is fitted; the KC-10 and MD-10 EGPWS speak.
The PAFAM's runway display is the DC-10's; the MD-10 relies on its FMA and the PFD for the autoland's progress.

parts.title: Landing and Go-Around
parts.summary: The Before Landing checklist, the landing and rollout with spoilers, reversers and brakes, the go-around, rejected and balked landings, and the local pattern.

blocks.content: A good landing is the end of a good approach: stabilized early, on the path at the target speed, it needs only a small flare and a firm touchdown in the zone, after which the deceleration is done by the ground spoilers, the reversers and the brakes, in that order of importance at high speed. The DC-10's long body and its pilots' high eye position shape the technique: the aircraft is not held off for a smooth touchdown, and the nose is flown onto the runway promptly, because both protect the tail and stop the aircraft sooner. The landing technique is described in more depth in [Landing technique](normal-techniques#landing-technique).
Once reverse thrust has been selected, a full stop landing must be made.

The PF calls for the gear and the landing flaps and then the Before Landing checklist; the second officer reads it. If a flaps 50 landing has been briefed, the checklist is held at Flaps & Slats until the flaps and slats show 50/LAND. Either flaps 35 or flaps 50 is a standard configuration.

blocks.title: Before landing flow (PM)
rows: Gear: confirms the green lights aloud

items: **Gear.** Down, three green (four on the -30 and -40); the second officer confirms aloud.
**Thrust computer.** GA, its light on, the N1 bugs agreeing with the digital readout. Never above 14,000 ft pressure altitude.

**Anti-skid.** With the gear handle down, the TEST button lights every ANTI-SKID FAIL light; released, they go out (the button is inoperative in the simulation). Leave the switch at ARM. With the anti-skid off, braking is proportional to pedal pressure with no skid protection: avoid locking the wheels.
**Spoilers.** The AUTO SPOILER DO NOT USE light out, the handle raised to ARM and staying up; the second officer confirms.

**Auto brakes.** With the ABS lights out, the selector to MIN, MED or MAX and the ARM-DISARM switch to ARM. They must be used, if available, on a CAT III approach. After landing they are taken out by depressing the brake pedals past about 40% of their travel, by advancing the throttles, by the ARM-DISARM switch or by turning the selector to OFF; retracting the spoilers releases them without disarming them.
**Flaps and slats.** The flaps at the setting, the slat LAND light on, the DISAGREE light out; the second officer checks.
**Lights (silent).** As required. In low visibility the landing lights may be left off at the captain's discretion, to cut the glare.

blocks.content: The flight engineer positions their seat so that they can do all the landing and go-around duties, and makes a last scan of their panel before landing. The PF commands "Gear down"; the PNF acknowledges and lowers it.

items: **Landing gear (1).** Down and green on the pilots' and the flight engineer's indications. The center gear is normally used for every landing; when it is not needed, the center gear switch to UP (lock pin removed and replaced) keeps it retracted and takes it out of the gear warning and lights. During the extension system 3's pressure may dip below 2,000 psi for a moment. An unsafe indication on only one of the two indicating systems does not demand a visual inspection.

**Spoilers (3).** Not armed until the gear is down. An AUTO SPOILER DO NOT USE light seen at any point in the flight, even one that has since gone out, rules out the automatic mode: leave the handle at RET and deploy the spoilers by hand after touchdown.
**Anti-skid, brake pressure and temperature (4).** The switch at ARM, then the test; both brake system pressures in the white band; note the brake temperature reading.

**Flaps/slats (5).** Normally 35; 50 on a short, wet or contaminated runway when the landing distance would otherwise suffer. A two-engine landing uses flaps 35. The final flap selection is made just before the glideslope or the final approach fix.

blocks.content: **Approach calls.** The PNF, backed up by the flight engineer, calls 1,000, 500 and 100 ft above the DH or MDA. At DH (precision) the PNF calls "Decision height"; on a non-precision approach "MDA", "VDP" and "MAP". The PF answers each and announces "Landing" or "Going around". If neither pilot has called passing DH, the flight engineer calls "Going below minimums".

blocks.title: Before landing
rows: Checks the speed below the gear limit and lowers the gear. With three green (four on the Series 30), raises the spoiler handle to ARM.
Before the final approach fix: "Flaps 35" (or "Flaps 50"), "set speed" unless in FMS speed. Slows to VREF + 5 for the configuration.
Checks the speed below the flap limit, sets the flaps and watches them run: "Flaps 35, speed set."
Cross-checks the altimeters with the PNF. Checks the EAD for alerts, reminders and the green box; calls for the Before Landing checklist.
Reads the Before Landing checklist and announces it complete. Receives the landing clearance.

blocks.content: The checklist is called for as the landing flaps are commanded. For flaps 50 it is started after flaps 35 is selected, and not completed until flaps 50 is confirmed. If the landing essential items box on the EAD shows LANDING GEAR in white with the handle down, check the primary gear lights: if they show safe, the gear is down and locked.
**Autobrake.** Not installed in the simulated MD-10; the item is answered "Not Installed".

Cross the threshold on speed with about 50 ft of wheel height; the radio altimeter is biased to read the main wheels' height, and its callouts are the best guide. On a normal final approach the sink rate is 650 to 800 ft/min. From 3° the flare is small: begin it at about 30 to 40 ft (MD-10) with about 2° of pitch, close the throttles (the autothrottle retards from 50 ft) and fly the aircraft onto the runway in the touchdown zone. Do not trim the stabilizer in the flare, and do not hold the aircraft off for a smooth touchdown: floating in ground effect uses runway fast, raises the pitch attitude toward a tail strike and ends in a long, hot landing. If the speed is high, put the aircraft on the runway near the 1,500 ft point anyway: deceleration on the ground is about three times that in the air.

blocks.title: Typical attitudes
rows: DC-10-10, flaps 35, mid CG, 2.5° glideslope, VREF + 5
Flaps 35 approach at maximum landing weight
About 6°; about 1° more at VREF over the threshold
8 to 9° (10° if flared to zero sink at idle to 1.25 VS)

blocks.content: **Bounce.** After a bounce, keep or regain the normal landing attitude with smooth pitch inputs and use thrust to stop the sink from building before the second contact. A high, hard bounce calls for a normal go-around instead; leave the gear down until the aircraft is clearly climbing, since it may touch the runway again first.
Large forward or aft column movements just before touchdown can strike the tail or damage the nose gear.

**Ground spoilers.** Armed, they deploy automatically: with the flaps in the landing range at main wheel spin-up, with less than landing flaps when the reversers are selected, and in a rejected takeoff on reverse thrust. Their deployment pitches the nose up, most at an aft CG; hold forward pressure on the column and fly the nose wheel smoothly onto the runway, then keep the pressure on for the steering. If the No. 2 throttle is not at idle at spin-up, the spoilers may deploy and immediately retract: then extend them by hand. If the handle does not come fully aft, the second officer (KC-10: the flight engineer, on the pilot's command) pulls it aft into the ground spoiler position and holds it there if it will not latch. Deploy the spoilers by hand only once the nose gear is on the runway.

The KC-10 manual describes a two-stage deployment: the handle moves to about 2/3 at main wheel spin-up and fully aft at nose gear touchdown, and if more than 8 seconds pass between the two the AUTO SPOILER DO NOT USE light comes on (on a touch-and-go with the spoilers armed and only the mains touching, that is the system working as designed). The simulation deploys the spoilers fully at spin-up, but keeps the 8-second watchdog and its light on the DC-10 and KC-10.

**Reverse thrust.** Reverse is most effective at high speed, so it is used at once. At main gear touchdown, check the throttles at idle and lift the reverse levers to the interlock (the amber REV U/L lights; on the MD-10 the REV legend on the EAD); hold a steady pull on the No. 1 and No. 3 levers while lowering the nose, so that reverse comes in smoothly when the interlocks release, without cycling the levers. The No. 2 reverser is held to reverse idle until the nose strut is compressed (FedEx: it cannot be used until the nose wheel is on the ground; in the simulation it does not deploy until then): once the nose wheel is down, bring its lever back to match. When the green REV THR lights show ("Reverse available"), take the levers to the reverse stop, or less as the runway allows.

At 80 kt start bringing the levers toward reverse idle, reaching it by 60 kt, and be at forward idle by the turn-off speed (MD-10: reverse idle at 80 KIAS, forward idle at 60 KIAS). Come out of reverse slowly: a quick move to forward idle from high reverse gives a surge of forward thrust. Check the reversers stowed before turning off. The PM calls "80 knots" and "60 knots".

blocks.title: Reverse thrust nominal limits
rows: The go-around N1; reduce to it if it is exceeded before the reverse stops
95% N1 at 0 °C, decreasing with temperature to below 85% at 50 °C TAT (the fuel control's reverse stop: 95% N2)

blocks.content: The flight engineer (DC-10, KC-10) watches the reversers and calls any REV THR light not on, an engine that does not spool up, an N1 above the limit or an excessive EGT rise. Reverse at high power and low speed invites compressor stalls and hot gas re-ingestion: be at reverse idle by 60 kt. Reverse is normally limited to 60 seconds. If directional control suffers in reverse, go back to reverse idle (or forward idle), regain control, and reapply.

**Brakes.** Aerodynamic braking is ineffective on the DC-10: the drag is about the same with the nose up as with the nose down and the spoilers out, and holding the nose up keeps weight off the wheels. With the nose wheel down and the spoilers deployed the brakes work best. Use the autobrake where fitted, or brake smoothly and progressively with the pedals. With the anti-skid inoperative, increase pedal force smoothly until the wanted deceleration is felt and do not release it until at taxi speed; do not pump the brakes. On a wet or icy runway the anti-skid can be defeated if the wheels do not spin up at touchdown, or slow too much during a release; if the brakes seem to push the aircraft along, release them completely for a moment to let the wheels spin up.

**Autobrake.** In the simulation the brakes come on once the ground spoilers deploy with throttles 1 and 3 retarded, the pedals released and the main wheels above 45 kt; MIN and MED wait about 4 seconds, MAX about 2, so the nose wheel is down first. To come off the autobrake without an abrupt stop, before the anti-skid cut-out at about 10 kt press the pedals gradually until the ARM-DISARM switch drops to DISARM and the ABS light comes on, then brake as needed. If the brakes do not work normally without the autobrake, release the pedals, anti-skid OFF, reapply, and use more reverse.

**Who has the aircraft.** With the first officer flying, the captain takes control as the aircraft slows to taxi speed and is ready to clear the runway (MD-10: when the reversers are stowed), or earlier if the captain judges it necessary.

Fly the final approach wings level, crabbed into the wind. From about 200 ft, align the fuselage with the runway with rudder and lower the upwind wing just enough to stop the drift (a forward slip). The worst case needs about 6° of bank, which leaves a good margin: with a 9° touchdown attitude and normal strut extension, the DC-10's wing tip touches at about 11.8° of bank on the -10 and 11.1° on the -30, and the tip (or the flaps at 50°) always touches before the engine nacelle. Do not hold the aircraft off: a low angle of attack keeps the lateral control. After touchdown keep straight with the rudder and the wings level with aileron; the landing gear and tail geometry make the aircraft weathercock into the wind, so expect it and correct at once. Consider flaps 35 in a strong crosswind.

FedEx limits the crosswind to 31 kt (the demonstrated value) with both rudders working, 15 kt with either rudder inoperative, and 10 kt with braking reported poor; the limits are in [Limitations](limitations).

A go-around and a rejected landing are the same procedure; a missed approach is a go-around that also flies a published or assigned route. Do not continue below the minimums unless the aircraft is in a position and condition to land normally; if it cannot land in the touchdown zone (the first 3,000 ft), go around. The decision is announced clearly and is irrevocable: no landing is attempted once a go-around has started.

blocks.alt: Side-view profile of a three-engine go-around for the DC-10 and KC-10 (with an MD-10 inset), not to scale: at DH or MDA "Go-around", TO/GA pressed, "Max power" (GA thrust), rotate to about 15° pitch (the FD's go-around limit), "Flaps 22"; "Positive rate", "Gear up"; "Set and arm missed approach altitude", "Set top bug" (0/RET minimum maneuvering speed); no turn below 400 ft AGL; bank limited to 15° below VREF + 10; 1,500 ft AGL "Climb power", autothrottle on; altitude capture: speed mode; flaps and slats retracted on schedule, After Takeoff checklist, bank unlimited at 0/RET. A side box shows the vertical speed go-around above 500 ft (1,500 ft/min on the wheel). FMA legends N1, ALT, G/A, G/A. Legible.
blocks.title: Go-around profile
Which go-around
rows: Precision approach above 500 ft AGL; non-precision approach at or above the MDA
Vertical speed go-around preferred (autopilot or manual)
Precision approach below 500 ft; non-precision approach below the MDA
Any autoland approach (SNGL or DUAL LAND)
TOGA go-around required: the vertical speed wheel is locked out
Manual TOGA go-around: the autopilot may not have the authority (see [Emergency procedures](emergency-procedures))

blocks.content:
**TOGA go-around, automatic.** Press TO/GA and advance the throttles to go-around thrust, calling "Go-around, max power, flaps 22". Monitor the autopilot and autothrottle: about 15° pitch and go-around thrust. With a climb established: "Positive rate" (either pilot), "Gear up", "Set and arm missed approach altitude", "Set top bug".

**TOGA go-around, manual.** Advance the throttles to go-around thrust, disconnect the autopilot, press TO/GA and rotate positively (2.5 to 3° per second) to 15°, calling "Go-around, max power, flaps 22"; then as above.

**Vertical speed go-around.** With the autopilot: "Go-around", the vertical speed wheel smoothly to about 1,500 ft/min up, "Flaps 22"; then the same calls. By hand: "Go-around, vertical speed to 1,500" while disconnecting the autopilot and starting the climb; the PM sets the wheel; then the same.

**Then.** The PM sets flaps 22, raises the gear on the call, refines the thrust, sets and arms the missed approach altitude and sets the speed bug to the 0/RET minimum maneuvering speed or 250 kt (or the 0/EXT speed or the holding speed if low holding is planned). Turn no earlier than 400 ft unless the procedure says otherwise, and keep the bank to 15° below VREF + 10. At 1,500 ft: "Climb power" (and "IAS hold" after a vertical speed go-around, at VAPP to VAPP + 10). At the altitude capture select the speed mode; moving the vertical speed wheel after ALT CAP cancels the capture. Retract the flaps and slats on schedule, call for the After Takeoff checklist, and unlimit the bank (25°) at 0/RET.

items: The flaps must be out of UP for TO/GA to select the go-around mode. TO/GA also switches the thrust computer to GA.
If both autopilots were in CMD for an autoland, AP 2 drops at the TO/GA press.
The aircraft holds the heading flown at the press; in a bank it rolls level and holds the heading at which the wings come within 3° of level.
The go-around mode commands at most 15° of pitch; if more is needed to hold the speed, the fast/slow shows fast with the bars centerd.
If the runway is touched during a coupled go-around, disconnect the autopilot and fly the rest by hand.

With an engine failed, level at 1,000 ft AGL, retract on schedule, select MCT and IAS HOLD and climb at the 0/EXT minimum maneuvering speed. Do not use the autopilot in CMD for a two-engine missed approach.

blocks.content: The PF announces the go-around and commands "Go-around power" and "Flaps 22"; the PF advances the throttles to about go-around thrust and presses TO/GA. The PNF sets the flaps; the flight engineer refines the thrust and disarms the spoilers. With the autopilot engaged, the PF checks it rolls the wings level and pitches to hold at least the approach speed (V2 + 10 kt on three engines); flying by hand, the PF rotates to center the pitch bar. At a positive rate on the TVSI, radio altimeter and altimeter: "Positive rate of climb, gear up"; the PNF confirms it and raises the gear. Fly the missed approach, holding the go-around speed with pitch and power; at the missed approach altitude, or clear of obstacles, lower the nose and retract the flaps above the flap retraction speed and the slats above the slat retraction speed. With obstacle clearance not a factor they may come up during the climb, provided the aircraft is accelerating past the retraction speeds and climbing faster than the procedure requires.

items: The flaps must be out of UP for the go-around mode; TO/GA switches the thrust computer to GA.
The maximum pitch in the flight director or autopilot go-around mode is 15°.
Do not use the autopilot for a go-around with an engine out; the flight director commands V2 on two engines.
The KC-10 has no autoland, so the vertical speed wheel also stays available for a go-around.

Push the GA switch and advance the throttles to go-around thrust. At the same time raise the pitch to the flight director's command, or watch the autopilot do it, to establish the climb and speed (15° nose up at most), and select flaps 22.
At a positive rate of climb, gear up; check the missed approach altitude, heading and speed are selected.
Follow the missed approach in heading select or NAV.
Hold the commanded speed to the clearance altitude: Vmin + 5 for flaps 22, or the speed when GA was pushed if that was higher. The altitude capture ends the go-around pitch mode.

blocks.content: The GA switch works below 2,500 ft radio altitude with the flaps or slats out, and is the only way out of DUAL LAND, SINGLE LAND or a dual-director APPR ONLY below 1,500 ft. If the ground spoilers have deployed on main wheel spin-up, the autothrottle will not advance the No. 2 throttle: advance all three by hand. See [Go-around](automatic-flight#toga-md10).

A **rejected landing** is discontinued at low height before touchdown: fly it exactly as the TOGA go-around (DC-10: the FMA should show N1, ALT, G/A, G/A). If the runway is touched, disconnect the autopilot and fly by hand.

A **balked landing** begins after touchdown but before the reversers are selected. Disconnect the autothrottle (with the ground spoilers deployed it will not advance the No. 2 throttle) and the autopilot, advance the throttles to go-around thrust, press TO/GA and call "Go-around, max power, flaps 22". The PM selects flaps 22 and makes sure the spoilers retract (they retract as the No. 2 throttle advances; if not, the PM retracts them by hand); the second officer backs up the spoiler retraction. At VREF - 10 rotate at 2.5 to 3° per second to about 15°. If the nose wheel was already on the runway, TO/GA gives TAKEOFF (22° maximum) rather than G/A (15°). Positive rate, gear up, and the normal missed approach calls; the speed settles near VAPP + 10.

items: With the ground spoilers extended, do not advance the throttles until the nose wheel is on the runway: the pitch-down as they retract can drop the nose hard.
Expect a slow and uneven spool-up from ground idle to go-around N1, 6 seconds or more; the ENGINE FAIL lights may flash.
The takeoff warning horn may sound for a moment while the flaps, spoilers and trim are moving.
An armed autobrake disarms as the spoilers retract (in the simulation the retraction only releases the brakes; advancing throttle 1 or 3 on the ground disarms it).
After an autoland's nose wheel touchdown, TO/GA is ignored until the autopilot is disconnected.

blocks.content: In the pattern (repeated approaches, touch-and-goes or full stop taxi-backs) every phase of a flight comes round every few minutes. Every crewmember must know before each approach whether it will end in a full stop, a touch-and-go or a go-around. Reverse thrust is never used on a touch-and-go: once a reverse lever leaves its stowed position, the landing becomes a full stop.

The local pattern checklists replace the Descent, Approach, Before Landing and Before Takeoff checklists for a series of approaches. If the normal After Takeoff/Climb checklist was done, the normal sequence is used for the first landing, and the pattern checklists after it; after the last landing, the normal After Landing and Parking checklists. **Full Stop Taxi Back** serves as both After Landing and Before Takeoff (done to the line before taking the runway); **Downwind** is done on the downwind leg or its equivalent; **Before Landing** is unchanged.

blocks.title: FULL STOP TAXI BACK (BELOW THE LINE)

items: **Landing data (Downwind 1).** Recomputed for the weather and for every 20,000 lb change in gross weight.
**Crew briefing (Downwind 2).** The type of approach, the missed approach, any simulated emergencies.
**Seat belt switch (Downwind 8).** AUTO.

blocks.content: The KC-10 manual's touch-and-go is flown normally to the touchdown. In training the pilot in command may choose not to arm the spoilers, but they are normally left in automatic to show their pitch effect as they extend and retract. The pilot in command briefs the calls, duties and the go-around and abort actions beforehand.

blocks.title: Touch-and-go duties (KC-10)
rows: At main gear touchdown keeps control and lowers the nose wheel smoothly but positively; disconnects the autothrottle if used. When ready: "Flaps 22, check trim in the green."
On command selects flaps 22 and resets the stabilizer trim in the green band if needed; checks the autothrottle disconnected.
After nose wheel touchdown confirms all three engines running, the flap handle and trim set and the autothrottle off.
When the configuration is confirmed: "Push them up" (or taps the PF's hand).
Advances the throttles to about the 12 o'clock position and lets the engines stabilize.
Checks the spoiler handle back at RET (it resets with an audible sound as the throttles go up) and the three engines accelerating together.
Makes sure the spoiler handle returns to RET.
On the commander's "Set takeoff power", advances to takeoff thrust.
Sets and refines the thrust (about 100% N1, up to go-around N1 if the runway or the conditions need it): "Power set."
Pushes TO/GA and rotates at no less than the salmon bug speed, to center the pitch bar or to climb at the threshold speed plus additives.
"Rotate" as the speed passes the salmon bug.

items: With the ground spoilers out, do not advance the thrust until the nose wheel is on the runway.
TO/GA pushed with both nose and main wheels on the runway gives TAKEOFF in pitch and roll (22° maximum); with the nose wheel off the runway, or too early for the ground sensing, GA (15° maximum).
The takeoff warning horn may sound for a moment while the flaps, slats and spoilers are still moving; following the sequence avoids it.
General Electric's preferred technique is to let the engines stabilize at the 12 o'clock position before taking them to touch-and-go thrust.
DC-10: FedEx's book has no local pattern checklists. After each go-around or touch-and-go, run the After Takeoff checklist, and on the next circuit the Approach and Before Landing checklists.

blocks.content: Between multiple approaches the MD-10 crew do, on the downwind leg, the checklist items the FCOM marks **: from After Takeoff the gear and lights, the spoiler handle and the autobrake; from Descent/Approach the landing data, the DH or MDA and the altimeters. The After Landing checklist waits until a taxi-back's 180° turn is finished.

items: The armed ground spoilers deploy automatically, straight to full extension: above 45 kt of wheel speed, on spin-up with flaps 30 or more and the wheels below about 7 ft, or on the ground with less flap as soon as two throttles are at idle or in reverse (no reverse is needed); and on the ground with two reversers selected if the wheels have not spun up. Moving the handle or advancing the No. 2 throttle releases them. The AUTO SPOILER DO NOT USE light and its 8-second timer are modeled on the DC-10 and KC-10; the MD-10 has neither.
The reversers latch only with the gear down and can be raised only from idle; the No. 2 reverser does not deploy until the nose strut is compressed.
The anti-skid TEST button does nothing in the simulation; the Before Landing item is answered without the test.

On the DC-10 and KC-10, TO/GA pressed on the runway selects TAKE OFF as soon as the main gear is on the ground (the books: once the nose wheel is down), even in an autoland's ROLL OUT with the autopilot still engaged. Disconnect the autopilot and autothrottle first, as the balked landing procedure says.
The autothrottle is not stopped from advancing the No. 2 throttle after the ground spoilers deploy; advance the throttles by hand on a balked landing all the same.
The autobrake is fitted to every DC-10 in the simulation; the KC-10 and the simulated MD-10 have none.
There is no engine cool-down or warm-up enforcement: the times are crew discipline.

parts.title: After Landing and Shutdown
parts.summary: The After Landing checklist, shutting down No. 2 for the taxi-in, parking and engine shutdown, and leaving the aircraft secured.

blocks.content: After the landing roll the aircraft is cleaned up for the taxi: the spoilers stowed, the flaps and slats retracted, the lights and radar set for the ground, and the APU started for the gate. At the gate the engines are shut down on ground power or the APU, the systems are left in their parked configuration, and the aircraft is secured: chocked, its brakes released, its covers on and, if it will stand, its power off.

At the end of the landing roll, slowed to a safe taxi speed, the captain calls for the After Landing checklist. It is silent: the first officer and the second officer do their flows, the second officer reads the checklist silently, checks every action, challenges aloud any item not done, and announces "After Landing checklist complete".

blocks.title: After landing flows
rows: Brake temperature indicator and OVHT lights

items: **Lights.** As required for the taxi: the landing lights off, the nose light at TAXI, the high intensity lights off; the logo lights stay on.
**Flaps and slats.** Handle UP, and the surfaces checked up and the slats retracted, not just the handle moved.
**Radar.** FedEx's "Off & Test": TEST selected with the indicators unpowered. The antenna is not switched OFF while the aircraft is moving.
**Transponder.** STBY, or left on if the airport's ground operations require it.
**Stabilizer trim.** 2° ANU, which closes an opening in the fuselage beside the stabilizer and keeps water and debris out of the stabilizer drive.
**Outflow valve.** Fully open. One pack stays on until the Shut Down checklist is done.
**APU.** As required: not used if the gate has external power, but its door may be opened in case it is needed.
**Brake temperatures.** The gauge normal, the OVHT and DIFF TEMP lights out.
**Engine limit pointers.** Within limits (and the digital EGT's recall light out); an exceedance is written up.

blocks.content: The pilot taxiing makes sure the aircraft is clear of the active runway before the After Landing checklist is started.

items: **IFF/WX radar (1).** The IFF to OFF, or to STBY for a through flight; the radar to STBY. The radar antenna can be damaged if it is switched OFF while the aircraft is moving.
**APU (2).** As required: started, and all APU GEN BUS switches ON.

**Anti-ice (4).** WING ANTI-ICE OFF, its DISAGREE lights out; ENG & ANT ANTI-ICE OFF, the engine DISAGREE lights cycling. With TAT below 6 °C and visible moisture, leave the engine anti-ice on until the engines are shut down.
**Spoilers (5).** The top of the handle hit down: RET, the spoiler positions DN.
**Flaps/slats (6).** UP/RET, the flaps up and the slat light out. After an approach in icing, or a landing on snow or slush, 22/EXT instead (the slat TAKEOFF light on).
**Trim (7).** 2° nose up on the LONG TRIM indicator.

**Hydraulic system (8).** Motor pump switches OFF (leave 1-3 or 2-3 armed if that system is being powered by it, to keep full steering and both brake systems). Left engine pumps OFF: the right pumps alone must hold each system; left pumps ON. Right pumps OFF: the left pumps alone; right pumps AUTO. Write up any pump that does not give at least 2,800 psi; a takeoff is permitted if either pump in a system gives 2,800 psi.
**Number 2 fuel lever (9).** See [Two-engine taxi-in](#two-engine-taxi-in).

**Brake pressure and temperature (10).** Both brake systems in the white band, the OVHT lights out and the temperature normal. One brake system alone brakes adequately. After heavy braking, forecast the peak brake energy from the chart; at 400 °C or an OVHT light, the abnormal brake procedure. The flight engineer reports the brake pressure and temperature when taxiing in congested areas.

blocks.content: Clear of the runway (after the 180° turn on a taxi-back), the first officer does the after landing flow and reads the After Landing checklist.

items.action: UP/RET (22 or more after an approach in icing, or with snow or slush on the runway)
NOSE LT to TAXI; HI-INT OFF; wing and runway turnoff and LDG LTs as required
OFF at the captain's discretion (throttle at idle first)

blocks.content: **Autobrake.** Not installed in the simulated MD-10. **APU.** The first officer pushes APU START/STOP and, once it is on speed, APU PWR so the APU can take the buses at shutdown.

If the thrust is not needed for the taxi, No. 2 may be shut down after the After Landing checklist, at the captain's decision. Consider the weight and the thrust the taxi will need: above 40% N1 and below 15 kt the wing engines' inlet vortex can lift debris, and their blast must be kept off people and equipment. Do not shut No. 2 down for the taxi with a hydraulic or engine-driven generator abnormality.

**Cool-down.** Run the engine at or near idle for at least 3 minutes before shutting it down, timed from when the reversers stow; taxi power, including short bursts, counts as idle. It may be shut down 1 minute after the landing roll if the EGT stayed below 650 °C from the outer marker to the flare and below 750 °C in reverse (or reverse was not used, or held at reverse idle).

items.item: No. 2 engine fuel lever (after the captain confirms)
No. 2 tank pump switches (if the APU will not be used)

items: The procedure is also used to shut No. 2 down during a long taxi-out or a delay; it is then restarted with the Delayed Engine Start procedure (see [Delayed number 2 start](normal-engine-start#delayed-engine-start)).
Before the fuel lever goes off, check the engine max pointers within limits (an exceedance is written up). After shutdown the fuel flow indicator may show a spurious flow.
The Virtual Crew does not run this procedure on the DC-10: do it yourself.

If the pilot decides to shut No. 2 down, the flight engineer moves the No. 2 FUEL lever to OFF and watches the EGT and fuel flow fall. If the fuel lever does not shut the fuel off at the engine, pulling the engine fire handle closes the shutoff valve at the tank.

With every APU GEN BUS switch ON, the APU must take bus 2 as the No. 2 generator drops off: AC BUS 2 OFF stays out and the AC BUS TIE 2 ISOL light comes on. If the APU does not pick up bus 2, power the generator buses from the APU or ground power before shutting all the engines down. With no APU, the AC tie bus powers generator bus 2 automatically.
All tank 2 pumps OFF except one for the APU (the right aft pump preferred); the No. 2 fuel pressure stays in the normal range.
The Virtual Crew's flight engineer, when on, asks "Shut down No. 2 engine?" at this item and does it on your yes.

blocks.content: At the captain's discretion, confirm the No. 2 throttle at idle and move the engine 2 FUEL lever to OFF; watch the EGT and fuel flow fall on the EAD. On narrow or contaminated taxiways use reduced power on the wing engines where possible.

At the gate, set the parking brake and keep it set until the ground crew confirm the chocks are in. Before the engines are shut down, ground power or the APU must be carrying the buses, or the aircraft goes to battery power as the generators drop off. The engines have their cool-down (see [Two-engine taxi-in](#two-engine-taxi-in)). The beacon goes off once the engines have run down: it is the ground crew's signal that it is safe to approach.

blocks.title: Shutdown flows
rows: Digital EGT memory, engine limit pointers
Lav and galley vent, cargo heat
Cargo vents, cargo fire and smoke detection, water system

items.item: Dig EGT Memory & Eng Limit Pointers

items: **Parking brake.** Set at block-in and not released until maintenance or the ramp crew confirm the chocks are in (by interphone or in person).
**Fuel levers.** OFF after the cool-down. If no external power is available and an engine must provide power, keep No. 2 running (its generator) and shut down Nos. 1 and 3.
**INS.** Checked (drift rate and residual ground speed) and off.

**Digital EGT memory and limit pointers.** Press the overtemp recall: any stored overtemperature is recorded and reported (only maintenance can clear it); reset the max pointers if a power transfer moved them.
**Debrief.** After each block-in, in the cockpit or another private place.

**Cabin doors (silent).** Disarmed only at the final parking spot, never one armed and the other disarmed. A door may be opened no more than 8 inches until the stairs are in place, to show the aircraft is depressurized.
**Hydraulic panel (silent).** Engine pumps L ON and R AUTO, rudder standby power OFF, the RMPs OFF.

**APU, fuel pumps, pneumatics (silent).** The APU as required; with the APU running a tank 2 aft pump (the right one) on and fuel pressure in system 2, the others off; the supplies and packs and the APU/ISOL valve as required for the gate; both isolation valves NORM.
**Crew oxygen (silent).** The selector left on the bottle with the lowest quantity; below 1,610 psi, check that bottle against the pressure-temperature chart.
**Trim air, lav and galley vent, cargo vents, cargo fire and smoke detection, water (silent).** Off; the water system depressurized.
**CVR circuit breaker (silent).** Pulled only after an accident, incident or other reportable event, to preserve the recording.

**Parking brakes (1).** Both brake pressures in the white band; push and hold the pedals, pull the PARK BRAKE handle aft, release the pedals: the pedals stay down, the handle stays aft, the PARK BRAKE ON and PARK lights on. If they release, set them again.
**Aux hydraulic pump (2).** If chocks are not readily available, start at least one aux pump to keep brake pressure.
**Electrical power (3).** APU PWR AVAIL on and the APU GEN BUS switches ON; or the EXT PWR switch to EXT PWR with the AC BUS TIE switches in NORM; the AC and DC BUS OFF lights stay out.
**Fuel levers (4).** OFF; the EGT and fuel flow fall.
**Exterior lights (5).** All off and the beacon OFF; the nav lights may stay on for safety during parking or maintenance.
**Fuel panel (6).** All pumps off (flow lights out, pressures to zero), except one tank 2 pump if the APU is running.
**Cabin doors (7A).** The boom operator disarms the slides before a door is opened.

items.action: Coordinated before shutdown and brake release
APU or ground power available before shutdown
OFF; EGT and fuel flow falling
NOSE OFF, LDG RET, WING & RUNWAY TURNOFF off, BCN OFF; logo and nav as required
AUTO (MANUAL: pumps off, transfer pumps off, crossfeeds closed)
APU BLEED out (APU air), 1-2 and 1-3 ISOL ON, PACKs ON; zone temperatures as required
Released once the chocks are confirmed in (press and release the pedals)
OFF if leaving the aircraft or changing crews

items: **Anti-skid.** The MD-10's anti-skid is an analog system and is switched off after every flight: left armed, it shortens the unit's life.

**Air conditioning at the gate.** Before conditioned air is connected, make sure the cabin pressure controller is in AUTO and the outflow valve open. With an external air source, the supplemental procedures apply.
**Tip-over.** The aircraft can tip onto its tail if the forward cargo is unloaded with the zero fuel weight CG near its aft limit.

blocks.content: If the aircraft will stand, it is left chocked with the parking brake released (a parked aircraft is not left on its brakes alone), the covers on, and its power off unless maintenance or the next crew want it. On the ramp, the chocks and the pitot and engine covers come from the EFB's Ground Ops app; see [Leaving the aircraft](ground-operations#leaving-the-aircraft).

FedEx's card ends at Shut Down; the EFB adds a Leaving Aircraft checklist in the order that keeps the aircraft safe: the chocks in first, then the parking brake released, then the covers, and the power off last.

items: **APU.** APU/ISOL valve closed, master switch OFF and its fuel pump off. The real APU runs on for 90 seconds to cool after the APU/ISOL valve closes (the simulated one stops at once). Turn off the tank 2 pump that fed it once it has stopped.
**External power, battery.** EXT PWR off, then the battery off once nothing else needs power.

The Virtual Crew's second officer, when on, puts the chocks in through Ground Ops, releases the brake only with them in and nothing running, puts the covers on and shuts the APU, external power and battery down.
**INUs (2).** Checked and off.
**WX radar (3).** OFF now that the aircraft is stopped.
**IFF, FMS, CDUs, crypto, SATCOM (4, 5, 8, 9, 18, 22).** Off, zeroized, secured or removed as the unit requires.
**Oxygen regulators (6).** OFF.
**Emergency lights (11).** As required.
**Windshield anti-ice and defog, pitot heat, engine anti-ice, anti-skid, aux pumps, cabin cargo smoke (12 to 17).** Off.

**APU (20).** As required: APU/ISOL valve to CLOSE, master OFF; the real APU runs on for 90 seconds to cool (the simulated one stops at once); then the pump that fed it and the APU GEN BUS switches off.
**Battery (21).** As required.
**Exterior walkaround (23).** Completed: the aircraft secure, the covers on, the chocks in.

blocks.content: The alert force's Power Off Cocking and Scramble checklists are in [Normal checklists](normal-checklists#kc10-non-standard).

items: **EMER LT.** OFF.

**APU (if not required).** The APU BLEED pushed in (USE ENG AIR), the isolation valves off (ON legends out) and the operating packs off (OFF legends lit); then push APU START/STOP for the cooling run and shutdown (the simulated APU has no cooling run).
**BAT.** If the aircraft is to be depowered: check the APU has shut down, raise the guard and push BAT.

The engine cool-down before shutdown is crew discipline: the simulation does not time it or penalize a hot shutdown. The APU has no cooling run either: it stops within a few seconds of being switched off.

With the Virtual Crew on, the DC-10's second officer starts the APU after landing unless a ground power unit is connected, and puts its power on the buses; the KC-10's flight engineer does the same. The MD-10's first officer starts the APU at After Landing.
The DC-10's two-engine taxi-in is not part of the EFB's card or the Virtual Crew's run; the KC-10's flight engineer offers it at After Landing.
The DC-10 Virtual Crew's first officer sets the radar to STBY at After Landing rather than the TEST position on FedEx's card.
The anti-skid OFF at shutdown matters on the real MD-10's analog unit; in the simulation it simply disarms the anti-skid.

blocks.content: For transition training: Full Stop Taxi Back after a full-stop landing, Downwind on each downwind leg, and the pattern Before Landing on each approach. Their use is described in [Local pattern](normal-landing#local-pattern).

blocks.title: FULL STOP TAXI BACK (BELOW THE LINE)

blocks.content:
A KC-10 on ground alert is **cocked**: preflighted by the crew with the normal checklists and scan patterns, then left ready for a scramble. Cocking is a coordinated effort, and the crew stays at the aircraft until the aircraft commander judges it complete. A cocked aircraft may instead be held at constant readiness with the crew on cockpit alert and power kept on from the APU or a ground cart.

The crew's preflight stays valid for 48 hours, or until the maintenance preflight expires if that is sooner. If the aircraft has to be uncocked for maintenance, the crew cock it again with the normal preflight checklists. To release it from alert, the crew run the After Landing, Parking and Leaving Aircraft checklists before handing it to maintenance.

items: **Pack function selectors (5).** Held at MAN HOT until the ram air doors have closed, then OFF.
**Aircraft forms (11).** The time the preflight was completed, with each preflight crewmember's name and position.
**Hatches, windows and doors (12).** If no stairs or stand are available, the ladder may be left installed with door 1L closed.

blocks.content: **Scramble.** On an alert notice the flight engineer runs the Scramble checklist and confirms each action; the crew chief may do the starred items. Then the crew run every normal checklist from Cockpit Preparation on. Responses of "Not applicable" or "Not required" may be given to items the scramble has already covered.

items: **Before electrical power (3).** After fuel servicing, the center accessory compartment must have been checked for leaks before power is first applied.
**MSUs (10).** Get them to NAV first: the alignment can take up to 15 minutes, and is the longest item before taxi.
**Codes (12).** May be loaded after takeoff.
**Boom pressurization (13 to 15).** The flight engineer and boom operator coordinate so the boom's hydraulics are pressurized for its 2 minutes.
**Cabin doors (19).** If the engines are started before door 1L is closed, the ladder is removed and every door closed and armed before taxi; the taxi is not delayed to stow the ladder.

parts.title: Techniques
parts.summary: Standard callouts, use of automation, thrust management, takeoff and landing technique, and taxiing a long, high-cockpit wide-body.

blocks.content: The procedures in this section say what is done and by whom. This part says how: the words the crew use, how the automation is shared between the pilots, how thrust is set and protected, and the handling technique the aircraft's size and geometry call for on the runway and the taxiway. Most of it comes from the operators' training material: FedEx's for the DC-10 and MD-10, the Air Force's for the KC-10. Where they differ, each is given for its own flight deck.

Standard callouts let each pilot know, without looking, that a task is done or a point has been reached, and they make a missing call an alarm in itself. As a rule the PM announces what has happened ("Standard power set", "80 knots") and the PF acknowledges the calls that need it. The flight engineer listens to every call, watches the same instruments, and makes any call the PM misses. A call that is not made when expected is a prompt to look: a pilot who does not answer may be incapacitated.

**Transfer of control** is always spoken. On the DC-10 the pilot giving up control says "You have the airplane" and the other answers "I have the airplane". On the MD-10 the pilot taking control announces "I have the aircraft" once their hands are on the controls, and the other then takes up the PM duties. Whichever words are used, there must never be a moment when both pilots, or neither, think they are flying.
**Go-around** is called aloud by whoever starts it, on every flight deck: "Go-around". The go-around procedures are in [Go-around](normal-landing#go-around).

blocks.content: Visual cues are called as they appear ("Approach lights", "Runway"). FedEx's DC-10s carried a GPWS that spoke the radio height at 1,000, 500 and 100 ft and from 50 to 10 ft, so the pilots made none of those calls. **The simulated DC-10's standard GPWS has no voice** (see [GPWS fits](surveillance#gpws-fits)), so fly it as FedEx flew an aircraft whose voice callouts were inoperative: the PM calls 1,000 and 500 ft from the radio altimeter, and the flight engineer calls 50, 40, 30, 20 and 10 ft on every approach that ends in a manual landing (not on an autoland). With the voice option fitted the GPWS calls 500 and 100 ft and 50 to 10 ft itself, and MINIMUMS at the radio altimeter's decision height; the PM still calls 1,000 ft.

**Exception callouts.** On an automatic approach, any departure from the expected sequence is called the moment it is seen, so the captain can decide whether the approach can continue: "Single land", "Approach only", "No align", "No flare", "No rollout", "Below minimums", "Below alert height", and "Steer left" or "Steer right" on the rollout. The autoland sequence they refer to is in [DC-10 autoland](automatic-flight#autoland-dc10).

The KC-10's EGPWS speaks the radio height from 500 ft down and MINIMUMS at the decision height set on the captain's radio altimeter (see [GPWS](surveillance#gpws-fits)).

On the MD-10 the PNF repeats each of the PF's commands as it is carried out, so the command and its execution are both heard. After any ATC clearance the PF repeats the cleared altitude and clearance limit aloud.

blocks.content: The MD-10's EGPWS speaks the radio height from 500 ft down, and MINIMUMS when the captain's EIS control panel has radio minimums selected (see [GPWS](surveillance#gpws-fits)). The approach calls of the DC-10 table ("Stable" at 1,000 ft, "Approaching minimums", "Minimums") are good practice on the MD-10 too.

Every new altitude clearance is checked by both pilots, so that a wrong altitude in the preselector is caught before the aircraft flies to it. The pilot who did not set the altitude always confirms it and says it aloud.

PF, and checks ALT in the ARM window
Checks the setting against the clearance and says it aloud ("230, set and armed")
If the confirmation does not come
The setter points at the readout, then asks "Confirm altitude"

blocks.content: Any doubt about the clearance is resolved with ATC at once. On the MD-10 the same principle applies to the FCP altitude window: whoever sets it, the other pilot confirms it against the clearance.

The autopilot, flight director and autothrottle are there to reduce workload and improve precision, and the pilots are expected to choose the level of automation the situation calls for: the autopilot in busy terminal airspace and on demanding procedures, so that the PF can manage the flight and the PM is free of panel inputs; hand flying where traffic is light and the procedure simple, so that the skill stays fresh. Whatever is engaged, the PF remains responsible for the flight path. Automation invites complacency: the priorities do not change because a machine is flying.

**The FMA is the authority.** Every input to the flight guidance panel or FCP is confirmed on the flight mode annunciator, and the FMA is checked whenever a mode changes. If the autopilot does something unexpected, or you are not sure it is doing the right thing, disconnect it, stabilize the attitude, retrim, and then re-engage the other autopilot if you want one.

**Engine failure.** The autopilot may fly with an engine inoperative, but not until the aircraft has been trimmed for the asymmetry. After an engine failure on takeoff, engage it only once trimmed and at the clean maneuvering speed.
