Setting climb thrust after takeoff or go-around
Always the PM, whatever the autopilot status

items: The two flight director switches are used together: both on or both off (unless one is deferred).
The autothrottle is normally used in every phase; the PM makes the autothrottle and FGP inputs when climb thrust is set.
FedEx engages the autopilot no lower than 500 ft above the ground.
In IAS HOLD or MACH HOLD the autopilot holds speed with pitch, so in turbulence or with thrust changes the speed and attitude wander as it corrects. That is normal.
FedEx does not take off in control wheel steering.

blocks.content: How the modes fit together through a flight is described in [Automatic flight](automatic-flight#operation-dc-kc).

children.title: MD-10: flight control panel and MCDU

items: With the autopilot engaged the PF works the FCP. When the PF is hand flying the PNF makes the FCP inputs at the PF's direction, and the PF checks each one.
The PNF works the MCDU. Any entry that changes the flight profile is agreed by both pilots before it is inserted (*INSERT).
AUTO FLIGHT is called for at or above 200 ft (400 ft with NAV armed) and engages the autopilot in the speed, roll and pitch modes already active; PROF or LEVEL CHANGE becomes available above 400 ft.
With PROF and FMS speed the aircraft flies the vertical profile within the FCP altitude window: the window must be reset before every climb and descent.

blocks.content: How the MD-10's modes fit together through a flight is described in [Automatic flight](automatic-flight#operation-md10).

**Use reduced thrust whenever performance allows.** Most of an engine's wear happens while takeoff thrust is set, and the hotter it runs the faster it wears: one full-thrust takeoff on a one-hour sector wears the engine about as much as a reduced-thrust takeoff on a three-hour one. Most takeoff engine failures happen at full thrust, so reducing thrust also reduces the chance of the very failure the takeoff data protect against. Full thrust is used when the performance data or the conditions require it (see [Mission planning](mission-planning)).

**Set it before 80 kt, then leave it.** The computed thrust must be set by 80 kt; after that the throttles are not touched except to stop an engine exceeding a limit. A CF6 blooms after takeoff thrust is set: as its internals heat up, N1 rises 1 to 2% with a matching rise in EGT, and falls back shortly after lift-off as temperatures settle. Pulling the throttles back to recover the original N1 would leave the engine short of the thrust the takeoff data assumed.

**DC-10.** The PF advances the throttles to about takeoff thrust and calls for the power; the PM sets each engine exactly and calls it set. The flight engineer watches the engines and the annunciators through the roll. If an EGT is racing toward its acceleration limit, the engineer says "Engine ___ approaching overtemp, adjusting throttle" and trims that throttle back just enough; a captain who needs the thrust overrides by word or by hand. Momentary ENG FAIL lights as the engines spool up at different rates are normal. The DC-10-40's JT9D engines are set on EPR instead of N1. Only the -15 and -30 computers have the T.O. FLX mode that gives standard power from an assumed temperature; on the -10 and -40 the card's standard power N1 or EPR is set by hand (the -40 offers an alternate takeoff rating instead).

**KC-10.** By the end of the lineup the throttles are at flight idle (about 40 to 45% N1), so the engines spool up together and the computed performance is achieved. The PF then advances the throttles toward takeoff thrust, and the flight engineer sets the computed N1 and calls "Power set". The analog pointers are watched while thrust is first set, the digital readouts for the fine adjustment. N1 may drift down slightly after about 2 minutes at takeoff thrust. A little oil quantity is lost at takeoff thrust and returns as thrust is reduced.

**MD-10.** The PF sets about 70% N1, checks the engines symmetrical and calls "Auto flight"; the autothrottle advances to T/O THRUST and the PNF trims it and calls "Thrust set". From 80 kt the FMA shows T/O CLAMP and the throttles stay where they are. The PF keeps a hand on the throttles until V1.

**Climb and cruise.** Climb thrust is selected at the acceleration height (DC-10, KC-10: by the PM on the thrust rating computer; MD-10: automatically at the CLB THRUST altitude). Thrust is always set to the parameter, not to a throttle position: each engine is rigged a little differently, and the throttles may be staggered. The thrust ratings, the thrust rating computer and the limits are described in [Setting thrust](engines#setting-thrust).
The thrust rating computer's modes and how to set an assumed temperature are in [Thrust rating computer](engines#thrust-rating-computer).
The MD-10's thrust limits are described in [MD-10 thrust limits](engines#md10-thrust-limits).

A **rolling takeoff** is begun without stopping: the aircraft is lined up at taxi speed and thrust is advanced as it rolls. A **static takeoff** is begun from a stop, with thrust run up against the brakes. Both are permitted, but the rolling takeoff is preferred: it uses less runway than a static takeoff made with a long, slow lineup, and it keeps the wing engines from ingesting debris while they are at high thrust and low speed. Line up on the centerline at normal taxi speed with the tiller, then change to the rudder pedals for the rest of the takeoff and move the left hand to the control wheel. Where there are centerline lights, offset slightly so the nose wheels do not run along them.

Start the roll with the control wheel slightly forward of neutral to keep the nose wheels firmly on the runway, and track the centerline with the pedals and rudder. The captain keeps a hand on the throttles until V1, ready to reject.

**DC-10-30.** The CF6-50C2 swallows so much air at high thrust that, at very low speed, a crosswind disturbing the flow into the inlet can stall its compressor. A static takeoff, where full thrust meets the wind before the aircraft is moving, is the worst case. FedEx therefore permits a static takeoff on the DC-10-30 only with the wind within 45° of the runway heading and a crosswind component of 23 kt or less; outside that, the takeoff must be rolling or made from another runway. A rolling takeoff is permitted at any time within the crosswind limit. The DC-10-10 has no such restriction. See [Limitations](limitations).

Take care with a rolling takeoff on a wet or icy runway: with high thrust the nose wheel steering may not be able to line the aircraft up. If the **takeoff warning** sounds as the throttles come up, reject the takeoff (unless the captain judges continuing safer), and find and correct the cause before trying again. Its conditions are in [Takeoff warning](warning-systems#takeoff-warning).

Takeoff performance depends on rotating at the right speed, at the right rate, to the right attitude. The PF checks VR on their own airspeed indicator rather than waiting for the call. Just before VR, ease the control wheel back to neutral so the rotation itself is a short, smooth movement; at "Rotate" pitch up in one continuous motion to the initial climb attitude. Lift-off comes at about 10° of pitch, depending on weight. Hold the initial attitude until the flight director's pitch bar is valid, then follow it, cross-checking the airspeed; do not rotate into the bar before it has settled, and do not chase the speed.

blocks.title: Rotation
rows: 2.5 to 3° per second, about 6 seconds from VR to the climb attitude
About 15°, giving V2 + 10 kt on three engines (V2 on two)
The attitude that holds V2 + 10 kt (V2 on two engines); the takeoff mode commands no more than 22°
V2 + 10 kt at 35 ft; not normally more than 22° nose up

blocks.content: **Tail strikes.** Rotated at the correct rate, the DC-10 has ample tail clearance. A tail strike comes from rotating too early or too fast: the attitude increases faster than the lift can build, and the tail reaches the runway before the aircraft has started to climb. A slow or late rotation is the opposite error: it costs runway. Bank is limited to 15° until the aircraft reaches its minimum maneuvering speed.

The geometry of the DC-10's landing gear and tail makes it weathervane strongly into a crosswind on the ground. Expect it, and correct at once with rudder. The upwind wing tends to rise as the roll begins: hold it level with aileron into the wind, applied as needed or set before the roll starts, and take it off progressively as the speed builds. Avoid large wheel oscillations, and do not swing between neutral and the correction. The result is a crossed-control takeoff: hold the wheel displaced through rotation to keep the wings level at lift-off, then recover gently from the sideslip once airborne.

The pilots sit high and far ahead of the main gear, and the aircraft lands nose high. The eye therefore crosses the threshold well above the wheels, and the wheels lag behind the point the pilot is looking at. A landing judged by eye alone tends to touch down short on an ILS and long after a float. The cure is to know the geometry, to aim at a fixed point, to flare little, and to let the radio altimeter (which reads the main wheels' height) and the callouts tell you the height.

blocks.alt: Side-view schematic of a DC-10 on a 3° approach crossing a runway threshold. Show three heights at the threshold, labeled: pilot's eye (highest), glideslope antenna (7 ft below the eye), main gear (lowest, about 30 ft below the antenna). Draw the ILS glideslope from a transmitter 1,000 ft past the threshold and the no-flare main gear touchdown point about 400 ft past the threshold. Below it, a second strip for a visual approach: aim point 1,500 ft past the threshold, eye about 80 ft and main gear about 40 ft above the threshold, no-flare touchdown about 800 ft in. Flat engineering-drawing style, labels in feet.
blocks.title: Eye, antenna and wheel heights at the threshold
Heights at the threshold and no-flare touchdown, DC-10-10 and -30, flaps 35, 3° path
rows: Glideslope antenna about 52 ft (the eye about 7 ft higher)
About 400 to 450 ft past the threshold
Visual (aim point 1,500 ft past the threshold)
About 780 to 820 ft past the threshold

blocks.content: The ranges are for forward and aft CG. On a flatter path (2.5°) the gear crosses the ILS threshold about 8 ft lower and touches down about 100 ft earlier; flaps 50 changes the heights by only a few feet but flies about 1° flatter in attitude. The lesson of the ILS row: flown to the ground with no flare, an ILS puts the wheels down only a few hundred feet past the threshold, so the flare matters, and in the last 100 ft or so the PF's eyes belong on the touchdown zone, not on the glideslope needle. On a visual approach, pick an aim point about 1,500 ft beyond the threshold and hold it fixed in the windscreen: the wheels will touch down about half that distance in. Do not duck below the path to land earlier.

**MD-10.** On a visual approach, aim about 1,700 ft past the threshold on a 3° path: the wheels cross the threshold at about 47 ft and touch down, with no flare, about 900 ft in. Be stabilized by 1,000 ft above the field and go around if not stabilized by 500 ft; below 1,000 ft the descent rate should not exceed 1,000 ft/min.

**Flare and touchdown.** The flare is small: about 2° of pitch, started at 30 to 40 ft, with the throttles closing from 50 ft. Do not trim in the flare and do not hold the aircraft off for a smooth landing; floating uses runway, ends in a higher attitude with less tail clearance, and leaves heavier braking to do. A firm touchdown in the zone, slightly below VREF, is the aim. Below about 10 ft, fully flared and sinking 2 to 4 ft/s, the basic technique is simply to hold the attitude; the more advanced one is to start lowering the nose by about 1° just before the mains touch.

**After touchdown** fly the nose wheel onto the runway without delay: holding the nose up for aerodynamic braking does nothing useful on this aircraft and costs tail clearance. Counter the pitch-up as the ground spoilers deploy, most noticeable at an aft CG, and keep forward pressure on the column for nose wheel steering. Reverse thrust may be selected at once and does most good at high speed; below 80 kt it adds little. The numbers and the deceleration sequence are in [Spoilers, reversers and brakes](normal-landing#spoilers-reversers-brakes), and the crosswind technique in [Crosswind landing](normal-landing#crosswind-landing).

The tail contacts the runway at about 13° of pitch with the struts compressed (MD-10). A high flare, a float or a bounce brings it close; large, quick pitch inputs just before touchdown can strike the tail or damage the nose gear.

Taxiing a DC-10 is much like taxiing any heavy jet, with three things to respect: the jet blast and the inlet suction of three large engines, the distance between the pilots and the wheels, and the height of the cockpit, which makes the aircraft feel slower than it is. In congested areas taxiing needs the whole crew's attention and close coordination with the ground crew.

items: To break away, release the brakes and smoothly add thrust; about 40% N1 should be enough. Then wait for the aircraft to respond before adding more. The common error is to keep adding thrust until it moves, which gives far more than needed.

Cold tires need about twice the thrust of warm ones to break away. Starting in a turn needs considerably more, and a hard turn can stall the aircraft, which then needs excessive thrust to restart: if a turn follows the breakaway, carry enough speed into it.
At light and medium weights idle thrust on three engines is more than enough, and may accelerate the aircraft. At high weights a little more than idle may be needed for short periods.

Do not exceed 40% N1 in congested areas. If 40% will not move the aircraft from a tight gate where jet blast could do damage, close the throttles and ask for a tow or for the area behind to be confirmed clear.
Away from congestion, use all three engines together, up to about 40% N1: less thrust from each means less blast and less debris drawn into the wing engines' inlets.

If something is behind No. 2, taxi on Nos. 1 and 3. If small aircraft are behind, use No. 2 alone. On narrow or contaminated taxiways, or with the wing engines over unpaved ground, ice or sand, keep the wing engines low and take any thrust above 40% N1 from No. 2.
Never use reverse thrust to slow down on the ground or to back the aircraft.
Taxiing burns about 110 lb of fuel a minute.

blocks.content: If the aircraft runs off the paved surface, do not try to power it out. The wing engine on that side is over the unpaved ground and will ingest debris, and high thrust can damage the landing gear.

Brake intermittently, with time to cool between applications, and never ride the brakes: hot brakes stop less well and can seriously reduce what is left for a rejected takeoff. The brakes are very sensitive at light weights, so anticipate and apply them gently. The anti-skid becomes inactive below about 10 kt, so the last few knots of every stop are on unmodulated brakes (see [Anti-skid](landing-gear#anti-skid)). If you have to stop and hold during the taxi, set the parking brake: it is too easy to become absorbed in a cockpit task and let the aircraft creep. Asymmetric thrust and differential braking wear the tires and the gear, and are kept for when nothing else will do.

The tiller turns the nose wheels up to 68° each side; the rudder pedals give 10° each side for small corrections and the takeoff and landing roll, and the tiller overrides them (see [Nosewheel steering](landing-gear#nosewheel-steering)). Move the tiller smoothly and bring it back to center gently while keeping hold of it: it is spring-loaded to center, and released quickly or worked jerkily it makes the aircraft lurch. Abrupt steering, or turning too fast, on a wet or painted surface makes the nose wheels scrub sideways instead of turning the aircraft. Use the largest radius the taxiway allows, for the sake of the tires and the gear, and center the nose wheels before stopping, so the aircraft does not need extra thrust to start again.

blocks.title: Geometry, pilot to wheels
rows: Ground first visible over the nose

blocks.content: Because the wheels are so far behind, the cockpit must overshoot every turn. Keep the nose gear on the centerline on straight taxiways (it appears to be under the seat of the pilot taxiing). Going from one narrow taxiway to another, start the turn when the cockpit is about halfway between the centerline and the edge of the taxiway (the MD-10 book's guide: when the new taxiway's extended centerline passes under your seat), and for a turn of 90° or more apply full tiller as soon as the turn begins. During the turn the cockpit may swing as far out as the edge of the taxiway; the main gear will then track inside the centerline. The sharper the turn, the further you must overshoot. Turns of more than 90° need fillets between the taxiways.

blocks.alt: Plan-view schematic of a 90° turn from one 75 ft wide taxiway into another, DC-10 outline shown at three positions through the turn. Draw three paths in different line styles: the captain's eye path (overshooting toward the outer edge of the taxiway), the nose wheel track (21 ft behind the pilots) and the main gear track (93 ft behind, 40 ft wide, cutting inside). Mark the point to start the turn, with the cockpit halfway between the centerline and the taxiway edge. Labels in feet, flat schematic style.
blocks.title: Turning from one taxiway into another

blocks.content: **Turning radius.** The tightest turn recommended for routine use, with symmetrical idle thrust and no differential braking, needs about 145 ft of pavement for a 180° turn on the DC-10-10 and MD-10-10, and about 150 ft on the DC-10-30 and MD-10-30 (the KC-10 is built on the -30 airframe). Maximum tiller with asymmetric thrust and light differential braking can tighten it, but should be kept for the occasional case. The MD-10-30's center gear has no noticeable effect on the way it taxis.

From 20 ft up, the aircraft seems to move more slowly than it does, and the natural tendency is to taxi too fast. Check the ground speed on the navigation system's readout where there is one, and look out of the side window from time to time, especially when stopping. The limits below keep the tire sidewalls from flexing and heating excessively.

Slow down considerably on ice, snow or a wet surface. In reduced visibility, brief the taxi route and the airport diagram first, to anticipate the routing and the lighting and to avoid a runway incursion.

Look for another route before planning a 180° turn on a runway. When it must be done, a 150 ft runway is wide enough with the right technique: about 300 ft before the end of the runway, turn about 15° away from the runway heading toward one edge, continue until the cockpit is over that edge, then turn back across the runway with full tiller and symmetrical thrust, keeping the aircraft moving. Done this way the nose wheels keep about 20 ft from the far edge and the main gear more. Done badly, the width needed grows quickly. Watch for obstructions along the runway edge, and remember that the nose wheels tend to skid on wet paint.

blocks.alt: Plan-view schematic of a DC-10-30 turning 180° on a 150 ft wide runway near its end. Show the aircraft starting on the centerline, angling 15° toward the left edge from a point 300 ft before the runway end, the captain's position reaching the runway edge, then the full-tiller turn back across the runway. Draw the nose wheel and main gear tracks and label the remaining clearances to the far edge (nose wheel about 20 ft, main gear more than 20 ft). Flat schematic style, labels in feet.
blocks.title: 180° turn on a 150 ft runway

blocks.content: From the normal seat position, fixed points on the cockpit frame show where the aircraft's extremities will track when taxiing straight ahead. The MD-10 book gives the references below; the FedEx DC-10 book marks the same items (wing tips, engines, nose and main gear) on the same windshield frame. They hold only with the eye at the design position (if you move the viewpoint, they move with it), and not at all in a large turn.

rows: Sight left along the second screw from the bottom of the vertical frame between the captain's side windows
The lower left corner of the captain's windshield
The light sensor on the captain's glareshield, or the inside of the captain's right knee
The lower right corner of the captain's windshield

blocks.content: The first officer uses the mirror image, starting from the right side (the nose gear by the left knee).

blocks.alt: View from the captain's seat at the design eye position on a straight taxiway centerline, looking forward and slightly left, daylight. Overlay labeled markers on the cockpit frame: the lower left windshield corner (No. 1 engine track), the lower right windshield corner (No. 3 engine track), the captain's right knee area (nose gear track), and the side window frame (left wing tip track). Taxiway edge lines visible so the references can be compared with the pavement.
blocks.title: Captain's taxi references

blocks.content: Shutting No. 2 down for the taxi in saves fuel and wear, but the wing engines then carry all the thrust. Keep their N1 low where debris could be drawn in (above 40% N1 and below 15 kt the inlet vortex reaches the ground) and remember their blast is now stronger. At high weights, with a tight turn or an uphill slope, the wing engines alone may need more thrust than is comfortable: then keep No. 2 running.

The same applies to a taxi out with No. 2 not yet started. The procedures are in [Delayed number 2 start](normal-engine-start#delayed-engine-start) for the taxi out and [Two-engine taxi-in](normal-after-landing-and-shutdown#two-engine-taxi-in) for the taxi in.
On the MD-10 the engine 2 FUEL lever is closed after landing at the captain's discretion; see [Two-engine taxi-in](normal-after-landing-and-shutdown#two-engine-taxi-in).

items: The simulation does not speak the PM's speed or approach callouts. With the Virtual Crew in the first officer's seat, its "Positive rate. Gear up." appears as a text prompt on the EFB once the aircraft is 50 ft up and climbing, and you raise the gear.

The radio height and MINIMUMS callouts come from the GPWS where it has a voice: the KC-10, the MD-10, and a DC-10 with the voice option. The standard DC-10 has none (see [GPWS fits](surveillance#gpws-fits)).
The visual references are for the design eye position. If you fly from a different viewpoint, recalibrate them on a straight taxiway before relying on them.

chapters.title: Performance and Mission Planning
chapters.summary: Weight and balance, takeoff, en-route and landing performance, fuel planning, and planning a flight in the simulation from the load sheet to the takeoff card.

blocks.content: This section is the aircraft's performance manual and loading manual brought together and adapted to the simulator. It explains how the aircraft is weighed and balanced, how its takeoff, climb, cruise, holding, descent and landing performance is worked out, how much fuel a flight needs, and how to plan a complete flight in the simulation, from the load sheet to the takeoff card. It corresponds to Section V of the KC-10's flight manual (Mission Preparation) with its performance volume, T.O. 1C-10(K)A-1-1, to chapters 5 and 6 of FedEx's DC-10 flight manual (Performance, Weight and Balance), and to the performance chapter of the MD-10 operating manual.

Two ideas run through all of it. The first is that **performance is a set of limits**, each protecting the aircraft against a specific failure: an engine failing at the worst moment of the takeoff roll, a stop on a wet runway, an obstacle in the climb-out path, a missed approach on two engines, a hold that lasts longer than planned. The weight a flight may carry is the lowest of those limits, and much of planning is finding which one governs today. The second is that **every number in this section comes from the aircraft's own books**: the EFB's Performance app evaluates their charts and tables exactly, and the tables printed here are read from the same data. None of them is derived from the simulator's flight model.

blocks.alt: Side-view profile diagram of a typical DC-10-30 freighter flight of 4,000 NM, distance along the bottom axis and pressure altitude up the side. From left: taxi (1,500 lb), takeoff allowance from brake release to 2,000 ft (2,500 lb, 8 NM), three-engine climb at 250 KIAS to 10,000 ft then 330 KIAS and Mach 0.82 to FL310 (top of climb 136 NM), cruise at Mach 0.82 at FL310, a 4,000 ft step climb to FL350 at about 1,390 NM and another to FL390 at about 3,600 NM, top of descent 130 NM from the destination, en route descent at Mach 0.82, 320 KIAS and 250 KIAS below 10,000 ft, approach and landing. A dashed branch after the destination shows the missed approach, the 200 NM flight to the alternate and a 30-minute hold at 1,500 ft. Labels give the fuel for each segment and the reserves (contingency, alternate, final reserve) as a stacked bar at the right.
blocks.title: A typical mission profile
blocks.caption: The worked example in Planning a flight in the simulation, drawn to scale. Fuel is planned backwards from the landing weight; the aircraft flies it forwards.

blocks.content: Planning follows the order in which each answer is needed by the next. The weight at the end of the flight decides how much fuel is needed to get there, the fuel decides the takeoff weight, the takeoff weight and the day decide the takeoff speeds and thrust, and the weight at each point of the cruise decides the best altitude to fly. The books therefore plan the fuel **backwards**, from the zero fuel weight and the reserves to the takeoff weight, and the crew then fly it forwards.

items: **Payload and zero fuel weight.** Add the payload (cargo, passengers, or for a tanker the offload fuel) to the basic operating weight and check the result against the maximum zero fuel weight and the zero fuel CG limits. See [Weight and balance](#weight-and-balance).

**Route and fuel.** Load the route, find the trip fuel and time for the planned speeds and altitudes, and add the reserves. See [Fuel planning](#fuel-planning) and [Climb, cruise and descent](#climb-cruise-descent).

**Weights and limits.** The zero fuel weight plus the takeoff fuel is the takeoff weight; less the trip fuel it is the landing weight. Check both against their structural limits, and the landing weight against the destination's landing performance. See [Landing performance](#landing-performance).
**Loading.** Load the fuel in the aircraft's schedule, then the cargo and passengers, and check the takeoff CG. See [Loading the aircraft with the EFB](#wb-loading-in-efb).

**Takeoff data.** With the actual weight, CG and the day's conditions, compute the takeoff card: the maximum weight for the runway, the flap setting, the thrust, the speeds and the stabilizer trim. See [Takeoff performance](#takeoff-performance) and [Takeoff data in the simulation](#efb-takeoff-data).
**Cockpit setup.** Set the speed bugs, the assumed temperature and the trim from the card, and brief the departure, the engine-out procedure and the emergency return.
**In flight.** Check the fuel against the plan, step climb as the weight comes off, plan the descent, and compute the landing data before the top of descent.

blocks.content: In the airline this work is shared: dispatch builds the flight plan and the fuel, the load control office builds the weight and balance, the flight engineer (second officer at FedEx) computes the takeoff data and the captain checks it. On the KC-10 the flight engineer computes all the performance data and coordinates the weight and balance with the boom operator, who is the aircraft's loadmaster. On the MD-10 the two pilots share it. In the simulation the EFB does the arithmetic of every step; the crew's work is to give it the right inputs and to understand what the answers mean.

children.title: The basis of the performance data

blocks.content: The DC-10 family was operated under two different rule books, and its performance data was written in two different ways. The **civil** aircraft, the DC-10 and MD-10, were certificated under FAR Part 25 and flown by airlines under FAR Part 121. Their takeoff and landing data are in the Airplane Flight Manual in the certification's own terms (balanced and unbalanced field lengths, a 35 ft screen height, net flight paths), and FedEx's crews computed them with a laptop program, the Airport Performance Laptop Computer, from the AFM's data and an airport database. The **military** KC-10A was operated by the US Air Force under its own flight manual and performance volume, T.O. 1C-10(K)A-1-1, whose takeoff data is built on the critical field length, a runway condition reading, and a reference engine-out climb gradient. Both describe the same physics; they draw the safety margins in different places.

blocks.title: Civil and military takeoff and landing criteria compared
rows: The greater of the distance to 35 ft with an engine failure recognized at V1, and 115 % of the all-engine distance to 35 ft; accelerate-stop distance not more than the runway plus stopway

Critical field length: accelerate on three engines to the critical engine failure speed, then either continue to liftoff on two engines or stop, in the same distance. Liftoff at the end of the critical field length
V1: the latest speed for the first action to stop; not less than VMCG nor more than VR or VMBE
V1: the higher of VCEF and VMCG, not more than VMBE
First segment at least 0.3 %, second segment at least 2.7 %, final segment at least 1.5 % (three-engine aircraft)
A reference gross gradient of at least 2.5 %, measured at the moment the gear is up
The net flight path (gross less 0.9 %) clears every obstacle in the departure fan by 35 ft
The climbout flight path chart gives the gross gradient needed to clear an obstacle at its height and distance from the liftoff point
Dry, wet or contaminated, with clutter limits
Runway condition reading (RCR) from 23 (dry) downward, and runway surface condition (RSC) for standing water or slush
The reported wind including gusts controls (FedEx)
50 % of a headwind and 150 % of a tailwind including gust; no headwind credit for takeoff except for mission accomplishment
The AFM distance from 50 ft at the threshold to a stop, multiplied by 1.67; FedEx's quick reference data use medium braking
Flare distance (with a 167 % factor) plus the ground roll at the runway's stopping distance ratio
FedEx's flight planning charts add 4 % for in-service deterioration; its cruise tables are unfactored book values
All fuel flows are 5 % above the engine specification

blocks.content: **What the simulation uses.** The only complete takeoff data available to the simulation is the KC-10's, so the EFB's Performance app computes the long-wing aircraft, the KC-10A, the DC-10-30 and the MD-10-30, from T.O. 1C-10(K)A-1-1. They share the long-span wing and the CF6-50C2 engines and fly at similar weights (590,000 lb for the KC-10, up to 580,000 lb for the heaviest -30s), so the charts describe their aerodynamics and thrust directly. The short-wing DC-10-10, MD-10-10 and DC-10-15 take their climb, cruise, holding, descent, approach and landing data, their stabilizer trim and (except the -15, whose engine is simulated with the CF6-50C2's ratings and takes the KC-10's N1) their takeoff N1 from FedEx's Series 10 performance chapter. FedEx computed its takeoff data only on the laptop, so no book gives a -10, -15 or -40 field length; for those aircraft the takeoff limits and speeds are read from the KC-10's charts at an equivalent condition. The DC-10-40 uses the KC-10's data with its own JT9D thrust ratings. The details are in [EFB: where the numbers come from](efb#performance-data).

The practical consequence is that a DC-10-30 or MD-10-30 in the simulation is dispatched by military criteria. The differences are small at normal weights, but they are real: the KC-10's V1 is a critical engine failure speed rather than a FAR 25 V1 chosen against a 35 ft screen, its obstacle method works from a single reference gradient, and its landing distances are those of a maximum-effort stop. Where this section quotes a civil figure (a FedEx speed schedule, a FAR 121 reserve, an MD-10 approach speed), it says so.

blocks.title: Simulation use only
blocks.content: The performance data in this section and in the EFB are for flight simulation. They are not approved data for any real aircraft and must not be used to plan a real flight.

sections.title: Weight and balance
sections.summary: The weights, the mean aerodynamic chord and the CG envelope, how a load moves the CG, and how the simulation and the EFB weigh the aircraft.

blocks.content: An airliner's weight decides almost every performance number it has, and where that weight sits decides whether the aircraft can be controlled at all. A DC-10 can carry more than half its takeoff weight as fuel and payload, and a freighter often operates close to its limits with heavy pallets that can be placed almost anywhere along a main deck well over 100 ft long. Weight and balance is therefore not paperwork: it is the first performance calculation of every flight, and FedEx's manual calls it the most critical of all the preflight tasks.

The calculation itself is simple statics. Every item aboard has a weight and an **arm**, its distance aft of a fixed reference plane; weight times arm is its **moment**. The aircraft's total weight is the sum of the weights, and its center of gravity is the sum of the moments divided by the total weight. Airline load sheets carry the moments as scaled **index** numbers so that crews can add small integers instead of millions of inch-pounds; a computer does the same sums directly. The answer is checked against two kinds of limit: structural weight limits, and a CG envelope that depends on the weight.

blocks.title: Weight terms
rows: The weighed empty aircraft plus everything it carries on every flight: the crew and their bags, manuals and navigation kits, unusable fuel, potable water, lavatory chemicals and galley supplies. FedEx's DC-10 BOW includes three crew members at 190 lb each. Also called dry operating weight. Every weight and balance calculation starts from it
What the flight is paid to carry: cargo, passengers and their baggage, and on a tanker the fuel it will give away
BOW plus payload, plus any ballast fuel, which is declared unusable and counted as part of the ZFW
ZFW plus all the fuel aboard at engine start
The weight at brake release: ramp weight less the fuel burned in taxi
TOGW less the trip fuel; at the destination it is the ZFW plus the reserves still aboard
The fuel aboard at brake release; the fuel burned from brake release to landing; the fuel that must remain at landing (see [Fuel planning](#fuel-planning))

blocks.content: Each structural weight limit protects a particular part of the structure. The **maximum taxi weight** is set by the landing gear, tires and pavement on the ground, and is a few thousand pounds above the takeoff limit to allow for the fuel burned in taxi. The **maximum takeoff weight** is the heaviest weight at which the structure has been shown to take the gust and maneuver loads of flight and the gear the loads of a rejected takeoff. The **maximum landing weight** is set by the landing gear: its design sink rate at touchdown is much higher at the landing limit than at the takeoff limit, and a landing above it takes energy the gear and the brakes were not designed to absorb. The **maximum in-flight weight with landing flaps** protects the flaps themselves.

The **maximum zero fuel weight** protects the wing. In flight the wing lifts the whole aircraft, and the weight it lifts is distributed along its span: fuel in the wing tanks sits close to where the lift is generated, so it bends the wing root very little, while everything in the fuselage hangs from the root. The heaviest load for the wing root is therefore the aircraft with full cabin and holds and empty wing tanks. Limiting the ZFW limits that bending moment, whatever the fuel; any weight above the MZFW must be fuel. This is also why the loading schedule fills the outer wing tanks first and empties them last.

blocks.title: Maximum weights, lb
rows: None stated; the CG envelope starts at 240,500

blocks.content: The -30 figures are three certification groups of the FedEx and MD-10 fleets, from the lightest to the heaviest. The DC-10-10 may land above 363,500 lb only with flaps 50, a brake energy limit. -30 takeoff weights above 555,000 lb need 28-ply or stronger tires on every main and center wheel. The DC-10-15 and DC-10-40 limits, and the limitations that go with all of these, are in [Limitations](limitations). The EFB's Performance app uses 440,000 lb (Series 10), 580,000 lb (Series 30) and 590,000 lb (KC-10) as the structural takeoff limits, and never shows a maximum takeoff weight above them.

Structural limits are not the only weight limits. On the civil aircraft the maximum zero fuel weight is also limited by performance: it may not exceed the lower of the approach-climb and landing-climb limiting weights at the departure field's conditions, less 42,300 lb of fuel that cannot be dumped. The reasoning is that an aircraft which must return immediately after takeoff can dump down to its ZFW plus that undumpable fuel, and must still be able to climb on two engines in the approach configuration from there. FedEx's laptop flagged this as a MAXIMUM ZFW message on hot, high days.

children.title: Center of gravity and the mean aerodynamic chord

blocks.content: Arms on the DC-10 family are measured in inches from **fuselage station 0**, a reference plane 239 in ahead of the nose, so that every station on the aircraft is a positive number. The nose gear stands at about FS 570 and the wing main gear at about FS 1481; the center gear (-30, -40, KC-10, MD-10-30) is about 7 in forward of the wing gear.

A CG expressed in inches says nothing about stability by itself, because what matters is where the CG sits relative to the wing's lift. It is therefore given as a percentage of the **mean aerodynamic chord** (MAC), the chord of an equivalent straight wing with the same area and the same aerodynamic properties. On the long-span wing the MAC is **295.8 in** long and its leading edge (**LEMAC**) is at **FS 1312.0**, so

CG (% MAC) = (CG station − 1312.0) ÷ 295.8 × 100

One per cent of MAC is about 3 in. The wing's aerodynamic center, about which its pitching moment does not change with angle of attack, lies near 25 % MAC, and the whole aircraft's neutral point, which includes the tail, lies further aft. The distance by which the CG lies ahead of the neutral point is the static margin, the measure of the aircraft's pitch stability.

The MAC length and LEMAC above are those of the -30 and KC-10 wing, from the KC-10's loading and weight and balance manuals. The -10 and -15 have the shorter-span wing, and their MAC is not the same. The simulation uses the long-span MAC for every airframe, so on the short-wing aircraft its percentages are a consistent scale rather than the -10 load sheet's own figures.

The **forward limit** is set by control power. The further forward the CG, the greater the nose-down moment the tail must balance and the more elevator and stabilizer it takes to rotate on takeoff and to flare on landing. In the flare the aircraft is slow, in ground effect (which reduces the tail's effectiveness), and the flaps add their own nose-down moment, so the landing configuration at a forward CG is usually what sets the limit. A forward CG also loads the nose gear more heavily and raises the stall speed slightly, because the tail's download must be carried by extra wing lift.

The **aft limit** is set by stability. As the CG moves aft the static margin shrinks, the aircraft becomes lighter and more sensitive in pitch, and at the neutral point it would have no natural tendency to return to its trimmed speed. The aft limit keeps a margin from that point, keeps enough nose-down control to recover from a high angle of attack, and on the ground keeps enough weight on the nose wheel for steering. With the CG aft of the main gear the aircraft would sit on its tail, which is why a freighter is loaded and unloaded in an order that keeps weight on the nose wheel throughout.

Both limits vary with weight, so the envelope is a polygon on a chart of weight against % MAC. On the -30 the forward limit bulges aft, to 12.0 %, between about 430,000 and 500,000 lb; the aft limit comes forward at both ends of the weight range, to 23.6 % at 583,000 lb and 25.0 % at 240,000 lb.

blocks.alt: Chart of gross weight (1,000 lb, 220 to 600, vertical axis) against center of gravity (% MAC, 5 to 35, horizontal axis) for the DC-10-30 at 580,000 lb takeoff weight, drawn from FedEx limitations 1-1-0-2: the forward limit at 8.0 % from 240,000 to 414,000 lb, curving to 10.0 % at 431,000, 11.7 % at 448,000, 12.0 % at 460,000 to 465,000, then 10.2 % at 500,000, 10.1 % at 520,000 and 9.9 % at 583,000 lb; the aft limit at 25.0 % at 240,000, 29.0 % from 280,000 to 460,000, 28.1 % at 500,000, 27.7 % at 520,000 and 23.6 % at 583,000 lb. A narrower shaded zero fuel weight CG band inside it, up to the 414,000 lb MZFW line. Two points plotted from the worked example: ZFW 329,500 lb at 19.4 % and TOGW 523,700 lb at 20.4 %, joined by an arrow labeled fuel loading, and a dotted line showing the CG travel in flight: aft to 22.8 % at 475,000 lb (center tank empty) and 24.3 % at 450,000 lb (tank 2 down to the wing tanks), then forward to 21.2 % at the 365,300 lb landing weight.
blocks.title: CG envelope, DC-10-30
blocks.caption: The envelope for the heaviest -30 group, with the worked example's loading and the CG travel as the fuel burns in schedule.

blocks.title: CG limits, DC-10-30, 580,000 lb takeoff weight (FedEx)

blocks.content: The lighter -30 groups (565,000 and 572,000 lb) have their own tables, close to this one; the aft limit at their maximum weights is 24.6 and 24.2 % MAC. The **KC-10A**'s envelope runs from 8.0 % MAC forward and 33.0 % aft at its 240,500 lb minimum weight, with an aft limit of 29.0 % from about 275,000 to 460,000 lb that closes to 27.8 % at 520,000 lb and 23.2 % at 590,000 lb; at its heaviest weights the CG must lie between about 19 and 23 %. Its forward limit has separate takeoff and in-flight lines between 8 and 12 % MAC. The tanker's manual also shows a narrower desirable ZFW CG envelope for cargo and dual-role missions, which leaves room for the CG movement of the fuel as it is burned and given away. The **MD-10**'s envelopes are those of the DC-10-10F and -30F freighters it was converted from. All of them are in [Limitations](limitations).

The envelope charts carry an inner band, the **zero fuel weight CG limits**, and a condition: if the aircraft is loaded within the ZFW limits and its fuel is used in the approved schedule, it will remain inside the gross weight envelope for the whole flight. The fuel is so large a share of the weight that its CG travel during the flight can be several per cent of MAC; checking the ZFW CG against the narrower band is how the load planner guarantees that every combination of fuel left in the tanks is safe, without plotting each one. When less fuel is carried the CG cannot travel as far, so the charts allow a wider ZFW band for a takeoff with, for example, 100,000 lb of fuel or less on the -30F, or 114,000, 102,000 and 80,000 lb on the -10F.

Adding a weight w at an arm a to an aircraft of weight W with its CG at c moves the CG to (W·c + w·a) ÷ (W + w): towards the new item's arm, in proportion to its share of the new total. Moving an item already aboard by a distance d moves the CG by w·d ÷ W. For example, moving a 10,000 lb pallet 100 in aft in a 500,000 lb aircraft moves the CG 2 in aft, or 0.7 % MAC. The same pallet moved 900 in (75 ft) moves it more than 6 %, a third of the envelope's width: where the heavy units go is the planner's main lever on the CG.

Fuel is the other lever, and it moves during the flight. Because the wing is swept, the further outboard a tank is, the further aft its fuel sits. The table gives the arms the simulation uses for each tank when full; the fuel's own CG therefore depends on how the tanks are filled, which is why the loading schedule matters for balance as well as for the wing's structure.

blocks.title: Fuel tank arms (full tanks)
columns: Effect of loading or burning it
rows: Far aft of any CG: adding fuel moves the CG aft, burning it moves the CG forward
Ahead of the leading edge of the MAC: adding fuel moves the CG forward, burning it moves the CG aft
Center auxiliary tank (-10 option, -15, -30, -40, MD-10-30; the KC-10's center wing tank)
Close to tank 2; burned first, so the CG moves aft early in a long flight
A powerful forward moment: the tanker keeps balance fuel in it

blocks.content: Taking the worked example in [Planning a flight in the simulation](#flight-planning-in-sim), a DC-10-30F with a ZFW of 329,500 lb at 19.4 % MAC: its 195,700 lb of fuel, loaded in schedule (tanks 1 and 3 full at 40,203 lb each, tank 2 full at 64,969 lb, 50,325 lb in the center tank), has its own CG near 22 % MAC and brings the ramp CG to about 20.4 %. As the center tank is emptied first the CG moves aft, to about 22.8 % when it is dry at about 475,000 lb. It keeps moving aft while tank 2, which also lies ahead of the CG, feeds down to the level of the wing tanks: about 24.3 % at 450,000 lb, the aft-most point of the flight. From there the three tanks are used together, their combined fuel lies far aft of the CG, and the CG comes forward again, to about 21.2 % at the 365,300 lb landing weight. The fuel system's part of this is described in [Fuel: CG management](fuel#cg-management).

**Passengers and cabin service** shift the CG too. A full DC-10 cabin standing up for the lavatories or the galley carts moving aft can move it a fraction of a per cent, which is why the CG envelopes leave margin and why some operators restricted cabin movement on aft-loaded flights. In the simulation every passenger weighs about 190 lb and is placed in the seat they board to.

An empty or lightly loaded freighter has its CG well aft: the tail engine is far behind the wing, and with no cargo forward nothing balances it. **Ballast** brings the CG forward. FedEx ferried an empty DC-10-30 with about 45,000 lb of **ballast fuel** in the upper auxiliary tank, which lies ahead of the CG; a -10, whose ballast fuel has little effect on its CG, carried a **ballast pallet** of at least 5,000 lb (10,000 lb preferred) in main deck position 1L or 1R instead. A ballast pallet, a container or a combination of pallet and fuel may be used on the -30, and a maintenance fly-away kit loaded far forward can make ballast unnecessary.

Ballast fuel is **declared unusable** and becomes part of the zero fuel weight. It appears on its own line of the load sheet between the BOW and the ZFW, and it must still be aboard at landing. Two consequences follow for the crew. The auxiliary tank's pumps must be off before its quantity reaches the ballast figure, in normal fuel management and in a fuel dump. And when the zero fuel weight is set into the flight engineer's gross weight indicator, which adds the total fuel on board to the ZFW set on it, the ballast must be subtracted from the manifest's ZFW first, or it is counted twice.

On the MD-10 ballast fuel may be carried in tank 2 (up to 25,000 lb) or, on the -30, in the upper auxiliary tank (up to 75,000 lb), in one tank only. The amount and the tank are entered on the FMS FUEL INIT page so that the FMS leaves the ballast out of its usable fuel and its predictions.

In the simulation, ballast fuel is simply fuel in the center tank that you do not use: load it on the EFB's Fuel page, include it in the zero fuel weight of your own load sheet, and manage the pumps so that it stays. The fuel system's handling of ballast, and what the simulation does and does not automate, are described in [Fuel: ballast fuel](fuel#ballast-fuel).

A tanker's payload is fuel, and the KC-10's weight limits are written so that it can be carried like cargo. Its 414,000 lb maximum zero fuel weight applies to the zero fuel weight **plus the fuel in the body tanks** (the center wing tank and the forward and aft body tanks). That fuel counts exactly as cargo does: it sits in or under the fuselage, and the wing root must carry it in bending. Only main tanks 1, 2 and 3 give the wing root its bending relief.

That defines the tanker's loading rules. When the zero fuel weight plus the body tank fuel exceeds 414,000 lb, or the gross weight exceeds 556,000 lb, the main tanks must be kept full, and tank 2 must never hold less than tank 1 or 3: the offload comes from the body and center tanks while the wing tanks stay full. The FWD body tank carries **balance fuel**, normally 15,000 lb, kept until tank 1 or 3 is down to about 5,000 lb, because its far-forward arm is what holds the CG within limits as the aft fuel is given away. A full AFT body tank leaves little margin for cargo in the rear of the main deck: the flight manual warns that even lightweight cargo can then exceed the floor's zone loading limits.

The weight and balance for a tanker mission is planned at several points: at takeoff, before and after each offload or onload, and at landing. Each must be inside the envelope, and the offload plan is built to make it so (see [Offload planning](#kc10-offload-planning)). The flight engineer works the CG movement and the fuel distribution with the boom operator, who is responsible for the cargo and passenger loading. The fuel system's side of this, the balance fuel stop and the scheduling lights, is in [Fuel: ballast fuel](fuel#ballast-fuel) and [Fuel: KC-10 tanker fuel system](fuel#kc10-tanker-fuel-system).

children.title: How the simulation weighs the aircraft

blocks.content: The simulator's flight model takes mass in two forms only: the fuel in its tanks and the weights at a fixed set of payload stations along the fuselage. The aircraft writes its own fuel quantities into the simulator's tanks once a second, and spreads every cargo unit and every seated passenger over the payload stations at the position where it actually is. The gross weight and the CG that the flight model flies are therefore the true sum of the empty aircraft, the fuel and the load, and they move as the fuel burns and as cargo rolls along the deck.

The simulator measures its own CG against a reference chord that is not the aircraft's MAC, and its raw percentage reads about 2 points higher than a load sheet would. The aircraft converts it, through the fuselage station, to the real MAC defined above, and that converted figure is what the EFB shows everywhere: on the Fuel page, in the Performance app, on the Virtual Crew page. Use the EFB's CG for planning, not the percentage on the simulator's own weight and balance page. The conversion uses the simulator's own nose position, which lies about an inch from the book's datum, so the EFB's CG may differ from a real load sheet's by up to about 0.4 % MAC.

**Gear loads.** The aircraft also works out how its weight divides between its landing gear legs, which the landing gear, brakes, steering and towing models use. With a center gear the aircraft stands on four legs in a line, and the share each carries cannot be found from the balance of forces alone; the simulation treats the airframe as rigid on four springs, each leg with the stiffness of its own oleo, and solves for the share that satisfies both the vertical force and the pitching moment. The center gear carries about a seventh of the weight. As the aircraft rotates for takeoff, the nose leg's share fades out above about 60 kt, so that the nose gear unloads through rotation as lift builds; on a parked aircraft on a slope nothing fades.

Do not change the payload stations on the simulator's own weight and balance page while the EFB's cargo or passengers are in use. The aircraft then assumes something else owns the payload and stops writing its own for the rest of the session: cargo and passengers loaded or moved after that no longer reach the flight model's weight and CG. Load fuel, cargo and passengers through the EFB. See [EFB: ground, fuel, cargo and passengers](efb#loading-apps).

children.title: On-board weight and balance system (MAC panel)

blocks.content: Some DC-10s carried an on-board weight and balance system that weighed the aircraft on its own landing gear. A transducer on each gear leg measures the load on it; a weight and balance computer in the avionics compartment adds the loads into a gross weight and, from the known stations of the legs, computes the CG in % MAC. An attitude sensor corrects for the aircraft not standing level, because tilting a body whose CG is 15 ft above the ground moves the CG over the wheels. The results show on the **MAC panel** at the flight engineer's station. It is an option on the DC-10s in the simulation, off by default: fit it in the EFB's Aircraft Configuration under the Engineer zone (see [EFB: Configuration](efb#configuration-app)). It is not offered on the firefighting air tankers. In this version the panel itself does not yet respond in the cockpit; see [Simulation notes](#mp-simulation-notes).

blocks.alt: DC-10-30 flight engineer's MAC (weight and balance) panel, close-up, powered and reading: the GROSS WEIGHT counter of three drums reading 5 2 4 (thousands of pounds) and the CG counter of three drums reading 2 0 4 (20.4 % MAC); the five-position SYSTEM CHECK selector at OPR (positions OPR, INST, CHAN, ATT, Z SET legible); the READ-STBY switch at READ; the power switch ON with its POWER light lit; the GO, NO-GO, DEG MODE and SYSTEM ON TEST lights unlit; the wind direction pointer. All legends legible.
