blocks.content: **Operation.** Switch the panel on at least five minutes before the reading is needed: the computer needs a five-minute warm-up and shows nothing reliable before it, and the warm-up restarts after any loss of power. With the warm-up complete, select INST and check that the counters run to 765,000 lb and 7.5 % with the GO light on; select ATT and check GO; return the selector to OPR and the READ-STBY switch to READ, and read the gross weight and CG. Compare them with the load sheet and the EFB. The system weighs the aircraft only while it stands on its wheels; in the air, with the struts extended, it keeps the last reading taken on the ground. Set STBY to freeze a reading, for example before engine start or during refueling.

A strong gusty wind loads the legs unevenly and makes the readings wander, which is why the panel has a wind pointer; a zero calibration (Z SET) attempted in a gale fails for the same reason. A failed gear channel drops that leg's share out of the sum, so the gross weight reads low rather than going blank; a degraded one lights DEG MODE. The weight and balance system is an independent check: the load sheet remains the reference.

children.title: Loading the aircraft with the EFB

blocks.content: The EFB loads the aircraft through its own systems: fuel through the refuel panel, cargo through the holds' rollers and locks, passengers through the doors to their seats. The screens are described in [EFB: ground, fuel, cargo and passengers](efb#loading-apps). What the EFB does not do is check the load against the zero fuel weight limit or the CG envelope: it enforces only the hardware's own limits, such as a tank's capacity or a cargo position's maximum weight. The load plan is the crew's.

items: **Know the BOW.** With no fuel, cargo or passengers aboard, the EFB Home screen's WEIGHTS widget shows the ZFW: that is the aircraft's basic operating weight as the simulator carries it. Note it, since it differs between variants and fits.
**Plan the payload against the ZFW limit.** BOW plus payload (plus ballast) must not exceed the maximum zero fuel weight, nor give a TOGW or LW above their limits with the planned fuel.

**Load the cargo and passengers.** Place heavy units to bring the ZFW CG inside the ZFW band, normally near its middle. The Cargo app shows each position's limits and the load's weight; see [EFB: Cargo](efb#cargo-app), [EFB: Passengers](efb#passengers-app) and, for how units are moved and locked, [Doors and cabin: loading cargo](doors-and-cabin#loading-cargo).

**Read the ZFW CG.** With the cargo and passengers aboard, type 0 as every tank's target on the Fuel page: the preview then shows the weight and CG without fuel, the ZFW and ZFW CG. Check them against the limits, then set the real targets.

**Plan and load the fuel.** On the Ground Ops Fuel page, type the block fuel or fetch it from SimBrief, press Distribute to spread it in the aircraft's loading schedule, and read the previewed FUEL, GW and CG before pressing Refuel or Instant. See [EFB: the Fuel page](efb#fuel-page).

**Check the takeoff weight and CG.** Ramp weight less taxi fuel is the TOGW. Check it and its CG against the envelope, and check that the CG stays inside the envelope through the flight (it will, if the ZFW CG was inside the ZFW band and the fuel is used in schedule).
**Compute the takeoff data** with that weight and CG (see [Takeoff data in the simulation](#efb-takeoff-data)).

blocks.alt: Two EFB screens side by side, portrait. Left: the Home screen's WEIGHTS widget on a DC-10-30F at the gate, GROSS WEIGHT 525.2 klb in large digits, a progress bar of fuel against gross weight, and FUEL 195.7 and ZFW 329.5 below. Right: the Ground Ops Fuel page after Distribute with a block fuel of 195,700 lb: Tank 1 40,203, Tank 2 64,969, Tank 3 40,203, Center aux 50,325 as targets, and the preview line FUEL 195,700, GW 525,200, CG 20.4 %.
blocks.title: Reading weights and CG in the EFB

blocks.content: Where to read the weights in flight: the EFB Home screen's WEIGHTS widget (gross weight, fuel and ZFW); the Performance app's GW and CG boxes, which take the aircraft's readings when left blank; on the DC-10 and KC-10 the flight engineer's fuel quantity and gross weight indicators, the gross weight being the ZFW set on the indicator plus the fuel totalizer (see [Fuel: controls and indicators](fuel#controls-and-indicators)); on the DC-10 the MAC panel if fitted; on the MD-10 the gross weight and CG on the system display and the FMS, from the ZFW and CG entered at initialization.

The horizontal stabilizer is set before takeoff so that the aircraft is close to trimmed at the climb-out speed and the elevator alone can rotate it at VR with a normal pull. The right setting depends on the **CG**, because a forward CG needs more nose-up trim to lift the nose against its larger nose-down moment, and on the **flap setting**, because more flap gives more nose-down pitching moment and needs a little more nose-up trim. The setting is a compromise: too much nose-up trim and the aircraft rotates early or pitches up sharply as it leaves the ground; too little and it is slow to rotate, uses more runway than the data assumes, and needs a hard pull. The takeoff data assume the correct setting.

blocks.title: Takeoff stabilizer setting, units (degrees) airplane nose up, long-span wing (KC-10, DC-10-30, -40, MD-10-30)
Takeoff stabilizer setting, units ANU, short-span wing (DC-10-10, -15, MD-10-10), FedEx

blocks.content: The relation is close to linear: on the long wing about a quarter of a unit per per cent of MAC, so a CG error of 4 % MAC is a trim error of about one unit. That is why the trim must come from the actual CG, not from a typical one, and why a late change to the load sheet means a new trim figure. The EFB's takeoff card gives the setting as STAB for the CG and flap entered.

The trim is set with the control wheel trim switches or the LONG TRIM handles and read on the LONG TRIM indicator on the pedestal (on the MD-10 also as STAB on the system display's configuration page). The indicator's **green band** marks the range allowed for takeoff: 2.0 to 10.0 units on the -10 and 2.5 to 9.4 units on the -30. Outside it the takeoff warning sounds when the throttles are advanced (the simulation's warning uses 2.0 to 10.0 units on every aircraft). The band is a gross error check, not a substitute for the card. The trim system is described in [Flight controls: horizontal stabilizer](flight-controls#horizontal-stabilizer).

With the Virtual Crew working, the captain sets the trim and the flaps at Before Takeoff, and the first officer (the copilot on the KC-10) checks them against the takeoff card the crew started the checklist with: the stabilizer within 0.3 units of the card's STAB and the flaps within half a degree of its setting. If they are not, that pilot says so and the item waits. With no card, the check is that the trim is inside the green band and the flaps in the takeoff range. See [Virtual Crew](virtual-crew).

In level flight the tail normally pushes down to balance the nose-down moment of the wing and the CG ahead of the lift. That download must be carried by the wing as extra lift, which costs induced drag, and the stabilizer's incidence adds trim drag of its own. Moving the CG aft shortens the lever arm between weight and lift, reduces the download and so reduces the drag: an aft CG is a fuel-efficient CG. The KC-10's cruise data, drawn for 24 % MAC, credit about 0.2 % of specific range for each 1 % MAC the CG lies further aft, a few per cent over the width of the envelope. An aft CG also lowers the stall and buffet speeds slightly, which is why buffet charts are drawn for a stated CG (24 % MAC on the KC-10's) and why a forward CG needs a few knots more margin.

The price is stability, which is why the aft limit exists, and why no operator plans to the aft limit: a loading error or a passenger moving aft must not put the aircraft outside it. The normal fuel schedule moves the CG aft in the first part of a long flight and forward in the second (see [How loading moves the CG](#wb-loading-effects)). A flight engineer can also trim the cruise CG with fuel transfers between tank 2 and the wing tanks, within the fuel system's own rules.

On the DC-10 the Virtual Crew's second officer will hold a target cruise CG for you, set on the EFB's Virtual Crew page, by moving fuel between tank 2 and tanks 1 and 3 in level cruise above 20,000 ft. How it is done and what stops it are described in [Fuel: cruise CG target](fuel#cruise-cg-target).

sections.title: Takeoff performance
sections.summary: Takeoff speeds, field length, the engine-out flight path, obstacle clearance, the optimum flap, reduced thrust and the brake and tire limits.

blocks.content: The takeoff is the most tightly constrained part of a flight, because the aircraft is at its heaviest, closest to the ground and slowest, and because it must be safe whether or not an engine fails at the worst possible moment. The maximum takeoff weight for a given runway on a given day is the lowest of several independent limits:

items: **Runway (field length).** The weight at which the runway is just long enough to stop after an engine failure at V1, or to continue and lift off. On the KC-10 data this is the runway available limiting weight (RALW).

**Climb.** The weight at which the aircraft can just achieve the minimum engine-out climb gradient after takeoff: the climb gradient limiting weight (CGLW). It depends on the day and the flaps, not on the runway.
**Obstacles.** The weight at which the engine-out flight path just clears the obstacles beyond the runway, which raises the gradient the climb limit must deliver.
**Tire speed.** The weight at which the liftoff ground speed reaches the tires' placard speed.
**Brake energy.** The weight at which a stop from V1 would exceed the energy the brakes are demonstrated to absorb.
**Structure, and the landing weight.** The maximum takeoff weight, and a takeoff weight low enough to arrive at the destination at or below its maximum landing weight.

blocks.content: Each of these limits changes with the pressure altitude, the temperature, the wind, the runway slope and surface, the flap setting and the bleed configuration. The rest of this part explains what each limit is and why it behaves as it does. How the EFB works them out is in [Takeoff data in the simulation](#efb-takeoff-data).

rows: Minimum control speed on the ground: the lowest speed at which a sudden wing engine failure can be controlled on the runway with rudder alone, the remaining engines at takeoff thrust, without deviating more than 30 ft from the centerline (FAR 25; the KC-10's definition uses 25 ft). FedEx's DC-10s were certificated with the rudder pedal nose wheel steering disconnected. The KC-10's charted VMCG is the wet or icy one; with an RCR of 10 or better, no standing contaminant and no more than 10 kt of crosswind, nose wheel steering is credited and VMCG is 10 kt lower for V1

Minimum control speed in the air: the lowest speed at which the aircraft can be controlled after a wing engine failure with full rudder and no more than 5° of bank. It does not limit the KC-10's takeoff performance
The speed at which the critical engine is assumed to fail
The decision speed. An engine failure recognized before V1: stop. At or after V1: continue. V1 may not be below VMCG nor above VR or VMBE
Critical engine failure speed (KC-10 data): the speed at which an engine failure leaves the same distance to stop as to continue to liftoff. V1 is the higher of VCEF and VMCG, not above VMBE
Rotation speed. Chosen so that a normal rotation reaches the climb-out speed by the screen height; the KC-10 data assume four seconds from VR to liftoff. Never below VR MIN
Minimum rotation speed (KC-10 data): the wet or icy VMCG, so that an engine failure after rotation from the three-point attitude can still be controlled

Takeoff safety speed, the climb-out speed with an engine inoperative. Civil: at least 1.2 times the stall speed and 1.1 times VMCA. KC-10: established at 50 ft, always above 1.15 times the 1 g stall speed, chosen for fuselage clearance at liftoff. If VR is raised to VR MIN, V2 rises by the same amount. The KC-10 can turn with 25° of bank at V2 + 10 kt
Maximum brake energy speed: the highest speed from which a stop does not exceed the brakes' flight-tested energy capacity. V1 may not exceed it
The tires' placard ground speed: 204 kt (235 mph) on the -30 and KC-10, 195 kt on the -10
The minimum speeds for retracting the flaps and the slats after takeoff
Minimum maneuver speed with flaps and slats retracted, the clean climb speed below 10,000 ft at heavy weights

blocks.content: The stall speed the civil rules use was measured in a stall maneuver in which the load factor falls below 1 g, which gives a lower figure than a stall at 1 g. The KC-10's data use the 1 g stall speed. That is why its V2 margin, 1.15, is smaller than the civil 1.2: the two criteria are of similar severity.

blocks.title: Typical rotation and climb-out speeds, long-span wing, sea level, 15 °C (KIAS)

blocks.content: Read from the KC-10's charts. The charted (wet or icy) VMCG at sea level and 15 °C is about 132 to 134 KIAS, depending slightly on the flap setting, and 10 kt less on a dry runway; it falls with altitude and temperature, because the engines make less thrust and so less yawing moment (122 to 124 KIAS charted at 5,000 ft and 30 °C). A heavy aircraft is therefore rarely VMCG-limited; a light one at a cold, low field on a short runway may be.

Imagine the takeoff roll with an engine failing at some speed. If it fails early, the aircraft has a long way still to accelerate on two engines before it can lift off, but stopping is easy: the **accelerate-go distance** is long and the **accelerate-stop distance** short. If it fails late, the reverse is true. Plotted against the engine failure speed, the go distance falls and the stop distance rises. Where the two curves cross, the distance to continue equals the distance to stop: that distance is the **balanced field length** (the KC-10's **critical field length**), and the speed is the balanced V1 (the KC-10's **VCEF**). Choosing V1 there makes the runway needed as short as it can be.

blocks.alt: Diagram of distance (vertical axis) against engine failure speed (horizontal axis). A falling curve labeled accelerate-go (continue on two engines to liftoff) and a rising curve labeled accelerate-stop (stop on the runway) cross at a point labeled critical field length / balanced field length, with the speed at the crossing marked VCEF. Vertical lines mark VMCG on the left, below which an engine failure cannot be controlled, and VMBE on the right, above which a stop exceeds the brakes' energy. A horizontal line marks runway available; where it lies above the crossing, the gap is runway margin. A second, lighter pair of curves for a heavier weight crosses higher, touching the runway available line: that weight is the runway available limiting weight.
blocks.title: Accelerate-go, accelerate-stop and the critical field length

blocks.content: The **runway available limiting weight** is the weight at which the critical field length equals the runway available. As the weight rises, both curves rise, the crossing moves up and to the right, and at the limiting weight it touches the runway available. The civil rules define the distances slightly differently (to a 35 ft screen height, with the all-engine distance multiplied by 1.15 as a separate check, and with optional stopways and clearways that make the field unbalanced), and FedEx did not use clearway or stopway to increase its takeoff weight. The KC-10's data put the aircraft at the end of the critical field length at liftoff, at 0 ft rather than 35 ft, and include the effect of reverse thrust on the stop; separate charts without reverse thrust apply when a reverser is inoperative.

Two more limits sit on V1. It may not be below **VMCG**: if VCEF is below VMCG, V1 becomes VMCG, the stop now starts later and needs more runway than the balanced field, and the KC-10's data give a **maximum allowable weight when V1 = VMCG** (MAW), the weight at which a stop from VMCG still fits. This is the light-weight, short-runway case. And V1 may not exceed **VMBE**: if VCEF is above it, V1 must come down to VMBE and the takeoff weight down until the go case still fits. This is the heavy, hot, fast case.

On the KC-10's data the runway the charts are entered with is not the paved length. **Runway available** is the length less the distance used lining up (300 ft at least, more after a 180° turn on the runway) and less any runway deliberately left unused for obstacle clearance. The charts then correct it for the CG, runway condition, slope, wind and bleed configuration to an **equivalent field length** (EFL), which may be longer or shorter than the runway available, and enter the limit charts with that.

After an engine failure at V1 the aircraft must not only get airborne but climb away from the ground and the obstacles around the airport on two engines. On a three-engine aircraft that means climbing with a third of its thrust gone. The climb gradient is the excess of thrust over drag divided by the weight, (T − D) ÷ W, so it falls quickly as the weight rises and as the air gets hotter and thinner. The flight path from liftoff to the clean configuration is divided into segments, each with its own configuration and required gradient.

blocks.alt: Profile diagram of the engine-out takeoff flight path, height against distance, not to scale. From brake release: ground roll, engine failure at V1, liftoff at the end of the critical field length; first segment from liftoff to gear up (gear retraction starting 3 s after liftoff, complete 10.5 s later; speed VLOF to V2; civil minimum 0.3 %); second segment at V2 with gear up and takeoff flaps from gear up to the acceleration height (civil minimum 2.7 %; KC-10 reference gradient at least 2.5 %); transition segment, level acceleration while retracting flaps at VFR and slats at VSR (civil 1.5 % capability); final segment climbing at VSR with maximum continuous thrust (civil 1.5 %), thrust reduced to MCT after 10 minutes or 2,000 ft above the field. Acceleration height marked, at least 400 ft engine-out and 800 ft with all engines. Below the gross flight path a dashed net flight path 0.9 % lower, and an obstacle inside the departure area cleared by 35 ft. Inset plan view of the departure funnel widening with distance either side of the extended centerline.
blocks.title: Engine-out takeoff flight path

rows: Liftoff to gear up; gear extended, takeoff flaps; VLOF to V2
Gear retraction starts 3 s after liftoff and is complete 10.5 s later
Gear up, takeoff flaps; V2; takeoff thrust on two engines
The reference gross gradient at gear-up must be at least 2.5 %, more if an obstacle requires it
Level acceleration at the acceleration height while the flaps and slats retract
Acceleration height from the chart, at least 400 ft engine-out (800 ft all engines)
Takeoff thrust for at most 10 minutes or to 2,000 ft above the field, then MCT

blocks.content: The **second segment** is nearly always the one that limits, because it is flown at the lowest speed with the flaps still out, and its gradient defines the climb limit weight. The KC-10's data express the requirement as a single gross gradient measured at the moment the gear is up, used to look up a whole altitude-distance profile on its climbout flight path charts; that reference gradient is not the slope of the actual path and must not be used as one. Bank costs gradient (the load factor must be paid for in thrust), and the data assume a straight climb-out: an engine-out departure that turns needs its own allowance.

The **acceleration height** is the height at which the climb is leveled to accelerate and clean up. It must be high enough for the flight path to clear the obstacles, so the chart gives it as a pressure height for the day; at sea level it is typically about 1,400 to 1,500 ft above the runway on the KC-10's data. Flying the computed speed matters more than following the flight director: the KC-10's manual warns that its takeoff mode does not command the CG-corrected V2, nor the higher V2 of a VMCG-limited reduced-thrust takeoff in which VR has been raised to VR MIN, and that the takeoff is flown on the airspeed indicator. See [Automatic flight](automatic-flight).

The civil rule protects against obstacles with a deliberately pessimistic flight path. The **net flight path** is the gross (actual) engine-out path with its gradient reduced by 0.9 % on a three-engine aircraft, to allow for a below-average aircraft, gusts and piloting. The net path must clear by 35 ft every obstacle in the departure area, a funnel that starts a few hundred feet either side of the extended centerline at the end of the takeoff distance and widens with distance. Because the 0.9 % margin grows with distance, the gross path must clear an obstacle 8,000 ft out by at least 35 ft plus 0.9 % of 8,000, or 107 ft.

The KC-10's data turn an obstacle into a climb gradient. The obstacle's height is measured **above the liftoff end of the runway available**, not above sea level, and its distance from that point; the climbout flight path chart then gives the gross gradient the aircraft needs, at the most limiting flap, to clear it. If that is 2.5 % or less, the obstacle does not limit and 2.5 % is used. A **screen height** at the runway's end is treated the same way, as an obstacle at zero distance. On a downhill runway whose departure end elevation is not known, the obstacle's height is corrected for the slope.

When an obstacle limits the weight, the KC-10's manual offers an optimization: deliberately use less runway. Cutting the runway available moves the liftoff point back, which makes the obstacle further away and the gradient needed smaller, while the shorter runway lowers the runway limit. Repeating the calculation with the runway cut back in steps (about 200 ft for obstacles up to 2,000 ft away, 500 ft beyond) finds the point where the two meet and the maximum takeoff weight is highest. The maximum allowable weight with V1 at VMCG is still worked with the full runway.

Flaps trade climb for runway. More flap gives more lift at a given speed, so the aircraft can lift off slower and the runway limit weight rises; but it also gives more drag, so the engine-out climb gradient falls and the climb limit weight falls. On the long-span aircraft the takeoff data cover any flap from 5 to 25°, set with the FLAP T.O. SEL thumbwheel (see [Flight controls: flaps and slats](flight-controls)), so the crew can choose the exact flap at which the two limits are equal. That is the **optimum flap**, and the weight there is the **maximum takeoff gross weight** (MTOGW) for the runway and the day.

blocks.alt: Chart of takeoff weight (1,000 lb, vertical) against takeoff flap setting (5 to 25 degrees, horizontal). A rising line labeled runway available limiting weight (RALW) from 484,200 lb at 5 degrees, and a falling line labeled climb gradient limiting weight (CGLW) reaching 556,100 lb at 25 degrees, for a DC-10-30 at Memphis runway 18R, 9,019 ft available, 28 °C, 341 ft. The lines meet near 24.8 degrees at 540,700 lb, marked optimum flap and MTOGW. A horizontal dashed line at the actual weight, 523,700 lb, crosses both, showing the margin. An inset shows the case where the CGLW line lies below the RALW line everywhere and peaks, with the optimum flap at its peak.
blocks.title: Optimum flap and MTOGW

blocks.content: The KC-10's charts make this practical with two reference numbers: the runway limit weight at 5° flaps and the climb limit weight at 25° flaps. On the third sheet of the takeoff chart, lines through those two values are followed until they meet, which gives the optimum flap and the MTOGW together. If the climb limit lies below the runway limit at every flap, the lines never meet and the optimum is the flap at which the climb limit peaks. A low flap setting means a higher liftoff speed, so on a hot, high day the **tire speed limit** can cap the weight at low flaps and push the optimum to a larger setting; at 20° and more it does not limit. The takeoff weight may then be anything up to the MTOGW; the further below it, the more room for reduced thrust.

columns: In the KC-10 data and the EFB
rows: Raises the field length and the speeds, lowers the climb gradient

Thinner air means less thrust and a higher true speed for the same indicated speed. The CF6-50C2 is **flat rated**: its takeoff thrust is constant up to a break temperature (about 30 °C at sea level), then falls
Takeoff data from −1,000 to 14,000 ft, within the environmental envelope of −54 to 50 °C and not above ISA + 40 °C
A headwind shortens the takeoff, a tailwind lengthens it
No headwind credit; 150 % of the tailwind including gust. No takeoff with more than 10 kt tailwind. A variable wind is taken at its worst
Downhill improves acceleration but lengthens the stop; uphill the reverse
RCR and RSC charts (see [Wet and contaminated runways](#wet-contaminated))
An aft CG reduces the tail's download, so the wing needs less lift: takeoff capability improves as the CG moves aft
Charts at 8 % MAC with corrections from 8 to 30 %
Bleed air taken from the engines costs thrust. Normal takeoff bleed is packs on, anti-ice off; a packs-off takeoff has more thrust and a higher MTOGW
AC and anti-ice entries; anti-ice corrections apply only at or below 8 °C
Add 0.08 % to the required gradient and take 0.6 % off the runway available (not computed)
Missing panels or fairings add drag
Reduce MTOGW by 2,000 lb per unit of drag index (not computed)
Take 400 ft off the runway available (not computed)
Frost on the lower wing over the fuel tanks
Permitted when caused by cold fuel; costs climb
CGLW penalty 0.8 % for 1/8 in of frost, 1.2 % for 1/16 in of ice; frost or ice elsewhere not permitted (not computed)
Engine cowl anti-ice valve failed open
Center gear retracted, one brake or anti-skid inoperative
Reduced stopping capability, lower weight limits
A configuration correction (CFCC) in the charts; not computed by the EFB
Reduce runway available 3.9 % (dry to RCR 3), add 0.52 % to the required gradient, then apply the pods' drag index (not computed)

blocks.content: Most takeoffs are made well below the maximum weight, and a takeoff at full thrust then has margin it does not need. Using less thrust lowers the turbine temperatures, which is where an engine's life is spent: the KC-10's manual states plainly that failing to use reduced thrust whenever conditions allow increases engine wear and shortens engine life. The DC-10 family uses the **assumed temperature** method (FedEx's standard N1 and assumed temperature; the KC-10's and the TRC's T.O. FLX; the MD-10's FLEX).

The idea is to find the **hottest day** on which the aircraft could still meet every takeoff limit at its actual weight on full thrust, and then set the thrust it would have on that day. Because the engine is flat rated, its thrust falls only above the break temperature, so the assumed temperature always lies above the break. Each limit is traced through the actual weight back to its temperature, and the lowest of those temperatures is the assumed temperature. The actual day is cooler than the assumed one, so the real air is denser and the true airspeeds and ground speeds for the same indicated speeds are lower, which shortens both the go and the stop: a reduced-thrust takeoff performs a little better than the calculation says, which is a built-in margin.

**Restrictions.** The takeoff data for temperatures beyond the environmental envelope exist for reduced thrust only. The EFB allows reduced thrust only with an RCR of 10 or better and no standing contaminant deeper than 0.10 in. The KC-10's manual also forbids it with the anti-skid or a main wheel brake inoperative, with windshear suspected or after Type II de-icing fluid; the EFB does not check these. With engine anti-ice on, the reduced-thrust N1 is read, and the thrust rating computer set, at an assumed temperature 3 °C lower than the one the limits gave. And there is one trap in the method: the minimum control speed was computed at the thrust of the assumed day, so after a wing engine failure on a reduced-thrust takeoff the remaining engines may be advanced to full takeoff thrust only above 135 KIAS. Below that, the extra asymmetric thrust could exceed what the rudder can hold.

A **derate** is a different thing: a lower thrust rating with its own certified data, including its own, lower minimum control speeds. The DC-10-40's thrust rating computer has an **ALTN T.O.** rating of this kind. The EFB offers it on the -40's card, but works it as the equivalent assumed temperature and does not take credit for its lower control speeds. FedEx's limitations call its reduced takeoff thrust derated (standard) thrust, and forbid the flight director's takeoff mode with it at weights below the one at which the minimum control speeds begin to set the takeoff speeds.

blocks.title: Maximum takeoff N1, % (packs as noted, anti-ice off)

blocks.content: The CF6-50C2 column is the KC-10's chart with the packs on; the CF6-6D column is FedEx's Series 10 table, which is drawn with the packs off. The rise of N1 with temperature up to the break and its fall beyond it is the flat rating seen from the cockpit: holding constant thrust in warmer air takes a higher fan speed, until the engine reaches its temperature limit and the thrust must come down instead. The reduced-thrust N1 for an assumed temperature is not simply the maximum N1 at that temperature: the KC-10's data carry it to the actual temperature at the same corrected fan speed. Thrust setting is described in [Engines: thrust limits and thrust setting](engines#thrust-rating).

A rejected takeoff from V1 at a heavy weight turns the aircraft's kinetic energy, half the mass times the square of the ground speed, into heat in the brakes within about half a minute. Doubling the speed quadruples the energy. **VMBE** is the speed above which a stop would exceed the energy the brakes have been shown to absorb; it falls as the weight, the field altitude, the temperature and a tailwind rise, because each adds energy at the same indicated speed. If VMBE is below VCEF, V1 is limited to VMBE and the weight must come down.

The brakes' capacity also depends on how hot they are before the takeoff. The KC-10's data give a **maximum allowable brake temperature**: the highest brake temperature at brake release, read on the brake temperature monitoring system (BTMS), from which the energy of a rejected takeoff from V1 can still be absorbed. After a landing the brakes reach their peak temperature 15 to 20 minutes after touchdown; the **brake cooling time** chart then gives the time to cool from that reading to the maximum allowable temperature. In the manual's example, 300 °C must cool to 200 °C, which takes 45 minutes. A second chart sorts the energy of a stop from V1 into **zones**: NORMAL; CAUTION, in which the brakes get hot enough to need cooling and inspection; and DANGER, in which the wheel fuse plugs may melt and the tires deflate, and a brake fire is possible. With the BTMS inoperative, assume 100 °C.

The **tire speed limit weight** is the weight at which the all-engine liftoff ground speed reaches the tires' placard speed. Ground speed, not indicated airspeed, is what spins the tires, so the limit bites at hot, high fields and with a tailwind, at low flap settings where the liftoff speed is highest; at sea level on a standard day it does not limit at any weight. Turnaround time matters too: FedEx's laptop flagged runways on which a -10 had to stay at the gate at least 30 minutes, and a -30 35 minutes, before the next takeoff, so that the brakes had cooled enough for a rejected takeoff. The brake temperature system is described in [Landing gear: brake temperature](landing-gear#brake-temperature).

The KC-10's data describe the runway surface by its **runway condition reading** (RCR), a measure of tire-to-runway friction from 23 (dry) downward, and its **runway surface condition** (RSC), the depth of standing water, slush or snow. Friction decides the stop; depth adds drag that slows the acceleration, until the tires hydroplane. The data come in separate sets for RCR 23 to 18, 17 to 12, 11 to 8 and 7 to 3, and for RSC 0.25 and 0.50 in. When the surface is in doubt, take the lower reading. Water 0.10 in deep or less makes a wet runway, taken at RCR 10 to 14 for takeoff, not a contaminated one.

blocks.title: Stopping distance ratio and crosswind limit by RCR (KC-10 data; the crosswind limits are the manual's estimated data)

items: No takeoff with more than 1/2 in of wet snow, slush or water, or more than 4 in of dry snow. Dry snow up to 2 in is taken as RSC 0.25 and from 2 to 4 in as RSC 0.50.
With any RSC, no takeoff with a wheel brake or the anti-skid inoperative or the center gear retracted.
With an RSC above 0.10 in, use RCR 6 for landing and for the crosswind limit.
FedEx: no takeoff with a tailwind when the runway is contaminated; 10 kt maximum crosswind with braking action reported poor; landing with up to 1 in of water or slush or 6 in of dry snow.
No reduced thrust with an RCR below 10 or an RSC above 0.10 in.

blocks.content: Cold weather operation, de-icing and contaminated runway technique are covered in [Adverse weather conditions](adverse-weather).

sections.title: Takeoff data in the simulation
sections.summary: How the EFB's Performance app works the takeoff card from the KC-10's charts, what to enter, how to read the answers, and where they go in the cockpit.

blocks.content: The EFB's **Performance** app computes the takeoff card on its **Takeoff** page. The page is the takeoff section of the KC-10's TOLD card worksheet and the TOLD card itself, and it works them in the order the KC-10's manual prescribes, with the manual's charts evaluated exactly. Its boxes and buttons are described screen by screen in [EFB: Performance, Takeoff](efb#takeoff-page). This part explains the method behind the page, the inputs that need care, how to read the answers, and how they reach the cockpit.

TAKEOFF COMPUTATIONS: COMP H8, X-WIND R0, CALC 0, CL GR 2.50, EFL 8821, 5 RALW 484.2, 25 CGLW 556.1, MTOGW 540.7, FLAP 24.8, ASSUMED RALW/TEMP 469.8/35, ASSUMED CGLW/TEMP 523.6/37, ASSUMED TEMP +34, TSLW NL, VMCG 120, VCEF 142, VMBE 182, MAW N/A, VR 157, VRMIN 130, V2 168, MAX BRAKE TEMP 292 C, BRAKE ZONE CAUTION, RWY REQ'D 8,940. TOLD CARD: GW 523.7, FLAPS 24.8, N1 111.9, ASSUMED TEMP +34; V1 142, VR 157, V2 168, VFR 196, VSR 241, 0/RET 275; STAB 5.4, ACCEL HT 1433; emergency return landing distance 5,958 ft at VTH 173. Set Bugs button at the foot.
blocks.title: Takeoff card for the worked example

items: **Wind.** The head or tail and cross components of the reported wind. The calculation wind gives no credit for a headwind and takes 150 % of a tailwind including the gust; a variable wind is taken at its worst, all of it as tailwind and as crosswind. More than 10 kt of tailwind, or a crosswind above the limit for the RCR, is a no-takeoff warning; wind more than 45° off the runway or a crosswind above 23 kt calls for a rolling takeoff, because the crosswind disturbs the airflow into the No. 2 engine's inlet.
**Obstacle.** The gross climb gradient the controlling obstacle needs, at the most limiting flap, never less than 2.5 % (CL GR).
**Runway.** The runway available corrected for CG, runway condition, slope, wind and bleed into the equivalent field length (EFL).

**The two limits.** The runway limit weight at 5° flaps (5 RALW) from the EFL and the day, and the climb limit weight at 25° flaps (25 CGLW) from the temperature, altitude, bleed, CG and the required gradient.

**Optimum flap and MTOGW.** The flap at which the two limits meet, searched across 5 to 25°, and the weight there. If an obstacle limits and the MTOGW is short of the gross weight, the runway is cut back in steps until the MTOGW stops rising.
**Tire speed.** The tire speed limit weight, not limiting at 20° and more.

**Thrust.** With reduced thrust selected and allowed, each limit is traced back through the actual weight to its temperature (ASSUMED RALW/TEMP and CGLW/TEMP), and the lower is the assumed temperature, never below the flat-rating break; otherwise the card is a maximum-thrust card.

**V1.** VMCG, VCEF and VMBE. V1 is the higher of VCEF and VMCG, not above VMBE; on a reduced-thrust card the assumed temperature is lowered until VMBE is at least VCEF. If VMCG sets V1, the maximum allowable weight with V1 at VMCG (MAW) is checked against the gross weight.

**Speeds, trim and thrust.** VR (never below VR MIN) and V2 with their corrections, the flap and slat retraction speeds and the clean minimum maneuver speed, the stabilizer setting, the acceleration height and the takeoff N1 (EPR on the -40), corrected for bleed the same way the thrust rating computer corrects it so that the card and the TRC agree.
**Brakes.** The maximum allowable brake temperature for a stop from V1, the brake energy zone of that stop from the BTMS reading (100 °C assumed when blank), and the runway the takeoff requires.
**Emergency return.** A landing back at the departure field at the takeoff weight: the landing distance, threshold and approach speeds and minimum maneuver speeds, for the return flap selected.

blocks.content: Where the manual leaves a choice open, the page takes the conservative side and says so: VMBE is read just below the chart's lines because it is a limit; the brake speed for the brake checks is V1; a headwind is never credited on takeoff. Each answer cell carries a note when it is limited, flagged or off the edge of a chart, and the status line under the buttons gives the warnings: a weight above MTOGW or MAW, a wind limit exceeded, a rolling takeoff required.
**Pull Aircraft Data** fills most boxes from the aircraft, the simulator's weather and its airport database. A few need the crew's judgment:

rows: The weight at **brake release**: the ramp weight less the taxi fuel. At the gate the aircraft's gross weight is still the ramp weight, so take off the planned taxi burn (1,500 lb is the standard allowance)
The takeoff CG from the load. It sets the runway correction, the climb correction, VR and V2 corrections and the stabilizer trim; a figure from a different load gives the wrong trim

Pull Aircraft Data fills the runway's full length. The KC-10's data expect the **runway available**: the length less the alignment distance (300 ft at least, more for a 180° turn on the runway) and less any part of it you will not use, such as an intersection departure. Correct the box yourself
The controlling obstacle's height **above the departure end of the runway** (not above sea level) and its distance from that end. Leave blank when there is none: the 2.5 % minimum then applies
The reported wind including gusts; VRB for a variable wind
23 for a dry runway; the reported or estimated reading otherwise. RSC for standing water, slush or snow over 0.10 in
As the takeoff will be flown. The anti-ice corrections apply only at 8 °C or below; the FedEx icing criteria are in [Ice and rain protection](ice-and-rain)

On for a normal takeoff with the packs running; Off for a packs-off takeoff, which gives more thrust and a higher MTOGW. The box shows Off until it is set or filled from the pack switches by Pull Aircraft Data: check it. With the Virtual Crew, this box decides how the crew sets the packs and bleeds
No if a reverser is inoperative: the page then uses the no-reverse charts
Reduced unless there is a reason not to (a contaminated runway, windshear, a known engine problem). The DC-10-40 also offers ALTN T.O.
The hottest brake's temperature, read after it has peaked, for the brake energy zone

blocks.content: Recompute the card whenever the inputs change: a different runway or intersection, a weight change, a new CG, a wind or temperature change, a change of runway condition, or a decision to take off with the packs off or anti-ice on. A card computed for one set of conditions says nothing about another.

The worked example's takeoff, a DC-10-30F at 523,700 lb with its CG at 20.4 % MAC, from Memphis runway 18R (9,319 ft long, 9,019 ft available after 300 ft of alignment, elevation 341 ft) at 28 °C with the wind 180/08, packs on, dry, reduced thrust:

rows: 8 kt of headwind, none of it credited
The runway the charts are entered with, after the corrections
Runway-limited at 5° flaps, climb-limited at 25°: the flap trade's two ends
The heaviest takeoff this runway allows today, and the flap to set on FLAP T.O. SEL
The runway limit falls to the actual weight at about 35 °C and the climb limit at about 37 °C; the lower governs, rounded down to a whole degree
V1 is VCEF; VMCG and VMBE do not limit
Flap retraction, slat retraction and the clean minimum maneuver speed
The trim for 20.4 % MAC at 24.8° flaps; the engine-out level-off height above the runway
The brakes must be below 292 °C at brake release; a stop from V1 would end in the caution zone
An immediate landing back at 523,700 lb: an overweight landing

blocks.content: The same takeoff on other days shows how the limits move. At **maximum thrust**, V1 is 141 and VR 156, N1 113.6 % and the runway required 8,450 ft: the thrust bought about 500 ft of margin that this takeoff did not need. With the **packs off**, the MTOGW rises to 556,500 lb and the assumed temperature to 39 °C (N1 110.6 %). With the CG at **15 %** instead of 20.4 %, the MTOGW falls to 535,700 lb and the trim rises to 6.8 units. At **35 °C**, past the flat-rating break, the MTOGW falls to 523,300 lb, just below the actual weight: the takeoff is no longer allowed on this runway without taking off weight, using the packs-off gain, or choosing a longer runway. On a **wet runway** (RCR 12) the MTOGW is 519,300 lb, again below the actual weight, and V1 drops to 132, because a slower V1 is what keeps the stop on the runway.

As a check on the method, the KC-10 manual's own worked example (520,000 lb, CG 26 %, 20 °C, 2,050 ft, an obstacle 99 ft above the runway's end at 3,200 ft) gives on the page the book's own answers: climb gradient 4.05 %, flap 15.3° (the book reads 15.2), VMCG 120, VCEF 146, VMBE 180, V1 146, VR 164, VR MIN 130, V2 177, VFR / VSR / VMM 195 / 240 / 274, STAB 3.4, acceleration height 1,456 ft (the book reads 1,460) and N1 114.1 %. For comparison with the civil method, FedEx's sample laptop output for a -30 on the same Memphis runway at 28 °C, with its own wind and the full runway, gives a runway-limited 535,200 lb at 20° of flap: the two methods agree within about one per cent.

children.title: From the card to the cockpit

blocks.content: The card's answers reach the aircraft in three ways: the crew set them, the EFB writes them, or the Virtual Crew uses them.

blocks.title: Where the card goes
rows: **Set Bugs** writes them to both airspeed indicators' bugs 1 to 5, in that order
**Send to Avionics** enters V1, VR and V2 on the FMS TAKEOFF page as crew entries; each PFD shows them
Set Bugs writes it to the glareshield SPEED select
Set by the crew on FLAP T.O. SEL and the flap handle
Sent to the FMS TAKEOFF page; set by the crew
Set by the crew; the Virtual Crew checks it
Set by the crew; the Virtual Crew checks it

On a reduced-thrust card, Set Bugs dials the assumed temperature into the TRC's ASSUMED TEMP thumbwheels on the aircraft with T.O. FLX (KC-10, -30, -15), 3 °C lower with engine anti-ice; selecting T.O. FLX remains the crew's press. On the -10 and -40, set the thrust by hand
FLEX is sent to the FMS TAKEOFF page as the card's assumed temperature; a maximum-thrust card sends none
Sent to the FMS TAKEOFF page
Briefed; the gross weight indicator carries the ZFW plus the fuel
Sent to WEIGHT INIT as TOGW and TOCG, with the fuel aboard as BLOCK (or a ZFW you have typed)

blocks.alt: DC-10-30 captain's airspeed indicator close-up after Set Bugs from the worked example's card: bug 1 at 142 (V1), bug 2 at 157 (VR), bug 3 at 196 (VFR), bug 4 at 241 (VSR), bug 5 at 275 (0/RET VMM); inset left, the glareshield SPEED select window reading 168 (V2); inset right, the center panel TAT/thrust rating indicator with the T.O. FLX button lit, the ASSUMED TEMP thumbwheels at 34 and N1 LIM 111.9.
blocks.title: Speed bugs and assumed temperature set from the card

blocks.content: Set Bugs writes once per press, so the bugs can be dragged afterwards; it drives the electromechanical airspeed indicators only. On a DC-10 fitted with flat-panel primary flight displays, set their speed references in those displays. The Landing page has its own Set Bugs for the approach (see [Landing performance](#landing-performance)).

**The Virtual Crew.** The takeoff card the Performance app holds is sent to the crew with each checklist they are asked to run, and three of its answers drive what they do. The flight engineer (DC-10 second officer, KC-10 flight engineer) sets the packs and bleeds from the AC box: a packs-off card is a packs-off takeoff, with the engine pneumatic supplies also off unless wing anti-ice is needed; with no card, the packs stay on. The anti-ice is set from the ANTI-ICE box: the engine anti-ice by the first officer (the KC-10's copilot) before taxi, and the wing anti-ice by the flight engineer. At Before Takeoff the first officer checks the captain's flap setting against the card's flap and the stabilizer against its STAB. On the MD-10 the first officer sets the anti-ice from the card after start. See [Virtual Crew](virtual-crew).

**Failures.** The EFB's Failures app can schedule an engine failure at V1 on the takeoff roll; by default it uses the V1 on the Performance card, so a practice engine failure arrives at the speed the card was computed for. See [EFB: Failures](efb#failures-schedule).

sections.title: Landing performance
sections.summary: Threshold and approach speeds, landing distance and its factors, autobrake selection, go-around climb limits, overweight landing and fuel dump.

blocks.content: The landing weight is limited three ways: by the structure (the maximum landing weight), by the ability to climb away from a missed approach (the approach and landing climb limits), and by the runway (the landing distance). The first two are checked at dispatch for the destination and the alternate; the third is checked again before the top of descent with the actual weight and the destination's weather. The EFB's **Approach** and **Landing** pages compute the speeds and the distance; they are described in [EFB: Approach and Landing](efb#landing-pages).

The **threshold speed** (VREF on the civil aircraft, VTH on the KC-10) is the speed at which the aircraft crosses the threshold at 50 ft in the landing configuration: 1.3 times the stall speed in that configuration, or 1.35 times with the slats retracted. The **minimum maneuver speeds** give the margin needed to maneuver in each intermediate configuration: 1.5 times the stall speed clean (0/RET) and with slats only (0/EXT), 1.4 times with 22° flaps and slats (22/EXT). Because the stall speed grows with the square root of the weight, each of these speeds rises by about half the percentage change in weight: at landing weights about 1 kt for each 5,000 lb for the threshold speeds and 1 kt for each 3,000 to 4,000 lb for the faster maneuver speeds.

The **approach speed** adds a margin for wind. On the DC-10 and MD-10 it is the threshold speed plus 5 kt or plus the **wind additive**, whichever is greater; the additive is half the steady wind above 20 kt or the full gust increment, whichever is greater, and never more than 20 kt. FedEx flew a 0/RET approach at VREF. The KC-10's manual adds the gust increment and half the steady wind above 20 kt, at most 20 kt, with no fixed 5 kt. The additive protects against a gust dropping away on short final. It is held until the flare begins, and the KC-10's data lengthen the ground roll for the faster touchdown it brings.

blocks.title: Series 30 landing speeds, KIAS (MD-10-30 and FedEx DC-10-30; the KC-10's card agrees within 1 kt)
Series 10 landing speeds, KIAS (MD-10-10; FedEx's DC-10-10 table, which the EFB uses for both, agrees within 1 kt)

blocks.content: Speeds above the landing weight limits are for an overweight landing or an emergency return; at the heaviest weights some of them exceed the flap limit speeds, and a lesser flap setting may be needed. The abnormal-configuration speeds (slats or flaps retracted, two engines inoperative) are in the procedures for those failures and in the EFB's Approach page. Above 2,000 ft pressure altitude the KC-10's threshold speeds rise slightly with altitude and come from its altitude charts; the EFB does this automatically.

**Set Bugs** on the Landing page puts bug 1 back to its rest position and sets bugs 2 to 5 to the threshold speed and the 22/EXT, 0/EXT and 0/RET minimum maneuver speeds, lowest first, because the bugs cannot pass one another on the dial. The SPEED select is left for the crew.

The landing distance has two parts. The **air distance** runs from 50 ft over the threshold to touchdown: the flare, roughly 1,000 to 1,300 ft as demonstrated on these aircraft (1,600 to 2,100 ft in the KC-10's charts, which factor it by 1.67). The **ground roll** runs from touchdown to a stop, and it is governed by energy: the kinetic energy at touchdown, proportional to the weight and to the square of the ground speed, must be absorbed by the brakes, the reversers and aerodynamic drag. Anything that raises the touchdown ground speed (weight, altitude, temperature, a tailwind, an approach speed additive not bled off) lengthens it with the square, and anything that reduces friction (a wet or contaminated runway) or deceleration (a reverser, the spoilers, the anti-skid or a brake inoperative) lengthens it directly.

blocks.alt: Profile diagram of a landing: the aircraft crossing the threshold at 50 ft at VTH, the flare (air distance) to touchdown, then the ground roll to a stop. Below, three bars of distance to the same scale for a DC-10-30 at 365,300 lb, sea level, 15 °C, flaps 35, calm: KC-10 data, dry (flare 1,881 ft factored, ground roll 2,381 ft, total 4,262 ft); KC-10 data, wet at RCR 12 (ground roll 3,648 ft, total 5,529 ft); and a civil bar showing the demonstrated distance multiplied by 1.67 to give the AFM landing field length. Labels list the factors that lengthen the roll: weight, density altitude, tailwind, downhill slope, runway condition, reverser, spoilers, anti-skid, brake or center gear inoperative.
blocks.title: How a landing distance is built

blocks.content: **The civil method.** The certificated landing field length is the distance from 50 ft at the threshold, at 1.3 times the stall speed, to a full stop with maximum braking and no reverse thrust, as demonstrated in flight test, multiplied by **1.67**. Put the other way, the demonstrated stop must fit in 60 % of the runway. The factor covers the difference between a test pilot's landing and a line landing in weather. For the crew's own in-flight checks FedEx used a **Quick Reference Landing Data** card, based on medium braking: find VREF for the weight and flaps, the airport's environmental region from its elevation and temperature, add the region's density correction and any tailwind to get the true ground speed, and read the approximate landing distance, dry and wet.

blocks.title: FedEx Quick Reference Landing Data examples (flaps 50, 1,000 ft, 30 °F, 4 to 5 kt tailwind)

blocks.content: **The KC-10 method.** The KC-10's landing distance is the flare distance, with a 167 % factor built in, plus the ground roll for the runway's stopping distance ratio, with reverse thrust on the operating engines. The roll is corrected for the threshold speed increment, the calculation wind (150 % of a tailwind; no headwind credit unless the landing is required for mission accomplishment), a downhill slope and the runway condition. Abnormal configurations enter as an **equivalent RCR**: center gear retracted, a wheel brake, the anti-skid or the spoilers inoperative each lower the effective runway condition, and several together take the lowest. A dual hydraulic failure multiplies the 50/EXT roll; a deactivated wing reverser adds 10 % to the roll. Standing water over 0.10 in lands at RCR 6, and a wet runway is taken at RCR 12 at best. The touchdown ground speed is also checked against the 204 kt tire limit and, when overweight or abnormal, the maximum brake energy speed.

blocks.title: Landing distance, long-span wing, KC-10 method (sea level, 15 °C, calm, reverse thrust), ft
The two methods are not interchangeable
blocks.content: The KC-10's distances are those of a maximum-effort stop with a factored flare; FedEx's quick reference figures assume medium braking. On FedEx's own Series 10 example the KC-10 method gives 3,724 ft against FedEx's 6,200. The EFB's Landing page gives the long-wing aircraft the KC-10's distance and the short-wing aircraft FedEx's quick reference distance. Treat the KC-10 figure as what the aircraft can do, not as what a normal landing uses: plan to land with a generous margin beyond it, and choose the autobrake setting (where fitted) for the runway you actually have.

The DC-10-10 may land above 363,500 lb only with 50° of flap, because with 35° the higher touchdown speed would exceed the brakes' energy capacity. On every series, 50° gives a slower threshold speed (about 5 kt) and a shorter landing; 35° gives a better go-around gradient, less noise and less fuel, and is the normal setting where the runway allows.

The DC-10's automatic brake system holds a selected deceleration after touchdown: MIN about 4.0 ft/s², MED about 5.4 ft/s², and MAX the full pressure of brake system 1 limited by the anti-skid (see [Landing gear: automatic brake system](landing-gear#autobrakes)). Because MIN and MED regulate the deceleration, more reverse thrust means less braking and cooler brakes, not a shorter stop. The choice is a balance: enough deceleration to stop with margin on the runway available in the conditions, and no more than needed, to save brakes, tires and the passengers' comfort and to make the planned turnoff.

FedEx published a stopping distance table for the -30's autobrakes at flaps 35 or 50: the distance from brake application to a stop at ISA with no slope, for the touchdown speed and the setting, with corrections for airport elevation and wind (as speed increments), for temperature (2.5 % for each 10 °F above ISA) and for a downhill slope (for each 1 %: 11 % at MIN, 7.5 % at MED and 4 % at MAX on a dry runway, 8 % at MAX or MED on a wet one). Its worked example: VREF + 5 of 140 kt, 2,000 ft, 5 kt tailwind, ISA + 20 °F, 0.5 % downhill, MED: 148 kt gives 5,740 ft, the temperature makes it 6,027 ft and the slope 6,238 ft.

items: **MIN** for a long, dry runway with a distant turnoff.
**MED** for a normal runway, or a wet one with margin.
**MAX** for a short or contaminated runway, a landing above the normal weight, or a failure that lengthens the stop.
On a CAT III approach FedEx requires the autobrakes when they are available.

blocks.content: A DC-10 fitted with the PMS has no autobrake: the PMS control display unit takes the AUTO BRAKE panel's place on the pedestal. Brake manually, with the deceleration the runway requires, as on the KC-10 and the simulated MD-10s, which have no autobrake either.

A landing weight must allow a go-around. Two certification climbs protect it. The **approach climb** is a climb on two engines at go-around thrust in the approach configuration (gear up, approach flaps 15/EXT or 22/EXT) at no more than 1.5 times the stall speed: the gradient must be at least **2.4 %**. The **landing climb** is a climb on all engines at go-around thrust in the landing configuration (gear down, flaps 35/EXT or 50/EXT) at no more than 1.3 times the stall speed: at least **3.2 %**. At most airports neither limits; at a hot, high field they can limit the landing weight below the structural limit, and the approach climb with an engine out is usually the tighter.

The same two limits set the civil MD-10's maximum zero fuel weight for performance, as described in [Weight definitions and structural limits](#wb-weights), so that an aircraft that must return just after takeoff can dump to a weight from which it can go around on two engines.

blocks.title: Go-around N1, CF6-50C2 (KC-10 data, entered at the total air temperature of the approach speed), %

blocks.content: Go-around thrust is set from the TRC's GA mode (the FMS on the MD-10), which the crew select before the approach. FedEx's Series 10 table is entered with the OAT, the KC-10's with the total air temperature, which at approach speeds is a few degrees higher. Missed approach procedures with an engine out and the two-engine approach are in [Abnormal procedures](abnormal-procedures) and [Emergency procedures](emergency-procedures).

An immediate return after takeoff usually finds the aircraft far above its maximum landing weight. The crew can land overweight, which FedEx permits only in an emergency, with a logbook entry and an inspection afterwards, or dump fuel to bring the weight down. An overweight landing can exceed the flap placard speeds, the tire speed and the brake energy limits, so the KC-10's manual asks the crew to check those whenever there is time. The TOLD card's emergency return section gives the landing data at the takeoff weight for this reason.

FedEx's DC-10s dump at about **5,000 lb per minute** with all tank, transfer and auxiliary pumps running and the crossfeeds open, so a -30 at 580,000 lb needs about half an hour to reach its 436,000 lb landing weight; FedEx's crews reviewed the dump time and weight as part of every takeoff briefing. Some fuel cannot be dumped: the dump stops by itself with about 40,000 lb left in the main tanks, fuel to reach a runway (the zero fuel weight rule in [Weight definitions and structural limits](#wb-weights) counts 42,300 lb). Dump speeds are limited on the -30 (325 KIAS below 28,000 ft, Mach 0.82 above). The procedure is in [Fuel: fuel jettison](fuel#fuel-jettison) and [Emergency procedures](emergency-procedures).

sections.title: Climb, cruise and descent
sections.summary: Speed schedules by series, climb, cruise and descent data, optimum and maximum altitude, buffet margins, step climbs, holding, and the engine-out case.

blocks.content: The en-route performance decides the trip fuel and time, and therefore much of the takeoff weight. The books give it in tables for a standard speed schedule: fuel, distance and time to climb from brake release to each cruise altitude, fuel flow and speed in the cruise for each weight and altitude, holding fuel flows, and fuel, distance and time to descend. The tables below summarize them; the EFB's **Climb**, **Cruise**, **Holding** and **Descent** pages evaluate them in full for any weight, altitude and temperature (see [EFB: Climb, Cruise, Holding and Descent](efb#enroute-pages)).

The long-span aircraft (KC-10, DC-10-30, DC-10-40, MD-10-30) are given the KC-10's data and the short-span aircraft (DC-10-10, -15, MD-10-10) FedEx's Series 10 data. The two books plan slightly differently: the KC-10's fuel flows are 5 % above the engine specification and its climb tables exclude the takeoff allowance from brake release to 2,000 ft; FedEx's climb tables include the takeoff allowance and a 4 % conservatism, and its cruise tables are unfactored book values.

A climb schedule is flown at a constant indicated airspeed until that speed reaches the chosen Mach number, then at the constant Mach. The indicated airspeed measures the impact pressure, and the Mach number depends on the ratio of that pressure to the static pressure; as the aircraft climbs and the static pressure falls, a constant IAS therefore means a rising Mach number (and the colder air lowers the speed of sound as well). The altitude at which the two meet is the **crossover altitude**. The best rate of climb would need a speed that changes continuously with weight and altitude, but the gain over a well-chosen constant schedule is negligible (the KC-10's manual puts a ±10 kt variance at no measurable effect), so each book uses one schedule for all weights.

blocks.title: Climb speed schedules
rows: 250 KIAS or 1.43 Vs, whichever is higher
KC-10, three engines (and the EFB's long-wing data)
250 KIAS or the minimum maneuver speed, whichever is higher

blocks.content: The 250 kt speed limit below 10,000 ft is an air traffic rule, and a heavy DC-10's clean minimum maneuver speed is above it: on the KC-10's data the climb speed below 10,000 ft is 250 KIAS up to about 433,000 lb, then 255 at 450,000, 268 at 500,000, 282 at 550,000 and 292 KIAS at 590,000 lb. FedEx's DC-10-30 schedule uses 1.43 times the stall speed for the same reason. The acceleration at 10,000 ft has its own fuel and distance, which is why the climb tables carry two 10,000 ft rows. The MD-10's flight management system computes its own climb speeds for the cost index entered (see [Flight management: Pegasus](flight-management#pegasus)).

**Thrust.** Climbs are flown at the maximum climb rating (CL on the thrust rating computer), two-engine climbs at maximum continuous thrust. The KC-10's **derated climb** uses maximum cruise thrust until the rate of climb falls to 500 ft/min, then climb thrust; it saves engine life at the cost of a slightly longer climb. At a constant throttle the N1 tends to rise during the climb, so the climb thrust must be watched; the autothrottle's N1 mode reduces the tendency. Climbing in vertical speed mode can command more climb than the aircraft has and bleed the speed away: monitor the airspeed. See [Automatic flight](automatic-flight) and [Engines: setting thrust](engines#setting-thrust).

blocks.title: Three-engine climb, long-span wing (KC-10 data): fuel, distance and time from sea level, standard day, zero wind; add 2,500 lb, 8 NM and 2.5 min for the takeoff allowance
Three-engine climb, DC-10-10 (FedEx): from brake release, ISA, zero wind, including the takeoff allowance and 4 %

blocks.content: A dash means the altitude is above the climb's useful ceiling at that weight. Above standard temperature the engines make less thrust and the climb takes longer: FedEx's -30 example, 480,000 lb to 31,000 ft, takes 18 minutes at ISA and 23 at ISA + 20 °C. A headwind shortens the distance over the ground; fuel and time are unaffected by wind. FedEx subtracts 0.4 minutes per 1,000 ft of departure field elevation from its times. A climb begun in flight, or a step climb, is read as the difference between two altitudes at the starting weight.

blocks.title: Service ceiling (100 ft/min), long-span wing, standard day (KC-10 data)

blocks.content: The **service ceiling** is the highest altitude at which the recommended climb speed still gives 100 ft/min with climb thrust (two engines: maximum continuous). The **cruise ceiling**, 300 ft/min with maximum cruise thrust, is lower and is the practical limit for a cruise level: an aircraft that can only just reach an altitude has no margin to hold it in turbulence or a turn.

The measure of cruise efficiency is the **specific range**: the distance flown per unit of fuel, true airspeed divided by fuel flow, given in nautical miles per 1,000 lb. For a given weight and altitude it has a maximum at the **maximum range cruise** speed. The KC-10's data define **long range cruise** as the speed giving 99 % of that maximum: one per cent of range buys several per cent of speed. In practice the books plan the jet aircraft at a constant Mach number: Mach 0.82 is the KC-10's and FedEx's planning speed, and FedEx's long range cruise starts near Mach 0.83 and slows as the weight comes off.

Specific range depends on altitude as well as speed. At a constant Mach the true airspeed hardly changes with altitude, but the dynamic pressure falls with the static pressure, so the wing must fly at a higher lift coefficient to carry the same weight. Low down it flies below the lift coefficient for its best lift-to-drag ratio, with more drag than the weight needs; climbing brings it towards the best one, and the engines, running at a higher fan speed in colder air, also burn less fuel per pound of thrust. Above the best lift coefficient the drag rises again: up to a point, higher is better. The **optimum altitude** is where the specific range is greatest for the weight; it falls as the weight rises, because a heavier aircraft reaches its best lift coefficient at a higher dynamic pressure, lower down. On the long-span wing the optimum altitude falls by about 2,500 ft for every 50,000 lb.

blocks.title: Optimum altitude, long-span wing, three engines, standard day (KC-10 data)

blocks.content: On the Series 10 the FedEx altitude-versus-weight placard gives the **optimum initial cruise weight** for each flight level at Mach 0.82: 440,000 lb (the maximum) at FL290 and FL310, 430,000 lb at FL330, 404,000 lb at FL350, 368,000 lb at FL370 and 334,000 lb at FL390. On the -10 the optimum altitude is always limited by maximum cruise thrust, so these weights are also the maximum recommended weights, and the best fuel mileage comes from climbing as high as maximum cruise thrust allows; the placard still leaves a 1.5 g buffet margin there. On the -30 placard the optimum initial weight is a separate, lower figure, the weight at which the specific range is slightly better than 4,000 ft above or below.

blocks.title: Cruise at Mach 0.82, long-span wing, three engines, standard day (KC-10 data): total fuel flow, lb/h / specific range, NM per 1,000 lb
Cruise at Mach 0.82, DC-10-10, three engines, ISA (FedEx): total fuel flow, lb/h / specific range, NM per 1,000 lb

blocks.content: A dash marks a cell beyond the maximum cruise thrust limit: the aircraft cannot hold Mach 0.82 there. The cells around each weight's optimum altitude show the shape of the specific range curve: flat near the top, so a level 2,000 ft off optimum costs little, and falling away faster above it than below. Engine anti-ice adds 1.3 % to the fuel flow and engine and wing anti-ice 2.2 % (FedEx -30). Above standard temperature the fuel flow rises a little for the same Mach, but so does the true airspeed, and the specific range hardly changes. The DC-10-40 has no cruise table of its own in any book the simulation has; the EFB gives it the CF6-50C2's fuel flows, which are an approximation for the JT9D.

blocks.alt: The EFB Performance app's Cruise page, portrait, on a DC-10-30F after Calculate Performance for the worked example's top of climb: GW 509.2, CRUISE ALT 31000, ISA DEV 0, CG 20.4 entered; results at Mach 0.82 on three engines: N1 97.7, IAS 306, TAS 481, fuel flow 7,082 lb/h per engine and 21,247 lb/h total, 22.6 NM per 1,000 lb; optimum altitude about 30,700 ft with the next 4,000 ft step; buffet margin 1.5 g or more. Clear Data, Pull Aircraft Data and Calculate Performance buttons at the top.
blocks.title: Performance, Cruise page

blocks.content: **Step climbs.** As fuel burns, the optimum altitude rises by about 500 ft for every 10,000 lb, so the best profile is a slow cruise climb. Air traffic control assigns levels, so the books plan **step climbs**: climb to the next level when the specific range there has become as good as the present one. For a 4,000 ft step that is roughly when the optimum altitude has risen 2,000 ft above the present level, or a little before, since the climb itself burns fuel. FedEx's -30 example: at Mach 0.82 the optimum initial cruise weight at 35,000 ft is 449,000 lb, so the step from 31,000 ft should begin about 3,000 lb heavier, at 452,000 lb, because the climb itself burns fuel. The books' 4,000 ft steps come from the semicircular level rules of their time; with reduced vertical separation, levels 2,000 ft apart in the same direction are available and allow smaller steps closer to the optimum.

blocks.alt: Chart of pressure altitude (28,000 to 42,000 ft, vertical) against gross weight (300,000 to 580,000 lb, horizontal, decreasing to the right as fuel burns) for the long-span wing at Mach 0.82, standard day. A curved line for the optimum altitude (27,800 ft at 580,000 lb to 41,300 ft at 300,000 lb); above it the 1.5 g, 1.4 g, 1.3 g and 1.2 g buffet-onset lines; a maximum cruise thrust line. A staircase marks the worked example's flight: FL310 from the top of climb at 509,000 lb, a step to FL350 at 456,600 lb, a step to FL390 at 376,400 lb, and the top of descent at about 367,000 lb. Shaded band around the optimum line where the specific range is within 1 % of the best.
blocks.title: Optimum altitude, buffet margins and step climbs

blocks.content: **Maximum altitude.** An aircraft can fly above its optimum, but not indefinitely. Two limits close in. The **thrust limit** is the altitude at which maximum cruise thrust can just hold the cruise Mach (or give 300 ft/min of climb), and it falls quickly in warm air. The **buffet limit** is the altitude at which the margin to buffet onset falls below what is needed to maneuver and to ride turbulence: the wing must be able to pull a certain load factor before it buffets. FedEx's -30 placard bases its maximum recommended weight on a **1.3 g** margin, enough for a bank of about 40° before buffet; above ISA + 15 °C maximum cruise thrust may limit first. The -10's placard is limited by maximum cruise thrust and leaves 1.5 g, about 50° of bank. The KC-10's optimum altitude line lies just below its **1.5 g** buffet line, so cruising at the optimum leaves at least 0.5 g of margin. For air refueling the KC-10 uses its 1.2 g buffet speed plus 5 kt as the minimum speed (see [Air refueling](air-refueling)).

blocks.title: Load factor to buffet onset at Mach 0.82 to 0.83, long-span wing, CG 24 % MAC (KC-10 data)

blocks.content: On the Series 10 the FedEx altitude capability at Mach 0.82, ISA, is about 39,800 ft at 320,000 lb, 37,400 ft at 360,000 lb, 35,200 ft at 400,000 lb and 32,000 ft at 440,000 lb (maximum cruise thrust), with the 1.5 g buffet altitude 700 to 1,300 ft above. A forward CG raises the buffet speed slightly, which is why the charts state their CG. The aerodynamics of buffet and high-altitude handling are in [Flight characteristics](flight-characteristics).

**Wind.** A better wind at a lower level can outweigh the specific range lost by flying below the optimum. FedEx's -10 wind trade chart gives the wind difference needed to justify it: at 340,000 lb at 35,000 ft, cruising 4,000 ft lower costs nothing in fuel mileage only if the headwind there is at least 34 kt less (or the tailwind 34 kt more). The comparison is always read at the higher of the two altitudes.
