children.title: Cost index and the performance computers

blocks.content: The cheapest speed is rarely the most economical in fuel alone. Time costs money too: crew pay, maintenance by the hour, connections. The **cost index** is the ratio of the time-related cost per hour to the cost of fuel; at a cost index of zero the economy speed is the maximum range speed, and as it rises the economy (ECON) speed rises towards the maximum operating speed. Long range cruise and the books' constant Mach 0.82 are fixed points in that range, simple enough to plan by hand.

rows: Economy climb, cruise and descent speeds and thrust targets for the entered cost index, optimum and maximum altitudes, step climb points and a descent profile to the bottom of descent. In the simulation it is advisory: the crew fly its targets. See [Flight management: PMS](flight-management#pms)
Lateral navigation and its own performance pages. See [Flight management: HT9100](flight-management#ht9100)
Navigation, performance and the mission (air refueling) functions. See [Flight management: KC-10 FMS](flight-management#kc10-fms)

ECON speeds for the cost index, optimum and maximum altitudes, fuel predictions, thrust limits and the vertical profile, all from the weights and fuel entered at initialization. See [Flight management: Pegasus](flight-management#pegasus)

blocks.content: None of these computers replaces the plan. They predict from the weight they were given: a wrong zero fuel weight gives wrong speeds, wrong optimum altitudes and wrong fuel predictions all the way to the destination. Initialize them from the load sheet, and check their fuel predictions against the flight plan at each waypoint.

In a hold the aim is the least fuel per hour, not per mile: **maximum endurance**. Endurance is best at the speed of minimum drag (strictly, minimum fuel flow), which is slower than the best range speed and rises with weight. Lower down the engines are less efficient, so holding is best done high when there is a choice; FedEx's holding charts shade the optimum altitude for each weight. Each book gives a recommended holding speed and target N1 with the fuel flow they produce.

blocks.title: Three-engine holding, long-span wing, clean, standard day (KC-10 data): straight-leg speed, KIAS / total fuel flow, lb/h

blocks.content: The turns cost more: the KC-10's tables give a separate speed and fuel flow for the bank angle used, read at the weight divided by the cosine of the bank, so a 25° bank turn is flown as if the aircraft were about 10 % heavier. The KC-10's mission planning uses the 25° bank figure throughout, which is how its manual gets 10,720 lb/h for a 249,100 lb aircraft holding at 10,000 ft. Holding with the slats extended at low altitude costs about 1,500 to 2,300 lb an hour more at 25° of bank.

FedEx's -30 holding fuel includes a 4 % conservatism: a hold of 45 minutes at 25,000 ft starting at 400,000 lb needs 11,000 lb, and at 360,000 lb and 20,000 ft, 9,000 lb of holding fuel lasts 41 minutes. Engine anti-ice adds 1 % and engine and wing anti-ice 3 %.

The descent is flown at idle thrust, so its fuel is small and nearly independent of weight and temperature; the planning question is where to start it. Begun too early, the aircraft levels off low and burns fuel at low altitude; too late, it arrives high and fast and must use the speed brakes, which on the DC-10 family are usable only with the flaps at 0. The books' tables give the fuel, time and distance to descend from each altitude for each schedule, valid for all weights and temperatures.

blocks.title: Descent to sea level, long-span wing (KC-10 data): fuel, lb / distance, NM (zero wind) / time, min
columns: Penetration (250 KIAS, gear and speed brakes below 20,000 ft)

blocks.title: Descent to sea level, DC-10-10 (FedEx), idle: fuel, lb / distance, NM (zero wind) / time, min

blocks.content: The KC-10's en route descent averages about 1,600 ft/min, its long range descent 1,400 ft/min, and its penetration descent 4,000 ft/min below 20,000 ft with the gear and speed brakes out. FedEx's -30 tables use the same low-speed and high-speed schedules as the -10. For a destination above sea level, FedEx subtracts 1 minute, 3 NM and 70 lb for every 1,000 ft of field elevation. If the descent starts later than planned, increase the rate of descent by 50 ft/min for every 10 NM late; if earlier, reduce it by the same. A headwind shortens the distance over the ground, a tailwind lengthens it: correct the top of descent for the descent wind.

After an engine failure in cruise the aircraft cannot hold a high cruise level on two engines at a heavy weight, and must **drift down** at the best two-engine speed with maximum continuous thrust to the altitude it can hold. On the KC-10's data the two-engine climb schedule is 300 KIAS and Mach 0.76, and the two-engine service ceiling ranges from about 36,600 ft at 350,000 lb to 27,400 ft at 500,000 lb and 21,800 ft at 590,000 lb (see the service ceiling table under [Climb](#climb)). Dumping fuel raises it.

The civil rules require that at every point of the route the **net** one-engine-out ceiling (the actual performance reduced by a set margin) clears all terrain within 5 statute miles of the track by 1,000 ft, or that the net driftdown path clears it by 2,000 ft. FedEx did not normally treat this as a dispatch limit, because fuel may be dumped after the failure; it had to be checked when dispatching with the fuel dump system inoperative, against the highest terrain on the route. For the continental United States a terrain clearance height of 15,500 ft covers the highest terrain. The procedures are in [Abnormal procedures](abnormal-procedures), the handling in [Flight characteristics](flight-characteristics).

sections.title: Fuel planning
sections.summary: The parts of a fuel plan and the reserves, planning backwards from the landing weight, typical fuel flows, tankering, the loading schedule, and tanker offload planning.

blocks.content: Fuel is the largest variable in the weight of a flight and the one that decides whether it arrives. A fuel plan has to answer three questions: how much fuel the flight will burn, how much must remain at the end in case the plan does not work out, and whether the result can be carried within the aircraft's limits. The civil aircraft were planned under FAR Part 121's fuel rules; the KC-10's performance manual uses its own mission reserves in its worked examples. This part gives both and the data for each component.

children.title: The parts of a fuel plan

rows: Engine start, taxi out, and any APU use on the ground

1,500 lb is the standard allowance (FedEx's load sheet and the KC-10's manual); the KC-10 adds 100 lb for each minute of engine ground running beyond 15. Engines on the ground burn about 120 lb/min in total at takeoff weights and 90 lb/min at landing weights; 80 lb/min at ground idle. An engine start takes about 30 lb per engine. The APU burns about 350 lb/h on the ground (500 lb/h at full load) and 300 lb/h in flight
Brake release to 2,000 ft, including clean-up and acceleration to the climb speed

KC-10 data: 2,500 lb, 8 NM, 2.5 min on three engines (4,000 lb, 16 NM, 5.5 min on two), added to its climb tables. FedEx's climb tables already include it: 2,000 lb (-10) or 2,500 lb (-30), 3 min, 8 or 10 NM
Climb, cruise and descent to the destination, and the approach
From the climb, cruise and descent data (see [Climb, cruise and descent](#climb-cruise-descent)). The KC-10's manual allows 3,000 lb for approach and landing, and 18,000 lb/h in a traffic pattern
Deviations from the plan: wind and temperature errors, routing, a level off optimum
FAR 121 international flights: fuel to fly 10 % of the total flight time to the destination, at normal cruise consumption (FedEx's chart assumes Mach 0.82 at 30,000 ft)
A missed approach at the destination, the climb, cruise and descent to the alternate, and an approach there

From the alternate's distance and the landing weight there. FedEx's -30 chart includes the missed approach and a straight-in approach at the alternate; the KC-10's manual gives the fuel, altitude and Mach for the distance
Fuel to hold when everything else is used
FAR 121 domestic: 45 minutes at normal cruise consumption. International: 30 minutes holding at 1,500 ft above the alternate. The KC-10's examples: 45 minutes holding at 10,000 ft at 25° bank
An international flight with no alternate
Two hours at normal cruise consumption instead of the alternate fuel
Expected traffic delays; the captain's discretion; tankering
From the holding data (FedEx's planned-hold chart) or as decided

blocks.content: Anti-ice costs fuel: FedEx adds 1.3 % to the destination fuel with engine anti-ice on and 2.7 % with engine and wing anti-ice, with no effect on the time. FedEx's flight planning charts already carry 4 % for the in-service deterioration of engines and airframes, so a direct comparison with a computer flight plan nearly always shows the charts asking for more fuel. The KC-10's data are 5 % above the engine specification throughout.

The fuel burned depends on the weight carried, and the weight carried depends on the fuel. The books break that circle by planning **from the end of the flight**. The zero fuel weight plus the reserves is the weight at which the aircraft must arrive. The trip fuel is then found for that landing weight, which makes the takeoff weight. FedEx's flight planning charts are drawn for exactly this: enter with the distance, correct it for the wind, go up to the landing weight, and read the trip fuel, with a correction if the cruise altitude is off the optimum. The KC-10's manual works its missions the same way, segment by segment from the destination backwards.

items: **Final reserve and alternate.** Start from the ZFW. Add the final reserve (computed at about the ZFW) and the alternate fuel (computed for the weight at the alternate).
**Contingency.** Add the contingency for the trip time. The sum is the planned landing weight at the destination.

**Trip.** Find the trip fuel and time for the planned speed and altitudes from that landing weight, with the en route wind as an equivalent still-air distance (a headwind lengthens it, a tailwind shortens it).
**Takeoff and ramp.** Landing weight plus trip fuel is the takeoff weight; plus taxi fuel, the ramp weight. Takeoff fuel is the trip fuel plus all the reserves.

**Check.** The takeoff weight against the structural and the performance limits for the departure; the landing weight against the destination's; the takeoff fuel against the tank capacity. If a limit is exceeded, payload must come off, the route or the alternate must change, or the flight needs a fuel stop.

blocks.content: FedEx's own examples show the scale. A -30 flying 2,500 NM with an 80 kt tailwind (2,150 NM in still air) at 25,000 ft at long range cruise, to land at 380,000 lb, needs 92,000 lb of trip fuel and 4 h 54 min. A diversion of 1,300 NM into a 40 kt headwind at 31,000 ft from 420,000 lb takes 49,000 lb and 3 h 03 min; for the -10, 650 NM into 50 kt at 35,000 ft from 380,000 lb takes 22,000 lb and 1 h 37 min. Those charts include FedEx's 4 % conservatism.

A flight plan from a service such as SimBrief does this arithmetic for you, with its own aircraft profile and the forecast winds, and the EFB can fetch its ramp fuel directly (see [Planning a flight in the simulation](#flight-planning-in-sim)). Its answer is only as good as its profile: check that the profile's basic operating weight, maximum weights and fuel capacity match your variant, and compare its trip fuel with the book figures in this section for a sense of its margin.

blocks.title: Typical fuel flows, standard day
rows: Climb to the initial cruise level
7,400 lb to FL290 at 400,000 lb; 12,000 lb to FL330 at 500,000 lb; plus 2,500 lb takeoff allowance
9,800 lb to FL330 at 340,000 lb, allowance included
Cruise, Mach 0.82 near the optimum altitude
11,500 lb/h at 300,000 lb, 15,100 lb/h at 400,000 lb (straight legs)
Descent from cruise to sea level

blocks.content: As a rule of thumb, a DC-10-30 on a long sector averages about 18,500 lb/h from brake release to landing: the worked example burns 158,400 lb in 8 h 34 min. A -10 on a domestic sector burns rather less, mainly because it is lighter. The DC-10-40's JT9D engines have no cruise data in any book available to the simulation; the EFB plans it with the CF6-50C2's fuel flows, which are only an approximation.

These are the books' figures, and the plans in this section use them. The simulated engines do not burn exactly the book's fuel: see [Simulation notes](#mp-simulation-notes). Plan with the book, then compare the actual burn against the plan at each waypoint, as a real crew would.

**Tankering** is carrying more fuel than the flight needs, to avoid buying fuel at the destination where it is expensive, scarce or slow to load. It is never free: the extra fuel is extra weight, and carrying weight costs fuel. The KC-10's cruise table shows how much. At Mach 0.82 between FL310 and FL350, every extra 10,000 lb raises the total fuel flow by roughly 240 to 650 lb/h, between 2.4 and 6.5 % of the extra fuel each hour; the cost rises with weight and altitude, steeply once the extra weight takes the aircraft above its optimum altitude. The extra weight also lowers the optimum altitude, so the flight spends longer at less efficient levels.

So 10,000 lb tankered on a five-hour flight at a typical 3 % per hour arrives as about 8,500 lb: about 1,500 lb has gone to carrying it. Tankering pays when the price saved on the fuel that arrives exceeds the cost of the fuel burned to carry it, and when the turnaround time saved is worth something. It is limited by the tanks, by the maximum takeoff weight and the departure's performance, and above all by the **maximum landing weight** at the destination: tankered fuel is fuel the aircraft lands with.

The **loading schedule** fixes how much fuel each tank holds for a given total, and the **use schedule** fixes the order in which it is burned. Both exist first for the wing's structure: fuel in the outer wing tanks relieves the wing's bending moment in flight, so those tanks are filled first and emptied last, and the zero fuel weight limit relies on it. Both also fix the CG travel, which the ZFW CG limits assume. The schedule gives each tank's quantity at the end of the fueling, not the order of filling.

rows: Load tanks 1, 2 and 3 equally until 1 and 3 are full, then tank 2
Tank 2 transfers to tanks 1 and 3 until the three are equal, then all three feed equally

As above until tank 2 is full, then the upper auxiliary tank until full, then the lower auxiliary tank where fitted (not on the -15 or -40). FedEx adds the auxiliary fuel as soon as tanks 1 and 3 are full
The auxiliary tank transfers to the main tanks, keeping them full, until it is empty; then tank 2 to tanks 1 and 3 until equal; then all three equally

5,000 lb in each main tank; 15,000 lb in the FWD body tank; the main tanks equally until 1 and 3 are full; tank 2 until full; the center wing tank and both body tanks equally until the FWD body tank is full; the center wing and AFT body tanks equally until the AFT tank is full; then the center wing tank until full

In general the body and center tank fuel is used or offloaded first, the main tanks kept full as the weight limits require and the FWD tank's balance fuel kept as the CG requires (see [Fuel: KC-10 fuel management](fuel#kc10-fuel-management))

blocks.content: The EFB's Fuel page **Distribute** button applies these schedules, and its preview shows the CG the fuel will give (see [EFB: the Fuel page](efb#fuel-page)). The **lateral imbalance** between tanks 1 and 3 is limited to 2,000 lb on FedEx's DC-10s, 2,900 lb (Series 10) and 2,500 lb (Series 30) on the MD-10, and 4,000 lb on the KC-10 (2,000 lb above 556,000 lb). Planning densities are 6.7 lb per US gallon; the MD-10 accepts 6.3 to 7.1 lb/gal, and its maximum takeoff weight comes down 2,500 lb for each 0.1 lb/gal below 6.5, because the tanks hold fewer pounds.

blocks.title: Total usable fuel as simulated
rows: 145,375 (DC-10-10 with the Extended Range center tank option: 178,102)
243,175 (DC-10-30 with the Extended Range aft auxiliary tank option: 265,375)

blocks.content: Capacity limits range as much as weight does. The worked example's -30F, at a 329,500 lb ZFW, can fill its tanks and still take off at about 571,000 lb, inside the heaviest -30's limit; with full tanks and full reserves it reaches about 4,900 NM in still air on the book's figures. A heavier payload makes the maximum takeoff weight the limit before the tanks are full, and a short sector with a heavy payload can be limited by the maximum landing weight. The tank-by-tank capacities are in [Fuel: capacities](fuel#capacities), and the fuel system itself, its pumps, transfer and crossfeed, in [Fuel](fuel).

A tanker's mission plan answers one more question: how much fuel can be given away. The method is the same backwards planning, applied segment by segment. Work from the destination: the zero fuel weight plus the reserves and the approach allowance is the weight overhead the destination; add the descent and the cruise and climb after the last offload to find the weight at the end of the offload. Then work forwards from takeoff to the start of the offload. The offload is the weight at the start of the refueling, less the weight at its end, less the fuel the tanker burns while refueling.

The KC-10's manual gives the data the segments need. The standard **orbit** speed while waiting for receivers is 275 KIAS or Mach 0.78, whichever is lower, but not below the orbit table's speed for the weight; at 25,000 ft and 540,000 lb that is 304 KIAS and 401 lb/min on a standard day, 407 lb/min at ISA + 10 °C. While refueling with the boom trailing, the drag reduces the specific range (by a factor of about 0.94 in the manual's examples). The KC-10 transfers fuel at up to **7,800 lb/min**, and as a receiver can pump about 1,000 lb/min back to a tanker. The planning base altitude for refueling is 25,000 ft, and the KC-10 is not planned to receive above 31,000 ft (25,500 ft when being filled to its maximum weight).

The manual's first worked mission shows the scale of it: a round robin of 4,400 NM, taking off at 590,000 lb with 345,400 lb of fuel and a zero fuel weight of 246,100 lb, flying 2,000 NM out at 29,000 ft, orbiting 15 minutes, refueling a C-5A over 200 NM at 20,000 ft, then returning at 37,000 and 41,000 ft with full reserves. It can give away **143,940 lb** of fuel, and burns 178,760 lb itself. Its second mission, a fighter deployment, plans six offloads and two onloads from another KC-10, and shows that the onload should be taken as late as possible, so that the tanker carries the extra weight for the shortest time.

The planning, rendezvous and refueling procedures are in [Air refueling](air-refueling) and its [Mission planning](ar-general-operations#ar-mission-planning). In the simulation there are no receiver aircraft, so no fuel is actually offloaded or onloaded: the tanker's weight changes only with its own burn, and an offload plan can be flown but not delivered.

The DC-10-40 Omega and the KDC-10 are air refueling tankers on the DC-10 button; their refueling procedures are in [Air refueling](air-refueling), and as on the KC-10 the simulation has no receivers, so their offload is planned but not delivered. The DC-10-10 and -30 **air tankers** carry their retardant as payload: the EFB's Fire Support app loads the three retardant tanks (2,700, 4,000 and 2,700 US gal) with retardant at 9.01 lb/gal or water at 8.34 lb/gal, so a full load of retardant weighs about 84,700 lb. The sortie, its weights and its drops are described in [Aerial firefighting: the firefighting mission](aerial-firefighting#vlat-mission).

sections.title: Planning a flight in the simulation
sections.summary: What the EFB needs, loading a route, and a worked DC-10-30F flight from the load sheet to the takeoff card and the landing data.

blocks.content: In the simulation the whole planning sequence is done on the EFB, with the route from SimBrief or the simulator's own flight planner. The EFB does the arithmetic; the crew decide the inputs and check the answers against the limits. This part lists what the EFB needs, shows how a route gets into the aircraft and the Performance app, and then works one complete flight.

rows: The variant loaded: the Performance app picks the airframe (and so the book) from it automatically
Route's Load from SimBrief, the Fuel page's SimBrief button, the MD-10's flight plan initialization
MSFS or Navigraph, in EFB Settings
The route loaded into the navigation unit
The simulator's METAR for the airport, and the aircraft's own readings on the ground
The simulator's airport database: heading, length, slope, threshold elevation
Pull Aircraft Data and Send to Performance
The aircraft, after loading through the EFB
Pull Aircraft Data, Performance's blank GW and CG boxes
Set Bugs, Send to Avionics, the Virtual Crew, the Failures app's V1 trigger

blocks.content: The EFB's **Route** app loads a flight plan into whichever long-range navigation unit the aircraft carries: an INS or the AINS-70, the HT9100, the KC-10's FMS or the MD-10's Pegasus. **Load from SimBrief** fetches your latest SimBrief flight plan; **Load from Sim** takes the route planned in the simulator. On a route longer than an inertial unit can hold, the route is cut into parts, and the crew load each part from the Route app as the aircraft nears the end of the one before. The **Navlog** page shows the SimBrief plan fix by fix, with the planned fuel on board at each, which is what the fuel check in flight compares against. How a route is loaded and what each unit does with it are in [EFB: Route](efb#route-app) and [Flight management: loading a route](flight-management#fm-route-loading).

blocks.alt: The EFB Route app's Load page, portrait, after a SimBrief import on a DC-10-30F: the route's two ends KMEM to the destination, the source SimBrief and the job's state LOADED as a badge; the unit's next step (the AINS-70's company route and waypoints); the FLIGHT PLAN PARTS boxes for a long route; and at the foot the Send to Performance button. An inset shows the Performance app's Climb page afterwards, with TOC ALT, ISA DEV and WIND filled from the plan and marked as such.
blocks.title: Route: Send to Performance

blocks.content: Once a route is held, **Send to Performance** on the Route app's Load page fills every Performance page with what the plan knows: the departure airport, runway and its data on Takeoff; the destination, arrival runway and its data on Approach and Landing; the top-of-climb level, the climb's average ISA deviation and wind on Climb; the initial cruise level and its ISA deviation on Cruise; the top-of-descent level, the destination elevation and the descent wind on Descent. It never fills a weight, a CG or the day's conditions: those come from the aircraft with Pull Aircraft Data once the aircraft is loaded. The **Fuel** page's SimBrief button takes the plan's ramp fuel and Distribute spreads it in the loading schedule.

On the MD-10, **Send to Avionics** on the Performance app's Takeoff page also fills the Pegasus F-PLN INIT page from the SimBrief plan (flight number, cruise level, cost index, alternate) and WEIGHT INIT from the card. It never sends a new FROM/TO, which would replace the route you have built. See [Flight management: Pegasus](flight-management#pegasus).

children.title: Worked example: a DC-10-30F from Memphis

blocks.content: A DC-10-30F at the heaviest -30 weights (580,000 lb takeoff, 436,000 lb landing, 414,000 lb zero fuel) departs Memphis runway 18R for a 4,000 NM sector. For simplicity the example assumes still air and a standard atmosphere en route, a 200 NM alternate, and FAR 121 international reserves. Every performance figure is from the books' data, as the EFB evaluates them.

rows: FedEx's sample -30F; read your own from the EFB with the aircraft empty
Inside the ZFW CG band; the cargo was placed to give it

blocks.content: Planned at Mach 0.82 with step climbs, worked backwards from the reserves and then flown forwards on the KC-10's tables:

blocks.title: Reserves and the fuel load
rows: 10 % of the trip time at Mach 0.82 cruise consumption
200 NM, with the missed approach climb, the descent and a 3,000 lb approach allowance
Trip plus reserves, worked unrounded (the rounded parts shown add to 194,100)

blocks.content: The steps fall where the optimum altitude passes 2,000 ft above the present level: 456,600 lb for FL310 to FL350 (FedEx's own -30 example gives 452,000 lb), and 376,400 lb for FL350 to FL390. FL310 is the initial level because at the 509,200 lb top-of-climb weight the optimum is about 30,700 ft and the buffet margin there is 1.5 g or more. The resulting weights: takeoff **523,700 lb** (limit 580,000), landing **365,300 lb** (limit 436,000).

Load the cargo first and confirm the ZFW and ZFW CG on the EFB. Then on the Fuel page enter 195,700 lb and press Distribute. The schedule fills tanks 1 and 3 (40,203 lb each) and tank 2 (64,969 lb), and puts the remaining 50,325 lb in the center auxiliary tank. The preview shows the fuel's own CG near 22 % MAC and a ramp CG of about **20.4 %**. Press Refuel (with ground power on the ground service bus) or Instant.

At 523,700 lb the -30's envelope runs from about 10.1 to 27.5 % MAC, so 20.4 % is comfortably inside. As the center tank empties in the first hours of the flight the CG moves aft, to about 22.8 % at 475,000 lb, and further aft as tank 2 feeds down to the level of the wing tanks, to about 24.3 % at 450,000 lb (the aft limit there is 29.0 %). With the three tanks then used together it comes forward, to about 21.2 % at the landing weight. Every point lies inside the envelope, as the ZFW CG band promised.

On the Performance app's Takeoff page: Send to Performance has filled the airport, runway, heading, length and elevation; Pull Aircraft Data fills the weight, CG, temperature, pressure altitude and wind. Correct GW to the brake release weight (523.7) and RWY AVAIL to 9,019 ft (9,319 ft less 300 ft of alignment). With 28 °C, wind 180/08, packs on, dry runway and reduced thrust, Calculate Performance gives the card described in [Reading the card: an example](#told-reading):

rows: Maximum 292 °C at brake release; a stop from V1 in the caution zone

blocks.content: In the cockpit: press **Set Bugs**, which sets the speed bugs and the SPEED select and dials 34 into the TRC's ASSUMED TEMP thumbwheels; set 24.8° (or the nearest setting) on FLAP T.O. SEL; set the stabilizer to 5.4 units. Before takeoff select T.O. FLX on the thrust rating computer and confirm N1 LIM 111.9. Brief the engine failure (V1 142, V2 168, level off at 1,433 ft) and the return: an immediate landing would be 87,700 lb overweight, about 18 minutes of fuel dumping.

At the top of climb at FL310 the aircraft weighs about 509,200 lb: Mach 0.82 needs about 97.7 % N1 and 21,250 lb/h. Check the fuel on board against the Navlog at each waypoint. Request FL350 around 1,390 NM from departure, when the weight is near 456,600 lb, and FL390 near 3,600 NM at 376,400 lb; a better wind at a lower level can justify staying (see [Cruise](#cruise)). On the DC-10 the PMS, where fitted, computes its own optimum altitudes and step points from its own model of the aircraft; expect them to differ somewhat from the book's.

Before the top of descent, compute the landing data on the Approach and Landing pages with the destination's weather. At 365,300 lb the 35/EXT threshold speed is 145 KIAS (approach 150 by the FedEx +5 rule; 145 in calm air by the KC-10's). At a sea-level destination at 15 °C in calm air the KC-10 landing distance is 4,262 ft dry with 35/EXT, 3,977 ft with 50/EXT, and 5,529 ft on a wet runway. With a gusty 15G25 kt wind the additive is 10 kt and the distance with 35/EXT grows to 4,724 ft. Start the descent 130 NM out (from FL390, en route schedule), set the landing bugs, and choose the autobrake for the runway.

items.item: Send to Performance, Pull Aircraft Data
GW (brake release) and RWY AVAIL (less alignment)

blocks.content: **Weight and CG.** The aircraft's mass is carried by the simulator's fuel tanks and payload stations, written by the aircraft from its own fuel system, cargo and cabin, so the flight model flies the true gross weight and CG. The EFB converts the simulator's CG to the real mean aerodynamic chord; its figure can differ from a real load sheet by up to about 0.4 % MAC, and the short-wing aircraft use the long-span wing's MAC. The gear load split is solved for every airframe. The MAC panel can be fitted and the weight and balance computer behind it is modeled, but in this version the panel in the cockpit is not yet connected: its switches, counters and lights do not respond. The computer's own CG also does not yet follow the loading (it assumes about 18.5 % MAC), and the gear load split uses the same value. Use the EFB's weight and CG.

**Performance data.** The EFB's numbers are the books' charts and tables, digitized and checked against the books' own worked examples; they are not derived from the simulator's flight model, and the flight model is not tuned to reproduce them exactly. The aircraft will not necessarily fly exactly the book's distances, gradients and fuel flows: plan with the book and keep the margins it builds in. The long-wing aircraft use the KC-10's military data. The DC-10-10, -15, -40 and MD-10-10 take their takeoff limits from the KC-10's charts at an equivalent condition, an approximation. The DC-10-15 is given the CF6-50C2's thrust, since its -50C2F rating is not modeled. The DC-10-40 is planned with the CF6-50C2's cruise fuel flows.

**Fuel burn.** The simulated CF6-50C2 has been compared with the KC-10's Mach 0.82 cruise table and tends to burn somewhat less than the book, of the order of 5 to 15 per cent depending on the bleed load; unlike the book, its cruise fuel flow hardly rises with temperature. The CF6-6D's cruise fuel flow has not been checked against cruise data. The DC-10-40's JT9D-59A shares the CF6-50's gas path model with its own ratings, and burns about a quarter less in cruise than a real JT9D: do not take its fuel flows as JT9D figures. Plan with the book and treat the difference as margin.

items: Pull Aircraft Data fills RWY AVAIL with the runway's full length; subtract the alignment distance yourself.

Not computed by the EFB: the configuration corrections for center gear retracted, a brake or the anti-skid inoperative on takeoff; drag index deviations; APU doors open; an inoperative ENG FAIL light; frost; an engine cowl anti-ice valve failed open; windshear takeoff speeds; the derated climb's temperature and wind corrections; the integrated range charts.
The EFB does not check the zero fuel weight or the CG envelope; plan them yourself.
The Aircraft Setup page's brake type (tri-metallic or carbon) and the Realism setting are stored but do not yet change any performance data.

The simulated KC-10 carries its wing refueling pods, but the KC-10's data are for an aircraft without them and the EFB does not apply the manual's pod corrections (3.9 % off the runway available, 0.52 % on the required climb gradient, and the pods' drag). On a limiting takeoff, enter a correspondingly shorter RWY AVAIL and keep a margin.
There are no receiver aircraft: a tanker's offload is planned but not delivered.
On the MD-10 the fuel controller does not hold entered ballast fuel back from its schedule; manage it yourself.
Do not edit the payload stations on the simulator's own weight and balance page while the EFB's loading is in use.

chapters.title: Flight Characteristics
chapters.summary: How the aircraft handles across its envelope: stability, stalls, high-speed flight, engine failures, heavy weights, abnormal configurations and control failures.

sections.title: Introduction
sections.summary: What this section covers, and the aircraft as a flying machine: a large, heavy, swept-wing tri-jet with powered controls and artificial feel.

blocks.content:
This section describes how the DC-10 family flies: its stability in each axis, how it approaches a stall and how it is recovered, how it behaves at high Mach number and high altitude, how it is controlled with one or two engines inoperative, how weight and configuration change it, and how failures of the flight control system change what the pilot feels and must do. It is the aerodynamic companion to [Flight Controls](flight-controls), which describes the hardware that moves the surfaces, and to the procedure chapters, which give the checklists. The KC-10's handling while refueling and the air tanker's handling in the drop are described under [Heavy-weight handling](#heavy-weight-handling).

The KC-10 flight manual, drawing on the type's flight test, describes its stall characteristics, its stability and its natural buffet warning as excellent throughout the weight and center of gravity range. Nothing in this section describes a dangerous aircraft. It describes a large one, whose behavior follows directly from its size, its wing and the arrangement of its engines, and whose pilots fly it best when they understand why it does what it does.

**The wing.** Every member of the family has a wing swept 35° at the quarter chord with 6° of dihedral, carrying leading edge slats along the whole span (in an inboard and an outboard group) and inboard and outboard trailing edge flaps that travel to 50°. The -10 and its derivatives have the short-span wing; the -30, -40, KC-10 and MD-10-30 add about 10 ft of span. At maximum takeoff weight the wing carries around 125 lb per square foot on the -10 and 155 to 162 lb per square foot on the long-span aircraft. High wing loading gives a smooth ride in turbulence, because a gust changes the lift on a heavily loaded wing by a smaller fraction of the weight, and it gives high approach speeds and long runways, because a heavily loaded wing must fly fast to make its lift.

**The controls.** Every primary surface is driven by hydraulic power control units, each surface from two of the three hydraulic systems, with no manual reversion. The forces the pilot feels are made by the feel system, not by the air: the column force comes from the elevator load feel system, scheduled with airspeed, and the wheel and pedal forces come from springs. The aircraft therefore has no natural force cues at all. What the pilot feels was designed to resemble a conventional aircraft, and it does so very well, but it does not change when the air does: it changes only when the feel system's inputs do.

**The engines.** Two engines hang below and ahead of the wings, about 27½ ft either side of the centerline and well below the center of gravity. The third sits in the fin root on the centerline, well above it. That arrangement shapes the handling more than any other feature of the design. A wing engine failure produces a large yawing moment; a center engine failure produces none at all, but changes the trim in pitch. Thrust changes on the wing engines and on the center engine push the nose in opposite directions. And because the center engine is mounted on the fin, an uncontained failure there is the one event that can reach all three hydraulic systems at once.

blocks.alt: Side-view schematic of a DC-10-30 in level flight, nose to the left. Marked: the center of gravity on the fuselage near the wing root; the wing's center of lift slightly aft of it; the horizontal stabilizer with a downward tail load arrow; the two wing engines' thrust line drawn below the center of gravity with a curved arrow showing the nose-up pitching moment of wing engine thrust; the No. 2 engine's thrust line in the fin root drawn above the center of gravity with a curved arrow showing the nose-down pitching moment of its thrust; the weight arrow from the center of gravity. A small inset plan view shows the wing engines' lateral arm (27 ft 7 in from the centerline) and the yawing moment one wing engine's thrust makes about the center of gravity. Labels legible, no numbers other than the arm.

blocks.caption: Wing engine thrust acts below the center of gravity and pitches the nose up; center engine thrust acts above it and pitches the nose down. A wing engine also has a long lateral arm; the center engine has none.

sections.title: General handling
sections.summary: Mass and response, pitch changes with thrust, trim and feel, ground effect, rotation and flare geometry, and crosswinds.

blocks.content: Pilots coming to the DC-10 from smaller jets describe it the same way: stable, solid, honest, and slow to be hurried. It goes where it is pointed and stays there. The skill it asks for is anticipation: a small correction made early does what a large correction made late cannot, and a large correction made late is followed by a second one to stop the first.

An aircraft of 400,000 to 590,000 lb, with a fuselage over 170 ft long and its engines and fuel spread far from the center of gravity, has large moments of inertia in all three axes. A control input produces an angular acceleration in proportion to the moment it makes divided by the inertia, so rotation starts slowly, and once started it takes an equal and opposite input to stop. The aircraft is not sluggish, because its control surfaces and their moment arms are scaled to its inertia, but it has a definite lag between input and response that a pilot must allow for.

In pitch the response comes in two stages. The column changes the elevator angle, which changes the angle of attack within a second or two (the aircraft's short-period response, which is quick and well damped). The changed angle of attack changes the lift, which bends the flight path, and the flight path follows the pitch attitude only after several seconds. Altitude follows the flight path later still. That is why the books ask for attitude to be flown precisely and for altitude and speed to be allowed to follow: a pilot who chases the altimeter with the column is always several seconds behind, and in a heavy aircraft that produces the slow pitch oscillation called a pilot-induced oscillation.

**Rotation.** The books ask for a smooth, continuous rotation at about **2.5 to 3° per second** to the initial climb attitude, taking about six seconds from VR, with lift-off at around 10° of pitch. The rotation rate matters because lift needs time to build: rotating too fast raises the tail-down attitude before the wing has lifted the main gear clear, which is how a tail strike happens on takeoff. Rotating too slowly lengthens the takeoff roll and erodes the margins the performance data assumes. At high weights a heavier than normal feel can be expected and the aircraft tends to settle after lift-off; FedEx gives 10° as the minimum pitch attitude in that case.

**Initial climb.** The initial climb attitude is about 15°: with all engines it gives V2 + 10 kt, and with an engine inoperative about V2. The all-engine pitch attitude normally stays below 22°. Bank is limited to 15° until the minimum maneuvering speed for the configuration is reached.

Thrust acting along a line that misses the center of gravity makes a pitching moment. The wing engines' thrust lines pass well below the center of gravity, so more thrust from Nos. 1 and 3 pitches the nose up and less pitches it down. No. 2's thrust line passes well above the center of gravity, so more thrust from No. 2 pitches the nose down and less pitches it up. With all three engines moving together the two effects partly cancel, and the books single out the case where they no longer do: with No. 2 inoperative, every thrust change on the wing engines needs elevator or trim.

items: **With No. 2 inoperative**, thrust changes on the wing engines are no longer offset, and each needs an elevator input or a stabilizer trim change (FedEx). The effect is greatest at low speed, where the tail has the least dynamic pressure to oppose it (the KC-10 manual notes that trim changes with thrust are larger at low speed).

**With the stabilizer jammed**, No. 2's throttle becomes a pitch control: varying its thrust can move the pitch attitude by more than 5° (FedEx). The stabilizer inoperative approach uses exactly that.
**With no hydraulic power at all**, wing engine thrust is the only pitch control left (see [Loss of all hydraulic power](#total-hydraulic-loss)).

**On the ground**, No. 2's reverse thrust pulls rearward high above the center of gravity and raises the nose; with only one set of elevators available, FedEx limits No. 2 to idle reverse for that reason. Ground spoiler extension also pitches the nose up, most noticeably at aft centers of gravity, and the pilot flying holds the nose wheel down with forward column.

**At low speed and high power**, as in a go-around from a light-weight approach, the nose-up moment of the wing engines arrives with the thrust and needs a positive forward input and nose-down trim to hold the target attitude.

blocks.content:
The aircraft is trimmed in pitch with the horizontal stabilizer, at two rates (the faster rate at low speed, where large trim changes accompany configuration changes, and the slower rate at high speed, where a small stabilizer movement makes a large moment). See [Horizontal stabilizer](flight-controls#horizontal-stabilizer). The column force the pilot holds is made by the elevator load feel system, which stiffens the column with airspeed: the force per degree of elevator rises with speed while the elevator needed for each g falls, so the force per g stays roughly constant across the speed range. A failure of the feel system leaves the column too light at high speed or too heavy at low speed, while the aircraft's actual response is unchanged; see [Elevator load feel](flight-controls#elf-auto).

Longitudinal stability shows itself to the pilot as the need for a push to fly faster than the trimmed speed and a pull to fly slower. Re-trimming relieves the force but does not change the stability. Two consequences follow, and both appear in the books' cautions. A pilot who trims away the warning force as the speed decays is removing the very cue that the aircraft is slowing; and an autopilot that trims nose up to hold altitude while the speed decays hands back an aircraft that is out of trim nose up at exactly the moment the pilot needs to push. That is why the stall recovery procedures begin with a warning to be alert for mistrim.

Aileron and rudder trim move the neutral point of the feel springs, so the surfaces and the controls both move to the new neutral. Rudder trim is used to hold the steady rudder of an engine-out condition, and should be returned to zero before touchdown on a normal landing. Aileron trim corrects small lateral asymmetries, such as an imbalance of fuel. Neither is used in turbulence or in an upset.

Close to the ground the wing's downwash cannot develop fully, because the ground blocks it. Within about half a span of the runway the wing's induced drag falls and its lift at a given angle of attack rises; the DC-10 begins to feel it at about 100 ft and the effect grows rapidly as the wheels approach the runway. Two consequences matter to the pilot. The aircraft floats if it arrives with excess speed, because less drag is slowing it. And the reduced downwash at the tail changes the tail's angle of attack and gives a nose-down pitching tendency, so the flare needs a little more back pressure than the same attitude change at height would. Close to the runway the elevator also feels noticeably more effective, most of all in a flapless landing (FedEx).

The books' flare technique follows from this. Aim 1,500 to 1,800 ft down the runway (the MD-10 FCOM gives about 1,700 ft for a 47 ft threshold crossing height on a 3° path), begin a slight flare at 30 to 40 ft of about 2°, do not trim during the flare, and fly the aircraft onto the runway rather than holding it off. Holding off to find a smooth touchdown makes the aircraft float through the touchdown zone, raises the pitch attitude as the speed decays, and reduces the tail's clearance. Deceleration on the runway is about three times what it is in the air, so a long float costs far more runway than a firm touchdown at the target.

blocks.alt: Two diagrams of a DC-10-30 on the runway with its main gear struts compressed. Left, side view: pitch attitudes marked against the runway line: about 10° at lift-off, 8° to 9° typical at touchdown, and about 13° where the aft fuselage contacts the runway, with the tail clearance angle shaded. Right, front view at 9° of pitch: bank angle to wingtip contact marked as 11.8° for the short-span wing and 11.1° for the long-span wing, with a note that the wingtip (or the flap at 50°) touches before an engine nacelle. Labels legible.
blocks.title: Tail and wingtip clearance
blocks.caption: Pitch and bank margins on the runway. The touchdown attitude is close enough to the tail contact angle that holding the aircraft off in the flare, or flaring late and abruptly from a high sink rate, can use it all.

blocks.content: **Tail and wingtip clearance.** In a normal flaps 35 approach at maximum landing weight the pitch attitude is about 6°; flared to zero sink at idle thrust the aircraft would touch down at about 10°, and a typical touchdown is at 8 to 9°. Flaps 50 lowers each of these by about 1°. The aft fuselage contacts the runway at about **13°** with the struts compressed (MD-10 FCOM), so the margin is a few degrees. It is consumed by holding the aircraft off, by flaring late and hard from a high sink rate, by large column movements just before touchdown, and by the nose-up moment of the ground spoilers if the nose is not promptly lowered. In bank, at a 9° touchdown attitude the wingtip contacts the runway at 11.8° (short-span wing) or 11.1° (long-span wing); the wingtip, or the flap at 50°, always touches before an engine nacelle. The forward slip of a strong crosswind landing needs at most about 6°.

The landing gear and tail geometry give the DC-10 a marked tendency to **weathervane** into a crosswind on the runway: the large fin and the long fuselage behind the main gear make the crosswind push the tail downwind and the nose into wind. On takeoff, the upwind wing tends to rise as the roll begins. The technique is the conventional swept-wing one: hold the column slightly forward of neutral to load the nose wheel, correct the weathervaning immediately with rudder, and hold enough aileron into wind to keep the wings level, a fixed amount set before brake release if preferred. The aileron needed decreases as speed rises. The result is a crossed-control sideslip, held through rotation and lift-off, and taken out smoothly after lift-off. Avoid large wheel oscillations, and do not alternate between neutral and the correction.

**Landing.** The recommended method is to fly the final approach wings level, crabbed into the wind, and at about 200 ft to align the fuselage with the centerline using rudder while lowering the upwind wing just enough to stop the drift. Avoid holding the aircraft off: the low angle of attack of a positive touchdown gives the best lateral control. After touchdown keep the wings level with aileron and the direction with rudder, and expect the weathervaning until the nose wheel steering and the brakes are effective.

The maximum demonstrated crosswind component is **31 kt**. With either rudder inoperative it falls to **15 kt**, and with braking action reported poor FedEx limits takeoff and landing to **10 kt**. On the CF6-50 aircraft (DC-10-30, MD-10-30) a static takeoff (power set against the brakes) is prohibited if the wind is more than 45° off the runway heading or the crosswind component exceeds 23 kt, because the engine's inlet is prone to compressor stall at high power and low speed in a wind across its face; a rolling takeoff is required instead. See [Contaminated and slippery runways](adverse-weather#contaminated-runways) for the effect of a crosswind on a slippery runway.
Strong crosswinds can make the nose gear steering angle large enough to skid the nose wheels on a slippery surface. If it does, hold the nose wheel straight and steer with rudder and brakes.

sections.title: Stability and control
sections.summary: Static and dynamic stability, the longitudinal modes, speed stability, transonic effects, lateral-directional stability, Dutch roll, the spiral mode and the use of rudder.

blocks.content: An aircraft's **stability** is its tendency to return to a trimmed condition after a disturbance, whether the disturbance comes from a gust or from the pilot. More stability means a stronger tendency to stay trimmed, and therefore a larger control force or deflection to make the aircraft do anything else. Good handling is a balance: enough stability that the aircraft holds its condition without constant attention, and not so much that maneuvering it is hard work. The KC-10 manual records positive static stability in every axis throughout the normal operating envelope, and the type's flight test found no transonic pitch instability up to the limit Mach number.

**Static stability** describes the aircraft's initial reaction to a disturbance, ignoring what happens afterwards. If the forces and moments that arise push it back toward trim, it is statically stable; if they push it further away, statically unstable; if they do neither and it simply stays where it was put, statically neutral.

**Dynamic stability** describes the motion that follows, over time. A statically unstable aircraft diverges, so it is also dynamically unstable. A statically stable aircraft may return in one of four ways: directly, without overshooting (a **subsidence**, the most stable case); or by oscillating about the trim condition, with oscillations that shrink (dynamically stable), stay the same size (dynamically neutral) or grow (dynamically unstable). Static stability is therefore necessary for dynamic stability but does not guarantee it: an aircraft that tries hard to return to trim can overshoot further each time.

blocks.alt: Six small time-history graphs, displacement from trim on the vertical axis against time on the horizontal, each with the trim line dashed. Top row, non-oscillatory: divergence (curve leaving trim, labeled statically and dynamically unstable), neutral (curve stepping off trim and staying there, labeled neutral static stability), subsidence (curve returning to trim without overshoot, labeled positive dynamic stability). Bottom row, oscillatory: damped oscillation decaying to trim (positive dynamic stability), undamped oscillation of constant amplitude (neutral dynamic stability), divergent oscillation growing in amplitude (negative dynamic stability). Titles legible.
blocks.title: Dynamic stability modes

blocks.content: A real aircraft responds to a disturbance in a mixture of **natural modes**, each with its own period and damping, and each tied to a particular axis or pair of axes. In pitch there are two: the quick **short-period** mode and the slow **phugoid**. Laterally and directionally there are three: the fast **roll subsidence**, the oscillatory **Dutch roll**, and the slow **spiral** mode. The sections below take each in turn.

Longitudinal static stability is the aircraft's resistance to a change of angle of attack. If a gust raises the angle of attack, the extra lift on the wing and on the horizontal tail acts at a point called the **neutral point**. With the center of gravity ahead of the neutral point, the extra lift makes a nose-down moment and the aircraft returns toward its trimmed angle of attack; the distance between them, as a fraction of the mean aerodynamic chord, is the **static margin**. The horizontal tail contributes most of the stability, which is why it is large and far aft. The fuselage, the nacelles and engine thrust each contribute too, some stabilizing and some not. The family is designed for positive static and dynamic longitudinal stability throughout its normal envelope.

To the pilot, static stability appears as the force needed to fly away from the trimmed speed: a push to fly faster, a pull to fly slower. The feel system shapes those forces, but the stability that makes them necessary is the aircraft's own.

**The center of gravity.** The CG moves the trade between stability and performance. A forward CG increases the static margin: the aircraft is more stable, heavier in pitch, needs more nose-up stabilizer to rotate and flare, and carries a larger tail download, which the wing must lift as well as the weight, raising the stall speed and the trim drag. An aft CG does the opposite: lighter forces, a smaller download, lower stall and buffet speeds and better fuel economy, with less margin of stability. The limits balance the two. At mid weights they run from about 8% MAC to about 31% MAC on the DC-10-10 and to about 29% on the DC-10-30, narrowing at the heaviest weights (see [Limitations](limitations)). The KC-10 manual encourages loading toward the aft part of the envelope for economy. The CG also shifts the stick shaker and buffet onset speeds: the KC-10's 1.2 g buffet speed rises by about 0.5 kt for each 1% MAC the CG moves forward.

**The short-period mode** is the quick pitch response at nearly constant speed: angle of attack and pitch rate change together and settle within a few seconds. It is heavily damped, because pitching the aircraft swings the tail up or down through the air and the tail's change of angle of attack opposes the motion. Pilots rarely see it as an oscillation; they see it as the crispness, or otherwise, of the aircraft's answer to the column.

**The phugoid** is a slow exchange between speed and height at nearly constant angle of attack. If the nose rises, the aircraft climbs and slows, its lift falls below its weight, the nose drops, it descends and accelerates, its lift exceeds its weight, and the nose rises again. The classical estimate of its period is π√2 times the true airspeed divided by the acceleration of gravity, which is roughly 0.23 seconds per knot of true airspeed: about 40 seconds on an approach and nearly two minutes in cruise. Its damping comes from drag, and is weak; an efficient airframe with a high lift-to-drag ratio has a lightly damped phugoid. On the DC-10 it damps out eventually without any pilot action. In normal flight the pilot and the autopilot suppress it without noticing. It matters in two places: when chasing altitude with the column, which can drive it, and when the elevators are lost and the phugoid has to be damped with thrust (see [Loss of all hydraulic power](#total-hydraulic-loss)).

children.title: Speed stability and the back of the drag curve

blocks.content: **Speed stability** is something different from static longitudinal stability, although the terms are often confused. It describes what happens to the speed after a disturbance when the pilot holds the flight path and leaves the throttles alone. It depends on how drag and thrust change with speed. Total drag is the sum of parasite drag, which rises with the square of the speed, and induced drag, which falls with it; the sum has a minimum at the **minimum drag speed**. Above that speed, a speed increase raises the drag and the aircraft slows back down: it is speed stable. Below it, a speed decrease raises the drag, the aircraft slows further, and only more thrust stops it: it is speed unstable. Because the thrust at a fixed throttle also falls a little as speed rises, the speed of neutral stability is slightly below the minimum drag speed.

blocks.alt: Graph of thrust required (total drag) against airspeed for a DC-10 at a fixed weight and altitude. The U-shaped total drag curve is drawn with its two components dashed: parasite drag rising with speed and induced drag falling with it. The minimum drag speed is marked at the bottom of the U. A slightly falling line for thrust available at a fixed throttle setting crosses the curve. Point A, just below the minimum drag speed where the slopes match, is labeled neutral speed stability. The region to the right is shaded and labeled speed stable (front side); the region to the left labeled speed unstable (back side, behind the drag curve), with point B on it. Small arrows at a point on each side show the speed returning on the front side and diverging on the back side. Labels legible, no numerical scales.
blocks.title: Speed stability

blocks.content: Flying on the **back side of the drag curve** is not dangerous, but it is more work: with the flight path held on the column, every speed correction has to come from the throttles, more thrust to recover lost speed and less to shed excess. The DC-10 approaches close to its minimum drag speed, where speed stability is about neutral; the flare, the slowest part of the approach, is never meant to be flown slow enough for a marked instability to appear. Slow refueling, holding and maximum endurance speeds can sit at or just below the minimum drag speed, and there an autothrottle in light chop can be seen hunting for the speed. FedEx suggests flying the throttles by hand in cruise when that hunting exceeds about ±3% N1.

Below its critical Mach number a swept wing's lift acts near its quarter chord. As the speed rises into the transonic range, regions of supersonic flow and their terminating shock waves form on the upper surface, the pressure distribution changes and the center of lift moves aft. With the center of gravity unchanged, that gives a growing nose-down pitching moment, and the push the pilot must hold to fly faster grows less steeply, or reverses. The effect is called **transonic tuck**, or Mach tuck. On an aircraft that has it strongly, an inattentive pilot could find the nose dropping and the speed building further, and some types carry a Mach trim compensator that biases the elevator nose-up with Mach number to hide it.

The DC-10 family's flight test found no transonic tuck within the flight envelope: the aircraft does not become unstable in pitch up to its MMO, and the KC-10 manual records that no mechanical compensation is required. The pilot will see the trim change progressively with Mach number, as on any swept-wing transport, but no reversal of the column force.

Lateral (roll) and directional (yaw) stability are treated together because each axis drives the other. Static stability in both is positive throughout the normal operating range.

**Directional stability**, or weathercock stability, is the aircraft's tendency to point into the relative wind. A sideslip puts the fin at an angle of attack, and its side force, acting far behind the center of gravity, yaws the nose back into the wind. The DC-10's fin, rudder and long tail arm give it strong directional stability, which shows on the ground as the weathervaning in a crosswind described above.

**Dihedral effect** is the rolling moment produced by sideslip, and it is what makes a wing that has dropped tend to come back up. On a swept wing, sideslip changes the effective sweep of the two wings: the wing advancing into the relative wind is less swept, generates more lift, and rolls the aircraft away from the sideslip. Geometric dihedral adds to the effect (the DC-10 has 6°). Because the sweep contribution is proportional to the lift coefficient, dihedral effect is strongest at low speed and high lift, short of the stall. It is also what lets a pilot pick up a wing with rudder: rudder makes sideslip, and sideslip makes roll.

On some aircraft dihedral effect can reverse at high Mach number, because the advancing wing's higher effective Mach number brings on shock-induced separation and a loss of lift. On the DC-10 family it stays positive throughout the normal envelope.

children.title: Dutch roll and the yaw dampers

blocks.content:
**Dutch roll** is a coupled oscillation in yaw and roll, usually set off by a gust or by an uncoordinated input. A yaw disturbance makes the aircraft sideslip; the dihedral effect rolls it away from the sideslip; the directional stability yaws the nose back, overshoots, and sets up a sideslip the other way; and the aircraft rocks and wags with a period of a few seconds, the wingtips tracing ellipses against the horizon. The roll lags the yaw by part of a cycle, which is why the motion looks like a skater's rhythm and why a pilot trying to stop it with a control input tends to arrive at the wrong moment.

Two features make it more pronounced on a swept-wing transport at altitude. Strong dihedral effect from sweep raises the ratio of roll to yaw, so the rolling part dominates. And the aerodynamic damping of the motion comes from the air the fin and wing push aside as they move, so it falls as the air density falls: the oscillation is least damped high up, at high weight and at low indicated speed.

blocks.alt: Diagram of the Dutch roll on a DC-10 shown in three rows over one full cycle at quarter-cycle intervals. Top row, plan view: the aircraft's heading swinging left and right of the flight path, with the sideslip angle between the nose and the relative wind arrow marked. Middle row, rear view: the bank angle rocking left and right. Bottom row: three sine curves on one time axis for yaw angle, sideslip angle and bank angle, showing the bank lagging the yaw by roughly a quarter cycle. A side panel shows the yaw damper loop: yaw rate gyro, washout filter, gain, and the series pistons moving the rudder against the yaw rate, with the rudder deflection curve drawn opposing the yaw rate curve. Labels legible.
blocks.title: Dutch roll
blocks.caption: The damper senses yaw rate and puts in rudder against it, removing energy from the oscillation on every cycle. It does not move the pedals.

blocks.content:
No stability augmentation is needed to control the aircraft in normal conditions. Near the maximum operating altitude, though, the Dutch roll damping weakens to the point where a pilot can still control the motion but the people in the back would not enjoy it, so **series yaw dampers** supply the damping the airframe lacks up there. Each rudder carries two damper channels, each limited to ±2.5° of rudder, acting in series with the pedals; the dampers sense yaw rate and move the rudder against it. See [Yaw dampers](automatic-flight#yaw-dampers) for the system and [Yaw dampers](flight-controls#yaw-dampers) for the rudder hardware.

At least two channels must be operative for takeoff (see [Limitations](limitations)). In flight with all dampers lost, the books impose no limitation and give no special technique: smooth flying avoids exciting the mode, and since the damping improves with air density, a lower cruising altitude improves it. Do not try to fight the oscillation with the rudder pedals. A pedal input arrives a part-cycle out of step with the motion it is meant to stop, and the KC-10 manual's warning about answering a roll with opposite rudder (see [Rudder use](#rudder-use)) applies here with full force.

blocks.title: KC-10 fuel slosh yaw oscillation
blocks.content: With certain loadings of the forward fuselage (body) tank, fuel slosh can drive a yaw oscillation of about 0.4 Hz (a period of about 2.5 seconds), usually above M 0.85. It is not a hazard to the aircraft. If it appears, transfer fuel out of the forward fuselage tank, preferably to the aft fuselage tank, until the oscillation is acceptable or gone.

The **spiral mode** is the slow tendency, after a small bank disturbance with the controls free, either to roll back to wings level (spirally stable) or to tighten gradually into a steepening, descending turn (spirally unstable). It is decided by a contest between the two lateral-directional effects. Directional stability turns the nose into the sideslip that a bank produces, which steepens the turn; dihedral effect rolls the wings level, which ends it. The parameters that improve one usually worsen the other, which is why the Dutch roll and the spiral modes are designed as a compromise: strong dihedral effect favors spiral stability and weakens Dutch roll damping, strong directional stability the reverse.

The usual design choice favors Dutch roll damping at some cost in spiral stability. The DC-10 family nevertheless has good spiral stability, and with the yaw dampers operating it is always spirally stable.

The rudder is sized to give directional control after an engine failure on takeoff and to handle the demonstrated crosswind. Its normal uses are exactly those: trim, engine failure, and crosswind takeoff and landing, and in those uses full rudder is well within the aircraft's structural capability. The flight control system descriptions show no rudder ratio changer or travel limiter (see [Rudder authority](flight-controls#rudder-authority)), although the KC-10 manual's note on rudder characteristics speaks of the available deflection being reduced by rudder limiting as speed rises. Fly as if full pedal can command full rudder at any speed: the side load on the fin from a given input grows with dynamic pressure.

A rudder input yaws the aircraft first and rolls it afterwards, because the roll comes from the sideslip, and sideslip takes time to build. A large, abrupt pedal input can therefore produce a sideslip far larger than the steady sideslip a slow input would settle at: the aircraft overshoots in yaw, and the overshoot amplifies the roll that follows. The lag between the input and the roll has surprised pilots into believing an outside force was rolling the aircraft. If the pilot answers that roll with a large rudder input the other way, the yaw and roll oscillations can grow quickly, and the loads from **full-authority rudder reversals** may exceed the structure's design limits even below the design maneuvering speed. No procedure requires such inputs. Large sideslip at high power can also surge the engines, and the loads reach other structure, such as the engine pylons.

items: A rudder input is never the right first response to a wake vortex encounter, a windshear, an upset, or a roll toward the stall. Use the ailerons and spoilers.

In a stall recovery, do not use rudder at all: the books found it unnecessary in flight test, and rudder near the stall produces a yaw-induced roll. Recover from the stall first; the ailerons and spoilers then give ample roll control for any attitude recovery that follows.
In an upset, consider rudder for roll only when the ailerons have proved ineffective and the aircraft is not stalled, and use it carefully.
Confine full application of rudder or aileron, and maneuvers near the stall, to speeds below the design maneuvering speed VA (see [Limitations](limitations)).

sections.title: Stalls
sections.summary: The swept wing at the stall, stall warning and its margins, the automatic slat extension, approach-to-stall recovery, upset recovery and spins.

blocks.content: In flight test the family stalled benignly in every configuration across its weight and center of gravity range, with little difference between a forward and an aft CG. It neither rolls off nor pitches up, the wheel keeps good lateral control up to the break, and buffet or the stick shaker gives a clear warning first. The procedures that follow are therefore about recognizing the warning early and recovering without fuss, and about the few configurations (slats retracted with flaps extended, high altitude, ice or damage on the leading edge) in which the margin is smaller.

children.title: The swept wing at the stall

blocks.content:
A wing stalls when its angle of attack exceeds the angle at which the flow over the upper surface can stay attached. The airspeed at which that happens is not fixed: in steady flight the stall speed rises with the square root of the weight, and in a turn or pull-up with the square root of the load factor (a 45° bank, 1.41 g, raises it by about 19%). It also depends on the configuration, on the center of gravity through the tail download, and at high altitude on Mach number, because compressibility lowers the maximum lift coefficient the wing can reach.

A swept wing has a natural tendency to stall at the tips first. The sweep drives a spanwise flow toward the tips that thickens the boundary layer there, and the outer wing runs at a higher local lift coefficient. On a swept wing the tips are behind the center of gravity, so a tip stall loses lift aft and pitches the nose up, deeper into the stall, and it takes away the ailerons' effectiveness as it goes. The DC-10's wing is designed against both. The inboard sections fly at a higher angle of attack than the outboard sections, and the slats are rigged so that, flown into a stall, the inboard wing stalls first: the lift lost is ahead of the tips, and the nose drops. With the slats extended, the outer wing keeps its flow and its ailerons through the stall.

**Nacelle strakes.** Each wing engine nacelle carries a pair of small ear-like strakes on the outside of its leading edge, set 45° either side of the vertical. At high angles of attack each sheds a strong vortex that crosses the pylon-wing junction and, close to the stall, presses flat against the upper surface, re-energizing the boundary layer and holding off the separation that the nacelle and pylon would otherwise trigger. The effect was discovered in the wind tunnel and the strakes were sized in flight test, where the stall speeds came out slightly better than predicted with landing flaps and several knots better with takeoff flaps, the configuration that matters most for second segment climb. Their cost in cruise drag is under 0.1%. On a humid day the vortex can be seen streaming back over the wing at rotation.

blocks.alt: Conceptual graph of wing lift coefficient against angle of attack for the DC-10, no numerical scales. Three curves: clean wing, rising and peaking at the clean stall; slats extended, continuing to a higher maximum lift coefficient at a higher stall angle; flaps and slats extended, shifted upward to the highest maximum lift coefficient. On each curve a marker below the peak shows the stick shaker point, and a shaded band between the shaker and the peak is labeled stall warning margin. On the clean curve, an arrow at the shaker point jumps up to a dashed curve labeled outboard slats auto-extended, showing the automatic slat extension raising the outer wing's stalling angle. A note at the flap curve: flap buffet can mask the natural stall buffet. Labels legible.
blocks.title: Lift curves and stall warning
blocks.caption: The shaker is scheduled on angle of attack for the configuration. In the clean configuration the shaker also extends the outboard slats.

blocks.content:
**Configuration changes the warning.** Some aerodynamic buffet precedes the stall in every configuration. It is strongest in the clean configuration and weakens as slats and flaps are extended. With the slats out, light buffet begins about 10 to 12 kt above the stick shaker speed. At lower flap settings the shaker is closely followed by a perceptible buffet that grows; at the landing flap settings the flaps' own buffet can mask the stall buffet almost completely, which is why the shaker is the definite warning there. Slowed further, the aircraft may show some rolling tendency and a nose-down pitch that increases with the deceleration.

In the clean configuration the approach to the stall is marked by considerable buffet and more lateral activity, a tendency to drop a wing that the automatic slat extension was introduced to remove (see below).

**With the slats retracted and the flaps extended**, as after a dual hydraulic failure, the stall is abrupt: there is no pre-stall buffet, and recovery must begin at the first indication. The MD-10 FCOM singles out flaps 22 with the slats retracted.

Ice, frost or hail damage on the wing's leading edges raises the stall speed and can bring the stall before the stick shaker, which knows only the angle of attack. Hail can also damage the angle-of-attack vanes. The approach speeds include a margin for the leading edge damage a hail encounter normally causes; fly them, and treat any buffet as a stall warning.

Certification requires a stall warning that is clear and distinctive to the pilot, given either by the aircraft's own buffet or by a device. On the DC-10 and KC-10 the device is the **stick shaker**: two angle-of-attack vanes, one each side of the forward fuselage, feed two stall warning channels in the autothrottle/speed control computers, each holding a schedule of shaker angle of attack against configuration. When a vane exceeds its channel's reference, both control columns shake. The shaker is set at, or above, the required margin over the certified stall speed; the KC-10 performance manual places it about **5 kt above the 1 g stall speed**, and charts the shaker speeds with their variation with center of gravity. The MD-10's flight control computers compute the same warning with compensation for the rate of change of angle of attack, roll and sideslip. The system and its tests are described in [Stall warning](flight-controls#stall-warning).

blocks.title: Which warning comes first
columns: First indication of the approach to stall
rows: The shaker may be preceded by low-speed buffet
The stall can occur before the shaker, with buffet as the only warning

blocks.content: The reason for the change with height is compressibility. At high altitude the aircraft flies at a high Mach number for its indicated airspeed, and the maximum lift coefficient, and the angle of attack at which buffet begins, both fall as the Mach number rises. The shaker's reference angle of attack does not. At low altitude the shaker leads the aerodynamic warning; high up, the buffet arrives first, and above about 25,000 ft the wing can reach its buffet-limited maximum lift before the vane reaches the shaker setting. At altitude, therefore, **buffet is the stall warning**. It must not be confused with high-speed buffet at high Mach number, which calls for the opposite response (see [Buffet boundaries](#buffet-boundaries)).

**Speed margins in normal operation.** The operating speeds are built on fixed margins over the stall speed for each configuration: VREF is 1.3 times the stall speed in the landing configuration, and the minimum maneuvering speeds are chosen to allow a 30° bank plus a 15° overshoot (45°, 1.41 g) at the heaviest weight. The speed control system's **alpha speed**, the floor below which the autothrottle in SPD will not let the speed fall and which the fast/slow indicator respects, uses the margins below (see [Speed control system](automatic-flight#speed-control-system)).

blocks.title: Alpha speed stall margins (multiple of the stall speed)

blocks.content: **MD-10 indications.** The MD-10's PFD shows how close the aircraft is to the shaker in three ways. The **pitch limit indicator** (PLI), a pair of feathered bars on the attitude display, stands above the aircraft symbol by the number of degrees of pitch the aircraft can gain before the shaker's angle of attack; it turns amber as the margin closes and red at the shaker. Because it is based on angle of attack it remains valid in a windshear, when speed-based cues are not. On the speed tape, the FMS's minimum speed (VMIN, normally 1.3 times the stall speed) and the shaker speed are drawn as limit columns, and the digital speed turns amber below the selected speed. The FCCs' low speed protection acts on VMIN (see [Vertical modes](automatic-flight#vertical-md10)).

blocks.alt: MD-10-30 captain's PFD during a level deceleration toward the stall with flaps 35 and slats extended. Attitude display: aircraft symbol at about 8° nose up, the pitch limit indicator's feathered bars just above it and colored amber. Speed tape: current speed in an amber digital box, the amber VMIN column above it and the red-and-black shaker column only a few knots below. FMA showing the autopilot and autothrottle disconnected. All legends and numbers legible.
blocks.title: MD-10 PFD approaching the stall

children.title: The automatic slat extension at the stall

blocks.content:
In the clean configuration, the signal that starts the stick shaker also extends the **outboard slats**, those outboard of the engines, to a predetermined position: about 13.5°, roughly half their takeoff travel, on the DC-10 (FedEx) and 14.35° on the MD-10. The slats raise the outer wing's stalling angle exactly where the swept wing is most likely to stall first, and with them extended lateral control is excellent up to and through the stall. The buffet still grows as the angle of attack increases, a firm deterrent to going further. The extension happens only in the clean configuration and only below the system's inhibit speed: about 260 KIAS on the DC-10s and the MD-10-10 (270 KIAS for the heaviest DC-10-30s, and on the MD-10-30), and 270 KIAS or M 0.55 on the KC-10; the arming conditions are tabled in [Automatic slat extension](flight-controls#auto-slat).

On the DC-10 and KC-10 the extension latches: the amber SLAT RESET light and the slat DISAGREE light come on, the slats stay out after the shaker stops, and SLAT RESET is pushed to retract them once the aircraft has accelerated to the slat retraction speed. The MD-10's computers retract them by themselves about 5 seconds after the condition clears. With the outboard slats out, the auto-slat limit speeds apply. See [Automatic slat extension](flight-controls#auto-slat).
The first indication of an approach to the stall can be any one, or any combination, of:

items: a rapid decrease of airspeed below the bug or selected speed (on the MD-10, the digital airspeed turning amber, the speed falling below VMIN toward the shaker column, or the PLI turning amber or red);
a rapid decrease of the rate of climb during takeoff or go-around;
a rapid increase of the sink rate on an approach;
aerodynamic buffet, which may be accompanied by light wing rock;
the stick shaker.

blocks.content: Any of them is treated as a stall warning, and recovery begins at once. The cure for a stall is a reduction of the angle of attack; thrust helps by limiting the height lost and by accelerating the aircraft away from the stall. Positive climb performance and a limited maneuver margin still exist at or near the shaker speed, which is why a recovery close to the ground (or in a windshear) uses high pitch attitudes; but pitch must never be raised so fast that the speed falls below the shaker speed.
**When ground contact is not a factor:**

items: Disengage the autopilot and the autothrottles (MD-10: disconnect auto flight). Be alert for a mistrim: an autopilot that was holding altitude as the speed decayed will have trimmed nose up.
At the same time apply the maximum available thrust (MCT or go-around). The PF calls for it.
Smoothly reduce the pitch attitude while leveling the wings, then adjust pitch to minimize the height lost. Use the ailerons alone for roll; rudder will produce a yaw-induced roll.
The PM monitors and calls out airspeed and the vertical flight path.

As the aircraft accelerates, keep adjusting the pitch to reach a safe flying speed with the least loss of height. At high altitude it may be necessary to lower the nose to or just below the horizon and accept a height loss to accelerate at all.
Once the buffet has stopped, choose a speed and altitude that give the weight an adequate buffet margin (FedEx uses 1.3 g).

blocks.content: **When ground contact is a factor:**

items: Disengage the autopilot and the autothrottles, and be alert for a mistrim.
At the same time apply **firewall thrust**: advance the throttles to their mechanical stops.
Level the wings and adjust pitch to recover from the stall with the least loss of height. Higher than normal column forces may be needed. Ailerons only for roll.
