Do not change the flaps until the recovery is complete, and do not retract the landing gear until a positive rate of climb is established.
Avoid abrupt control inputs, which can provoke a secondary stall. As the aircraft accelerates, keep adjusting pitch to reach a safe flying speed.

blocks.content: Firewall (overboost) thrust takes the engines past their limits. After it has been used, record which engine parameters exceeded which limits and for how long, for maintenance.

**Clean configuration at altitude.** Where performance is limited, accept a loss of altitude while accelerating to the clean minimum maneuvering speed, then reconfigure and return to the desired altitude and speed. Below the slat limit speeds the KC-10 manual extends the slats as part of the recovery; on every aircraft the automatic slat extension will already have brought the outboard slats out at the shaker. A premature recovery invites a secondary stall, or leaves the aircraft unable to accelerate to its cruise Mach number on the thrust available. A recovery not begun promptly can cost thousands of feet, into levels assigned to other traffic.

**Takeoff, approach, landing or go-around configuration.** Apply the maximum available thrust and adjust pitch to minimize the height lost or to clear obstacles, without going below the shaker speed. The KC-10 keeps the existing flap, slat and gear configuration until it has accelerated to the minimum maneuvering speed for that configuration, then reconfigures. FedEx's practiced recovery from the landing configuration calls for maximum power and the go-around flap setting of 22° together, and raises the gear only once the aircraft is climbing.

Climbing at altitude in VERT SPD, the autopilot holds the selected rate of climb regardless of the airspeed, trimming the stabilizer and moving the elevator to do it. At high weight and high altitude the engines may not have the thrust to hold the speed. Monitor the airspeed closely in any vertical speed climb.

**After a stall.** Heavy or prolonged stall buffet at high altitude can wrinkle the outboard elevators' skins, and in extreme cases throw off their balance weights through the interaction of the buffet with the weights' inertia. Losing a balance weight is not an immediate hazard: either of the two hydraulic systems on each elevator holds it stiffly enough to prevent coupled flutter with the stabilizer. Any stall, or any heavy buffet encounter, needs a maintenance entry and an inspection.

blocks.title: Practice approaches to the stall (FedEx training maneuvers)
rows: Stabilize at 0°/RET minimum maneuvering speed. Autopilot and autothrottles off, throttles to idle, hold heading and about 500 ft/min climb; trim to relieve back pressure, then hold the decaying speed with the column.

At the first warning: Max Power, level wings. Shaker and automatic slats come in. Hold attitude if accelerating, otherwise lower the nose toward 5° nose up. Accelerate to the slat retraction speed and push SLAT RESET; regain altitude at 0°/EXT speed; complete at 0°/RET minimum maneuvering speed.
Stabilize at the 22°/EXT minimum speed. Autopilot and autothrottles off, throttles 50% N1, 20° bank, 500 ft/min climb.
Max Power, level wings. The aircraft normally accelerates away before the target attitude is reached. Hold attitude to the bug speed, then rotate to hold it, not above 22° pitch.
Stabilize at VREF + 5. Autopilot and autothrottles off, throttles 80% N1, slight climb.
Max Power, Flaps 22°. Hold attitude if accelerating, otherwise lower the nose toward 5° nose up. Accelerate to VREF + 5 and hold it, not above 15° pitch. Gear up with a positive rate of climb.

blocks.content: The practice maneuvers are entered with the IN RANGE checklist complete and the bugs set as for a normal landing. Common faults: letting a descent develop before the warning; lowering the nose too far and then pulling it back up abruptly, which brings the shaker back through the load factor; too much aileron rolling out; not enough thrust; calling for the gear too early; and using rudder instead of aileron, which can produce an abrupt roll.

An **upset** is an unintended excursion beyond any of: **25° nose up**, **10° nose down**, **45° of bank**, or an airspeed inappropriate to the conditions inside those limits. Treat the steps below as options taken in order of need rather than a fixed sequence; once the recovery is under way some will not be needed. They assume the aircraft is **not stalled**. A stall can exist at any attitude, and is recognized by continuous stick shaker together with buffet (which may be heavy), a lack of pitch or roll authority, or an inability to stop the descent. If the aircraft is stalled, recover from the stall first, by applying and holding nose-down elevator until the shaker stops; only then deal with the attitude.

Excessive use of pitch trim or rudder can aggravate an upset, cause loss of control, or impose high structural loads. Use pitch trim sparingly. Consider rudder to help roll control only if the ailerons are ineffective and the aircraft is not stalled.
**Nose high:**

items: Recognize and confirm the situation.
Disconnect the autopilot and the autothrottles.
Apply nose-down elevator, up to full nose-down.
Apply nose-down stabilizer trim as appropriate.
Set thrust as appropriate.
If the nose will not come down, roll, adjusting the bank up to 60°, to obtain a nose-down pitch rate.
Complete the recovery: as the nose approaches the horizon, roll wings level; check the airspeed and adjust thrust; establish a pitch attitude.

blocks.content: **Nose low:**

items: Recognize and confirm the situation.
Disconnect the autopilot and the autothrottles.
Roll the shortest way to wings level. If the bank exceeds 90°, unload first and then roll.
Recover to level flight: nose-up elevator, nose-up trim if needed, and thrust and drag as needed.

blocks.content:
Rolling is an effective way to bring a high nose down because tilting the lift vector away from the vertical lets gravity pull the flight path, and the nose, down toward the horizon without asking the wing for negative g. Unloading before rolling out of a steep bank does the opposite job: with the wing at low lift, the ailerons roll the aircraft without the lift vector pulling the nose further down.

**Spins** are prohibited. Inadvertent spins are best avoided by recovering at once from any stall, by keeping an adequate margin above the stall, and by avoiding large yaw rates when flying with an engine inoperative. The KC-10 manual gives a spin recovery for completeness: thrust to idle, full rudder against the spin, speedbrakes retracted, flaps and slats to 0°/EXTEND, gear up, nose-down elevator with aileron into the spin, and asymmetric thrust against the rotation if it will not stop; neutralize the rudder as the rotation stops, return the throttles to idle, and recover from the dive with elevator, stabilizer and speedbrakes to limit the speed build-up.

sections.title: High-speed and high-altitude flight
sections.summary: Compressibility and the Mach limits, the buffet boundaries and margins, overspeed, and the narrowing envelope at high altitude.

blocks.content: The DC-10 cruises at Mach numbers where the air over the upper surface of its wing is already supersonic. That is efficient, because the wing was designed for it, but it brings the effects of compressibility into normal flight: a drag rise that grows steeply above the cruise Mach number, a high-speed buffet that limits both speed and maneuver at the top of the envelope, and an envelope that narrows with altitude until the slowest and the fastest speeds the wing will accept meet.

As the aircraft accelerates, the air speeding over the wing's upper surface reaches the speed of sound locally before the aircraft itself does; the flight Mach number at which that first happens is the **critical Mach number**. Above it a pocket of supersonic flow grows on the upper surface and ends in a shock wave. A weak shock costs little, and the wing's sweep and section shape are designed to keep it weak through the cruise range. As the Mach number rises further the shock strengthens and moves aft, the boundary layer behind it is pushed toward separation, and the drag rises steeply (the **drag rise** or **drag divergence**). The engines' thrust and fuel flow tell the story: the specific range charts show fuel mileage falling sharply above about M 0.84 to 0.86, and the economical cruise Mach numbers sit below that knee, the long-range cruise Mach number near M 0.82 on the -10 and M 0.83 on the -30.

Sweep raises the critical Mach number because the wing responds mainly to the component of the airflow normal to its leading edge, which is slower than the flight speed by the cosine of the sweep angle. It also explains some of the swept wing's character at low speed: the spanwise flow, the tip-stall tendency and the strong dihedral effect described elsewhere in this section.

**VMO and MMO.** The maximum operating speed is an indicated airspeed limit at lower altitudes and a Mach number limit higher up. Climbing at a constant indicated airspeed the Mach number rises, so the two meet at a **crossover altitude**, between about 25,000 and 28,000 ft depending on the series, above which the MMO is the controlling limit and the indicated airspeed limit falls with altitude. Neither may be deliberately exceeded in any phase of flight. The overspeed warning (clacker) sounds above VMO or MMO; see [Overspeed](warning-systems#overspeed-warning).

The KC-10's MMO is M 0.88; its full speed schedule, and those of the -15 and -40, are in [Limitations](limitations). The design maneuvering speed **VA**, below which full control deflections and maneuvers near the stall are confined, also varies with altitude: on the DC-10-30 it rises from about 310 KIAS at sea level to about 343 KIAS at 25,000 ft and falls above that, to about 245 KIAS at 42,000 ft.

**Low-speed buffet** is the shaking of flow separation approaching the stall: at a given weight and altitude, the speed below which the wing cannot make the lift asked of it without separating. **High-speed buffet**, or Mach buffet, is the shaking of shock-induced separation at high Mach number. Both depend on the lift the wing is being asked to make, so both move with weight, altitude and **load factor**: in a turn or a pull-up the wing must make more lift, the low-speed buffet speed rises and the high-speed buffet Mach number falls. The **buffet margin** is the load factor the aircraft can pull at its present weight, altitude and speed before buffet begins.

In a level turn the load factor is the reciprocal of the cosine of the bank angle, so a buffet margin can be read as the bank the aircraft could hold without buffet:

blocks.title: Load factor and bank angle in a level turn
rows: KC-10 minimum air refueling speed: the 1.2 g buffet speed + 5 kt (+10 kt with wing pods)
FedEx DC-10-30 maximum recommended cruise weight; the margin to recover to after a stall
KC-10 margin 2,000 ft above optimum altitude
Minimum maneuvering speeds: 30° of bank plus a 15° overshoot
KC-10 margin at optimum altitude; FedEx DC-10-10 at its maximum recommended weight (about 50° of bank)

blocks.content:
The cruise altitude a crew chooses sets the margin. On the DC-10-30, FedEx's maximum recommended weight for each flight level is the weight at which 1.3 g of buffet margin remains, about 40° of bank. On the DC-10-10, with less thrust, the weight is limited by maximum cruise thrust instead and leaves 1.5 g. The KC-10's charts give about 1.5 g at the optimum altitude and 1.35 g 2,000 ft above it. In practice, staying at or below the optimum altitude for the weight keeps a generous margin for turbulence and maneuver; climbing above it to top weather trades that margin away (see [Turbulence and thunderstorms](adverse-weather#turbulence-thunderstorms)).

The natural warning of the approach to either boundary is good in every configuration: an early, light buffet, followed by buffet strong enough to discourage going further. Operation in moderate to heavy buffet should be avoided; it can damage the airframe, and a heavy buffet encounter calls for an inspection.

blocks.alt: Conceptual buffet boundary chart for a DC-10-30 at a fixed weight: pressure altitude (up to 42,000 ft) on the vertical axis against Mach number (0.5 to 0.9) on the horizontal axis. Drawn: the 1.0 g low-speed buffet boundary rising steeply from lower left; the 1.0 g high-speed buffet boundary rising from lower right and leaning slightly left; the two meeting at a point near the top labeled aerodynamic ceiling (coffin corner); a second pair of curves inside them labeled 1.3 g, meeting lower; the MMO line at M 0.88 vertical; the stick shaker line just right of the low-speed boundary at low altitude, crossing it near 25,000 ft with a label 'above here, buffet before shaker'; a shaded band between M 0.81 and 0.84 near the top labeled buffet curves peak near M 0.825: small Mach changes give low- or high-speed buffet; and the optimum and maximum recommended cruise altitudes marked as horizontal ticks. No numerical buffet values other than those quoted. Labels legible.
blocks.title: Buffet boundaries and the coffin corner
blocks.caption: Both boundaries move with weight and load factor. The 1.3 g pair, not the 1 g pair, is the one to cruise inside.

blocks.content: **Buffet near the top of the envelope.** The buffet curves peak at about **M 0.825**. Between about M 0.81 and 0.84 the aircraft can be close to both boundaries at once: a small increase in Mach number brings high-speed buffet, a small decrease brings low-speed buffet. The books' guidance depends on the Mach number at which buffet is met:

items: **Between M 0.81 and 0.84:** level the wings to unload the wing. If the buffet persists, descend to a lower altitude at M 0.82 to 0.83.
**Above M 0.84:** the buffet is high-speed buffet, not a sign of an impending stall. Level the wings and reduce speed, but not below M 0.825. If it persists, descend at M 0.82 to 0.83.
**Well below M 0.81 at altitude:** treat buffet as a stall warning and recover as in [Approach-to-stall recovery](#approach-to-stall-recovery).

blocks.content: High-speed buffet in severe turbulence at high altitude is not a stall. Pushing the nose down to 'recover' from it raises the Mach number and deepens the buffet. Level the wings, hold attitude, and descend if needed to gain margin.

Inadvertent overspeeds usually have outside causes. At altitude, a sudden increase of headwind or a sudden drop in temperature raises the indicated airspeed or the Mach number faster than the autothrottle can respond, and an autopilot holding Mach in IAS/MACH HOLD will let the speed wander in unstable air while it corrects. In a descent, a steep path with high thrust builds speed quickly, and a shallowing of the descent rate with the thrust unchanged does the same. A heavy aircraft at a high true airspeed carries a lot of momentum, and it slows only slowly once it is fast.

The books publish no separate overspeed procedure; the response follows from the limitations and from the techniques for turbulence and upsets. Reduce thrust. If the speed is still rising, raise the nose smoothly to stop the acceleration, keeping the load factor modest: an abrupt pull at high speed loads the structure, and at high altitude it can push the wing into buffet. Use the speedbrakes, which are permitted in flight with the flaps up, to help. Above all avoid large or abrupt control inputs: VMO and MMO are set below the speeds the aircraft was designed and demonstrated to, so that an inadvertent excursion is survivable, and a violent correction can do more harm than the overspeed itself. Record any overspeed for maintenance.

**High-speed descents.** The emergency descent is flown at M 0.82 to 0.85 and then 320 to 350 KIAS, straight ahead or in a turn of up to 30° of bank, pitch about 10° nose down, avoiding negative g. If structural damage is suspected, or turbulence is present, the speed is reduced: the MD-10 FCOM limits it to M 0.85 or 287 KIAS on the Series 10 and M 0.85 or 310 KIAS on the Series 30, and FedEx tells crews to keep the speed at or below what it was when the damage occurred.

As altitude rises, a given indicated airspeed corresponds to a higher Mach number. The low-speed buffet boundary, an indicated airspeed for a given weight and load factor, therefore climbs to higher and higher Mach numbers, while the high-speed buffet boundary stays near the same Mach number or falls slightly. The two converge, and at the aircraft's **aerodynamic ceiling** for its weight they meet: the **coffin corner**, where any slower speed brings low-speed buffet and any faster brings high-speed buffet. Long before that point the margin between them is too small for practical flight, which is why the books limit cruise weights by buffet margin rather than by the ceiling itself. The maximum operating altitude is 42,000 ft.

items: **Thrust.** Thrust falls with air density, and at high altitude the margin of thrust over drag is small. Climbing too high for the weight leaves the aircraft unable to accelerate if it slows, or to hold altitude in a turn. Fly the optimum altitude for the weight and step-climb as fuel burns off; FedEx's altitude and weight placard gives the maximum recommended and optimum weights for each flight level and cruise Mach number.
**Speed stability.** Near the maximum altitude for the weight the cruise speed can approach the minimum drag speed, where the speed is unstable and the autothrottle hunts.

**Engine response.** The engines accelerate more slowly at altitude. Move the throttles smoothly and slowly from a stabilized setting, and do not reverse a throttle movement while the engines are still spooling: retarding and then advancing during a deceleration, or the reverse, risks compressor stall.
**Dutch roll** damping is weakest at high altitude and low indicated speed; the yaw dampers make it a non-event (see [Dutch roll and the yaw dampers](#dutch-roll)).
**Stall warning** may come from buffet before the shaker above about 25,000 ft (see [Stall warning and its margins](#stall-warning-and-margins)).
**Turbulence** at high altitude can produce high-speed buffet, and climbing to top a turbulent layer brings the aircraft closer to both boundaries. Descending is usually the better choice.

sections.title: Engine-out handling
sections.summary: Asymmetric thrust, minimum control speeds, wing and center engine failures, engine-out approaches and go-arounds, and flight on one engine.

blocks.content: A tri-jet loses a third of its thrust with any engine, but which engine it loses decides what the pilot has to do. A **wing engine** failure leaves the remaining thrust off-center and yaws the aircraft hard toward the failed side; it is a directional control problem first and a performance problem second. A **center engine** failure leaves the thrust symmetrical; it is a performance problem with a change of pitch trim, and it may be noticed first on the ENG FAIL light or the gauges rather than in the seat. Losing two engines on a tri-jet is a case of its own, and it too depends on which two.

Each wing engine is 27 ft 7 in from the fuselage centerline. When one fails at takeoff thrust, the other wing engine's thrust (51,800 lb installed on the CF6-50C2, about 40,000 lb on the CF6-6D) acts on that arm, a yawing moment of over a million foot-pounds, joined at once by the drag of the failed engine as it runs down and windmills. The only thing that balances it is the side force of the rudders. That force grows with the dynamic pressure, the square of the airspeed, while the engine's yawing moment does not; so at high speed a little rudder holds the failure easily, and at low speed it takes all there is. The speed at which full rudder only just holds it is the **minimum control speed**.

If the yaw is not stopped, the aircraft sideslips toward the live engine's side, and the dihedral effect rolls it toward the dead engine. Holding the wings level with aileron alone does not cure that: it leaves the aircraft sideslipping, with its drag high, and on this aircraft the aileron input also raises roll spoilers on the down-going side, adding drag and losing lift. The correct input is **rudder**, enough to stop the yaw: in FedEx's words, the correct amount keeps the slip ball centerd, and a nearly centerd control wheel is the sign that the rudder input is right. A small bank toward the live engine changes the balance further. Wings level, the rudder's side force has to be balanced by a sideslip, and the fin's weathercock stability in that sideslip opposes the rudder. Banked toward the live engine, part of the weight acts sideways in the aircraft's own axes and balances the rudder's side force instead, so the aircraft can fly with less sideslip and needs less rudder for the same yawing moment. The definition of the air minimum control speed allows up to 5° of such bank, and the published VMCA figures depend on it.

blocks.alt: Engine-out control diagram for a DC-10-30 with No. 1 engine failed. Left, plan view: thrust arrow from No. 3 engine at its 27 ft 7 in arm, drag arrow at the failed No. 1 nacelle, the resulting yawing moment arrow (nose left), the rudder deflected right with its side force arrow at the fin, the center of gravity, and the flight path arrow with a small sideslip angle. Right, two small rear views: (a) wings level, rudder holding the yaw, slip ball centerd and control wheel nearly centerd, labeled normal technique; (b) the aircraft banked 5° toward the live No. 3 engine, with the weight vector split into a component along the lift vector and a small sideways component balancing the rudder's side force, labeled VMCA definition. A small graph inset: rudder side force available rising with the square of airspeed against the constant yawing moment from asymmetric thrust, crossing at VMC. Labels legible.
blocks.title: Engine-out control: rudder and bank
blocks.caption: Rudder stops the yaw, with the slip ball centerd and the wheel nearly neutral. The minimum control speed is defined with up to 5° of bank toward the live engine, where a sideways component of the weight balances the rudder's side force.

blocks.content: **VMCG**, the ground minimum control speed, is the lowest speed at which the aircraft, on the ground, can suffer a sudden failure of a wing engine with the others at takeoff thrust and be kept on the runway with the aerodynamic controls alone, deviating no more than 25 ft from the centerline (the KC-10's definition; civil certification allows 30 ft). It assumes maximum thrust on the tail engine and on the other wing engine, and the failed engine windmilling. Because it is set by thrust, it falls as the air gets hotter or thinner, and it is lower at high-elevation, hot airports. The KC-10's charted VMCG lies roughly between 100 and 140 KIAS, depending on temperature, pressure altitude and flap setting. The charted value assumes a wet or icy runway, where the nose wheel steering cannot help; with a good runway (RCR 10 or more, no contaminant) and a crosswind component of 10 kt or less, the KC-10 subtracts 10 kt for the help the nose wheel steering gives, and with engine and wing anti-ice on it adds 1.2 kt. V1 is never less than VMCG.

During a reduced thrust takeoff VMCG is computed for the assumed temperature, not the actual one. If a wing engine fails, advancing the remaining engines to full takeoff thrust before about 135 KIAS (the KC-10's worst-case wet or icy VMCG) can create more asymmetry than the rudder can hold, and the aircraft may leave the runway.

**VMCA**, the air minimum control speed, is the lowest speed at which the aircraft can suffer a wing engine failure in the air and hold direction with full rudder and no more than 5° of bank. With both rudders working it does not limit the KC-10's takeoff performance, which its other speed requirements already exceed. It becomes important when a rudder is lost: each rudder is on a different hydraulic system, and with one of them gone much less rudder side force is available and VMCA rises sharply. The books then forbid slowing below VMCA until the landing is assured: below it, the thrust of a go-around could not be held straight.

blocks.title: VMCA with one rudder inoperative (KIAS)
rows: By landing weight: 201 at 260,000 lb, 190 at 280,000 lb, 179 at 300,000 lb, 172 at 320,000 lb and above

blocks.content:
The lower-rudder VMCA of the long-span aircraft falls as the weight rises. The reason is the 5° bank the definition allows: in that bank a component of the weight acts sideways and balances part of the rudder's side force, so less sideslip is needed, and a heavier aircraft gets more of that help from the same bank. With only one rudder, that help makes up a larger share of what is needed. With one rudder inoperative the maximum crosswind component is also reduced, to 15 kt.

**All engines out.** With every engine flamed out the hydraulic systems are powered only by the windmilling engines, and the limiting speed becomes the one that keeps enough hydraulic power for the controls. FedEx tabulates it by weight and configuration for the DC-10-10 (155 KIAS at most weights in the takeoff configurations, rising to over 200 KIAS clean at the highest weights) and never less than 155 KIAS. See [Emergency Procedures](emergency-procedures).

Below V1 an engine failure is a rejected takeoff. A wing engine failure yaws the aircraft toward the failed side and may bank it a little, depending on the speed; directional control is held with rudder pedal steering, with slight forward pressure on the column to keep the nose wheel on the runway, and the pitch-up from the spoilers and reverse thrust is anticipated. On a slippery runway use symmetrical reverse thrust as far as the stopping distance allows. See [Thrust reversers](engines#thrust-reversers) and [Brake energy](landing-gear#brake-energy).

At or after V1 the takeoff is continued. The technique:

items: **Directional control first**, primarily with the rudder, keeping slight forward pressure on the column. Announce the decision to continue so that there is no doubt.

**Thrust.** If a reduced (standard) thrust takeoff is in progress, the pilot flying may call for maximum takeoff power, and if continued flight is in doubt, for firewall thrust; but see the VMCG warning above.

**Rotate at VR**, not at the moment of the failure, smoothly at the normal rate, to the initial climb attitude: about 15° on the DC-10 and KC-10, 12 to 15° depending on weight on the MD-10, aiming for V2 at 35 ft. Initially disregard the flight director's pitch bar, which commands a higher pitch than needed and leads to over-rotation; aim for the target attitude, hold it, then adjust for the target speed. The airspeed indicator is primary.

**Speed.** If the failure occurs before V2, accelerate to and hold V2. If it occurs between V2 and V2 + 10, hold the speed at the moment of failure. Above V2 + 10, reduce to V2 + 10. Do not exceed 20° of pitch.
**Gear up** on a positive rate of climb, called by either pilot.

**Heading** within ±5°, using rudder to hold it and trimming the rudder to relieve the pedal force. Avoid large aileron inputs, which raise spoilers. Bank no more than 15° until the minimum maneuvering speed for the configuration.

**Engine-out acceleration height** (1,000 ft above the field unless the departure says otherwise; the MD-10's EO ACCEL default is 800 ft): level off or reduce the climb, accelerate, retract the flaps and then the slats on schedule, and set maximum continuous thrust. Trim as the aircraft accelerates; insufficient nose-down trim lets the aircraft climb instead of accelerating.
Follow the engine-out departure procedure if one is published for the runway and the failure occurred before its first turn point.

blocks.content: Outside the autoland modes the autopilot commands no rudder beyond the yaw dampers' few degrees, which are not meant to hold an asymmetry. Trim the aircraft with rudder trim before engaging an autopilot. FedEx's engine failure profile engages the autopilot only once the aircraft is level, in trim and at the 0°/RET minimum maneuvering speed.

On the MD-10 the autopilot can be engaged above 200 ft. In the takeoff mode the MD-10 engages a parallel rudder servo that holds rudder for an engine failure, and reverts to series rudder when the roll mode changes; the FCOM warns the pilot flying to be ready to hold the rudder before the parallel rudder disengages.

Common errors in the maneuver: over-controlling the rudder or the wheel; trying to keep the wings level with aileron instead of rudder; rotating at the failure instead of at VR; failing to recognize a No. 2 failure; trimming poorly while retracting the flaps and slats so that the aircraft climbs and does not accelerate; neglecting heading; delaying the gear.

No. 2's thrust acts on the centerline, so its failure makes no yaw and needs no rudder. A No. 2 failure on the takeoff roll is usually first recognized by the ENG FAIL light, not by any movement of the aircraft, and the crew must look for it. What does change is the pitch trim: No. 2's thrust line passes above the center of gravity, so its thrust was holding a nose-down moment, and losing it gives a nose-up change that must be trimmed out. With No. 2 inoperative, thrust changes on Nos. 1 and 3 change the pitch trim without the offsetting effect of No. 2 (see [Thrust and pitch](#thrust-and-pitch)), and an engine-out approach with the center engine out calls for elevator and stabilizer trim with each thrust change where a wing engine failure calls for rudder trim.

No. 2 also drives hydraulic system 2's engine pumps and supplies its own bleed system. And because the engine sits in the fin, with all three hydraulic systems' lines running past it to the tail surfaces, an uncontained No. 2 failure is the one engine event that can damage all three systems together. The aircraft carries protection for that case (see [Loss of all hydraulic power](#total-hydraulic-loss)). The No. 2 reverser cannot be used until the nose wheel is on the ground.

Stabilize the speed and the profile early, so that few thrust changes are needed close in. FedEx's profile calls for flaps 22 and the gear before the final approach fix (or at 1½ dots below the glideslope), and flaps 35 once below their limit speed, decelerating to arrive at the approach speed at or soon after glideslope capture: **VREF 35°/EXT + 10** is held after flap extension to 35° (flaps beyond 35° are not used on an engine-out approach). With a wing engine inoperative each thrust change needs a matching rudder or rudder trim change, which should be anticipated; with the center engine inoperative, each needs elevator and stabilizer trim. The landing itself is normal. Use reverse thrust on the operating engines with discretion; asymmetric reverse yaws the aircraft.

With an outboard engine inoperative, the autopilot may not have enough rudder authority to begin a controlled go-around. Make a manual go-around: disconnect the autopilot, press TO/GA, set maximum power and rotate by hand. FedEx prohibits the autopilot during a go-around with an engine failed. As thrust is increased to level off at a minimum descent altitude, the rudder available on the autopilot may also be insufficient; disconnect it if needed to keep directional control.

An engine-out go-around is flown as the engine failure after takeoff: about 15° of pitch, flaps 22, gear up with a positive rate of climb, acceleration and clean-up at 1,000 ft above the field, bank limited to 15° until the minimum maneuvering speed. See [Go-around](automatic-flight#go-around) for the guidance modes.

With two engines out, a third of the aircraft's normal thrust remains, and it may not hold level flight with the flaps, slats or gear extended. Which two are lost changes the handling. With **both wing engines** out the remaining thrust is on the centerline: no yaw, but No. 2's high thrust line pitches the nose down as its thrust is increased, and the pitch trim changes with every thrust change. With **a wing engine and No. 2** out, the remaining wing engine at maximum continuous thrust makes the full asymmetric case, held with rudder and rudder trim. In either case two engine-driven hydraulic systems have lost their engine pumps (see [Hydraulics](hydraulics)).

items: Immediately advance the remaining engine to maximum continuous thrust and dump fuel. If a malfunctioning engine is still producing thrust, consider accelerating to the 0°/RET minimum maneuvering speed before shutting it down.

Trade altitude for airspeed. Fly clean (speedbrakes retracted, flaps and gear up, slats retracted on schedule) at the 0°/RET minimum maneuvering speed, which gives the best balance of thrust required against thrust available. The slats can be retracted only once the aircraft has the energy to fly clean.

Do not hurry the approach. Maneuver to final in the clean configuration with altitude hold, heading select and a 15° bank limit. About two miles before the descent, extend the slats and slow to the 0°/EXT speed (on an extended final, delay the slats to about the outer marker altitude).
Descend at about 1,000 ft/min. Speedbrakes are available to slow down.

At 1,000 ft above the ground, with the runway assured, disconnect the autopilot and extend the gear; its drag is about three times that of the slats. Disconnect the autothrottles before setting the bug to VREF plus additives, and bleed the speed off to cross the threshold at that speed. Zero the rudder trim when the runway is assured. Do not let the aircraft float.
After touchdown, lower the nose promptly and brake; reverse the operating engine with discretion.

blocks.content: Do not attempt a go-around after the gear has been lowered or at or below 1,000 ft above the ground. Above that point, a go-around with the slats extended is flown by setting go-around thrust, retracting the slats and continuing to descend at 700 to 800 ft/min until the 0°/RET speed is reached, and only then climbing; begun at 1,000 ft it costs about 500 ft. Do not trim during the slat retraction: the trim competes for the limited hydraulic flow. Below 14,000 ft FedEx permits go-around thrust for five minutes (the KC-10 manual, ten).

A second engine failure during an engine-out climb, before the aircraft is clean, is handled the same way: set go-around thrust on the remaining engine and begin a shallow descent to accelerate to the 0°/RET minimum maneuvering speed, reconfiguring on schedule. On the KC-10, refueling with an engine shut down is permitted only as command directives allow; see [KC-10A two-engine refueling](ar-emergency-abnormal#two-engine-refueling).

sections.title: Heavy-weight handling
sections.summary: Takeoff and landing at high weight, the wing's structure and its fuel, the air tanker in the drop, and the tanker while refueling.

blocks.content: Between its lightest and heaviest weights a long-range DC-10-30 or KC-10 more than doubles in mass, and its handling changes with it. Every speed tied to the stall rises with the square root of the weight; every distance on the runway rises faster than the weight; the aircraft's inertia grows; and its buffet margin at a given altitude shrinks. None of this changes the technique, but it changes the margins, and the books' high-weight cautions are about keeping them.

children.title: Takeoff and landing at high weight

blocks.content: **Takeoff.** At high weight VR and V2 are high and the takeoff run long. A heavier than normal feel can be expected in the rotation, and the aircraft tends to settle after lift-off; FedEx gives **10°** as the minimum pitch attitude in that case. The rotation rate is the normal 2.5 to 3° per second: a faster rotation at high weight raises the tail-down attitude before the lift has caught up with the weight, which is the classic takeoff tail strike, while a slow one uses runway the performance data did not allow for. High weights bring the other takeoff limits closer: the **tire speed** limit (a liftoff ground speed of 195 kt on the DC-10-10, 204 kt on the DC-10-30 and KC-10) at hot and high airports, the **brake energy** limit for a rejected takeoff (see [Brake energy](landing-gear#brake-energy)), and the climb gradient limits with an engine out.

**Landing.** The maximum landing weights (436,000 lb for the KC-10 and the heaviest -30s; 363,500 lb for the DC-10-10, or 375,000 lb with flaps 50, which FedEx requires above 363,500 lb) are set by the landing gear and structure at the design sink rate of 10 ft per second (600 ft/min). A landing above the maximum landing weight is an overweight landing, made only when operational necessity or an emergency requires it: the KC-10 manual limits the touchdown sink rate to 6 ft per second (360 ft/min) and the flaps to 35°, and requires an inspection afterwards. Dump fuel where possible. At high landing weights approach speeds, landing distances and brake energies are all high; plan the longest suitable runway and use the autobrakes (see [Autobrakes](landing-gear#autobrakes)).

**In flight.** A heavy aircraft needs higher minimum maneuvering speeds, has less buffet margin at a given altitude, and so cruises lower; its first step climb comes later. It rides turbulence more smoothly, because a gust changes its lift by a smaller fraction of its weight, but it is slower to respond to any input, and its thrust margin for acceleration is smaller.

children.title: The wing's structure and its fuel

blocks.content:
In flight the wing carries the fuselage. The lift on each wing bends it upward about its root, and the wing's own weight, the engine and the fuel in its tanks bend it downward: the **inertia relief** of the mass spread along the span. Fuel in the wing therefore unloads the wing root, and the wing tanks are the last to be emptied for that reason. On the KC-10, when the gross weight exceeds 556,000 lb, or the zero fuel weight plus the fuel in the body tanks exceeds 414,000 lb, the main tanks must be kept full for structural reasons. In turbulence, keeping fuel in the outboard compartments of the wing tanks until it is needed improves the spanwise distribution of the load.

The wing is flexible. Its first bending mode, measured in a NASA ground vibration test of a DC-10-10 with empty tanks (fitted with experimental winglets for the test), has a natural frequency of about 1.6 to 1.7 Hz, and in cruise the tips ride well above their position on the ground. That flexibility smooths the ride: part of each gust's energy goes into bending the wing rather than accelerating the fuselage. On a full aircraft parked at the gate the tips sit lower than on an empty one.

children.title: The air tanker in the drop

blocks.content: The DC-10-10 and -30 Tankers fly firefighting drops at high weight and low level, often in turbulent air over terrain, and the drop itself changes the aircraft's weight and balance in seconds. Up to about 85,000 lb of retardant leaves the aircraft, at more than 10,000 lb a second at the highest coverage levels. Two effects arrive together: the aircraft is suddenly lighter, so at the same speed and angle of attack it climbs; and the load's centroid was ahead of the wing, so the center of gravity moves aft by as much as about 13% MAC and pitches the nose up. Crews meet the combined nose-up pitch and climb with nose-down trim at the start of the drop and forward pressure through it. A ganged drop moves the CG smoothly; a sequenced drop moves it in steps. The details, with the FAA differences training figures, are in [Handling in the drop](aerial-firefighting#handling-in-the-drop).

The run-in is the aircraft's most demanding condition: heavy, slow for its weight, low, and often turning. Every degree of bank adds load factor and raises the stall speed (a 30° bank raises it by about 7%, a 45° bank by about 19%), and turbulence near terrain adds gusts on top. Keep the speed well above the minimum maneuvering speed for the configuration, keep the turns moderate, and plan every run with an escape route that works with an engine failed, because two-engine climb capability at drop weight is limited. Jettisoning the load (the emergency drop empties the tanks in about two seconds) restores it. After the drop the aircraft is much lighter, climbs and accelerates well, and its escape performance is far better than its run-in performance.

A tanker's handling task during refueling is to be a steady platform: constant speed, constant heading or a gentle constant-bank turn, and no abrupt changes in either, so that the receiver can hold position. The autopilot does most of it, and the procedures for using it, the autothrottles and the heading changes are in [Flying the tanker during refueling](ar-general-operations#ar-tanker-flying). This applies to the KC-10 and to the DC-10 tankers with wing pods; see [Air Refueling](air-refueling).

items: **Speed and buffet.** Slow receivers bring the tanker down to its minimum air refueling speed: the 1.2 g buffet speed for its weight, altitude and center of gravity plus 5 kt, or plus 10 kt with wing refueling pods fitted. At that speed a bank of more than 25° can bring moderate buffet. Never let the speed fall below the corrected 1.2 g buffet speed.

**Speed stability.** Minimum refueling speeds are at or slightly below the minimum drag speed, on the speed-unstable side of the drag curve. Small speed losses grow unless thrust is added, and an autothrottle there works hard. Change speed slowly, in small steps.

**Weight and balance.** The tanker gets lighter throughout the offload, so at a fixed speed its angle of attack falls and its trim changes; fuel transferred from the body tanks to the boom or hoses moves the center of gravity. Fuel management keeps the CG within limits while the autopilot follows the trim.

**Receivers in close proximity.** A receiver flying under the tanker is in the tanker's downwash and upwash fields, which can draw the two together, and an overrunning receiver's low-pressure field can reach the tanker's static ports and make its autopilot read a climb, and descend. Closure from precontact to contact is made slowly so that both aircraft can absorb the trim changes, and a receiver that is not stable is told to break away.

blocks.content: **Slat oscillation.** The KC-10 manual describes an oscillation of the slats when they are extended and the aircraft holds an angle of attack of about **8.5°**. It is a property of the slat system and is aggravated by slat cable stretch after long periods with slats extended, and by the wing refueling pods. Without pods it should not occur and, if it does, needs a maintenance entry for slat rigging. With pods it is considered normal and needs no entry if it is stopped. Because it depends on angle of attack, slow-speed refueling is where it is met, and the books ask crews to accelerate and retract the slats between slow-speed refuelings rather than staying slats-out for long periods. Small changes of angle of attack normally stop it:

items: If possible, increase the airspeed by 3 to 5 kt, which lowers the angle of attack.
If that is not possible, or does not stop it, reduce the airspeed by 3 to 5 kt, which raises the angle of attack.
If changing speed does not work, extend 5° of flaps, if possible, which lowers the angle of attack.

If sustained oscillation cannot be stopped, accelerate to a speed at which the slats can be retracted, discontinue operations that need long periods with the slats extended, and make a maintenance entry.

blocks.content: Slowing down stops slat oscillation only for a while. As fuel is offloaded and burned the aircraft lightens, its angle of attack falls, and it passes back through 8.5°. Expect to repeat the corrective steps.

**As a receiver**, the KC-10 closes on the tanker from the precontact position very slowly, so that both aircraft can compensate for the trim changes as it moves into the tanker's flow field. The contact position is held with small, well-anticipated corrections: the movement of the tanker's nose as a guide for elevator, aileron to keep the wings parallel to the tanker's, small amounts of rudder for alignment only, and power for fore and aft position. Rough use of the controls by either pilot starts a chain of growing corrections. Improper or excessive rudder creates lateral alignment problems. Approaching the boom limits at high rates can bind the nozzle so that it will not disconnect.

sections.title: Flight in abnormal configurations
sections.summary: Flap and slat asymmetry, flapless and slatless approaches, the inoperative stabilizer, and the pitch and drag effects of spoilers and gear.

blocks.content: The procedures for each configuration failure are in [Abnormal Procedures](abnormal-procedures) and [Emergency Procedures](emergency-procedures). This section explains how the aircraft flies in each configuration, and why the procedures ask for what they do.

**Flaps.** The two inboard flaps are tied together so that the sides move symmetrically, and the outboard flaps follow them. If one side's drive is disconnected, that side stops while the other runs on, and the wing with more flap makes more lift: the aircraft rolls toward the wing with less flap. The FLAP DISAGREE indication appears at a 5° split (FLAP DISAG at 4° on the MD-10). The roll is held with aileron and aileron trim, and the procedure returns the flap handle to the last position at which the flaps were symmetrical; if the asymmetry appeared during a retraction, a further extension may be tried. Expect a higher approach speed and a landing with less than normal flap.

**Slats.** An outboard slat group left retracted while the rest extend is a more insidious asymmetry. At normal speeds it shows only as a slight roll; its danger is at high angle of attack, because the wing without its outboard slats reaches its stalling angle first and loses lift and roll control at its tip, the very behavior the slats are there to prevent. Fly the speeds the SLAT DISAGREE procedure gives, keep well clear of the stall warning, and treat any buffet or wing drop as a stall.

With neither flaps nor slats the landing speed is the clean VREF, which is abnormally fast and can approach the maximum tire speed, so the gross weight is reduced as far as practical by dumping fuel, and the longest suitable runway is chosen. The landing gear is extended early with the **alternate gear extension lever**, which helps stabilize the speed and also unlocks the outboard ailerons; they would otherwise stay locked out, because neither the flaps nor the inboard slats leave their retracted position. At high weights (about 360,000 lb and above on the DC-10) the clean minimum maneuvering speed is above the 230 kt alternate extension limit, which is a further reason to reduce weight.

items: Fly a wide pattern, or a longer than normal localizer intercept, at the minimum maneuvering speed until the base turn. Bleed off speed in level flight, and arrive on final at the clean VREF with a level segment for speed stabilization before the glidepath.

The aircraft decelerates slowly and accelerates quickly in this configuration. Do not fly a flat approach or drag the aircraft in: a normal glidepath angle gives the best chance of finding the normal touchdown point.

Crossing the threshold, the elevator becomes noticeably more effective in ground effect. Throttles to idle, a slight flare to reduce the sink rate, and fly the aircraft onto the runway: flaring causes a long float.

On touchdown, lower the nose wheel positively, which destroys lift and loads the wheels for braking, and use reverse thrust at once, most effective at high speed. Reverse thrust also deploys the ground spoilers in this configuration.
In this configuration the stall is abrupt, with no pre-stall buffet. The fast/slow indicator is referenced to 1.5 Vs and will read slow throughout the approach.

blocks.content: Landing with the flaps extended and the slats retracted is, in FedEx's words, the most demanding of these configurations. The flaps raise the lift at a given angle of attack, but without slats the wing still stalls at a low angle; the aircraft therefore flies its approach **5 to 7° flatter in pitch** than normal, at a flat or slightly nose-down attitude, and the flaps 35/RET VREF is high enough to approach the maximum tire speed. The stall in this configuration is abrupt, without the warning buffet of the slatted wing.

items: Plan a slightly wider pattern for a longer final. Precise speed control is imperative.

Entering the pattern, select flaps 15/RET and slow to 210 kt, the flaps 22 limit. Before the base turn, flaps 22/RET, the bug to the 22/RET speed, gear down and the BEFORE LANDING checklist. Stabilized on final heading in level flight, flaps 35/RET and the bug to the 35/RET VREF plus additives.
Fly a normal glide path, using an ILS or VASI to hold it; do not flatten the approach.
At the threshold, flare slightly to reduce the sink rate and raise the nose to at least a level attitude, so that the main gear touches first; reduce thrust and do not float.
Use reverse thrust at once and hold forward pressure on the column. Depending on the failure that caused the configuration, the anti-skid may be inoperative.

blocks.content:
If the stabilizer stops in climb, cruise or descent, the column force needed to hold the aircraft at that speed is small; it grows as the speed is reduced for the approach, because the stabilizer is no longer moving nose-up to follow the speed down. The pull can reach about **30 lb**, especially if the stabilizer stopped near its cruise setting. Slewing the elevator feel manually to its minimum reference speed reduces it but does not remove it (see [Manual elevator feel](flight-controls#elf-manual)), and the other pilot may help to hold it.

Avoid high sink rates and steep body angles on the approach: with the stabilizer fixed, the elevator alone may not have the authority for a large pitch change at low speed. Control pitch and descent together with thrust and elevator; No. 2's throttle alone can move the pitch attitude by more than 5°. Flaps 35 is normally used, because it needs less nose-up trim and its higher speed gives the elevator more authority; but if the stabilizer stopped with the aircraft in trim at flaps 50, land at 50. An additive to VREF may be needed, depending on where the stabilizer stopped. In a go-around, fly no slower than the flaps 35 VREF.

**Speedbrakes** are used in flight only with the flaps up (slats extended or retracted); the SPEED BRAKE light flashes if the spoiler handle is out of its retracted position with the flap handle at 3° or more in flight. The ground spoilers must not be extended in flight. Spoiler extension costs lift as well as adding drag, so at low speed it raises the stall speed; and the spoilers' roll function adds drag on the down-going wing whenever large wheel inputs are made, which is why the books ask for rudder, not aileron, to hold an engine failure. See [Spoilers](flight-controls#spoilers).

**Landing gear** extension gives a nose-up pitching tendency and a large increase in drag, about three times that of the slats; on a two-engine-inoperative approach it is therefore delayed until the landing is assured. With no hydraulic power the gear's nose-up pitch upsets the aircraft in pitch, and its drag then steadies it (see below).

sections.title: Handling with control system failures
sections.summary: How hydraulic, feel, trim and control failures change the aircraft's handling, and flight with no hydraulic power at all.

blocks.content: Every primary surface is powered from two hydraulic systems, the two rudders from different systems each with a standby motor-pump, and the stabilizer from two motors on two systems. The architecture is designed so that any single failure changes almost nothing the pilot can feel, and any double failure leaves control in every axis. What each combination does to each surface is tabled in [Effect of hydraulic system losses](flight-controls#hydraulic-failure-effects). This section describes the result as the pilot meets it.

children.title: Failures and their effect on handling

rows: Nothing in normal maneuvering. Some surfaces move at half rate; flaps or slats extend at half rate
Allow for slower flap or slat extension; follow the procedure's landing configuration

No flaps. Outboard elevators unpowered and streamlined: less pitch authority, more column for the flare. Upper rudder lost, lower rudder on its standby pump. Left outboard aileron unpowered; only the No. 3 spoiler panels remain. Stabilizer trim at half rate
Flaps-up landing with slats; higher speeds; one-rudder crosswind and VMCA limits; roll mostly from the ailerons; trim sparingly
No slats; flaps at half rate. Right inboard elevator and aileron unpowered
Slats-retracted landing (see above); stall is abrupt without pre-stall buffet
Lower rudder lost. Left inboard elevator, left inboard and right outboard ailerons unpowered; roll authority reduced with the flaps up
Extending the flaps unlocks the outboard ailerons; one-rudder limits
Do not slow below the one-rudder VMCA until the landing is assured; crosswind 15 kt maximum
Column force wrong for the speed: too light if the feel is set for a lower speed, too heavy if set for a higher one. The aircraft's response is unchanged
Slew the feel manually toward the reference speed; fly smoothly by attitude
Growing pull as speed is reduced
Flaps stop at 20° until the limiter is overridden
Override; land with the flaps the procedure allows
A small steady rudder deflection on that rudder, partly opposed by its partner channel; possible yaw
Isolate the channel by its effect on the handling, as the procedure describes
Loss of control by conventional inputs
Wheel, column or pedals move no surface on that axis; trim, yaw damper and autopilot still work
Engage the autopilot and fly through its modes

blocks.content: Unpowered elevator segments stream with the airflow, so pitch authority falls roughly in proportion to the segments lost, and each lost segment changes the trim slightly. An unpowered rudder trails with the air and adds nothing. Without hydraulic power the ailerons tend to float trailing edge up over a period of time, while the elevators and spoilers float very little and the rudders not at all. A spoiler panel whose system has failed can float up under the air load; that is why the procedures for some hydraulic failures limit the landing flaps to 35°, and why spoiler float may need aileron to hold.

An uncontained No. 2 engine failure is the one credible event that can cut the hydraulic lines of all three systems in the tail. It happened to a DC-10, and two things followed. The first was a change to the aircraft: hydraulic system 3 now has an electrically operated shutoff valve in its supply to the tail, aft of the rear pressure bulkhead, with a check valve in the return and a quantity switch in the reservoir. If system 3 leaks behind the bulkhead, the valve closes, isolating the elevators' system 3 chambers and preserving system 3 forward of the bulkhead, and the crew see **HYD SYS 3 ELEV OFF** (DC-10, KC-10) or **HYD 3 ELEV OFF** (MD-10). The second was a technique for flying an aircraft with no flight control power at all.

blocks.title: Systems 1 and 2 failed with system 3 isolated aft
rows: Both rudders; all elevators; all spoilers except No. 3; flaps; one stabilizer trim motor; the autopilots; the 3-2 standby motor-pump
Ailerons, each on its system 3 actuator (both inboards, and the right outboard once unlocked); aileron trim; No. 3 spoilers; slats; stabilizer trim at reduced rate; pitch control by thrust

blocks.content: In that case roll is controlled conventionally with the ailerons, and aileron trim can take out any rolling moment from damage; without rudder a slight sideways force remains, easily held with a very small bank. Pitch is controlled with stabilizer trim and thrust. With the autothrottles off and the throttles moved together, the crew can give full attention to pitch. The stabilizer trims slowly, and an input must be anticipated and stopped early, often by reversing it briefly.

**With nothing left at all**, the wing engines are the only control. Their thrust acts below the center of gravity, so a net increase pitches the nose up and a decrease pitches it down; asymmetric thrust yaws the aircraft, and through the dihedral effect rolls it (more thrust on the right engine rolls the aircraft left). Airspeed is set by the pitch trim and configuration, not directly by the pilot. The aircraft's natural behavior in pitch is the **phugoid**: left alone after a disturbance it climbs and slows, then sinks and speeds up, in a slow oscillation that the DC-10's own stability eventually damps. The pilot's task is to damp it faster with thrust: apply power as the nose is coming down and reduce it as soon as the nose is rising. Aggressive inputs (a rapid acceleration followed by a quick throttle chop) work best; thrust applied out of phase makes the oscillation grow.

blocks.alt: Time-history diagram over about three minutes of a DC-10 phugoid with no flight control power. Top trace: pitch attitude oscillating slowly with a period of about a minute, with the oscillation decaying in the lower half of the figure. Second trace: airspeed oscillating a quarter cycle out of phase with pitch (lowest speed after the highest pitch). Third trace: wing engine thrust, showing short bursts of power applied as the nose passes through level going down, and throttle chops as the nose passes level going up. A dashed alternative thrust trace marked out of phase is paired with a growing pitch oscillation, with a cross through it. Labels legible, no numerical scales other than the time axis.
blocks.title: Damping the phugoid with thrust
blocks.caption: Power as the nose falls, power off as the nose rises. Thrust applied the other way round drives the oscillation instead of damping it.

items: **Regain level flight** with the conventional controls for as long as the hydraulic power lasts: disconnect the autopilot and autothrottles, level the wings, hold pitch for level flight.
**Assess the damage** by any means available, including a chase aircraft if the weather allows.
**Use asymmetric thrust** for heading; the high throttle may have to stay near maximum continuous thrust to limit the descent.

**Transfer fuel** laterally to level the wings so both wing engines can run at the same setting, which lets one hand change heading by moving both throttles; and aft (from No. 2 tank or the auxiliary tanks to Nos. 1 and 3) to move the center of gravity aft, which lowers the trim speed and with it the landing speed.

**Choose the landing site** for runway length and width, approach aids, weather, terrain and rescue cover, but above all for the degree of control. With confidence in the structure and the control, it can be better to stay airborne to reach a better airport than to land hastily nearby. The gear cannot be raised again once lowered, and its drag shortens the range.

**Extend the gear** with the alternate extension lever, early enough for the pitch upset it causes to settle before the approach; once settled, the gear's drag makes the aircraft more stable. On the long-span aircraft the center gear may also be extended, for its braking and its energy absorption.

**Approach** long and flat, using every aid at the landing site. Arrive near the outer marker (5 to 7 miles out) at approach altitude, aligned and with the gear down, then fly slightly below the glideslope (about half a dot, but no flatter than 2½ to 3°): a steeper path means a higher sink rate close to the ground, and the higher thrust of a flatter path makes the engines respond faster. Remember there is more thrust available at lower altitude. Bias the flight director bars out of view low down if they distract from the attitude.

**Ground effect** begins at about 100 ft and grows rapidly; without elevators its nose-down tendency can be checked only with a sharp burst of power followed by a throttle retard. Move the aim point toward the far end of the runway: in simulator trials this brought the touchdown into the first third.

**Land** if the approach is stable from 500 ft, with the PM calling radio altitude, sink rate and its trend. Do not try for a smooth landing; reduce the sink rate as much as possible. A go-around is made by adding enough power to start a moderate climb, keeping any thrust asymmetry that was holding the wings level.

blocks.content: If thrust asymmetry is holding the wings level, both throttles must keep that asymmetry through every power change. Retarding both to idle together starts a roll. Watch also for the engines accelerating unevenly, which is more likely when the throttles are moved up from idle than from approach power.

After touchdown in the system 3 isolated case: apply full brake pedal, and as the nose comes down use reverse thrust on the wing engines; monitor brake system pressure and the anti-skid. The No. 3 spoilers are powered and are deployed at nose gear touchdown. Restricted nose wheel steering is available for directional control down to taxi speed.

sections.title: Simulation notes
sections.summary: Where the handling comes from, how the stall and high-speed flight are modeled, the stall warning margins, and what is and is not modeled.

blocks.content: **Where the handling comes from.** The aerodynamics (lift, drag, stability in each axis, the response to the controls, the stall, ground effect, and the moments of symmetric and asymmetric thrust) are the simulator's flight model, configured for this aircraft. The short-span and long-span wings are modeled separately, with their own span, area and moments of inertia. The aircraft's own systems drive the flight model: the flaps, slats and spoilers reach it from the modeled high-lift and spoiler systems, with their real rates, half rates and asymmetries (the spoilers as one mean deflection per wing, roll augmentation included). The simulator's own roll spoiler function is also still active: with more than about half aileron, it adds roll spoiler of its own on top of the modeled panels, so at large wheel inputs the flight model sees more roll power and more spoiler drag than the aircraft would have. Pitch, aileron and rudder trim reach it only through the modeled stabilizer and trim mechanisms; and the primary surfaces follow your inputs directly unless a surface loses all its hydraulic power or a control link is failed, when the modeled surface positions are written instead. See [Flight Controls simulation notes](flight-controls#simulation-notes).

**Lift, drag and the stall.** The flight model's maximum lift in each flap and slat configuration has been derived from the KC-10 performance manual's own threshold and stall speeds, so the stall speeds, and the speeds built on them, follow the book closely in every configuration. Its drag in each configuration, with the gear and with the speedbrakes or ground spoilers, has been fitted to the same manual's climb, descent and specific range data, and its transonic drag rise to the specific range charts between M 0.82 and 0.88. With the throttles at their stops in cruise the aircraft will accelerate through MMO; do not leave it there.

The stall itself follows the books' description: the inner wing stalls before the tips, the break is gentle rather than abrupt, the center of lift moves aft at the stall to give a nose-down tendency, and buffet grows as the angle of attack increases past the stall. The flight model knows the aircraft's maneuvering load factor limits (+2.5 to −1.0 g clean, +2.0 to 0 g with flaps or slats extended). With the simulator's aircraft damage options on, flaps or slats extended at speeds well above their placards can be damaged.

**Stall warning margins.** The flight model uses one lift curve for every flap and slat setting, so its stalling angle of attack does not rise when the slats are extended, as the real wing's does by several degrees; measured on that model it falls slightly with each step of high lift. To keep a warning ahead of the stall in every configuration, the DC-10 and KC-10 stall warning uses a shaker angle of attack of about 14° clean and about 13.5° with all slats extended, set against the simulator's own curve rather than the real aircraft's. The margin between the shaker and the simulator's stall is then about:

columns: Stalling angle of attack in the simulator

items: At flaps 50 the shaker leads the simulator's stall by **less than 1° of angle of attack**, a few knots. Treat the first shake as the stall, and in the practice approaches to the stall in the landing configuration expect the stall to follow the shaker closely. Fly the published approach speeds, which keep you well clear of either.

The automatic slat extension extends the outboard slats to their takeoff position (about 20°) rather than to the smaller auto-extend angle of the aircraft. Because the flight model's stalling angle does not change with slats, the extension changes the model's lift and drag but does not delay its stall; the shaker stays on its clean reference after an automatic extension, since only the outboard slats are out.

On the MD-10 the stick shaker follows the simulator's own stall warning, while the pitch limit indicator on the PFD measures the margin to the stall warning system's reference angle of attack above. The two may not agree exactly.

Ice or damage on the leading edges does not change the shaker reference, as on the aircraft. Whether airframe ice penalizes the flight model's lift depends on the simulator's own icing assistance option (see [Ice and rain simulation notes](ice-and-rain#simulation-notes)).

The engines model inlet distortion at very high angles of attack: well past the stall, above about 27° at high power, they can surge. Crosswind and tailwind distortion of the inlet flow on the ground is not modeled.

blocks.content: **High-speed flight.** The flight model does not reduce the wing's maximum lift with Mach number, and it does not model the high-speed (Mach) buffet. At high altitude, therefore, the simulator's low-speed buffet and stall come at the same angle of attack as lower down, and the stick shaker still leads them, where on the aircraft buffet can come first; and nothing but the drag rise and the overspeed warning marks the approach to the high-speed buffet boundary. Use the buffet margins in this section and the performance data when choosing a cruise altitude, as the books do; the simulator will not shake to tell you that you are too high. The flight model also reduces the effectiveness of the primary controls progressively at high airspeed, so they are noticeably less powerful near VMO than on an approach.
**Other differences and simplifications:**

items: **Center of gravity height.** The flight model places the aircraft's vertical center of gravity far too low: below the bottom of the fuselage and, empty, even below the wheels (fuel raises it, but not to where it belongs). With the mass hung that low, the wing engines' thrust line passes above the modeled center of gravity instead of below it, so in the simulation more thrust on Nos. 1 and 3 can pitch the nose slightly down rather than up, and No. 2's nose-down moment is larger than the aircraft's: the thrust and pitch couplings in [Thrust and pitch](#thrust-and-pitch) are weaker, or reversed, in the simulation. The roll damping and the coupling between roll and yaw ([Lateral and directional stability](#lateral-directional-stability)) are affected too. The longitudinal center of gravity, which sets stability, trim and stall speeds, is the aircraft's, and moves with the fuel, cargo and retardant the systems carry.

**Mach trim.** Above about M 0.82 the simulation applies a small nose-down elevator bias that grows with Mach number (about 2½° of elevator at M 0.88). The aircraft has no such device: its flight test found no transonic tuck and the KC-10 manual says no compensation is required. With the hydraulics working, the bias shows on the surface position indicator and the exterior model but does not reach the handling.

**Overspeed warning.** The VMO/MMO schedule behind the overspeed warning and the maximum speed indications is a single fleet-typical schedule (about 365 KIAS and M 0.88) on every variant. On the DC-10-10 and MD-10-10, whose MMO is M 0.85 and VMO 340 KIAS, the warning comes late. On the DC-10-30 (VMO 350 KIAS at sea level, 375 KIAS from 10,000 to about 25,000 ft) it comes about 15 kt late near sea level and about 10 kt early in that band. Fly the limits in [Limitations](limitations).

**Yaw dampers.** With any damper channel engaged in flight, the rudder the simulator flies is the modeled rudder command, your pedals plus the damper pistons, so the dampers genuinely damp the flight model's Dutch roll, within their real authority. With all four channels off, the Dutch roll you see is the flight model's own. Turn coordination by the dampers is not modeled.

**Rudder.** The simulation has no rudder limiter; as with the other primary controls, the flight model's rudder simply grows less effective at high airspeed. No pedal or wheel forces are computed, so the rudder's force cues come only from your hardware.

**Engine failures.** The yaw and roll from asymmetric thrust and the aircraft's controllability at low speed are the flight model's. The VMCG and VMCA figures in this section are the aircraft's own, from its manuals; the simulator's minimum control speeds have not been verified against them. On the MD-10 the parallel rudder servo that holds rudder for an engine failure in the takeoff and go-around modes is not modeled: trim the rudder and hold it yourself before and after engaging the autopilot.

**Hydraulic failures.** A single system loss is not felt. With a surface's hydraulic power gone, the flight model receives the modeled surface positions; with no power at all the inboard ailerons streamline with the airflow in flight (and droop trailing edge down at rest), rather than floating trailing edge up over time as FedEx describes. The tail area hydraulic isolation valve and its light are modeled.

**Wing bending** is modeled as the wing's first bending mode, calibrated to the ground vibration test frequency and loaded by the lift, fuel, engines and load factor. The model bends the tips about a meter at 1 g; the exterior shows only part of that steady bend in cruise, while gusts, pull-ups, the touchdown and the runway's bumps show in full. It does not feed the flight model.

**Not modeled:** slat oscillation; the KC-10's fuel slosh yaw oscillation; aerodynamic interaction with a receiver or tanker (the simulation has no receiver aircraft); the elevator balance weight damage from heavy buffet.

blocks.content: **Practicing.** The failures that change the handling can be injected from the EFB's failures app: engine failures and fires, hydraulic system losses and leaks, the flight control failures (flap and slat jams and disconnections, flap limiter, elevator feel, stabilizer, loss of control inputs), the yaw damper hardover and the stall warning vane fault. See [EFB](efb) and [Flight Controls simulation notes](flight-controls#simulation-notes).

chapters.title: Adverse Weather Conditions
chapters.summary: Operating in cold, heat, icing, turbulence and wind shear, on contaminated runways, in heavy rain and near volcanic ash.

sections.title: Introduction
sections.summary: What this section covers, the principles behind it, and where the systems involved are described.

blocks.content:
This section supplements the normal procedures for operation in cold weather and icing, in heat and at high elevation, in turbulence and near thunderstorms, in wind shear, on contaminated and slippery runways, in heavy rain and hail, and near volcanic ash. Weather varies without limit, and no set of procedures fits every case: these are the techniques the books give for the conditions they describe, and the reasoning behind them, so that a crew can apply them to the weather it actually meets.

Three ideas run through all of it. The first is the **clean aircraft**: frost, ice or snow adhering to the wings, tail or control surfaces at takeoff is never acceptable, because even a thin rough layer on a wing raises its stall speed and cuts its climb. The second is **avoidance**: thunderstorms, known wind shear, severe icing, freezing rain and volcanic ash are to be avoided, not flown through, and most of the procedures for them are about recognizing them early. The third is that **most cold weather difficulties are met on the ground**, before takeoff, where time and care solve them.

blocks.title: Where the systems are described
rows: Contaminated wings; cold-soaked systems; slippery ramps
Ice on probes, engine inlets and fans, and unprotected surfaces
Reduced thrust and climb; high true speeds; brake and tire heat
Upset and structural loads; hail; lightning
Loss of airspeed and climb close to the ground
Long stops, weathervaning, hydroplaning, slush damage
Engine rollback or flameout; erroneous airspeed; abrasion

blocks.content: The handling of the aircraft in these conditions is described in [Flight Characteristics](flight-characteristics); the operating limits (crosswind, tailwind, runway contamination, temperature and altitude envelopes, turbulence penetration speeds) are in [Limitations](limitations); and the checklists for the non-normal situations weather can cause are in [Abnormal Procedures](abnormal-procedures) and [Emergency Procedures](emergency-procedures).

sections.title: Cold weather operation
sections.summary: The cold-soaked aircraft, the clean-aircraft preflight, de-icing and anti-icing with holdover, engine start, taxi and takeoff on snow and ice, and the arrival and parking.

blocks.content: Cold weather brings two kinds of problem: low temperature itself, which stiffens fluids, weakens batteries and freezes water wherever it collects; and snow, ice and frost on the aircraft and on the ramps, taxiways and runways. Most of the difficulties are met on the ground, and the most effective protection against ground icing is a complete de-icing and anti-icing of the aircraft as close to departure as the operation allows. Before engine start the crew's part is mostly to check what maintenance has done: de-icing itself is a maintenance task, but the captain accepts the aircraft and remains responsible for its condition until takeoff.

An aircraft that has stood for hours in severe cold takes time to bring back to life. After six hours or more below −45 °F, and sometimes after no more than a light coat of snow, ice or frost, parts of the emergency escape and safety equipment may not work as intended. The batteries for the escape slide lights and the emergency lights are likely to be low or flat; keep warm flashlights at hand until the interior has warmed, which normal lighting needs (to about 20 °F). Doors, hatches and the clearview windows can freeze shut: check that each opens freely.

items: **APU.** Ice in the inlet areas, or ice ingested, upsets the APU. In very low temperatures it may not start at the first attempt; shut it down, wait at least 5 seconds after the APU DOOR OPEN light goes out, and try again (KC-10). The second attempt should succeed.
**Cabin warm-up.** Warm the interior with the packs. Remove snow from the fuselage first: snow melted by a warming cabin can refreeze on the skin.

**Hydraulics.** Bring each system up one pump at a time and let its pressure and quantity stabilize before starting the next. After a severe cold soak watch for pump cavitation: violent pressure fluctuations, pressure that will not build, or heating. Shut down a system that shows it; brief restart attempts may cure it, or the reservoir, pump or lines may need heating. Hydraulic pressure must be established before engine start, to protect the engine pumps, and the KC-10 manual asks for the systems to be pressurized for 30 minutes before takeoff.

**Engines and oil.** Oil pressure may be very high immediately after a cold start; that is normal if it comes back into the normal range as the oil warms. FedEx asks for the oil temperature to be in its normal range (65 to 160 °C) before takeoff. On the MD-10 an ENG OIL FILTER alert at low oil temperature can be disregarded if the oil pressure is normal and the alert goes out as the oil warms.

**Navigation and avionics.** Inertial alignment can take several minutes longer when the equipment is cold-soaked (about 4.8 minutes longer on the KC-10). Built-in tests may fail until the equipment has warmed; let it warm and test again.
**Instruments.** Make sure the instruments have warmed enough to operate normally.

blocks.content: **Preparing for a cold soak.** If the aircraft is to stand for a long time in severe cold: park with the brakes released and the wheels chocked fore and aft (moisture in a brake can freeze it on), the nose wheel straight and the aircraft rolled a few feet forward to relieve side loads, and if the cold soak will be severe, on sand or small twigs to stop the tires freezing to the ramp. Install the covers and plugs if there is any chance of blowing snow. Have the water systems drained if the aircraft will not be heated. Remove the batteries if they will see very low temperatures for long periods (the KC-10 manual gives below −20 °F for four hours or more; the MD-10 FCOM, an extended layover below 0 °F): a cold battery gives less and will not charge until warmed. The MD-10 FCOM also leaves the stabilizer at 2° ANU.

**KC-10 cold soak preparation.** For a layover of more than four hours below 0 °F the KC-10 manual adds: both isolation valves to manual open, the generator switches off, every door, window and hatch closed, the emergency light charging, ARO rack cooling fan and center accessory compartment fan breakers and the INS battery breakers opened, the INS batteries removed and stored warm, and the air conditioning inlet and outlet doors driven to full hot. Before the boom operator's preflight, the boom hydraulic selector is left at BOOM for 30 minutes and the ARO compartment allowed to warm to 32 °F.

Before takeoff the fuselage, wings, tail, control surfaces and their actuators, engine inlets, landing gear and gear doors must be inspected and cleared of ice, frost and snow; on the KC-10 the refueling boom as well. A hard coat of frost on the wing's upper surface makes it rough enough to raise the drag and lower the stall margin significantly. When in doubt, call for de-icing.

blocks.title: What may remain at takeoff
rows: Frost, ice or snow adhering to the wings, tail or control surfaces
Thin frost on the upper surface of the fuselage, with every vent and port clear

Yes. Thin frost is a uniform white deposit through which paint lines, markings or lettering can still be seen. Rime ice formed on windward surfaces in freezing fog is not thin frost and is not acceptable
Frost on the lower wing surface in the fuel tank area, caused by cold fuel

Yes, if not thicker than 1/8 in (3.2 mm). The KC-10 manual also accepts ice up to 1/16 in (1.6 mm) there, with a second segment weight penalty of 0.8% for the frost or 1.2% for the ice. Anything thicker must be removed
A light coating of loose, dry, powdery snow that would blow off in the takeoff roll
Yes (KC-10, MD-10), but only if the surface beneath is free of adhering ice or refrozen snow. FedEx: do not assume snow will blow off; there may be ice underneath
Snow, slush or ice in the cavities ahead of the control surfaces or on the leading edge behind the slats
No. Remove it before powering the hydraulic systems, or the surfaces and structure can be damaged
