blocks.alt: Plan and side view diagram of a DC-10-30 marking the areas for the cold weather exterior inspection. Shaded red: wing upper surfaces, horizontal stabilizer, vertical fin and all control surfaces, labeled no adhering frost, ice or snow. Hatched amber: the lower wing surface over the fuel tanks, labeled cold-fuel frost acceptable up to 1/8 in. Shaded light blue: the upper fuselage, labeled thin frost acceptable with vents and ports clear. Callouts to: the No. 2 engine inlet and the fuselage top ahead of it (inspect for ice and snow that No. 2 could ingest); the wing engine inlets and fans (free to rotate, no internal ice); pitot probes, static ports and angle-of-attack vanes; pack inlets and outflow valves; fuel tank vents; the slat and flap cavities. Labels legible.
blocks.title: The clean aircraft: what to inspect

items: **No. 2 engine and the top of the fuselage.** Ice or snow on the fuselage ahead of the tail engine can be ingested by it. If the aircraft has stood in freezing rain, snow or sleet, the top of the fuselage and the full length of the No. 2 inlet are inspected, and cleared, before No. 2 is started. On the DC-10-10 this is a maintenance inspection required by an airworthiness directive.

**Engine inlets and fans.** Every inlet must be free of ice and snow, and every fan free to rotate, before start. Snow can migrate forward through the bypass duct into the inlet even with covers on, and water from snow melted in a hangar can refreeze in an inlet and be ingested on takeoff.
**Probes and ports.** Pitot probes, static ports and vanes are heated, but check them carefully anyway, especially after reverse thrust has been used in loose snow.
**Other openings.** Clear ice and snow completely from the radome, the windshields, the pack inlets and outlets, the outflow and pressure relief valves, and the fuel tank vents.
**Heat.** If hot air is used to remove snow, apply it long enough to dry the area completely, or the melt will refreeze somewhere more critical. Take care not to overheat the structure.

**Flight controls.** After clearing ice and snow, move the controls through their full travel, with the flaps and slats at the takeoff setting so that the outboard ailerons unlock, coordinating with the ground crew. Never force a frozen control: the balance panel seals are damaged if the controls are moved while they are frozen.

blocks.content:
**De-icing** removes frost, ice or snow to leave clean surfaces. **Anti-icing** protects clean surfaces against frost or ice forming, and snow or slush accumulating, for a limited time: the **holdover time**. A **one-step** procedure does both with one heated fluid. A **two-step** procedure de-ices with one fluid and then anti-ices with another, normally a hot Type I fluid to clean and a thickened fluid to protect.

**Type I** fluids are unthickened glycol solutions applied hot. They clean well and protect mainly against refreezing when nothing more is falling: their holdover time is short. **Type II and Type IV** fluids are thickened. They stay on the wing as a film that absorbs precipitation and so protect for much longer, and they are designed to shear off the wing during the takeoff roll. (Military specification fluid types do not follow the same numbering: a military Type II fluid does not imply a longer holdover than a military Type I, and no holdover times are published for them.) On the KC-10, commercial Type II fluid is approved only for full-thrust takeoffs.

**Holdover time** is the time the fluid's protection is expected to last, counted from the **start of the final application**. It depends on the fluid and its concentration, the type and rate of precipitation, the temperature (of the air and of the fuel under the wing skin), the wind, and the exposure of the surfaces to jet blast. The published holdover tables are for planning only. Protection is shortened by heavy precipitation, by high wind or jet blast, by fuel much colder than the air, and by thickened fluid applied with forced-air equipment, which can come out thinner and aerated. The tables do not replace looking at the wing.

After de-icing, the ground crew report the **anti-icing code**: the fluid type, the fluid-to-water mixture (fluid first, by volume, for example 75/25), the local time the final application began, and the date. The holdover clock starts at that time. In the simulation, de-icing is ordered from the EFB as a ground service; see [De-icing and holdover](ground-operations#de-icing).

blocks.alt: Concept diagram of de-icing fluid holdover. Left: a cross-section of a wing upper surface with a layer of anti-icing fluid, drawn as a reservoir being filled by falling precipitation; when the fluid is diluted past its freezing point it fails and ice begins to form. Right: a graph of remaining fluid protection (vertical axis, from full to fluid failure) against time since the start of the final application (horizontal axis). Three falling lines: Type I (steep), Type IV in light precipitation (shallow), Type IV in heavy precipitation (steeper), each reaching the failure line; the time at which each crosses is labeled holdover time. Vertical markers on the time axis: taxi, pre-takeoff contamination check within 5 minutes of takeoff, and takeoff, with a note at rotation that the thickened fluid shears off the wing during the takeoff roll. Labels legible, no numerical holdover values.
blocks.title: Holdover: how anti-icing fluid protects, and why it runs out
blocks.caption: The fluid absorbs what falls on it until it is diluted past its freezing point. Heavier precipitation uses up its capacity faster, so the holdover time shortens.

blocks.content: In continuing icing conditions take off as soon as possible after anti-icing. Whatever the fluid, the wings must be inspected immediately before takeoff, within five minutes of it (KC-10). The inspection should be an external walk-around or from a lift by qualified personnel; as a last resort the crew can inspect from inside the aircraft through the cabin doors and overwing windows, from which the wings and the right horizontal stabilizer can be seen. If there is any doubt that the aircraft is clean, it is not: return for further de-icing.

items: **Fumes.** De-icing fluid that enters an engine or APU inlet sends white, acrid smoke into the cabin through the air conditioning. Turn the packs and the engine bleeds off before spraying, and let the APU and engines run at least **3 minutes** after the spraying before using any pneumatic source for air conditioning.
**Fire.** Glycol is flammable. Fluid sprayed carelessly around the engine and APU exhausts can ignite when they start; fluid ingested in quantity can damage hot sections.
**Transparencies.** Some fluids craze or soften acrylic windows.

**Residues.** Repeated applications of thickened fluid without a hot Type I or hot water application between them can leave residue in aerodynamically quiet areas, which can rehydrate and freeze and restrict the flight controls.

**Configuration.** During spraying the horizontal stabilizer is set to **2° ANU**, which keeps fluid and water out of the elevator balance panel bays, and the other control surfaces are neutral. The flaps and slats are normally retracted. If there is snow or slush in the flap or slat areas, or ice or snow of extreme thickness that may adhere to the fixed leading edge below the slats, the aircraft is de-iced with the slats (and flaps) at the takeoff setting. Ice is not chipped or scraped off.
**Movement.** Once de-icing has begun, any movement of the aircraft or change of configuration must be coordinated with the ground crew.

items.item: APU/ISOL VALVE switch (APU running, at the gate)

items.action: MAN, FULL HOT, then PACK OFF

blocks.content: Driving the packs to full hot before selecting them off closes the ram air doors, which keeps fluid out of the heat exchangers. Wind may make it wise to shut the air conditioning down earlier, before reaching a spray facility, so that fumes from the previous aircraft's spraying do not enter. When spraying is complete, taxi clear at low power to limit fluid ingestion, return the CAB PRESS MAN/AUTO handle to AUTO, and after at least 3 minutes purge the pneumatic ducts:

items.item: No. 1 and No. 3 ENG PNEU SUPPLY selectors

blocks.content: Do not spray into the engines, and avoid spraying the outflow valve opening and the brakes. When spraying is complete, set the APU BLEED switch ON and the BLEED AIR switches as required, and taxi clear at minimum power. Clear of the facility, set the PACK and BLEED switches as required.

items.action: CYCLE TO 50/EXT, THEN SET FOR TAKEOFF

blocks.content: Cycle the ailerons and rudder through their full travel, pausing briefly at each stop, so that fluid and water drain. If slush may be thrown up into the flaps and slats on the way to the runway, leave them retracted and set them for takeoff only before entering the runway; the BEFORE TAKEOFF checklist is then completed after they are set. Throughout the taxi the captain judges, from the reported weather and what the crew can see, whether the protection is holding, and returns for further de-icing if it is not.

items: **Chocks.** On a slippery ramp, chock the nose and main wheels in front and behind before starting; chocks may not hold on ice unless it is sanded. Crossbleed starts call for more care still. Where there are no chocks, sand the area and clear it for possible movement, and make sure the tires are not frozen to the ground.

**Inlets.** Do not start an engine with snow or ice in its inlet. Wherever snow or ice may have collected in a fan duct, make sure the fan is turning before the fuel lever goes ON. N1 rotation must be seen before N2 reaches stabilized idle; if it is not, terminate the start and find out why.

**Starter air.** Cold weather starting tests found that, whatever the variations in flame propagation and starting fuel flow, the engines always started with at least **30 psig** of starter air. After a cold soak below −18 °C, **35 psig** gives better assurance. A slight increase above 30 psig greatly helps the start.
**Hung starts** are the typical cold-weather start problem: the fuel-air mixture lights unevenly, and the start stalls short of idle. More starter air is the cure.
**White smoke** during the start of a cold-soaked engine is unburned fuel vapour, and soon clears.
**Oil pressure** may be extremely high just after start; idle the engine until it is no longer above its maximum. It is normal provided it comes into the normal range as the oil warms.

**Engine anti-ice** goes on as soon as practicable after start whenever icing conditions exist on the ground (see [Icing conditions](#icing-conditions)), and stays on until they no longer exist. (DC-10 in the simulation: the ENG anti-ice toggles do not move on screen, although a click or the anti-ice key bindings sets them; confirm by the ENG ANTI-ICE lights. See [Ice and rain simulation notes](ice-and-rain#simulation-notes).)

blocks.content: On the MD-10, with the APU in its standby mode, more pneumatic pressure can be had by increasing the electrical load, but carefully: in standby there is no N1 regulation against overspeed, and the APU may shut itself down if its normal limits are exceeded.

Breaking away from a snow- or slush-covered stand needs a little more thrust than usual. Advance the throttles to about **40% N1** and give the aircraft a few seconds to respond; if it does not move, add power until it does, and then reduce to the least that keeps it moving. Avoid high thrust: it blows snow, slush and ice against other aircraft and equipment, and the wing engines, low and wide, act as vacuum cleaners for anything on the surface (including sand spread on the taxiways).

items: Taxi as slowly as practical on slippery surfaces, at **5 kt or less** in turns. Braking is reduced, and excessive speed brings problems in stopping and turning.

Use the nose wheel steering smoothly and at a moderate rate, entering turns slowly; watch the nose wheel and reduce the angle at the first sign of skidding. Nose tires skid most readily on wet paint. On contaminated surfaces a center of gravity at or forward of about 23% MAC improves nose wheel steering (KC-10).
A crowned slippery taxiway can make the aircraft slide sideways; taxi on the centerline.
Blasted snow and ice can do damage at considerable distances. Keep increased separation behind other aircraft, and expect them to make engine run-ups too.
Do not taxi through deep snow or slush, and beware of snowbanks with the flaps extended.
Plan the shortest route: taxi on snow and ice takes longer, burns fuel, and the engines' ice fog can bring the visibility below takeoff minimums.

Keep the flaps and slats retracted until approaching the takeoff position, so that slush and ice are not thrown into the gaps between the slats, flaps, vanes and wing. When they are extended, watch the flap indication closely: if the flaps stop, put the handle immediately at the position indicated, to protect the flap system, and have the cause found before takeoff. The flight control check waits until the flaps and slats are out.
Exercise the flight controls frequently to check that they are free.

In icing conditions with engine anti-ice on, run each engine up to about **60% N1 for 30 seconds** every 30 minutes of ground operation, and once more in the takeoff position, to shed ice from the fans and spinners. The surfaces around the aircraft should be clear before running up. If the surface or the traffic does not allow 60%, use as much as is practical for as long as possible.

blocks.content: Compute takeoff performance with the anti-ice selection that will be used and with the runway condition. Where there is snow, slush or standing water on the runway, the contaminated runway limits and techniques in [Contaminated and slippery runways](#contaminated-runways) apply as well. If freezing rain or drizzle is falling, takeoff is not permitted unless the airframe is known to be free of ice and precautions have been taken to keep it so (MD-10 FCOM).

items: **Before brake release**, with anti-ice required, make a static run-up to about 60% N1 for 30 seconds and check every engine parameter. On a slippery surface, make sure the parking brake is released before setting takeoff power.

**Set symmetrical thrust.** Advance all three throttles together to an intermediate setting (about 70% N1 on the MD-10), check that the engines are accelerating evenly, then advance smoothly to takeoff thrust. That minimizes any thrust asymmetry from differences in acceleration and prevents overshooting the setting. Throttles aligned at part power may not be aligned at takeoff power; watch for uneven spool-up.

**Directional control.** Expect a lag in the nose wheel steering and a possibility of the nose wheels skidding. Hold a little nose-down elevator to keep weight on the nose wheels. Maintain heading with small rudder pedal steering inputs, detecting any deviation early: on ice, 3° or more of nose wheel angle can make the nose wheels slip. Keep the wings level with aileron; between about 60 and 100 kt the KC-10 manual notes that control wheel deflection toward the desired turn gives a useful aerodynamic turning moment. Do not use differential thrust.

**Wing anti-ice** cannot open on the ground. Selected ON before takeoff, its valves open at lift-off, and the extra bleed reduces the engines' thrust. On aircraft whose thrust rating computer corrects for it, use the corrected setting; do not advance the throttles to make up the loss, which would overspeed the engines. On a packs-off takeoff FedEx's DC-10 technique arms the wing anti-ice with the 1-2 ISOL VALVE open and turns Nos. 2 and 3 ENG PNEU SUPPLY to AUTO after 80 kt, so that wing anti-ice is available as the nose wheel leaves the ground.
**Engine anti-ice** selected for takeoff only under the temperature/dewpoint icing criterion may be turned off at 250 KIAS if no other icing conditions exist (FedEx).

**After takeoff** from slush or wet snow, cycling the gear once, clear of obstacles, can shed accumulations that might freeze the gear doors or prevent a free fall. On the KC-10, cycle the receptacle (UARRSI) doors as soon as practical.
**Snow on the radome** blows back onto the windshield and restricts visibility at the worst moment; hard snow or ice left on the fuselage can come off in flight and strike the tail or No. 2 engine.

blocks.content: A rejected takeoff on a snow- or ice-covered runway can cause serious foreign object damage to the wing engines if reverse thrust is carried to low speed. Cleared runways often have chunks of ice, snow or sand left on them, and a fan engine draws a great deal of air. Follow the reverse thrust procedures strictly unless the safety of the aircraft demands otherwise.

items: **Descent.** Turn the engine anti-ice on before entering icing conditions. If icing is met unexpectedly, turn it on one engine at a time; shed ice ingested all at once can make the engines unstable. If possible, turn the wing anti-ice on to clear the wing before extending the slats. When the destination reports temperature/dewpoint icing conditions, turn the engine anti-ice on when descending below 10,000 ft into the approach and leave it on through the landing and taxi (FedEx).

**Landing.** On a short, wet or contaminated runway the KC-10 manual recommends flaps 50 where landing distance is a concern, and FedEx makes flaps 50 the preferred setting for a contaminated runway. The approach and landing technique is in [Contaminated and slippery runways](#contaminated-runways).

**Taxi-in.** If the approach was flown through icing conditions, or the runway was covered with slush or snow, do not retract the flaps beyond 22° until they have been inspected at the stand; ice in the flap and slat structure can damage it if they are fully retracted. Slush in puddles can be deeper than the takeoff limits, so inspect the aircraft after each landing in slush or snow, especially around the landing gear, for damage from ice and slush. Taxi carefully on crowned slippery surfaces.

**Parking.** Park into wind if practical, particularly in driving rain or snow. Do not set the parking brake on hot brakes; chock the wheels instead. Install the covers and plugs. See [The cold-soaked aircraft](#cold-soak) for a long stop.

sections.title: Operation in icing conditions
sections.summary: What counts as icing conditions, the use of engine, wing and windshield anti-ice, fan ice and the ice shedding procedure, iced probes, and refueling in icing.

blocks.content: Ice forms on an aircraft when it flies through supercooled water: cloud droplets or rain below 0 °C that freeze on impact. The protected areas, and the physics of how fast each one ices, are in [Ice and Rain Protection](ice-and-rain#icing-physics). The aircraft's ice protection is designed as **anti-icing**, to keep ice from forming, not as de-icing, to shed ice already there; so it must be on before ice builds, and the procedures turn it on at the conditions, not at the ice. Flight in freezing rain or severe icing is to be avoided.

**Icing conditions** exist when the outside air temperature on the ground and for takeoff, or the **total** air temperature in flight, is **6 °C or below** and visible moisture in any form is present, or the temperature and dewpoint are within 3 °C of each other. In flight the static air temperature is not used as the reference, because the wing's leading edges and the probes are warmed by the air's compression toward the total temperature, and it is that temperature at which they ice or stay clear. Icing conditions also exist on the ground at 6 °C or below where snow, ice, standing water or slush on the ramps, taxiways or runways may be thrown up into the engines or freeze on the engines or nacelles.

**Visible moisture** means clouds; a ceiling below 1,500 ft; fog or mist (the MD-10 FCOM uses a visibility of one mile or less); and precipitation of any kind or intensity: drizzle, rain, snow, snow grains, ice crystals, ice pellets, hail or small hail, including blowing, drifting, showery or freezing forms.

items: The warmer the air, up to 6 °C, the more liquid water the cloud can hold and the more severe the icing.
Below about −20 °C icing is usually lighter, because most of the cloud water has already frozen to crystals that bounce off.
Heavy icing has nevertheless been reported at temperatures as low as −60 °C. Watch the unheated parts of the aircraft visible from the flight deck (the windshield frames and wiper arms) for ice.
**When in doubt, turn on ice protection.**

blocks.content: Engine anti-ice heats each inlet cowl's lip with high-stage bleed air (see [Engine anti-ice](ice-and-rain#engine-anti-ice)). It is used whenever icing conditions exist or are expected, on the ground and in flight, and turned on **before** entering them: on the ground as soon as practicable after each engine is started, and in flight ahead of the cloud. Turn the switches on one engine at a time, pausing after each, so that each engine's response can be seen to settle. If icing is met unexpectedly, the one-at-a-time rule matters more still: any ice already in the inlets is shed and ingested as each cowl warms, and ice taken by all three engines at once can make them unstable together.

items: The bleed costs thrust. On aircraft whose thrust rating computer carries the correction, the N1 limit it displays already allows for it; on the KC-10 an N1 penalty is applied with engine anti-ice on until the TAT falls below 8 °C. Use the displayed setting; with the computer inoperative, correct the thrust from the performance data.
The ice protection works at flight idle. There is no need to carry power above idle in flight to keep it effective.

If ice builds on a cowl lip anyway, through a malfunction or icing beyond the system's capability, run that engine at the lowest practical power until the ice has been ingested, to limit compressor damage.

When engine anti-ice was turned on for takeoff only because of the temperature/dewpoint rule, FedEx allows it off at 250 KIAS if no other icing conditions exist. When the destination reports the temperature/dewpoint condition, it goes on when descending below 10,000 ft and stays on through the taxi-in.
Anti-ice raises fuel burn. FedEx plans about 1.3% more destination fuel for engine anti-ice, and about 2.7 to 3.5% for engine and wing anti-ice together, depending on the series.

blocks.content: In the simulation the three ENG anti-ice toggles on the DC-10 pilots' overhead do not move on screen. A click still sets them, as do the simulator's anti-ice key bindings (all three, or one engine at a time), and the system responds normally: confirm the selection by the ENG ANTI-ICE lights rather than the toggles. See [Ice and rain simulation notes](ice-and-rain#simulation-notes).

children.title: Wing anti-ice and ice on the airframe

blocks.content:
Wing anti-ice heats the leading edges of the outboard slats, ahead of the ailerons, where ice would most affect roll control and the stall (see [Wing anti-ice](ice-and-rain#wing-anti-ice)). It is used for takeoff and in flight whenever the temperature is 6 °C or below with visible moisture, and should be on for flight whenever icing conditions are expected. It cannot open on the ground: selected ON before takeoff, it is armed, and its valves open at lift-off.

If icing is encountered, turn the wing anti-ice on, where possible, to clear the outer wing before extending the slats. In a holding pattern in icing conditions the slats are normally retracted. There is otherwise no configuration restriction in icing, and no need to remove ice before retracting the flaps or slats.

**Unprotected surfaces.** Only the outboard slats, the engine inlets, the windshields and the probes are heated; the inboard slats, the flap and tail leading edges and the radome are not. In icing conditions ice can build on them however the anti-ice is set. Ice on a wing or tail leading edge raises the stall speed and lowers the stalling angle of attack, while the stick shaker's reference angle of attack does not change; and snow or ice accumulation adversely affects climb performance, stall speed and handling. Treat buffet as the stall warning with ice on the airframe, keep the speeds up, and remember that the airframe ice may remain into the approach.

**Windshields.** Select windshield anti-ice to NORM when icing is imminent, and to HIGH only for the duration of moderate to heavy icing. Windshield defog is normally on in all conditions (see [Windshield anti-ice](ice-and-rain#windshield-anti-ice)).

The engine anti-ice heats the inlet cowl only, not the fan blades or the spinner. In moderate or severe icing, ice can build on the fan and spinner whether engine anti-ice is on or off, especially when the engine runs for a long time at low power. When it sheds, it is flung into the acoustic panels in the fan case and can damage them, and an unbalanced fan vibrates. Running the engines above **70% N1** gives the best protection against the build-up; at low power, in cruise, holding or descent, the ice is shed deliberately and in a controlled way. See [Fan ice](ice-and-rain#fan-ice).
In moderate to severe icing with N1 settings below 70% for a prolonged period, do the following **every 10 minutes**, one engine at a time, until clear of icing conditions:

items.action: REDUCE TOWARD IDLE, THEN ADVANCE SLOWLY TO AT LEAST 70% N1 FOR 10 TO 30 SECONDS
REDUCE TOWARD IDLE, THEN ADVANCE TO AT LEAST 70% N1 FOR 10 TO 30 SECONDS

items.item: ENG IGN OVRD push-button (anti-ice no longer required)

items: Reduce **one engine at a time**: the ignition override protects against flameout while the ice is ingested, but the aircraft must never have all three engines in the shedding cycle together.
If fan or spinner ice is shed, N1 vibration may rise as thrust is applied, then return to normal as the ice clears.
On the MD-10 the MCDU may show the *CONFIRM ENG OUT CLEAR* prompt during the procedure; it does not mean that an engine has failed.
On the ground the equivalent is the 60% N1 run-up for 30 seconds every 30 minutes (see [Taxiing on snow and ice](#cold-taxi)).

blocks.content: Do not run the ice shedding procedure with a receiver in the precontact position or closer, and tell the receiver before beginning it.

**Induction icing** is fan and spinner icing in clear or moist air, favored by a TAT between +10 and −40 °C, visible moisture or high humidity, low speed and high angle of attack: the conditions of slow-speed air refueling near freezing. Prolonged exposure can damage the high-bypass engines even with engine anti-ice on. Turn the anti-ice on before the conditions. If it is inoperative, climb or descend to where the TAT is warmer than +6 °C or colder than −20 °C, avoid clouds between 0 and −20 °C TAT where possible, and fly faster than 400 KTAS. Record any prolonged exposure for maintenance.

A pitot probe or its drain can ice up through a heater failure, a failure of the heater's power, or icing heavier than the heater can handle. Recognizing the signature quickly matters, in instrument conditions above all, because the airspeed feeds the autopilot, the overspeed and stall-related systems and the elevator feel as well as the indicators:

items: **Pitot inlet blocked, drain open:** the pressure in the line leaks away toward static, and the indicated airspeed and Mach fall toward zero, whatever the aircraft is doing. Systems fed by that air data try to correct for a speed loss that is not happening.

**Pitot inlet and drain both blocked:** the pressure is trapped. In level flight the airspeed simply stops changing (a perfectly steady third digit of the Mach number is suspicious). In a climb the static pressure falls and the indicated airspeed rises falsely; in a descent it falls. The airspeed indicator has become an altimeter, and a crew following it can stall or overspeed the aircraft. False overspeed warnings are possible.

**Static port blocked:** the altimeter and vertical speed indicator freeze at their readings when the port blocked, and the airspeed errs the opposite way to the trapped pitot case: low in a climb, high in a descent.

blocks.content: Cross-check both pilots' instruments against the standby instruments, the attitude and the thrust, and look at the heater indications (PITOT HEAT INOP and the heater current meter on the DC-10 and KC-10, the air data alerts on the MD-10). Two systems seldom fail together unless the icing exceeds what the heaters can supply. If the airspeed is unreliable, fly attitude and thrust from the tables in the unreliable airspeed procedure (see [Abnormal Procedures](abnormal-procedures)). How each sensor fails when iced is described in [Iced sensors](ice-and-rain#iced-probes).

items: **Boom.** The boom has no ice protection. Refueling may continue in icing conditions, but when ice forms on the boom or its control surfaces, check the boom's flight control effectiveness and stability: further ice can reduce it. Terminate refueling unless operational necessity dictates otherwise. If it continues with reduced control effectiveness, reduce the envelope limits to less than the maximum reached in the control check, or the receiver's limits, whichever is less. If the boom controls do not respond to commands or the surfaces are erratic, go to the abnormal procedure.

**Wing pods.** Avoid using the wing refueling pods in icing conditions except in a fuel emergency. If ice is reported on any part of a pod, its hose or drogue, rewind the hose as soon as possible and terminate refueling unless operational necessity dictates otherwise; do not trail the hose again for 5 minutes after rewinding.

**Cold soak of a trailed hose.** With the static air temperature between −47 and −58 °C, a pod hose must not stay trailed for more than 15 minutes before fuel transfer, and is rewound after transfer unless another is about to begin. Below −58 °C it is not trailed except in a fuel emergency.

blocks.content: See [Air Refueling](air-refueling) for the refueling procedures and envelopes.

sections.title: Hot weather and high elevation
sections.summary: Performance in thin, hot air, the engines' flat rating and EGT margin, brakes and tires, cooling the aircraft, and sand and dust.

blocks.content: Heat and altitude act on the aircraft the same way: they thin the air. Thinner air gives the wing less lift and the engines less thrust at a given indicated airspeed and throttle, and every true airspeed and ground speed is higher for the same indicated airspeed. The penalties must be worked out before takeoff from the performance data, and on a short runway they can cost payload. High temperatures, especially with high humidity or blowing sand and dust, also make the aircraft and its crew work harder on the ground.

children.title: Performance in heat and at altitude

blocks.content: **Thrust and EGT margin.** Each engine is **flat rated**: up to its flat rating temperature it gives its full rated takeoff thrust, at a turbine temperature below its limit; above it, the thrust that can be had falls as the temperature rises, because the turbine is then at its temperature limit and every further degree of inlet temperature takes thrust away. The CF6-50C2 and the JT9D-59A are flat rated to 30 °C, the CF6-6D to about 20 °C. The margin between the operating EGT and its limit, the **EGT margin**, shrinks with heat, with altitude and with the engine's age and wear, and on a hot day at a high airport the engines run close to their limits throughout the takeoff. The thrust rating computer sets the N1 limits for the actual temperature and altitude (see [Thrust rating](engines#thrust-rating)); with it inoperative, take them from the performance data.

items: **Takeoff distances** grow significantly with temperature and with airport elevation: lift-off is at the same indicated airspeed but a higher true and ground speed, and there is less thrust to get there. Adhere strictly to the recommended takeoff and climb speeds.

**Tire speed** can become the limit at hot, high airports: the lift-off ground speed must stay below the tires' rating (195 kt on the DC-10-10, 204 kt on the DC-10-30 and KC-10). See [Wheels and tires](landing-gear#tires-and-wheels).
**Climb.** The rate of climb falls and the climb time, fuel and distance rise above standard temperature. Engine-out climb gradients fall too, and may limit the weight.
**Minimum control on the ground** (VMCG) is lower when the engines give less thrust, so it seldom limits a hot, high takeoff.

**Approach and landing.** The true airspeed, and with it the touchdown ground speed, is higher for the same indicated speed. Fly the normal approach speeds, never less than the computed threshold speed over the runway end, and expect a longer ground roll. Avoid heavy braking, which overheats the brakes.

blocks.title: Temperature and altitude envelope (FedEx DC-10)
rows: Takeoff and landing, airport at −1,000 to 2,500 ft
Takeoff and landing at the highest airport altitude

blocks.content: Temperature limits vary linearly between the altitudes shown. The KC-10's standard certified takeoff and landing envelope extends to 8,500 ft, and an envelope to 14,000 ft is approved for its performance data; it may land, and go around, at outside air temperatures up to 55 °C. The MD-10s follow their own environmental envelope charts. See [Limitations](limitations).

children.title: Brakes and tires in the heat

blocks.content: A brake absorbs the aircraft's kinetic energy as heat and then has to lose that heat to the air, and on a hot day it loses it slowly. Heat that a cool day would shed between flights accumulates, and a brake already warm from taxiing and a previous landing has less capacity left for a rejected takeoff. The brake cooling charts and the brake energy limits are in [Brake energy](landing-gear#brake-energy).

items: Use the brakes as little as possible while taxiing.
Avoid excessive braking on landing.
At the stand, have the chocks in as soon as the aircraft stops and release the parking brake, which helps the brakes cool. Do not set the parking brake on hot brakes.

After a maximum-performance landing or heavy braking, everyone stays clear of the main landing gear until the brakes have cooled; use the brake temperature indications to judge it. The wheel fuse plugs can release the tire pressure minutes after the stop.
Inspect the tires and shock struts for correct inflation, and the accumulators for their air charge, more closely in hot weather. An under-inflated tire flexes more and heats much faster during taxi.

blocks.content:
Keep the interior as cool as possible. Keep the doors closed as far as possible, and the cargo doors open no longer than necessary. At transit stops in high temperatures, consider turning off heat sources that are not needed, such as window heat and electronic equipment. On entering the aircraft in high humidity, check the instruments and electrical equipment for excessive moisture.

Ground air conditioning on a hot day needs the packs' full flow, from the APU or a ground cart and then from the engines; see [Air Conditioning](air-conditioning) for the pack controls.
The MD-10 FCOM gives a hot weather air conditioning start, which brings the packs on line as each engine is started, in the order 3, 1, 2, instead of waiting until all three are running:

items.item: After engine 3 is started: 1-3 ISOL switch
After engine 1 is started: 1-2 ISOL switch
After engine 2 is started: BLEED AIR 2 switch

blocks.content: If pack 1 or pack 3 is inoperative, pack 2 can be selected after engine 2 is started.

items: Clean dust and sand from the shock struts, the other hydraulic pistons and the limit switches. Look for hydraulic leaks, and for door seals deformed or damaged by heat. Remove every cover and plug.

Position the aircraft so that it will not sandblast other aircraft or equipment during start and run-up, and keep a good distance from other aircraft while taxiing, so that sand and dust are not blown into the engines.
Check for dust in the flight deck's controls, instruments and electronic equipment.

If blowing sand or dust is expected, park facing into the forecast wind with the flaps and slats retracted, which keeps sand out of the trailing edges and the aileron, flap and spoiler mechanisms. Protect the equipment inside with dust covers if doors must be left open.
Except in dust or rain, leave the doors open for ventilation when the aircraft is parked, with the wheel well doors open.

sections.title: Turbulence and thunderstorms
sections.summary: How turbulence loads the aircraft, the penetration speeds and technique, the severe turbulence procedures, and thunderstorm avoidance.

blocks.content: Flight through thunderstorms, or through known severe turbulence, is not recommended and should be avoided whenever possible. Turbulence penetration procedures exist for the encounter that cannot be avoided, and they have two aims at once: to keep the aircraft's attitude within reasonable bounds, and to keep the structural loads within limits.

A vertical gust changes the wing's angle of attack, and so its lift, suddenly. The resulting increment of load factor is proportional to the air density, the true airspeed, the lift curve slope and the gust's vertical velocity, and inversely proportional to the wing loading. Two consequences follow. **The faster the aircraft flies through a given gust, the larger the load**: halving the speed halves the load factor increment. And **a heavily loaded wing feels a given gust less**: the DC-10's high wing loading and its flexible swept wing, which bends and absorbs part of each gust, give it a smooth ride by comparison with lighter aircraft.

That would argue for flying slowly in turbulence, and in moderate turbulence a low speed is satisfactory and may feel comfortable. In severe turbulence it is not. Close to the low-speed buffet boundary, the big swings of angle of attack in severe gusts drive the wing into heavy, frightening buffet, whose drag costs altitude and invites large thrust changes; the trim changes with thrust are larger at low speed; the aircraft is on the back side of the drag curve; and it is more easily upset laterally and directionally.

The experience of the industry is that structural failures in severe turbulence have almost always followed a severe upset: the combination of the turbulence and the loads of an abrupt recovery maneuver, rather than the turbulence alone. The penetration technique is therefore built around **attitude control**, and the penetration speed around giving the best compromise between the margin from the stall buffet and the margin from structural limits and high-speed buffet. The aircraft also tolerates higher gust intensity with the flaps retracted (its limit load factors are +2.5 to −1.0 g clean, against +2.0 to 0 g with flaps or slats extended): delay flap extension in known turbulence as long as possible. Keeping fuel in the outboard compartments of the wing tanks until it is needed improves the spanwise load distribution (KC-10).

blocks.alt: Diagram of the turbulence penetration speed window for a DC-10-30 at a fixed altitude below 35,000 ft. Horizontal axis: indicated airspeed. On the left, a shaded region bounded by the 1 g low-speed buffet speed and, further right, the speed at which a severe gust's angle-of-attack increase would reach buffet, labeled stall buffet margin. On the right, a shaded region bounded by VMO and labeled structural and high-speed margin, with an arrow showing gust load increasing with speed. Between them a green band labeled turbulence penetration speed 290 to 310 KIAS, with a note: fly the high side of the band; do not chase airspeed. A small inset shows a gust arrow changing the angle of attack of a wing section. Labels legible.
blocks.title: The turbulence penetration speed window
blocks.caption: The penetration speed leaves room for severe gusts in both directions: away from the stall buffet on one side and from structural loads and high-speed buffet on the other.

blocks.title: Turbulence penetration speeds
rows: 280 to 287 KIAS or M 0.80 to 0.85, whichever is lower
DC-10-10, flaps up: 250 KIAS up to 430,000 lb, rising with weight (about 252 KIAS at 440,000 lb, 257 KIAS at 460,000 lb). MD-10-10: the greater of 250 KIAS and the climb speed
290 to 310 KIAS or M 0.80 to 0.85, whichever is lower
DC-10-30: 250 KIAS or 1.5 Vs, whichever is greater. MD-10-30: the greater of 250 KIAS and the climb speed
290 to 310 KIAS or M 0.80 to 0.85, whichever is lower

blocks.content: The Mach range applies at high altitude (FedEx gives it above 35,000 ft). There, most turbulence is not severe and does not need a speed reduction at all; reducing from M 0.85 to 0.82 at 35,000 ft lowers the true airspeed by only about 15 kt, the aircraft is better controlled at the higher Mach numbers, and less time is spent in the turbulent air. In severe turbulence the speed range gives latitude, with the maneuvering and structural margins needed. Fly the high side of the range rather than the low side, and expect large, rapid airspeed fluctuations: some of what the instruments show is the turbulence acting on the pitot-static system, not a real change of speed. Do not chase the airspeed with the elevator or the throttles.

items: **Attitude** is the primary reference, on the attitude indicator. Rapid and large aileron inputs are acceptable to hold the wings level, but control pitch with small to moderate elevator inputs only: apply elevator smoothly against motion away from the desired attitude and return it toward neutral as the aircraft comes back. The aircraft's own stability works to keep the loads down; since nobody knows the size, direction or timing of the next gust, holding the attitude loosely, or even leaving the column alone, usually does less harm than trying to pin it.
**Do not trim the stabilizer.** The next draft is likely to reverse the last, and trim applied for the first exaggerates the out-of-trim condition in the second.

**Thrust.** Set thrust for near-level flight at the penetration speed in smooth air (FedEx gives about 90% N1 as an initial setting in an emergency) and leave it. Move the throttles only to correct an excessive speed trend or to stay inside the engine limits, slowly and deliberately. At high altitude, never reverse a throttle movement while the engines are still accelerating or decelerating.

**Altitude.** Updrafts and downdrafts will move the aircraft hundreds or thousands of feet. Allow the altitude to vary; sacrifice altitude to hold attitude and speed. Chasing the altimeter produces large load variations and speed excursions.

**High-speed buffet** at high altitude in severe turbulence may be unavoidable. It is not a stall: a rapid push-over to 'recover' raises the Mach number and makes it worse. Severe high-altitude encounters have produced up to about 2.5 g; following the attitude technique keeps the loads down. Climbing to top a turbulent area that cannot be fully topped invites high-speed buffet; descending improves the buffet margin.
**Configuration.** Flaps retracted unless needed; the aircraft tolerates gusts better clean.
**Occupants.** Have everyone strapped in well before entering forecast or suspected turbulence.
If severe turbulence persists, diversion away from the area is the best policy.

blocks.content: **TURB mode (DC-10, KC-10).** Pushing either TURB pushbar drops the autopilot from CMD to CWS, disengages the autothrottles, and removes the flight director bars; the pitch window shows TURB and the other windows are blank. In TURB the autopilot's pitch response is softened and its automatic pitch trim inhibited, and trimming disconnects it. It holds the attitude while the thrust stays where the crew set it, so the aircraft does not chase gusts with the throttles. See [Vertical modes](automatic-flight#vertical-dc-kc).

blocks.title: Severe turbulence or heavy rain (DC-10, KC-10)

items.item: AP lever (if the autopilot is in use)

items.action: TURB; BARS OUT OF VIEW; AP LEVER AT CWS

items.item: AP and ATS red warning lights

blocks.content: If the autopilot is not in use, set the ATS levers to OFF and fly the rest of the procedure by hand. The anti-ice is turned on because the extra bleed demand increases the compressors' stall margin (on the DC-10 in the simulation the ENG anti-ice toggles do not move on screen when set; confirm by the ENG ANTI-ICE lights, see [Ice and rain simulation notes](ice-and-rain#simulation-notes)). When the turbulence mode is no longer needed, move the AP lever to CMD or OFF; from CWS to CMD the autopilot engages in its basic modes.

blocks.title: Severe turbulence and/or heavy rain ingestion (MD-10)

blocks.content: In areas of turbulence fly the FMS optimum altitude when possible, for buffet margin and economy, and descend if needed to improve the margin. Use the autopilot, monitor it closely, and disconnect it only if it does not hold an acceptable attitude. **Never apply force to the control wheel or column while the autopilot is engaged**: it disconnects on sustained force, and the surfaces then jump to match the force being held, giving an abrupt and unpredictable response. If it does disconnect, take control smoothly, fly attitude, sacrifice altitude, disregard the flight director pitch bar and do not trim by hand. When the turbulence or heavy rain no longer exists: ENG and WING ANTI-ICE off, autothrottles on (AUTO FLIGHT switch), ENG IGN OVRD off.

A thunderstorm combines nearly every weather hazard in one cell: severe turbulence and the upsets it brings, hail, heavy rain, icing above the freezing level, lightning, and the downdrafts and outflow that make wind shear near the ground (see [Wind shear](#windshear)). The policy is to avoid them, by visual sighting where possible and by the weather radar; early detection is what makes a sensible course of action possible. As a storm is approached, adjusting the radar's mode, range, antenna tilt and gain is needed for the best picture. Remember that heavy rain close to the aircraft attenuates the radar beam, so the area behind a strong cell can paint weaker than it is, or not at all. See [Weather radar](surveillance#weather-radar), its [theory of operation](surveillance#wxr-theory) and [attenuation](surveillance#wxr-attenuation).

items: **Hail** can damage the radome and the pitot probes, giving unreliable airspeed, and the wing leading edges, raising the stall speed and degrading handling near the stall; with certain damage the aircraft can stall before the stick shaker. Damage to a large part of the radome brings noise and a low-frequency buffet that does not change much with speed or attitude, unlike stall buffet. Fly attitude and thrust if the airspeed is suspect.
**Heavy rain and hail** can flame out the engines at low power (see [Heavy rain and hail](#heavy-rain-hail)).
**Turbulence** in and near a storm may be severe; fly the penetration technique above.
**Lightning** can strike the aircraft, and static discharge (St Elmo's fire) on the windshields is common near storms.

blocks.content: When the departure, en route or arrival path may take the aircraft near lightning, keep the refueling boom full of fuel, as a precaution against ignition of fuel vapour in the boom by a strike. Coordinate with the boom operator before filling the boom, because the boom may extend. The boom filling procedure is in [Air Refueling](air-refueling).

sections.title: Wind shear
sections.summary: What wind shear is and why it is dangerous close to the ground, recognizing and avoiding it, precautions, the recovery maneuver, and the alerts on each flight deck.

blocks.content: **Wind shear** is a change of wind speed or direction over a short distance along the flight path, often with vertical air movement (updrafts and downdrafts) mixed in. The books define **severe wind shear** as a rapid change in wind direction or speed that produces an airspeed change of more than **15 kt** or a vertical speed change of more than **500 ft/min** (FedEx adds a pitch change of more than 5°). Close to the ground, on takeoff and approach, it can leave a heavy aircraft with too little energy to stay airborne, and the crew may have only **5 to 15 seconds** to recognize it, react and fly out of it. The first defense is to avoid it.

children.title: How wind shear affects the aircraft

blocks.content:
An aircraft flies relative to the air, but its inertia is relative to the ground. When the headwind suddenly decreases, or the tailwind increases, the aircraft keeps its ground speed for a moment and so loses airspeed: a **loss shear**, or decreasing-performance shear. Lift falls with the airspeed, the aircraft sinks, and the pilot's instinct, to lower the nose and regain the speed, costs height it may not have. A **gain shear** (an increasing headwind or decreasing tailwind, or an updraft) does the opposite: a sudden rise in airspeed and lift that tempts the crew to cut the thrust and lower the nose, just before the shear reverses. A downdraft lowers the flight path directly, and at the same time tilts the relative wind down, reducing the angle of attack and the lift.

The most dangerous form is the **microburst**: a column of air plunging out of a convective cloud, a few kilometers across, that spreads out in all directions when it reaches the ground. An aircraft flying through it meets first an increasing headwind (a gain shear, which lifts it above the path and invites a thrust reduction), then the downdraft in the core, then a strong tailwind on the far side, with the loss of airspeed and lift coming just when it is lowest. Microbursts can be **wet**, inside heavy rain, or **dry**, beneath high-based clouds with little or no rain reaching the ground, which makes them hard to see and nearly impossible to detect with conventional radar.

blocks.alt: Cross-section diagram of a microburst on the final approach path of a DC-10. A convective cloud above with a downdraft column descending and spreading horizontally near the ground in a ring vortex. The aircraft's intended 3° glide path is drawn from left to right through it. Position 1, entering the outflow: increasing headwind arrow, airspeed and lift increase, aircraft rising above the glide path (label: gain shear; do not reduce thrust). Position 2, the core: downdraft arrow, aircraft sinking. Position 3, exiting: strong tailwind arrow, airspeed and lift decrease, aircraft well below the glide path (label: loss shear). A dashed actual flight path shows the danger. Labels legible, no numerical values.
blocks.title: A microburst on the approach
blocks.caption: The headwind on entry lifts the aircraft above the path and invites a thrust reduction just before the downdraft and the tailwind take the energy away.

blocks.content: **The energy view.** A useful way to think about a shear is as a rate at which the air is taking energy away from the aircraft. Windshear detection systems compute a hazard index for this, the **F-factor**: the rate of change of the horizontal wind along the flight path (tailwind positive) divided by the acceleration of gravity, minus the vertical wind (updraft positive) divided by the airspeed. It is the equivalent, in climb gradient, of the energy the shear is removing. A transport aircraft at full thrust has a climb gradient margin of only a tenth or so to spare, so a shear whose F-factor approaches that leaves the aircraft unable both to hold its speed and to climb. The recovery technique follows from it: put every bit of available thrust into the energy balance at once, and spend airspeed (down to the stall warning) for height, never the reverse.

blocks.title: Causes of wind shear accidents
rows: Thunderstorms and convective clouds, including rain and snow showers
Other: temperature inversions, mountain waves, sea breeze fronts, unknown

blocks.content: No single signal, short of a reliable report from another aircraft, proves that wind shear is present. The danger signals are cumulative: the more of them there are, the more reason to delay the departure or the approach. They include pilot reports of airspeed loss or gain (actual shear can be up to twice what a report says, because microbursts intensify quickly; note the type of aircraft reporting), low-level wind shear alerting system warnings (not fully reliable), virga, visual signs of strong outflow near the surface (blowing dust, rings of dust, dust devils), lightning, heavy precipitation on the radar, moderate or greater turbulence, a large temperature/dewpoint spread in hot weather, and forecasts of convection. At night many of the visual signs are missing.

blocks.title: Microburst wind shear probability (within 3 NM of takeoff or landing, below 1,000 ft)
rows: Convective weather near the flight path, with localized strong winds (reported, or seen as blowing dust, rings of dust, tornado-like features)
Convective weather near the flight path, with heavy precipitation (seen, or on radar as red, contour or an attenuation shadow)
An onboard windshear alert, reported or observed
Pilot report of an airspeed loss or gain of 15 kt or more
Convective weather near the flight path with a rain shower, lightning, virga, or moderate or greater turbulence
Convective weather in hot air (above about 27 °C) with a temperature/dewpoint spread of about 17 to 28 °C
Pilot report of an airspeed loss or gain of less than 15 kt

blocks.content: A **high** probability calls for a decision to avoid: delay, divert or hold. A **medium** probability calls for avoidance to be considered and precautions taken. A **low** one is to be noted, but does not usually call for avoidance. The hazard grows with closeness to convective weather, and the assessment must be kept up to date. The policy is to **avoid known wind shear**: delay the takeoff until conditions improve, divert around the area in flight, and go around if wind shear is indicated on the approach.
**Takeoff precautions** when wind shear is possible:

items: Use maximum takeoff thrust, not reduced thrust, and the longest suitable runway, away from the suspected shear.

Consider a higher rotation speed: compute the speeds for the actual weight, but rotate at the VR for the performance-limited weight (FedEx's performance computer gives it; the MD-10 FCOM limits the increase to 20 kt and to the runway-limited VR). Rotate normally to the normal initial climb attitude and hold it until clear of the ground and obstacles. If shear is met at or beyond the normal VR, do not wait for the higher speed: rotate at once, and in no case later than **2,000 ft before the end of the usable runway**.

On the DC-10 and KC-10, do not use the flight director's speed-referenced pitch guidance for takeoff, which has no windshear logic and can command a pitch reduction in a loss shear. On the MD-10, the windshear guidance makes the flight director usable.

Be alert for airspeed fluctuations on the roll and in the initial climb; they may be the first sign. Minimize any reduction from the initial climb attitude until terrain and obstacles are cleared. With an increasing tailwind the balanced field data may no longer be valid, and a rejected takeoff before V1 may not be possible.

Below V2 + 10 kt in a shear, unusually high column forces (20 to 30 lb) may be needed to stop the pitch attitude decreasing. Respect the stick shaker at all times. Do not change the configuration, and do not retrim.

blocks.content: **Approach precautions:**

items: Stabilize the approach by 1,000 ft above the ground at the latest.
Use the minimum flap setting authorized for a normal landing: flaps 35 on the DC-10 and KC-10, which gives the best overall recovery performance.
Use the most suitable runway away from the suspected shear, within the crosswind and tailwind limits.
Add an airspeed correction, applied like a gust correction, up to 20 kt.

Use the autopilot and autothrottles for more monitoring and recognition time, but back up the throttles by hand: be ready to disconnect the autothrottles if they are slow to add thrust, and do not let them pull the thrust far back in a gain shear.
Avoid large thrust reductions or trim changes in response to sudden airspeed increases; a decrease may follow.
Do not let the aircraft get low on the glideslope, or leave the throttles at idle for long.
Ensure the touchdown is in the normal touchdown zone.

blocks.content: **Standard techniques**, used on every takeoff and approach whether or not wind shear is expected, are what prevent a dangerous flight path from developing unnoticed: know the normal all-engine pitch attitude, rotation and airspeed build-up on takeoff, and the normal vertical speed, thrust and pitch on the approach; make a continuous rotation at the normal rate; cross-check the flight director against the raw vertical flight path; and have the pilot monitoring (and the flight engineer) watch the vertical speed, altimeters and glideslope and call out deviations. Use the inertial or FMS ground speed on the approach.

**Reference ground speed.** Comparing the actual ground speed with a computed reference is a proven way of detecting low-level shear before it arrives. Take the approach indicated airspeed (threshold speed plus wind additives), convert it to a true airspeed for the airfield's pressure altitude and temperature, and subtract the reported runway headwind component (or add the tailwind) to get the **reference ground speed**. For example, an approach speed of 145 KIAS at an airfield 5,000 ft high on a warm day is about 160 kt true; with a reported headwind of 20 kt the reference ground speed is 140 kt. If the aircraft is making only 120 kt over the ground, the headwind is 20 kt stronger than reported: if it stops abruptly, 20 kt of airspeed will go with it, so fly a higher indicated speed and hold the ground speed at its reference. If the aircraft is making 160 kt, the shear to expect will raise the airspeed: hold the approach speed, and resist the temptation to pull the thrust off. Keep the reference up to date as conditions change, and once stabilized on the glidepath with a safe landing assured, fly the approach speed to the flare.

The KC-10 manual applies the technique formally: approach IAS and the reference ground speed are both minimum speeds on final, and the flight engineer monitors the No. 3 FMS CDU's wind and calls significant deviations (10 kt of ground speed or of headwind/tailwind component, or a direction change of 20° or more). If more than VAPP + 20 kt would be needed to hold the reference ground speed, seriously consider not starting, or discontinuing, the approach; below 500 ft, discontinue it. The FMS wind may be wrong below about 130 KTAS. Takeoff is not attempted when severe loss shear is reported or forecast at or below 2,000 ft, or when wind shear is associated with convective activity. Unlike FedEx and the MD-10 FCOM, the KC-10 manual does not recommend the autopilot or autothrottles for a takeoff or approach in suspected wind shear; if they are used on an approach, be ready to override the autothrottles if they are slow to add thrust, and do not let the N1 fall too low late in the approach, which lengthens the time to accelerate.

Begin the recovery **immediately**, without waiting to analyze the situation, on a windshear warning (where fitted) or whenever the flight path control becomes marginal below 1,000 ft on takeoff or approach. As a guide, marginal flight path control means uncontrolled changes from the normal steady condition of more than:

items: ±15 KIAS;
±500 ft/min of vertical speed;
±5° of pitch attitude;
±1 dot of glideslope displacement;
an unusual throttle position held for a significant time.

items.item: Vertical flight path and radio altitude

blocks.title: Wind shear recovery: approach and landing (DC-10, KC-10)

items.item: Vertical flight path and radio altitude

blocks.content: If the aircraft is descending or the terrain clearance is not enough, increase the pitch attitude gradually until the stick shaker comes on, and at the same time apply firewall thrust (throttles to their mechanical stops). Thereafter fly at the onset of the shaker, with intermittent shaker as the limit and pitch changes as smooth as possible. Stop the rotation at once if the shaker or buffet comes in before 15°. Disregard the flight director's pitch bar: in a go-around it tries to hold V2 + 10 kt and will trade height for speed, and with the autopilot in CMD in G/A it can fly the aircraft into the ground.

items.action: AS NECESSARY (MAXIMUM IF GROUND CONTACT IS IMMINENT)
DISCONNECT (unless windshear guidance is engaged and followed)
TOWARD 15° AT THE NORMAL RATE; PLI AND INTERMITTENT SHAKER AS THE LIMIT
FOLLOW WINDSHEAR GUIDANCE, OTHERWISE OFF OR DISREGARD

blocks.content: On the MD-10, on approach, pushing the **GA switch** when a shear is detected engages the windshear guidance: the flight director (popping up if it was off) and the autopilot fly an energy-conserving path, and the autothrottles advance to go-around thrust. If more than go-around thrust is needed, disconnect the autothrottles and push the throttles further. On takeoff the guidance is automatic once the nose strut extends. The pitch limit indicator shows the margin to the shaker angle of attack and remains valid in the shear, where the speed tape's cues may not be. Follow the guidance even when the PLI moves rapidly above and below the aircraft symbol. Without guidance, fly the manual technique: on takeoff, if the all-engine pitch attitude was already established, hold it until the shear is exited or the shaker comes; if the descent or height loss is still unacceptable at 15°, raise the pitch in small steps (about 2° at a time), never beyond the shaker's angle of attack. See [Windshear alert and guidance](automatic-flight#windshear-md10).

items: **Do not lower the nose to regain airspeed.** Airspeed is the energy to be spent; height is what must be kept.

**Do not retrim** to the lower speed, and do not change the flaps, slats or gear until terrain contact is no longer a factor and a positive rate of climb is established. A flap change might in principle help, but the risk of moving the flaps the wrong way or too far is judged greater than the benefit.
**Be ready** for further areas of horizontal shear and vertical wind on the way out.

**Rapidly changing vertical winds** can make the shaker come on momentarily at any attitude. If the pitch was limited below 15° to stop the shaker, increase it toward 15° again as soon as the shaker stops. Make pitch changes smoothly, in small steps, to avoid overshooting.

**On the takeoff roll**, a shear before V1 is a reason to reject (the MD-10 FCOM requires it on a windshear alert); after V1, continue, and if the shear is a loss shear and VR has not been reached 2,000 ft from the end of the runway, rotate there, with maximum thrust.

**Once climbing** and clear of the ground, regain airspeed by cautious reductions of pitch. Report the shear to ATC (the airspeed change, location and altitude, and the aircraft type) as soon as practical, and make a maintenance entry with the parameters exceeded. Consider landing at the nearest suitable airport if damage is suspected.

blocks.alt: Windshear recovery profile on a go-around, drawn as three aligned time traces over about 30 seconds above a side-view flight path. Flight path panel: the aircraft entering a loss shear at about 400 ft on approach, the recovery initiated, a shallow minimum height reached and a climb out. Pitch trace: rotation at a normal rate to 15°, then increased in small steps up to the stick shaker limit (a dashed line labeled intermittent shaker = upper limit), then reduced cautiously after climbing. Thrust trace: an immediate step to go-around thrust, then to firewall (mechanical stops) when descending. Airspeed trace: falling toward the shaker speed and recovering only after the shear is exited. Annotations: do not lower the nose to regain speed; do not change configuration; do not retrim; disregard the flight director (DC-10, KC-10). Labels legible.
blocks.title: Wind shear recovery

blocks.content: **DC-10 and KC-10.** Where the enhanced GPWS is fitted it carries a reactive windshear function, with a split windshear light in front of each pilot: **WND SHR** on the FedEx DC-10, **W/S** on the KC-10. It is active from rotation to 1,500 ft on takeoff and in a missed approach, and from 1,500 ft down to 10 ft on approach (KC-10). A **windshear warning** (decreasing performance) lights the red half and sounds a siren followed by WINDSHEAR, WINDSHEAR, WINDSHEAR: begin the recovery at once. A **windshear caution** lights the amber half (with CAUTION, WINDSHEAR spoken on the KC-10; silent on the FedEx DC-10) and marks an increasing headwind, decreasing tailwind or updraft: be alert for the loss of airspeed and the downdraft that may follow. After rotation, a caution calls for maximum takeoff thrust if a reduced thrust takeoff was in progress, and for holding the takeoff pitch attitude, disconnecting the autopilot and autothrottles if necessary; on final, for adding the wind and gust allowances to the approach speed, more thrust, and disconnecting the automatics if necessary. All factors considered, a go-around may be the right answer to a caution. The W/S FAIL light (KC-10) or WINDSHEAR FAIL light (DC-10) shows that the function is lost. The basic DC-10 GPWS has no windshear function; recognition is then by the instruments alone. See [GPWS](surveillance#gpws).

**MD-10.** The windshear alert and guidance system (WAGS) in the flight control computers detects shear from 80 kt on the takeoff roll to 1,500 ft, and on approach from 1,500 ft to 50 ft. A decreasing-performance shear shows a red **WINDSHEAR** at the top left of the PFD with an alert tone and TAILWIND SHEAR spoken three times; an increasing-performance shear shows it in amber, with HEADWIND SHEAR; red has priority, and the legend flashes three times and then stays steady. Detection is delayed in a sustained bank of more than 15° or while the flaps are moving. Do not wait for it: if the pilot recognizes the shear first, begin the manual recovery, and the guidance will follow once the system detects it. Aircraft with **predictive windshear** fitted (it must be on for takeoff where installed) give WINDSHEAR AHEAD, WINDSHEAR AHEAD on the runway (reject the takeoff, or do not start it), GO AROUND, WINDSHEAR AHEAD on approach (go around at once), or MONITOR RADAR DISPLAY with an icon (consider the shear's position and avoid it).

sections.title: Contaminated and slippery runways
sections.summary: Tire friction and the anti-skid on slippery surfaces, hydroplaning, the contamination limits, and takeoff and landing technique on wet, slushy, snowy and icy runways.

blocks.content: Water, slush, snow and ice on a runway do three things to an aircraft. They reduce the friction the tires can develop, which lengthens every stop and weakens the nose wheel's grip against a crosswind. Deep, loose contaminants also drag on the wheels and spray up against the airframe, which slows the takeoff acceleration and can damage flaps, gear doors and engines. And standing water or slush can lift the tires off the runway altogether. A landing on, or a dispatch to, a runway with poor braking action is undesirable and should not be planned unless it is unavoidable.

A braked tire develops its friction by slipping: its surface turns slightly slower than the runway passes under it. Friction rises with slip to a peak, then falls away as the wheel approaches a lock, when the tire is sliding, its braking and its sideways grip collapse, and it can flat-spot and burst. The anti-skid system holds each wheel near the peak by releasing pressure at each incipient skid (see [Anti-skid](landing-gear#anti-skid)). On a contaminated surface the whole curve is lower and its peak flatter and earlier: the pressure the anti-skid can allow is much lower, its releases are more frequent and more pronounced, and the varying patches of ice and snow add more releases still. Tests have shown that at high ground speed on a wet runway the braking is only about **one third** of its dry value, and in slush about **one fifth**. Braking action reports and runway friction readings (RCR) express how much remains.

blocks.alt: Graph of tire braking friction coefficient (vertical axis, 0 to about 0.8) against wheel slip ratio (horizontal axis, 0 = free rolling to 1 = locked wheel). Four curves: dry runway, rising steeply to a high peak near 10 to 20% slip and then falling gradually toward the locked-wheel value; wet runway, a much lower peak; slush, lower still; ice, a low, flat curve. A band at the peak of each curve is labeled anti-skid operating region; the locked-wheel end is labeled skid: braking and cornering lost. A small inset shows cornering (side) friction falling as braking slip increases, with a note that a sliding tire cannot resist a crosswind. Labels legible, approximate shapes only.
blocks.title: Tire friction on contaminated runways
blocks.caption: Every contaminant lowers the friction curve. The anti-skid can only hold the wheel near the peak of the curve it is given.

items: **Use full pedal and hold it.** The anti-skid works best with the brake pedals fully depressed: it then modulates from the most pressure available. On a slippery runway apply full brake pressure smoothly and hold it constant until the aircraft has slowed to a safe taxi speed. Modulating or pumping the pedals only makes the anti-skid's job harder.

**A slick patch with partial pedal.** With partial pedal, a sudden drop in friction can make the anti-skid release so much pressure that the braking seems to stop altogether. The answer is more pedal, to full if needed. On leaving the slick patch with full pedal applied, an abrupt deceleration may follow, but this technique gives the best braking available.

**Spin-up.** The anti-skid needs the wheels to spin up on touchdown before it can control them, and on a very slippery surface they may not. A wheel that has not spun up, or that slows almost to a stop in a release cycle because the runway cannot turn it back up, can be braked as if the aircraft were parked, and lock. If the aircraft seems to accelerate when the brakes are applied, release them completely for a moment to let the wheels spin up, then reapply.

**Autobrakes.** Where fitted, use the autobrakes at their maximum setting on a contaminated runway (FedEx, MD-10 FCOM). They wait for the ground spoilers, so a delayed spin-up delays them too. See [Autobrakes](landing-gear#autobrakes).

**Without anti-skid.** Apply the brakes smoothly, increasing pedal force gradually until the deceleration is felt, and increase it further as the aircraft slows; do not release pressure until at taxi speed, and do not pump.
**Reverse thrust** is most effective at high speed, where the wheels are least effective, and its retarding force does not depend on the runway. Use it early and symmetrically.

blocks.content: Partial or total **hydroplaning** is possible whenever water or slush stands on the runway, at depths as small as 0.1 in on some surfaces. It happens when a tire cannot squeeze the fluid out of its footprint fast enough. The faster the tire rolls, the further a wedge of fluid is driven into the front of the footprint, and the pressure it builds lifts that part of the tire off the surface; the dry contact patch shrinks until, at the total hydroplaning speed, none is left and the tire is carried by the fluid alone. There is no sharp threshold: friction is already reduced well below that speed. And once a tire is fully up on the fluid it tends to stay there as the aircraft slows below the speed at which it began. The speed at which it begins rises with the tire pressure; see [Wheels and tires](landing-gear#tires-and-wheels) for the approximate figures.

blocks.alt: Side-view diagrams of an aircraft main gear tire rolling to the right through standing water at three increasing speeds. Low speed: the full footprint on the runway, water displaced forward and sideways, a bow wave ahead of the tire. Medium speed: a wedge of water penetrating the front of the footprint, the remaining contact area shaded smaller, labeled partial hydroplaning, bow wave still present. Total hydroplaning speed: the tire lifted entirely onto the water film, no runway contact, the bow wave gone, labeled total hydroplaning, braking and steering lost. A small inset compares a ribbed tread draining water through its grooves with a worn smooth tread. Labels legible.
blocks.title: Hydroplaning

items: **Evidence.** In water or slush each wheel pushes a bow wave ahead of it, and the drag of pushing it grows with speed. When the wheels ride up onto the fluid at the hydroplaning speed, the bow wave vanishes and so does much of that drag.

**Tread and wear.** Tread grooves give the fluid an escape path, so smooth or worn tires hydroplane sooner; fluid deeper than the grooves leaves a good tire no better off than a bald one. Wear makes no difference to friction on a dry runway, but on a wet one a badly worn tire loses a great deal.

**Runway surface.** Grooved or textured pavement drains the footprint and resists hydroplaning; a crowned runway sheds water and rarely builds deep water except in heavy downpours. Slush does not drain as readily as water, and hydroplaning in slush can be expected even on a crowned runway.

**Reverted rubber hydroplaning** starts with a locked-wheel skid: frictional heat turns the water under the tire to steam, the rubber in the footprint softens back toward raw latex and seals the tread grooves, and the tire glides on its own steam with almost no friction, sometimes nearly to a stop. A textured runway hardly helps; what prevents it is not letting a wheel lock.

**Effects.** Braking is lost or greatly reduced, and applying more brake to wheels that have already spun down does not restore it. Nose wheel steering is lost with the tire's grip, and the tires can no longer resist a crosswind. In a crosswind a hydroplaning aircraft points its nose into wind while its path curves toward the downwind edge of the runway, and only the rudder and the other aerodynamic controls, if they have enough authority at that speed, can keep it on the pavement. Reverse thrust, which does not depend on the tires, is an effective way to reduce the effect.

blocks.title: Runway contamination limits
rows: Not more than 1/2 in (12.7 mm) of water, slush or wet snow, or 4 in (10 cm) of dry snow
Not more than 1 in of water or slush, or 6 in of dry snow
Tailwind takeoff on a contaminated runway
Not permitted (FedEx: with clutter on the runway; MD-10: wet or contaminated). The limiting tailwind component is otherwise 10 kt
Reduced thrust takeoff on a wet or contaminated runway
Not permitted (MD-10 FCOM); use maximum takeoff thrust
Takeoff with the anti-skid inoperative on a wet or contaminated runway
Crosswind with braking action reported poor

blocks.content:
Takeoff and landing performance on a contaminated runway comes from the contaminated runway data in the performance manuals. The MD-10 FCOM's convention is typical: with less than 1/4 in of water, slush or wet snow use the 1/4 in data; between 1/4 and 1/2 in use the 1/2 in data; and treat 2 in of dry snow like 1/4 in of slush, and 4 in like 1/2 in. Slush in puddles and low spots can be much deeper than the reported average. Slush thrown up at high speed can do significant structural damage, particularly to the flaps and gear doors; avoid puddles and slush where possible, and inspect the aircraft after operating through them.

A chemical de-icer freshly applied to an icy runway forms a watery film over the snow and ice that gives **extremely poor** braking until it has worked.

The technique for the takeoff roll itself (symmetrical thrust set in two stages, slight nose-down elevator, small rudder pedal steering inputs, no differential thrust) is in [Takeoff in cold weather](#cold-takeoff). On a slippery runway a loss of directional control is possible after a rejected takeoff at any speed, especially in a crosswind. On contaminated runways the KC-10 manual recommends a center of gravity at or forward of 23% MAC for taxi, takeoff and landing, which improves the nose wheel steering.

items: **Displacement drag.** The wheels must push the contaminant aside, and the spray strikes the gear and airframe. Both retard the aircraft more as speed rises, until the hydroplaning speed, so acceleration is slower and the distances longer than on a dry runway. The performance data accounts for this; ordinary dry-runway data does not.

**Rejected takeoff.** Both nose wheel steering and differential braking are less effective on a slippery runway, especially in a crosswind. Reverse thrust is recommended to shorten the stop, but it can also reduce directional control: apply it gradually and symmetrically, as far as directional control allows. If directional control becomes a problem, reduce the reverse thrust, to reverse idle or forward idle if necessary, regain control, and reapply.

**Engines.** High reverse thrust at low ground speed on a contaminated runway can flame out the wing engines by ingesting spray, slush or snow, and on a cleared runway can throw ice chunks and sand into them.

blocks.content: Before the approach, consider the runway length available, the visibility of the runway markers and lights, snowbanks and drifts along the runway, the wind and the crosswind's effect on directional control, the braking action, the effect of spray and slush on the aircraft (engine ingestion, damage to flaps and gear doors), and the possibility of hydroplaning. Use the most favorable runway for its surface, wind and weather, land into the wind if possible, and use the landing distances from the performance data. Maximum flap (flaps 50) is recommended where braking is reduced.

items: **Approach.** Fly a stabilized approach early, with precise control of drift and speed and no excess speed. Execute a missed approach if a zero-drift condition cannot be established before touchdown.

**Illusions.** Blowing or drifting snow in a crosswind can give a false impression of the aircraft's movement over the ground, including an impression of no drift when there is a great deal. Use the runway lights and markings and the inertial drift information as references.
**Touchdown.** Fly the aircraft firmly onto the runway at the normal touchdown point; do not hold it off or let it float.

**Spoilers.** Make sure the ground spoilers deploy, and be ready to deploy them by hand, because a delayed wheel spin-up can delay the automatic deployment. The automatic ground spoilers also have an ice and water mode that deploys them on reverse thrust when the wheels have not spun up (see [Ground spoilers](flight-controls#ground-spoilers)).
**Nose down.** Lower the nose wheels to the runway at once and hold forward pressure on the column to keep the wheels loaded and the nose wheel steering effective.

**Brakes.** Autobrakes at MAX where fitted; otherwise smooth, constant brake pressure. If wind is not a factor and there is no lateral control problem, full braking with the anti-skid gives the shortest stop.

**Reverse.** Apply reverse thrust smoothly and symmetrically on all engines, to the maximum allowable, as soon as possible. Never use asymmetric reverse for directional control. Below about 60 kt on dry snow, reverse can blow snow forward and take away the forward visibility, and can melt snow that refreezes on cold surfaces; use it with that in mind. Avoid a rapid return to forward thrust with the engines at high speed, which can make the aircraft accelerate.
