**Direction.** Keep directional control primarily with the rudder and nose wheel steering, with differential braking as needed. In a strong crosswind the rudder needed can turn the nose wheels to an angle at which they skid; it may then be better to hold the nose wheel straight and steer with rudder and brakes. Using the steering wheel to correct a skid at high speed is extremely hazardous.
**Turn off** only when the speed is low enough to turn without skidding, using as much of the runway as necessary.

blocks.alt: Plan-view vector diagram of a DC-10 rolling out on a slippery runway with a crosswind from the left. The aircraft has weathervaned so its nose points left of the runway centerline into the wind. Reverse thrust arrows from the three engines point forward along the fuselage axis, and their resultant is resolved into a braking component along the runway and a side component pushing the aircraft toward the right (downwind) edge. A crosswind force arrow also points downwind. The aircraft's track is drawn curving toward the downwind edge. A second inset: reverse reduced to idle, the nose realigned with the runway using rudder, the side force gone, then reverse and braking reapplied. Labels legible.
blocks.title: Reverse thrust in a crosswind on a slippery runway
blocks.caption: With the aircraft weathervaned into wind, reverse thrust pushes it toward the downwind side, adding to the crosswind. Reduce reverse, realign, then reapply.

blocks.content: **Skids and drift.** If the aircraft begins to slide toward the downwind side, the reverse thrust is making it worse: with the aircraft weathervaned into wind, the reverse thrust's side component acts in the same direction as the wind. Disarm the autobrakes, release or reduce the braking, reduce the reverse thrust to reverse idle and if necessary forward idle, use the rudder and nose wheel steering to bring the aircraft back in line with the runway, and then reapply braking and reverse to complete the stop.

sections.title: Heavy rain and hail
sections.summary: Visibility in heavy rain, what water and hail do to the engines, and continuous ignition.

blocks.content: **Visibility.** In rain the view through the windshield can be badly reduced. In heavy rain the pilot flying stays on instruments until reaching the minimums, whether or not the pilot monitoring has the runway in sight, and both are ready to go around if any part of the approach is in doubt. Use the windshield wipers (not on a dry windshield, and not at high speed for more than 30 minutes); see [Rain removal](ice-and-rain#rain-removal).

**Engines in heavy precipitation.** In extremely heavy rain the N1 indications can wander up or down by as much as 6% at a constant throttle setting. Up to a point, the water lowers the compressor inlet temperature and raises the air the core demands, so N1 rises. Beyond that point the water reaches the combustor, where it takes heat out of the flame: the cycle temperature falls, less work is available to drive the fan, and N1 falls. The water also raises the fuel flow the flame needs to stay alight. An engine at high power has plenty of margin and ordinary heavy rain changes little; an engine near flight idle in an extreme cell, especially one carrying hail, can roll back or flame out. See [Flameout](engines#flameout).

items: **Continuous ignition.** In heavy rain (and severe turbulence) select the ignition to continuous: CONT A or CONT B on the DC-10 and KC-10, ENG IGN OVRD ON on the MD-10. With the igniters firing, a flame that blows out while the core is still turning fast relights at once on the compressor's own air, often with no more than a brief rollback. (The MD-10's ignition override has no time limit, though excessive use shortens the igniters' life.)

**Throttles.** No other action is needed unless the N1 must be reduced to stay within its limits. Move the throttles slowly and deliberately, accept momentary changes in N1, and readjust the thrust as the rain eases.
**Anti-ice.** The FedEx and MD-10 severe turbulence and heavy rain procedures turn the engine and wing anti-ice on: the extra bleed demand increases the compressors' stall margin.
**Hail** can also damage the radome, the pitot probes and the wing leading edges (see [Thunderstorms](#thunderstorms)). Fly attitude and thrust if the airspeed becomes suspect.

blocks.content: The full procedure is in [Severe turbulence or heavy rain](#turbulence-penetration). On the runway, heavy rain means standing water, with the braking and hydroplaning considerations in [Contaminated and slippery runways](#contaminated-runways).

sections.title: Volcanic ash
sections.summary: What ash does to the engines and the air data, how to recognize it, the encounter procedure, restarts, and operating from ash-contaminated airfields.

blocks.content: Flight through known volcanic ash clouds should be avoided whenever possible; plan routes to keep clear of known volcanic activity, and stay on the upwind side of any active volcano or reported ash cloud. The checklist for an inadvertent encounter is in [Abnormal Procedures](abnormal-procedures); this section explains what the ash does and why the procedure asks for what it does.

**Erosion.** Volcanic ash is highly abrasive: in a dense cloud, at high rotor speed, a minute can be enough to wear down the tips of the rotating blades. The high-pressure compressor and turbine suffer most, the tips of the high-pressure turbine blades above all, where tight clearances, high temperatures and high rotor speed combine: the loss of turbine efficiency (about 7%) shows afterwards as slower accelerations, higher EGT on starting, and a permanent upward shift of EGT and fuel flow.

**Glazing.** More immediately dangerous, ash can melt at temperatures below those in the combustor, and the melted ash resolidifies on the first-stage high-pressure turbine nozzle guide vanes. The deposit builds up and partly chokes the engine, reducing its stall margin: at high power the engine stalls and rolls back to flight idle or below, and its EGT can rise toward the limit, in less than a minute after climb thrust is applied. Low thrust keeps the combustor cooler, slowing or preventing the build-up and delaying any stall; more bleed demand increases the stall margin.

**Air data.** Ash commonly contaminates the pitot probes and gives abnormally low indicated airspeeds, or erratic and unreliable indications, or none. An autothrottle chasing a falsely low airspeed would command more thrust, raising the combustor temperature and speeding the glazing; that is why the procedure turns the autothrottles off.

**Other effects.** The windshields can be sandblasted, reducing forward visibility, and the wipers scratch the glass if used to clear ash; electrostatic discharge can disturb communications; ash and sulphurous fumes can enter the cabin through the air conditioning.

**Recognition.** An ash cloud is hard to see by day and almost impossible to see at night. The weather radar cannot be relied on: the particles are too small to return a usable echo, and the cloud may look like an ordinary overcast. The signs are:

items: an outside environment darker than normal;
smoke or dust entering through the air conditioning, or an acrid odour like electrical smoke, or of sulphur;
a white or orange glow at the engine inlets, St Elmo's fire on the windshields, or an unusual amount of static discharge;
landing lights casting sharp, distinct shadows;
on the engines: falling N1, N2 and fuel flow with rising EGT, surges, torching from the tailpipe, or flameout.

blocks.content: If an ash cloud is entered, act as quickly as possible. Exit by the shortest route at the lowest practical thrust: an immediate descending 180° turn is often the quickest way out. The aims of the procedure are to keep the turbine temperatures down, to protect against surges and flameout, and to be ready to restart.

items.action: IDLE, OR AS LOW AS PRACTICABLE
ON (WING AND ENGINE ANTI-ICE, PACKS, PNEUMATICS)

items.item: Oxygen masks (ash or sulphur odour in the flight deck)

blocks.content: The autopilot may be re-engaged later at the captain's discretion. On the KC-10, the ENG PNEU SUPPLY selectors go to HI for the most bleed. On the DC-10 in the simulation the ENG anti-ice toggles do not move on screen when set; confirm by the ENG ANTI-ICE lights (see [Ice and rain simulation notes](ice-and-rain#simulation-notes)). Do not attempt an APU start after an all-engine flameout; the air driven generator is available for electrical power if needed (see [Electrical](electrical)). Consider smoke goggles. If an engine flames out, or its EGT rises toward or beyond its limit, shut it down and restart it with the in-flight shutdown and restart procedures; several attempts may be needed.

If an engine has flamed out or stalled, or its EGT is beyond or rising rapidly toward its limit, move its FUEL lever OFF and then ON; with N2 below 20%, pull its ENGINE START switch. Do not use the windshield wipers, which scratch the glass and make the night approach difficult.

items: **Airspeed.** Expect erratic or lost airspeed indications. If the air data is unreliable, fly pitch attitude and thrust from the unreliable airspeed tables.

**Restarts.** An engine restarted and accelerated at altitude is slower than on the ground, and the slowness can be mistaken for a hung start or an ash-related malfunction. If it does not start, try again; repeated attempts help to dislodge the glazed ash from the turbine nozzles, and a successful start may not be possible until clear of the cloud and within the normal start envelope.

**After the encounter**, avoid rapid throttle movements; expect a marked upward shift in EGT and fuel flow. If the aircraft was damaged or an engine behaved abnormally, land at the nearest suitable airport.

**Report** the encounter to ATC as a pilot report: position, altitude, drift of the cloud, and the details of the volcanic activity report. Record the encounter for maintenance: location and time, altitude, speed, phase of flight, engine power, weather, duration, indications, actions taken and any unusual engine or aircraft response.

blocks.content: The KC-10 manual allows a hung or aborted restart in ash to exceed the normal EGT limit provided it does not exceed 945 °C. If the EGT approaches or exceeds that, abort the start and restart at once (fuel lever OFF, then ON as soon as the EGT falls): the engine is more likely to restart that way than by being left stalled or hung at a climbing EGT.

children.title: Ground operations on an ash-contaminated airfield

blocks.content: These recommendations are for engines that have not ingested ash, operating from an airfield where ash has fallen.

items: **Preflight.** Remove all covers. Clear the engine inlets and exhausts of ash (with brooms or vacuum cleaners), and clear the ash from the ground within about 25 ft of each inlet.
**Starting.** Dry motor each engine for at least 2 minutes before moving the fuel lever ON, while it is motoring. Expect a cooler than normal start.

**Taxi.** Consider towing to the runway. Do not exceed about 40% N1 to break away or while taxiing, which limits the inlet vortices that pick up ash; consider taxiing on No. 2 alone. Keep well clear of other aircraft's exhaust.
**Takeoff.** Use a rolling takeoff, and avoid setting takeoff thrust below about 30 kt. Do not use the autothrottles for takeoff: the airspeed indications may not be reliable.
**Landing.** Use as little reverse thrust as possible, and avoid more than idle reverse below 60 kt unless it is needed for safety. Forward visibility may be reduced by ash-abraded windshields.

**Leaving the aircraft.** Install the pitot covers and all engine inlet covers, and cover the exhausts if possible. Close every door, hatch and window, the pack inlet and exhaust doors and the outflow valve, and cover the static ports.

sections.title: Simulation notes
sections.summary: How the simulator's weather reaches the aircraft's systems, what is modeled in depth and what is not.

blocks.content: **The weather comes from the simulator.** Temperature, pressure, wind, turbulence, cloud and precipitation are the simulator's live weather. The aircraft's systems read them: the air data and the engines from the temperature and pressure; the ice and rain protection from the temperature, the cloud and the precipitation rate; the engines from the precipitation rate as water (or frozen precipitation) ingested; the MD-10's windshear detection from the winds. What the weather does to the aircraft's aerodynamics (turbulence, gusts and wind changes, and ice on the airframe if enabled) is the simulator's flight model.

**Icing.** The aircraft's own ice model grows ice on every zone separately and drives the probe failures, the indications and the ice drawn on the airframe; the simulator's own structural icing is what penalizes the flight model, and only with the simulator's icing assistance option on. The aircraft drives the simulator's anti-ice switches from its own systems, so the two agree. See [Ice and rain simulation notes](ice-and-rain#simulation-notes).

**Ground contamination and de-icing.** Frost (including frost from cold-soaked fuel), snow, freezing rain and freezing fog collect on the wing upper surfaces of a parked or taxiing aircraft, and are drawn on the wing and shown on the EFB's ICE page. De-icing is a ground service from the EFB (Type I alone, or a two-step Type I and Type IV application) or from GSX's trucks; see [De-icing and holdover](ground-operations#de-icing). The holdover is modeled as the fluid's capacity to absorb what falls on it, used up faster by heavier precipitation and frost and, for Type I, by the fluid running off; the ICE page shows the remaining holdover, and the fluid shears off during the takeoff roll. The holdover times this produces are typical of the published guidance but are not the official tables. Contamination on the wing does not by itself change the flight model: a takeoff with a contaminated wing is not penalized aerodynamically in the simulation. Treat it as the books do, and do not take off with it.

items: Fumes from de-icing fluid ingested by the engines or APU, and thickened fluid residues, are not modeled. The de-icing configuration and the pneumatic duct purge can be flown, but the purge's WING ANTI-ICE TEST position does not open the valves on the ground.

Cold soak effects are modeled in part: the engines' idle schedule and oil follow the temperature, hydraulic fluid temperature follows the ambient and affects the pumps, and the batteries lose some voltage when cold and are not charged below about −30 °C until they warm. Cold-fluid pump cavitation, slow inertial alignment and frozen doors are not modeled.

On the DC-10 the three ENG anti-ice toggles on the pilots' overhead do not move on screen in the current release, although a click or the simulator's anti-ice key bindings still sets them; confirm by the ENG ANTI-ICE lights. The KC-10's and MD-10's switches work normally.

Engine anti-ice bleed is a real load on the engines and pneumatics. The thrust rating computer applies the performance manual's anti-ice bleed corrections to its takeoff and go-around limits on the CF6-powered aircraft; the DC-10-40's JT9D limits carry none.

Fan ice on the engines is modeled: it builds in freezing precipitation, more at low power, and is thrown off by centrifugal force as N1 rises, unevenly enough to show as a short rise in N1 vibration. The ice shedding procedure therefore works as described. In the simulation the engines' fan ice builds from precipitation rather than from cloud alone, and begins to shed above about 45% N1, so it accumulates mainly at idle and in holding.

blocks.content:
**Heavy rain and hail.** The simulator's precipitation rate reaches the engines. Water and frozen precipitation take heat out of the combustor and raise the fuel flow needed to keep the flame alight, so an extreme cell at flight idle can roll an engine back or flame it out, while heavy rain at climb or takeoff thrust changes little. Continuous ignition relights a flame that blows out at power. The wipers work at their real rates; rain repellent is not modeled.

**Turbulence and thunderstorms.** Turbulence is the simulator's. The weather radar shows the simulator's precipitation (see [Surveillance simulation notes](surveillance#simulation-notes)); attenuation behind heavy cells, turbulence detection and the MD-10's predictive windshear are not modeled, and on the MD-10 the radar picture is not yet drawn on the navigation display. Lightning strikes and St Elmo's fire are not modeled. The DC-10 and KC-10 TURB mode works, but in the simulation it flies the autopilot's control wheel steering law, holding altitude with automatic pitch trim; the softened pitch response and the trim inhibit of the aircraft's turbulence mode are not modeled. Bear that in mind in severe turbulence: the autopilot will work to hold the altitude rather than let it vary.

**Wind shear.** Wind shear is whatever wind changes and vertical air movement the simulator's weather produces. On the MD-10 the windshear alert and guidance system detects it from the aircraft's own measurements of the wind along the flight path and the vertical air movement, with a typical industry threshold rather than the aircraft's own, and its guidance is modeled; the TAILWIND SHEAR and HEADWIND SHEAR voice is not sounded. On the DC-10 and KC-10 the GPWS windshear function is not modeled: the WND SHR (KC-10: W/S) lights and the windshear voice appear only in the GPWS self-test, so recognition is by the instruments, as on an aircraft without the function.

**Runways.** Runway friction, wet or contaminated, is the simulator's, and the simulated tires do not hydroplane. The aircraft's anti-skid, autobrakes and ground spoilers (including their ice and water mode) are modeled. Spray lifted from a wet runway by the engines and reversers is drawn, but the aircraft does not model slush drag, slush impingement damage or the ingestion of spray by the engines.

**Volcanic ash** is not modeled.

chapters.title: Air Refueling
chapters.summary: Tanker and receiver air refueling: planning, rendezvous, boom, drogue and wing pod procedures, emergencies and abnormals, and how to fly them in the simulation.

blocks.content: This section covers air refueling from the planning to the end of the refueling: the general operating rules, the rendezvous, the tanker crew's and the boom operator's procedures for the boom, the centerline hose and the wing pods, the KC-10A as a receiver, and the refueling emergencies and abnormals. The last part explains how to fly it all in the simulation. How the systems work is in [Air refueling systems](air-refueling-systems); the refueling limits are in [Limitations](limitations).

blocks.title: Who this section applies to
rows: Tanker with the boom, the centerline hose and drogue, and two wing pods; receiver through its UARRSI
Tanker with the boom (no fuel offload in the simulation)
Tanker with two wing pods, worked by the flight engineer

blocks.content: Crew designators: **PF** and **PM**, the pilot flying and the pilot monitoring; **FE**, the flight engineer; **BO**, the boom operator; **ALL**, every crew member. The procedures follow the KC-10A's flight manual; the Omega's pods are worked from the flight engineer's panel, and where a pod procedure names the boom operator, the Omega's flight engineer does it.

There is no receiver aircraft in the simulation, so there are no contacts and no fuel is offloaded or onloaded. The boom's signal system can be exercised with test inputs once they are bound to buttons, the KC-10A's own receiver system cannot reach READY, and most of the rest up to the contact works. Short notes in the procedures mark what cannot be done; the full picture is in [Flying air refueling in the simulation](ar-in-the-simulation).

parts.title: General operations
parts.summary: Planning, speeds and altitudes, communications, signals, lighting and the refueling envelopes.

blocks.content: Tanker and receiver crews must both know every aspect of the refueling. The tanker crew should study the forecast for the refueling area, so that an alternate track can be used if the primary is unsuitable, and should know the receiver's route to the track, so that late changes can be passed on. Have a plan for a late receiver. Annotate the crew chart with the refueling track or anchor and its altitude limits, the air refueling initial point (ARIP) or entry point, the air refueling control point (ARCP) or anchor point, the rendezvous point (RZ) and its initial point (RZIP) if used, and the end of air refueling (EAR) or exit point.

items: **Base altitude.** Normally 25,000 ft for the tanker's orbit and the refueling. Altitudes up to 2,000 ft below the receiver's end-of-refueling optimum altitude may be used. Lead a two-tanker formation at least 2,500 ft below the receiver's optimum, and a three-tanker formation at least 3,000 ft below it.
**The KC-10A as receiver** does not refuel above 31,000 ft.
**Fuel without icing inhibitor** (FSII) is not offloaded without the receiver's agreement.

**Formation departures.** Below 10,000 ft the planned climb speed is 250 KIAS unless the heaviest aircraft's minimum maneuvering speed requires more. Above 10,000 ft it is 290 KIAS for formations with KC-10s below 500,000 lb and 310 KIAS at or above 500,000 lb. Avoid climb schedules that leave a KC-10 climbing with slats extended. Set TCAS to TA/RA before takeoff; TA may be selected during the join-up to avoid resolution advisories.

blocks.content: **Minimum refueling speed.** Find the 1.2 g buffet-onset speed for the weight and altitude from the cruise buffet boundary chart and add 5 kt, or 10 kt if wing pods are installed. Bank is limited to 15° at that speed. The buffet characteristics are discussed in [Limitations](limitations).

blocks.title: Refueling envelopes (summary)
rows: 180 KIAS from sea level to 20,000 ft, then linear to M 0.88 at 37,000 ft
350 KIAS or M 0.88, whichever is lower, to 37,000 ft
200 KIAS from sea level to 20,000 ft, then linear to M 0.88 at 37,000 ft
280 KIAS or M 0.88, whichever is lower, to 35,000 ft
230 KIAS from sea level to 33,000 ft, then linear to M 0.74 at 35,000 ft
Wing pods: hose extension and retraction
Retract at 280 KIAS or less. Maximum speed with a hose extended 350 KIAS

blocks.content: The boom can be flown as slowly as 180 KIAS, but below 200 KIAS its response is slightly reduced, particularly to rapid up commands above 30° elevation, and it overshoots by 2° to 3° after rapid or evasive commands. The centerline's upper limit is set by the reel response system, which cannot keep up at higher speeds; avoid refueling at a receiver's higher buddy-cruise speed. The full limitations, including the wing pod environmental limits, are in [Limitations](limitations).

With flaps or slats extended, a wing pod hose must not be trailed from stowed or wound fully in: it can strike the lower wing surface. Do not use the centerline drogue at the same time as either wing pod.
With flaps or slats extended, a wing pod hose must not be trailed from stowed or wound fully in: it can strike the lower wing surface.

**Receiver speeds and data.** Each receiver type has a published optimum refueling altitude, airspeed and Mach, a rendezvous speed, an overrun speed and its preferred offload rate, and for the boom its disconnect limits and disconnect delay. On the KC-10A and the KDC-10, the EFB's Air Refuel app lists them under Refueling Setup.

Unless directed otherwise, tanker and receivers keep the ability to talk throughout the rendezvous and the refueling, but voice transmissions are held to the minimum the **emission option** (EMCON) allows. The options run from unrestricted communications (option 1), through limited transmissions (option 2, the normal procedure for rendezvous and refueling) and a silent rendezvous without the 15-minute call (option 3), to no emissions at all (option 4). Agree the communications plan before flight. The assigned refueling frequency is normally the interplane frequency.

items: Monitor UHF Guard at all times. With two UHF radios working, turn Guard off on the one used for refueling. While refueling, the pilot flying and the boom operator listen only to interphone and the refueling frequency.
At least one UHF radio is on the refueling frequency. Positive radio transfer between the pilot and the boom operator takes place at 1/2 NM and after the refueling.
Except in breakaway calls, tactical call signs may be shortened to the number: Tank 11 is 11.
If radio contact between the boom operator and the receiver pilot is lost or unreadable, no contacts are attempted except in an emergency fuel situation.

blocks.content: Do not transmit on HF when in contact with, or close to, the KC-10A's boom. HF transmissions can cause uncommanded boom movement, endangering both aircraft.
Do not transmit on HF when in contact with, or close to, the boom. HF transmissions can cause uncommanded boom movement, endangering both aircraft.

blocks.title: Mandatory receiver calls
rows: Initial radio contact: call sign, altitude, timing, Mode 3
At least 15 minutes before the rendezvous control time. The tanker answers with its call sign, refueling altitude, timing and Mode 3.
If not at that altitude at the 15-minute call
Before using manual, emergency or override boom latching

blocks.content: Radio-silent refueling uses visual signals, which are also used as much as possible under emission option 2:

items: **Boom.** The boom operator lights a red pilot director panel and its letter with the coaching switch to direct the receiver: steady for a large correction, flashing for a small one, in the direction shown.
**Breakaway (boom).** BREAKAWAY SIG flashes the pilot director lights for 10 seconds.

**Disconnect request (boom).** The boom operator holds the disconnect signal switch, which puts all the pilot director lights out, until the receiver disconnects and the nozzle is clear of the receptacle.

**Breakaway (hoses).** BREAKAWAY SIG flashes the red external drogue light and the red pod signal lights. On the KC-10A, the boom operator can also send a drogue receiver back to precontact with the drogue signal while resetting the reel response.

blocks.content: The pilot director lights and the hoses' external signal lights are not driven in the simulation; see [Simulation notes](air-refueling-systems#sim-not-modelled).

For a rendezvous the tanker shows its navigation lights at full bright, the high-intensity lights, both beacons, and formation lights if required, from at least 15 minutes before the latest receiver ETA for the rendezvous point. A single tanker shows red/white in both beacons; in a tanker formation number 1 shows red, number 2 white, number 3 red-white. Night refueling lighting is set before the receivers reach 1 NM in trail. Once a receiver is visual and closed to 1/2 NM, the tanker turns its lower beacon and high-intensity lights off. At the observation and precontact positions the tanker adjusts its lights as required or as the receiver asks, and the receiver adjusts its own as the boom operator asks.

blocks.title: KC-10A exterior lighting for refueling (typical night settings)

blocks.content: For night training both aircraft should use all their refueling lighting; a KC-10A receiver should have its upper fuselage floodlight and receptacle light working, set at the tanker boom operator's discretion. Refueling with less than the best lighting calls for great care: depth perception and visual cues are reduced.

The disconnect limits are set well inside the boom's mechanical limits, so a disconnect normally happens before any structural damage. Set the adjustable limits and the receiver disconnect delay for each receiver type, and reset them before refueling a different type. During a receiver pilot's demonstration of the envelope limits, the boom operator states the limit, gives the boom's position in increments of 2 as the receiver approaches it, and warns the receiver as it nears the limit. The boom's structure and limits are described in [Structural limits and the disconnect envelope](air-refueling-systems#boom-envelope).

blocks.alt: Side and rear diagram of a large receiver in the boom contact position behind and below a KC-10A: boom at about 30° elevation, telescope extended about 12 ft, receiver's receptacle under the nozzle. Overlaid: the disconnect envelope in elevation (upper limit band 20° to 27°, lower limit 40°), in telescope (inner 6 ft, outer 21 ft) and, in the rear view, the left and right roll limits (11° to 25°), with the contact position near the middle. Labels for precontact (about 50 ft behind and below, stabilized) and observation positions.
blocks.title: Boom refueling positions and envelope

blocks.content: A receiver that reaches a boom limit quickly can jam the nozzle in its receptacle so that the disconnect fails, with damage to both aircraft; the risk is greatest with the receiver rolled well over and the boom at low elevation. Contacts are not attempted with more than 10° of boom roll.

**Centerline hose (KC-10A).** 80 ft of black hose painted with 12-inch white bands, every 10 ft along its length and every 5 ft within the refueling range. Wider 24-inch bands show where fuel starts to flow, the recommended refueling position and the inner limit; the range itself extends from about 5 ft to 40 ft in from full trail. Use only the first 20 ft of travel where possible, to keep the receiver's nose clear of the tanker's tail.

blocks.alt: Diagram of the KC-10A centerline hose at full trail and pushed in, with the hose markings drawn to scale: 12-inch white bands every 10 ft, 5-ft bands through the range, 24-inch bands at fuel flow initiation (5 ft in), recommended refueling position and the inner limit (40 ft in). Below: the external signal lights' state at each position: amber at full trail, amber out and green on in range, amber flashing beyond the forward limit.
blocks.title: Centerline hose markings and refueling range

blocks.content: **Wing pod hose.** 79 ft long, of which 74 ft trails, black with white and orange bands. Pushed in 5 ft by the receiver, it puts the pod's amber light out; 12 ft further the light flashes, and roughly 9 ft beyond that the fuel valve shuts, leaving about 21 ft of usable range. The tensators can take up hose only between about 46 ft and full trail: push it in further and the hose goes slack and may loop.

blocks.alt: Diagram of a wing pod hose from full trail (74 ft) pushed in: 69 ft (refuel range entered, amber out, valve opens), 57 ft (amber flashes approaching the inner limit), about 48 ft (inner limit, fuel valve closes, green out), about 46 ft (tensators stop, dead hose). The white and orange hose bands drawn, and the pod's red, amber and green signal lights shown at each position.
blocks.title: Wing pod hose positions

items: A serviceable autopilot is engaged for every refueling except authorized autopilot-off training. The pilot flying rests one hand on the column and keeps the other near the throttles, ready for an autopilot fault or a breakaway.
Do not engage or disengage the autopilot with a receiver in the contact position except in an emergency: unscheduled attitude changes can follow.
Do not use the autopilot's navigation modes during refueling.

Use HEADING SELECT with care: changing the reference heading can produce abrupt bank. Set the bank selector to 5° until a turn is started, change the heading slowly to reach the bank wanted, and return the bank selector to 5° after the turn. Turns can be made in contact if no large or abrupt control or throttle movements are made by either aircraft.

Autothrottles may be used with most receivers, but are not recommended with large receivers and must not be used in turbulence. Check that the speed is above ALPHA speed before engaging them. Change speed slowly, in 1-kt steps. Mind the heading knob's closeness to the speed knob. Disengage the autothrottles if a breakaway is called.
If the tanker is more than 10 kt off the refueling speed inside 1 NM of closure and must accelerate or decelerate, tell the receiver before changing speed.
Do not let the speed fall below the 1.2 g buffet speed corrected for the conditions.

blocks.content: Two aircraft stacked close together vertically are in danger: the flow around each can pull them together, and a receiver that overruns beneath the tanker creates low pressure that corrupts both aircraft's static sources, so airspeed and altitude read wrongly. The tanker's autopilot can take that pressure drop for a climb and descend onto the receiver. Call a breakaway for a receiver that cannot settle in precontact or is starting to overrun.

When an emergency or abnormal condition that affects the tanker's stability or controllability occurs during refueling, disconnect immediately and tell the receiver to stay clear until it is corrected. Discontinue refueling when the in-flight visibility is not enough for safe operation, and consider moving the track, altitude or heading if the sun, cloud or precipitation are making the closure difficult.
Stow the boom or hose when more than 10 minutes will pass between refuelings. When receivers accelerate and climb on the refueling heading after the refueling, avoid flying through their jetwash.

blocks.title: Mandatory maintenance write-ups after refueling
rows: Boom retracted against the stops with the emergency retraction
Boom will not trim to 0° roll or 30° elevation
A significant event on a hose: an observable hose whip or sine wave or a dead hose after contact, or a contact that damages either aircraft or the drogue

blocks.content: After a significant event on a hose, discontinue refueling with it unless there is an emergency. The hose's stability and strength are unknown and it could fail at any time.

parts.title: Rendezvous procedures
parts.summary: The tanker orbit, the point parallel rendezvous and its geometry, the FMS refuel pattern, alternate means, closure, overrun and missed rendezvous.

blocks.content: Unless briefed otherwise the tanker waits in a racetrack flown to the left at the assigned refueling altitude: two-minute straight legs joined by 25° bank turns. One leg lies along the receiver's inbound track, and the ARCP (or anchor point) sits at its far end. Orbit at 275 KIAS or M 0.78, taking the lower, without going below the refueling orbit speed; with A-10s the figure drops to 255 KIAS, which may require 0/EXT. A heavy KC-10 may have to orbit faster, which is agreed before the flight. If the wait will be long, fly the holding procedures from the performance manual instead.

blocks.alt: Plan view of the typical tanker orbit: a left-hand racetrack with 2-minute legs and 25° bank turns, the ARCP at the downstream end of the inbound leg, which lies along the receiver's ARIP-to-ARCP track; the ARIP upstream on that track; the tanker's offset to the left of the receiver's track marked; wind arrow and the drift correction noted.
blocks.title: Typical tanker orbit pattern

items: A right-hand orbit, or a pattern that drift and true airspeed carry more than 18 NM from the ARIP-ARCP track, needs its own ATC clearance.
With no orbit delay expected, the rendezvous turn may be flown at the higher of maximum endurance speed and 275 KIAS (255 KIAS with A-10s).
Refueling is normally done in level flight. A power-limited receiver may need a descending flight path: see [Toboggan](ar-tanker-procedures#tk-toboggan).

Lead normally passes from number one to number two to number three, but every pilot must be ready to take the formation at any time; announce a change of leader to the whole formation. After the rendezvous the lead tanker keeps the radar weather watch and steers the formation clear of hazardous weather.

blocks.content: Have the rendezvous equipment on and checked 30 minutes before the control time (ARCT or RZ), and the air-to-air TACAN 15 minutes before it. The KC-10A carries an I-band double-pulse rendezvous beacon, UHF direction finding and an air-to-air TACAN that gives both bearing and range; its normal method is the **FMS used together with the TACAN in beacon-inverse mode**. Keep the backups ready throughout: airborne radar and beacon, UHF/ADF, TCAS, a shared ground TACAN or VORTAC, FAA or GCI controllers, and timing, each weighed against the emission option in force.

Have the rendezvous equipment on and checked 30 minutes before the control time (ARCT or RZ), and any air-to-air TACAN 15 minutes before it. Keep every backup ready: airborne radar, UHF/ADF, TCAS, a shared ground TACAN or VORTAC, FAA or GCI controllers, and timing.

**Air-to-air TACAN.** By 15 minutes before the ARCT the tanker and one receiver in each formation have the assigned pair of Y channels set, the receiver on the lower-numbered one and the tanker on the higher. The mode depends on the pairing: a KC-10A receiving from a KC-135 selects beacon-inverse, behind a KC-10A beacon-normal, and a KC-10A tanker meeting another KC-10A selects beacon-inverse. A TACAN range that agrees with the TCAS or radar range confirms the right aircraft. Once the rendezvous no longer needs it, set REC or T/R so that it does not disturb other formations.

In a point parallel rendezvous the tanker aims to be at the ARCP a quarter of an hour ahead of the ARCT. With no radio contact by the ARCT it is overhead the ARCP at that time and waits there for at least 10 minutes (longer if directives say so) before going to the missed rendezvous procedure.

Receivers that reach the ARCP first fly the tankers' orbit pattern and timing over it, stacked below the tanker altitude with 1,000 ft between the highest receiver and the lowest tanker. Once the tanker is there and in sight, they join from the orbit into precontact, and contact is made after the formation has rolled out on the refueling track.

In the **point parallel** rendezvous the receiver flies the refueling track inbound from the ARIP toward the ARCP at its rendezvous altitude, 1,000 ft below the refueling altitude, while the tanker flies its orbit at the ARCP. The receiver monitors the range. When the range between the two reaches the **turn range**, the tanker begins its final turn onto the refueling track, rolls out ahead of the receiver at the planned **rollout range**, and slows to the refueling speed. The tanker's FMS keeps the **offset**, the lateral distance between the orbit's outbound leg and the refueling track; the air-to-air TACAN is the primary range source. Once the tanker has rolled out the receiver is the maneuvering aircraft.

blocks.alt: Plan view of a point parallel rendezvous. The receiver flying the ARIP-to-ARCP track at rendezvous altitude (1,000 ft below). The tanker on the reciprocal outbound leg, offset laterally by the offset distance, at the moment it starts its 25° bank final turn: the turn range drawn as the slant line between the two aircraft, with its along-track and offset components; the tanker's turn path as a semicircle drifted by the wind, rolling out on the refueling track 3 NM ahead of the receiver (rollout range). The relative bearing of the receiver from the tanker's nose at the turn start marked. Wind arrow from the left of the inbound course, showing the drift that widens the offset.
blocks.title: Point parallel rendezvous geometry

blocks.content: **Theory: turn range and offset.** At a constant bank φ and true airspeed V, the tanker's turn has a radius R = V² / (g·tan φ); at 400 KTAS and 25° that is about 5 NM, and the 180° turn takes about 2 minutes 20 seconds. In still air the tanker's turn displaces it sideways by 2R, which is why the offset is about 10 NM at 400 KTAS. During the turn the receiver keeps closing along the track at its own speed, so at the start of the turn it must be the distance it covers in the turn plus the rollout range behind the rollout point: about 16 NM plus 3 NM in the example. The slant range between them at that moment, combining that along-track distance with the 10 NM offset, is the turn range: about 21 to 22 NM. A crosswind changes both: wind from the pattern side across the turn carries the tanker further and lengthens the turn by twice the drift angle, widening the offset and the turn range; wind from the other side narrows them. That is why both charts are entered with the ARIP-to-ARCP drift, and why the bank must be held constant: the computed offset only rolls the tanker out on the track if the turn is flown at the bank it was computed for.

blocks.title: Turn range, NM, for a 3 NM rollout (excerpt)

blocks.content: Enter the charts with the drift on the ARIP-to-ARCP track (R: track to the right of heading), with its sign reversed when the orbit or final turn is to the right. Where no rendezvous TAS was agreed with the receiver, use the tanker's overrun CAS for that receiver converted to TAS; the turn range and offset are then good to within 1 NM. Each additional tanker adds 1 NM to the turn range. The 1/2 NM rollout used with A-10s and the 1 NM rollout behind a C-130 have rows of their own.

items: If the receiver must descend through the refueling altitude and the range between the aircraft is unknown, the tanker holds off its final turn until the receiver reports level at its rendezvous altitude.
In close-interval stream operations, do not use orbit delays to control timing.

During the tanker's turn the forward range from a radar skin paint is the range that counts, not the TACAN's slant range; without a skin paint, carry on with the beacon. Act at once on any sign of an overrun.
Receivers do not leave the rendezvous altitude until they have the tanker in sight. Discontinue the closure if visual contact cannot be kept at the range specified for the aircraft type.
A KC-10A receiver stays at its separated altitude until it is within 1 NM with the tanker in sight, then climbs slowly toward precontact, still at least 500 ft below at 1/2 NM.
In formation, the last tanker turns its beacon to operate, single code, on rolling out on the refueling heading.

sections.title: Flying the rendezvous with the FMS refuel pattern

blocks.content: The KC-10A's FMS flies the tanker's part of the point parallel rendezvous: it lays the orbit at the computed offset, flies it, turns outbound for the rendezvous, and shows where the receiver should be when the final turn begins. The pages are described in [Flight management](flight-management); this is how they are used.

items: MSN, then <REFUEL. On REFUEL 1/4 enter the AR IDENT (or find it through CATALOG in the installed refueling database), or build the pattern: ENTRY (IP, CP or ENTR), TRACK or ANCHOR, and the ALTITUDE block.

On REFUEL 2/4 check the INITIAL POINT, CONTROL POINT and EXIT POINT loaded from the database, and the track checkpoints. Do not delete the IP from the flight plan. If the CP is omitted, the flight plan waypoint the pattern is attached to becomes the CP.

On REFUEL 3/4 leave the OFFSET to be computed (it is recomputed at each CP passage from the TAS, the wind and the bank on the FGS bank selector) or enter one; select the turn direction (L TURN is the default); enter the ORBIT LENGTH (default 14 NM) and an ORBIT ETD if wanted; select the entry method (AUTO, OUTB, INB or FIX).

On REFUEL 4/4 set the ROR MODE (LEAD or TRAIL) and the roll-out range (default LEAD, 3.0 NM), and enter the receiver's TAS. The FMS then shows the TURN REL BRG and TURN REL RANGE: where the receiver should be, relative to the tanker's nose, when the final turn starts.
<LEGS, then INSERT REFUEL BEFORE? at the waypoint wanted, and EXEC.
Set the FGS bank angle selector to 25°: the orbit is computed for, and only rolls out on track at, the selected bank.

With the CP the active waypoint, select ORBIT MODE to ORBIT on REFUEL 4/4. The pattern executes: the aircraft diverts to the midpoint of the inbound or outbound leg (MODE IND shows which), then flies the orbit. ORBIT ACTIVE shows while it does; REFUEL BNDRY EXCEED shows if the aircraft leaves the track's boundary or its altitude block.

For the rendezvous select ORBIT MODE to RDVZ. On the inbound leg the aircraft turns at once to capture the outbound leg; on the outbound leg it keeps flying outbound. There is no waypoint alert in RDVZ.

Start the final turn when the receiver is at the TURN REL BRG and RANGE, confirmed by the air-to-air TACAN, radar and the turn range chart. Select ORBIT MODE to TRACK: the aircraft turns at once at the selected bank onto the inbound course and holds it until a Direct-To or a return to ORBIT.

Leave the pattern only by a Direct-To. A Direct-To to a waypoint other than the CP removes the CP from the plan; a Direct-To to the CP deactivates the pattern, which re-engages when the CP is crossed.

blocks.alt: KC-10A FMS CDU showing the REFUEL 4/4 page: ROR MODE LEAD, ROR 3.0NM, ORBIT MODE with ORBIT/RDVZ/TRACK/DISABLD and ORBIT selected in green, RCVR TAS 420KT, TURN REL BRG -27° and TURN REL RANGE 22.4NM, LEGS and SEC LEGS prompts. Text legible.
blocks.title: FMS REFUEL 4/4 page during an orbit

blocks.content: Once the pattern is in the flight plan only its length, offset and turn direction can be changed (not the direction once it is executing), and once it is active only its length and offset. ORBIT MODE and the REFUEL 4/4 rendezvous data take effect at once without EXEC. A new pattern starts with ORBIT MODE at DISABLD, in which the CP is flown through like any waypoint. TURN REL BRG is negative for a receiver on the left: for the default left-hand orbit the receiver is ahead and to the left at the turn.

Do not use the autopilot's navigation modes during refueling. Once rolled out on the refueling track and with the receiver closing, fly the track in heading select, with the bank selector at 5° between turns.

When the primary means are unavailable or lost, the aircraft fly the same profiles using whatever else is available, preferably several together, and with as few radio calls as possible. If primary means come back, or radar skin paint is obtained in the final phase, tell the other aircraft and use them. If the alternate rendezvous fails, fly the missed rendezvous procedure.

items: **FAA or GCI** facilities for vectors and separation advisories.
**Common TACAN or VORTAC**: exchange DME and radial, and start the final turn when the DME difference equals the turn range.
**FMS distance**, when both aircraft have reliable navigation: insert the ARCP or another common point to measure the range between them.

**UHF/ADF direction finding**, provided the tanker hears of it before the receiver is within 40 NM of the rendezvous point. As the receivers leave the ARIP the tanker heads for, or flies, the reverse of their inbound track. The receiver keys for about 10 seconds in each 20 (a tone or an open microphone, finishing with its call sign). The tanker calls its turn when the receiver's bearing reaches the computed value, 26° left of the tanker's heading in still air, which corresponds to about 21 NM of turn range at the nominal 9.5 NM offset. From then on the tanker transmits so the receiver can steer on it until radar or visual contact.
**Timing**, always available as a cross-check but a primary method only when nothing else is left; start or correct it from a trustworthy head-on separation with the tanker on the reciprocal heading.

**Receiver-directed rendezvous**, when the tanker's TACAN and radar are unusable: the tanker turns toward the receiver as it crosses the ARIP and keeps the offset; the receiver flies the inbound track and calls the tanker's turn.

blocks.title: UHF/ADF/TACAN cross-check bearing, 9.5 NM offset, no wind (excerpt)

blocks.content: Ask for a block of three adjacent altitudes. The tanker normally takes the middle one and the receiver the lowest, so the two are at least 1,000 ft apart while they close and the joined formation has 1,000 ft clear above and below it. Fighters need a fourth, giving them 1,000 ft of room below for maneuvering; if only three can be had, the tanker moves to the top and the receivers are told. Formations of tankers and receivers, or several fighter elements, need more altitudes, always keeping 1,000 ft between the lowest tanker and the highest receiver. An altitude reservation or an en-route formation clearance gives the same separations within its block.

Under emission option 3 there is no 15-minute call, and the rendezvous carries more risk. Fly it clear of cloud where possible; where not, both aircraft confirm their altitudes at once. The two inbound tracks to the RZ or ARIP should differ by 30° or more, each at least 40 NM long. Both aircraft work to the same RZ time and meet at the RZ or ARIP, the receiver 1,000 ft below the tanker. Choose an ARIP-to-ARCP time that lets each aircraft fly near the middle of its speed range. The planners agree in advance the rendezvous altitudes, the RZ time and ARCT, the inbound courses, and the time at which radio silence ends if the rendezvous is missed.
In a **turn-on rendezvous**, flown under the joint procedures, receivers keep 1,000 ft below the base refueling altitude until they have the tanker in sight.

The tanker holds the contact refueling speed during the receiver's closure. Use speedbrakes for deceleration with great care, and only when certain the receiver will not overrun. When one tanker refuels one or more receivers and rolls out further ahead than wanted, closure can be speeded up by the tanker flying a series of double-drift turns; with more than one tanker, differential airspeed is the only way.

blocks.title: KC-10A receiver closure speed schedule
rows: From the ARIP (descend to 1,000 ft below the refueling altitude at about 2,500 ft/min, no later than the ARIP)

blocks.content: Hold the schedule during the deceleration. A KC-10A receiver more than 4 NM in trail may increase speed to close, and resumes the schedule at 3 NM. Keep the rendezvous altitude until it is certain an overrun will not happen. If the initial refueling speed has been changed, keep the same relative schedule. Closure inside 1 NM (2 NM for formations) does not continue without visual contact.

blocks.alt: Profile diagram of a receiver's descent, closure and climb to contact: level at the planned altitude to the ARIP, descent to 1,000 ft below the refueling altitude at about 2,500 ft/min, level closure with the speed schedule (2 NM, 1 NM, 1/2 NM), visual contact at 1 NM and a gradual climb to 500 ft below at 1/2 NM, then the precontact position about 50 ft behind and below the boom nozzle, and the contact position. The tanker at the refueling altitude ahead.
blocks.title: Receiver descent, closure and contact

blocks.content: After an overrun, and once the two aircraft are clear of each other, the receiver holds its track and altitude and slows, but not below its 0/RET minimum maneuvering speed. The tanker speeds up to 335 KCAS at its own altitude, adjusts its track to pass the receiver, and once ahead slows to 290 KCAS (or the refueling speed) so the receiver can make its final closure. Used above 14,000 ft, the 0/RET minimum maneuvering speeds, though not corrected for altitude, give at least 25° of bank protection below the standard-day cruise ceiling.

With no contact made, the tanker is at the ARCP at the ARCT. An aircraft that gets there with the other not in sight orbits to the left, timing the pattern to pass over the ARCP every 8 minutes after the ARCT, and goes on looking. Mission planning sets how long to wait and when radio silence may be broken.
**Condition:** in flight, approaching the rendezvous. Complete no later than 30 minutes before the ARCT or RZ time unless stated.

Set the air-to-air TACAN no later than 15 minutes before the ARCT. Pilots monitor UHF; the flight engineer monitors the HF backup refueling frequency. Altimeters are set to 29.92 at or above the transition altitude, over water, or as the procedures require; otherwise to the briefed or reported setting. On the KC-10A, set up the FMS refuel pattern as above.

parts.title: Tanker procedures
parts.summary: Crew duties, preparation for contact, boom, centerline drogue and wing pod procedures, toboggan, and after refueling.

rows: Flies a stable platform on the autopilot, with one hand on the column and one free for the throttles. Holds the refueling speed and heading, turns and toboggans gently, and is ready for a breakaway.
Rendezvous equipment, radios and the radio transfer with the boom operator, TCAS, thrust rating and beacons. Monitors the BOOM/DROGUE ENGAGED lights (KC-10A).

Sets up the offload fuel system and the hydraulic pumps, monitors the offload, fuel flow and pressure, the CG, and the hydraulic and refueling status lights, and coordinates with the boom operator. Tells the boom operator when the cockpit's preparation for contact is complete. On the Omega, works the wing pods.

Prepares and works the boom, the centerline hose or the wing pods (KC-10A, KDC-10); talks to and directs the receiver; keeps the pilot informed of the receiver's position and closure; initiates disconnects and breakaways.

blocks.content: In the simulation the Virtual Crew does not run the refueling checklists; you fly them yourself, moving between the flight deck, the flight engineer's station and the boom operator's station. See [Flying air refueling in the simulation](ar-in-the-simulation).

sections.title: Tanker preparation for contact (receiver 1/2 NM in trail)

blocks.content: **Condition:** the receiver is approaching 1/2 NM in trail. Complete before the receiver reaches the precontact position. **Objective:** a stable tanker, the hydraulic and fuel systems set for the method in use, and the crew ready for contact and for a breakaway.

items.item: Seat belt sign (crew and passengers advised)

items.action: SET for the method in use
REC or T/R when no longer needed

blocks.content: For boom or drogue refueling, when the BOOM/DROGUE HYD PRSRZ light comes on, move the 2-3 HYD PUMP selector to ON. If the 1-3 and 2-3 pump valve open lights do not come on, or flicker continuously, verify the pump with the [2-3 pump valve verification](ar-emergency-abnormal#abn-2-3-pump-verification) before refueling.

If any hydraulic pressure gauge fluctuates between 3,000 and 2,400 psi at regular intervals, move that system's ENG HYD PUMP 2 switch to ON. If it drops below 2,400 psi, move ENG HYD PUMP 2 to ON, start the AUX PUMPS and move the 1-3 HYD PUMP to ON. If it stays below 2,400 psi, or the fluid temperature rises abnormally, turn off the AR pumps that system drives.

**KDC-10.** The boom runs directly on hydraulic system 2: keep system 2's engine-driven pumps on, with the 2-3 HYD PUMP armed to hold system 2 pressure if its pumps fail. There is no fuel panel setup; no fuel passes through the KDC-10's boom.
Do not use the autopilot's navigation modes during refueling. Do not let the aircraft slow below the 1.2 g buffet speed corrected for the conditions.

items.action: OPEN (if offloading from the CTR WING tank)

blocks.content: Armed pumps start when the boom makes contact, in the FPCU's sequence. (In the simulation there is never a contact, so armed pumps do not start and no fuel moves; the CONTACT MADE TEST does not start them either.) Select by priority: from system 3, R FWD, R CTR, L AFT; from system 1, L FWD, L CTR; from system 2, R AFT; if possible no more than two pumps from system 3. When operating in AR PUMP OVRD, turn the AR pumps on after the BOOM VALVE is open and the BOOM/DROGUE ENGAGED light is on; when using transfer pumps for the offload, turn them on after the ALTN TRANS and BOOM valves are open and BOOM/DROGUE ENGAGED is on. If all the fuel in the forward tank is to be offloaded, take the AR PUMP OVRD action before the forward tank falls to 15,000 lb.

The drogue valve and the hose reel bleed valve are interlocked through the fuel range position switch. The drogue valve may be armed before contact but does not open until the hose is pushed in about 5 ft; at the disconnect it closes, and the bleed valve opens as the hose returns to trail. Trapped pressure in the hose can prevent a contact: if the normal bleed does not relieve it, open the drogue valve and scavenge the AR manifold until the pressure is below 10 psi (the boom operator holds REEL RESP RESET while the drogue valve is operated with the hose at full trail), then return MANF SCAV to OFF. Closing the drogue valve before the receiver disconnects prevents trapped pressure for the next contact.

items.item: ALTN TRANS and ISOL valves (tank system to be used)

blocks.content: If both pods are to be used, open both the forward and aft tank systems. Transfer or engine-feed pumps may be used as an alternate supply where fuel separation allows. The center wing tank's AR pumps can feed the pods, but the extra pressure can shut pumps down. With the AR pumps feeding the pods, do not open the engine crossfeed valves under normal conditions. The pod's fuel valve will not open until a receiver has pushed the hose in about 5 ft. If a pod's FUEL INLET PRESSURE LOW comes on during the refueling, add pumps.

children.title: Fuel panel: Omega wing pod refueling

blocks.content: The Omega has no AR pumps: the crossfeed manifold that feeds each pod is pressurized only by the boost pumps through the X-FEED valves. With the X-FEED valves shut the pods are dry whatever the WING DROGUE VALVES say.

sections.title: Boom refueling
sections.summary: KC-10A and KDC-10.

blocks.content: **Condition:** boom refueling planned. Complete before the receiver reaches 1 NM in trail, up to establishing radio contact; for buddy refueling, at least 5 minutes before the ARCT.

blocks.title: Boom operator's preparation for contact: boom

items.action: ON (FREE FLT on, FAIL and caution lights out)

items.item: RCVR DISC DELAY and disconnect limits

items.action: COMMON or PRIVATE (receiver without boom interphone: OFF)

items.item: BOOM HOIST lever (boom stopped at about 0°)

blocks.content: If the boom moves uncommanded, uncontrollably or does not respond, move FLT CONT to OFF immediately and do not move it back to ON; go to the [uncommanded boom](ar-emergency-abnormal#abn-uncommanded-boom) procedure. If FLT CONT is moved to ON with HYD SEL at OFF or DROGUE, ELEV and both RUD FAIL lights and the aural warning come on: set HYD SEL to BOOM and cycle FLT CONT OFF and ON.

Guard the flight control stick while the boom is lowered. Do not apply a DOWN command with the hoist lever at LWR: the cable can fail. Do not move HYD SEL from BOOM to OFF with the boom deployed and the hoist at FREE WHEEL; if it happens, set the hoist to RAISE until the cable is taut before returning HYD SEL to BOOM.

**Amplification.** The boom will not lower to trail unless the hoist is at FREE WHEEL and ELEV POSN at REFUEL. Below 200 KIAS it can move very quickly from about 14° above horizontal to trail. **Flight control check:** extend the telescope to 12 ft and fly the boom smoothly through 18° to 40° elevation and 0° to 25° roll each way. If it cannot reach those positions but everything else is normal, continue, set the adjustable limits within what was reached, and disconnect before the receiver reaches the largest position attained. One check per mission is enough. **TLSCP AT DISC** shows MAN for C-130s, the 737 AEW&C and fighters, without normal disconnect capability, and with manual boom latching; AUTO otherwise. **Radio check:** under emission options 1 and 2 the boom operator calls an astern check (for example "25, 27") and the receiver acknowledges ("25"); it may be made anywhere between 1/2 NM and the astern position. Use **OVRD** only for Boeing-type receptacles or when the mission or a failure requires it.

blocks.title: In the simulation
blocks.content: BOOM COIL TEST has no needle to read in the 3D model, the refueling exterior lights are not drawn, the FUEL OFFLOAD counter stays at zero, and on the KDC-10 the boom operator's oxygen regulator is inert. The rest of this checklist works as written.

blocks.title: In the simulation
blocks.content: There is no receiver. A contact can be simulated only with the CONTACT MADE TEST or EMER CONTACT MADE, and those switches, like DISC and RESET TO READY, work only once bound to buttons: see [Contact, disconnect and reset inputs](ar-in-the-simulation#sim-stick-switches). The armed AR pumps do not start, no fuel flows, and the stick shaker and stick force changes of COUPLED are not felt.

When the receiver is stabilized in the precontact position, clear it to contact ("Receiver call sign, cleared to contact") and watch its approach. Extend the boom slowly and accurately into the receptacle; nozzle cocking is least likely with the receiver stable in the proper contact position. A receptacle on a fighter or a UARRSI-equipped aircraft is a small target needing a precise contact, and a UARRSI's slipway can cock the nozzle. At night keep the boom left or right of center, so the nozzle light does not dazzle the receiver pilot.

items: Contact gives CONTACT and one beep; COUPLED follows about a second later, the pilots' BOOM/DROGUE ENGAGED comes on, and the armed AR pumps start. Watch the refueling system's failure and caution lights, the fuel flow and pressure, the receiver and the boom position instruments.

If the signal system stays in READY/FREE FLIGHT after the nozzle is in the receptacle, initiate a disconnect if there is no oscillation; otherwise pull and hold EMER CONTACT MADE until the nozzle is free, and disconnect. Give the receiver verbal instructions to stay in the envelope until the nozzle and receptacle separate.

Guard the flight control stick. Boom controls are extremely sensitive in COUPLED: large abrupt inputs can exceed a structural limit or strike either aircraft. Do not try to maneuver the receiver with the boom or the telescope.
Watch the receiver closely and be ready to disconnect or call a breakaway before it reaches a position where the nozzle could bind.

Some fuel spray at contact and at disconnect is normal; if it persists, tell the receiver, whose pilot decides whether to continue. Excessive spillage: disconnect, and discontinue except in an emergency. If fuel siphons, have the FE turn the AR pumps off.

Told of a boom flight control failure while in contact, hold the flight control stick in line with the boom and talk the receiver to a safe position (about 0° roll, moving down and back, allowing for any axis that still works) before disconnecting.
Advise the FE if the fuel flow or pressure reads zero. The pilot director lights and the automatic disconnect limits are not active in READY/COUPLED (coupled by a nozzle load without a contact).

blocks.content: The boom operator or the receiver pilot may start a disconnect. The receiver holds its contact position until someone, the boom operator or one of the receiver's crew, has seen the nozzle come out of the receptacle; it then drops back to precontact, or to a steady position behind the boom, and waits to be cleared in again. Push RESET TO READY once the nozzle is clear and before the next contact; do not push it while the telescope is moving.

items: If the nozzle stays captured after a normal disconnect, use the IDS (the disconnect trigger through its second detent). If the boom is oscillating, pull and hold EMER CONTACT MADE until the nozzle is free, then disconnect.
With TLSCP AT DISC at MAN, avoid fast retraction: if the boom has not been released, it pulls the receiver forward.

Even with a disconnect signal the nozzle can stay jammed in the receptacle, especially with the receiver rolled well over and the boom at low elevation. If it binds or may be binding, neutralize the boom flight controls and avoid abrupt inputs.

The boom may oscillate if the nozzle stays captured after the flight controls have returned to FREE FLIGHT. Releasing EMER CONTACT MADE starts the return to FREE FLIGHT: once the receiver disconnect delay has run, ALAS stops working, the stick shaker drops out and the stick forces go back to their selected values.
The tanker's breakaway capability is reduced above 20,000 ft, above 570,000 lb, and near the 1.2 g buffet speed; tell the receiver that the breakaway will then depend on its own actions.

blocks.content: **Condition:** centerline drogue refueling planned. Complete before the receiver reaches 1 NM in trail, up to establishing radio contact; for buddy refueling, at least 5 minutes before the ARCT. Whether a probe receiver connects depends on its pilot's skill, on visibility and turbulence, on how steady the tanker and the drogue are, and on how the receiver is loaded. In light turbulence the drogue wanders about 1 ft below 250 KIAS and 2 to 3 ft above that speed; at 35,000 ft and over 250 KIAS it tends to trace an ellipse of about 2 ft, one cycle every two seconds. Plan with the receiver unit: drogue engagement rates and the reel response's limits must be understood.

blocks.title: Boom operator's preparation for contact: centerline drogue

items.action: PWR (DROGUE POSN STOW, HYD PRESS LOW on)
MON (RESP INOP on about 1 s, then out)

items.item: REEL RESP RESET (at refueling altitude, attitude and speed)

blocks.content: **Trailing.** DROGUE POSN shows a barber pole as the hose is released. As soon as the hose is visible, check that the paradrogue trails smoothly and that neither hose nor canopy is frayed or cut. DROGUE POSN shows TRAIL and READY comes on about 5 s after full trail; if RESP INOP comes on, TRAIL does not show or READY does not come on, go to the abnormal procedures. **Response check:** after READY comes on, move HOSE REEL TEST to SYS: READY goes out, the hose rewinds to the forward limit of the range and redeploys to full trail, READY returns about 5 s after full trail, and RESP INOP stays out. Do it before the first refueling and after every deployment. **Reel response reset:** READY goes out when the button is pushed and returns about 5 s after release; if it comes on at once on release, push and hold it about 5 s. Reset before each contact and see READY on before clearing the receiver. The hose may rewind partly as the tanker decelerates: push REEL RESP RESET and let it redeploy before it rewinds fully.

If the canopy does not inflate, select REWIND, see DROGUE POSN show STOW and abandon the drogue refueling. If the hose or canopy shows fraying or cuts, discontinue centerline refueling except in an emergency.
Do not refuel if the hose response system check fails, except in an emergency. Do not move HOSE REEL TEST to SYS with a receiver connected.

blocks.title: In the simulation
blocks.content: HOSE REEL TEST has only its MON position, so the response check at SYS cannot be done; the [55-knot check](#tk-reel-response-check) works and exercises the same response system. No receiver engages the drogue, no fuel flows, the offload counter stays at zero, and the refueling exterior lights and the drogue's signal lights are not drawn.

children.title: Reel response speed reduction check (55-knot check)

blocks.content: **Condition:** centerline refueling required with the hose reel monitor removed or deactivated. The check proves the response system works before the first refueling. The tanker must start at least 60 kt above its 1.2 g buffet speed.

items.action: REDUCE to 270 KIAS at about 1 kt/s

blocks.content: Watch the drum through the ARO compartment's hose drum viewing mirror. If the reduction takes more than 60 seconds, repeat it. If the check fails at 325 to 270 KIAS, repeat it from 310 to 255 KIAS, at an altitude where the aircraft can hold speeds as low as 240 knots.
Do not refuel if the 55-knot check fails, except in an emergency. Do not decelerate below the 1.2 g buffet speed corrected for the conditions.

items: Tell the receiver flight lead about the 3-kt closure limit; receivers close on the drogue at no more than 3 kt. Use visual signals as much as possible and voice when needed for safety. Clear the receivers from astern to contact.

No contact is attempted with the red signal light or the HYD PRESS LOW light on. Contacts are improbable with the hose pressurized, or with the drogue hit off center above 275 KIAS. A drogue hit off center or stabbed can become unstable and damage either aircraft.
Do not push REEL RESP RESET with a receiver in contact. If a reset is needed after a failed contact or a speed change, send the receiver back to precontact first.
Use only the first 20 ft of hose travel where possible, to avoid nose-to-tail overlap. The reel response is marginal with the receiver low in the envelope.

RESP INOP may flicker as a receiver first engages, or as it moves the hose between the aft limit and full trail with READY on: that is normal. If a caution light comes on, act and go to the abnormal procedures.
Coordinate contacts and disconnects with the FE; watch the fuel flow, pressure and quantity, and tell the FE when the flow or pressure reads zero.
Terminate the refueling if a crimp or a fuel leak is seen in the hose, except in an emergency.

For a planned disconnect the receiver eases power off and drops back; with READY on, its pilot may try again. A small amount of spray at contact and disconnect is normal. Fuel may flow by gravity to a receiver in the range with the drogue valve open; the green signal light then comes on.
A power-limited receiver may not make an effective contact if the hose stays pressurized after a disconnect; coordinate with the FE to depressurize it.

sections.title: Wing pod refueling
sections.summary: KC-10A and DC-10-40 Omega.

blocks.content: **Condition:** wing pod refueling planned. Complete before the receivers reach 1 NM in trail, up to establishing radio contact; for buddy refueling, at least 5 minutes before the ARCT. On the KC-10A the boom operator works the pods and the FE their fuel; on the Omega the FE does both from their panel.

items.action: FUEL PRESS LOW out, HOSE STOWED on, counter zero
FUEL INLET PRESSURE LOW out, FUEL OFFLOAD zero
SET for wing pods (X-FEED, WING DROGUE VALVES)
FUEL PRESS LOW out, HOSE STOWED on, counter zero
FUEL INLET PRESSURE LOW out, FUEL OFFLOAD zero

blocks.content: If the pod's lights or indications are not as listed, do not deploy that pod's hose: turn its POD POWER off. Do not deploy a hose from stowed, or fully retract one, with the flaps or slats extended.

**Trailing.** After a 5-second delay HOSE STOWED goes out, the canopy inflates, the hose deploys steadily, HOSE TRANSIT flashes until the hose stops, and READY comes on at full trail. If the hose reaches full trail and READY does not come on, cycle POD POWER. If the hose stops short of full trail and READY does not come on, increase speed (not above 300 KIAS). A FAIL on the counter means a failure of the fuel control valve, the RAT blade control or the data bus; a blank counter means the pod's processor has failed: go to the [abnormal procedures](ar-emergency-abnormal#abn-pod-fail-blank-counter). **SIG/FLOOD:** for day refueling set the signal lights bright and the floods off; at night, signals dim and floods on, with the underbody lights bright for the sighting and dimmed as receivers reach the observation position.

blocks.title: In the simulation
blocks.content: No receiver engages a pod drogue, so the pod fuel valve never opens and the counters stay at zero; the pod signal lights and floodlights are not drawn. Trailing, rewinding, the pod's lights, counters and BITE all work.

items: Tell the receiver flight lead about the 3-kt closure limit, and clear receivers from astern to contact. Watch each pod's lights, its offload counter and the receivers' positions in the envelope; coordinate contacts and disconnects with the FE.

About 5 ft of push opens the pod's fuel valve (READY out, pilots' L or R DROGUE ENGAGED on, DROGUE ENGAGED on the F/E's panel once fuel flows). Roughly 12 ft more and READY flashes as a warning that the inner limit is near; a few feet beyond, the fuel stops.
The reel's take-up works only from about 46 ft to full trail. Pushed further in, the hose goes dead and a loop forms that can damage the receiver.
A drogue contacted off center or stabbed can become unstable. If retracting it would cause damage, jettison the hose or land with it in trail.
For a planned disconnect the receiver reduces power and backs out; contact may be reattempted if READY is on.

blocks.content: Do not move HOSE TRAIL/REWIND to REWIND with a receiver connected to the drogue.

When a receiver needs more thrust than it has, which happens as it gets heavier or as the altitude and temperature change, the tanker and receiver toboggan: the formation descends so that gravity supplies the missing thrust. It is a coordinated maneuver:

items: The receiver pilot asks for a toboggan while there is still some military power in hand.
The tanker pilot reduces power very gently and starts a descent of about 300 ft/min, holding the refueling speed.
If the receiver still needs more thrust than it has, it asks for a higher rate of descent.
At the level-off altitude the tanker raises the nose and adds power very gradually, so that the receiver can stay connected.
If an element in a formation must toboggan, the tanker leader takes the whole formation down.

blocks.content: Drogue refueling is not done while tobogganing, except in an emergency.

blocks.alt: Side-view diagram of a toboggan: a tanker and a receiver in contact flying level, the receiver unable to hold speed and altitude, the pair descending together at 300 ft/min or more, then leveling off.
blocks.title: Toboggan

blocks.content: **Condition:** refueling finished. The receiver decelerates and descends to clear the tanker.

**Fuel panel (KC-10A).** Close the ALTN TRANS and ISOL valves and the AR ISOL VALVE. Push the BOOM or DROGUE VALVE switch and see the fuel flow indicator and the valve's lights go out. For boom or drogue refueling, set MANF SCAV to TANKER; when MANF SCAV PRESS LOW comes on steady (no more than 10 minutes; it may flicker meanwhile), set it OFF. Normal fuel transfer can start while the manifold is scavenged, since it uses different lines. After wing pod refueling, coordinate with the boom operator once the fuel panel is set so the pods can be shut down. Resume normal fuel management. **Report:** the fuel transferred if not as briefed, the ARTCC frequency, Mode 3 and instructions, the position at the end of refueling, and anything else requested.

**Fuel panel (Omega).** Close the POD FUEL VALVES and the WING DROGUE VALVES and return the X-FEED valves and boost pumps to the normal fuel management configuration. **Report:** the fuel transferred if not as briefed, the ARTCC frequency, Mode 3 and instructions, the position at the end of refueling, and anything else requested.

If the boom operator reports HOSE WILL NOT REWIND, a speed reduction of 80 kt or more may let the reel response wind the hose in: go to [Centerline hose will not rewind](ar-emergency-abnormal#abn-centreline-will-not-rewind). Do not slow below the 1.2 g buffet speed.

blocks.title: Boom operator's post air refueling: boom

items.action: STOW (telescope retracts, boom up to about 0°)
RAISE (ELEVATION at the STOW mark when seated)
LWR: no movement on ELEVATION, then HOLD

blocks.content: Guard the controls while the boom rises toward the stowed position so it does not rise too fast, and avoid abrupt commands after ELEV POSN goes to STOW. If ELEVATION shows movement with the hoist at LWR, the latch is not closed: move the latch to UNLOCK and repeat the stow. If the boom has to be flown to its stowed position, go to [Broken boom hoist cable](ar-emergency-abnormal#abn-broken-hoist-cable). If more refuelings follow, the lights may be left on.

blocks.title: Boom operator's post air refueling: centerline drogue

items.action: REWIND (READY out, barber pole, then STOW)
OFF (if the drogue deploys, back to DROGUE at once)

blocks.content: If the hose does not fully rewind, trail it again and repeat the rewind; a speed reduction may be needed to stow it. If it still will not rewind, tell the pilot and go to [Centerline hose will not rewind](ar-emergency-abnormal#abn-centreline-will-not-rewind).

items.action: REWIND (READY out, HOSE TRANSIT flashing, HOSE STOWED steady)

items.item: POD FUEL VALVE and WING DROGUE VALVE

items.action: OFF (after the fuel panel is set)

blocks.content: Rewind at 280 KIAS or less. If a hose does not fully rewind, trail it again and repeat; a speed reduction may be needed. On the KC-10A, the boom operator then closes the sighting door, sets the oxygen regulator OFF and 100%, and tells the pilot "drogue stowed, leaving position".

parts.title: Receiver procedures
parts.summary: The KC-10A as a receiver behind a boom tanker.

blocks.content: The KC-10A refuels as a receiver through its UARRSI receptacle above the flight deck, from any boom tanker, including another KC-10A. This part covers the receiver from the rendezvous to the end of the refueling. The receiver system is described in [Receiver system (UARRSI)](air-refueling-systems#receiver-system), the rendezvous and closure in [Rendezvous procedures](ar-rendezvous).

blocks.title: In the simulation
blocks.content: There is no tanker aircraft in the simulation, and the UARRSI door crank, AR RESET, the AR RECP LATCH test and the UARRSI hydraulic shutoff valve are not connected, so these procedures cannot be flown to a contact. They are given for reference. See [Receiver system](air-refueling-systems#sim-receiver-status).
**Condition:** approaching the rendezvous. Complete at least 30 minutes before the ARCT or RZ time unless stated.

Set the radar to beacon mode and its tilt to show the tanker's rendezvous beacon, and cross-check the air-to-air TACAN's range and bearing for a positive identification. Pilots monitor UHF and the FE the HF backup refueling frequency. When refueling from a tanker with boom interphone (every KC-10 and KC-135), the receptacle audio is set to NORM. No later than the ARIP, descend at about 2,500 ft/min to 1,000 ft below the assigned refueling altitude and fly the closure speed schedule in [Descent and closure](ar-rendezvous#rv-closure).
If weather may affect the rendezvous, a capable receiver is designated to keep the radar weather watch and keep the formation clear of hazardous weather.

sections.title: Receiver preparation for contact (complete before 1/2 NM)

items.item: Main tank fill valves, body tank ISOL and fill valves

items.action: REC or T/R when no longer needed

blocks.content: Set the receptacle lights full bright; at night, dim them approaching astern and adjust further as the boom operator asks. When gross weight is planned to exceed 556,000 lb, or zero fuel weight plus body tank fuel to exceed 414,000 lb, keep the main tank fill valves open for normal fuel management. For dry contacts at 556,000 lb or more, or a zero fuel weight above 414,000 lb, one transfer pump may be used to keep the wing tanks full; coordinate with the tanker so the boom valve is closed first. If a tank will be filled near its capacity, perform a high-level float test once the onload starts.

Do not select WX, MAP 1, MAP 2 or BCN on the weather radar close to the tanker, and do not operate the radar during receiver refueling. If both autothrottle and speed control circuit breakers are open, the ATS disconnect buttons on the throttles give no A/R disconnect.
If one or both autothrottle and speed control systems malfunction and the READY light will not stay on, opening the affected system's circuit breaker may restore the READY.

Start the deceleration early enough to stabilize in the precontact position with zero closure; a higher-than-normal refueling speed for the receiver's weight must be agreed before flight.
