In precontact, align with the tanker's fuselage centerline, stop any sideways drift between the aircraft, and check by eye that READY is lit and the tanker shows it is ready. Close from precontact to contact very slowly, so both aircraft can compensate for the trim changes. Use the tanker's forward fuselage, wings and pilot director lights to establish and hold position. If lateral movement, pitch oscillation or closure becomes excessive, reduce power, move back to precontact and stabilize. In the contact position, stabilize until the LATCHED light comes on.

If the receiver cannot stabilize in the precontact position, or an overrun is developing, call a breakaway. Failing to do so can cause a midair collision. Flying close under the tanker is unsafe: upwash, downwash and the low pressure between the aircraft affect both aircraft's control and their static ports.

The contact position is held with small, anticipated corrections. The movement of the tanker's nose is a guide for elevator inputs. Keep the wings parallel to the tanker's with the ailerons, and use small amounts of rudder to stay aligned with the stripe on the tanker's belly; improper or excessive rudder causes lateral alignment problems. Base power corrections on the size and direction of any fore-and-aft movement. Rough control by either pilot sets off a chain of ever larger corrections: develop a smooth technique, and avoid disconnects at extreme azimuth, roll or elevation. Turns may be made in contact without disconnecting if neither aircraft makes large or abrupt control or throttle movements.

items: Flight tests found 320 KCAS optimum at 590,000 lb. A proven technique is to start refueling and let the tanker accelerate during the transfer, without changing its power, until about 320 KCAS (about 320 KIAS behind a KC-10A).

Behind a KC-135, its digital autopilot may disengage without warning when large out-of-trim conditions arise (large power or speed changes, rapid movement of a large receiver), and the tanker may descend abruptly into the receiver's path: be ready for a breakaway. KC-135s with standard-speed booms are limited to 330 KCAS.
If the pilot director lights fail and the refueling continues, ask the boom operator for verbal corrections. Contacts with reduced refueling lighting are at the boom operator's discretion.
Fatigue is among the worst hazards: a pilot who is tiring disconnects, drops back and hands over to the other pilot in precontact for a few minutes.

Sun, cloud and precipitation can lead to an overrun or loss of visual contact. If safe separation cannot be kept in contact, call for or initiate a disconnect, and ask the boom operator to help you back out. Maneuvering in the envelope to avoid glare must be done with care: the boom's aerodynamics can change the tanker's speed and position.

blocks.content: Approaching a boom limit at a high rate can prevent the disconnect: the nozzle can bind in the receptacle. If the binding is not relieved before the disconnect, structural damage and foreign object ingestion in the number 2 engine can follow.

Disconnects are planned (by the receiver pilot, copilot or the boom operator) or inadvertent (an envelope limit exceeded, a high receiver rate of movement, a fuel pressure surge, or a malfunction). At a disconnect the DISCONNECT light comes on, LATCHED goes out, and the boom operator retracts the boom. For another contact, reset the signal amplifier by pressing and releasing AR RESET once the boom is clear of the receptacle: READY comes on and DISCONNECT and LATCHED go out. The pilots are ready to press A/R DISC (the ATS disconnect buttons) at all times during the refueling.

items: Stay stabilized in the contact position until the pilot monitoring sees the DISCONNECT light and the boom clear. Back out smoothly and slowly, to avoid trim changes in both aircraft.
After a failed contact and after each disconnect, move back to precontact and stabilize, reset the system, and confirm READY and that the tanker is ready before returning to contact.
If an emergency or abnormal condition affecting controllability occurs, disconnect at once and stay clear of the tanker until it is resolved.
With manual boom latching (AMPL OVRD), the receiver initiates every disconnect.

blocks.content: The KC-10A's boom is fly-by-wire; some failures leave an axis uncontrollable and the boom operator unable to steer it clear of the receiver. When told that a boom flight control system has failed, do not disconnect unless the boom operator directs it, and follow the boom operator's instructions exactly. It may be necessary to stay stabilized after the disconnect while the boom's surfaces fair.
**Condition:** refueling finished. Decelerate and descend to clear the tanker.

items.action: AS REQUIRED (TA in formation, TA/RA alone)
RCVR, then OFF when MANF SCAV PRESS LOW is steady

blocks.content: The receiver manifold scavenge should take no more than 10 minutes. If fuels that must be kept apart were onloaded, set MASTER FUEL ISOL, the AR ISOL VALVE and the forward, center wing and aft tank ISOL VALVES to ISOL as applicable. Then resume normal fuel management.
The UARRSI hydraulic shutoff valve must stay closed in flight except when refueling: the UARRSI hydraulics run in the flight deck overhead.

parts.title: Emergency and abnormal procedures
parts.summary: Breakaway and the other refueling emergencies, and the abnormal procedures for the boom, the fuel system, the centerline drogue and the wing pods.

blocks.content: These are the procedures particular to air refueling. The aircraft's other emergency and abnormal procedures are in [Emergency procedures](emergency-procedures) and [Abnormal procedures](abnormal-procedures). In each refueling procedure the first action in contact is usually to get the receiver off the boom or hose safely: disconnect, or have it disconnect, before working the problem. The systems behind these procedures are described in [Air refueling systems](air-refueling-systems), whose failure table links back here.

Air refueling failures cannot be scheduled from the EFB's Failures app. Some arise in the simulation from hydraulic and electrical failures or from how the systems are operated; others (receiver-related events, a lost drogue) cannot occur. See [Failures you can practice](air-refueling-systems#sim-failures).

Where a procedure uses the boom operator's stick switches (DISC and IDS, RESET TO READY, EMER CONTACT MADE, CONTACT MADE TEST), they work only once bound to buttons: see [Contact, disconnect and reset inputs](ar-in-the-simulation#sim-stick-switches). HOSE REEL TEST at SYS, the telescope stick's BREAKAWAY SIG, the receiver's AR RESET, AR RECP LATCH test and UARRSI door and hydraulic controls, and the external signal and pilot director lights are not available.

**Condition:** any crew member of either aircraft sees a situation that needs immediate separation: a receiver that cannot stabilize, a closure overrun, an erratic receiver, a controllability problem, or damage to either aircraft about to happen. The aircraft do not have to be in contact. **Objective:** separate the aircraft vertically and longitudinally at once, the tanker forward and up, the receiver down and back.

items.action: ADVANCE to the thrust limit, accelerate in level flight
MAINTAIN until the receiver is clear
CLEAR of the receiver; STOW as applicable
REPORT to the pilot; "clear to climb" when vertically clear

blocks.content: In the simulation the BREAKAWAY SIG on the telescope control stick is not available. On the KC-10A the drogue panel's BREAKAWAY SIG works, but the signal and pilot director lights it flashes are not drawn. The disconnect trigger works only once bound to a button (see [Contact, disconnect and reset inputs](ar-in-the-simulation#sim-stick-switches)).

items.item: A/R DISC (autopilot release or ATS disconnect)

items.action: DROP AFT until the tanker is entirely in sight
MONITOR: call if not descending or below 0/RET minimum maneuvering speed

blocks.content: Receiver: do not overrun the tanker, and make no turns until separation is positive. If the tanker goes out of sight, keep descending to 1,000 ft below the refueling altitude until definitely aft with the tanker in sight. Level off from a heavy-weight breakaway with care: an accelerated stall and airframe damage are possible.

**Terminating.** In a toboggan, the tanker levels off once the receiver is well clear. When the boom operator calls "clear to climb", the tanker starts a slow climb, keeping its bank and not letting its speed fall below the speed at the start of the climb. When the boom operator reports the receiver "well clear", the tanker transmits its call sign and "terminate emergency separation" and waits for the receiver's acknowledgement before slowing to the refueling speed. If visual contact is lost, help the receiver find the tanker with the air-to-air TACAN, the rendezvous beacon and the navigation lights. Breakaway effectiveness is reduced above 20,000 ft, above 570,000 lb and near the 1.2 g buffet speed.
**Condition:** receiver refueling with an engine shut down. Only as command directives allow. The refueling envelopes, speeds and altitudes are unchanged except as noted.
With only two engines, refueling to weights above 436,000 lb or above 25,000 ft is not recommended. The recommended altitude is 20,000 ft. Use all three throttles with an engine shut down.

children.title: Towing fighters
children.summary: KC-10A and KDC-10.

blocks.content: **Condition:** a fighter receiver asks to be towed. The tanker pilot and the boom operator acknowledge the request.

items.action: CLEARED to the tow position (very slowly)

blocks.content: The receiver moves to the tow position very slowly, to avoid a brute force disconnect. With the envelope limits inactive the receiver disconnect delay logic does not advance the signal system to disconnect; disconnects are made by the boom operator or the receiver pilot after coordinating.

children.title: Pressure refueling
children.summary: KC-10A and KDC-10.

blocks.content: **Condition:** an emergency fuel shortage aboard a receiver whose toggles will not hold the nozzle. The boom is held in the receptacle by extend pressure alone. Not attempted otherwise.

Brief the receiver that the contacts will be made with boom extend pressure, that a slight power increase may be needed to avoid being pushed beyond the outer limit, and that it must be ready to reduce power at once if the nozzle comes out. Apply only the extend pressure needed to keep the nozzle sealed, and retract the nozzle before the receiver exceeds a disconnect limit. When the transfer is complete, tell the receiver you are relieving the extend pressure, relieve it, and initiate the disconnect.

Boom controls are extremely sensitive in CONTACT/COUPLED. If the nozzle comes out before the transfer is complete, reset the signal system to READY before re-establishing contact. Excessive extend pressure can overstress the telescope or push the receiver beyond the outer limit.

children.title: Landing with boom or drogue in trail

blocks.content: **Condition:** the boom or a hose cannot be stowed or jettisoned, or the crew has decided to land with it in trail. Confirm that the boom operator has completed [Boom preparation for landing with the boom in trail](#abn-boom-in-trail-landing-prep).
**Drogue in trail:** land at the slowest practical speed, clear the runway as required and stop for maintenance.

items.action: Normal 35/EXT, normal reverse and braking; stop on the runway

blocks.content: Do not use 50/EXT with maximum braking, or reduced braking for a gentle stop, to shorten the landing roll. BOOM/DROGUE DEPLOYED is on, and BOOM/DROGUE NOT STOWED comes on when the gear is lowered (on the KC-10A, with the FUEL cue light). The aft body tank item applies to the KC-10A.

sections.title: Boom abnormal procedures
sections.summary: KC-10A and KDC-10.

blocks.content: An **inadvertent** brute force disconnect is any unplanned disconnect in which the receiver moves rapidly to the aft limit and the aircraft separate mechanically, or a boom pull-out at 38° elevation or below. A **controlled tension** (coordinated) brute force disconnect is a deliberate one above 38°, made by the receiver moving gradually to the aft limit until the boom pulls out smoothly under tension. It is a last resort, used only after every other normal and emergency method has failed.

items: The receiver pilot must not jerk the boom out with a rapid thrust reduction: a gradual power reduction is enough. Stay stabilized at contact altitude until certain the nozzle is clear of the receptacle and slipway.
After a brute force disconnect, refueling for that receiver is terminated except in a fuel emergency or when operational necessity requires.
A receiver that has had a brute force disconnect lands as soon as practical: the damage cannot be assessed in flight, and maintenance must check for foreign object damage before the next flight.
Every brute force disconnect is a mandatory maintenance write-up stating which type it was.

children.title: Boom FAIL light on, or flight control stick failure

blocks.content: **Condition:** ELEV FAIL, L or R RUD FAIL, or TLSCP FAIL on, with the aural warning; or a flight control stick failure: a five-second tone, ROLL or ELEVATION ALAS INOP, and the stick limp in that axis.

items.action: NOTIFY of the malfunction, DIRECT to a safe position, disconnect as applicable

blocks.content: With a limp stick, align it with the boom's position immediately. Control authority starts to return a second after FLT CONT comes back on, and the boom moves to wherever the stick is commanding unless that surface's FAIL light is on.
If every FAIL and ALAS INOP light is now out, check the affected system's control; if it is normal, continue refueling. Otherwise go to the item for the light that remains:

items: **ELEV FAIL.** Discontinue refueling and stow the boom. It will not fly up when ELEV POSN goes to STOW: use the hoist.

**RUD FAIL (one).** Continue as operational necessity dictates. Rudder effectiveness is reduced: do a flight control check at refueling speed and set the roll limits below the largest roll reached in the check, or the receiver's limit, whichever is less. Stow the boom when finished (or at once with both RUD FAIL lights).
**TLSCP FAIL.** Discontinue refueling. The receiver must not try to push the boom in. Retract the telescope with the emergency retraction: pull the telescope control to full retract. Stow the boom.
**Flight control stick failure.** Discontinue boom refueling except in an emergency; if it continues, set the roll limits to 15°. Stow the boom.

blocks.content: A limp stick has no back-drive and no centering feel in the failed axis: large inputs that can damage the boom or the receiver are easy to make.

Do not let the boom strike the retract shock absorber when using the emergency retraction on the ground or with the boom stowed. A hard landing with the telescope extended in the stowed position can damage the boom or the latch.

**Condition:** the boom moves on its own, will not follow the stick, or does not respond. A failed or biased gimbal position transducer makes the control unit fly the boom against a position that is not there, which can drive it violently into its stops.
After moving FLT CONT to OFF for an uncommanded, uncontrollable or unresponsive boom, do not move it back to ON.
The boom will not fly up when ELEV POSN goes to STOW: stow it with the hoist. Discontinue boom refueling and complete the boom operator's post air refueling checklist.

children.title: FLT CONT DEGRADED or MAINT REQD light on

blocks.content: **FLT CONT DEGRADED.** The refueling may continue; complete this procedure before the next contact.

If the light goes out, continue boom refueling. If not, do a flight control check to judge the boom's control and stability: in CONTACT/COUPLED the boom behaves normally, but in FREE FLIGHT its sensitivity and response are degraded and precise control may be hard. If it is controllable and stable, continue, with the roll limits set below the largest roll reached in the check or the receiver's limit, whichever is less. If not, discontinue and stow the boom.
**FLT CONT MAINT REQD.** Flight control performance is not affected; boom refueling may be done.

children.title: ROLL or ELEVATION ALAS INOP light on

blocks.content: If the light goes out, continue. If not, continue only as operational necessity dictates: set the roll limits to 15°, leave ALAS at ENABLE, and track the receiver and alleviate the nozzle loads by hand in the failed axis. The higher stick force gradient after contact makes the job easier. HI NOZZLE LOAD and the stick shaker do not work in the failed axis.
Large boom misalignment can load the nozzle enough to stop it retracting from the receptacle, or damage the receiver once the nozzle is free.

children.title: LTS & EMER TLSCP INOP light on

blocks.content: With LTS & EMER TLSCP INOP on, the emergency telescope retraction, all four FAIL lights and the aural warning are inoperative.

items.item: BOOM EMER RET & FAIL ANNUN circuit breaker
items.action: CHECK: if open, reset after 90 seconds; if closed, pull and reset

blocks.content: If the light goes out, continue the refueling mission. If it stays on, discontinue boom refueling except in an emergency.

children.title: Boom control unit shutdown after a power interruption

blocks.content: **Condition:** after a DC or AC interruption, all four FAIL lights and the aural warning are on and the stick is limp (DC: the signal system's status lights out; AC: the position instruments at their unpowered positions and both ALAS INOP lights on). A momentary interruption only blinks the lights and gives a small stick transient; no action is needed. See [Monitoring, power interruptions and shutdown](air-refueling-systems#boom-bcu-monitoring).
If the fuel flow or pressure reads zero afterwards, tell the FE. If the boom does not recover, stow it with the hoist and discontinue boom refueling.

children.title: HYD PRESS LOW light on (main, boom or drogue)

blocks.content: **Condition:** MAIN HYD PRESS LOW, BOOM HYD PRESS LOW or the drogue panel's HYD PRESS LOW comes on. The FE may direct the boom operator to disconnect and stow the boom or drogue during any hydraulic malfunction.

items: **Main.** Confirm the state of hydraulic system 2 with the FE. If its pressure and quantity are normal, continue the refueling mission. If not, continue only as operational necessity dictates.
**Boom.** Stow the boom, then FLT CONT OFF.

**Centerline drogue (KC-10A).** If DROGUE POSN shows STOW, do not deploy the hose. When the receiver is clear of the drogue, set HYD SEL to OFF and tell the FE. The FE's analysis of the hydraulic system decides whether refueling can continue; if it does, repeat the preparation for contact.

blocks.content: BOOM HYD PRESS LOW may cycle momentarily when the boom's pressure comes from the 2-3 motor pump (KC-10A). On the KDC-10 the boom's supply is system 2 itself.
**Condition:** the signal system does not work in NORM (for example no READY light), or a normal disconnect is not obtained.

**Coil GOOD:** disconnect capability exists; continue. If a normal disconnect is not then obtained, treat the reading as OPEN or SHORTED for that receiver. With a good coil, both aircraft's signal systems advance to disconnect if an envelope limit is exceeded.

**Coil OPEN or SHORTED:** set TLSCP AT DISC to MAN. If the INDEP DISC gauge reads 1,000 psi or more, disconnect capability exists (through the IDS); continue. If not, there is no tanker disconnect capability: continue only as operational necessity dictates. The boom operator initiates an IDS disconnect before the receiver reaches a normal limit; receiver-initiated disconnects, when feasible, save the IDS.

Brief the receiver: "Receiver call sign, the following contacts will be made in tanker manual override. Receiver's air refueling system will remain in normal and receiver pilot must initiate all disconnects. Tanker call sign, ready." To make a manual contact, with the receiver stable in the contact position insert the nozzle, pull EMER CONTACT MADE, see CONTACT and COUPLED come on, and call "Tanker call sign, contact".

The tanker's signal system still advances to disconnect if an envelope limit is exceeded, but call for the disconnect before the receiver reaches a normal limit, to free the nozzle from the receptacle.
**Condition:** the receiver's own signal system has failed and it latches the boom manually (its amplifier override).

Brief: "Receiver call sign, the following contacts will be made in manual boom latching and receiver pilot must initiate all disconnects. Tanker call sign, ready." Call "Tanker call sign, contact" when CONTACT and COUPLED are on. The tanker still advances to disconnect at an envelope limit, but call for, or make, an IDS disconnect before the receiver reaches a normal limit. Receiver-initiated disconnects save the IDS.

children.title: Boom remains at 0° after ELEV POSN to REFUEL

blocks.content: Repeat until the boom descends to 35°, then cycle FLT CONT once more. Before attempting a contact, push the CONTACT MADE TEST: if the signal system advances to CONTACT/COUPLED and then, with the disconnect, to DISC/FREE FLIGHT, continue boom refueling. If not, fly the boom lower than 35° (but not below 40°), cycle FLT CONT and repeat the test. If it still fails, stow the boom (with the hoist if it will not fly up), discontinue boom refueling and complete the post air refueling checklist.
**Condition:** the hoist cable has parted. The boom can be stowed only by flying it into its chock with its own elevator.

items.action: 300 KIAS or more, below 20,000 ft, wings level
FLY to the stowed position and HOLD it there

blocks.content: If a broken cable could damage the boom or the receiver, discontinue boom refueling except in an emergency; otherwise continue as operational necessity dictates. Avoid abrupt up commands after ELEV POSN goes to STOW. The boom may not fly to the stowed position above 20,000 ft or in a turn, and several attempts may be needed. If it cannot be latched, go to [Landing with boom or drogue in trail](#landing-boom-drogue-in-trail); if it latches, complete the post air refueling checklist.

The hoist at RAISE keeps the boom from creeping down. On the ground the boom support sling must be fitted before hydraulic system 3 is depressurized. BOOM/DROGUE DEPLOYED stays on, and BOOM/DROGUE NOT STOWED comes on with the gear down.
With the boom unlocked, depressurizing hydraulic system 3 lets the boom fall.

children.title: Boom preparation for landing with the boom in trail

items.action: RETURN to the cockpit for landing

blocks.content: Coordinate the boom scavenge with the FE; flying the boom above 0° helps it drain. If there is a long time before final approach, move ELEV POSN to REFUEL meanwhile, and do not turn FLT CONT off until ready for the final approach. Then fly [Landing with boom or drogue in trail](#landing-boom-drogue-in-trail).

rows: Continue the mission. The computer tolerates the loss of cooling flow for several hours at moderate temperatures. Turn AR MASTER PWR OFF when the boom is not needed, to prevent heat build-up.
Continue refueling with care: some fighters move forward in the envelope when the AR pumps stop, and power-limited receivers may not stay within the telescope envelope.

Initiate a disconnect; the FE tells the boom operator. The affected bypass valve is closed by its manual override in the ARO compartment, after which refueling can continue. With both lights on, discontinue boom refueling. A light on when not in contact is normal.

blocks.content: **Condition:** the 1-3 or 2-3 pump valve open light does not come on, or flickers, during the preparation for contact. The check proves the 2-3 motor pump can carry hydraulic system 2, and so the boom, before refueling.

items.action: NOTIFIED: stow the boom or drogue
OFF (No. 2 ENG HYD PRESS LOW on, No. 2 pressure zero)

blocks.content: If system 2's pressure is not in the normal range, the 2-3 motor pump is inoperative: set it OFF and do not refuel unless an emergency exists. If it is normal, return the No. 2 engine pumps to PUMP 1 ON and PUMP 2 AUTO, and leave the 2-3 HYD PUMP ON until the refueling is complete; if it is moved out of ON, it must be checked again before further refueling.

Reverse refueling, from the receiver back to the KC-10A through its boom, is not a normal operation but is available when operational necessity calls for it. The tanker rendezvouses and hooks up normally. When BOOM/DROGUE ENGAGED is on, the FE opens the BOOM VALVE and an ALTN TRANS valve, decides which tanks to fill, and opens their fill valves (forward or aft body tanks) or the ISOL valve (main and center wing tanks), then asks the receiver to start the transfer. At the end, the receiver stops, the boom operator disconnects, and the FE closes the fill, ISOL, ALTN TRANS and BOOM valves, scavenges the manifold and resumes normal fuel management. A tank filled near capacity needs a high-level float test, which requires AR MASTER on.

The maximum reverse refueling rate is 300 GPM (about 2,000 lb/min); one AR pump gives it. More pumps produce higher flows and can cause unacceptable surge pressures at a tension disconnect. The boom operator should not hold the telescope control in retract during reverse refueling: it opens the bypass valves and sends the incoming fuel to the aft body tank.

children.title: Receiver system does not advance to LATCHED

blocks.content: Recycle the receptacle door to make sure system 1 pressure is reaching the UARRSI, and confirm the UARRSI hydraulic shutoff valve is open. If LATCHED still does not come on, the Amplifier Override at OVRD bypasses the amplifier and moves the signal system to DC bus 3 (manual boom latching): tell the boom operator first, and remember that the receiver must then initiate every disconnect. With hydraulic system 1 lost, the UARRSI toggles are inoperative.

children.title: HOSE REEL NOT LOCKED light on

blocks.content: **Condition:** HOSE REEL NOT LOCKED with DROGUE MASTER PWR off. If boom refueling is in progress, disconnect, send the receiver to the observation position on the left wing, stow the boom and set FLT CONT OFF: the hose could deploy and strike a receiver astern.

If the light is now out, continue the mission. If the drogue starts to deploy when HYD SEL goes OFF, return it to DROGUE at once. If the reel will not lock, leave DROGUE MASTER PWR at PWR and HYD SEL at DROGUE and discontinue boom refueling. BOOM/DROGUE DEPLOYED stays on.
With the reel unlocked, moving HYD SEL from DROGUE to OFF or BOOM can let the hose deploy rapidly and be damaged or torn away.

children.title: DROGUE POSN shows barber pole or STOW with the hose trailed

blocks.content: If READY is on, continue drogue refueling. If not, select REWIND and let the hose rewind fully, then TRAIL again. If TRAIL shows and READY comes on, continue. If not, ask the receiver pilot to check the external amber light; if it is on, continue. Otherwise rewind and stow the hose and discontinue drogue refueling.

children.title: Hose slack or whip after the receiver engages

blocks.content: Initiate a disconnect and tell the receiver to disconnect and stay clear of the hose. Unless the receiver declares a fuel emergency, discontinue drogue refueling and complete the post air refueling checklist. To continue in an emergency: push REEL RESP RESET, and once READY is on run the response check (HOSE REEL TEST to SYS); push REEL RESP RESET again; brief the receiver that the reel response is inoperative, hose whip or failure may occur, and to use the slowest practical closure; watch the approach with extreme caution and be ready to call a breakaway. A RESP INOP that comes on after the receiver makes contact is an indication failure, not a system failure: no disconnect is needed; push REEL RESP RESET after the receiver disconnects and before the next contact.

Tell the receivers to stay clear of the hose: it may oscillate severely. Push REEL RESP RESET as soon as the separation is seen, since the hose may rewind rapidly with the switch at TRAIL, and have the FE close the DROGUE VALVE. Ask the pilot to slow as much as possible without lowering the flaps. If the hose is stable, rewind it and set HYD SEL to OFF as soon as the end of the hose enters the chute (the reel does not stop by itself with no drogue at the stop switch), then DROGUE MASTER PWR OFF; DROGUE POSN keeps showing a barber pole. If the hose is not stable, select TRAIL and jettison it.

items.action: REDUCE as slow as practical (up to 80 kt)

blocks.content: Watch the drum in the hose drum viewing mirror: DROGUE POSN shows TRAIL until DROGUE MASTER PWR is switched off. If the drogue rewinds to stowed, set HYD SEL to OFF while watching the drogue at the chute (back to DROGUE at once if it deploys), then DROGUE MASTER PWR OFF, and complete the post air refueling checklist. If it does not, decide between jettisoning the hose and landing with it in trail; consider landing in trail if the hose is stable. To land in trail: HYD SEL OFF, DROGUE MASTER PWR OFF, post air refueling checklist, then [Landing with boom or drogue in trail](#landing-boom-drogue-in-trail).

**Hose in trail:** push and hold REEL RESP RESET for at least 2 seconds; READY and RESP INOP go out, and READY returns about 5 seconds after release. If RESP INOP stays out, continue drogue refueling.

If it comes back, and the refueling must continue in an emergency: HYD SEL DROGUE, HOSE TRAIL, REEL RESP RESET held at least 2 seconds, then the response check (HOSE REEL TEST to SYS). If RESP INOP persists, or the hose is stowed with RESP INOP on, the reel response or hose reel monitor is improperly set or inoperative: do not refuel except in an emergency, set HOSE REEL MONITOR OFF, and brief the receiver: "Receiver call sign, the hose reel response system is inoperative. Hose whip may occur during contact. Use slowest closure rate practical. Tanker call sign, ready."
An undetected loss of reel response or of the hose reel monitor can cause severe damage to the tanker and the receiver.

items.item: HOSE JTSN (when cleared by the pilot)

blocks.content: If the hose does not jettison, also close the sighting door and return to the forward position, and plan to land with the drogue in trail. After a jettison BOOM/DROGUE DEPLOYED stays on and DROGUE POSN shows the barber pole. A jettisoned drogue is a mandatory maintenance write-up.
Do not jettison the hose over a populated area unless the aircraft's safety requires immediate action.

sections.title: Wing pod abnormal procedures
sections.summary: KC-10A and DC-10-40 Omega.

blocks.content: On the Omega the flight engineer performs the boom operator's items.

children.title: Wing pod hose will not rewind

blocks.content: If FUEL TEMP HIGH is on, or a RAT overspeed has occurred or may have, do not use this procedure until just before landing unless the aircraft's or crew's safety is paramount: the pod pump's cooling circulation stops once the hose is jettisoned or POD POWER is off.

First make sure the speed is below 280 KIAS and try the rewind again; if it rewinds, complete the normal post refueling procedure. If the hose will not rewind because of a FAIL that does not clear, cycling POD POWER may clear it.

Decide between jettisoning the hose and landing with it in trail. Unless the aircraft's safety is compromised, do not jettison. **To jettison:** receivers clear; when the pilot clears it, HOSE JTSN to JTSN (no longer than half a second), then POD POWER OFF. The hose must be at full trail for the jettison to work. **To land in trail:** POD POWER OFF, and fly [Landing with boom or drogue in trail](#landing-boom-drogue-in-trail).
If the hose does not separate immediately it may jettison at any time without further action. Do not jettison over a populated area unless safety requires it.

children.title: FAIL or blank fuel offload counter

blocks.content: **Hose stowed:** POD POWER OFF; do not deploy that pod. **Hose deployed:** tell the receiver to disconnect, and verify the hose reaches full trail (its trail rate may be restricted, and a receiver may be disconnected before it gets there). The pod resets automatically at full trail if the failure has cleared: if the counter is normal, continue refueling.

**FAIL still shown:** cycle POD POWER OFF and ON; if the counter is then normal, continue; if not, discontinue use of that pod. **Blank:** the pod's processor has failed, and every signal and annunciator light may be out with it; if it does not recover at full trail, discontinue use of that pod.

children.title: RAT overspeed: HOSE STOWED, FUEL PRESS HIGH and FUEL PRESS LOW flashing

blocks.content: **Condition:** with the hose stowed, HOSE STOWED, FUEL PRESS HIGH and FUEL PRESS LOW flash together; with the hose deployed, only FUEL PRESS HIGH and FUEL PRESS LOW flash.

items.action: NOTIFIED: RAT overspeed, rpm and temperature

blocks.content: BITE pressed under 2 seconds shows the RAT's speed, pressed again the fuel temperature; COUNTER RESET returns to the offload. Watch both while the speed comes down. If they return to normal: POD FUEL VALVE and WING DROGUE VALVE CLOSE, POD POWER OFF (leave POD POWER on to keep watching them if you continue refueling on the other pod). If they do not: WING DROGUE VALVE OPEN, crossfeed manifold pressurized, POD FUEL VALVE CLOSE, POD POWER ON: fuel pressure in the manifold is what keeps the pump from overheating.

Land as soon as possible if the pod's fuel temperature cannot be kept below 200 °C. A blade may separate above 10,000 rpm: keep the RAT below 10,000 rpm unless the tanker's or the receiver's safety would suffer.

children.title: Pod FUEL PRESS LOW light on

blocks.content: Tell the receiver to disconnect, verify the hose is at full trail, and confirm with the FE that the WING DROGUE VALVE is open and the crossfeed manifold is pressurized (on the Omega, the X-FEED valves open and the boost pumps on). If the light goes out, continue. If not, discontinue use of that pod and go to [Wing pod hose will not rewind](#abn-pod-will-not-rewind) if needed: with FUEL PRESS LOW on and the hose deployed, the hose cannot be stowed.

children.title: Pod FUEL PRESS HIGH light on

blocks.content: Tell the receiver to disconnect and verify the hose reaches full trail (its rate may be restricted). The pod resets automatically if the fault clears: if FUEL PRESS HIGH goes out and READY comes on, continue. If not, rewind the hose and discontinue use of that pod.

children.title: Pod FUEL TEMP HIGH light on

blocks.content: If FUEL TEMP HIGH goes out and READY comes on, continue. If not, rewind the hose and check the RAT speed and fuel temperature with BITE. If they are normal, close the POD FUEL VALVE and WING DROGUE VALVE and turn POD POWER OFF. If not, ask the pilot to slow until the RAT is below 2,000 rpm and the fuel below 50 °C, then shut the pod down the same way. If they still will not come down: WING DROGUE VALVE OPEN, crossfeed manifold pressurized, POD FUEL VALVE CLOSE, POD POWER ON, to keep fuel circulating through the pump.
Land as soon as possible if the fuel temperature cannot be kept below 200 °C.

children.title: Loss of a wing pod drogue

blocks.content: Tell the receivers to stay clear of the hose. The hose rewinds by itself until about 46 ft is left out, and then can be neither stowed nor jettisoned (the jettison needs full trail). Have the FE close the POD FUEL VALVE and the WING DROGUE VALVE (fuel spills as the hose rewinds through the refuel range with the pod valve armed), ask the pilot to slow as much as possible without flaps, turn POD POWER OFF, and land with the hose in trail.
Hose oscillation grows until it can damage the aircraft if the flaps or slats are extended. If possible fly a no-flap, no-slat approach and landing.

children.title: Pod READY light does not come on

blocks.content: Without READY, fuel cannot be transferred and the jettison is not enabled. If the hose has reached full trail, cycle POD POWER. If it has not, increase speed (not above 300 KIAS). If it then reaches full trail, continue; if not, rewind the hose and discontinue use of that pod.
Do not select REWIND unless the drogue is stable and not moving in or out.

parts.title: Flying air refueling in the simulation
parts.summary: What works, the ARO Input control intercept, the EFB's Air Refuel app, and practice sessions for the boom, the centerline hose and the wing pods.

blocks.content: The simulation has no receiver aircraft, so there is no contact and no fuel offload. Most of what comes before that point works as on the real aircraft, with the exceptions listed in [Simulation notes](air-refueling-systems#simulation-notes), and the boom's signal system can be taken through a contact and its disconnect with the test inputs once they are bound to buttons. A tanker session is therefore a mission of its own: plan and fly the track and orbit, prepare the boom or hoses, fly the boom through its envelope, trail and rewind hoses, run the checks, and handle the failures that can arise.

rows: Boom (flown by you), its signal system with test contacts, IDS, limits; centerline hose with its response system, monitor and guillotine; both wing pods with their RATs, DRCUs, counters and BITE; the offload fuel system's pumps and valves; the FMS refuel orbit and rendezvous; the receiver system's AR MASTER, AMPL OVRD and lights (the receiver cannot reach READY)
Boom operator's station (boom, centerline, pods), F/E panel (fuel, hydraulics, WING AERIAL REFUEL), flight deck (FMS, autopilot), EFB Air Refuel app
Boom and its station, on the DC-10-30's own buses and hydraulic system 2. No fuel side
Boom operator's station, EFB Air Refuel app
Both wing pods, fed by the boost pumps through the X-FEED valves

sections.title: The ARO Input control intercept
sections.summary: KC-10A and KDC-10.

blocks.content: The boom is flown with your own flight controls. The **ARO Input** switch at the top of the EFB's Air Refuel app hands your joystick, throttle and trim from the aircraft to the boom; switching it off hands them back. While the boom has them, the aircraft's own controls are held: the autopilot keeps flying pitch and roll, the yaw damper keeps the rudder, and the thrust levers stay where you left them unless the autothrottle is engaged and moving them.

blocks.title: Your controls while ARO Input is engaged
rows: Forward is boom down. A position command about the trail: centerd returns the boom to trail.
The boom operator faces aft: stick left swings the boom to your left as you look aft, which is the tanker's right.
A position command: lever travel 0 to 100 % is 0 to 22 ft of extension. The last lever moved wins.
In the boom operator's frame, like the stick.

items: **The autopilot must be in command.** ARO Input engages only if, at the moment you switch it on, the aircraft is airborne with the autopilot in CMD (not CWS) flying both pitch and roll. Otherwise the app shows refused: engage CMD, then switch ARO Input off and on again.

**If the autopilot drops out of CMD, the controls stay on the boom.** The aircraft's pitch and roll then have no one flying them. The app's card turns red with Return controls to the cockpit, and a banner shows over every other app: switch ARO Input off at once and fly the aircraft. Nothing hands the controls back by itself.

**Telescope pick-up.** A throttle lever does not spring back, so it commands the telescope only after you have brought it to where the telescope already is; with the telescope retracted, that is the idle stop. After every automatic retraction at a disconnect (TLSCP AT DISC at AUTO), bring the lever back to idle before it extends the telescope again. The telescope answers only with ELEV POSN at REFUEL.
**Engage the autothrottle** (from the glareshield or the app's Aircraft Control page) before taking ARO Input, so the tanker holds its speed while your throttle is the telescope.
When you hand the controls back, they stay where the hold left them until your hardware sends a new input: move each axis through center.

sections.title: The EFB Air Refuel app
sections.summary: KC-10A and KDC-10.

blocks.content: The Air Refuel app appears on the tankers only. The KC-10A and the KDC-10 also carry a second EFB at the boom operator's station, which mirrors the flight deck's, so the app is at hand where you need it. See [EFB](efb).

blocks.alt: The EFB at the boom operator's station showing the Air Refuel app: the ARO Input switch at the top reading BOOM (engaged); below it the Refueling Setup page with a boom receiver selected, the ARO's three disconnect limits and RCVR DISC DELAY read back and matching the receiver, a Set ARO button, and the receiver data (optimum altitude, airspeed and Mach, rendezvous speed, overrun speed, offload rate, disconnect limits and delay, notes).
blocks.title: Air Refuel app: ARO Input and Refueling Setup

items: **ARO Input** at the top: off, the boom, refused (the autopilot was not flying in CMD), or autopilot lost.

**Aircraft Control** mirrors the glareshield's autopilot panel: the flight mode annunciators with the flight data under them, the SPEED, HEADING, ALTITUDE and V/S selectors (typed, and sent on Enter), their push and pull functions, the bank limit, the mode keys, the autopilot levers and the autothrottle. It lets you fly the tanker's autopilot from the boom operator's station.

**Refueling Setup** lists the receivers of the published KC-10 receiver tables, for the boom and, on the KC-10A, the drogue. Choosing a boom receiver sets the ARO's three disconnect limit knobs and the RCVR DISC DELAY at once; the page reads the ARO back, shows when it differs from the receiver (a reload resets the knobs) and offers Set ARO. Below are the receiver's data: optimum refueling altitude and speed first, then rendezvous and overrun speeds, offload rate, radios, and its notes. A drogue receiver sets nothing: the hoses have no receiver settings.

sections.title: Contact, disconnect and reset inputs
sections.summary: KC-10A and KDC-10.

blocks.content: The switches on the boom operator's hand controllers are not on the 3D station. The disconnect trigger (DISC, and the IDS through its second detent), RESET TO READY, EMER CONTACT MADE and the CONTACT MADE TEST are provided as bindable inputs for external control-binding utilities; assign them to buttons on your stick to use them. Without them you can still lower, fly and stow the boom and set it up, but you cannot take the signal system out of READY.

With them, the CONTACT MADE TEST or EMER CONTACT MADE gives CONTACT with its beep, COUPLED a second later (not with ELEV POSN at STOW), the pilots' BOOM/DROGUE ENGAGED (KC-10A), and arms the envelope limits: fly the boom to an armed limit and the control unit disconnects by itself, with three beeps and, at AUTO, the telescope's 10 ft/s retraction. DISC disconnects; through the second detent it also fires the IDS and spends part of the bottle; RESET TO READY returns to READY.

sections.title: A boom session
sections.summary: KC-10A and KDC-10.

items: **Preflight.** At the boom operator's station: AR MASTER PWR to PWR (READY on), the station inspection settings, limits at 25° and 20°, INDEP DISC 1,500 psi or more, BOOM COIL TEST (its indicator has no needle in the 3D model). With the FE, HYD SEL to BOOM for about two minutes, then OFF. Boom stowed and latched.

**To the track.** On the KC-10A, build and insert the refuel pattern in the FMS and fly it to the orbit with ORBIT MODE at ORBIT (see [Flying the rendezvous with the FMS refuel pattern](ar-rendezvous#rv-fms-refuel-pattern)). Level at the refueling altitude, about 275 to 300 KIAS, autopilot in CMD, autothrottle holding the speed.

**Cockpit preparation.** Fly the tanker preparation for contact: hydraulic pumps, 2-3 HYD PUMP ON when BOOM/DROGUE HYD PRSRZ comes on (KC-10A), fuel panel for boom refueling (KC-10A), autopilot in heading and altitude hold.
**Boom operator's preparation.** At the station, the boom checklist down to FLT CONT ON and ELEV POSN STOW. In the Air Refuel app pick a receiver under Refueling Setup.
**Lower the boom.** HOIST RAISE, LATCH UNLOCK, HOIST LWR: the boom settles at about 0°. HOIST FREE WHEEL, ELEV POSN REFUEL: it flies to about 30°.
**Take the boom.** ARO Input on (it shows the boom). Bring the throttle to idle to pick up the telescope. Trim the boom to 0° roll and 30° with the trim inputs if needed.
**Flight control check.** Extend the telescope to 12 ft and fly the boom smoothly through 18° to 40° and 0° to 25° roll each way. Watch the limit cursors and the boom outside.

**Contact drill** (with the inputs bound). CONTACT MADE TEST: CONTACT, COUPLED. Guard the stick. Fly slowly to an armed limit and watch the automatic disconnect and retraction; RESET TO READY; repeat with TLSCP AT DISC at MAN, and with DISC.

**Stow.** Throttle to idle, ELEV POSN STOW (the telescope retracts and the boom flies up to about 0°), ARO Input off, HOIST RAISE to the chock, LATCH LOCK, HOIST LWR to check, then HOLD; FLT CONT OFF, HYD SEL OFF, sighting door closed.

blocks.content: Never hold the stick forward with the hoist at LWR: you can break the hoist cable. Then the only way to stow the boom is to fly it into its chock at 300 KIAS or more, low and wings level, as in [Broken boom hoist cable](ar-emergency-abnormal#abn-broken-hoist-cable); it is good practice for that procedure, too.

items: At the station: DROGUE MASTER PWR to PWR (DROGUE POSN STOW, HYD PRESS LOW on), HOSE REEL MONITOR ON, HOSE REEL TEST (RESP INOP for about a second), HYD SEL to DROGUE (HYD PRESS LOW out).
HOSE to TRAIL: watch the canopy open in the stream and the hose trail out; DROGUE POSN TRAIL, READY about 5 seconds after full trail.
Settle at the refueling condition and push REEL RESP RESET: READY goes out and returns.

**55-knot check.** Accelerate to 325 KIAS, reset, then slow at about 1 kt per second: the reel starts winding the hose in as the drag falls below its pull. READY goes out as the hose enters the range, and the pilots' BOOM/DROGUE ENGAGED comes on. The rewind stalls short of stowed: push REEL RESP RESET and the hose returns to trail.
Change speed without resetting and watch the hose reel monitor light RESP INOP; hold REEL RESP RESET 2 seconds to clear it.
HOSE to REWIND, then HYD SEL OFF, HOSE REEL MONITOR OFF, DROGUE MASTER PWR OFF.

sections.title: A wing pod session
sections.summary: KC-10A and DC-10-40 Omega.

items: **Fuel.** On the KC-10A, open an ALTN TRANS and an ISOL valve, set AR PUMP OVRD, run the AR pumps in that tank, and open the WING DROGUE VALVES. On the Omega, run the boost pumps and open the X-FEED valves and the WING DROGUE VALVES.
POD POWER ON: HOSE STOWED on, FUEL PRESS LOW out, FUEL INLET PRESSURE LOW out, counter zero. Arm the POD FUEL VALVES if you like.
Above 230 KIAS, slats and flaps up, HOSE TRAIL/REWIND to TRAIL: 5 seconds' delay, HOSE TRANSIT flashing, READY at 69 ft, the hose stopping at full trail. Watch the RAT spin up.
BITE (a short press) shows the RAT's speed, again the pump's fuel temperature; COUNTER RESET returns to the offload.
At 280 KIAS or less, REWIND: HOSE TRANSIT flashes, HOSE STOWED steady. POD POWER OFF, valves closed.

Try a trail below 230 KIAS and watch the hose stall short of full trail without READY; speed up and it reaches full trail. Try trailing with the WING DROGUE VALVE shut (or, on the Omega, the X-FEED valves shut): FUEL PRESS LOW, a FAIL after 10 seconds, and a hose that cannot be rewound until the pressure is restored.

sections.title: The flight engineer's role and the Virtual Crew

blocks.content: The flight engineer's refueling duties are the fuel panel set-up and its scavenge afterwards, the hydraulic pumps and the 2-3 motor pump, the AR hydraulic and status lights, the CG, the offload record, and, on the Omega, the pods themselves. The Virtual Crew does not perform them: it runs the normal checklists, and on the KC-10A its flight engineer does the normal checklist's boom items (telling the boom operator, and on a scramble AR MASTER PWR and HYD SEL to BOOM for two minutes). For a refueling session, take the flight engineer's seat yourself for the fuel and hydraulic set-up before going to the boom operator's station. See [Virtual Crew](virtual-crew).

chapters.title: Glossary
chapters.summary: Abbreviations, acronyms and technical terms used in this manual, with a one-line meaning for each.

blocks.content: This glossary spells out the abbreviations and acronyms used in this manual and defines the technical terms it relies on. Panel and display legends are listed where they are abbreviations (ISOL, OVRD, XFEED, CONSEQ); switch positions that are plain words, such as ON, OFF, AUTO, NORM and ARM, are not.

An entry that belongs to one aircraft, series or equipment fit says so in parentheses at the start: (MD-10), (DC-10, KC-10), (KC-10), (AINS-70), (DC-10 air tanker). Where an abbreviation has more than one meaning, each is given, separated by semicolons. Where the manual explains a term in depth, the entry links to the page that does.

Entries are in alphabetical order under their first letter, with capitals and lower case sorted together. Entries that begin with a digit or a symbol, such as %MAC, the series designations and the flap/slat configurations, come first under Numbers and symbols. The V-speeds are under V.

rows: The DC-10 series. -10: short span, CF6-6D. -15: -10 airframe with CF6-50C2F engines for hot and high airfields. -30: long span, center gear, CF6-50C2. -40: long span, center gear, JT9D-59A. See [Aircraft General](aircraft-general).
The freighter versions of the DC-10 series, with the main-deck cargo door.
Center of gravity position as a percentage of the mean aerodynamic chord, measured aft from its leading edge (LEMAC). See [Mission Planning](mission-planning).
Flap/slat configurations as the handle and the speed cards name them: flap angle in degrees, then slats retracted (RET) or extended (EXT). See [Flight Controls](flight-controls).
The two reversible motor pumps, which pass hydraulic power between system 3 and systems 1 and 2 in either direction without exchanging fluid. See [Hydraulics](hydraulics).
Door designations: doors are numbered from front to rear on each side, L for left and R for right.

The two non-reversible motor pumps: each is driven by the first-numbered system and pressurizes a standby loop of the second, giving the rudder segments and one stabilizer trim motor a second source. See [Hydraulics](hydraulics).
The nominal voltage of the DC system, supplied by the transformer-rectifiers and the battery.
The main AC system: three-phase, 115 V phase to neutral and 200 V phase to phase, at 400 Hz. See [Electrical](electrical).
(KC-10) The USAF cargo pallet system; the KC-10's cargo floor takes the HCU-6/E 463L master pallet only.
The air-driven generator's line contactor, which connects the ADG to the ADG bus. See [Electrical](electrical).
Automatic brake system; the ABS DISARM light shows the autobrakes disarmed. See [Landing Gear](landing-gear).
Above (the TCAS or ETCAS display envelope that extends further above the aircraft; BLW is below).
Aircraft (as in the MD-10's A/C STATUS page).
Aircraft communications addressing and reporting system, an air-ground datalink. Not fitted in the simulation.
Acceleration, as in ACCEL HT (acceleration height) and the FMS's EO ACCEL altitude.
The distance to accelerate, lose an engine at a given speed, continue the takeoff and reach the screen height. See [Mission Planning](mission-planning).
The distance to accelerate, lose an engine at a given speed, and bring the aircraft to a stop on the runway. See [Mission Planning](mission-planning).
The height at which the climb is leveled to accelerate and retract the flaps and slats, high enough for the flight path to clear the obstacles. See [Mission Planning](mission-planning).
A vessel in which a gas charge stores hydraulic fluid under pressure, to smooth pump pulses and to supply brakes or other users when pump pressure is lost. See [Hydraulics](hydraulics).
Air cycle machine: the turbine-driven refrigeration unit in each air conditioning pack. See [Air Conditioning](air-conditioning).
Audio control panel: each crew station's panel for choosing the transmitter and the receivers to monitor. See [Communications](communications).
(KC-10) Automatic communications system: the menu-driven control system for the HF radios; SELCAL is one of its modes.
Active (FMS route or page in use, as opposed to MOD or SEC).
Auxiliary data acquisition unit, part of the AIDS.
(KC-10) ARO DC bus transfer relay, which feeds the boom operator's DC bus from DC bus 3 or DC bus 1.
The Carousel IV-A's card reader (not modeled).
Automatic direction finder: an LF/MF receiver whose needle points to the tuned NDB or broadcast station. See [Navigation](navigation).

Air-driven generator: a ram-air turbine generator deployed into the airstream after the loss of all generators, to power the right emergency AC bus or auxiliary hydraulic pump 1. See [Electrical](electrical).
Attitude director indicator: the attitude instrument carrying the flight director command bars. See [Flight Instruments](flight-instruments).
(MD-10) Air data inertial reference system and its three units (ADIRU 1, 2 and AUX), which supply position, attitude, heading and velocities. See [Navigation](navigation).
Automatic dependent surveillance–broadcast: the transponder's periodic broadcast of position (Out only, on the KC-10's IFF).
The altitude at which, for the weight, the low-speed and high-speed buffet boundaries meet. See [Flight Characteristics](flight-characteristics).
The simulation's towbar tractor for pushback and towing, of the TLD TMX-550 class. See [Ground Operations](ground-operations).
Airplane flight manual: the certificated document that contains a civil aircraft's limitations and performance.

(MD-10) Automatic flight system: the MD-11-derived autopilot, autothrottle and flight director system of the two flight control computers, controlled from the FCP. See [Automatic Flight](automatic-flight).
(MD-10) Ancillary fuel system controller, the backup to the fuel system controller.
(MD-10) Automatic flight system control panel on the overhead, with the FLAP LIMIT and ELEV FEEL controls.
(KC-10) The USAF aircraft forms record, in which any operation beyond a limit is entered.
AC ground service tie relay: connects the AC ground service bus to generator bus 2; interlocked with the GSR so that external power is never paralleled with generator 2.
Agent (fire extinguishing), as in the AGT 1 LOW and AGT 2 LOW lights.
The relay that connects the air-driven generator to auxiliary hydraulic pump 1 when the ADG is selected to HYD. See [Electrical](electrical).
Anti-ice (MD-10 alert legends, for example ENG 1 A-ICE DISAG).
Aircraft integrated data system: an optional flight data monitoring and recording system (DMU, acquisition units, DAR, FDEP and printer). See [Warning Systems](warning-systems).

Area inertial navigation system (DC-10 fit): three inertial sensor systems and two navigation computers that blend inertial, radio and air data into one area navigation position. See [Navigation](navigation).
Aeronautical information regulation and control: the 28-day cycle on which navigation databases are issued.
The engine starter: a small turbine driven by pneumatic air that turns the high-pressure spool through the accessory gearbox. See [Engines](engines).

(KC-10) Automatic load alleviation system: when enabled and coupled, senses the radial loads on the boom nozzle and drives the boom to follow the receiver. See [Air Refueling Systems](air-refueling-systems).
Align: an inertial alignment mode or status; in an autoland, the decrab phase before the flare.
(DC-10, KC-10) The speed control system's angle-of-attack floor, below which the autothrottle in SPD will not let the speed fall. See [Automatic Flight](automatic-flight).
Altitude (ALT HOLD, ALT CAP); on some legends, alternate.
Lowering the landing gear without hydraulic power: the uplocks are released mechanically and the gear falls and locks under gravity and airloads. See [Landing Gear](landing-gear).
Amplitude modulation (VHF voice and an HF mode).
(KC-10) Amplifier: AMPL OVRD (AMPL OVERRIDE) selects manual boom latching, in which the receiver initiates every disconnect.
(KC-10) The IFF transponder of the simulated KC-10A.
The angle between the wing's chord and the relative airflow. Lift, the stall and the stall warning depend on it. See [Flight Characteristics](flight-characteristics).
Actual navigation performance: the FMS's estimate of its position accuracy, compared with the RNP. See [Flight Management](flight-management).
Collins radio area navigation system offered on early -10s, single (ANS-70S) or dual (ANS-70D); simulated as the AINS-70's interface without inertial platforms. See [Navigation](navigation).
Antenna (radar ANT TILT; the ADF's ANT mode).
The brake control that releases a wheel's brake when it starts to skid, so each wheel brakes close to the best available friction. See [Landing Gear](landing-gear).
Aircraft nose up (stabilizer trim units and direction).
(DC-10, MD-10) The autoland status that allows a coupled approach to minimums but no automatic landing, for example when one autopilot failed the preland test.
Auxiliary (APU) power relay: one per generator bus, connecting the APU generator to that bus. See [Electrical](electrical).
Autopilot pitch trim; also airport (FMS and EFB fields).
Auxiliary power unit: the gas turbine in the tail cone that supplies electrical power and bleed air. See [APU](apu).
Air refueling (as in A/R DISC, the receiver's disconnect).
Air refueling; on the KC-10 also the ARO station's AR panel.
Air refueling control point: the planned point on the refueling track (or the anchor point) at which the receiver should reach the tanker. See [Air Refueling](air-refueling).
Air refueling control time: the planned time at the ARCP or rendezvous point.
Aeronautical Radio Inc., whose standards define avionics data and navigation databases (ARINC 424 leg types).
Air refueling initial point: the entry point of the refueling track. See [Air Refueling](air-refueling).
(KC-10) Aerial refueling operator: the boom operator's station in the aft fuselage, and the ARO AC and DC buses that serve it.
(MD-10) Automatic slat extension; SLATS ASE on the PFD shows the slats extended by the flight control computers.

A reduced-thrust takeoff method: thrust is set for an air temperature higher than the actual one, up to the temperature at which the runway would just be limiting. See [Mission Planning](mission-planning).
Air start unit: the ground cart that supplies pneumatic air for engine starting.
Air Transport Association; its chapter numbers group an aircraft's systems (ATA 24 electrical, ATA 29 hydraulics and so on).
Air traffic control; also the ATC transponder.
Autothrottle system (ATS levers, ATS disconnect switches).
(DC-10, KC-10) Automatic throttle/speed control: the autothrottle and speed control computers. See [Automatic Flight](automatic-flight).
Attitude: the failure flag, and the inertial reversion that supplies attitude only.
The automatic brake system, which applies the brakes on landing at a selected deceleration, or at full pressure in a rejected takeoff. See [Landing Gear](landing-gear).
An automatic approach and landing: localizer and glideslope tracking, align, flare and rollout (DC-10 and MD-10; the KC-10's LAND switch is inoperative). See [Automatic Flight](automatic-flight).
Automatic extension of the outboard slats at stall warning onset with the wing clean, to restore stall margin. See [Flight Controls](flight-controls).
Avionics circuit breaker panel, as a breaker location (AV B-13).
An error in the heading an inertial platform found during alignment; it makes the computed track slightly wrong, so position error grows with distance flown. See [Navigation](navigation).
back side of the drag curve
Flight below the minimum drag speed, where a loss of speed raises the drag and only more thrust stops the speed falling further. See [Flight Characteristics](flight-characteristics).
The runway length at which the accelerate-go and accelerate-stop distances are equal for the chosen V1 (the KC-10's critical field length). See [Mission Planning](mission-planning).
(KC-10) Fuel kept in the forward body tank to hold the center of gravity inside limits.
Fuel carried only to hold the center of gravity forward, declared unusable and added to the zero fuel weight (for example in the -30's upper auxiliary tank). See [Fuel](fuel).
The barometric altimeter setting, or the knob that sets it.
The essential DC bus, normally fed by TRs 2A and 2B through diodes, with the battery behind it through the CBR. See [Electrical](electrical).
The DC bus connected straight to the battery, live whenever the battery is connected.
(KC-10) Boom control unit: the digital fly-by-wire computer between the boom operator's stick and the boom's control surfaces. See [Air Refueling Systems](air-refueling-systems).
The weather radar effect at long range, where a beam wider than the storm averages in clear air, so the cell paints weaker and larger than it is. See [Surveillance](surveillance).
Beat frequency oscillator (an ADF mode for identifying unmodulated stations).
Built-in test equipment: a unit's self-test.
Air taken from the engine or APU compressors for the pneumatic system: air conditioning, pressurization, anti-icing and engine starting. See [Pneumatics](pneumatics).
Doors that fold into the fan duct when the thrust reverser deploys, turning the fan air out through the cascade vanes. See [Engines](engines).
Ballast (FMS fuel entries BLST FUEL and BLST TANK).
(KC-10) Boom operator, the crew member who flies the boom and operates the drogue systems from the ARO station.

The air cycle in which the ACM's own compressor raises the pressure of the cooled bleed air before its turbine expands and chills it; compressor, turbine and fan share one shaft. See [Air Conditioning](air-conditioning).
The heat the brakes must absorb in a stop, rising with the square of speed; it limits V1 (VMBE) and turnaround time. See [Landing Gear](landing-gear).
Bus tie relay: connects a generator bus to the AC tie bus. See [Electrical](electrical).
Bus tie relay–external power, which connects external power to the AC tie bus.
The load factor the aircraft can pull at its present weight, altitude and speed before buffet begins. See [Flight Characteristics](flight-characteristics).
The ratio of the air the fan sends around the core to the air that passes through it. See [Engines](engines).
(MD-10) Center accessory compartment, the equipment bay whose duct leak and airflow alerts are CAC MANF FAIL and CAC AIR FLO OFF.

Central air data computer: one of two computers that derive airspeed, Mach, altitude, vertical speed and air temperature from the pitot-static and TAT probes. See [Flight Instruments](flight-instruments).
(MFD fit) The display control panel mode that turns the EADI into the combined attitude and navigation picture.
Capture (FMA modes such as ALT CAP, LOC CAP and G/S CAP).
Calibrated airspeed: indicated airspeed corrected for position and instrument error.
The rows of turning vanes in the nacelle wall that direct reversed fan air forward when the translating cowl moves aft. See [Engines](engines).
Category II and III: precision approaches with decision heights below 200 ft, flown on the autoland system. See [Automatic Flight](automatic-flight).
(MD-10) Central aural warning system, which pairs each warning tone with a voice message. See [Warning Systems](warning-systems).
Charger battery relay: connects the battery to the battery bus or to its charger.
Control display unit: the keyboard and screen of an inertial navigation system (DC-10; C/DU on the Carousel IV-A) or of the KC-10's FMS. See [Navigation](navigation).
The third main landing gear under the fuselage of the -30, -40, KC-10 and MD-10-30. See [Landing Gear](landing-gear).
General Electric high-bypass turbofan: CF6-6D (DC-10-10, MD-10-10), CF6-50C2F (DC-10-15), CF6-50C2 (DC-10-30, KC-10, MD-10-30). See [Engines](engines).
FedEx's DC-10 flight manual, one of the sources this manual follows.
Climb gradient limiting weight: the heaviest takeoff weight that meets the required engine-out climb gradient.
Change; on the battery meter, charge.
(KC-10) The FMS navigation solutions blending INU 1 or INU 2 with a civil GPS receiver.
Carousel IV-A: Delco inertial navigation system (DC-10 fit), fitted three to an aircraft. See [Navigation](navigation).
Climb (the thrust rating computer's climb mode); also coverage level, and CL GR, climb gradient.
(DC-10, KC-10) The autothrottle takeoff mode from 80 kt: the servo brake holds the throttles where they are through rotation and the initial climb. See [Automatic Flight](automatic-flight).
Climb (thrust limit, FMS page or key).
The rule that no frost, snow or ice may adhere to the wings, tail or control surfaces at takeoff. See [Adverse Weather](adverse-weather).
Command: the autopilot engage position; on the thrust rating computer, the command N1 or EPR bugs.
The first phase of inertial alignment, in which the gyros spin up and the platform levels while it waits for a present position.
The altitude at which low-speed buffet and high-speed buffet meet for the weight, leaving no speed margin. See [Flight Characteristics](flight-characteristics).
Fuel chilled during cruise that keeps the wing skin below freezing after landing, so frost and clear ice can form in air well above 0 °C. See [Adverse Weather](adverse-weather).
Compass; on the vibration monitor, compressor.
The unit of a compass system that slaves the directional gyro to the flux valve's magnetic reference. See [Flight Instruments](flight-instruments).
The region directly above a VOR station where the radial changes rapidly and is unreliable. See [Navigation](navigation).
Configuration (on the MD-10, a system display page).
(MD-10) Consequences: the SDCP switch and system display page that list what the current failures take away.
(MD-10) The effects of a failure on other systems, shown on the system display beside the alerts. See [Warning Systems](warning-systems).
(DC-10 air tanker) Control of the tank doors so retardant leaves at a constant rate, laying an even coverage level along the line. See [Aerial Firefighting](aerial-firefighting).
A TCAS resolution advisory that calls for a change of vertical speed. See [Surveillance](surveillance).
The ratio of time-related cost to fuel cost that sets the FMS's economy speeds.
(DC-10 air tanker) The density of the retardant laid on the ground, in US gallons per 100 square feet. See [Aerial Firefighting](aerial-firefighting).
Cruise (the thrust rating computer's cruise mode).
(KC-10) The balanced field length: the runway needed when the engine fails at VCEF.
The flight Mach number at which the local airflow somewhere on the aircraft first reaches the speed of sound. See [Flight Characteristics](flight-characteristics).
Feeding an engine from a tank other than its own through the crossfeed valves and manifold. See [Fuel](fuel).
Copying data from one FMS unit to another (HT-9100 NDB CROSSLOAD).
The altitude, about 25,000 to 28,000 ft, above which MMO rather than VMO is the limiting speed.
(MD-10) Communication radio panel: three identical panels on the aft pedestal, each able to tune any VHF radio.

Constant speed drive: the hydromechanical drive between engine gearbox and generator that holds the generator at constant speed, and so at 400 Hz, whatever the engine speed. See [Electrical](electrical).

(DC-10, KC-10) One of the amber ELEC, FUEL, HYD and PNEU lights on the pilots' annunciator panel that point to a caution light at the flight engineer's station. See [Warning Systems](warning-systems).
(MD-10) A switch on the system display control panel that calls up a system's synoptic page; it lights white when that system has an alert.
Control valves 1 and 2 of the horizontal stabilizer trim: CV-1 feeds trim motor 1 from hydraulic system 3, CV-2 feeds motor 2 from the system 1 standby loop. See [Flight Controls](flight-controls).
Control wheel steering: the autopilot mode in which the pilot maneuvers through the control wheel and the autopilot holds the attitude when it is released. See [Automatic Flight](automatic-flight).
Drift angle: the angle between heading and track.
(MD-10) The overhead panel philosophy in which every switch light is out when its system is normal, so anything lit needs attention. See [Warning Systems](warning-systems).

The McDonnell Douglas three-engine wide-body transport; in this manual also the aircraft button covering the -10, -15, -30 and -40 with their freighters and tankers. See [Aircraft General](aircraft-general).
The removal of the crab angle just before touchdown, so the aircraft lands with its nose on the runway heading; in an autoland, the ALIGN (ALGN) phase.
Definition (the INS-61B's L/L DEF and NAV DEF keys).
(KC-10) The navigation solution (INU only, or INU blended with civil or military GPS) that each FMS side is set to fly. See [Flight Management](flight-management).
Decision height: the radio altitude at which a precision approach is continued only with the required visual reference.
Differential (as in DIFF TEMP, the brake temperature difference light).
The rolling moment produced by sideslip that tends to raise a dropped wing; on a swept wing it comes largely from the sweep. See [Flight Characteristics](flight-characteristics).
The heading gyro of a compass system, slaved to the flux valve by the compass coupler. See [Flight Instruments](flight-instruments).
Disagree: a valve, surface or gear not where it was commanded.
Disconnect, as in GEN DRIVE DISC (the CSD disconnected) or the autopilot and autothrottle disconnects.
Distance measuring equipment: gives the slant range to a ground station. See [Navigation](navigation).
Data management unit, the computer of the AIDS.
The steep rise in drag above a certain Mach number as shock waves form and separate the flow. See [Flight Characteristics](flight-characteristics).
Digital refueling control unit: the controller in each wing air refueling pod. See [Air Refueling Systems](air-refueling-systems).
Dead reckoning: position computed from heading, airspeed and the last known wind, without a navigation fix.
The descent after an engine failure in cruise to an altitude the remaining engines can hold. See [Emergency Procedures](emergency-procedures).
Desired track (INS-61B DSRTK/STS selector position: desired track and status).
Display unit: on the MD-10, the six screens numbered 1 to 6 from left to right.
(DC-10, MD-10) The fail-operational autoland status (DUAL LAND), with both autopilots engaged and healthy. See [Automatic Flight](automatic-flight).
The oscillation in which the aircraft yaws and rolls out of phase, the nose tracing a flat figure eight; the yaw dampers suppress it. See [Flight Characteristics](flight-characteristics#dutch-roll).
(MD-10) Engine and alert display: display unit 3, showing the engine indications and the alerts. See [Warning Systems](warning-systems).
Electronic attitude director indicator (KC-10; DC-10 with the MFD fit).
End of air refueling (the exit point of the track).
The speed that minimizes the total cost per mile for the cost index: fuel cost plus time-related cost. See [Flight Management](flight-management).
(MD-10) EIS control panel: one at each end of the glareshield, for that pilot's barometric setting, minimums and ND mode and range.
Environmental control system (air conditioning and pressurization).
(APU) Electronic control unit, which sequences the APU start, governs its speeds and shuts it down on a fault. See [APU](apu).
(DC-10 air tanker) Emergency dump of the retardant load; the E-DUMP PSI lights show that the emergency dump accumulators are charged.
Emergency escape breathing device: a smoke hood.
Electronic flight bag: the aircraft's in-sim tablet for loading, performance, ground services, failures and the Virtual Crew. See [EFB](efb).
The aircraft, series or equipment a piece of content applies to; marked in this manual by the aircraft badges and by the series in parentheses. See [Aircraft General](aircraft-general#effectivity).
Equivalent field length: the runway available corrected for condition, slope, wind and bleed configuration, used to enter the takeoff limit charts. See [Mission Planning](mission-planning).
Estimated fuel on board (at a waypoint).
Enhanced ground proximity warning system: GPWS with a terrain database, terrain display and look-ahead alerting. See [Surveillance](surveillance).
Exhaust gas temperature, the engine's main temperature limit. See [Engines](engines).
Electronic horizontal situation indicator (KC-10; DC-10 with the MFD fit).
Engine indicating display system: the two liquid-crystal engine displays offered on the DC-10 (the Digital engine instrument choice).
(MD-10) Electronic instrument system: the six display units and their source switching. See [Flight Instruments](flight-instruments).
Elevator; elevation (field elevation, or boom elevation on the KC-10).
Elevator load feel: the system that sets the elevator feel spring rate from airspeed, and limits flap extension at high speed (ELF/flap limiter). See [Flight Controls](flight-controls).
Emission control: the option, from 1 (unrestricted) to 4 (no emissions), that limits radio and radar transmissions during a rendezvous. See [Air Refueling](air-refueling).

The left and right emergency AC and DC buses, which carry the loads needed to fly, navigate and communicate, and which the battery, static inverter and ADG can keep powered. See [Electrical](electrical).
Envelope (the KC-10 boom's BOOM ENV LIMITS switches).
Engine out (EO ACCEL, the FMS's engine-out acceleration altitude).
External power (the nose wheel well external power panel).
(MD-10) Electrical power control unit: the controller that configures the electrical system automatically. See [Electrical](electrical).
(MD-10) Electrical power generating system; EPGS FAULT is raised by each automatic generator reset.
(KC-10) Emergency passenger oxygen system: a self-contained hood at each support seat.
Engine pressure ratio (Pt7/Pt2), the thrust-setting parameter of the JT9D (DC-10-40); also external power relay. See [Engines](engines).
(KC-10) Estimated position uncertainty: the FMS's position accuracy figure in military mode.
The slow torque applied to a vertical gyro to keep its spin axis aligned with the apparent vertical. See [Flight Instruments](flight-instruments).
(KC-10) Enhanced TCAS: TCAS with formation and rendezvous awareness, served by the IFF transponder. See [Surveillance](surveillance).
Execute (FMS key that makes a modified route active).
An autoland that continues to touchdown after a single failure (DUAL LAND). See [Automatic Flight](automatic-flight).
An autoland in which a single failure disconnects the system without a significant deviation, leaving the pilot to land manually (SNGL LAND). See [Automatic Flight](automatic-flight).
The valve that meters cool fan air through the precooler to hold the bleed air below its temperature limit. See [Pneumatics](pneumatics).
Federal Aviation Regulations (FAR Part 25, the transport category).
(DC-10, KC-10) The pointer on each ADI showing the speed error from the target speed. See [Automatic Flight](automatic-flight).
(MD-10) Flight control computer: one of the two computers of the AFS, which also run automatic functions such as auto slat extension. See [Automatic Flight](automatic-flight).
Flight crew operating manual (the MD-10 FCOM).
(MD-10) Flight control panel: the glareshield panel for speed, heading, altitude and vertical speed selection and the autopilot and autothrottle controls. See [Automatic Flight](automatic-flight).
The AIDS report of flight controls, control forces and hydraulic temperatures.
Fuel control valve (in each wing air refueling pod).
Flight deck access system (not fitted in the simulation).
Fire detection control unit: monitors the two detector loops in a fire zone. See [Fire Protection](fire-protection).
Flight data entry panel: the AIDS control panel on the flight engineer's upper panel No. 3.
(AINS-70) Flight data storage unit: the tape unit holding each computer's database.
FedEx (its ICAO code), used to mark FedEx limits and data.
Federal Express, operator of the MD-10 conversions and of many of the DC-10s whose procedures this manual follows.
Flight engineer: the third crew member of the DC-10 and KC-10, at the side-facing station; FedEx calls this crew member the second officer.
Flight guidance control (the glareshield flight guidance panel's lighting).

(DC-10, KC-10) Flight guidance system: two independent systems, each with roll, pitch and yaw computers, providing the autopilots and flight directors, controlled from the glareshield FGS panel. See [Automatic Flight](automatic-flight).
The second phase of inertial alignment, after the present position is entered, in which the platform levels precisely and finds north by gyrocompassing.
The throttles advanced to their mechanical stops, accepting engine limit exceedance (stall and windshear recovery).
The reduction of the rate of descent just before touchdown; in an autoland, the FLARE mode at about 50 ft. See [Automatic Flight](automatic-flight).
An engine rating that holds takeoff thrust constant up to a break temperature (about 30 °C at sea level for the CF6-50C2), above which it falls with temperature. See [Engines](engines).
Reduced takeoff thrust by the assumed temperature method (T.O. FLX on the thrust rating computer; FLEX on the MD-10 FMS).
The higher idle speed scheduled in flight, which keeps the engines ready to accelerate quickly for a go-around. See [Engines](engines).
The magnetic sensor in each wingtip that measures the direction of the earth's field for a compass system. See [Flight Instruments](flight-instruments).
Flight mode annunciator: the display of the engaged and armed autopilot, flight director and autothrottle modes. See [Automatic Flight](automatic-flight).
(MD-10) Flight management function: one of the Pegasus FMS's two FMFs; if one fails the other becomes master.
Flight management system: on the KC-10 the three-CDU FMS; on the MD-10 the Honeywell Pegasus. See [Flight Management](flight-management).
First officer; the right seat (on the KC-10 the copilot).
Cross-controlled flight with the wing lowered into the wind and opposite rudder, used to keep the nose on the runway heading in a crosswind; the autoland's decrab.
(KC-10) Fuel pressure control unit: regulates the air refueling delivery pressure and sequences the refueling pumps.
Flat panel display system: the DC-10 attitude display fit with one wide screen per pilot carrying a PFD and an ND.
The disk in each wheel that releases tire pressure at about 350 psi, so over-inflation cannot burst a tire.
(DC-10 air tanker) The Trotter Controls FRDS GEN II drop control system: a master sequencer and three tank controllers. See [Aerial Firefighting](aerial-firefighting).
Fuselage station: a distance in inches along the fuselage from the reference datum.
(MD-10) Fuel system controller: does the flight engineer's fuel management automatically. See [Fuel](fuel).
A plug in each main and center wheel that melts at about 224 °C and releases the tire's pressure before an overheated brake can burst it. See [Landing Gear](landing-gear).
Go-around (the go-around thrust limit, mode or switch).
Ground-controlled intercept: a military radar control facility.
